> If the intellect is divine compared with man, then the life lived according to the intellect is divine compared with ordinary human life. # THE
# GENERAL PREFACE.

---

1. The author's excuse for the alterations he has made in this edition of his books.
2. The general scope of this entire volume.
3. The excellence and necessity of reason for maintaining the truth of the Christian religion.
4. His apology for frequently weaving *Platonism* and *Cartesianism* <note>Platonism refers to the philosophy of Plato; Cartesianism refers to the philosophy of René Descartes.</note> into his writings.
5. Certain notices for the more profitable reading of his books.
6. Divine insight <note>original: "Sagacity"</note> is a principle that must come before <note>original: "antecedaneous to"</note> successful reason in contemplations of the highest importance.
7. The aforementioned principle further illustrated and confirmed from *Aristotle*.
8. The author's excuse for omitting, in his *Antidote*, a refutation of the weak <note>original: "unconcluding"</note> arguments some people use to prove the existence of God.
9. His excuse for not adding a treatise on *Superstition* to the one on *Enthusiasm* <note>In the 17th century, "enthusiasm" usually referred to a claim of private, direct divine inspiration, often viewed with suspicion as religious fanaticism.</note>.
10. That it should be no offense to the knowledgeable and open-minded that men feel a shyness and suspicion toward such truths as they have not been acquainted with.
11. Certain remarkable facts concerning *Descartes* and his writings.
12. Certain considerations brought together which completely prevent all imaginable objections against the idea of a spirit occupying space <note>original: "Extension of a Spirit." This was a major philosophical debate: whether spirits are "extended" in space like matter or are non-spatial.</note>.
13. The properties and roles of the *Spirit of Nature* further cleared and confirmed. A logical conclusion <note>original: "Consectary"</note> concerning the guidance of souls by the Spirit of Nature.
14. That the ancient *Jewish Kabbalah* <note>original: "Judaical Cabbala"</note> consisted of what we now call *Platonism* and *Cartesianism*, made further probable by the lineage of the *Pythagorean School*.
15. Particular considerations from *Pherecydes*, *Parmenides*, and *Aristotle* that might move one to believe that the whole *Pythagorean philosophy*—both *physical* and *metaphysical*—was the ancient wisdom of the Jews.
16. The unfortunate separation of the *physical part of the Kabbalah* from the *metaphysical* in the works of *Leucippus*, *Democritus*, and *Epicurus*; along with the author's serious endeavor to reunite them.
17. That what he applies to the text of *Moses* in his *Philosophic Kabbalah*, he believes is rational and is assured that it perfectly fits the text, but he continues to deliberate further concerning its ultimate truth.
18. The testimony of several holy persons who either plainly asserted, or at least did not dislike, the doctrine of the soul's *pre-existence*: *Clement of Alexandria*, *Origen* <note>original: "Origenes Adamantius"</note>, *Clement's* scholar, *St. Basil* and *Gregory Nazianzen*, *Synesius* (Bishop of Cyrene), *Arnobius*, *Prudentius*, *St. Augustine*, the author of the *Book of Wisdom*, and our blessed Savior.
19. That there is not the least conflict between *pre-existence* and the inheritance of original sin from *Adam*.
20. That mathematical certainty in purely philosophical speculations does not require any man's conscience to make a public profession of them.

->READER,<-

<margin>
The author's excuse for such alterations as he has made in this edition of his books.
</margin>

1. <image-desc>Decorative drop cap T featuring floral scrolls and foliage.</image-desc> *So that these writings, which you find bound up in one volume, may also appear to be held together by some common purpose, I thought it not inappropriate to say something by way of a general preface to them all. Therefore, if your curiosity makes you eager to ask what I have done in these new editions of my books, I am ready to inform you that I have taken the same liberty in this intellectual or theoretical garden of my own planting that men usually take in their natural ones: which is to plant or pull up, to transplant and graft <note>original: "inoculate"; in 17th-century gardening, this referred to grafting a bud from one plant onto another</note>, where and what they please. Therefore, if I have erased some things (which are very few), transposed others, and inserted others, I hope I shall seem harmful to no man in organizing and cultivating this philosophical plantation of mine according to my own disposition and liking.*

<margin>
The general scope of this entire volume.
</margin>

*2. But these are smaller matters, and hardly any part of what I was going to say. The great bond <note>original: "Cement"</note> that holds these various discourses together is one main design which they jointly aim for, and which, I think, is admittedly noble <note>original: "generous"</note> and important: namely,* THE KNOWLEDGE OF GOD, *and through that, of* TRUE HAPPINESS, *so far as* REASON *can cut her way through those darknesses and difficulties she is burdened with in this life. Though these difficulties are many and great, I would misrepresent <note>original: "belie"</note> the sense of my own success if I were to call them insurmountable; also, if I were deprived of that sense of success, I would lose many pleasures and enjoyments of mind that I am now conscious of. Among these, none is as significant as that quiet reflection within myself regarding what real service might come <note>original: "redound"</note> to* RELIGION *from these labors of mine. For what greater satisfaction can there be to a rational spirit than to find himself able to appeal to the strictest rules of* REASON *and* PHILOSOPHY *to show that those doctrines of the* EXISTENCE OF GOD *and the* IMMORTALITY OF THE SOUL *are true? And what greater* support <note>original: "Establishment"</note> *to* RELIGION *can there be than to discover these two grand* PILLARS *so firm and stable, even upon those very grounds that our own mental faculties naturally agree are true? This cannot help but bring much honor and reverence to the* PRIESTHOOD *and silence the mouths of shallow and profane* WITS <note>original: "Wits"; here meaning intellectuals or skeptics who used their cleverness to mock religion</note>, *who are so prone to look upon every* PRIEST *as either a* FOOL *or an* IMPOSTER.

<margin>
The excellence and necessity of reason for maintaining the truth of the Christian religion.
</margin>

*3. Nor would I be thought to limit the reasonableness of our religion to those two main points only, as if the rest were not reasonable too. For I believe the* CHRISTIAN RELIGION *is rational throughout, and I think I have proved it to be so in my* Mystery of Godliness. *This, I must confess, was the main—if not the only—purpose of my so long and anxious search into* REASON *and* PHILOSOPHY; *without this goal, I would have proven to be only a lazy and negligent inquirer into the nature of things. For to heap up a great deal of reading, ideas <note>original: "Notions"</note>, and experiments without some such noble and important* PURPOSE *would have been, as I imagined, like making my mind or memory a shop of cheap trinkets <note>original: "small-wares"</note>. But having this so eminent a goal in my view, and taking up that noble resolution of*

<meta>This page continues the "Preface General," where Henry More explains his philosophical and theological goals. He focuses here on the necessity of reason in the priesthood, using the symbolic garments of the High Priest Aaron to argue that a clergyman should also be a philosopher.</meta>

<page-num>v</page-num>
<header>The GENERAL PREFACE.</header>

Marcus Cicero said, "I will follow reason wherever it leads me" <note>original: *Rationem, quòd ea me cunque ducet, fequar*</note>. I considered that I then began to honor my profession <note>original: "adorn my Function"</note> and, among other priestly garments, specifically to put on the *Rationale* <term>the Rationale: from the Latin *rationalis*, this refers to the "Breastplate of Judgment" worn by the High Priest Aaron (Exodus 28:15). More uses the name to link the garment to the concept of Reason (*Ratio*).</term>, the priestly breastplate. This garment rightfully claims its place in that region which is the seat of the heart, as the simplicity and sincerity of the heart are the root and wellspring of the soundest and purest reason. 

Truly, I cannot well imagine any other moral reason why Aaron’s robes should be such an exact representation of the universe—
<margin>* Philo, *On Monarchy*</margin>
"a representation and a kind of imitation of the world" <note>original: *ἀπεικόνισμα καὶ μίμημά τι τοῦ κόσμου*</note>, as Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BCE – 50 CE), a Jewish philosopher who sought to harmonize the Torah with Greek philosophy.</note> calls it—unless it is that every priest should endeavor, according to his opportunity and capacity, to also be as much as he can a rational man or philosopher. (Certainly, this is the reason why universities were first established and continue to this very day.) Philo himself suggests something to this purpose: 
"For the Law wishes the high priest to have an image resembling the universe, so that by continuous contemplation he may make his own life worthy of the nature of the whole" <note>original: *Βούλεται γὰρ τὸν ἀρχιερέα εἰκόνα τοῦ παντὸς ἔχειν ἐμφερῆ, ἵνα ἐκ τῆς συνεχούς θέας ἄξιος παρέχῃ τὸν ἴδιον βίον τῇ τῶν ὅλων φύσεως*</note>. 

This means that the High Priest, by continually reflecting upon his attire which represented the universe, might be reminded not to do or speak anything contrary to its laws, or in opposition to the rules of eternal Reason. This eternal Reason is that everlasting High Priest, as 
<margin>* In his *On Dreams*.</margin>
Philo elsewhere suggests: "For there are, it seems, two temples of God: one is this universe, in which the High Priest is His first-born, the Divine Logos <term>Logos: Greek for "Word" or "Reason." In Christian philosophy, it refers to the second person of the Trinity (Christ) as the organizing principle of the universe.</term> or eternal Wisdom; the other is the rational soul, whose priest is the true man" <note>original: *Δύο γάρ, ὡς ἔοικεν, ἱερὰ Θεοῦ· ἓν μὲν ὅδε ὁ κόσμος, ἐν ᾧ καὶ ἀρχιερεὺς ὁ πρωτόγονος αὐτοῦ, ὁ Θεῖος λόγος· ἕτερον δὲ ἡ λογικὴ ψυχή, ἧς ἱερεὺς ὁ πρὸς ἀλήθειαν ἄνθρωπος*</note>. That is to say, the priest is the Intellect (as Plotinus <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 CE), the founder of Neoplatonism.</note> says somewhere), which is the image of the Divine Logos, as 
<margin>*Stromat.* book 5.</margin>
Clement <note>Clement of Alexandria (c. 150–215 CE), a Christian theologian who integrated Greek philosophy with Christianity.</note> has expressed it: "For the image of God is the Divine and Royal Logos, the impassible Man <note>original: *ἄνθρωπος ἀπαθής*; a man not subject to suffering or shifting emotions</note>; but the image of this image is the human intellect" <note>original: *Εἰκὼν μὲν γὰρ Θεοῦ λόγος Θεῖος καὶ βασιλικός, ἄνθρωπος ἀπαθής, εἰκὼν δ' εἰκόνος ἀνθρώπινος νοῦς*</note>.

So, although the Divine Reason or *Logos* is that eternal High Priest who was to be incarnated in time—and of whom Aaron in his priestly robes was only a type and figure—nevertheless, because man is an image of Him (and every priest in a more special manner), he is to endeavor to adorn himself with such accomplishments as are represented by those rich and precious garments of Aaron. Among these, the *Rationale* (the breastplate) had a chief place. 

For while it belongs to that everlasting *Logos* alone to be the Maker of the world, to fill every part of it with His presence, and to be (in a sense) vitally clothed with it; yet, through the goodness of God, every Christian priest may share in being invested and adorned with the knowledge of the laws and measures of creation. He may take notice of the "reasons of nature," of which the eternal *Logos* is the Maker and Governor. This is very consistent with what Philo writes regarding the shape of the *Rationale* or priestly breastplate, which he says was square: "Because it is necessary that both the reason of nature and the reason of man should stand firm on all sides and not be shaken in any way" <note>original: *ὅτι χρὴ καὶ τὸν τῆς φύσεως λόγον καὶ τὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου βεβηκέναι πάντη, καὶ κατὰ μηδὲν κραδαίνεσθαι*</note>. Just as these things were symbolized in Aaron and are fulfilled perfectly in Christ, so they are also to be fulfilled in their own measure in the Christian priesthood. For if it were not lawful to offer up a blind or lame animal under the Old Law, surely the priest himself ought

<page-num>vi</page-num>
<header>The GENERAL PREFACE.</header>

...to be neither beneath the Gospel, nor even beneath the People (so far as is possible) whom he presents to God.

->Therefore, to take away Reason—under whatever fanatical <note>original: "Fanatick"</note> pretense—is to strip the priest of his robes and rob him of his Breastplate <term>the Rationale: as mentioned on the previous page, this is the "Breastplate of Judgment" (Exodus 28:15) symbolizing the use of Reason (*Ratio*).</term>. Worst of all, it robs Christianity of the special privilege it has over all other religions in the world: namely, that it dares to appeal to Reason. Anyone who understands the true interest of our religion will not fail to stick closely to this; to do the opposite betrays religion to the unjust suspicion of falsehood and makes it equal to every empty imposture. For if you take away Reason, all religions are equally true—just as when light is removed, all things are the same color. Indeed, worst of all, the religion that is the truest will seem the falsest in this artificial darkness, if it strictly and positively declares itself to be the only true one. This claim will not be accepted, nor can it be verified, in that region of midnight where everything looks the same.<-

<margin>His defense <note>original: "Apologie"</note> for so frequently interweaving Platonism and Cartesianism into his writings.</margin>

->4. These serious and weighty considerations urged me to search to the very bottom of things with all possible care and vigor, so that my heart might not fail me in the day of trial. Much of the result of that investigation is included in this volume. While I have gained great satisfaction myself regarding those major points I have tried to clarify, I am also eager that nothing in these pages causes the slightest dissatisfaction to others. I think it will be impossible for anything to do so, if they will only notice my design. My goal is not to "theologize" within philosophy, but to build an external fence <note>original: "Exoterick Fence"</note> or outer fortification around theology. By defending those outer works against the assaults of the confident Atheist—and his massive attacks <note>original: "Gigantick batteries," an allusion to the giants of mythology who attempted to storm heaven</note> raised against the belief in God’s existence and a reward in the world to come—I might show him what a man of vanity and recklessness he is. He imagines in his unskilled thoughts that it is an easy thing to overrun the Holy City and Sanctuary, yet he is easily beaten back from the walls. This is the true and genuine meaning of my frequent interweaving of Platonism <note>The philosophy of Plato and his followers, emphasizing the existence of abstract forms and the soul.</note> and Cartesianism <note>The philosophy of René Descartes, which sought to use rational doubt and mathematics to reach certain knowledge.</note> into these writings: I use these hypotheses as invincible bulwarks against the most cunning and harmful efforts of Atheism. I am certain that if the ideas I have chosen from those two philosophies are taken as true (and let our adversaries prove them false if they can), there is no objection Atheism can make against the doctrines mentioned above that I cannot answer fully and irrefutably.<-

->Therefore, it is not hopeless to think that as we put many to flight, the rest might voluntarily surrender as prisoners. They may be led captive by the power of Reason into a true belief in the core principles of faith. Once their hopes of escaping punishment after death <note>original: "After-Impunity"</note> are cut off by a clear conviction of the Soul’s Immortality, they may be prompted to become real Christians in the simpler aspects of the faith. They may be willing to remain in the Outer Court—though, because of their current weak vision, they may not yet be fit to enter the more sacred incense smoke of the Temple. Since I am so faithfully and, I believe, usefully occupied in managing these "outer works," as I call them, I will not attribute any criticism to even over-hasty zeal, but<-

<page-num>vii</page-num>
<header>The GENERAL PREFACE.</header>

*...but I attribute it to mere mishap if I am pelted behind my back by any shots of slander <note>original: "Obloquie"</note> from any unknown servant of the Sanctuary <note>A fellow member of the clergy or the church.</note>. I presume that if I am hurt, the pain will be greatest for those who did it, once they realize they have wounded a true and faithful friend—and even then, at a time when he was so busily and watchfully employed in facing the common Enemy <note>Likely referring to atheism or materialism.</note>.*

<margin>Certain advice for the more profitable reading <note>original: "perusing"</note> of his books.</margin>
*5. If anyone expects or desires any general instruction or preparation for more profitably reading these writings of mine, I must declare that I can give none that is unique to them, except what would fit all writings written with freedom and reason. And this one Royal Rule I would recommend for all: **Not to judge the truth of any proposition until we have a settled and definite understanding <note>original: "apprehension"</note> of its terms.** Although this law is so necessary and indispensable, there is none so frequently broken. The result of this neglect is those many heaps of voluminous writings and foolish <note>original: "inept"</note> oppositions and controversies that fill the world. These would be impossible if men had not developed a habit of fluttering mere words against one another without noticing any definite sense. They fight, as it were, with many Hercules' clubs made of cardboard <note>original: "Pastbord"</note>, which make a great sound but do no execution toward ending disputes. For just as no man will ever be so wild as to claim that a triangle is a quadrangle, or a square a circle, once he has the distinct ideas of those figures in his mind; so it would be just as impossible for him to pronounce anything else falsely and absurdly if he had as perfect and settled a notion of the things he is speaking about. But since this first and main principle of wisdom is neglected, it is no wonder that men clash as ridiculously and without cause as those two country clowns who, in their cups, almost came to blows because one called himself a* Lutheran *and the other a* Martinist <note>The joke here is that both terms refer to the followers of Martin Luther; the clowns are fighting over two names for the same thing because they do not understand the terms.</note>.*

*I might also add another piece of advice (which will contribute much toward a greater conciseness <note>original: "Compendiousness"</note> in controversies) which I think I have hinted at elsewhere: namely, **That what will prove anything will prove nothing.** If this were thoroughly understood, it would not only enable a man to defeat the apparent force of countless irrelevant assaults, but also keep him—if he has any honesty <note>original: "ingenuity"</note> in him—from attacking, or rather disturbing or interrupting, the composure and silence of another man’s mind with the empty noise of such weak and groundless arguments. I mean those arguments that could infer or maintain falsehood just as easily as truth. All such arguments ought to be rejected, especially in philosophy. I think if this kind of weapon were once out of fashion, conflict would soon be at an end, and such a victory would follow that everyone would be a gainer by it.*

<margin>Divine Insight <note>original: "Sagacity"</note>: A principle prior <note>original: "antecedaneous"</note> to successful Reason in contemplations of the highest importance.</margin>
*6. But in the third and last place (which, though it has some considerable influence everywhere, is more particularly required when reading writings on subjects such as these I treat of), I would recommend to those who wish to philosophize successfully the belief in and pursuit of a certain principle more noble and inward than Reason itself. Without this, Reason will falter, or at least reach only to mean and frivolous things. I have a sense of something in me while I speak this which I must confess is of so hidden <note>original: "retruse"</note> a nature that I lack a name for it, unless I should venture to term it* **Divine Insight** <note>original: "Divine Sagacity"</note>*, which is the first source of successful Reason, especially—*

*...especially in matters of great complexity and importance, without which a man is, as it were, in a dense forest. He may make infinite promising attempts but can find no exit into the open countryside <note>original: "Champain"</note>, where one may freely look about in every direction (the "plain of truth" <note>original: "πεδίον τῆς ἀληθείας" (pedion tēs alētheias)</note>) without the safe guidance of this good Genius.*

<margin>* Enneads, book 1, chapter 2 <note>A reference to the works of the Neoplatonist philosopher Plotinus.</note>.</margin>
*All pretenders to philosophy will indeed be ready to magnify Reason to the skies, to make it the light of Heaven and the very Oracle of God. But they do not consider that the Oracle of God is not to be heard except in His Holy Temple—that is to say, in a good and holy man, thoroughly sanctified in spirit, soul, and body. For there is a sanctity even of the body and physical temperament <note>original: "Complexion"</note> which the sensually-minded do not even dream of. Did not Aaron’s Breastplate <note>original: "Rationale"; a reference to the high priest's breastplate described in Exodus.</note>, his Oracle <note>original: "Λόγιον" (Logion)</note> or Oracle of Reason, include within it the Urim and Thummim—purity and integrity of the will and affections, as well as the light of the understanding? Was not that breastplate square, not only in reference to the firmness of logical reasoning <note>original: "Ratiocination"</note>, as Philo suggests, but also to denote the evenness and uprightness of the spirit of one who takes it upon himself to pronounce great truths? He must be, as Aristotle says somewhere, "a good man, square and without reproach" <note>original: "ἀνὴρ ἀγαθὸς καὶ τετράγωνος ἄνευ ψόγου" (anēr agathos kai tetragōnos aneu psogou)</note>. This squareness is not only according to the standard of the city but of the Sanctuary; it is not only a political degree of virtue, but a "purifying" <note>original: "Cathartical"</note> virtue, or rather that which \** Plotinus places "in being purified" <note>original: "ἐν τῷ κεκαθάρθαι" (en tō kekatharthai)</note>, implying a soul that is already purged.*

*A man may adorn himself as well as he can with the history of universal nature (represented by the long priestly robe), but if this breastplate with the Urim and Thummim is missing, he may act the part of a priest, but he will necessarily fail to prove himself a sound philosopher. He will be unable to utter any oracles himself and will be poorly equipped to receive them when they are uttered by another. For if this Divine Sagacity <note>A term for an intuitive, God-given insight.</note> is lacking because of the impurity of a man's spirit, he can neither find the right scent <note>original: "sent"</note> of things himself, nor easily pick it up or rightly pursue it when he is shown the path by someone else. This odd position of mine might make those who have made the contempt of morality a part of their philosophy fret and storm; they may think themselves uncivilly treated to be declared unqualified <note>original: "incompetent"</note> judges of such things as they took for granted were within their own reach. Yet I could not conceal so important <note>original: "concerning"</note> a truth, especially since it is not at all unphilosophical in itself.*

<margin>The aforementioned principle further illustrated and confirmed from Aristotle. *On Subtlety* <note>original: *De Subtil.*</note>, exercise 307, section 25.</margin>
*7. For is it not the saying of that universally-applauded Aristotle: "For the divine within us moves all things in a certain way, and the beginning of reason is not reason, but something better" <note>original: "Κινεῖ γάρ πως πάντα τὸ ἐν ἡμῖν θεῖον, λόγου δ' ἀρχὴ οὐ λόγος, ἀλλά τι κρεῖττον" (Kinei gar pōs panta to en hēmin theion, logou d' archē ou logos, alla ti kreitton)</note>? What Plato—nay, what Chrysostom or Augustine—could have spoken more heavenly language? Scaliger, transported by the sight of this text, breaks out into this enthusiastic <note>original: "Encomiastick"</note> question: "What do you say, divine man? Is there something divine in us that is more excellent than reason itself? Were even the rays of the Holy Spirit known to you?" <note>original: "Quid ais, divine vir? Estne in nobis aliquid divinum quod sit præstantius ipsâ ratione? An tibi quoque noti fuerunt ipsi radii Spiritûs Sancti?"</note> &c. And so that we do not think that this "divine thing within us" <note>original: "τὸ ἐν ἡμῖν θεῖον" (to en hēmin theion)</note> is any part of ourselves, it appears both from what goes before and what follows after that it is the Deity itself. For having asked the question, "What is the beginning of motion in the soul?" <note>original: "τίς ἡ τῆς κινήσεως ἀρχὴ ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ?" (tis hē tēs kinēseōs archē en tē psychē?)</note>, the full answer follows thus:* <margin>Aristotle, *Eudemian Ethics*, book 7, chapter 14.</margin> *"It is clear that just as God is in the whole universe, so all things are in Him. For the divine within us moves all things in a certain way; and the beginning of reason is not reason, but something better. What, then, could be better even than knowledge..."* <note>original: "Δῆλον δὴ ὥσπερ ἐν τῷ ὅλῳ θεὸς, καὶ πᾶν ἐκείνῳ. κινεῖ γάρ πως πάντα τὸ ἐν ἡμῖν θεῖον· λόγου δ' ἀρχὴ οὐ λόγος, ἀλλά τι κρεῖττον. τί οὖν ἂν εἴη κρεῖττον καὶ ἐπιστήμης" (Dēlon dē hōsper en tō holō theos...)</note>

...except God? <note>original: "πλὴν θεός;" (plēn theos)</note> It is evident, he says, that it is—as in the Universe—God himself, and all things are in him. For it is the same divine power <note>original: "Numen"</note> within us that moves all things in some way or another. And the beginning of Reason is not Reason itself, but something which is better. But what can be better than knowledge <note>original: "Science"</note> except God? *The subject of the chapter is a question concerning good fortune <note>original: "περὶ εὐτυχίας" (peri eutychias)</note>, whether it occurs by nature, by reason, or by some inspiration <note>original: "φύσει, νόῳ, ἢ ἐπιπνοίᾳ τινί" (physei, nōi, ē epipnoiai tini)</note>—that is to say, whether it happens by Nature, Reason, or by the care of some good spirit, or a "pilot" <note>original: "δαίμων ἀγαθός· κυβερνήτης" (daimōn agathos; kybernētēs)</note>. These are Aristotle's own words, which I cite particularly because it is the only place I know where there is such express mention of spirits <note>original: "Dæmons"</note>. Yet he does not even assert it here; but because of this subject, his mind swelled higher and rose at last to such a height that he uttered this aphorism so much admired by Julius Scaliger: namely, that there is something before and better than reason, from which reason itself originates.*

*Though Aristotle mainly applies this to external affairs, I must (and may with equal right) transfer it also to the activities of the mind and the success of pure contemplation <note>original: "Speculation"</note>. In this realm, "divine success" <note>original: "ἡ θεία εὐτυχία" (hē theia eutychia)</note>, as he calls it, is more likely to continue and prove constant (because of the natural bond between Truth and an unpolluted soul) than it is in external business. This intellectual success, therefore, comes from the presence of God, who moves all things in some way <note>original: "κινεῖν πως πάντα" (kinein pōs panta)</note>, but residing in the undefiled spirit, moves it in the most excellent manner. He grants it that "Divine Sagacity" I spoke of, which is a more internal, direct, and comprehensive presentation of truth. This always precedes that Reason which, in theories of greatest importance, later proves itself to be most solid and perfect in every way upon the most exact examination. This is truly that wisdom which is specifically called the gift of God, and is hardly suitable <note>original: "competible"</note> for anyone but those of a pure and unspotted mind. It is of such great importance to sincerely strive to be holy and good.*

<margin>
The author's excuse for omitting, in his *Antidote*, the refutation of the weak reasons some use to prove God exists.

**8.** *This is all I thought appropriate to preface in a more general way. I will briefly look over the various parts of this present volume to see if anything occurs that I should excuse, complete, or clarify. For instance, some may consider it an omission in my book, *An Antidote against Atheism* <note>original: "Antidote"</note>, that I did not include and refute the slippery <note>original: "lubricous"</note> or inconclusive arguments that some use to prove the existence of a Deity. But I think it is not unbecoming for one who is faithful to the cause not to be overly industrious in revealing the weakness of such arguments intended to create in men's minds a belief in that Truth—a truth so necessary and of such vast importance for mankind to be convinced of. For I charitably assume <note>original: "surmise"</note> that the first inventors of those reasons thought they were conclusive, or else they would not have used them. It follows, then, that those arguments may still have power for people who are at the same intellectual level as their first proposers. And he who guesses correctly and continues his journey will just as surely reach his destination as he who perfectly knows the way. I must confess I have been more free in my criticism of Descartes' <note>original: "Des-Cartes"</note> second and third arguments, but less harm is done there since they are not as popular. Besides, it was appropriate to show my impartiality, because I have*

...with that confidence, I declared the solidity of the first argument. The more I considered it, the more firm I found it to be; nor have I to this day met with any man or book that could produce anything material toward the **refutation** <note>original: "Confutation"</note> of it.

<margin>His excuse for not adding a treatise on **Superstition** to that of **Enthusiasm**.</margin>

9. I cannot easily predict <note>original: "presage"</note> what **defect** anyone might find in my ***Treatise of Enthusiasm***. Nor can I protect myself from appearing deficient to a reader who, considering the usefulness of that work, feels I have failed by not adding another treatise on ***Superstition***. But I have naturally and unintentionally followed that judicious advice of the Poet:

---

-> —And those things which<-
-> *you despair can be made to shine through handling, leave behind.* <note>original: "Et quæ Desperas tractata nitescere posse relinque" — Horace, *Ars Poetica*.</note> <-

For I must confess I do not look upon that subject as something I can refine, as it is an argument better suited for rhetoric than philosophy. Besides, I never found my mind low or abject enough to sink into any feeling or concept of that state, nor to experimentally discover what lies at the bottom of it. I must frankly confess that I have a natural touch of ***Enthusiasm*** in my **temperament** <note>original: "Complexion"</note>, but it was one that—thank God—was always governable enough, and which I have eventually found to be perfectly controllable. By virtue of this victory, I know better what is inside ***Enthusiasts*** than they do themselves; therefore, I was able to write what I wrote with vitality and judgment, and I hope I shall contribute significantly to the peace and quiet of this kingdom because of it.

But having had such a notion of God from my very youth—one that represented Him to me as the most noble and excellent Being possible—it could never enter my mind that He was either easily provoked or easily appeased by the omission or performance of any lowly or insignificant services. Such services neither perfect human nature nor are they the genuine result of that perfection. Therefore, I had an early belief that he serves God best who is least envious, worldly, or sensual; who delights most in the common good of the **Universe**; and who has the strongest faith in the bounty and mercy of God—of which His Son **Jesus** is the most tangible pledge He could show to the **world**. This constant frame of spirit made me entirely incapable of even the slightest **trace** <note>original: "Tincture"</note> of **Superstition**. For it is the **ignorance** of better things that causes those anxieties and distresses of mind regarding matters of less importance.

The end of religion is human **happiness** and **perfection**; he who serves God while imagining Him to lack anything of his own, instead of honoring Him, actually insults Him. Therefore, **superstition** is always accompanied by **ignorance** or **hypocrisy**. The first occurs when people do not know what that "good and acceptable will of God" is—which is to become like Him ("You will honor God best if you make your mind like God," <note>original: "Τιμήσεις τὸν Θεὸν ἄριστα ἐὰν τῷ Θεῷ τὴν διάνοιαν ὁμοιώσῃς" (Timēseis ton Theon arista ean tō Theō tēn dianoian homoiōsēs)</note> as **Pythagoras** taught). Instead, they express their zeal and devotion in things that benefit neither themselves nor anyone else. The second occurs when these same trifles are offered up to God, not so much out of ignorance of what is better, but out of a kind of silent fraud and cunning deception of God—as if making an unequal exchange with Him, or rather, forcing it upon Him. Although they may pacify their false hearts and consciences for a while with these delusions, in the meantime, they really only provoke God with these "sacrifices of fools" <note>A reference to Ecclesiastes 5:1.</note>.

This is the sum of what I am able to conceive regarding this other **disease** of

Superstition—which I understand only through logical deduction <note>original: "mere collection of Reason"</note>, as I have had no personal experience with it to stimulate <note>original: "quickening"</note> my writing style or expand my thoughts on the matter. However, I think I may safely affirm, as I have elsewhere, that it is **Superstition** (unless it is vainglory, self-interest, or something worse) when men have an excessive <note>original: "over-proportionated"</note> zeal for or against things in religion that **God** places little or no value upon, whether they are performed or omitted. If this were seriously and conscientiously considered, it would go a long way toward calming or preventing the usual storms <note>original: "blusters"</note> of **Christendom**. And there could be no better result from writing an entire book. But I must confess that the success and growth of the Church is a **profound secret** <note>original: "Arcanum"</note> that lies deeper in Providence; it is a **mystery** of life rather than of external **reason**. Paul may plant and Apollos may water, but **God** gives the growth <note>original: "increase"</note>.

<margin>It should not offend knowledgeable and honorable people that men are shy or jealous toward truths they are not familiar with.</margin>
10. As for the letters that follow next, they speak for themselves regarding their purpose. I have added the one addressed to **V. C.** <note>likely a Latin abbreviation for "Vir Clarissimus" or "Most Illustrious Man," referring to a specific correspondent</note> for several reasons, but chiefly to encourage a better opinion in those who are not well-acquainted with **Descartes** and his writings. It is inevitable that even men of excellent spirit may struggle with prejudice against such a worthy **author** due to the misrepresentation of his ideas. I must confess that novelty alone is enough cause for even the most honorable people to hesitate; for anything strange carries the face of something hostile. This is why **enemy** <note>original: "Hostis"</note> and **foreigner** <note>original: "Peregrinus"</note> once had the same meaning, as **Cicero** observes. Furthermore, it is a sign of rudeness and a lack of skill in understanding both the nature of things and the perfection of Divine Providence (who has generally implanted in us a stubborn attachment to what we are used to, so that the human mind might be a safer container once it finds what is best) to imagine that just because a **truth** is self-evidently proven, its opposite will immediately surrender the **castle**. Considering this should ensure that honorable people maintain sincere civility and respect even toward those who suspiciously doubt or oppose new truths; it makes it seem a piece of surprising ignorance or inhumanity to feel otherwise toward them.

<margin>Certain remarkable things concerning Descartes and his writings.</margin>
<margin>* Letters of Mr. Descartes. Volume 2, letters 75, 76, 80.</margin>
11. Nothing specific regarding that letter comes to mind now, except perhaps to applaud the luckiness of my guess concerning **Descartes**'s distortion of the true and natural idea of motion. I believe he did this because of **Galileo’s** misfortune, who was so harshly treated by a Council of Cardinals for his hypothesis on the **motion of the earth**. It is now very evident from several of his letters to **Mersenne** that Descartes had this in mind. I had no knowledge of those passages until a few days ago, and my own letter was written before this second volume of **Descartes**'s letters was published. In the meantime, I cannot help but notice the harm this external force and fear causes to the community of learning, and how many innocent and deserving young minds have been mentally tortured <note>original: "put upon the Rack"</note>, just as **Galileo** was put into prison. For his imprisonment frightened **Descartes** into such a distorted description of **motion** that no man’s **reason** could make good sense of it, yet no man's **modesty** would allow him to imagine anything as **nonsense** <note>original: "Non-sense"</note> in such an excellent **author**.

My main goal in my letter was to clear **Descartes** <note>original: "Cartesius"</note> from that flighty and groundless suspicion of **atheism** (which surely could only be believed by the most unrefined and vulgar **spirits**), which I believe I have done fully...

...and to effectively stop all such rumors in the future, even among the weakest and most skeptical of those who doubt him. I could have added even more from his first volume of letters: namely, that he not only believed in the existence of God, but also in His specific Providence, which he felt and acknowledged in the special inspiration and success he experienced in his philosophical studies. I am not surprised by this, as he began so piously in his youth. His first writing was on that excellent theme, *The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom* <note>Proverbs 9:10</note>. I was informed of this by letters from Mr. Clerselier in Paris when he sent me a list <note>original: "Catalogue"</note> of the writings Descartes <note>original: "Cartesius"</note> left behind. <margin>
Letters of Mr. Descartes. Volume 2. Letter 24.

But what delights <note>original: "enravishes"</note> me the most is that, although we both started from the same starting point <note>original: "Lifts"</note> and took different paths, we eventually meet at the same goal. One of us traveled the lower road of Democritism <note>original: "Democritisme"; the philosophy of Democritus, which focuses on physical matter and atoms</note>—amidst the thick dust of atoms and flying particles of matter—while the other followed the high and airy hills of Platonism in the thin and subtle region of immateriality. Yet we meet at last (certainly not without the hand of Providence) at the same goal: the entrance of the Holy Bible. We dedicate our joined labors to the use and glory of the **Christian Church**. We lay at its feet what we believe to be the truest and most acceptable philosophical interpretation of the first three chapters of *Genesis* ever offered to the world since the loss of the ancient **Jewish Kabbalah** <note>original: "Judaical Cabbala"; refers to an ancient mystical or secret oral tradition</note>. This is not just a rhetorical flourish on my part, but a frank acknowledgment—or rather, a serious boast—by **Descartes** himself. In a letter to a certain friend, he confessed that he found his own philosophy to be surprisingly consistent with the text of Moses, more so than any other interpretation. I have fully demonstrated this in the defense of my *Philosophic Kabbalah*, doing so even more thoroughly than Descartes could have, unless he had happened upon the same key that I used.

<margin>
Certain considerations laid together which completely prevent all imaginable objections against the extension of a spirit.
</margin>
12. Regarding my work *The Immortality of the Soul*, I will address only two points of dissatisfaction. Although these seem like major issues to some, they never seemed so to me. The first is that I have allowed for a kind of **extension** <note>The property of taking up space</note> in the nature of a **spirit**. The second is that I have not allowed for perception in the **Spirit of Nature** <note>More’s term for a non-conscious plastic power that governs the physical world</note>. Regarding the first point, I can rightly defend myself by saying that *necessity knows no law*. If they consider the clear evidence of these two conclusions—first, **that there is an immaterial substance fundamentally and specifically distinct from the body**; and second, **that nothing real exists that is not in some sense extended**—they will find it impossible not to conclude, as I have, that a **spirit** is also extended in some way. Therefore, it is a poorly constructed complaint to criticize the conclusion without examining the strength of the premises. I appeal to any impartial <note>original: "indifferent"</note> reader to judge whether I have not mathematically demonstrated the truth of the first point in both my *Antidote* and my *Treatise of the Soul’s Immortality*.

I shall now, for the reader's fuller satisfaction, demonstrate the second point more precisely: namely, that neither the soul nor anything else can be **wholly in** <note>original: "Totum in"; part of the Scholastic phrase "totum in toto, et totum in qualibet parte," meaning "the whole is in the whole, and the whole is in every part"</note>

<meta>catchword: in</meta>

<summary>The author highlights the shared religious foundations of his and Descartes' philosophies, arguing that both eventually lead to a biblical understanding of creation. He also defends his controversial view that spirits must possess "extension" (occupy space) to exist as real entities.</summary>

--- Page 21 ---
<meta>This page continues the general preface, specifically the author's argument regarding the nature of spirits and their presence in space. He is refuting the traditional Scholastic view that a spirit is "wholly in the whole and the whole in every part" of the space it occupies.</meta>

<page-num>xiii</page-num>
<header>The PREFACE general.</header>

...wholly in the whole, and the whole in every part <note>original: "in toto, and totum in qualibet parte"</note>, but that this *Assertion* (as I once had occasion to write to an *ingenious friend of mine*) is a mere *ringing* <note>original: "chiming"</note> *contradiction.* Which I proved to him like this: *namely, That the Whole* <note>original: "Totum"</note> comprehends all that belongs to a thing both in a *positive sense* and (*consequently*) in a *negative* sense. That is to say, if all of *A* is in *B*, there is nothing left to be in *C*, which is distant from *B*. For it is as if one should say: there is nothing of *A* except what is contained within *B*, and yet at the same moment not only something of *A*, but all of *A*, should also be in *C*. This is impossible for any singular or individual *Essence*; and *Universals* are not real *Things*, but merely *Notions* <note>term: concepts existing in the mind rather than as independent physical realities</note>.

To which we may further add, that this *Supposition* makes the thing it describes as small as the smallest thing imaginable. For if the *Whole* <note>original: "Total"</note> is in every point, it is plain that the size <note>original: "amplitude"</note> of this *Whole* is no bigger than the point it is in. This is an unbearable <note>original: "intolerable"</note> idea when applied to the *Deity* <note>term: God</note>, and ridiculous when applied to anything else.

Therefore, since it is so *Mathematically* provable that there is something properly called *Spirit*, and that no *Being* at all can be totally present in separate points or parts of Matter at once, it unavoidably follows that a *Spirit* is, in some way, extended <note>term: occupying space or having dimensions</note>.

But you will further argue: If *Spirit* is extended as well as *Body*, how shall we imagine *Perception* as being more compatible with a *Spirit* than with a *Body*? To which I briefly answer that I have already demonstrated that *Perception* is incompatible with a *Body*—a challenge I dare anyone to meet regarding a *Spirit*. And I further ask those who imagine <note>original: "phansy"</note> a *Spirit* is totally present in every part of *Matter* whether they can better understand the immediate reason for the power of *perception* by that theory. I also ask those who say it is neither like a *Mathematical point*, nor totally present, nor extended, whether they imagine it any more capable of that *vital Sympathy* and *Coactivity* <note>term: the ability of parts to work together instantly and harmoniously</note> that transmits *Objects* in their exact circumstances to the *common Percipient* <note>term: the part of the soul or mind that receives and unifies sensory information</note>. I dare say, if they will speak honestly <note>original: "speak what they find"</note>, they will not fail to answer that they gain no advantage in understanding the immediate reason for either *simple Perception* or the *above-mentioned vital Sympathy* through such suppositions.

And therefore, in the third place, I will take the boldness to inform <note>original: "advertise"</note> them that the truth of my *9th Axiom*—which declares that some powers and properties belong directly <note>original: "immediate"</note> to a *Subject*—has already fully accomplished my purpose. For since there are other properties in *Body* <note>term: physical matter</note> that prevent it from having the capacity to perceive, it was necessarily left to some *Incorporeal Substance* <note>term: a non-physical reality; a spirit</note> to be the direct *Subject* of the power of *Perception*. For perception must be the direct power of some *Subject* or other, as far as our understanding can reach; nor can we find any other adequate cause besides the *Subject* itself which is precisely *perceptive*. It is true that we are conscious within ourselves that the *Being* which is *perceptive* must be very *Unitive* <note>term: having the quality of oneness or being a single unit</note>. *Reason* makes it evident to us that being *One* in a deeper way than *Matter* is *one* (which is *one* only by the *placing of parts side-by-side* <note>original: "juxtaposition of parts"</note>) is a necessary requirement for whatever is capable of the function of *Common-Percipiency*, and therefore it comes first in nature. But that which is as much "one" as anything can be without a contradiction—that is to say, is so much one that it has, by its very nature, *vital Sympathy* and *coactivity of parts*, so to speak,

For I believe every Spirit may be thus unified; but I am not certain that every Spirit has perception, but rather on the contrary that some have not. Therefore, although everything that is perceptive must be a Spirit, every Spirit does not need to be perceptive. From this, perception must be an immediate power in that rank of Spirits that are perceptive; and therefore it must be an argument of no small <term>unskilfulness</term> <note>original Greek: ἀπαιδευσία (apaideusia), meaning a lack of education or ignorance</note> to ask or expect a reason why it is so.*

*Nor can we give any account of that vital <term>Oneness</term> <note>original: Onenesse</note> in every Spirit—consisting of sympathy and shared activity of parts—unless we should argue that it is very fitting, seeing the nature of a Spirit is opposite to that of Matter, that the first and most immediate consequences of their natures should be opposite also. Therefore, it being here acknowledged that Matter is inert <note>original: stupid, meaning lacking sensation or life</note>, or destitute of vital sympathy and shared activity, Spirit must be vital, and endowed with such properties. Or we could argue that, as Matter (which lacks that Essential Unity consisting of the inability to be divided) is also devoid of this vital <term>Oneness</term>, so Spirit (which has this Essential Unity) should consequently be endowed with the vital kind. But this is not entirely according to the strict <note>original: severity</note> manner of reasoning which I prefer; though the argument is in no way contemptible if we consider the immediate opposition of the two species, and that it is but the first degree and most immediate emergence of vitality which we are arguing for in this comparison.*

*But I did not care to rely on such kinds of <term>logical arguments</term> <note>original: ratiocinations</note>, being well assured that I had already finished my task by merely demonstrating that what I assert belongs to Spirit was incompatible with Matter or Body; and that therefore Spirit must necessarily be acknowledged both to exist, and to be also the subject of such powers and properties—namely, of vital sympathy and shared activity of parts, and, which is the flower of all, of the faculty of perception. And who can question but that they are rightly placed there?*

*For I think there is no one but will acknowledge that there is generally in all men either a vague intuition <note>original: confused presage</note>, or a more definite idea <note>original: Notion</note>, that whatever has this power of sympathy and perception is the most refined <note>original: subtil</note> and unified thing there is. Now I dare appeal to anyone, if he can conceive of anything more refined or more unified than the essential idea of a Spirit, as it is immediately defined in contrast to Matter. For can there be anything more unified than what is utterly incapable of being divided into parts? Or more refined than what is not only able to penetrate Matter, but also itself, or things of its own kind? For Spirit will penetrate Spirit, though Matter cannot penetrate Matter. Therefore, there being no <term>resistance</term> <note>original Greek: ἀντιτυπία (antitypia), the quality of matter that prevents other matter from occupying the same space</note> in a Spirit—neither to its own kind nor to anything else—it is evident that it is the most refined thing there is. Therefore, the communication of vital impressions (and all impressions here are vital, though not all are perceptions, nor any of them physical motions) is not made by the bumping or crowding of parts, but by spiritual sympathy, which is more loose and free from those restrictions that are in the mechanical laws of Matter.*

*Of which the natural <term>logical consequence</term> <note>original: Consectary</note> is, that to resolve a phenomenon into sympathy is not always to take refuge in the "Asylum of Fools" <note>a phrase used to describe a lazy explanation that avoids true scientific inquiry</note>. For it is the result of very refined and laborious <note>original: operose</note> demonstration to come to the certain knowledge of the existence of spiritual beings; which once granted, their*

*To conclude briefly: I have demonstrated with evidence as clear as a mathematical proof that there are incorporeal <note>non-physical or spiritual</note> substances, and that all substance is in some sense extended <note>original: extentional</note>. This is because there is no substance that is not—or at least cannot be—essentially present to Matter. It necessarily follows from this that incorporeal substance is in some way extended in space. Consequently, a soul or spirit is capable of no other unity or "oneness" than that which consists in <term>indiscerpibility</term> <note>the quality of being impossible to divide or pull apart</note> and in a vital shared activity and sympathy of its parts. Therefore, finally, when we experience phenomena in ourselves or observe them in other things that exceed the mere mechanical laws of matter, resolving them into this "Vital Oneness" (consisting of shared activity and sympathy) is not a useless repetition or simply saying a thing is so because it is so. Instead, it is a clear indication of the proper and immediate cause. All these things, when laid together and seriously considered, will easily prevent whatever objections anyone might otherwise imagine against the idea of a Spirit having extension in space.*

<margin>The properties and duties of the Spirit of Nature further clarified and confirmed.</margin>

13. The *second point of dissatisfaction* concerns the *Spirit of Nature*, specifically that I have not granted it the *power of perception*. I believe I have demonstrated as clearly as anything can be shown in philosophy that there is a *Spirit of Nature*—that is to say, an *incorporeal substance* that involves itself in bringing about the more general *phenomena* of the world. Nor can a man doubt that it is an *universal principle* if he considers the nature of God and the divine fruitfulness, and the use of this Spirit wherever there is matter that can be managed for some useful end for the good of the whole creation. Furthermore, there are testimonies of its "omnipresence," so to speak, as it performs the same actions at vast distances.

For example, *it pulls a stone down toward the center of the Earth just as well when the Earth is in the constellation of Aries as when it is in Libra; it prevents the waters from bulging out from the Moon; it constrains the matter of the Sun into a round shape (which would otherwise be oblong); it restrains the crusty parts of a star from flying into pieces into the surrounding ether; it carries along those large regions of looser particles together with the comets in their travels from one vortex to another; and everywhere it directs magnetic atoms on their right path.* This is in addition to all the *molding roles* <note>original: Plastick services; refers to the formative force that grows and shapes biological life</note> it performs in both plants and animals.

This Spirit, therefore, being a silent copy of the *eternal Word* (that is, of that *Divine Wisdom* which is entirely present everywhere), is naturally appointed in every part to perform the best services that Matter is capable of. It acts according to specific modifications and according to that blueprint of which it is the *transcript*—by which I mean the *understanding* and *purpose* of those *Ideas* of things which exist in the *eternal intellect* of God. From this it is plain that there is no need for any other <term>seminal forms</term> <note>original Greek: λόγοι σπερματικοὶ (logoi spermatikoi), the generative principles or "seeds" of things in Stoic and Neoplatonic philosophy</note> than this one, which virtually contains all others everywhere, and is therefore rightly called *The Universal Spirit of Nature*. This philosophy, which now deserves to be called *Cartesianism* because *Descartes* so successfully recovered it back into view, was originally part of the ancient *Jewish Cabbala*. It was part of the philosophy of *Pythagoras*, which he obtained (as is abundantly testified by ancient writers) from the *Jews*. I omitted setting down the succession of the *Pythagorean School*, which would have been relevant to our purpose; therefore, I will provide that list here from *Diogenes Laertius*, who calculates the descent as follows: *Pherecydes, Pythagoras, Telauges, Xenophanes, Parmenides, Zeno of Elea, Leucippus, Democritus*, and then *many others*, among whom were *Nausiphanes* and *Naucydes*, and the last of all, *Epicurus*.

<margin>* Appendix to the Defense of the Philosophical Cabbala, chapter 7, section 5.</margin>
This school was called the *Italian School*. The first in this succession, *Pherecydes*, is said to have obtained certain secret writings from the *Phoenicians* or *Hebrews*, as I have already observed from *Hesychius*. Nor do I need to repeat those ample testimonies that prove that *Pythagoras*, the immediate successor of *Pherecydes*, received his philosophy from the *Jews*. I also need not repeat how the *Cabbala* <note>a mystical Jewish tradition that More believed contained the core of all physical and spiritual truth</note> was kept entire by him and some of his successors. By this, I mean that the *physical* or *mechanical part* was not separated from the *theological* or *metaphysical part*—the body was not separated from the soul. This separation seems to have occurred in the work of *Leucippus* and *Democritus*, and finally, the philosophy became like a corpse and foul-smelling in the hands of *Epicurus* and all those who have followed in his footsteps to this very day.

<margin>Particular considerations from Pherecydes, Parmenides, and Aristotle, that might move one to believe that the whole Pythagorean philosophy, both physical and metaphysical, was the ancient wisdom of the Jews.</margin>
15. In the meantime, I cannot help but note that this succession of that school is a strong confirmation of two things: first, that the philosophy of *Pythagoras* was the ancient *wisdom* of the *Jews*; and especially that the *Atomic* or *Mechanical Philosophy* (such as I have applied to the *text of Moses*) was also part of that wisdom. It is unnecessary here to repeat what I have already noted to show how *Pythagoreanism* relates to the *Book of Genesis*. But besides what I have observed regarding *Pherecydes* mentioning *Ophioneus* as the ringleader of the *apostate spirits* <note>original: "Apostate Spirits"; referring to fallen angels or demons</note>, the beginning of a book of his, which *Laertius* recites, seems to me like a fragmented reflection of the *beginning of Genesis*.

"God and Time and the Ground were always; and the name of the Ground became Earth when God gave it honor." <note>original Greek: Ζεὺς μὲν καὶ χρόνος εἰς ἀεὶ καὶ χθὼν ἦν· χθονὶ δὲ ὄνομα ἐγένετο γῆ, ἐπειδὴ αὐτῇ Ζεὺς γέρας δίδοι.</note>

The easy English translation of this is: *God and Time (I suppose he means Duration) and the Ground existed eternally: But the Ground, upon God's adorning it, was called Earth.* The latter part was, in all likelihood, a reference to the work of the third day of Creation. But the first part, which affirms that the *Ground is eternal*, reflects upon the first day. For this "Ground" <note>original Greek: χθὼν (chthon)</note> is *Hyle* <term>Hyle</term> <note>a Greek term for "prime matter" or the raw material of the universe</note>, which *Plotinus* calls a *foundation* <note>original Greek: ὑποβάθρα (hypobathra)</note> and *the ancient nature* <note>original Greek: ἡ ἀρχαία φύσις (he archaia physis)</note>. This *Hyle*, or the *possibility of the external creation being eternal*, is nonetheless a kind of non-existence, and yet it is the lowest foundation of actual being.

According to this sense, *Parmenides* (the fifth in this *Italian succession*) is also to be understood when he makes the two first principles *Fire and Earth*, as appears from *Aristotle*:

"He posits two principles, the hot and the cold, speaking of them as fire and earth; of these, he ranks the hot under 'Being,' and the other under 'Non-being'." <note>original Greek from Aristotle's Metaphysics, Book 1, chapter 5: Δύο τὰς ἀρχὰς τίθησι, θερμὸν καὶ ψυχρὸν, οἷον πῦρ καὶ γῆν λέγων· τούτων δὲ τὸ μὲν κατὰ τὸ ὂν τὸ θερμὸν τάττει, θάτερον δὲ κατὰ τὸ μὴ ὄν.</note> <margin>Aristotle's Metaphysics, Book 1, chapter 5.</margin>

Though this seemed like a somewhat daring exploit—not unlike raising the dismembered Hippolytus <note>In Greek mythology, Hippolytus was killed when his horses were spooked by a sea monster, but was later brought back to life</note> from the dead—even the consideration of the fate of Asclepius <note>original: "Æsculapius"; the god of medicine who was struck by Zeus's thunderbolt for the "crime" of raising the dead</note> could not deter me from so glorious an enterprise. My free profession that this was a "design" rather than a completed "achievement" gave me enough assurance that I was safely sheltered from any thunderbolt of either misdirected zeal or burning envy.

<margin>He believes that what he applies to the text of Moses in his *Philosophical Cabbala* is rational and fits the text perfectly, though he considers its truth further.</margin>
17. Yet, so that I do not hide what cannot be concealed: the Platonism and Cartesianism <note>The philosophy of René Descartes, which was then a revolutionary new system of science and logic</note> which I have applied to the text of Moses is, I believe, very rational in itself. *And I must further add—and I dare not hide or disguise it, as I believe it is for the interest and safety of religion for me to profess it openly and earnestly—that what I have applied fits the text perfectly and without exception, from beginning to end, as I have demonstrated in the "Defense of that Cabbala" and in its Appendix. This is not an empty boast of mine, but a serious statement of the truth, drawn from me by the great sense I have of the service this work provides to the dignity and authority of the Church. For I am convinced in my own judgment that what I have applied is very consistent with human understanding. Considering also how far that philosophy has already gained a foothold in Christendom, and how easily those victories are won which provide pleasure and satisfaction to the conquered (and such is truth to the soul of man); and also considering how extremely disadvantageous it would be for religion and theology to seem to be left so far behind, or to appear opposite to that which I foresee might probably become the common philosophy of the learned; therefore, to prevent all contempt and petty objections <note>original: "cavil"</note> against the sacredness of Christianity—as if it held anything against the solid truths of proven reason and philosophy—I thought it necessary, and an indispensable duty of the faithfulness I owe to the Christian Church, to declare publicly: If anyone presumes they have found such points of Cartesianism or Platonism (as I have applied to the writings of Moses) to be really true upon examination, I dare confidently tell them that, if they are so, those truths were always lodged within the text of Moses. No philosopher has the slightest excuse to puff himself up against religion and the Church of God, where such rich theories have always been stored, even though men have not had the leisure or opportunity to unlock them for many ages until now. I believe this consideration is of primary importance for silencing atheistic wits and winning unspeakable honor and reverence for religion and the Church among those who are knowledgeable and sincere.*

Therefore, I must and ought to affirm this: what I have applied fits the text of Moses perfectly. I hope I may also add, without being immodest, that it is rational; but it must be the result of a longer deliberation with myself to affirm that it is true. For—

I must admit that although I feel I have a key in my hand whose design and shape are perfectly fitted to every part of the lock of this Mosaic Treasury <note>The "Mosaic Treasury" refers to the hidden philosophical knowledge More believes is contained within the writings of Moses.</note>, and which turns easily—locking and unlocking so that I can see within what I believe to be priceless riches of knowledge—yet I dare not believe my own eyes. I cannot conclude whether it is a real vision or a dream, not knowing for certain whether this is undoubtedly that ancient golden key of the Cabbala <note>The Cabbala (or Kabbalah) here refers to a tradition of mystical and philosophical interpretation of the Hebrew Scriptures.</note>, or one made of a cheaper metal. Indeed, a person's suspicion <note>original: "Jealousy"; in this context, it means suspicion or caution.</note> might well be increased by the fact that it immediately opens upon those two dazzling paradoxes: the motion of the Earth <note>The idea that the Earth orbits the sun (Copernicanism), which was still scientifically and religiously controversial in the 17th century.</note> and the preexistence of the soul <note>The theory that the soul exists in a heavenly realm before the body is conceived.</note>. These are enough to make even the boldest observer step back in sudden amazement, a state in which I confess I remain to this very day. No one can rightly wonder at my hesitation if they consider how cautious the ancient Church Fathers were about the roundness <note>original: "Globosity"</note> of the Earth and the existence of people living on the other side of it <note>original: "Antipodes"</note>. That the Earth is a sphere was the opinion of Pythagoras in ancient times, but it has become the certain knowledge of this present age.

<margin>The testimony of several holy people who either clearly supported, or at least did not dislike, the doctrine of the soul's preexistence.</margin>
18. Besides, I must honestly admit that I know of nothing more or better to be argued for the motion of the Earth and other main points of Cartesianism <note>The philosophy of René Descartes, which combined physics and metaphysics.</note> than what I have included in my *Letter to V. C.*, nor anything more conclusive regarding the preexistence of the soul than what I have produced in my *Treatise on her Immortality*. I brought these ideas into view (as I did with anything else in my writings that might seem to deviate from common opinion) to provide a broader subject for more precise evaluation, which contributes greatly to a correct decision about what is true. Nor did anything occur to my mind that seemed worth adding concerning that latter subject of preexistence, except for one point. Beyond showing that it was the opinion of all philosophers who held the soul to be immortal—and particularly of Plato, Aristotle, and Cicero, who are authors assigned to us by the very statutes of our University, which is enough to make the opinion respectable—I also noted how harmless and inoffensive that doctrine was during the early, untainted <note>original: "intemerate"</note> ages of the Church.

<margin>Clement of Alexandria <note>A prominent Christian theologian of the late 2nd century.</note>.</margin>
For I find Clement of Alexandria describing it in several places without the least hint of any dislike, such as in the first book of his *Stromata* <note>original: "Stromata's"; a series of writings by Clement titled "Miscellanies" or "Patchwork".</note>. Writing there about the Barbarians (whose wisdom he seems to prefer over the Greeks, perhaps to favor the Hebrews), he speaks thus: <note>original Greek: "Δῆλοι δ᾽ ἐισὶν οἱ βάρβαροι διαφερόντως τιμήσαντες τοὺς αὐτῶν νομοθέτας τε καὶ διδασκάλους, θεοὺς προσήποντες. ψυχὰς γὰρ ἀγαθὰς, κατὰ Πλάτωνα, καταλιπούσας τὸν ὑπερουράνιον τόπον ὑπομεῖναι ἐλθεῖν εἰς τόνδε τὸν τάρταρον, καὶ σῶμα ἀναλαβούσας τῶν ἐν γενέσει κακῶν ἁπάντων μετασχεῖν ὑπολαμβάνουσι, κηδεμόνας τοῦ τῶν ἀνθρώπων γένους, αἳ νόμους τε ἔθεσαν, καὶ φιλοσοφίαν ἐκήρυξαν."</note> "It is clear that the barbarians particularly honored their own lawmakers and teachers, calling them gods. For they conceive, along with Plato, that certain good souls, leaving their celestial mansions, endured coming into this Tartarus <note>A deep abyss in ancient Greek mythology used as a dungeon of torment; here used to refer to the physical world or a lower state of existence.</note>, and by taking on bodies, they shared in all the miseries that accompany physical birth. They did this because they were entrusted with the care of mankind, to whom they gave laws and preached philosophy." Clement is so far from rejecting this opinion that he introduces his discussion on the philosophy of the nations with this wonderful comparison: "That just as the parts of the universe, though they disagree one..."

*...true, which we find in* Eusebius. <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD) was a historian of the early Christian Church whose works are the primary source for Origen’s life.</note> *For certainly (to say nothing of his extraordinary talents and abilities, which even his greatest* adversaries *will not deny), it will be very hard to find another example of such sincere and zealous devotion to the cause of* Christ, *even to the point of a contempt for death and a desire for* martyrdom. *This was not just a thoughtless outburst of youthful passion in him, but a permanent faithfulness and fortitude of* spirit. *It was usual for that holy man to assist and encourage all the* martyrs, *those unknown to him as well as his acquaintances; he would openly accompany them to their execution, friendly embracing them and administering to them all the comfort he could, often at the risk of being stoned by the angry crowds.*

*It will seem a lesser matter to take notice of his constant reading and meditating on the Holy* Scripture *day and night, and his complete neglect of the* world *for the pleasure of divine contemplation and the service of the* Church *of* Christ. *Consider his excessive* charity *to the poor, his frequent* fastings *and sleeping on the ground, his endurance of cold and nakedness, his walking barefoot on hard stones, his abstinence from wine, and his singular* temperance <note>original: "Temperance"; meaning moderation and self-restraint.</note> *in all the pleasures of* nature. *His great example of an* ascetic *life gained many disciples for the* Church *and raised and equipped many undaunted* champions *of the* Christian faith, *who willingly laid down their lives for the love of the* Lord Jesus. *Among those from* Origen's school *were* Plutarchus, *the two* Sereni, Heraclides, Heron, Rhais, *and* Basilides, *who received the* crown of martyrdom <note>A traditional term for the spiritual reward and honor granted to those who die for their faith.</note> *through the intercession of that illustrious* virgin-martyr Potamiæna. *What dreadful calamities* Origen *himself also underwent in the* Decian Persecution, <note>The persecution of Christians under the Roman Emperor Decius, around 250 AD.</note> *what* shackles *and* torments *of* body, *what throwings into* prisons *and* dungeons, *what stretching and racking of limbs, what terrors of fire and burnings—all these are to be read in the records of* Church history.

<meta>This page continues Henry More's defense of Origen, specifically addressing the criticisms and "ridiculous additions" that later followers and enemies attached to his name, before moving on to list other Church Fathers who supported the doctrine of the preexistence of the soul.</meta>

...so expressly declaring that the Soul of the Messiah <note>original: "Messias"</note> never sinned. And lastly, to omit several others, there is the claim of his transferring the souls of men into the bodies of animals <note>original: "brutes"</note>: which I do not doubt, and could easily prove, to be falsely attributed <note>original: "fathered"</note> to Origen, just as it was to Pythagoras. Rather, some fanciful followers of both did attach these unbecoming and ridiculous additions <note>original: "Appendages"</note>, thinking every vain addition to be an improvement of those pure doctrines which were anciently delivered to the world. And such was the state of the doctrine of Preexistence in the Church of the Jews, where no such foolishness was mixed with it. And if it had so continued among the followers of Origen, certainly it would never have fallen under public censure. Though I dare not lay the blame solely upon them, as his spiteful enemies took enough liberty to charge Origen with things that had no basis in fact at all. 

One such example was that formal story of his burning incense on the altar of an idol, supposedly being forced to choose between that or the sexual abuse of his body by an Ethiopian. This is nothing but a <margin>* See the Epitome of Spondanus, Year 253, section 19. <note>Henri de Sponde (1568–1643) was a French historian who summarized the "Annals" of Baronius.</note></margin> * mere romance built upon the greatness of Origen's name and virtues. While his reputation may seem much tarnished by that public censure in the fifth General Council, anyone who considers that the details of his condemnation were entirely removed from the records of that Council by the same power that first caused his censure, may easily find evidence that will repair Origen's credit in great measure—and this without any damage to the authority of that great assembly. For it was their *wrong* (meaning they were misled), not their *fault*, that they were misinformed.

<margin>St. Basil and Gregory Nazianzen.</margin>
It also appears that St. Basil and Gregory Nazianzen <note>Two of the "Cappadocian Fathers," highly influential 4th-century theologians.</note> were no enemies to the opinion of the soul's preexistence, but rather favored it. This is evident from the great esteem they had for Origen, and particularly from the gift that Nazianzen gave to Theodorus Tyaneus: a book of excerpts from Origen’s writings, compiled by himself and St. Basil, which is titled *The Philocalia of Origen* <note>original: "Ὡριγένες Φιλοκαλία"</note>. In this work, there are several passages that plainly imply or directly affirm the preexistence of the soul.

<margin>Synesius, Bishop of Cyrene.</margin>
The next open supporter <note>original: "Assertor"</note> of the soul's preexistence is Synesius, Bishop of Cyrene. In a letter to his brother, he seriously professes that he cannot accept the honorable position offered to him without the liberty of enjoying—nay, I may say of professing—certain opinions of his which had been rooted in him for a long time based on well-considered reasons. At the head of these, he names this doctrine of the preexistence of the soul. <margin>* Letter 105.</margin> * "In good earnest," he says, "I shall never consent to the idea that the soul is of later existence than the body or matter" <note>original Greek: "Ἀμέλει τ. ψυχὴν ἐκ ἀξιώσω ποτὲ σώματΘ. ὑσερογενῆ νομίζειν"</note>. He deals so openly that he gives directions to his brother to share the letter with the "Scholastics" (as he calls them), so that it might be communicated to that reverend Father who offered him the position. Despite his freedom in professing this opinion, it was no obstacle to his promotion.

<margin>Arnobius.</margin>
To these you may add the authority of two Latin Fathers, Arnobius and Prudentius. The former writes explicitly concerning this point, <margin>* Against the Heathen, book 1. <note>original: "Advers. gent. lib. I."</note></margin> * "Do we not all owe this very first thing to God: that we exist, that we are called men, and that—having been either sent by Him or having fallen through blindness—we are held within the bonds of this body?" <note>original Latin: "Nonne Deo omnes debemus hoc ipsum primum quod sumus, quod esse homines dicimur, quod ab eo vel missi, vel lapsi cæcitate, hujus in corporis vinculis continemur?"</note> <margin>Prudentius.</margin> The other says this, in his *Hymn for the Burial of the Dead* <note>original: "Hymnus in Exequiis Defunctorum"</note>:

This last verse matches exactly the expression used by Synesius <note>Synesius of Cyrene (c. 373–414 AD), a philosopher-bishop who blended Neoplatonism with Christianity.</note> in his *Hymns*, where he calls his soul a *wandering exile* <note>original Greek: φυγὰς ἀλῆtis</note> because it left Heaven and wandered into this lower world.
