*St. Augustine* also speaks very favorably of this opinion in his work *On Free Will* <note>original: "de Libero arbitrio"</note>, where he writes: "Whether the soul lived in some other life before joining with this body is a great question, a great secret." <note>original: "Utrùm ante conſortium hujus corporis aliâ quâdam vitâ vixerit animus, magna quæstio est, magnum secretum."</note> And then in another place of the same treatise, speaking again of the soul's *preexistence*, he tells us freely and honestly: "If we think something about God other than what He is, our intention will lead us not to happiness <note>original: "beatitatem"</note> but to vanity. But regarding the creation <note>original: "creatura"</note>, if we think something other than how it is, as long as we do not hold it as something definitely known and perceived, there is no danger." <note>original: "Si de Deo aliud ſenſerimus quàm est, intentio nostra non in beatitatem ſed in vanitatem compellet. De creatura verò ſiquid aliter quàm ſeſe habet ſenſerimus, dummodo non id pro cognito perceptoque teneamus, nullum periculum."</note> And in a third place, in his discussion of that fourfold inquiry <note>original: "Quære"</note>—namely, whether souls are passed down through birth <note>original: "propagated"</note>, created, sent from God out of some hidden storehouse <note>original: "Repository"</note> where they already existed, or fell here of their own accord—he says, "Either this question has not yet been explained and illustrated by Catholic commentators of the divine books, as its obscurity and complexity deserves; or, if it has already been done, such writings have not yet reached our hands." <note>original: "Aut nondum iſta quæstio... à divinorum librorum Catholicis tractatoribus pro merito ſuæ obſcuritatis & perplexitatis evoluta atque illustrata est; aut, ſi jam factum est, nondum in manus nostras ejusmodi literæ pervenerunt."</note> From this, I think it is very clear that the early ages of the Church did not have a negative view of the opinion of the soul's *preexistence*.

implied in the question; I say, a man may derive a proof from this: **that there is no harm in the opinion, no poison or danger in it. Otherwise, surely our Savior, having such a perfect opportunity, would not have failed to point it out.**

<margin>That there is not the least clashing between Preexistence and the derivation of Original Sin from Adam.</margin>
19. **And I am as certain that there is no evil, conflict, or clash between this *hypothesis*** <note>original: "Hypothesis"—a proposed explanation or theory.</note> **and the ordinary, literal meaning of *Scripture* and the *universally-acknowledged standards of faith*, as I am that clear *air* does not block the light of the *sun*, but both can exist in the same space. That which it seems most opposed to is the derivation of *Original Sin* from *Adam*. But those who assert the *Preexistence of the Soul* do not understand the mystery correctly if they assume all souls—which enter these *earthly dwellings* according to natural *order*—were in a state of silence first. This makes it seem as though they did not exist before, and that the whole story of things evidently begins with *Adam*. In reality, God placed Adam's soul into such a *paradisiacal* body that it naturally encouraged his mind toward the possibility of not falling (just as traditional *theology* assumes Adam to have been). God intended for this same advantage to be passed down to his *descendants* if he had remained faithful. From this, it is clearly manifest that Adam's fall was the cause of what we now call *Original Sin*—that is to say, of that excessive *proneness* and almost irresistible *inclination* toward what is evil. Thus, the *hypothesis of Preexistence* is far from clashing with the derivation of *Original Sin* from *Adam*.**

**In fact, I will add further: what is said in *Scripture* about the first and second *Adam* cannot be understood as clearly as it can through the *hypothesis of Preexistence* and the idea of a previous fall of souls in another state. I ask anyone to consider without prejudice what better meaning there can be for those words** 
<margin>Romans 5:14.</margin>
**of *St. Paul*, where he says that *Adam* was the figure of him who was to come—that is to say, of *Christ*. He means that the office of *Adam* was a preliminary and *symbolic* version of the office of *Christ*. This comparison would be very weak if it only meant that Adam was a public figure, without any responsibility for the *redemption* of humanity. Therefore, the office of *Adam* was to transmit a healthy and *paradisiacal constitution* of body to his *offspring* (in the way our ordinary *theology* describes it). By doing so, he was meant to be, as it were, the *savior* and *redeemer* of his descendants from the ill effects of that former fall they had experienced [before this life]. This is why he was so exactly the figure of him who was to come. But this earthly *Adam* failing in his office, the Heavenly Adam was substituted in his place, who is** <margin>* Hebrews 7:25.</margin> **able to save to the uttermost. In my mind, this *hypothesis* makes *St. Paul* and this part of the *mystery* of our *religion* wonderfully easy and intelligible.**

**These and similar arguments may be alleged on behalf of that ancient point of *Platonism*: The Preexistence of the Soul.**

<margin>That mathematical certainty in mere philosophical speculations need not oblige any man's conscience to profess them against the wishes of his superiors.</margin>

<margin>Herodotus, Book 5, section 63.

*But so that I do not seem to harm my own reputation or cause offense to others by such a free confession, I am forced to add this: the conscience of every holy and sincere Christian is as strictly bound in matters of religion—those plainly and expressly determined by the infallible word of God—as it is free in philosophical speculations. And although, for the sake of his own peace or out of a respectful regard for the authority of the Church (which every honorable spirit naturally feels), he may strongly desire to say, profess, and do as they would have him, yet in cases of this kind—where anything is expected of him that goes against the plain and express meaning of those Divine Writings—he cannot help but find himself restricted. He will certainly be forced **to value the things of God more than the things of men** <note>original: "τὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ πρεσβύτερα ποιέεσθαι ἢ τὰ τῶν ἀνδρῶν"</note> (as the Lacedaemonians <note>term: Lacedaemonians—the ancient Spartans.</note> are said to have done, though based on a religious mistake). <margin>Matthew 10:33.</margin>
*These are the unbreakable <note>original: "Adamantine"</note> laws and bonds of religion, which no one can complain about without complaining against the very existence of God, or against His absolute right to be served first and to bind our consciences to believe (and our tongues to profess) whatever truths He has miraculously shared with the world on those terms. As it is written: "Whoever denies me before men, I will also deny before my Father who is in heaven." But in philosophical theories—such as the preexistence of the soul, the motion of the earth, and similar ideas—where God has not required our public profession, nor is our eternal interest at stake, nor is the source of the idea infallible; even if we imagine we have mathematical certainty of our conclusions, I must admit (as I said before) that I do not see how anyone is bound by conscience to assert them against the authority of the Church they live under. If the Church authorities should dislike these theories at any time, a person may with a safe conscience compromise with his superiors and use their language and phrasing regarding such matters. For if it was a virtue in that holy and respected lawgiver, Moses, to use such wisdom and fatherly kindness to adapt his message to the understanding of the common people <note>original: "Capacity of the Vulgar"</note> by describing the creation of the world according to how things appeared to them, then it certainly cannot be a vice in us—out of humble submission and respect for the governors of the Church—to adopt their official ways of speaking in those matters where God has not bound us to the contrary (no matter what our private judgment might be).*

<margin>That if the philosophy which he has applied to the text of Moses is true, it is a genuine restoration of the Mosaic Cabala <note>term: Cabala—here referring to a secret or traditional oral interpretation of the scriptures.</note>.</margin>

Once these theorems are accepted as true, they will necessarily be acknowledged as most lovely and glorious;*

# THE PREFACE.

1. *The author's defense <note>original: "Apologie"</note> for writing this treatise, since there are already so many books on this same subject.* 2. *That what he has written are the natural outpourings <note>original: "proper Emanations"</note> of his own mind, and may be especially useful for people of a similar temperament.* 3. *That he does not use fancy rhetoric, nor literary scholarship <note>original: "Philologie"</note>, nor the impressive number of more popular arguments, but rather solid and irresistible reason in a clear method.* 4. *That he has undeniably demonstrated the existence of God, provided this one assumption <note>original: "Postulate"</note> is admitted: That our mental powers <note>term: "Faculties" refers to the senses and the ability to reason</note> are reliable.* 5. *His unique management of the first argument of Descartes <note>original: "Des-Cartes"</note>:* 6. *And the reasons why he rejected the rest of Descartes' arguments.* 7. *His caution and care in managing arguments drawn from the more general phenomena <note>original: "Phænomena"</note> of nature:* 8. *As also in those arguments involving animals.* 9. *His careful choice of historical accounts that tend to prove the existence of spirits.* 10. *His confidence in that kind of argument.* 11. *The reason why he avoids repeating the miraculous stories of Holy Scripture.* 12. *His intentional effort to meet the atheist on their own ground <note>original: "Condescension and compliance"</note> to win them over from their atheism.*

->READER,<-

1. Regarding the reasons I was led to publish this present treatise, despite the large number of writings of this kind, I would rather leave it to your own keen observation <note>original: "quick-sightedness"</note> to discover them, than be forced into the immodesty of saying anything that might seem to claim it is superior <note>original: "precellency"</note> to what is already available in the world on this subject. I may only say this much: that I purposefully avoided reading any treatises concerning this subject so that I might write the natural thoughts of my own mind more undisturbed. I did not want to be carried away from what would naturally occur to me by filling my thoughts beforehand with the inventions of others.

2. I have written, therefore, following no copy but the eternal nature <note>original: "Characters"</note> of the human mind and the known phenomena of nature.

<sig>A 4</sig>

<summary>In this preface, Henry More introduces his philosophical approach to proving the existence of God, emphasizing original thought over existing literature and relying on human reason and natural phenomena.</summary>
<keywords>Henry More, preface, Descartes, atheism, reason, natural phenomena, philosophy of mind, methodology</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the Preface, where the author justifies adding another book to the existing literature on the existence of God. He explains that while he doesn't use the same flowery language or vast number of arguments as others, his focused and logical approach offers a unique contribution for different types of readers.</meta>

# THE PREFACE.

<sig>A</sig>

Nature. Since everyone looks to those who try to write sensibly—even though everyone does it differently—it was inevitable that I would address the same topics <note>original: "Heads"</note> as previous authors. Although those authors may deserve very high praise for their learned achievements <note>original: "atchievements"</note>, I hope my efforts have been such that, while they might not be rivals <note>term: "corrivals" refers to those competing for the same prize or status</note> or partners in their fame and reputation, I am confident <note>original: "do not distrust"</note> they will still contribute to the public good that such works usually claim to aim for.

What encouraged <note>original: "embolden"</note> me to publish this present treatise was not, as I said before, because I flattered myself with the idea <note>original: "Conceit"</note> that it was flashier or more appealing than what is already available to people; rather, it is because it is of a different kind and has its own unique usefulness and advantages, separate and distinct from others. I may admire the specific excellence of those other works from a distance, but I do not dare to compare mine with them in any way. Therefore, there is no repetition <note>term: "Tautology" refers to the unnecessary repetition of an idea</note> committed in recommending what I have written to the public, nor does it diminish the work of others by offering the fruit of my own. Considering there are so many different personalities and dispositions <note>original: "complexions and tempers"</note> of people in the world, I am confident that, just as what others have done has been very welcome and helpful to many, this work of mine may be well-received by some, and so not seem to have been written in vain.

3. For though I cannot promise my reader that I shall entertain him with as much charming *Rhetoric* and pleasant *scholarship* <note>term: "Philology" here refers to wide literary learning or the study of classical texts; original: "Philologie"</note> as he may find elsewhere, I hope he will acknowledge, if his mind is unbiased, that he encounters sound and plain reason and an easy and clear *Method*.

These arguments will only seem weak <note>original: "slight"</note> to those who consider them carelessly and superficially. For I did not borrow them from books, but drew them from the very nature of reality itself and from the permanent <note>original: "indeleble"</note> *ideas* within the human soul.

By relying on my own thoughts, I took nothing from the vast wealth of other writers’ work. As for what I might have remembered from others, I could not include it if I judged it to be open <note>term: "obnoxious to evasion" means vulnerable to being dodged or dismissed by a clever opponent</note> to being dismissed. My goal was not to trick <note>original: "impose upon"</note> the *Atheist*, but to truly convince him. <margin>
By the **objective reality** of an idea, I mean the reality of the thing represented by the idea, insofar as it exists within the idea itself. For whatever we perceive as being in the objects of our ideas is present in the ideas themselves *objectively*. <note>original: "Per Realitatem objectivam Ideae intelligo entitatē rei representatã per Ideam quatenus est in Idea. Nam quaecunque percipimus tanquam in Idearum objectis, ea sunt in ipsis Ideis objectivé. Cartes. Resp. ad Object. 2. Metaphys. Defin. 3."</note>

6. But as for his following reasons—which assume that the **objective reality** <note>term: "Objective reality" here refers to the content or "thing" represented by a thought, rather than the thought's existence as a mental event.</note> of the idea of God exceeds the creative power <note>original: "efficiency"</note> of the human mind; and that the human mind, if it did not come from another, would have bestowed upon itself all the perfection it can conceive of; and, lastly, that because the mind has no power to sustain itself, and because the present and future have no necessary connection to each other, the mind must be continually reproduced (that is, preserved) by some higher cause, which must be God—I say, since these grounds are so easily avoided by the atheist, I did not dare trust them, unless I had the author’s <note>The author is referring to René Descartes.</note> wit to defend them, for he was skillfully able to justify anything. But these arguments seem to me to be vulnerable to certain evasions that I cannot prevent.

For the atheist will readily reply that the human mind may be able, by itself, to form such an actual **idea** of God as is discussed there. This idea would merely be a current state <note>original: "modification"</note> of the mind, like any other notion, and an effect of the mind's own essence and power—that power being a fundamental property of its nature. Thus, there is no "effect" that exceeds the "cause," even if we look no further than the mind itself; for the mind forms this notion of God as naturally, and as much without the help of a higher cause, as it does anything else.

And as for the mind contributing those perfections to itself that it can imagine: if the mind existed by its own power, the atheist will say that such a claim implies a contradiction. It assumes that a thing, before it exists, could consult about the advantages of its own existence. But if the mind exists by its own power, it is simply what it finds itself to be, and it can be no other way.

And therefore, lastly, if the mind finds that it exists, it can no more destroy itself than it can create itself. Nor does it need anything to continue its being, provided that there is nothing in nature that can act against it and destroy it; for whatever exists continues to be as it is, unless there is some cause to change it.

# The Preface.

the mind of man, my careful choice made very large deductions <note>original: "defalkations"</note>; insisting rather upon such things as might be otherwise, and yet are far better as they are, than upon such as were necessary and could not be otherwise. As for example: when I considered the distance of the Sun, I did not believe that the fact he was not placed as low as the Moon, or as high as the fixed stars, was any great argument for Providence. This is because it might be replied that it was necessary for it to be between those two distances, otherwise the Earth would not have been habitable; and so mankind might have waited for a state of being until the agitation of **Matter** had worked things into a more tolerable fitness or posture for their production.

Nor is the annual motion of the *Sun*, or rather of the *Earth*, simply any argument for Divine Providence in itself; it is as necessary as a piece of wood being carried down a stream, or straws around a whirlpool. But the **Laws** of her motion are such that they very clearly convince us of a Providence; and therefore I was inclined to let go of the former argument and insist more extensively upon the latter.

Nor did I think it fit to use rhetorical flourishes <note>original: "Rhetoricate"</note> in proposing the great variety of things and the excellence <note>original: "precellency"</note> of one above another. Instead, I chose to press closely upon the design and the subordination of one thing to another, showing that—whereas the crude motions of **Matter** (by a thousand-to-one chance) might have cast it otherwise—the actual productions of things are such that our own reason cannot help but approve of them as being for the best, or as we ourselves would have designed them.

8. And so in the consideration of *Animals*, I do not so much urge my reasons from their diversity and survival <note>original: "subsistence"</note> (though the framing of **Matter** into even the bare survival of an animal is the effect of no less a cause than one which has some skill and counsel); but what I aim at is the exquisite design <note>original: "contrivance"</note> of their parts, and that their structure is far more perfect than what would merely serve for their bare existence and continuance in the world. This is an undeniable demonstration that they are the effects of **Wisdom**, not the results of Fortune <note>original: "Fortune"; here meaning random chance.</note> or fermented matter. <note>The author is likely referring to "spontaneous generation," an old theory that life could arise from the "fermentation" or chemical brewing of non-living matter.</note>

# CHAPTER I.

1. *That the tendency of these ages of the world to free themselves from the fear of superstition makes it a suitable time to try to steer them away from atheism.* 2. *That those who follow religion only in a superstitious and habitual way will easily turn into atheists if those ties once fail.* 3. *The usefulness of this present treatise even to those who are seriously religious.*

<margin>1.</margin>
The great truth which we are now to be employed with and to prove is, *That there is a God.* I chose this subject as very appropriate for the times we are in, and those that are coming, wherein Divine Providence is more generally freeing the minds of men from the fear and tyranny of mere customary superstition <note>original: "Superstition"; in this context, it refers to unthinking religious habits or dogmas held without personal conviction</note>, and permitting a freer investigation of religious matters than in former ages. In this environment, the Tempter <note>original: "the Tempter"; a reference to Satan</note> would take advantage, where he can, to carry men captive out of one dark prison into another—out of *superstition* and into *atheism* itself.

<margin>2.</margin>
2. This is something feasible enough for him to accomplish in those men who have followed religion only in a purely external way, either for the sake of fashion or in blind obedience to the authority of a church. Thus, being emboldened by the tottering and falling of what they previously took for the main structure of religion, they will gladly, in their imagination, also cast down the very object of that religious worship after it. They will conclude that there is no God, just as there is no religion; that is, they wish there were none, so that they might be free from all

### CHAPTER II.

*1. That nothing is so demonstrable that the human mind can rationally conclude it is impossible for it to be otherwise. 2. That the human soul may give full assent to something that might nonetheless possibly be otherwise, illustrated by several examples. 3. A similar example of dissent. 4. The reasons why he has so diligently established this point. 5. That the atheist gains no advantage from the author's free confession that his arguments are not so convincing that they leave no possibility of the matter being otherwise.*

1. **B**ut when I speak of demonstrating that there is a God, I would not want to be suspected of such vanity and boastfulness that I am thought to mean I will bring only those arguments that are so convincing that a person's understanding shall be forced to confess it is impossible to be otherwise than I have concluded. For, for my own part, I am inclined to believe that there is nothing at all that can be demonstrated in that way. For it is possible that *mathematical evidence* itself might be nothing but a constant, undiscoverable delusion to which our nature is necessarily and perpetually liable <note>original: "obnoxious unto"; in this context, it means vulnerable to or subject to</note>. It could be that, either by fate or by chance, there has been in the world since time immemorial such a being as we call *Man*, whose essential quality is to be most mistaken precisely when he believes something to be most evidently true. And why might this not be as likely as anything else, if one insists that all things are fated or accidental without a God? For there can be no check on this wild idea except by supposing that we ourselves exist because of some higher Principle that is absolutely *good* and *wise*—which is the same thing as acknowledging *that there is a God*.

2. Therefore, when I say that I will demonstrate *that there is a God*, I do not promise that I will always produce arguments so strong that the reader will be forced to confess it is utterly impossible for it to be otherwise. Instead, they shall be such as deserve *full assent* and win *full assent* from any unprejudiced mind. For I believe that we may give *full assent* to something that might nonetheless possibly be otherwise, which I shall illustrate with several examples. Suppose two men climbed to the top of Mount *Athos* <note>A mountain in northeastern Greece, famous in antiquity and later as a center of monasticism</note>, and there

...viewing a stone in the form of an altar with ashes on it, and the footsteps of men on those ashes, or some words, if you like—such as "To the Best and Greatest" <note>original: *Optimo Maximo*</note>, or "To the unknown God" <note>original: *τῷ ἀγνώστῳ θεῷ* (*tō agnōstō theō*)</note>, or the like—written or scrawled out upon the ashes; and one of them should cry out, "Assuredly some men have been here and have done this." But the other, more fastidious than wise <note>original: "more nice than wise"</note>, should reply, "No, it may possibly be otherwise; for this stone may have naturally grown into this very shape, and the seeming ashes may be no ashes—that is, no remains of any fuel burnt there—but some unexplainable and imperceptible motions of the air, or other particles of this fluid matter that is active everywhere, have worked some parts of the matter into the form and nature of ashes, and have flickered and played about so that they have also shaped those meaningful characters in them." Would not anyone deem it a sign of weakness, no less than senility <note>original: "dotage"</note>, for the first man to withdraw even slightly from his previous understanding? Instead, he should agree as fully as ever with what he first pronounced, despite this bare possibility of the matter being otherwise.

->2. The same applies to **anchors** that have been dug up, either in open fields or mountainous places, as well as **Roman urns** with ashes and inscriptions, such as *Severianus*, *Julius Linus* <note>original: *Ful. Nor can any man ever so demonstrate that those coins, anchors, and urns were once the **workmanship** <note>original: "Artifice"</note> of men, or that this or that skull was once a part of a living man, that he could force an acknowledgment that it is *impossible* for it to be otherwise. But yet, I do not think that any man, without doing obvious violence to his **faculties**, can at all withhold his agreement. He must freely and fully agree that this or that skull was once part of a living man, and that these anchors, urns, and coins were certainly once made by human skill, despite the possibility of it being otherwise.<-

->3. And what I have said of **Agreement** <note>original: "Assent"</note> is also true of **Disagreement** <note>original: "Dissent"</note>. For the mind of man, if not broken or prejudiced, will fully and irreconcilably disagree by its own natural wisdom <note>original: "sagacity"</note>, even where no wit of man can prove that the thing it so resolutely and undoubtedly rejects is impossible to be true. Imagine such a fiction as this: that **Archimedes**, with the very same body he had when the soldiers killed him, is now safely focused on his **geometrical figures** underground at the center of the Earth, far from the noise and din of this world that might disturb his meditations or distract him in his intricate drawings <note>original: "curious delineations"</note> he makes with his staff in the dust. No man living can prove this is impossible; yet if any man does not as irreconcilably disagree with such a fable as this as he would with any falsehood imaginable, assuredly that man is on the verge of madness or senility, or does enormous violence to the free use of his faculties.<-

<page-num>12</page-num>
<header>An Antidote against Atheism. BOOK I.</header>

Therefore, it is clear that there can be a very firm and unwavering *agreement* <note>original: "Assent"</note> or *disagreement*, even when the thing we agree with might possibly be otherwise, or when the thing we disagree with cannot be proven impossible.

4. I have spent quite some time exploring this point in various ways to make a better impression on my reader. It is very useful and important for two reasons. First, it informs the reader that the arguments I will present—though I do not use the boastful term *demonstration* <note>In this context, a "demonstration" is a formal logical proof that carries mathematical certainty.</note> for them—can still be just as effective for winning a *firm and unshaken agreement* as if they were strictly proven in the most technical sense. Second, it serves to remind him that if these arguments are so strong and so well-suited to the human mind that he has no reply other than "it might possibly be otherwise," he should give his free and full *agreement* to the conclusion. If he does not, he should suspect some personal bias, prejudice, or weakness in himself, rather than a lack of strength in the arguments.

5. But if the *atheist*, on the contrary, tries to twist my honesty and fair dealing, imagining he has gained some advantage because I freely confessed that my arguments are not so undeniable as to rule out all other possibilities, let him calculate his supposed gains. He must add this limitation: that being wrong is no more possible than the idea that the clearest *mathematical evidence* might be false (which is impossible, if our mental faculties are reliable); or, it is no more possible than the idea that the *Roman urns* and *coins* mentioned earlier were the work of *Nature* rather than human skill. Our minds find this so improbable that it is impossible for them not to fully agree with the opposite. When he has finished his calculations, it will be clear that only his gross ignorance of this kind of "arithmetic" would embolden him to think himself the winner.

---

### CHAPTER III.

> 1. *We must first have a settled idea of what God is before we attempt to prove that He exists.* 2. *The definition of God.* 3. *There is an idea of an absolutely perfect Being in our minds, whether the atheist accepts it as the idea of God or not.* 4. *The fact that this idea might be triggered by external events does not mean it is not natural to us.*

1. Now that I have laid this groundwork, I will move closer to my actual goal. In pursuing this, it is necessary for me to first define *what God is* before I proceed to prove *that He exists*. It is natural for human reason to find arguments for the impossibility, possibility, probability, or necessity of a thing's existence by first explaining its essence <note>original: "Essence"; the fundamental nature or "what-ness" of a thing.</note>.

<summary>More concludes that "moral certainty" is a valid basis for belief and begins Chapter III by stating that one must define God's essence before proving His existence.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the general nature of logical certainty to the specific task of defining God. Henry More addresses the atheist directly, arguing that one cannot deny or doubt a concept without first having a clear definition of it.</meta>

<page-num>13</page-num>
<header>CHAPTER III. *An Antidote against Atheism.*</header>

1. Now that I have arrived at this point, I ask any atheist who denies there is a God, or anyone who doubts whether there is one, what *idea* or *notion* they form of the thing they deny or doubt. If they choose to be overly particular or hesitant <note>original: "nice and squeamish"</note> and claim they can form no *notion* of such a thing, I would gladly ask them why they then deny or doubt something they do not understand. For it is necessary that anyone who wishes to rationally doubt or deny a thing must have some settled *notion* of the thing they are doubting or denying. But if they claim that the very reason they deny or doubt God's existence is because they can form no *notion* of him, I shall immediately remove that excuse <note>original: "Allegation"</note> by offering them a notion that is as specific to God as any notion is specific to anything else in the world.

2. I define God, therefore, in this way: *An Essence or Being who is fully and absolutely perfect*. I say *fully and absolutely perfect* to contrast him with the kind of *perfection* that is not *full and absolute*, but rather the *perfection* of this or that *species* or *kind* of finite *being*—for instance, of a lion, a horse, or a tree. But to be *fully and absolutely perfect* is to be at least as perfect as the human understanding <note>original: "apprehension of a man"</note> can conceive without a contradiction. For whatever is inconceivable or contradictory is nothing at all to us; we are not meant to step a single atom beyond the limits of our natural abilities <note>original: "Faculties"</note>. However, what I have proposed is so far from being beyond our abilities that I dare appeal to any atheist who still has any command of sense and reason left in him: is it not very easy and intelligible at first sight? And if there is a God, must he not be thought of by us as this *idea* or *notion* sets forth?

3. But if he stubbornly denies that this is the proper *notion* of God, let him indulge his own whim. This yet remains undeniable: that there is in man an *idea* of a *Being who is absolutely and fully perfect*, which we construct by attributing to it every conceivable *perfection* that does not imply a contradiction. And this *notion* is natural and essential to the soul of man; it cannot be washed out nor taken away <note>original: "conveigh'd away"</note> by any force or clever argument <note>original: "trick of wit"</note> whatsoever, as long as the mind of man is not broken <note>original: "craz'd"</note> but has the ordinary use of its own faculties.

4. Nor will it matter if someone claims that *this notion* is not innate <note>original: "connatural"</note> and essential to the soul because she formed it based on external experiences <note>original: "occasions from without"</note>. For all those undeniable conclusions in geometry—which might be helped and triggered by something external—are nonetheless so natural and essential to the soul that you might as soon separate the soul from itself <note>original: "unsoul the Soul"</note> as divide her from her perpetual agreement with those mathematical truths, provided no disease or violence is done to her faculties. As for example, she cannot help but acknowledge within herself the several distinct *ideas* of the *five regular solids* <note>original: "five regular Bodies"; these are the Platonic solids: the tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron, and icosahedron.</note>, as well as the fact that it is impossible for there to be any more than five. And this *idea* of a *Being who is absolutely perfect* is as distinct and permanent <note>original: "indeleble"</note> an *idea* in the soul as the *idea* of the *five regular solids* or any other *idea* whatsoever.

It remains undeniable, therefore, that there is an inseparable *idea* of a *Being who is absolutely perfect* always residing in the soul of man, even if it is not always active.

## CHAPTER 4.

1. What notions are more particularly comprised in the idea of a being absolutely perfect. 2. That the difficulty of framing the conception of a thing ought to be no argument against its existence; the nature of physical matter being so perplexed and intricate, yet all men acknowledge it exists. 3. That the idea of a spirit is as easy a notion as that of any other substance whatsoever. What powers and properties are contained in the notion of a spirit. 4. That eternity and infinity, if God did not exist, would be attributed to something else; so that atheism cannot free the mind from such complexities. 5. Goodness, knowledge, and power, notions of highest perfection, and therefore necessarily included in the idea of a being absolutely perfect. 6. As also necessity, since it establishes greater perfection than contingency <note>original: "Contingency" — the state of existing by chance or depending on something else, rather than existing by necessity.</note>.

1. But now, to lay out more particularly the perfections comprehended in this notion of a *being absolutely and fully perfect*, I think I may confidently name these: *self-subsistence* <note>original: "Self-subsistency" — the ability to exist independently without being created or sustained by another.</note>, *immateriality*, *infinity* of both *duration* and *essence* <note>original: "Essence" — the fundamental nature or core reality of a thing.</note>, *immense goodness*, *omniscience* <note>all-knowing</note>, *omnipotence* <note>all-powerful</note>, and *necessity of existence*. Let this, therefore, be the description of a *being absolutely perfect*: That it is a *spirit*, *eternal*, *infinite in essence and goodness*, *omniscient*, *omnipotent*, and of *itself necessarily existing*. All these attributes are characteristics of the highest perfection that the human understanding can grasp. Since they have no discoverable imperfection mixed with them, they must by necessity be attributed to that which we conceive as absolutely and fully *perfect*. 

If anyone says that this is merely dressing up a concept from my own imagination, which I then slyly suggest is the concept of a *God*, I answer this: no one can discuss or reason about anything without referring to settled notions written in his own mind. To make such an objection implies the most contradictory absurdities imaginable; it is as if a man should reason from something that never entered his mind, or that is utterly beyond the reach of his own faculties. Such groundless allegations only reveal an unwillingness to acknowledge one's own ability to think of God. They show a heavy tendency to sink into a total forgetfulness of him, becoming as dull and senseless in divine matters as the very animals.

2. But others, perhaps, will not look on this notion as contemptible because it is easily composed of familiar concepts the human mind normally forms. Instead, they might reject it because of certain difficult terms within it, such as *spirit*, *eternal*, and *infinite*. They claim they can form no concept of a *spirit*, and they do not know how to position their minds to understand how anything could be *eternal* or *infinite*. Therefore, some would argue there is no such thing as a *spirit* in the world.

But if the difficulty of forming a conception of a thing must take away

...the existence of the thing itself, there will be no such thing as a *body* left in the world, and then all will be *spirit*, or nothing. For who can form such a clear notion of a *body* as to free himself from the entanglements that the *extension* <note>original: "Extension" — the property of taking up physical space.</note> of it will bring along with it? For this extended *matter* consists of either indivisible points, or of particles divisible *infinitely* <note>original: "in infinitum" — to infinity.</note>. Take whichever of these two you will (and you can find no third option), and you will be wound into the most notorious absurdities possible. 

For if you say it consists of points, from this position I can necessarily demonstrate that every *spear* or *church steeple*, or whatever long body you choose, is as thick as it is long; that the tallest *cedar* is not as high as the lowest *mushroom*; and that the *Moon* and the *Earth* are so near one another that the thickness of your hand will not fit between them; that *rounds* and *squares* are all the same figure; that *even* and *odd numbers* are equal to one another; and that the clearest *day* is as dark as the blackest *night*. 

And if you choose the other side of the *alternative* <note>original: "Disjunction" — a choice between two logical possibilities.</note>, your imagination will be little better at ease; for nothing can be divisible into parts it does not have. Therefore, if a *body* is divisible into infinite parts, it has infinite extended parts; and if it has an infinite number of extended parts, it must be a difficult mystery to the imagination of man that infinite extended parts should not amount to one whole infinite *extension*. And thus a *grain* of *mustard seed* would be as infinitely extended as the whole *matter* of the *universe*, and a thousandth part of that grain as well as the grain itself. 

These things are more inconceivable than anything in the notion of a *spirit*. Therefore, we are not to scornfully and contemptuously reject any notion for seeming at first to be clouded and obscured with some difficulties and intricacies of conception; since that of whose being we seem most assured—matter—is the most entangled and perplexed in its conception of anything that can be proposed to the understanding of a man. 

But here you will reply that our *senses* are struck by such manifest impressions from *matter* that, though its *nature* is difficult to conceive, its *existence* is palpable to us by how it acts upon us. Why then, all that I desire is this: that when you are reminded of some *actions* and *operations* that come to the notice of your sense or understanding which (unless we do violence to our faculties) we can never attribute to *matter* or *body*, you would not then be so fastidious <note>original: "nice" — picky or overly particular.</note> and averse to admitting such a substance as is called a *spirit*, even though you imagine some difficulty in conceiving of it.

3. But for my own part, I think the *nature* of a *spirit* is as conceivable and easy to be defined as the nature of anything else. For as for the very *essence* or bare *substance* of anything whatsoever, anyone who is not a complete novice in speculation acknowledges that it is utterly unknowable. However, the *essential* and *inseparable properties* are as intelligible and explicable in a *spirit* as in any other *subject* whatever. 

As for example, I conceive the entire *idea* of a *spirit* in general (or at least of all finite, created, and subordinate *spirits*) to consist of these several powers or properties: namely, *self-penetration* <note>The ability of a spirit to occupy the same space as another entity without displacing it.</note>, *self-motion*, *self-contraction* and *dilation* <note>Expansion.</note>, and *indivisibility*. These are those that I reckon more absolute. I will add also that which has relation to another, and that is the power of

*Penetrating, Moving, and Altering Matter.* These properties and powers, when put together, form the *Notion and Idea* of a *Spirit*. By these, it is plainly distinguished from a *Body*, whose parts cannot penetrate one another, is not *self-moving*, and can neither contract nor expand itself. A body is divisible and its parts can be separated from one another; but the parts of a *Spirit* can no more be separated—even though they may be expanded—than you can cut off the *rays of the sun* with a pair of *scissors* made of *clear crystal*. This will suffice for establishing the *Notion* of a *Spirit*; the proof of its *Existence* does not belong in this section. From this *description*, it is plain that a *Spirit* is a concept of greater *Perfection* than a *Body*. Therefore, it is more fitting to be an *Attribute* of that which is *absolutely Perfect* than a body is.

4. But now, concerning the other two difficult terms, *Eternal* and *Infinite*: if anyone would excuse himself from agreeing to the *Notion of a God* because of the *incomprehensibility* of those *Attributes*, let him consider this: he will be forced, whether he wants to or not, to acknowledge that something is *Eternal*—either *God* or the *World*—and the complexity is the same in either case. And though he might try to brush off the trouble of understanding an *Infinite Deity*, he will never untangle himself from the complexities of *Infinite Space*; that *notion* will stick as closely to his *Soul* as his own power of *Imagination*.

5. Now, it will be undoubtedly concluded if a man consults his own faculties—and I know of nothing else he can consult—that *Goodness, Knowledge, and Power* (the three following attributes) are *Attributes of Perfection*. At the very least, this will be returned as infallibly true: that a *Being who is absolutely Perfect* possesses these, or possesses something that contains these in a superior way. It is manifest that *Knowledge*, or something like it, is in *God*, because without *awareness* <note>original: "Animadversion" — the act of noticing or perceiving; conscious attention.</note> in some sense or another, it is impossible to be *Happy*. And it is just as impossible for a *Being* to be *absolutely Perfect* and yet not *Happy*. But *Knowledge* without *Goodness* is only *cold shrewdness* <note>original: "dry Subtilty"</note> or *malicious craft*; and *Goodness* combined with *Knowledge* but devoid of *Power* is merely lame and ineffective. Therefore, whatever is *absolutely Perfect* is *infinitely Good, Wise, and Powerful*.

6. Lastly, it is a greater *Perfection* for all of this to be *Stable, Unchanging, and Necessary* rather than *accidental* or merely *Possible*. Therefore, the *Idea of a Being who is absolutely Perfect* represents to our minds that the subject of that *Idea* must necessarily exist; and that which by its own nature necessarily exists must never fail to be. Whether the *Atheist* chooses to call this *absolutely Perfect Being "God"* or not makes no difference; I do not care <note>original: "I list not" — I do not desire or care to.</note> to argue about words. But I think any other person, at first sight, will say that we have discovered the true *Idea of God*.

<header>CHAPTER 5. An Antidote against Atheism.</header>

# CHAPTER 5.

1. *What has caused various men to imagine that the Soul is a blank slate* <note>original: *abrasa tabula*</note>. 2. *That the Mind of Man is not a blank slate, but has actual knowledge of her own, and in what sense she has it.* 3. *A further illustration of the truth of this.*

1. Now that we have discovered this *idea* of a *Being who is absolutely perfect*, it will be useful to briefly touch upon a notable point in *philosophy* before we apply that idea further. This point is: *whether the human soul is a blank slate* <note>original: *abrasa tabula*</note>—*a notebook in which nothing is written—or whether she has some innate notions and ideas within herself*. It so happens that because the soul first begins to think when prompted by external objects, some men’s judgments have been so misled that they have imagined the soul has no knowledge or notions except what are *passively* impressed or drawn upon her by the objects of our *senses*. These men do not distinguish carefully enough between *external occasions* <note>external triggers or circumstances</note> and the primary *causes* of things.

2. But the human mind, being more free and better practiced in closely observing its own operations and nature, cannot help but discover that there is an *active* and *actual knowledge* in a person. The outward objects we encounter are merely *reminders* of this knowledge, rather than its original creators or planters. When I say *actual knowledge*, I do not mean that there is a set number of *ideas* flaring and shining to the *attentive faculty* <note>original: *animadversive faculty*; the part of the mind that notices things</note> like so many *torches* or *stars* in the sky to our outward sight. Nor do I mean there are any *figures* occupying distinct places, legibly written there like the *red letters* or *astrological symbols* <note>original: *astronomical characters*</note> in an *almanac*. Instead, I mean an active wisdom in the soul—a kind of quick recollection—whereby a small hint causes her to immediately develop a much clearer and larger concept.

3. I cannot describe her condition better than this: suppose a skilled *musician* has fallen asleep in a field of grass. While asleep, he does not dream of anything concerning his musical talent; therefore, in one sense, there is no *actual skill*, notion, or representation of anything musical within him. But his friend, who is sitting by him and cannot sing at all, jogs him awake and asks him to sing this or that song, giving him only the first two or three words. The musician immediately takes the song from his friend's mouth and sings the whole piece based on that slight and slender hint. In the same way, the *human mind*, being jogged and awakened by the *impulses* of outward *objects*, is stirred up into a fuller and clearer understanding of what was only imperfectly hinted to her by external circumstances. I venture to call this faculty *actual knowledge*, in the same sense that the sleeping musician’s skill might be called *actual skill* even when he was not thinking about it.

### CHAPTER VI.

1. *Various examples arguing for actual knowledge in the soul: such as her having a more accurate idea of a circle and triangle than matter can show her.* 2. *And that, upon one single observation, she assures herself of the universal properties of a triangle.* 3. *The same is argued from the nature of mathematical and logical notions, which do not enter through the senses, as they are not physical properties of matter;* 4. *Because they are produced without any physical motion upon the matter;* 5. *And that contrary kinds may be entirely in one and the same part of matter at once.* 6. *That there are certain sure complex notions of the mind for which she was not indebted to the senses.*

1. That this is the condition of the soul is discoverable by several observations. For example: show the soul the figure of a *circle* through the outward senses; she recognizes immediately that this is one kind of *figure*, and can promptly add that if it were perfect, all the lines drawn from one central point to the *perimeter* <note>The outer boundary or edge of a shape</note> must be exactly equal. In the same way, show her a *triangle*; she will straightway pronounce that if that is the correct figure it aims to be, the *angles* must be closed in indivisible points. But this level of accuracy, either in the *circle* or the *triangle*, cannot be found in any material *object*. Therefore, it remains true that she has a more full and exquisite knowledge of things within herself than *matter* can display before her.

2. Let us consider a third example: suppose someone demonstrates that this *triangle* described in *matter* has its three angles equal to two right angles <note>A fundamental rule of geometry: the sum of the angles in any triangle is 180 degrees, which equals two 90-degree right angles</note>. "Why yes," says the soul, "this is true—and not only in this particular *triangle*, but in all plain triangles that can possibly be described in *matter*." And thus, you see, the soul sings out the whole song upon the first hint, as if she knew it very well beforehand.

3. Besides this, there are a multitude of *relative notions* or *ideas* in the mind of man—both mathematical and *logical*—and if we prove these cannot be the impressions of any material *object* from the outside, it will necessarily follow that they come from the soul herself within, and are the natural equipment of human understanding. These include notions such as *Cause, Effect, Whole* and *Part, Like* and *Unlike*, and the rest. So too are *Equality* and *Inequality*, *ratio* <note>original: λόγος (logos)</note> and *analogy* <note>original: ἀναλογία (analogia)</note>, *Proportion* and *Analogy, Symmetry* and *Asymmetry*, and such like. I shall easily prove all these *relative ideas* to be no material impressions from the outside world upon the soul, but rather her own active conceptions proceeding from herself while she takes notice of external *objects*. It is plain that these *ideas* can make no impression upon the outward senses because they are not *sensible* <note>perceptible by the senses</note> nor *physical properties of matter*. And how can something that is not a *physical property of matter* affect our bodily organs of *sense*?

Now, that these *relative ideas*, whether *logical* or *mathematical*, are not *physical properties of matter* is manifest from these two arguments:

arguments. First, these notions may be produced when there has been no **physical motion** or alteration in the **subject** to which they belong; indeed, they can arise when nothing at all has been done to the **subject** to which they apply. For example, suppose one side of a room is whitened while the other is not touched or meddled with; this other side has thus become unlike the first, and the notion of being <term>dissimilar</term> <note>original: *Dissimile*</note> necessarily belongs to it, even though nothing at all was done to it. Likewise, suppose you have two pounds of **lead**, which are two **equal** pieces of that **metal**. If you cut away half from one of them, the other pound—without anything being done to it at all—has lost its notion of being **equal** and has acquired a new notion of being **double** the size of the other. 

It is useless to argue that although nothing was done to this pound of **lead**, something was done to the other. That does not weaken the logic; rather, it shows that the notion of being <term>half</term> <note>original: *Sub-double*, meaning a 1:2 ratio</note>, which applied to the lead that was cut, is merely our **mode** of conceiving it. The same applies to the other piece. These are not **physical properties** that strike the physical organs of the **body** in the way that **hot** and **cold**, **hard** and **soft**, or **white** and **black** do. Therefore, the **ideas** of **equal** and **unequal**, **double** and **half**, **like** and **unlike**, and the rest, are not external impressions upon the senses. Instead, they are the soul's own active way of conceiving those things discovered by the outward senses.

5. The second argument is that one and the same part of **matter** is capable, at the exact same time, of representing two contrary **ideas of this kind**. For example, any piece of matter that is a <term>middle proportional</term> <note>In mathematics, a value between two others that maintains a consistent ratio, such as 4 in the sequence 2, 4, 8.</note> between two other pieces is both **double** (relative to one) and **half** (relative to the other), or **triple** and **one-third** at once. This is a clear sign that these **ideas** are not **properties of the matter** itself and therefore do not affect our senses. If they did, they would also affect the senses of **beasts**, and animals might then become good geometricians and mathematicians. Since these ideas do not affect our physical senses, it is plain that we possess some **ideas** for which we are not indebted to our senses. They are instead the simple exertions of the mind, occasionally awakened by the stimuli of outward objects—much like how the person who woke a **musician** to sing did not actually teach him his skill.

6. And now, in the third and last place, it is manifest that besides these single **ideas** I have proved to exist in the mind, there are also several complex **notions** in the same. Examples include: ***The whole is greater than the part***; ***If you take equal amounts from equal amounts, the remainders are equal***; and ***Every number is either even or odd***. These are recognized as true by the soul at the very first proposal, as anyone of sound mind plainly perceives.

## CHAPTER VII.

1. *The Mind of Man is not unfurnished with **Innate Truth**; we should confidently listen to its natural and unprejudiced dictates and suggestions. 2. Some notions and truths are at least naturally and unavoidably assented to by the Soul, whether it has **actual knowledge** within itself or not. 3. The definition of an **absolutely Perfect Being** is one such truth. 4. This **absolutely Perfect Being** is **God**, the Creator and Designer of all things. 5. The certainty and stability of this Idea.*

1. And now that we see so clearly that the Soul is not unfurnished for dictating Truth to us, I ask anyone: why should he be so hesitant or fearful as to be afraid to trust his own faculties? Why, under the pretense that the Soul has nothing of its own and can be molded into believing anything—or that it arbitrarily and randomly organizes the various impressions it receives from the outside world—would he refuse to accept the **natural emanations** <note>original: "Emanations," meaning the natural outputs or insights arising from the mind itself</note> of his own mind as faithful guides?

2. But if the point I am arguing for—namely, that the Soul has **actual knowledge within itself** in the sense I have explained—seems too subtle (even though it is not), then surely this at least will be admitted as true: the nature of the Soul is such that it will certainly and fully agree to some conclusions, no matter how it came to know them, unless it does obvious violence to its own faculties. These truths must therefore be concluded to be not accidental or arbitrary, but **natural** to the Soul. I have already named examples, such as: *Every finite number is either even or odd*; or *If you add equal parts to equal parts, the wholes are equal*. There are also principles that are not as simple as these, but which stick just as closely to the Soul once they are understood, such as: *The three angles in a triangle are equal to two right angles*; *There are exactly five regular bodies, neither more nor less* <note>The "five regular bodies" refer to the Platonic solids: the tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron, and icosahedron</note>; and similar principles which we declare to be necessarily true according to the light of Nature.

3. Therefore, let us now revisit what we laid aside for a moment: the **Idea of an absolutely Perfect Being** proposed earlier. Because it is presented in such a way that a person cannot get it out of his mind—and must acknowledge it to be indeed the **Idea** of such a **Being**—it follows that it is no arbitrary or accidental concept <note>original: "conceipt"</note>, but a **necessary** one. Therefore, it is natural to the Soul, even if it is not always consciously present.
Wherefore it is clear that when we consult our own natural light concerning the notion of an **absolutely Perfect Being**, this inner wisdom tells us that it is: *A spiritual substance, eternal, infinite in essence and goodness, omnipotent, omniscient, and of itself necessarily existent.*
This answer is such that if we understand its meaning, we cannot find a way to deny it; therefore, it is true according to the light of Nature.

<page-num>21</page-num>
<header>CHAPTER VIII. An Antidote against Atheism.</header>

A being that is all-knowing and all-powerful is the root and origin of all things. For **Omnipotence** <note>original: "Omnipotency," the quality of having unlimited power</note> signifies a power that can achieve anything that is not logically contradictory; and **Creation** implies no such contradiction. Therefore, this perfect **Being** can create all things. However, if this being found **Matter** or other **Substances** already existing on their own, this omnipotence and power of creation would be useless. Indeed, a complete omnipotence would not reside in this supposedly absolute power—an idea that the free and unbiased faculties of the human mind cannot accept, viewing it instead as a contradiction. Therefore, the natural notion of a **Being who is absolutely Perfect** implies that the same **Being** is the **Lord** and **Maker** of all things. According to the natural light of reason, a being of this nature is to be adored and worshipped with all humility and thankfulness by everyone who knows of him. And what is this, if not to acknowledge him as God?

5. Therefore, I believe I have sufficiently demonstrated that the notion or idea of God is as natural, necessary, and essential to the soul of man as any other notion or idea. It is no more arbitrary or made-up than the notion of a **Cube** or a **Tetrahedron** <note>original: "Tetraedrum," a three-dimensional shape with four triangular faces</note>, or any of the other **Regular Bodies** <note>original: "Regular Bodies," referring to the five Platonic solids in geometry</note> in geometry. These are not invented for our own pleasure (for such imaginary fictions and monsters are infinite), but for these geometric shapes, it can be proven that there can be no more than **five** of them. This shows that their concept is necessary, not an arbitrary collection of whatever we please.

And thus, having fully established the notion of God—*what he is*—I proceed now to the next point, which is to prove *that he is*.

## C H A P T E R VIII.

1. *That the very idea of God implies his necessary existence.* 2. *That his existence is not just hypothetically necessary, but absolutely so, with a note on the common excuse used to avoid this truth.* 3. *That to acknowledge God as a being who necessarily exists according to his true definition, and yet to say he might not exist, is a plain contradiction.* 4. *That "necessity" is a logical term and implies an unbreakable connection between a subject and what is said about it <note>original: "Subject and Prædicate"</note>, from which this axiom is necessarily and eternally true:* God does exist. 5. *A further demonstration of his existence from the fact that "happening by chance" or "being impossible" is incompatible with his nature or idea.* 6. *That necessary self-existence belongs either to God, to Matter, or to both.* 7. *The great inconsistencies that follow if we assume Matter exists by its own power.* 8. *An answer to an excuse.* 9. *That a number of deities existing by their own essence <note>original: "Self-essentiated"</note> plainly denies the existence of the true God.* 10. *The only undeniable demonstration of the Unity of the Godhead.* 11. *The absurdity of admitting that **Matter** exists by its own power while denying that **God** does.* 12. *That this absurdity cannot be excused by the fact that **Matter** can be felt by the senses, since the **Atheist** himself is forced to admit things that cannot be sensed.* 13. *That it is just as foolish a*

The **factious stubbornness** <note>original: "factious Humoursomeness," referring to a biased or self-willed temperament</note> of the **Atheist** in siding with **some Faculties** of the **Soul** and rejecting the **rest**, even though they are all equally competent **judges**.

1. **AND** now, truly, looking upon the true **Idea** of God which we have discovered, I seem to myself to have delved deeper into this matter than I realized. For if this **Idea** or **Notion** of God is true, as I have undeniably proved, it is also undeniably true that he does **exist**. For this **Idea** of God is not an arbitrary invention made up for pleasure, but the necessary and natural outgrowth <note>original: "Emanation"</note> of the human mind. If it shows us that the notion and nature of God implies **necessary existence**—as we have shown it does—then, unless we choose to ignore our own **natural light** <note>original: "natural Light," the innate capacity for reason and intuition</note>, we must acknowledge without any further doubt **that God does exist**.

2. Nor is it a sufficient reason to doubt the strength of this argument just because our imagination can try to diminish it <note>original: "shuffle in this Abater"</note> by saying: "Indeed, this **Idea** of God shows us that his existence is necessary *if* God exists, but it does not show us that he *actually* necessarily exists." For whoever answers this way does not realize the prejudice that enables them to make such a reply. Because they are accustomed to imagining the nature or notion of every other thing without **existence**—and thus always easily separating **Essence** and **Existence** in those things—they unintentionally take the same liberty here. They divide **Existence** from that **Essence** to which **Existence** itself is essential. That is the clever fallacy their lack of care has entangled them in.

3. Again, we contend that the true **Idea** of God represents him as a **Being necessarily existent**, and therefore that he does exist. To avoid the force of this argument, you reply, "If he existed at all." By this answer, you involve yourself in a manifest contradiction. For first, you agree with us that the nature of God is such that its very notion implies its **Necessary Existence**. But then you take it back by suggesting that, despite this true **Idea** and **Notion**, God might not exist. Thus, you acknowledge that what is **absolutely necessary** according to the free operation of our mental faculties might actually be otherwise. This is a clear contradiction regarding us and our faculties—and we have nothing more internal or immediate than these to guide ourselves by.

4. To make this even clearer, or perhaps stronger: when we say that the existence of God is necessary, we must note that **Necessity** is a **logical term**. It signifies such a firm connection between the **Subject** and **Predicate** (as they are called) that it is impossible for them to be separated or fail to hold together. Therefore, if they are affirmed of one another, they create a **necessary axiom** <note>original: "Axioma Necessarium"</note>—an axiom that is necessary or eternally true. Therefore, since there is a **necessary connection** between **God** and **Existence**, this axiom—**God does exist**—is an axiom that is necessarily and eternally true. We shall see this yet more clearly...

We can understand this if we compare *Necessity* and *Contingency* together. For just as *Contingency* signifies not only the *manner of existence* in something that is *contingent* according to its *Idea*, but also suggests a *possibility of actual existence*; so (to complete the clear and simple analogy), *Necessity* does not only signify the *manner of existence* in that which is *necessary*, but also implies that it *actually exists*, and could never possibly do otherwise. For *to be necessary* <note>original: "ἀναγκαῖον εἶναι"</note> and *to be impossible not to be* <note>original: "ἀδύνατον μὴ εἶναι"</note> are considered one and the same by *Aristotle* and all other *logicians*. But the *atheist* and the *enthusiast* <note>In the 17th century, an "enthusiast" was someone who claimed irrational or private divine inspiration</note> are usually such declared enemies of *logic*—the one merely out of an obsession with outward, physical senses, the other out of a devotion to his rigid and wild *imagination* <note>original: "Phansy"</note>, that source of mysteries and clever ideas.

5. Thirdly, we may further add that we must attribute to the *Idea of God* either *contingency*, *impossibility*, or *necessity of actual existence* (as one of these must belong to every imaginable *Idea*). Since *contingency* is incompatible with the *Idea of a being absolutely perfect*, and *impossibility* even more so—given that the *Idea of God* is composed only of notions that are possible according to the *light of nature* <note>The innate human capacity for reason</note>, to which we now appeal—it follows that *necessity of actual existence* must be assigned to the *Idea of God*. Therefore, God *actually exists*.

6. Fourthly and finally, if this seems too subtle—though it is no less true for it—I will now propose something so obvious that it is impossible for anyone in their right mind to deny it. I say, therefore, that either God, or this *physical* <note>original: "corporeall"</note> and *perceivable world* must necessarily exist of itself. Or put another way: *either God, or matter, or both* necessarily exist by themselves. If *both* exist, then we have reached our goal: the *existence of God*.

7. However, to acknowledge that *matter* exists necessarily by itself does not align well with the *light of nature*. For if anything can exist *independently of God*, then all things can. This would not only mean that God's *omnipotence* <note>unlimited power</note> might be useless, but it would also allow for every imaginable confusion and disorder. Indeed, it would allow for some great devil of equal power and as much command as *God* himself; or, if you prefer, six billion <note>original: "six thousand Millions"</note> such monstrous, giant spirits, filled with various and wicked passions and armed with immense power. In a fit of anger or whim, these spirits might appear in massive forms, snatch up the planets in their enormous claws, and pelt one another with them like boys throwing snowballs. The only reason this hasn't happened yet would be that the mood hasn't struck them; but the structure of nature and the creation of things would constantly be at risk of such ruin and disorder. This shows how dangerous it is to ignore the natural connections between our *innate ideas and concepts*.

I have already abundantly proved that there is other knowledge and perception in the soul besides that of the *senses*. Therefore, it is very unreasonable—since we have other faculties of knowledge besides the *senses*—that we should consult only the *senses* about matters of knowledge and exclude those faculties that penetrate beyond sense. This is something that the self-proclaimed atheists themselves will not do when they are in the mood for *philosophizing*; for their principle of *atoms* is a concept that does not fall under the *senses*, as *Lucretius* <note>Titus Lucretius Carus (c. 99–55 BC), a Roman poet and philosopher who championed the idea that the world is made of tiny, invisible atoms</note> admits at length.

### CHAPTER IX.

The existence of God argued from the **final cause** <term>final cause</term>: the purpose or end for which something exists or is done. of the implantation of the **idea** of God in the soul. 2. An evasion of the argument by supposing all things to be as they are by **chance**. 3. That this evasion is either impossible or only barely possible, and therefore of no weight. 4. 1. Up to this point, I have argued from the natural **notion** or **idea** of God as it relates to that of which it is the **idea** or **notion**. I shall now try to see what advantage may be gained from the relationship it bears to our **souls**, which are the **subject** in which this idea resides. I demand, therefore: who imprinted this **indelible character** <note>original: "Indeleble Character"; a permanent mark or seal</note> of God upon our souls? Why, and for what purpose, is it there?

2. Do not think to brush me off by saying, "We must take things as we find them, and not inquire about the **final cause** of anything." Some might argue that things are necessarily as they are of themselves, and that their guidance and arrangement come from no principle of wisdom or counsel. Instead, they would say every substance is now, and always was, of whatever nature and capacity it is found to have, originating from nothing other than itself. They might claim that all the changes and varieties we see in the world are merely the result of an "eternal struggle of competing causes," each doing its best to maintain itself in its current state; and that by acting and being acted upon by others, these different things appear in the world. But they would argue that every particular substance, with its essential properties, is self-originated and independent of any other.

3. To this, I answer that the very best that can be made of all this is that it is merely and barely possible—indeed, if we consult our own **faculties** and the **idea** of God, it is utterly impossible. But even admitting it were possible, this bare possibility is so vague, so weak, and so indeterminate a consideration that it should have no power to move the mind of anyone who has any reasonable use of their own reason. It should have no more power than the faint breath of a light breeze has to shake a mountain of brass. For if bare possibility could at all entangle our belief or disbelief, we could not fully disbelieve the most absurd fables in **Aesop** or **Ovid**, or the most ridiculous fictions that can be imagined. For example, we might have to imagine *that ears of corn in the field hear the whistling of the wind and the chirping of the birds; that the stones in the street feel pain from being ground down when carts go over them; that the sunflower* <note>original: "Heliotrope"</note> *watches the sun and actually sees him, as well as turning around with him; or that the meat of a walnut, because it carries the physical resemblance of a brain, is endowed with imagination and reason.* I say...

<page-num>27</page-num>
<header>Cʜᴀᴘ. IX. An Antidote against Atheism.</header>

No one can fully disbelieve any of these absurdities if bare **possibility** is allowed the slightest power to tip the scales one way or the other. For none of these, nor a thousand more like them, imply a perfect and obvious contradiction; therefore, they will all claim their right to be considered **possible**.

4. But we are not to pay attention to what is simply **possible**, but to what our **natural faculties** <term>natural faculties</term>: our innate human abilities to think, reason, and perceive. direct and determine us toward. For example, suppose the question were, **whether the stones in the street have senses or not**. We should not leave the point as indifferent—or as something that could be argued either way—just because it is **possible** (and implies no obvious contradiction) that they might have **senses**, and even a painful **sense**. Instead, we are to consult our **natural faculties** and see which way they lean. They plainly settle the controversy by telling us that whatever has **senses** and is capable of **pain** ought also to have **progressive motion**, so that it can avoid what is harmful and painful. We see this is true in all beings that have any significant degree of **senses**. Even **Aristotle**, who was no worshiper <note>original: "doter"; someone excessively or foolishly fond of something—here, Aristotle is noted for his scientific rather than religious focus.</note> of a **Deity**, frequently assumes this principle: "Nature does nothing in vain" <note>original: "Ἡ φύσις οὐδὲν μάτην ποιεῖ"</note>. This is either an acknowledgment of a **God** or an appeal to our own **rational faculties**; and I am indifferent as to which it is, for I get what I want from either. For if we appeal to the natural suggestions of our own faculties, they will assuredly tell us **there is a God**.

<margin>* See Chapter 8, sections 7, 8, and 9.</margin>

5. I therefore ask once more—and I desire to be answered without prejudice or any restraint laid upon our natural faculties—to what purpose is this **indelible image** or **idea of God** in us if there is no such thing as **God** existing in the world? Or who stamped so deep an impression of that **character** <term>character</term>: a distinctive mark, sign, or quality. upon our minds?

If we were traveling in a desolate **wilderness** where we could discover neither man nor house, and we should meet with **herds of cattle** or **flocks of sheep** upon whose bodies were branded certain **marks** or **letters**, we would conclude without any hesitation that these have all been handled by some man who has set his name upon them. And truly, when we see written in our souls in such legible characters the **name**, or rather the **nature** and **idea** of God, why should we be so slow and backward in making the same reasonable inference? Assuredly, he whose **character** is signed upon our souls has been here and has marked us this way, so that we and everyone else may know to whom we belong: *That it is he who has made us, and not we ourselves; that we are his people, and the sheep of his pasture* <note>A reference to Psalm 100:3.</note>. It is also clearly evident from the **idea** of God, which includes **omnipotence** in it, that we could be made by none other than he, as I have demonstrated before. Therefore, there was no better way than by sealing us with this **image** to make us acknowledge ourselves to be his, and to give that **worship** and **adoration** to him that is due to our mighty **maker** and **creator**—that is, to our **God**.

Therefore, since these things harmonize so naturally and easily together according to the free suggestions of our natural faculties, it is as stubborn and forced an act to withhold belief as it would be to doubt whether those **Roman urns** and **coins** I mentioned, dug out of the earth, were the works of nature or the craftsmanship of men.

<meta>This page continues the argument that human reason and our natural faculties lead us toward the existence of God. It transitions from discussing the innate "Idea of God" to other psychological and social evidence, such as conscience and universal worship.</meta>

<page-num>28</page-num>
<header>An Antidote against Atheism. BOOK I.</header>

6. But if we cannot yet, despite all this, give free assent to this *position*, *that God exists*, let us at least have the patience for a while to suppose it is true. I ask, therefore: assuming God did *exist*, what could the human mind imagine that this God could do better or more effectively to make himself known to a creature such as man—who is endowed with specific faculties—than what we find has already been done? For God, being a *Spirit* and *Infinite*, can never make himself known necessarily and adequately by any appearance to our outward *senses*. For if he were to manifest himself in any outward figures or shapes, portending either love or wrath, terror or protection, our faculties could not assure us that this was *God*, but rather some particular *spirit* <term>genius</term>: a local or specific supernatural being, which could be good or bad. Besides, such dazzling and frightening external forces are neither becoming of the *Divine Nature* nor suitable for the *condition of the human soul*. God engages with our *better faculties* and our free will; he does not force or amaze us by using a coarse and overwhelming power upon our weak and animalistic *senses*. What remains, therefore, but that he should manifest himself to our *inward man*? And what way imaginable is more fit than the indelible impression of the *Idea* of himself? This is not *divine life* or spiritual sensation itself (for that is a higher prize laid up for those who can win it), but a natural representation of the Godhead and a notion of his *essence*. By this, the soul of man could conceive of him in no other way than as an *eternal spirit*, *infinite in goodness*, *omnipotent*, *omniscient*, and *necessarily existing of himself*. But *this*, as I have fully proved, we find is actually <note>original: "de facto"</note> done within us. Therefore, since we are dealt with in every way as if there were an *existing* God, and no faculty discovers anything to the contrary, what should hinder us from concluding that he really does *exist*?

1. *Several other characteristics or properties in the human soul that argue for the being of God. 2. Such as natural conscience. 3.
