...what we may observe to be deeply rooted in man's nature; such as *Natural remorse of Conscience*, and a fear and disturbance arising from committing acts that, despite being unpunishable by human laws, still cause inner turmoil. We also see a *Natural hope* of being prosperous and successful when doing things we conceive to be good and righteous; and lastly, *Religious Veneration*, or *Divine worship*. All of these are fruits that grow naturally and easily out of the nature of man; and if we rightly understand their meaning, they all suggest *that there is a God*.

2. And first, regarding *Natural Conscience*: it is clear that it is a fear and confusion of mind arising from the foreboding of some harm that may befall a man outside the ordinary course of nature or the usual occurrence of affairs, simply because he has done this or that. It is not that something supernatural or absolutely extraordinary must necessarily happen to him, but that at least the ordinary calamities and misfortunes of the world will be directed and aimed at him eventually, because he has committed an evil act against his *Conscience*. In times of heavy *Adversity*, a mighty *Tempest* at sea, or dreadful thunder on land (though these arise from *Natural Causes*), men naturally reflect upon themselves and their actions. They are then either overcome with fear or remain untroubled, depending on whether they condemn or acquit themselves in their own *Consciences*. From this comes that magnificent expression of the poet concerning the just man:

> *Nor the mighty hand of thundering Jove,*
> <note>original: *Nec fulminantis magna Jovis manus*. A reference to Horace’s Odes (3.3), describing a man of integrity who does not fear the wrath of the gods or the elements.</note>

This suggests that the just man is not afraid of *Thunder* and *Lightning* being hurled down from *Heaven*. But this *fear*—that one person should be struck rather than another, or at this specific time rather than another, because a man has done wrong—is a natural acknowledgment that these events are guided and directed by some discerning Principle. This is the same as confessing *that there is a God*. It does not matter that some argue that sailors curse and swear the loudest when a storm is at its peak; this is only because being accustomed to such dangers has made them lose their sense of *danger*, not their innate sense of *God*.

3. It is also very natural for a man who honestly follows the dictates of his own *Conscience* to be full of *good hopes*, and to feel much at ease and secure that all things at home and abroad will go well for him. This is true even though his actions or the sincere intentions of his mind have no physical power over nature or the course of the world to change them. Therefore, this implies there is an *Overseeing Principle* <term>Superintendent Principle</term> over nature and the material structure of the world, which ensures that nothing happens except what is consistent with the good and welfare of honest and conscientious men. And if things do not work out for them according to their expectations in this world, it naturally leads to a belief in a world to come.

4. Nor does it at all weaken the strength of this argument that some men have lost the sense of the difference between *Good* and *Evil*—if indeed any are truly so degenerate. But even if we suppose such a person exists, he is a monster, and, I suspect, one of his own making. This does not undermine my goal, which is to argue from the *Natural constitution* of man for the *Existence*

of a **God**, then if, because **Democritus** <note>original: "Democritus" — an ancient Greek philosopher who, according to legend, blinded himself to avoid being distracted by the world so he could focus on his thoughts.</note> put out his eyes, some are born blind, or others drink away their eyes and cannot see, you should not conclude that there is neither **Light** nor **Colors**. Therefore, I conclude from the **natural conscience** in a man—which fills him with hope and fear regarding **Good** and **Evil** based on what he does or fails to do—that there is an **Intelligent Principle** over all of nature that takes notice of the actions of men. That is, **that there is a God**. Otherwise, this **Natural Faculty** would be false and useless, since these actions and omissions do nothing to change the physical course of Nature or the material affairs of the world.

5. Now, as for **Adoration** or **Religious Worship**, it is as universal as mankind. There is no nation under the canopy of Heaven that does not perform divine worship to something or other, and through it to God, as they conceive Him. Therefore, according to the ordinary **natural light** <note>original: "natural light" — the innate human capacity for reason and basic moral or logical truths.</note> that is in all men, there is a God.

6. Nor can the force of this argument be avoided by saying it is merely a universal tradition that has been spread among the nations of the world since time immemorial. For even if that were so (which cannot be proven at all), the fact that it is universally received shows it is according to the **light of Nature** to acknowledge there is a God. For whatever all men admit as true—even if someone else first proposed it—is undoubtedly to be called true according to the **light of Nature**. For example, many hundreds of **Geometrical Demonstrations** <note>original: "Geometrical Demonstrations" — the mathematical proofs of Euclid and others.</note> that were first the inventions of a single man have passed undeniably through all ages and places as true according to the **light of Nature** to those who were only learners, not inventors, of them. It is enough to make a thing true according to the **light of Nature** that no one, upon understanding what is proposed and the reasons for it (if it is not clear at first sight and needs reasons to support it), will ever hesitate to acknowledge it as a truth. Therefore, even if there were any nations that lacked the knowledge of a **God** (just as they might lack the basics of **Geometry**), as long as they will accept the knowledge of one as well as the other when it is properly presented, the acknowledgment of a **God** is just as much according to the **light of Nature** as the knowledge of **Geometry** which they receive in this way.

But even if it did not stand still, this does not apply to our case. ...the impressions of *sense*; otherwise, we would, like *Epicurus* and *Lucretius*, have to admit that the sun and moon are no wider than a sieve, and that the stars are no bigger than an ordinary candle flame. Thus, we gain at least this much: that there are in the universe some more subtle and immaterial substances that take notice of human affairs; and this is as unwelcome to a dull-witted <note>original: "slow"</note> atheist as believing that *there is a God.*

As for the *adoration* some show to the *sun and moon*, I cannot believe they do it thinking of them as merely *inanimate bodies*; rather, they take them to be the homes of some *intellectual beings*, as the poem plainly suggests to us:

->The Sun, who sees all and hears all,<-

*The Sun that hears and sees all things:* and this is very near the true notion of a *God*.

9. But whatever this *universal religious worship* may be, however absurd you choose to imagine it, it still goes a long way toward proving the existence of a *Deity*. For there are no *natural faculties* in creatures that do not have a corresponding *object* in the world; just as there is food as well as *mouths*, sounds as well as *hearing*, colors as well as *sight*, and dangers as well as *fear*. In the same way, there ought to be a God as well as a *natural inclination* in men toward *religious worship*, since God alone is the proper *object* of that worship.

The strength of this argument is not weakened by the fact that this deeply-rooted <note>original: "radicated"</note> trait of *religion* in man—which cannot be lost—displays itself so clumsily and ridiculously in mankind.

For just as a dog moves its feet in its sleep as if it were chasing game, and a young lamb butts its head before it even has horns or enemies to fight—actions that would not exist in nature if there were no such thing as a hare to be hunted or a horned enemy to be fought—so there would not be such a *universal* practice of *religious worship* in the world (no matter how clumsily or foolishly it is performed) if there were not a real, appropriate *object* of this *worship*, and a capacity in man to perform it correctly. This could not be the case unless there were a *God*.

This, therefore, implies that these poor, uncivilized souls once had the true knowledge of *God* and his *worship*, and through some hidden providence, they may be restored to it again. This is more likely than that this inclination toward *religious worship*, which appears so clearly in them, should be completely in vain—as it would be for them and all other men if there were no *God*.

1. *An investigation concerning the essence of the human soul.* 2. *That the soul is not merely a modification of the body, as the body is incapable of such operations as are usually attributed to the soul, such as spontaneous motion, awareness <term>Animadversion: The power of the mind to perceive or attend to things</term>, memory, and reason.* 3. *That the animal spirits <term>Animal spirits: In early medicine, these were believed to be subtle fluids that traveled through the nerves to facilitate sensation and movement</term> are incapable of memory, and consequently of reason, awareness, and moving the body.* 4. *That the brain cannot be the source of spontaneous motion, having neither muscles nor sensation.* 5. *That imagination <note>original: "phansy"</note>, reason, and awareness are located neither in any pore nor any particular part of the brain; nor is the whole brain shaped into this or that concept, nor every particle of it.* 6. *That the shaping of one part of the brain is not reflected to the rest, demonstrated from the location of things.* 7. *That the brain has no sensation, further demonstrated from anatomical experiments.* 8. *How ridiculously the operations of the soul are attributed to the pineal gland <term>Conarion: The pineal gland, which René Descartes argued was the seat of the soul</term>.* 9. *The conclusion that the impulse for spontaneous motion comes neither from the animal spirits nor the brain.* 10. *That the soul is not any physical <note>original: "corporeal"</note> substance distinct from the animal...*

### CHAPTER XI. *An Antidote against Atheism.*

*10. The interaction between **Animal Spirits** and the body; 11. And therefore the soul is a **non-physical** substance. 12. The discovery of the nature of the soul, and how useful it is for easily conceiving the nature of God. 13. And how there may be an Eternal Mind that possesses both understanding and the power of moving the matter of the universe.*

1. We have finished discussing all those more obvious abilities of the human soul that naturally lead to the discovery of God's existence. Before we leave our inner selves and launch out into the vast ocean of the external *phenomena* of *nature*, let us briefly consider the nature of the *soul* itself: what it is, whether it is a mere function of the body or a substance distinct from it; and then whether it is *physical* or *non-physical*. For by clearing up this point, we may perhaps be convinced that there is a spiritual substance really distinct from matter. Anyone who acknowledges this will be more easily induced to believe there is a God.

2. First, then, if we say that the *soul* is a mere function <note>original: "Modification"</note> of the *body*, then the *soul* is nothing but one universal ability of the *body*, or many abilities joined together. Consequently, those *operations* usually attributed to the *soul* must necessarily be attributed to the *body*. I ask, therefore: to what in the *body* will you attribute <term>spontaneous motion</term>? <note>The power of moving oneself voluntarily.</note> By this, I mean a power within ourselves to move or keep still most parts of our body—for example, our hand or little finger. If you say that it is nothing but the sending of *spirits* into various *muscles*, I would dearly like to know what *sends* these *spirits* and *directs* them so precisely. Is it the spirits themselves, or the *brain*, or that particular piece of the brain they call the <term>conarion</term> <note>original: "Conarion or Pine-kernel"; today known as the pineal gland.</note>? Whatever it is, that which sends and directs them must have <term>animadversion</term> <note>The faculty of conscious awareness or the power to take notice.</note>; and whatever has the power of awareness also has *memory* and *reason*. Now, I want to know whether the *spirits* themselves are capable of awareness, memory, and reason; for that seems altogether impossible. These <term>animal spirits</term> <note>In early science, these were thought to be very thin, liquid substances that acted as messengers between the brain and the body.</note> are nothing but very thin and liquid matter. Their nature consists of all their particles being in *motion*, moving and shifting about according to how they are agitated.

3. I therefore now ask: which of the particles in these many loosely moving parts possesses *awareness*? If you say that they all have it when put together, I appeal to the person who answers this way: how unlikely is it that something so utterly incapable of *memory*, and consequently of *reason*, could have awareness? For it is as impossible to imagine *memory* belonging to such a subject as it is to imagine how one might write characters in water or in the wind.

4. If you say the *brain* sends and directs these *spirits*, how can it so freely and spontaneously move itself or something else when it has no *muscles*? Besides, anatomists tell us that although the *brain* is the instrument of sense, it has no sensation at all in itself. How then can something that has no sensation spontaneously and arbitrarily direct the *animal spirits* into any part of the body? Such an act plainly requires specific sensation and

perception. But let the anatomists conclude what they will, I think I shall almost demonstrate that the **brain** has no **sense**. For the same thing in us that has **sense** also has the power of **conscious attention** <note>original: "Animadversion"</note>; and that which has **conscious attention** in us also has a faculty of free and voluntary **imagination** <note>original: "Phansy"</note> and **reason**.

5. Let us now consider the nature of the **brain** and see how compatible those operations and powers are with such a subject. Truly, if we take a proper look at this loose pith or marrow in a person's head, neither our **senses** nor our **understanding** can discover anything more in this substance that could pretend to such noble operations as **free imagination** and the wise deductions of **reason** than we can find in a cake of suet <note>animal fat</note> or a bowl of curds. For this loose pulp that is wrapped up within our **skull** <note>original: "Cranium"</note> is merely a spongy and porous body. It is permeable not only to the animal spirits <note>In 17th-century science, "animal spirits" were thought to be a very fine fluid that traveled through the nerves to communicate sensation and motion.</note> but also to thicker juices and liquids. Otherwise, it could not be well nourished; at least, it could not be so softened and dampened by drunkenness and excess that it makes the **understanding** clumsy and foolish in its operations.

Therefore, I now ask: in this soft substance we call the **brain**—whose softness implies that it is somewhat **liquid**, and liquidity implies the separate **motion** of loose parts—in what part or piece of it do **imagination**, **reason**, and **conscious attention** reside? In this loose structure that lies like a net heaped up in water, I ask: in what knot, loop, or space within it does this faculty of free **imagination** and active **reason** reside? I believe you would be ashamed to point out any single part in particular.

And if you say it is in **all the parts together**, you must then say that the whole **brain** is shaped into this or that representation. This would cancel out **memory** and take away any possibility of there being distinct markers or places for the various **types** <note>original: "Species"</note> of things represented there.

But if you say that this power of **conscious attention** and **imagination** is in **every part** of the brain, you must remember that the **brain** is somewhat like a **liquid body**. We must then ask how these loose parts understand each other's various **attentions** and **ideas** <note>original: "Notions"</note>. And if they could—which is quite inconceivable—and if they could therefore do anything to **send in** <note>original: "Immission"</note> and **direct** the **animal spirits** into this or that part of the body, we must consider that they would have to do it (after knowing one another's minds) by a joint effort of strength. It would be like many men lifting or tugging together at a signal to move a body so massive that the strength of one person alone could not handle it. But this is to turn the various particles of the **brain** into so many individual **persons**—an idea more fit for laughter than for even the slightest belief.

6. Besides, how is it that these **many attentions** seem like only **one** to us, if our mind is made up of them as is supposed? Or rather, if the shape or image in one part of the **brain** is communicated to all the rest, why does the same **object** not seem to be located behind us, before us, above, beneath, on the right, and on the left—every way that the impression of the **object** is reflected against all the parts of the **brain**? appearing to us as but one **conscious attention** <note>original: "Animadversion"</note>, just as there is but one **arrangement of things**, it is a sufficient argument that there is **but one** perceiver. Or if there are **many**, it is clear that they do not communicate with one another across their various parts, and therefore there can be no such joint effort toward a single design. From this, it is manifest that the **brains** cannot **send in** <note>original: "immit"</note> nor **direct** these ***Animal Spirits*** <note>In 17th-century science, these were thought to be a subtle fluid that carried instructions from the brain to the muscles.</note> into whichever part of the body they please.

7. Moreover, there is no small argument for the fact that the ***Brain* has no sense**, and therefore cannot spontaneously impress any motion on the ***Animal Spirits***. This is proven by the fact that some people, when dissected, have been found **without brains** at all; and ***Fontanus*** <note>Nicholas Fontanus, a 17th-century Dutch physician.</note> tells us of a boy in ***Amsterdam*** who had nothing but clear water in his head instead of ***brains***. Generally, ***brains*** are easily dissolved into a **watery consistency**, which agrees with what I suggested before. Now I appeal to any unbiased judge: how likely is it that these **liquid** particles possess the nature and power to organize and knit themselves together for a moment, supporting themselves with such a joint struggle of strength as to cause a voluntary **dispatching** <note>original: "ablegation"</note> of the ***spirits*** into this or that specific part of the body? I have already sufficiently hinted at the absurdity of this.

Lastly, the ***nerves***—I mean the marrow within them, which is of the exact same substance as the ***brain***—have **no sense**, as is demonstrable from a ***catalepsis*** or ***catochus*** <note>Archaic medical terms for a trance or seizure state involving muscle rigidity and a total loss of sensation.</note>. But I will not pile up arguments in a matter so obvious.

8. As for that little stunted piece of the ***brain*** which they call the ***conarion*** <note>The pineal gland. René Descartes famously argued that this small gland was the seat of the soul because it is one of the few parts of the brain that is not paired.</note>, the idea that this should be the very substance whose natural faculty is to move itself—and by its motions and nods to determine the course of the ***spirits*** into this or that part of the body—seems to me no less foolish and fabulous than the story of the man who could change the wind as he pleased by setting his cap on one side of his head or the other.

If you heard only the magnificent stories told of this little lurking **mushroom**, you would hear how it not only hears and sees, but imagines, reasons, and commands the whole structure of the body more dexterously than an ***Indian*** boy guides an elephant. You would hear what an acute ***logician***, subtle ***geometrician***, prudent ***statesman***, skillful ***physician***, and profound ***philosopher*** he is. And then, afterward, by dissection, you discover this worker of miracles to be nothing but a poor, silly, contemptible knob or protrusion, consisting of a thin membrane containing a little pulpy matter, much of the same nature as the rest of the brain;

->If you were admitted to see this, friends, could you hold back your laughter?<-
<note>original Latin: "Spectatum admissi risum teneatis amici?" (Horace, Ars Poetica)</note>

Would you not sooner laugh at it than go about trying to disprove it? And truly, I may better laugh at it now, having already disproved it in my previous arguments concerning the rest of the ***brain***.

9. I shall therefore make bold to conclude that the impulse for ***spontaneous motion*** is neither from the ***animal spirits*** nor from the ***brain***, and therefore those operations usually attributed to the ***soul*** are really **incompatible** <note>original: "incompetible"</note> with any part of the body. Therefore, the ***soul*** is not a mere **modification** <note>In this context, a "modification" means a specific physical state or arrangement of matter.</note> of the body, but a **substance distinct** from it.

10. Now we are to enquire whether this **distinct substance** from what...

10. Whether what we normally call the *Body* is itself a *Physical* <note>original: "Corporeal"</note> *Substance*, or whether it is *Incorporeal* <note>existing without a physical body</note>. If you say that it is a *Physical Substance*, you can understand it as nothing other than *Matter* more subtle and tenuous than the *Animal Spirits* themselves, mingled with them and dispersed through the vessels and pores of the *Body*; for there can be no "Penetration of Dimensions" <note>A philosophical principle stating that two physical objects cannot occupy the same space at the same time.</note>. But I need no new arguments to refute this foolish conceit, for what I said regarding the *Animal Spirits* before is applicable with all ease and fitness to this present case. Let it be sufficient that I inform you of this, and so be excused from repeating the same things over again.

11. It remains, therefore, that we conclude that the thing which triggers *Spontaneous Motion* <note>voluntary movement</note> upon the *Body*—or more immediately upon the *Animal Spirits*—and that which *imagines*, *remembers*, and *reasons*, is an *Immaterial Substance* distinct from the *Body*. This substance uses the *Animal Spirits* and the *Brain* as instruments for such operations. And thus we have found a *Spirit*, in the proper sense and meaning of the word, that clearly possesses these faculties: it can both *understand* and *move Physical Matter*.

12. And now the prize that we have won will prove to be of very great significance for our purpose. For it is obvious here to observe that the human soul is, as it were, *an image of God* <note>original Greek: ἄγαλμα Θεοῦ (agalma Theou)</note>, a small-scale *statue of the Deity*; her substance is a solid *likeness* <note>original: "Effigies"</note> *of God*. Therefore, just as we easily consider the substance and motion of the vast *Heavens* on a little *sphere* or *globe*, we may with similar ease contemplate the nature of the *Almighty* in this little *medal of God*, the human soul. We simply enlarge to infinity what we observe in ourselves when we attribute it to God; just as we imagine those *circles* which we see on a *globe* to be vastly larger when we imagine them as they are described in the *Heavens*.

13. Therefore, being assured of this—that there is a spiritual substance within ourselves in which both of these properties reside, namely *Understanding* and *moving Physical Matter*—let us simply expand our minds to conceive as well as we can of a Spiritual Substance that is able to *move and drive all Matter* whatsoever, no matter how far extended, and in whatever way and manner it pleases. And let us conceive that it has not only the *knowledge* of this or that particular *thing*, but a distinct and full *cognizance* <note>original: "Cognoscence"</note> *of all things*. In doing so, we have indeed a very competent apprehension of the nature of the Eternal and Invisible God. He, like the human soul, does not fall under the reach of our *Senses*, but operates everywhere in such a way that His presence is easily gathered from what is discovered by our outward senses.

...with me a while on the wide theater of this *external world*, and diligently attend to those many and most manifest marks and signs that I shall point out to him in this external structure of things, which naturally signify to us *that there is a God*.

And now, first, to begin with what is most general, I say that the *phenomena* <note>original: "Phænomena"</note> of *day* and *night*, *winter* and *summer*, *spring-time* and *harvest*, the manner of the *rising* and *setting* of the *sun*, *moon*, and *stars*—all these are signs and tokens to us that there is a God. That is, things are so framed that they naturally imply a principle of *wisdom* and *counsel* in their *author*. And if there is such an *author* of external nature, there is a *God*.

2. But here it will be replied that the mere *motion* of the *universal matter* will at last necessarily grind itself into those more rough and general outlines <note>original: "delineations"</note> of nature that are observed in the circuits of the *sun*, *moon*, and *stars*, and their general consequences. But if the *mind* of man grows so bold as to imagine <note>original: "conceit"</note> any such thing, let him examine his faculties to see what they naturally conceive of the *motion* of *matter*. And truly, the great master of this *mechanical hypothesis* <note>Referring to René Descartes</note> does not suppose or admit any *specific difference* in this *universal matter* from which this outward structure of the *world* should arise. Neither do I think that anyone else will easily imagine anything other than that all the *matter* of the *world* is *of one kind* in its very *substance* or *essence*.

Now, therefore, I ask concerning this universal, uniform *matter*: does *motion* or *rest* naturally belong to it? If *motion* belongs to it, and the matter is acknowledged to be *uniform*, it must be moved in the same way in every part or imaginable particle of it. For if this *motion* is natural and essential to the *matter*, it is the same everywhere within it, and therefore has loosened every *atom* of it to its utmost capacity; so that every particle is alike and moved alike. And therefore, because there is no dominance <note>original: "prevalency"</note> at all in any one *atom* over another in size or *motion*, it is manifest that this *universal matter*—to which *motion* is so essential and internal—will be ineffective for producing any variety of appearances in *nature*. Consequently, no *suns*, *stars*, *earths*, or *vortices* <note>A key concept in Cartesian physics where the universe is filled with whirling particles of matter</note> can ever arise out of this infinitely thin and still *matter*. It would thus eternally remain imperceptible to any of our *senses*, even if our *senses* were ten thousand million times more subtle than they are. Indeed, there could not be any such thing as *man* or *sensation* in the world. But we see this *matter* shows itself to us in an abundance of varieties of appearance; therefore, there must be another principle besides the *matter* to order its *motion* in a way that allows these varieties to appear. And what will that prove to be but a *God*?

3. But if you say that *motion is not of the nature of matter* (as indeed it is very hard to conceive it, assuming the *matter* is homogeneous <note>original: "homogeneal"</note>), but that it is inert and mindless <note>original: "stupid"</note> of itself, then it must be moved by something else. Thus, of necessity, we shall be led to a *God*, or at least a *spiritual substance* animating <note>original: "actuating"</note> the *matter*. This is something atheists are as much afraid of as children are of *spirits*, or as they themselves are of a *God*.

Therefore, <note>Continuing from the previous page: "Therefore..."</note> it may be that they will not hesitate to affirm that either the parts of Matter are *specifically different* <note>original: "Specifically different"; meaning different in their essential nature</note>, or—even if they are not—that some are naturally *movable* while others are inclined toward *rest*, and have always been so. They might say it just happened to be that way, even if there is no reason for it in the thing itself. However, to say this is to wound our mental faculties with such a wide gap that they would afterward admit anything, and it would take away any claim to have principles of knowledge at all.

But to wrestle and combat with them in their own dark caverns: even if we let the *universal matter* be a heterogeneous chaos of confusion, moved variously and by chance, I say there is no likelihood that this mad *motion* would ever result in such a wise contrivance as is visible even in the general outlines of nature. In fact, it would not even result in the natural appearance of what we see and what is considered easiest to happen this way—namely, a round *sun*, *moon*, and *earth*. For it is strongly suspected that if there were no *superintendent* <note>An overseer or divine guide</note> over the motions of those *ethereal whirlpools* <note>original: "Æthereall Whirle-pools"; referring to the "vortices" in Cartesian physics</note> which the *French philosophy* <note>The mechanical philosophy of René Descartes</note> proposes, the shape of the *sun* and the rest of the *stars* would be *oblong*, not *round*. This is because matter recedes all along the *axis* of a *vortex* as well as from the *center*; therefore, the space left for the finest and subtlest element of all (which the *sun* and *stars* consist of) would naturally be *long*, not *round*. Therefore, this *round* figure we see them in must come from some higher principle than the mere *agitation* of *matter*. Whether that principle is simply *formative* <note>original: "Spermatical"; referring to a biological-style organizing force</note>, or also *sensitive* and *intellectual*, I will leave to the investigation of others who have more leisure to deal with such curiosities.

5. The task I have at hand to prove is this: taking for granted what these great naturalists <note>Scientists or natural philosophers</note> would have us allow—namely, *that the earth moves around the sun*—I say the laws of its motion are such that if they had been imposed on her by human reason and deliberation, they would be no different than they are. So, appealing to our own faculties, we must confess that the *motion of the sun and stars* (or of the *earth*, as our naturalists would have it) comes from a *knowing principle*, or at least has passed the approval and allowance of such a principle.

For just as *art* takes what *nature* provides for its purpose and completes the rest itself, so the *Eternal Mind*—which set the *universal matter* into motion (as I conceive most reasonable), or, if the *matter* moved itself confusedly (as the atheist stubbornly contends)—this *Eternal Mind*, I say, takes the easy and natural results of this general impulse of *motion* where they serve his purpose; where they do not, he rectifies and completes them.

He does this so that the *intellect* <note>original: "Wit"</note> of man, whom God has made to contemplate the *phenomena* of nature, may have a more suitable object to exercise itself upon. # BOOK II. An Antidote against Atheism.

This would not have been the case if God had deliberately avoided what **Matter** naturally provided through **Motion**, or if He had cancelled the laws of nature in every instance. Besides, to have altered or added anything further where it was not needed would have been to *multiply entities to no purpose* <note>original: "multiply Entities to no purpose"; a reference to the principle of parsimony, or Occam's Razor, suggesting that a simple explanation is better than a complex one.</note>.

This is how it works with Divine Providence: whatever the initial push of motion upon the **Universal Matter** <note>The primary, formless substance from which all things were thought to be made.</note> can provide that is useful and good, Providence allows and includes. Whatever motion might have failed at, or could not achieve on its own, Providence directs or supplies. It is like finding small pieces of wood naturally curved like a person's elbow; a carver does not straighten the wood, but instead carves a hand at one end and shapes it into the complete form of a human arm.

Therefore, what I am arguing is this: regardless of how **matter is moved**, the **appearances** of things are such that they clearly suggest they are either all specifically planned, or at least approved, by a **Universal Principle of Wisdom and Counsel**.

And you must answer me that it is better to have it *steady* and *parallel*; for in this lies the necessary foundation for the arts of *navigation* and *sundial making* <note>original: "Dialling"; the mathematical art of creating sundials to tell time</note>. For that steady stream of particles which is supposed to keep the *axis* of the Earth *parallel* to itself provides the sailor with both his *Cynosura* <note>original: "Cynosura"; a term for the North Star or the constellation Ursa Minor, used as a guide</note> and his *compass*. Both the *loadstone* <note>original: "Load-stone"; a naturally magnetic rock used in early compasses</note> and the *lodestar* <note>original: "Load-star"; the guiding North Star</note> depend on this, and *sundial making* could not exist at all without it.

Both of these arts are beneficial, and navigation is especially of great importance to mankind. Through it, there is an orderly measuring of *time* for our affairs at home and an opportunity for trade abroad with the most remote nations of the world. Thus, there is a mutual supply of the various goods of all countries, in addition to the broadening of our understanding through the vast experience we gain of both people and things. Therefore, if we were to consult our reason as to whether the *axis* of the Earth should be held *steady* and *parallel* to itself or be left to chance, we would conclude that it ought to be *steady*. And that is how we find it to be *in fact* <note>original: "de facto"</note>, even though the Earth moves floating in the fluid heavens. So, by appealing to our own mental faculties, we must affirm that the constant direction of the Earth’s *axis* was established by a principle of *wisdom* and *deliberation*, or at least approved by it.

2. Furthermore, since there are several possible positions for this steady direction of the Earth’s *axis*—namely, either *perpendicular* to a plane passing through the center of the Sun, *coincident* with it, or *inclining* toward it—I ask: which of all these would reason and knowledge choose? Reason would not choose a *perpendicular* posture. If it did, both the pleasant variety and the great convenience of *summer* and *winter*, *spring* and *harvest* would be lost. Because the Sun would never approach them, those parts of the Earth that now bring forth fruit and are habitable would be incapable of ever producing anything, and consequently could support no inhabitants. Meanwhile, those parts reached by the full heat of the Sun—because the Sun would beat down on them always the same way, without any annual retreat or break—would eventually become tired and exhausted. Besides, consulting our own faculties, we observe that an orderly change <note>original: "vicissitude"; here meaning the regular, predictable rotation of the seasons</note> in things is most pleasant to us and much more satisfies the *contemplative* nature in humanity.

For if the *axis* lay in a plane that passes through the center of the Sun, the *ecliptic* <note>the apparent path of the Sun across the sky</note> would pass through the *poles* of the Earth, like a *colure* <note>original: "Colure"; one of the two main circles on the celestial sphere that intersect at the poles</note> or one of the *meridians*. This would put the world's inhabitants in a miserable condition. Even those who fare best in the *temperate zone* would be burdened with very long, tedious nights—no less than forty days long. And those who now never have a night longer than twenty-four hours—such as people in *Friesland* <note>a province in the Netherlands</note>, *Iceland*, and the farther parts of *Russia* and *Norway*—would be deprived of the Sun for over a hundred and thirty days straight. We ourselves in *England*, and others in the same climate, would be locked in darkness for no less than a hundred or eighty continuous days, and the same would apply proportionally to everyone else, both inside and outside the *temperate zones*. # CHAPTER II. *An Antidote against Atheism.*

Even if we were to grant that the confused agitation of the parts of **Matter** might form a round, hard heap like the **Earth**, and more thin and liquid bodies like the **Ether** and **Sun**—and that the **Earth** might swim in this liquid **Ether** like a roasted apple in a great bowl of wine, carried about like straws or grass cast upon a whirlpool—it is still absurd to believe its **Motion** and **Position** would be so perfectly directed and balanced. We ourselves, using our **Reason** upon due consideration, would want it to be exactly as it is. To suggest this order does not come from something that is **Knowing** and, in some sense, **Reasonable**, is as discordant <term>original: absonous; meaning out of harmony with reason</term> and absurd to our faculties as anything can be. Since it would have been easier for the universe to be chaotic, why should it be this way, if some **Superintendent Cause** did not oversee and direct the motions of **Matter**, allowing nothing within it except what our **Reason** admits serves a very good purpose?

7. That the previously mentioned phenomena are not the result of chance or luck, but are directed and achieved by the aforementioned **Superintendency**, will be even more convincingly confirmed if we consider two other phenomena in nature. These are very plain and simple, yet they violently contradict the purely **Mechanical** powers of **Matter**. The first is **Gravity**, or the descent of heavy bodies toward the **Earth**; the other is what is commonly called the **Abhorrence of a Vacuum** <note>original: "Fuga Vacui"</note>. Regarding the latter, I shall provide an example from that noble and ingenious gentleman's experiments with his **Air pump** <note>A reference to Robert Boyle (1627–1691), who conducted pioneering experiments on air pressure</note> that will plainly demonstrate there must be some **Immaterial Being** that exercises its **directive activity** on the **Matter** of the world. But first, I shall return to and briefly discuss the nature of **Gravity**.

<margin>Book 3. chapter 13.</margin>

In my *Treatise on the Immortality of the Soul*, I have clearly and fully demonstrated that if we suppose the **Earth** rotates every twenty-four hours, it would violently fling off everything lying upon it—unless there were some other **Substance** distinct from **Matter** that resists its **Mechanical** powers. If we consider more particularly the strong pull a massive bullet (of lead or brass, for example) must exert to move away from the surface of the **Earth**—following that primary **Mechanical** law where motion persists in a straight line—the bullet would be moving so swiftly that it would cover fifteen miles in one minute. It must appear, then, that a wonderful power is required to curb it, regulate it, or command it back to the **Earth** and keep it there despite the strong resistance of that first **Mechanical** Law of **Matter** that would urge it to fly away. This manifests not only the marvelous power of **Unity** and **Indiscerpibility** <term>The quality of being impossible to divide or separate into parts</term> in the **Spirit of Nature**, but also that there is a decisive and even forceful execution of an **All-comprehensive** and **Eternal Counsel** for ordering and guiding the motion of **Matter** in the **Universe** toward what is best. This phenomenon of **Gravity** is of such good and necessary consequence that there could be neither **Earth** nor **Inhabitants** without it, in the current state of things.

As for the **Air**, whether a man is so delirious as to imagine it is all endowed with perception and the free will to resist as it pleases, or that it is interspersed with some subtler **Matter** so qualified—which they must ridiculously turn into either a disjointed or else a spongy and perforated **Deity**—all...

# BOOK II. An Antidote against Atheism.

Any resistance that this loose and scattered element <note>The air.</note> could make—call it natural or divine (for words alone have no power)—could no more keep the aforementioned bullet from moving away from the Earth than an army of the smallest flies could stop a cannonball flying through the air, no matter how stoutly they resisted it. This *phenomenon* of *gravity* is such a plain demonstration that there is a *Spirit of Nature* <note>Henry More’s term for an immaterial, non-conscious force that acts as God's "deputy" to organize matter.</note> which is the representative power of God over the *motion* of the *matter* of the *universe*.

<margin>* The Honorable Robert Boyle, Esq., his treatise titled *New Experiments Physico-Mechanical touching the Air*.</margin>

8. In my opinion, it is plainly manifest that neither the *air* itself has any such *power*, *knowledge*, or liberty of *will*, nor are there any such "divine particles" interspersed in the *air* that possess them. This is clear from the second and thirty-second experiments in the previously mentioned treatise by that learned gentleman. In the first of those experiments, the brass key or stopper <note>original: "Stopple"</note> of the cover of the *receiver* <note>The glass vacuum chamber of Robert Boyle’s air pump.</note>, after the *receiver* is well emptied of air, is lifted up with great difficulty. In the other experiment, if you apply a tapering brass valve to the lower branch of the stopcock of the *receiver* (emptied of air as before) and turn the key of the stopcock, the external *air* will beat like a forceful stream upon the valve to get inside. It will suddenly both shut the valve and keep it shut so strongly that it will support a ten-pound weight. These are evident arguments of an earnest endeavor in nature to fill the *receiver* again with air, as it was naturally before. However, this motion—by which it attempts so strongly to get in—actually excludes the air more accurately. From this, it is apparent that neither the *air* itself, nor any more subtle and "divine" matter (which is more densely packed <note>original: "throngly congregated"</note> together in the *receiver* after the air is pumped out) has any freedom of *will*, or any knowledge or perception to do anything. They are completely puzzled, acting so foolishly <note>original: "fondly"</note> and preposterously in their attempts to refill the *receiver* with air.

For if the external *air* and that subtler *matter* in the *receiver* had been knowing and free agents, there would have been cooperation between them. The external *air* would have suspended or withdrawn its pressure from the outside, and the subtle and divine matter within would have directed its motion against the stopper and valve to let in the air, according to the intention of Nature. Or, if only that subtle body were *free* and *knowing*, it alone—by mutual correspondence (the part in the air outside holding off the pressure of the outward air against the *receiver*, and the part within pushing against the *valve* or *stopper*)—would let in the *air*, according to the earnest and serious purpose of Nature. But because their actions are so clearly contrary to the intended goal, and their attempts so clumsy <note>original: "inept"</note> (even though the task would be easily done if there were *knowledge* and free agency in either the *air* or any other more subtle matter), it is a demonstration that the *force* <note>original: "impetus"</note> of *motion* in all *matter* is blind and inevitable. There is no *matter* at all that is free and knowing; instead, matter moves and acts by itself (unless directed by some other *immaterial principle*) according to the mere *mechanical laws* of *motion*.

<margin>* See Mr. Boyle's *New Experiments Physico-Mechanical*, Experiment 23.</margin>

<meta>This page continues Henry More’s critique of mechanical explanations for air pressure. He is examining the experiments of Robert Boyle to argue that "elastic power" alone cannot account for the behavior of air, suggesting instead the presence of an immaterial Spirit of Nature.</meta>

# CHAP. II. An Antidote against Atheism.

In the *air-pump*, once the cylinder is well emptied of *air*, it should draw up more than a hundred-pound weight, moving upward as if by its own accord. As the ingenious experimenter <note>Robert Boyle.</note> observed in his third experiment, this forceful attempt of the *air* to enter <note>original: "subingression"</note> is not caused by the pressure of the surrounding *air* being strengthened by the addition of the *air* sucked out. If that were the case, the person operating the pump would find the resistance of the *air* increasing as the sucker <note>The piston or plunger of the pump.</note> is drawn lower, which is not what is observed. To this we may reasonably add that since *air* is nothing but a thin body or collection <note>original: "Congeries"</note> of small particles in perpetual motion, whatever is pumped out will naturally spread into the distances where it can move more freely—that is, into those spaces where the *air* is thinner. Consequently, almost instantly, all the *air* becomes of one and the same consistency. Therefore, any new pressure (based on the idea that the *air* nearest the pump becomes thicker) cannot be factored into the calculation in this case.

10. The most plausible *mechanical solution* therefore that can be given for this *phenomenon* is the *hypothesis* which the excellent author himself has used, and which would apply universally to *air* even in its own natural state: namely, that there is an *elastic power* in the *air*. You might explain this in the *Cartesian* way <note>Referring to the philosophy of René Descartes, who argued that particles move in vortices or "whirls."</note>, by the playing and whirling of every particle, through which they attempt to occupy a larger space; or you might suggest there is a compression of the particles like the hairs in a lock of wool, which will expand once whatever was pressing against it recedes.

But whether this *elastic power* consists of this or of something else, although the solution looks very hopeful and promising at first glance, I must confess (while deferring to better judgments) that the *effect* attributed to the *hypothesis* in this experiment seems to me a *demonstration* <note>A proof.</note> against the *hypothesis* itself. For according to the experiment, this *elastic power* has no less pressure than a hundred-pound weight or more. This pressure (as in all flexible bodies that have a *spring-power* in them) is perpetual and exists everywhere in the *air*, if it is there at all. And therefore, any cylinder of *air* at the same height from the ground, and of the same diameter as the sucker of the pump, will press as forcefully as a hundred-pound weight.

Now, imagine a lump of butter in a pair of wooden scales having the same diameter as the sucker of the *air-pump*. It is obvious that this butter would be pressed with the force of two hundred pounds—one cylinder of *air* pressing from below and another from above, each with a force of one hundred pounds. This would necessarily follow if this *elastic power* existed in the *air*. But the butter is not pressed at all, as appears by the fact that no watery fluid <note>original: "serose humour"</note> is squeezed out of it; nor is it at all flattened or spread out by any such compression, although it should have the force of two hundred pounds pressing it according to this *hypothesis* of the *elastic power* of the *air*.

11. Nor can I think up <note>original: "excogitate"</note> any excuse against this demonstration, unless it is argued that the *spring* of the *air* presses against the sides of the butter as well as the bottom and top, which keeps it from flattening. But it is

<meta>This page continues Henry More’s critique of the mechanical philosophy. He is using the behavior of common substances (like butter) and the results of Robert Boyle’s air-pump experiments to argue that physical phenomena cannot be explained by the "air-spring" (air pressure) alone, but instead require an immaterial "Spirit of Nature."</meta>

11. It is easily answered that this "air-spring" still cannot prevent the squeezing on all sides, nor the pressing out of the milky and serous <note>original: "serose"; watery</note> fluid in the butter, if there were indeed any such pressure as is supposed. To this you may further add: suppose a lump of butter were flattened into the shape of a round trencher <note>A flat wooden plate or board used for serving food.</note>, where the thickness of its edge is a hundred or two hundred times smaller than the surface area of its two sides. If it were then placed between two thin, light trenchers broad enough for the purpose and hung freely in the *air* with strings, as if in a scale, the force of pressure from above and beneath would exceed the pressure against the round edge of the butter a hundred or two hundred times. Yet, despite this, the butter will not be pressed any closer by the *spring of the air*, nor will it have any more effect upon it than it had before—even though the butter is so soft and yielding that a very small force from our own hands would easily press it between the two trenchers.

12. This is not because our strength is added to the force of the *spring of the air*. The excess of the force of the *spring of the air* against the sides of the trenchers (compared to the force against the round edge of the butter) is far greater than the additional force of our hand pressing against the trenchers—and yet, the air alone produces no effect.

Furthermore, in places where this *air-spring* supposedly does not reach—such as inside a pail filled with water—you can place a lump of butter, and it will yield as easily to the pressure of your hand there as it does in the *air* itself. Thus, it is irrefutably evident that there is no such *spring of the air* as some learned men have supposed—at least, not one so strong as to master a hundred-pound weight, as it is thought to do in this remarkable experiment of the *air-pump*.

13. But just as the *phenomenon of gravity* is completely at odds with the very first *mechanical laws of motion*—even though gravity is a *universal law of terrestrial bodies* imposed on them by something that is not only non-terrestrial, but *immaterial*—so too is this rising of the sucker <note>The piston or plunger of the air-pump.</note> of the *air-pump* with over a hundred pounds of weight attached to it. It is such a glaring and violent breach of that *universal law of gravity*, and so powerful, that it is apparent there is a *principle* transcending the nature and power of *matter* that umpires and rules all. This principle directs the *motion* of every part and parcel of *matter* backward, forward, and in contrary ways, in pursuit of such *general* designs as are best for the *whole* world. No less a goal than the *living* and *breathing* of *animals* is intended by this industrious and constant effort to keep the parts of the *air* together, as is well observed by this virtuous and judicious author <note>Robert Boyle</note> in his 41st experiment.

Therefore, it is manifest that there is a *principle* in the *world* that tugs so stoutly and resolutely against the *mechanical laws of matter*, and that so forcibly resists or cancels one common law of nature for the more appropriate exercise of another. This, I say, is a very sure pledge to us that when things are done rightly—even if not with this apparent violence and persistence—they are the *effects* of the same *immaterial principle* (call it the *Spirit of Nature* or what you will) which is the *vicarious <note>Acting as a deputy or representative; God's "agent" in the physical world.</note> power of God* upon this great *automaton* <note>A self-operating machine; here, the physical universe.</note>, the *world*.

# An Antidote against Atheism. BOOK II.

1. Let us therefore quickly travel over the *valleys and mountains*, sound the depths of the *sea*, roam through the *woods and forests*, and dig into the *depths* <note>original: "entrails"</note> of the *earth*. Let the *atheist* tell me which of all these places are silent and say nothing of a *God*. Even those things that are most silent will at least agree with the rest: that all things exist by the guidance and determination—no matter how *matter* moves—or at least by the allowance and approval of an *Intelligent Principle* <note>original: "Knowing Principle"</note>. Just as a *mason* building a wall sometimes finds a *stone* that requires no cutting, and so, simply approving of it, he places it in his work; or as a piece of *timber* may happen to be cracked in the exact place where the *carpenter* wants to split it, so he does not need to join it first only to split it apart later. Therefore, if the mere *motion* of *matter* can produce any simple thing of good consequence, let it stand as acceptable. But we shall also discover those things which so clearly show *design and counsel* <note>The author uses "counsel" to mean "deliberate planning."</note> that we cannot naturally withhold our agreement, but must say, *There is a God*.

2. And now let us turn ourselves to the search, and see if all things are not exactly as our *reason* would desire them to be. To begin at the top first: even those randomly scattered *mountains*, which seem like nothing more than *cysts* <note>original: "Wens"</note> and *unnatural growths* upon the face of the *earth*—if you consider their consequences, you may see them as ornaments as well as useful features once you understand their purpose.

For these are *nature’s distilleries* <note>original: "Stillatories"</note>. In their hollow *caverns*, ascending vapors are condensed into that universal *water of life* <note>original: *Aqua vitæ*</note>—that good fresh water, the liquid of life that sustains all living *creatures* in the world. This water is carried to all parts of the *earth* through the winding *channels* of *brooks and rivers*. *Geography* proves this through many examples. I will only mention three or four: the *Ana* <note>The Guadiana River</note> and the *Tagus* run from *Sierra Molina* in *Spain*; the *Rhine* <note>original: *Rhenus*</note>, the *Po* <note>original: *Padus*</note>, and the *Rhone* <note>original: *Rhodanus*</note> from the *Alps*; the *Don* <note>original: *Tanais*</note> from the *Riphean Mountains*; the *Garonne* <note>original: *Garumna*</note> from the *Pyrenean Mountains*; the *Achelous* from *Mount Pindus*; the *Maritsa* <note>original: *Hebrus*</note> from *Mount Rhodope*; the *Tigris* from *Mount Niphates*; the *Orontes* from *Mount Lebanon* <note>original: *Libanus*</note>; and the *Euphrates* from the *mountains* of *Armenia*; and so it is with the rest. But I will not dwell on this; I will now turn to what more forcefully declares an *Eye of Providence* directing and determining—as well as approving—the results of the supposed movement of the parts of *matter*.

3. And so that you may better feel the strength of my *argument*, let us first briefly consider the *nature* of *humanity*: what *abilities* <note>original: "Faculties"</note> we have, and what our rank is in respect to the rest of the *creatures*. Indeed, though the human body is weak and unarmed, our inward abilities of *reason* and *skillful invention* <note>original: "Artificial contrivance"</note> are admirable. Mankind is much given to *contemplation* and the viewing of this *stage of the world* <note>original: "Theatre of the world"</note>, to trade and commerce with foreign *nations*, to the building of *houses and ships*, to the making of elaborate <note>original: "curious"</note> instruments of *silver, brass, or steel*, and the like. In a word, man is the flower and chief of all the products of *nature*.

Certainly, agitated *matter*, unless there were some special, overpowering guidance over it, might just as easily have missed these necessary and useful things as hit upon them.

## CHAPTER IV.

1. *The distinction between Land and Sea is not without a Providence.* 2. *As also the consistency of Sea-Water, which allows it to support ships.* 3. *The great convenience and pleasure of navigation.* 4. *The admirable series of fit provisions in Nature for gratifying the intelligence of man in such a significant curiosity.*

### CHAPTER V.

1. *That the Form and Beauty, Seed and Signature of Plants are Arguments for a Providence.* 2. *That though the mere motion of Matter might produce certain Weather Phenomena, such as Hail, Snow, Ice, etc., it does not follow that the same is the complete cause of Animals and Plants.* 3. *That it would be no great flaw or gap in Nature if some more basic Phenomena were acknowledged as the results of the mere Mechanical Motion of Matter.* 4. *That the Form and Beauty of Flowers and Plants come from a higher Principle.* 5. *That there is such a thing as Beauty, and that it is the Object of our Intellectual Faculties.* 6. *From which it follows that the beautiful Forms and Figures of Plants and Animals come from an Intellectual Principle.*

1. Hitherto we have only considered the more basic and rough outlines <note>original: "rude and careleſs ſtrokes and delineaments"</note> of Divine Providence in the world, shown in those larger **Phenomena** of **Day** and **Night**, **Winter** and **Summer**, **Land** and **Sea**, **Rivers**, **Mountains**, **Metals**, and the like. We now come to a closer view of God and **Nature** in **Vegetables** <term>In this period, "vegetables" referred to all plant life, not just those we eat.</term>, **Animals**, and **Man**.

And first regarding **Vegetables**, I shall touch only on these four topics: their **Form** and **Beauty**, their **Seed**, their **Signatures** <term>The "Doctrine of Signatures" was the belief that plants were "signed" by God with physical features that indicated their medicinal use (e.g., a heart-shaped leaf for heart ailments).</term>, and their great **Use** for both **Medicine** and **Sustenance**. 

In order that we may better understand the advantage we have in this closer contemplation of the works of Nature, we must first take notice of the condition of that **Substance** which we call **Matter**. Consider how fluid, slippery, and undefined it is by itself; or, if it is hard, how unfit it is to be changed into anything else. Therefore, all things must rot into a moisture before anything can be generated from them, just as we soften wax before we press a Seal into it.

2. Therefore, we should not be so foolish as to conclude that because simple motion can do something, it must do everything. For example, some say the uniform motion of the **Air** (or some more subtle physical element) might compress a small amount of vaporous moisture so equally that it forms into round drops, as is seen in **Dew** and other **Experiments**. 

But to claim that mere rough and undirected **Motion**—simply because it naturally produces some basic results—could reach the level of a wise and planned arrangement <note>original: "contrivance of Counſel"</note>, is a ridiculous **Sophism** <term>A fallacious or deceptive argument.</term>. As I have already suggested, such an idea is more fit to fool the thoughtless souls of children than men of mature Reason who are well-practiced in Philosophy. Let us admit that **Rain**, **Snow**, **Wind**, **Hail**, **Ice**, and similar **Meteors** <term>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomena, including weather events.</term> may be the products of **Heat** and **Cold**, or of the **Motion** and **Rest** of certain small particles of **Matter**; yet that the

# CHAP. V. *An Antidote against Atheism.*

...the useful and beautiful design <note>original: "contrivance"</note> of the branches, flowers, and fruits of **Plants** should also be a result of random motion (to say nothing yet of the bodies of **Birds, Fish, Beasts,** and **Men**) is as ridiculous and lazy a conclusion as to infer that, because mere heat and cold can soften and harden wax into some shape or other, that therefore this mere heat and cold—or motion and rest—without any art or direction, also made the **Silver Seal** and engraved upon it so skillfully a **Coat of Arms**, or the shapes of **Birds** or **Beasts** such as an **Eagle** or a **Lion**. Indeed, this inference is far more reasonable than the other, as the works of human **Art** are much simpler and less grand than those of **Nature**.

<margin>
* Concerning these *seminal reasons* <note>original: *Rationes seminales*</note>, whether they are distinct principles or one common Spirit of Nature, see Book 3, chapters 12 and 13, in the *Discourse on the Immortality of the Soul*.
</margin>

3. Nor is it a flaw or gap at all in the works of **Nature** that some particular **phenomena** are merely the simple results of that **general motion** given to **matter** by **God**, while others are the effects of more skillful **design**, or of **Divine Art** or **Reason**—specifically the *seminal reasons* <note>original Greek: *λόγοι σπερματικοί* (*logoi spermatikoi*); these are the "rational seeds" or blueprints that guide the growth of living things</note> incorporated into **matter**. This is especially true since **matter** itself is, in some sense, vital; otherwise, it would not continue the **motion** it is set upon when it is moved one way or another. Besides, since the **Nature of God** is the most perfect fullness of **Life** that can possibly be imagined, it is very fitting that this furthest and most distant shadow of Himself—the physical world—should be in some way vital, however obscurely. 

Therefore, as things descend by degrees from the highest **Perfection**, it is a smooth and proportionate step to descend from the **top** of this outward **Creation**—**Man**, in whom there is a principle of finer and more reflective **Reason**. This reason continues (though not in the same way) in the more perfect kinds of **Brutes** <note>animals</note>, just as **Sense**—unwilling to be confined to too narrow a space—extends even to some kinds of **Zoophytes** <term>organisms like corals or sea anemones that appear to be halfway between plants and animals</term>. In the rest of the plants, no further traces of a **perceptive** <note>original: "animadversive"</note> form are discovered, though they show the effects of an **unaware form**—a **materialized reason** <note>original Greek: *λόγος ἔνυλος* (*logos enylos*); a "word in matter" or unconscious formative principle</note> or **seminal reason**. I say, it is no uneven leap to pass from these faint and obscure examples of **seminal life** to the more basic effects of **general motion** found in **minerals, metals**, and various **weather phenomena** <note>original: "meteors"</note>, whose simple and rough shapes may have no need for any **principle of life** or **seminal form** distinct from the rest or motion of the particles of **matter**.

4. But there is such an **intricacy** <note>original: "curiosity"</note> of **form** and **beauty** in the more noble kinds of **Plants**, which harmonizes so well with the refined sense and wisdom of the **Soul of Man**, that he cannot help but acknowledge—as his **intellectual intuition** <note>original: "Intellectual Touch"</note> is so sweetly satisfied by what it perceives in such **objects**—that some hidden **Cause**, much like his own **intellectual** nature, is the designer and perfecter of these pleasant sights in the world.

5. Nor is it at all useful to object that this matter of **beauty** and **proportion** is merely an imaginary notion <note>original: "conceit"</note> because some men do not recognize it, and all things seem equally handsome to them even though they have the use of their eyes as well as others. For I say, this actually supports our point: that **beauty** <note>original: "pulchritude"</note> is indeed conveyed by the outward **senses** to the **soul**, but it requires a more **intellectual**...

The intellectual faculty is what relishes it; just as a *geometrical diagram* <note>original: "Scheme"</note> is perceived by the *eyes*, but the *demonstration* is understood by *reason*. And therefore it is more rational to claim that some *intelligent principle* <note>original: "Intellectual Principle"</note> was the author of this *beauty* <note>original: "Pulchritude"</note> of things, than that they should be fashioned this way without the help of that principle. To say that there is no such thing as *beauty* because some men's souls are so dull and stupid that they respond to all objects the same way in that respect is as absurd and groundless as to conclude there is no such thing as *reason* and *demonstration* because a natural fool cannot grasp it. 

But that there is such a thing as *beauty*, and that it is acknowledged by all generations of men to exist in *trees*, *flowers*, and *fruits*, is shown by the ample and undeniable evidence of the decorating and beautifying of *buildings* in all ages. For what is more common for people than to include *flowers* and *fruit patterns* <note>original: "Fruitage"</note> to garnish their work? Besides, I appeal to any man who hasn't sunk into such a wretched state of degeneracy that he is as stupid toward these things as the lowliest of beasts: whether, for example, a correctly-cut *tetrahedron* <note>original: "Tetraedrum"; a four-sided triangular pyramid</note>, *cube*, or *icosahedron* <note>original: "Icosaedrum"; a twenty-sided polyhedron</note> has no more beauty in them than any rough, broken stone lying in a field or on the highway. Or, to name other solid *figures* which—though they are not "regular" in the strictly mathematical sense—yet have a settled *idea* and nature, such as a *cone*, *sphere*, or *cylinder*: ask whether the sight of these does not please the minds of men more and claim more elegance of shape than those rough cuttings or chips of sandstone <note>original: "free-stone"</note> that fall from a mason’s hands. Those chips serve for nothing but to fill up the middle of a wall, and are thus hidden from the eyes of man because of their ugliness. 

It is also notable that if Nature shapes anything close to this *geometrical* accuracy, we take notice of it with much satisfaction and pleasure. For example, consider the stones found to be exactly round (such as the abundance of stones found between two hills in *Cuba*, an island of *America*), or those that are naturally *five-angled* <note>original: "Quinquangular"</note>, or have *parallel* sides even if the *angles* are unequal (as is seen in some small stones and in a kind of *alabaster* found here in *England*). These stones, I say, please our sight because they have a closer connection <note>original: "cognation"</note> with the soul of man, which is rational and intellectual. Therefore, the soul is well pleased when it meets any outward object that fits and agrees with those *innate ideas* <note>original: "congenite Ideas"</note> with which her own nature is equipped. For *symmetry*, *equality*, and the *correspondence of parts* are recognized by *reason*, not merely by the *senses*, as I have previously proven.

6. Now, therefore, it being evident that there is such a thing as *beauty*, *symmetry*, and *comeliness of proportion* (to say nothing of the delightful mixture of colors), and that this is the proper object of the *understanding* and *reason* (for these things are not noticed by *beasts*), I think I may safely infer this: whatever is the first and principal cause of changing the fluid and unformed *matter* into shapes so comely and symmetrical as we see in *flowers* and *trees* must be an *intelligent principle* <note>original: "Understanding Principle"</note>. This principle knows both the nature of man and the *objects* it presents to his sight in this outward and visible world. These things cannot come by chance, or by a diverse, random attempt of the parts of matter acting upon themselves. If that were the case, it would be likely that the species of things (though some might happen to turn out right) would mostly be malformed and ridiculous;

...ridiculous; but now there is no lack of purpose <note>original: "ineptitude"</note> in anything, which is a sign that the fluidity of *Matter* is guided and determined by the overpowering counsel of an *Eternal Mind*, that is, of a *God*.

If it were not unnecessary, I might now give examples of various kinds of *Flowers*, *Herbs*, and *Trees*. But since these objects are so obvious, and every person's imagination <note>original: "phansy"</note> is filled with the memory of *Roses*, *Marigolds*, *carnations* <note>original: "Gilly-flowers"</note>, *peonies* <note>original: "Pionyes"</note>, *Tulips*, *Pansies*, *Primroses*, the leaves and clusters of the *Vine*, and a thousand such things—all of which they cannot help but confess possess beauty, symmetry, and pleasing proportions—I consider it redundant to weary you with any longer list of examples <note>original: "Induction"</note>. ---

### CHAP. VI.

1. *Providence argued from the Seeds of Plants.* 2. *An Objection answered concerning stinking Weeds and poisonous Plants.* 3. *The Signature of Plants an argument of Providence.* 4. *Certain Instances of Signatures.* 5. *An Answer to an Objection concerning such Signatures in Plants as cannot refer to Medicine.*

---

1. **I** say, therefore, that because every *Plant* has its own *Seed*, it is a clear sign of *Divine Providence*. Since it is not a necessary result of the movement of *Matter*—just as the entire design of the plant is not—and because it is of such great consequence that they have *seeds* for the continuation and propagation of their own *species*, and also for the benefit of human skill, industry, and needs (for much of farming and gardening depends on this), it must be an act of wisdom to provide the various kinds of *plants* with their *seeds*. This is especially true because the Earth is of such a nature that, although at first it might have produced all kinds of *plants* (as some believe it also produced all kinds of *animals*), it would eventually grow so sluggish that without the advantage of those small, concise principles of generation—the grains of *seed*—it would produce no such life. It would be no different than a pump that has grown dry and will not yield any water unless you pour a little water into it first; then, for one basin-full, you may draw up many large buckets full <note>original: "Soe-fuls"; a "soe" was a large wooden tub or bucket</note>.

2. Nor is it a significant objection to say that *stinking weeds* and *poisonous plants* bear *seeds* just as the most pleasant and useful plants do. For even those *stinking weeds* and *poisonous plants* have their uses. First, human industry is exercised by the need to weed them out where they are harmful. If this reason seems trivial, let us consider that if human industry had nothing to struggle against, the fire of the human spirit would be half-extinguished by the flesh. Then we shall acknowledge that the point I have made is not so contemptible or weak.

But secondly, who knows but it is the same with poisonous **Plants** as is commonly imagined <note>original: "phansied"</note> regarding **Toads** and other poisonous **Serpents**—that they lick the venom from off the Earth? In this way, poisonous **Plants** may well draw to themselves all the harmful juice and nourishment so that other plants may be more pure and cleansed <note>original: "defæcate"</note>. This is similar to how there are **Receptacles** and **Emunctories** <term>Emunctories: organs or canals in the body that carry off waste or secretions</term> in the human body to drain away superfluous **Choler**, **Melancholy** <note>In the medical theory of the time, these were two of the four "humors" or bodily fluids—yellow and black bile—that governed health.</note>, and the like.

But lastly, it is very well known by those who know anything of Nature and Medicine <note>original: "Physick"</note> that those **Herbs** which the unrefined and ignorant would call **Weeds** are the ingredients of very powerful medicines. It is reported that *Aconitum hyemale* <note>original: "Winter-wolfs-bane"</note>, which is otherwise a rank poison, is extremely effective against the bites of vipers and scorpions, a fact which **Crollius** <note>Oswald Croll (c. 1563–1609), a celebrated German alchemist and physician.</note> agrees with. Furthermore, that plant which carries "death" in its very name, *Solanum lethiferum* <note>original: "deadly nightshade"</note>, prevents death by inducing sleep if it is correctly applied during a fever. Nor should those things be considered useless whose purpose we do not yet know; for all things are not to be known at once, so that future ages may always have something left to discover for their own benefit.

3. We come now to the **Signatures** <term>Signatures: the ancient "Doctrine of Signatures" held that the physical shape or color of a plant indicated its medicinal use (e.g., a heart-shaped leaf for heart ailments).</term> of Plants. These seem no less an argument that the highest origin of the works of Nature is some **Intelligent Mind** <note>original: "Understanding Principle"</note> than the careful provision of their **Seed**. Indeed, this relates to us even more specifically and appropriately than the other, and is a certain key to introduce Man to the knowledge and use of the treasures of Nature. I ask, therefore, whether it is not a very easy and natural inference to observe that several **Herbs** are marked with some **mark** or **sign** that suggests their **virtue** <note>In this context, "virtue" means the specific medicinal power or quality of a plant.</note> and what they are good for. Since there is such a creature as Man in the world who can read and understand these **signs** and **characters**, we can conclude that the Author of both Man and the plants knew the nature of them both. For it is like the **Inscriptions** on pharmacists' <note>original: "Apothecaries"</note> boxes that the Master of the shop writes so that the Apprentice may read them. In fact, it is even better, for here the very **nature** and **use** of the **Herbs** is inscribed, not just the mere **name**. 

Nor is it necessary that all plants should be signed in this way, even if some are; for the rarity of it provides delight. Otherwise, it would have been dull and tiresome <note>original: "cloying"</note>—too much "harping upon the same string." Besides, Divine Providence intended only to initiate and introduce mankind into the useful knowledge of her treasures, leaving the rest to employ our industry, so that we might not live like idle loafers and truants. For the **Theater** of the world is intended for the exercise of Man’s wit, not as a lazy **Polyanthea** <term>Polyanthea: a common type of reference book or encyclopedia in the Renaissance that compiled quotes and knowledge for easy access.</term> or book of commonplaces. Therefore, all things are in some measure obscure and intricate, so that the diligence of that "divine spark"—the Soul of Man—may have the opportunity for conquest and triumph, once he has performed bravely with the additional assistance of his God.

4. But to prove that there are some **Plants** that carry a very evident **Signature** of their **nature** and **use**, I shall fully demonstrate this with the following examples:

*Capillus Veneris* <note>original: "Venus’s Hair" or Maidenhair fern.</note>, *Polytrichon* <note>original: "Many-haired," likely referring to hair-cap moss.</note>, or **Maiden-hair**: the liquid <note>original: "lye"</note> in which it is boiled or infused is good for washing the head and making hair grow in places that are thin and bare.

### CHAPTER VII.

1. *That the usefulness of plants argues for a Providence, particularly those that afford timber.* 2. *As also such herbs and plants as serve as medicine for men and beasts.* 3. *Of plants fit for food.* 4. *Of the color of grass and herbs, and of the fruits of trees.* 5. *The notable provisions in nature for husbandry and tillage, with the universal usefulness of hemp and flax.* 6. *The marvelous usefulness of the Indian nut-tree.*

1. We have finally reached the fourth and last consideration of *plants: their use and usefulness.* We shall say nothing now of those larger *trees* that are suitable for *timber*, and are the necessary materials for the *building of ships and magnificent houses* to adorn the earth and make the life of man more splendid and delightful; as also for the erecting of those *holy structures* consecrated to Divine worship. Among these, we must not forget that famous edifice, that glorious **Temple at Jerusalem**, consecrated to the great God of Heaven and Earth. Indeed, it was most fitting that He—whose guidance and Providence did not allow the strength of the earth to waste itself on worthless gravel and pebbles instead of quarries of stone, nor on briars and brushwood instead of pines, cedars, and oaks—that He should eventually have the most stately and magnificent temples erected to Him that the wit and industry of man and the best of those materials could provide. It is the most suitable expression of thanks for that act of Providence that can be imagined. This is the very consideration that moved that pious **King David** to plan the building of a temple to the God of Israel:
