# CHAPTER VII. An Antidote against Atheism.

Medicine <note>original: "Physick"</note> and food, and then pass on to the consideration of **animals**. Regarding their **medicinal uses**, the large herbals that are everywhere available are such ample evidence of them that I have said enough just by reminding you of them. What is most notable here is that brute beasts share in their benefits as well as **humans**. For the **toad**, when overwhelmed with the poison of the **spider** (as is commonly believed), seeks out the **plantain leaf**. The **weasel**, when she is about to fight a **serpent**, prepares herself by eating **rue**. The **dog**, when he is sick to his stomach, knows his cure; he eats **grass**, vomits, and is well. **Swallows** use **celandine**, and the **linnet** uses **eyebright** <note>original: "Euphragia"</note> to repair their **sight**. And the **donkey**, when he is oppressed with melancholy <note>In the medical theory of the time, melancholy was linked to an enlarged or "heavy" spleen</note>, eats the herb **spleenwort** <note>original: "Asplenium" or "Miltwaste"</note> and so eases the swelling of his spleen. And **Virgil** reports of the **Cretan Dittany** <note>original: "Dictamnum Cretense"</note> that wild **goats** eat it when they are shot with darts or arrows; for that herb has the power to work them out of their bodies and heal the wound.

->Those grasses are not unknown to wild goats,<-
->when winged arrows have stuck in their backs.<-
<note>original Latin: *non illa feris incognita Capris Gramina, cùm tergo volucres hæsere sagittæ.*</note>

I consider these things to be a clear indication <note>original: "indigitation"—literally, a pointing out as if with a finger</note> of **Providence**. Because they do by instinct and nature what humans—who possess free reason—cannot help but acknowledge as very relevant and fitting (indeed, such that the most skilled **physician** would approve), and because these creatures have no such reason or skill themselves to act as **physicians**, it must be concluded that they are enabled to do these things by the power of that **Principle** <note>Meaning God, the first cause</note> that designed them and made them with the nature they possess. Therefore, that **Principle** must have **skill** and **knowledge**—that is, it must be **God**.

3. We come now to the consideration of plants as they provide **food** for both humans and beasts. Here we may observe that just as there was a general provision of **water**—by opening up the mountains and hills <note>original: "setting the Mountains and Hills abroach"—a metaphor for piercing a cask to let liquid flow</note> so that through the **springs** and continuous streams drawn together (which later formed larger rivers with long, winding distributions) all the creatures of the Earth quench their thirst—so **Divine Providence** has spread her table everywhere. She has covered it not with a dry green carpet, but with juicy **herbage** and nourishing **grass** on which most of the beasts of the field feed. Those that do not feed on it feed on those that eat it, and so the generations of them all are continued.

4. But because this seems **necessary** rather than a matter of choice, I will not dwell on it. For I admit that **Counsel** <note>Intentional design or purposeful planning</note> is most clearly implied where we see variety and the possibility of things being otherwise, yet the **best** option is chosen. Therefore, I will only suggest this much: although it was necessary that something like **grass** should exist if there were to be such creatures in the world, it was not at all necessary that **grass** and **herbs** should have that **color** which they have. They might have been **red** or **white**, or some other color that would have been very offensive and harmful to our sight. But I will not dwell on

...these things; let us now consider the *fruits of trees*, where I think it will appear very clearly that there was one and the same Author for both man and trees, and that he certainly knew what he was doing when he made them. For could *apples*, and *oranges*, and *grapes*, and *apricots*, and such like fruit, be intended for *beasts* that hold their heads downward and can scarcely look up at them, much less know how to reach them? When we feed our dogs, we set the dish or plate <note>original: "trencher"</note> on the ground, not on the table. But you will say that eventually these fruits will fall down, and then the beasts may come to them. But for one thing, there are not many beasts that desire them, and so they would rot upon the ground before they were eaten, or be wasted in a moment, as might easily happen with the most precious of plants, the *vine*. 

But *man*, who knows the worth of the *grape*, knows how to preserve it for a long season (for it is both *eaten* and *drunk* some years after the harvest) just as he also gathers the rest of the fruits of the earth and stores them up for both himself and his cattle. Therefore, it is plainly discoverable that man's coming into the world is not a matter of *chance* or *necessity*, but a *design*, like the bringing of worthy guests to a well-furnished table.

5. And what I have suggested concerning the *vine* is as clearly—if not more clearly—observable in the ordinary kinds of grain, such as *wheat* and *barley*, and the like. These also, like the *vine*, are made either *edible* or *drinkable* <note>original: "potable"</note> by man’s art and industry. But that is not the thing I care so much to observe. What I am aiming at now is this: that *bread-corn* <note>A general term for cereal grains like wheat or rye used to make bread</note>, which yields such a considerable increase through *tillage* and *husbandry* <note>Farming and management of resources</note>, would scarcely exist at all without them. For that which grows wildly on its own is worth nothing; but because it is such a wholesome and strengthening food, the fact that it yields such a plentiful harvest—and that this harvest requires human art and industry—plainly suggests that there is a *Divine Providence* that intended to exercise the intelligence of man in *husbandry* and *tillage*. 

We may be even more firmly assured of this if we add to it the careful provision of *instruments* so exactly suited for this employment: namely, the hardworking *ox* and the strong but easily manageable *horse*; *iron* for the plowshare; and *ropes* <note>original: "roaps"</note> for the horse-harness to pull by. It is very appropriate to take notice of this last point, as it belongs to this consideration of the *profitableness of plants*. 

I appeal to anyone who will take the pains for a moment to consider how great the use and consequence of *cordage* <note>Ropes and cords</note> is in the affairs of men, whether it was not a clear act of Providence to send such plants out of the earth that would provide it. For we can discover no necessity in nature that there must be such plants as *hemp* and *flax*. Therefore, if we will only follow the simple suggestions of free *reason*, we must credit it to *Providence*, which has provided mankind with such a commodity. Upon this material depend no fewer affairs than all the *tackling* of ships, their *sails* and *anchor cables* <note>original: "cable-roaps"</note>, and what not? And consequently all foreign *trade* <note>original: "traffick"</note>, as well as the transportation of wood and stone and other necessary materials for building, or the carrying of them by land in *wagons* <note>original: "wains"</note> and *carts*, besides the ordinary use of *pulleys* or other *engines* <note>In this context, mechanical devices or machines</note> for lifting heavy weights, which the strength of man without these helps would not easily master;

### CHAPTER VII.

master; besides what I hinted before concerning the use of *cordage* <note>original: "Cordage"; ropes and cords used on ships or in farming</note> in *husbandry* <note>farming and agriculture</note>, in plowing and carrying home the fruits of the Earth. The *uses* indeed of the aforementioned *plants* are so universal, and play a part in every affair of Man, that if it were lawful to be a little merry in so serious a matter, a man might not unfittingly apply that verse of the Poet to this so general a commodity:
> *All things for man hang by a slender thread;* <note>original Latin: "Omnia sunt homini tenui pendentia filo"</note>
meaning that all the businesses of Men do very much depend upon these little long flakes or shreds of *hemp* and *flax*. Or if you will say that some scrambling shift might be made without them—using long chains of *iron*, or sails of *wool*, and the like—yet seeing ourselves provided for infinitely better, we are in all reason to judge it to proceed from no worse a principle than *Divine Providence*.

6. I might now reach out to *exotic plants*, such as the *cinnamon* tree, the *balsam* tree, the tree that bears the *nutmeg* enveloped with the *mace*, as also the famous *Indian nut tree* <note>the coconut palm</note>, which provides almost all the necessities of life at once. For if they only cut the twigs at evening, a plentiful and pleasant juice comes out, which they receive into *bottles* and drink instead of *wine*, and out of which they extract such a *water of life* <note>original: "Aqua vitæ"; a strong distilled spirit or medicinal brandy</note> as is very effective against all manner of sicknesses. They make their *houses* of the branches and boughs; and the body of the tree, being very spongy within though hard without, they easily fashion into the frame and use of their *canoes* or *boats*. The kernel of the nut serves them for *bread* and *meat*, and the shells for *cups* to drink from; and indeed they are not mere empty *cups*, for there is found a delicious cooling *milk* in them. 

Besides, there is a kind of *hemp* <note>coir or coconut fiber</note> that encloses the nut, of which they make *ropes* and *cables*, and of the finest of it, *sails* for their ships. The leaves are so hard and sharp-pointed that they easily make *needles* or *bodkins* <note>thick, blunt needles used for leather or heavy fabric</note> of them, for stitching their *sails* and for other necessary purposes. And so that *Providence* may show herself kind as well as wise, this notable *plant* is not restricted to one coast of the world—such as the *East Indies*—but is found also in some parts of *Africa*, and in all the islands of the *West Indies*, such as *Hispaniola* and *Cuba*, as well as upon the continent of *Carthagena* in *Panama*, *Norumbega* <note>a legendary settlement in northeastern North America, often associated with New England</note>, and several other parts of the *New World*.

But I thought it fit not to insist upon these things, but to keep myself within the scope of such *objects* as are familiarly and ordinarily before our eyes, so that we may better take the opportunity to return thanks to him who is the bountiful *Author* of all the supports of life.

### CHAPTER VIII.

1. *The designed usefulness of animals for man, specifically the dog and the sheep.*
2. *Also concerning the ox and other animals.*
3. *Concerning man’s subduing of creatures to himself.*
4. *Concerning those animals that are as of yet untamed.*
5. *The excellent usefulness of the horse.*
6. *The usefulness of some animals that are enemies to those animals that are hateful or annoying to man.*

We have now come to take a view of the nature of animals. In contemplating them, we shall use much the same method we did with plants; for we shall consider in them also their *beauty*, their *birth*, their *make* and *fabric* <note>original: "Fabrick"; referring to the anatomical structure</note> of body, and their *usefulness* to mankind. 

To address this last point first: it is wonderfully easy and obvious that almost all animals are made in some way or other for human use. Some are so notoriously and evidently designed for us that, without doing great violence to our own reason, we cannot possibly deny it. To give examples of things that are most obvious and familiar: when we see in the solitary fields a *shepherd*, his *flock*, and his *dog*, how well they are fitted together; when we knock at a farmer's door, and the first to answer is his vigilant *mastiff*, whom because of his job he ordinarily names "*Keeper*." 

I remember *Theophrastus* <note>A Greek philosopher and student of Aristotle</note> in his character sketch *On Obsequiousness* <note>original: "Περι ἀρεσκίας" (Peri areskias)</note> tells us that a master, when he has let a stranger in, <note>original: "δηλαδὴ μετὰ & ρύγχες" (delade meta rhynches); literally "clearly by the snout"</note> taking his *dog* by the snout, will relate long stories of his usefulness and the services he does for the house and those in it: "*This is he that keeps the yard, the house, and the property*" <note>original: "Οὕτω φυλασσὸ τὸ χωρίον & ὴ οἰκίαν & τὸν βίον" (Houto phylasso to chorion kai he oikian kai ton bion)</note>. 

Lastly, when we view in the open countryside a brace of swift *greyhounds* chasing a good, stout, and well-breathed *hare*, or a pack of well-tuned *hounds* and *huntsmen* on horseback pursuing their game with pleasure and alacrity; or when we hear them blowing their horns near a woods-side, so that the whole wood rings with the echo of that music and the cheerful yelping of the eager *dogs*—to say nothing of *duck-hunting*, *fox-hunting*, *otter-hunting*, and a hundred more such sports and pastimes that are all performed by this one kind of *animal*—I say, when we consider this diverse harmony and fitness of things in reference to ourselves, how can we stop ourselves from inferring that the Power which made *dogs*, *ducks*, *hares*, and *sheep* made them with a reference to us, and knew what it was doing when it made them? 

And though it is possible to imagine it otherwise, it is highly improbable that the flesh of *sheep* was not designed for food for men. It is also improbable that *dogs*, which are such familiar and domestic creatures to man, should not be intended (among other clever feats they do for him) to fill the role of a servant too, and to take away the bones and scraps so that nothing might be lost. And unless we should expect that Nature should make *jerkins* <note>A close-fitting jacket, often sleeveless</note> and *stockings* <note>original: "Stockens"</note> grow out of the ground, what could she do better than afford us such fit materials for *clothing* as the wool...

# CHAPTER VIII.

...wool of the sheep, there being in man the wit and art to make use of it? To say nothing of the *silkworm*, which seems to come into the world for no other purpose than to furnish man with more costly clothing, spinning away her very entrails to make him fine on the outside.

2. Again, when we view those large bodies of *oxen*, what can we better imagine them to be than so many living and walking pickling tubs? <note>original: "powdring-Tubs"; vessels used for salting and preserving meat.</note> We might say they have *a soul in place of salt* <note>original Latin: "animam pro Sale"</note>, as *Philo* <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher.</note> says of *fishes*: that their life is merely like salt, to keep them sweet and fresh until we have need to eat them. Besides, their *hides* afford us *leather* for *shoes* and *boots*, just as the *skins* of other beasts also serve other uses. Indeed, man seems to have been brought into the world on purpose so that the rest of the creation might be improved to its utmost usefulness and advantage. For was it not better that the *hides* and *flesh* of beasts should be put to such considerable use as to *feed* and *clothe* men, than that they should rot and stink upon the ground? Without man, they would fall short of such a noble improvement as being the subject for the exercise of human wit, and providing him with the necessary conveniences of life. For if man did not make use of them, they would either die of old age or be torn to pieces by more cruel masters. Therefore, we plainly see that it is an *act of reason* and *divine counsel* to have made man, so that he might be a lord over the rest of the creation and maintain good order among them.

3. And being furnished with fit materials to make himself weapons, as well as with natural *wit* and *valor*, man offered battle to the very fiercest of animals. He either chased them away into solitudes and deserts, or else brought them under his subjection and gave laws to them. Under these laws, they live more peaceably and are better provided for (or at least might be, if men were good) than they could be when they were left to the mercy of the *lion*, *bear*, or *tiger*. And what if he does occasionally and in an orderly way kill some of them for food? Their death is quick, and so less painful than the paw of the bear, the teeth of the lion, or the tedious melancholy and sadness of old age, which would first torture them and then kill them, leaving them to rot upon the ground, stinking and useless.

Besides, all the wit and philosophy in the world can never demonstrate that the killing and slaughtering of a beast is anything more than the striking of a bush where a bird's nest is: you scare away the bird, and then seize upon the empty nest. <note>The author suggests the animal's soul or life-force departs, leaving only the "nest" of the body behind.</note> So, if we could see through to the final *resolution* <note>original: "Catastrophe"; used here in the classical theatrical sense of a final event or conclusion.</note> of things, the whole cycle might prove to be but a *tragic-comedy*.

4. But as for those *rebels* <note>Wild animals that have not been domesticated.</note> that have fled into the *mountains* and *deserts*, they are to us a very pleasant subject of natural history. Furthermore, we make use of them as much as serves our purpose; they are not only ornaments of the universe, but a continual exercise for man's wit and valor whenever he pleases to encounter them. To expect and wish that there were nothing but such dull, tame things in the world that would neither bite nor scratch is as groundless and childish as to wish there were no *bile* <note>original: "Choler"; one of the four bodily humors, associated with anger and heat.</note> in the body, nor *fire* in the universal compass of nature.

5. I cannot dwell upon the entire result of this war, nor must I forget how that generous animal the *horse* at last had the wit to yield himself up, to his own great advantage and ours. And truly, he is so fitly made for...

6. For not all men and women are exquisitely handsome—indeed, very few are—so that those who are may raise greater admiration in the minds of others and sharpen their natural abilities toward brave adventures, whether in valor or poetry. But as for the brute *creatures*, though some of them have a *hateful appearance*, such as the *toad*, the *swine*, and the *rat*, these are merely like *discords* in music, intended to make the following chord sound more pleasant. Indeed, most of those momentary inconveniences that human life encounters from time to time only give a sharper edge and vigor to one's enjoyments.

2. However, it is not difficult to find many *creatures* that are either *beautiful things* <note>original: καλὰ χρήματα (kala chremata)</note> or *elegant* <note>original: ἀστεῖα (asteia)</note>, as the Philosopher distinguishes; they are either very grand and *beautiful*, or at least *elegant* and *pretty*, as most *birds* are. But for *stateliness* and *majesty*, what can compare to a *horse*? This is true whether you look at him alone, with his mane and tail waving in the wind and hear him racing and neighing in the pastures, or whether you see him with some gallant *hero* on his back, gracefully performing useful maneuvers and *practicing* his exploits of *war*. Who can help but conclude that a *Providence* brought these two together? They are so well-fitted to each other that they seem like one complete spectacle of *nature*. This sight deceived the unrefined people near *Thessaly* <note>A region in Greece famous in antiquity for its horsemen.</note> and gave rise to the fable of the *Centaurs*, as if they had been a single living *creature* made up of *horse* and *man*.

3. The point I am driving at is this: there is a *goodliness* in the bodies of *animals*, such as in the *ox*, *greyhound*, and *stag*; or a *majesty* and *stateliness*, as in the *lion*, the *horse*, the *eagle*, and the *rooster*; or a grave *awfulness* <note>In the sense of inspiring awe or respect.</note>, as in the best breed of *mastiffs*; or *elegance* and *prettiness*, as in smaller *dogs* and most kinds of *birds*. All of these are various *modes of beauty*. Since *beauty* is an intellectual *object*, just as *symmetry* and *proportion* are (which I proved sufficiently in my discussion of the *beauty of plants*), it naturally follows that the *Author* or *Original* of these *creatures* deemed *beautiful* must himself be *Intellectual*, having designed such pleasing *objects* for the *mind* or *intellect* of *man*.

4. After their *beauty*, let us touch upon their *birth* or manner of *propagation*. Here I appeal to any man: is the design of *male* and *female* in living *creatures* not a genuine *effect* of *wisdom* and *deliberation*? For it is perfectly obvious that these are made for one another, and both are made for the continuation of the *species*. Even if we should admit, along with *Cardan* <note>Gerolamo Cardano (1501–1576), an Italian polymath who speculated on spontaneous generation.</note> and other *naturalists*, that the *earth* at first brought forth all kinds of *animals* as well as *plants*, and that they might have been fastened by the *navel* to their common *mother* the *earth* (just as they are now to the *female* in the *womb*), we see that she has grown sterile and barren, and her births of *animals* are now very insignificant. Therefore, what can it be but *Providence* that ensured, while the earth was still fertile, she sent out *male* and *female*? This way, when her own *procreative power* was exhausted, she might still serve as a dry *nurse* or a helpful *grandmother* to thousands of generations. And I say it is *Providence*, not *chance* nor *necessity*; for what can be imagined in the parts of *matter* that...

...that they should necessarily fall into the structure of even an *Animal*, much less into so careful a provision of different *Sexes* for their continual propagation?

5. Nor was it the frequent attempts of moving Matter that first happened upon *Animals*—which would have perpetually and suddenly become extinct for want of the difference of *Sexes*—and afterward by *chance* differentiated their *Sexes* as well, from which their kinds have continued. For what is perpetual is not by *chance*; and the births that now occur by putrefaction <note>original: "putrefaction"; the early modern belief that some life forms arose spontaneously from decaying matter</note> show that it is perpetual, for the Earth still constantly brings forth both *Male* and *Female*.

6. Nor is it at all relevant to reply (if you will make so large a leap as to cast yourself from the land into the water to dive for *Objections*) that the *Eel*, according to *Pliny* and *Aristotle*, though it is a <gloss>blood-bearing animal <note>original: "ζῶον ἔναιμον" (zōon enaimon)</note></gloss>, an *Animal so perfect as to have blood in it*, yet has no distinction of *Sexes*. For if it does not, there is good reason for it: that creature arises out of the kind of Matter that will never fail to generate. There will be such Mud as will serve this purpose as long as there are Rivers, and longer too; and Rivers will not fail as long as there is a Sea. Therefore, this actually supports the idea of a discerning Providence that knew the nature and course of all things beforehand and made her contrivances accordingly, doing nothing superfluously or in vain.

<margin>See Pliny's *Natural History*, book 10, chapter 63; and Aristotle's *History of Animals*, book 6, chapters 14 and 16; also book 4, chapter 11, and book 9, chapter 30.</margin>

7. But in other *Generations* that are more hazardous, even though they are sometimes produced by putrefaction, Nature still makes them *Male* and *Female*, as is plain in *Frogs* and *Mice*. Nor should we be scandalized that such careful provision is made for such contemptible *Vermin* as we perceive them to be. For this feeling only comes out of pride and *ignorance*, or a haughty presumption that because we are encouraged to believe that in some sense all things are made for Man, they are therefore not made at all for themselves. 

But he who pronounces this is ignorant of the nature of God and the knowledge of things. For if a good man is merciful to his beast, then surely a good God is bountiful and kind, and takes pleasure in the fact that all his Creatures who have life and *sense* <note>term: "sense" refers to the ability to feel or perceive</note> enjoy themselves and are capable of any enjoyment. So, regarding the swarms of little *Vermin*, *Flies*, and innumerable such *diminutive Creatures*, we should rather celebrate their coming into Being than murmur sullenly and scornfully against their *Existence*. For they find nourishment in the world which would be lost if they did not exist, and they are, in turn, convenient nourishment themselves to others that prey upon them.

Besides, *Life* being divided into such infinite numbers that have their distinct *sense* and *pleasure*, and are sufficiently provided with contentment, those little *Souls* are, in a way, just as significant for receiving the overflowing goodness of the Creator as the *Ox*, the *Elephant*, or the *Whale*. For it is *sense*, not *size*, that makes things capable of enjoyment.

Therefore, it was fitting that there should be a safe provision made for the propagation and continuance of all *kinds* of living *Creatures*—not only of those that are *good*, but also of those that we rashly and inconsiderately call *evil*. For they are at least good enough to enjoy themselves and to partake of the bounty of their Creator. But if they grow troublesome and—

# CHAPTER IX. An Antidote against Atheism.

If animals become troublesome to us, we have both the power and the right to curb them; for there is no question that we are worth more than they are, or any of the brute creatures.

8. But to return to the present point at hand: there are also other manifest footsteps of *Providence* which the *generation* <note>The process of procreation or biological reproduction.</note> of living creatures will discover to us; as, for example, the manner of *procreation* of *fishes* and *birds*. For there being that notable difference in animals—that some of them are *oviparous* <note>Egg-laying.</note>, others *viviparous* <note>Giving birth to live young.</note>—the fact that "the creatures of the water" <note>original: τὰ ἄναλα (*ta anala*). Philo of Alexandria used this term to describe aquatic creatures.</note> (as *Philo* comprehends them by that general term), and that *fishes* and *birds* should be *oviparous*, is a plain sign of *counsel* and *providence*. For though it will be granted that their *species* might continue and subsist even if they had been *viviparous*, yet it would have reduced their individuals to very small numbers.

For as for *fishes*, since *grass* and *herbs* are not the fruit of the sea, it was necessary that they should feed upon one another, and therefore that they should multiply in very great plenty. They could not have done this in anything near the fullness they now do if they had been *viviparous* as four-footed beasts are. But being now *oviparous*, and the lesser kinds of them being so many at first and sending forth such infinite numbers of *spawn*, their generations are neither extinct nor limited, but are as plentiful as any creatures on the land.

And the reason why *birds* are *oviparous* and lay *eggs*, but do not bring forth their young alive, is so that there might be a greater plenty of them also, and so that neither the birds of prey, the serpent, nor the fowler <note>A bird hunter.</note> should restrict their generations too much. For if they had been *viviparous*, the burden of their womb (if they had brought forth any significant number at a time) would have been so big and heavy that their wings would have failed them, and so everyone would *have had the wit to catch the mother bird*. Or, if they brought forth only one or two at a time, they would have been troubled all year long with feeding their young or bearing them in their womb. Besides, there would have been a necessity for too frequent *sexual mating* <note>original: "venery."</note>, which would have been very prejudicial to their dry bodies. It was very reasonable, therefore, that *birds* should propagate by the laying of *eggs*.

9. But this is not all the advantage we shall make of this *consideration*. I demand further: what is it that makes the *bird* prepare her *nest* with such *artifice* <note>Skillful craftsmanship.</note>, to sit upon her *eggs* when she has laid them, and to distinguish between these and her useless *excrement*? Did she learn it from her mother before her? Or rather, does she not do she knows not what, but yet what ought to be done by the appointment of the most exquisite *knowledge* that exists? Therefore, something else has *knowledge* for her, which is the *Maker* and *Contriver* of all things, the *omniscient* and *omnipotent God*.

And though you may reply that the *hatching* of their *eggs* is necessary, otherwise their generations would cease, I answer that all the circumstances and curiosities of *brooding* them are not necessary. For they might have made do on the ground in the *grass*, and not made themselves such curious and safe *nests* in *bushes* and *trees*. Besides, if all things...

<summary>The author argues that the egg-laying nature of fish and birds is evidence of divine design, as live births would hinder their survival and population density. He further asserts that the complex nesting instincts of birds prove the existence of an omniscient Creator.</summary>

# BOOK II.

If things were left to *Chance*, it is far easier to conceive that there should have been no such things as *Birds*, than that blind *Matter* should ever have stumbled on such lucky *Instincts* as those that seem barely necessary for survival.

10. But you will object that the *Ostrich* lays *Eggs* and does not hatch them herself, so that these things happen by *Chance* rather than *Providence*. But this actually argues for a more exquisite and discerning *Providence* rather than being an *Argument* against it. For the heat of the ground (like those *ovens* in *Egypt* <margin>Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian who described Egyptian artificial incubation.</note> speaks of</margin>) where she lays them proves effective for the production of her young. Thus *Nature* does not tie the *Female* to this tedious service where it is needless and useless; as is also seen in *Fish*, who, when they have spawned, are discharged of any further trouble. This is a most manifest discovery of a very curious and watchful *Eye* of *Providence*, which suffers nothing to be done ineptly or in vain.

11. I will only take one more advantage of this *Speculation* on the *Birth of Animals* and then pass on to what remains. It is observed by those who are more attentive watchers of the works of *Nature* that the <margin>•</margin> *fetus* <note>original: "fœtus"</note> is framed out of some *homogeneous* <note>original: "homogeneal"; meaning uniform or of the same kind throughout.</note> *liquid* or *moisture* in which there is no variety of parts of *Matter* to be organized into bones and flesh. For *Example*, in an *Egg*, about the third day the *Hen* has sat on it, in that part where *Nature* begins her work of formation <note>original: "efformation"</note>, all is turned into a *crystalline liquid substance* around it. Similarly, several *Insects* are bred from little drops of *dew*. In all other *Generations* <note>The process of biological reproduction or coming into being.</note>, it is supposed by these observers that *Nature* first wipes the *writing tablet* <note>original: "Table-book"; a metaphor for a blank slate.</note> clean and then portrays upon it whatever she pleases. 

And if this is her course—to break down the subject *Matter* into as perfect a *Deprivation* <note>original: "Privation"</note> of *Form* as possible, making it as *homogeneous* as she can, yet *liquid* and pliable to her *Art* and *Skill*—it seems to me very highly probable, if not necessary, that there should be something besides this *fluid Matter* that must change, alter, and guide it into that wise arrangement of parts that we afterwards find. For how should the parts of this *liquid Matter* ever come into this exquisite *Structure* <note>original: "Fabrick"</note> of themselves? This may convince any *Atheist* that there is a *Substance* besides *corporeal Matter*, which he is as loath to admit as he is to admit that there is a *God*.

For there being nothing else in *Nature* but *Substance* <note>original: "Substantia"</note> or *Mode* <note>original: "Modus"; a philosophical term for the way a substance exists or is arranged.</note>, and this power of arranging the *liquid Matter* into such order and shape being incompatible with the *liquid Matter* itself, it must be the *Mode* of some other *Substance* hidden <note>original: "latitant"</note> in the *fluid Matter* and really distinguishable from it. This is either the *Soul*, or some *seminal Form*, or *Archeus* <note>A term used by Paracelsus and the "Chymists" to describe a vital force or "internal chemist" that directs life processes.</note>, as the *Chemist* calls it. They are all the same to me at this time, as I am aiming here only to prove a *Substance* besides *Matter*, so that the *Atheist* may then be more easily led to acknowledge the *Existence of a God*.

12. Nor can the force of this *Argument* be escaped by saying the *Matter* is touched and infected by the life of the *Female* while she bore the *Egg*, or that her *Imagination* <note>original: "Phansie"</note> gets down into her womb.

For what life or *imagination* has the *Earth*, which, as they say, generated all *Animals* at first, and some still? And what similarity is there between a *Bee* and—

It is but some rude and general suitability of vital preparation that sets this *Archeus* <note>original: *Archeus*; in Paracelsian philosophy, this was the vital force or "internal chemist" that directed the growth and functions of a living body.</note> to work rather than another. It is just as mere *choler* <note>original: *Choler*; one of the four bodily humors, associated with yellow bile and a fiery, angry temperament.</note> engages the *fancy* <note>original: *Phanſie*; the creative or imagining faculty of the mind.</note> to dream of firing guns and fighting armies; *sanguine* <note>original: *Sanguine*; the blood humor, associated with a cheerful and amorous disposition.</note> shapes the imagination into the representation of fair women and beautiful children; *phlegm* <note>original: *Phlegm*; the cold, moist humor, associated with water.</note> transforms her into water and fishes; and the shadowy *melancholy* <note>original: *Melancholy*; the black bile humor, associated with sadness and fear.</note> entangles her in struggles with old hags and hobgoblins, and frights her with dead men's faces in the dark. ### CHAPTER 10.

1. *That the structure of the bodies of animals argues for a Deity: namely, the number and location of their eyes and ears; 2. As also of their legs. 3. The armor of beasts, and their use of it. 4. Of the general structure of birds and fishes. 5. The admirable structure of the mole. 6. Cardan's* <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), an influential Italian polymath and physician.</note> *rapture upon the consideration of it. 7. Of the hare and greyhound. 8. Of the structure of the body of the camel.*

1. I come now to the last consideration of animals: the outward shape and structure of their bodies. When I have shown you that they might have been made otherwise, and yet are made according to the most exquisite level of reason that the wit of man can conceive of, it will naturally follow that they were really made by wisdom and providence, and consequently that there is a God. And I ask first, in general, concerning all those creatures that have eyes and ears: might they not have had only one eye and one ear apiece? To make the supposition more tolerable, they might have had the eye on one side of the head and the ear on the other; or the ear on the crown of the head and the eye in the forehead. They might have lived and survived even if they had been no better provided for than this. But it is evident that their having two eyes and two ears, placed as they are, is safer, more attractive, and more useful. Therefore, since that choice is constantly made which our own reason deems best, we must infer that the choice proceeded from reason and counsel.

2. Again, I desire to know why there are no three-footed beasts (when I speak thus, I do not mean monsters <note>original: *Monſters*; in this period, "monsters" referred to individual biological deformities or "freaks of nature" rather than mythical creatures.</note>, but a constant species or kind of animals). Such a creature as that would make a limping attempt to live just as well as those that have four feet. Or why do some beasts not have more than four feet—suppose six, with the two middlemost shorter than the rest, hanging like the two legs of a man on horseback by the horse's sides? It is no harder a thing for Nature to make such frames of bodies than others that are more elegant and useful. But since the works of Nature are neither useless nor unfit, she must either be wise herself, or be guided by some higher...

# BOOK II.

higher principle of *knowledge*: just as a man who does nothing foolishly throughout his life is either wise himself or consults with those who are.

3. And then again, regarding the *armature* <note>original: "Armature"; here meaning natural defenses or weaponry</note> of *beasts*, who taught them the use of their *weapons*? The *lion* will not kick with his *feet*, but he will strike such a blow with his *tail* that he will break the back of his opponent with it. The *horse* will not use his *tail*, except against busy flies, but kicks with his *feet* with such force that he lays his enemy on the ground. The *bull* and *ram* know the use of their *horns* as well as the *horse* knows his *hoofs*. So the *bee* and *serpent* know their *stings*, and the *bear* the use of his *paw*. They know these things merely by natural instinct, just as the male knows the use of the female. For they do not gather this skill by observation and experience; rather, the very frame of their nature carries them to it. This is manifest in young *lambs* that will butt with their heads before they even have *horns*. Therefore, it is some higher *Providence* that has made them with this nature. This is also evident in *birds* that will *flutter* with their wings when there is only a little down upon them, while they are still utterly useless for flying.

4. And now that I have mentioned this kind of creature, let me take advantage of the general structure observable in them: the form of their *heads* being *narrow* and *sharp* so that they may better cut the air in their swift flight; and the spreading of their *tails* parallel to the *horizon* to better support their *body*. Their tails might have been perpendicular, like the *tails* of *fishes* in the water. It does not matter that the *owl* has such a broad face, for her flight was not intended to be so swift or so frequent.

As for *fishes*, to say nothing of how handsomely their *gills* supply the place of *lungs* and are replenished with a similar plenty of *veins* and *arteries*—so that their blood may be cooled by the *water* just as it is in the *lungs* of other animals by the *air*—we will take notice of more simple and common considerations. Who can say that the bladder of air found in their bodies was placed there by chance, rather than being designed for their easier swimming? Consider also the design of their *fins*, which consist of a number of gristly bones, long and slender like pins and needles, with a kind of skin between them. This is for greater precision and makes them thin and flat like *oars*. This perfect craftsmanship and accuracy might have been omitted, and they still might have managed to move up and down in the water.

But I have stumbled upon a subject that is infinite and inexhaustible. Therefore, so that I am not too tedious, I will confine myself to a few observations regarding ordinary *beasts* and *birds* (since what is most well-known and obvious serves our purpose best), and then I shall come to the contemplation of *man*.

5. And indeed, what is more common and ordinary than a *mole*? And yet, what is a more palpable argument for *Providence* than she? The members of her body are so exactly fitted to her nature and manner of life. Because her dwelling is underground where nothing is to be seen, Nature has so obscurely equipped her with *eyes* that *naturalists* <note>Early scientists or students of biology and the natural world.</note> can scarcely agree whether she has any *sight* at all. But to make amends, what she is...

### CHAPTER X.

[The abilities] that she is capable of for her defense and warning of danger, she has very eminently conferred upon her; for she is exceedingly quick of hearing. And then her *short tail* and *short legs*, but broad *fore-feet* armed with *sharp claws*—we see by the result for what purpose they exist: she so swiftly works herself underground, like the *rat* or *mouse* (to which she is related), but is forced to dig herself a dwelling there. And since she makes her way through so thick an element, which will not yield easily like the *air* or the *water*, it would have been dangerous to have drawn so long a train behind her; for her enemy might fall upon her *rear* and pull her out before she had completed or gained full possession of her tunnels.

6. *Cardan* <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), an influential Italian polymath and physician.</note> is so much taken with this contemplation that, though I find him often wavering, yet here he very fully and firmly professes that the contrivance of all things comes from *Wisdom* and *Purpose*. His words are so noble and significant that I consider them worth transcribing: "It is therefore evident that Nature has been wonderfully careful in all things, and has provided everything not by chance, but according to a deliberate plan. Humans—who possess this benefit above all others, that they may discover the First Cause of things—share in that primary Nature; nor is the Nature that established these things of a different kind from the minds of those who have been able to fully understand the reason why they were made so." <note>original Latin: *Palam est igitur, Naturam in cunctis sollicitam mirum in modum fuisse, nec obiter, sed ex sententia omnia providisse; hominesque, quibus hoc beneficium prae caeteris est, ut Causam rerum primam inveniant, participes esse illius primae Naturae, neque alterius esse generis Naturam quae hac constituit, ab illorum mente qui causam eorum cur ita facta sint plenè assequi potuerunt.*</note> Thus forcibly has the proper contemplation of Nature carried him beyond Nature and himself, and made him write like a man caught up in a divine *ecstasy*.

7. But there are as manifest footsteps of *Divine Providence* in other creatures as in the *mole*: as for example, the *hare*, whose temperament and frame of body are plainly fitted on purpose for her condition. For why is she made so full of *fear* and *vigilance*, always rearing up and listening while she is feeding? And why is she so exceedingly *swift of foot*, and has her *eyes* so *prominent* and placed so that she can see better behind her than before? It is because her flight is her only safety; and it was necessary for her to perpetually watch her pursuing enemy, against whom she dared never stand and fight, having nothing but her long, soft, flexible *ears* to defend her. Therefore, he who made the *hare* made the *dog* also, and guarded her with these properties from her eager foe, so that she might not be too easy a prey for him, and thus never be able to save herself or afford the spectator any significant pastime <note>The author refers to the historical "sport" of hare coursing.</note>. And so that the *hare* might not always get away from the *greyhound*, see how exquisitely his shape is fitted for the *chase*: for the narrowness and slenderness of his parts are made for speed; and that seemingly useless long *appendix* of his body, his *tail*, is made for more nimble turning.

8. There are other *animals* also whose particular physical structure clearly appears to be the effect of *Providence* and *Purpose*, though naturalists cannot agree whether it is for the benefit of the *beast* thus framed,

## CHAPTER XI.

1. Regarding Providence, I shall content myself by taking notice only of the outward frame of a few kinds of creatures that familiarly come into our sight, such as the *cock*, the *duck*, the *swan*, and the like.

2. I ask, therefore, concerning the *cock*: why does he have *spurs* at all? Or, having them, how do they come to be so fittingly placed? For he might have had none, or had them so misplaced that they would have been utterly useless, and thus his courage and pleasure in fighting would have been to no purpose. Nor are his *comb* and his *wattles* in vain, for they are an *ornament* becoming his martial spirit; indeed, they are a form of *armor* <note>original: "Armature"</note> too, for the pecking and tugging of those parts often protects the more vital parts of his head from harm. Thus fittingly does Nature gratify all creatures with accommodations suitable to their temperament, and nothing is in vain.

3. Nor should we complain at the red, puckered attire of the *turkey*, and the long *fleshy growth* <note>original: "Excrescency"</note> that hangs down over his bill when he swells with pride and anger. For it may be a receptacle for his heated blood, which has such free recourse to his head; or he may please himself in it, just as the uncivilized *Indians* <note>The author refers to indigenous peoples of the Americas, reflecting 17th-century perspectives.</note> whose *jewels* hang dangling at their *noses*. And if the bird is pleased, we should not be displeased, being always mindful that creatures are made to enjoy themselves as well as to serve us; it is a gross piece of ignorance and rudeness <note>original: "Rusticity"</note> to think otherwise.

4. Now for *swans* and *ducks*, and similar *water birds*, it is obvious to notice how well they are fitted for that manner of life. For those that swim, their *feet* are framed for it like a *pair of oars*, their *claws* being connected with a fairly broad *membrane* <note>webbing</note>; and their *necks* are long, so that they may dive deep enough into the water. This is also true of the *neck* of the *heron* <note>original: "Hern"</note> and similar *fowl* who live on *fish* and are required to frequent that element. They also walk on long stilts, like the people who dwell in the *marshes*; but their *claws* have no such *membranes*, for they would have been only a hindrance to those kinds of birds that only wade in the water and do not swim.

<margin>* And it happens in these places that the neck is long and the beak is sharp, like a fishing rod and line.</margin>
<margin>* Aristotle, *On the Parts of Animals*, Book 4, Chapter 12.</margin>
<margin>* Chapter 13 of the same book.</margin>

Aristotle is clever in comparing the long necks of these *water-fowls* to a *fishing rod* <note>original: "Angle-Rod"</note>, and their long *bills* to the *line* and *hook*. He also adds another observation concerning their *long legs*: that their *tails* are therefore shorter. However, I do not much admire his reasoning, as he claims they are short for want of biological matter that was instead spent upon the *legs*. Rather, the reason is because they are birds that fly less often; and besides, the posture of their *long legs* cast backward while they fly performs the office of a larger <term>rudder</term> <note>original: "ὀππόπλοιον" (oppoploion)</note>, and so they are helps to their flying, whereas otherwise they would be a trouble and hindrance. Therefore, as I said, their *tails* are so short not because the matter was spent upon their *legs*, but because their *legs* perform the office of the *tail*, according to that excellent aphorism of *Aristotle*: *Nature does nothing in vain or superfluously* <note>original: "ἔτε περίεργον ἐδὲν ἔτε μάτω η φύσις ποιεῖ"</note>.

This is the reason *fish* have no *legs*, though they have *fins*; and why the *torpedo* <note>an electric ray</note> has no *fins* at the sides of its round body, but only at the sides of its *tail*, the breadth and flatness of its body serving it instead of fore-fins to swim with. But this speculation on *water-fowls* has engaged me among the *fish* further than I intended.

9. To his great impatience against their *manner of incubation* <note>The process of sitting on eggs to hatch them.</note>, they would perhaps return this answer: that the method is not ridiculous, but perhaps rather *necessary*, based on what *Aldrovandus* <note>Ulisse Aldrovandi (1522–1605), a renowned Italian naturalist.</note> himself not only acknowledges but insists upon—namely, that they *have no feet at all*. For from this it is manifest that they cannot land on the ground, nor rest anywhere on their bellies and be able to take flight again. They cannot creep out of holes in rocks as *Swifts* and similar short-footed birds can, because they have no feet at all to creep with. Besides, as *Aristotle* well argues concerning the long legs of certain *water-fowl*, they were made so long because they were intended to wade in the water and catch fish, 
<margin>On the Parts of Animals, Book 4, Chapter 12.</margin> adding that excellent aphorism, *Nature creates the organs for the task, not the task for the organs* <note>original: "Τὰ γὰρ ὄργανα πρὸς τὸ ἔργον ἡ φύσις ποιεῖ, ἀλλ' ἐκ τοῦ ἔργου πρὸς τὰ ὄργανα"</note>. So may we rationally conclude, they will say, that just as the long legs of these *water-fowl* imply a design for haunting the water, the lack of *legs* in these *Manucodiata's* <note>An archaic name for the Bird of Paradise, derived from the Malay "manuk dewata," meaning "bird of the gods."</note> argues they are never to come down to the earth, because they can neither stand there, nor walk, nor take off again. And if they never come to the earth or any other resting place, where can their eggs be laid or hatched but on the back of the male?

Besides, *Cardan* <note>Gerolamo Cardano (1501–1576), an Italian polymath.</note> pleases himself with that *harmony of opposites in nature* <note>original: "Antiphonie in Nature"</note>: that just as the *Ostrich* is a bird yet never flies in the air, so this *Bird of Paradise* should always be in the air and never rest upon the earth. And as for *Aldrovandus's* presumption based on the five different *Manucodiata's* he had seen—in which he could observe no physical structure that implied a fitness for such a *manner of incubation*—*Cardan* would answer: "I myself have seen three, and *Scaliger* <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger (1484–1558), a scholar and physician.</note> has seen one, and we both agree against you."

10. However, you see that *Cardan*, *Aldrovandus*, and the rest all jointly agree in allowing the *Manucodiata* no feet, as well as in furnishing her with two strings hanging from the rear parts of her body; which *Aldrovandus* claims are in the female as well as the male, though *Cardan's* experience did not go that far.

11. But *Pigafetta* <note>Antonio Pigafetta, an explorer who accompanied Magellan.</note> and *Clusius* <note>Carolus Clusius (1526–1609), a pioneering botanist.</note> will easily end this great controversy between *Cardan* and *Aldrovandus*, if what they report is true, and if they are speaking of the same kind of Birds of Paradise. For they both affirm, with all imaginable confidence, that they have feet a palm's length long.

# CHAPTER XI.

But *Nierembergius* <note>Juan Eusebio Nieremberg (1595–1658), a Spanish Jesuit and naturalist.</note> on the contrary affirms that an eyewitness, who had picked up one of these birds newly dead, told him that it had no feet at all. *Johnston* <note>John Jonston (1603–1675), a Polish scholar and physician.</note> also gives his support to *Nierembergius* in this, though he agrees with *Aldrovandus* <note>Ulisse Aldrovandi (1522–1605), an Italian naturalist.</note> in rejecting the supposed method of their *incubation* <note>The process of hatching eggs.</note>.

However, they could only raise themselves from the ground by the stiffness of some of their wing feathers, or perhaps by those fibrous strings which they might have the power to stiffen while alive by sending "spirits" <note>In early physiology, "spirits" were thought to be fluids or vapors that animated the body.</note> into them. These might serve as well as legs to lift them from the ground, or to hang from the branches of trees (since a very slight thing can raise or hold up their light, feathery bodies in the air, just as a small twig will support us in the water). Unless this is the case, I would rather lean toward the testimony of *Pigafetta* and *Clusius* <note>Antonio Pigafetta and Carolus Clusius, explorers and botanists who argued the birds actually had legs.</note> than to the judgment of those sailors. The sailors told *Nierembergius* that the legs are pulled off by those who catch the birds, who then disembowel <note>original: "exenterate"</note> them and dry them in the sun, either for their own use or for sale.

<margin>*History of Animals, Book 1, Chapter 1.*</margin>
This conclusion would best protect the reputation of *Aristotle*, who long ago so decisively declared: *There is no bird that only flies, just as there is no fish that only swims.* <note>original Latin: "Ois anoron monon eden esin, osper psarion monon kinichthus" (transliterated Greek). Aristotle argued all animals must have a means of resting on a surface.</note>

12. Thus, our Bird of Paradise has quite flown away and vanished into a myth or fable. But if anyone mourns the loss of such a convincing argument for a divine *Providence* <note>The protective care of God or nature as a spiritual power.</note>—which fits one thing to another—I must take the liberty to tell him something. Unless he is a greater admirer of novelty than a seeker of the logical connection between things, I shall provide his meditations with something of this nature that is just as strongly conclusive. I remind him that it will be his own fault if he cannot see as clear an inference from an ordinary *truth* as from either an *uncertainty* or a *fiction*. In this regard, bringing this doubtful story into the discussion is not without purpose, as it carries with it a serious and corrective bit of irony.

The idea of the *Manucodiata* <note>An old name for the Bird of Paradise, derived from the Malay "manuk dewata," meaning "bird of the gods."</note> living on dew is not the part of the story that proves a *Providence*. Rather, it is the bird being so excellently provided with wings and feathers—*adorned with such a collection of lightness* <note>original Latin: "tanta levitatis supellectile exornata"</note> (as *Nierembergius* says). It is so well furnished with every advantage for buoyancy that it seems harder for it to sink down (as he imagines) than to be carried up in the air. That a bird thus fitted for that region should have no legs to stand on the earth would be a significant sign of a discerning *Providence* that intentionally avoids all uselessness and excess.

The other remarkable point—and it is a famous one—is the cavity on the back of the male and in the breast of the female for *incubation*.

And the third and last is the use of those strings, as *Cardan* <note>Gerolamo Cardano (1501–1576), an Italian polymath.</note> supposes, for better keeping the pair together during this *incubation*.

If these details of this strange story strike you so strongly as to convince you of a *Providence*, consider it a matter of whim and not judgment if the ordinary facts I offer in their place do not have the same force with you.

13. For is not the **fish's** lack of feet (as we observed before)—she being sufficiently supplied with **fins** in so thick an element as the **water**—as great an argument for **Providence** as a bird's lack of feet in that thinner element of the **air**? Especially since the extreme lightness of the bird's feathers is proportioned to the thinness of that element? And is not the same **Providence** seen, and just as conspicuously, in allotting only very short legs to those birds called **Apodes** <note>original: "Apodes" (Greek for "footless"); a term used by ancient naturalists for birds like swifts that appeared to lack feet.</note> (mentioned by both **Pliny** and **Aristotle**), upon whom Nature has bestowed such large and strong wings and the power of flying so long and fast? This is surely as much a sign of design as giving no legs at all to the **Manucodiata** <note>The Bird of Paradise, which was historically (and incorrectly) believed to lack feet and remain perpetually in flight.</note>, who has an even greater power of wing and lightness of body.

And as for the cavities on the back of the male and in the breast of the female <note>Referring to a myth that Birds of Paradise mated and nested in mid-air using specialized body cavities.</note>, is that design of Nature any more certain and plain than in the reproductive parts of males and females in every kind of animal? What greater argument of **counsel** and **purpose**—of fitting one thing for another—can there be than that? And if we should make a more inward search into the workings of these parts in an ordinary **hen**, and consider how, or by what force, an **egg** of such great growth and size is transmitted from the **ovary** through the **funnel** <note>original: "Infundibulum"</note> into the **uterus** (the membranes being so thin and the passage appearing so very small), the **principle** of that motion cannot be thought of as anything less than **Divine**. And if you would compare the **protruding** paps or teats in the females of beasts with that **cavity** in the breast of the **Manucodiata**, which of them do you think is the clearer pledge of a knowing and designing **Providence**?

And lastly, regarding the strings that are imagined to hold together the male and female during their **brooding** <note>original: "Incubiture"</note>, what a trivial thing it is if compared with those invisible links and ties that compel ordinary birds to sit upon their eggs, despite having no visible reward for such a tedious service?

1. But we did not need to have wandered so far into the works of Nature to seek out arguments to prove a God, since we are so plentifully furnished with evidence at home which we took the pains to seek abroad. For there can be no more ample testimony of a **God** and **Providence** than the **frame** and **structure** of our own **bodies**. The admirable **artifice** <note>original: "Artifice"; here meaning skilled craftsmanship or design</note> of the body so captivated **Galen** <note>A prominent Greek physician and philosopher in the Roman Empire (c. 129–216 AD) whose views dominated Western medical science for 1,300 years.</note>, though he was a mere **naturalist**, that he could not help but award the honor of a **hymn** to its wise **Creator**. The **contrivance** of the **whole** and **every particular** part is such an evident **argument** of **exquisite skill** in the **Maker**, that if I were to pursue everything that suits my purpose, it would fill an entire **volume**. I shall therefore only hint at a few things, leaving the rest to be supplied by **anatomists**. I think there is no man who has any skill in that **art** but will confess that the more diligently and accurately the **frame** of our **body** is examined, the more it is found to be exquisitely conformable to our **reason, judgment,** and **desire**. So much so, that if we had the same matter our **bodies** are made of, and it had been in our own power to make ourselves, we would have framed ourselves no differently than we are.

2. To give a specific example: consider our **eyes**. Their **number**, **location**, and **fabric** are such that we can think of nothing to be added or altered, whether for their **beauty, safety,** or **usefulness**. As for their **beauty**, I will leave that to the delicate wit and pens of **poets** and lovers, rather than venture upon such a tender and refined **subject** with my more severe **style**. I will only note how **safely** they are **guarded** and **fitly framed** for their **intended use**. The **brow** and the **nose** save them from harder **blows**. However, because a part as delicate as the **eye** is necessarily vulnerable to injury from smaller things, the **sweat** of the **forehead** is kept away by those two wreaths of hair which we call the **eyebrows**. Furthermore, the **eyelids** are fortified with little stiff **bristles**, like **palisades** <note>original: "Palisadoes"; a fence of wooden stakes used for defense</note>, against the **assault** of **flies**, **gnats**, and similar bold **tiny animals** <note>original: "Animalcula"</note>. Besides this, the **upper lid** immediately snaps down and is as good a defense as a **portcullis** <note>A heavy sliding gate in a fortress</note> against the **attacks** of the **enemy**. This happens every night, whether there is an active assault or not; it is as if **Nature** kept a garrison in this **Acropolis** <note>The ancient citadel of Athens; here used to mean the "fortress" of the human head</note> of **man's body**, the **head**, and ensured that such laws were duly observed as were most necessary for his **safety**.

3. Now, regarding the **use** of the **eye**, which is **sight**: it is evident that this **organ** is so **exquisitely framed** for that purpose that not the slightest **refinement** <note>original: "curiosity"</note> could be added. For, first, the **fluids** <note>original: "Humour"</note> and **membranes** <note>original: "Tunicles"</note> are purely **transparent** to let in **light** and **colors** unpolluted and pure, without being distorted by any internal tint. And then again, the **parts** of the **eye** are made **convex**, so that there might be a **direction** of many **rays** coming from one point...

Thirdly, the *Tunica Uvea* <note>The iris and ciliary body.</note> has a *muscular* power, and can dilate and contract that round hole in it which is called the *Pupil* of the *Eye*, for the better moderating the transmission of light. Fifthly, the *Tunica Arachnoides* <note>The capsule of the lens.</note>, which envelops the *Crystalline Humour*, by virtue of its *ciliary processes* <note>original: Proceſſus Ciliares</note> can thrust forward or draw back that precious useful part of the *Eye*, as the nearness or distance of the object shall require. 4. And the *Eye* is already so *perfect* that I believe the reason of man would have easily rested here and admired its own contrivance; for he, being able to *move* his whole *head* upward and downward and on every side, might have unawares thought himself sufficiently well provided for. But Nature has added *muscles* also to the *Eyes*, so that no perfection might be wanting. For we often have occasion to *move* our *eyes* while our *head* remains unmoved, as in reading and viewing more particularly any object set before us; and so that this may be done with more ease and accuracy, she has furnished that *organ* with no less than six several *muscles*.

5. And indeed this framing of *muscles* not only in the *eye*, but in the whole *body*, is admirable. For is it not a wonder that even all our flesh should be so handsomely contrived into distinct pieces, whose origins and insertions should be placed with such advantage that they serve with such ease to move some part of the *body* or another? And the parts of our *body* are not moved only so conveniently as will serve us to walk and subsist by, but they are able to move every way imaginable that will advantage us. For we can fling our *legs* and *arms* upwards and downwards, backwards, forwards, and round, like those who spin, or those who would spread a molehill with their feet. I will say nothing of *respiration*, the constriction of the *diaphragm* for keeping down the *guts* and so enlarging the *thorax* <note>The chest cavity.</note> so that the *lungs* may have play, and the assistance of the inward *intercostal muscles* in deep *sighs* <note>original: Suspirations</note>, when we take larger gulps of air to cool our heart overcharged with love or sorrow. Nor will I speak of the curious fabric of the *larynx*, so well fitted with *muscles* for the modulation of the *voice*, tunable *speech*, and delicious *singing*; nor, lastly, of Nature's so industriously perforating the *tendons* of the second *joints* of both *fingers* and *toes*, and her so careful transmitting of the *tendons* of the third *joints* through them.

6. You may add to these the notable design of the **Heart**, its two **ventricles** <note>The main chambers of the heart.</note> and its many **valves**, so formed and situated as is most fit for the reception and transmission of the **blood**. The blood circulates through the **heart** and is sent away warm to comfort and cherish the rest of the **body**. For this purpose also, the **valves** in the **veins** are made so that the blood may more easily ascend upwards.

7. But I will rather insist upon such things as are easy and intelligible even to **uneducated people** <note>original: "Idiots," used here in the archaic sense of private persons or those lacking professional knowledge.</note>. If they can but count the **joints** of their **hands** or know the use of their **teeth**, they may easily discover it was **purposeful design** <note>original: "Counsel"</note>, not **chance**, that created them. For why do we have three **joints** in our **legs** and **arms**, as also in our **fingers**, except that it was much better than having only two or four? And why are our **front teeth sharp** like chisels to cut, but our **inner teeth** broad to grind, except that this is more excellent than having them all **sharp** or all **broad**, or the **front teeth** broad and the others **sharp**? We might have managed to survive, though in a much worse condition, otherwise. Again, why are the **teeth** so luckily placed? Or rather, why are there not **teeth** in **other bones** as well as in the **jawbones**? For other bones might have been as capable of holding them as these. But the reason is, **nothing is done foolishly or in vain**; that is, there is a **Divine Providence** that orders all things. Again, to say nothing of the internal complexity of the **ear**, why is there that outward frame of it, if not for the certain purpose of improving our **hearing**?

8. I might add to these that **Nature** has made the **hindmost parts** of our **body** which we sit upon most **fleshy**, providing for our **comfort** and making us a natural **cushion**, as well as providing **muscles** <note>original: "instruments of Motion"</note> for our **thighs** and **legs**. She has made the **back** of the **head** stronger, as it is otherwise unprotected against falls and other accidents. She has made the **backbone** of several **vertebrae**, as it is more fit to bend, more tough, and less in danger of breaking than if it were all one entire bone without those **cartilaginous joints** <note>original: "gristly Junctures"</note>. She has strengthened our **fingers** and **toes** with **nails**, whereas she might have allowed that hard substance to grow out at the end of the first or second **joint**, which would not have been as **attractive** <note>original: "handsome"</note> or **useful**, but rather somewhat **troublesome** and **hurtful**. And lastly, she has made all the **bones** devoid of **sensation**, because they were to bear the weight of themselves and of the whole **body**. Therefore, if they had possessed **sensation**, our life would have been continually painful and full of suffering.

9. And what she has done for **us**, she has done proportionately in the design of all other **creatures**; so that it is manifest that a **Divine Providence** permeates all things.

10. And therefore, since things are designed with such exquisite **detail** <note>original: "Curiosity"</note> as if the most watchful **Wisdom** imaginable attended to them, to say they are thus framed without the assistance of some **intelligent Principle**, and that they come to pass from **chance** or some other blind, unknowing **source**, is to stubbornly and moodily assert a thing simply because we wish to assert it. Under the pretense of avoiding **superstition**, one falls into the only thing that makes **superstition** itself hateful or ridiculous: a willful and groundless adhering to ideas without any support of **reason**.

<summary>The author argues that the specific anatomical features of the human body—such as heart valves, tooth shapes, and the placement of flesh and nails—prove that humanity was designed by a wise Creator rather than by blind chance. He concludes that denying this divine design is a stubborn rejection of reason.</summary>

# An Antidote against Atheism. BOOK II.

11. And now that I have considered the fitness of the parts of the human body for the good of the whole, let me briefly consider the fitness of the *passions* of the *mind*—whether they are unique to man or shared with the rest of the *animals*—as well as the fitness of the *whole man* as he is a *part of the universe*; and then I shall conclude.

And it is manifest that *anger* so activates the spirits and heightens the courage of men and beasts that it allows them to break through the difficulties they encounter with more ease. *Fear* also exists for the avoiding of danger, and *hope* is a pleasant anticipation of enjoyment, such as when a dog waits until his master has finished picking a bone. But there is neither *hope*, nor *fear*, nor *hate*, nor any peculiar *passion* or *instinct* in *brutes* <note>original: "brutes"; meaning non-human animals</note> that is in vain. Why then should we think that Nature should fail more in *us* than in any other creature? Why should she be so careful in the construction of our *body*, and yet so forgetful or unlucky in the framing of the faculties of our *souls*? It would be strange if that *fear* which is so uniquely natural to *us*—namely, the *fear of a Deity*—should be in vain, or if that pleasant *hope* and those heavenly *joys* of the *mind* which man is naturally capable of, along with the earnest direction of his spirit toward God, should have no real object in the world. If so, the *religious affection* which Nature has so plainly implanted in the *soul* of man would be of no use, except to make him either ridiculous or miserable. Yet we find no *passion* or *affection* in *brutes*, whether common or unique, that is not for their good and welfare.

12. For it is not for nothing that the *hare* is so *fearful* of the *dog*, and the *sheep* of the *wolf*. And if there are instances of *fear* or *enmity* in some *creatures* for which we cannot easily discern a reason regarding themselves, yet we may well accept it as reasonable in regard to *us*, and as serving a good purpose. But I think it is manifest that *sympathy* and *antipathy*, *love* and *enmity*, *aversion*, *fear*, and the like, are notable sharpeners and quickeners of the spirit of life in all *animals*. Their being subject to *dangers* and *encounters* more closely knits together their vital *powers* and makes them more sensibly relish their present *safety*; they are more pleased with an *escape* than if they had never met with any *danger*. Their greedy assaults upon one another, while there is *hope* of *victory*, also highly gratify them both. If one is conquered and slain, the *conqueror* enjoys a fresh improvement of the pleasure of life: the *triumph* over his *enemy*. These things seem to me to be contrived even for the sake of these *creatures* themselves, so that their vital heat and moisture may not always merely simmer in one sluggish tone, but sometimes boil up higher and seethe over, the fire of life being more than ordinarily kindled by some emerging occasion.

13. But it is beyond controversy that many of these peculiar *passions* of animals are *useful* to *men* (such as the *lizard's* enmity against the *serpent* <note>A common folklore belief of the era was that lizards would warn humans of approaching snakes.</note>). All of them highly gratify man's *contemplative* faculty, and some seem purposely contrived to make his *worship* <note>original: "worship"; here meaning his honor or his position as a superior being</note> merry. For what else could Nature intend in that *antipathy* between the *ape* and the *snail*? It is a marvel that a beast which seems so boldly to claim kinship with man due to the resemblance of his outward shape should have so little wit or courage...

<summary>The author argues that human emotions, specifically the innate desire for God, must have a real purpose just as animal instincts and passions serve their survival and vitality. He suggests that even the conflicts and fears of animals contribute to the "fire of life" and provide utility or contemplation for mankind.</summary>

14. But that Nature should implant in Man such a *strong propensity* toward *Religion*, which is the *reverence of a Deity*, when there is neither *God* nor *angel* nor *spirit* in the world, would be such a *blunder* committed by her that no excuse could possibly be devised. For if there were a higher *species* of beings to laugh at us as we do at the ape, it might seem more tolerable. But there can be no end—neither humorous nor serious—for this religious property in Man, unless there is something of a higher nature than himself in the world. Therefore, since religion is suitable to no other species of things besides Man, it ought to be beneficial at least for himself. But supposing there were no God, there could be nothing worse for Man than religion.

15. For we may look at the *external effects* of it, such as bloody *massacres*, the *disturbance* and *overthrow* of *commonwealths, kingdoms*, and *empires*, the most savage *tortures* of individuals, and the *extermination* and *dispossession* of whole *nations*. This has happened in *America*, where the remorseless *Spaniards*, under the pretense of being educated in a better *religion* than the *Americans* <note>Referring here to the Indigenous peoples of the Americas.</note>, devalued the poor *natives* so much that they thought nothing of knocking them on the head merely to feed their dogs with them, along with many such unheard-of *cruelties*. 

Or we may consider the great *affliction* that this severe *governess* of human life brings upon those *souls* she seizes: by frightening them with the *horrors* of *conscience*; by puzzling and making fools of them in the free use of their *reason*; by putting a barrier against more extensive searches into the pleasing knowledge of *nature*; by anxious cares and disquieting fears concerning their *state* in the *life to come*; by *curbing* them in their natural and healthy enjoyments of the *present life*; and by making *bitter* all the *pleasures* and *contentments* of it through checks of *conscience* and suspicions that they are doing something now for which they may suffer eternally hereafter. 

Besides these, there are those inexpressible *agonies of mind* undergone by those who are more generously *religious* and strive to participate in the *Divine Nature*. These people are willing, though with unspeakable pain, to be torn away from their own desires to become one with that *Universal Spirit* that ought to guide all things. Through an insatiable desire for that just and proper temper of mind—whereby all *arrogance* should utterly cease in us, and everything we have or can do should be vividly and sensibly attributed to God, while we fully and heartily acknowledge ourselves to be nothing (that is, to be as little prideful, and to no more relish the glory and praise of men, than if we had done nothing or did not exist at all)—they plunge themselves into such slumps and *deadness of spirit* that to be buried alive would be far less torture than such dark *privations* of all the *joys* of life, and such sad and heart-sinking *mortifications* <note>original: "Mortifications"; here meaning the subduing of physical desires or the "killing off" of the ego.</note>. 

I say, whether we consider these inward *pangs* of the *soul* or the external *outrages* caused by *religion*—and *religious* pretense will animate men to commit such violences as bare *reason* and the simple passions of the mind, unsupported by the fury of superstition...

For the fear of the **Civil Magistrate**, the convenience of mutual aid and support, and the natural scourge and plague of diseases would contain men within such bounds of **Justice**, **Humanity**, and **Temperance** as would make them more clearly and undisturbed happy than they are now capable of being—considering any advantage **Religion** does to either the public State or private person—supposing there were no **God**.
