# ANTIDOTE
## AGAINST
### ATHEISM.
#### BOOK III.
##### CHAPTER I.

*1. Because good men do not always fare best in this world, the great examples of Divine Vengeance upon wicked and blasphemous persons are not always convincing to the obstinate Atheist. 2. The irreligious jests and sacrileges of Dionysius of Syracuse. 3. The cause of the Atheist's disbelief in supernatural or miraculous things. 4. That there have been true miracles in the world as well as false ones. 5. And what are the best and safest ways to distinguish them, so that we may not be deceived by history.*

I. Hitherto I have insisted upon such arguments for proving the existence of God as were taken from the ordinary and known phenomena <note>original: "Phenomena"</note> of nature; for such is the history of plants, animals, and man. I shall come now to such effects discovered in the world as are not deemed natural, but extraordinary and miraculous. I do not mean unexpected discoveries of murders, or a conspicuous vengeance upon proud and blasphemous persons—such as Nicanor, Antiochus, Herod, and the like, of which all histories, both sacred and secular, are very full. All of these tend to impress this divine precept of the poet upon the minds of men:

->*“Be warned; learn justice and do not slight the gods.”* <note>original Latin: "Discite Iustitiam moniti & non temnere Divos." From Virgil's Aeneid.</note><-

For although these examples cannot help but move impartial men to an acknowledgment of <term>Divine Providence</term> <note>The belief that God intervenes in the world to guide events and uphold justice.</note> and a <term>Superior Power</term> above and different from physical matter; yet I am now dealing with the obstinate and stubborn <term>Atheist</term> <note>One who denies the existence of God.</note>, who, though an obdurate scorner of the <term>Deity</term> <note>God.</note>, finding himself...

<meta>This page continues the author's exploration of arguments for the existence of God by addressing common atheistic counter-arguments regarding divine justice and the apparent lack of punishment for the wicked.</meta>

# CHAPTER I.

A man who considers himself safe and well at ease will brush all these things aside by asking a question similar to the one posed to the Priest of Neptune. When the priest showed him the many *offerings* <note>original: "Donaria"</note> hung up in the temple by *devotees* <note>original: "Votaries"</note> who had been saved from shipwreck—boasting much of the power of that God of the Sea—the man replied: *“But what has become of all those who, despite their vows, were lost?”* So I say, the atheist, to evade the force of this argument, will whisper to himself: *“But how many proud, blasphemous, atheistical men like myself have escaped, while those accounted good have died untimely deaths?”*

Such were *Aesop* and *Socrates*, the *Prophets*, *Apostles*, and *Martyrs*, along with various other wise and good men in all ages and places. These men, not being fully aware of the ill condition and resistance of this wicked world—of which they truly professed themselves not to be citizens, but strangers—suffered the greatest mischiefs that can happen to human nature because of their innocent intentions and their meddling in *a foreign state* <note>original: "aliena Republica"; referring here to the secular or corrupt affairs of the world</note>. It has usually been safer to craftily and cautiously undermine the honor of God than to plainly and honestly seek the good and welfare of men.

2. Furthermore, the atheist will reply that outrageous affronts intentionally committed against religion have not only been applauded by the world, but have gone unpunished by Divine Justice. This is notorious in the case of that sacrilegious wit, *Dionysius of Syracuse*. When he robbed *Jupiter Olympius* of his costly robe, which was very stiff and heavy with gold, he added this mocking apology for his sacrilege: "This golden garment is too heavy for the summer and too cold for the winter, but one made of wool would fit both seasons."

3. Likewise, at *Epidaurus*, he commanded the golden beard of *Aesculapius* to be cut off and carried away, alleging that it was very unfit for the son to wear a beard when his father, *Apollo*, wore none.

Another of his sacrilegious jests was no less bold: when he took away the golden cups and crowns held out by the hands of the statues of the gods, he excused himself by saying that he only received what they gave him of their own accord. He added that it would be a gross piece of foolishness to pray to the gods for all good things and then not take them when they so freely offer them with their own hands.

*Dionysius* played these and other such irreligious pranks, yet he fared no worse than the most serious and innocent of men, dying no other death than what other mortals usually do. It was as if in those ages there was as great a lack of *wit* as there once was of *Latin* here in England, and that he escaped a more severe sentence by the "benefit of his clergy" <note>A historical legal loophole where literacy—specifically the ability to read Latin—could exempt a person from the death penalty</note>. Others think he was paid back and punished through his son who succeeded him. But the atheist will reply that this is merely "whipping the absent," as *Aristotle* wittily said to someone who told him that a certain person was unmercifully slandering him behind his back.

Therefore, I hold it more convenient to omit such arguments that may entangle us in such endless disputes. Instead, I will bring forward only those arguments that cannot be explained by <term>natural causes</term> or imagined to happen by <term>chance</term>, but are so <term>miraculous</term> that they imply the presence of some free, subtle, understanding <term>essence</term> distinct from brute <term>matter</term> and the ordinary power of <term>nature</term>.

->3. And<-

<meta>This page continues the author's argument regarding the existence of God and spirits, specifically addressing the skepticism surrounding miracles and supernatural phenomena.</meta>

3. Regarding these *miraculous effects*: while nothing is more convincing if they could be believed, there is also nothing harder for the *atheist* to believe. Because *religionists* <note>original: "Religionists"; here meaning people who are professionally or zealously religious, often used by the author to imply those who might manipulate faith</note> have—for "pious purposes," as they claim—forged so many false *miracles* to trick and exploit credulous people, they have caused the *atheist* to lose all belief in those miracles that are actually true. Furthermore, the childish and superstitious *fear of spirits* found in *melancholic* <note>original: "Melancholick"; in the 17th century, this referred to a physical imbalance of "black bile" thought to cause depression, hallucinations, or paranoia</note> persons—who create strange *monsters* and terrible *apparitions* for themselves in the dark—has provided the atheist with a further excuse: to attribute all *specters* and strange *apparitions* to mere *melancholy* and a disturbed *fancy* <note>original: "Phanſie"; imagination</note>.

4. But to me, the greatest *miracle* of all is that there should be such universal talk and fear of something that never was, is not, and could never be in the world.

For if there had not been *true miracles* at some time or other, it is very improbable that priests and cunning deceivers would have ever been able to impose upon the people so easily with *false* ones. (Indeed, there ought to be true miracles, unless the natural faculties of man—which so easily listen to and accept such things—were created in vain.) Just as an *alchemist* would never attempt to adulterate *metals* and pass them off as *true gold* and *silver* unless it were already acknowledged that *true gold* and *silver* exist in the world, the very attempt to delude people with *false miracles* is a sign that *true* ones have existed and may exist still.

5. But you will say there is a *touchstone* <note>a stone used to test the purity of gold and silver; figuratively, a standard for testing authenticity</note> by which we may discern the truth of *metals*, but there is no way to discover the truth of *miracles* recorded everywhere in *history*. To this I answer: there is a way, and it is this:

First, if what is recorded was confirmed by persons who had *no personal goal or interest* in claiming such things.

Secondly, if there were many *eye-witnesses* to the same matter.

Thirdly and lastly, if these things—which are so strange and miraculous—leave any *perceivable effect* behind them.

While I will not claim that all *stories* lacking these conditions are *false*, I dare affirm that it is mere whim and stubbornness for a man to reject the *truth* of those that do possess them. To do so is to believe nothing except what he sees himself; from which it would follow that he should read nothing of *history*, for there is neither pleasure nor any use in it if it deserves no belief.

Husband, who being in the flower of his age, in good health and very cheerful, went out of his house in the morning with the intent to return for dinner. ### CHAPTER III.

1. That winds and tempests are raised upon mere ceremonies or forms of words. 2. The unreasonableness of Wierus's doubting of the Devil's power over the meteors <note>In this period, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomena, including rain, snow, and lightning.</note> of the air. 3. Examples of that power in rain and thunder. 4. Margaret Warine discharged upon an oak tree during a clap of thunder. 5. Amantius and Rotarius cast headlong out of a cloud onto a house-top. 6. The Witch of Constance seen by shepherds riding through the air. 7. That he might add several other instances from eyewitnesses of the strange effects of invisible demons. 8. His concise rehearsal of the most remarkable exploits of the "Devil of Mascon" <note>A famous 17th-century account of a haunting or poltergeist in Mascon, France.</note> in place of those instances. 9. The reasons for giving himself the trouble of this rehearsal.

1. Wierus <note>Johann Weyer (1515–1588), a physician who argued that many accused witches were actually suffering from mental illness.</note>, that industrious advocate for witches, recites several ceremonies that they use for the raising of tempests. He acknowledges that tempests do follow the performance of those ceremonies, but claims they would have happened anyway without them. He argues that the Devil, foreseeing the weather, excites the deluded women to use those magic rites so they may be better persuaded of his power. Whether there is any causal connection between those ceremonies and the ensuing tempests, I will not meticulously decide. But that the connection between them is supernatural is plain at first sight.
<margin>Wierus, *On the Deceptions of Demons*, Book 3, Chapter 16.</margin>
For what is the casting of flint stones behind their backs toward the West, or flinging a little sand into the air, or striking a river with a broom and sprinkling the water toward heaven, or the stirring of urine or water with their finger in a hole in the ground, or boiling hogs' bristles in a pot? How are these fooleries effective by themselves to gather clouds and cover the air with darkness, and then to make the ground smoke with peals of hail and rain, and to make the air terrible with frequent lightning and thunder? Certainly, they have no power at all. Therefore, the occurrence of these tempests after such ceremonies must be either from the foresight of the Devil (as Wierus would have it) who set the witches to work, or else from the power that the Devil has in his "Kingdom of the Air."

2. And it seems strange to me that Wierus should doubt this power when he grants the Devil a greater one. For what is the transporting of vapors
<margin>*On the Deceptions of Demons*, Book 3, Chapter 1, and Book 4, Chapter 19.</margin>
or driving them together, compared to the carrying of men and cattle through the air (of which Wierus is a confident supporter), unless it simply requires larger devils or greater numbers of them? And that there are sufficient numbers of such spirits
<margin>See Bodin, *On the Demon-Mania of Witches*, Book 2, Chapter 4.</margin>
will seem as credible to anyone as the idea that there are any spirits at all. Now, regarding the truth of this—that certain words or ceremonies seem at least to cause an alteration in the air and raise tempests—Remigius <note>Nicolaus Remy (c. 1554–1612), a French magistrate and witch-hunter.</note> writes that he had this witnessed to him by the free confession of nearly two hundred men that he examined. He adds a story or two in which, there being neither fraud nor melancholy <note>original: "Melancholy"; here meaning clinical depression or mental delusion.</note> to be suspected, I think them worth mentioning.

3. The first story concerns a **Witch** who, in order to satisfy the curiosity of those who had the power to punish her, was set free so that she might provide proof of the power she claimed to possess to raise **tempests** <note>original: "Tempests"; violent storms</note>. Once she was released, she immediately went to a place densely filled with trees, scraped a hole in the ground with her hands, **filled it with urine, and stirred it around for so long that she finally produced a thick, dark cloud filled with thunder and lightning, to the terror and fright of the onlookers.** But she told them to be of good courage, for she said she would command the cloud to discharge its rain upon whatever location they chose; she then proved this true in the sight of the spectators.

The other story is of a **young girl** who wished to please her father when he complained of a drought. Guided and helped by that "evil master" <note>referring to a demon or the Devil</note> to whom her mother had devoted and consecrated her, she raised a **cloud** and watered her father's ground only, while all the surrounding land remained as dry as before.

4. Let us add to these the account of **Cunius** and **Margaret Warine**. While this **Cunius** was busy making hay, there suddenly arose great **thunder and lightning**, which made him run toward home and abandon his work. He saw six **oaks** near him overturned from their very **roots**, and a seventh shattered and torn to pieces. In his haste, he lost his hat and had to leave his pitchfork or rake behind. Despite his speed, another crack of thunder overtook him and rattled about his ears. Immediately after that thunderclap, he spotted **Margaret Warine**, a reputed witch, on the top of an **oak tree**, and he began to scold her. She begged for his secrecy and promised that no injury or harm would ever come to him from her at any time.

<margin>See Remigius's *Demonolatry*, Book 1, Chapter 29.</margin> This **Cunius** testified to this under oath before a magistrate, and **Margaret Warine** acknowledged the truth of it several times before her death—and at the moment of her death—without any force being used against her. **Remigius** <note>Nicholas Rémy (c. 1530–1612), a French magistrate and famous hunter of witches</note> believes she was dropped onto the top of the **oak** during that last **thunderclap** and hung there among the branches; he is led to believe this because of two stories he tells afterward.

Running into the woods for shelter, they suddenly saw two countrymen on the tops of the trees nearest to them. These men were so dirty, in such a mess, and so out of breath that it looked as if they had been dragged up and down through thorns and muddy places. But as soon as the herdsmen looked closely at them, the men vanished in a moment, and the herdsmen did not know how or where they went. These herdsmen spoke of the incident, but the truth of it came out not long after. The voluntary confessions of those two men they had seen agreed so exactly with what the herdsmen had reported that the whole matter became clear and certain.

6. I will only add one more account of this nature, and that is of a witch of **Constance** <note>A city in Germany, famous for its 15th-century Church Council.</note>. # An Antidote against Atheism. BOOK III.

There are already published and available to us such narrations as will provide us with enough examples of this kind.

8. Among these, the account by Mr. *Francis Perreand* concerning an unclean spirit that haunted his house at *Mâcon* in *Burgundy* is of primary use, both for the variety of its subject matter and the authenticity of the story. For although this *demon* never appeared visible to the eye, his presence was clearly detectable by many antics and pranks that he played. These included drawing the curtains at midnight and plucking off the blankets; holding doors shut and rolling logs of wood; knocking and flinging things against the wood paneling; whistling tunes such as those taught to *birds*, and singing profane and lewd songs; repeating aloud the Lord's Prayer and the Creed; and imitating the voices and dialects of several people, as well as the cries of huntsmen, the croaking of frogs, and the speeches of jugglers and street performers. He was also known for scoffing, jeering, and uttering witty remarks, such as the one about *Pays de Vaud*, where he said they made fine *carbonados* <note>original: "Carbonado's"; a carbonado is a piece of meat scored and grilled over coals—here a dark joke about burning witches</note> of witches, and laughed very loudly afterward. He brought greetings from distant friends and told stories of fights and murders. He revealed things done in private to the people who had done them, and even reproached a grave clergyman for singing a lewd song in a tavern.

He tossed a roll of cloth fifty ells <note>An "ell" is a traditional unit of measurement, roughly 45 inches</note> long; he disordered skeins of yarn and pulled men backward by their coats while they were at work. He flung a man's hat at his face while he was asleep in his house and snatched a candlestick out of a maid's hand. He entangled and tied things in such knots that it was impossible for anyone to untie them, yet he himself untied them in a moment. He tumbled the bed into the middle of the floor as soon as it had been made and took down books from their shelves in the study. He made a noise like a volley of gunfire and imitated the sound of four hemp-dressers beating together. He made music with two little bells he found among rusty iron in the house, which he used not only there but in several other places; the people could hear the sound passing by them in the air, though they could see nothing. He hid a goldsmith's jewels and tools for a while and then dropped them out of the air onto the table. He flung stones about the house without causing hurt, as in the previous narration. He often beat a new maid in her bed and poured water on her head until he had forced her to leave. And lastly, he pulled a certain lawyer by the arm into the middle of the room, whirled him about on his tiptoes, and then flung him to the ground.

This is a short *summary* <note>original: "Epitome"</note> of the most remarkable exploits of that invisible *devil* of *Mâcon*. As I remember, he was not seen even once in any shape during all this time, unless it was he whom *Lullier* and *Repay* met at a street corner in the guise of a *country woman* spinning by moonlight, who vanished from their sight as they approached.

9. I have taken the trouble of transcribing these particulars partly because they contribute so much to discovering the nature of these kinds of *spirits*. <margin>This was not written by only one person. For Marcelin, a Preacher then at Mascon, wrote the same story; and Ternus, who was a frequent eyewitness of the pranks of this Demon, left an account written and signed with his own hand, which Perreand kept with him.</margin>

...partly for both the abundance and the suitability of the story to the present theme; but lastly and chiefly, for the unquestionable truth and authenticity of the narration. The observation of these strange events was made not by one solitary person, but by many together; nor by a person of suspected integrity, but of singular gravity and exemplary life. It was not recorded carelessly or credulously, but cautiously and diligently, by searching every corner of the house and setting bolts and barricades to all its doors and windows—even stopping up the cat-holes in the doors—leaving nothing that might allow for a suspicion of fraud <note>original: "Imposture"</note>. 

A candle also burned every night, all night long. During the day, various people searched the places from which the voice originated and examined the objects within. When one Simeon Meissonier had, among other things, carried away a bottle, the Devil began laughing that Meissonier should think him such a fool as to enter it, as he would then be liable to be trapped inside by a finger. Lastly, this experience occurred not once or twice, but essentially every day for a quarter of a year.

To the truth of the miraculous nature of the story, the silence of the dog also provides further evidence. The dog was otherwise very watchful and ready to bark at the slightest noise, yet he never barked at the loud speaking and hideous noises of the Demon. The profane Goblin himself took notice of this, mischievously claiming it was because he had made the sign of the Cross on the dog's head; for he was then in a merry mood <note>original: "on a merry pin"</note> and full of jeering.

To all of this, you may further add the authority of the Reverend and Learned Mr. P. Du Moulin (father to the current Dr. Du Moulin) and the sharp, judicious reasoning of his accomplished son in his preface to Mr. Perreand’s account: namely, that this familiar conversation with the Devil did not happen in a corner or in a desert (where the melancholy of witches is supposed to make them imagine they converse with him), but in the midst of a great city, in a house where there was a daily resort of people coming to hear him speak. There, men of opposing religions met together; their natural inclination to bring disgrace upon dissenting parties led to the narrow examination and full confirmation of the truth, both by the Magistrate and by the Bishop <note>original: "Dioceſan"</note> of the place.

And lastly, so that nothing may be lacking to convince the skeptical, we add the testimony of that excellently learned and noble gentleman, Mr. R. Boyle <note>Robert Boyle (1627–1691), the famous natural philosopher and chemist.</note>, who spoke with Mr. Perreand himself at Geneva. There, he received from him as a gift a copy of his book before it was printed, and had the opportunity to inquire about both the writer and several passages of his book. He was so well satisfied that he professes all his settled reluctance to believe strange things was overcome by this special conviction.

### CHAPTER IV.

1. The supernatural *effects* observed in the bewitched children of Mr. *Throgmorton* and Mrs. *Mulchamp*.
2. The general *remarkable details* in them both.
3. The *possession* of the *religious virgins* <note>Nuns</note> of *Werts*, *Heffimont*, etc.

1. WE will now pass to those *supernatural effects* which are observed in *persons* that are *bewitched* or *possessed*. These include: *foretelling* things to come; *telling* what such and such *persons speak* or *do* as exactly as if they were standing by them, even when the *possessed* party is at one end of the town inside a house, and those parties acting and talking together are outside at the other end of the town; being able to see *some* people and *not others*; playing at *cards* with one certain person and not perceiving anyone else at the table besides him; acting, talking, walking about, and predicting the outcome of events and what is happening during those *fits of possession*; and then, as soon as the *possessed* or bewitched party comes out of the fit, remembering nothing at all, but asking about the welfare of those whose faces he seemed to be looking at just moments before while in his *fits*. 

All of these can be no symptoms or signs of anything else but the *Devil* having entered the body of a man, taking over all the operations of his soul, and then acting, speaking, and sporting as he pleases in the miserable tenement <note>The human body viewed as a temporary dwelling</note> he has crowded himself into. He makes use of the organs of the body at his own pleasure to perform such pranks and feats as are far above the capacity, strength, or agility of the party thus *bewitched* or *possessed*. All these things are fully confirmed by long and tedious observations recorded in *The Discovery of the Witches of Warboys in Huntingdonshire, 1594*, the memory of which is still kept fresh by an *anniversary sermon* preached at *Huntingdon* by some of the Fellows of *Queen's College* in *Cambridge*.

There has also lately been published a *narrative* of how one Mrs. *Mulchamp's children* were treated in *Cumberland*, which is very similar to this account of Mr. *Throckmorton's children* of *Warboys*.

2. That which is generally observed in them both is this: that in their *fits* they are as if they had no *soul* at all in their *bodies*. Whatever operations of *sense*, *reason*, or *motion* seem to be in them do not belong to them at all, but belong entirely to that *stranger* <note>The possessing spirit</note> that has entered them. For as soon as their *fits* are over, they are as if they had been in so profound a sleep that they did not even dream; they remember nothing at all of what they either said or did, or where they had been, as is manifest by an infinite number of examples in the previously mentioned accounts.

From this, she gained for herself the reputation of a very **holy woman** and a great **prophetess**. 

But other things happened through her, or for her sake, that were no less strange and miraculous. For instance, during the celebration of the holy **Eucharist** <note>The Lord's Supper or Mass</note>, the priest would always find himself missing one of his round wafers. This was secretly conveyed to **Magdalen** by the administration of **angels**, as was supposed; and receiving it into her mouth, she ate it in the view of the people, to their great astonishment and high reverence for the **saint**. At the elevation of the Host <note>The raising of the consecrated bread during Mass</note>, while Magdalen was nearby but with a wall between them, the wall was believed to open to show Magdalen to the view of those in the chapel, so that she could partake of the consecrated bread. 

When this **abbess** came into the chapel herself upon some special day, she would set off the solemnity of the occasion with some notable and conspicuous **miracle**. For she would sometimes be lifted up above the ground three or four cubits <note>A cubit is about 18 inches; three or four cubits is roughly 4.5 to 6 feet.</note> high. At other times, while bearing the **image of Christ** in her arms and weeping piously, she would make her hair increase to such a length and thickness that it would reach her heels and cover her entirely, along with the image of Christ in her arms; yet shortly afterward, it would shrink back to its usual size. She performed many such impressive, though useless, **miracles**.

2. *Wierus* <note>Johann Weyer (1515–1588), a Dutch physician and occultist.</note> also tells of a person who was possessed—of which he himself was an eyewitness—who vomited up pieces of cloth along with *pins, nails, needles*, and similar items. He argues that these do not come from the stomach, but are merely placed into the mouth by a deceptive trick of the Devil.

<margin>Cardan, *On the Variety of Things*, Book 15, Chapter 80.</margin>
*Cardan* <note>Gerolamo Cardano (1501–1576), an influential Italian polymath.</note> relates a similar story about a good, simple country fellow and friend of his. This man had been troubled for a long time by vomiting up *glass, iron, nails,* and *hair*. At the time he told *Cardan* about it, he was not yet so perfectly restored that something did not still crash in his belly, as if there were a *bag of glass* inside him. I might seasonably add to this what is so credibly reported of *Mrs. Muschamp’s child*, who was seen to vomit up pieces of *wood* with *pins* stuck in them.

<margin>Wierus, *On the Deceptions of Demons*, Book 1, Chapters 4 and 8.</margin>
3. But I will conclude all with the story of about thirty *children* who were so strangely handled at *Amsterdam* in 1566, the truth of which *Wierus* professes himself very well assured. They were tortured very much and cast violently upon the ground; but when they recovered from their fits, they knew nothing, thinking they had only been asleep. To remedy this mischief, they sought the help of *physicians, wizards,* and *exorcists*, but without success. Only while the *exorcists* were reading did the *children* vomit up *needles, thimbles, shreds of cloth, pieces of pots, glass, hair*, and other things of a similar nature.

4. Now, the use I would make of these accounts is this: since these extraordinary and supernatural effects are so obvious and permanent, they are not at all subject to the *excuses* <note>original: "subterfuges"</note> that *atheists* usually resort to—such as blaming *melancholy* <note>A common 17th-century medical explanation for hallucinations or depression.</note> or a disturbance of the *imagination* <note>original: "phanfie"</note> in those who claim to see such strange things, or alleging *fraud* or *imposture* in those who act them out.

5. All that can be alleged with any show of reason is this: that such parties, in their fits of *distraction* <note>A state of mental derangement or frenzy.</note>, might devour the things they later vomit up, or at least put them into their mouths. But those standing by could easily see that, as distracted people do things carelessly and openly. Furthermore, these things happen to those who are treated this way against their wills; and just as they are not caught doing any such things themselves, they do not confess to it afterward when they have returned to their right senses. Ordinarily, it is discovered that some *woman* or other, through *sorcery* or *witchcraft*, was the cause of it.

<margin>Wierus, *On the Deceptions of Demons*, Book 4, Chapter 13.</margin>
Besides, it is evident that there can be no mistake at all in some of these passages. For how can an *iron nail* get between the skin and the flesh without the skin being ripped or touched at all? Or how is it possible for anyone to swallow down *knives* and *pieces of iron* a span <note>About 9 inches.</note> long? This, besides the story of *Ulricus Neuffesser*, is confirmed in another account of a young *girl*. After she had cleaned a pair of shoes with a *knife*, which she then put in her bosom, she later searched for it but it could not be found anywhere. At length, it began to reveal itself in a swelling on her left side, and was finally pulled out from there by a *surgeon* <note>original: "chirurgion"</note>. You may read the whole account in *Wierus*. It happened at *Levensteet* in the *Dukedom of Brunswick* in 1562. An old *woman* had come to the house...

## CHAPTER VI.

1. The *apparition Eckerken*. 2. The *story of the Pied Piper*. 3. A *Triton* or *sea-god* seen on the banks of the *Rubicon*. 4. 1. BUT it is now high time to move from this dim and cloudy discovery of *spirits* into more distinct and clear *apparitions*, according to what I first proposed. And these I shall divide into two ranks: those that appear near to us on the *ground*, or those that are seen far off, high in the *air*. And here again, to begin with small things first: near *Elton*, a village half a mile distant from *Emmerich* in the Dukedom of *Cleves*, there was a thing that haunted the area which they called *Eckerken*. There never appeared more than the shape of a *hand*, but it would beat *travellers*, pull them off their horses, and overturn carriages. This could be no *fancy*, as such real *effects* followed it.

<margin>*On the Deceptions of Demons*, Book 1, Chapter 16.</margin>

For the event is very religiously kept among their ancient records, painted also in their church windows, and is an *epoch* <note>A significant date used as a reference point for time</note> joined with the year of our Lord in their bills, legal contracts, and other law instruments.

3. There is also an account that seems to me beyond all exception or evasion, which *Suetonius* <note>A Roman historian (c. 69 – c. 122 AD) known for his biographies of the Caesars.</note> relates regarding a *Specter* appearing on the banks of the River *Rubicon*. The story is as follows: *Julius Caesar* had marched with his army to this river, which divides *Cisalpine Gaul* <note>original: "Gallia citerior"; the region of Northern Italy inhabited by Gauls.</note> from *Italy*. Being very doubtful and hesitant whether he should cross over into *Italy* or not, a man of a prodigious stature and form was seen on the riverbank playing on a reed pipe. The strangeness of his person, as well as the pleasantness of his music, drew several shepherds toward him, as well as many of the soldiers, among whom were some *trumpeters*. This *Triton* (as *Melanchthon* <note>Philipp Melanchthon (1497–1560), a German Protestant reformer and scholar.</note> ventures to call him) or *Sea-god* observed them closely. He nimbly snatched one of the *trumpets* out of their hands, leaped immediately into the river, and sounded a "March" with such strength and violence that he seemed to tear the heavens. He made the air ring with the mighty force of the blast, and in this manner, he passed over to the other side of the river. Whereupon *Caesar*, taking this as an *Omen*, ceased all further debate with himself. He led his army across and entered *Italy*, confident of success because of such manifest tokens of the favor of the Gods.

4. To confirm the truth of *Apparitions*, we need only admit the free confessions of *Witches* concerning their *Imps* <note>Small demons or spirit familiars believed to serve witches.</note>, whom they so frequently see and converse with, know by their names, and show obedience to. If we did, the point would be put quite beyond all doubt; the proofs would be so numerous that no volume would be large enough to contain them. But, of course, some claim these must all be *Melancholy* <note>In this period, "melancholy" was often used as a medical diagnosis for delusions or depression.</note> old women who have grown senile and bring themselves into danger by their own *fancies* and *imaginations*. However, I am better assured that they are not senile than I am of the sanity of those who say they are. To satisfy my own curiosity, I have examined several of them myself, and they have spoken as cleverly and rationally as anyone of their social standing and education. From what I have read and observed, I discern they serve a very treacherous Master, who often plays tricks on them specifically to betray them. But that is only a side note.

5. I ask regarding these *Witches*—who confess to their contract and frequent conversation with the *Devil*, some seeing him in one shape and others in another—whether mere *Melancholy* and *Imagination* can physically put *powders*, *rods*, *ointments*, and such things into their hands and tell them how to use them? Can imagination impress *marks* upon their bodies so deep that they lose all feeling in that spot? Can it put *silver* and *gold* into their hands, which afterwards commonly turns out to be only *counters* <note>Imitation coins or tokens.</note>, *leaves*, *shells*, or some other useless matter? These real *effects* cannot be caused by mere *Melancholy*. For if a man receives anything into his hand, whatever it may be, there must have been someone who gave it to him. Therefore, when a *Witch* receives a real object from this or that shape that appeared to her, it is an evident sign that what she saw was an external reality, not a mere figment of her *melancholy fancy*. There are innumerable examples of this kind; but the thing is so common and ordinary that it requires no specific proof. I will only set down one instance, in which there is the apparition of three spirits.

"Having seven shillings in it, for which he suspected someone in the family where he lived, he says that on a Friday, while he was making hay-bundles <note>original: "hay-bottles"; a "bottle" of hay is a bundle or truss</note> in the barn, and swore and cursed and raged, and wished to himself that some *wise* person <note>original: "wife body"; likely a transcription error for "wise body," meaning a person with occult knowledge or a 'cunning' person</note> would help him find his purse and money again, there appeared to him a *Spirit* in the shape of a Bear, but not as large as a rabbit <note>original: "Coney"</note>. To suggest that all these things should be a mere dream is a notion more slight and foolish than any dream could possibly be. For the receiving of his purse was a palpable and tangible pledge of the truth of all the rest. And it is incredible that such a *series* of *circumstances*, backed by twenty-nine years of experience of being sucked and visited daily—sometimes in the day-time, but most commonly by night—by the same three *Familiars*, should be nothing but the joining together of so many *Melancholy Whims* <note>original: "Melancholy Conceits"</note> and *Fancies*."

7. Nor does the sealing of *Covenants* and writing with *Blood* make such stories as these more suspicious. For it is not at all unreasonable that such ceremonies should pass between a *Spirit* and a *Man*, when similar tangible rites are used for the more firmly tying of Man to God. For whatever is physical <note>original: "crass"</note> and external leaves a stronger impression upon the *Imagination* <note>original: "Phansie"</note>, and the remembrance of it strikes the mind with more effectiveness. So it is certain that the *Devil* has a greater hold <note>original: "hanck"</note> upon the soul of a *Witch* or *Wizard* who has been persuaded to complete their *Contract* with him in such a gross, sensory way; it keeps them more securely from revolting against him than if they had only contracted in bare words.

### CHAPTER VII.

1. To the story of John Winnick, it will not be out of place to add a more recent and more notable narrative concerning one Anne Bodenham, a witch who lived in Fisherton Anger, adjacent to the city of New Sarum <note>modern: Salisbury</note> in the county of Wiltshire, who was arraigned and executed at Salisbury in 1653. He who has a mind to read the story at greater length may consult Edmond Bower, who was an eyewitness and ear-witness of several passages. But I shall only set down here what is most relevant to our present purpose, partly from him and partly from others who were then at the Assizes, and who also had private conferences with the witch and spoke with the maid who gave evidence against her.
    This Anne Bodenham, it seems, did not conceal her skill in foretelling things to come, helping men find their stolen goods, and other such feats that the more notable sort of wizards and witches are said to claim and practice.

2. Among others who sought her out, there was one *Anne Styles*, a servant to Richard Goddard, Esq., of the Close in New Sarum. She placed in the circle an earthen pan of coals, into which she threw something that, when burned, caused a very foul stink. She told the maid that she should not be afraid of what she would then see, "for now they would come" (those are the words she used). And so, calling "Beelzebub, Tormentor, Satan, and Lucifer, appear," there suddenly arose a very*

Then the spirit gave a piece of silver (which he first bit) to the witch, who gave it to the maid. He also stuck two pins in the maid's head-cloths <note>a head covering or kerchief</note> and told her to keep them and to be gone. The witch also said, *"I will vex the gentlewoman well enough, just as I did the man in Clarington Park, whom I made walk about with a bundle of pales <note>wooden stakes or fencing</note> on his back all night in a pond of water; he could not lay them down until the next morning."*

7. All these things the maid deposed upon oath. I think it is now evident beyond all controversy that, unless she knowingly committed perjury, these things are certainly true; for they cannot be attributed to any dreaming, fancy, or melancholy <note>term: melancholy; in this period, often used to describe hallucinations or mental illness caused by an imbalance of "black bile"</note>. Now, many arguments present themselves to prove that the maid did not commit perjury or invent these narrations she swore to.

First, it is altogether unlikely that a lowly girl <note>original: "sorry Wench"</note> who could neither write nor read should be able to devise <note>original: "excogitate"</note> such magical forms and ceremonies, with all the specific circumstances of their effects, and declare them so precisely, had she not indeed seen them done before her eyes.

Secondly, if she had been so cunning at inventing lies, she would have had enough wit to frame them better for her own advantage, and for the advantage of those by whom she was employed; or she would have told only as much of the truth as would not have prejudiced herself or anyone else by its revelation.

8. For in brief, the case stood thus: her mistress either had, or pretended to have, a suspicion that her two daughters-in-law, Mistress **Sarah** and Mistress **Anne Goddard**, were plotting to poison her. Thereupon, this maid, **Anne Styles**, was sent to the witch under the pretense of finding out when this poisoning would happen and how to prevent it. During the second time she consulted her, the witch sent her to the apothecary's to buy some white arsenic and bring it to her. Taking it, the witch told her...

That what the boy heard and saw was no fancy of his own, but a real object of his senses, is clearly argued by the witch's condition in another chamber at the same time. 10. But to return to the maid, from whom we may draw further arguments relating also to the witch. For instance, when the maid had not taken any rest for many days and nights together, and was then under most grievous hurryings <note>original: "hurryings" — violent agitations or seizures</note> and tortures of the body, the witch was brought into the room where she lay. The maid did not know of this plan or the time of the witch's entry; yet, as soon as the witch had set one foot into the room, the maid gave a most hideous glance with her eyes and shut them immediately after. She fell asleep in a moment and slept for about three hours so deeply that when they tried to waken her, they could not by any art or violence whatever—such as stopping her breath, putting things up her nostrils, holding her upright, striking her, and the like. The witch also declared her unwillingness that the maid should be wakened, crying out:

> *O, I pray you, by no means awake the maid; for if she should awake, I should be torn in pieces, and the Devil would fetch me away bodily.*

And a further evidence that this sleep of the maid depended in some way upon the witch is that as soon as the witch had gone from under the roof where she was, the maid wakened on her own. As soon as the maid wakened and was at ease (the Devil, as she said, having gone out of her stomach, doing her no violence but only making her body tremble a little), the witch began to roar and cry out:

> *The Devil will tear me in pieces.*

These things you may read more fully and particularly in the narration of *Edmond Bower*, who was an eyewitness to them. ### CHAPTER VII.

11. ...Moreover, it would have been argument enough to any unprejudiced person that she swore to nothing but what she was certain was true. Those floods of tears and her bitter weeping after sentence was passed on the witch, her bewailing of her own wickedness and madness, and her profession of willingness—if it could be done without sin—that the witch might be reprieved, should further wash away all suspicion of either fraud or malice.

12. Nor can the witch’s denial (even to her dying day) of what the maid swore to weaken her testimony. For the maid tells the whole truth as it was, even at the hazard of her own life; whereas the witch denies it only to save her own. It is no wonder that someone who would call down a curse <note>original: "bid a pox on"</note> upon the hangman when he asked her to forgive him at her death would lie and impudently deny anything to save her life.

But you will object that this reputed witch may indeed be wicked enough, and willing enough to do anything, but since the power of her wickedness could not reach such performances as the maid witnessed against her, we should believe her rather than the maid. The sense of which objection, if I understand it, can be nothing but this: that either this *Anne Bodenham* was no witch, or else the things charged against her were absolutely impossible. The meaning of the latter is surely that it is impossible for anyone to be a witch, because there are no such things as *spirits* to be conjured up by them. This is an unskillful argument—to let go of the premises because they are too strong, and instead quarrel with the conclusion.

13. But if the meaning is (admitting that *witches* exist) that she was not one, I think it may be clearly proved that she was, based on what she undoubtedly both did and said. For example, she showed the maid in a glass <note>A scrying glass or mirror used for divination.</note> the shapes of various persons and their actions and postures in several rooms of her master's house. When the maid returned from the witch, she told the family exactly what they had been doing in her absence; this made *Elizabeth Rosewell*, one of the family, declare that she thought *Mrs. Bodenham* was either a witch or a woman of God. 

Besides this, what happened to her regarding the maid's fits—which has already been discussed—creates strong suspicions of her being a witch. There was also her boasting to *Mr. Tucker's clerk* concerning a *purse that hung about her neck on a green string, claiming she could do many feats with it; and that if he would give her half a dozen pots of ale, she would make a toad spring out of it*. 

She confessed to *Mr. Lang* of *Sarum* <note>Salisbury</note> that she lived with *Dr. Lamb* <note>John Lambe (c. 1545–1628), a notorious astrologer and advisor to the Duke of Buckingham, often accused of sorcery.</note> and learned the art of raising *spirits* from him. She also confessed this to *Edmond Bower*, to whom she acknowledged her skill in curing diseases by *charms* and *spells*, and that she could discover stolen goods and show anyone the thief in a glass. When asked by him for the *Red Book*—which was half-written in blood and served as a *catalogue* of those who had made a pact with <note>original: "sealed to"</note> the *Devil*—she did not deny knowing of the book, but said it was with someone in *Hampshire*. She also professed that she used many "good" *prayers*, that she said the *Creed* backwards and forwards, and that she prayed to the *planet Jupiter* for the curing of diseases.

There was found on her shoulder a certain mark or teat about the length and size of a woman's nipple; it was hollow and soft like a nipple, with a hole on the top of it. <note>In the 17th century, such "witch's marks" were believed to be used by demons or familiars to suckle blood from the witch.</note>

14. Therefore, to conclude: since there were found upon her, and done and spoken by her, such things as clearly indicate <note>original: "indigitate"</note> that she is a witch and has the power of raising spirits; and since she was accused of raising them by a witness who could not likely have invented <note>original: "excogitate"</note> such magical forms, effects, or circumstances as are described above; and since this witness tells her story so impartially that it incriminates herself nearly as much as the witch; and since upon her revealing the villainy she was physically afflicted in a way that was plainly beyond any imaginable natural illness—it must, I say, gain the full agreement of any man whom prejudice and stubbornness have not utterly blinded, that what the maid confessed concerning herself and the witch is most certainly true.

# CHAPTER VIII. An Antidote against Atheism.

->CHAPTER VIII.<-

1. *Two memorable stories, and their credibility.* 2. *The first concerns a shoemaker of Breslau <note>Modern Wrocław, Poland</note> who cut his own throat.* 3. *His appearance after death in his usual clothing, and his troublesome haunting of the entire town.* 4. *That upon being dug up after being buried for eight months, his body was found intact and fresh, and his joints were supple and flexible.* 5. *That the apparition ceased once the body was burned.* 6. *A similar event happened regarding one of his maidservants, after she had annoyed and disturbed people for an entire month.* 7. *That the narrator of the story lived in the town at the time these events occurred.*

1. I have dwelt so long upon the previous narrative partly because it is very recent—so that any man who doubts such things may satisfy himself concerning its truth—and partly because it is so notorious that it is hardly matched by any account we find in other writers, considering all the circumstances. And yet, if they were as recent, I do not know but that those accounts by Martinus Weinrichius <note>A 16th-century German physician</note>, a Silesian physician and philosopher, might seem just as convincing. These accounts are included as a preface to Pico della Mirandola's *The Witch* <note>original: *Strix*</note> or *On the Deception of Demons* <note>original: *De Ludificatione Daemonum*</note>.

The stories are two and very memorable. They are all the more credible because the events happened during the lifetime of the narrator, only a few years before he wrote them down, and in his own country; he vouches for them with all imaginable confidence as being most certainly true. The first of them is this:

2. A certain shoemaker in one of the chief towns of Silesia, in the year 1591, on September 20th—early on a Friday morning—cut his own throat with his shoemaker's knife in the back part of his house, near a small garden. To cover up the shame of the deed and to ensure no disgrace fell upon his widow, the family claimed he died of a stroke <note>original: "Apoplexie"</note>. They turned away all visits from friends and neighbors. In the meantime, they washed him and arranged linens so neatly around him that even those who saw him afterward—such as the parson and others—had not the slightest suspicion that he died of anything else. Thus, he received a respectable burial, complete with a funeral sermon and other honors fitting for someone of his rank and reputation.

Six weeks had not passed before such a strong rumor broke out—claiming he had not died of a disease but had committed suicide <note>original: "laid violent hands upon himself"</note>—that the local government <note>original: "Magistracy"</note> was forced to call everyone who had seen the corpse for a strict examination. At first, the family brushed the matter off as well as they could with many polite excuses on behalf of the deceased to remove suspicion of such a' heinous act. But when the matter was pressed more deeply to their consciences, they finally confessed he died a violent death. However, they pleaded for mercy and clemency for his widow and children, who were not at fault, adding also that it was uncertain whether he might have been killed by some outside accident, or...

or if he had killed himself in some irresistible fit of frenzy or madness. Thereupon the Council deliberated on what was to be done. When the widow heard of this, she feared they might be determining something harsh that would discredit her husband and herself. Being also encouraged by some busybodies, she made a great complaint against those who raised these reports about her husband. She resolved to take legal action against them, earnestly contending that there was no reason—based on mere rumors and idle slanders by malicious people—that her husband's body should be dug up or treated as if he had been either a *Magician* <note>original: "Magician"; here meaning a practitioner of black magic or witchcraft</note> or a *Self-murderer*. This boldness and persistence of the woman, even after the fact had been confessed, did to some extent influence the Council and caused them to hesitate.

3. But while these things were being debated, to the astonishment of the inhabitants of the place, a *Spectrum* <note>original: "Spectrum"; a ghost or apparition</note> appeared in the exact shape and clothing of the deceased, and that not only in the night, but at midday. It terrified those who were asleep with horrible visions; those who were awake it would strike, pull, or press, lying heavy upon them like an *Ephialtes* <note>original: "Ephialtes"; a nightmare or a "night-hag" sensation where one feels a heavy weight on the chest</note>. Consequently, there were perpetual complaints every morning throughout the whole town regarding their previous night's rest. But the more pranks this *Spectrum* played, the more diligent the friends of the deceased were to suppress the rumors, or at least to hinder the effects of those rumors. Therefore, they made their appeals to the President, complaining how unjust it was that so much weight should be given to idle reports and blind suspicions. They beseeched him to prevent the Council from digging up the corpse of the deceased and from all shameful treatment of him. They added that they intended to appeal to the Emperor's Court, so that their Wisdoms <note>The high judges of the imperial court</note> might decide the controversy, rather than having the cause determined here based on the light conjectures of malicious men.

But while the business was still delayed by these means, there were such stirs and tumults all over the town that they are hardly possible to describe. For no sooner did the sun hide its head than this *Spectrum* would be sure to appear, so that everyone was forced to look about him and stand on his guard. This was a painful trouble to those whom the labors of the day made more sensitive to the lack of rest at night. For this terrible *Apparition* would sometimes stand by their bedsides, sometimes throw itself upon the middle of their beds, would lie close to them, would miserably suffocate them, and would so strike and pinch them that not only blue marks, but plain impressions of his fingers would be found upon various parts of their bodies in the morning. Indeed, such was the violence and force of this Ghost, that even when men abandoned their beds and stayed in their dining rooms with candles lighted—many of them staying in company together to better secure themselves from fear and disturbance—he would still appear to them and have a bout with some of them, despite all this preparation against it. In short, he was so troublesome that the people were ready to abandon their houses and seek other dwellings. The magistrates were so awakened by the perpetual complaints that they finally resolved, with the President's agreement, to dig up the body.

# CHAPTER VIII.

4. He had lain in the ground for nearly eight months, namely from September 22, 1591, to April 18, 1592. When he was dug up in the presence of the town magistrates, his body was found entire and not at all putrid. There was no foul smell about him, except for the mustiness of the grave clothes. His joints were limber and flexible, like those of a living person. His skin was merely flaccid, but a fresher layer had grown in its place. The wound in his throat was gaping, but contained no pus or corruption. A <term>magical mark</term> <note>original: "Magical mark"; likely referring to a "witch's mark" or sign of a pact with the devil</note> was also observed on the big toe of his right foot—an <term>excrecence</term> <note>a distinct growth or protrusion</note> in the shape of a rose. His body was kept out of the earth from April 18 to the 24th, during which time many people from the town and elsewhere came daily to view him. These unquiet disturbances did not cease despite this; the authorities later attempted to appease the spirit by burying the corpse under the gallows, but in vain. The hauntings continued as much as ever, if not more, and he now did not even spare his own family. Consequently, his widow finally went to the magistrate herself and told them she would no longer oppose them if they thought it fit to take more strict proceedings regarding her husband.

5. Therefore, on the seventh of May, he was dug up again. It was observable that he had grown noticeably more fleshy since his last interment. To be brief, they cut off the head, arms, and legs of the corpse, and opening his back, they took out his heart, which was as fresh and entire as that of a newly killed calf. These parts, together with his body, they placed on a pile of wood and burned to ashes. Carefully sweeping the ashes together and putting them into a sack (so that no one could obtain them for wicked purposes), they poured them into the river. After this, the <term>specter</term> <note>a ghost or apparition</note> was never seen again.

6. A similar thing happened with his maid, who died after him. She appeared within eight days of her death to her fellow servant and lay so heavily upon her that she caused a great swelling in the servant's eyes. She also so grievously handled a child in the cradle that if the nurse had not come to his aid, he would have been completely harmed. However, when the nurse crossed herself and called upon the name of **Jesus**, the <term>specter</term> vanished. The next night, she appeared in the shape of a **hen**. When one of the maids of the house, thinking it was a real bird, followed her, the hen grew to an immense size and suddenly caught the maid by the throat. This caused her throat to swell so that she could neither eat nor drink well for a long time afterward. She continued these disturbances for a whole month, slapping some people so smartly that the strokes were heard by those standing nearby, and pulling the beds out from under others. She appeared sometimes in one shape and sometimes in another—as a woman, a dog, a cat, or a goat. But at last, her body being dug up and burned, the apparition was never seen again.

7. These events took place at **Breslau** in **Silesia** <note>modern-day Wrocław, Poland</note> where <term>Weinrichius</term> <note>Martin Weinrich, a 16th-century physician and philosopher who recorded these events</note> lived at the time, which makes the narration more credible. I believe he concealed the names of the parties involved out of civility toward his deceased townsman, the widow, and their family.

### CHAPTER IX.

1. *The second story of one Cuntius, whose first biographer not only lived in the town, but was a distressed sufferer in the tragedy.*

13. *How difficult it will be for the atheist to find an excuse to dismiss this story.*

1. The other story he records, he is not the original writer of (though the events occurred in his time, and, as I understand it, some time after what has been related above, as a passage in the narrative seems to suggest). Instead, he transcribed it from someone who not only lived in the place, but was often harassed by the foul encounters of that troublesome ghost which caused so much mischief to the town where he lived. The account is somewhat long; I shall condense it into as small a space as I can.

2. Johannes Cuntius, a citizen of Pentsch in Silesia <note>A historical region in Central Europe, mostly in modern-day Poland.</note>, nearly sixty years of age and one of the aldermen of the town, was very respectable in his behavior and blameless, in the opinion of men, throughout his entire life. Having been sent for to the Mayor's house (being a very knowledgeable man and skilled at handling business) to settle some disputes concerning certain wagoners and a merchant from Pannonia <note>A province of the Roman Empire, roughly modern-day western Hungary and parts of its neighbors.</note>, and having finished those affairs, he was invited by the Mayor to supper. He obtained permission first to go home to settle some business, leaving this sentence behind him: *“It is good to be merry while we may, for mischiefs grow up fast enough daily.”*

This Cuntius kept five strong geldings <note>Castrated male horses.</note> in his stable. He commanded one of them to be brought out, and its shoe being loose, had it tied to the nearest post. He and a servant busied themselves by lifting the horse's leg to look at its hoof; the horse, being wild and high-spirited, struck them both down. Cuntius received the worst of the blow. Someone standing nearby helped them both up again. As soon as Cuntius was up and regained consciousness, he cried out, *"Woe is me, how I burn and am all on fire!"* which he repeated often. But when the women were sent out of the room and the parts of his body he complained of most were searched, no sign of any strike or injury was found on them. To be short, he fell downright—

3. The night he died, his eldest son watched over him. He gave up the ghost about the third hour of the night. No sooner was *Cuntius* dead than a great tempest arose, which raged most fiercely at his very funeral; there were such impetuous storms of wind and snow that it made men's bodies quake and their teeth chatter in their heads. But as soon as he was buried, all was suddenly calm.

When he finally returned, he accused his wife; she confessed to the deed and identified her companions, who were subsequently burned with her.

2. So the husband of the Witch of Lochia—whom she brought into a similar assembly—by saying, "O **my God**, where are we?" made everything vanish. He found himself alone and naked in the field, a fifteen days' journey from home. 

Bodin sets down several other narrations to this purpose. These tangible effects—being so far distant from home and being found naked in the fields—show these events to be no freaks of **melancholy** <note>original: "Melancholy"; here meaning clinical depression or a delusional state of mind</note>, but certain truth. The ordinary confession of **witches** (who are discovered and convicted in this way) is that the **Devil** appears to the guests in these "junketings" <note>festive gatherings or feasts</note> in the form of a **satyr**, a **black goat**, or sometimes in the shape of an ill-favored **black man**.

<margin>See Remigius, *Demonolatry*, Book 1, Chapter 14.</margin>
3. I will only add a story or two out of Remigius concerning these kinds of **conventicles** <note>secret or unlawful religious meetings</note>, and then I will proceed to some other proofs. 

**John of Hembach** was carried by his mother, who was a witch, to one of these meetings. Because he had learned to play the **pipe** <note>a flute-like instrument</note>, he was commanded by her to exercise his talent and to climb up into a tree so that they might better hear his music. While doing this and looking upon the dancers—seeing how uncouth and ridiculous they were in their motions and gestures—he was struck with wonder at the novelty of the matter and suddenly burst out with these words: "Good **God, what a mad company have we here!**" No sooner was this said than down came John, pipe and all, hurting his shoulder in the fall. When he called to the company to help him, he found himself alone, for they had all vanished. John of Hembach told what had happened, but people did not know what to make of it until some of that "mad crew" who danced to his pipe were apprehended on other suspicions—such as **Catharina Prævotia**, **Kelvers Orilla**, and others. These women confirmed every bit of what John had previously told (though they knew nothing of his statement beforehand), adding more particularly that the place where he piped to them was **Maybuch**.

<margin>*Demonolatry*, Book 1, Chapter 14.</margin>
4. The other memorable story that I shall relate out of Remigius is this. The posture of their bodies was so uncouth and unusual that it made her view them more attentively, whereby she discerned some of them to have cloven feet like oxen or goats. (It would seem they were **spirits** in the shape of lusty **satyrs**.) Being astonished with fear, she cried out, "**Jesus**, help me, and send me well home." She had no sooner said so than they all vanished, except for one **Peter Grofpetter**, whom a little after she saw snatched up into the air. He let fall his **maulkin** <note>original: "Maulkin"; a tool used to clean out ovens</note>, and she herself was driven so forcibly by the wind that it made her almost lose her breath. She was forced to keep to her bed for three days afterward.

5. This Peter (though at first he tried to sue Nicolea for slandering him) afterward freely confessed and identified others of his companions, such as **Barbelia**, the wife of **Joannes Latomus**, and **Mayetta**...

### CHAPTER XI.

Mayetta, the wife of *Laurentius*, confessed that she danced with those cloven-footed creatures at the same time that *Peter* was among them. And for further evidence of the matter, *John Michael*, a herdsman, confessed that while they danced in this way, he played upon his *crooked staff* and struck upon it with his fingers as if it had been a pipe, sitting upon a high bough of an oak tree. ### CHAPTER XI.

We may add a third point, which may perhaps better explain the other two; and that concerns your <term>lycanthropes</term> <note>original: *Λυκανθρώπες*</note> (which the Germans call **Werewolves**, the French *Loups-garous*): men transformed into **wolves**. The same reasoning applies to other **transformations**. I shall not trouble you with many histories of them, though I could produce many. But both those who hold that it is but a delusion of the **Devil** and mere tragedies in dreams, as well as those who say they are real transactions, acknowledge that those parties who have confessed to being thus transformed have been weary and **sore** from running, have been **wounded**, and the like.

<margin>Nicolas Rémy, *Demonolatry*, Book 2, Chapter 9.</margin>
**Bodin** is also deserted here by **Rémy**, who is of the same mind as **Wierus**—that sly, smooth physician and faithful patron of witches. Wierus is sure to load the **Devil** with as much blame as he can, the Devil's shoulders being more able to bear it, and so he eases the **hags** <note>Wierus argued that "witches" were actually mentally ill women being deceived by the Devil, rather than powerful criminals.</note>.

<margin>* Johann Wierus, *On the Deceptions of Demons*, Book 3, Chapter 10; Book 1, Chapter 24; Book 2, Chapter 8; Book 4, Chapter 20.
* Nicolas Rémy, *Demonolatry*, Book 2, Chapter 5.</margin>
3. For my own part, though I will not undertake to decide the controversy, I think it is not wrong to declare that **Bodin** may very well prove his point, despite anything those others allege to the contrary. For the points that **Wierus** and **Rémy** seem to insist upon—that it is too great a power for the **Devil** to have, and too great an indignity to man that he should be able to transform him—are, in my mind, but slight rhetorical flourishes, not sound arguments.

For what is that outward misshaping of the body compared to the inward deformity of their **souls**, which the Devil helps along so notoriously? And since they have given themselves over to him so completely, why may he not use them this way here, when they shall be treated even worse by him hereafter? As for changing the **species** of things: if that were a power too great to be granted to the **Devil**, yet it is no more done here when he transforms a man into a **wolf** than when he transforms **himself** into the shape of a **man**. For this **wolf** is still a **man**, and that **man** is still a **devil**. It is just as the poet says it was with **Ulysses'** companions whom **Circe** turned into **hogs**: they had the head, the voice, the body, and the bristles of **hogs**;

->*—But their mind remained stable as it was before—*<-
<note>original Greek: *Αὐτὰρ ὁ νοῦς ἦν ἔμπεδος ὡς τὸ πάρος περ*</note>

but their understanding was unchanged; they had the mind and memory of a man as before. As **Petrus Bourgutus** professed: when his companion **Michael Verdung** had anointed his body and transformed him into a **wolf**, and he looked upon his hairy feet, he was at first afraid of himself.

4. Therefore, since it is plain that no material evidence is alleged to the contrary, and since **men** confess they are turned into **wolves** and acknowledge the savage cruelties they then committed upon children, women, and sheep—and they find themselves exceeding **weary** and sometimes **wounded**—it is more natural to conclude they were really thus transformed than that it was a mere delusion of **fancy**.

For I conceive the **Devil** gets into their body, and by his subtle substance—more active and searching than any fire or putrefying liquid—melts...

melts the yielding *structure* <note>original: "Compages," meaning the complex framework or joining together of parts</note> of the body to such a consistency, and so much of it as is fit for his purpose, and makes it pliable to his imagination. Then it is as easy for him to work it into what *shape* he pleases, as it is to work the air into such forms and figures as he ordinarily does. Nor is it any more difficult for him to soften what *is* hard, than it is to harden what is as soft and fluid as the air.

5. And for him who has this power, we can never *hesitate* <note>original: "stick"</note> to grant him that which is lesser: namely, to *instruct* men how they *shall for a time forsake their bodies* and come back in again. For can it be a hard thing for *him that can* thus melt and take apart the particles of the body, to *have the skill* and power to loosen the soul—a *substance* really *distinct* from the body and separable from it? This is, after all, done by the *easy course of nature* at that final dissolution of soul and body which we call *death*. But no course of nature ever transforms the body of man into the *shape of a wolf*; therefore, that transformation is more difficult and further removed from the *order of nature* than the other.

6. "Ah," but you will say, "the *greatness* and *incredibility* of the *miracle* is this: that there should be an actual *separation* of *soul* and *body*, and yet no *death*." But this is not at all strange if we consider that *death* is properly a disjunction of the soul from the body by *reason of the body's unfitness* any longer to host the soul. This may be caused by extreme *diseases*, outward *violence*, or *age*. If the *Devil* could restore such *bodies* as these to life, it would be a *miracle* indeed. But this is not such a miracle, nor is the body properly dead, even though the soul is out of it. For the *life of the body* is nothing else but that *fitness* to be activated by the soul. The *preservation* <note>original: "conservation"</note> of this fitness is helped, as I conceive, by the *anointing* of the body before the *ecstasy* <note>original: "Ecstasie," here referring to a trance-like state where the soul leaves the body</note>. This ointment, filling the pores, keeps out the cold and keeps in the heat and spirits, so that the frame and temperament of the body may continue in a fit state to host the soul again upon her return. Thus, the vital *vapors* <note>original: "steams"</note> of the body not yet being spent, the original operations of life are immediately *rekindled*. It is like a *candle* newly blown out that is still smoking; it suddenly catches fire from the flame of another, even at some distance, as the light glides down along the smoke.

7. Therefore, since there is nothing in the nature of the thing that should make us skeptical, and since these *sorceresses* so confidently declare that they are *out of their bodies* at such times—seeing and doing various things, meeting one another, bringing messages, discovering secrets, and the like—it is more natural and easy to conclude they are really *out of their bodies than in them*. We should be even more easily induced to believe this if we could give credit to that *story* <note>original: "Narration"</note> *Wierus* <note>Johann Weyer (1515–1588), a physician and occultist who wrote about witchcraft</note> tells of a *soldier*. While he was asleep, a thing in the shape of a *weasel* came out of his mouth. It nudged along in the grass and finally came to a brook side, busily attempting to get over. Not being able to cross, one of the bystanders who saw it made a bridge for it with his sword. The creature passed over it, and coming back, made use of the same bridge, and then entered into the *soldier's* mouth again while many people looked on. *When* he awoke, he told how he dreamed he had gone over an *iron bridge*, and other...

*Wierus* <note>Johann Weyer (1515–1588), a physician who argued against the persecution of witches.</note> acknowledges the truth of the account, but insists that it must be the *Devil*, not the *Soul* of the *Man*. He does this out of a tender regard for *Witches*, so that from such a truth as this they might not be made so vulnerable to the suspicion that their *Ecstasies* are not mere *Dreams* and *Delusions* of the *Devil*, but are accompanied by *real effects*.

8. I will not take it upon myself to decide such a delicate controversy; I will only make so bold as to intervene this far: to pronounce that the opinion of *Bodinus* <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596), a French jurist and writer on demonology.</note> is not at all unworthy of a rational and wise man. Even though he was much addicted to such speculations and might attribute some natural effects to the ministry of *Spirits* when there was no need to do so, his judgment in other things of this kind is no more to be dismissed than that of *Descartes* <note>original: "Cartesius"</note>. That stupendous mechanical mind is not to be rejected in those excellent inventions regarding the causes of the more general *Phenomena* of Nature just because his success emboldened him to enlarge his principles too far—even to assert that *Animals* themselves were mere *Machines*. He is like *Aristoxenus* the Musician, who made the *Soul* nothing else but a *Harmony*; of whom *Tully* <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero</note> pleasantly observes, *that he did not depart from his own art* <note>original: "Quòd non recessit ab arte sua"</note>.

Every *Genius* and *Temperament*, like the various sorts of beasts and living creatures, has its own proper waste product; it is the part of a wise man to take notice of it, and to choose what is profitable as well as to abandon what is useless and dross.

It should have a more keen and piercing cold because it consists of more subtle particles than those of *Water*, and therefore is more fit to penetrate, and more accurately and stingingly to affect and touch the nerves.

3. Therefore, since *Witches* confess so frequently as they do that the *Devil* lies with them, and at the same time complain of his tedious and offensive *coldness*, it is a strong presumption that he does lie with them indeed, and that it is not a mere *Dream*, as their friend *Weyer* <note>original: "Wierus"; Johann Weyer was a physician who argued that many witchcraft confessions were the result of mental illness or "melancholy."</note> would have it.

4. From this we may also discover the folly of that opinion which claims the very *Essence of Spirits* is *Fire*. It is plain at first sight how unfit fire would be to coagulate the *Air*. It would melt and dissolve these consistencies rather than constrict and freeze them, in a manner of speaking. Instead, it is manifest that the *Essence of Spirits* is a substance specifically distinct from all corporeal matter whatsoever. But my intent is not to philosophize concerning the nature of *Spirits*, but only to prove their existence.

5. The *Specter* at *Ephesus* may be a further argument for this. This could be no imposture caused by *Melancholy* <note>A common historical explanation for hallucinations or depression.</note>, nor the *Fraud* of any priest. And the learned *Grotius* <note>Hugo Grotius, a famous Dutch jurist and philosopher.</note>, a man far from all levity and vain credulity, is so certain of the truth of *Apollonius's* *Miracles* that he does not hesitate to call anyone impudent who has the face to deny them.
