2. This person—a holy and pious man, as it would seem, and an acquaintance of *Bodin's* <note>original: "Bodinus's"; referring to Jean Bodin, a famous 16th-century French jurist and philosopher</note>—freely told him that he had a certain *Spirit* that perpetually accompanied him. He first became aware of it when he had attained about thirty-seven years of age, but he believed that the said *Spirit* had been present with him his entire life, as he gathered from certain *warning dreams and visions* <note>original: "Monitory Dreams and Visions"</note> by which he was forewarned of various dangers and vices. This *Spirit* revealed itself to him after he had earnestly prayed to God for a whole year to send a *good Angel* to him to be the guide and governor of his life and actions. He added also that before and after prayer, he used to spend two or three hours in meditation and reading the Scriptures, diligently asking himself which *religion*, among the many that are debated in the world, might be the best, and beseeching God that He would be pleased to direct him to it. He noted that he did not approve of the methods of those who, at all costs, pray to God to confirm them in the opinions they have already formed, whether they are right or wrong. 

While he was thus occupied with matters of *religion*, he came across a passage in *Philo Judaeus* <note>A Hellenistic Jewish philosopher</note> in his book *On Sacrifices* <note>original: "De Sacrificiis"</note>, where he writes that a *good and holy man* can offer no greater nor more acceptable sacrifice to God than the offering of himself. Therefore, following *Philo's* counsel, he offered his soul to God. After that, among many other divine *dreams and visions*, he once seemed to hear the voice of God saying to him in his sleep:
> I will save your soul; I am he who appeared to you before.

Afterward, the *Spirit* would knock at his door every day around three or four o'clock in the morning. Although he would rise and open the door, he could see nobody; yet the *Spirit* persisted in this habit and would continue to rouse him unless he got up.

3. This trouble and rowdiness made him begin to imagine that it was some *evil spirit* that haunted him in this way. Therefore, he daily prayed earnestly to God that He would be pleased to send a *good Angel* to him; he also often sang *Psalms*, having most of them memorized.

Consequently, the *Spirit* afterward knocked more gently at the door and one day revealed itself to him while he was awake. This was the first time he was assured by his physical senses that it was the Spirit; for it often touched and moved a drinking glass that stood in his chamber, which amazed him quite a bit.

Two days later, when he was entertaining a certain friend of his at supper—a Secretary to the *King*—this friend was greatly startled when he heard the *Spirit* thumping on the bench right next to him and was struck with fear. But the man told him to be of good courage, as no harm was intended; to better reassure him, he told him the truth of the whole matter.

Therefore, from that time on, says *Bodin*, the man affirmed that this *Spirit* was always with him and always notified him of things by some physical sign. For example, it would strike his right *ear* if he did anything wrong, and his left ear if he acted rightly. If anyone came to deceive him, his right—

### CHAPTER XIV.

1. Certain *inquiries* upon the preceding *narration*; such as, what these *guardian spirits* <note>original: "Genii"</note> may be. 2. Whether one or more of them are allotted to every man, or to some none at all. 3. What may be the reason for *spirits* appearing so seldom. 4. And whether they have any settled *shape* or not. 5. What their manner is of assisting men in either *devotion* or *prophecy*. 6. Whether every man's temperament <note>original: "complexion"</note> is capable of the *society* of a good *spirit*. 7. 1. It is outside my present purpose, as I have already declared, to enter into any more particular and curious *investigations* <note>original: "Disquisitions"</note> concerning the nature of *spirits*, my aim being only to demonstrate their *existence* by those strange *effects* recorded everywhere in *history*. But this last *narration* is so extraordinarily remarkable that it would be a piece of disrespect to dismiss it without at least some *inquiries* into such *problems* as it naturally offers for our consideration; though it may well seem plainly beyond the power of human *intellect* <note>original: "Wit"</note> or the laws of *modesty* to determine anything for certain therein.

In the first place, therefore, it cannot but amaze a man's mind to think what these helpful <note>original: "officious"; in the 17th century, this meant "eager to serve" rather than "meddlesome"</note> *spirits* might be that so willingly sometimes offer themselves to associate with a man. Whether they may be *angels* incapable of inhabiting human *bodies* (as is commonly conceived); or whether they are the *souls* of the deceased, they having more affinity with mortality and human frailty than the others, and so being more sensitive to our necessities and infirmities, having once felt them themselves. 2. Secondly, we are invited to inquire whether *every man has his own Guardian Genius <note>A protective spirit or "guardian angel" assigned to a person.</note> or not*. That *Witches* have many—such as they are—their own *confessions* testify. The *Pythagoreans* <note>Followers of the philosopher Pythagoras.</note> were of the opinion that *every man has two Genii, a good one and a bad one*. *Muhammad* <note>original: Mahomet</note> has taken this into his *Religion*, adding also that they sit on men's shoulders with notebooks in their hands, and that the one writes down all the *good*, and the other all the *evil* a man does. But I look upon such expressions as symbolic rather than literal. I think it more reasonable that when a man changes the state of his mind, he changes his *Genius* as well. Or rather, unless a man is very sincere and single-hearted, he is left to common *Providence*; just as, if he is not desperately wicked or deplorably miserable, hardly any particular *evil Spirit* interposes or offers himself as a perpetual *Assistant* in his affairs and fortunes. 

But extreme *Poverty, irksome old Age, want of Friends, and the Contempt, Injury*, and *Hard-heartedness* of evil neighbors, working upon a *Soul* sunk low into the *Body* and wholly devoid of the *Divine life*, sometimes kindle so sharp, so eager, and so piercing a desire for *Satisfaction* and *Revenge*, that the shrieks of men while they are being murdered, the howling of a *Wolf* in the fields at night, or the squeaking and roaring of tortured *Beasts*, do not so certainly call to them those of their own kind, as this powerful *Magic* of a pensive and complaining *Soul* in the bitterness of its affliction attracts the aid of these over-officious *Spirits*. So it is most probable that those who are the quickest to *hang Witches* are the very ones who *made* them. They have no more goodness nor true piety than those they so willingly prosecute; they are as wicked as the witches, though with better luck or more discretion, offending no further than the *Law* will permit them. Therefore, they securely starve the poor helpless *man*, yet with a great deal of clamor about *Justice*, they will revenge the death of their *Hog* or *Cow*.

3. Thirdly, it would be worth our investigation to ask why *Spirits* so *seldom* appear nowadays, especially those that are *good*. Whether it is the wickedness of the present *Age*, as I have already hinted; or the general *prejudice* men have against all *Spirits* that appear, assuming they must immediately be *Devils*; or the *frailty* of human nature, which is not usually able to bear the appearance of a *Spirit*, any more than other *Animals* are. For we see what agonies *Horses* and *Dogs* are cast into upon their approach, which is a good sign to distinguish a *real Apparition* from our own *Imaginations*. Or lastly, whether it is the *condition* of *Spirits* themselves, who perhaps cannot become visible without some violence done to their own nature; it being perhaps as troublesome a thing for them to keep themselves in one steady, visible consistency in the air as it is for men who dive to hold their breath in the water.

But some proofs being more palpable than others, and more suited to awaken the dull and slow belief of the Atheist into the acknowledgment of a God, it will not be amiss to take notice of what *evasions* <note>original: "Evasions" — excuses or logical loopholes used to avoid a conclusion.</note> he attempts to make for the extricating himself out of those that he fancies most sensibly entangle him and most strongly hinder his escape.

And such are especially these last two I insisted upon: the curious frame of **Man's Body** and **Apparitions**.

2. And the force of the former some endeavor to evade thus: "That there have ever been **Man** and **Woman** and other *species* in the world, and so it is no wonder that like should propagate its like; and therefore there is no want of any other invisible or material cause but the *species* of things themselves. And so these admirable contrivances in Nature must imply no divine *Wisdom* nor *Counsel*, nor any such thing."

3. But here I demand: whether there were *ever* any **Man** who was *not mortal*, and whether there be any mortal who had *not a beginning*? And if he had a beginning, it must be either by *Generation* <note>Reproduction through parents.</note> or *Creation*. If by *Creation*, there is a *God*. If by equivocal *Generation* <note>The archaic theory that living things could arise from non-living matter, like insects from mud.</note>—such as rising out of the *Earth*—our argument will still hold good notwithstanding this *evasion*. But if you will say there was never any man in the world who was not born of a *Woman*, this must amount to nothing more than this: that there has been an infinite number of *successions* of births. If anything more than this is meant by it, it will not make sense.

4. For though our *fancy* <note>original: "Phanfie" — our imagination or ability to visualize.</note> cannot run through an *infinite series* of *effects*, yet our *reason* is assured there is no *effect* without a *cause*. And let the *progress* of *causes* and *effects* be as infinite as it will, at last we resolve it naturally into some *First*. He who denies this seems to me to willfully wink against the light of *Nature* and do violence to the faculties of his *mind*. And therefore, of necessity, there must be at least one *first Man* and *Woman* who are *first in the order of Nature* <note>original: "ordine Naturæ"</note>, even if they seem infinite to our limited understanding. And these who are thus *first* in order of *Nature* or *causality* must also exist *first* before there can be any other *men* or *women* in the world. And therefore, concerning these *first* people, it being manifest that they were born of no parents, it follows they were *created* or rose out of the *earth*, and so the *evasion* will be frustrated.

5. Besides, if you affirm that there was *never* any *man* in the world but who was born of a *woman*, and so grew to *man's estate* <note>Adulthood.</note> by degrees, it will fall to some man's share to be both a *babe* and a *man* at once, or to be both *father* and *child*. For as soon as *mankind* existed (let it be from *Eternity*, and beyond *Eternity* is nothing), those who then existed were begotten by *somebody*; and if there was *nothing* before them to beget them, then they begot *themselves*.

6. But that they should at once then have been *perfect men*—their substances being of alterable and passive matter that is wrought diversely and by degrees into the frame it has, according to the perpetual testimony of *Nature*—is as rash as if they should say that *boots* and *shoes* and...

However, it is manifest that there must be an orderly interval of time before these things can exist; there must first be the killing and flaying of oxen and sheep, as well as tanning, spinning, cutting, and many more such circumstances. So, it is enormously ridiculous to say that *mankind* might have existed all at once from all *eternity*, unless the *omnipotence* of a God—who can do whatever we can imagine and more—should, by his irresistible *command* <note>original: "Fiat"</note>, cause such a thing in a moment as soon as he himself existed (which was forever), for he never lacked either power or skill.

But that fluid and blind *matter* could have raised itself up from all *eternity* into such complete *species* of things is entirely groundless and irrational. I say, that there should ever be such a thing in the world as a *man* existing of himself all at once in this physical frame we see—who nevertheless afterwards died like other mortals—is a fable beyond all poetic fictions whatsoever. It is more incredible than the most foolish legend that any religion ever offered to the *atheist's* belief.

7. Others, therefore, abandoning this way of *evasion*, betake themselves to another, which, though it seems more plausible at first glance, is just as frivolous. They say, "That all the *species* of things, *man* himself not excepted, first came out of the earth by the diverse attempts of the particles of *matter* upon one another; these particles finally happened upon such a lucky construction and fabric of the bodies of creatures as we see. They argue that, having an infinite *series* <note>original: "series"</note> of time to try all possible combinations, they would of necessity eventually arrive at the state they are in."

But I answer: first, that these particles might commit infinite *repetitions* <note>original: "Tautologies"</note> in their collisions and motions, and therefore there was no such necessity at all of falling into those forms and shapes that appear in the world. Again, there is such excellent contrivance in the *body*—of a *man*, for instance, as I have previously shown—that it can only be the effect of very accurate *knowledge* and *wisdom* <note>original: "Counfel"</note>.

And lastly, regarding this collision of *atoms*, since they are left without a guide, it is a miracle beyond all understanding that they should produce no *unfit* <note>original: "inept"</note> *species* of things. For example, creatures that by their own nature had only three legs, one eye, or one ear, or rows of teeth along the *vertebrae* <note>original: "Vertebræ"</note> of their backs, and the like, as I have mentioned above. These *unfit forms* <note>original: "Ineptitudes"</note> would be much easier to happen upon than such accurate and faultless frames of creatures.

8. The monsters, not being as well provided with either limbs or senses as the others, were never able to hop fast enough away from them, or to detect in time the approaching dangers that were constantly coming upon them." The accusations cast upon God and Nature will be easily discovered and proven false if we only consider:

First, that **trees, herbs**, and **flowers**, which do not move from their places or exercise fierce cruelty upon one another, are all in their several kinds **handsome** and **elegant**, and have no **ineptitude** <note>original: "ineptitude"; meaning lack of fitness or poor design</note> or **defect** in them.

Secondly, that all creatures born of **putrefaction** <note>original: "putrefaction"; the historical belief in "spontaneous generation," where living things were thought to arise from decaying matter</note>, such as **mice** and **frogs** and the like, as well as those many hundreds of **insects**, such as **grasshoppers, flies, spiders**, and others—these also have a most accurate **contrivance** <note>original: "contrivance"; purposeful design or mechanical arrangement</note> of **parts**, and there is nothing framed rashly or poorly in any of them.

Lastly, in more perfect **creatures**, such as the **Scotch Barnacles** which **historians** write of; even if there is any doubt about those, **Gerard** <note>John Gerard (c. 1545–1612), a famous English herbalist and author of "The Herball, or Generall Historie of Plantes."</note> relates from his own knowledge (which is as admirable and as much to our purpose) that there is a kind of **fowl** which in **Lancashire** are called **Tree-Geese**. They are bred out of rotten pieces of broken ships and trunks of **trees** cast upon a little island in **Lancashire** they call the **Pile of Foulders** <note>Now known as Piel Island, near Barrow-in-Furness.</note>. The same **author** says he has found the like also in other parts of this kingdom. Those **fowls**, though bred thus of **putrefaction**, are in all respects of as exact a **fabric of body** and as fitly designed for the functions of such a living **creature** as any of those produced by **propagation** <note>original: "propagation"; sexual reproduction</note>. (And that they are thus bred is undeniably true, as any man, if he please, may satisfy himself by consulting **Gerard**, the very last page of his **History of Plants**). Nay, these kinds of **fowls** themselves also propagate, which has so fooled some people that they have denied the other way of their generation; whereas being generated one way does not exclude the other, as is seen in **frogs** and **mice**.

Therefore, since these productions out of the **earth** and from **putrefaction** are as perfect and accurate in all points as any others, it is a manifest discovery that Nature never framed any **species** of things poorly or foolishly. Therefore, she was always guided by **counsel** and **providence**—that is, that **Nature** herself is the effect of an all-knowing God.

9. Nor does this consideration only take away this present **evasion**, but it more palpably and intelligibly weakens the former argument. For what does it profit them to fly to an infinite propagation of **individuals** in the same eternal **species**, as they imagine, so that they might always be able to assign a **cause** answerable to the **effect**? For here are such **effects** and **products of putrefaction** where **wisdom** and **counsel** are just as conspicuous as in others. Thus, they are nonetheless necessarily trapped <note>original: "illaqueated"; ensnared or entangled</note> in that same inconvenience which they thought they had escaped by such a clever subtlety.

### CHAPTER XVI.

1. *The Atheist's excuses against apparitions: first, that they are mere products of the imagination.*
2. *Next, that even if they are external realities, they are caused by the force of imagination; with a refutation of these ideas.*
3. *Their foolish idea that skirmishes seen in the sky are caused by the "shedding of films" <note>original: "exuvious Effluxes" — a theory that objects shed thin layers or skins that float through the air</note> from physical things; with a refutation of this.*

5. *Based on the rough surface <note>original: "rude Politure"</note> of the clouds.*
6. *Based on the clouds' inability to reflect even the image of the stars, which would be much easier; first, because the stars' size does not diminish.*
7. *Then, because of the purity of the stars' light.*
8. *Thirdly, because of the position of our eye within the shadow of the Earth.*
9. *Lastly, because the stars are scattered, ready to be reflected from every part of the sky if the clouds had any such reflective quality.*
10. *That if clouds did have enough reflectivity to show battles from such a great distance, it would have to be by some supernatural craftsmanship <note>original: "Artifice"</note>.*
11. *That this craftsmanship has its own limited laws.*
12. *Therefore, at least some of these aerial battles cannot be reflections from the Earth.*
13. *Machiavelli’s opinion concerning these fights in the air.*
14. *Nothing is as demonstrable in philosophy as the existence of a God.*
15. *The source from which that narrow-minded <note>original: "Pedantick"</note> affectation of atheism likely arose.*
16. *The true causes for being genuinely prone to atheism.*
17. *That men ought not to pit their mere personal moods <note>original: "complexional humours"</note> against the principles of reason and the testimonies of nature and history. The author's apology for being so detailed in reciting stories of spirits.*

Now, as for the excuses by which they would dodge the force of the argument for spirits drawn from apparitions: these excuses are so weak and silly that one may be almost certain the atheists were actually convinced in their judgment of the truth of such stories. Otherwise, it would have been better to flatly deny them than to invent such idle and vain reasons for them.

For first, they say these apparitions are nothing but imaginations, and that there is nothing real outside of ourselves in such sightings.

2. But when they are forced away from this shallow explanation—because many people see the same thing at once—they then flee to a "miraculous" power of *fancy* <note>imagination</note>. They claim fancy is able to change the air into a real shape and form, so that others may behold it just as well as the person who created it by the power of his own *fancy*.

Now I ask any man: is this not a more difficult mystery, and more inconceivable, than all the magical transformations <note>original: "Metamorphoses"</note> of devils or witches? For it is far easier to conceive that some intelligent being in the air should transform the air into this or that shape (being present in the very part of the air it transforms) than that the imagination of...

He attempts to explain these *phenomena* <note>original: "Phænomena"</note> thus: that the *vapors of men's bodies*—and it seems of *horses* too—are carried up into the *air* and fall into a certain proportional arrangement of parts, and so imitate the figures of them high among the *clouds*.

But I ask: how do the *vapors* of the *horses* find the *vapors* of their *riders*? And when and how long are they traveling to meet each other? And do they not often appear before there are any *armies* in the field to send up such *vapors*? And do *harness* and *weapons* send up *vapors* too, such as *swords, pikes*, and *shields*? And how do they happen to land so luckily into the hands of those *aerial men of war*—especially the *vapors of metals* (if they have any), which are in all likelihood heavier than the steam <note>original: "reek"</note> of *animals* and *men*? 

And lastly, how do they come to *fire* at one another and to *fight*, there being neither life nor soul in them? And do *sounds* also have their own *shed layers* <note>original: "Exuviæ"</note> that are reserved until these ceremonies? For at *Aldeburgh* in *Suffolk* in 1642, there were heard in the *air* very loud beatings of *drums, the shooting of muskets* and *artillery* <note>original: "Ordnance"</note>; just as in other such *prodigies* <note>A "prodigy" is a marvelous or prophetic sign.</note> there has been heard the sounding of *trumpets*, as *Snellius*

The *shed layers* of *fiddles*, it seems, fly up into the *air* too; or were those *musical notes* <note>original: "Accents"</note> frozen there for a time, and then, at the heat and firing of the *cannons*, the *air* relented and thawed, becoming so harmoniously vocal? With what vain conceits are men intoxicated who willfully blink against the light of nature and are estranged from the true knowledge and acknowledgment of a God!

It is so evident that they are unfit for this, as they fail at things of far less difficulty. For we never find them able to reflect the image of a *star*, whereas not only glass, but every troubled pool or dirty puddle of water in the highway usually does so.

6. But several reasons will sufficiently inform us that it is far easier for a *star* than for any of these *objects* here upon Earth to be *reflected* to our eyes by those rough natural looking-glasses placed among the clouds.

For first, the stars do not diminish at all from their *usual magnitude* in which they ordinarily appear to us by this reflection; a difference of many hundreds of leagues makes no difference in their size. Indeed, the distance of the *diameter* of the *orbit of the Earth* makes none, as must be acknowledged by all those who admit the *annual motion* of the Earth. But a very few miles exceedingly diminish the *usual size* of the *image* of a horse or man, even to such smallness that they become invisible. What then will become of his *sword, shield*, or *spear*? And in these cases we now speak of, I have mentioned before how great a journey the *images* must travel from the Earth to the cloud that reflects them.

7. Secondly, it is manifest that a *star* has preeminence over these *earthly objects*, in that it is as pure a light as the Sun (though not so large), while they are but opaque, colored bodies; therefore, there is no comparison between the vigor and strength of the *image* of a star and of them.

8. Thirdly, in the *nighttime*, the eye being placed in the shadow of the Earth, those *reflections* of a star will be even more easily visible; whereas the great light of the Sun by day must necessarily weaken these reflected *images* of *objects* upon the Earth, as his beams strike our eyes with such *strong vibrations*.

That discerning wit Descartes <note>original: "Cartesius"</note> was well aware of these laws and boundaries. He generously and judiciously declared: *A burning-glass—where the distance of its focus from the glass is not smaller in proportion to its diameter than the distance of the Earth from the Sun is to the Sun's diameter—will burn no more intensely than the direct rays of the Sun would without it. This remains true even if the glass were as exactly shaped and carefully polished as could be expected from the hand of an angel.*

13. His own words are so free and candid, and his judgment so significant (though he does not pretend to be a philosopher) regarding the reason for these strange sights, that I think it worth the while to transcribe them:

14. I have now completed this present *Treatise* against *Atheism* in all its three parts. As I cast my eye upon it and view that clear and irrefutable evidence of the cause I have undertaken—the external appearances of things in the world so faithfully supporting the undeniable dictates of the innate principles of our own minds—I cannot but confidently assert that there is no single notion in all philosophy more certain and demonstrable than that there is a God. And truly, I think I have ransacked all the corners of every kind of philosophy that can claim any influence in this controversy with such diligence that I may safely pronounce that it is mere brutish *ignorance* or *impudence*, not *skill* in *nature* or the *knowledge* of things, that can encourage any man to profess *atheism*, or to embrace it when proposed by those who make a profession of it.

15. But I conceive the situation is this: at first, some famously learned men, because they were not as indiscreetly zealous and superstitious as others, were mistaken by idiots <note>term: "ideots" here refers to uneducated or ignorant people rather than a clinical diagnosis</note> and slandered as *atheists*. Then, ever after, some vain-glorious fool or another has pretended to be atheistical, as far as he safely could, so that he might be reputed as more learned or a more profound *naturalist* <note>term: a scientist or student of the natural world</note>.

16. But I dare assure any man that if he only searches into the bottom of this "enormous disease of the soul," as Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: "Trismegist"</note> truly calls it, he will find nothing to be the cause of it but either *vanity* of mind, or brutish *sensuality* and an untamed desire to satisfy one's own will in everything; a guilty *conscience* and a base *fear* of divine *vengeance*; ignorance of the narrowness and insufficiency of secondary causes; a jumbled *foulness* <note>original: "seculency"</note> and *disorder* of the spirits caused by perpetual intemperance and luxury; or else a dark, deadening *melancholy* that so starves and kills the perception of the *soul* (especially in divine matters) that it makes a man as unfit for such contemplations as if his head were filled with cold earth or dry grave-mold.

17. And for such slow constitutions as these, I shall not wonder if, just as the first part of my discourse must seem marvelously subtle, so the last appears ridiculously incredible. But they are to remember that I do not...

<page-num>142</page-num>
<header>An Antidote against Atheism. BOOK III.</header>

I do not here appeal to the *physical* humors <note>original: "Complexional humors"; referring to the four humors of ancient medicine believed to dictate temperament</note> or the peculiar *tastes* of men that arise out of the temperament of the *body*. Instead, I appeal to the known and unalterable *Ideas of the Mind*, to the *phenomena* of *Nature*, and to the records of *History*. 

If I have insisted somewhat more fully upon this last point—historical records—it should not be attributed to any vain credulity on my part, nor to the idea that I take pleasure in telling strange stories. Rather, I thought it necessary to fortify and strengthen the faith of others as much as I could. I am well assured that a contemptuous disbelief of such narrations concerning *Spirits*, and any effort to make them all appear ridiculous and incredible, is a dangerous prelude to *Atheism* itself; or else, it is a more secretive and crafty profession and suggestion of it. 

For certainly, that saying is no more true in politics—*No Bishop, no King*—than this saying is in metaphysics: *No Spirit, no God*.

## CHAPTER I.

1. The Author's reason for adding this Appendix to his Antidote. 2. A list of the chief objections made against the First Book of the treatise.

1. Suspected innocence and doubted truth can win no greater credit than by the strictest examination. The world is thereby more fully assured of the blamelessness of the one and the solidity of the other than it could possibly be without such a public trial. Therefore, so that such a great advantage may not be lacking to the weighty cause we have in hand, I was not content only to set down such reasons for the existence of God which, in my own judgment, I conceived to be irrefutably firm. Rather, so that their firmness may appear more conspicuous to all men, I have brought into view the chief and most material objections I could find. These include objections raised by those who have personally taken exception to any argument I used, as well as those who were invited to more carefully search and discover any weakness or inconsistency <note>original: "inconsequency"</note> in any reasoning throughout the whole treatise. The chief exceptions and objections against the First Book are these:

2. First, that the ground of our demonstration of the existence of God from his Idea is the claim that there are innate ideas <note>Innate ideas: Concepts or knowledge present in the mind from birth, rather than learned through experience.</note> in the mind of man; which, they say, is false.

Secondly, that there is no such Idea of God at all as we have described;

Thirdly, That *Existence* is not a term of *Perfection*, and therefore is not so inseparably involved in the notion of a *Being absolutely Perfect*, or of *God*.

Fourthly, That though *Necessary Existence* be included in the *Idea* of *God*, yet our inferring from that that he does *exist* is but a *Sophism* <note>original: "Sophism" — a clever but false argument</note>; because a *Being absolutely Evil*, as well as *absolutely Perfect*, includes *necessary existence* in its *Idea*.

Sixthly, That *God* did not put this *Idea* of himself into the *Mind* of *Man*, but rather the subtler sort of *Politicians*, who have always used *Religion* as a mere engine of *State*.

Seventhly, That the *Fear* and *Hopes* of *Natural Conscience* are nothing indeed but these *Passions* raised upon a belief in a *God* which men have received by *Tradition* or *Education*.

Lastly, That these arguments by which we prove the *Incorporeity* <note>original: "Incorporeity" — the state of having no physical body; being purely spiritual</note> of the *Soul* of *Man* will also conclude the *Incorporeity* of the *Soul* of a *Beast*, and that therefore they are *Sophistical*.

To these I shall answer in order with as little pomp and luxury of words, and as much plainness and clarity, as I may, in such a subtle and difficult matter.

But from what we have written, he must plainly see that the weight of our argument is not based solely upon this notion of **Innate Ideas** <note>Ideas present in the mind from birth rather than learned through experience.</note>, but upon that confessed truth: that there are some things so plain that, however the soul came to the knowledge of them, she cannot help but assent to them and acknowledge them to be undeniably true.

2. Now, the **Idea of a Being absolutely Perfect** is such that it must be acknowledged—according to the light of Nature—to be indeed the true **Idea** of such a Being. Whether you call it **Innate** or not, it is all one; the demonstration will follow as inevitably as if it were acknowledged to be an **Innate Idea**. We shall discern this more plainly if we look at examples in other **Ideas**; for instance, in the **Idea of a Triangle**, of a regular geometric body, and of a round **Solid**. For the nature of these **Ideas** is such that the mind of man cannot possibly deny that they are distinct **Ideas**, and that certain properties belong to them. 

For example: 
* That every **Triangle** is either **Equilateral** <note>original: "Isopleuron"</note>, **Isosceles**, or **Scalene** <note>original: "Scalenum"</note>; so that there are exactly **three kinds** of them in reference to their sides, and no more.
* That there are **Five regular Bodies** in Geometry, neither more nor less: namely, the **Cube**, the **Tetrahedron** <note>original: "Tetraedrum"</note>, the **Octahedron** <note>original: "Octaedrum"</note>, the **Dodecahedron** <note>original: "Dodecaedrum"</note>, and the **Icosahedron** <note>original: "Eicosaedrum"</note>. 
* That there is only one kind of **round Solid**, namely, the **Sphere or Globe**. 

And so, by contemplating the **Idea of a Being absolutely Perfect** (whether the **Idea** is innate or not innate, it does not matter), we cannot help but conclude that there can be **only one such being in existence**, and that this one being also cannot fail to exist, as we have demonstrated at length.

3. However, although we need no such **Principle** as **Innate Ideas** to carry out our demonstration, I still believe it to be true. I thought it important to encourage the reader to attend to the **Notions** of his own mind and to appreciate the excellence of that "Judge" <note>The human intellect or reason.</note> we are to appeal to; therefore, I held it appropriate to insist upon it somewhat. I am ready now to prove that this **Principle** is true, despite anything I find alleged against it.

4. In the sixth chapter of this first book, I contend that the exact **Idea of a Circle or a Triangle** is hinted to us by those shapes described in physical matter, rather than being taught to us by them. This remains true despite the **Objection** that such shapes seem exact to our **outward senses** when we look at them carelessly, even though they are not actually perfect. For we plainly correct ourselves afterward, not only because of the physical figure (which we may always perceive as imperfect), but by our **Innate knowledge**. This knowledge tells us that the **outward Triangle** cannot be an exact **Triangle**, because an **indivisible point**—in which the angles must end—is utterly invisible to the **outward sense**.

Besides, it should be considered that even if we admitted a **Triangle** could be drawn so perfectly that it seemed exact to our **outward sense** (even if we looked as closely as possible through **Microscopes**), those who have never seen or noticed such an accurate drawing still form the exact **Idea of a Triangle** in their own minds upon seeing much rougher drafts. Since they have not learned this perfection from any **outward object**, it must be the inward representation of their own minds.

<summary>The author argues that whether or not the idea of God is "innate," its perfection and logical necessity are as undeniable as the mathematical properties of triangles and geometric solids. He maintains that our minds possess an internal standard of perfection that exceeds what we observe in the physical world.</summary>

# An Appendix to the foregoing Antidote. CHAPTER II.

5. But now for other objections: namely, that a blind man would be able to discourse about colors if there were any *innate ideas* <note>Innate ideas: The philosophical concept that the mind is born with certain ideas or knowledge, rather than being a "blank slate" at birth.</note> in his soul. I say, it does not follow at all; because these *ideas* that I contend to be in the soul are not *sensible* <note>Sensible: Relating to the physical senses (sight, touch, etc.) rather than "reasonable."</note>, but *intellectual*. Such are those many *logical, metaphysical, mathematical*, and some *moral notions*. All of these we employ as our own *modes* <note>Modes: Ways or methods of processing information.</note> of considering *sensible objects*, but they are not the *sensible objects* themselves. We have no *idea* of those objects, but only a capacity—by reason of the organs of our body—to be affected by them. The reason, therefore, for a blind man's inability to discourse about *colors* is only that he has no *substratum* <note>Substratum: An underlying layer or foundation; here, the raw sensory data of sight.</note> or *phantasm* <note>Phantasm: A mental image or sensory impression.</note> of the *subject* of the discourse. He lacks the sensory data upon which he would use these *innate modes* or frame of *notions* that are naturally in his mind, and which he can make use of in the contemplation of various other *sensible objects*.
<margin>See Book 1, chapter 6, Section 3.</margin>

6. And whereas it is further objected that these *logical* and *mathematical notions* also entered through the *senses* because *brutes* <note>Brutes: Animals, as distinguished from humans.</note> have knowledge of them—and we will not bestow so rich an inward furniture as these *innate ideas* upon animals—I answer that *brutes* do not have the knowledge of any such *notion*. Instead, what they do arises from a mere *concatenation* <note>Concatenation: A chain or linking together.</note> of *sensible phantasms* representing things *pleasurable* or *unpleasant* to the *senses*. To give an instance in those particulars that are objected: a *dog* will bark at one noise, suppose the knocking at the door, and not at another, such as the falling of a stool or of a dish from a shelf; he will follow one scent, such as that of the *hare*, and neglect another, and the like. These are all done not because he has any *notion* of *effect* and *cause*, but by a mere *linking* of *mental images* representing things as *pleasurable*, *unpleasant*, or neutral to his *senses*, in which case he is not moved at all. And if a *dog* snaps at the bigger morsel, it is not because he considers the *notion* of *inequality*, but because that *sensible object* more powerfully moves his appetite. So, if he takes one single side of a *triangle* to reach the corner where a piece of bread is placed, it is not because he considers that a *straight line* is the shortest distance between two points. Rather, he *sensibly* feels that by going *directly* to it, he shall be there sooner than if he went around. Zeno <note>Zeno: Likely referring to the ancient philosopher Zeno of Elea.</note> gave a good example of this with an *ass* at one corner of a *pasture* and the fodder in the other: the ass would go *directly* to the corner where the fodder lay. Zeno thought this was a marvelous, witty jab at *Euclid's demonstration* <note>Euclid's demonstration: A reference to Euclid's Elements, specifically the theorem that any two sides of a triangle are together greater than the third side.</note> that any two sides of a *triangle* are larger than the *third*, as it was a *truth* so plain that even an *ass* could not miss it.

7. But by the favor of such a *critical philosopher*, we may very well suspect that neither *dog* nor *ass* that moves toward any *object* goes *directly* in a *straight line* because he considers that a *crooked one* is further around. He does so because his *line of sight* guides him *straight* to the *object* he looks at. He moves in that direction naturally, without any reflection upon *mathematical notions*, just as a stone cast out of a sling endeavors of its own accord to steer its course with a *rectilinear motion* <note>Rectilinear motion: Movement in a straight line.</note>. Since a stone does not even have *senses*, we can in no way suspect it to be capable of even the simplest *notion* in *geometry*.

8. Therefore, it is a mere fallacy to argue that *brutes*, because they do things that are *reasonable* or *mathematical*, therefore do them...

1. That the souls of men—the lowest dregs of all the *intellectual orders*—should be plunged into confusion and puzzled by the close and accurate study of *spiritual* and *intellectual* things is only reasonable. This is especially true considering that even matter itself—in which they tumble and wallow, which they feel with their hands and engage with all their senses—seems unimaginable and full of contradictions if they once attempt to contemplate it in an *intellectual* and *rational* manner. Their imaginations are so clouded in this dark state of imprisonment in these earthly bodies, as I have already argued at great length.

2. But the *notion* of a *spirit*, which some claim obscures the clarity of the *idea* of God, is not such an inconsistent and inconceivable *notion* as some would have it. I hope I shall sufficiently prove this by answering the shrewdest objections that I think can be made against it.

# An Appendix to the foregoing Antidote. CHAPTER III.

2. Therefore, since we have defined a Spirit (referring primarily to a created one) by its absolute powers of **self-contraction** and **expansion** <note>original: "dilatation"</note>, as well as by its relative faculties of **penetrating**, **moving**, and **altering matter**, we will now address the objections made against both.

Against the first point, it is objected that it is impossible for the human mind to imagine any substance possessing the power of **self-expansion** and **contraction** without it also being extended in space. The argument follows that **extension** cannot be imagined without a **diversity of parts**, nor can a **diversity of parts** exist without the possibility of **dividing** or **separating** them. This is because a diversity of parts in any substance implies a diversity of distinct substances, and a diversity of substances implies they are independent of one another. From this, it would follow that **indivisibility** is incompatible with a **spirit**, even though we included it in our definition.

I admit this objection is very clever and forcefully argued. However, I also believe the difficulty is easily resolved if we acknowledge that the nature of a **spirit** contains something similar to what thousands of scholars have acknowledged in the nature of **intentional species** <note>In medieval and early modern philosophy, "intentional species" were the forms or images through which the mind perceives objects, thought to be present in the air or the senses without taking up physical space.</note>. We will therefore represent the property of a **spirit** using this **symbol** or **hieroglyph** <note>meaning a visual metaphor or sacred representation</note>.

Suppose a **point of light** from which a luminous **sphere** <note>original: "orb"</note> radiates according to the known principles of **optics**. This sphere of light closely resembles the nature of a **spirit**, which is diffused and extended, yet remains indivisible. For we shall suppose that in this **spirit**, the center of life is indivisible, yet it diffuses itself by a kind of **circumscribed omnipresence**, just as the **point of light** is detectable at every point within the **luminous sphere**. And yet, assuming that central shining **point is indivisible**, there is nothing divisible in that entire **sphere of light**. It would be ridiculous to think that by any **machine** <note>original: "engine"</note> or **skill** whatsoever, one could separate the luminous rays from the shining **center** and keep them apart by themselves; any person who carefully considers the nature of the thing we are discussing will acknowledge this.

Now, there is no difficulty in imagining such a sphere as a **substance** rather than just a **quality**. Indeed, this **sphere of light** itself—since it does not reside in any physical object within the space it occupies—looks much more like a **substance** than a mere **accident** <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a property that cannot exist on its own, like "redness" or "tallness."</note>. We often thoughtlessly assume that **light** and **colors** behave this way—that any point of them will radiate in a circle—but it is more rational to apply this concept to **spiritual substances**. Their central essence spreads out into a **secondary substance**, just as luminous rays are understood to shoot out from a shining **point**. 

From this, we are able to provide an answer to the greatest difficulty in the previous objection: namely, that the perceived parts of a **spirit** have an inseparable dependence upon its central **essence** from which they flow and in which they are fundamentally contained. Therefore, although there is an **extension** of this entire substantial power, one part is not separable or "discerptible" <note>term: "discerptible" means capable of being torn asunder or pulled apart</note> from another. Instead, the entire **substance**—the **secondary** as well as the **primary** or **central**—is **indivisible**.

3. But let us again look at this shining **point** and radiating **sphere** we have used as an example. It is obvious that those rays which are prevented from shooting...

Therefore, there is no generation of a new ray, but an emission of what actually existed before. By this, we are well-equipped with an answer to a further objection, which would insinuate that this <term>emanation</term> <note>original: "Emanation" — a flowing out from a source</note> or <term>efflux</term> <note>original: "Efflux" — an outward flow</note> of the <term>secondary substance</term> <note>The extended part of a spirit, as opposed to its central core.</note> from the <term>central</term> is <term>creation</term> properly so called, which is deemed impossible for any creature to perform.

But we answer that both the <term>central</term> and <term>secondary substance</term> of a <term>spirit</term> were created at once by God, and that these free, active <term>spirits</term> only have a power within them of contracting and dilating their vital rays, not of annihilating or creating them. For we also added to the definition of a <term>spirit</term> the property of *self-penetration*, or the running of one part into another (if we may call them parts). And I hold this answer to be so satisfactory that I think it needless to allege the opinion of *Durandus* <note>Durandus of Saint-Pourçain (c. 1275–1334), a philosopher and theologian known for his independent thinking.</note>, who contends that <term>creation</term> is not incompatible with a creature, provided it is acknowledged to be done by virtue of a gift from the first Creator and in inevitable obedience to His laws. We might also further question whether any <term>emanation</term> may be properly called <term>creation</term>, but enough has been already said to satisfy this objection.

4. But we are further urged concerning this <term>self-contraction</term> and <term>dilatation</term> <note>expansion</note>; for it is asked why the <term>soul</term> of man, which we acknowledge to be a <term>spirit</term>, does not contract itself or withdraw itself from those parts of the body that are in pain, or why she does not dilate herself beyond the bounds of the <term>body</term>. To which it is answered: that the <term>plantal faculty</term> <note>The unconscious, life-sustaining power of the soul that governs growth and physical union.</note> of the <term>soul</term>, by which she is united to this terrestrial <term>body</term>, is not arbitrary <note>subject to will</note>, but fatal <note>determined by fate or necessity</note> or natural. This union cannot be dissolved unless the bond of life is loosened, and that <term>vital congruity</term> <note>The fitness or harmony between the soul and the body that allows them to remain joined.</note> (which is in the <term>body</term> and necessarily holds the <term>soul</term> there) is either hindered for a time or utterly destroyed.
<margin>See my *Immortality of the Soul*, Book 2, chapter 11, section 10; also Book 3, chapter 2, sections 3 and 4.</margin>

5. The last objection against the <term>self-extension</term> of a <term>spirit</term> is that there would be as many <term>wills</term> and <term>understandings</term> as there are <term>parts</term>. But in that <term>symbolical representation</term> I have used, I have represented the <term>extension</term> of a <term>spirit</term> in such a way that it is also acknowledged to be <term>indivisible</term>. Thus, the objection is answered as soon as it is proposed, that engine <note>rhetorical device or argument</note> lying in readiness to receive all such assaults.
<margin>See also this Appendix, chapter 10, sections 9 and 10.</margin>

6. Now, regarding the objections made against the <term>relative faculties</term> of a <term>spirit</term>—namely, the power of *penetrating, moving,* and *altering* <term>matter</term>—there is mainly this one: that <term>matter</term> cannot be altered except by <term>motion</term>, nor <term>motion</term> be communicated except by <term>impulse</term> <note>physical striking</note>, nor <term>impulse</term> without <term>impenetrability</term> in the thing striking. Therefore, it is argued that it is impossible to imagine how a <term>spirit</term> should move <term>matter</term> which it simply penetrates.

But I answer, first, that what our <term>imagination</term> is baffled by, either our outward <term>senses</term> or inward <term>reason</term> often prove to be true. As for example, our <term>reason</term>, considering the nature of an exact <term>globe</term> and <term>plane</term> <note>flat surface</note>, will undoubtedly pronounce that they will touch only at a single point, and that they may be moved one upon another. But our <term>imagination</term> cannot help but make this exception: that the <term>globe</term> thus drawn upon the <term>plane</term> describes a line

...which must necessarily consist of *points*, point perpetually following point in the whole description; how monstrous it is to admit this, I have already intimated in the previous Discourse.

So likewise the *Angle of Contact* <note>The angle between a curve and its tangent line.</note> included between the *Periphery* <note>The circumference or outer boundary of a circle.</note> and a *Perpendicular* falling on the end of the *Diameter* of a *Circle*, Geometricians demonstrate by *Reason* to be less than any acute *Angle* whatsoever. This is so much the case that a line cannot fall between the *Periphery* and the *Perpendicular*. Because of this, the *Fancy* <note>original: "Phanfy"; the faculty of imagination or mental picturing.</note> cannot help but imagine this *Angle* to be indivisible; yet this is a perfect contradiction and goes against the definition of an *Angle*, which is not the *coincidence* <note>The state of occupying the same space.</note> but the *inclination* of two lines. Besides, if a smaller *Circle* is inscribed within a larger one so that it touches at one point, through which a common *Diameter* for both is drawn, and then a Perpendicular is dropped on that end of the *Diameter* where the *Circles* touch; it will be evident that one *Angle of Contact* is bigger than the other. Yet both were acknowledged by our *Imagination* before to be indivisible. Thus, one and the same *Angle* will be both divisible and indivisible, which is again a plain contradiction.

And just as *Imagination* is puzzled by things we are sure of by *Reason*, so is it also in things we are certain of by *Sense*; for who can imagine how it comes about that we see our image behind the *Looking-glass*? For it would be easier to fancy that we should perceive our faces either on the very surface of the glass, or else in the place where they actually are. For if the reflected rays were enough to explain it, then we should find the distance of our image no greater than that of the glass; but if we are affected also by the direct rays, it seems to me we should be led by them to the original place from which they came, and find our faces in the real position where they are.

7. But to provide instances that will come closer to our purpose: We see in some kinds of *Matter* an almost invincible union of parts, as in *Steel*, *Adamant* <note>A legendary stone of impenetrable hardness, often identified with diamond.</note>, and the like. What is it that holds them so fast together? If you say some inward *Substantial form* <note>A philosophical term for the essence that makes a thing what it is.</note>, we have found what we looked for: a *Substance* distinct from the *Matter*. If you say it is the quality of *Hardness* in the *Matter* that makes it thus hard, that is no more than to say it is so because it is so. If you say it is a more perfect rest of parts one by another than there is in other *Matter*; if that be true, it is still a thing utterly unimaginable. 

As an example: suppose that upon *Matter* exactly plain—more plain and solid than a *Table of Marble*—a man laid a little *Cube* of similar plainness and solidity. The idea that this *Cube*, by merely touching the *Table* immediately, should have as firm a union with it as the parts of the *Cube* have with one another, is something that the *Fancy* of man cannot accept. For suppose at first you drew this *Cube* along the *Table*, as it would easily go since both surfaces are so exactly smooth; and then you stopped moving it. That these two smooth bodies should presently stick so fast together that a *Hammer* and a *Chisel* could scarcely sever them is a thing utterly unimaginable. 

Therefore, since the *union* between the parts of *Matter* is so strong, and yet it is so unimaginable how this comes to pass, why should we not admit an equally strong or stronger union between a *Spirit* and a *Body*? This is true even though our *Fancy* suggests the spirit would simply pass through the body, just as it suggests that smooth bodies will...

...will ever lie loose, unless there be some cement to hold them together? And once this union is admitted—*Motion*, *Activity*, and *Agitation* being such easy and natural ways to conceive of the properties of a *Spirit*—it will as easily and naturally follow that it does *move* or *agitate* the *Matter* to which it is thus united.

8. But again, to answer more closely, I say that this present objection is nothing else but a sophism <note>original: "Sophism of the Phansy"; a logical fallacy created by the imagination.</note> of the *Imagination*, conceiving a *Spirit* as a *Body* going through some porous hole or passage that is too wide and open for it, in which it therefore cannot stick or be firmly settled. To this *Imagination* we will oppose the idea that, although *Spirits* do penetrate *Bodies*, they are not such thin and weak things that they must of necessity run through them, or be unable to take hold of them or be united with them. Rather, they may fill up the capacity of a *Body* that is penetrable by *Spirits*. When this *penetrability* of a *Body* or *Matter* is saturated or filled, that *Spirit* which thus fills it is more strongly riveted in, or united with, the *Body* or *Matter* than one part of *Matter* can be with another.

And therefore, we will acknowledge one special faculty of a *Spirit* which, after penetration, it exerts either naturally or by its own will: which is to fill the *Receptivity* or *Capacity* of a *Body* or *Matter* so far as it is capable or receptive of a *Soul* or *Spirit*.

And this quality of a *Spirit* we will make bold to call, for the sake of brevity, by one Greek term: *Hylopathia* <note>original: "ἀνοπάθεια" (anopatheia). The author likely intended "Hylopathia" (matter-affecting), as used later in the paragraph, to describe the spirit's capacity to interact with matter.</note>. So that there may be no suspicion of any fraud or affected foolishness in words, we will define it as plainly as we can: *A power in a Spirit of offering so near a corporeal emanation from the Center of life, that it will so perfectly fill the receptivity of Matter into which it has penetrated, that it is very difficult or impossible for any other Spirit to possess the same; and therefore of becoming hereby so firmly and closely united to a Body, as both to actuate it and to be acted upon, to affect it and be affected by it.*

And now let us appeal to *Imagination* herself: does *Matter* not fit as close—nay, closer—to a *Spirit* than any one part of *Matter* can do to another? For here, *union* pervades through the whole, whereas there, *conjunction* is only on a common *Surface* <note>original: "Superficies"</note>, as is usually imagined and acknowledged. And this *Hylopathia* <note>term: Hylopathia; from the Greek words for "matter" and "feeling/affection," referring to the soul's ability to be affected by or to affect physical matter.</note> which we thus suppose in a finite *Spirit* or *Soul*, I further add, may well correspond by analogy to that power of creating *Matter* which is necessarily included in the *Idea of God*.

9. But lastly, if the manner of how a *Spirit* acts upon a *Body*, or is affected by a *Body*, seems so intricate that it must be given up as inexplicable; yet consider the mobility of a perfect *Globe* upon a *Flat Surface* <note>original: "Plane"</note>. This is admitted as an evident and undeniable property by our *Understanding*, even though we cannot imagine how it—always touching only at a single point—should by its motion describe a continuous line. (The same may be argued from other following instances of *Complexity* and *perplexedness*.) So, supposing there are such manifest operations in *Nature* that *Reason* can demonstrate do not come from the *Matter* itself, we must acknowledge there is some other *Substance* besides the *Matter* that acts in it and upon it, which is *Spiritual*, even if we do not know exactly how *Motion* can be communicated to *Matter* from a *Spirit*.

<summary>The author argues that spirits can unite with and move matter by "filling" its capacity, a faculty he calls Hylopathia. He asserts that even if the mechanics of this interaction are difficult to imagine, reason dictates that a spiritual substance must exist to account for natural operations that matter alone cannot perform.</summary>

# An Appendix to the foregoing Antidote. CHAPTER III.

10. The strength of this, our third and last answer, consists in this: that there are indeed several operations that clearly transcend the power of **Matter**. We will only briefly repeat the main points here, having discussed them more fully in the previous treatise.

First, I will point to a general principle acknowledged by **Descartes** himself, who attributed the laws of **Matter** to the highest **Effects** that any man ever rationally could. It is this: that the **Matter** from which all things are made is, in itself, uniform and of one kind. From this, I infer that matter by itself must either be entirely at **rest** or entirely in **motion**. If it were all at **rest**, there must be something besides **Matter** that **moves** it, which is necessarily a **Spirit**. If it were all in **motion**, it would be impossible for anything to join together; every imaginable particle would be loose from every other. Therefore, a Substance besides **Matter** is required to bind together what we find fixed and joined.

The second instance is found in that admirable **Wisdom** discoverable in all the works of Nature, which I have insisted upon at length in my Second Book. These works clearly prove that all things are designed by a **wise** Principle. Who but a fool would say that **Matter** is **wise**? And yet, out of the decaying parts of the Earth itself—as well as out of drops of dew, rotten pieces of wood, and similar materials <note>original: "geer"</note>—the bodies of Animals arise. They are so skillfully and exquisitely framed that the Reason of Man cannot contemplate them without the greatest pleasure and admiration.

Thirdly, those many and undeniable stories of **Apparitions** clearly prove that an Understanding dwells in various **Airy** bodies. It is utterly impossible that **Air** could be so arbitrarily changed into shapes and held together as a living vessel <note>original: "actuated vehicle of life"</note> if there were not something besides the **Air** itself that possessed and controlled it—something that could expand, contract, and guide it as it pleased. Otherwise, it would be no better formed nor more steadily kept together than tobacco smoke or the steam from chimneys.

Fourthly and lastly, it is manifest that the part of us which **understands**, **remembers**, and **perceives** is the same thing that **moves** our bodies. These **Cognitive Faculties** <note>original: "Cognoscitive Faculties"; the abilities related to knowledge and perception</note> cannot be an operation of mere **Matter**. From this, it is evident that there is in our **Bodies** an **Intellectual spirit** that **moves** them as it pleases, as I have proved extensively enough in the last chapter of the First Book of my *Antidote*, and shall further confirm when we address the objections made against it.

<summary>The author argues that matter alone cannot account for motion, biological complexity, apparitions, or human consciousness, concluding that an immaterial spirit must exist to organize and move physical substance.</summary>

# CHAPTER IV.

1. That *Existence* is a *Perfection*, verified from *common examples*. 2. *Further proved from Metaphysical Principles*. 3. *An Appeal to ordinary Reason*. 4. *That at least Necessary Existence is a Perfection, if bare Existence is not*. 5. *An Illustration of that last Conclusion*.

To avoid the necessity and evidence of our demonstration of the *Existence* of *God*—drawn from the inseparable connection of the *Notion* of God with his *Idea* (we urging *that necessary Existence must needs be included in the Idea of a Being absolutely Perfect*)—there are some who do not hesitate to affirm that *Existence* is not a *term of intrinsic Perfection* <note>original: "Term of intrinsecall Perfection"; meaning a quality that inherently makes something better</note> to anything. For, they say, imagine two pieces of *Gold* equal in weight, purity, and all other respects, differing only in duration or necessity of *Existence*; we cannot justly, without being moody or fanciful, attribute superiority to one more than to the other. To which I answer: just as two pieces of *Gold* are better than one, so one piece of *Gold* that will last twice as long as another is twice as good as the other, or at least much better than the other. I think this is so evident that it requires no further proof.

1. But further, so that we may not only apply ourselves to answering objections, but absolutely confirm the present *Truth*, *That Existence is a Perfection*: First, it is palpably plain, according to that sensible *Aphorism* of *Solomon*, *A living dog is better than a dead lion* <note>Ecclesiastes 9:4</note>.

2. But then again, to argue more generally, the *Metaphysicians*, as is very well known, look upon *Existence* as the formal and actual part of a *Being*; and *Form* or *Act* is acknowledged as the more noble and perfect *Principle* in every *Essence*. Therefore, if they can be distinguished in *God*, it is so there also; if they cannot, then it is thereby confessed that we cannot think of the *Idea* of *God* without it immediately informing us that he does *Exist*. And I recommend it to the inquiry of the *Hebrew Critics* whether <term>havah</term> <note>original: הוה; the root of the verb "to be"</note>, from which comes <term>Jehovah</term> <note>original: יהוה; the Tetragrammaton, the personal name of God in the Hebrew Bible</note>, does not signify *Existence* rather than *Essence*.

3. Thirdly, let the *Metaphysicians* conclude what they please; it is evident to ordinary *Reason* that if there is one conception better than another which implies no imperfection in itself, it must be attributed to what is most perfect. But *Existence* is better than non-*existence* and implies no imperfection; therefore, it must be attributed to the *Idea* of a *Being absolutely Perfect*.

4. Fourthly and lastly: even if it were possible to quibble over the single *Notion* of *Existence*—arguing that it indicated neither *Perfection* nor *Imperfection* nor belonged to either—yet there can be no appearance of an exception against the highest and most perfect manner of existing. That manner is naturally and undeniably included in the *Idea* of a *Being absolutely Perfect*; and therefore, we only rightfully contend that *necessary Existence* is inseparably contained in the *notion* of *God*.

<summary>The author argues that existence is an inherent perfection and must therefore be a defining characteristic of an absolutely perfect being (God). He uses logical analogies, biblical aphorisms, and metaphysical principles to show that necessary existence is inseparable from the concept of divinity.</summary>

5. For example, while it is confessed that *Matter* is finite and cannot be otherwise, for a *Body* to have a specific shape implies neither *Perfection* nor *Imperfection*, but is a natural and necessary characteristic of it. Yet, to be orderly shaped is undoubtedly a *Perfection* of a *Body*. In the same way, even if it were admitted that mere *Existence* is neither *Perfection* nor *Imperfection*, yet so noble a *Mode* <note>original: "Mode" — a specific way or state of being</note> of existence as to *Exist* necessarily must, without any hesitation, be acknowledged as a notion of *Perfection*. Therefore, it naturally belongs to the *Idea* of a *Being* who is absolutely perfect.

## CHAPTER V.

1. That there is a vast difference between arguing from forced *fictions* <note>original: "Figments"</note> or *fancies* and from the natural *Ideas* of our own *Minds*. 2. That the *Idea* of a *Being* who is absolutely *Evil* does not imply necessary *Existence*, whether it signifies a *Being* that is absolutely *Imperfect*, 3. Or absolutely *Wicked*, 4. Or absolutely *Miserable*, 5. Or absolutely *Mischievous*. 6. That if by a *Being* absolutely *Mischievous* one meant only the *Infinite power* of doing hurt, this is *God*, whose absolute *Goodness* prevents the execution of it. 7. That the right *Method* of using our *Reason* is to proceed from what is plain and unsuspected to what is more obscure and suspicious. 8. That according to this *Method*, being assured first of the *Existence* of a *Being* absolutely *Perfect* from his *Idea*, we are thereby enabled to answer that *Impossibility* of *Existence* belongs to a *Being* who is either absolutely *Miserable* or absolutely *Mischievous*. 9. That the *Phenomena* <note>original: "Phænomena" — observable facts or events</note> of the *World* further prove the *impossibility* of the *Existence* of a *Being* absolutely *Mischievous*. 10. And that the *Counsels* and *Works* of *God* are not to be measured by the vain *Opinions* of *Men*.

1. As for those who admit that necessary *Existence* is included in the *Idea* of a *Being* who is absolutely *Perfect*, but want to show that our *Inference* from that—namely, *that this perfect Being does Exist*—is false and sophisticated because necessary *Existence* is contained in the *Idea* of a *Being* absolutely *Evil*, which we nevertheless will not admit to *Exist* (for, they say, that which is absolutely *Evil* is immutably and ever unavoidably such, and cannot but be so, and therefore it cannot but *Exist*, and has always *Existed*): To these people we answer, that we shall easily discover the great difference between such *arbitrary* and forced *fictions* and fancies as these, and the natural and consistent *Ideas* of our own *Mind*. We can do this if we look more carefully and curiously into the *Nature* of what these *Objectors* <note>original: "Objects"</note> have ventured to utter, and sift out what they themselves mean, or what must necessarily be understood by this *Idea* of a *Being* absolutely *Evil* which they have thus forged.

2. By the *Idea* of a *Being* absolutely *Evil*, one must mean either the *Idea* of a *Being* absolutely *Imperfect*, or absolutely *Wicked*, or absolutely *Miserable*, or absolutely *Mischievous*. Now, the *Idea* of what is absolutely *Imperfect* removes from it whatever—

It is as if all *Perfectness* were 1000; then this *Idea* removes from this absolutely *imperfect* being every unit of these 1000, allowing not so much as a unit or fraction of a unit—no, not even the possibility of them—to what is thus absolutely *imperfect*. So that what is absolutely *imperfect* is impossible to *Exist*. But *necessary Existence* is a *term* of *Perfection*, as was plainly demonstrated before.

3. The *Idea* of a Being absolutely *Wicked* removes from it all manner of *Goodness, Equity, Decorum, and Righteousness*. It implies a firm and immutable aversion of the Will from all these, and a settled and unchangeable purpose of doing things wickedly. However, it intimates nothing regarding either the *Necessity* or *Contingency* <note>original: "Contingency"; the quality of being possible but not certain to occur, or depending on something else.</note> of the *Existence* of the *Substance* of this Being; that being neither here nor there to its moral deformity, as is evidently plain at first sight.

4. The *Idea* of a Being absolutely *Miserable* is the *Idea* of a Being that sustains the fullest and most complete torments that are conceivable; and this must be in a knowing, passive, and reflexive Subject. Now, I say, this torture arises partly from the sense of present pain, and partly out of reflection on what it has suffered, and a full belief that it shall suffer thus eternally. This *miserable Being*, though but a *Creature*, is as perfectly tormented as it could possibly be if it necessarily existed of itself. For if it always existed—even if only contingently and dependently on another—the torture is equally perfect; and therefore *necessary Existence* is not included in the *Idea* of it.

Again, the Objector must prove that a Being wholly *Immaterial* can suffer any torture. Until he does so—it seeming more reasonable that it cannot—I shall flatly deny that it can. Therefore, I assert that a torturable Being is a *Spirit* incorporate <note>original: "Spirit incorporate"; a spirit joined to a physical body.</note>. I affirm also, as a most rational thing, that if this *Spirit* experienced such great pain that it were better for him not to exist at all than to be in it, that anguish would be so increased by its continuance (pain infinitely overpowering the vital vigor and outweighing the contents of life and sense) that it would die to the *Body* in which it is thus tormented. But if it is not in so ill a state as to change its condition of conjunction, and the torture proves tolerable, then *necessary Existence* would not be its misery, but rather some part of happiness. So, there can be no such thing as a Being absolutely *Miserable* in the world. For *Misery* racked up to the highest would make the thing cease to be. Just as a man cannot speak of an "absolutely big *Triangle*," for a *Circle* will always be bigger; or rather, no Figure can be absolutely big, because its nature is to be limited.

Thirdly, the *Idea* of a Being absolutely *Perfect* is composed of *Notions* of the same denomination, all of them in themselves establishing absolute *Perfection*. But the *Idea* of a Being absolutely *Miserable* is not compiled of *Notions* that establish absolute *Misery* in themselves. For what *Misery*, rather than good, is there in *necessary Existence*? Therefore, if we should contend that an inference from the *Idea* of a thing to its *necessary Existence* is only warrantable where the *Idea* consists of *Notions* of one denomination, the Objector must disprove that distinction.

Or, to speak more plainly, Absolutely *necessary Existence* and *Self-existence*...

existence is one and the same notion. But self-existence is the most high and perfect mode of existence that is conceivable, and therefore proper only to what is most absolutely perfect. Therefore, to transplant self-existence to so pitiful an *idea* as the *idea* of a "being absolutely miserable" is as absurd <note>original: "absonous"</note> and monstrous as to attach the head of a lion to the body of a snail. Indeed, it seems even more contradictory; for the lion-snail is merely a misplacing of physical body and figure, but this is the implantation of an inward property into the wrong subject—indeed, it places infinitely contrary properties in the same subject.

5. Fourthly and lastly, as for a "being absolutely mischievous," it seems indeed to include necessary and unavoidable existence as well as *omnipotence* and *omniscience*; otherwise, this *sovereign mischief* is not as full and absolute as our minds can conceive. These attributes, added to a stubborn and unchangeable desire or will to do all mischief possible for mischief's sake, fully complete the notion of this *absolutely mischievous* being.

But how false and unnatural this *idea* is, is evident in that it again forcibly ties together notions of a quite contrary nature: the greatest imperfection with the highest perfections. It joins the incommunicable attributes of God with a character that is perhaps worse than we can prove to exist in any devil; indeed, it joins qualities that seem to be a contradiction in any subject whatsoever.

Therefore, as I suggested before, if any man claims our argument to be a *sophism* <note>a clever but false argument intended to deceive</note>, and attempts to expose the fallacy by applying it to some other matter, he must exactly observe the laws of the argument in his imitation. He must construct an *idea* of notions that all agree with the same title, just as they perfectly do in the *idea* of a "being absolutely perfect"; for in that idea, there is no notion that does not represent the highest perfection.

But in this *idea* of a "being absolutely mischievous," there is nothing that of its own nature signifies mischief except for that wicked and malicious desire of doing mischief merely for mischief's sake. This is a degree of imperfection sunk into the borders of inconsistency and contradiction. Furthermore, to be able accurately to destroy all good whatsoever implies, on the other hand, an *omnipotence* in power and an *omniscience*. But what is omnipotently and absolutely mischievous must also destroy itself; just as an infinitely large triangle implies no triangle at all. So, this *idea* is not free from the entanglement of many various contradictions in its very conception.

6. But if by a "being absolutely mischievous" one meant a being that has the power and skill to do all mischief imaginable—and indeed far above all the imagination and thought of man—and to do so effectively and universally that nothing can possibly prevent him; this is indeed the Eternal God. He is necessarily of himself and precedes all things, and his actions can be limited by none but himself. But because He is that absolute and immutable *Good*, and full and pure Perfection, He cannot but include in His *idea* that precious attribute of *benignity* <note>kindness and well-wishing</note>. Therefore, acting according to His entire nature, He is not only *Good* himself, but, by the prerogative of His own Being, He keeps out such *mischievous sovereignties*...
