7. Therefore, to bring our answer to a conclusion, I say that we ought to use the natural method in this speculation that men who know how to use their faculties observe in all others: namely, to assent first to what is most simple, easy, and plain, and of which there can be no doubt that the concept is harmonious and consistent. Such is the *Idea of a Being absolutely Perfect*. This is no arbitrary or accidental fiction, nor a forced compilation of concepts that clash with one another, or which might be justly suspected (if not proven) to be incoherent and contradictory—such as, for example, a *walking tree*, or an *intelligent stone*, or the like. Instead, it is a concept wherein the ideas naturally and necessarily come together to complete the conception of a single title, being uniform and essential to it.

8. And then, what I contend for is this: that by attending to this natural *Idea of God*, or a *Being absolutely Perfect*, we unavoidably discover the necessity of *actual existence* as inseparable from him, because it is necessarily included in this *Idea of absolute perfection*. This is even more undeniably established in the final point of my argument, where I urge that either *impossibility, contingency, or necessity of actual existence* must belong to a *Being absolutely Perfect*. But since neither *impossibility* nor *contingency* <note>original: "Contingency"; the state of existing by chance or being able to not exist.</note> apply, it must be *necessity of actual existence*.

Therefore, being so well secured in this truth, I require the objector to bring his argument to this final and clearest framework. Let him also argue that either *impossibility, contingency, or necessity of actual existence* belongs to either a *Being absolutely miserable* or *absolutely mischievous*. I shall confidently answer: *impossibility of existence*. I will give him a further reason beyond what I suggested before regarding the inconsistency of the concepts themselves: it is also repugnant to the *existence of God*, whom we have already demonstrated to exist by attending to the natural and undistorted suggestions of our own faculties without any obstacle or doubt.

9. And to make our answer even more certain concerning a *Being absolutely mischievous*, it is most evident that he does not exist. Therefore, since he must exist by his own power if he exists at all, it is impossible that he should exist. That he does not exist is plain, because things would then be infinitely worse than they are, or not exist at all; whereas I dare say things are now as well as it is fit or possible for them to be, if we only had the wisdom to conceive or comprehend the whole counsel and purpose of *Providence*, and knew clearly and particularly what is past and what is to come.

### CHAPTER VI.
1. *That the sense of his argument from the Idea of God in its first position is not simply that the Idea is true, and that if God were, his existence would be necessary; but that this Idea, being true, exhibits to our mind an absolute necessary existence as belonging to Him.* 2. *That the Idea of the God of the Manichees <note>The Manicheans were a dualistic religious group who believed in two opposing powers: one perfectly good and one perfectly evil.</note> does not include in it necessary existence.* 3. *That to say that necessary existence included in the Idea of a Being absolutely perfect is only conditional, is a contradiction.* 4. *The second position of his argument is confirmed, and that by virtue of its form, the existence of the Manichean God cannot be concluded.* 5. *The convincing evidence of the third position of his argument, even in the judgment of his antagonist himself.* 6. *That the force of his argument in the fourth and last position is not that we conceive the Idea of Matter without necessary existence; but that, look as closely as we can, we find no necessary existence included therein, as we do in the Idea of God.* 7. *That the faculties of our mind, to which he perpetually appeals, are to be assumed, not proved, to be true.*

1. AND now, having thus clearly satisfied the objection taken from the *Idea of a Being absolutely Evil*, it will be easy to turn back the edge of any argument of a similar nature, no matter how skillfully and cunningly it is directed against us. Such as that which I received from an ingenious hand, which, because it seems very witty to me as well as invincible to the objector, I shall propose in his own words; the tenor of which runs thus:

*If a man may have a true Idea or Notion of that which is not—yes, and of that which is not and yet would necessarily be if it were—then your argument for the existence of God, based on necessary existence being comprehended in his Idea or Notion, is inconclusive. How you can deny this argument, I cannot possibly conceive, since the substance of your first argument from the Idea of God is contained therein in its first position.*

*But a man may have a true Notion of that which is not—yes, and of that which is not and yet would necessarily be if it were; as, for instance, of the Evil God of the Manichees.*

<margin>Antidote, Book 1. chapter 8. sections 1, 2.</margin>But I answer briefly to the proposition thus: That it does not reach our case. This is because we argue God does exist, not because the *Idea* of him is true and that if he did exist he would necessarily exist (for conditional necessary existence, being less perfect than absolute necessary existence, cannot belong to a *Being absolutely Perfect*); but because this true *Idea*, without any *If* or *And*, suggests to our natural faculties that necessary existence is involved in his *Idea* alone. Since the same does not happen in any other *Idea* besides, without any more ado, he does of himself absolutely and really exist.

To the premise <note>original: "Assumption"; a logical term referring to the second part of a syllogism.</note> I answer that the *Manichaean God*, if he could exist at all, would do so necessarily; and my reason is that God would never create such a foul monster.

2. But if you still urge that the *Idea* of this *Evil God* of the *Manichaeans* includes *necessary existence* within it—it being the notion of a "god," yet he does not exist—and that therefore the true God cannot be proved to exist simply because *necessary existence* is involved in his *Idea*; I further answer: The notion of the *Manichaean God* does not naturally include *necessary existence* because it is not the notion of a Being *absolutely Perfect*. The notion of an *Evil God* is a mere forced or accidental fiction <note>original: "fortuitous Figment"</note>, and makes no better sense than a *Wooden God* <note>An idol made of wood; the author argues that such a concept is a contradiction in terms because a true God cannot be a lifeless object.</note>, whose *Idea* implies not *necessary existence*, but an *impossibility of existence*.

<margin>*Antidote*, Book 1, chapter 8, section 3.</margin>
3. But the objector proceeds, and we must follow his movements. However, before he reaches the second position of our argument, he takes notice of my charge: I accuse all those of self-contradiction who acknowledge that *necessary existence* is contained in the *Idea of God* (or a Being *absolutely Perfect*), signifying that *necessary existence* belongs to him, and yet take it back again by adding, "*If he exists at all*." I answer that my charge is true. For to say that *necessary existence* belongs to a Being, while simultaneously claiming he may not exist after all, is to admit a contradiction. In doing this, our mental faculties acknowledge the same thing to be both *necessary* and *contingent*—that is, that it "cannot but be" and yet "it may not be." If that is not a contradiction in this case, I do not know what is; for nothing less than *absolutely necessary existence* must be comprised in the Idea of a Being *absolutely perfect*.

<margin>*Antidote*, Book 1, chapter 8, section 4.</margin>
4. But the argument will appear even clearer in its second position. For if there is any fraud or fallacy, it lies in this term, *Necessary*, which I have truly explained (and it is not denied) to signify nothing else but an inseparable connection between the *Subject* and the *Predicate*. Therefore, since *existence* has an inseparable connection with God, it must follow that this axiom—*God exists*—is eternally and immutably true. But to reply here, "*If he did exist*," is to insinuate that despite this, he may not exist. This is the same as saying that what is immutably true is *not* immutably true, which is a palpable contradiction.

But the objector here flies for aid to the God of the Manichaeans, asking me to substitute the *Manichaean God* in place of the God whose *existence* I want to prove, so that I might see my own sophism <note>A clever but false argument.</note>. Well, if it is not idolatry, let us place him there; but you may understand from what I said before how puny <note>original: "shrimpish"</note> and unfit he is to fill this place. The *Manichaean God* no more implies *necessary existence* in his notion than a *Wooden God* does; in fact, he rather implies the *impossibility* of existence. For the notion of *God* is the same: a Being *absolutely Perfect*, which must involve the most absolute *goodness* possible. Now, bring the *Manichaean God* into view and let us look at his description: *He is an evil that is absolutely good*. This, as I said before, is in my opinion far worse sense than a *Wooden God*, and therefore *impossibility*, and not *necessity of existence*, is contained in his *Idea*.

Since I argue that either *Impossibility*, *Contingency*, or *Necessity of Actual Existence* belongs to a *Being absolutely Perfect*, he admits here that the *Manichaean God* <note>The Manichaeans were an ancient religious group who believed in two equal and opposing powers: one perfectly good and one perfectly evil. But afterward, having reconsidered, he notices that if God does not exist, it is impossible for Him to exist; and therefore, I say, it is only fair that we expect the person who denies God’s existence to prove His Being impossible—especially since the force of our argument so necessarily pushes him to that point. In my opinion, however, he would do better to save his effort than to venture upon such a pointless undertaking. He may remember that the *Idea of this Being absolutely Perfect* is so framed that, in the judgment of any man who has the use of his mental faculties, there is no contradiction or impossibility within it, nor the least shadow of cause for suspicion or hesitation. Furthermore, since the "impossibility of existing" is the most imperfect <term>relation <note>original: "σχέσις" (schesis); a Greek term meaning the state, relation, or connection one thing has to another.</note></term> that any being can have toward existence, it must be an outrageous inconsistency to attribute it to a *Being absolutely Perfect*. Such a state naturally and undeniably belongs to a *Being absolutely Imperfect*, as has been noted before.

Therefore, if either the doubting or stubborn *Atheist* says the *Existence of God* is impossible, that will not prove any weakness or vanity in my argument, but rather reckless boldness and blind insolence in the man who offers such an irrational answer.

6. But I answer: This does not address the strength of our argument. No matter how carefully and skillfully you look into the *Idea of Matter*, you can discover no such property as *necessity of existence* within it. And then again, the weight of my reasoning lies mainly in this: that "necessity of *Self-existence*" is so plainly and unavoidably discoverable in the *Idea of a Being absolutely Perfect*, but not at all discernible in the *Idea of Matter*. We clearly violate our own faculties when we acknowledge *Self-existence* in *Matter* (even though no faculty informs us it is so) while denying it in *God* (even though the *Idea of God* so clearly informs us that *necessary Self-existence belongs to Him*). So, all I contend for is this: that he who denies a God goes against the light of his natural faculties, to which I constantly appeal.

7. But if you still say, "Perhaps our faculties are deceptive," I reply that this might be true if there were no God by whom we were made. If that were the case, we would be exactly as we find ourselves and could look no further; nor could we assure ourselves that we were not of such a nature as to be then mistaken...

## CHAPTER VII.

1. *That the necessity of existence which seems to be included in the idea of space is really the same necessity that presents itself to our minds in the more complete and perfect idea of God.* 2. *That the same reasoning applies to eternal duration, whose immediate subject is God, not matter.* 3. *That space is merely the possibility of matter, measurable only in the same way that many different possible species of things are countable.* 4. *That distance is not a physical property of anything, but only a conceptual one.* 5. *That the distance between bodies is only a lack of physical contact, measurable by parts, just as other absences of qualities are measured by degrees.* 6. *That if empty space remains a real thing after matter is removed, it is actually that necessary Being represented by the idea of God.* 7. *That self-existence and contingency are terms inconsistent with each other.*

2. Now, there is the same logic regarding *Time* (by *Time* I mean *Duration*) as there is for *Space*. For we cannot imagine anything other than a continuous *Duration* that has no beginning or interruption. Anyone would say it is nonsense for there to be such a necessary duration when there is no real Essence that must, of itself, always exist and endure forever. To whom or to what, then, does this eternal, uninterrupted, and never-fading duration belong? No Philosopher can answer more appropriately than the holy *Psalmist*: *From everlasting to everlasting, you are God.* Therefore, I say that those unavoidable mental images of the necessity of an *Infinite Space*, as they call it, and *Eternal Duration*, are not proofs of *Self-existent Matter*, but rather faint indications of the *necessary existence of God*.

3. There is also another way of answering this objection: the mental image of *Space* is not the image of any real thing, but only of the vast and immense capacity for the potentiality of *Matter*. We cannot free our minds from this concept, but must necessarily acknowledge that there is indeed such a possibility for Matter to be measured upward, downward, and in every direction to infinity <note>original: "in infinitum"</note>, whether this physical *Matter* were actually there or not. Even though this potentiality of *Matter* or *Space* can be measured by furlongs, miles, or similar units, it implies a real Essence or Being no more than when a person counts up various types of *possibilities*; the count or number of them does not prove they actually exist.

4. But if they push us further, arguing that there would be a real distance even in *Space* devoid of *Matter*—for example, if three balls of brass or steel were placed together in this empty *Space*, it is utterly unimaginable that there would not be a triangular distance between them—it may be answered that *Distance* is not a real or *physical* property of a thing, but only a conceptual one <note>original: "notional"</note>. This is because more or less distance can be attributed to an object even when nothing at all has been done to the object itself. For instance, suppose one of the balls mentioned was initially an inch away from another; this distance between them could be increased to many miles, and yet one of the balls might not be touched or moved at all, even though its distance from the other has increased.

5. But if they continue to push us, contending that this distance must be some *real* thing because it keeps those balls apart—supposing two of them are two miles apart in empty *Space*, and one lies in the middle; if the ball two miles away were to reach the other as quickly as the one only one mile away, it would have to move with double the speed <note>original: "celerity"</note> to complete its journey. I answer briefly: *Distance* is nothing else but the lack of *physical contact* <note>original: "privation of tactual union"</note>. The greater the distance, the greater the lack of contact; and the greater that lack, the more work must be done to regain the former *positive* condition of touching. This lack of *physical contact* is measured by parts, just as the lack of other qualities is measured by degrees. 6. But if this does not satisfy you, it does no harm to our argument. For example, if Matter existed *of itself*, it is clear that it exists necessarily and could not have been otherwise. For *Self-existence* prevents all obstacles by which a thing might have been in danger of failing to actually exist.

And as for God, it is equally clear that it is either impossible for him to exist, or else he exists of himself. And if he exists of himself, his existence is unavoidable and necessary—as anyone must acknowledge who understands the terms they venture to pronounce.

# CHAP. VIII.

-> 1. *That the Idea of God is a natural and indelible Notion in the Soul of Man.* 2. *That even if there were some small obscurity in the Notion, it does not prevent it from being natural.* 3. *That the Politician's abuse of the notion of God and Religion proves them to be his own invention no more than natural affection, the love of Honor, or Liberty are; all of which he abuses in the same way.* 4. *A twofold Answer to an Objection concerning God's implanting his Idea in us through deliberate counsel or design.* <-

All the *Attributes* of this Idea are consistent with the general title of *Perfection* to which they belong, and this is undoubtedly and immutably true.

# An Appendix to the foregoing Antidote. CHAP. VIII.

A part of the world never had any such *Idea*; and that those who have had it, have blotted it out of their souls; and those who have it most deeply imprinted upon them are not as sure of it as that two and two make four. I briefly answer that all people always have had, and still have, this *Idea* in their souls; it is no more in their power to blot it out than it is to blow out the sun with a pair of bellows. Interest, the distraction of their minds by other matters, or the distemper of the body caused by sensuality or melancholy, may hinder the actual contemplation or discovery of this *Idea* in the mind, but it cannot radically erase it.

2. Regarding the last claim—that it is not as clear as "two and two make four"—even if that were true, it does not invalidate our position. The truth we are contending for is natural and undeniable. Many truths that fall short of that level of ease, or at least clarity, must nonetheless be acknowledged as naturally and undeniably true.

3. But now to come closer to the matter at hand, and that major suspicion held by *Atheists*: that this notion of a God is only a crafty fiction created by *Politicians* <note>original: "Politicians" — in this context, the author refers to cynical power-seekers or "statists" who use social engineering to control the public</note>, by which they intend to keep the people in obedience, and that it is they who, through their cunning and power, have impressed this character upon the minds of men. I answer that what is already naturally within man, they cannot put there. They may, I confess, make a *Political* use of it; indeed, it is as dreadful and detestable as it is true that mere statesmen have no conscience about prostituting the most sacred things for their own lowly, trivial designs. But to argue, therefore, that there is no such thing as *Religion* or a *God*—simply because they so abominably abuse the acknowledgment of them for *political* purposes—is as irrational as if we should argue that there is no natural self-love, no love of wife and children, and no desire for liberty, riches, or honor except for what *politicians* and statesmen have placed into the hearts of men. Because by applying themselves skillfully to these existing affections, they lead and manipulate the people as they please; and by inflaming their spirits with plausible speeches, they often hurry them into the hazard of losing the very capacity to enjoy those hopes that were so fairly and fully spread out before them.

4. The most significant objection I can imagine being made against our second argument (derived from the *Idea of God* as it exists within our soul) is this: that this *Idea* is such a plain and obvious truth that it must exist in any *intellectual* subject. Therefore, we cannot easily argue (as we did in the ninth chapter of our first book) that this *Idea* in our soul was placed there specifically so that we might come to the knowledge of our Maker; for if it is there by necessity, then it is not there by specific counsel or purpose.

But to this I answer, first: that our bodies might have been of such a frame that our minds were forever hindered or diverted from attending to this *Idea*, even though it could not possibly be absent from the soul itself.

And in the second place: it is no inconvenience for us to acknowledge that the *Idea of God* is such that no *intellectual* being can be conceived without it—that is, one cannot imagine a being of an *intellectual* nature that does not necessarily acknowledge, upon due consideration, that this *Idea* is

# CHAP. IX.

1. *That the natural structure of Conscience is such that it suggests fears and hopes which imply that there is a God. 2. That the ridiculous nature of various religions is not any proof that being affected by religion is not an innate faculty of the human soul.*

1. THE strength of my argument from *Natural Conscience* is this: that people naturally fear *misfortunes* and *hope for success* according to how they behave. But I must confess that this proof or reason is the most slippery <note>original: "lubricous"</note> and unmanageable of any that I have used, as it is so clearly vulnerable <note>original: "obnoxious"</note> to the objection or evasion that the *fears and hopes of conscience* do not come from any *natural knowledge* of God, but from the power of *education* (upbringing), which is like a "second nature." Now, since there is hardly any nation that has not awed its children with some basic elements or other of religion, we are not able to provide a pure example that would fitly demonstrate the validity of our argument; we can only help ourselves by using a hypothetical case.

We will therefore suppose a man of an ordinary sort (for I admit that some people are born so enormously deformed in their intellect <note>original: "ingeny"</note> or inward nature that a man can no more judge human intellectual or moral properties by them than he can judge the normal shape of a body by a *deformed growth* <note>original: "Mole"</note> or a *biological monster*) who has not had any principles of religion, or explicit or formal <note>original: "Catechistical"</note> doctrine of a God, drilled into him. Suppose he is only of such a temperament (whether by nature or education, it is all the same) that he deems some things fit and right to be done, and others unfit and unjust. For what is *just and unjust, good and evil, lovable and detestable* <note>original: "amiable and execrable"</note> is—according to the judgment of some—more obvious and plain than the *existence of a Deity*. I say, suppose such a man should commit what he considers very heinous and abominable crimes—such as *murdering his father or mother, incest with his sister, betraying his truest friends*, or the like—and should not be punished by the hand of the law (having done these things so cunningly that they escaped its notice). But suppose that immediately thereafter he is continually unfortunate: his barns and haystacks are burned by lightning from heaven, his cattle die in his fields, and he himself is afterward tormented with the most offensive <note>original: "noisome"</note> and painful diseases. Although all of these things happen to many in the natural course of life, I appeal to anyone: do you think it at all probable that this man would not naturally and unavoidably be so touched in his conscience that he would suspect these misfortunes fell upon him as a *punishment* from some invisible Power or Divine hand that orders all things justly?

An Appendix to the preceding Antidote. CHAPTER 10.

Regarding religious veneration—namely, the many ridiculous religions in the world. From this, it is inferred that the human mind has no innate principle of *religion* at all, but is moldable into any shape or form of worship that the supreme power in every country chooses to propose. I answer this as follows:

First, if every religious person would look upon foreign religions with the same respectful openness and solemn seriousness that they do their own, they might find them more worthy of pity for their falsehood than laughter for their ridiculousness. However, it no more follows that all religions are false because so many are, than it follows that no philosophical opinions are true because so many are false.

Second, the multitude of *various* and (if you will) *foolish* <note>original: "fond"</note> *religions* in the world—into which the nations of the earth are moldable—is actually better for our argument, no matter how ridiculous they are. We contend that *religion* is a *natural property* of man. The necessity of it being part of our nature is more clearly proven by this: humans can no more be without *religion* than *matter* can be without *shape* <note>original: "Figure"</note>. Although few parts of matter have the good fortune to be framed into something *regular* or *orderly* <note>original: "Ordinate"</note>, or to have any beauty or proportion in their shape, yet break the *matter* however you will, it will still take some shape or another.

<meta>This page continues the "Appendix to the preceding Antidote." The author is arguing against the materialist view—specifically the ideas of René Descartes—that the soul or "common sense" is merely a physical part of the brain called the pineal gland.</meta>

# CHAPTER 10. An Appendix to the preceding Antidote.

1. ...conveniently placed near the center of the **brain**; and if the transmission of motions which act upon the organs did not have some such single part to terminate in, it is conceived by some (though I suspect more cleverly than solidly) that because these outward organs of sense are two, the objects would seem to be two as well—which is contrary to experience.

But though the **Conarion** <term>The pineal gland; René Descartes argued this was the seat of the soul.</term> may be the organ of various perceptions from physical objects, and the tent or pavilion where the soul is chiefly seated, we utterly deny that without an **immaterial** inhabitant, this **arbitrary motion** <note>original: "arbitrarious Motion"; voluntary movement guided by will.</note> which we are conscious of could be performed in us or by us at all. For if we attend to the condition of our own natures, we cannot help but acknowledge that whatever **moves** our body thus **arbitrarily** does not only **perceive** sensible objects, but also **remembers**, and has a power of free imagination and of **reason**.

2. And to begin with the first of these: I say that mere **perception** of external objects seems incompatible with the **Conarion**. Because it is of a similar nature to the rest of the **brain**, it is not only divisible but, in a way, actually divided into particles; otherwise, it could not be as soft as it is (though it is somewhat harder than the rest of the **brain**). Now I say, because the images of sensible objects spread across a certain space on the surface of the **Conarion** which they hit, one part of the **Conarion** has the **perception**, for instance, of the **head** of a man, another of a **leg**, a third of an **arm**, and a fourth of his **chest**. Therefore, even if we should admit that every particle of such a space on the **Conarion** may perceive such a **part** of a man, there is nothing to perceive the **whole man**, unless you say they communicate their perceptions to one another. But this communication seems impossible; for if **perception** occurs by impression from the external object, no particle in the **Conarion** shall perceive any part of the object except that which it receives an impression from. But if you still say that every part of the object presses upon every part of the **Conarion** where the image is, it will be utterly impossible for the whole image not to be confused, and the distinctness of colors would be lost, especially in smaller objects.

3. Now, regarding the faculty of **remembering** things: we prove that it cannot be in the **Conarion** in this way. It is plain that **memory**, which is the standing seal or impression of external objects, is not there. For if it were, it would spoil the representation of things **present**, or rather, subsequent objects would be sure to deface all former impressions whatsoever. But if you say that **memory** is in the **brain**, but **reminiscence** <note>The intentional act of recalling a memory.</note> is in the **Conarion**, I answer: these impressions or signatures made by outward objects in the **brain** must also of necessity be wiped out <note>original: "obliterated"</note> by subsequent impressions. For whether these images or impressions consist of a certain posture or motion of the **flexible fibers** <note>original: "Plicatile Fibres"; the tiny threads thought to make up brain matter.</note> or subtle threads of which the **brain** consists, it is evident that they cannot help but be canceled and erased by the thousands of objects that invade our senses daily, which must necessarily displace them or give them a new motion different from what they had before.

But suppose **memory** were thus sealed upon the **brain** and transmitted its image through the **animal spirits** <note>Fluid or "vapors" believed to flow through the nerves to transmit signals.</note> in the cavities <note>original: "ventricles"</note> of the brain, as an outward...

3. ...Object sends its images <note>original: "species"; in early modern science, these were the "visible forms" or qualities thought to be transmitted from an object to the senses.</note> through the air to the eye; since **perception** is caused by an impression, and that impression was lost in the **Conarion** <term>The pineal gland; then thought to be the seat of the soul.</term> even though it was retained in the **brain**, how can the **Conarion** ever say that it had any such impression before? For once the impression is wiped out, it is as if it never existed, and therefore the gland can never remember that it had it. Besides, the **perception** of this image in the **brain** is as incompatible with the **Conarion** as the **perception** of any external object, a point upon which we have already insisted.

4. And thirdly, regarding the power of free **imagination**, by which the **Conarion** is supposed to invent the various forms or shapes of things which it never saw; I ask, is it the thin membrane, or the inward and somewhat soft and fuzzy pulp it contains, that raises and represents these arbitrary inventions and fantasies <note>original: "Figments and Chimeras"</note> to itself? And then, what part or particle of either of them can perform these impressive feats? And (what is most important) since these representations are physical, is it not necessary for the **Conarion** to be affected or impressed just as it is by external physical objects? 

Then I ask how this passive, soft substance should be able to impress or mark itself, or how one part of this body should be able to act upon another for this purpose? Furthermore, since there is also a **memory** of these invented impressions, how can they be stamped upon the **brain**, which is the seat of **memory**? For even if we admit that the **Conarion** imitates the way external objects make impressions when it invents images of its own, if it then presses these images upon the **brain**, it would be like using the impression of a seal on a hard material to stamp something softer; in that case, the two impressions will be notoriously different, as the parts that protrude in the first will be recessed in the second.

5. Fourthly, concerning **Reason**: besides the fact that it is obvious when we use reason that we comprehend at once the images or mental phantasms of not only different but contrary things in the very same part or particle of the **Conarion**—for if they are in different parts, what shall judge between them both?—as when, for example, we conclude "hot is not cold," or "a crooked line is not a straight line," which cannot be conceived without a confusion of both impressions. There is also another consideration of **notions** that are plainly immaterial, which do not impress themselves upon the **Conarion**, nor any part of the **brain**, nor on the **outer organs** from sensible objects, but are our own innate **conceptions** used in the contemplation of things. Such are various **logical**, **metaphysical**, and **mathematical notions**, as I have proved elsewhere. Therefore, it seems altogether incredible that the **Conarion**, being such a gross and tangible body as it is, should have any notions or conceptions that are not physical and conveyed to it from material objects from the outside.

6. But fifthly and lastly, it is very difficult to conceive how the **Conarion**, if it were capable of sense and perception, should—being only a mere pulpy, protruding knob—be able by its tilts or jolts to drive the **animal spirits** <term>In early medicine, these were refined fluids or gases thought to travel through the nerves to cause motion.</term> so precisely as to never miss the "key" that leads to the movement of the smallest joint of our body. How could it drive them in so forcibly and smartly as to enable us to strike such fierce blows as we see men do, especially those...

### CHAPTER X. An Appendix to the foregoing Antidote.

Since **animal spirits** <term>Subtle, fluid particles then believed to transmit sensory information and movement through the nerves.</term> are so thin and fluid, and the **Conarion** <term>The pineal gland; then thought to be the seat of the soul.</term> is so broad and blunt, it leads to two problems. First, we can imagine that the spirits—especially when only faintly struck by the **Conarion** (as they likely are and certainly sometimes must be)—would simply swirl gently throughout the cavities <note>original: "ventricles"</note> of the **brain**. They would not be directed toward any specific "key" or channel that leads to the **muscle** of a particular joint of the body. Second, if the impulse from the **Conarion** were strong enough to drive the **spirits** forward, that "wind" would force open many doors at once. Yet, we see that we can move a single finger or toe with significant force while the rest of our body remains still.

We might also add that it is difficult to imagine how this **pineal gland** <note>original: "Pineal Glandula"</note> could move itself spontaneously without **muscles** and **spirits**, or some similar mechanical setup. And if it does move itself, why would **Nature** have taken such great care to include **muscles** and **animal spirits** in the structure of **animals**? If it does *not* move itself, we must look further for the **source of motion** and ask what moves the **animal spirits** that are supposed to move the **Conarion**. In the study of **physical motion** <note>original: "Motion corporeal"</note>, it is an accepted **maxim** <note>original: "Maxime"</note> that **whatever is moved, is moved by another** <note>original: *Quicquid movetur, ab alio movetur*</note>. Thus, it is demonstrable in every way that the first principle of our voluntary motion is not—and cannot be—located in any part of our body. Instead, it must reside in a substance entirely distinct from the body, which people usually call the **Soul**.

7. Furthermore, the strength of our argument is not weakened by the claim some make that our reasoning is flawed <note>original: "Sophistical"</note> because it would also prove that **animals** <note>original: "Beasts"</note> have an **immaterial substance** <note>original: "Incorporeal substance"</note> just as **humans** do.

To this, I first answer that these arguments prove absolutely that there is an **immaterial soul** in **humans** because we are certain humans perform actions that clearly require such a nature. We are not so certain about what happens within **animals**. Very knowledgeable men with a more mechanical **disposition** <note>original: "Genius"</note> have at least doubted whether **animals** have any **thought** <note>original: "Cogitation"</note> at all. However, these same men have stated they are sure that if animals *did* think, they would also need to have **immaterial souls** distinct from their **bodies**.

Secondly, even if we admit that our arguments prove there are **souls** in **animals** <note>original: "Brutes"</note> distinct from their bodies, is this any different from what all **philosophers** and **scholars** <note>original: "School-men"</note> have acknowledged, either explicitly or implicitly, when they held the theory of **substantial forms**? <term>A philosophical concept suggesting that the "form" or "soul" of a thing gives it its essential properties.</term> But if these souls are **immaterial**, some say they must also be **immortal**, which they find ridiculous. If by **immortal** they mean "indestructible," just as **matter** is, why shouldn't they be as indestructible as matter itself? This active substance of the **soul**—even the soul of an **animal**—is a more noble **essence** and shares more in its **Creator’s** <note>original: "Makers"</note> perfection than dull, easily scattered **matter**.

However, if by **immortality** they mean the potential for eternal life and happiness after the death of the body, that is an absurd conclusion of their own making. We are happy to let the authors of that idea laugh at it; it does not affect us or our current argument. For we believe that the **soul** of an **animal** may be of such a nature that it can only be active within a **physical body**. Once outside the body, it may have neither sense nor perception of anything, so that, for all intents and purposes, it utterly perishes.

### CHAPTER X. An Appendix to the foregoing Antidote.

8. There is an objection of greater significance: since there are properties that must be acknowledged to exist in a **body** or **matter**, and yet these properties imply strange contradictions in how we conceive of them—for example, that complicated property of **divisibility**, which must result in either finite points or go on **to infinity** <note>original: *in infinitum*</note>, both of which confuse our imagination when we think of them—why may we not acknowledge that a **body** may also have **sense** and **understanding**, even though it seems ever so contradictory when considered closely? 

But I answer: this argument is very fallacious <note>original: "Sophistical"</note>, because by the same logic we should admit that the head of an **onion** understands and perceives as well as the **pineal gland** <term>Conarion</term> in a human. For you can bring no stronger argument against the onion than that it is contradictory and offensive to reason for it to be so. But you will reply that we plainly see that some part of the human body must have **sense** and **understanding** in it, but we perceive no such thing in an onion. But I ask: by what faculty do we perceive this? If you answer, "Our own senses tell us so," I say that our own senses, if we did not correct them, would confidently suggest to us that our **finger feels** and our **eye sees**; whereas it is plain they do not. For the very same thing that feels and sees also moves our body; but neither our eye nor our finger moves the body, and therefore they neither feel nor see.

And yet without our **eye** we cannot see in this state of union [of soul and body], just as without the proper structure and condition of our **brain** we cannot well understand. But it no more follows from this that the **brain understands**, rather than **something distinct from it**, than it follows that the **eye sees**. Therefore it is apparent that there is no faculty within us that can clearly inform us that any part of our body is endowed with **sense** and **understanding**.

From this we see the great difference between admitting the **divisibility** of matter (however complicated that notion may be) and admitting **sense** and **understanding** in a **body** (which actually brings more confusion than the former, if looked into very accurately). This is because we are fully assured by **sense**, and I may say by **reason** too, that **matter is divisible**; but no faculty at all can claim to assure us that a **body** is capable of either **sense** or **reason**.

9. But there seems to be an even worse objection still remaining, which is this: that though we have clearly proved the impossibility of there being either **sense**, **understanding**, or **spontaneous motion** in **matter** or a **body**, we are no closer to the truth. For similar difficulties may be raised against there being any **sense** or **understanding** in a **spirit**, since a **spirit** must be **extended**, and if extended it must be **divisible**, and if divisible it must be **incapable of sense or understanding**, just as we argued before against **matter**.

But to this I answer: If by **extension** one means a **side-by-side placement of parts** <note>original: "Juxta-position of parts"</note>, or placing them one by another as it is in **matter**, I utterly deny that a **spirit** is **extended** in this sense at all. But if you mean only a certain **amplitude of presence**—that it can be present in every part of a given amount of **matter** at once—I say it **is extended**. However, this kind of **extension** does not imply any **divisibility** in the substance extended in this way. For the **side-by-side placement of parts**, **impenetrability**, and **divisibility** go together; and therefore where the

9. But when I speak of *Indivisibility*, so that the *imagination* does not create new troubles for herself, I do not mean the kind of *indivisibility* imagined in a mathematical point; rather, I mean what we imagine in a *sphere* of light created from a single glowing point or radiant *center*. For that *sphere* or *orb* of light, although it is in some sense *extended*, is truly *indivisible*, assuming the *center* is so. There is no imaginable way to tear apart <note>original: "discerp"</note> or separate any single ray from this *orb* and keep it separate by itself, disconnected from the *center*.

10. Now, to slightly flip the properties of this glowing *orb* when we apply it to a *soul* or *spirit*: just as any change in the radiant *center* necessarily affects every part of the *orb*—for instance, if it became redder, everything would be redder; if dimmer, everything dimmer, and so on—there is also a unity and indivisibility between the outer parts (if I may call them that) of a *spirit* or *soul* and their innermost *center*. If any of these outer parts are affected, the *center* of life is necessarily affected as well. When these outer parts of the *soul* are affected by the parts of an *object* exactly as they are, the inward *center* receives everything with those same details. Thus, it necessarily possesses the complete and clear images of things from the outside, even though they are gathered into such a small space and exist within the very center of this *spiritual substance*.

I used this *symbolic representation* before, and I cannot devise <note>original: "excogitate"</note> anything that better illustrates the *nature of a spirit*. It implies a power of receiving many specific shapes into one indivisible *principle of sense*, where all are perfectly united into one *subject* and yet distinctly represented. This cannot be performed by the *pineal gland* <term>Conarion</term> itself, as I have demonstrated; therefore, it follows that this process must belong to a *soul*, whose primary *seat* of perception may perhaps be located there.

11. But if anyone takes advantage of our attempt to help (or at least satisfy) his *imagination* through this *symbolic representation* by imagining this *center of the soul* as merely some dull, divisible point in *matter*, and of no greater power—or by thinking its vital or willful *extension* implies that its parts are as divisible and separable as a *body*—to prevent such petty arguments, we will set aside those thorny difficulties <note>original: "spinosities"</note> regarding the *extension* or *indivisibility* of a *soul* or *spirit* and conclude briefly like this:

The many contradictions and inconsistencies we find in the nature of *matter*—showing it is unable to either think or move itself spontaneously—assure us that these operations do not belong to it, but to some other *substance*. Therefore, since we find these operations within ourselves, it is obvious that we have an *immaterial being* within us that is truly distinct from the *body*, which we commonly call a *soul*. While contemplating the soul's pure *essence* may puzzle us, the *properties* we find that are incompatible with a *body* inform us enough about her different *nature*. For it is clear she is a *substance* endowed with the power of *thought* <note>original: "cogitation"</note> (that is, of perceiving and thinking about *objects*), as well as the power of penetrating and spontaneously moving a *body*. These *properties* are as essential to her...

## CHAPTER XI.

1. *That Subtlety is not inconsistent with the strongest Truth.* 2. *That the subordinate usefulness of things in the world are in the things themselves, not merely in our Fancy.* <note>original: "Phanſy"</note> 3. *That the difficulty of obtaining such useful commodities is rather an Argument for Providence than against it.* 4. *That Beauty is no necessary Result from the mere Motion of Matter.* 5. *That it is an intellectual Object, not noticed by Brutes.* <note>The author uses "Brutes" to refer to non-human animals, which he believes lack the capacity for aesthetic appreciation.</note> 6. *That the preying of Animals one upon another is very well consistent with the Goodness of the First Cause.* <note>The "First Cause" is a philosophical term for God.</note> 7. *As also the Creation of offensive Animals, there being curbs and correctives to their increase.* 8. *That the immediate Matter of the Fetus is homogeneous.* <note>original: "homogeneal"</note> 9. *That the notion of the Vital Principles* <note>original: "Archei" (Latin), referring to the internal forces that govern the growth and function of living organisms</note> *or Seminal forms is no such intricate Speculation.*

1. WE have now gone through all the Objections against the First Book of our *Antidote*; at which if the more coarsely complexioned <note>meaning those with a less refined or more materialistic mindset</note>, so they may still seem to have something further to object, shall scoffingly cavil, as if we had used over-much *subtlety* in the management of our Arguments, I can only advise <note>original: "advertiſe"</note> them of this: That *Subtlety* is as consistent with *Truth* as the most coarse *Theories*; as is manifest in many *Mathematical Speculations*, than which there is nothing more certain nor undeniable to the Reason of Man. But that the coherence of Notions that are subtle in themselves should be as easily plain and conspicuous as the broad Objects of *Sense*, is a very incongruous conceit <note>an "incongruous conceit" is a nonsensical or ill-fitting idea</note>, and can be the expectation of none but those who are utterly unskilled in the nature of such like contemplations.

But the defense of our Second Book will be not only shorter, but less obscure, our Arguments there for the most part being such that even the unlearned can judge of them, and few of them but so evidently convincing <note>original: "convictive"</note> that there can be nothing material alleged against them. But such Objections as there are I shall briefly set down and answer.

2. And the first is made against our reasoning for Providence from the excellent *Usefulness* of *Stones, Timber, Metals, the Magnet, etc.* For those long and subordinate chains <note>original: "concatenations"</note> of instrumental usefulness of such things, say they, is but our fancy, no design of any *First Cause*. And how easy a thing is it for the wit of Man to bring things together that are of a distant nature in themselves, and to imagine many *Series of means and ends* in matters that have no dependence one of another but what he himself makes? But I answer, that the several *Useful dependencies* of various matters of this kind we only find them, *not make them*. For whether we think of it or no, it is for example manifest that *Fuel* is good to continue *Fire*, and *Fire* to melt *Metals*, and *Metals* to make *Instruments*,

...instruments, to build ships or houses, and so on. Therefore, since it is true that there is such a subordinate *usefulness* in the things themselves that are provided for us, it is only reasonable for us to attribute it to a Cause that was aware of the *usefulness* and *utility* <note>original: "Serviceableness"</note> of its own works.

3. Nor should we complain <note>original: "cavil"</note> because these *useful* things—such as *stones*, *metals*, *coals*, and the like—must be obtained with so much labor, when people might prefer to be released from such drudgery so they could have more time to contemplate the world, seek after God, and exercise the higher faculties of human nature. For we see plainly that in the fallen state of humanity <note>original: "lapsed condition of Man," referring to the theological concept of the Fall of Adam</note>, *idleness* does not encourage virtue or piety, but rather fosters animalistic behavior <note>original: "beastliness"</note> and indulgence in the senses. Furthermore, few people have a mind so *contemplative* <note>original: "Speculative"</note> that they can find great pleasure in meditations that would justify leaving a more *practical* and hardworking life—a life which, in itself, does not prevent anyone from being pious and honest, as no calling does. Therefore, the fact that for most people all *useful* things are hard to come by is actually an argument for *Providence*; it shows that the Cause that framed the Earth knew beforehand what the nature of earthly man would be.

4. The second objection is against our argument from the *beauty* of *plants*, which I maintain originates from an *intelligent Cause* <note>original: "Intellectual Cause"</note>, because *beauty* itself is an object perceived by the intellect. However, two things are objected to this. First, that *beauty* is a necessary result of the mere motion of *matter*. Second, that it is not an *intellectual object*, since *women* and *children* seem to be more captivated by it than *men*, and *animals* <note>original: "Brutes"</note> as much as either. <note>The author’s grouping of women and children with animals regarding their capacity for intellectual appreciation reflects the social and philosophical hierarchies common in the 1600s.</note>

The former point they attempt to prove this way: they say it is plain that *color*—which is one part of *beauty*—is the result of mere *matter*, as seen in the *rainbow*, which is certainly such a purely natural result. And as for *symmetry*—the other part of *beauty*, which in *plants* consists of their *leaves* and *branches* matching each other in parallel, as do the various parts of the same *leaf*—they say there is a kind of natural necessity for such a uniform correspondence. They argue that nourishment must follow the path of the *vessels* in the *seed*, which, being regular in their first formation, cause the *branches* and *leaves* that sprout out to also be regular. Now, they claim this regular formation of the seed came from the uniform motion of particles in the *mother-plant*; and finally, that the first *mother-plant* of any kind came from the regular motion of *matter*.

But I answer that, although the *position* <note>original: "Positure"</note> as well as the *colors* of the *rainbow* are necessary results of mere *matter*—being nothing but the reflection and refraction of the Sun's light in the round drops of a dewy cloud <note>original: "rorid cloud", from the Latin *roridus*</note>, as Descartes <note>original: "Cartesius", the Latinized name for the philosopher René Descartes</note> has admirably demonstrated—nothing more is required for this except the position of our eyes in a line drawn from the Sun and continued to this dewy cloud. If the cloud is spread out so that the colored circle has a *radius* of about forty-two or fifty-one degrees, then this *effect* will necessarily follow; and if this dewy cloud extends itself so far in every direction that there

Because of this dewy state of the air, two **Rainbows** will necessarily appear at once, as has been frequently seen. So, I admit, given certain conditions, the **Colors of Flowers** will be a necessary result of **Matter** in such a motion or posture. 

Yet for all this, the **variety of the placement of these Colors of Flowers** cannot but show that it is something either **fortuitous** <note>original: "fortuitous," meaning accidental or happening by chance</note> or **arbitrarious** <note>original: "arbitrarious," meaning decided by will or choice rather than necessity</note>. But since they always somehow please the beholder, it is a sign that it is not **fortuitous**; therefore, it must be **arbitrarious**, coming from some Purpose <note>original: "Counsel"</note> that contrived them this way.

But what I insist upon most—and contend proceeds from an **intelligent** <note>original: "Intellectual"</note> principle—is their **Symmetry**. The objection against this seems very weak, the reason for it being this: you can plainly see that the regular **Motion** of **Matter** made the **first Plant** of every kind. For we ask: What regulated its **Motion** so as to guide it to form itself into such a state that it finally appears as a very pleasant **Intellectual** spectacle? It would be exceedingly hard (if not impossible) to achieve this without some other **Director** distinct from blind **Matter**. 

A person will easily believe this if they do not think so much about the **Trunks and Branches of Trees** (whose growth out of the ground, and then having arms shooting out of the trunk and branching themselves into many subdivisions, is not so difficult to imagine) as they do upon their ***Blossoms, Fruits, and Leaves***. Consider the **Leaf** of the **Oak** and of **Holly**, and the abundance of **leaves of Herbs and their Flowers**. Look at **Monkshood, Snapdragon, and various types of Fly-flowers**—such as the **Fly-flower** properly so called, the **Butterfly-Satyrian**, the **Gnat-Satyrian**, to which we can add the **Wasp-Orchis**, the **Bee-flower**, and the like <note>These are types of orchids that resemble insects to attract pollinators</note>. **Matter** could never have stumbled upon such difficult and yet regular **shapes** had it not been regulated by something besides itself. Since the harmony of these figures pleases us who are **Rational**, we ought in all reason to conclude that they came from an **Intelligent Principle**.

5. But it was objected in the second place that **Beauty** is no **Intellectual Object**, because **Women** and **Children** are more taken with it than **Men**, and **Animals** <note>original: "Beasts"</note> as well as either. To which I answer, that **Children** are not so much taken with **Symmetry** as with the **vividness of colors** <note>original: "gayness of colours"</note> in things that are counted beautiful, just as **Larks** are greatly pleased by the shining of the **Glass** that a **Lark-catcher** exposes to their view. 

However, if children can also discover a lack of **Symmetry** and correspondence—as when a **Flower** has some leaves torn off—then that **Spirit** within them being **Intelligent**, it is not at all unreasonable that it should exercise itself upon such easy **Objects** as these early on. But the reason **They** or **Women** are taken more with **outward beauty** than **Men** is because **Men** employ their **intellectual faculties** <note>original: "Intellectuals"</note> about **harder tasks**, and so cannot attend to these smaller matters. Otherwise, there is no question that if they could be free from other employments, they would be as devoted admirers of **beauty** as **Women** themselves, and be as well pleased with their own beauty, if they have any, as women are with theirs.

But as for **Animals**, I deny that they have any sense of so noble an Object...

subject as *Beauty* is, or take any notice of the chief requisite in it, which is *Symmetry* and concinnity <note>original: "concinnity," meaning a harmonious arrangement of parts</note> of parts, or of any order of colors, but only of the *colors themselves*. And it is no wonder that as the sight of *red* stockings will inflame the spirits of a *turkey-cock* with anger, as also the sight of the *blood of grapes* or mulberries provoke the *elephant* to fight <note>A reference to ancient warfare where elephants were reportedly shown red juice to incite their battle rage; see 1 Maccabees 6:34.</note>; so other fresh colors of various sorts may please and exhilarate the spirits of several *animals*, just as *light* does for most. And therefore, if the *horse* prances and carries himself proudly when he has gay and glittering furniture, it is for no other reason than what we have already declared. And if a *dog* barks at a ragged *beggar* more than at a handsomely-clad *gentleman*, it is to be inquired into whether a beggar's *cur* <note>original: "Curre," a common dog or mutt</note> will not bark more at a *gentleman* than at a beggar—the sense of *beauty* neither pleasing nor provoking this *animal*, but the unusualness of the object stirring up his choler <note>original: "choler," meaning anger or agitation</note>. And the fact that *birds* prune their feathers is not out of any delight in decency and comeliness, but to rid themselves of that more uncomfortable and harsh sensation they feel in their skins caused by the disorder of their ruffled plumes. So for the choice of their *mates* in either *birds* or *beasts* for copulation, it is very hard to prove that they are guided as much by *sight* as by *scent*; and even if by *sight*, it is likely color rather than the exact symmetry of parts that moves them.

And lastly, if we should admit at any time that *brutes* <note>original: "Brutes," meaning non-human animals</note> may be more pleased with a *beautiful object* (taking "beauty" in its entire definition) than with one less beautiful, it is but a confused delight. Nor do they any more relish it as *intellectual* than *children* do the exact cuttings and carvings of the characters and lines of *geometrical* instruments (which are often made of brass or ivory or similar materials), seeing them as rational and mathematical. Children are ordinarily well pleased to see the instruments themselves, but do not understand their higher purpose. And therefore we may very well conclude that the beauty of bodies is naturally intended no more for *brutes* than such *mathematical* instruments are for *children*: but all such objects are directed to *intellectual creatures* from that *Eternal Intellectual Principle* <note>The author's term for God or the Divine Mind.</note> that made them.

6. The third objection is against animals *preying upon one another*, and man preying upon them all. For this, they say, is inconsistent with that *Eternal Goodness* that we profess to have created and ordered all things. To which I answer, that it is not at all inconsistent: for the nature of that *Absolute Universal* and *Eternal Goodness* is not to dote upon any one *particular* being as we do. Our temperaments perhaps may make us more than ordinarily compassionate—though most men have too little of that natural kindness—and our short-sightedness plunges us too much into the feelings of what is happening in the present moment. Instead, this Goodness takes a full and free view of the capacities for *happiness* in these kinds of creatures and contrived their condition to be such as was best for the generality of them, even though the *necessity* and *incompossibility* <note>original: "incompossibility," a philosophical term meaning the impossibility of two things existing together at the same time.</note> of things would be sure to load some particular creatures with greater inconvenience than the rest.

And therefore, so that several kinds of terrestrial creatures might more perfectly be happy in their animal nature, this *Sovereign Goodness* was content to let it be so, that every now and then something that the *animal* sense would necessarily account tragical and miserable should fall upon

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Divine Providence, specifically addressing the existence of predation and the survival of species despite individual deaths.</meta>

...some few; the *species* of things in the meantime being still copiously enough preserved, and marching on safely in this theater <note>original: "Theatre"</note> of the world in their several successions.

Now it is evident that the *main powers* of the *animal life* are *natural craft, strength,* and *activity* of body, and that any achievement <note>original: "purchace"</note> made by these is far more pleasant to a living creature than what comes easily without them. Therefore, what can be more gratifying to a terrestrial animal than to hunt its prey and to obtain it? But all kinds of creatures are not capable of this special happiness. Some, therefore, are made to feed on the fruits of the Earth, so that they may not only enjoy themselves but occasionally afford game and food to other creatures. In this, nonetheless, the *wisdom* of God as well as His *goodness* is manifest; for while they are thus a sport and prey to others, they are still abundantly preserved in their several generations. But I have so fully and methodically treated all such doubts against Providence in my *Inquiry into the Causes and Occasions of Atheism* <note>Referring to More's own work, "An Antidote against Atheism" (1652)</note>, that we will content ourselves with this short mention of an answer here.

We will only add that if the *souls of brute animals prove immortal* <note>original: "Souls of Brutes"; More, like some other Platonists, entertained the idea that animals might have immortal souls, which would make their deaths in nature less problematic</note> (which the best of philosophers have not been against), the tragedy is even less horrific. Yet, that ought not to encourage us to recklessly or petulantly <note>original: "cauſleſly and petulantly," meaning without good reason or out of spite</note> kill them, because we do not know how long it will be until they have an opportunity to form new *bodies* for themselves; and the interval of time in between is, to them, a perfect death, wherein they have neither the sense nor enjoyment of anything. For my own part, I think that he who slights the life or welfare of a brute creature is naturally so *unjust* that if outward laws did not restrain him, he would be just as cruel to humans.

7. *The fourth objection* is against our **argument for Divine Providence** drawn from the consideration of that happy *mitigation* <note>original: "Mitigation," meaning the lessening of a burden or nuisance</note> of the trouble and *offensiveness* of some animals by *others* that bear an *enmity* toward them and feed upon them as their prey—as the *cat*, for example, does to the *mouse*. Now, critics say, it would be a more exact sign of Providence if there were no such *offensive* creatures in the world to trouble us at all, rather than bringing on the trouble by making these animals and then taking it away again by making others to *correct* the mischief that would follow.

But no man would argue this way if he had not over-carelessly adopted this false principle: *that the world was made for man alone*. In truth, the blessed and benign Maker of all things intended that *other living creatures* should enjoy themselves as well as *humans*, which they could not do if they did not exist. Therefore, *Providence* is more exact in that she can thus spread out her *goodness* further, even to the enjoyment of the more inferior ranks of creatures, without any considerable inconvenience to the more noble and superior ones.

Besides, all these creatures that are thus a *prey* to others provide their sport and sustenance, and so give pleasure to others by their death, just as they enjoy themselves while they are still alive and free from their enemies. This is to say nothing of how they are all, in some way or another, *useful* to man himself, and therefore would sometimes be missed if they were absent.

8. The fifth and last objection is against our concluding that there is a *substance* distinct from the *body* based on the *homogeneity* <note>original: "Homogeneity"; the quality of being uniform or composed of parts that are all of the same kind</note> of that immediate *crystalline matter* from which the *fetus* <note>original: "Fœtus"</note> is *formed* <note>original: "efformed"</note>—for example, in an *egg*—which is also observable in other types of generation. To avoid the force of this argument, it is denied that there is any such *homogeneity* of parts. Instead, it is argued that there are various *heterogeneous* <note>original: "Heterogeneal"; diverse or consisting of different kinds of parts</note> particles, though invisible to us, which are set in motion by the heat of the *hen* or some similar warmth. According to this view, like particles will be driven toward their like, and so the *chicken* will be *formed*. But it is claimed that to acknowledge any other *vital spirit* <term>original: "Archeus"; a term from Paracelsian medicine referring to the internal force or "master workman" that governs the formation and life of an organism</term> brings inextricable difficulties with it. For where, they ask, were all the *vital spirits* that shaped the *wasps* out of a *horse’s carcass*? <note>More refers to the then-common belief in "spontaneous generation," the idea that complex organisms like wasps or maggots could be born directly from decaying flesh without parents.</note> Are they parts of the *horse’s soul*, or new intruding guests arriving after the old ones were ejected? If the former, then the *soul* of a *horse* is divisible and consequently material—or, if you will, truly *matter*. If the latter, where were those little *intruders* before? Or are they so many sprigs or branches of the *common soul of the world*? <note>original: "common Soul of the world"; also known as the Anima Mundi, a concept in Platonism suggesting a single spirit animates all of nature.</note> But if so, why do they not all share one common sense of pain and pleasure? To all these points, I answer in order.

To the first part of this objection, I say that it must be a very strong presumption that *Nature* intends an absolute *homogeneity* of *matter* before she begins her work of *formation*. She so constantly brings it to as perfect a *homogeneity* as we can possibly discern with our *senses*. And since there is no conceivable benefit at all in having a *heterogeneity* of parts at that stage, I think the conclusion is not rash if we assert that the immediate *matter* for the *formation* of the *fetus* is either accurately *homogeneous*, or, if there is any *heterogeneity* of parts in it, that it is only by accident. It contributes no more to the initial work of *forming* or organizing the *matter* than those *atoms* of dust that land on a painter’s <note>original: "limners"</note> colors contribute to the better drawing of a *picture*. For to say that those various sorts of particles, set in motion by external warmth, gather together by virtue of their similarity to one another is to claim something without any foundation at all, against all grounds of *reason*.

For what can this *similarity of parts* consist of, if not in the likeness of *shape*, or in the equality of *motion* or *size*? Now, *bodies* of the like *shape* being set in motion will not direct their courses toward one another any more just because they are alike in shape. Indeed, *bodies* of like *shape*, motion, and size, in a state of confused agitation, may very likely go together, as we see happen in certain cases: in the thinner spirits of distilled liquors that all mount upward; in the *tartarous* parts of *wine* that are driven outward to the sides of the vessel; in the sediment <note>original: "feculency"</note> of *urine* that sinks to the bottom of the glass; and in the settling <note>original: "subsidency"</note> of this dreg-like part of the world, the *Earth*—if it may be said to settle and be at the bottom as much as it is in the midst of the more refined and subtle *elements*. In like manner, the *fermentation* of the matter which precedes the *formation* of *creatures* may perhaps arrive at some such crude effect as is seen in those examples; but it can never amount to such an artistic arrangement of *organs* as are found in living *creatures*.

But if by *Likeness of Parts* they mean only a *fitness of parts for shape and motion*, where both are so structured and moderated that, upon external warmth, their agitation will necessarily cause them to lock into one another and be linked into this admirable and useful frame of an animal's body—that artistry would be so particularly precise and curious that it is utterly inconceivable. It must imply either the attendance, or at least the initial contrivance, of a *Knowing Principle* <note>original: "Knowing Principle"; an intelligent or conscious agent, such as God or a presiding spirit</note> that put the *matter* into such a wonderful order as to be able, by such precise laws of *shape* and *motion*, to exhibit such noble objects to our senses and understandings. And thus, our adversaries will gain nothing by this supposition.

<margin>* See my Treatise on the Immortality of the Soul, Book 3, chapters 12 and 13.</margin>
But though this may seem barely possible, I conceive it is very improbable that such an infinite number of particles—which must concur to make up a *fetus* <note>original: "Fœtus"</note>—should have such a particular shaping and law of motion impressed upon each of them as to enable it to take its right station or posture in the structure of a living creature. For it seems to me that this is taking the long way around, whereas the more direct way would be to make use of some *Immaterial Substance*, such as those conceived to be the *seminal forms* <term>original: "Seminal Forms"; the internal "blueprints" or spiritual patterns that guide the growth of plants and animals</term> of plants and animals, or the *Archei*, as others call them. For this *form* or *Archeus* <term>original: "Archeus"; a term from Paracelsian medicine referring to a vital force or "internal master-workman" that governs life processes</term> is a thing more simple and plain, and it requires a more simple and plain qualification of the subject it works upon: namely, that the matter be only uniform and yielding to the tender assaults of that substantial power of life that resides in it.

9. Nor is this opinion of the *Archei* or *Seminal Forms* entangled in any such difficulties that cannot be easily answered.

For as for those many pretended intricacies in the example of the formation of *wasps* out of the carcass of a horse, I say the *Archei* that framed them are no parts of the horse’s soul that is dead. Rather, they are several distinct *Archei* that join as naturally with the *matter* of the horse's body (when it is decayed and prepared for them) as crows come to eat its flesh.

But you ask where these *Archei* were before. To which I answer: Can there be a lack of room for such small pieces of *spirituality* in so vast a compass as the reach of the *universe*? I shall rather reply, where were they *not*? The *world of life* is excluded from no place, and the various sorts of souls are as plentiful and as obvious there as those *magnetic* particles are in this physical world; you can scarcely place your *lodestone* <note>original: "Loadstone"; a naturally magnetized mineral used as a magnet</note> and *iron* anywhere without finding their presence by their noticeable effects. Or, if you prefer a coarser comparison, they are as cheap and common as dust flying in the air in a dry and windy summer.

<margin>* This is the usual phrase of the Ancients, but how far it is justifiable, see "Immortality of the Soul," Book 3, chapter 16, section 8.</margin>
To the last puzzle proposed—whether these *Archei* are so many offshoots of the *common Soul of the world* <note>original: "Soul of the world"; the *Anima Mundi*, a concept of a single spirit animating all nature</note> or particular independent substances themselves—there is no great inconvenience in acknowledging that it may be either way. For it does not follow that if they are so many branches or distinct *rays of the great *Soul of the world*, they are therefore that very Soul itself; and if they are not, they may have their pleasures and pains distinct from one another. And what is pleasure and pain to them may perhaps be neither to their source, disturbing her no more than the chirping of a cricket disturbs those who are listening to a full concert.

...as much as a consort of loud music, or the biting of a flea, affects a man being tortured on a rack.

But suppose we say they are as many *substances* as independent of the *Soul of the World* <note>original: "Soul of the world" or *Anima Mundi*; the concept of an animating spirit within the universe</note> as *matter* itself is (though all depend on God). There is no difficulty or inconvenience at all in that position. Nor do we need to worry about where they are or what becomes of them—either before they activate this or that part of *matter*, or after they have finished activating it—any more than we worry about the parts of *matter* they activate. For just as every particle of *matter* is safely kept within the boundaries of the physical world, whether it is acted upon by a *soul* or an *Archeus* <term>original: "Archeus"; a vital principle or spiritual force believed to govern life and growth</term> or not; so too every *Archeus* or *soul* is just as safe in the *world of life*. They are secure from being expelled from the realm of *immaterial beings*, whether they act upon any part of the material world or not. For *substance*, whatever its nature may be, cannot perish without a *miracle*. And I do not think anyone can think of any *reason* why God should annihilate something that, in the course of *time*, might again have the opportunity to play its part and prove useful to the world.

## CHAP. XII.

1. *Objections against the story of the Charmer of Salzburg.* 2. *And of the bewitched children at Amsterdam, with some others of that kind.* 3. *As also against the stories of John of Hembach and John Michael Pipers regarding the grotesque dances of devils.* 4. *Also against the disappearing of the assembly of witches at the naming of God.* 5. *And against a certain passage in the story of the Guardian Spirit related by Bodinus* <note>original: "Bodinus"; Jean Bodin (1530–1596), a French jurist and writer on demonology</note>.

1. The passages challenged in my third book are either *historical* or *philosophical*. The *historical* ones are mainly these: First, against the account of the *Charmer of Salzburg*, it is objected that the last and largest *serpent* might not have been the *Devil*, but simply a regular *serpent*. To this I answer that it is very probable that this *serpent* had more to it than an ordinary, natural snake. This serpent presented himself last and brought such a sad fate upon the *charmer*—as if he intended to take revenge for the deaths of so many of his own kind, or to spiritedly mock <note>original: "flurre"; to mock, slight, or treat with contempt</note> the glory and victory of their now almost triumphant enemy. That is, it was either the *Devil* transformed into that shape, or a *serpent* controlled and guided by him. We will believe this more easily if we consider that the whole business of *charming* has no natural power, but is supernatural, if it has any effect at all.

2. The second *objection* is against those *stories* of several possessed people who seemed to vomit strange materials out of their stomachs, as if it might be done by some *sleight of hand* and *cunning*, only to get money. In answer to this, I must confess that there are no real strange *effects* or *events* in the *world* but that someone or other, if possible, will either...

And as for the children at *Amsterdam*, the sight was so miserable, and their reported torture so great—and the parties involved so many, and all attempts of science or religion so fruitless <note>original: "frustraneous"</note>—that it seems very incredible that there should be either fraud or foolishness in the matter.
