Therefore, in such cases, the judgment and wisdom of the first storytellers is to be assumed, as in that story that Fernel <note>Jean Fernel (1497–1558), a French physician who introduced the term "physiology."</note> tells us of a demoniac <term>demoniac: a person believed to be possessed by an evil spirit</term> in his time who spoke Greek and revealed the secrets of the physicians. The spirit mocked their ignorance because they had half killed a man by administering medicine <note>original: "Physick"</note> based on the false assumption that he had a natural disease.

3. The third objection is against the *mirth* of some of the stories recorded, such as those of the pipers *John of Hembach* and *John Michael*. But these narrations should seem no less incredible for those passages of humor, if we consider that those fallen spirits <note>original: "Apostate Spirits"</note> who haunt this lower air and earth have fallen in various ways into an excessive love and liking of the *animal life*, having utterly forsaken the *Divine*. We must also consider that there are such passions and emotions in them as are found in wicked men and beasts. Some of them especially relate to an unfallen angel in the same way an ape or monkey relates to a sober man; thus, all their pleasure is in unlucky, ridiculous tricks. Even those who are more ferocious <note>original: "ferocient"</note>, if they ever relax into *mirth*, it is foolishly clownish <note>original: "antick"</note> and distorted, as is obvious in all those stories of their dances and nightly revels. For they harbor a secret hatred for whatever is beautiful and proper; in a constant mockery of it, they twist all their actions to the opposite style, praising themselves only for their unlimited freedom and for doing whatever their foolish or foul imaginations suggest to them. They care for nothing but the satisfaction of their own wills and the power to make themselves wondered at and feared.

4. The fourth objection is against those passages of the *Nocturnal Gatherings* <note>original: "Conventicles"; meetings often associated with secret religious groups or, in this context, witches.</note> of witches *disappearing at the naming of God or Jesus*. For critics say the devils are not at all afraid of these *Names*, but can name them themselves in mockery or abuse and apply them to their own persons. But this objection is easily satisfied if we simply distinguish between the intentions <note>original: "mindes"</note> of the speakers of these words. Therefore, I say it does not follow that because they can tolerate the pronouncing of these words among themselves, they can also do so when they are named with an honest heart and due devotion.

Besides, it is not irrational (even if they could withstand the power of these *Names* and the devotion of those who use them) that there may be a mandatory ceremony among them not to continue their gatherings if anyone is near or present who makes an open and serious profession

5. The fifth and last objection is against a vision or dream in which a man—who for many years had the company of a **Guardian Genius** <term>Guardian Genius: a protective spirit or "good angel" assigned to a person, similar to a guardian angel</term> or **Good Angel**—seemed to hear these words: *I will save your soul; I am he who appeared to you before.* This makes it seem as if this **Genius** or **Angel** had claimed to be the Eternal God Himself. But this should not cause any doubt. First, because no physical shape was presented to him in this vision, it may simply be a divine suggestion from the Spirit of God, assuring him of His love and providence now, just as He had done in previous visions or dreams.

Secondly, even if we admit that the **Angel** spoke those words to him, the **Angel** in this case is not properly said to speak as a **Person**, but as an **Instrument**. This is similar to how a man’s **Tongue** speaks, even though the man’s **Soul** (or the man himself) is more truly the speaker than the tongue. Therefore, if God takes such full possession of all the powers and faculties of an **Angel** that the Angel briefly loses the sense of his own personality and becomes a mere passive **Instrument** of the **Deity**—acting as the **Eye** or **Mouth of God**—then whatever he speaks in that state is to be understood as coming from God, not from himself.

In this way, I hope I have resolved the difficulties regarding all the **historical passages** of this **Third Book** that remain in it. I must confess that, upon a closer review, I have removed some passages that did not seem to agree accurately enough with the rules I set for myself. This is not because I know them to be false, but because they lacked that consistency; therefore, I must acknowledge they are not convincingly true.

## CHAPTER XIII.

# An Appendix to the foregoing Antidote. Chapter XIII.

12. That if spirits or demons be nothing but mere collections of airy or fiery atoms, every devil would be many millions of devils. 13. The superiority of arguments drawn from the history of spirits over those drawn from the operations of the soul in the body for proving the existence of an immaterial substance.

1. THE first philosophical objection is against the **transformation** of a human body into the shape of, for instance, a **wolf** or any similar creature. It is thought that this cannot be done without a great deal of pain to the person being transformed. To this I answer that although this **transformation** is performed in a very short time, it may be done without any pain at all. For that part in the head which is the seat of **common sense** <term>common sense: in early modern psychology, the "sensus communis" was the faculty that integrated data from the five senses into a single perception</term> is, I believe, very small. (Suppose it to be the **conarion** <note>original: "Conarion"; the pineal gland, which many 17th-century thinkers, including Descartes, believed was the seat of the soul</note>; it is not very large.) Therefore, if the Devil gets into the body of a man and takes possession of that part along with the rest, he can intercept or block all the transmissions of motion from other parts of the body. Thus, let him do what he will with them, the person will feel no **pain** at all. He may soften all the other parts of the body into whatever consistency he pleases and mold it into any form, just as he can his own **vehicle of air** <term>vehicle of air: the subtle, semi-material body that spirits were thought to inhabit and manipulate</term>, and the person will not be aware of it the whole time. There is the same reason for returning the body to its own shape again, which is just as painless to the person who undergoes it. Nor is there any fear that the body, once loosened in this way, will forever remain in this loose, melting condition. For it is acknowledged even by those who oppose **Bodin** <note>original: "Bodinus"; Jean Bodin (1530–1596), an influential French jurist and demonologist</note>—whose cause I undertake—that a **spirit** can **stop** and fix a body just as well as **move** it. Therefore, I say that when the Devil has **fixed** the body again in its original shape, it will, according to the undeniable laws of nature, remain in that state he left it, until something more powerful unsettles and changes it—and every body is overpowered at last, and we must all yield to death.

2. The second objection is against our acknowledging an **actual separation of soul and body without death**. Death, as we properly define it, is a separation of the soul from the body because the body is **unfit** to house the soul any longer, which may be caused by extreme disease, outward violence, or old age. Now, they say, what is **violence** if this is not—for the Devil to take the soul out of the body? But the answer is easy: any separation by violence is not **death**, but rather such a violence in separation that it makes the body **unfit** to house the soul again. This is the case when blood is drained by wounding the body, or when the course of the **spirits** <term>spirits: "vital spirits," thought to be subtle fluids that carried life and motion through the nerves</term> is hindered by strangling, drowning, or the like. To revive such a body as this would indeed be a miracle in these cases, because death has seized upon the body in a true and proper sense; and then none but God Himself can thus kill and make alive.

3. The third objection is against the notable **coldness** of the bodies of demons. For at the great trial of witches at the **St. Edmundsbury Assizes** <term>assizes: periodic courts held in English counties to handle serious crimes</term> in August 1645, I heard some of them openly confess at the bar—says the objector—that when the Devil lay with them, he was **warm**. To which I might answer, if I had a mind to dodge the issue rather than precisely satisfy the

But to answer more directly to the point, I admit the **bodies of demons** may be not only **warm**, but **scorching hot** <note>original: "findgingly hot"</note>, as was the case with the spirit that took one of **Melanchthon’s** <note>Philipp Melanchthon (1497–1560), a German theologian and key figure in the Protestant Reformation</note> relatives by the hand and scorched her so badly that she bore the mark of it until her dying day. However, examples of **cold** spirits are more frequent, as in the famous story of **Cuntius**. When he touched the arm of a certain woman of **Pentsch** as she lay in her bed, he felt as cold as ice; and the same was true of the spirit’s claw felt by **Anne Styles**. There are many other stories of that nature. Yet, I will not deny that their bodies may also be **warm**; otherwise, it is impossible to understand how those two wretched **magicians** <note>original: "Magi"</note> could reap such inexpressible pleasure—one from his **Armellina**, the other from his **Florina**—as they claimed to have done in a certain dialogue by **Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola** <note>original: "Franciscus Picus"</note>. This work is titled *The Witch, or On the Deceptions of Demons* <note>original: "Strix, or De Ludificatione Dæmonum"</note>; he assures us in his preface <note>original: "Epistle"</note> that it is a true history and that he records only things he has either seen with his own eyes or heard from the confessions of **witches** themselves.

The weight of the objection, therefore, is directed against something we do not actually claim—namely, that the bodies of demons are found only to be cold. What we would suggest is simply this: their bodies are nothing but **condensed or compressed air**. When they arrange themselves in such a way that they compress their vehicles <term>vehicle: the semi-material body or "envelope" that a spirit inhabits to interact with the physical world</term> much more than they agitate its individual particles, the body will then seem not only **cold**, like frozen water, but more piercingly and stingingly cold because of the fineness of its parts.

But when they not only strongly compress their vehicle as a whole but also fiercely agitate its individual particles, their body will become **scorching hot**. In this state, it will imitate, in some measure, heated **brass** or **iron**, where the particles stay close together and yet every one is moving rapidly within itself. This is clear to us if we spit upon such heated metals; they will make the spittle hiss and bubble, as the particles of the metal communicate their motion to the spittle lying upon them. Such heat will turn all liquid into vapor, as we commonly see when burning **vinegar** and **rose-water** in a room to perfume it. For what is this perfuming but the process of setting the watery, separable parts of the liquid into such strong motion that they rise into the **air** and disperse as fumes, caused by the fierce and strong agitation of the inseparable parts of the heated **fire-shovel**?

Lastly, if a spirit uses its **moving** <note>original: "Agitative"</note> power moderately and its **compressing** power strongly enough to feel solid or tangible to the man or woman he deals with, he may not only feel **warm**, but more pleasantly and agreeably warm than any earthly or fleshy body can be. Because of the fineness of the **matter**, it will more precisely strike and more powerfully reach the **sensory organs**, and more exquisitely and delightfully stimulate the **nerves** than any terrestrial body possibly can. But in the meantime, the **spirit** himself is neither hot, nor warm, nor cold, nor anything else that belongs to a **body**; he is a **substance** specifically distinct from all physical...

### An Appendix to the Foregoing Antidote. CHAPTER 13.

4. The fourth objection is against our assertion that it is an inconsistent and self-contradicting position to hold *that there never was any man who was not born of a woman*, even if we should admit that the *successions* of mankind were *infinite*. For, the objectors say, the contradiction only exists if you can find a *First*. But in an *infinite succession*, there can be no *First* in any sense at all; for if there were a *First*, then there would be a *Second*, and so on to our own times. Thus, the *series* would be countable and consequently finite; which is a contradiction, for then the *succession* would be both *finite* and *infinite*.

But I answer, first, that I can demonstrate that there is a *First* in *infinite succession* based on principles that the atheist either does grant or must necessarily grant. That principle is that matter exists *from eternity* <note>original: "ab Æterno"</note>, and that at least some part of it moved *from eternity*. Now, it is plain that this matter which moved *from eternity* either moved on its own or was moved by another. If the latter, then we have a *First* in an *infinite succession* of motions: for whatever moved this matter from eternity is first in the order of causality, as is undeniably clear to anyone with common sense.

But you will say that this *matter* which moved *from eternity* was moved by itself. Even if that were so, no part of it can move in this full ocean of *matter* (which is excluded from no space) without hitting some other part of *matter* as soon as it moves, and that part hitting another, and so on. And thus, there might be a *succession* of motions from eternity or an infinite succession, and yet still a first in the order of causality. For that original motion of the *matter* is clearly first and the cause of all the rest. Our understanding can never be at rest until it has reached some such "first" in the order of causes.

Secondly, regarding that subtle argument that would prove this *infinite succession* would be both *finite* and *infinite*, I answer that it is a mere sophism <note>a clever but false argument</note> arising from the ambiguity of the term *first*. The word signifies either *priority of succession* (coming first in a line) or *priority of causality* (being the primary cause). In the first sense, if we admit a *first*, the *succession* will be *finite* according to our own faculties; for we cannot help but look beyond it, finding the succession bounded by that *first*. But in the second sense, *first* sets no bounds to succession, but leaves it free and infinite.

Or we may answer this way: that beginning from this moment and going back to the original primordial motion—calling this present moment *first*, and the moment before it *second*—the sequence will amount to a number truly infinite that our understanding can never fully grasp. However, even though God’s understanding can grasp it, it does not follow that the number is therefore *finite*; for an infinite mind may well comprehend an *infinite number*. But for us, whose capacities are *finite*, if we dared to name a "first" in an infinite succession, we should call it the *first infinitesimal* <note>original: "πρῶτον ἀπειροσὸν"</note>, and acknowledge ourselves unable to complete the count, our understandings being finite.

5. The fifth and last objection is against the story taken from Gerard <note>John Gerard (c. 1545–1612) was a famous English botanist and author of "The Herball" (1597), which famously described "barnacle geese" growing from trees</note> concerning the *tree-geese* on the island of the *Pile of Foulders* <note>now known as Piel Island, or the Piel of Fouldrey, in Cumbria</note>. For it was objected by someone who inquired of people living near that place that the story was not confirmed to him; instead, they told him only that at that time of the year it was...

More is referring to the Barnacle Goose, which was long believed to hatch from barnacles attached to driftwood rather than laying eggs.</note> which he gathered in their shells from an old rotten tree upon the shore of our English coast between *Dover* and *Romney*. He brought many of them with him to *London*, and opening the shells, which were somewhat like *mussels*, he found these birds in several degrees of development <note>original: "maturation"</note>; in some, only shapeless lumps; in others, the form of birds but bare; in others, the same form and shape and with down also upon them, their shells gaping and they ready to fall out.

I might add a third kind described to me by a gentleman from *Ireland*, which he has often observed upon those coasts; but it is not necessary to insist upon describing it. All that I aim at is this: that this truth of *birds being bred from decaying matter* <note>original: "putrefaction." This refers to the theory of spontaneous generation, where living things were thought to arise from non-living matter.</note> is very certain. I am as well assured of this by this gentleman's information as by that account from *Gerard*, so I must confess that for my own part I cannot doubt it at all. And it might support my willingness to believe—if I could be justly suspected of that fault here—that the objector himself, upon further inquiry, is at last fully satisfied concerning this same truth.

6. We have now answered all the objections, both *philosophical* and *historical*, made against those particular passages in my *Third Book*. There remains only one of a more universal nature, and indeed of such importance that if I do not satisfy it, it would utterly subvert the main design of our whole *Third Book* against *Atheism*. In that book, we intended to persuade men toward an easier belief in a God through the *history* of *spirits*. For even admitting all those stories to be true, the objectors say it does not at all follow that there are *spirits* in the sense that I define them—the notion used in my explanation of the *Idea of God*. That is, they deny there is an *immaterial or incorporeal substance that can penetrate and act upon matter*. They argue that "spirits" are actually just a thinner kind of *body*, such as *air* or *fire*, or some similar subtle element, and not *pure spirit* according to our definition.

If this were true, I must confess that our last book against *Atheism* has no efficacy at all and can do nothing toward the end for which it was intended. For if there is a *God*, by necessity he must be a *spirit* properly so called; otherwise he cannot be *infinite*. Nor can he be this *universal matter* in the world, even if we suppose it to be boundless, because he could not then be *perfect*. Instead, he must be an *essence* on which this *matter* depends, and in which he exists, penetrating and possessing all things. Which any one will—

7. For I appeal to anyone who knows what *Fire* and *Air* are: are they not truly a mere collection <note>original: "aggregation"</note> of loosened particles of *matter*, just like a heap of sand? They are only so small that they are invisible and undetectable in their individual parts; however, they are as truly *disjoined atoms* (if I may use that term for what is still divisible) as the *grains of sand* we are discussing.

8. Now, assuming this is true—and only *ignorance* could deny it—we shall clearly see that the things done by *Spirits* (as we usually call them) are completely incompatible with any structure <note>original: "compages"</note> made of these small grains or *Atoms* of *Matter* of which *Air* and *Fire* consist. For first:
Either all these *grains* or *atoms* possess *Sense*, *Imagination*, and *Understanding*, or only a few do, or only one does. If all or some few possess them, it is clear that they are many distinct intelligent beings, and a distinct intelligent being is a *Person*. Thus, this one person would actually be many persons; which is clearly a contradiction, or at least foolishly ridiculous. But if the seat of *Sense*, *Imagination*, and *Understanding* is placed in only one atom, how is it possible for that one atom to *move all the others by its own will* <note>original: "spontaneously to move"</note>? The same logic applies if we were to seat *Sense* and *Reason* in a few internal atoms. For how could they pull along those behind them, carry those beside them, or drive those before them without the group splitting apart and leaving atoms behind? 

And yet, there is a strong suspicion that the *Seat of Sense* is confined to a small area within the *Vehicle* <note>original: "Vehicle"; in Neo-Platonic philosophy, this refers to the subtle, non-fleshly body that a soul or spirit inhabits</note> of a Spirit, just as it is in the *Body of a Man*. For if it were not—if every part of the *Vehicle* had *Sense* in itself—then an external object would appear in God knows how many places at once. The images of things would either be utterly confused, or the *atoms*, when they began to move, would lose their target; by following their own individual senses, they would necessarily break away from each other and destroy the whole spirit.

9. Again, it is manifest that whatever has the power of *Sensation* in a *Spirit* also has the power of *Memory*. Otherwise, they could not remember the objects of *Sense* unless it were one and the same thing in them that possessed both *Sense* and *Memory*. And that which remembers also *imagines*; and that which *imagines* uses the power of imagination to transform the *Vehicle* into various shapes and figures, holding it in that shape as long as it sees fit.

Now I ask: how can this possibly be done by either one or a few particles or atoms residing in any part of the *Vehicle*? How can they either hold the others together or grip them to restrain and compress <note>original: "constringe"</note> them into this or that form—suppose of a dog, a young horse <note>original: "colt"</note>, or a *man*? But to say that *imagination* exists in every part of the *Vehicle*, and to admit that those particles can *imagine* even if they do not have so much as *Sense* (as the far greater part seem not to have, based on what was just implied), is altogether unreasonable.

He assumes the soul is a collection <note>original: "congeries"</note> of little *atoms*, much like the *spirits* described here...

Fourthly and lastly, the transportation of cattle and of witches themselves to their nightly gatherings <note>original: "Nocturnal Conventicles"; referring to the "Witches' Sabbath," a legendary midnight meeting of those suspected of witchcraft.</note> through the air would be completely impossible if *Spirits* or *Devils* were merely a collection of subtle *Airy* or *Fiery atoms* without an internal <term>Immaterial Principle</term> <note>A non-physical soul or essence that provides unity and purpose to a being.</note> that has the power to hold the particles together. For it is evident that the weight of a *man* or a *beast* will sink through the *air* and never rest until they reach the *earth*. They would do the same through the "vehicle" <note>In Neo-Platonic philosophy, a "vehicle" is the semi-material body or "carrier" that a spirit inhabits to interact with the physical world.</note> of a *spirit*—which is as subtle, fluid, and yielding as the *air* itself—were there not an internal essence and principle that was able to bind <note>original: "constringe"</note> and hold together this fluid body or vehicle of the *spirit*, and so make it sustain the weight. For all bodies, whether hard or fluid, are equally impenetrable; therefore, if any power should hold the air together so as to restrain it within one compass or space, and yet not change its usual consistency, it would be like wind in a bladder. A man might lie upon it as safely as upon a soft bed and never fear sinking through.

But in this loose composition of *atoms* which they say is all that is in a *spirit* (even though we should admit that ridiculous supposition that *every atom can imagine* and apply itself to one joint design of holding everything close together), yet it is hard to conceive that this actual division of the whole into so many subtle, tiny, and invisible particles does not so enfeeble the spontaneous efforts toward sustaining and carrying away the burden that their endeavors would always prove futile <note>original: "frustraneous"</note>.

12. But I need not insist upon that which, perhaps, may seem a point somewhat more slippery <note>original: "lubricous"; meaning an argument that is difficult to hold onto or prove definitely.</note>, when we have what is more palpably absurd presenting itself to our view. For if this compilation of *Airy* or *Fiery particles* is the only substance acknowledged in a *spirit*, and every atom has *Imagination* and *Reason* in it to apply itself to one joint design, they must be (as I have hinted before) as properly many distinct *persons* as the grains of sand are many distinct individuals of matter. Therefore, every single Devil is indeed five billion <note>original: "5000 millions"</note> Devils and more; a thing that a man would little dream of, or admit to be any more than a dream, if he thinks of it while waking. But if such things as these will not be acknowledged as absurd, but shamelessly admitted and swallowed down as true, I must confess that there is no proof <note>original: "Demonstration"</note> against impudence and stubbornness. I would not be able to prove to such people that either animals have life, or that the dust motes <note>original: "moats"</note> that play in the sunbeams are devoid of *Sense* and *Reason*.

#### THE PREFACE.

1. The author's apology <note>original: "Apologie"; here meaning a formal written defense of his reasons for writing.</note> for writing this treatise, since there are already so many on the same subject. **page 1**
2. That what he has written are the proper outpourings <note>original: "Emanations"</note> of his own mind, and may have their own particular usefulness for men of a similar intellectual nature <note>original: "Genius"</note>. **ibid.**
3. That he does not strive for rhetoric, nor philology <note>original: "Philologie"; the study of language and classical texts</note>, nor the pompous abundance of more popular arguments, but solid and irresistible reason in a clear method. **2**
4. That he has undeniably demonstrated the existence of God, provided this one postulate <note>A basic assumption required as a starting point for an argument.</note> is admitted: That our mental faculties are true. **3**
5. His unique management of the first argument of <term>Descartes</term> <note>René Descartes (1596–1650), the French philosopher famous for "I think, therefore I am."</note>: **ibid.**
6. And the reasons for his rejection of the rest. **4**
7. His caution and selectivity in managing such arguments as are drawn from the more general phenomena <note>original: "Phænomena"</note> of nature: **ibid.**
8. As also in those arguments drawn from animals. **5**
9. His careful choice of such histories as tend to prove the existence of spirits. **6**
10. His confidence in that kind of argument. **ibid.**
11. The reason for his declining to recite the miraculous stories of Holy Scripture <note>original: "Holy Writ"</note>. **ibid.**
12. His intentional condescension <note>In this context, "condescension" means a voluntary lowering of oneself to the level of the listener to be better understood.</note> and compliance with the atheist to win him over from his atheism. **7**

<column-break/>

#### BOOK I.

CHAPTER I. 1. That the inclination <note>original: "Proneness"</note> of the current age to free their minds from the fear of superstition makes it reasonable to attempt to steer them away from atheism. 2. That those who adhere to religion in a merely superstitious and habitual way easily turn into atheists if that tie once fails. 3. The usefulness of this present treatise even to those who are seriously religious. **p. 9.**

CHAPTER II. 1. That there is nothing so demonstrable that the mind of man can rationally conclude it is impossible to be otherwise. 2. That the soul of man may give full agreement <note>original: "Assent"</note> to that which, nonetheless, may possibly be otherwise—proven by several examples. 3. A similar example of disagreement. 4. The reasons why he has so diligently <note>original: "sedulously"</note> proven this point. 5. That the atheist has no advantage from the author's free confession that his arguments are not so absolutely convicting that they leave no possibility of the thing being otherwise. **10**

CHAPTER III. 1. That we must first have a settled notion of what God is before we go about demonstrating that he is. 2. The definition of God. 3. That there is an idea of a being absolutely perfect in our mind, whether the atheist will allow it to be the idea of God or not. 4. That it is no prejudice to the natural character <note>original: "Naturality"</note> of this idea that it may be framed <note>This sentence continues onto the next page.</note>

**CHAP. IV.** *1. What concepts <note>original: "Notions"</note> are more particularly comprised in the idea of a Being absolutely perfect. 2. That the difficulty of imagining <note>original: "framing the conception"</note> a thing ought to be no argument against its existence; the nature of physical <note>original: "corporeall"</note> matter being so perplexed and intricate, which yet all men acknowledge to exist. 3. That the idea of a spirit is as easy a concept as that of any other substance whatsoever. What powers and properties are contained in the concept of a spirit. 4. That eternity and infinity, if God did not exist, would be attributed to <note>original: "cast upon"</note> something else; so that atheism cannot free the mind from such complexities. 5. Goodness, knowledge, and power—concepts of the highest perfection, and therefore necessarily included in the idea of a Being absolutely perfect. 6. As also necessity, it establishing greater perfection than contingency <note>original: "Contingency"; the state of being possible but not certain, or existing by chance.</note>.*

**CHAP. VI.** *1. Various instances arguing for actual knowledge in the soul: such as that she has a more accurate idea of a circle and triangle than matter can show <note>original: "exhibite"</note> to her. 2. The same argued from the nature of mathematical and logical concepts, which do not enter through the senses, as they are no physical properties <note>original: "Physical affections"</note> of the matter. 4. Because they are produced without any physical motion upon the matter. 5. And that contrary kinds may be entirely in one and the same part of matter at once. 6. That there are certain sure complex concepts <note>original: "Complex Notions"</note> of the mind for which she was not indebted to sense.*

And that the definition of a Being absolutely perfect is such. 4. And that this absolutely perfect Being is God, the creator and designer <note>original: "Contriver"</note> of all things. 5. The certainty and stability of this idea.*

**CHAP. VIII.** *1. That the very idea of God implies his necessary existence. 2. That his existence is not theoretically <note>original: "hypothetically"</note> necessary, but absolutely, with the occasion noted of that slippery excuse <note>original: "Evasion"</note>. 3. That to acknowledge God as a necessarily existent Being according to the true concept of him, and yet to say he may not exist, is a plain contradiction. 4. That "Necessity" is a logical term and implies an unbreakable connection between Subject and Predicate <note>The "subject" is the topic of the sentence (God), and the "predicate" is what is stated about it (existence).</note>, from which again this axiom is necessarily and eternally true: God does exist. 5. A further demonstration of his existence from the incompatibility of contingency or impossibility with his nature or idea. 6. That necessary self-existence belongs either to God, or to matter, or to both. 7. The great inconsistencies <note>original: "Incongruities"</note> that follow the admission of the self-existence of matter. 8. An answer to an excuse <note>original: "Evasion"</note>. 9. That a number of self-created <note>original: "Self-essentiated"</note> deities plainly takes away the being of the true God. 10. The only undeniable demonstration of the unity of the Godhead. 11. The absurdity in admitting actual self-existence in matter while denying it in God. 12. That this absurdity cannot be excused by the perceptibility <note>original: "sensibleness"</note> of matter, since the atheist himself is forced to admit such things as do not fall under the senses. 13. That it is as foolish a thing to reject the existence <note>original: "Being"</note> of God because he does not immediately fall under the senses, as it would be to reject the existence of matter because it is so incomprehensible to the imagination <note>original: "Phansy"</note>. 14. ### Chap. IX.
1. The existence of God argued from the final cause <note>original: "Finall cause"; the ultimate purpose or "why" something exists.</note> of planting the idea of God in the soul. 2. An avoidance of the argument by assuming all things are as they are by chance. 3. That this excuse is either impossible or barely possible, and therefore carries no weight. 4. That we should not focus on what is simply possible, but on what our natural faculties determine. 5. He emphasizes again the final cause of the permanent <note>original: "inde-leble"</note> idea or image of God in the soul, illustrating its force through a comparison <note>original: "Similitude"</note>. 6. That, assuming God did exist, he would have dealt with us no differently than we are in fact <note>original: "de facto"</note> dealt with; which therefore again proves that He does exist. 26

### Chap. X.
1. Several other qualities <note>original: "Affections"</note> or properties in the human soul that argue for the being of God. 2. Such as natural conscience. 3. A pious hope or confidence of success in one's affairs when dealing righteously with the world. 4. An answer to an objection: that some men are completely lacking these divine senses. 5. That the universality of religious worship proves the knowledge of God's existence comes from the light of nature. 6. An answer to an objection: namely, that this general acknowledgment of a God among the nations may be nothing but a universal tradition. 7. Another objection answered: namely, that what is universally accepted by all nations may nevertheless be false. 8. An objection taken from the general falsehood and corruption of world religions. The first answer is by way of a defense <note>original: "Apologie"</note>. 9. The second answer, assuming the religions of the nations are as depraved as you please. 10. A further objection regarding the long duration of those false religions and the hopelessness of ever escaping them, with a brief answer. 28

<column-break/>

### Chap. XI.
1. An important <note>original: "concerning"</note> inquiry regarding the essence of the human soul. 2. That the soul is not a mere arrangement <note>original: "Modification"</note> of the body, as the body is incapable of such operations as are usually attributed to the soul, such as voluntary motion <note>original: "Spontaneous Motion"</note>, perception <note>original: "Animadversion"</note>, memory, and reason. 3. That the "spirits" <note>original: "the Spirits"; in 17th-century physiology, these were subtle fluids thought to carry signals through the nerves.</note> are incapable of memory, and consequently of reason, perception, and moving the body. 4. That the brain cannot be the source of voluntary motion, having neither muscles nor sense. 5. That imagination <note>original: "Phansy"</note>, reason, and perception are located neither in any pore nor any particular part of the brain; nor is the entire brain (or every particle of it) shaped into this or that concept. 6. That the shaping of one part of the brain is not reflected to the rest, demonstrated by the position <note>original: "Site"</note> of things. 7. That the brain has no sense, further demonstrated by anatomical experiments. 8. How ridiculously the operations of the soul are attributed to the pineal gland <note>original: "Conarion"</note>. 9. The conclusion: that the drive <note>original: "Impetus"</note> of voluntary motion comes from neither the animal spirits nor the brain. 10. That the soul is not any physical <note>original: "Corporeal"</note> substance distinct from the animal spirits and the body. 11. And therefore, the soul is an immaterial <note>original: "Incorporeal"</note> substance. 12. The discovery of the soul's essence is very useful for more easily understanding the nature of God. 13. And how there may be an eternal mind that has both understanding and the power to move the matter of the universe. 32

...the laws of the Earth's motion are not accidental or by chance <note>original: "casual or fortuitous"</note>. 6. That there is a Divine Providence that at least approves, if not directs, all the movements of matter; with a reason why she [Providence] allows the effects of purely mechanical motion to go as far as they can. 37

**Chapter II.** 1. The constant parallelism <note>The fact that the Earth's axis always points in the same direction as it orbits the Sun.</note> of the Earth's axis is a clear argument for Divine Providence. 2. The great inconveniences that would occur if the position of this axis were perpendicular to the plane of the ecliptic <note>original: "Ecliptick"; the path of the Sun's motion as seen from Earth.</note>. 3. Or if it were aligned with that plane. 4. The excellent advantages of its actual tilted <note>original: "inclining"</note> position, and what a clear demonstration of Providence this is. 5. The same argument presented using the Ptolemaic hypothesis <note>original: "Ptolemaical Hypothesis"; the older theory that the Earth is the stationary center of the universe.</note>. 6. A further consideration of the Earth's axis and the Moon's crossing of the celestial equator <note>original: "Æquinoctial Line"</note>. 7. A demonstration from the phenomenon of gravity that there is a guiding principle distinct from matter. 8. That neither the air, nor any more subtle matter within the air, possesses knowledge or free agency. 9. A notable demonstration from the piston <note>original: "Sucker"</note> of an air pump lifting a great weight, showing there is a substance distinct from matter in the world. 10. That this phenomenon cannot be explained <note>original: "salv'd"</note> by the elasticity of the air, as shown by the phenomenon itself. 11. An excuse <note>original: "Evasion"</note> presented and answered. 12. Another excuse anticipated. 13. That this undeniable force of nature, which goes against the basic laws of mechanical motion and gravity, is clear evidence that when things turn out well, an immaterial guide is at work, even when the force on the matter isn't as obvious. 14. The ridiculous false reasoning <note>original: "Sophistry"</note> of the atheist—who argues from minor effects of simple matter in motion that there is no higher principle—is clearly exposed and rightly mocked. 15. Providence is proven by the laws of day and night, winter and summer, etc. 40

<column-break/>

**Chapter III.** 1. That nothing exists in nature except what is approved by a conscious, knowing principle. 2. The great usefulness of hills and mountains. 3. The status <note>original: "Condition"</note> of man in relation to the rest of creation. 4. The intentional usefulness of stone quarries, timber, metals, and minerals. 5. How the glory and magnificence of both peace and war depend on these resources. 6. As well as the defense of humans against wild animals. 47

**Chapter IV.** 1. The division of land and sea is not without the work of Providence. 2. Also, the density <note>original: "Consistence"</note> of seawater, which allows it to support ships. 3. The great convenience and pleasure of sailing <note>original: "Navigation"</note>. 4. The admirable series of natural provisions designed to satisfy human ingenuity <note>original: "Wit"</note> in such an important pursuit <note>original: "Curiosity"</note>. 50

**Chapter V.** 1. That the form, beauty, seeds, and signatures <note>The "Doctrine of Signatures" held that plants resemble the body parts they are meant to heal.</note> of plants are arguments for Providence. 2. That although the simple motion of matter might produce certain atmospheric events <note>original: "Meteors"</note> like hail, snow, and ice, it does not follow that it is the sufficient cause of animals and plants. 3. That it would be no great flaw <note>original: "botch"</note> in nature if some cruder phenomena were acknowledged as the results of simple mechanical motion. 4. That the form and beauty of flowers and plants come from a higher principle. 5. That beauty exists and is something recognized by our intellectual faculties. 6. From which it follows that the beautiful forms and shapes <note>original: "Figures"</note> of plants and animals come from an intellectual principle. 52

**Chapter VI.** 1. Providence argued from the seeds of plants. 2. An objection answered regarding smelly weeds and poisonous plants. 3. The "signatures" of plants as an argument for Providence. 4. Certain examples of signatures. 5. An answer to an objection regarding signatures in plants that do not seem to relate to medicine. 55

## Book III.

**Chapter I.** 1. That, because **good men do not always fare best in this world**, the great examples of **divine vengeance** upon wicked and blasphemous persons are not always convincing to the stubborn <note>original: "obstinate"</note> **atheist**. 2. The irreligious mockery <note>original: "Jeers"</note> and sacrileges of **Dionysius** of **Syracuse**. 3. The cause of the **atheist's** disbelief <note>original: "incredulity"</note> in supernatural or miraculous things. 4. That there have been true **miracles** in the world as well as false ones. 5. And what are the best and safest ways to distinguish them, so that we may not be deceived <note>original: "impos'd upon"</note> by **history**. 86

**Chapter II.** 1. **The moving of a sieve by a charm.** Coskinomancy <note>original: "Coskinomancy"; a form of divination using a sieve and shears</note>. 2. A **magical cure** of a **horse**. 3. The **charming of serpents**. 4. A strange example of someone **struck dead** as he walked the streets. 5. A story of a **sudden wind** that nearly knocked down the gallows at the hanging of two **witches**. 89

**Chapter III.** 1. That **winds and tempests** are raised by mere ceremonies or forms of words. 2. Examples of that power in **rain and thunder**. 4. **Margaret Warine** thrown <note>original: "discharged"</note> upon an **oak tree** during a **clap of thunder**. 5. **Amantius** and **Rotarius** cast headlong out of a cloud onto a house-top. 6. The **Witch of Constance** seen by shepherds riding through the air. 7. That he might add several other instances from eyewitnesses of the strange effects of invisible **demons**. 8. His brief retelling <note>original: "compendious Rehersal"</note> of the most remarkable exploits of the **Devil of Mascon** <note>A famous case of a poltergeist or "speaking spirit" in Mascon, France, in 1612</note> instead. 9. The reasons for giving himself the trouble of this retelling. 91

**Chapter IV.** 1. The **supernatural effects** observed in the bewitched children of **Mr. Throgmorton** and **Mrs. Muschamp**. 2. The general remarkable facts in both cases. 3. The **possession** of the religious virgins of **Werts, Hessimont**, etc. 4. The story of that famous **Abbess Magdalena Crucia**, her useless and playful <note>original: "ludicrous"</note> miracles. 5. That she was a **sorceress**, and was married to the **Devil** for thirty years. 6. How convincing <note>original: "The Convictiveness"</note> these accounts are. 5. Objections against their persuasiveness answered. 6. Of a **girl possessed by a demon** <note>original: "Maid Demoniack"</note> speaking **Greek**; and of the miraculous binding of another's hands by an invisible power. 98

## *Enthusiasm Triumphed Over;* <note>original Latin title: "Enthusiasmus Triumphatus"</note>

->OR,<-

### A BRIEF DISCOURSE

->ON<-

### The Nature, Causes, Kinds, and Cure

->OF<-

# ENTHUSIASM.

### By HENRY MORE, D. D. <note>Doctor of Divinity</note>

### SECTION I.
### *The Great Affinity and Correspondence between Enthusiasm and Atheism.*

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter 'A' featuring floral motifs and a border.</image-desc>

Atheism and *enthusiasm* <note>enthusiasm: in the 17th century, this term referred to a state of being "possessed by a spirit," often used pejoratively to describe people who falsely claimed direct divine inspiration or revelation</note>, though they seem so extremely opposite to one another, yet in many things they agree very closely. For, to say nothing of their joint conspiracy against the true knowledge of God and religion, they are commonly entertained—though successively—in the same temperament <term>complexion: a person’s physical and mental constitution or character</term>. For that temperament which disposes a man to listen to the authoritative <term>magisterial: dictatorial or overbearing</term> dictates of an overbearing *fancy* <note>original: "phansy"</note>, more than to the calm and cautious suggestions of free *reason*, is a subject that by turns very easily houses and shelters these mischievous guests.

For just as *dreams* are the *fancies* of those who sleep, so *fancies* are but the *dreams* of men awake. And these *fancies* by day, like those *dreams* by night, will vary and change with the weather and the current state <term>temper: the balance of bodily fluids or physical condition</term> of the body. Thus, those who have only a fiery, *enthusiastic* acknowledgment of God may, through a change of diet, the foulness <term>feculent: murky, foul, or full of dregs</term> of old age, or some current bouts of melancholy <note>melancholy: in this period, seen as a physical imbalance of "black bile" that caused depression, anxiety, or delusions</note>, just as confidently imagine in their *fancy* that there is no God as they ever imagined that there is one. And then, having lost the use of their more noble faculties of *reason* and *understanding*, they must—according to the course of nature—be as bold *atheists* now as they were confident *enthusiasts* before.

Nor do these two unruly guests only take turns inhabiting the same person, but they also send mutual reinforcements to one another when housed in separate people. For the *atheist's* pretense to *wit* and natural *reason* (though the foulness of his mind makes him fumble very foolishly <term>dotingly: acting as if mentally weakened by age or obsession</term> in the

[The] use thereof makes the *enthusiast* <note>enthusiast: in the 17th century, this referred to someone who wrongly believed they were receiving direct, private revelations from God</note> certain that *reason* is no guide to God. And the *enthusiast’s* bold claims, presenting the careless ravings of his own tumultuous *fancy* <note>original: "phansy"</note> as undeniable principles of divine knowledge, confirms to the *atheist* that the whole business of religion and the concept of God is nothing but a troublesome fit of overly curious melancholy. Therefore, since there is such a close alliance and mutual connection between these two enormous disorders of the mind—atheism and enthusiasm—I believe it is very suitable and convenient, having already treated the former, to add this brief discourse on the nature, causes, kinds, and cure of this latter disease.

### S E C T. II.

->*What Inspiration is, and what Enthusiasm.*<-

I leave the etymology <term>etymology: the study of the origin of words</term> and the various meanings of the word *enthusiasm* to critics and grammarians; but you shall fully understand what we mean by it here after we have defined what *inspiration* is. For *enthusiasm* is nothing else but a misconception of being *inspired*. Now, to be *inspired* is *to be moved in an extraordinary manner by the power or Spirit of God to act, speak, or think what is holy, just, and true.* From this, it will be easily understood what *enthusiasm* is, namely: **A complete but false persuasion in a person that they are inspired.**

---

### S E C T. III.

->*A search of the Causes of Enthusiasm in the Faculties of the Soul.*<-

We shall now inquire into the causes of this disorder—how it happens that a person should be so fooled by their own imagination. And truly, unless we were to provide less satisfaction than the subject allows, we must not only discuss melancholy here, but also the *faculties of the human soul*. By doing so, it may be better understood how the soul can become vulnerable <term>obnoxious: in this context, exposed to harm or subject to influence</term> to such disturbances of melancholy, through which she has completely lost her own judgment and freedom, and can neither keep out nor distinguish between her own fancies and real truths.

---

### S E C T. IV.

->*The several Degrees and Natures of her Faculties.*<-

We must therefore take notice of the several degrees and natures of the soul's faculties. The lowest of these she exercises without even a perception of what she does, and these operations are

...inevitable <note>original: "fatall"</note> and natural to her as long as she is in the body; in these functions, a man differs little from a plant, which you may therefore call the *Vegetative* or *Plant-like* faculties of the soul.

The lowest of those faculties whose present operations we can *perceive* are the outer *senses*. When an object comes into contact <note>original: "pertingencie"</note> with a sensory organ, these senses cannot fail to act. That is, the soul cannot help but be affected by them, nor is it in her power—or at least, it is very difficult—to suspend her *perception*.

From this, it is plain that the soul's nature is such that she may sometimes awaken inevitably and necessarily into *phantasms* and *perceptions* without any will or consent of her own.

This is also found to be true in *imagination*, though that faculty is freer than the previous one. For what are *dreams* but the imaginations and perceptions of someone asleep? Yet these steal upon the soul or rise out of her without her consent. This is most obvious in those dreams that torment us and cause extreme pain until we wake up.

Similar sudden intrusions <note>original: "obreptions"</note> or unavoidable, persistent *thoughts*—which offer or force themselves upon the *mind*—can be observed even during the day, depending on the nature or strength of our body's physical constitution <note>original: "complexion"</note>. However, how the body engages the mind in *thoughts* or *imaginations* is most obvious in *sleep*. Depending on which of the four humors—*choler*, *sanguine*, *phlegm*, or *melancholy*—is dominant, the scene of our *dreams* will change. This happens without any check or restraint of doubt concerning the truth and existence of the things that appear.

We can imagine no other reason for this than the fact that the *inner seat of sense* is very fully and vigorously affected. This is just like how objects affect us during the day; our ordinary assurance of their real existence comes from the fact that they strike or affect our *sensitive faculty* so strongly. This faculty does not reside in the external organs—no more than a craftsman's skill resides in his tools—but in some more inward *recesses of the brain*. Therefore, since the *true and real seat of sense* is affected in our *sleep* just as much as when we are awake, it is less of a wonder that the soul believes her dreams to be real transactions rather than dreams while she is dreaming.

## S E C T. V.
### *Why Dreams, until we awake, seem to be real transactions.*

Now, the reason the inward sense is so vigorously affected in these *dreams* proceeds, I believe, from this: the *brain*, *animal spirits* <note>animal spirits: in 17th-century medicine, these were thought to be very fine fluids or essences that carried signals between the brain and the body</note>, or whatever the soul works upon during her *imaginative* operations, are not significantly moved, altered, or agitated by any external motion. Instead, they entirely and fully maintain that shape or modification into which the soul necessarily and naturally molds them during our *sleep*. Therefore, the belief in the truth of what is represented to us in our *dreams* comes from this: *imagination* at that time (that is, the internal shaping of our brain or spirits into this or that representation) is far stronger than any motion or agitation from *outside*, which to those who are awake <meta>catchword: diminishes</meta>

...dims and obscures their inward imagination, just as the light of the sun does to the light of a candle in a room. Yet even in this case, according to Aristotle, *fancy* <note>original: "Phanfy"</note> is "a kind of weak sensation" <note>original: "αἴσθησίς τις ἀσθενὴς"</note>.

But if the imagination were so strong that it could hold its own against all the encounters <note>original: "occursions"</note> and impulses of outward objects—so that it was not disrupted, but remained complete and equal in splendor and vigor to things presented from the outside, and did so not by choice but by necessity and unavoidably, as has already been suggested—then the person affected would certainly mistake their own imagination for a real object of sense. This happened in a case mentioned by Descartes <note>original: "Cartesius"</note> (and there are several other examples of this kind) regarding a man who had his arm amputated. While blindfolded <note>original: "hoodwinkt"</note>, he complained of pain in one finger or another, even though he had lost his entire arm. 

Another example can be found in mad or melancholic men <note>original: "Melancholy men" — in the 17th century, "melancholy" was a medical diagnosis believed to be caused by an excess of black bile, often resulting in hallucinations or delusions</note>, who have confidently claimed to have met with the Devil or conversed with angels, when it was nothing but an encounter with their own imagination.

# SECTION 6.
*The Enormous Strength of Imagination as the Cause of Enthusiasm.*

Therefore, it is the enormous strength of *imagination*—which is actually a weakness or lack of control in the soul, by which she sinks so far into phantoms <note>original: "Phantasmes"</note> that she cannot recover her ability to use her freer faculties of *reason* and *understanding*—that so decisively forces a man to believe a lie. 

And if the imagination is strong enough to convince us of the presence of some external object that isn't really there, why might it not be just as effective in creating a belief in internal perceptions? Such cases have been reported of mad and fanatical men who have so firmly and unchangeably imagined themselves to be *God the Father, the Messiah, the Holy Ghost, the Angel Gabriel,* the *last and greatest Prophet* that God would send into the world, and similar things. 

For their thoughts are not so pure or spiritual <note>original: "immateriall"</note>, nor solid or rational, that these words aren't always accompanied by some powerful phantom or vivid imagination. The fullness and clarity of this image (as in the case mentioned just before) naturally overwhelms the soul into believing in the truth and existence of what she so vigorously perceives. Being so completely immersed in this delusion <note>original: "conceit"</note> and so strongly affected by it, the soul either lacks the patience to consider any evidence against it, or if she does consider it and finds herself trapped by logic, she will view it as a piece of human trickery <note>original: "sophistry"</note>. She will then prefer her own "infallibility"—or the "infallibility of the Spirit"—over all "carnal reasonings" whatever. 

This is similar to those whose imaginations <note>original: "Phanfies"</note> are strengthened by long habit and education in some absurd point of a false religion; though they are wise enough in other matters, they will firmly hold to their conclusion despite the clearest proof to the contrary. Now, what custom and education achieve gradually, a disordered <note>original: "distempered"</note> [state of the body...]

*Fancy* <note>original: "Phansy"</note> may do in a shorter time. But the case in both is much like that in *dreams*, where what is represented is necessarily taken as true because nothing stronger weakens <note>original: "enervates"</note> the perception. Just as the suspension <note>original: "ligation"</note> of the outward organs of sense keeps away the fluctuations or waves of motion from outside that might break or hide these images during sleep, so too do prejudice and confidence in a personal idea <note>original: "conceit"</note> when a man is awake. These keep his foolish <note>original: "fond"</note> imagination vigorous and whole against all the assaults of reason that would cause any doubt <note>original: "dubitation"</note>.

It is no more surprising that his intellect <note>original: "Intellectuals"</note> should be sound in other matters, even though he is delirious on one specific point, than it is for a man who thinks he sees the devil in a forest to be completely accurate about the location—seeing the very same path, flowers, and grass that a person in their right mind sees there as well as himself.

To be brief, therefore, the origin of such absolute <note>original: "peremptory"</note> delusions that mankind is prone <note>original: "obnoxious"</note> to is the enormous strength and vigor of the *imagination*. This faculty, although it is somewhat in our power—just as *breathing* <note>original: "Respiration"</note> is—will also work without our permission, as I have already shown. Consequently, men become mad and fanatical whether they want to or not.

## SECTION 7.

### *Various Natural and Physical Causes that Necessarily Affect the Imagination.*

Now, exactly what it is within us that captivates our *imagination* and carries it far out of the reach or hearing of that freer and superior faculty of *reason* is difficult to define specifically. But experience sufficiently proves that there are various physical <note>original: "material"</note> things that most certainly change our mind or fancy.

<margin>*On the Geography of the World*, book 2, chapter 2.</margin>
<margin>*Antiquities of the Jews*, book 11, chapter 4.</margin>
For our *imagination* changes as our blood and "spirits" <note>In 17th-century medicine, "spirits" (or animal spirits) were thought to be subtle fluids that traveled through the nerves to communicate between the soul and the body.</note> are altered (as I have mentioned and shown with the example of our *dreams*). Indeed, very small things will alter them even when we are awake: a mere change of weather, various states of the air, or even a little smoke or incense <note>original: "reek or suffumigation"</note>. An example is the seeds mentioned by *Pomponius Mela* which the *Thracians* (who did not know how to use wine) used to throw into the fire at their feasts; this intoxicated them into as much joy as those who drink freely of the "blood of the grape" [wine]. The power of wine is so great that, as *Josephus* phrases it, it seems to create a new soul in the person who drinks it: *For it transforms and sweetens the souls when it enters into them* <note>original Greek: Μεταποιεῖ γὰρ καὶ μεταγλυκᾷ τὰς ψυχὰς ἐν αὐταῖς γινομένη</note>, or as it is often said, *it transforms and regenerates the soul into a new nature.*

But it most certainly brings a new "scene" of thoughts into the minds of those who use it. This led the *Persians* to never undertake any serious matter or agree to a significant deal without first considering it both while nearly drunk <note>original: "fuddled"</note> and while sober. For if they liked the idea in all the ways those two opposite moods <note>original: "tempers"</note> presented it to their minds, they thought themselves

<margin>* *Practical Medicine*, book 1, part 2, chapter 17.</margin>
And yet *Wine* does not always change our thoughts and alter our temperament so much as heighten it, so that its effect sometimes proves contrary only because of the diversity of persons; some being weeping drunk, others laughing, some kind, others raging. This also happens in those who are stung by the *Tarantula* <note>The bite of the tarantula spider was historically believed to cause "tarantism," a form of uncontrollable dancing mania.</note>: "Some laugh perpetually, others sing, others weep," <note>original: "Alii perpetuò rident, alii canunt, alii plorant"</note> and so on, as *Sennertus* observes from the writings of *Matthiolus*. But what they both seem to admire most is that the imagination <note>original: "Phansie"</note> of those afflicted by the *Tarantula* should be so powerfully carried away by music; for they not only forget their pain, but dance incessantly. Regarding this, *Epiphanius Ferdinandus* tells a very remarkable story of an old man ninety-four years of age, who could scarcely crawl with a staff, yet after being bitten by the *Tarantula*, immediately upon hearing music, he leaped and skipped like a young goat <note>original: "kid"</note>.

Related to this is that kind of madness which they call *St. Vitus's Dance* <note>A disorder characterized by rapid, uncoordinated jerking movements, often historically linked to religious or physical causes.</note>. *Sennertus* rightly claims this disease proceeds from a certain malignant humor <note>In ancient and early modern medicine, "humors" were bodily fluids believed to control health and temperament.</note> generated in the body that is closely related to the poison of the *Tarantula*. This will help us explain the *causes* of even stranger workings on the *imagination* than have yet been mentioned; for example, in Lycanthropy, Galeanthropy, and Cynanthropy <note>original: λυκανθρωπία, γαλεανθρωπία, and κυναнθρωπία</note>, which are distempers of the mind where men imagine themselves to be *wolves, cats, or dogs*.

## SECTION 8.

### *The power of Foods to change the Imagination.*

<margin>* In his *Medical Institutions*, book 2, part 3, Section 2, chapter 4.</margin>
There are several accounts in the previously mentioned *author* <note>referring to Sennertus</note> concerning the power that *nourishment* has to affect the *imagination*, and to change a person's disposition into the nature of the creature whose blood or milk nourishes them.

A young woman at Wrocław <note>original: "Breslaw"</note> suffered from epilepsy after seeing an executioner cut off a criminal's head. When several other remedies failed, she was persuaded by some to drink the blood of a *cat*. After doing this, the girl not long after took on the nature and characteristics of that animal: she cries and jumps like a *cat*, and hunts mice with the same silence and watchfulness they do, pursuing them as closely as she could to their very holes. He transcribes this account from the writer *Weinrichius*.

He also briefly mentions another account in the same writer of someone who, having been fed on swine's blood for a long time, took special pleasure in wallowing and tumbling in the mud. Similarly, there was a girl raised on goat's milk who would skip like a goat and browse on trees as goats typically do.

We might add a fourth example of one who, by eating the brains of a *bear*, developed a *bear*-like temperament; but we will not dwell on smaller considerations.
