## SECT. IX.

### *Baptista Porta’s Potion to act upon the Fancy.*

Baptista Porta carries the matter much further, claiming that he was acquainted with someone who could, whenever he pleased, so alter a man's *Imagination* that he would make him fancy himself to be this or that *Bird*, *Beast*, or *Fish*; and that in this madness the person thus deluded would move his body, as far as it was capable, just as such *Creatures* are accustomed to do; and if they were vocal, he would also imitate their voice.

This intoxicating Potion is made of the extract of certain herbs, such as *Solanum manicum*, Mandrake, and others, together with the heart, brain, and some other parts of this or that *Animal* with whose image they wished to infect the Fancy of the person. And he affirms from his own experience that, trying this feat upon some of his comrades when he was young, one who had gorged himself on *beef*, upon taking the potion, strongly imagined himself to be surrounded by *Bulls* that were constantly running at him with their horns.

---

## SECT. X.

### *The power of Diseases upon the Fancy.*

WHAT happens here in these cases where we can trace the *Causes*, sometimes occurs where we cannot so plainly and directly find the reason. For Physicians take notice of such kinds of *Madnesses* as make men confidently imagine themselves to be *Dogs*, *Wolves*, and *Cats*, even when they have neither eaten the flesh nor drunk the blood of any *Cat*, *Dog*, or *Wolf*, nor taken any such artificial potion as we just spoke of to bring them into these diseases.

The causes of this cannot be better guessed at than has been done by *Sennertus* regarding *St. Vitus's dance*. For just as there the Body is conceived to be infested by some malignant humor closely related to the poison of the *Tarantula*; so in these distempers we may well conclude that such fumes or vapors arise into the Brain from some foulness in the Body (though we do not understand the particular causes) which have a very close analogy to the harmful humors or exhalations that move up and down and mount up into the Imagination of those who have drunk the blood of *Cats*, or have been nourished with the milk of those *Animals* named above, or have taken such intoxicating potions as *Baptista Porta* has described.

--- Page 254 ---
## SECT. XI.

*Concerning the power of Melancholy, and how it often imposes a single absurd delusion upon the Mind, while the person remains sober in all other matters.*

We have given several instances of the mighty power that *natural Causes* have to act upon and unavoidably change our *Imagination*. We will now mention something more general, whose nature is nonetheless so various and changeable—like *Vertumnus*—that it can account for almost all specific cases, and that is *Melancholy*. *Aristotle* testifies to this, noting that according to its various degrees and temperaments, men vary wonderfully in their constitutions. It makes some slow and dull, others wild, clever, and amorous, prone to anger and lust; others it makes more eloquent and talkative, and others it raises even to the level of madness and *Enthusiasm*. He gives the example of one *Maracus*, a poet of *Syracuse*, who never composed verses so well as when he was in his fits of distraction.

But it is most observable in *Melancholy*, when it reaches the level of a disease, that it fixes one particular absurd delusion upon the Mind so firmly that no amount of evidence from Reason to the contrary can remove it, even though the persons affected are in other matters as sober and rational as other men. This is so well-known and frequent that *Aretaeus*, *Sennertus*, and other Physicians define *Melancholy* by this very effect.

---

## SECT. XII.

*Several Examples of the foregoing Observation.*

Aristotle provides us with no examples of this kind, but others do. *Democritus junior*, as he chooses to style himself, recites several stories from authors to this purpose. For instance, from *Laurentius*, he tells of a French *Poet* who, while using *Unguentum populeum* during a fever to rub on his temples to induce sleep, developed such a fixation against the smell of that ointment that for many years afterward he imagined everyone who came near him smelled of it. Therefore, he would let no man talk with him except from a distance, nor would he wear any new clothes because he fancied they smelled of that ointment; yet in all other things he was wise and discreet, and would talk as sensibly as other men.

He has another story (from *Anthony Verduer*) of a Gentleman of *Limosin* who was persuaded he had only one leg, having been frightened into that delusion by having that part struck by a wild boar, though otherwise he was a man in his right mind.

A third he has from *Platerus*, concerning a countryman of his who, having by chance fallen into a pit where there were frogs and frog-spawn and having swallowed a little of the water, was afterward so fully persuaded that there were young frogs in his belly that for many years following he could not correct his delusion. He betook himself to the study of

--- Page 255 ---
of Medicine for seven years together to find a cure for his disease: He traveled also in *Italy*, *France*, and *Germany* to confer with Physicians about it, and meeting with *Platerus*, consulted him along with the rest. He imagined the rumbling of his guts to be the croaking of frogs; and when *Platerus* tried to deceive him by putting live frogs into his excrement so that he might think he had passed them and was cured, his own knowledge of medicine made that trick ineffective. Except for this one vain delusion, the man was, as he reports, a learned and prudent man.

We will add only a fourth example from *Laurentius*, which is of a Nobleman of his time, a man of reason and discretion in all other things, except that he imagined himself made of glass; and though he loved to be visited by his friends, yet he took special care that they should not come too near him, for fear they should break him.

Not much unlike this is the story of a Baker of *Ferrara*, who thought he was composed of butter, and therefore would not sit in the sun nor come near a fire, for fear he should be melted.

It would be an infinite task to set down all these cases at length. *Sennertus* has given some hints of the variety of this distemper, referring us to *Schenckius*, *Marcellus Donatus*, *Forestus*, and others for more full narrations. Some, he says, are vexed and tormented with the fear of death, thinking they have committed some crime they never actually committed; some imagine they are eternally damned, and even complain that they are already tormented with hellfire; others believe themselves to be dying, others imagine themselves quite dead, and therefore will not eat; others fear that the heavens will fall upon them, others dare not clench their hands for fear of crushing the world between their fists; some imagine themselves to be roosters, some nightingales, some one animal, some another; some engage in conversation with God or his Angels, others imagine themselves bewitched, or that a black man or Devil perpetually accompanies them; some complain of their poverty, others imagine themselves persons of honor, Dukes, Princes, Kings, Popes, and what not? Much to this purpose you may see in *Sennertus*, and more in *Democritus junior*.

---

### SECT. XIII.

#### *A seasonable application of the foregoing Examples for the weakening of the authority of bold Enthusiasts.*

That which is most observable and most useful for the present matter in hand is, that notwithstanding there is such an enormous lapse of the Imagination and Judgment in some *one thing*, yet the party should be of a sound mind in *all others*, according to his natural capacities and abilities; which all Physicians acknowledge to be true, and are ready to prove by innumerable examples. This I conceive to be of great importance to consider more thoroughly.

I do not mean *how* it may come to pass (for that we have already explained) but *what excellent use* it may be of to prevent that easy and...

--- Page 256 ---
and ordinary sophistry which imposes upon many, who, if an *Enthusiast* speaks eloquently, and perhaps rationally and piously (you may be sure zealously and fervently enough, and with the greatest confidence imaginable), are so credulous that, because of this visible dress of such laudable accomplishments, they will believe him even in that which is not only improbable, but vain and foolish—nay, sometimes very mischievous and impious to believe. Such claims include: that the party is immediately and extraordinarily inspired by God; that he is a *special Messenger* sent by Him, the last and best Prophet, the *Holy Ghost* come in the flesh, and similar stuff as this, which has been set on foot time and again in all ages by some *Enthusiast* or other.

Amongst whom I do not deny but there may be some who, regarding the main practical light of Christianity, might have their judgments as consistent as those *Melancholists* named above had in the ordinary practical affairs of the world. But as for this one particular of being supernaturally inspired, of being the *last Prophet*, the *last Trumpet*, the *Angel in the midst of Heaven with the Eternal Gospel in his hand*, the *Holy Ghost incorporated*, *God come to judgment*, and the like—this certainly in them is as true, but far worse, dotage than to fancy oneself either a *Cock* or a *Bull*, when it is plain to the senses of everyone else that he is a *Man*.

## SECT. XIV.

### *That the causality of Melancholy in this distemper of Enthusiasm is more easily traced than in other extravagancies.*

BUT it being of such weighty concern, I shall not satisfy myself with this more general account of *Enthusiasm*: that it may very well be resolved into that property of Melancholy whereby men become delirious in some *one point*, while their judgment stands untouched in *others*. For I shall easily further demonstrate that the very nature of *Melancholy* is such that it may more fairly and plausibly tempt a man into such conceits of *Inspiration* and supernatural light from God than it can possibly do into those more extravagant conceits of being *Glass*, *Butter*, a *Bird*, a *Beast*, or any such thing.

## SECT. XV.

### *Melancholy a stubborn and religious complexion.*

FOR besides that which is most general of all—that *Melancholy* inclines a man very strongly and peremptorily to either believe or disbelieve a thing (as is plain in that passion of *Suspicion* and *Jealousy*, which upon little or no occasion will win such full assent of the mind that it will engage a man to act as vigorously as if he were certain that his jealousies were true)—it is very well known that this complexion is the most religious...

--- Page 257 ---
... gious complexion that exists, and will be as naturally tampering with Divine matters (though in no better light than that of her own) as Apes and Monkeys will be imitating the actions and manners of Men.

Neither is there any true spiritual *Grace* from God but this mere natural constitution, according to its various tempers and workings, will not only resemble, but sometimes seem to *outstrip*, by reason of its fury and excess; and that not only in *Actions*, but very commonly in *Eloquence* and *Expressions*; as if here alone were to be found that lively sense and understanding of all holy things, or at least as if there were no other state to be compared to it.

The result of which must be, if a very great measure of the true Grace of God does not intervene, that such a *Melancholist* as this must be very highly puffed up, and not only fancy himself *inspired*, but believe himself to be such a special piece of *Light* and *Holiness* that God has sent into the world, that he will take it upon himself to reform, or rather annul, the very *Law* and *Religion* he is born under, and make himself not at all inferior to either *Moses* or *Christ*, though he has neither any sound *Reason* nor visible *Miracle* to compel belief.

---

### S E C T. XVI.

*That men are prone to suspect some special presence of God or of a Supernatural power in whatever is Great or Vehement.*

BUT this is still too general; we shall yet more particularly point out the Causes of this Imposture. Things that are *great* or *vehement*, People are subject to suspect they rise from some Supernatural cause; insomuch that the Wind cannot be more than ordinarily high, but they are prone to imagine the Devil raised it, nor any sore Plague or Disease occur, but they imagine God in an extraordinary manner to be the Author of it.

So rude Antiquity conceived a kind of Divinity in almost anything that was extraordinarily great. For this reason some have worshipped very tall Trees, others large Rivers, some a great Stone or Rock, others high and vast Mountains; hence the Greeks confound *great* and *holy* in that one word *ἱερος*, which signifies both; and the Hebrews by the *Cedars of God*, the *mountains of God*, the *Spirit of God*, and the like, understand high Cedars, great Mountains, and a mighty Spirit or Wind. We may add also what is more familiar: how old Women and Nurses are accustomed to tell little Children when they ask concerning the *Moon*, pointing at it with their fingers, that it is *God's Candle*, because it is so great a Light in the night. All of these are arguments or intimations that man's nature is very prone to suspect some special presence of God in anything that is *great* or *vehement*.

From this arises a strong temptation for a Melancholist when he feels a storm of devotion or zeal come upon him like a mighty wind, his heart being full of affection, his head pregnant with clear and sensible representations, and his mouth flowing and streaming with fit and powerful...

--- Page 258 ---
powerful expressions, such as would astonish an ordinary audience to hear, it is, I say, a strong temptation to him to think that it is the very Spirit of God that then moves supernaturally in him; whereas all that excess of zeal, affection, and fluency of words is most clearly to be attributed to the power of Melancholy, which is a kind of natural intoxication.

And that there is nothing better than Nature in it is evident both from the experience of good and sensible men, who have found their own zeal, devotion, and eloquence to vary strangely as Melancholy has been more or less predominant in them; and also from what everyone may observe in those who have been wicked, mad, and blasphemous, and yet have excelled in this mistaken gift of Prayer; as is notorious in Hacket, who was so infatuated with a conceit of his own zeal and eloquence that he imagined himself to be the Holy Ghost.

---

### SECT. XVII.

*The mistake of heated Melancholy for holy Zeal and the Spirit of God.*

AND when men talk so much of the Spirit, if they notice what they ordinarily mean by it, it is nothing else but a strong and impetuous motion by which they are zealously and fervently carried away in matters of Religion: so that Fervour, Zeal, and Spirit are in effect all one. Now no Complexion is so hot as Melancholy when it is heated, being like boiling water, as Aristotle observes ("If it be sufficiently heated, it is like that which boils," etc.) so that it surpasses the flame of fire; or it is like heated stone or iron when they are red hot, for they are then much hotter than a burning coal. We shall omit playing the Grammarian here, and taking notice of how well Aristotle's term for "boiling" suits with the very word "zeal" of which we speak; but we shall look more carefully at the things themselves, and find a parallel from the same Philosopher between what they call Spirit and what he affirms to be contained in Melancholy: "The humor and the temperament of black bile is full of spirit (or wind)."

The Spirit, then, that wings the Enthusiast in such a wonderful manner, is nothing else but that Flatulency which is in the Melancholy complexion, and rises out of the Hypochondriacal humor upon some occasional heat, like wind out of an Aeolipile applied to the fire. This fume, mounting into the head after being first activated, energized, and somewhat refined by the warmth of the heart, fills the mind with a variety of imaginations; it so quickens and enlarges invention that it makes the Enthusiast admirably fluent and eloquent, he being as it were drunk with new wine drawn from that cellar of his own that lies in the lowest region of his body. He is not aware of this, but takes it to be pure Nectar and those waters of life that spring from above. Aristotle makes a long parallel between the nature and effects of Wine and Melancholy, to which both Fernelius and Sennertus refer.

--- Page 259 ---
### SECT. XVIII.

*The Ebbs and Flows of Melancholy as a further Cause of Enthusiasm.*

BUT this is not the only advantage that Melancholy provides toward *Enthusiasm*—to thus unexpectedly and suddenly surprise the mind with such vehement fits of *Zeal*, and such streams and torrents of *Eloquence* in either exhorting others to piety or in devotions toward God; it also adds a greater weight of belief that there is something supernatural in the matter, because the same temperament reveals itself to those who live under it in such contrary *effects*.

For just as it is thus vehemently hot, it is also as stupidly cold; which makes the person prone to melancholy become faithless, hopeless, disheartened, and almost witless. These *ebbs* of his constitution must necessarily make its *overflowing* seem more miraculous and supernatural. Furthermore, these *cold* and *dejected* fits also make him very perceptibly and winningly *rhetorical* when he speaks of *disconsolation*, *abandonment*, *humility*, *mortification*, and the like, as if he were truly and voluntarily passing through such experiences; whereas only the fatal necessity of his temperament has violently dragged him through the mere shadows and resemblances of them.

But when he later finds himself, beyond all hope or any sense or forewarning of any power in himself, lifted aloft again, he does not doubt that anything less than the immediate arm of God from heaven has thus exalted him as the cause of this unexpected joy and triumph; when in truth it is nothing but a *paroxysm* of Melancholy, which is like the breaking out of a flame after the long smoking and reeking of new rubbish laid upon a fire. But because such returns as these do not occur at set times, nor make men feel sick, but rather delight them, they think there is something *divine* in them, and that they do not arise from *natural causes*.

---

### SECT. XIX.

*The notorious mockery of Melancholy in reference to Divine love.*

THERE is also another notorious mockery in this temperament: *Nature* confidently claiming to be *God*, whom the Apostle calls *Love*, as if it were His very essence; when indeed it is here nothing else but *Melancholy* that has put on the garments of an angel of light.

Nothing is more true than that *love* is the *fulfilling of the law* and the highest *perfection* attainable by the soul of man; this is also so plain and unavoidable a truth that a man may be mad to a very high degree and yet not fail to agree with it. Nay, I dare say Melancholy itself would act as his monitor to remind him of it, if there were any possibility that he should forget so manifest and palpable a truth.

For the sense of *love* in a general sense is eminently contained within the temperament of the person prone to melancholy, *Melancholy* and *wine* being of so similar a nature...

--- Page 260 ---
one to the other. *But wine makes men amorous*; which the Philosopher proves by the fact that a man influenced by wine will kiss such persons as a sober man would scarcely touch with a pair of tongs, because of their age and ugliness. And assuredly it was the fumes of *Melancholy* that infatuated the imagination of a recent, trendy *Religionist*, when he sat so affectionately by a *Gypsy* under a hedge, and put his hand into her bosom in a fit of devotion, and boasted of it afterward as if it had been a very pious and meritorious action.

---

### SECT. XX.

*That Melancholy partakes much of the nature of Wine, and from what temperament Poets and Enthusiasts arise, and what the difference is between them.*

**But** now that *Melancholy* partakes much of the nature of *Wine*, he demonstrates from the fact that it is so *spirited*; and that it is so *spirited*, from the fact that it is so *foamy*: and that *Melancholy* is flatulent or *spirited*, he appeals to the Physicians, who say that windy and hypochondriac disorders are melancholy.

Therefore the Philosopher assigns another companion to *Venus* besides the plump youth *Bacchus* whom the Poets bestow upon her, who, though seemingly more somber, will yet prove as faithful an attendant as the other, and this is *Melancholy*. And most melancholy people are lustful, for the sexual act is driven by internal air.

Now besides this *Flatulence* that incites lust, there may be such a proper dash of the *Sanguine* humor in the *Melancholy*, that the temperament may prove stupendously ravishing. For that more sluggish *Sweetness* of the blood will sometimes be so quickened and activated by the fierceness and sharpness of the *Melancholy* humor (just as the cloying sweetness of Sugar is by the acidity of *Lemons*) that it will afford far more perceptible pleasure; and all the imaginations of *Love*, of whatever kind, will be far more lively and vigorous, more piercing and rapturous, than they can be in the pure *Sanguine* temperament itself.

From this temperament arise *Poets*, and the more high-pretending *Enthusiasts*: Between whom this is the great difference, That a *Poet* is an *Enthusiast* in jest, and an *Enthusiast* is a *Poet* in good earnest; *Melancholy* prevailing so much with him that he mistakes his merely *Poetic* fits and fictions for divine Inspiration and real Truth.

### SECTION XXI.

#### *That a certain dose of the Sanguine temperament mixed with Melancholy is the spirit that usually inspires Enthusiasts, proven by a large gathering of examples.*

**BUT** it is a purely natural, vaporous, and spirited temperament—a specific *dose of the Sanguine* <note>The "Sanguine" humor (blood) was thought to make a person cheerful and amorous, while "Melancholy" (black bile) made them serious or delusional.</note> added to their *Melancholy*—and not the pure *Spirit of God* that drives them. This is clearly discovered not only in their language, which is very sweet and melting (as if they had sugar-plums under their tongue), but also from the notorious circumstances of their lives. In my view, it will be sufficient proof of this *truth* if we look at those who have most highly claimed to possess the *Spirit*, and who have had the greatest power to deceive the people.

The *pride* and arrogance of mind by which they are so confidently driven to claim, as well as to believe, such high things of themselves—that no lesser *title* will serve them than that of *God*, the *Holy Spirit* or *Paraclete* <term>Paraclete: A title for the Holy Spirit, meaning "advocate" or "helper."</term>, the *Messiah*, the last and greatest *Prophet*, the *Judge of the living and the dead*, and the like—all of this comes from *Melancholy*. This is made manifest by the lower-level effects of that same physical *temperament*.

To begin with the first of these impostors, *Simon Magus* <note>A biblical figure (Acts 8) and early legendary heretic who attempted to buy the power of the Holy Spirit.</note>, who claimed that he was *God the Father*: he proved himself to be but a wretched, lustful man by his inseparable companion, *Helena*. He called her *Selene* <note>original: "Selene," a Greek name for the Moon.</note> and claimed she was one of the *Divine powers*, when she was in fact no more than a common prostitute.

There was also *Menander*, a Samaritan, who boasted that he was the *Savior* of the world, while maintaining the same licentious and impure opinions as *Simon*.

*Montanus* <note>A 2nd-century leader of a prophetic movement known as Montanism.</note> claimed to be the *Spirit of God*; but it was clearly the *Spirit of Melancholy* that infatuated him, as his two mistresses, *Prisca* and *Maximilla*, demonstrate. It is said they left their own husbands to follow him. We might add a third, a woman named *Quintilla*, who was of no better reputation and was an intimate acquaintance of the other two; because of her, the *Montanists* were also called *Quintillians*.

*Manes* <note>The founder of Manichaeism.</note> also considered himself to be the true *Paraclete*, but he left behind a sect instructed in all sorts of licentious and filthy principles.

*Mahomet* <note>The author uses "Mahomet" for the Prophet Muhammad, reflecting 17th-century Western spelling and biases.</note> was more successful than any—the last and greatest *Prophet* ever to come into the world (if you believe him). That he was *melancholic* is evidenced by his epileptic fits, and by his permission of a plurality of wives and concubines, and his sensual descriptions of the joys of Heaven or Paradise.

But I must confess, I strongly doubt whether he actually believed himself to be a *Prophet* or not. To me, he seems more like a pleasant, witty companion and a shrewd *politician* than a mere *enthusiast*. He was wise enough not to bet his reputation or success on his own whims alone; instead, he built upon the most significant principles of the religions of the *Jews* and *Christians*—such as *that God is the Creator and Governor of the world, and that there are...*

# A brief Discourse of Enthusiasm. SECT. XXI.

...angels and spirits, that the soul of man is immortal, and that there is a judgment and an everlasting reward to come after the natural death of the body. So it seems that Islam <note>original: "Mahometism"</note> is merely an abuse of certain principles of the teachings of Moses and Christ for a political purpose. Therefore, in itself, it is far better than the vain and idle enthusiasms of David George <note>David George (c. 1501–1556), also known as David Joris, was a Dutch Anabaptist who claimed to be the "third David" and a new Messiah.</note>. George was so highly conceited regarding his own "light" that he hoped to upstage Muhammad <note>original: "put Mahomet's nose out of joint"</note>, claiming for himself that he was the last and greatest prophet. However, left to the intoxication of his own melancholy and sanguine humors, he believed in neither heaven nor hell, neither reward nor punishment after this life, neither devil nor angel, nor the immortality of the soul. Although he was born a Christian, he followed the example of Muhammad in this: he also indulged in a plurality of wives.

It would seem that such a dark and cloying <note>original: "fulsome"</note> dash of blood was mixed with his melancholy that, although the one made him a pretended prophet, the other would not allow him to believe in anything beyond this mortal life.

<margin>See my *Explanation of the Mystery of Godliness*, Book 5, chapter 8; also Book 6, chapter 17.</margin>
There is another who is said to follow in his footsteps <note>Likely referring to Hendrik Niclaes, founder of the "Family of Love."</note>, speaking so magnificently of himself as if he had come to judge both the living and the dead. By an unwise distorting and forcing of plain, substantial passages of Scripture—which assure us of the existence of angels, spirits, and a life to come—he carries his own condemnation within himself. He proclaims to all the world that he is more a priest of Venus <term>priest of Venus: a metaphor for someone driven by sexual lust rather than spiritual devotion.</term>, or a mere "star-driven" <note>original: "Sydereal"</note> preacher speaking out of the sweetness and power of his own natural physical temperament, than a true prophet of God or a friend of the mystical bridegroom, Jesus Christ. The Church, as his spouse, owes all reverential love and honor to Christ's very person as her Lord and Sovereign.

But such bloated and egotistical enthusiasts, who are so grand in the conceit of their own inward worth, have little sense or belief in this duty. Instead, they imagine themselves to be either equal or superior to Christ—even though God has declared Christ the supreme head over men and angels. Yet they would dethrone him and set themselves up, though they can show no title to authority except for an unsound kind of popular eloquence, a collection of flighty and soft words, and rolling, streaming repetitions <note>original: "tautologies"</note>. If these words ever carry any true meaning, it is only what every ordinary Christian already knew; but what they often imply indirectly is abominably false, as surely as Christianity itself is true.

Yet such foolishness <note>original: "fopperies"</note> as these seem like fine things to the careless and the weak-willed. But surely Christ will raise such a discerning spirit in his Church that—by evidence and the conviction of reason, not by force or external power—such mock-prophets and false Messiahs will be discredited and hissed off the stage. No man who knows himself to be a Christian will receive them.

# SECTION XXII.

->*More examples for the same purpose.*<-

I think we have, by a sufficient investigation <note>original: "Induction"</note>, discovered the condition and causes of this mysterious mockery of *Enthusiastic Love* in its highest workings. We have shown how it is, in effect, merely a *natural temperament* <note>original: "Complexion," referring to the balance of bodily humors</note>, just as *Religious Zeal* in general is often discovered to be. This is also observable in the tumultuous *Anabaptists* in *Germany*; for among other things they contended for, this was not the least: namely, a *freedom to have many wives*. So it would seem that for the most part, this *religious heat* in men—since it arises merely from Nature—is like *exploding gold* <note>original: "Aurum fulminans," a volatile chemical compound of gold; the author is punning on its tendency to "fly upward" but exert force downward</note>; though it flies upward somewhat, its greatest force when ignited is found to go downward.

This made that religious *sect* of the *Beguards* <note>original: "Beguardi," a medieval lay religious group often accused of heresy</note> imagine that it was a sin to kiss a woman, but no sin at all to lie with her. The same provided *Carpocrates* and *Apelles*—two busy *sectaries* <note>members of a sect, often used disparagingly</note> in their time—the one with his *Marcellina* and the other with his *Philumena*, on whom to spend their lust.

---

# SECTION XXIII.

->*Concerning Enthusiastic Joy.*<-

But enough of this. Closest to this *enthusiastic affection of Love* is that of *Joy* and *Triumph of Spirit*, with which *enthusiasts* are several times filled <note>original: "actuated withall"</note>, much to their own great admiration. But we have already suggested the near similarity between *melancholy* and *wine*, which *cheers the heart of God and Man*, as is said in the Parable. And certainly *melancholy*—which at first lies smoldering <note>original: "smoaring"</note> in the heart and blood—once *heat* has overcome it (consisting as it does of solid particles which are then put into motion and agitation), is more strong and vigorous than anything else that moves in the blood and spirits. It comes very near to the nature of the highest *cordials* <note>stimulating medicines for the heart</note> that exist. <margin>Aristotle, Problems, section 30.</margin> Aristotle also witnesses this, asserting that *melancholy*, while it is cold, causes sadness and despondency of mind; but once heated, it causes *ecstasies and raptures with triumphant joy and singing* <note>original Greek: ἐκστάσεις καὶ τὰς μετ' ᾠδῆς εὐθυμίας</note>.

---

# SECTION XXIV.

->*Concerning the mystical Allegories of Enthusiasts.*<-

There are *three delusions* still remaining which I will not omit to speak of, because they have come to my memory: namely, *mystical interpretations of Scripture*, *quakings*, and *visions*. All of these are easily explained as...

into the effects of **melancholy**. For as for the first point, we have already shown that **melancholy**, just like **wine**, makes a person **rhetorical** or **poetical**. Everyone knows how full of **fancy** <note>original: "Genius"</note> that state is, and how it is filled with **allusions**, **metaphors**, and fine resemblances. What greater difficulty is there in applying **moral** and **spiritual** meanings to the **history** of the **Bible** than to the **history** of **nature**? There is no **rhetorician** or **poet** who does not do that constantly. Or how much easier is it to make up a **story** to illustrate a **moral** meaning, than to apply a **moral** sense to such **stories** as are already well-known? Regarding the former, **Aesop** was excellently skilled at it without any suspicion of **inspiration**; and the latter, **Sir Francis Bacon** has admirably performed in his *Wisdom of the Ancients* <note>original: "Sapientia Veterum"</note>, without any such peculiar or extraordinary influxes <note>original: "illapses"</note> of a divine **spirit** into him—a claim, I dare say, he never dreamed of, and any man who understands him will willingly be his **character witness** <note>original: "Compurgatour"</note>.

### SECTION XXV.
->Of **quaking**, and of the **Quakers**.<-

**And** as for **quaking**, which deluded souls take to be an infallible sign that they are moved by the **Spirit** of **God**, it is apparent that it may be only an **effect** of their **melancholy**. For none have such high **passions** as **melancholics**; and it cannot be denied that **fear**, **love**, or **veneration** at their height will cause great **trembling**. None are nearly as vulnerable <note>original: "obnoxious"</note> to these **passions** as those of a **melancholy temperament** <note>original: "Complexion"</note>, because of the deepness of their feelings <note>original: "resentments"</note> and apprehensions.

That **fear** causes **trembling** is completely obvious; and it is just as true of **love**, which the **comic playwright** <note>referring to the Roman playwright Terence</note> has judiciously noted in that passage where **Phaedria**, upon seeing his beloved **Thais**, says to **Parmeno**: "I am trembling all over, and I shuddered as soon as I saw her" <note>original Latin: "Totus tremo, saies he, horreóque postquam aspexi hanc"</note>.

As for **veneration**, which consists in a way of these two emotions mixed together, it is a **passion** that **melancholy** men are deeply immersed in whether they want to be or not. When they are to address any person of honor or worth, or to perform some solemn or weighty task in public, they will quake and tremble like an **aspen leaf**; some have been struck silent, and others have fallen down to the ground.

And it is well enough known that **fancy** <note>imagination</note> in other cases will work upon the **spirits** <note>the "vital spirits" or subtle fluids thought to move through the body</note> and cause a tumultuous and disorderly commotion in them, or so suffocate the **heart** that motion will be almost entirely extinct, and the person will fall down dead. These things are so commonly known that it is enough only to mention them.

Therefore, it is no wonder that the **enthusiast**, imagining these natural **fits** <note>original: "Paroxysms"</note> that surprise him to be extraordinary **visits** from the **Deity** and **descents** <note>original: "Illapses"</note> of the **Holy Ghost** into his **soul**, receives them with the highest **veneration** imaginable. It is no wonder, I say, that **fear**, **joy**, and **love** should make such a confusion in his **spirits** as to put him into a fit of trembling and quaking. In such a case, the **fervor** of his **spirits** and the **heat** of his **imagination** may be wrought up...

## SECTION XXVI.
### That **melancholy** disposes a person toward **apoplexy** and **epilepsy**.

Both philosophers and physicians acknowledge that **melancholy** itself makes a person prone to **apoplexy** and **epilepsy**. For whatever is **narcotic** and deadens the motion of the **animal spirits** <note>original: "Spirits"; these were thought to be subtle fluids that traveled through the nerves to produce movement and sensation.</note>, if it is powerful enough, also leads to **apoplexy**. Furthermore, thick vapors stopping the **carotid arteries** <note>original: "Arteriæ Carotides"</note> and the **choroid plexus** <note>original: "Plexus Choroïdes"; a network of blood vessels in the brain.</note>, and so hindering the flow and supply of spirits, may do the same. Some would illustrate this using the example of **charcoal** fumes, which have often made men fall down dead. But whether you consider any or all of these causes, **melancholy** is as likely to produce such harmful vapors as any other physical **temperament** <note>original: "Temper"</note> whatsoever. It is very reasonable that an **epilepsy** may arise from such causes, as these two diseases are closely related—as **Galen** <note>A famous Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries.</note> writes. It is also evident from the sudden and easy passing of the fit that the disease-causing matter is "a certain spiritual substance like a breeze" <note>original: "πνευματική τις ὀσία ὥσπερ αὔρα"</note>, as Galen's master **Pelops** expresses it.
<margin>Sennert, *Medical Institutions*, Book 2, Part 3, Section 2, Chapter 6.</margin>

---

## SECTION XXVII.
### On the nature of **enthusiastic** **revelations** and **visions**.

Since in both these conditions the outward senses are suspended <note>original: "ligation of the outward senses"</note>, whatever is then represented to the mind is essentially a **dream**. But because these fits are not as common as our natural sleep, the rash and unskillful are quick to imagine these to be extraordinary and supernatural representations, which they call **revelations** or **visions**. However, there can be no certainty in these at all, any more than there is in a **dream**.

---

## SECTION XXVIII.
### On **ecstasy**; its nature and causes.

The mention of **dreams** reminds me of another **melancholy** symptom, which physicians call <term>ecstasy</term>. This is nothing more than "a sleep deeper than nature intended" <note>original: "Somnus præter naturam profundus"</note>. Its causes are the same as those of natural sleep, but more intense and excessive. The result is the **delusion** <note>original: "deliration"</note> of the person after they awake, for they mistake their **dreams** for true histories and real events. The reason for this, I believe, is the extraordinary clarity and

Because there are no interferences or conflicting physical movements from a body so deeply overwhelmed and deadened with sleep, what the *Imagination* then produces on its own is as clear as broad daylight. The *perception* of the Soul is at least as strong and vigorous as it is at any time when one is awake. Therefore, *Memory* is as thoroughly impressed by it as it is by the sensation of any external object.

The vigor and clarity of these *Visions* differ from those in ordinary sleep as much as the liveliness of images projected artificially into a perfectly darkened room <note>This likely refers to a camera obscura, a device that projects an external image through a small hole into a dark room.</note> differs from those in a room carelessly darkened, where some chinks or crevices let in light where they should not.

But strength of perception is no sure ground for truth. Such *Visions* as these, let them be ever so clear, are still in the nature of *Dreams*. 
> *And he who relies on dreams is like one who catches at a shadow or follows after the wind*, as *Siracides* <note>original: "Siracides"; referring to Jesus ben Sirach, the author of the Book of Ecclesiasticus.</note> speaks.

## SECT. XXIX.

### *Whether it is in a person's power to cast themselves into an Enthusiastic Apoplexy, Epilepsy, or Ecstasy.*

Whether it is in any person's power to fall into these *epilepsies*, *apoplexies*, or *ecstasies* <note>In this period, "ecstasy" (from the Greek *ekstasis*) meant a trance-like state where the soul was believed to leave the body.</note> whenever they please is neither a useless nor an impossible question. We may find a probable solution from what has already been suggested.

An *Enthusiast* <note>original: "Enthusiast"; at this time, the word often referred to someone who wrongly believed they were receiving direct revelations from God due to a physical imbalance like melancholy.</note> in one of his melancholy-induced trances (which he may speed up through solemn silence and intense, earnest meditation) finds himself in a state far beyond his normal self. He may believe it to be a perceptible presence of God and a supernatural manifestation of the Divinity. This must necessarily raise that passion of *veneration* and most powerful *devotion* which consists of *Love*, *Fear*, and *Joy*. These individual passions alone have been able to kill people or cast them into a trance. How, then, can they fail to cast the Enthusiast into *tremblings*, *convulsions*, *apoplexies*, *ecstasies*, and so forth, if they are pursued by the imagination and a desire for a closer union with this inward light? *Melancholy* is easily changed into these symptoms. It is very probable that this may be the condition of some of those they call *Quakers*.

But as for *St. Augustine's African Presbyter* (who was named *Restitutus*) who could be cast into such an *ecstasy* by a lamenting voice or a mournful tone, he is the only one known for that. He is hardly able to be imitated, as it arose from some unique physical constitution of his own.

<margin>In his *Medical Institutions, book 2, part 3, section 2, chapter 4.* See also *Bodin’s Demon-mania of Sorcerers, book 2, chapter 5.*</margin>
I can as easily believe that *Cardan* <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), a famous Italian polymath who claimed to have various supernatural abilities.</note> and his father *Facius* could cast themselves into an *ecstasy* whenever they wanted as I can believe the *Laplanders* <note>original: "Laplanders"; a historical term for the Sámi people, who were often described in early modern texts as having shamanic powers.</note> could. In my own judgment, I attribute both cases to one cause. *Sennertus* notes that *Cardan* suggests somewhere regarding his father that he had an *attendant spirit* <note>original: "δαίμονα πάρεδρον" (daimona paredron); a familiar or guardian spirit who assists a practitioner.</note>. I believe this is also the case with the worse...

...worse sort of *Quakers*. But I do not focus as much on this kind of *enthusiasm* <note>original: "Enthusiasm"; in the 17th century, this term usually referred to a misguided belief that one was directly inspired by God.</note> as on that which is *natural*.

As for those *visions* that *enthusiasts* see while awake, we have already attributed their causes to the strength of *imagination* in a *melancholy spirit* <note>original: "Melancholy"; then considered a physical ailment or temperament caused by an excess of "black bile," often linked to religious mania.</note>.

## SECTION 30.
### Of Enthusiastic Prophecy.

**As** for that *fervor of mind* which carries people so confidently to predict the future, it can be shown that there is nothing *supernatural* about it. Either some probable reasons that common sense can discover might lead them to think one thing or another (with the intensity of their own melancholy giving them as much confidence in their prediction as if God himself had placed it in their spirit); or else it is because they most often predict incorrectly, and therefore when they do happen to be right, it is rightly attributed to chance. Like a man who dreams at night, it would be a strange thing if, in many years of dreaming, he did not happen upon some *clear and direct dreams* <note>original: εὐθυονειρίας (*euthyoneirias*)</note>, as they are called, which are plainly and directly true. It is *just as those who throw often frequently succeed* <note>original: καθάπερ οἱ πολλὰ βάλλoντες ἐπιτυγχάνουσι πολλάκις (*kathaper hoi polla ballontes epityngchanousi pollakis*)</note>—or as those who shoot often may sometimes hit the mark (as *Plutarch* says)—but it is more by luck than by skill.

---

## SECTION 31.
### Of the prediction of a person’s own heart from a supernatural impulse felt by themselves, but inexplicable to others; where this may occur, and why it is not properly "Enthusiasm."

<margin>* See *Descartes’* letter to Princess *Elizabeth*, where he discusses the "Spirit" of Socrates <note>original: "ou il est parlé du Genie de Socrate"</note>.</margin>
<margin>* Proverbs 16:10 and 21:1.</margin>
<margin>Ecclesiasticus 37:14.</margin>
**And** yet, I humbly believe—and I hope I may do so without any suspicion of being a *fanatic* <note>original: "Fanaticism"; here meaning someone who claims direct divine revelation without reason or evidence.</note>—that there may be such a premonition in the spirit of a person who is to act in matters of very high importance to themselves (and even more so in public affairs) that it serves as a sure guide to them, especially if they remain consistently sincere, just, and pious. For it is not at all improbable that those who act in significant public affairs—where Providence <note>God's guiding hand or divine intervention in the affairs of the world.</note> has a more direct role—may receive a special assistance and inspiration from Her while carrying out Her designs. Others do not feel this, and so they cannot imagine how it works. This is the situation, I think, where the words of *Siracides* <note>Jesus ben Sirach, author of the biblical book of Ecclesiasticus.</note> may be proven true: *“A person's own heart will tell them more than seven watchmen on a high tower.”*

But this is *enthusiasm* in the positive sense, and therefore not the focus of our discussion, since we are not speaking of what is true, but of what is a mistake. Having fully explained its causes, we will now consider the different kinds of enthusiasm, though only briefly and so far as it suits our current purpose.

Therefore, putting aside all technical precision, we will satisfy ourselves by dividing it—based on the type of person in whom it exists—into *Political* and *Philosophical*. For *enthusiasm* <note>original: "Enthusiasm"; the 17th-century belief that one is directly inspired by God, often viewed by the author as a psychological delusion.</note> usually works according to the *natural character* <note>original: "Genius"</note> of the person it overcomes.

## SECTION 32.

### Several Examples of Political Enthusiasm.

Therefore, those whose temperament draws them most toward *political* affairs—who love power and honor, and have a strong sense of civil rights—find that when their melancholy <note>original: "Melancholy"; then considered a physical condition where an excess of "black bile" could heat the brain, leading to mania or delusions.</note> heats them up, it sometimes makes them imagine themselves to be great princes (at least by divine appointment) and deliverers of the people sent from God. Such were likely the false *Messiahs* who deceived the *Jewish* people, such as *Theudas* and that *Egyptian Impostor*, as well as *Barchocab*, *Jonathas*, *Dositheus*, and several others. Since it was common knowledge among the *Jews* that the *Messiah*, the Deliverer, was expected to arrive around that time, they—driven by the heat and eagerness of their own melancholy—imagined themselves to be him. This is easier to believe when we consider several historical examples of people who imagined themselves to be *monarchs*, *popes*, and *emperors*, when in reality they were only *servants*, *grooms*, and *footmen*.

If one suspects there might be as much *villainy* as *melancholy* in some of these false *Messiahs*, that suspicion will be hard to disprove. However, there was a *German* man, whom we may more safely use as an example, who was here in *England* not many years ago. He called himself a *Warrior of God*, *David II*, and out of deep compassion for the suffering of his country, he was very eager to gather a few forces here to take across the sea. He was confident that with these forces, he could have silenced the enemy and established peace throughout all *Germany*.

The man seemed to be very religious and a great hater of tyranny and oppression; he seemed quite sane in all other matters. His only problem was this weakness: he imagined himself to be that *David* whom the *prophets* foretold—the peaceable *prince* and great *deliverer of the Jews*. He published a short pamphlet that I had the chance to see, which was full of religious zeal and biblical eloquence. I saw him in person in *London*, if the man who pointed him out to me was not mistaken. He was a tall, handsome man of middle age, but with a very pale, haggard, and melancholy expression.

I also happened to meet another man in recent years whose conversation was not only rational but pious, and he seemed to have his wits about him. I could not find the slightest sign to the contrary, except for this one flaw: he believed he was appointed by God to be that *Fifth Monarch* <note>The "Fifth Monarchy Men" were a radical religious group in mid-17th-century England who believed that the four earthly empires of the Bible were ending and that Jesus was about to return to establish a fifth, eternal kingdom.</note> of which there is so much talk in this age. This delusion had so taken hold of him that he would sometimes have his servant serve him entirely on *silver plates* and *on bended knee*, as a very learned and religious friend of mine later told me.

## SECTION 33.

*David George's prophecy of his rising again from the Dead, and the manner in which it was fulfilled.*

Therefore, I do not consider this man to be as rational as the previous one, nor is either of them comparable to that *David* <note>David Joris (c. 1501–1556), a major Anabaptist leader who claimed to be the "third David" and the true Messiah.</note> who was born at *Delft*, lived first in lower *Germany* with those of his sect, and later came to *Basel* in the year 1544. He died there in 1556 and was dug up again in 1559. In this event, his prophecy about himself was fulfilled in an unfortunate way; for, in order to sustain the wavering minds of his followers—whom he wanted to persuade that he was immortal—he told them at his death that he would rise again within three years. He thus predicted for himself something that he denied would ever happen to anyone else. <note>The prophecy "came true" when his body was exhumed by the city authorities of Basel three years after his death so that his remains could be publicly burned for heresy.</note>

## SECTION 34.

*A description of the person, manners, and doctrine of David George.*

This *David George*, a man of very humble origins, was nevertheless, in the judgment of even his enemies, a man of notable natural talents, a handsome person to look upon, and possessed of a graceful presence. He was also well-built, yellow-bearded, with bright and shining gray eyes, and was grave and calm in his speech. In short, all his movements, gestures, and behaviors were so respectable and becoming that he seemed to be entirely dedicated to honesty and godliness. He lived very splendidly and magnificently in his house, yet without the least commotion or disorder. He was a religious attender of the Church, a generous helper of the poor, a comforting visitor of the sick, obedient to the magistrates, kind and approachable to all people, and discreet in all things. He was very clever in some matters, such as his secrecy and reserve regarding his doctrine while among the people of *Basel* where he lived—to whom he did not communicate even a single tiny detail <note>original: "Iota"</note> of it. Yet, he diligently spread his teachings in the further parts of *Germany* through both books and letters. You shall hear the main points of his doctrine as follows:

1. That the doctrine delivered until now by *Moses*, the *Prophets*, *Christ* himself, and his *Apostles*, is flawed and incomplete. It was published only to keep men in a childish obedience for a time, until the fullness and perfection of *David George's* doctrine should be shared with the world—which is the only doctrine that can make mankind happy and fill them with the knowledge of God.
2. That *David George* is the true *Christ* and *Messiah*, the dear Son of God, born not of the flesh, but of the Holy Ghost and the Spirit of *Christ*. He claimed God had reserved this Spirit in a secret place—his [Christ's] body having been reduced to nothing—and has now infused it entirely into the soul of *David George*.
3. That this *David* the *Messiah* is to restore the house of *Israel* and rebuild the Tabernacle of God, not through the *Cross*, afflictions, and death,

### SECTION 35.

### *The evident Causes of that power of speech in David Joris.*

As for his own writings, which are greatly admired by some—his moving eloquence and his powerful encouragements <note>original: "animations"</note> toward the great duties of godliness—I have already established such **natural** principles that these qualities may be easily explained without needing to credit any **supernatural** spirit. For an illiterate man, as he was, but one of good natural ability, will naturally develop a more winning and commanding rhetoric <note>The art of persuasive speaking or writing.</note> through constant reading of the **Bible** than those who are formally learned. The mixture of multiple languages and artificial phrases often ruins the style of scholars, making it sound more like the work of men—though there may usually be more of God in their writing than in that of the **Enthusiast** <note>In the 17th century, an "enthusiast" was a person who falsely believed they were receiving direct, private revelations from God, often seen as a symptom of mental imbalance.</note>.

nothing in all this but what his own <term>Sanguine: In the medieval theory of the four humors, a "sanguine" temperament was associated with blood, making a person naturally cheerful, social, and energetic, but also prone to lust and over-optimism.</term> temperament may suggest without any inspiration from God.

For there is no Christian **Virtue** to be named which concerns manners, but that one's physical temperament <note>original: "Complexion"</note> will afford a **spurious imitation** of it. Because these imitations look so much like the real thing, it is an easy thing to disguise these mere **mock-graces** with **Scriptural phrases**. Thus, a person who possesses only these natural temperamental **virtues** and a **Scriptural style** will, among the less skillful, look like an **Apostle** or **Prophet**; but among the uneducated multitude, he may boast himself to be whatever he wants without suspicion or contradiction.

The most unlikely of all these imitations is **self-denial**, which seems completely opposite to a sanguine temperament. But **Enthusiasm** <note>In this period, "Enthusiasm" referred to the delusional belief that one was receiving direct revelations from God.</note> is not without a mixture of **Melancholy** <note>The "melancholy" humor was associated with black bile, making a person serious, imaginative, or prone to obsession.</note>, and we are speaking now of **Enthusiastic Sanguine**, in which fiercer passions also reside. Therefore, this **self-denial** and **mortification** <note>The practice of self-discipline or overcoming physical desires.</note> may be nothing more than the **Sanguine temperament's conflict** and **victory** over a **most harsh and fierce Melancholy**.

That this is the reign of the sanguine temperament, and not the rule of the Spirit, is discoverable both from the physical appearance of the leader of this sect, as well as from the general disposition of his followers. It is seen in that tender love they bear for their own dear bodies <note>original: "carkases"</note>, who would not, I dare say, suffer the least aching of their little fingers as an external martyrdom for any religion. Therefore, their prudence and discretion consist mostly of trickery <note>original: "juglings"</note>, evasions, and subtle excuses <note>original: "tergiversations"</note>—peaceable compliance with anything rather than suffering in body or goods. This is the natural command of the **Sanguine** temperament when it is in control.

Yet this dominion seems far better than the tyranny of **Choler** <note>The "choleric" humor, associated with yellow bile, made a person angry, aggressive, and ambitious.</note> and **Melancholy**, whose active ferocity can neither benefit itself nor be just to others. Such temperaments are prone to impose their views and are just as quick to avenge the refusal of every frivolous and irrelevant foolishness <note>original: "foppery"</note> or hated falsehood with inhumane and cruel persecutions.

->That **David Joris** <note>original: "David George"</note> was a man of a **Sanguine Temperament**.<-

# SECTION 38.

### Further and more certain proofs that David George was of a Sanguine temperament.

But two surer signs still remain regarding this "Prophet’s" natural constitution: his denial of a life to come and the existence of angels or spirits, and his promotion of the plurality or community of wives <note>original: "community of Wives"; this refers to the practice of polygamy or the sharing of partners within a religious sect</note>.

I must confess that I cannot attribute the former—his denial of the afterlife—to anything other than a rich and heavy mixture of the **Sanguine** humor <note>The "sanguine" temperament was thought to be caused by an excess of blood, leading to a person being overly focused on physical pleasures and the material world.</note> within his **Enthusiastic** <note>In this context, an "Enthusiast" is someone who believes they are directly inspired by God, often viewed by the author as a form of mental or physical delusion.</note> complexion. For nothing so effectively dampens a man’s desires, or kills his belief in a more **spiritual** and **immaterial** state of being, as this sweet excess of blood. It so thickens and clouds the spirits that the mind cannot imagine or predict anything beyond the present concerns of this mortal **body**.

As for the latter—his views on wives—I think it is generally acknowledged that no cause is as likely as this same **sanguine** temperament, which disposes men so strongly toward the love of women.

---

# SECTION 39.

### That it was a dark, heavy Sanguine temperament that hid the truth of the great promises of the Gospel from his eyes.

Therefore, this **Enthusiast**, being overwhelmed by the power of his own physical constitution, fell into disbelief regarding those great **promises** of **eternal life** set forth in the Scripture. He assumed the Holy Writers were either mistaken or only intended to use **allegories** <note>Symbolic stories where the literal meaning represents a hidden spiritual or moral truth.</note> in what they wrote. 

Because he felt a **fervor** within himself for **love**, **peace**, **equity**, and similar virtues, it boiled so high that it convinced him he was **inspired**. He even imagined his disbelief in those precious **promises** of **immortality** and **glory** in the heavens to be a special form of **enlightenment** <note>original: "Illumination"</note>. He claimed the **resurrection** of the dead was nothing more than being raised into a state of passion for these earthly virtues, similar to his own, and sharing his disbelief in that **heavenly crown** mentioned by the Apostle Paul. 

Thus, because he was unable to raise his mind to heaven through faith, he brought heaven down to earth in his vain imagination. This required less effort than **Muhammad** <note>original: "Mahomet." The author is referencing the proverb "If the mountain will not come to Muhammad, Muhammad must go to the mountain."</note> took, who was obliged to walk to the mountain when he saw the mountain would not move toward him.

## SECTION 40.

### *The exact likeness between David George and the Father of the modern Nicolaitans, with the Author’s judgment of them both.*

This is a brief account of David George <note>original: "David George"; the English name for David Joris (c. 1501–1556), a radical Anabaptist leader who claimed to be the "third David."</note>, whose errors the Father of our modern Nicolaitans <note>The "Nicolaitans" refers here to the "Family of Love" (Familists), a mystical sect founded by Hendrik Niclaes. The author is linking Joris’s ideas to Niclaes.</note> drank in so carefully, as if he were reluctant to let a single drop spill to the side. Never was the proverb of Solomon so clearly proven as in these two men: *As a face is reflected in water, so the heart of one man reflects the heart of another.* <note>Referencing Proverbs 27:19.</note>

Therefore, concerning them both, I dare to declare that even though they placed themselves on the same level as Christ and made themselves judges of the living and the dead, they were actually more lacking in true judgment regarding religion than the lowliest of sincere Christians. And though they have so "deified" or (as they phrase it) **begodded** <term>begodded</term> <note>A term used by the Family of Love to describe a mystical union where a human becomes divine or "godded with God."</note> themselves all over—I might even say bedaubed themselves with the fake and counterfeit paint of arrogant, empty words to amaze the common people—they were in truth merely men. They were men of shallow minds and indulgent <note>original: "liquorsome"; meaning prone to physical appetites or sensory pleasures.</note> bodies, clinging to the pleasures of the flesh and so deeply enjoying the sweetness of *this present life* that all hope or desire for *that better life* was completely dead within them. Therefore, their settled and deep-rooted ignorance made them so **Enthusiastically** confident in their own error.

## SECTION 46.

->That Paracelsus has given cause for the wildest philosophical enthusiasms that have ever yet been set in motion.<-

These are the rampant and delirious fancies of that great boaster of Europe, Paracelsus. His unbridled imagination and his bold, confident forcing of his strange and lazy inventions upon the world has, I dare say, given cause for the wildest **philosophical enthusiasms** <note>original: *Philosophic Enthusiasms*; here meaning irrational or delusional systems of thought mistaken for divine wisdom</note> that were ever started by either Christian or Heathen. Some have tried to **allegorize** <note>to interpret a text as having a hidden spiritual or symbolic meaning rather than a literal one</note> that last idea of his (just as the Persians do with the **Quran** <note>original: *Alcoran*</note>, because they are ashamed of its literal sense). However, in my view, they do it so coldly and poorly that it would only convince a person further that the literal meaning was the one intended. If one compares it with what he writes of nymphs, giants, and fairies in his *Astronomical Science* <note>original: *Scientia Astronomica*</note>, he will have no further doubt about it.

## SECTION 47.

->That Paracelsus’s philosophy, though he himself did not intend it, is one of the safest refuges for the atheist and the very support of ancient paganism.<-

I admit there is some show of religion in his writings, and far more in his followers, who believe themselves to be taught by God. However, I plainly see that their brains are merely heated and infected by this strong spirit of **phantastery** <note>original: *Phantastrie*; the state of having a mind filled with wild, unrealistic fancies or hallucinations</note> that breathes through Paracelsus’s books. I know it is not wise to speak lightly of those whom others admire; but "prudence" in that case is merely craftiness that commands an unfaithful silence. I do not see how any honest man can fulfill his conscience by carefully ignoring such falsehoods when he sees them ensnaring the minds of men. These ideas not only abuse people's intellects with foolish and ridiculous concepts, but they also introduce dangerous and harmful—

...mischievous opinions that undermine and destroy the very fundamentals of the Christian religion.

For I ask anyone: what is closer to ancient **paganism** than what this bold writer has said concerning the **stars**? Or what refuge is so safe for the atheist who mocks and avoids all religion, as such a miraculous **influence** of the heavens as **Paracelsus** describes in his *Astronomical Science* <note>original: *Scientia Astronomica*</note>? Therefore, I would be very amazed at the madness and inconsistency of him and his followers—who constantly criticize **heathen philosophy** while including its very dregs in their own writings (namely, the crude principles of ancient **pagan superstition** and idolatry)—if I did not remember that they are **enthusiasts** <note>original: *Enthusiasts*; in this era, this term referred to people who wrongly believed they were receiving direct divine revelations, often leading to irrational or fanatical ideas</note> who follow the strength of their **imagination** <note>original: *Phansy*</note> rather than the guidance of **reason**.

->*Jupiter is whatever you see, etc.* <note>original: *Jupiter est quodcunque vides, &c.*; a quote from the Roman poet Lucan, expressing a pantheistic view that God is everything in the physical world</note><-

Taken in its coarsest sense, I have no doubt that this was the main principle from which so many varieties and impurities of **pagan** superstition flowed. They imagined they met God in every object of their senses. Our outrageous **enthusiasts** claim that "everything is God," whether in love or in wrath. If I understand anything at all, this is no better than **atheism**. For it implies that God is nothing else but the **universal matter of the world**, dressed in various shapes and forms, and in different properties and qualities—some pleasant, some unpleasant; some holy, some profane; some wise, some mindless; some weak, some strong, and so on. But to slice God into so many parts is to wound and kill him, and to make him no God at all.

***

### SECTION 48.

### *How the Paracelsian philosophy justifies the heathens' worship of the stars, detracts from the authority of our Savior’s miracles, makes the Gospel ineffective for establishing belief in God and a particular providence, and pleases the self-proclaimed atheist Vaninus in the very thing he celebrates most, as it serves his purpose best to avoid all religion whatsoever.*

Again, look at how **Paracelsus** justifies the heathens' worship of the stars! He portrays them as such knowing, powerful, and compassionate spectators of human affairs. And why might people not pray to them—as **Anne Bodenham** <note>a woman executed for witchcraft in 1653 who reportedly invoked planetary spirits</note> the witch did to the planet **Jupiter** to cure diseases—if they have so much power and knowledge that they can create men here below and bestow gifts upon them? For doing so would be no more than asking a father or godfather for a blessing. If it is admitted that any one nation is created by the stars, the atheist will surely assume that all nations are.

Furthermore, how shall we repair the loss and damage done to the authority of our blessed Savior's miracles? Through these miracles, not only Christianity but the very foundations of all true religion are powerfully established—namely, **the discovery of a special and particular providence of God**...

<meta>This page continues Henry More’s critique of the dangers of radical "enthusiasm," specifically how astrological theories—like those of Paracelsus and Cardan—can unintentionally provide arguments for atheists by suggesting that even the greatest religious figures were merely products of the stars rather than divine providence.</meta>

...and a hope of a *life to come*. For if the stars can create living creatures out of prepared matter—beings that possess sense and understanding but lack **immortal** souls and simply return to dead matter—then why wouldn’t the same be true for humans? And if the stars can provide the power for such wonder-working wisdom as was seen in **Moses** and in **Christ** (or something very close to it), what evidence remains to prove that there is any **God** or **spirits**? In such a view, everything can be explained by the power of the **stars**. This is a concept that the zealous and industrious atheist **Lucilio Vanini** <note>original: "Cæsar Vaninus"</note> triumphs in exceedingly in his *Amphitheater of Eternal Providence* <note>original: *Amphitheatrum æternæ Providentiæ*</note>. In that work, he cites several **astrological** passages from **Gerolamo Cardan** <note>original: "Cardan"</note> under the pretense of refuting them; in these passages, Cardan traces the origins of those three eminent lawgivers—**Moses**, **Christ**, and **Muhammad** <note>original: "Mahomet"</note>—to the influence of the stars.

The Law of **Moses** comes from **Saturn**, says Cardan; that of **Christ** from **Jupiter** and **Mercury**; that of **Muhammad** from the **Sun** <note>original: "Sol"</note> and **Mars**; and the law of the **idolaters** from the **Moon** and **Mars**.

In another place, **Cardan** attributes that sweetness, meekness, wisdom, and eloquence found in our Savior—by which he was able to debate in the Temple at twelve years of age—to the influence of **Jupiter**.

**Pietro Pomponazzi** <note>original: "Pomponatius"</note> also acknowledges the wisdom and miracles of **Christ**, but refers them all to the stars. I believe he was a man who had collapsed as far into **atheism** as Vanini himself. Thus, these wild fancies of the **enthusiasts** are, in truth, the primary supports or shelters that atheists use to uphold or defend themselves. But let any man who possesses patience and sober reason judge just how fanciful and confused the logic of astrology really is.

## SECTION XLIX.

### *That Paracelsus and his followers are neither atheistical nor diabolical; and what makes the chemist ordinarily so pitiful a philosopher.*

<margin>See my *Explanation of the Mystery of Godliness*, Book 7, chapters 15, 16, 17.</margin>
I do not say these things because I think either **Paracelsus** or his followers are atheists in this way. Rather, I say them to show their **fancifulness** <note>original: "Phantastrie"</note> and **enthusiasm**. They heatedly claim to represent matters of Christianity and religion, yet they handle them so crudely and indiscreetly. They blurt out any flashy foolishness that enters their minds, even if it is entirely contrary to the **consistency** <note>original: "Analogie"</note> of faith or lacks any ground in solid reason, simply to make the world stare and wonder at them.

The result is that while some people admire them, others curse them as men of an impious and diabolical spirit. I confess that I think this is too harsh a judgment; well-meaning men are just as susceptible to **melancholy** <note>original: "Melancholy"; here referring to a clinical state of mental imbalance or depression</note> and **madness** <note>original: "Lunacies"</note> as they are to **chills** <note>original: "Agues"</note> and burning **fevers**. Yet, a person should be very far from thinking better of a "truth" just because it was discovered by an **enthusiastic** spirit. On the contrary, for that very reason, one should suspect it. This is because the temperament that makes men **enthusiastic** is the greatest enemy to reason.

This is as ridiculous a project, in my judgment, as that of a man who, finding a piece of a broken oar on the sand, busied his brains beyond all measure to try to turn it into an entire ship.

### SECTION L.

->*The writer of this discourse is no enemy to either the theosophist or chemist; he only excuses himself from being over-credulous regarding either.*<-

WHAT I have spoken so far I would have understood as coming from one who neither despises the well-meaning of the *theosophist* <note>A philosopher who claims to have direct knowledge of God through mystical insight</note>, nor rejects the industry of the *chemist*; but I shall always excuse myself from giving any credit to either, any further than some powerful <note>original: "lusty"</note> miracle, extraordinary medicine, or solid reason shall force it from me.

### SECTION LI.

->*The cure of enthusiasm through temperance, humility, and reason.*<-

WE have spoken of the *kinds* of *enthusiasm* so far as we held it useful for our purpose; we shall now touch upon the *cure* of *this disease*. Here, waiving all pretense to a knowledge of *medicine* <note>original: "Physick"</note> or acquaintance with the *apothecary's* shop, we shall set down only such things as fall under a *moral* or *theological* consideration, giving only instructions for the guidance of a man's life in reference to this great error of *enthusiasm*: which a sober man cannot easily decide whether it is more ridiculous, or more deplorable and mischievous.

Now the most sovereign medicine that I know against it is this *triple-remedy* <note>original: "Diatrion"; a medical term for a compound of three ingredients</note>, or *composition of three* excellent ingredients: namely, *temperance*, *humility*, and *reason*. I do not despair that these may recover those who are somewhat far gone in this *enthusiastic* distemper,

### SECT. LII.

->What is meant by Temperance.<-

By Temperance, I mean a measured abstinence from all "hot" or stimulating <note>original: "heightning"</note> foods and drinks, as well as from all sexual <note>original: "venereous"</note> pleasures and physical delights of the body, and from all softness and lack of discipline. I mean a constant and firm commitment to the highest degree of *Chastity* in single life, and of *Constancy* <note>original: "Continency"</note> in marriage, that can be achieved. For it is clear from many examples of *Enthusiasm* <note>original: "Enthusiasm"; in More's time, this specifically meant the false belief that one is receiving direct private revelations from God</note> mentioned above that the more hidden and lurking fumes of *Lust* had corrupted the imaginations <note>original: "Phansies"</note> of those who claimed to be *Prophets* or *Inspired*.

We will also add to these: moderate physical exercise, regularly taking in the fresh air, and the wise and careful use of Devotion, which helps the blood circulate <note>original: "ventilated"</note> and purges it of dark, oppressive vapors. A temperate diet, if not fasting, must also accompany this. Otherwise, the more hot and zealous our religious addresses are, the more likely they are to bring mischief upon our own heads. Such zeal stirs up the impurities <note>original: "feculency"</note> of our lack of moderation and sends them into the most precious parts of the body—the *Brains* and *Animal Spirits* <note>original: "Animal Spirits"; in early modern medicine, these were believed to be a subtle fluid that transmitted messages between the soul and the body</note>—thereby intoxicating the mind with madness and wild behavior.

### SECT. LIII.

->What is meant by Humility, and the great advantage thereof for<-
->Wisdom and Knowledge.<-

By Humility, I mean a complete submission to the will of God in all things. It is a state of being "dead" to any sense of one's own excellence or superiority over others. It is a total lack of any desire to be unique or to attract people's attention to oneself. It involves caring as little for one's own praise or glory in the world as if one had never been born into it. Instead, one should be entirely satisfied with this one thing: that his own will is being brought under the Will of God. With thankfulness and reverence, he receives whatever Divine Providence brings to him—whether it is sweet or sour, or whether it goes with the grain or "against the hair" <note>original: "against the hair"; an idiom meaning against one's natural inclination or "against the grain"</note>. It is all the same to him; for whatever he cannot avoid, he sees as God's gift to the world intended for a greater good.

But I must admit that the person who is affected this way—since he does not seek knowledge just to please himself—cannot help but become the *most knowledgeable man* alive. He is surrounded by the beams of Divine Wisdom, just as the low-lying Earth is surrounded by the rays of the stars. His deeply and profoundly humbled soul becomes the center of all heavenly enlightenment, just as this little globe of the Earth is the center of those celestial influences. I confess I stand amazed while I consider the ineffable advantages
