Consider how calm, how comprehensive, how quick and aware <note>original: "sensible"</note> a mind is when it is submitted to the Divine Will; notice how free, how wise, and how refined her touch and judgment are in all things. Whereas *Pride* and strong desire ruffle the mind into uneven waves and boisterous fluctuations, so that the eternal light of *Reason*—concerning either *Nature* or *Life*—cannot imprint its perfect and distinct image or character there. Nor can such subtle and delicate motions and impressions be perceived by an Understanding that is disturbed and agitated by such a violent storm.

Therefore, that person who has attained this *Humble* frame of *Spirit*—which is of such great importance for acquiring all kinds of *Wisdom*, both *Natural* and *Divine*—cannot possibly be so foolish as to be mistaken about that which is the natural result of an opposite temperament. Such is the nature of *Enthusiasm* <note>original: "Enthusiasm"; in More's time, this referred specifically to the deluded belief that one is receiving direct, private revelations from God</note>, which puffs men up with the opinion that they have a more than ordinary influence from God acting upon their spirits, and that He designs them by special appointment to be *new Prophets*, *new Law-givers*, *new Davids*, *new Messiahs* <note>original: "Messiafes"</note>, and what else? In reality, it is nothing but the working of the "old man" <note>original: "old man"; a biblical term from Romans 6:6 referring to the unregenerate, sinful human nature</note> within them in a fanatical manner.

# SECT. LIV.

->What is meant by Reason, the danger of abandoning that guide, and the<-
->mistake of those who expect the Spirit not to suggest things<-
->that are rational.<-

By Reason, I understand such a settled and cautious composure of mind that it will suspect every high-flown and bold Fancy <note>original: "Fancy"; here meaning wild imagination or delusional thoughts</note> that endeavors to carry away one's agreement before a deliberate examination. Reason does not endure being tricked <note>original: "gulled"</note> by the vigor or flashiness of a representation, nor will she be at all beaten down by its weight or strength. Instead, she patiently tests the idea by the known faculties of the soul. These are: *Common notions* <note>original: "Common notions"; self-evident truths or first principles that all rational people agree upon</note> that all men in their right minds agree upon; the *Evidence of outward Sense*; or else a clear and distinct *Deduction from these*.

Whatever is not agreeable to these three is *Fancy*, which proves nothing of the *Truth* or *Existence* of anything. Therefore, it ought not—and cannot—be accepted by anyone except madmen or fools.

Those who talk so loudly of that higher principle, *The Spirit*, while excluding these rational tests, betray their own ignorance. While they use their wild rhetoric to dissuade men from the use of their rational faculties—under the pretense of waiting for a higher and more glorious Light—they act as madly, in my mind, as a group of men traveling by night with torches <note>original: "links"</note> and lanterns. Imagine if some furious orator among them, through his wonderful strains of eloquence, should so fool them into a misconception of their current condition by comparing it to the sweet and cheerful splendor of the day. If he caused them, through impatience and indignation, to smash their torches and break their lanterns to pieces against the ground, they would then choose instead to walk in the dark at the risk of hitting their noses against the next tree...

But the *Enthusiast's* mistake is not only in leaving his current guide before he has a better one, but in having a false idea of the guide he expects. For certainly, that *Spirit of illumination* which lives in the souls of the faithful is a principle of the *purest Reason* that can be communicated to human nature. And whatever this *Spirit* possesses, he receives from Christ (as Christ himself testifies), who is the eternal *Logos* <note>original: *λόγος*; the Word or Divine Reason</note>, the all-encompassing Wisdom and Reason of God. In this Reason, he sees through the natures and *Ideas* of all things, including all their relationships of dependency and independence, agreement and disagreement, or whatever connection <note>original: "Habitude"</note> they have to one another, all in one continuous glance.

Whatever *Intellectual light* is shared with us is derived from this source; in us, it manifests as *individual reason*, or *reasoning in sequence*, or piece by piece. Furthermore, the *Holy Spirit* never suggested anything to anyone that was not agreeable to—if not demonstrable by—what we call *Reason*. I leave it to anyone to judge how powerful a restraint <note>original: "Curb"</note> this conviction will be against the excessive impressions and impulses of melancholy and *enthusiasm* <note>the 17th-century term for the deluded belief that one is receiving direct, private revelations from God</note>.

### SECTION LV.

#### Further Helps against Enthusiasm.

In addition to these three significant and general helps, we might add some specific considerations by which we may guard ourselves against this *enthusiastic stubbornness* <note>original: "pertinacity"</note>, or recognize it when it has taken hold of others. For example: if someone claims to discover a truth through *Inspiration* that is of no benefit or importance to the Church of God, it is to me nearly a demonstration that he is *fanatical*. If he piles up *falsehoods* along with *truths* and claims to be *inspired in everything*, it is evidence to me that he is *inspired in none* of those *mysteries* he offers to the world.

### SECTION LVI.

#### Of the elevated language of Enthusiasts, and of what may extraordinarily fall from them.

There are also certain advantages that *enthusiasts* possess which should be noted, as they have deceived many people. For instance, they may speak in a very elevated and divine manner—which has certainly happened to several people just before they went completely mad. The fact that they might hit upon something extraordinary is no guarantee <note>original: "pledge"</note> of the truth of the rest of their claims.

For this unquiet and tumultuous spirit of melancholy, shaking the whole bodily frame, is like an earthquake to a person in a dungeon; for a brief moment, it makes the very walls gape and split open, and so lets in light for a while through those cracks. But then everything closes up again suddenly, and the prisoner is confined to his accustomed darkness. This, therefore, was a chance occurrence in nature, not a gracious visit from the Spirit of God.

### SECTION LVII.

*Regarding Enthusiastic Prophecy that usually happens to fools and madmen, and the reason why; as also why ecstatic men foresee things to come, and concerning the uncertainty of such predictions.*

To this you may also add the "luck" of prophecy, whether it occurs while sleeping or waking. Such things have happened to madmen and fools, and *Aristotle* offers a clever reason that may explain both: "For the minds of such people are not preoccupied with thought, but are like a desert, empty of all things; once set in motion, they are led by whatever moves them" <note>original Greek: Ἡ γὰρ διάνοια τῶν τοιούτων οὐ φροντιστική, ἀλλ’ ὥσπερ ἔρημος καὶ κενὴ πάντων, καὶ κινηθεῖσα κατὰ τὸ κινοῦν ἄγεται</note>. To which he also adds why *ecstatic* men foresee *future things*: "Because their own internal motions do not disturb them, but are brushed aside; therefore they are especially aware of external ones" <note>original Greek: Ὅτι αἱ οἰκεῖαι κινήσεις οὐκ ἐνοχλοῦσιν, ἀλλ’ ἀποῤῥαπίζονται, τῶν ξενικῶν οὖν μάλιστα αἰσθάνονται</note>.

All of this suggests that a detachment <note>original: "alienation"</note> of the mind, and a rest from our own mental activity, prepares us to receive impressions from something else. By a quick sense and touch, we may be notified—through a communication of motion from the *Spirit of the world* <note>The "Anima Mundi," or a natural collective spirit that connects all things in the universe, according to some ancient philosophies</note>—of what is happening at a distance, or what causes are conspiring to bring this or that to pass. However, these causes might change direction, making the *prediction* false; for not everything that attempts to happen actually comes into being. Therefore, all these *presages* are not "sent from God" <note>original: Θεόπεμπτα</note>, but may only be "daemonic" <note>original: δαιμόνια; in the sense of being driven by natural spirits or forces rather than the highest God</note>. "For nature is daemonic, not divine" <note>original: Ἡ γὰρ φύσις δαιμονία, οὐ θεία</note>—these are the words of *Aristotle*, but they are such that some skillful *Platonist* could very easily explain.

All that I aim to show is this: that *prophecy* can arise from something far below the level of the pure and infallible God. It is our mistake to think that because a *prediction* turns out to be true, it was certainly foreknown by the *foreteller*. For the current conspiracy of causes that enters the vacant mind may later be corrupted, altered, or blown away like clouds that at first seem to promise the farmer a following rain.

*That if an Enthusiast should cure some diseases by touching or stroking the diseased party, it might still be no true miracle.*

But there is yet a stronger lure than *prophecy* to draw people into believing an *Enthusiast*, and that is the appearance of performing a miracle, such as curing some desperate disease—as happened very lately in this nation. And the spirits of melancholic men being more heavy and weighty, when they are so highly refined and activated by an extraordinary heat and vigor of the body, may prove a very powerful elixir—nature having surpassed the usual claims of *chemistry* in this case.

### SECTION LIX.
### *Regarding the Willingness and Patience of Enthusiasts to Suffer.*

<margin>* *Attic Nights*, book 9, chapter 5.</margin>
Their willingness to suffer, or their patience in suffering, may also seem to provide an extraordinary testimony for some *enthusiasts* <note>In the 17th century, an "enthusiast" was someone who falsely believed they were directly inspired by God.</note>, as if there were something divine or supernatural in them. But our admiration will decrease if we consider how passionately some people hate the feeling of *pleasure*, accounting it the *highest evil* <note>original Latin: "Summum malum"</note>. For this paradox, *Antisthenes* is noted in the writings of *Aulus Gellius*, as well as for his suitable motto: "I would rather be mad than feel pleasure" <note>original Greek: Μανείην μᾶλλον ἢ ἡσθείην</note>—as if outright *madness* were more tolerable than pleasure. There are others who, by their mere temperament, love to struggle with troubles and dangers; such are those who undergo warfare and sea voyages with a natural delight. Others make it their study, and pride themselves on it, to become insensitive to pain, or to bear it as if they were not affected by it at all; this condition became a technical term among the *Stoics*, who call this power "apathy" <note>original Greek: 'Απάθεια</note> and "insensitivity to pain" <note>original Greek: 'Αναλγησία</note>.

But this is nothing more than a *Spartan* hardening of the mind, backed by a sense of shame, a desire for glory, or the satisfaction of being conscious of one's own toughness and endurance. A notorious instance of this is the *Spartan* <note>original: "Lacedæmonian"</note> boy, who, having hidden a stolen fox under his coat, would not cry out even though it was gnawing at his very entrails.

<margin>Nonnus in his *Collection of Histories* on Gregory Nazianzen's *Invectives* against Julian the Apostate.</margin>
*Anaxarchus's* pain, though it does not seem as sharp, yet his courage appears just as great; he was able to philosophize so freely while he was being crushed in a mortar by the cruelty of *Archelaus* <note>More likely refers to the tyrant Nicocreon; Anaxarchus was a philosopher who was famously pounded to death.</note>. From there he cried out in the midst of their thumping upon him, "Pound, pound the sack of Anaxarchus; for you do not pound Anaxarchus himself" <note>original Greek: Πτίσσε, πτίσσε 'Αναξάρχου θύλακον, οὐ γὰρ πτίσσεις τὸν 'Ανάξαρχον</note>. He added wit to his philosophy, comparing his body to a sack, but making his soul as good as absent and the sack empty, by his professed insensitivity to the blows and unconcern for what happened to his body. Yet, setting aside his natural intuition of the soul's immortality, this was nothing but a sullen and reckless *Stoicism*. For his body had more reason to defy their blows than his soul, since she alone was capable of...

<summary>Henry More argues that the "miraculous" healing powers and extreme endurance of enthusiasts are natural phenomena caused by bodily heat or a stubborn, Stoic mindset rather than divine intervention. He cites historical examples of extreme physical endurance, like the Spartan boy and the philosopher Anaxarchus, to show that such feats are products of human will and temperament.</summary>

...pertaining to sensation and pain. So it is clear that the special support for his mind was nothing but a deep-seated error and imagination.

We can also see how **anger** and **outrage** will sustain the spirit against **fear** and **pain** in the brief example of **Theano** <note>Theano was a Pythagorean philosopher; legend says she bit off her tongue to avoid revealing secrets under torture.</note>, who, being forcibly urged to betray the secrets of her country, bit out her tongue and spat it in the face of the tyrant. These are examples evident enough of that sought-after and not entirely unattainable power of **insensitivity to pain** <note>original: "Indolency"</note> among the ancients.

<margin>*Attic Nights*, Book 12, Chapter 5.</margin>
I do not know what to call that which **Gellius** reports of a certain gladiator belonging to **Caesar**, who would laugh while his wounds were being dried and cleaned. It seems to be more than a simple **insensitivity to pain** <note>original Greek: 'Αναλγησία (*analgesia*)</note> or **lack of feeling** <note>original Latin: *Indolentia*</note>. But from these examples and considerations, it is manifest that there is no such divinity or supernatural holiness in the stout and stubborn bearing of pain, nor any necessity for divine assistance in it. Either a simple resolution of the mind based on some absorbed **doctrine** <note>original: "Dogma"</note>, or the power of some hidden passion, may enable someone to endure everything.

And yet these are but small things in comparison to what the **enthusiast** is armed with due to his peculiar condition. For besides the fact that his very **temperament** <note>original: "Complexion," referring to the balance of bodily "humors."</note> makes him stiff, inflexible, and unyielding—for there is no temperament so sturdy and stubborn as **melancholy** <note>In 17th-century medicine, melancholy was thought to make a person cold, dry, and mentally rigid.</note>, even in less important matters—there is a further force added to it. This comes from the strong delusion he has of being **inspired**, and consequently, the belief that his cause is infallibly good. This naturally tends to make him invincible in his sufferings, as he is conscious of the absolute goodness of his cause (as he perceives it) and the necessity of his duty in adhering to it. To this, you may add the certain expectation of future glory and happiness for his **martyrdom**. It is quite plain, then, that there is nothing supernatural or miraculous in the case.

---

## SECTION LX.
### *That the determined sufferings for mistaken points in religion is no good argument against the truth of all religion.*

I must confess that a casual reflection upon this **resolution** to **suffer** to the utmost extremity—even by persons who are mistaken in the points they suffer for—cannot help but make those who are **inclined toward atheism** think that there is no truth or certainty at all in religion. They see that even where men seem so certain to themselves that they dare to, and actually do, stake their lives upon it, they are still grossly mistaken. It is plain they are mistaken because people of contrary persuasions suffer with the same confidence and to the same extremity, choosing to lose their lives rather than their opinions and their party. This is found to be true among **Jews**, **Muslims** <note>original: "Mahometans"</note>, **Catholics** <note>original: "Papists"</note>, and **Protestants**.

At first sight, this indeed appears to have no small show of reason. However, if it is looked into more closely, it will prove to be but a weak and sorry **logical fallacy** <note>original: "Sophism"</note>. For if this reasoning were solid, it would follow that there was nothing true in...

<summary>More argues that the ability to endure pain is a product of human temperament and firm belief rather than divine favor, and he begins to counter the "atheist" argument that conflicting martyrdoms prove all religion is false.</summary>
<keywords>Theano, Aulus Gellius, analgesia, melancholy, martyrdom, atheism, religious conflict, temperament</keywords>

--- Page 289 ---
<meta>This page continues the argument from Section LX regarding the nature of martyrdom and religious conviction. The author is responding to the skeptical "atheist" argument that because people are willing to die for opposing religious beliefs, all religion must be based on mere imagination or education rather than truth.</meta>

<page-num>43</page-num>
<header>SECTION LX. A Brief Discourse on Enthusiasm.</header>

...nor in philosophy either. For assuredly men are as firmly convinced of opposing views in philosophy as they are in religion, and yet only one side can be true. The reason they are not so persuaded by these matters that they will die for them is not because they do not firmly believe their philosophical opinions, but because those opinions carry no moral obligation <note>original: "obligation of Conscience"</note> or concern for eternal life as religion does. Otherwise, if it were a matter of religious conscience to be a **Copernican**, **Tychonist**, or **Aristotelian** <note>These terms refer to the three major competing models of the universe: the sun-centered model of Copernicus, the hybrid model of Tycho Brahe, and the earth-centered model of Aristotle.</note> regarding the system of the world, I think there is no question that there would be martyrs for them all—at least for two of them; the one being so perfectly in line with **reason**, and the other so crudely fitted to the **senses**.

Besides, I cannot help but notice that it is very simplistic and illogical for these **atheistic intellectuals** <note>original: "Atheistical Witts"</note> to appeal to such a minor legal standard as mere **human testimony** when judging these noble propositions about the existence of God and the truth of religion. For in their arguments, they treat the sufferings of martyrs in opposing religions as if laying down one's life were nothing more than placing a large wager. This is a topic that some have sarcastically called the **argument of fools**.

But whatever weight **human testimony** carries in these cases, it is so far from helping the atheist's cause that it actually works against him. For even if we admit that these **anti-martyrs** (as I may call them) testify against one another individually, they collectively testify against the atheist by confirming with their blood **that there is a God and a life to come**. I believe this is not only the **effect of education**, but of a **natural insight** in the better sort of men and a natural inclination to think so. When this is further strengthened by the principles of religion—especially one as clear and persuasive as **Christianity**—it may very well gain the power to engage a person’s conscience to lay down their life, even for things impressed upon them by mere **education** or some **gloomy delusion** <note>original: "Melancholy conceit"</note>. But the firm foundation and support of it all, without which they would not suffer for anything, is the sincere and unshaken belief **that there is a God, and a happiness to be expected after this life**. Therefore, the conscience being careful and not daring to act or agree to things it strongly suspects to be evil or false, chooses the **safer way** for its main interest: namely, to suffer rather than to sin.

So, it is not so much the firm belief in the specific points they die for (whether they are Catholic or Protestant) as it is the care to do nothing they suspect is sinful that makes them undergo martyrdom.

Thus, the very basis of the atheist's **logical fallacy** <term>original: "Paralogism"; a piece of false reasoning</term> is shown to be invalid. It is not evident from their suffering that they are absolutely certain about the false points for which they die. But even if we admit the **enthusiast** <note>In the 17th century, an "enthusiast" was someone who believed they were directly inspired by God, often viewed with suspicion as being "fanatical."</note> is certain, **fanaticism** is merely a disease of religion. It no more proves that there is no religion than **madness** proves there is no **reason**, or than a **physical disease** proves that **health** or the **human body** do not exist in the world.

### *On the Far-fetched Ideas, Mysterious Style, and Moving Eloquence of Enthusiasts.*

Whatever credit the *enthusiast* might gain for himself through his moving eloquence, his *mysterious style*, and *unexpected ideas*, they can easily be traced back to that principle of *melancholy* <note>original: "Melancholy." In the 17th century, melancholy was considered a physical condition caused by an excess of "black bile," which was thought to trigger intense imagination, hallucinations, or religious delusions.</note> mentioned above. The feelings produced by this temperament <note>original: "Complexion"</note> are so deep and powerful that they inevitably enable the speaker to tell their story with great passion and energy. Furthermore, the *imagination* is so unrestrained that it is much easier for it to wander off and bring back some bizarre, distorted concept from a remote, obscure corner of the mind than to think about what is more immediate and commonly understood.

But these matters are so fully and clearly explained by the *general causes of enthusiasm* we have already stated—besides what we have specifically touched on before—that it will not be worth our effort to dwell on them any longer. Once we have addressed a concern or two regarding what we have said about *melancholy* and *enthusiasm*, I believe we will have covered everything essential to this present study.

---

## S E C T. LXII.

### *How to Distinguish Between Pure Religion and Natural Temperament.*

AND the first question is: how can we distinguish between *religion* and *melancholy*, given that we have attributed such notable effects to the latter? The second is: have we not insulted and disparaged all *enthusiasm* entirely, and thereby invited men toward a cold, *Pharisaic* <note>Referring to the Pharisees of the New Testament, implying a rigid, soulless adherence to the letter of religious law without any inner spiritual life.</note> stupidity—acting merely according to the written word without an inner testimony of life?

The focus of the first concern must be limited to things that appear praiseworthy and acceptable on the surface; that is, whether such actions arise from a *divine* or a *natural* principle—whether from *God* or from one’s own *temperament*. For actions that are clearly blameworthy from the very first glance are obviously not from *God*.

I answer, therefore, that there are three main ways to distinguish between the *Spirit* and even the most *impressive natural temperament*. The first is that the *piety* or *goodness* which comes from the *Spirit* of God is *universal*; it roots out every vice and omits nothing that is truly a divine virtue.

The second is a belief in those *Holy Oracles* <note>The scriptures of the Bible.</note> contained in the *Old and New Testaments*, provided they are interpreted correctly. In particular, it requires belief in this article of faith: that *Jesus Christ*—the very one who died on the cross at *Jerusalem* between two thieves—is the *Son of God* and *Sovereign of men* and *angels*, and that he will come again in person to judge the living and the dead.

He begins to establish criteria for distinguishing true religion from physical temperament, emphasizing universal virtue and adherence to orthodox Christian scripture.</summary>

<header>SECTION LXIII. A brief Discourse of Enthusiasm.</header>

The third and last indicator is a *universal prudence*. By this, a person neither accepts nor acts upon anything that is not fundamentally rational at its foundation, and for which they can provide a clear explanation, regardless of the outcome. Anyone who finds themselves moved in this way can be certain it is the *Spirit of God* ruling within them, rather than the influence of their physical temperament <note>original: "Complexion"</note> or natural instincts. However, to others who are skeptical—those so unrefined and unprepared that they are not capable of *reason*—such a person means nothing to them unless he can perform a *miracle*. How foolish <note>original: "vain"</note> then is the *enthusiast* who lacks both reason and miracles? But those ancient records of *miracles* performed on behalf of Christianity are sufficient proof of the truth of our religion to those whose hearts are properly prepared for it.

## SECTION LXIII.
### *That the devotional enthusiasm of holy and sincere souls has not been criticized at all in this discourse.*

Regarding the second concern, I answer that not a single word has been spoken all this time against that *true* and *justifiable enthusiasm* of devout and holy souls. These people are remarkably moved by the intense *love* they bear toward God and the indescribable *joy* and *peace* they find in Him. They are modest and sensible in all of this; they testify to the world of nothing other than what others may experience for themselves, and what is clearly stated in the Holy Scriptures: *That the Kingdom of God is righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit*.

In none of these matters do they claim to be equal to Christ—whom God has exalted above men and angels—but instead acknowledge the power of His Spirit within them for the praise and glory of God, and for the comfort and encouragement of their discouraged neighbors. But anything beyond this, if it lacks clear *reason* or a *miracle*, is most rightly judged to come from no supernatural help, but rather from some *hypochondriacal* disorder <note>original: "Hypochondriacall distemper." In the 17th century, this referred to a physical imbalance of "black bile" thought to cause delusions or obsessive thoughts.</note>.

What I have said on behalf of Christians applies also, in its own measure, to those more divine philosophers like *Plato* and *Plotinus*. You will find that when they experienced more than ordinary visits of divine love and beauty descending into their captivated souls, they described themselves as being moved in ways that phrases such as "to be stirred up," "to be in a divine frenzy," or "to be inspired" <note>original: "ἀνακινεῖσθαι, ἐκβακχεύεσθαι, ἐνθουσιᾶν or ἐνθουσιάζειν"</note> express. I declare myself a friend to this kind of enthusiasm—which is simply the triumph of the human soul rejoicing, as if intoxicated by the delightful experience of the divine life, that blessed root and origin of all holy wisdom and virtue. I am as much a friend to this as I am a declared enemy to common, fanatical enthusiasm. Let eternal shame silence anyone who dares to deny that the fervent love of God and the beauty <note>original: "pulchritude"</note> of virtue provide the human spirit more joy and triumph than has ever been tasted in any lustful pleasure—even though the pens of immoral writers praise such pleasures so highly in both poetry and prose.

### SECTION LXIV.

->*That the fuel for devotion, even in legitimate and sincere enthusiasm, is usually melancholy.*<-

Furthermore, regarding these rapturous and enthusiastic emotions *even in those who are truly good and pious*, it cannot be denied that their *fuel is usually natural or acquired melancholy*; <note>In the 17th century, "melancholy" was one of the four "humors" or temperaments. It was associated with deep thinking and spiritual intensity, but also with a tendency toward gloom or delusion.</note> any person who is *religious* can see this, unless their soul and body are so intertwined that everything is confused. This is the case with mistaken *enthusiasts*, who attribute to God what actually belongs to nature.

<margin>James, chapter 5, verse 13.</margin>
But melancholy usually prepares the mind, and the soul *perfects* the action through the power of the Spirit. A wise and holy person knows how to use this opportunity, according to that warning of the Apostle:
> *If a man is sad, let him pray; if he is cheerful, let him sing psalms.* <note>original: "If a man be sad, let him pray; if chearfull, let him sing Psalmes." This is a paraphrase of James 5:13.</note>

---

### SECTION LXV.

->*That there is a unique advantage in melancholy for divine contemplation, and a response to the atheist's objection to this.*<-

But there is also a unique advantage in *melancholy* <note>original: "Melancholy"</note> for *divine contemplation*. And yet, the mysteries that result from it should no more be suspected of being mere fantasies—simply because they may occasionally arise from such a physical temperament—than *mathematical truths* are. These truths owe their birth to a *mathematical temperament* <term>complexion</term>; <note>The author uses "complexion" to mean a person's physical and psychological constitution, determined by their bodily humors.</note> which is just as much a physical constitution as the *religious* temperament is, and yet no sensible person will deny the truth of its theorems. Just as it would be foolish and incorrect to claim that such a *temperament* teaches someone mathematics, it would be equally wrong to claim that melancholy is the sole mother of religion.

---

### SECTION LXVI.

->*How it happens that people are so quick and skillful at finding the truth in some things, and so slow and heavy in others; and that the dullness of the atheist's perception in divine matters is no argument against the truth of religion.*<-

It is most certain, and observation will confirm it, that human souls, while they are in these mortal bodies, are like so many prisoners confined in separate prisons. They have only single loopholes looking out in various directions, and therefore can only speak of what their specific view allows them to see. In the same way, the different physical temperaments <term>complexions</term> of men's bodies prepare or invite them to an easy and successful discovery...

### SECTION LXVII.

*That the enthusiast, though he is necessarily affected by his own temperament, is not affected irresistibly; and that, therefore, the guilt for his wild behavior lies at his own door.*

With the brevity I intended, I have now run through the *Nature*, *Causes*, *Types*, and *Cure* of *Enthusiasm*. Looking back carefully over the path I have taken, I believe all my steps are complete, except perhaps for the section concerning the causes of this disorder. The list might seem lacking because I omitted the influence of the Devil and the deliberate wickedness of the human mind, and instead attributed everything to "complexion" <note>original: "Complexion"; in the 17th century, this referred to the balance of the four humors (physical temperament) that determined a person's health and personality.</note>, or the current condition—or rather, the disorder—of the body arising from natural causes that necessarily affect it. Because of this, people may judge my discourse as much an excuse for this disease of *Enthusiasm* as it is a discovery of it.

But I answer that although these causes act necessarily upon the body, and the body necessarily upon the mind, they do not act irresistibly—unless a man has brought himself to such a state of weakness by his own fault. This is like a man who, through his own lack of self-control, has brought a fever upon himself and then inevitably becomes subject to its laws. And though the Devil may do much on his own, he can do no more than God permits. God will suffer no man to be tempted beyond what he can bear, provided he is sincere and faithful, and does not give himself over to fanatical fits out of pride or for some deceitful projects in the world. For people like these, enthusiasm may prove to be "the Devil's bath" <note>original: "Balneum diaboli"</note>, as is commonly said of melancholy; whereas, on the contrary, it may be the washing of regeneration <note>original: "laver of Regeneration"; a reference to spiritual cleansing and rebirth.</note> to those who sincerely love and fear God, and strive to be

This refers to the debate over whether animals have souls or are merely "beast-machines."</note>
4. *The response of* **René Descartes**.
5. *The second letter of* **Henry More** *to* **René Descartes**, *in which he refutes the responses to his previous objections with many new examples, and proposes various questions about the extension of the universe, the nature of motion, striated particles, the union of the soul with the body and its command over the body, the conversion of ethereal globules into the first element, the flexibility of water particles, and finally, the self-motion* <note>original Greek: αὐτοκινησίᾳ (autokinasia)</note> *of matter.* <note>"Striated particles" (particulis striatis) were screw-like particles used in Cartesian physics to explain magnetism.</note>

7. **Henry More's** *third letter to* **René Descartes**, *in which he briefly reviews what has been debated so far, then proposes various points from the "Principles of Philosophy" that are either to be proven or explained.* <note>Referring to Descartes' major work, "Principia Philosophiae."</note>
8. **Henry More's** *fourth letter to* **René Descartes**, *which likewise proposes various points from both the "Dioptrics" and the "Meteors" to be either proven or clarified.* <note>These were scientific treatises published alongside Descartes' "Discourse on Method."</note>
9. *A fragment of* **René Descartes'** *response to the third letter of* **Henry More**, *which deals with the perception of angels and the separate mind, the contraction and expansion of spirit, the immensity of God, the rest and motion of matter, etc.*

11. *A letter from* **Henry More** *to a most distinguished gentleman,* <note>original: "V. C." for Virum Clarissimum</note> *which includes a defense of* **Descartes**, *and which could serve as an introduction to the entire Cartesian philosophy.*

<header>Letter of Claude Clerselier to Henry More.</header>

## *To the Most Distinguished Man*

# HENRY MORE.

I have read, excellent sir, and reread with the greatest pleasure your objections <note>original: "difficultates"</note> to Mr. Descartes, which you proposed to him on December 11, 1648; March 5, 1649; July 23, 1649; and October 21, 1649. I admired both your intellect and your great kindness; relying on that kindness, I have dared to write back to you confidently to inform you of what I intend to do, and to obtain from you what I need to bring the work I have undertaken to its conclusion.

You should know, therefore, that I have in my hands the primary original manuscripts which the incomparable philosopher Mr. Descartes left with Mr. Chanut <note>Hector-Pierre Chanut was a French ambassador and Descartes' close friend and brother-in-law.</note>, formerly the ambassador to the Most Serene Queen of Sweden, and now the highly deserving ambassador to the Dutch. He is my relative, and it was at his home in Sweden that Descartes passed away. Among these papers are the letters which Descartes wrote back to many of his friends. I am collecting the most important of these—specifically those that touch upon his philosophy, concern the works he had undertaken to complete, or solve the difficulties proposed to him by many great men (among whom you hold a prominent place). My goal is to publish them all, which I hope to accomplish shortly.

However, because those letters that respond to objections can hardly be understood unless the letters that prompted such a response are published alongside them, and because it did not seem honorable for me to do this without the permission and license of those who wrote to him, I have requested and obtained this permission from several others. I hope that, given your great kindness and incredible devotion to Descartes, you will also grant this to me.

But furthermore, I would like you to send me copies of all the letters you received from Mr. Descartes. I only have two in my possession: the first corresponds to your letter dated December 11, and the second to the one written on March 5. There remains, therefore, a third letter which I lack, and which ought to address your letters of July 23 and October 21. That letter must surely be a masterpiece <note>original: "pulcherrima"</note> and contain many things most worthy of knowing, since it must respond to so many of your great objections and questions drawn from both the *Principles of Philosophy* and the *Dioptrics*. I found only two pages of it, which only attempt to address your immediate examples and do not contain a single word regarding your questions on the *Principles* and the *Dioptrics*.

Therefore, I greatly desire and earnestly pray that you grant me permission to print your letters together with the responses, and that you also send me the letters you have from Mr. Descartes. In this way, we may serve the benefit of future generations and honor our friend’s fame and memory. Besides these original letters, I have many other notable records of that most celebrated man, each of which will be published in its own time. I believe these will bring you no small pleasure, as you seem so diligent in studying Cartesian writings. If I had been permitted to use my native tongue <note>Clerselier's native language was French.</note>, I would have explained my meaning more aptly and elegantly; but...

<meta>catchword: lest</meta>

Paris, December 12,

### Response
## OF HENRY MORE.

Your letter, most distinguished Sir, sent from Paris on December 12, 1654, did not reach my hands before April 15 <note>original: "decimum septimum Calendarum Maii" — the 17th day before the Kalends of May, which is April 15.</note>. I am surprised that so much time has passed between its sending and arrival. I was then staying at Grantham in Lincolnshire, for I had retired to the countryside both for other reasons and to improve my health. I was truly delighted after I understood your excellent plan to publish all of Descartes' writings that you have in your possession. By doing so, you will best serve not only the fame and memory of that most noble philosopher, but also the common benefit of all learned people. For that saying of Horace fits no one more aptly than that divine man:

---
->*Who attempts nothing foolishly.*<-
<note>original: "Qui nil molitur ineptè" — from Horace’s *Ars Poetica*.</note>

---

For this reason, if I were your advisor, nothing of what he attempted in any way regarding philosophical matters, or successfully brought to a conclusion, would be suppressed; instead, all of it would see the light of day for the greater benefit of the Republic of Letters <note>original: "Reipub. Literariæ" — the international community of scholars and intellectuals.</note>. And therefore, so that there might be no obstacle to such a useful and noble purpose, I would even voluntarily grant you the opportunity to publish my first and second letters written to Descartes. As you correctly point out, his responses cannot be so easily understood without them. I do not deny it would also be quite relevant if you published my third letters at the same time, since they contain the response to those other letters from Descartes. 

However, since my fourth letters do not respond to any of his letters, nor was any reply made to them by him—as he was snatched away by an unexpected death—I hesitate somewhat whether I should make them public. Nevertheless, all doubt would be removed if one of his friends or associates, who visited and spoke with him frequently or lived closely with him, could take his place in responding. In that case, I have little doubt that it would be worthwhile to bring those into the light as well. 

But if this cannot be achieved at present, I might still be persuaded to grant you the right to publish them if there were a probability that my third and fourth letters would entice one of the more skilled followers of Cartesian philosophy to respond to all the difficulties I proposed to Descartes himself. You will perhaps be able to guess the likelihood of this happening better than I can. So that I do not delay you with many words, I leave this whole business to your judgment and integrity, so that you may do what needs to be done. It is incredible with how much grief I was affected upon hearing of the premature death of Descartes, for his genius...

# The Response of Henry More to the Letter of Claude Clerselier.

[The genius] and virtues of that incomparable man I have deeply loved and admired. Furthermore, there arose in me a great desire to read through his responses—which I had been expecting—to my third and fourth letters, which survey his entire *Philosophy*. I understand from you that he had begun a complete response to my letter dated July 23 <note>original: "10. Cal. Aug." — the 10th day before the Kalends of August.</note>. I conjecture that he wrote this fragment while he was at *Egmond* in *Holland*. However, as he informed me through his friends, he ceased the undertaking because his mind, being very busy with preparations for his journey to *Sweden*, could not find the time for such subtle difficulties and inquiries of such great importance (as he himself said). But he constantly promised his friends that he would return the following spring, and then explain everything to me fully and clearly. 

But since envious death has snatched everything else away from us, I would not want even that *Fragment* of two pages, which you mention, to be lost. As for those more substantial works <note>original: "monumenta"</note> of *Descartes* which you claim to have, and which, as you promise, will see the light of day in their own time, my mind truly rejoices at such happy and welcome news. In the meantime, I eagerly desire, if it is not a burden to you, that you list the arguments or titles of each of the books in your next letter. For that former passion for *Cartesian Philosophy* has been revived in me since I received your recent letter; it had cooled down a bit after the death of our most missed Friend, since new material to read was not available. But, to confess the truth frankly, that was not the only cause, but rather certain particular studies which had called my mind elsewhere. For such is the weight of the subject matter, the beauty of truth, the breadth of genius and sharpness, and finally that admirable order and agreement of all the theorems in the *Cartesian* writings, that even when read a thousand times they do not become stale <note>original: "fordescant"</note>—no more than the light of the *Sun*, whose rising the birds, the cattle, and even humans themselves contemplate with joy every day.

Certainly, this *Cartesian Philosophy* is not only pleasant to read but especially useful—whatever others may mutter or babble—for that highest end of all *Philosophy*, namely *Religion*. For while the *Peripatetics* <note>original: "Peripatetici" — followers of Aristotle's philosophy, dominant in medieval universities.</note> contend that there are certain "substantial forms" <note>Aristotelian concept of an internal principle that gives a thing its properties.</note> which arise from the power of matter and which merge with matter in such a way that they cannot exist without it, and therefore necessarily return at last to the power of matter (to which class they assign the souls of almost all living things, even those to whom they attribute sensation and thought); the *Epicureans* <note>Followers of Epicurus, who argued that everything is made of atoms and that the soul is material.</note>, on the other hand, having exploded those "substantial forms," determine that the power of sensing and thinking resides in matter itself. 

*Descartes* alone, as far as I know, has stood out among the *Physiologists* <note>original: "Physiologos" — here meaning natural philosophers or scientists.</note> as the one who removed those substantial forms, or souls arising from matter, from *Philosophy*, and plainly stripped matter itself of all faculty of sensing and thinking. From this, if one stood by *Cartesian* principles, there would be a most certain way and *Method* of demonstrating both that *God* exists and that the human soul cannot be mortal. These are those two most solid foundations and pillars of all true *Religion*. I note these things briefly, though I could add many other things here that look toward the same goal. But I will say in summary: no philosophy exists (unless perhaps you except the *Platonic*) that so firmly blocks the way for *Atheists* against those perverse quibbles and excuses to which they usually retreat, as does this *Cartesian* philosophy, if it is understood more deeply. From this I hope that all good men will more kindly tolerate those most ample praises with which I heap the incomparable Man in those letters I wrote to him; and I believe that whatever this pre-

<page-num>60</page-num>
# The Response of Henry More to the Letter of Claude Clerselier.

Whatever the present age has felt about Descartes <note>original: "Cartesio"</note>—for just as envy never spares the living, so it rarely spares the memory of the recently deceased—posterity will surely receive him with all praise and veneration, and will recognize the excellent value of his philosophy. I declare this all the more willingly to further encourage you to proceed in that noble undertaking of publishing all the philosophical writings of Descartes which you possess. By doing so, you will place many others under a great debt of gratitude, and me above all, as I am accustomed to perceiving such great pleasure in studying them.

If it should seem right to you to publish my letters to Descartes, I strongly request this of you: that it not be done using those copies you already have, because I am preparing much more corrected versions for you. For I have discovered, after reading them more attentively, quite a few things needing correction which escaped me unawares due to too much mental fervor and haste when I was writing to Descartes. I have also struck out certain of the "Inquiries" in my third and fourth letters, but the first and second remain complete.

As for the fact that almost a month has now passed since I received your letter and I have not yet written back, this has certainly happened through no negligence or lack of care. For I cannot help but value you highly, both because of your exceptional intellect—which is shaped for all fairness and kindness, as I have clearly seen from your letters—and because of the honorable devotion toward the late Descartes shown by your most illustrious brother, Chanut <note>Pierre Chanut was a French ambassador and a close friend of Descartes</note>, formerly an ambassador to the Swedes and now, as you say, a most deserving ambassador to the Dutch <note>original: "Batavos"</note>. 

But all the time that has passed was spent partly on business that kept me occupied in the country, and partly on correcting and transcribing my letters to Descartes after I had returned to the University. I did not think it would be worthwhile to write back to you before I had finished those tasks. Now, however, everything is ready—copies of my own letters as well as those of Descartes. Yet I am sending neither to you this time, as I thought I should first test how safely these letters I have now written reach your hands; as soon as I know they have arrived, I will send the others to you immediately. In the meantime, I would very gladly hear from you how far you have progressed in that noble business you wrote that you have undertaken. You will do me a truly pleasing favor if you inform me about that matter in your next letter. Farewell, most illustrious man, and may you successfully carry out that noble work you are laboring upon. So wishes:

Cambridge, from Christ’s College,
the day before the Ides of May, 1655. <note>May 14, 1655</note>

->Most devoted to you and to<-
->all Cartesians,<-
->**HENRY MORE.**<-

### ->*To the Most Illustrious Man*<-
# RENÉ DESCARTES
## FROM HENRY MORE, ENGLISHMAN.

With how much pleasure my mind was filled, most illustrious Sir, in reading your writings, no one but you alone can possibly imagine.

Indeed, I would dare to assert that I exulted no less in recognizing and understanding your excellent theorems than you did in discovering them. I hold those most beautiful "offspring" of your genius <note>original: "ingenii tui foetus"—a common 17th-century metaphor for an author's books or ideas</note> just as dear and love them as much as if my own mind had brought them forth. And certainly, my mind seems to have done so in some way, by exerting and unfolding itself into the very same senses and thoughts which your noble mind first conceived and demonstrated. These ideas are truly of such a kind that, since they are so well-suited to my own intellect and judgment, I do not hope to ever encounter anything more closely related or "kindred" to my own thinking. Truly, they could not be foreign to the mind of anyone whose own intellect is not foreign to right reason.

I will say freely what I feel: all the Masters of the Secrets of Nature <note>original: "Arcanorum Naturae Antistites." An "antistes" was a high priest or overseer; More uses it to describe great scientists and philosophers of the past</note> who have ever existed, or even exist now, if compared to your magnificent talent, seem plainly to be Dwarfs and Pygmies. After I had studied your philosophical works even once, I suspected that your most illustrious disciple, the most Serene Princess Elizabeth <note>Princess Elizabeth of the Palatinate (1618–1680) was a brilliant philosopher who conducted a famous long-term correspondence with Descartes</note>, had become far wiser than all other Europeans—not only women, but men and even philosophers. This I soon perceived more clearly when I began to examine and understand your writings a little more deeply.

For at last, the **Cartesian Light** <note>original: "Cartesiana Lux"</note> clearly shone upon me—that is, a free, distinct, and self-consistent Reason which has wonderfully illuminated both Nature and your own pages. It has done so such that there remain either no hiding places at all, or very few, which that noble torch has not revealed; or at the very least, it will soon reveal them with the slightest effort whenever I wish. Everything in your *Principles of Philosophy*, *Dioptrics*, and *Meteors* <note>These are three of Descartes' major works: *Principia Philosophiae* (1644), *Dioptrique*, and *Météores* (both 1637)</note> is so elegant, and so beautifully consistent with itself and with Nature, that the human mind and reason could hardly hope for a more pleasant or joyful sight.

In your *Method* <note>Referring to the *Discourse on the Method* (1637)</note>, through a certain playful but truly elegant kind of modesty, you show yourself to be a man so sweet and amiable in character and genius that nothing more excellent or noble could be imagined or desired.

But why all this? Not because I thought, most illustrious Sir, that it mattered either to you or to the Republic of Letters <note>The "Republic of Letters" was the long-distance intellectual community of scholars in the 17th century</note> that I should write these things; rather, it is because the consciousness of that wonderful pleasure and benefit I received from your writings wrung from me this testimony, such as it is, of a grateful mind toward you. Furthermore, I wrote to assure you that even among the English there are those who value you and your works highly, and who deeply respect and admire the divine gifts of your mind. No man can love you more fervently than I, nor embrace your exceptional philosophy more closely.

<meta>This page continues the first letter from the English philosopher Henry More to René Descartes, dated December 11, 1648. More is transitioning from polite praise of Descartes' brilliance to a respectful critique of specific points in Descartes' "Principles of Philosophy" (1644).</meta>

<header>First Letter of H. More to R. Descartes.</header>

But truly, most illustrious Descartes, to hide nothing: although I am deeply enamored with the beautiful structure and essence of your philosophy, I must confess that a few points in the second part of your *Principles* <note>original: *Principia Philosophiae*, Descartes' major work on physics and metaphysics</note> have escaped me. Either my mind is a bit too dull to grasp them, or it is too resistant to accept them.

However, the overall merit of your excellent philosophy is not endangered by this. These points are of such a nature that, even if they were judged false or uncertain, they do not affect the essence or foundations of your system; your philosophy can stand perfectly well without them. If it is not too tedious for you, I will now briefly explain what these points are.

First, you establish a definition of **Matter** or **Body** that is much broader than is appropriate. For God seems to be an **extended thing** <note>original: *res extensa*—Descartes' term for substance that takes up space</note>, as is an Angel, and indeed any thing that exists on its own. Thus, extension and the absolute essence of things seem to be bounded by the same limits, though this extension can vary according to the variety of the essences themselves. Indeed, I believe it is clear that God is extended in His own way, precisely because He is omnipresent and intimately occupies the entire machine of the world and each of its particles. For how could He impart motion to matter (which you admit He did once and continues to do) unless He touched the matter of the universe closely, as it were, or at least had touched it at some point? He certainly could never have done this unless He were present everywhere and occupied every region. Therefore, God is extended and expanded in His own way, and is consequently an "extended thing."

Yet He is not that "body" or "matter" which your ingenious mind—the true craftsman—has so skillfully shaped into globules and grooved particles <note>original: *striatasque particulas*. Descartes' physics imagined matter as consisting of various shaped particles, including screw-like "striated" ones that explained magnetism</note>. Therefore, the category of "extended thing" is broader than that of "body."

I am further encouraged to disagree with you on this point because, in confirming your definition, you use such a *clumsy and almost sophisticated* <note>original: *scævum... & ferme sophisticum*. More is calling Descartes' logic "clumsy" or "awkward"</note> *argument*. You argue that a body can be a body without softness, hardness, weight, or lightness, etc.; for if those and all other qualities felt in corporeal matter are removed, the thing itself remains intact. This is just like saying that a pound of wax remains a pound of wax even if it is stripped of a spherical, cubic, or pyramidal shape—and therefore it can remain a pound of wax while having no shape at all. Yet that is impossible. For although this or that specific shape is not so tightly bound to the wax that the wax cannot shed it, it is a supreme and absolute necessity that the wax always has *some* shape. In the same way, although matter is not necessarily soft, hard, hot, or cold, it is absolutely necessary that it be *sensible* <note>perceptible to the senses</note>; or, if you prefer, *tangible*, as Lucretius so excellently defines it:

> For nothing can touch or be touched, except a body. <note>original: *Tangere enim, & tangi, nisi corpus nulla potest res.* From Lucretius, *De Rerum Natura*, 1.444</note>

This notion certainly should not be foreign to your mind, since your philosophy—along with those ancients mentioned in Theophrastus’s *On Sense Perception* <note>original Greek: περὶ αἰσθήσεως (*Peri aistheseos*)</note>—clearly establishes every sense as a form of touch. I would very easily admit that nothing is truer than this. But if you are reluctant to define "body" by its relation to *our senses*, then this Tangibility becomes broader and more diffuse: it signifies that mutual contact and power of touching between any bodies whatsoever, whether they are animate or inanimate, being the immediate juxtaposition of the surfaces of two or more bodies. This also implies another condition of matter or body...

More is arguing that Descartes’ definition of "matter" as simply "extension" is too broad, because it would mistakenly include God and angels, who are also extended throughout space but are not material.</meta>

<page-num>63</page-num>

...condition, which you might call **impenetrability**; namely, that a body can neither penetrate other bodies, nor be penetrated by them. From this, the difference between divine and corporeal nature is most clear, since the former can penetrate the latter, while the latter cannot penetrate itself. Therefore, it seems to me that Virgil <note>Publius Virgilius Maro, the Roman poet</note> philosophizes more successfully along with his fellow Platonists than Descartes himself does, when he sang according to their opinion:

->*Mind, infused through the limbs,*<-
->*moves the whole mass and mingles itself with the great body.*<-
<note>original: *Totámque infusa per artus / Mens agitat molem, & magno se corpore miscet.* — Virgil, *Aeneid*, Book 6, lines 726-727. More uses this to argue that God is "extended" through the physical world.</note>

I set aside other more notable conditions of Divine extension, as there is no need to explain them here. These few points will suffice to show that it would have been much safer to define matter as a **tangible substance**, or **impenetrable** (in the way explained above), rather than simply as an **extended thing**. For what is called **tangibility** or **impenetrability** applies perfectly and exclusively to body; but your definition fails the law of the **first universal** <note>original: <term>καθ’ὅλου πρῶτον</term> (*kath’olou proton*) — an Aristotelian logical rule that a definition should be exactly co-extensive with the thing defined, neither broader nor narrower</note>, for it is not interchangeable with the thing being defined.

Second: When you suggest that it is not possible, even by divine power, for a **vacuum** (properly so-called) to exist, and that if all body were removed from a vessel, the sides would necessarily come together—these things seem to me not only false, but also inconsistent with your previous statements. For if God imparts motion to matter (as you taught above), can He not push back against the motion and prevent the sides of the vessel from meeting? You argue that it is a contradiction for the sides of the vessel to be distant and yet have nothing lying between them. However, learned antiquity—Epicurus, Democritus, Lucretius, and others—did not think so. 

But to set aside that lighter kind of argument, I contend that **Divine extension** lies between the sides, and that your assumption here—that only matter is extended—is weak. The sides would indeed come together, but not by logical necessity; rather, they would do so by natural necessity. Only God could prevent this joining. For since particles (especially those of the first and second elements) are agitated by such a furious motion, they must necessarily rush headlong wherever space is yielded, dragging other nearby particles with them.

It is unfortunate, therefore, that you support such a fine theorem on the method of **rarefaction and condensation** (which I certainly believe to be true for other reasons) with such a slippery foundation.

Third: I do not grasp that singular subtlety by which you prove that **atoms**—that is, particles by their nature indivisible—do not exist. For as you say, even if God had made those particles so that they could be divided by no creatures, He certainly could not take away from Himself the power of dividing them, because it is impossible for Him to diminish His own power. By the same argument, you might prove that God never made yesterday's sun rise, because His power can no longer bring it about that yesterday's sun had not risen; nor can He kill the lowliest fly,

->*If only he who has perished could not have perished,*<-
<note>original: *Si modò qui periit, non periisse potest* — Ovid, *Tristia*, 3.4.7. The poet is lamenting that the past cannot be undone.</note>

as Ovid cleverly said of himself. Or you might argue that He did not create matter, since it is divisible into things that are always further divisible, and therefore God could never finish or complete this division. A part always remains undivided, however divisible it may be, and thus divine power is perpetually eluded, unable to fully exert itself or reach an end.

Fourth: I do not understand your **indefinite extension** of the world. For that indefinite extension is either simply infinite, or infinite only as far as we are concerned.

<page-num>64</page-num>
<header>First Letter of H. More to R. Descartes.</header>

If you mean an extension that is simply infinite, why do you obscure your mind with such overly restrained and modest words? If you mean it is only "infinite relative to us" <note>Descartes preferred the term "indefinite" to avoid the theological implications of "infinite."</note>, then the extension is actually finite; for our mind is the measure of neither things nor truth. And therefore, since there is another simply infinite expansion—namely, that of the divine essence—the matter of your vortices will recede from its centers, and the entire machine of the world will break apart into scattered atoms and wandering dust motes.

And truly, I wonder all the more at your modesty and fear here, because you are so careful to avoid the infinity of matter, even though you yourself recognized that particles are both actually infinite and divided in Articles 34 and 35. Even if you had not done so, it seems this could still be forced from your logic in this way: for since any quantity is divisible into infinity, it must have parts that are actually infinite. Just as it is completely impossible <note>original: <term>ἀμήχανον</term> (*amēchanon*)</note>—or rather, unfeasible—to mechanically dissect a body with a knife or any other instrument into tangible parts that are not already actually such; so too, to divide a quantity in the mind into parts that do not really and actually exist within the whole is clearly irrational <note>original: <term>ἄλογον</term> (*alogon*)</note> and contrary to reason.

To these points can be added the following: this hypothesis—that the world is simply and truly infinite—has equal power to explain and confirm the reasoning for **rarefaction** and **condensation** <note>Rarefaction is the thinning of matter; condensation is the thickening or crowding of matter.</note> that you proposed earlier in Articles 6 and 7, as well as that principle: *extension belongs to body alone, and nothingness cannot be extended*. For what logical or contradictory necessity achieves there, physical or mechanical necessity will certainly achieve here.

For since everything, all the way to infinity, is full and packed with matter or bodies, the law of impenetrability will prevent any distance from being bare of bodies during rarefaction, or any movement of parts toward each other during condensation, without the expulsion of the particles lying between them.

And so far, what I have said seems most clear to my reason and mind, and far, far more certain than your own views.

However, because of my own soft and tender nature, there is no opinion of yours from which my mind shrinks more than that murderous and throat-cutting sentiment you delivered in your *Method* <note>René Descartes, *Discourse on the Method* (1637)</note>, where you snatch away life and feeling from all "brute" animals—or should I say, you forestall it? For you do not even allow that they ever lived. Here, I do not so much admire the glittering edge of your genius as I dread it, being concerned for the fate of living creatures. I recognize your sharp wit as being not merely subtle, but as rigid and cruel as steel; with a single blow, as it were, it dares to strip almost the entire race of living beings of life and feeling, turning them into marble statues and machines.

But let us see, I pray, what reason you have for passing such a harsh sentence on "brute" animals. They cannot speak, of course, nor argue their case before a judge; and, what aggravates the "crime," they have the physical organs for speech, as is clear in magpies and parrots. For this reason, you claim they should be deprived of life and feeling.

But truly, how could it be that either parrots or magpies imitate our voices unless they heard and perceived what we are saying through their senses? "But they do not understand," you say, "what those words mean which they babble out in imitation." Yet why shouldn't they understand enough of what they themselves want—namely, the food they get from their masters through this trick? They think, therefore, that they are begging for food,

...show <note>original: <term>dicare</term></note> that they so often achieve their desires through that vocalization. And why, I ask, is there that attention and listening in songbirds, which they display, if there is no sensation or awareness in them? From where does that cleverness and wisdom of foxes and dogs come? How is it that threats and words restrain fierce beasts? When a hungry dog has stolen something by stealth, why does he slip away secretly as if conscious of the deed, and walking fearfully and distrustfully, greet no one he meets, but continues on his way with his snout turned away and held low, suspiciously cautious lest he pay the penalty for the crime committed? How can these things happen without an internal consciousness of the deed? That vast collection of stories, by which some attempt to demonstrate that reason exists in brute animals, will at least prove that sensation and memory exist in them. But it would be endless to weave together such little tales here. From which I know many are of such a kind that their force cannot be escaped by even the most subtle wit.

But I see clearly what has driven you to this point—to consider brute animals as machines. It is the method of demonstrating the immortality of our souls, which, since it supposes that a body can in no way think, concludes that wherever there is thought, a substance really distinct from the body must be present, and therefore immortal. From which it follows that if brutes think, they must have immortal substances joined to them.

But I beseech you, most perceptive man, since from that method of demonstration it was necessary either to rob brute animals of sensation or to gift them with immortality, why did you prefer to establish them as inanimate machines rather than bodies animated by immortal souls? Especially since the former is not at all consistent with the phenomena of nature and has been completely unheard of until now; while the latter was established and approved by the wisest of the ancients—**Pythagoras**, **Plato**, and others. And certainly, this would give courage to all **Platonists** to persist in their opinion on the immortality of brutes, since such an outstanding genius is reduced to such straits that, if the immortality of brute souls is not granted, he must necessarily establish all brutes as unfeeling machines.

These are those few points (great **Descartes**) in which I thought it lawful for me to disagree with you. All other things so please and flatter me that I find nothing more delightful; and they are so harmonious and related to the innermost feelings of my mind that I am confident I could not only explain them easily to the slower-witted, but even successfully defend them against the most combative opponents, if necessary.

As for what remains, I must beg you, most illustrious man, to take these our thoughts in good part, and not to suspect me of any lightness or vain ambition, as if I were striving for the familiarity and friendship of famous men; since I myself, if I could, would not wish to become famous, judging fame to be a turbulent thing and very hostile to private leisure.

Nor indeed, although my mind is very inclined and favorably disposed toward you, would I ever have signaled this to you, unless urged by others; but I would have been content to follow you and your works with hidden love and silent veneration.

Nor do I urgently demand that you write back, since I assume you are most occupied with extremely difficult contemplations, or with performing experiments that are as useful as they are difficult.

I therefore allow you to use your own judgment here, so that I may not be injurious to the public. If...

### *To the Most Learned and Kindest Man*
## **HENRY MORE**
# RENÉ DESCARTES.

The praise you heap upon me, most kind sir, is evidence not so much of any merit of mine—since no merit could equal such praise—as it is of your goodwill toward me. This goodwill, developed solely from reading my writings, shows the clarity and generosity of your mind so openly that it binds me entirely to you, though we were previously unknown to each other. Therefore, I will most gladly answer the questions you have asked.

1. The first question is why, in defining a body, I say it is an **extended substance** <note>original: <term>substantia extensa</term>. In Cartesian philosophy, "extension" means taking up space in three dimensions (length, width, and depth), which Descartes argued was the essential nature of all physical matter.</note> rather than a **sensible** <note>original: <term>sensibilem</term>. In this context, "sensible" means "perceivable by the senses" (touch, sight, etc.), not "reasonable."</note>, **tangible**, or **impenetrable** one. But the logic of the matter reminds you that if it were called a "sensible substance," it would then be defined by its relationship to our senses. By that reasoning, only one of its properties would be explained, not its entire nature; for since a body can exist even if no humans exist, its nature certainly does not depend on our senses. Consequently, I do not see why you say it is highly necessary that all matter be sensible. On the contrary, there is no matter that is not completely imperceptible <note>original: <term>insensibilis</term></note> if it is simply divided into parts much smaller than the particles of our nerves, and if each part is moved quickly enough on its own.

And that argument of mine, which you call **clumsy** <note>original: <term>scævum</term>, literally "left-handed" or "awkward."</note> and **almost Sophistical**, I used only to refute the opinion of those who believe, as you do, that every body is sensible; in my judgment, it refutes that view clearly and demonstratively. **For a body can retain its entire nature as a body even if it is not soft, hard, cold, or hot to the touch, nor even has any sensible quality at all.**

Now, to fall into the error you seem to want to attribute to me—using the **comparison of wax**, which, although it can be neither square nor round, cannot help but have some shape—I would have had to conclude that a body could exist even if none of its particles were in motion or at rest. This follows from my principle that all sensible qualities consist solely in the fact that the particles of a body move or rest in certain ways. But such a thought never entered my mind. **Therefore, a body is not correctly defined as a sensible substance.**

Let us see now whether perhaps it can be more aptly called an **impenetrable** or **tangible** substance, in the sense you explained.

But again, that tangibility and impenetrability in a body is only as...

In a human being, the capacity for laughter is a "property of the fourth kind" <note>original: <term>proprium quarto modo</term>. In Aristotelian logic, this refers to a characteristic that belongs to every member of a species and only to that species, but is not part of its essential definition.</note>, according to the common rules of logic. It is not a true and essential difference, which I contend consists in **extension**. Therefore, just as a human being is defined not as a "laughing animal" but as a "rational animal," so I have not defined a body by its **impenetrability**, but by its extension. This is confirmed by the fact that tangibility and impenetrability relate to parts and presuppose the concept of division or boundaries. However, we can conceive of a continuous body of indeterminate or indefinite magnitude in which nothing besides extension is considered.

But, you say, even God and angels, and any other self-subsisting thing, are extended; therefore, your definition is broader than the thing being defined <note>More argued that if God is everywhere, God must have "extension," making Descartes' definition of matter too vague.</note>. I do not usually argue about names, and so if someone says that because God is everywhere, He is in some way extended, I will not object. Yet I deny that **true extension**, as it is commonly understood by everyone, is found in God, or in angels, or in our minds, or indeed in any substance that is not a body.

For by an "extended being," most people commonly understand something **imaginable** (whether it is a mental concept or a real thing, I leave that aside for now). In such a being, the imagination can distinguish various parts of a specific size and shape, where one part is in no way another. One can also imagine transferring some parts into the place of others, yet cannot imagine two parts existing together in one and the same place. 

However, nothing of this sort can be said of God, or even of our minds; for they are not imaginable, but only **intelligible** <note>In Cartesian philosophy, the "imagination" deals with sensory-like mental images of physical things, while the "intellect" understands abstract truths like God or math.</note>. Nor are they divisible into parts, especially not parts that have specific sizes and shapes. Finally, we easily understand that the human mind, and God, and several angels all at once can be in one and the same place. 

From this, it is clearly concluded that no incorporeal substances are "extended" in the proper sense. Instead, I understand them as certain virtues or powers; although these powers apply themselves to extended things, they are not themselves extended—just as fire within a piece of glowing-hot iron does not mean that the fire is the iron. 

As for why some people confuse the notion of "substance" with the notion of an "extended thing," this happens due to a false prejudice: they think nothing exists, or *is intelligible, unless it is also imaginable*. In truth, nothing falls under the imagination that *is not in some way extended*. 

Now, just as one might say that "health" belongs only to a human being, even though by analogy medicine, temperate air, and many other things are also called "healthy"; so too I say that only that which is imaginable—having parts distinct from other parts, with a specific size and shape—is truly "extended," even though other things are called extended by analogy.

2. To move on to your second difficulty: if we examine what this "extended being" I have described actually is, we will find it is exactly the same as **space** <note>original: <term>spatium</term></note>. The common people think of space as sometimes full, sometimes empty, sometimes real, and sometimes imaginary. In space, however imaginary or empty it may be, everyone can easily imagine various parts of specific size and shape, and they can *mentally transfer some parts into the place of others*. But there is no way to conceive of two parts mutually penetrating each other in one and the same place at the same time, because it involves a contradiction for this to happen without any part of the space being removed. Since I considered that such real properties can only exist in a real body, I dared to affirm that no...
