...no completely empty space exists, and that every extended being is a true body. I have not hesitated to differ in this matter from great men such as *Epicurus, Democritus, and Lucretius* <note>ancient Greek and Roman philosophers who proposed "Atomism," the idea that the universe consists of tiny indivisible particles moving through empty space</note>. For I saw that they did not follow some firm reason, but rather a false prejudice with which we have all been imbued from our earliest years. Indeed, although our senses do not always show us external bodies exactly as they are in every respect, but only insofar as they relate to us and can benefit or harm us (as I warned in Article 3 of Part 2 <note>Refers to Descartes' book, *Principles of Philosophy*</note>), we nevertheless all judged when we were still children that there was nothing else in the world except what was shown by the senses. Consequently, we believed there was no body unless it was sensible <note>original: <term>sensibile</term>; meaning "perceivable by the senses"</note>, and that all places in which we sensed nothing were empty. Since this prejudice was never rejected by *Epicurus, Democritus, or Lucretius*, I ought not to follow their authority.

However, I marvel that a man who is otherwise most clear-sighted <note>referring to Henry More</note>, when he sees that he cannot deny that some substance exists in all space—since all the properties of extension are truly found in it—would nevertheless prefer to say that "divine extension" fills a space in which there is no body, rather than admit that no space at all can exist without a body. For, as I have already said, that pretended "extension of God" can in no way be the subject of the true properties which we perceive most distinctly in all space. For God is not "imaginable" <note>Descartes uses "imaginable" to mean something that can be represented as a mental image with physical dimensions</note>, nor is He divided into distinguishable parts that are measurable and shaped.

But you easily admit that no vacuum exists naturally. You are concerned, however, about divine power, which you think could remove everything that is inside a vessel and simultaneously prevent the sides of the vessel from coming together. Yet, since I know that my intellect is finite and God's power is infinite, I never determine anything regarding this power. Instead, I consider only what can or cannot be perceived by me, and I take diligent care that my judgment does not disagree with my perception. Therefore, I boldly affirm that God can do everything that I perceive to be possible; but, on the other hand, I do not boldly deny that He can do what is repugnant to my concept. I simply say that it involves a contradiction. Thus, because I see it is repugnant to my concept for all body to be removed from a vessel while "extension" remains in it (extension being conceived by me no differently than the body previously contained in it), I say that **it involves a contradiction for such extension to remain there after the body is removed**, and therefore the sides of the vessel must come together. **This is entirely consistent with my other opinions.** For I say elsewhere that **no motion occurs except in a circular fashion**; from which it follows that it cannot be distinctly understood that God removes a body from a vessel without it being simultaneously understood that another body, or the sides of the vessel themselves, succeed into its place by a circular motion.

3. In the same way, I also say it involves a contradiction for any "atoms" to exist **which are conceived as extended and yet simultaneously indivisible**. For although God could have made them such that they could not be divided by any creature, we certainly cannot understand that He could deprive Himself of the faculty of dividing them. Nor is your comparison valid regarding things that have been done and cannot be "undone" <note>original: <term>infecta</term></note>. For we do not take it as a sign of powerlessness that someone cannot do what we do not understand to be possible; rather, we only say someone cannot do something among those things which we perceive distinctly as possible. But we certainly perceive it to be possible for an atom to be divided, seeing as we suppose it to be extended; and therefore, if we were to judge that it cannot be divided by God,

<meta>This page continues Descartes' argument that the material world is "indefinite" in extent and divisibility, distinguishing it from the "infinite" nature of God. He responds to Henry More's critiques regarding God's power and the nature of space.</meta>

...otherwise, we would be judging that God cannot do something which we nevertheless perceive to be possible. We do not perceive it as possible, however, for what has been done to be undone <note>original: *factum est fit infectum*</note>; on the contrary, we perceive this to be plainly impossible. Therefore, it is no defect of power in God that he does not do it. As for the divisibility of matter, the reasoning is not the same. For even if I cannot count all the parts into which it can be divided, and therefore call their number "indefinite," I still cannot affirm that their division is never completed by God. This is because I know that God can do more than I can encompass in my thought. Indeed, I conceded in Article 34 <note>referring to *Principles of Philosophy*, Part 2</note> that this indefinite division of certain parts of matter actually occurs.

4. It is not out of false modesty, but out of what I judge to be necessary caution, that I call certain things "indefinite" rather than "infinite." For God alone is the being whom I understand, in a positive sense, to be infinite. Regarding other things—such as the extension of the world, the number of parts into which matter is divisible, and similar things—I profess not to know whether they are *simply infinite or not*. I only know that I recognize no end in them, and therefore, from my perspective, I say they are "indefinite."

And although our mind is not the measure of things or of truth, it certainly ought to be the measure of what we affirm or deny. For what is more absurd or thoughtless than wanting to pass judgment on things that we confess our minds cannot reach or perceive?

I am surprised, however, that you not only seem to want to do this when you say, *"if the extension is only infinite to us, it will actually be finite,"* etc.; but that you also imagine a certain "divine extension" which reaches further than the extension of bodies. You thus *suppose that God has parts outside of parts <note>original: <term>partes habere extra partes</term>; a philosophical phrase describing how physical objects occupy space by having distinct parts in distinct locations</note>, and is divisible, and you attribute the entire essence of a physical thing to him.*

Lest any doubt remain here: when I say that the extension of matter is indefinite, I think this is sufficient to prevent anyone from imagining a place outside of it into which the particles of my "vortices" <note>original: <term>vortices</term>; Descartes' theory that planets and matter are moved by circular whirlpools of subtle matter</note> could escape. *For wherever that place may be conceived, there—according to my opinion—some matter already exists.* By saying it is indefinitely extended, I am saying it extends further than anything a human can conceive.

But I nevertheless believe *there is a vast difference between the magnitude of that physical extension* and the magnitude of the divine—I will not say "extension," since properly speaking it has none—but substance or essence. Therefore, I call the divine magnitude simply "infinite," while I call the other "indefinite."

Furthermore, I do not accept what you kindly grant me—namely, that my other opinions could remain valid even if what I wrote about the extension of matter were refuted. *For this is one of the principal, and in my judgment, most certain foundations of my Physics.* I profess that no reasons satisfy me in Physics unless they involve that necessity which you call "logical or contradictory" <note>meaning something is true because its opposite would be a logical contradiction</note>; provided you except only those things which can be known through experience alone, such as the fact that there is only one Sun or one Moon around this Earth, and similar things. Since you do not disagree with my views in other matters, I hope you will easily agree to these as well, if only you consider it a prejudice that many people think an extended being—in which there is nothing to move the senses—is not a true physical substance, but merely a vacuum...

...merely a vacuum; and that no body exists unless it is perceptible to the senses, and no substance exists unless it can be imagined, and is therefore extended.

5. But there is no prejudice to which we have all become more accustomed than the one that has persuaded us since our early years that brute animals think. Indeed, no reason moved us to believe this except that, seeing most of an animal's limbs do not differ much from our own in external shape and movements, and believing there is only a single principle for these movements in us—namely the soul <note>original: *anima*</note>, which both moves the body and thinks—we did not doubt that some such soul could be found in them.

After I noticed, however, that two different principles of our movements must be distinguished—one that is purely mechanical and corporeal, which depends solely on the force of the animal spirits <note>original: *spirituum* – in 17th-century physiology, these were refined fluids in the blood thought to control movement</note> and the structure of the limbs, and can be called the "corporeal soul"; and another that is incorporeal—namely the mind, or that soul which you define as a thinking substance—I searched more diligently to see whether the movements of animals arise from these two principles, or from only one. Since I clearly perceived that all movements could arise from the one that is corporeal and mechanical alone, I held it as certain and demonstrated that it can in no way be proven by us that there is any thinking soul in brute animals. Nor do I pause over the cunning and cleverness of dogs and foxes, nor anything else done by animals for the sake of food, sex, or fear. *For I profess that I can very easily explain all those things as having proceeded solely from the configuration of their limbs.*

Although I hold it as demonstrated that it cannot be proven that there is any thought in animals, I do not therefore think it can be demonstrated that there is none, because the human mind does not penetrate their hearts. But by examining what is most probable in this matter, I see no reason to argue for animal thought except for this one: that *since they have eyes, ears, a tongue, and other sensory organs like us, it is likely they feel as we do*; and because thought is included in our way of feeling, a similar thought must be attributed to them. This reasoning, being very obvious, has occupied the minds of all people from their earliest age. However, there are many other much stronger reasons—though not so obvious to everyone—which persuade us of the opposite. Among these, it holds its place *that it is not as probable that all worms, gnats, caterpillars, and other animals are endowed with an immortal soul as it is that they move like machines.*

First, because it is certain that in the bodies of animals, as also in ours, there are bones, nerves, muscles, blood, animal spirits, and other organs so arranged that, by themselves and without any thought, they can trigger all the movements we observe in animals. This is evident in convulsions, when, against the mind's will, the machinery of the body often moves itself more violently and in more diverse ways than it is accustomed to move with the help of the will.

Next, because it seems consistent with reason—since art is an imitator of nature, and humans can build various automata <note>original: *automata* – self-moving mechanical devices</note> in which there is movement without any thought—that Nature should also produce its own automata, far more excellent than those made by art, namely all the brute animals; especially since we recognize no reason why, where there is such a configuration of limbs as we see in animals, thought must also be present; and

...therefore, it is more worthy of admiration that a mind is found in every human body than that none exists in any brute animals.

But of all the reasons that persuade us that beasts are devoid of thought, the chief one in my judgment is this: although among animals some are more perfect than others of the same species—just as among men, as can be seen in horses and dogs, some of whom learn what they are taught much more successfully than others—and although all of them very easily signal their natural impulses to us, such as anger, fear, hunger, and the like, by voice or other bodily movements; nevertheless, it has never yet been observed that any brute animal reached such a level of perfection that it used true speech. That is, that it *indicated anything, whether by voice or signs, which could be referred to thought alone, and not to a natural impulse.* <note>Descartes argues that while animals communicate emotions or needs, they do not use language to discuss abstract ideas.</note> For this speech is the only certain sign of a thought hidden in a body, and all men use it—even the *most stupid and insane*, and those deprived of tongue and vocal organs—*but no brute animal does*; and therefore, one may take this as the true difference between men and beasts.

I omit here, for the sake of brevity, the remaining reasons for denying thought to beasts. I would, however, like it to be noted that I am speaking of thought <note>original: *cogitatio*</note>, not of life or sensation. For I deny life to no animal, since I establish that it consists solely in the heat of the heart; nor do I deny sensation, insofar as it depends on a bodily organ. Thus, my opinion is not so much cruel to beasts as it is favorable to men who are not addicted to the superstition of the Pythagoreans <note>The followers of Pythagoras believed in the transmigration of souls between humans and animals, and therefore practiced vegetarianism.</note>, for it absolves them from the suspicion of crime whenever they eat or kill animals.

I have perhaps written all these things at greater length than your sharp intelligence required; but I wanted to testify in this way that the objections of very few people have been as welcome to me as yours, and that your kindness and sincerity have greatly indebted me to you.

Egmond, near Alkmaar,
*February 5, 1649.*

<header>The Second Letter of Henry More to René Descartes.</header>

...I take your most rich letters as the surest proof of that favor. However, so that you do not regret showing such kindness to me—as if it were bestowed upon a slave—and so that my zeal and love for you do not seem cheap, as if they came from a low and groveling mind, I will openly and clearly state, as becomes a free man, the ways in which your answers satisfied me. Yet, to avoid causing too much trouble for you or myself, I will set aside long, elaborate compositions of speech and condense the whole matter into certain brief *Instances*, or at least short notes, regarding each individual point of your responses.

## Regarding the Response to the First Difficulty

### Instance I.
### *To be defined by its relationship to our senses, etc.*

Here it may be replied: Since the root and essence of all things lies buried in eternal darkness, everything must necessarily be defined by some relationship. This relationship can be called a "property" in substances, since it is not the substance itself. I freely acknowledge that some properties are more primary than others, but I only meant to say that it is better to define a thing by any adequate property than by a so-called "form" that is broader than the thing being defined. Furthermore, when you yourself define a "body" as an *extended thing*, I also note that this extension consists in a certain relationship of parts to one another, insofar as they are spread out beyond each other. It is clear that this relationship is not an absolute thing.

### II.
### *Even if no human beings existed.*

If all mortals were to close their eyes at once, the sun would still not lose its capacity to be seen as soon as they opened their eyes again; just as an axe would not lose its capacity to cut as soon as wood or stones were placed before it.

### III.
### *Much smaller than the particles of our nerves.*

I believe, however, that God the Creator <note>original: *Deum artificem*</note> could adapt nerves small enough for those tiny particles of matter, and therefore the "sensibility" (the ability to be sensed) of matter remains intact even when it is broken down in this way. Furthermore, these particles can stop moving and cluster together, and in this way they become sensible once again to *our* nerves. This is in no way true regarding an incorporeal (immaterial) substance.

### IV.
### *Although it may not be soft to the senses, etc.*

It is certain that it would be hard or soft to our sensory nerves—or at least to the kind of nerves that God could create if He wished, as I just mentioned. This is sufficient for a definition, even if God were never going to create such nerves. It is like how the parts of the earth toward the center are visible in themselves, even if they are never to be pulled out into the light of the sun, and no one will ever go down there with a torch or a lamp.

### V.

# V.

->*It is only a property of the fourth kind, like “risibility” is in a human.*<-
<note>original: "proprium quarto modo." In Scholastic logic, a "property of the fourth kind" is a characteristic that belongs to all members of a species, only that species, and at all times (e.g., the ability to laugh in humans).</note>

If reason were also shared by other animals, a human would be more correctly defined as a "laughing animal" <note>original: "animal risibile"</note> than a "rational animal." *Furthermore, no one has yet demonstrated that tangibility or impenetrability are properties essential to extended substance, although anyone would rightly acknowledge them to be properties of a body.* Indeed, I can clearly conceive of an extended substance that has no tangibility or impenetrability in any way. Therefore, tangibility or impenetrability does not immediately follow from "extended substance" simply because it is extended.

# VI.

->*But I deny true extension, etc.*<-

By "true extension," you mean that which is accompanied by tangibility and impenetrability. I myself also deny that this kind of extension is found in God, or in a bare mind, or in an Angel. However, meanwhile *I assert that there is another extension that is equally true, although not as common or well-worn in the Schools* <note>The "Schools" refers to the traditional university curriculum based on Scholasticism and Aristotle.</note>. This extension, in Angels and the human mind, has boundaries and even a shape, but these are variable according to the command of the Angel or the mind. Our minds (or souls) and Angels can contract themselves and expand again to certain limits while their substance remains exactly the same.

# VII.

->*Nothing is intelligible unless it is also imaginable, etc.*<-

Indeed, I am somewhat more inclined toward that opinion of Aristotle: *that it is not possible to think without mental images.* <note>original Greek: "ὅτι ἄνευ τῶν φαντασμάτων οὐκ ἔστι νοῆσαι" (hoti aneu tōn phantasmatōn ouk esti noēsai)</note> But here, let everyone test the powers of their own mind.

---

# Regarding the Response to the second Difficulty

## Instance I.

->*To transfer some parts into the place of others by the imagination.*<-

My own imagination cannot do this; nor can it even conceive that if they were transferred, *some parts of empty space would not absorb others, and completely coincide and penetrate each other.*

## II.

->*Nor is it doubted by great men, Epicurus, Democritus, etc.*<-

I have no doubt that you are perfectly right to disagree, since (in my opinion) you are far greater and much more majestic than not only those men, but all interpreters of Nature.

## III.

->*But that there is some substance in every space, etc.*<-

*I certainly conceded that for the sake of peace.* But it is not clearly established to me. For if God were to annihilate this entire universe, and much later create another from nothing, *that "Intermundium" <note>original: "Intermundium" – a term used to describe the space between worlds or the void.</note>, or the absence of the world, would have its own duration which so many days, years, or centuries would have measured.* Thus, there is a duration belonging to something that does not exist, and duration is a kind of extension. And therefore the amplitude of "Nothingness"—namely, of a Vacuum—can be measured by yards or paces, just as something non-existent in its own...

...the duration of non-existence is measured by hours, days, and months. But I concede—though not yet forced by the weight of your argument—that some substance exists in all space. However, it does not follow that this substance is bodily, since divine extension or presence can be the subject of measurability. For example, I assert that the divine presence or extension occupies one or two fathoms <note>original: "orgyam" — an ancient unit of length roughly equal to six feet</note> in this or that vacuum; yet it does not follow at all that God is bodily, as is clear from what was said above in Objection 5. But this matter must be discussed elsewhere.

### IV.

->*I say it involves a contradiction for such extension, etc.*<-

But here I would gladly ask whether it is necessary that extension must either be as you conceive it in a body, or not exist at all. Then, since you have conceded that other things besides bodies are extended in their own way, does not that "analogical extension," as you call it, take the place of bodily extension, and thus blunt that contradictory force? This is especially true since this analogical extension comes so close to extension properly so-called that it is measurable and occupies a certain number of feet or ells <note>original: "ulnarum" — a traditional unit of measurement, usually about 45 inches</note>.

### V.

->*That no motion is given, except in some way circular.*<-

I concede that this follows necessarily—by physical necessity, at least—assuming only that all things are full of bodies and that no other extension exceeds the entire extension of the world. On this point I am fairly certain; but I confess I have not yet fully grasped this "unassailable force" of contradiction you mention.

## To the Response concerning the third Difficulty.

->*Which things are conceived as extended and at the same time indivisible.*<-

Since you have explained your meaning in this way, there is no controversy between us.

## To the Response concerning the fourth Difficulty

### Objection I.

->*Whether they are simply infinite or not, I profess that I do not know.*<-

Yet it cannot be hidden from you that they are either simply infinite or actually finite, even if you cannot so easily determine which of these they are. Moreover, the fact that your "vortices" <note>Descartes' theory that planets are carried by massive whirlpools of celestial matter</note> do not break apart and fall to pieces seems a clear sign that the world is actually infinite. Meanwhile, I freely profess that although I can boldly agree with this axiom—*the world is finite, or not finite (or, what is the same thing here, infinite)*—I cannot fully grasp the infinity of any thing in my mind. 

Instead, what happens to my imagination here is what Julius Scaliger <note>A famous 16th-century Italian scholar and physician</note> writes somewhere about the expansion and contraction of Angels: namely, that they cannot extend themselves into infinity, nor can they squeeze themselves into the "unity" <note>original Greek: ἑνότητα (henoteta) — oneness or unity</note> of a single point. Now, if someone acknowledges God as "positively infinite" (that is, existing everywhere), which you rightly do, I do not see why—if allowed free use of reason—he would hesitate to also admit that God is nowhere idle. He would admit this with the same right and the same ease as he does for this part of the world where we live, or as far as our eyes and our minds...

...goes on to have produced matter everywhere. But I was going to treat this more at length than I planned; I suppress this impulse, lest I be more troublesome to you.

### II.

*When you say, "if it is infinite only in relation to us, it will in reality be finite."* <note>original: "Cùm ais, si tantùm quoad nos sit infinita, revera erit finita."</note>

I say, and I add moreover, that the consequence is most manifest, because the word (*only*) plainly excludes all infinity from a thing that is said to be infinite only in relation to us; and therefore extension will in reality be finite. My mind, however, touches here upon those things about which I pronounce judgment, since it is most clearly evident to me that the world is either finite or infinite, as I suggested a little earlier.

### III.

*And thus to suppose God to have parts outside of parts, and to be divisible, and to attribute to Him every essence of a bodily thing.* <note>original: "Atque ità supponere Deum habere partes extra partes, & esse divisibilem, omnémque prorsus rei corporeæ essentiam illi tribuere."</note>

I attribute no such essence. For I deny that extension belongs to a body insofar as it is a body, but insofar as it is a being, or at least a substance. Furthermore, since God (as far as the human mind can grasp God) is whole everywhere, and His entire essence is present in all places or spaces and in every point of those spaces, it does not follow that He would have "parts outside of parts," <term>parts outside of parts: a philosophical phrase (Latin: *partes extra partes*) meaning that the parts of an object are spatially distinct from one another, like bricks in a wall</term> or, consequently, that He is divisible—even though He occupies all places tightly and closely, leaving no gaps. From this, I recognize the divine presence (or "amplitude," as you call it) as measurable, but God Himself as in no way divisible.

That God occupies every single point of the world is admitted by everyone, from the unlearned <term>unlearned: original "idiotæ," referring to common people or those without formal philosophical training</term> to the philosophers; and I clearly and distinctly perceive and embrace this in my mind. Now indeed, the divine essence is the same inside and outside the world. Thus, if we imagine the world to be enclosed by the visible starry sky, the center of the divine essence and His total presence would be repeated outside the starry sky in the same way we clearly conceive it to be repeated and reiterated inside. It is appropriate that this repetition of the divine center, which occupies the world, should expand infinite spaces with itself further beyond the visible sky. Unless your "indefinite matter" accompanies this expansion, your theory of vortices <note>original: "vortices" — Descartes' theory that planets were carried by whirlpool-like movements of matter</note> will be finished. But so that these things may seem more gentle, let us test our agreement regarding the successive duration of God.

God is eternal—that is, the divine life encompasses all the evolutions of ages and the reasons of things (past, future, and present) at once. Yet this eternal life also sits within and, as it were, "rides" <note>original: "inequitat" — literally to ride upon, suggesting mastery or presence over time</note> upon every individual moment of time; so that we may rightly and truly say that God, relying on His eternity, exists through so many days, months, or hours. For example, if we suppose the world was created a hundred years ago, has not that whole and all-embracing eternity of God endured through successive hours, days, months, and years (say, one hundred) up to this very day? But truly, God is no different since the creation of the world than He was before the creation of the world.

Therefore, it is manifest that, besides infinite eternity, a succession of duration also applies to God. If we admit this, why should we not also attribute to Him an extension filling infinite spaces, just as we attribute to Him an infinite succession of duration?

Indeed, whenever I think more deeply and searchingly with myself about these matters, those...

I am of the opinion that both types of extension, of space as well as time, can apply to non-beings as well as beings. <note>original: "sum in sententia, quòd utraque extensio, tam spatii quàm temporis, Non-entibus juxtà atque Entibus competere possit"</note> I suspect it may equally be a result of prejudice—since all those things we handle and perceive with our senses, being thick and corporeal, are always extended—that we immediately conclude all extended things are corporeal. On the other hand, no such sensory prejudice forces us to think that some things which are not corporeal are extended.

Now, as to why extension might apply to a non-being, <note>In this context, "non-being" (Latin: *non-ens*) refers to things like a vacuum or empty space, which some philosophers argued had no "real" existence but still occupied space.</note> we gather this from the fact that *to be extended* implies nothing other than *parts existing outside of parts*. <term>parts existing outside of parts: (Latin: *partes extra partes*) A philosophical definition of extension, meaning that one part of a thing occupies a different location than another part.</term> But "part" and "whole," "subject" and "attribute," "cause" and "effect," "opposites" and "relatives," "contradictories" and "privations"—all such universal categories are logical notions, and we apply them to non-beings just as much as to beings. Therefore, it does not follow that whatever we conceive of as having "parts outside of parts" must be conceived of as a real, physical being.

But how often do human minds here struggle with their own shadows, or, like playful puppies, play with their own tails? For such battles and games are surely set up for themselves by our minds whenever they fail to notice that the logical reasons and modes by which they consider external things are merely their own modes of thinking. Instead, thinking these modes are something in the things themselves distinct from the mind, the mind chases its own tail, so to speak, playing until it is exhausted and miserably entangled. But I have blurted out more here than I intended; I hurry on to the rest.

### IV.

->*For wherever that place may be conceived, there is some matter.*<- <note>original: "Ubicumque enim locus ille concipiatur, ibi aliqua materia est."</note>

Truly, you are a cautious man here, and elegantly modest; yet you finally admit the world is infinite, if Aristotle rightly defined the infinite in his *Physics*, book 3, as "that which always has something outside it." <note>original Greek: ᾧ ἀεί τι ἔξω ἐστίν</note> There is nothing now that should cause us to doubt further.

### V.

->*But nevertheless, I think there is a very great difference between the amplitude of that bodily extension, etc.*<- <note>original: "Sed nihilominus existimo maximam esse differentiam inter amplitudinem istius corporeæ extensionis, &c."</note>

I also think there is a massive difference between divine amplitude <note>The "vastness" or "extension" of God.</note> and corporeal extension. First, because the former cannot be perceived by the senses, while the latter can. Second, because the former is uncreated and independent, while the latter is dependent and created. Furthermore, the former is penetrable, pervading through all things, while the latter is thick and impenetrable. Finally, the former arises from the ubiquity of a total and entire essence being repeated everywhere, while the latter arises from the external but immediate application and side-by-side placement of parts. Thus, no one—unless they are completely leaden-headed <note>original: "plumbeus," meaning dull-witted or dense.</note> and remarkably slow—could suspect,

> *That we are entering upon the unholy elements of reason, and starting*
> *on a path of sin,* (as the poet says.) <note>original: "Impia nos rationis inire elementa, viámque / Indogredi sceleris." A quote from the Roman poet Lucretius, warning against thinking that philosophy leads to impiety.</note>

This is especially true since there are theologians—who are perhaps otherwise quite scrupulous—who nevertheless acknowledge that God, if He had wished, could have created the world from eternity. And yet it seems just as "absurd" to attribute infinite duration to the world as it does to attribute infinite size.

### VI.

->*“For it is one of the chief, and in my judgment most certain, foundations of my Physics.”*<-
<note>original: "Unum enim est ex præcipuis, meóque judicio certissimis, Physicæ meæ fundamentis."</note>

I fully understand that it is an absolutely necessary foundation for your Physics that matter is at least indefinitely extended and that there is no vacuum. I certainly do not doubt that this is true. However, I am uncertain whether you have followed the correct line of reasoning to prove it. The starting point of your demonstration is that *everything extended is real and corporeal*; I confess this is not yet clear to me, for the reasons I gave above. <note>More argued on the previous page that "extension" (occupying space) could also apply to God or to space itself, not just to physical matter.</note>

In fact, to speak frankly about a thought that has just come to mind: if neither empty space (as your demonstration requires) nor God is extended at all, then your philosophy does not even need an indefinitely large amount of matter; *a certain and finite number of miles* <note>original: "stadiorum," referring to stadia, an ancient unit of distance</note> would suffice. In a finite world, the "sides" would have nowhere to move back to, and the central <term>vortices</term> <note>Descartes believed the planets were carried around the sun by "vortices" or whirlpools of invisible matter.</note> could not gape open, since there would be no intermediate space to be stretched out, and "non-being" cannot take on new dimensions.

Nevertheless, a natural impulse drives me to another conclusion: namely, a faith in divine fecundity. Since God is never idle, He has produced matter everywhere, in all places, skipping over no intervals, however narrow.

Because I admit these points so easily, your philosophy will not collapse in my estimation for lack of that particular foundation. I clearly see that the truth of your Physics does not reveal itself so much in one specific point or another, but rather shines out from the entire thread and texture of the whole work, as you yourself very rightly point out in Part 4, article 225. If anyone views the entire face of your philosophy at once, it is so harmonious and consistent—both with itself and with the observed phenomena of nature—that they might rightly imagine they have seen Nature herself, the craftswoman, shining out from this polished mirror.

# In Response to the Final Difficulty

## Point I.

->*“But there is no prejudice to which we have all become more accustomed, etc.”*<-
<note>original: "Sed nulli præjudicio magis omnes assuevimus, &c."</note>

This is more than clear to me regarding myself, for I feel that I cannot in any way free myself from the snares of this prejudice. <note>The "prejudice" mentioned here is the human tendency to believe that animals have feelings and souls similar to humans.</note>

## II.

->*“For I profess that I can very easily explain all those things as having*<-
->*proceeded from the configuration of the limbs alone.”*<-
<note>original: "Profiteor enim me posse perfacilè illa omnia ut à sola membrorum conformatione profecta explicare." Here, Descartes claims he can explain all animal behavior as pure mechanics without needing a soul.</note>

What a happy and pleasant task that would be! If you accomplish this—and I believe that, as far as human genius is capable, you will do so in the fifth or sixth parts of your Physics—it will be a great feat. I hear those parts are almost finished and perfected by you now; I expect them so eagerly and ask so passionately that they see the light of day as soon as possible (or rather, that we may see the further light of nature within them).

But back to the matter: if you accomplish this, I say, I will acknowledge that you have demonstrated that no one can prove there is a soul in animals. But in the meantime, as you yourself suggest, you have not yet demonstrated that there is *no* soul in animals, nor can you demonstrate it in any way.

### III.
#### *“Except for this one [reason], that since they have eyes, ears, etc.”*
<note>original: "Præter hanc unam, quòd cùm habeant oculos, aures, &c." More is quoting Descartes’ argument that physical organs do not prove the presence of a soul.</note>

The strongest argument, in my judgment, is that animals protect themselves and look ahead with such cleverness. If I had the time, I could demonstrate this with stories that are as true as they are remarkable. However, I believe you have encountered similar histories yourself, and my own accounts are not found in any published books.

### IV.
#### *“That it is not so probable that all worms, gnats, caterpillars, etc. [possess immortal souls].”*
<note>original: "Quòd non sit tàm probabile omnes vermes, culices, erucas, &c." Descartes argued it was unlikely that every tiny insect possessed a soul like a human does.</note>

This would be true, unless perhaps we imagine that such souls are like the sand or dust of the **Life of the World** <note>original: "Mundi Vitæ." More refers to the Neoplatonic concept of the *Anima Mundi* or World-Soul.</note> (as *Ficino* <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), an influential Italian philosopher who revived Neoplatonism.</note> calls it). We might imagine that nearly infinite swarms of souls from that "storehouse" are always gliding, by a certain fatal impulse, into matter that has been prepared for them. But I admit that such things are easier to say than to prove.

### V.
#### *“That [an animal] might indicate something by voice or gestures, etc.”*
<note>original: "Ut aliquid voce vel nutibus indicaret, &c." Descartes claimed animals do not use signs to express thought.</note>

Do not dogs "nod" with their tails, just as we do with our heads? Do they not frequently beg for food at the table with short barks? Indeed, they sometimes touch their master's elbow with a paw as reverently as they can, using this gentle sign to remind him of their presence when he seems to have forgotten them.

### VI.
#### *“Even those who are most stupid and mindless... but no brute animal [speaks], etc.”*
<note>original: "Quàm maximè stupidi ac mente capti, &c. non autem ullum brutum, &c." Descartes argued that even the most impaired human can use language, while the most "perfect" animal cannot.</note>

Neither do any infants speak for at least many months, even though they cry, laugh, and get angry. Yet I do not think you doubt that infants are animated and possess a thinking soul.

These are the responses, Illustrious Sir, which I felt I should offer to your distinguished answers. I cannot predict whether they will be as welcome to you as my recent objections.

Your kindness, which I have seen directed toward these thoughts, and my long-standing familiarity with your writings, have made me bolder. I fear I may have been too long-winded and troublesome.

In truth, I had almost forgotten my primary purpose. It was not to engage in endless back-and-forth arguments with you, but rather to take this opportunity to calmly experience the judgment of such a great man on the philosophical matters that arise—and especially to hear your own interpretation whenever a difficulty emerges while reading your books. If you would graciously and willingly grant me this favor, I will be greatly indebted to you.

And indeed, since I am certain you will gladly share your extraordinary skill and expertise with me, I will now test it with a few specific questions.

First, I ask: could God have ordained, or could it have happened in any other way, that the world was **finite**—that is, limited by a certain fixed number of miles? It seems to be a significant argument that the world *can* be finite, given that almost everyone else thinks it is impossible for it to be infinite.

Secondly, if someone were sitting near the edge of this world, I ask: could he thrust a sword through the walls of the world right up to the hilt, so that the whole...

...almost as if a sword were sticking out beyond the world’s walls. For while it seems easy to imagine there is nothing outside the world to resist it, it seems impossible, from that perspective, that there is no *extension* outside the world to receive it.

**Thirdly** (regarding Article 29, Part 2): If a body **A B** is transferred from a body **C D**, I ask how it is established that the translation is reciprocal. Let us imagine that **C D** is a tower, and **A B** is a west wind blowing past the sides of the tower. The tower **C D** either remains at rest, or at least does not move away from the wind **A B**. If it did move away, or—as you say—was transferred by motion, it would surely be moving toward the west. But it is not carried toward the west, since both the Earth and the wind are carried toward the east. Therefore, it seems to be at rest with respect to the wind, since it receives no motion from it. Yet you say that the translation (which is indeed the translation of motion) is reciprocal between the tower and the wind. Thus, the tower would be both moving and at rest with respect to the same wind, which is very close to a contradiction. A clear sign of this is when someone walks away from me while I am sitting—say, for a thousand paces—they might turn red or become tired, whereas I, sitting still, experience neither redness nor fatigue. This shows that they alone were in motion, and I was resting during that time. Therefore, I undergo only a <term>notional</term> <note>original: "notionalem" — existing only in the mind or as a concept, rather than as a physical reality.</note> change of distance regarding that motion, but no real and physical motion.

**Fourthly**, Article 149, Part 3: *And so it will also cause the Earth to rotate around its own axis, etc.* How will the Moon cause the Earth to complete its rotations in a single day, when the Moon itself takes nearly 30 days to complete its own cycles? I do not believe the things written in Article 151 address this question.

**Fifthly**, concerning those twisted particles which you call **striated** <note>original: "striatas" — grooved or fluted. Descartes used these screw-shaped particles to explain magnetism.</note>: How could they be twisted in such a way without breaking into infinite fragments and atoms? What softness or tenacity can we imagine in that primary matter, which is supposedly uniform and the same everywhere? From what did those particles first soften, and how did they then become hard?

**Sixthly**, Article 189, Part 4: *the soul, or mind, is intimately joined to the brain*. I would very gladly hear your opinion on the union of the soul with the body: Is it joined to the whole body, or to the brain alone, or is it confined solely within the <term>pineal gland</term> <note>original: "conarium"</note> as if in some tiny prison? For I acknowledge, having been taught by you, that this gland is the common seat of the senses and the **stronghold** <note>original: "ἀκρόπολιν" (akropolin)</note> of the soul. Yet I doubt whether the soul does not pervade the entire body. Furthermore, I ask you, since the soul has no particles that are branched or hooked, how is it so tightly united with the body? And I ask further: is there not something at work in nature for which no mechanical explanation can be given? That **free will** <note>original: "αὐteξousion" (autexousion) — the power of self-determination.</note> of which we are conscious within ourselves—how does it arise? And what is the reason for our soul’s command over the **animal spirits** <note>original: "spiritus animales" — in early modern physiology, these were subtle fluids that carried signals between the brain and the muscles.</note>, by which it can send them to any part of the body? How do the spirits of witches, which they call "familiars," adapt and constrain matter so aptly to themselves that they show themselves as visible and tangible to those wretched old women? That this happens was confessed to me not only by old women, but by many young witches, quite of their own accord and without any force. Moreover, do we not experience this very thing in some way in our own souls, when we can stir or stop, project or withdraw our animal spirits at our own whim? I ask, therefore, whether it would be unbecoming for a philosopher to acknowledge some incorporeal substance in the universe, which...

### The Second Letter of Henry More to René Descartes.

...can it [the soul] impress all, or at least most, corporeal properties upon some body, just as bodies themselves do to each other? I mean properties such as motion, shape, and the arrangement of parts. Indeed, since the existence of motion is well-established, we should immediately add those things that follow from motion: such as dividing, joining, scattering, binding, and shaping particles—arranging shaped particles, rotating those that are arranged, moving them in any way, or holding those together that are rotating. From these, light, colors, and the rest of the objects of the senses must necessarily arise, according to your excellent philosophy.

Furthermore, since nothing—whether corporeal or incorporeal—can act upon another thing except through the application of its essence, it must be concluded that whether it is an Angel, a Demon, a soul, or God who acts upon matter in these ways, the essence of each must, as it were, "ride upon" <note>original: "inequitet"</note> those parts of matter on which it acts, or upon others that act on these by the transmission of motion. Indeed, the essence must sometimes be present to the whole of the matter it governs and modifies, as is evident in the case of Spirits <note>original: "Geniis" — here referring to spiritual beings like angels or demons.</note>, whether good or evil, who have revealed themselves to human eyes. Otherwise, how could they constrain matter and hold it in this or that shape?

Finally, since an incorporeal substance has such an astounding power that through the mere application of itself—without ropes or hooks, without slings or wedges—it can constrain, unfold, divide, throw, and simultaneously hold matter, does it not seem likely that it could contract into itself (since no impenetrability stands in the way) and spread itself out again, and so forth?

I ask these things of you, most learned sir, as much as your leisure permits, that you might deign to explain them; for I know you have searched out the most internal and external mysteries of Nature and can interpret them skillfully.

**Seventh**, I ask about the **ethereal globules**: If God had created the world from eternity, would these globules not have been crushed and broken into indefinitely fine parts many years ago by mutual collisions or friction? Would they not have taken on the appearance of the "first element" long ago, so that the entire world would have turned into one immense flame many centuries ago?

**Eighth**, regarding your **water particles**—which are long, smooth, and flexible—do they have pores? This certainly does not seem probable to me, since they are simple bodies and primary particles not composed of any other particles, but are fragments struck out from whole and primary matter, and therefore entirely homogeneous. Hence, I doubt how they could be bent without the <term>penetration of dimensions</term> <note>original: "penetratione dimensionum" — a philosophical concept where two bodies or parts of a body occupy the same space simultaneously. More is arguing that for a solid, poreless particle to bend, its inner parts would have to overlap or "penetrate" each other.</note>. For let us suppose they are sometimes bent into the shape of a ring; the concave surface will be smaller than the convex surface, and so on. You understand the point well; there is no reason for me to dwell on it here.

Yet even if you were to argue that they have pores (which I do not think you will ever do), it would not remove the difficulty. This is because the question would then be raised about the edges or sides of the pores: for something without pores must necessarily be bent.

And this difficulty applies not only to your oblong particles but also to those branch-like ones, and almost all others that must be bent without being broken.

**Ninth and finally**: whether matter—whether we imagine it to be eternal or created only yesterday—if left freely to itself and receiving no impulse from elsewhere, would move or remain at rest. Furthermore, whether rest is a <term>privative</term> <note>original: "privativus" — a state defined by the absence of something; in this context, whether rest is merely the absence of motion or a positive state of its own.</note> mode of the body...

...whether it is privative or actually positive. And whether you prefer it to be positive or privative, it is not clear how either is established. Finally, I ask whether any thing can naturally and of itself possess any quality <note>original: "affectionem" — here meaning a characteristic or property</note> of which it can be entirely deprived, or which it can adopt from elsewhere.

So far, I have played—or should I say labored?—around the general foundations of your illustrious Physics. I intend to proceed hereafter to more specific matters, if your kindness and courtesy invite or at least permit me to do so. You will surely bear with me more patiently, since we are dealing here with first principles, if I have examined everything with superstitious care, moving forward slowly and at a snail’s pace, feeling my way as if by touch and handling each point with great curiosity. For I see that the human mind is so constructed that it discerns what follows a premise far more easily than it discerns what is primarily true in nature. Our common condition is not much different from that of Archimedes: *"Give me a place to stand, and I will move the earth."* <note>original Greek: "δὸς ποῦ στῶ, καὶ κινήσω τὴν γῆν"</note> We are much more concerned with finding where to first plant our foot than we are with how to proceed further once we have found it.

As for those wondrous structures you have built from those general principles, although at first glance they seemed so sublime and remote from our view that everything appeared shrouded in clouds and darkness, time has diminished the difficulties. Those obscurities have gradually vanished, so that now very few remain in sight compared to what was there before.

However, I felt it necessary to confess this so that you do not expect me to create trouble for you forever. Instead, I hope you will write back to me more willingly and receive these inquiries of mine with the same kindness with which you received the first objections I sent. If you do this (most illustrious Descartes), you will make me more indebted to you than words can say.

Cambridge, from Christ's College,
March 5, 1649. <note>original: "3. Nonarum Martii" — using the Roman calendar</note>

->*A most devoted admirer*<-
->*of your humanity and wisdom,*<-

## To the most Illustrious and Learned Man,
# HENRY MORE,
## FROM RENÉ DESCARTES.

Most illustrious sir, I received your most welcome letter, dated March 5th, at a time when I am distracted by so many other occupations that I am forced either to write back in great haste this very hour or to delay my response for many weeks. But the side that persuades me to haste shall win; for I would rather appear less skillful than less dutiful.

->Regarding the first points of insistence.<-

Regarding your point that some properties are prior to others, etc.: "Sensibility" <note>The capacity of an object to be perceived by the senses.</note> seems to me to be nothing in the sensible thing itself except an "extrinsic denomination" <note>original: "denominatio extrinseca" — a Scholastic term for a description based on a thing's relationship to something else (like being "seen") rather than its own internal nature.</note>. Nor is it...

<meta>This page continues René Descartes's point-by-point response to Henry More’s second letter. Descartes is defending his view that "extension" (taking up space) is the fundamental essence of matter, whereas Henry More argues that spirits and God also have a type of extension.</meta>

<language>Latin</language>
<page-type>text</page-type>
<page-num>82</page-num>
<header>René Descartes’s Response to the Second Letter of Henry More.</header>

...equated. For if we refer to our senses, this does not fit the tiniest particles of matter. If we refer to other imaginary senses—such as those you believe God could create—perhaps they would also apply to Angels and Souls. I do not find it any easier to understand sensory nerves so subtle that they can be moved by the smallest particles of matter than I do some faculty by which our mind could immediately sense or perceive other minds. Although we easily comprehend the relationship of parts to one another in extension, I seem to perceive extension best even when I do not think of the relationship of parts at all. You ought to admit this even more than I do, because you conceive of extension in a way that applies to God, yet you admit no parts in Him.

*It has not yet been demonstrated that Tangibility or Impenetrability are proper characteristics <note>original: "affectiones" — properties or attributes</note> of extended substance.* If you conceive of extension through the relationship of parts to one another, you cannot seem to deny that every part touches its neighbors. This "tangibility" is a true and intrinsic property of the object, not merely the sensation we call "touch" <note>original: "tactûs"</note>.

It is also impossible to imagine one part of an extended thing penetrating another part of equal size without simultaneously understanding that the middle portion of that extension is removed or annihilated. Since something that is annihilated cannot "penetrate" anything else, I believe this proves that impenetrability belongs to the essence of extension <term>extension: the property of taking up space</term>, and not to any other kind of being.

*I assert that there is another extension that is equally true.* At last, then, we agree on the matter; the question remains about the name—whether this latter extension should be called "equally true." For my part, I understand no extension of substance in God, Angels, or our mind, but only an extension of power <note>original: "potentiae" — meaning the range of action or influence</note>. This means an Angel can exert his power now in a larger, now in a smaller part of corporeal substance. If no body existed, I would understand no space to which an Angel or God would be co-extended. I believe that anyone who attributes extension—which belongs only to power—to substance is under a prejudice, assuming that every substance, even God Himself, must be imaginable <term>imaginable: something that can be pictured in the mind as having shape, size, or location</term>.

### Regarding the second set of objections.

*Whether some parts of empty space might absorb others, etc.* Here I repeat: if they are absorbed, then the middle part of the space is removed and ceases to be; and what ceases to be does not penetrate another. Therefore, impenetrability must be admitted in all space.

*That "interworld" <note>original: "intermundium" — a term for a void or space between worlds</note> would have its own duration, etc.* I think it involves a contradiction for us to conceive of any duration occurring between the destruction of the previous world and the creation of a new one. For if we refer that duration to the succession of divine thoughts or something similar, it will be an error of the intellect, not a true perception of any real thing. I have already responded to what follows by noting that the extension attributed to incorporeal things belongs to power only, not to substance. Since this power is only a "mode" <term>mode: a specific state or way of being</term> in the thing to which it is applied, once the extended thing with which it coexists is removed, that power cannot be understood as being extended itself.

# Regarding the penultimate points.
<note>original: "Ad penultimas Instantias" — referring to More's second-to-last set of arguments</note>

*God is positively infinite, that is, existing everywhere, etc.* I do not admit this "everywhere." For you seem to place the infinity of God in the fact that He exists everywhere; I do not agree with this opinion. Rather, I think that God is everywhere by reason of His power, but by reason of His essence, He has absolutely no relation to place. Since in God power and essence are not distinguished, I think it is better in such matters to reason about our own minds or Angels—as being more commensurate with our perception—than about God. 

All the following difficulties seem to me to have arisen from a prejudice: we have become too accustomed to imagine all substances, even those we deny are physical bodies, as being extended <term>extended: taking up space or having physical dimensions</term>. We also tend to philosophize immoderately about beings of reason <note>original: "entibus rationis" — concepts that exist in the mind to help us categorize things, but do not have independent physical existence</note> by *attributing the properties of a being or a thing to a non-being.* But one must correctly remember that *non-being* can have no true attributes, nor can *part and whole, subject, adjunct, etc.* be understood of it in any way. Therefore, you correctly conclude that the mind plays with its own shadows when it considers logical beings.

*A certain and finite number of stages would suffice, etc.* <note>original: "stadiorum" — a Greek measurement of distance</note> But it is repugnant to my concept to assign any limit to the world, and I have no other measure of what I ought to affirm or deny than my own perception. Therefore, I say the world is "undetermined" or "indefinite" because I recognize no boundaries in it; but I would not dare call it "infinite," because I perceive God to be greater than the world—not by reason of extension (of which, as I have often said, I understand none to exist in God), but by reason of perfection.

# Regarding the final points.

*If you perform this, etc.* I am not certain that the continuation of my philosophy will ever be published, because it depends on many experiments; I do not know if I will ever have the opportunity to perform them. However, I hope to publish a short treatise on the *Passions* <note>original: "Affectibus" — the soul's emotions or responses to the body; this refers to his work "The Passions of the Soul" (1649)</note> this summer. From this, it will be clear how I believe that all the movements of the limbs that accompany our passions are performed in us not by the soul, but solely by the machinery of the body. 

As for the fact that *dogs wag their tails, etc.*, these are only movements that accompany passions, and I think they must be accurately distinguished from speech, which alone demonstrates the thought hidden within the body. *Nor are there any infants, etc.* The case for infants is different from that of animals. I would not judge infants to be endowed with a mind, were it not that I see they are of the same nature as adults; but animals never grow up to the point where any certain sign of thought can be detected in them.

# Regarding the Questions.

*To the first.* It is repugnant to my concept—or, what is the same thing, I think it involves a contradiction—for the world to be finite or bounded. This is because I cannot help but conceive of space beyond any presupposed limits of the world; and for me, such space is a true body. Nor do I care that by others...

<meta>This page continues René Descartes’s response to Henry More’s second letter. Here, Descartes addresses More's specific objections regarding the finitude of the world, the nature of motion, and how incorporeal substances (like the soul or God) interact with physical matter.</meta>

<page-num>84</page-num>
<header>René Descartes’s Response to the Second Letter of Henry More.</header>

...is called "imaginary" by others, and for that reason the world is thought to be finite; for I know from what prejudices this error has proceeded.

*Regarding the second point.* By imagining a sword thrust beyond the boundaries of the world, you show that you also do not conceive of the world as finite; for every place that the sword reaches, you actually conceive of as a part of the world, even though you call that which you conceive "vacuum" <note>original: *vacuum* — a void or empty space</note>.

*Regarding the third point.* I cannot better explain the reciprocal force in the mutual separation of two bodies from each other than if I place before your eyes a small boat stuck in the mud next to a river bank, and two men: one standing on the bank pushing the boat with his hands to move it away from the land, and in exactly the same way another man standing in the boat pushing the bank with his hands to move that same boat from the land. For if the forces of these men are equal, the effort of the one who stands on the ground—and is therefore joined to the ground—contributes no less to the motion of the boat than the effort of the other who is being carried along with the boat. From this, it is clear that the action by which the boat recedes from the land is no less in the land itself than in the boat. Nor is there a difficulty regarding the person who has moved away from you while you were sitting; for when I speak here of translation <note>original: *translatione* — displacement or the change of position of a body relative to those touching it</note>, I only mean that which occurs through the separation of two bodies that are immediately touching each other.

*Regarding the fourth point.* The motion of the Moon determines the celestial matter <note>Descartes believed space was filled with a "plenum" of subtle matter rather than being a vacuum</note> (and consequently also the Earth contained within it) so that it turns toward one direction rather than another—namely, in the figure placed there, as from A toward B rather than toward D—but it does not give it its speed of motion. And because this speed depends on the celestial matter, which is roughly the same near the Earth as it is near the Moon, the Earth ought to revolve twice as fast as it does (so that it would complete its circle about sixty times in the time the Moon runs through its own circle, which is sixty times larger) if its size did not stand in the way, as was said in Article 151, part 3 <note>Referring to Descartes's *Principles of Philosophy*</note>.

*Regarding the fifth point.* I assume there is no sluggishness <term>sluggishness: *lentorem*, a lack of fluidity or a resistance to flow</term> and no stickiness in the smallest particles of matter, except in the same way as in sensible and large things: namely, that which depends on the motion and rest of the parts. But it should be noted that the "striated particles" <term>striated particles: *particulae striatae*, grooved or channelled particles that Descartes hypothesized to explain magnetism</term> themselves are formed from the most subtle matter, divided into innumerable or indefinitely many tiny pieces which are joined together to compose them. Thus, I conceive of more diverse tiny pieces in each single striated particle than common people do in other very large bodies.

*Regarding the sixth point.* I have attempted to explain the greatest part of what you ask here in my treatise on the passions <note>original: *de affectibus* — likely referring to his work *The Passions of the Soul*</note>. I add only this: nothing has occurred to me so far regarding the nature of material things for which I cannot very easily devise a mechanical explanation. And just as it is not unbecoming for a philosopher to think that God can move a body, even if he does not think God is corporeal <term>corporeal: having a physical body</term>; so too it is not unbecoming for him to judge something similar about other incorporeal substances. And although I believe that no mode of acting belongs to God and his creatures in the same sense <note>original: *univoce* — "univocally," meaning the term is applied with the exact same meaning to both</note>, I nevertheless confess that I find no idea in my mind that represents the way in which God or an Angel can move matter that is different from the idea which shows me the way in which I am conscious that I can move my own body through my own thought.

<summary>Descartes argues for an indefinite world where "voids" are actually matter, explains motion as a reciprocal relationship between bodies, and posits that the mind's ability to move the body is our best model for understanding how God or spirits interact with matter.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes René Descartes’s response to Henry More’s second letter and begins More’s third letter to Descartes. Descartes finishes his explanations regarding the nature of motion, the composition of matter, and the divisibility of particles before More takes up the pen to express his gratitude and continue their philosophical debate.</meta>

<page-num>85</page-num>
<header>Third Letter of Henry More to René Descartes.</header>

Neither can my mind extend or contract itself in relation to place by its own substance, but only by its power, which it can apply to larger or smaller bodies.

*Regarding the seventh point.* If the world had existed from eternity, this Earth undoubtedly would not have remained from eternity; rather, other earths would have been produced elsewhere, and not all matter would have turned into the First Element <note>original: *primum Elementum* — in Cartesian physics, the finest, most fluid matter that fills the spaces between larger particles</note>. For just as some of its parts are crushed in one place, others coalesce <note>original: *coalescunt* — join together or grow into one</note> in another at the same time; and there is no more motion or agitation in the entire universe at one time than at another.

*Regarding the eighth point.* It follows evidently from the way I described the Earth's production—namely, from particles of the matter of the first element coalescing together—that particles of water and all others on Earth have pores. Since this First Element consists of no particles except those that are infinitely divided, it follows that we must conceive of pores existing down to the last possible division in all bodies formed from it.

*Regarding the ninth point.* From what I said just before about the two men (one who moves along with the ship, and the other who stands unmoved on the bank), I think I have sufficiently shown that I believe there is nothing more positive <note>original: *positivum* — having a real, independent existence rather than being a mere lack of something</note> in the motion of the one than in the rest of the other.

I do not quite understand what you mean by your last words: *Whether any thing can naturally and by itself have a characteristic of which it can be entirely deprived, or which it can acquire from elsewhere.*

Furthermore, I want you to be certain that it will always be a great pleasure for me to receive whatever you might ask or object to regarding my writings, and I will answer them to the best of my ability.

Egmond, April 15 <note>original: *17. Kalendis Maii* — the 17th day before the Kalends of May, which is April 15th</note>, 1649. 

->Yours most devotedly,<-
->RENÉ DESCARTES.<-

# RENÉ DESCARTES,

## FROM HENRY MORE.

I could scarcely restrain myself (Distinguished Sir) from writing back to you immediately upon receiving your letter. However, that would have been quite impolite of me, as I understood well enough from your letter that you would be very busy with business for many weeks. Furthermore, many things happened to me at that time due to my father's death which called me away elsewhere, and hindered me so much that I could not easily perform what I most desired. 

But now, having returned to you and your works and found enough leisure, I am writing back. I give you the greatest thanks for so freely and kindly granting me the full right to ask whatever I please about your writings and to raise objections.

However, lest I seem to abuse this great kindness of yours with overly long disputes (for so far we have been engaged in that part of philosophy which...)

<page-num>86</page-num>
# Third Letter of Henry More to René Descartes.
<note>original: *Epistola Tertia H. Mori ad R. Cartesium*</note>

...was more prone to word-battles <note>original: λογομαχίαις (*logomachiais*)</note> and slippery subtleties, existing as it does on the borders of Physics, Metaphysics, and Logic) I hasten toward those matters that allow for a more certain and firm judgment.

I will note only in passing, and first regarding your response to my initial objections: As for Angels and separate souls, if they perceive each other's essences immediately, *that cannot properly be called "sensation" if you imagine them to be entirely incorporeal*. For my part, I am happy to join with the Platonists, the ancient Church Fathers, and almost all the Sages <note>original: *Magis* — referring to the "Magi" or wise men of antiquity</note> in recognizing that all souls and spirits, whether good or evil, are clearly corporeal. Consequently, they possess sensation in the proper sense of the word—that is, sensation arising through the medium of the body they inhabit. Truly, since I expect nothing but greatness from your genius, it would be most welcome if you would briefly share your conjectures on this matter with me, which I believe will be highly ingenious given your renowned wisdom and sharp mind. 

As for those who boastfully pride themselves on not admitting any so-called "separate substances"—such as demons, angels, and souls surviving after death—and who applaud themselves here as if they had performed a great feat and become far wiser than other mortals, I do not value their opinion at all. For as I have often observed, these people are, for the most part, either men of "bull-like blood" <note>original: *Taurini sanguinis* — a reference to the four humors; a person with "bull's blood" was thought to be heavy, dull, or overly melancholic</note> and hopelessly depressed, or they are immensely devoted to the senses and pleasures—in short, atheists, or at least they would be if religion (upon which they rely only out of superstition) did not force them to acknowledge God. But I am not ashamed to profess openly that, even if the authority of religion were removed, I would of my own accord acknowledge that spirits and God exist. Yet I could not admit any other kind of God except the sort that every best and wisest person would wish to exist, even if He did not. Thus, I have always suspected that atheism is the triumph of reckless wickedness and extreme stupidity. The boasting of atheists is just as if a foolish population were to cheer and congratulate one another over the murder of a most wise and kind Prince. But I have wandered off on this tangent by some impulse. I return to the point.

Secondly, regarding that demonstration of yours by which you conclude that every extended substance is tangible and impenetrable: it seems to me that I can counter with this: namely, that in some extended substance, parts can exist "outside of parts" <note>original: *partes extra partes* — a philosophical phrase meaning the parts are spatially distinct</note> without any mutual resistance <note>original: ἀντιτυπίᾳ (*antitypia*) — the quality of a solid object that prevents another object from occupying its space</note>; and thus, tangibility (properly so called) disappears. Furthermore, extension can be folded back into other extension and substance along with its own substance, and is no more lost than that part of the substance which is retracted into another. Thus, that "Impenetrability" fails—an idea which I profess I can conceive clearly and distinctly in my mind. Moreover, it is clear from your own principles regarding motion that *something real can be enclosed (without any decrease in itself) within smaller or larger boundaries*. For according to your view, the same numerical amount of motion occupies now a larger, now a smaller subject. I, however, conceive with equal ease and clarity that a substance can be given which can dilate and contract without any lessening of itself, whether it does this by its own power or by some outside force.

Lastly, therefore: I am indeed astonished that it cannot even enter your understanding how either the human mind or an Angel could be extended in almost this same way, as if it involved a contradiction. For I would rather think it involves a contradiction that the *power* of the mind is extended while the mind *itself* is not extended in any way. For since the power of the mind is a mode of the mind...

<summary>In this letter, Henry More argues against Descartes' view that spirits are entirely incorporeal, suggesting instead that souls and angels possess a form of extension and subtle corporeality. He also challenges Descartes’ definition of matter, arguing that substance can be extended without being impenetrable or tangible.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Henry More's critique of René Descartes' metaphysics and physics. Having previously discussed the nature of the soul and spirits, More now transitions to debating the omnipresence of God and the definition of physical motion.</meta>

<page-num>87</page-num>
<header>Third Letter of Henry More to René Descartes.</header>

...within the mind, it is not outside the mind itself, as is evident. And a similar reasoning applies to God: hence a similar wonder strikes me that, in your response to the next-to-last objections, you concede that **he is everywhere by reason of his power, not by reason of his essence** <note>original Latin: *eum ubique esse ratione potentiæ, non ratione essentiæ*</note>; as if the Divine power, which is a mode <term>mode: a specific quality or state of being</term> of God, were situated outside of God, since every real mode is always intimately within the thing of which it is a mode. Therefore, it is necessary for God to be everywhere if his power is everywhere.

Nor can I suspect that by "the power of God" you mean to imply an effect transmitted into matter. But even if you mean this, I do not see why the matter does not fall back to the same point. For this effect is not transmitted except through Divine power, which touches the receiving matter—that is, it is united with it in some real way, and therefore is extended; yet in the meantime, it is not separated from the Divine Essence itself. For it seems, as I said, a clear contradiction. But I must not dwell on these points.

I fly to the questions, after having noted how the despair of continuing your philosophy saddens my mind. But equally, the certain hope of that most desired treatise which this summer is bringing forth <note>referring to Descartes' *Passions of the Soul*</note> revives me; I hope it comes to light quickly and successfully.

# Regarding the Response to the Questions.

To the first and second questions, you respond quite consistently and agreeably with your principles, which I both expect and praise in anyone, unless a better opinion prevails.

Regarding the third: From that little boat of yours <note>original: *navigiolo*—referring to Descartes' thought experiment in *Principles of Philosophy* II.24-32 regarding the movement of a man in a boat</note> I have acquired these goods for myself:
1. That in motion, there is a mutual struggle <note>original: *renixum*—can also mean counter-pressure or resistance</note> of those things which are said to be moved.
2. That rest is an action—namely, a certain struggle or resistance.
3. That for two bodies to be moved is for them to be immediately separated.
4. That this immediate separation is that motion, or transfer, strictly speaking.

When, indeed, two bodies disentangle themselves from each other, unless you add a force in both that is "disentangling" and "tearing away" to the notion of transfer or motion, this motion will be only an external relation <note>original: *respectus*</note>, or perhaps something even slighter. For "to be separated" either means that the surfaces of bodies which were just touching each other are now distant (and the distance of bodies is only an external relation), or it means not to touch what they were just touching, which is merely a deprivation or negation. Certainly, your opinion on this matter is not sufficiently clear to me.

However, if I were left to my own judgment, I would judge motion to be that force or action by which the bodies you say are moved mutually disentangle themselves from each other; and that the immediate separation of those same bodies is the effect of the said motions, even if it is only a bare relation or deprivation. But it seemed otherwise to you to philosophize in the explanation of the definition of Motion, *Article 25, Part 2* <note>Descartes, *Principles of Philosophy*, Part II, Art. 25</note>, where I do not fully grasp your meaning.

To all the remaining questions I proposed, you have responded clearly and appropriately. But for a fuller understanding of what I gathered for the sixth question, I am waiting until your most desired little book on the Passions <note>original: *de Affectibus*—referring to *Les Passions de l'âme*</note> comes out.

Otherwise, as for those last words of mine, *Whether any thing, etc.* was bringing forth...
