Indeed, my mind was pursuing some fleeting subtlety, which has now escaped me, and it is not in my interest to recall it.

I will only ask this again: ***Whether matter, left freely to itself—that is, receiving no impulse from elsewhere—would move or remain at rest.*** If it moves by itself naturally, since matter is homogeneous <term>homogeneous: uniform in structure or composition throughout</term>, and for that reason motion would be equal everywhere, it follows that as soon as all matter existed, it would be scattered into parts so infinitely small that nothing could ever be further rubbed off from any particle. For whatever you imagine could be rubbed off has already been scattered and dissolved, due to the deep force of motion pervading—or if you prefer, inherent in—all matter. Nor would some parts cling to each other more than others, or turn their course elsewhere more than others, since they are all exactly alike according to every imaginable reason. For no roughness or angularity of shape can be imagined that has not already been ground down to the ultimate degree that motion can achieve. Nor should any inequality of motion be placed in any particles, since matter is supposed to be perfectly homogeneous. If, therefore, matter moved naturally, there would be no Sun, no Heaven, no Earth, no vortices <term>vortices: in Cartesian physics, these were large circular currents of "fine matter" that carried planets around stars</term>, nor anything heterogeneous—whether perceptible or imaginable—in the nature of things. And therefore, your wonderful artifice for building the heavens, the earth, and other perceptible things would perish.

But if you say that matter is at rest by itself unless it is moved from elsewhere, and that this rest is something positive, then matter would suffer an eternal force from that impulse, and its natural state would be destroyed forever so that a contrary state might dominate—which seems a bit harsh. Yet perhaps it would be no safer to define rest as the privation or negation of motion; for then all action of resisting would fail in resting matter, which you nevertheless acknowledge. Though even that itself gives my intellect no small amount of trouble. For while you establish rest as an action of matter, you must also establish that motion is the same; since matter does not act except by moving, or at least by striving toward motion. These scruples truly trouble me, and I beg you to remove them as soon as you can.

Furthermore, I weigh these first principles so carefully that a new difficulty now arises for me regarding the nature of motion. ***Specifically, since the motion of a body is a mode <term>mode: a specific quality or state of being, like shape or position, that cannot exist independently of the object</term>, like its shape or the arrangement of its parts, how can it pass from one body to another, any more than other bodily modes can?*** And universally, my imagination cannot grasp how anything that cannot exist outside of a subject (as all modes are) can migrate into another subject. Next, I ask: when one body strikes another smaller body that is at rest and carries it along, does the "rest" of the resting body similarly migrate into the body that carries it, just as the motion of the moving body migrates into the one at rest? For rest seems to be such an idle and lazy thing that it would be weary of the journey. Yet since it is just as real as motion, reason would compel it to "pass over." Finally, I am quite amazed when I consider that such a trivial and lowly thing as motion—which can be separated from a subject and is transmissible, and of such a weak and vanishing nature that it would perish immediately unless supported by a subject—could nevertheless twist a subject so powerfully and drive it so forcefully this way or that. Indeed, I am more inclined to the opinion that there is no transition of motions at all, but rather that by the impulse of one body, another body is "awakened" into motion, much as the soul is awakened to a thought on this or that occasion; and that...

...a body does not so much "receive" motion, as it exerts itself into motion when prompted <note>original: *commonefactum*</note> by another body. As I mentioned a little earlier, motion relates to the body in the same way that thought relates to the mind: namely, neither is "received" from outside, but both arise from the subject in which they are found. I hold that everything called "body" is <note>original: *stupidè & temulentè esse vivum, utpote quod ultimam infimámque Divinæ essentiæ, quam perfectissimam vitam autumo, umbram esse statuo ac idolum*</note> *stupidly and drunkenly alive, as I maintain it is the ultimate and lowest shadow and idol of the Divine essence—which I consider the most perfect life—* yet it is nevertheless devoid of feeling and awareness.

Furthermore, your idea of the transfer of motion from one subject to another—and from a larger to a smaller body, and vice versa—perfectly represents the nature of my **Extended Spirits**. As I mentioned above, these spirits can contract and expand again; they can very easily penetrate matter without filling it; and they can stir and move it in any way, yet without any mechanical devices or the need for physical hooks to link them. Truly, I have lingered on this point longer than I intended; I will hurry on to my purpose, which is to propose new questions regarding those specific Articles in your *Principles of Philosophy* <note>Descartes' *Principia Philosophiae* (1644), a landmark text in early modern physics and metaphysics</note> whose force I do not yet fully understand.

### Regarding Part 1, Article 8

*We see clearly, etc.* We do not see clearly that extension, shape, and local motion belong to our nature, nor do we see clearly that they do *not* belong to it. I wish you would briefly demonstrate here that no body <term>body: in this context, "body" refers to physical matter</term> is capable of thought.

### Regarding Article 37

Is it not a greater perfection for a human to be able to will only what is best for themselves, rather than also being able to will the opposite? For it is always better to be happy than to be occasionally—or even always—extolled with the highest praise for one's choices.

### Regarding Article 54

Here I repeat again: it was necessary to demonstrate that nothing "extended" <term>extended: taking up space or having physical dimensions</term> can think, or—what might seem easier—that no body can think. For this is an argument worthy of your genius.

### Regarding Article 60

Although the mind can contemplate itself as a "thinking thing," excluding all physical extension from this concept, this does not prove anything other than that the mind *could* be either corporeal <term>corporeal: physical or bodily</term> or incorporeal. It does not prove that it is, in fact, incorporeal. Therefore, I must ask you again to demonstrate, from some operations of the human mind that cannot be performed by a physical nature, that our mind is indeed incorporeal.

### Regarding Part 2, Article 25

*Not the force or action that transfers, so that I may show it is always in the thing moved, etc.* Is it not the case, then, that the force and action of motion itself reside within the thing being moved?

### Regarding Article 26.

Is there, therefore, in bodies at rest a certain perpetual staying force <note>original: *vis statoria*</note>, or an action of holding themselves steady and strengthening themselves against all impacts by which their parts might be torn apart and scattered, or the whole body carried off and moved elsewhere? Could Rest, then, be rightly defined as a certain internal force or action of a body, by which the parts of the body are tightly bound to one another and compressed, and are thereby defended from being divided or moved by the impact of another body? From this, a conclusion would arise that is not at all foreign to my own understanding: namely, that Matter is a kind of obscure life (since I consider it to be the ultimate shadow of God), and that it does not consist in the mere extension of parts, but always in some kind of action—that is, in either rest or motion, both of which you yourself concede are actually actions.

### Regarding Article 30.

This article seems to contain a very evident demonstration that translation—or local motion—is not reciprocal in any way (unless we are merely considering the external relationship between bodies).

### Regarding Article 36.

I ask, does the human mind increase the total motion of the universe when it ignites the animal spirits <note>original: *spiritus*; in 17th-century physiology, "animal spirits" were volatile fluids thought to travel through the nerves to facilitate thought and movement</note> through intense and prolonged thinking, and additionally heats the body itself?

### Regarding Article 55.

Suppose a perfectly hard and perfectly flat cube were moved across a table that was also perfectly hard and perfectly flat. At the very moment the cube stops moving, would it bond as firmly to the table as the parts of the cube or the table are bonded to themselves? Or does it remain separate from the table, either forever or at least for a time, after coming to rest? For there is no pressure forcing the cube onto the table, since we are imagining this motion occurring as if in a vacuum, located outside the walls of the world if such a thing were possible (and therefore in a place where there is no gravity or weight), and the motion is stopped from the direction toward which the cube was heading. It seems, therefore, by the laws of nature—since the cube and the table are already separate and there is no real action by which they are joined—that they would always remain actually divided.

### Regarding Articles 56 and 57.

I do not see why it is necessary for you to describe such wide loops and plays of particles around body B. It seems sufficient if we suppose that individual particles of water are moved with a similar impulse by the "subtle matter" <note>original: *materia subtili*; in Cartesian physics, a fine, fluid matter that fills the gaps between larger particles</note>, and that the sizes of the particles are equal. For from this, when body B is struck from every side by the very short loops or semi-loops (or by any other means) of the motion of the nearest adjacent particles, it will necessarily remain at rest; it will not be moved in one direction more than another.

### Regarding Article 57, line 19.

*They will not travel along such straight lines, etc.* Why is this? Is it because they now approach a more circular shape, whereas previously they reflected a more oval one? I do not fully understand this point.

### Regarding Article 60.

*But that they <note>the particles of matter</note>, insofar as they are driven more swiftly, are carried toward any other parts.* Can the speed of a motion and its direction <note>original: *determinatio*; in Cartesian physics, "determination" refers to the specific direction of a body's movement as distinct from its speed</note> really undergo a divorce? For it seems just as if we were to imagine a traveler running who directs his course toward London, but the speed of his running is nonetheless "carried" toward Cambridge or Oxford. This is a subtlety that neither University will grasp, unless perhaps by "being carried" you mean that the motion exerts itself, or strives <note>original: *niti*</note>, so that motion might occur in some direction.

### Regarding Article 16 of the Third Part.

Would not the light of Venus, according to the Ptolemaic hypothesis <note>The older model of the universe where the Earth is at the center; More is asking if Venus would show phases like the Moon in that system</note>, now decrease and now increase in the manner of the Moon, although not by the same measurements and laws?

### Regarding Article 35.

How does it happen that all the planets do not revolve in the same plane—namely, in the plane of the Ecliptic <note>The path of the Sun across the sky</note>—and likewise the sunspots; or at least in planes parallel to the Ecliptic, including the Moon itself; or in the Equator, or in a plane parallel to the Equator, since they are directed by no internal force but are carried only by an external impulse?

### Regarding Articles 36 and 37.

I would also like you to indicate to me the reason for the Aphelia <note>original: *Apheliorum*; the points in a planet's orbit furthest from the sun</note> and Perihelia <note>original: *Periheliorum*; the points in an orbit closest to the sun</note> of the planets, and for what reason each one changes its position from time to time. Most importantly, since all the planets are in the same vortex <note>Descartes proposed that planets are carried around the sun by a swirling "vortex" of invisible matter</note>, why are the Aphelia and Perihelia of all the primary planets not found in the same places? Also, how does the precession of the equinoxes arise from your principles? For here you will be able to explain the true and natural causes of these phenomena <note>original: *Phænomenωv* (Greek)</note>, while others only set forth fictional hypotheses.

### Regarding Article 55.

*Those things which are driven in a circle.* But how did such immense spaces of matter first begin to be rolled into circles and become vortices?

### Regarding Article 57.

*That part of it which is impeded by the sling, etc.* It seems harder to perceive that the stone A is hindered from moving toward D, since it is never actually carried there in fact, nor would it naturally proceed there if the hindrance were removed; for it would proceed entirely toward C.

### Regarding Article 59.

You say here that a new force of motion is acquired, and yet the effort <note>original: *conatus*; in Cartesian physics, this refers to the "striving" or pressure exerted by a body to move</note> is renewed: I do not know how well these things hold together. For if a new force is acquired and added on top, it is not a "renewal" of motion, but an "increase." But if globule A, by moving, increases the motion while remaining at the same point on the rod (for this example refers to the globules of the vortex), why does motion not always ignite and increase itself simply by moving? If that were the case, everything would have turned into flame long ago.

### Regarding Article 62.

Here I ask: since the effort of the globules, in which light and luminosity consist, occurs through the entire width of the vortex, so that the base of the triangle BFD could be much larger than DB, and from the extremities of the produced diameter DB (made perhaps ten or a hundred times larger) the globules are pushed back by an oblique effort toward a point at F (the eye of any observer)—why then does the light, such as that of the Sun, not appear larger than what is contained within the circle DCB?

### Regarding Article 72.

I do not fully understand this mechanism <note>original: *artificium*</note> of twisting the matter of the "first element" <note>In Descartes' system, the "first element" consists of the finest, most agitated particles that fill the spaces between larger globules</note> into spiral or screw-like shapes; especially in places somewhat distant from the axis. This seems impossible unless it happens not because the globules are twisted around the particles of the first element, but rather because the first element itself—perhaps slightly directed into a gyration by those very globules—twists itself within those triangular spaces and describes spiral lines within itself. I beg you to explain your thinking here more fully. But another doubt also arises here: since these twisted particles consist of the smallest and most rapidly agitated particles, how do those tiny particles coalesce into any larger form or size, especially since that distortion and obliquity of motion occurs while these striated particles <note>original: *particulae striatae*; screw-shaped particles Descartes used to explain magnetism and other phenomena</note> are being formed?

### Regarding Article 82.

*Both the highest and the lowest, etc.* This rapid course of the highest globules seems like a marvel <note>original: *prodigii instar*; something monstrous or supernatural</note> to me (especially if compared with the middle ones), and one that far exceeds the causes you put forward in the following Article. If you can find anything further by which this doctrine might be made more palatable <note>original: *mollius*; literally "softer" or more gentle</note>, it would indeed be a pleasure to hear it.

### Regarding Article 84.

*Why the tails of comets, etc.* I impatiently thrust upon you every opportunity to explain anything: I ask that you also briefly settle this matter in this place.

### Regarding Article 108.

Thirdly and finally: since the celestial globules are carried around the axis of the vortex <term>in parallel</term> <note>original Greek: *παραλλήλως* (parallēlōs)</note> both to the axis and to each other, and they do not lose this parallelism while they change position somewhat among themselves, it seems impossible that any twisting of the **striated particles** <note>original: *particularum striatarum*; these were screw-shaped particles Descartes used to explain magnetism</note> could occur at all—unless those striated particles are rotated around their own axes within those triangular spaces. Meanwhile, other strings that are closer and even looser, or strings on the same instrument that are taut, do not move at all. This is a common and very well-known experiment. Indeed, no "sympathy" seems to me to escape mechanical explanations more than this agreement of musical strings.

...you might plead a lack of experiments here. For regarding our bodies, I have heard from trustworthy sources that you have most accurately explored everything pertaining to human anatomy. As for the soul, since you possess one that has awakened into the most sublime and grand operations, and you possess the most agile and subtle spirits, your noble mind—relying on its innate power and celestial vigor, like the fire of the chemists <note>original: "igni Chymicorum"—a reference to alchemical fire used for transformation</note>—will so exert itself and transmute into various forms that it can easily be its own workshop for infinite experiments.

### Regarding Article 195.

*“And I explained in the Meteors,”* etc. <note>original: "Et Meteoris explicui"—referring to Descartes' work *Meteors* (1637)</note> You have indeed explained the theory of colors in the *Meteors* most beautifully. However, there is a certain stubborn difficulty regarding that matter which causes great trouble for my imagination. Since you establish that the variety of colors arises from the proportion of the globules' circular motion to their straight-line <note>original: "rectilinearem"</note> motion, it must necessarily happen that sometimes, in those same globules, the circular motion exceeds the straight-line motion, while the straight-line motion also exceeds the circular at the very same time.

For example: Between two opposite walls, one of which is covered in red and the other in blue, the intervening globules—because of the red wall—will move faster in a circle than in a straight line. Yet, because of the blue wall, they will move faster in a straight line than in a circle, and at precisely the same time; these things are clearly <term>inconsistent</term> <note>original: ἀσύστατα (*asystata*)—meaning logically incompatible or impossible</note>. 

Or consider this: On the same wall where one part (say, the right) is red, the middle is black, and the left is blue, since a crossing over <note>original: "decussatio"—the intersection of light rays</note> always occurs at the eye, all the globules will take on a proportion of motion—specifically circular to straight—resulting from the meeting of the rays of every individual globule. Consequently, it is necessary that all the colors be mixed and confused at the back of the eye. 

I cannot think of any way to untie this knot, unless perhaps it must be assumed that this circular motion is merely a certain brief and rapid striving toward circulation, rather than a full motion, as actually occurs in the straight-line motion of the said globules. 

As for almost all the other difficulties I have proposed to you, I might perhaps have been able to extract some solutions by my own effort. But your kindness has granted me this liberty, and your singular skill in untying knots of this kind—which I perceived in your recent letters—has further invited me. (For although I see you acted briefly, due to the constraints of time into which you were then cast, you nevertheless satisfy me so fully and move my mind's senses as strongly as if you were present, pressing finger to finger.) Finally, since your explanations will carry greater authority, both with me and with others if there be a need, I thought it would be to our advantage to propose all these difficulties to you. When you have solved them, unless I am greatly mistaken, I shall most deeply understand all the principles of your philosophy. 

How much I value this is scarcely believable. When you have cleared up these present riddles <note>original: "gryphos"—referring to the Sphinx's riddles or complex puzzles</note> for me (and the sooner the better, because of that uncontrollable love by which I am carried away toward your work), you will soon receive other questions drawn from your *Dioptrics* from:

->The most devoted student of your philosophy,<-
->HENRY MORE.<-

->To the most illustrious man and supreme philosopher,<-

# RENÉ DESCARTES,

## HENRY MORE.

Truly, I am deeply grieved, most illustrious sir, that you have been snatched away from our neighborhood so suddenly and led away to such distant shores. However, to hide nothing, I have the means to mitigate this sorrow and distress of mind and to console myself. Certainly, it is no small thing that such honor has been granted to you, who so well deserve it, even among the most remote nations. The brightness of your name has penetrated so powerfully even to the thickets and dense mists of the North. Nor—and this is the main point—has it done so in vain, since such a great love of letters and learned men has filled the noble heart of that most illustrious heroine, the most serene Queen of the Swedes <note>Queen Christina of Sweden (1626–1689), who invited Descartes to Stockholm in 1649</note>. Not content with your fame and your books, she never stopped writing to you, urging you to visit her, until she attained her wish. I believe this will result in great benefit and honor to that kingdom.

For these reasons, I confess I have borne your departure from these regions of ours less harshly, as well as the loss of that most desired letter which I was expecting from you before your departure, as you promised. I am so far from giving up all hope of recovering it that, on the contrary, I strongly trust that you will soon reply not only to those things I wrote before but also to this present letter once it reaches your hands. Relying on this confidence, I proceed to your *Dioptrics* <note>original: "Dioptricen"—Descartes' 1637 work on optics</note>; soon I shall move on to the *Meteors* <note>original: "Meteora"—Descartes' 1637 work on atmospheric phenomena</note>, if any difficulty should happen to occur there, so that I may finally unburden my mind of all those things which I thought would be to our advantage to propose to you more fully. For I hope that in this way, when everything on my part that ought to be performed is completed, I will win a gentler peace for my soul and find myself less anxious in the future.

### Regarding *Dioptrics*, Chapter 2, Article 4, line 21.

*“In no way opposed to it.”* The cloth **CE** seems to be opposed to the ball **B**, at least in some way, even as the ball is carried to the right. This will be shown as follows:

<image-desc>A geometric diagram consisting of a circle with a horizontal diameter labeled G-H passing through a central point B. A diagonal line passes through the center from point A to point C. A vertical line segment connects point C to a point E on the right side of the circle's interior. Dashed lines connect point B to point E and other areas of the circumference. The diagram illustrates a vector or force problem involving a "pila" (ball) and "linteum" (cloth/surface).</image-desc>

For **GH** is fully opposed to the ball **B**, and perfectly hinders its course, both toward **HE** and toward **CE** (that is, downward). Since, therefore, **CE** approaches so closely to the position of **GH** that only the angle **HBE** (or **GBC**) is missing for a perfect opposition to its tendency toward **HE**, then **CE**, even while keeping its position, will be somewhat opposed to the ball **B**, even as it tends its course toward **HE**. This will appear even more clearly if we imagine **CE** to be a surface of moist clay and the ball (say, made of bronze) from...

The ball is carried from A to B <note>original: "A ferri ad B"—More is referring to a specific diagram in Descartes' *Dioptrics* where a ball represents a light ray</note>, where it will penetrate to some extent, but the force of its movement will be immediately stifled both toward HE and toward CE. This, however, would not happen if the ball were carried along the line CBE, but would instead proceed without hindrance toward HE, especially if no weight were present in the ball. From this, it is clear that the plane CE opposes the ball B descending from A, even insofar as it is carried toward HE, which was the point to be demonstrated.

*Let it lose half its speed, line 27.* I willingly grant that some part of the speed is lost here. However, I do not understand why you suppose—both in this Article and in the one immediately following—that this part of the speed is lost only toward CE and not toward FE. For since there is only one real motion of the ball (even though we can imagine various "tendencies" <note>original: "tendentias"—the directional components of motion</note> or goals of this motion at our pleasure), if this motion is diminished, it will move more slowly than before the motion was lessened, regardless of which way you imagine the ball proceeding. Therefore, the cause of the ball's tendency toward I rather than toward D should not be sought from the slowness or speed of the motion, but from the resistance of that large angle CBD and the weakness of that smaller angle EBD. The edge of the smaller angle, because of its thinness and the fluidity of its matter, yields more easily to the projected ball than the obtuse angle CBD. Otherwise, if the cause were attributed to speed or slowness, a ball descending from H to B would also deflect its course. Consult your diagram here, if necessary, on page 84.

->Regarding Article 6, line 7.<-

*It strikes so obliquely that the line FE having been drawn, etc.* This perpetual method of yours for demonstrating where the ball will go possesses a charming subtlety, but it does not seem to reach the actual cause of the matter. For the true and real cause is to be understood from the width of the angle CBD, the thinness of the angle EBD, and also the size of the ball. The larger the ball is, the less "depression" of line AB toward CE it requires to bounce back toward the air L. A larger ball does not as easily lift and open the point of the sharper angle to enter the water (for example), but rather, by striking against it, it flies across, reflected.

*Which may increase the force of its motion, line 22.* An increase in motion will do nothing to turn the ball's intended course unless there is a physical position of some body that determines said course toward another direction. I suspect this happens in those media which you imagine admit a ray more easily, such as crystal, glass, and so on. Namely, since the edge of the angle EBD in such substances is so hard and stubborn that it does not yield, the ray striking the compact and sloping edge of the angle is turned aside somewhat from its intended course and driven inward toward the perpendicular. Therefore, both refraction and reflection seem to me to be a kind of reflection, or at least a beginning of reflection. 

And just as in full and free reflection the "determination" <note>original: "determinatio"—in 17th-century physics, this refers to the direction of a force or motion</note> was changed without any slowing of the ball's course, so here a new slowness or speed does not seem necessary to diminish or change the direction. Only the diminished or increased determination itself is sufficient for either type of refraction. For when the ball arrives at the surface CE, it does not bend its course because it is faster or slower, but because it strikes a body that changes its direction. Otherwise, if only speed or slowness were added, the ball would always proceed straight from B to D.

In the first refraction, then—namely, away from the perpendicular line—the downward "determination" <note>original: "determinatio"—in 17th-century physics, this refers to the specific direction or tendency of a movement, distinct from its speed</note> is necessarily decreased, while the ball is slowed down only incidentally because of the softness of the material that changes its course. In the second type of refraction, the downward determination is increased; if the ball is accelerated, it is accelerated only incidentally because it passes more easily through the new medium. Therefore, the change in determination and its cause are absolutely necessary for both refraction and reflection; the speed and slowness of the motion itself are merely secondary, or rather, completely unnecessary. 

Indeed, regarding this new acceleration of the ball (or small globe) in a "faster" medium, it seems quite difficult to perceive how that works. This is because the new medium does not supply new degrees of motion; it only allows the ball to keep the degrees of motion it still has left without further decrease, since the medium does not seize or soak up any of that motion. It seems just as absurd to claim that new degrees of motion—or, if you prefer, the original degrees—are restored to a ball entering an easier medium, as it is to allow that a ball might stop for a moment at the point of reflection before it bounces back, an idea which you rightly reject in Article 2 of this chapter.

## Chapter 6. On Article 9.

> *but from the mere position of the small parts of the brain, etc.*

Are these kinds of small parts actually visible when dissecting a brain, or do you only conclude by logic that there must be such parts intended for this use? To me, there seems to be no need for them; rather, the same organs that transmit the motion necessarily inform the soul of where that transmission of motion is coming from, provided there is no obstacle in the way.

## On Article 13.

> *Similar to that by which Geometers, using two stations, etc.*

This comparison seems a bit forced and obscure, and it matches in nothing except that in both cases "two stations" are used. For Geometers—or, if you prefer, land-surveyors <note>original: "Geodaetae"</note>—take their stations along a straight line drawn directly from a tree or a tower. But the eye, if I understand the matter correctly, changes its position along a transverse line that is roughly parallel to the object.

## On Article 16.

> *From the knowledge or opinion we have of the distance, etc.*

It would perhaps be very difficult to explain the exact causes of the apparent size of objects. But I believe it consists mostly in one thing: namely, in the size or smallness of the angle of decussation <note>original: "decussationis anguli"—the angle at which light rays cross each other as they enter the eye</note>. For the larger that angle is, the larger the size of that body will appear; the smaller the angle, the smaller the body. 

Next, it is very worthy of observation that when you move an object—your thumb, for instance—to within the distance of a single grain <note>original: "grani"—a small unit of measurement, likely a "barleycorn" or about 1/3 of an inch</note> from your eye, this angle of decussation will be four or five times larger than the one formed when the thumb is about ten grains away. And if the thumb is moved further from the eye by several dozen grains, the angle of decussation will always become narrower, but by a smaller and smaller proportion for every ten grains of distance. It always turns out somewhat narrower than before, until fi-

...it indeed becomes so narrow that it is understood to have the character of a single straight line. Hence, no one will wonder if he finds his thumb to be much larger when it is only one grain <note>original: "grano"—a small unit of measurement, similar to a barleycorn</note> away from the eye than when it is ten grains away. Furthermore, after it has been moved many dozens of grains away, it does not lose much of its size for every ten grains added; yet it can be moved so far away that it eventually ceases to appear at all. This is because the distance between the "legs" of the internal angle of decussation <note>original: "decussationis"—the point where lines of sight cross each other, like an 'X', within the eye</note> can become smaller than the diameter of a single filament of the optic nerve. However, I little understand what the opinion regarding distance—compared with the size of the image—actually accomplishes here. Nor do I know for certain how either the eye or the soul initiates such a comparison within itself. As for how I conceive the perception of magnitude to arise from the aforementioned angle, I believe I can explain it as follows:

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating optical theory and perspective. A large vertical line on the left represents an object labeled 'C' at the top and 'D' at the bottom. A smaller parallel line between the object and the focal point is labeled 'E' and 'F'. Lines of sight from C and D converge at a central point of decussation labeled 'G'. Beyond point 'G', the rays diverge and strike two vertical lines representing the retina (the back of the eyes). The first line is labeled 'H' at the top and 'I' at the bottom; the second, further line is labeled 'K' at the top and 'L' at the bottom.</image-desc>

Let **H I** and **K L** be the back of two eyes <note>original: "fundi duorum oculorum"—the retinas</note>, namely a larger one and a smaller one. Let **C D** be a larger and more distant object, and **E F** a smaller but closer object. Let **E G F** or **K G L** be the angle of decussation.

First, I establish here that there is a certain effort <note>original: "nisus"—a term in 17th-century physics for pressure or the internal tendency toward motion</note>, or a transmission of motion from **E** into **L** and from **D** into **K**. My attention <note>original: "animadversionem"—the faculty of the soul that "notices" sensory input</note>, running out directly through the line **K G F D**, encounters one extremity of the object **C D** (namely **D**) in the place where it actually exists. Similarly, through the line **L G E C**, it encounters the other extremity of the object **C D** (namely **C**) in its own place as well. The same applies to all other parts, both the outermost and those in between, of the object **C D**. Therefore, by this direct outgoing of my attention, I perceive the presented size of the object, the measure of whose apparent diameter is the angle **E G F**. 

Thus, while keeping the same straight lines through which my attention runs out, and the same size of the angle in eye **H I** as was just in **K L**, I say that the object **D C** appears just as large as it did in eye **K L**. From this, I later conclude that the apparent size of the object is referred to the magnitude of the angle of decussation, and not to the size of the image on the retina. 

Finally, just as the apparent size of an object does not arise from the size of the image on the back of the eye (as is further evident from the fact that the size of the smaller object **E F** is the same as the larger object **C D**, in both eye **H I** and eye **K L**), so it does not arise simply from the size of the angle of decussation alone. Otherwise, the object **E F** would appear just as large as the object **C D**, since the angle of decussation is the same. But once the smaller object **E F** is removed, the object **C D** will in fact appear much larger than the object **E F** just did, even though both were seen under the same angle of decussation. From this, it can rightly be concluded that the apparent size of any object arises partly from the angle of decussation and partly from the real magnitude of the body. Nor is it surprising that my attention, proceeding through those straight lines of effort or transmitted motion, penetrates that far and stops itself there where this motion first begins: namely,

### Regarding Article 19.

*Since we are accustomed to judge, etc.* <note>original: "Quoniam sumus assueti judicare, &c." — This refers to Descartes' argument that our perception of distance is a learned habit rather than a purely mechanical process.</note> What, then, do you think of that man born blind from birth whom Christ healed, if a flat mirror had been placed before him before habit had corrupted his judgment? Would he have perceived his face on this side of the mirror, or beyond it, or behind the mirror? This "play" of the image behind the mirror has wonderfully twisted and fatigued my imagination, and I confess I do not yet sufficiently understand its causes. For this explanation of a "corrupted habit of judging" does not satisfy me in any way. If you can devise real and more mechanical reasons and share them with us, you will be doing a most welcome thing.

### Regarding Article 20, last line.

*From which it follows that their diameter, etc.* Why should the diameter of the Sun or Moon not appear to be one foot <note>original: "pedalis"</note> or two feet <note>original: "bipedalis"</note> wide, due to the angle of decussation <note>original: "angulum decussatorium" — the X-shaped crossing point of light rays in the eye</note> being diminished in that proportion? Such a proportion is suited to represent bodies of the same real size as the Sun and Moon under this apparent size of one or two feet at those distances.

### Regarding Article 21.

*Because both toward the Horizon and toward the vertex, etc.* Therefore, the Sun and Moon appear larger at the Horizon than they ought to appear relative to their distance. And that should rather be called the "true" apparent size—or the one that is not deceptive—which is subject to a certain law, rather than that which is altered by some external circumstances.

### Regarding Chapter 9, Article 5, page 185, line 10.

### Regarding Chapter 10, Article 4, line 17.

If it touches the outermost circles of the wheel’s width, it will not, however, fit the inner ones; for it will be too large to match them. Hence, the point of this instrument will not touch the rotating wheel in the middle sections of its width.

Regarding the *Meteors* <note>original: *Meteora*; referring to Descartes’ 1637 treatise *Les Météores*, which explained weather and atmospheric phenomena through physics.</note>, the difficulties that arise there are fewer and, I think, of less importance. You will soon hear what they are.

### *Meteors*, Chapter 1, Article 4, page 210, line 7.

*And finally, [that it is hotter] near the earth than near the clouds.* You assert this regarding both direct and reflected rays. But I do not see how direct rays could increase the power of heat, unless they are reflected and folded back again upon themselves near the Earth. In that case, they are not simply direct rays, but direct rays joined with reflected ones. Indeed, it seems rather that the force of heat in the air near the earth should be diminished, since the ethereal globules <note>In Cartesian physics, light and heat were explained as the motion or pressure of tiny, invisible spheres ("globuli") that filled all space.</note> communicate some of their motion to terrestrial particles; therefore, near the earth, their motion would be slower and weaker than in the upper regions of the air. It would not be out of place, then, if you explained here why the air becomes hotter near the Earth than near the clouds. And could it not be that, although the motion is less near the Earth than in the upper parts of the air, a greater heat is nevertheless felt because of the inequality <note>original: *inaequalitatem*; More suggests that "heat" might be caused by irregular or turbulent motion rather than just speed.</note> of this motion?

### Chapter 7, Article 6, page 283, line 4.

*But also the lower [clouds] are so thin and extended, etc.* But when they are so thin, how can they catch other clouds falling onto them and stop them there? It seems rather that, because of their thinness <note>original: *tenuitate*</note>, they would let them pass through to the Earth, if they were otherwise headed that way.

### Regarding Article 7, line 2.

*Because of the resonance of the air placed all around, etc.* Indeed, Paracelsus <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a famous Swiss physician and alchemist known for his eccentric theories.</note> imagines that thunder bellows and moans so monstrously because of the "arched temples of heaven," in a manner not unlike if someone were to explode a brass machine <note>A cannon.</note> loaded with gunpowder <note>original: *nitrato pulvere* — nitrate powder.</note> under a vaulted roof. But you, I know well, do not hold that the heavens are enclosed by any such ceilings. Therefore, it would seem more likely that the further the strike is from the Earth, the weaker the sound would be; for resonance does not occur as easily when the place where the sound might reverberate is so far from the objects being struck.

### Chapter 9, Article 2, line 19.

*Because only a few rays, etc.* Is it then the fewness of rays that generates the color blue? This seems hardly consistent with what came before. For above, you established that colors arise from the varying proportion of the rotation of the little spheres compared to their straight-line motion—specifically that blue comes from a rotation slower than the forward movement, as if the very nature of the color blue consisted in that. Yet now you attribute the cause not so much to a lack of rotation, but to the small number of rays bouncing back from the surface of the sea. Here, therefore, I ask whether you feel there is no other [cause] of colors...

<header>Fragment of the Response of René Descartes to the Third Letter of Henry More.</header>

...to determine anything by reason, and to allow room for conjectures. I approve of your statement that God should be considered only as the kind of being that all good people would wish Him to be, if He were lacking.

2. Your example regarding the acceleration of motion is ingenious, used to prove that the same substance can occupy a larger or smaller space at different times. However, there is a great disparity here, because motion is not a substance but a mode <note>original: *modus*; in Cartesian philosophy, a "mode" is a quality or state of a substance, like the shape of a piece of wax.</note>. Indeed, it is a mode of such a kind that we can intimately conceive how it can be decreased or increased in the same place. Each individual entity has its own proper notions, by which they must be judged on their own terms, rather than by comparison with others. Thus, what applies to motion does not apply to shape, nor does what applies to both apply to an extended thing <note>original: *rei extensæ*; physical matter.</note>. Anyone who has once clearly perceived that "nothing" has no properties—and therefore that what is commonly called "empty space" <note>original: *spatium vacuum*</note> is not nothing, but a true body stripped of all its accidents <note>original: *accidentibus*; non-essential qualities that can change without destroying the object, like color or temperature.</note> (those things that can be present or absent without the destruction of the subject)—and who has noted how every part of that space or body is distinct from all others and impenetrable, will easily perceive that the same divisibility, tangibility, and impenetrability cannot apply to any other thing.

3. I said that God is extended by reason of His Power <note>original: *Potentiæ*</note>, because that Power exerts itself (or can exert itself) in an extended thing. It is certain that God’s essence must be present everywhere so that His power can exert itself there. But I deny that He is there by way of an extended thing—that is, in the way I described an extended thing just a moment ago.

4. Among the "merchandise" <note>Descartes uses a metaphor here: More had previously described taking ideas from Descartes' "little ship" or published works.</note> which you say you acquired for yourself from my little ship, two seem to me to be "counterfeit." One is the idea that rest is an action or a certain resistance. For although a resting thing, by the very fact that it rests, has that resistance, the resistance itself is not the same thing as the rest. The other is that for two bodies to be moved is for them to be immediately separated. For often, of those things that are so separated, one is said to move and the other to stay at rest, as I explained in Articles 25 and 30 of Part 2 <note>This refers to Descartes' *Principles of Philosophy*.</note>.

5. That "translation" <note>original: *translatio*; here meaning the movement of a body from one place to another.</note> which I call motion is a thing of no less entity than shape is; specifically, it is a mode in a body. The moving force, however, can be that of God Himself, who conserves as much translation in matter as He placed in it from the first moment of creation. Or it can be the force of a created substance, such as our mind, or any other thing to which He gave the power of moving a body. And indeed, that force in a created substance is its mode, but it is not a mode in God. Because this cannot be easily understood by everyone, I did not wish to treat this matter in my writings, lest I seem to favor the opinion of those who consider God as a "soul of the world" <note>original: *animam mundi*</note> united to matter.

6. I consider matter, when left freely to itself and receiving no impulse from elsewhere, as being entirely at rest. However, it is impelled by God, who conserves as much motion or translation in it as He placed there from the beginning. Nor is this translation more "violent" to matter than rest is. In fact, the name "violent" refers only to our own will, which is said to suffer violence when something happens that is contrary to it. In nature, however, nothing is violent; it is just as natural for bodies to push or strike each other, when that happens, as it is for them to rest. I think you find difficulty in this matter because you conceive of a certain force in a resting body through which it resists motion, as if that force were something positive—namely, a certain action distinct from the rest itself—when in fact it is nothing other than a modal entity.

# Henry More’s Response to the Cartesian Fragment.

7. You rightly notice that motion, insofar as it is a mode <note>original: *modus*; in Cartesian philosophy, a "mode" is a state or quality of a substance, like the shape of a piece of wax</note> of a body, cannot pass from one thing into another. But I did not even write that; rather, I think that motion, as such a mode, is constantly changing. For the mode at the first point of body A is one thing—because it is separated from the first point of body B—and it is another thing when it is separated from the second point, and another from the third, and so on. However, when I said that the same amount of motion always remains in matter, I meant this concerning the force <note>original: *vi*; the underlying power or energy that causes movement</note> impelling its parts. This force applies itself now to some parts of matter, and now to others, according to the laws proposed in Article 45 and the following sections of the second part [of the *Principles of Philosophy*]. Therefore, there is no need for you to be worried about the migration of "rest" <note>original: *quietis*; the state of being at rest</note> from one subject to another, since not even motion, as the mode opposite to rest, migrates in that way.

8. What you add—namely, that it seems to you that the body is "stupidly and drunkenly alive"—I consider these things to be pleasantries. And by the freedom you grant me, I will say here once and for all: nothing holds us back more from finding the truth than if we decide certain things are true which no positive reason, but only our own will, persuades us to believe. This happens specifically when we have devised or imagined something, and afterward the invention pleases us—as is the case with you regarding corporeal angels, the "shadow of the Divine essence," and similar ideas. No one ought to embrace such things, because by doing so he blocks his own path to the truth.

***

## Response to the Fragment of Descartes, from a Letter of
### Henry More to Claude Clerselier.

That my recent letters pleased you so much (most Distinguished Sir) is surely to be attributed to no charm or wit of theirs, but to your singular kindness. Of this you have given an even richer proof: you sent that most welcome Fragment of a Cartesian Letter to me, though I neither requested nor expected it; and you yourself so kindly attempted to satisfy some of those difficulties which I proposed to Descartes. This favor I can repay in this way or not at all: namely, if I respond briefly to all those things which both of you have written.

1. First, then, regarding those Cartesian matters concerning the senses of separated souls and angels when they are entirely deprived of any body: it is agreed between us that neither has "sense" in the proper meaning of the word. However, the fact that some of them turned out evil by their own will is a sign that angels were always clothed in very subtle bodies. For a spirit that is purely and perfectly immaterial seems to be subject to no failing or "fall"; since it is so simple, there is nothing from which it could be tempted to desert its station.

# Henry More’s Response to the Cartesian Fragment.

<margin>* Natural Philosophy, Book 1, Chapter 5.</margin> He himself teaches in clear words that motion is transferred from body to body, and his disciple and interpreter *Henricus Regius* <note>original: *Henricus Regius*; Henri de Roy, a Dutch physician and early follower of Descartes who eventually diverged from him</note> affirms that it passes in the same way that an inheritance passes from Stichus to Seius <note>Stichus and Seius were conventional names used in Roman law, similar to "John Doe" and "Richard Roe"</note>. Nor does that disparity matter—that motion is only a mode <note>original: *modus*; a temporary state or quality of a substance</note> while a spirit is a substance—since both are real things. Indeed, it actually favors our cause, since it is impossible for the numerically identical mode to occupy now this subject and now that part of a subject, whereas the numerically identical spirit can do so quite conveniently. I wonder, therefore, at the misfortune of Regius’s intellect; although he allowed the same numerical motion to wander so freely from body to body, he nevertheless so inhumanly imprisoned the human soul in a foul corpse, and would not permit it to fly out even after the bonds of Nature were worn away or consumed. As for the idea of space and that often-repeated aphorism, *Nothing has no attributes* <note>original: *Nihili nullam esse affectionem*; a core Cartesian principle meaning that if we can perceive properties or "extensions," there must be a real substance there</note>, I have responded to those points so fully and extensively in my previous letters to Descartes that I consider it clearly unnecessary to add anything here.

3. Regarding what they call the "Omnipresence of God," there remains no disagreement between us, since he acknowledges that God is everywhere and exerts his power upon the underlying matter. Furthermore, he agrees that a certain kind of extension belongs to God, but one far different from that which belongs to a divisible and impenetrable body.

4. I have not "adulterated" <note>original: *adulteravi*; corrupted or faked</note> any cargo on the Cartesian ship. He complains that I so mix and confuse the resistance <note>original: *renixum*; the counter-pressure or tendency to stay still</note> of a resting body with "rest" itself that I admit no distinction between them; I contend that this was done with the best of reasons. For if it is not "rest," what else is there by which a resting body defends itself from being carried away or "translated"—which is what he calls motion? Therefore, that resistance is nothing other than rest itself, preserving the resting thing in a state of rest; that is, it perseveres in the state it is in according to the laws of Nature, until some stronger cause changes it. But if this resistance, or constancy, were some kind of action of rest, then since every bodily action is motion, rest would also be a kind of motion—which seems entirely contrary to reason. I therefore suspect instead that the incomparable Philosopher—perhaps through the fault of others who act with too much authority—has "adulterated" the definition of motion. He likely did this so that he would not seem to assert the "motion of the earth" (which the superstitious Peripatetic school <note>original: *Peripateticorum schola*; the traditional followers of Aristotle who held that the Earth was stationary</note> considers almost a sin), even while he acknowledges that the Earth is carried around the Sun in the common vortex of all the Planets.

That other charge of "adulteration" is also dismissed with equal ease. For since Descartes himself establishes that motion (or "translation") is reciprocal, yet claims there is no force or action in the bodies that are separated and moved, what, I ask, can motion be except the immediate separation of bodies? If motion is the immediate separation of bodies, it follows immediately that for two bodies "to move" is for them "to be immediately separated." However, to say that one of these is "at rest" is surely a groundless statement, since it is impossible. Indeed, unless the Earth (labeled E F G H) stays at rest while body A B is moved from E toward F, and C D from H toward G, the Earth would be moved in opposite directions at one and the same time. This shows again that Descartes himself has corrupted the genuine notion of motion. See Part 2, Article 30 [of the *Principles of Philosophy*].

5. "Translation" <note>meaning the physical movement from one place to another</note> seems to have less "entity" or reality than "Figure" <note>Shape</note>, because shape is a more absolute quality of the body it is in, while translation is merely a relation to something else. As for the "motor force" <note>original: *vim motricem*; the force that causes motion</note>, whether in God or in the Divine Mind...

...divine <note>The text begins mid-sentence, likely completing a thought on divine power</note>, whether he places it in the *Soul of the World* <note>original: *Anima Mundi*; a Platonic concept of an animating spirit permeating all nature</note> with the *Platonists*; nevertheless, it was excellently done that so distinguished a *Philosopher* [Descartes] did not attribute this power to matter itself, but to some other subject, which therefore cannot be anything but immaterial or incorporeal. For without doubt, that most clear-sighted man saw that—unless one were to take the liberty of rashly and arbitrarily affirming or denying anything—it was necessary to recognize that all matter is by its nature homogeneous <note>of the same kind or nature</note>, according to the idea of it present in our minds, especially since no cause can be imagined for any diversity within it. From this it follows that all worldly matter, by its own nature, is either in motion or at rest. But if it were all moved by itself, no object would have a permanent structure, even for a moment; its particles would immediately and spontaneously flow away from each other, or rather, they would never have joined together in the first place. I have already proved this sufficiently in my *Letters to Descartes*.

6. Therefore, *Descartes* openly professes—along with *Ficino* <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), a central figure in the revival of Platonism</note> and the other *Platonists*—that he considers matter, when left to itself and receiving no impulse from elsewhere, to be completely at rest. I agree with him that this impulse is not "violent" <note>forced or unnatural</note> in a literal sense. This is not only because the term "violent" properly refers only to our own will (which is said to suffer violence when something happens against its wishes), but because matter is, in a way, perfected by this motion or impulse. Furthermore, that "resistance" which is imagined to exist in resting matter is no obstacle, since it is not properly an "action," but merely the persistence of a resting thing in its state of rest, as *Descartes* himself suggests in this passage.

7. He says correctly here that I notice that motion, insofar as it is a "mode" <note>a temporary state or quality</note> of a body, cannot pass from one body into another, and that he never wrote such a thing. However, *Regius* <note>Henricus Regius, a former disciple of Descartes</note> deliberately explains the matter as if it were an error to think otherwise, as I mentioned above. Indeed, the words of *Descartes* himself seem to carry this meaning very clearly in *Part 2, Article 40* [of his *Principles of Philosophy*], where he asserts that a body having greater force to continue its path moves another body along with it, and loses as much of its own motion as it gives to the other. In fact, that "force" he discusses there seems to me to be the same thing as motion itself. But let every Author have the right to interpret his own writings.

8. As for those "sweet things" of mine (as he calls them), if they were mixed with his "severe things," I believe an excellent temperament <note>a balanced mixture</note> would be created from them. Nevertheless, in the meantime, I do not reluctantly admire and embrace the beautiful rigor of the *Cartesian* intellect, even though I have often noted this: namely, that those who so stubbornly strive for mathematical certainty in all things have, most unfortunately of all, wavered in certain areas. For that method of reasoning which puts on the appearance of a demonstration <note>a logical proof</note>, as soon as it is discovered not to be a legitimate demonstration, is rightly judged to be an argument of no value.

Furthermore, in using certain allusions and metaphors, there can be no deception, provided we remember that things are not being called by their proper names, but by figurative ones. The matter (or the universal body of the world) is not literally a "shadow" just because I suggested it is like a shadow of the divine essence. This allusion does not teach that the body is actually a shadow, but that it depends on God just as a shadow depends on a body. Then, just as a shadow reflects some image of the body, though a very dark and degraded one, so there are in body or matter certain blind and vanishing traces of the Divine essence, which when, as I said,

<page-num>108</page-num>

<header>Henry More’s Response to the Cartesian Fragment.</header>

Even if life is most perfect in its highest forms, analogy itself demands that matter is not entirely deprived of every image of life. It mimics a certain kind of life in this: when two bodies meet, their motions can be so adjusted that—as if by a mutual warning—one is accelerated and the other slowed, until both finally converge in the same rhythm of motion. The same reasoning applies to the other laws of transfer. For *Descartes* <note>original: *Cartesius*</note> himself hardly dares to affirm that the motion which is in one body actually passes into another.

As for his addition that there is some external force—whether it comes from God or from some incorporeal substance created by God—by which matter is stirred into motion, I also praise this, since it is undoubtedly most true in a general sense. However, if he understood the matter as if that Divine force immediately pushed every individual body that moves, there would be a great difficulty; for the mutual collisions of bodies would then be in vain. Experience proves that one body pushes another, as can be seen in stones thrown by hand, or iron globes discharged from a war machine <note>original: *machina bellica*; likely referring to a cannon or catapult</note>. If that Divine force excites certain parts of matter, but does not immediately excite others, those parts moved by God will then stir others into motion by their own impulse. Since no motion actually passes from one body to another, it is manifest that one body "awakens" the other, as if from sleep. In this way, the awakened bodies transfer themselves from place to place by their own power. I consider this property of a body to be a certain shadow and image of life. Therefore, it is clear at last that we are not chasing empty shadows, but rather concepts that have their use and best illustrate a truth that can be demonstrated through a more rigorous method of argument.

As for that other pleasant topic concerning corporeal angels: their existence is testified to by more than six hundred histories of demons—not fables, but most true accounts. As for those wandering and vagrant spirits being necessarily corporeal—that is, being clothed in "corporeal vehicles" <note>original: *vehiculis corporeis*; a Neo-Platonic concept that spirits require a subtle material body to interact with the physical world</note>—I believe I have sufficiently demonstrated this myself above.

25. How the inner nature of Light and Colors became known to him from this.
26. Which observations of philosophers invited him to believe that the Earth was once a Sun or a fixed Star.
27. An enumeration of certain properties of the Magnet, and a general conclusion from them: That, if the Earth is a magnet, it must have once been located in the axis of some Vortex.
28. The same conclusion specifically inferred from the hardness of the magnetic Earth.
29. Also inferred from the subtlety of magnetic particles and pores.
30. Descartes’ modest and sober nature.
31. That he nevertheless indulged his "Mechanical Genius" too much, but to the immense benefit of the **Republic of Letters** <note>original: *Reipublicæ literariæ*; the international community of scholars.</note>.
32. Those who complain that nothing can be known do not so much bring shame to philosophy as excuse their own laziness.
33. That Descartes clearly taught that something can be known in natural things.
34. Those who determine that things serving to cultivate the mind contribute nothing to human life are openly professing that they live like beasts.

1. You ask a great thing of me, Distinguished Sir, namely that I give my opinion on the "Triumvirate" of the most distinguished philosophers of this century. Of two of them, I can determine nothing clearly, as I have not yet read them thoroughly; nor do I believe it would be worth my while to ever do so. I wonder indeed that you ask me what I think of that third one <note>René Descartes</note>, since I have more than once publicly testified to the high opinion I have formed of him. But while you further inquire for what reasons in particular I have so greedily embraced his philosophy, your somewhat persistent questioning provides me with the subject for a fuller response. For it is not a single and simple question, but one armed with the sting of a certain minor accusation, as if I were admitting and fostering all Cartesian ideas without selection.

But the matter is much different than you suspect. For although this incomparable philosopher is so happy and ingenious in his discoveries and reasonings—almost everywhere surpassing the human lot—that we seem forced to believe he has succeeded everywhere; yet Nature has formed me with such a slow and hesitant mind that no mortal's authority could ever so dazzle my mental vision that, bound by this spell, I would give faith to those theorems whose truth is not supported by sufficiently solid arguments—much less to those which are repugnant to my own senses and reason. Therefore, I will say briefly: I am so far from greedily devouring all Cartesian things, "raw or cooked" alike <note>An idiom meaning accepting everything without processing or critique.</note>, that I thought I should freely profess to you that I have observed several things in his writings which I cannot swallow by any means. These I think will be worth recounting to you so that after you have read Descartes—which you write you will do shortly—I may test your judgment, whether you feel the same as I do about these theorems.

# Letter of Henry More to a Most Distinguished Man
<note>original: *Epistola H. Mori ad V. C.*</note>

2. We can trace whatever errors Descartes made to three types of causes. Namely: either to simple and plain oversight, the kind that happens to almost all mortals; or to an excessive desire for either prudence or a certain "honest shrewdness," for which not many people are guilty; or finally, to a certain enormous affectation for mathematical certainty and necessity in every one of his conclusions—a goal to which very few have yet aspired in natural matters, and absolutely no one has reached it, nor perhaps ever will.

3. To the first category <note>original: *Ad primum genus*; referring to simple oversight.</note> can be referred the method by which he explains Refraction in *Dioptrics*, chapter 2, and the explanation of the position of images in Reflection, chapter 6, along with a few other points about which we will perhaps say more shortly.

4. Two notable examples of the second category <note>Referring to "honest shrewdness" or strategic caution.</note> occur. The first is his explanation of the nature of **Motion**, which he says is always reciprocal. This notion has always seemed to me to be tangled in obvious contradictions. However, he preferred to obscure knowledge with words in this way rather than appear to attribute less motion to the Earth than either Copernicus or Tycho <note>Tycho Brahe (1546–1601) and Nicolaus Copernicus (1473–1543) represented competing models of the solar system. Descartes was trying to navigate the theological dangers of claiming the Earth moved.</note> did. Indeed, he even removed all motion from the Earth so that he might win greater favor for his philosophy and better protect himself from those men with whom long-standing custom and blind authority carry more weight than even the clearest demonstration. For undoubtedly, the fate of Galileo remained fixed deep in his mind—who, by attributing such free orbits to the Earth around the Sun, lost his own freedom and restricted his own steps within the limits of a prison. <note>Galileo was sentenced to house arrest by the Roman Inquisition in 1633 for supporting the Copernican heliocentric model.</note>

The second example concerns brute animals, whom he imagines to be lifeless **Machines** and unfeeling **Automata**. <term>animal machines</term> <note>Descartes famously argued that animals lack souls and consciousness, functioning as complex biological robots.</note> He found it necessary to devise this witty invention so that he would not have to conclude, from his own method of philosophizing, that the souls of brutes are immortal just like ours. Since he firmly held that not even the lowest act of thinking can occur in **Matter** (no matter how it is modified), if he had acknowledged that brutes possess sensation, he would also have had to grant that they possess a substance really distinct from matter—that is, an immortal soul. Therefore, he preferred to deprive brutes of sensation rather than imagine himself entangled and tortured by the hateful, petty questions of unfeeling and captious men regarding the status of brutes after death.

To this category should also be added what he remarks in passing in his *Principles*, part 3, article 2, about not investigating the "ends" <note>original: *finibus*; referring to "final causes" or God's purposes for creating things.</note> of those things we see in the complex of Nature. By this warning, he undoubtedly protected himself from those troublesome inquiries that idle men might press upon him concerning the whole class of Comets as well as Planets, and also concerning the Stars, which he clearly recognizes to be just as many Suns. For it was very easy to ask further: for what purpose did God create so many Suns, and for whom would they shine? And, since in all the Planets—which have almost the same origin (having been formed from "encrusted" suns) and the same method of production—there is earth, sea, air, magnets, gold mines, etc., one might ask further whether there are not also brute animals and those more noble inhabitants, humans, in each of them. Finally, one might ask whether it is not credible that the Planets passing through space and seeking a home for themselves in some **Vortex** <term>vortex</term> are the rough foundations of new Earthly worlds. From these thorny questions, Descartes hoped he could most easily free himself by warning early on that the counsel of God is so deep...

# Letter of Henry More to V. G. 111

...ends in the works of Nature, so that it is a mark of extreme recklessness to attempt to investigate their limits. For a very shrewd man <note>original: *nasutissimus*; literally "sharp-nosed," meaning someone with a keen sense or wit.</note> knows that a pretense of ignorance is much better than a poorly timed display of knowledge.

**5.** Regarding the third category <note>Referencing the "mathematical disease" or craving for absolute certainty mentioned on the previous page.</note>, we must consider what he applies to demonstrate that **Rarefaction** and **Condensation** occur in the manner of a sponge. Specifically, he claims that Distance, or space, and body are really the same thing, and that no extension can be imagined anywhere that is not a real property of some body. This foundation greatly pleased Descartes, because it confirms his method of Rarefaction and Condensation with a certainty that is (if possible) more than mathematical. Furthermore, it wonderfully supports his entire doctrine concerning the **Vortices** <note>original: *Vorticibus*; Descartes' theory that space is filled with swirling matter that carries the planets.</note>, which are immense in number and magnitude, and his theory of the particles of the "first element" being divided into infinity. To me, however, that foundation is in no way appealing. This is partly because the reasons Descartes brings forward for it are not valid enough (as I have proved at length in my letters), and partly because it implies that Matter either exists independently by itself, or at least has existed from all eternity alongside God—necessarily produced by Him and co-eternal with Him. The first of these ideas is plainly inconsistent <note>original: *ἀσύστατον* (asustaton); unstable or incompatible.</note> with a true concept of God, and the latter is harsh and rash. Nevertheless, it cannot be denied that there have always been, and still are, those who seriously combine either opinion with the existence and religious worship of God.

Furthermore, we must attribute to this "mathematical disease" and craving <note>original: *pruriginem*; literally an "itch."</note> for extreme certainty that magnificent promise of Descartes: that conclusions are to be perpetually deduced from the mechanical necessity of motion throughout his entire Philosophy. For that most sagacious man did not think himself sufficiently secure in the certainty of those methods by which he asserts the phenomena of Nature occur, if Divine plans (which could display the same phenomena in various ways) were mixed with the laws of Matter and Motion. But this immense passion and eagerness for deducing every single thing from this certain and inevitable law of Matter and Motion—which remains always at the same measure in the entire Universe—so fascinated Descartes' noble genius that he not infrequently imagined too hastily that he had achieved what he so passionately desired to achieve everywhere. Omitting others, I will produce only one example, but one that is very clear and of the greatest importance: namely, the formation of **striated particles** <note>original: *particularum striatarum*; screw-shaped particles Descartes used to explain magnetism and other physical effects.</note> and their motion. It is so far from the case that they are necessarily formed in the way he explains that it seems highly improbable, and perhaps even impossible, that they are formed that way, or that once formed, they move according to such laws.

We could experience the same thing here in any matter, especially in something both round and long, placed in some tube or channel parallel to the Earth's axis. Thus, every excuse seems to be blocked here for anyone inventing empty answers.

Therefore, these triangular small columns will proceed in a straight but very swift course through those triangular spaces without any twisting of themselves, provided that the corners of the spaces are found in almost the same lines in a continuous series.

But if the corners of these triangular spaces are not found in the same lines, but the corners and sides mutually cut across each other alternately—which indeed seems more likely to happen, as the globules would slip into a more stable and compact arrangement in that position—let us see finally whether the matter succeeds more happily in this way. Let us see if there is any mechanical necessity for the said small columns to be twisted into a **screw-like shape** <note>original: *formam cochlearem*; Descartes' "striated particles" were vital to his explanation of magnetism and other phenomena.</note>. 

Suppose, therefore, that the matter of the **first element** <note>The finest, fastest-moving matter in Descartes' system, which fills the gaps between larger particles.</note>, by passing through the triangular space **A B C**, has acquired a triangular shape for itself. And suppose that another triangular space, **D E F**, immediately meets this formed matter, with its corners cutting the sides of the previous space, if they were joined in that position.

Although the speed of their passage and the tenderness of the newly formed particles make it in no way probable, let us suppose it were so. It would still follow that it is entirely a matter of chance which way these small columns are twisted—namely, whether they follow the order of **Vortex G H**, or the opposite. For since the ethereal globules <note>original: *globuli ætherei*; the small, spherical particles of the second element in Cartesian physics.</note> lying closest to one another are of the same size, those triangular spaces will be equal and will intersect each other equally. Thus, when angle A strikes side FD, it must necessarily fall exactly in the middle of that side, and so on for the rest. Consequently, there is no reason why those triangular columns should be twisted toward H more than toward G, or vice-versa. Therefore, one might rightly conclude that the **striated particles** <note>original: *particulas striatas*; screw-shaped particles with grooves, which Descartes believed flowed through the Earth to create magnetic force.</note> would be twisted now this way and now that during their formation, and that not all those coming from the same pole would be twisted in the same direction. If this were the case, those well-known laws of **Magnetism** would be utterly overturned, and the phenomena of the world would be changed. For this reason, it is necessary to call upon some higher and more divine cause than purely mechanical **Matter and Motion** for this work—if indeed those triangular columns are to be twisted into a screw-like shape <note>original: *cochlearem*; literally snail-like or spiral.</note> so skillfully, with such constant craftsmanship, and for such useful purposes.

The same conclusion must be reached concerning the course and tendency of these particles once they have been twisted in this way. For they are supposed to proceed toward certain parts according to a fixed law, which nevertheless cannot be mechanical. For example, when they pass through the **subtle matter** of a star that is just beginning to be covered in a crust <note>Descartes theorized that stars could become "encrusted" with cooler matter, eventually turning into planets or comets.</note> (or is already nearly encrusted): unless some directing force more divine than mechanics rules and moderates the course of the striated particles, it is impossible for them not to be thrown from the axis of the star toward the sides. In that case, with one end stretched out, they would strike the crust in a line that is not parallel to the axis of the star, but rather cutting across it at nearly right angles. For it is incredible that one end of the striated particles does not usually outweigh the other or is not more solid. This much at least is manifest: since these striated particles rotate along with the star, they would necessarily recede from the axis and be pushed in a mass toward those parts of the star closest to the **Ecliptic**. Consequently, the greatest force of magnetism would be found toward the Earth's Equator, and almost none toward the Poles. Furthermore, if the matter of the **first element** <note>the finest, most fluid matter in the universe according to Descartes.</note> has become less pure and has grown somewhat sticky from contracted filth, the striated particles would lose their motion on such a long journey by having to cleave a path for themselves through this sticky and thicker consistency of matter.

But even if we grant that everything happens correctly and successfully on the inside, let us see what becomes of these striated particles when they have burst out with full force. Certainly, I cannot believe—if they had no other moderating force besides purely mechanical law—that they could repeat their circuits with such a successful exit and return. For even if I ignore how easy it would be for **Southern** particles to strike **Northern** pores and vice-versa, and how those impacts would foully deform the magnetic passages (especially while they are tender and newly formed), this certainly seems to me to be placed above every law of mechanics: that they return from Pole to Pole in such a constant course, having formed into what look like ranks, and do not instead fly straight forward into the free ether like thrown spears or arrows. For it would be more consistent with the laws of mechanics for them to bore a path through the air (even if we imagined it to be somewhat thicker) and to spend their motion and force on these efforts by...
