# Letter of Henry More to V. C.

...they would lose their way, rather than, as if by design, laboring to return and directing their course toward the other pole so far distant. For once they have projected themselves from the magnetic parts of the Earth into the air, they are immediately enclosed by parts of the air that are similar in every way, just as those that lie closest to one another. From this it is manifest that nothing corporeal can be the cause of why these particles, surrounded in this way by homogeneous parts of air on all sides, should break out here rather than there, or why they would prefer to return rather than complete their journey in a straight line or be carried upward. Instead, there must be some deeper and more divine Principle <note>More refers here to his concept of the "Spirit of Nature," an incorporeal force that moves matter toward specific ends.</note> that recalls the wanderers and everywhere moderates and governs their motions and courses toward certain and destined ends.

Finally, you might refer to this mathematical hair-splitting <note>original: *κυμοπορισίαν* (cymoporisia) or *μικρολογίαν* (micrologia); Greek terms for triviality or excessive attention to small details.</note> that cautious and scrupulous Principle: namely, that there is not even a tiny bit more or less motion in the Universe at one time than another. This can be defended by no reasons, as far as I know, except those that are begged or fabricated. Two of this kind occur to me. The first is that neither Spirits nor human Souls can move matter, but only determine its motion toward this or that direction. This is clearly a baseless assertion—to say that any active and operative Essence (which is how everyone regards a spiritual substance) has the power of restraining, stopping, and governing moved matter, and yet can never have even the slightest power to move that same matter in any way. The second is that a body which impresses motion upon another body always loses as much of its own motion as it gives to the other, and that the same numerical part of motion it loses passes into the other body. I believe that, if I had the time, I could very easily refute this from the study of what they call the **Mechanical Powers** <note>original: *Potentiarum Mechanicarum*; the laws of simple machines and forces.</note>. But since this opinion—that exactly the same amount of motion, both in number and measure, always remains in the World—belongs more to certain followers of Descartes than to the man himself, the fault of this rashness should be blamed on them rather than on him.

You see at last how I do not swallow with indiscriminate greed all those feasts with which Descartes so sumptuously entertains his friends.

6. Since I have cleared away this suspicion, I would gladly answer your question, if you would slightly change your words and meaning. That is, if you would not reproach me for such greedy and tight embraces of Cartesian inventions, but only ask why I profess to study Cartesian philosophy with such great zeal and pleasure. For I have many answers ready at hand.

First, I have no doubt that everything which reaches our senses from the sensible world (that is, from external Objects, which are commonly called **Phenomena**, and by which our senses are affected) is nothing other than bodily motion modified in various ways by the size, shape, and position of the parts of Matter. This will become clearly evident to anyone who examines all the senses and their objects.

Regarding **touch**, it is obvious; it is not affected except by the pressure, friction, impact, or collision of some body, and the like. Furthermore, it is equally clear that the fact that what is applied to our body seems soft or hard, hot or cold, and other things of that sort, must be attributed to motion. For sugar, stones, and iron, when broken by friction and reduced to fine powders, become soft; but water, from the deprivation of motion and the union of its parts...

...and when it is quiet and compacted into ice, it is hard. From this, it is established that hardness consists in the firm union of parts at rest, while softness consists in their separation—provided they are small enough—and that softness will be even greater if motion is added to that thinness. This could be demonstrated at length if it were necessary. It is also clear that the same reasoning applies to heat and cold; as motion rises to this or that degree, heat is excited, and when that degree of motion is relaxed, heat is either diminished or removed. We see this clearly in water boiling over a fire in a vessel. 

Indeed, we clearly perceive that the nature of fire itself consists in the most vehement <note>original: *vehementissima*; meaning intense or violent</note> agitation of particles, from the fact that it consumes the greatest part of its fuel into flame, which is carried upward by intense motion and agile vibration. It even separates the ashes themselves into the smallest parts, which is why they also become soft to some extent. By the same reasoning, the remaining tactile qualities <note>The "tactile qualities" are the physical properties we feel through touch, such as texture or temperature.</note> could be explained by the nature of motion, but that would be the work of a full volume, not of one short letter.

<margin>Aristotle, *On the Soul*, Book 2, Chapter 9.</margin>
Since it is certain that touch is nothing other than corporeal motion affecting the body, we can be confident that the same happens in taste. Taste is itself a kind of touch (as even **Aristotle** agrees), and its perceptions arise from the physical contact of the Object and the Organ, varying according to the different effects of motion in the Object. For all foods, through various uses of fire (the nature of which was just proved to consist in the intense agitation of particles), take on different flavors and affect the taste in various ways. This is equally true of both the flavors and the medicinal powers of drugs. Both are increased, diminished, or changed by the art of fire—which, as I have often said, is nothing other than a certain modified motion of Matter. Moreover, the Sun itself is fire, and by its heat, all the fruits of the earth reach their various stages of maturity.

As for the sense of smell, although there does not seem to be the same direct contact between the organ and the Object, it is nonetheless clear that sensation occurs by corporeal motion. We know this because odors are carried by the wind to the nostrils and are occasionally diverted. Thus, it is obvious that odors are certain particles floating in the air and striking the organ of smell. This appears even more clearly in fumigations <note>The practice of burning substances to produce smoke or medicinal vapors.</note>, where the agitation of fire excites odors in greater quantity, causing them to strike the nostrils more forcefully.

Sounds are also carried through the air; they are deflected by physical obstacles and hindered by contrary winds. From this, they clearly reveal their nature, indicating that they are specific motions transmitted through the air. This appears even more plainly from how they are generated. A sound is never heard except from the collision of some bodies, as is obvious in the voices of animals, in the striking or blowing of musical instruments, and in any disordered noises and crashes. Even the Echo herself sings in harmony with this truth; an echo is nothing other than sound reflected or bounced back from a concave body. But what, I ask, can be reflected from a body if it is not itself a body? Therefore, sound is nothing other than a specific motion of the air, and an Echo is nothing but the reverberation of this motion.

Just as we perceive from the Echo that sound is a type of corporeal motion, so by the same reasoning we can conclude that what reaches our eyes from visible objects is nothing other than this kind of...

...[the same] kind of motion modified by certain distinct laws. For everyone agrees that those so-called "visible species" <note>original: *species illas visibiles*; in older philosophy, these were the "images" or "forms" thought to be physically emitted by objects so they could be seen.</note> are reflected from bodies. We have already pointed out that it is self-evident that nothing can be reflected from a body unless it is itself a body. Therefore, it is universally true that sensation is nothing other than the perception of bodily motion.

This theorem <note>A "theorem" here refers to the principle that sensation is just perceived motion.</note> (I note in passing) is remarkably useful for refuting those who dream up certain "specific differences" of matter. They imagine certain clusters of particles that—setting aside all power of shape, motion, solidity, and position—display the various phenomena of the world to our senses based solely on their immediate and unchangeable "specific nature." For it is perfectly clear from what has been said, and from many other points that could be added, both that all material forms of this kind are constantly changing, and that our senses are only affected by them through certain laws of shape, motion, size, and position within the particles themselves.

Certainly, regarding the first point: no one who invents these "specific differences" in matter—unless they wish to philosophize recklessly and without reason—can deny that things which the senses judge to be extremely different must also differ in their "species" <note>In this context, "species" refers to the fundamental category or type of a substance.</note>. Now, I ask you, what greater difference ever meets our senses than that which exists between a star and this dark earth we walk upon? This would be a magnificent argument for demonstrating that the exact same matter undergoes the most opposite forms, and therefore that matter never differs in its fundamental type, if the Cartesian hypothesis <note>René Descartes (1596–1650) proposed that stars and planets were made of the same matter, and that planets were essentially "dead" stars that had cooled down and become covered in a thick crust.</note> about the transformation of stars into planets were not a mere hypothesis, but a recognized truth. 

In this way, it would be established that any terrestrial body, no matter how hard and thick, is composed of the most subtle matter of all. This matter originated from the fragments <note>original: *ramentis*; literally "shavings" or "scraps"</note> of the ethereal globules which are everywhere uniform (as is clear from our uniform perception of light). And if it cannot be done by human art, at least by Nature and the passage of time and fate, it could be worn down and dissolved into those same tiny fragments. However, setting hypotheses aside, that solid observation of sunspots <note>original: *macularum Solis*; the discovery of sunspots challenged the ancient idea that the heavens were made of a perfect, unchanging substance different from Earthly matter.</note> has nearly equal force; these sunspots are undoubtedly made from those most subtle particles, thinner than the ether itself. Furthermore, things seen closer at hand testify to the same: such as the transformation of thick bodies like tallow, wax, and wood into thin and shining flames; or the conversion of grass and herbs into blood, flesh, bone, and the hides of cattle or sheep. For grass, if we consult our senses, differs immensely from those parts of animals, and therefore, according to the principle stated above, they differ "specifically."

As for that second point—concerning particles of matter being distinct in species as if they showed the variety of phenomena to our senses by this "specific power" alone, excluding motion, position, rest, shape, and other modifications of matter—I believe it is abundantly refuted by the previous observations. From those, it was clearly established that everything reaching our senses is bodily motion, modified in various ways by the size, shape, and similar properties of the parts of matter. There is no need to add anything further here, once you notice how clearly an instance of this truth shines forth from the nature of light and colors. It is evident that light arises from motion because, if it is intense or nearby, a perceptible heat accompanies it.

<summary>Henry More argues that all sensation is merely the perception of matter in motion, refuting the idea that different substances have unique, unchangeable "natures." He cites the uniformity of matter across the universe, using examples like sunspots, the transformation of food into animal tissue, and the relationship between light and heat.</summary>

...is perceived. It is established from the rainbow <note>original: *Iride*</note> and the prism that colors are not certain specific qualities, but rather motion modified by certain laws. This is because no color actually exists within those dewy drops of the clouds, nor in the prism itself (since they are transparent); instead, light—refracted or reflected in specific ways—degenerates into that variety of colors. This is a clear indication that no specific colors exist within opaque bodies either. Rather, light is reflected from their surfaces in different ways depending on the position of the exterior particles. When this position is changed, the colors change immediately. This is evident in copper, iron, and other metals, whose surfaces change color when attacked and pitted by corrosive waters or saline particles in the air. For it is necessary that at least the position of the particles on the surface of the copper or iron, if not their shapes, is changed by this assault and impact. Consequently, the ethereal globules <note>original: *globulíque ætherei*; in Cartesian physics, these were the small, spherical particles of the "second element" that transmit light.</note> are reflected differently from polished copper than from tarnished or rusted copper.

Therefore, since it is so clearly established that all the phenomena of the world—insofar as they are open to our senses—are achieved by motion, it certainly seems to me that the person who observes the truest laws of philosophy is the one who investigates the causes of these phenomena so accurately and deeply that he can tell us precisely by what position, what thinness, and what shapes of particles all those motions (which affect our senses in various ways) are modified. This was performed for us in a stupendous manner by **Descartes**, who can never be praised enough by me.

7. Furthermore, there is no one who has even a moderate understanding of the nature of matter and motion who does not plainly see that from the single fact that God impressed a certain degree of motion into matter (the same degree, for instance, that we now experience in the world), various phenomena would necessarily emerge from it. For it is impossible for that measure of motion not to break matter apart and grind it into small fragments so that—although some things might remain hard (which would happen where there is a lower degree of motion)—other things would appear soft, some cold to the sense, others hot, and others clearly fiery. I believe that God intentionally allowed these two simplest principles of things <note>Matter and motion.</note> their own free and wandering cycles, so long as they were contained within those limits that would be just as convenient for the nature of things as if their force were restrained by some more divine power and law. This was done so that the contemplation of natural things would be all the more pleasing to the human mind.

For I think there is no physicist who, if he truly knows his own mind and purpose, will not acknowledge that he is searching for the corporeal efficient causes of things. He seeks these, if possible, as a long series of deductions, linked together in a necessary chain. Certainly, no such causes would be found if God—acting through some superior power—constantly and diligently obstructed the natural and internally necessary laws of bodily motion. In that case, no investigation of an efficient cause could exist except for something immaterial and least of all intelligible to us—such as the <term>Peripatetic substantial form</term> <note>original: *Peripateticorum forma substantialis*; the "Peripatetics" were followers of Aristotle. They explained an object's properties by claiming it had a "substantial form" (an internal essence) that made it what it was, which More considered a circular and empty explanation.</note>. This "form" wanders through individual things with almost the same definition as its name; it indicates nothing to us except our own ignorance and trifling. Such people would not be ashamed to respond with raised eyebrows to someone asking what water, fire, and similar things are (and from where they come), by saying that fire is fire and water is water because certain "substantial forms" which constitute fire and water have crept from the "womb of matter" into some unknown parts of matter, and in that way presented those two elements to the world. Away with these frivolous and idle trifles!

<summary>Henry More argues that colors and physical properties result from the mechanical motion and arrangement of particles, praising Descartes' mechanical philosophy while mocking the Aristotelian concept of "substantial forms" as a hollow explanation for natural phenomena.</summary>

...by which all the industry of human genius is put to sleep and hindered, and all its sagacity and sharpness is blunted and rendered useless! God did not present us with such a sluggish object for our natural contemplation; rather, He wisely permitted just enough to the necessary laws of motion and matter to excite us to investigate the causes of natural things, and to delight us with the pleasure of discovery. Consequently, it is not necessary to take refuge everywhere in that blind asylum of laziness and ignorance, namely, *internal substantial forms* <note>original: *internas formas substantiales*; in Scholastic philosophy, these were the "essences" thought to give things their specific properties, which More viewed as an empty explanation.</note>. 

For among those who call themselves philosophers, who—if asked about the phases of the moon or the eclipses of both the Sun and Moon—would ignore those clear and necessary reasons of mathematics and nature? If he were to reply instead that all these things proceed from the "internal principles and essential forms" of the Moon and Sun—which supposedly cause them to be deprived of light at certain times or cause the Moon to appear in different phases at set intervals—who, I ask, from that herd of philosophers would not be greeted with loud laughter for giving such a cold and meager response?

What would this poor little fellow do if the question were about the stations, directions, and retrograde motions of the planets? He cannot retreat to the **Ptolemaic hypothesis** <note>The ancient system where the Earth is the stationary center of the universe.</note>, as it overflows with the most obvious contradictions, as everyone now knows who has even tasted astronomy with the tip of their lips. Suppose then the **Tychonic system** <note>The system of Tycho Brahe, where the Sun orbits the Earth while the other planets orbit the Sun.</note> succeeds it, where all the planets complete their circuits in the free ether. Let us ask this man of ours: what is the cause that **Mars**, **Jupiter**, and **Saturn**, after having proceeded more hurriedly according to the order of the Zodiac signs, suddenly stand still as if fixed in a silent gaze, and then—as if they had suddenly remembered something they had forgotten—unexpectedly run backward? 

Undoubtedly, he would always strike the same string and say that this happens because of the "internal forms" of these planets which God implanted in them at the first creation; he would claim all their movements, progressions, regressions, and pauses are natural to them from their own constitutive principles—just as downward motion is innate to a stone and upward motion to fire. A splendid answer indeed, and one perfectly suited to the laziness and ignorance of such a respondent! 

Having dismissed this most trifling trifler, let us see how this question can be satisfied by the clear and admitted laws of matter and motion, which **Descartes** rightly established as being entirely common to both nature and mechanical art.

It is established from its phases that **Venus** performs its circuits on both sides of the Sun (sometimes closer, sometimes further), and the same reasoning applies to **Mercury**. No one so far has doubted that **Mars**, **Jupiter**, and **Saturn** are carried around the Sun. It is manifest, then, that these five planets go and return around the Sun. Next, we must ask whether they move by cutting a path for themselves through the matter of the ether, or whether they are carried along by the motion of the ether itself. 

It is clear that the first is not the case, because the resistance of the celestial matter would hinder such rapid planetary transits; they would lose their motion in a very short time by transferring it to the fluid ether. It remains, therefore, that they are carried along by the motion of the ether itself, and all the celestial matter in which they float is twisted like a **vortex** <note>original: *vorticis*; Descartes proposed that planets were carried around the Sun by massive whirlpools or "vortices" of celestial matter.</note> around the Sun. Finally, let us investigate what happens to the **Earth**, which is undoubtedly found within the limits of this vortex. Will she stand still in this rapid river, or will she move? With what hooks, what ropes and anchors...

...will it be held at the bottom of this sea? <note>original: *fundo hoc mari*; More is comparing the "ether" or celestial matter filling space to a vast ocean.</note> But let us imagine that the Earth is held stable and fixed by some supernatural and immaterial force. Good God! What storms would this admission excite against the most holy laws of Nature? For the celestial matter, like a most rapid torrent, would strike the face of the Earth with such assault and force that it would demolish animals, trees, towers, and every building whatsoever, carrying them away with it. Indeed, it would strip the entire Earth bare, shattering it deep down even to the metallic regions, and would carry the broken pieces away with it into this vast ocean of ether, like the debris of a terrible shipwreck. Therefore, we must allow the Earth to be carried around the Sun according to the laws of Nature and motion, just like the other planets that float peacefully in the ether.

And lest you should be anxious about the Moon—since it is certain that she travels around the Earth every month like a constant attendant, and since this cannot happen except by the power of a vortex <note>original: *vorticis*; in Cartesian physics, a vortex is a whirlpool of fine matter that carries planets and moons along in their orbits.</note> (as has already been demonstrated)—it is necessary that the Moon is carried around by its own particular vortex centered on the Earth. Since the Earth itself is in the middle of this vortex, and the celestial matter that swirls in this particular whirlpool passes through all the Earth's pores, it is impossible by the laws of Nature for the Earth not to be swept into a spin around its own axis by the force of this vortex. To put it briefly: if we consult the laws of bodily motion, it is impossible for the Earth not to be carried by that daily and yearly motion which Pythagoras, the wisest of the pagans, once taught, and whose doctrine Nicolaus Copernicus brought back to light a century or two ago.

You see from such clear and simple principles how we are led, even against our will, to that hypothesis—if it should even be called a "hypothesis," since it is necessarily contained within the real structure of Nature. By establishing this, the reasons and causes of nearly all the phenomena <note>original Greek: *Phænomenων* (phenomenon)</note> that have tortured the minds of astronomers for so many centuries are clearly revealed, not as mere possibilities or probabilities, but as necessary and inescapable facts. For our body does not cast a shadow in the Sun more necessarily than all those well-known planetary phenomena—which we will soon briefly review in order—follow from this Pythagorean system of the world which we have demonstrated.

These phenomena include:

The motion of Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Mercury, and Venus in their epicycles <note>original: *Epicyclis*; an epicycle is a small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one. In the old system, these were used to explain complex orbits.</note>; yet, meanwhile, the Sun is free of such clutter.

The fact that these five planets appear "direct" (moving forward), "stationary" (standing still), and "retrograde" (moving backward) in their epicycles; yet the Moon will appear neither stationary nor retrograde in her own epicycle.

The fact that the cycles of the epicycles of Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars have such a relationship to the motion of the Sun that they are always completed in the span of time that elapses from one conjunction with the Sun to the next; and that in each of these conjunctions with the Sun, they are found at the highest points of their epicycles <note>original: *Apogeis*; the point in an orbit farthest from the center.</note>, but in their oppositions they are at the lowest points <note>original: *Perigeis*; the point in an orbit closest to the center.</note>.

Furthermore, that the periods of Saturn’s epicycle are faster than Jupiter’s, and Jupiter’s faster than Mars’; but that the retrograde movements of Mars are greater than Jupiter’s, and Jupiter’s greater than Saturn’s.

Moreover, that Venus and Mercury are never far distant from the Sun, and the centers of both their epicycles seem to <term>run the same course</term> <note>original Greek: *ἰσόδρομα* (isodroma); meaning "traveling at the same speed" or "following the same path."</note> as the Sun.

Finally, that the nodes of the Moon <note>the two points where the Moon's orbit intersects the path of the Sun.</note> become mobile, and the eclipses of both lights...

He asserts that the Copernican/Pythagorean system is the only one that logically explains the observed movements and cycles of the planets.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Henry More’s defense of the Copernican (or "Pythagorean") system, explaining how the Earth's motion accounts for astronomical phenomena more simply than the old model. ...that it can occur in different signs of the Zodiac. This is to say nothing of the phenomena arising from the Earth's daily rotation: that all the stars and planets—even though they are separated from the Earth and from one another by immense distances—would otherwise have to be whirled around the Earth at an unspeakable speed and with opposite force every twenty-four hours.

This simple Pythagorean hypothesis <note>original: *Pythagoræ Hypothesis*; referring to the heliocentric model, which was often attributed to Pythagoras in the early modern period.</note> provides such clear and necessary explanations for all these phenomena (and others besides) that no one could doubt them—unless they were utterly foolish or deluded, or unless they wished to imagine that God deliberately disrupts the laws of Nature without any necessity. We can be as certain that this theory is true as we are that leaves falling from a tree into a river are carried downstream rather than upstream. We have already sufficiently shown how absurd such a notion of a "disturbed" nature would be.

At last you see, my Distinguished Friend, <note>original: *V. C.* (Vir Clarissime), a common formal address to a peer.</note> how beautiful and deeply satisfying to the human mind is this method of philosophizing based on the immutable and necessary laws of Nature. In this field, René Descartes <note>original: *Cartesius*</note> has surpassed all other mortals by infinite leagues <note>original: *parasangis*; an ancient Persian unit of distance used here metaphorically to mean a great distance.</note>.

<margin>Lucretius, *On the Nature of Things*, Book 3.</margin>
> He surpassed the human race in genius, and outshone all others,
> Just as the rising sun of the heavens outshines the stars.

You should not wonder, then, if I allow myself to indulge in reading his writings somewhat frequently.

8. Nevertheless, although I am quite certain that many of Nature’s phenomena can be demonstrated through mechanical laws, I am equally convinced that not everything—not even a thousandth part—can be explained in that way. First, if the structure of the whole world (including plants, the bodies of animals, and even humans) were formed solely because God set matter in motion to a certain degree, then the creation of the Universe would have to be attributed only to Divine Goodness and Omnipotence, excluding His Wisdom. This is unless someone were to argue that it shows no less wisdom to have deliberately created world-matter that would emerge into this beautiful form of things through the necessary laws of mechanics alone, rather than creating matter that would require countless corrections and adjustments for its wandering motions.

Furthermore, these laws of motion are so simple and behave so similarly everywhere that it seems utterly incredible that such a wonderful variety of things could arise from them. For what does motion ever accomplish except that it moves in a straight line, or at least attempts to do so? Or that one part of matter is reflected by another, or carries it along, or communicates part of its own motion to it? Or finally, that it is broken into various tiny pieces distinguished by size, shape, and position? 

Break any hard body you like, then, and crush it into powder with a pestle, and then examine the individual grains with a microscope <note>original: *microscopio*; the microscope was a relatively new invention in the 17th century, used here to argue against purely mechanical explanations of life.</note>. You will undoubtedly see that the shapes of these dust particles are no different from fragments of rubble, except that they are smaller. Nor do the particles of the "first and third elements" <note>original: *primi tertiique elementi*; terms from Cartesian physics referring to different sizes of particles that make up the universe.</note> differ from these dust motes, except that they are much smaller still. Now go and judge for yourself what beautiful forms of things will arise from the blind collisions, impacts, and coalitions of these confused fragments—or with what artistry they could paint either the wings of butterflies or the tails of peacocks! This is to say nothing of the stupendous design of the Divine Mind in forming...

<page-num>121</page-num>

...forming the internal parts of all animals: where nothing is admitted clumsily, but every single part is perfected with such accurate skill that it is necessary to acknowledge some Principle—far more holy and divine than Matter or bodily motion—watches over this domain. Although we might concede (which I will in no way concede) that certain lower, simpler creatures could be produced in this mechanical way, it is entirely impossible that all species of animals were produced this way, and that none were clumsily formed by such a blind and accidental principle; as I have demonstrated at length in my *Treatise against the Atheists* <note>Referring to More's work *An Antidote against Atheism* (1653).</note>.

Therefore, simply because the motion of Matter can explain some natural occurrences, to trust that everything can be achieved this way seems to me not a legitimate way of philosophizing. Rather, it is a most low sort of <term>Hylolatreia</term> <note>original Greek: $\dot{\upsilon}\lambda o\lambda\alpha\tau\rho\epsilon\acute{\iota}\alpha$</note>—that is, a ridiculous and superstitious adoration and worship of blind Matter. While I have always been sufficiently convinced of this, I have certainly become even more convinced after reading René Descartes <note>original: *Cartesius*</note>. I do not doubt that this incomparable Philosopher has achieved as much as human genius can possibly achieve through the mechanical explanations of things. However, I find that he quite often failed to live up to those great promises of total certainty regarding conclusions deduced from the necessary laws of Mechanics. This happened even when he was explaining the cruder and more general phenomena of Nature <note>original: *Phænomenων*</note>, for he had not yet proceeded beyond those limits. What then do we think he would have done if he had attempted to demonstrate the creation of the human body or any other Animal from those mechanical principles alone?

Whether Descartes wavers or stands his ground, both outcomes are a very pleasant sight to me. For if he proceeds firmly, I have gained a necessary and purely natural speculation. If he stumbles, I also count that as a gain. This does much to prove the truth and certainty of Metaphysics and the demonstration of an Essence entirely distinct from Matter. For if phenomena are found in the world whose creation exceeds the laws of Matter, it is necessary that we introduce an immaterial and incorporeal Principle, which people commonly call Spirit. Everyone knows how some of the bearded and elderly pseudo-philosophers <note>original: *philosophastri*</note> of this age shudder at that word, just as children do at a ghost.

9. But lest any injustice be done to the wonderful genius of Descartes—even though every part of his philosophy does not hold together by this mechanical and plainly necessary connection in a single, continuous chain—it must nevertheless be confessed that many such "small chains" are found that are truly golden and skillfully made. From all of these (which are not bound by the naked laws of Matter alone, but by some more divine force), a beautiful and firm connection of all his conclusions is formed. For example: *Although we cannot be certain from the laws of Mechanics that those "striated particles" <note>In Cartesian physics, these were channeled particles used to explain magnetism and other forces.</note> are formed solely by the twisting of a vortex, as we have already said;* yet we can easily suppose a certain force. Unless we are seized by <term>Hylomania</term> <note>original Greek: $\dot{\upsilon}\lambda o\mu\alpha\nu\acute{\iota}\alpha$; "madness for matter" or the obsession that everything is material.</note> and wish to be so insane as to boldly claim that every single phenomenon in the universe—not even exempting plants, let alone animals—is produced by bodily motion alone, we can easily, I say, suppose some force analogous to that power by which animal fetuses are formed (whether in the mother's womb or in the womb of the Earth, the common parent of all) with such admirable skill...

<header>Letter of Henry More to a Distinguished Man <note>original: *Epistola H. Mori ad V. C.*</note></header>

...are formed by skill, and that they reign in *heaven* just as they do on earth—that is, that *Divine Providence* is excluded by no places or spaces, but is present everywhere. It stands ready to moderate the motions of thinned and subdued *Matter*, so that nothing is omitted or occurs anywhere that does not contribute either to the utility or the beauty of the *Universe*. From this power (whether you prefer to call it the *Soul*, following *Descartes*, or a *Spirit*) which diligently looks after everything and everyone, and exhibits its primary effects in the most subtle and fluid parts of *Matter*, those <term>spoon-shaped particles</term> <note>original: *cochleares illas particulas*. More is referring to Descartes' "striated particles"—screw-shaped bits of matter used to explain magnetism.</note> were timely formed. Without these, the *parallelism of the Earth’s axis*, the *turning points of the seasons*, the *Magnet*, *Navigation*, and the *commerce of Nations* could not exist.

Once the formation of these particles is proven (or at least assumed), all the other things that the distinguished Philosopher teaches—right up to those rich demonstrations concerning magnetic virtues—agree with one another wonderfully. However, I would not wish to swear an oath here that the *Universal Mechanics* are everywhere linked by a plain necessity, as I warned above. But on the contrary, to speak briefly, I suspect rather that in producing almost all *Phenomena* where one sees a sufficiently great variety of parts conspiring toward some notable utility or beauty, the crude impulses and blind inclinations and attempts of *Matter* are always governed and perfected by that divine power. 

As for *Halos and Rainbows* <note>original: *Halones Iridésque*</note> and other things of that kind which have their own beauty, they are created by very simple causes; that variety of parts I mentioned is not found in them in any way. But the *Peacock’s feather* <note>original: *Pavonis pluma*</note>, which seems to represent either an eye or a burning lamp, deserves much more admiration. Its craftsmanship consists of so many distinct threads, so many pleasant colors—now fading, now resuming, and so skillfully blended to form that multi-colored *Ellipse*—that to attribute such a laborious effect to the brute motion of *Matter* or to chance, rather than to design, seems to me a sign of extreme stupidity or madness.

Therefore, the same series of things found in *Descartes* can be safely acknowledged, but not the same connection of this series everywhere. For it is necessary that the *Divine Providence*, the *Governess of the World* and of the generation of things, should interpose itself from time to time.

10. Although *Descartes* did not achieve what I hold for certain no mortal can achieve—namely, that the causes of all natural things be deduced in one continuous and kindred series from head to heel, with no other force interposed except that mechanical and entirely bodily one (the knowledge of whose effects must undoubtedly be considered the pure and simple science of *Nature*)—nevertheless, to the immense pleasure and benefit of the philosophical community, he has at least accurately accomplished this: he has made us clearly understand the immediate efficient causes (which are always kindred and purely bodily) of almost all sensible things which he discusses. This is certainly a difficult province to govern, and none but him have undertaken it who did not rightly regret ever having done so. You perceive at last for how many and how weighty reasons I value *Descartes* so highly.

11. But to hide nothing from you, I still have one peculiar reason which, although it might perhaps seem quite paradoxical to others, nevertheless wins no small favor for *Cartesian Philosophy* with me. That is its conformity with the *Mosaic creation of the World*. You will say I am telling a wonderful thing,

...you tell me. But believe me, it is very likely. For, as you know, there has been a consistent rumor that *Pythagoras* borrowed his wisdom from the *Jews*. Furthermore, in almost every century, there have been those who worked to apply various principles of *Philosophy* now to these and now to those parts of the *Mosaic* text <note>The "Mosaic text" refers to the Five Books of Moses, specifically the creation story in Genesis.</note>. As to their success, I would rather others judge than myself. Therefore, by the common consent of all, one should expect some *Philosophical* meaning to be found there; I add, a meaning worthy of *Moses* and of God. For it is not to be believed that that most intimate Friend of the all-wise God hid cheap or childish things behind that most holy veil of the Letter, but rather things so grand, so noble, and so brilliant that it was rightly feared the eyes of the common people could not bear them. Yet *Moses* and his successors—I mean the *Prophets* and *Priests*—freely communicated these things both to the most proven and wise men of their own nation and to those of other nations.

This *Cabbala* <note>original: *Cabbalam*. More uses "Cabbala" here in its literal sense of "received tradition," referring to an esoteric or philosophical interpretation of scripture supposedly passed down from Moses.</note>, received from the *Jews* and wrapped in numbers representing the works of each day, was highly valued by *Pythagoras*. He did not allow the Secret to leak out to the common people, even if his disciples might sometimes have gossiped about it to the unskilled, hiding the meaning behind those symbolic numbers. Therefore, keeping the kernel for themselves, they threw the fragments of the shell to the <term>uninitiated</term> <note>original: *αμυήτῳ* (uninitiated or unlearned)</note> people; some received these with laughter, others with resentment, and others with a certain suspicious veneration. From this, they committed to writing many truly *Pythagorean* names and powers of numbers. You will ask, "To what purpose is all this?" I will tell you briefly. Indeed, I believe I have found and recovered the kernel itself with the help of these fragments of the shell. For while I was seriously meditating on the *Philosophical* sense of the *Mosaic* creation, casting my eyes here and there—now upon what I judged to be the truest principles of *Philosophy*, now upon the Text itself—I could find none that agreed so precisely with the *Mosaic* page as those *Cartesian* principles.

I discovered that his three Elements <note>Descartes proposed three types of matter: the first (fire/light), the second (air/globules), and the third (earth/heavy particles).</note> were contained there, with not only their number but their natures clearly indicated. I also observed that the Earth revolves around the Sun; indeed, that it and the other Planets are of such a nature as if they themselves had once been Suns. Finally, I saw that the Earth, Moon, and all the other stars were generated from celestial matter. All these things, according to the modest skill in Hebrew words that I possess, I have shown in my *Defense of my Philosophic Cabbala* to agree so well with the *Mosaic* Text that no one—provided they were as certain of the truth of *Cartesian Philosophy* as many claim to be regarding *Aristotelian Principles*—would fail to recognize immediately that I have acted as a most true and faithful Interpreter. If they then notice how exactly the things I assigned to each day agree with the names and powers of those *Pythagorean* numbers, they will surely rejoice in having found a new and significant argument for trusting *Cartesian Philosophy*. They will marvel that this most laborious invention of the human mind is so clearly confirmed by divine reckoning. Yet, I do not dare to trust such demonstrations too much myself. I preferred to call it a *Conjecture*, and I have settled nothing at all, but left the whole matter to the mature judgments of the wisest men.

13. These three points look upon one another with such a wicked expression and a deceitful wink, as if they were seriously conspiring to drive God and Providence out of the world. But there is absolutely nothing to be feared from their plans or their power. For I believe I have sufficiently, thoroughly, and solidly refuted that first opinion in my letters to Descartes <note>original: *Carteſium*</note>. As for the second, the entire second part of my *Treatise Against Atheism* is a constant and unassailable refutation. But I have replied and organized my thoughts elsewhere. I say, therefore, that he held those first two opinions not from any "Atheistic disease," but—as I warned above—solely from an unrestrained itch to conclude everything with purely mathematical certainty. As for the third opinion, he held it out of an excessive zeal for "prudence" <note>Descartes argued humans are too finite to understand God's infinite purposes.</note>. There is no need to dwell on these points any longer, since you can gather a very full response for yourself from what was said above.

14. For concerning the existence of God, the first argument he employs is not only the best that human reason can devise, but is in truth an absolute and perfect demonstration. It is the one Descartes most relied upon, as can be seen in various places in his *Metaphysical Objections and Replies*. From this, it is clear that he brought in those other two arguments (which conclude less firmly, though they do not lack probability and cleverness) primarily for show, so that he would not seem to stand alone in the field.

15. In demonstrating the immortality of the soul, he hardly missed the mark by even a hair's breadth <note>original: *latum quidem pilum*</note>. Since he came so close to the target, I cannot doubt in any way that he firmly believed he had actually hit it. This confidence was further strengthened by the particular bent of his genius; he was so devoted to contemplating the mechanical properties of matter that he could imagine nothing in it except local motion, position, shape, and similar qualities. Therefore, he was certain that thought—which is as different from these as the entire sky—must be attributed to some other substance entirely.

16. <page-num>125</page-num>

### Letter of Henry More to a Distinguished Man <note>original: *Epistola H. Mori ad V. C.*</note>

...[the soul is] clearly distinct from Matter, very many things occur in his writings (where the circumstances themselves sufficiently prove that he acts without any trickery or deceit) by which he is clearly found to contradict himself <note>More means that if Descartes were an atheist, these points would contradict his own alleged materialism.</note>. Such points are:

1. That matter is everywhere one and perfectly homogeneous <term>homogeneous</term><note>Meaning matter is made of the same uniform substance throughout the universe.</note>.
2. That we are certain of this: that we were not born by chance, but were created by a most kind God.
3. That a "substance" is that which exists by its own power; therefore, the term "substance" does not apply to God and his creatures in the same sense <note>original: *univocè*; in philosophy, "univocal" means using a word with exactly the same meaning in different contexts.</note>, yet it does apply in the same sense to both Matter and our mind.
4. That Thought constitutes "thinking substance," while Extension <term>extension</term><note>The property of taking up space, which Descartes defined as the essence of physical matter.</note> constitutes "body." And just as local motion, position, and shape are "modes" <note>original: *modi*; temporary states or qualities of a substance.</note> of the body, so imagination, memory, and will are "modes" of the thinking substance.
5. That imagination is twofold: corporeal and incorporeal. The former uses the brain to exercise our mind, while the latter does so without its help.
6. That we possess free will, and that true nobility <note>original: *generositas*; often translated as "generosity" in Cartesian ethics, referring to a greatness of soul.</note> consists in its legitimate use.
7. That we have a perception of visible objects through a certain image—not a large one, to be sure, but nonetheless extended into various parts—impressed upon the **pineal gland** <note>original: *Conarióque*; Descartes believed the pineal gland was the "seat of the soul" where mind and body interacted.</note>.
8. That there are in our minds certain common notions and ideas of things that are not drawn from the senses, but are clearly innate <note>original: *connatas*; ideas we are born with, like the idea of God or geometry.</note> to the mind itself.
9. Finally, that we conceive of sizes and shapes in one way, but of pains, colors, and similar things in an entirely different way.

All of these points are so intimately connected, partly with the existence of God and partly with the soul's real distinction from the body, that unless Descartes was completely insane, it is impossible that he did not hold both beliefs from his heart.

Regarding the first point, it is manifest from the light of Nature <note>The "light of Nature" refers to truths that are self-evident to human reason.</note> that the same properties, in both kind and degree, belong to simple substances of the same species. For example, just as we are certain that for any circle of any size, the ratio of the diameter to the circumference is always the same everywhere; so we can be sure that the same properties exist in every particle of Matter. Therefore, if Matter were moved immediately by its own nature, it would follow that all Matter—at least if not held back by some force—would be agitated with the same degree of motion. From this, it would be necessary for the Earth and the other planets to melt into a matter equal in thinness and fluidity to the air, or even the ether; or rather, they would never have thickened into such a dense consistency.

It is obvious, therefore, that Matter is naturally at rest—which that most clear-sighted Philosopher <note>René Descartes.</note> openly declared to me in his letters. Thus, it is impossible that he does not inwardly acknowledge some omnipotent Mover of Matter, which is God. Indeed, he must also acknowledge the soul's real distinction from the body, unless he wished to claim that all Matter can feel—which would be utterly ridiculous and unworthy of such a great Philosopher.

Furthermore, he values that second principle so highly that he seriously acknowledges it to be the chief foundation of that certainty which he believes he has regarding all his demonstrations of natural things, as you may see in the *Principles of Philosophy*, Part 4, Article 206.

If you weigh these things correctly and observe the distinct and sober way of writing he uses (in Part 1, Articles 51, 52, 53, 54 of his *Principles of Philosophy*), you will not suspect that he described the third and fourth theorems <note>referring to the previous page's points about God and substance</note> as a joke or a play, but in good faith. This is especially true if you consider it highly unlikely that he would have chosen to prefix a summary of his Metaphysics to his *Principles of Philosophy* unless he felt that, in this way, the entire system would hold together as if by a single, very strong and firm thread.

The fifth conclusion is clearly Platonic, which is the most religious of all philosophies. And the remaining four are of nearly the same kind, clearly arguing that something far superior and far more divine than Matter lives within us.

18. I could gather many more points here that occur throughout his *Letters*, some of which I think it worthwhile to review for you, so that you may see how consistent and unified Descartes is everywhere. Points of this kind include:

1. That it is the soul that sees, not the eyes.
2. That the soul, because of its union with the body, represents certain "goods" to itself as being greater than they actually are.
3. That our free will makes us, in a certain way, equal to God. <margin>To the Queen of Sweden <note>Queen Christina of Sweden</note>, Letter 1.</margin>
4. That there is less harm in losing one's life than in losing the use of Reason. This is because Philosophy alone—even without the teachings of Faith—inspires in us the hope of a better state after death. It makes our soul foresee that nothing would be quite as burdensome as being tied to a body that completely takes away its freedom.
5. That there are two kinds of pleasures: one belonging to the soul alone, and the other to the Human (that is, to the soul insofar as it is united to the body). The latter are fleeting and decaying, while the former, like the soul itself, are immortal.
6. That three things are especially necessary to know for a happy life: the existence of God, the immortality of our souls, and the immensity of the Universe. <margin>To Princess Elizabeth <note>Elizabeth of the Palatinate</note>, Letter 6.</margin>
7. That the soul—when it deliberately thinks of things that can be imagined as well as those that can only be understood—marks the brain with a new impression. This is an "action" of the soul, not a "passion," <term>passion</term><note>In early modern philosophy, a "passion" is a state where the mind is acted upon by the body, whereas an "action" originates in the soul's own will.</note> and this is properly called "imagination."
8. That God’s providence embraces all things, the smallest as well as the largest. <margin>To the same, Letter 8.</margin>
9. That love is twofold: either Intellectual or Corporeal. The latter is properly a passion, while the former belongs to the soul even when it is separated from the body.
10. That God is Spirit, or a Thinking Thing of infinite perfection, and our soul is a sort of dim image of Him. <margin>To Mr. Chanut <note>Pierre Chanut, French ambassador and friend of Descartes</note>, Letter 35.</margin>
11. That a human being does not "understand" with the body. For the mind, even if it is hindered by the body, cannot be helped by the body at all in understanding immaterial things, but can only be impeded. <margin>To Henricus Regius, Letter 81.</margin>
12. That in corporeal things, all action and passion consist in local motion alone... <note>original Latin text: *In rebus corporeis omnem actionem & passionem in solo motu locali*</note>

Many other points remain that support this, both in his *Letters* and in his *Treatise on the Passions* <note>original: *Tractatu de Affectibus*</note>; however, I gladly skip over them so as not to be endless. I only add that it is by no means likely that a mind so pure and refined—filled with such modesty, humanity, and integrity of character—could have fallen into such a foul pit and stinking abyss as atheism.

19. Nothing therefore remains, as far as I know, for which Descartes could be suspected of Atheism, unless it is because he is rightly regarded as the most excellent of all Philosophers. For there is a certain fanatical type of people who believe that the wiser and more knowledgeable of Nature someone becomes, the further they must be from all Religion. It is as if they believe that the more ignorant and stupid a person is, the more fit he is for the worship of God.

Ancient nations once invented the story that the Jews worshipped a statue with a donkey’s head, and they hoped by this means to bring great disgrace upon them. In the same way, those people seem to me to insult God himself when they imagine that He cannot be rightly worshipped by anyone except "Donkey-heads" <note>original: *Onocephalis*; a reference to the "onolatry" myth, a common ancient slur against Jews and early Christians</note>. Truly, it is not at all necessary to bring ignorance and lack of knowledge to divine worship, but rather an Innocence that is whiter than any snow or light.

20. The other objections which you write are frequently raised are more tolerable, but no less ridiculous: specifically, that this incomparable Philosopher was out of his mind and seized by dizziness. I believe those foolish people were alluding to his doctrine of **Vortices** <note>Descartes' theory that the planets are carried around the sun by "whirlpools" of celestial matter</note>. A fine joke indeed, and worthy of Descartes' detractors! 

But they seriously insist that such unexpected, wandering, and far-fetched inventions are found in his writings that they could not possibly belong to any man unless he was insane. "For who is there," they say, "among sober and careful men, who would ever dare to explain the way the Sun, Stars, and Planets were formed? Or to define in detail by what shapes and motions of Matter light and individual colors are created? Or finally, to openly state that this hard and opaque Earth we walk upon was once a shining Star?" 

But I have no doubt that I can easily prove that it is not Democritus <note>More uses the name of the ancient Greek atomist to represent the "mad" scientist archetype</note> who is insane, but the public. It should not be attributed to any madness of Descartes that he discovered such wonderful Paradoxes, but rather to the laziness and stupidity of others that they had not stumbled upon similar thoughts themselves.

21. For Descartes thought of nothing in all these matters except what was very easy to think for a sharp mind, partly from obvious experiments and partly from new and accurate observations and conclusions of both this and recent centuries. Various Philosophers and Astronomers—acting as workers of a lower order—had already cleared the rubble and prepared the material for this sublime and truly architectural genius.

<page-num>128</page-num>
<header>Letter of Henry More to a Distinguished Man <note>original: *Epistola H. Mori ad V. C.*</note></header>

...space had been reduced to fluid ether. Most of the more noble astronomers and philosophers had with one voice approved the ancient doctrine concerning the motion of the Earth, which was renewed by Copernicus. They placed the Earth itself on the list of planets by common consent, for they discovered it not only turning around the Sun, but also (like the Moon) reflecting the Sun's light—even back onto the Moon itself—during eclipses and new moons. **Galileo** established that the Sun is a fixed star, and that the fixed stars are themselves so many suns. With his optical tube <note>original: *Tubo suo optico* (the telescope)</note>, he discovered Jupiter surrounded by four satellites running around it, like so many little moons. **Scheiner** <note>Christoph Scheiner (1573–1650), a Jesuit astronomer who studied sunspots.</note>, in an immense volume, provided a full and perfect teaching on solar spots: their creation, dissipation, and motion around the Sun, as well as the Sun's rotation on its own axis. Many had observed that some of the fixed stars appear now larger, now smaller—and indeed, that entirely new ones sometimes appear and then soon vanish. **Tycho** himself and others demonstrated by the most certain signs that comets, equal to or larger than the Earth, travel through the region of the planets. Finally, **Gilbert** <note>William Gilbert (1544–1603), author of *De Magnete*.</note> not only explained the powers of the magnet with the greatest skill and industry but—what is the heart of the matter—he confirmed with the most evident arguments that the Earth itself is one giant magnet.

22. Let us now diligently consider, I ask you, how **Descartes** derived conclusions from these findings that were neither wandering nor far-fetched, but obvious and closely linked with the observations of the most respected philosophers. We will see that the chief foundation of his philosophy was laid in a fact that the perigee of Mars and the phases of Venus had forced even an unwilling Tycho to admit: namely, the **fluidity of the heavens**. For Descartes understood perfectly what it means to be fluid; he realized it cannot happen unless matter is broken into the smallest particles by a violent motion pervading all its parts, shaking and separating them in every direction. The largest part of these particles (having been worn down by constant shaking and collisions) cannot help but become round over time. Nor can the triangular gaps between them fail to be filled by much smaller particles of matter, which were scraped off during the formation of the round ones. Finally, these fragments are so much more abundant than the triangular gaps between the round ones that those spherical particles, which he calls *globules*, can float loosely in this most subtle matter of all.

<margin>* See Section 7.</margin>
23. Furthermore, since it is admitted by all that the heaven is not only fluid, but that the Earth and the planets are carried around the Sun in this liquid heaven; and since it is contrary to the laws of nature * for either the Earth or the planets to be carried around the Sun in any way other than being conveyed by the motion of the celestial matter itself; it was clearly evident to Descartes that this huge mass of celestial matter, in which the planets and the Earth are found, is necessarily swept into a circuit <note>original: *vortex*</note> around the Sun. A further indication of this could be the rotation of the Sun itself around its own axis, just as a vortex of water carrying straws and leaves on its edge is a familiar and easy example of that phenomenon.

24. Lastly, from this sweeping motion of the celestial matter which we now find occurring around the Sun, he could not help but be reminded that the Sun itself was once generated, following that obvious experiment of a lead weight whirled in a sling. It was necessary...

<meta>This page continues Henry More’s explanation of René Descartes' cosmological system. Having established that the heavens are fluid and the Earth moves, More now explains how the Sun and stars were formed within "vortices" of matter and how light and color are produced mechanically.</meta>

<page-num>129</page-num>
<header>Letter of Henry More to a Distinguished Man <note>original: *Epistola H. Mori ad V. C.*</note></header>
<page-type>text</page-type>

It followed, therefore, that he concluded that as the more solid particles of the sky—namely the ethereal globules—receded from the center of the vortex, the most subtle matter (which we said was somewhat in excess) occupied their place. This matter filled that entire space where we now see the Sun; or, if you prefer, that space filled with this subtle matter in this way is nothing other than the very Sun we behold. Truly, when he observed such a great affinity between the Sun and the fixed stars—since both possess light in themselves and neither move from their place—it was an easy and natural task, following the example of **Galileo**, to number our Sun among the fixed stars. He attributed the same mode of production to both equally, and thus divided the entire matter of the visible world into almost infinite vortices, according to the number of the stars.

<margin>* See Section 6.</margin>

25. Once these points were proved, the intimate nature of light and brightness common to the stars and the Sun immediately became known to him. He saw that it consists in this: that the celestial globules, pushed partly by their own motion and partly by the motion of the subtle matter, are pressed toward our eyes. He could be most certain of this because it was clearly evident to him—and can easily be evident to all others except those who are completely dull—that sensation is nothing other than the perception of bodily motion, modified by certain laws and transmitted from an object into a sense organ. Furthermore, having thoroughly seen into the nature of light, the nature of colors revealed itself spontaneously. For it was very natural for him to think that if the perception of motion transmitted through these globules is *Light*, then by varying this motion, the perception itself would be varied. No variation occurred to him as easy and obvious as the ratio of the circular motion of the globules to their straight-line motion; and he demonstrated so solidly and ingeniously through the experiment of the prism that he had guessed correctly in this matter, that he left no room whatsoever to doubt the certainty of this theorem in the future.

26. And as for that final and greatest paradox of all—namely, that this Earth which we tread with our feet and handle with our hands was once a Sun or a fixed star—certainly there are many things that not only invited but almost forced him to think so. For even now, all but the lowest-ranking philosophers boldly profess that the Earth is a planet. Moreover, the satellites of **Jupiter** indicated clearly that Jupiter once reigned upon a throne of light, just like the Sun (which is now surrounded by so many planets); and that those faithful companions who once played around him while he was shining did not desert him even after he lost his light and fell. From this, no small suspicion could occupy his mind that Suns or fixed stars can be changed into planets as the centuries proceed.

He easily understood the method by which this could happen from the spots on the Sun <note>original: *maculis Solis* (sunspots)</note>, which have sometimes so covered its face that its heat was scarcely sufficient for ripening the crops, and fearful mortals thought the final fate of the world was at hand. **Virgil** also mentions this saddest of events in the *Georgics*:

> -> *When he covered his bright head with dark rust,* <-
> -> *And the impious ages feared eternal night.* <-
> <note>original: *Cùm caput obscurâ nitidum ferrugine tinxit, / Impiáque æternam timuerunt secula noctem.* Virgil, Georgics 1.467-8.</note>

But it was also very easy for him to predict that stars or suns are actually sometimes so covered and encrusted with spots that they are deprived of all light and harden into a manifold crust, as seen from those new stars in **Cassiopeia**, **Cygnus**, and elsewhere that appeared unexpectedly...

<summary>Henry More explains Descartes' theory that the Sun and stars are centers of vortices made of subtle matter and that light is a mechanical pressure. He also argues that planets like Earth and Jupiter were once glowing stars that became "crusted over" by sunspots until they lost their light.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Henry More’s explanation of René Descartes' cosmology, specifically detailing how stars become "encrusted" and turn into planets or comets, and how Earth's magnetism serves as evidence for its solar origins.</meta>

<page-num>130</page-num>
<header>Letter of Henry More to a Distinguished Man <note>original: *Epistola H. Mori ad V. C.*</note></header>

...seen appearing and then vanishing again after some time had passed. To these you may add that one of the seven Pleiades was struck out <note>original: *elisam*; referring to the "Lost Pleiad," a star in the cluster that ancient observers noted had disappeared.</note>.

Furthermore, what could happen afterward to such encrusted and opaque globes, he conjectured with equal ease from the nature of the **Vortices**, which he understood perfectly. For he knew well that once a star is extinguished, its vortex languishes and is greatly weakened; from this, it must necessarily be plundered and snatched away by neighboring vortices flooding toward its center. The encrusted star would soon be carried away by the strongest of them; then, depending on its own solidity, it would either escape from the "hand" of the captor or descend so close to the center that it would be forced to orbit around that Star or Sun.

This conjecture was confirmed both by the Planets—which rotate around the Sun at different distances according to their different solidity, especially Jupiter, Saturn, and the Earth (whose attendance by moons <note>original: *satellitium*</note> suggested they were once Suns or Stars)—and by the path of Comets wandering in the highest part of our Sun’s vortex. For it was easy for him to guess from the size and distance of the Comets that they were encrusted fixed stars, or wandering Planets, seeking a fixed seat for themselves in some vortex and attempting to descend to our region of Planets. What, then, could a man of such sagacious and free intellect do here? How could he withhold his assent when lured by so many flattering and likely signs?

<margin>See Section 5.</margin>
27. Nor have we yet reached the peak of the matter. Thus far, those phenomena only suggested to him from a distance that it was possible all Planets had once been Suns. But when he contemplated this planet of ours (I mean the Earth) up close, and discovered it to be a Magnet according to the doctrine of **Gilbert** <note>William Gilbert (1544–1603), who proposed that the Earth itself is a giant magnet.</note>, he realized it could only be so if it were wrapped in layers of iron or material harder than iron. He saw that the primary power of a Magnet consists in this: that certain insensible particles are formed with such a shape that those which enter through one pole of the Magnet cannot enter through the other. (This was certain to him, both from the mutual repulsion of Magnets when their like poles are brought together, and from the traces of the Magnetic Vortex marked in iron filings.) Furthermore, he saw that these particles were so subtle that they could penetrate wood, glass, gold, and any other body, no matter how solid. 

The direction of the Earth’s poles indicated to him that these particles even flow down from the sky. He was persuaded that their greatest force and abundance are found around the axes of the celestial Vortices, both by the size of the particles already formed and the manner of their formation. For they must be formed where the Matter of the "first element" <note>In Cartesian physics, the "first element" consists of the finest, most mobile particles that form the sun and stars.</note> begins to grow sluggish due to the slower motion of the vortex (which undoubtedly happens near the axes of the vortices, and especially toward the poles). Once formed, if they ever wander far from the axes of the vortices (since they are larger and slower than the other particles of the first element), they are pushed back again toward the axes. When **Descartes** saw all these things so clearly, it would have been a wonder if he had not acknowledged—not so much lured as compelled—that the Earth was once positioned in the axis of some Vortex, and there, as if in the most opportune place of all, it acquired its magnetism.

28. But to return to the other main points of the arguments: an even greater necessity for concluding this way weighed upon him, because he had divided the entire matter of the visible world—and that with the greatest judgment—into so many vortices...

--- Page 377 ---
<meta>This page continues Henry More's defense and analysis of René Descartes' cosmological theories, specifically focusing on the composition of the Earth and the mechanical evidence—such as magnetism—that suggests the Earth was once a star at the center of a vortex.</meta>

<page-num>131</page-num>
<header>Letter of Henry More to a Distinguished Man <note>original: *Epistola H. Mori ad V. C.*</note></header>

...that stars consisted of only two elements: namely, the most subtle matter <note>the "first element" in Cartesian physics, consisting of the finest, most fluid particles</note> and globules <note>the "second element," which forms the light-carrying ether</note>. He demonstrated that the globules could in no way bond together because of their shape and smoothness. However, he clearly showed that the most subtle matter could do so very easily, as evidenced by those spots so often observed on the Sun <note>sunspots</note>. To someone weighing every detail according to the laws of Nature, it seemed utterly impossible to find such a vast quantity of this matter—enough to compose the massive bulk of the Earth—anywhere except in the center of some **Vortex**.

Nor could he evade the force of this argument by imagining that those extremely hard magnetic crusts of the Earth were not actually "overlaid" crusts, but that the interior of the Earth is now, and always has been, a part of matter that is naturally solid and hard—that is, matter not yet broken into minute particles by that universal motion which tests all things. Indeed, this fabrication is contradicted both by the Earth's steady orbit around the Sun and by magnetism itself. For if the Earth were so solid, it would immediately break out of this Vortex, be cast into another, and continually escape from that one as well; thus, it would wander forever from vortex to vortex, never entering any except by "Cato’s law"—only to leave immediately <note>original: *Catonis lege*; a legal reference to a person who enters a place merely to satisfy a formality before departing.</note>. Furthermore, it could not be a Magnet in any way. For how could those slender magnetic particles hollow out channels for themselves in such a solid body?

29. It was therefore very clear to him that the interior crusts of the Earth must have been soft at some point—that is, they must have bonded together from certain minute particles. And not just any particles, but the smallest of all. He understood from experiments conducted before his own eyes that the subtlety of magnetic particles is such that he clearly perceived no body joined together from particles larger than those of the <term>first element</term> <note>the finest grade of matter</note> could be capable of forming channels with such thin and delicate craftsmanship. Any larger gaps would be too loose, and the particles themselves too hard—and perhaps not wide enough—to be bored into that twisted, screw-like shape. Any matter consisting of a coarser thread and texture than that most subtle matter of all would be far less fit for receiving these tiny (yet distinctly crafted) channels than a rough piece of oak or ash would be for receiving the images of the Caesars, which are usually carved with equal precision in the smallest space of the most precious gemstones. In this way, he demonstrated to himself that the magnetic crusts of the Earth clearly consist of the matter of the first element. Since he could not find a sufficient quantity of this matter to build the Earth anywhere outside the centers of the Vortices, it was necessary that the primary matter of the Earth was once located in the very axis of some Vortex. In this way, the Planet Earth could be a Magnet, after it had ceased to be a Sun or a Star.

30. If, therefore, Descartes was "insane," it must be said that he was insane with the highest degree of reason. But he was not so insane as to conclude anything more from such clear indications than that the nature of things is so arranged *as if* this Earth, which we inhabit, was formerly a Sun or a fixed Star. You see Descartes’ character—how cautious and modest it is, and how solid and sober in every respect.

31. But if this most noble Philosopher is not to be greatly blamed in most things, I believe he is chiefly to be criticized for this: that he indulged his mathematical and mechanical genius far too much in explaining the phenomena of Nature. Yet, meanwhile, I recognize the good fortune of such great minds, so that even their faults and errors possess a certain appearance of virtue...

<meta>This page continues Henry More’s letter, moving from his specific defense of Cartesian physics to a broader discussion of how these scientific discoveries support his metaphysical project (his "Cabbala") and help defend religion against skepticism and vice.</meta>

<page-num>132</page-num>
<header>Letter of Henry More to a Distinguished Man <note>original: *Epistola H. Mori ad V. C.*</note></header>

...and fruit. Indeed, it seems entirely incredible to me that he <note>Descartes</note> would have ever attempted so many great things, or successfully completed them, unless he had been motivated by that vast hope of demonstrating nearly all the phenomena of the world through the necessary laws of mechanics. His work has succeeded so well that I cannot help but suspect he has largely restored the ancient science regarding nature. If a perceptive and peaceful posterity judges that I have guessed correctly in this matter, they will place even greater trust in the rest of my *Cabbala* <note>More refers to his work *Conjectura Cabbalistica*, where he tries to reconcile Cartesian science with Platonic and Jewish tradition</note>. 

In that work, however—just as in the physical part—they will find that I have only pointed out a few conclusions or principles of metaphysics. Vast and gaping holes remain between them, which must be filled primarily from Platonic writings—or at least by someone whom a later fate may present to the world with a mind even greater than Plato’s. This person would search more deeply into the nature of God and other incorporeal <note>immaterial or spiritual</note> things. They would examine their countless states, looking both forward and backward, and measure their immense cycles. Finally, by weighing everything based on the attributes of the Supreme Being and the specific powers of immaterial orders, they would easily solve those riddles and traps with which wicked and idle men often entangle devoted religious followers. 

Consequently, in the future, nothing—except perhaps a miserable narrowness of mind, a contemptible stupidity, or an uncontrollable and deplorable urge to commit crimes (along with the agonizing fear of future punishment resulting from those crimes)—could prevent mortals from embracing the primary foundations of religion with sincere and unshakable agreement. I admit it may not seem very glorious to some that I have spoken of these hopes and of matters that we ourselves may not be able to fulfill in any part. Yet, I do not doubt that it is honorable to have shown, in passing, one's passion and zeal for promoting the public good of humankind, and to have held out a torch, in some small way, for the centuries to follow.

32. Regarding those who, as you say, look down on all philosophy because of the "trifles" of Aristotle, and who assume that none of the things philosophers write about can be known with certainty—or that, even if known, they contribute little to the common use of life—I have no better response than what Scaliger <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger (1484–1558), a renowned Renaissance scholar</note> once threw back at men of that sort: *“Ignorant people usually find no greater pleasure in their ignorance than a ready and disdainful contempt.”* <note>original: *Nullam utique majorem ignaris inscitiam parere solere voluptatem quàm expeditam fastidiosúmque contemptum.*</note> 

Truly, however, that should not be considered a "pleasure" so much as a kind of consolation and a lessening of the pain they might feel from the sense of their own loss and the forfeiture of the best things. Nature has implanted in all of us a great desire to know; it is a significant part of our natural conscience that we should not be as stupid and ignorant as cattle. Yet, we are not expected to know impossible or useless things. Thus, it is clear that those who complain so loudly that nothing can be known are not so much insulting the speculations of philosophy as they are seeking an honorable pretext for themselves. They want to excuse the fact that they spend almost their entire lives on luxury, greed, or ambition.

33. However, René Descartes has taught so clearly that something *can* be known in natural matters, that no one can doubt it any more than they can doubt mathematical demonstrations...

<meta>catchword: demonstrations <note>original: *strationibus*</note></meta>
