<meta>This page concludes Henry More’s letter. He has been arguing that Descartes' mechanical explanations of the universe do not lead to atheism, but rather clarify the boundaries between the physical and the spiritual, ultimately supporting More's own philosophical and religious project.</meta>

<page-num>133</page-num>
<header>Letter of Henry More to a Distinguished Man <note>original: *Epistola H. Mori ad V. C.*</note></header>

...demonstrations, the same man must necessarily doubt. Rather, to speak more freely—and setting aside this harmful modesty—if we stay within the shared boundaries of both philosophies, we must conclude that Descartes knew as much about investigating the causes of nature as Aristotle failed to understand. We should not judge what a serious and insightful mind can achieve in philosophy based on the work of a man who was certainly clever, but lacked substance—a man who had not even discovered the first principles of true philosophy.

34. "But suppose," they say, "that Descartes did find those true principles and brought to light the natural and immediate causes of all phenomena <note>original: *Phænomenων* (Greek)</note>—things that clever little Greek <note>Aristotle; More uses the diminutive *Graeculus* dismissively</note> never knew; what practical use do these things have for life?" If by "practical use" they mean honors, wealth, and physical pleasures, I freely admit that his work contributes little to those things. Yet I maintain that in the true way of philosophizing, one finds something far more excellent than honors, more precious than wealth, and ultimately much sweeter and far more enjoyable than all bodily pleasures. Those who believe that the things which nourish, adorn, and cheer the mind with a divine joy contribute nothing to human life seem to have entirely forgotten that they even possess a mind. They are practically admitting that they live the lives of mere animals <note>original: *belluinam*</note>.

Farewell, most distinguished sir <note>original: *V. C.* (Viro Clarissimo)</note>. If I have perhaps discussed these matters with you more at length and more freely than I should have, please forgive this excessive eagerness to please you, and continue to hold me in your affection as you always do.

->H. M. <note>Henry More</note><-

<page-num>131</page-num>

For these reasons, he must necessarily doubt. Indeed, to speak more freely—once we have set aside that internal modesty and humility <note>original: *ταπεινότητι* (Greek)</note>—if we were to keep ourselves strictly within the common boundaries of philosophy, we would perhaps need to diminish our investigation into the causes of Nature as much as we do in the lazy, idle versions of philosophy. We must not judge what can be achieved in philosophy by a light or sluggish mind, or by the claim that a man has such a pious faith that he can discover the principles of a solid and true first philosophy.

But let us grant, I say, to that most Excellent Christian <note>referring to René Descartes</note> that he discovered those true causes, and those natural and immediate effects of the Creator's phenomena <note>original: *Phænomenon*</note>. Even if he did not so much bring them to light as struggle to behold them; if by "struggle" one means seeking honors, wealth, or bodily pleasures, I admit he did not achieve much toward those ends. But is there not something far more excellent than honor, more pleasing than greed, and far more enjoyable than even the health and pleasures of the body to be found in the true order of things and the true way of philosophizing? Those who think that things which lead the mind toward a divine level and bring the light of truth contain nothing useful for life seem to have entirely forgotten that they possess a mind; they are content to endure a life fit only for animals <note>original: *belluinam*</note>.

Farewell, most Distinguished Man <note>original: *V. C.* for *Vir Clarissime*</note>. If this discourse—perhaps more trivial and unrestrained than is proper—should settle upon you like a cloud, please forgive this token of my respect; do not judge all my future works by this one.

->H. M.<- <note>Henry More (Latin: *Morus Henricus*)</note>

### To the Right Honorable
# **EDWARD**,
### Lord Viscount
## **CONWAY** and **KILULTA**.

My Lord,

Although I am not unaware of your Lordship’s distaste <note>original: "averness"</note> for all addresses of this kind—whether it is because your Lordship has noticed the common vanity of those who dedicate books, trying to win over their patrons with overly generous praise that far exceeds the worth of the person they so immeasurably commend; or whether it comes from a natural modesty that cannot bear even a fair description of your own virtues and abilities; or finally, from a very accurate observation that very few treatises are written today that are anything more than mere transcriptions or collections from other authors whose writings were already dedicated to the name and memory of other worthy people long since deceased (so that they effectively rob the dead to provide themselves with gifts to offer the living)—yet despite this distaste, or whatever reasons might be imagined for it, I could not stop myself from making this present dedication. 

I confess I do it not so much to please your Lordship (though that might not be the most polite compliment) as for my own satisfaction and contentment. For I take no greater pleasure in anything than in the awareness <note>original: "conscience"</note> of the appropriateness and suitability of my own actions. Among these actions, I can find none more perfectly just and appropriate than this dedication, as there are many reasons that give you a unique right and title to the patronage of this present discourse. For besides your skill in philosophy and

and a real sense of piety—two such qualities as are rarely found together (especially in people of high rank), yet without which matters of this nature can neither be read with any enjoyment <note>original: "relish"</note> nor easily understood. There are also other, more specific reasons that naturally guide and lead me to the choice I have made. 

For whether I consider the many kindnesses from yourself and your closest relatives—especially from your noble and virtuous lady <note>Anne Conway (1631–1679), a brilliant philosopher and More’s pupil, who later wrote "The Principles of the Most Ancient and Modern Philosophy."</note>, whom I can never think of without admiration nor mention without the highest respect; or whether I recall the first occasion of occupying my thoughts with this subject, which was when I had the honor and pleasure of reading René Descartes’ *The Passions of the Soul* <note>original: "Des-Cartes his Passions"</note> with your Lordship in the Luxembourg Gardens to pass the time (in which treatise, though there is nothing but what is elegant and clever, yet everything did not seem so perfectly solid and satisfactory to me that I was not forced to seek answers for myself regarding some principal matters); or finally, if I call to mind that pleasant retreat I enjoyed at Ragley Hall <note>The Conway family estate in Warwickshire, which became a center for the Cambridge Platonists.</note> during my stay with you there—the polite treatment I received from that perfect and faultless example of a truly noble and Christian matron, the Right Honorable Lady your mother; the solemnity of the place; those shady walks; those hills and woods where, having often lost sight of the rest of the world and the world of me, I discovered in that hidden solitude the best theories in the following discourse—I say, whether I considered all these circumstances or any one of them, I could only judge them to be more than enough to lead me to choose such a worthy patron.

Nor could the previously mentioned suspicions <note>referring to the reasons for Lord Conway’s distaste for dedications mentioned on the previous page, such as flattery or unoriginality.</note> drive me from my plan, as they do not apply to this case at all. For my part, I am such a great lover of the truth and so little an admirer of common eloquence that neither the prospect of any material gain <note>original: "gross Advantage"</note> could ever make me stoop so low as to expose myself to the vile infamy or suspicion of becoming a flatterer; nor could the tingling sensation of applause and vanity make me seek the hollow <note>original: "puffy"</note> name and title of an orator. Thus, your Lordship may be certain regarding that first suspicion.

And truly, regarding the second point: although I admit I would not be at all opposed to providing a fair and accurate description of your virtues and accomplishments, when I consider how great they are and how poor my own writing <note>original: "Rhetorick"</note> is, I realized it is not even within my power to offend <note>original: "entrench upon"</note> your modesty, even if I wanted to. Therefore, I must leave it to a more talented writer to give both you and the world the credit you deserve, whether you like it or not.

And finally, regarding that concern about the theft or petty sacrilege committed by various plagiarists <note>More is likely referring to the common 17th-century practice of writers copying heavily from earlier scholars without credit.</note>—who, in a sense, rob the monuments of the dead to decorate the living—this is the only thing I can state without vanity: what I offer you is truly my own. By that, I mean the invention, application, and arrangement of the reasons and arguments contained in this book—whether they are used to disprove or support a point—are the genuine result of my own careful and thoughtful mind. It is not old material stolen or borrowed from other writers. It would be too arrogant for me to decide beforehand how much truth and weight <note>original: "solidity"</note> there is in my principles and reasoning. This must be left to the judgment of independent and discerning minds <note>original: "free and discerning spirits"</note> like your Lordship’s. If what I have written finds acceptance or a favorable review <note>original: "censure"</note> from you, it will be an even greater honor and encouragement to,

->My Lord,<-

->Your Lordship's humbly devoted servant,<-

->HENRY MORE.<-

<header>The Epistle Dedicatory.</header>

And finally, regarding the second point: although I admit I would not be at all excessive in providing a fair and accurate description of your virtues and accomplishments, when I consider the basis of those virtues and the nature of my own education, I realized it is not within my power—even if I wished to—to offend <note>original: "encroach upon"</note> your modesty. Therefore, I must leave it to a more talented writer <note>original: "able Pen"</note> to give both you and the world the credit you deserve, whether you like it or not.

And finally, regarding that concern about the style <note>original: "Draught"</note> or habit of various authors <note>original: "Figures"</note> who, in a sense, rob the monuments of the dead to decorate the living—this is the only thing I can state without vanity: what I offer you is truly my own. By that, I mean the invention, application, and arrangement of the reasons and arguments contained in this book—whether they are used to prove or disprove a point—are the genuine results of my own careful <note>original: "anxious"</note> and thoughtful mind, and not stolen or borrowed from other writers. It would be a piece of arrogance for me to judge how much truth and weight <note>original: "solidity"</note> there is in my principles and reasoning. This must be left to the judgment of independent and discerning minds <note>original: "free and discerning Spirits"</note> like your Lordship’s. If what I have written finds acceptance or a favorable interpretation <note>original: "construction"</note> from you, it will be the greatest honor and encouragement to,

->My Lord,<-

->Your Lordship's most devoted servant,<-

->HENRY MORE.<-

## The CONTENTS of the Preface.

1. The *Title* of the *Discourse* and how it is to be understood. 
2. The *Author's* submission of his entire *treatise* to the infallible rule of *Holy Scripture* <note>original: "Sacred Writ"</note>. 
3. A plain and concise <note>original: "compendious"</note> demonstration that *matter* consists of indivisible <term>indiscerpible</term> parts. 
4. An answer to an objection regarding his demonstration against the *Sun's* control <note>original: "superintendency"</note> over the affairs of the Earth. 
5. A confirmation of Mr. *Hobbes's* <note>original: "Hobbs"</note> opinion: that *perception* is actually the same as *physical motion* and *reaction*, if there is nothing but *matter* in the world. 
6. A defense <note>original: "Apologie"</note> of the "vehicles" <note>In More's philosophy, these are the subtle, quasi-physical bodies used by spirits</note> of *demons* and *separated souls*. 
7. As well as for his precise description of the state of the afterlife, and his detailed <note>original: "curiously"</note> definition of the nature of an individual *spirit*. 
8. That the *Elysiums* <note>The paradises of the afterlife</note> he describes are not at all *sensual*, but *divine*. 
9. That he has not made the condition of the wicked too easy for them in the other world. 
10. A demonstration through the act of memory that it is not *one universal soul* that hears, sees, and reasons in every person. 
11. Regarding the *Spirit of Nature*; that it is not an obscure principle, nor is it introduced without good reason. 
12. That he has absolutely demonstrated its existence. 
13. That accepting that principle need not hinder the progress of *mechanical philosophy* <note>The study of the natural world through physical laws and mechanisms</note>. 
14. The great pleasure of that study for religious and rational people. 
15. The great importance it would have if *Descartes* <note>original: "Des-Cartes"</note> were generally read in all the *universities* of *Christendom*. 
16. An apology for the length <note>original: "prolixity"</note> of his preface, arising from his earnest desire to serve the public without giving the least offense to any rational or noble <note>original: "ingenuous"</note> mind.

*In order that this* treatise *may be received more freely and smoothly by readers, without causing any offense or doubt to the good and pious, or giving any real reason for objection or petty criticism from those whose* claims *to* reason *are greater than their* religion; *I shall attempt in this* preface *to prevent such issues by bringing into view, and more fully explaining and clearing, whatever I believe might be subject to their misunderstandings or verbal attacks <note>original: "obloquies"</note>.*

1. *Indeed, I cannot be certain that even the* title *of my* discourse *won't be disliked by both groups. And therefore they may perhaps claim that such an ambitious* title *seems to compete with the high* privilege *of* Christianity, *which has brought life and immortality to light.*

# The PREFACE.

<margin>Book 3, chapter 14.</margin>

...their belief that they are wholly mortal. For unless they will ridiculously imagine <note>original: "conceit"</note> themselves to be inspired—even though they almost as little believe there is either **God** or **Spirit** as they believe they have an **Immortal Soul** in them—they must either claim the experience of **Sense** or the clarity of **Reason**. The former is impossible, because these bold deniers of the **Immortality of the Soul** have not yet experienced whether we survive <note>original: "subsist"</note> after **Death** or not. But if they want us to believe they have reached this conclusion on rational grounds, I challenge them to produce any stronger **Reasons** for their **Cause** than those I have set down for them, and to see if I have not fully and fundamentally answered them. 

If they say their confidence comes from the weak arguments of the opposing party, I answer that it is foolish of them to be so sure that **Truth** is on their side rather than their opponents', especially when their own arguments are just as inconclusive as they imagine their adversaries' to be. But this only applies to those versions of the **Cause** they have already seen and criticized. That has nothing to do with me, as I could never feel I stood securely except on my own feet. Therefore, I only ask them to read through what I have written before they venture to judge it. After they have read it, if they declare that I have not demonstrated the **Cause** I have undertaken, I think it is only reasonable and just that they specifically show in which part or joint of my **Demonstration** they see such a weak connection that it emboldens them to still disagree with the **Conclusion**.

<margin>Book 5, chapters 1, 2, and 3. Also Book 6, chapter 11, section 13, and Book 8, chapter 17.</margin>

But to others, I answer with more modesty and submission: the **Title** of my **Book** does not necessarily imply a promise of such a full and perfect **Demonstration** that nothing more could be added for a firmer assurance of the **Truth**. Rather, it implies only that one may expect as clear a **Proof** as **Natural Reason** <note>The human capacity for logic and understanding without divine help</note> can provide us. From this, they should instead infer that I do acknowledge a further and more obvious evidence contained in the **Christian Religion**. This religious evidence is more understandable and convincing to the general **World**, who have neither the time nor the desire to deal with the complexities <note>original: "spinosities"</note> and anxieties of human **Reason** and **Philosophy**. However, I declined to use that **Argument** at this time; partly because I intend to speak more fully on it in my treatise on the ***Mystery of Christian Religion***, if **God** permits; and partly because it was unsuitable for the current **Title**, which claims to handle the matter only within the bounds of **Natural Light** <note>Human reason unassisted by supernatural revelation</note>, unassisted and unguided by any miraculous **Revelation**.

2. This will be a pleasant sight to those who have a natural talent <note>original: "Genius"</note> for these kinds of **Contemplations**, and it is entirely without danger. As long as they remember that it is the voice of **Reason** and **Nature** (which, being subject to corruption, may very well be defective or erroneous in some things), and therefore never trust its dictates and suggestions where they clash with the **Divine Oracles** <note>The Holy Scriptures</note>, they will certainly be safe from all deception. Though, I must say, I do not know of anything I assert in this **Treatise** that disagrees with them. But if anyone more perceptive than myself discovers anything not according to that **Rule**, it may be an occasion for humble thankfulness to **God** for the great privilege of being born under a higher and more exact light. By that light, those who are most perfectly trained in it are enabled to correct what is distorted <note>original: "perverse"</note> as well as to supply what is lacking in the light of **Nature**. They have my full permission in advance to do both thoroughly throughout the following **Discourse**.

# The PREFACE.

This may serve as a more general defense. But so that nothing is missing, I will also proceed to justify certain specific details—as many as are necessary to further clarify and confirm.

3. In the First Book, there are only two such points that I am aware of. The first concerns the **Center of a particular Spirit**, whose concept <note>original: "Idea"</note> I have described and proved to be possible. The other concerns my demonstration of the impossibility of the **Sun** seeing anything on Earth, assuming the Sun is merely physical <note>original: "corporeal"</note>. In justifying the former, I have taken the liberty to assert that **Matter** consists of **indiscerpible** <term>indiscerpible: atoms or particles that are indivisible and cannot be torn apart</term> parts. By "indiscerpible parts," I mean particles that actually take up space <note>original: "real extension"</note>, but are so small that they cannot be any smaller and still exist; therefore, they cannot be actually divided. You may call this tiny measurement **"Essential Extension"** (since without that specific measure, the very existence of Matter cannot be maintained). In contrast, you may call the measurement of any Matter made up of these particles **"Integral Extension,"** because the parts of this compound matter are actually and really separable from one another.

I confess that this assertion must seem like a paradox at first glance, even to the most clever and sensible people. But I shall plainly and briefly demonstrate here (in addition to what I have said in the treatise itself) that there are such indivisible particles into which Matter is divisible—namely, those that have "Essential Extension" and yet have parts that are utterly inseparable—by using this short syllogism:

->*That which is actually divisible as far as actual division can possibly be made, is divisible into parts that are indivisible.*<-

->*But Matter (I mean that compound Matter) is actually divisible as far as actual division can possibly be made.*<-

It would be foolish to try to prove either my premise <note>original: "Proposition"</note> or my assumption, as they are both so clear that no "common notion" in **Euclid** <note>Euclid of Alexandria, the "Father of Geometry," whose 'common notions' are foundational mathematical axioms.</note> is clearer, and all mathematical demonstrations are built upon those.

It must be admitted, therefore, that Matter consists of indivisible particles, and that physically and in reality, it is not divisible **to infinity** <note>original: "in infinitum"</note>, even though the parts that make up an indivisible particle are real and can be divided intellectually. It is part of the very essence of whatever exists to have parts or to take up space <note>original: "Extension"</note> in some measure or another. To take away all extension is to reduce a thing to a mathematical point, which is nothing but a pure negation or a non-entity. Since there is no middle ground between being "extended" (occupying space) and "not-extended," any more than there is between being a thing and being nothing, it is plain that if a thing exists at all, it must take up space. Therefore, there is an "Essential Extension" belonging to these indivisible particles of Matter, which was the second property I intended to demonstrate.

I know that an unruly **Imagination** <note>original: "Fancy"</note> will cause trouble here and cry out against this conclusion as impossible. "For a finite measurement," she will say, "must necessarily have a shape, and a shape has parts that stick out <note>original: "extuberancy of parts"</note> at such a distance that we cannot help but imagine them still being divisible." But we answer that when Matter is once actually divided as far as it possibly can be, it is a total contradiction to say it could be divided any further—just as it is a contradiction to say it cannot be divided as far as it can be divided. And no stronger...

<meta>This page continues the author's preface, moving from a discussion of "indiscerpible" (indivisible) particles to addressing objections regarding the nature of the Sun and the existence of immaterial substances.</meta>

This demonstration then, which they use against us, can be countered by either imagination <note>original: "Fancy"</note> or reason. Therefore, assuming our reasoning were merely equal to theirs, this is enough for me to win the argument <note>original: "give me the day"</note>, as I am only arguing for the *possibility* of the thing. For if I provide just as good a **demonstration** that it *is* possible as the other side does that it is *not*, no one can deny that the possibility remains on my side.

But to answer the argument mentioned above—even though they can never answer ours—I say that those **indiscerpible** <term>indiscerpible: atoms or particles that are indivisible and cannot be torn apart</term> particles of **Matter** have no **shape** <note>original: "Figure"</note> at all. Just as infinite **greatness** has no shape, infinite **smallness** has none either. A **cube** that is infinitely small in the strictest sense is as much a perfect contradiction as a **cube** that is infinitely large in that same sense of **infinity**; for the **corners** <note>original: "Angles"</note> would be the same size as the **faces** <term>Hedræ: the faces or flat surfaces of a geometric solid</term> of the cube.

Furthermore, wise men are certain of many things that their **imagination** cannot help but play tricks on them with—such as the **infinity** of **duration** and of **matter**, or at least of **space**. Although they are completely certain of the truth of these things, yet if they consider this infinite **matter**, **space**, or **duration** as being divided, for example, into three equal parts (all of which must be infinite, or else the whole would not be so), the middle part of each will seem both finite and infinite, because it is bounded at both ends. But every thing has two handles, as **Epictetus** <note>Epictetus (c. 50–135 AD) was a Stoic philosopher who taught that we should approach situations by the "handle" that makes them bearable.</note> notes; and he is a fool who will burn his fingers with the hot handle when he may hold safely by the other, which is more manageable and cool.

4. Concerning my **demonstration** of the **impossibility** of the **Sun** being a **spectator** of our particular affairs upon **Earth**, there is only this one objection: namely, that although the **Sun**, because of its great distance, cannot see any particular thing upon **Earth** if it remained in the ordinary shape we assume it would have if it lacked senses; yet, since it has life and perception, it might change some part of its **body** (as we do our **eye** when contracting or dilating the pupil) into such an advantageous **shape** that the **Earth** might be made to appear as large to it as it pleases.

Though some would be more ready to laugh at, rather than answer, such an odd suspicion—which imagines the **Sun** blinking and peering so curiously into our affairs as if through a **telescope**—yet because it arises in the course of reasoning, I shall have the patience to seriously return this **reply**:

First, that this objection can claim no strength at all unless the **body** of the **Sun** were **organized** <note>original: "Organical"</note> with organs like ours. Instead, it is nothing but **fluid light**. Therefore, unless the Sun has a spiritual **being** within it, for which this **light** serves only as a **vehicle**, this arbitrary shaping of its fluid **matter** cannot be achieved. But to grant that there is any such incorporeal **substance** in the **Sun** is to concede exactly what I am arguing for: namely, that there are **immaterial substances** in the **world**.

But it is apparent that there is no such **divine principle** in the Sun by which it can either see us or aim to produce any appearance on the **Earth** regarding any one of us through the activity of a **spirit** within it. This is clear from the scum and spots that lie upon it. The existence of sunspots is as great an **argument** that there is no such **divinity** in the Sun (as some would attribute to it, such as **Pomponazzi**, **Cardano**, **Vanini**, <note>Pietro Pomponazzi, Gerolamo Cardano, and Giulio Cesare Vanini were Renaissance philosophers often associated with naturalism or controversial views on the soul and divinity.</note> and others) as the dung of **owls** and **sparrows** found on the faces and shoulders of **idols** in **temples** is clear evidence that they are but dead **images**, not true **deities**.

<meta>This page continues the author's defense of his philosophical principles, specifically addressing objections to his axioms concerning the nature of matter and the necessity of immaterial substances.</meta>

Lastly, even if we were to suppose that the Sun had a particular sensing and intelligent spirit within him, the consideration of the vast distance of the **Earth** from him, and the thickness of her **atmosphere**, along with other disadvantages I have already mentioned in my **treatise**, makes it unbelievable that he would be able to shape his **body** into any **figure** so refined as to overcome these insurmountable difficulties.

5. In my second book, the first exception concerns the twentieth **Axiom** <term>Axiom: a self-evident truth or a statement that is widely accepted as being true</term>, which critics say I have not proved, but only brought in the testimony of **Mr. Hobbes** <note>original: "Mr. Hobbs"; Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679), a philosopher who argued for materialism, the idea that only physical matter exists</note> to support it. They argue this only allows me to debate Hobbes based on his own principles, which others might feel do not apply to them. But I answer, first, that it will affect all his followers as well as himself. Therefore, it is no small victory to demonstrate to all those confident **deniers of immaterial substances** <note>original: "Exploders of Immaterial Substances"; in this context, "exploders" are those who reject or drive out an idea with contempt</note> that their own acknowledged principles necessarily lead to the conclusion that such substances **exist** in the **world**. But furthermore, it will not be hard to provide undeniable reasons to prove the truth of the above-named **Axiom**: namely, *that sensation and perception in matter—assuming there is nothing but matter in the world—is actually the same thing as physical motion and reaction.*

For this is plain in **sensation**, as there is always external motion from objects when our senses are affected. And that internal **thought** <note>original: "Cogitation"</note> is performed in this way appears from the heat that **thinking** produces in a person. Therefore, generally all **thought** is accompanied by physical motion. And if there is nothing but **body** or **matter** in the **world**, then **thought** itself is actually the same thing as **physical motion**.

Moreover, just as in **sensation** the **physical motion** comes first and **perception** follows, it is necessary that in all internal **thoughts** as well, certain **physical motions** immediately precede those **perceptions**, even if we admitted that **matter** could move itself. For no **sense** would arise from that movement without the resistance of something it hit against. Consequently, the finest or most subtle **matter**, if it encountered no resistance or impact, would be no more capable of **thought** than a **wedge of gold** or a **block of lead** <note>original: "Pig of Lead"; an ingot or large casting of metal</note>. And therefore, if we will only admit (what no one but a madman would dare to deny) that a **block of lead** or a **wedge of gold** has no **thought** or **perception** at all without some knock or collision <note>original: "allision"</note> proportional to its size and solidity, the most subtle **matter** must likewise have none without some proportional impact or resistance. From this it is plain that physical **reaction** or **collision** always precedes **perception**, and that every **perception** is a kind of feeling that lasts as long as this resistance or impact of motion lasts; but when that ceases, perception is extinguished, the **matter** then being as senseless <note>original: "stupid"</note> as a **block of lead**. Therefore, just as there is generally always **physical motion** wherever there is **thought**, the variation of this motion and collision causes the variation of thoughts. They run hand in hand perpetually; one is never introduced without the other leading the way, nor does it last longer than the other. But just as heat is lost (which involves a significant motion or agitation of some very subtle **matter**), so our **understanding** and **imagination** decay, and our senses themselves fail, either because they cannot be moved by the impact of outward objects, or because they are not in a proper state of fluidity and agility. Therefore, in death, our **bodies** become as senseless as a lump of clay.

# The PREFACE.

*All sensation and perception, therefore, are really the same as the motion and reaction of matter, if there is nothing but matter in the world.*

*Furthermore, it is plain that every piece of matter must perceive according to how it is moved—whether by itself (if that were possible) or by physical impact from other parts. This is because matter has no subtle rays, nor any power or flow streaming beyond itself—like what the Scholastic philosophers call* **intentional species** <note>original: "species intentionales"; in traditional philosophy, these were the images or "forms" of objects that were thought to travel through the air to the senses</note>—*nor any union more mysterious than the mere* **juxtaposition** <note>original: "Juxta-poſition"; the act of placing physical things side-by-side without any deeper internal connection</note> *of its parts.*

*From this, it is manifest that no impact received or felt by one part of matter can be communicated to another part at a distance except by bumping or crowding the parts that lie in between. Therefore, in every respect, physical motion or reaction—provided the parts are sufficiently fine and the motion lasts long enough—will be the complete cause of all perception, if there is nothing but matter in the world. I think this should be enough to convince any impartial person of the truth of this part of* **Mr. Hobbes's** <note>original: "Mr Hobbs"; Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679), a philosopher known for his materialist views</note> **assertion**, *if he could only prove his other claim: that nothing exists in nature except what is purely physical. However, using this first part, which is his own acknowledged principle, I have undeniably demonstrated that there is indeed something more.*

6. The other objection is against the opinion I seem to embrace regarding the **vehicles** <term>vehicles: the subtle, physical "bodies" or vessels that spirits or souls were thought to inhabit to interact with the world</term> of **demons** <note>original: "Dæmons"; in this context, the term refers generally to spirits or intermediate beings, not necessarily evil ones</note> and departed souls; in this, I have allegedly offended against the authority of the **Schools** <note>original: "the Schools"; the Scholastic philosophers of the Middle Ages whose teachings still dominated many universities</note>. I confess this is the only reason I can imagine for their objection to my **assertion**. 

But they may, if they please, remember that the Schools trespass against an authority more ancient than themselves: namely, the **Pythagoreans**, **Platonists**, **Jewish Doctors**, and the **Church Fathers**, who all hold that even the purest angels have physical vehicles. It will be difficult for the Schools to produce any ancient authority for their own opinion. For **Aristotle**, their great **oracle**, is utterly silent on this matter, as he did not even believe in the **existence** of **demons** in the world (as **Pomponazzi** and **Vanini** <note>original: "Pomponatius" and "Vaninus"; Pietro Pomponazzi and Giulio Cesare Vanini were Renaissance philosophers known for their skeptical and naturalistic interpretations of Aristotle</note>, his sworn disciples, have noted to their great satisfaction). 

Therefore, being left to their own dry, overly-subtle reasoning, the Scholastics have declared all intellectual beings that are not coarsely earthly (as humans are) to be purely **immaterial**. In doing so, they create a hideous **chasm** or gaping breach in the order of things—one that no moderate judgment would ever allow. This has made them very vulnerable to being defeated by **atheistic** wits, who are skilled enough to draw out the absurd consequences hidden in false suppositions, as **Vanini** does in this case. For he argues—not foolishly—from the supposed pure immateriality of **demons** that they can have no knowledge of specific things on Earth. Such purely incorporeal essences would be incapable of receiving impressions from physical objects and therefore would not have the "species" or mental image of any particular physical thing in their minds. From this, he infers that all apparitions, prophecies, wonders, and whatever miracles are recorded in ancient history are not to be attributed to spirits, but to the influence of the stars; he thus concludes that there are indeed no such things as **demons** in the universe.

By this same kind of reasoning, it is also easy for the **Psychopannychites** <term>Psychopannychites: those who believe that the soul "sleeps" or is unconscious from the moment of death until the final resurrection</term> to support their opinion of the **sleep of the soul**. They argue that since the soul is utterly cut off from everything physical and has no vital union with any matter at all,

<margin>* Chapters 5, 6, 7.</margin>

7. These are the main **objections** my **First** and **Second Book** seem to face. I suspect my **last** book may be even more **offensive** <note>original: "obnoxious"; in this context, it means likely to cause offense or strong disagreement</note>. But the most common **objection** I foresee is that I have taken it upon myself to describe the state of the other **world** so precisely and in such detail, as if I had recently visited it. For **over-elaboration** may seem to **smell of trickery and fraud**. Just as we often feel **distrust** <note>original: "diffidency"</note> when we hear something that perfectly suits our **desires**—being ready to think it **too good to be true**—we are also prone to **suspect** **notions** that seem **too perfectly fitted** to our **intellectual faculties** and align most naturally with them, especially regarding things that at first seemed **very obscure and intricate** to us. For this reason, it is also very likely that the **concept** of a particular **spirit**, which I have so accurately described in my **First Book**, may seem less credible to some because it is now made so clearly understandable. They think it utterly improbable that these things, which have always been considered **inextricable puzzles**, should suddenly be made clear and familiar to anyone with enough **patience** and **reason** to study the **theory**.

But for my own part, I will not be so arrogant as to claim that the **indiscerpibility** <note>original: "Indiscerpibility"; the quality of being impossible to divide or tear apart</note> of a **spirit** arises exactly in the way I have described—that is, that **God** created a particular **spirit** in precisely the manner I have outlined. For His **wisdom** is infinite, and therefore it would be an **impious** act of boldness to limit Him to one specific way of forming the nature of a **being**, or of granting it the **attributes** that are **essential** to it, as **indiscerpibility** is to the **human soul**. But to have only said in general, "*It is possible there may be a particular essence that is naturally penetrable and indivisible, without describing exactly how it could be so*," might have seemed lazy and unsatisfactory to many; as the **proverb** says, **deceit lurks in generalities** <note>original: "Deceit lurking in Universals"</note>. Therefore, to fully convince those on the **opposing side**, I thought it best to provide a precise description of one way the **human soul** or a **spirit** <note>original: "Dæmon"; in the classical sense, a spirit or supernatural being, not necessarily evil</note> might be conceived as necessarily **indivisible**, even if it can be **expanded** <note>original: "dilatable"</note>. I am not overly concerned whether it happens in exactly that way or not, but I am well assured that it is either **that way or something even better**. But this one example shows that the thing is **possible in general** (just as the simple design of an **Indian canoe** <note>original: "Indian Canoa"</note> might prove that **navigation** is possible). And that is all I aimed for in that section; except that I also felt a **zeal** to defend the reputation of the **Platonists**, whose imaginative **insights** <note>original: "presages"</note> I have often observed to be in faithful agreement with the strictest **reason**. I believe I have demonstrated here that their **imagination** <note>original: "Fancy"</note> is not at all irrational when they so frequently compare **form** or **spirit** to radiant **light**.

Similarly, in my description of the state of the other world, I am not overly concerned with whether things are exactly as I have described them; but because

7. Some people completely disbelieve these things because they can form no specific concept of what the reception and activities <note>original: "Entertains"</note> of those **aerial inhabitants** <note>spirits or angels dwelling in the atmosphere</note> might be, or how they pass their time, along with many other complexities that tend to entangle this theory. I thought it of great importance to remove this objection against the life to come—namely, that because no one can conceive what it is, it therefore does not exist at all (which is the same common objection used against the existence of all **incorporeal substances** <note>beings without physical bodies</note>). I aim to do this by providing a detailed <note>original: "punctual"</note> and rational description of this future state. I exhibit this to the world as an intelligible **hypothesis** <note>a logical theory</note>, and one that may very well be true according to the dictates of our own faculties. In the meantime, I am fully assured that things are either exactly like this, or arranged in an even better and more precise order. But, as I said, I thought it very useful to propose a specific, probable way for those who totally distrust these matters mainly because they believe we can provide no rational representation of them to human understanding.

8. But there are also specific objections. The first of these is against my **aerial** and **ethereal Elysiums** <note>Elysium: a place of happiness in the afterlife; ethereal refers to the highest, purest heavens</note>. To make their reproach seem more clever, some will compare these to the **Islamic Paradise** <note>original: "Mahometan Paradise"; historically, Western writers often criticized the Islamic concept of heaven as being too focused on physical or "sensual" pleasure</note>. However, besides the fact that I suspend my own ultimate agreement in the very place where I describe them, there is nothing offered in my description that—if it were accepted—would not be suitable for the most refined spirit in the world. For nothing is more certain than that the **love of God** and our **neighbor** is the greatest happiness we can achieve, either in this life or the one to come. Whatever things are described there are either the causes, effects, or companions of that noble and divine passion. 

Neither should the external attractions I mention be wrongly deemed "sensual"; they are instead **intellectual**. For even sensible beauty—whether it shows itself in features, music, or whatever graceful behaviors and comely actions—is essentially intellectual, as **Plotinus** <note>a major Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 204–270 AD)</note> has well defined. As for those things that are not strictly intellectual, such as fragrances <note>original: "Odours"</note> and flavors <note>original: "Sapours"</note>, a certain spirit may be infused into the **vehicles** <note>the "bodies" or vessels used by spirits to interact with the world</note> of these **aerial inhabitants** through them, which may raise their **intellectual faculties** into action more than ordinary. Anyone who observes how our thoughts and inclinations depend immediately on a certain subtle matter within our own bodies will not hesitate to acknowledge this as true. Therefore, whatever my **Elysiums** may seem like to the rash and uncritical, they are really nothing other than pure **paradises** of **intellectual** pleasure; **divine love** and blameless **friendship** are the only delights of those places.

9. The next objection concerns the state of the wicked, as if I had made their condition too easy for them. But I think any man might be deterred from this view if he would only consider that I make the torture <note>original: "rack"</note> of **conscience** worse than a perpetually repeated death. It is all too credible that this will happen there, since we see what execution the passions can perform upon us even in this life; the **Sicilian tyrants** <note>ancient rulers of Sicily, like Phalaris, famous for inventing horrific torture devices like the "Brazen Bull"</note> never found a more exquisite torture than these passions. As for those souls who have lost all sense of conscience (if any can do so), I have assigned other punishments that are more physical <note>original: "corporeal"</note>, and little inferior to the fire of that great Hell prophesied as the portion of the devils and the damned at the Last Day.

10. The final two exceptions are: the first concerning the **Soul of the World**, and the other concerning the **Spirit of Nature**. The first is an objection against my overly-favorable representation of the opinion held by those who claim there is only *one Soul in the whole Universe*, endowing it with sense, reason, and understanding. They believe this single Soul acts in all animals, including **demons** <note>original: "Dæmons"; in this context, these are supernatural beings or spirits, not necessarily evil</note> themselves. In all of these beings, they say, it is one and the same Universal Soul that hears, sees, reasons, understands, etc. I believe I have refuted <note>original: "confuted"</note> this opinion in the third book as effectively as any error in all **natural philosophy** <note>the study of nature and the physical universe; the precursor to modern science</note> can be refuted. The favorable representation I gave it there contains within it the means for anyone—unless they are very careless—to easily demonstrate the falsity of that supposition. For we may well enough imagine that if the body remains unchanged, and this Soul of the Universe is exactly the same everywhere, a person could move to another place and shift into another part of the World Soul while retaining the same opinions, imaginations, and reasonings (at least those that do not depend on memory), because this Universal Soul would raise itself to the same thoughts given the same occasions. Yet memory is incompatible with a part of the soul that did not previously perceive the thing being remembered. For memory necessarily includes a sense or perception that we have *previously* had a perception or sense of the thing we now remember.

To be brief, therefore, and to strike this opinion dead with one blow: those who say there is only one Soul of the World, whose perceptive power is everywhere, must assert either that what one part perceives, all the rest perceives; or else that perceptions in demons, men, and beasts are confined to that specific part of the Soul that is within them while they perceive this or that. If they claim the former, they are proven wrong by common sense and experience. For though all animals are "steeped," as it were, in that subtle matter which runs through all things and is the immediate instrument of sense and perception, we are not conscious of one another’s thoughts, nor do we feel one another’s pains—nor do we feel the pains and pleasures of animals, even when they are at their highest intensity. Nor do the demons feel one another’s emotions, or necessarily agree with one another’s opinions, even though their "vehicles" are exceedingly **permeable** <note>original: "pervious"; meaning easily passed through or transparent</note>. If they did, they would all be **Averroists** <note>followers of the philosopher Averroes, who proposed that all humans share a single, collective intellect</note>, as were the spirits that appeared to **Fazio Cardano** <note>original: "Facius Cardanus"; the father of the famous mathematician Girolamo Cardano, who claimed to have been visited by seven spirits</note>, assuming any such beings existed. Therefore, we may generally conclude that if there were such a Universal Soul, its particular perceptions would be restricted to the specific part in which they are made; this contradicts the **unity of a soul**, as I have already stated in its proper place.

<margin>Book 3, chapter 16, section 2.</margin>
But let us grant the point for a moment (*for indeed we have demonstrated it must be so, if there is such a Universal Soul and nothing else*); then the grand absurdity I mentioned before arises. Namely, that a part of the Soul of the World which never perceived a thing shall, nonetheless, remember it. That is to say, it shall perceive that it *has* perceived what it *never* perceived. And yet, a person in **Japan** might remember a countryman who arrived there, whom he had not seen or thought of for twenty years before.

*Nay, what is even more to the point: assuming the* **Earth** *moves, what I write now—while the* **Earth** *is at the beginning of* **Aries** <note>The zodiac sign Aries; the author is referencing the Earth's position in its orbit around the Sun</note>—*I shall remember having written when the Earth is at the beginning of* **Libra**. *This is true even though that part of the* **Soul of the World** <note>original: "Soul of the World"; a philosophical concept suggesting a single spirit animates the entire universe</note> *which occupies my* **Body** *then will be twice as far from the part guiding my hand now as the* **Earth** *is from the* **Sun**.*

*Nor can the clarity of this demonstration be escaped by any* **evasion** *whatsoever. For* **first**, *even if we should admit that there are certain* **marks** *sealed in the* **Brain** *when we see or consider an* **object**—*by which the* **Soul** *might impress the* **memory** *of it more deeply upon herself—the ability to remember would still depend on her having once joined such a* **thought** *or* **representation** *with such an* **impression** *or* **mark**. *Otherwise, it would be useless. Therefore, if the* **Soul of the World** *at point* **B** *had not joined that* **representation** *with the* **mark** *in the* **brain** *as she did at point* **A**, *she could remember nothing by it. It is utterly inconceivable how any* **shape** *or* **motion** *in the* **brain** *could represent a* **perception** *to the* **Soul** *as something "perceived before" if the* **Soul** *herself never had that* **perception** *to begin with. There can be no* **basis** *for this reflective and comparative* **act** *other than the previous* **perception** *of which the* **Soul** *is still conscious; and she cannot be conscious of it if she never perceived it. From this, it is plain that these supposed* **marks** *cannot trick the* **Soul of the World** *at point* **B** *into imagining she had a* **perception** *of a thing when, in fact, she never did.*

*But then again, **secondly**, it is very evident that the power of* **Memory** *does not consist of such* **marks** *or* **figures** *in the* **brain**, *nor in any* **vibration** *or* **motion** *there, as I have sufficiently proved in the following* **discourse**. *This further assures us that* **Memory** *resides entirely in the* **Soul** *herself, and that* **she** *is the sole* **repository** *of all the* **perceptions** *she has had. Therefore, the* **Soul of the World** *cannot perceive herself to have perceived something when she has not actually perceived it.*

*And **thirdly** and finally, it is also manifest from this—I mean from* **Memory** *being located only in the* **Soul** *herself (though she acts in this, as in all other functions, only by virtue of a fit state of* **spirits** *and the proper condition of the* **brain**)—*that as the* **body** *changes locations from* **A** *to* **B**, *the part of the* **Soul of the World** *inside it at point* **B** *would have memories of things that were never perceived at point* **A**. *Conversely, it would forget, or rather have no knowledge of, what the* **Soul** *perceived there. Thus, by changing locations, a man might suddenly become an excellent* **physician**, **mathematician**, *or the like—or suddenly become a* **fool** <note>original: "Sott"; a dull or foolish person</note> *and lose all his learning, which is the more likely of the two. For the* **fruits** *of that* **meditation** *and* **study** *are lost once the* **body** *has left that part of the* **Soul of the World** *which did the studying and meditating. It is therefore impossible that every man should not have a particular soul of his own.*

*Nor can this* **error** *in the* **Soul of the World**—*of perceiving she has perceived something when she has not—be argued as possible based on the persistent mistakes of our* **outer senses**. *For example, we might feel a pain in our finger, or see white upon a wall, even though there is neither "white" in the wall nor "pain" in the finger, but only in our* **common percipient** <note>the central faculty of the mind that processes and interprets sensory data</note> *which is confined within our* **brain**. *For it is apparent that even if this is an* **error**, *there is a clear and necessary* **foundation** *for it.*

*For just as when we thrust a* **cane** *against the ground, we necessarily feel different sensations—one when against* **gravel**, *another against* **stone**, *and a third against* **mud** *or* **earth**—*and we feel them at the distance of the* **cane**'s *length: so it is also with* **colors**. *The* **medium** <note>The intervening substance, such as air, through which a force or perception acts</note> *between the* **object** *and the* **eye** *is like the* **cane**, *and the variety of sensations at the end of the* **cane** *is like that variety of* **colors**. *There is a necessary cause for this in the different surfaces of the objects, which the* **perceiving mind** *must necessarily perceive, and at the distance where the* **medium** *engages it, just as it was before with the length of the* **cane**. *So, to perceive such differences at the distance where they causally exist is not so much an error as a truth. The same logic applies to tickling or pricking in any part of the* **body**: *for it is true that those differences are also caused there, and therefore our perception is rightly directed there. There is a harshness and disharmony to* **nature** *in that spot, which the* **soul** *cannot perceive except as a harsh and painful sensation—not only because of its vital union with the* **body**, *but also from the special nature of the perception itself.*

*So it seems to me a harsh judgment to say the* **soul** *is mistaken in these perceptions. And if she is mistaken in some way, we can still trace the necessary and certain cause, which is both very obvious and very understandable. But regarding this error of the* **Soul of the World** *perceiving—suppose at point* **B**—*that she has perceived what she nevertheless never actually perceived: this is a thing of a completely different kind. It is a total and certain mistake for which no imaginable cause can be produced that would lead her into it. From this it follows that she never commits such an error; and therefore the reflexive* **act of memory**, *which firmly assures us of a previous perception (and no other faculty has any power or reason to prove the contrary), necessarily implies that every man has a particular soul of his own. Such a* **Universal Soul**, *as the* **Averroists** <note>original: "Avenroists"; followers of the medieval philosopher Averroes, some of whom argued that all humans share a single, universal intellect</note> *imagine, will not explain all* **phenomena**.

*And yet I dare say this wild opinion is more defensible than the views of those who believe there is nothing but mere matter in the world. *It might be argued that matter, being devoid of all sensation and perception and therefore incapable of planned design, should be considered unfit to organize itself into such exquisite structures. *To those who claim that the introduction of this Principle is poorly timed, I ask them: when will they think the time is right? This simple guess—that although all the mechanical solutions for certain* <term>phenomena</term> <note>original: "Phænomena"; observable facts or events in the natural world</note> *offered to the world so far are demonstrably false, future ages may still discover the truth—can be seen by the wise as nothing but a pitiful excuse for fearful* <term>souls</term>. *Such people are very reluctant to let such a frightening concept as an* <term>immaterial</term> *or* <term>spiritual substance</term> *into the world, for fear that the next step must be the acknowledgment of a* <term>God</term>, *from whom they would gladly hide themselves behind this weak and shaky pretense. For that admirable master of* <term>mechanics</term>, <term>Descartes</term>, *has improved this approach to the highest level that I believe human wit can reach regarding the* <term>phenomena</term> *he attempted to explain. Yet, I have noted both in the previous and following chapters, and elsewhere, how he falls short in several passages. I will give only one example here: the phenomenon of* <term>gravity</term>. *Regarding gravity, I believe I have perfectly demonstrated that both he and* <term>Mr. Hobbes</term> <note>Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679), an English philosopher known for his materialist views</note> *are completely wrong, and that the causes they assign are plainly false. 12. *But you will say that even if these thinkers are all mistaken, it does not follow that there might not arise some brilliant mind who will give a true mechanical solution to this problem. To this I answer: I have not only refuted their reasons, but I have also demonstrated—using mechanical principles accepted by all sides and confirmed by experience—that the descent of a stone, a bullet, or any such heavy body is entirely contrary to the laws of* <term>mechanics</term>. *According to those laws, if such objects were loose, they would necessarily move away from the Earth and be carried out of our sight into the farthest parts of the air, if some power greater than mechanics did not restrain that motion and force them downward toward the Earth. So it is plain that we have not introduced a Principle arbitrarily; rather, it is forced upon us by the undeniable evidence of demonstration. To withhold our agreement from this until future ages have improved mechanical philosophy to a greater height is as ridiculous as doubting the truth of any plain and easy demonstration in the first book of* <term>Euclid</term> <note>The ancient Greek mathematician; specifically his work "The Elements," the foundation of geometry</note> *until we have traveled through the entire field of the immense study of* <term>mathematics</term>.

## CHAPTER I.

1. *The usefulness of the present contemplation for understanding Divine Providence and managing our lives for our greatest happiness;* 2. *For the moderate bearing of the death and disasters of our friends;* 3. *For producing true magnanimity* <note>original: "Magnanimity"; greatness of spirit or courage</note> *within us;* 4. *and for peace and tranquility of mind.* 5. *That so weighty a theory is not to be handled superficially.* <note>original: "perfunctorily"</note>

<margin>1.</margin>

Of all the contemplations <note>original: "Speculations"</note> the **Soul** of man can engage in, there is none of greater importance, or of closer concern to her, than this regarding her own **Immortality** and **Independence** from this **Earthly Body**. For by this, not only are the complexities and difficulties of **Providence** <note>God's guidance and care for the world</note> made easier and smoother for her to understand—becoming able, by unravelling this thread from beginning to end, to pass safely back and forth through this labyrinth where many anxious or careless spirits have lost themselves—but also (which touches her own interest more particularly), once she is raised into the knowledge and belief of so significant a conclusion, she may see from this perspective the most certain and direct way to her own **Happiness**. This path consists of maintaining a very moderate affection for whatever tempts her during the time of this, her pilgrimage, and a careful preparation of herself for her future condition through such noble actions and heroic qualities of mind as shall make her most welcome in her own country <note>Referring to the soul's heavenly home</note>.

<margin>2.</margin>
This belief and purpose of hers will make her utterly incapable of either **envying the life or successes** of her most bitter **enemies**, or of **excessively mourning the death or misfortunes** of her dearest **friends**. She will have no friends except those who are friends of God and virtue, and whose afflictions will prove to be advantages for their future happiness, and whose departure from this life is but a passage to the immediate possession of that joy.

This will not be achieved by using many words, but by using them more sparingly; letting nothing fall from our pen except what relates closely to the matter, while omitting nothing essential for proving its truth.

For those who are not in such a strange state of hopelessness, but think they know something already and may learn more, I do not doubt that by a timely <note>original: "seasonable"</note> recourse to these few rules, along with others I shall set down in their proper place, they will be persuaded—if not forced—to count this truth of the *Immortality of the Soul* among those that must appear undeniable to those who have enough skill and leisure to accurately examine and thoroughly understand what I have written here to demonstrate it.

### AXIOM I.

*Whatever things are in themselves, they are nothing to us except in so far as they become known to our faculties or cognitive powers <note>the mental abilities used for perceiving and reasoning</note>.*

2. This axiom is self-evident at its first proposal. For just as nothing, for example, can concern the *visual* <note>original: "Visible"</note> faculty except in so far as it is *visible*, so there is nothing that can claim any influence on—much less determine—our *cognitive powers* in general, except in so far as it is *knowable* <note>original: "cognoscible"</note>.

### AXIOM II.

*Whatever is unknown to us, or is known only as a mere possibility, is not to move or influence us in any way, nor make us undecided; instead, we are to rely on the present light and plain determination of our own faculties.*

<margin>See *Antidote*, Book 1, chapters 2 and 9.</margin>
3. This is an obvious logical consequence <note>original: "Consectary"</note> from the previous axiom. For the existence of that which is *merely possible* is utterly unknown to us as an actual *fact*, and therefore it should have no weight against any conclusion, unless we wish to condemn ourselves to eternal *skepticism*. For example, if after a man has argued for a *God* and *Providence* based on the wise design found in the bodies of all *animals* on earth, someone should reply that there may be, despite this, animals on *Saturn*, *Jupiter*, or some other planets with very clumsy structures—suppose horses and other creatures with only one eye and one ear (and both on one side, with the eye placed where the ear should be), and with only three legs; or bulls and rams with horns on their backs, and the like. Such claims as these, according to this axiom, are to be held of no force at all for weakening the conclusion.

### AXIOM III.

*Not all our faculties have a right to vote <note>original: "suffrage"</note> in determining truth; only common notions, external sense, and the evident and undeniable deductions of reason have that right.*

4. By "common notions," I mean whatever is *intellectually* <note>original: "Noëmically"</note> true—that is to say, true at first sight to all men in their right minds upon a clear perception of the terms, without any further discussion or rea-

### AXIOM IV.

->*Whatever is not consistent with all or some of these faculties is mere fancy, and is of no importance for proving truth or falsehood, regardless of how vivid or confusing it may be.*<-

<margin>See *Antidote*, Book 1, chapter 4, section 2.</margin>
5. I say *mere fancy* <note>original: "mere Fancy"</note> in contrast to those representations which—although they are not the pure impressions of a real object—are nevertheless created by *rational deduction* from them, or from *common notions* <note>fundamental truths or self-evident principles</note>, or from both. Those representations that are not built upon such grounds I call *mere fancies*; these have no value at all in determining the truth. For if the *intensity of imagination* <note>original: "Vigour of Fancy"</note> could prove a thing true, then all the dreams of madmen would have to be accepted as oracles. And if the *confusing nature of the imagination* <note>original: "Perplexiveness of Imagination"</note> could prevent us from agreeing to a fact, we would have to reject mathematical demonstrations; for instance, the 16th Proposition of the 3rd Book of *Euclid* would be confidently judged to contain a contradiction.

### AXIOM V.

->*Whatever is clear to any one of these three faculties is to be held as undoubtedly true, provided the others have no evidence to the contrary.*<-

6. Otherwise, a person could not be certain of any physical object they encounter, nor could they firmly agree to such truths as: *It is impossible for the same thing to both be and not be at the same time*; *Whatever exists is either finite or infinite*; and similar statements.

### AXIOM VI.

->*Whatever is rejected by one faculty, while none of the other faculties provide evidence for it, should be considered a falsehood.*<-

7. Otherwise, a person might accept such impossibilities as truth, or doubt whether they are true or not—for instance: *The part is greater than the whole*; *There is something that is neither finite nor infinite*; *Socrates is invisible*; and the like.

## AXIOM VIII.

*The subject, or the bare essence or substance of a thing, is completely inconceivable to any of our mental faculties.*

9. To prove this truth, one needs only to quietly reflect on one's own mind to see if it is not so. If you take away all <term>capacities</term> <note>original: "Aptitudes"</note>, <term>operations</term>, <term>properties</term>, and <term>modifications</term> from a *subject*, your concept of it vanishes into nothing—or at best into the idea of a mere <term>undifferentiated substance</term> <note>original: "Undiversificated Substance"</note>. In that state, one *substance* cannot be distinguished from another; it can only be distinguished from <term>accidents</term> <note>properties that are not essential to a thing's nature</note> or <term>modes</term>, which have no independent existence of their own.

## AXIOM IX.

*There are some properties, powers, and operations that belong directly to a thing, for which no reasons can be given and none should be demanded. Furthermore, the way or manner in which these attributes connect to the subject cannot be visualized or imagined in any way.*

10. The evidence for this axiom follows from the previous one. For if the bare substance of a thing is so completely inconceivable, then no connection can be perceived between it and its primary properties. Examples of this are <term>actual divisibility</term> and <term>impenetrability</term> in <term>matter</term>. By <term>actual divisibility</term>, I mean <term>discerpibility</term> <note>original: "Discerpibility"; the capacity to be physically torn, shredded, or cut into separate pieces</note>—the gross tearing or cutting of one part from another. These are *immediate properties* of *matter*. But no man can pretend to give a reason why they should exist there rather than in any other *subject*, nor can anyone ask for a reason with any credibility. For *immediate attributes* are indemonstrable; if they could be proven by something else, they would not be "immediate" (fundamental).

11. Similarly, the *immediate properties* of a *spirit* or <term>immaterial substance</term> are <term>penetrability</term> and <term>indiscerpibility</term> <note>the quality of being impossible to tear or divide into separate parts</note>. The necessary connection of these attributes to the *subject* is just as impossible to demonstrate as the previous example. For I must assert what I cannot but see as evidently true: that there is no *substance* that does not have, in some way or another, <term>three dimensions</term> (length, breadth, and depth). This *substance* which we call *matter* could just as easily have been penetrable as impenetrable while still remaining a *substance*. But as it stands, it certainly and irresistibly prevents one part of itself from passing through another, and we do not know why. There is no necessary connection to be seen between a *substance* having three dimensions and its being <term>impenetrable</term>. Some argue that it implies a contradiction for an <term>extended substance</term>...

<summary>This page establishes that the core essence of any substance is unknowable and that fundamental properties—such as matter being impenetrable or spirit being indivisible—must be accepted as primary facts that cannot be further explained or proven.</summary>

<page-num>20</page-num>
<header>The Immortality of the Soul. BOOK I.</header>

substance should run one part into another; for so part of the *Extension*, and consequently of the *Substance*, would be lost. This, I say, (if examined closely) is of no force. For the *Substance* is no more lost in this case than when a string is doubled and redoubled, or a piece of wax reduced from a long shape to a round one. The dimension of *length* <note>original: "Longitude"</note> is in some part lost, but without any damage to the *Substance* of the wax. In the same way, if one part of an *Extended Substance* runs into another, something of its *length*, *width* <note>original: "Latitude"</note>, and *depth* <note>original: "Profundity"</note> may be lost, and yet all the *Substance* remains there; just as length was lost in the other case without any loss of *Substance*.

And just as what was lost in *length* was gained in *width* or *depth* before; so what is lost here in all or any two of the dimensions is kept safe in <term>Essential Spissitude</term> <note>More’s term for a "fourth dimension" of spirit, allowing it to compress or occupy the same space as matter without losing its essence.</note>. For that is what I will call this *Mode* or *Property* of a *Substance* that is able to receive one part of itself into another. This *fourth Mode* is as easy and familiar to my understanding as the *three dimensions* are to my senses or <term>imagination</term> <note>original: "Phansy"</note>. For I mean nothing else by *spissitude* but the redoubling or contracting of Substance into less space than it sometimes occupies. Analogous to this is the presence of two different kinds of substances in the same place at the same time.

To both of these, the terms <term>Reduplication</term> and <term>Saturation</term> may be applied. The former occurs when *Essence* or *Substance* is redoubled only once into itself or into another substance; the latter occurs when it is redoubled so many times that it will not easily admit anything more. And it is plain that more than one *Extension* can be equal to the same space at the same time, because *Motion* exists in the same space as the *Subject* in which it resides, and both exist within *Space* itself. And *Motion* is not "nothing"; therefore, two things can occupy one Space at once.

12. Now, then, *Extended Substance* (and all substances are extended) is in itself indifferent to <term>Penetrability</term> or <term>Impenetrability</term>. We find one kind of Substance (matter) to be so *impenetrable* that one part will not enter another at all; however, we might just as reasonably expect to find the parts of a substance so irresistibly united that nothing in the world could tear them apart. (For this <term>Indiscerpibility</term> <note>The quality of being impossible to divide or separate into parts.</note> is as logically connected to Substance as *Impenetrability* is. Neither of them can be proven by pure reason or demonstration; rather, they are *Immediate Attributes* of such a subject. For a man can no more argue from the *Extension* of a substance that it is <term>Discerpible</term> <note>divisible into parts</note> than he can argue that it is *Penetrable*. *Extension* is just as capable of being *Penetrated* as it is of being *Divided*.) I conceive, I say, that we may therefore as easily admit that some Substance may be inherently *Indiscerpible* as we admit others are *Impenetrable*. And just as there is one kind of *Substance* which by its own nature is *Impenetrable* and *Discerpible* (Matter), so there may be another that is *Indiscerpible* and *Penetrable* (Spirit). A man can give no other account for either of these than to say they are the immediate properties of such a Subject.

## AXIOM X.

*The discovery of some Power, Property, or Operation, which is incompatible with one Subject, is an infallible argument for the Existence of some other subject to which it must be compatible.*

<margin>Iamblichus, *On the Life of Pythagoras*, Chapter 18. Philostratus, *On the Life of Apollonius*, Book 6.</margin>
13. As when *Pythagoras* was spoken to by the River *Nessus* while he passed over it, and when a Tree (at the command of *Thespesion*, the chief of the <term>Gymnosophists</term> <note>original: "Gymnosophists"; a sect of ancient Indian philosophers who practiced asceticism and went naked.</note>) saluted *Apollonius* in a distinct and articulate voice, though small like a woman's; in these cases, I say, it is evident that there was something present that was neither *River* nor *Tree* to which these salutations must be attributed, since no *Tree* nor *River* has any faculty of *Reason* or *Speech*.

### CHAPTER III.

*1. The general Notions of Body and Spirit. 2. That the Notion of Spirit is altogether as intelligible as that of Body. 3. Whether there be any Substance of a mixed nature, between Body and Spirit.*

1. THE greatest and most significant obstacle to the belief in the *Immortality of the Soul* is the confident opinion held by some that the very notion of a *Spirit* is a piece of nonsense and a perfect contradiction in terms. Therefore, to proceed by degrees toward our main design, and to lay our foundation low and sure, we will first present the genuine notion of a *Spirit* in its general sense, and afterward describe several kinds of *Spirits*. This is so it may appear to all how unjust that <term>cavil</term> <note>An unfair or trivial objection.</note> is against *Incorporeal Substances*, as if they were mere impossibilities and contradictory inconsistencies. I will therefore define a *Spirit* in general as: *A substance penetrable and <term>indiscerpible</term>* <note>From the Latin "discerpere" (to tear into pieces); More means a substance that cannot be divided or torn into separate parts.</note>. The fitness of this definition will be better understood if we divide *Substance* in general into these first kinds: *Body* and *Spirit*. We then define *Body* to be *A Substance impenetrable and <term>discerpible</term>* <note>Able to be separated into distinct, physical parts.</note>. Thus, the opposite kind to this is fitly defined as *A Substance penetrable and indiscerpible*.

2. Now I appeal to any man who can set aside prejudice and has the free use of his faculties: is every term in the definition of a *Spirit* not just as intelligible and agreeable to Reason as those in the definition of a *Body*? For the precise notion of *Substance* is the same in both; in which, I believe, is comprised *Extension* and *Activity*, either <term>connate</term> <note>Inborn or natural.</note> or communicated. For *Matter* itself, once moved, can move other *Matter*. And it is as easy to understand what *Penetrable* is as *Impenetrable*, and what *Indiscerpible* is as *Discerpible*. Since *Penetrability* and *Indiscerpibility* are as immediate to *Spirit* as *Impenetrability* and *Discerpibility* are to *Body*, there is as much reason to be given for the attributes of the one as of the other...

<meta>catchword: Axiom</meta>

<summary>More defines "Spirit" and "Body" by their opposing logical properties—penetrability and indivisibility versus impenetrability and divisibility—arguing that the concept of a spirit is no less rational than the concept of physical matter.</summary>
