# CHAPTER 4. The Immortality of the Soul.

## CHAPTER 4.

*1. That the concepts of various kinds of immaterial beings contain no inconsistency or incongruity. 2. That the nature of God is as intelligible as the nature of any being whatsoever. 3. The true concept of his ubiquity <note>original: "ubiquity," meaning omnipresence or being everywhere at once</note>, and how intelligible it is. 4. Regarding the union of the Divine Essence. 5. Regarding his power of creation.*

**I. WE** have shown that the concept of a *spirit* in general is not at all inconsistent or impossible. It is equally consistent, coherent, and understandable in its *various forms; such as God, angels, the souls of humans and animals, and the* <term>seminal reasons</term> <note>original: λόγοι σπερματικοὶ (logoi spermatikoi); these are the generative principles or underlying blueprints that determine the form of living things</note> *or seminal forms of things.*

2. The concept of God—though knowledge of it is much hindered by the confusion and stupidity of either superstitious or worldly men—remains clear. These men delight in their lengthy, grand rhetorical speeches concerning the unthinkability and utter incomprehensibility of the **Deity**. One group does this through a devotional exaggeration of the transcendence of His nature; the other does it to make the belief in His existence seem ridiculous, craftily and perversely suggesting that there is no God at all, by making the very concept of Him appear to be nothing but a bundle of inconsistencies and impossibilities. Nevertheless, I shall not hesitate to affirm that His *idea* or concept is as easy to understand as any other concept whatsoever, and that we may know as much of Him as of anything else in the world. For the *very essence* or naked *substance* of nothing can possibly be known, according to Axiom 8. <note>The author refers to his own list of logical principles established earlier in the work.</note> But as for *His attributes*, they are as clear as the attributes of any subject or substance whatever. From these, a person may easily define Him thus: *God is a Spirit who is eternal, infinite in essence and goodness, all-knowing, all-powerful, and necessarily existing of Himself.*

I appeal to any person to say if every term in this definition is not sufficiently understandable. For as for *spirit*, that has already been defined and explained. By *eternal*, I understand nothing here but duration without end or beginning. By *infiniteness of essence*, I mean that His *essence* or *substance* has no bounds, any more than His *duration*. By *infinite in goodness*, I mean such a kind will in God that it results in boundless and innumerable acts of kindness. By *omniscience* and *omnipotence*, I mean the ability to know or do anything that can be imagined without a clear contradiction. By *self-existence*, I mean that He receives His being from no one else; and by *necessary existence*, I mean that He cannot fail to exist. What terms of any definition are clearer than these? Or what subject can be more accurately defined than this is? For the naked *subject* or *substance* of anything is known in no other way than this. And those who eagerly seek after any other theoretical knowledge of God beyond what is derived from His *attributes* and *actions* may have their heads and mouths filled with many hot, burning fantasies and words, and may go mad from the unruliness of their own imagination, but they will never arrive at any sober truth.

<sig>I i</sig>

3. Thus I have delivered a very explicit and understandable concept of the *nature of God*. I might also more briefly define Him as *an absolutely perfect essence*, in which all the terms of the previous definition are included—and more than I have named or thought necessary to mention, much less insist upon. These include His *power of creation* and His *omnipresence* or *ubiquity* <note>original: "ubiquity," the state of being everywhere at once</note>, which are necessarily included in the *idea of absolute perfection*. Some ancient philosophers, endeavoring to describe this latter quality, have defined God as a *circle whose center is everywhere and whose circumference is nowhere*. By this description, they certainly meant nothing else than that the Divine Essence is *everywhere present* with all those adorable attributes of *infinite and absolutely perfect goodness, knowledge, and power*, according to the sense in which I have explained them. This ubiquity or omnipresence of God is just as understandable as the way *matter* spreads out to fill all places.

4. But if anyone asks here how the "parts" (as I may call them) of the Divine vastness hold together, since *matter* is so easily <term>discerpible</term> <note>original: "discerpible," meaning capable of being torn apart or divided into pieces; a key concept for More, who argued spirits cannot be divided like physical objects</note>, it might be enough to remind him of what we have already said concerning the general concept of a *spirit*. But besides that, a specific logical explanation can be given: it implies a contradiction that an *absolutely perfect essence* should be either limited in its presence or change its place in part or in whole. Both of these are obvious signs or symptoms of imperfection, which is inconsistent with the nature of God. No better or more compelling reason can be given for anything than that it would be a logical contradiction for it to be otherwise.

5. Regarding the power of creating things from nothing, there is a very close connection between that and the *idea of God*, or of a *being absolutely perfect*. For this Being would not be what He is conceived to be if He lacked the *power of creation*. Therefore, this attribute is so consistent with the subject that it is a contradiction for it not to exist in Him, just as was observed regarding the previous attribute of *indiscerpibility* <note>original: "indiscerpibility," the quality of being impossible to divide or break into parts</note> in God. To claim that a person cannot imagine how God could create something from nothing, or how the Divine Essence holds so closely and invincible together, is to violate the 3rd, 4th, and 5th axioms, and to appeal to a mental faculty <note>More refers here to the imagination, which he believes is often misled by physical analogies, whereas Reason can grasp these truths</note> that has no right to judge the case.

# CHAPTER V. The Immortality of the Soul.

<margin>Book 1, chapter 4, section 3.</margin>
The properties of a *Spirit*, as it is a concept common to all these things, I have already listed in my *Antidote*: *Self-motion*, *Self-penetration*, *Self-contraction and expansion*, and *Indivisibility* (by which I mean <term>indiscerpibility</term> <note>original: "indiscerpibility," the quality of being impossible to tear, divide, or separate into distinct parts</note>). To these I added *Penetrating*, *Moving*, and *Altering matter*. We may therefore define *this kind of Spirit* we speak of as *a substance that is indiscerpible, that can move itself, that can penetrate, contract, and expand itself, and can also penetrate, move, and alter Matter*. We will now examine every term of this definition, from which it shall appear that it is as consistent and intelligible as those definitions made of things that all people, without any doubt, acknowledge to exist.

2. Regarding the *Indiscerpibility* of a *Spirit*, we have already given rational grounds to prove it is not impossible, as it is an *immediate attribute* of it—just as *impenetrability* is an attribute of a *Body*. It is as conceivable or imaginable that one *Substance* by its own nature may invincibly hold its parts together so that they cannot be disunited or severed, as it is that another substance may keep out another substance so strongly and irresistibly from entering into the same space or place as itself. For this *resistance* <note>original Greek: "$\alpha\nu\tau\iota\tau\upsilon\pi\iota\alpha$" (antitypia), meaning a pushing back or the quality of being solid and impenetrable</note> or *impenetrability* is not at all contained in the precise concept of a *Substance* as *Substance*, as I have already indicated.

But besides the fact that *Reason* may thus easily understand that it may be so, I shall slightly indulge the *Imagination*—and perhaps *Reason* too—by offering the *manner* in which it is so, in this kind of *Spirit* we now discuss. That ancient concept of *Light* and <term>intentional species</term> <note>original: "intentional species," a term from medieval philosophy referring to the forms or images that objects emit so they can be perceived by the senses</note> is so far from being a plain impossibility that it was formerly generally accepted, and is still by very many people looked upon as a truth—that is, that *Light* and *Color* radiate in the way they are described in <term>Aristotelian philosophy</term> <note>original: "Peripatetical Philosophie," referring to the school of Aristotle</note>. Now, it is observable in *Light* that it is most vigorous near its source and grows fainter by degrees. But we will simplify the matter to *one point of light*, which, according to the acknowledged principles of Optics, will fill a distance of space with its *rays of light*. These rays may indeed be reflected back toward their *center* by placing some opaque body in their way, and thus this *sphere of light* may be contracted; but, according to the *Aristotelian Hypothesis*, it was always considered impossible that they should be "clipped off" or cut from this *point of light* and be kept apart by themselves.

3. But if anyone objects that the *shining center of this sphere*, or the *Primary Substance* (as I \* elsewhere call it), is either *divisible* or *absolutely indivisible*; and if it is *divisible*, that regarding the *innermost part of a Spirit*, this representation is not at all useful to illustrate its nature by showing how the parts there may hold together so indiscerpibly; but if it is *absolutely indivisible*, that it seems to be nothing: to this I answer what <term>Scaliger</term> <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger (1484–1558), a famous Renaissance scholar and physician</note> somewhere has noted: *That what is infinitely great or infinitely...*

<meta>This page continues the discussion on whether a Spirit—an indivisible substance—can logically exist in a physical world. The previous page explored how "indiscerpibility" (indivisibility) is as reasonable a property for a Spirit as "impenetrability" is for a physical Body.</meta>

...infinitely small, the imagination of man is at a loss to conceive it. This certainly is the ground of the complex problem concerning Matter: whether it consists of points, or only of particles that are divisible <note>original: "in infinitum"</note> to infinity.

But to come more closely to the business: I say that though we should acknowledge the *inmost center of life*, or the very *first point*, as I may call it, of the *Primary Substance* (for this *Primary Substance* exists in degrees) to be *purely indivisible*, it does not at all follow—even according to *Imagination* itself—that it must be nothing. For let us imagine a *perfect plane*, and on this *plane* a *perfect globe*. We cannot conceive of this except that the *globe* touches the *plane*, and does so in what we ordinarily call a *point*; otherwise, one would not be a *globe*, or the other would not be a *plane*. Now it is impossible that one body should touch another, and yet touch one another in nothing. This *inmost center* of life, therefore, is something. It is something so full of essential vigor and power that, though it gradually diminishes, it can still fill a certain sphere of space with its own presence and activity, just as a spark of light illuminates the dim air.

Wherefore, there being no greater complexity or subtlety in the consideration of this *center of life* (or the *inmost part of a Spirit*) than there is in the *atoms of matter*, we may by *Axiom 7* rightly conclude that *indiscerpibility* <term>the quality of being impossible to tear or divide into parts</term> has nothing in its definition that is inconsistent with the possible existence of the thing to which it belongs.

## CHAPTER VI.

*1. Axioms that tend to demonstrate how the Center or First point of the Primary Substance of a Spirit may be Indiscerpible. 2. Several others that demonstrate how the Secondary Substance of a Spirit may be Indiscerpible. 3. An application of these Principles. 4. Of the union of the Secondary Substance considered transversely. 5. That the concept of a Spirit has less difficulty than that of Matter. 6. An Answer to an objection from the Rational faculty. 7. Answers to Objections suggested from Fancy. 8. A more brief explanation concerning the concept of a Spirit.*

I. And thus we have fairly well satisfied the *curiosity* of the inquisitive concerning the *Extension* and *Indiscerpibility* of a *Spirit*. But we shall advance even higher and demonstrate the possibility of this concept to the most rigorous Reason using these following principles.

### AXIOM XI.

*A Globe touches a Plane in something, even if it is the smallest thing imaginable to be real.*

### AXIOM XII.

*The smallest thing imaginable is so small that it cannot be conceived to be divisible <note>original: "discerpible"</note> into anything smaller.*

### AXIOM XIII.

*As small as this point is, the repetition of it will amount to a considerable size.*

For example, if this globe is moved across a plane, it creates a *line*. A cylinder moved across a plane—or that same *line* multiplied by itself—creates a *surface*, and so on. No one can deny this; in fact, the more one thinks about it, the more certainly true he will find it to be.

### AXIOM XIV.

*Size cannot arise out of things that have no size.*

If you multiply *nothing* ten billion times by nothing, the *product* will still be *nothing*. Furthermore, if the point where the globe touches a plane were more than just *indiscerpible*—that is, if it were purely *indivisible*—it is obvious that a *line* would consist of *mathematical points*. <note>A mathematical point is defined as having position but no size (length, width, or depth).</note> To say that a line is made of such points is the greatest absurdity allowed in philosophy and the most contradictory thing imaginable.

### AXIOM XV.

*The same thing, because of its extreme smallness, may be utterly indiscerpible <term>impossible to physically pull apart or divide</term>, even though it is intellectually divisible.*

This clearly follows from the previous principles. Every quantity is *intellectually* divisible; however, I have already demonstrated that something *indiscerpible* is still a quantity and therefore conceptually divisible. If it were not, then physical size would be made of mathematical points. 

Thus, I have found a logical basis for the concept of the *Center of a Spirit*. It is not a mathematical point, but a substance. In its size, it is so small that it is *indiscerpible*; yet in its power, it is so great that it can emit from itself a large sphere of *secondary substance* (as I call it). This sphere is able to animate and move large proportions of *matter*, while the entire sphere of life and activity remains, in itself, utterly *indiscerpible*.

2. I have stated this, and I shall now prove it by adding a few more principles. These are so evident that even the most rigorous reason will be unable to deny them.

### AXIOM XVI.

*An "emanative cause" is a concept of a possible thing.*

By an *emanative cause*, we mean a cause that produces an *effect* simply by *existing*, without any other activity or separate process coming between them. It is clear that this is possible because it can be demonstrated that there is, in fact <note>original: "de facto"</note>, some such cause in the world. This is because something must be able to move itself. Now, if there is no such thing as *spirit*, then *matter* must necessarily move itself. In that case, you cannot imagine any activity or cause other than the bare essence of the matter itself.

<summary>Henry More argues that spirits have a "center" of substance that is physically indivisible yet conceptually divisible, and that spirits act as "emanative causes" which influence matter simply by existing.</summary>

<margin>See the Appendix to the Antidote, chapter 13, section 4.</margin>
...matter from which this motion comes. For if you were to suppose some prior motion that might be the cause of this, then we might with just as much reason suppose some prior motion to be the cause of that, and so on *to infinity* <note>original: in infinitum</note>.

### AXIOM XVII.

*An emanative effect <term>an effect that flows directly and naturally out of a source, like light from a candle</term> exists at the same time as the very substance that is said to be its cause.*

This must be true because that very substance which is said to be the cause is the sufficient and immediate cause; it needs nothing added to its basic essence to produce the effect. Therefore, for the same reason that the effect exists at any point in time, it must exist at all times—or at least as long as that substance exists.

### AXIOM XVIII.

*No emanative effect that does not exceed the virtues and powers of its cause can be said to be impossible for that cause to produce.*

This is so clear that nothing needs to be added for either explanation or proof.

### AXIOM XIX.

*There may be a substance of such high virtue and excellence that it can produce another substance through emanative causality, provided that the produced substance is inferior to its cause in proper, gradual proportions.*

This is clear from the previous principle. There is no contradiction or impossibility in a cause producing an effect less "noble" (or perfect) than itself; indeed, this gives us better assurance that the effect does not exceed the capacity of the cause's own powers. Nor is it inconsistent for one substance to cause something else that we might, in some sense, call a "substance"—even if it is only a "secondary" or "emanatory" one. 

We recognize the primary substance as the direct object of God's creation, but the secondary substance can also be traced back to the primary (or central) substance through a causal relationship. For example, suppose God created matter with the immediate power to move itself. God is indeed the prime cause of both the motion and the matter, yet the matter is still rightly said to move itself. Finally, this secondary or emanatory substance can rightly be called a "substance" because it is an entity endowed with certain powers and activities, and it does not exist merely as an "accident" <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a property that cannot exist on its own, such as the color red or the shape of a table.</note> within another substance or matter. Instead, it could maintain its place even if all matter (or any other substance) were removed from the space it occupies, provided its primary substance remained safe.

3. From these four principles I have added here, we can gain a rational—rather than merely imaginary—understanding of the part of a spirit that we call its **secondary substance**. Its extension <term>the space it occupies</term> arises by gradual emanation from the first and most fundamental essence, which we call the **center of the spirit**. (This is not an impossible supposition, according to Axioms 16, 18, and 19).

More argues that this secondary extension is a true substance because it can exist independently of matter, provided its central source remains.</summary>

Based on these Axioms, we are led to a necessary acknowledgment of the perfect **indiscerpibility** <term>the quality of being impossible to tear apart or separate into pieces</term> of a spirit's parts, even if they are not **intellectually indivisible** (according to Axiom 17). For it implies a contradiction that an **emanative effect** <term>an effect that flows directly and naturally out of a source, like light from a candle</term> should be disjoined from its original source.

4. Thus, I have demonstrated how a *Spirit*—considering its "lineaments" (as I may call them) from the center to the circumference—is utterly *indiscerpible*. But now, if anyone is curious enough to ask how its parts hold together in a line drawn across these (from the center outwards), since *Imagination* might suggest they all lie loose, I answer that the conjecture of *Imagination* here is partly true and partly false, depending on how it is interpreted. For if "loose" means "actually disunited," then the idea is false and ridiculous. But if it only means "discerpible" in the sense that one part may be moved away from another, that may not only be true, but—supposing the essential rays are not fully reinforced from within—plainly necessary. Otherwise, a Spirit could not contract one part and extend another, which is a hypothesis that must be admitted. Therefore, this objection is so far from weakening the possibility of this notion that it provides an opportunity to more fully declare its exact **concinnity** <term>an elegant and harmonious fitting together of parts</term>.

To be brief, therefore, a *Spirit* is utterly *indiscerpible* from its center to its circumference; but in lines crossing this path, it is closely coherent, though not necessarily *indiscerpibly* so. This cohesion may consist in an immediate union of these parts, and a transverse penetration and crossing of **Secondary Substance** <term>the extended "body" or aura of the spirit that emanates from its central point</term> through this whole "sphere of life" which we call a *Spirit*.

<margin>Aristotle, *Nicomachean Ethics*, Book 10, chapter 7.</margin>
Nor should we wonder that so full an orb should swell out from such a subtle and small point as the *center of this Spirit* is supposed to be. "For even if it is small in bulk, in power and value it far surpasses all things," <note>original Greek: Εἰ γὰρ καὶ τῷ ὄγκῳ μικρόν ἐστι, δυνάμει καὶ τιμιότητι πολὺ μᾶλλον ὑπερέχει πάντων</note> as *Aristotle* says of the human mind. And besides, it is no more than what is seen by the eye in the nature of light: how a tiny spark can illuminate a large sphere of air.

5. This is the pure **Idea of a created Spirit** in general. If there is still any objection to be made against it, it can be none other than the same objection made against **Matter**: namely, the difficulty of imagining points and the smallest particles, and how something that is "discerpible" (divisible) can hang together at all. But since this difficulty does not prevent *Matter* from actually existing, there is no reason it should imply that the existence of a *Spirit* is impossible, according to Axiom 7.

However, the most **slippery** <note>original: "lubricous"</note> supposition we rely on here is not nearly as intricate as those difficulties found in *Matter*. For if it is granted—and I find no absurdity in it—that a particle of *Matter* may be so small that it is utterly incapable of being made smaller, it is plain that one and the same thing, though intellectually divisible, may yet be really indiscerpible. And indeed, it is not only possible, but it seems necessary that this should be true. For even if we were to acknowledge that *Matter* were discerpible *to infinity* <note>original: in infinitum</note>, yet if we suppose a Cause of infinite and distinct perception and infinite power (and God is such a cause), this Cause can turn this capacity for infinite division of *Matter* into reality; that is to say,

<meta>catchword: say,</meta>

<summary>Henry More argues that a spirit is "indiscerpible" (inseparable) from its center to its edge because it is an effect flowing from a source, though it remains flexible enough to contract and expand. He compares the spirit's expansion from a tiny center to a spark illuminating a room and argues that spirits are no more conceptually difficult to accept than the existence of matter.</summary>

--- Page 416 ---
<meta>This page continues the philosophical argument regarding the nature of substance. Having discussed the "indiscerpibility" (inseparability) of Spirit on the previous page, the author now transitions to a proof that even Matter, at its most fundamental level, must consist of particles that cannot be physically divided further, even if we can still divide them in our minds.</meta>

<page-num>30</page-num>
<header>The Immortality of the Soul. BOOK I.</header>

say, actually and at once **tear it apart** <term>original: "discerpt"</term> or **disjoin** it into as many particles as it is **separable** <term>original: "discerptible"</term> into. From this, it will follow that one of these particles, reduced to this **absolute smallness** <term>original: "perfect Parvitude"</term>, is then utterly **inseparable** <term>original: "indiscerptible"</term>. Yet, it remains intellectually divisible; otherwise, **Size** <term>original: "Magnitude"</term> would consist of mere points <note>In geometry, a "point" has no size. The author argues that if you couldn't mentally divide the smallest particle, it would be a point, and you cannot build a physical object out of things with zero size.</note>, which would imply a contradiction.

We have therefore plainly demonstrated by reason that **Matter** consists of parts that are **inseparable** <term>original: "indiscerptible"</term>. Since there is no other faculty to testify against this—for neither **Sense** nor any **Common Notion** <term>a self-evident truth</term> can contradict it—it remains true according to Axiom 5.

6. Some would object from **Reason** that if these **absolute smallnesses** are acknowledged to be still intellectually divisible, they must still have parts into which they can be divided, and therefore still be separable. To this, it is answered that the **division into parts** does not imply any **separability** <term>original: "discerptibility"</term>. This is because the parts conceived in one of these **smallest physical particles** <note>original: "Minima Corporalia"</note> (as I may call them) are **essential** or **formal** parts rather than **structural** <term>original: "integral"</term> parts. They can no more be actually severed than **Sense** and **Reason** can be severed from the **Soul of a man**. For it is part of the very **Essence of Matter** to be **divisible** <note>mentally</note>, but it is not at all required by its essence to be **separable** <note>physically torn apart</note>. Therefore, where the ability to be torn apart fails, there is no necessity that the ability to be mentally divided should also fail. See the Preface, Section 3.

7. As for the trouble of false suggestions or representations from the **Imagination** <term>original: "Phansy"</term>—such as the idea that these **absolute smallnesses** were **Round** bodies, and that there would therefore be **triangular gaps** <term>original: "intervalls"</term> between them, void of Matter—these are of no importance in this case. The imagination always represents a **separable size** instead of an **inseparable** one. Therefore, since she brings in false evidence, her testimony is to be rejected. Indeed, even if she could perplex the cause far worse, she was not to be heard, according to Axiom 4.

Therefore, since **Imagination** is unable to show the object we are considering in its proper light, for all we know, these **absolute smallnesses** may lie so close together that they have no **gaps** between them. Indeed, it seems necessary for this to be so; for if there were any such **gaps**, they would be capable of containing particles even smaller than these "smallest of all," which is a contradiction in **Reason** and a thing utterly impossible.

But if we should gratify the **Imagination** so far as to admit these gaps, the greatest absurdity would be that we must admit an invisible **Vacuum** <term>an empty void</term>, which no faculty will ever be able to disprove. But it is most rational to admit *none*, and more consistent with our determination concerning these **smallest physical particles** <note>original: "Minima Corporalia"</note>. Their size is to be limited to the smallest real touch of either a **Globe** on a **Plane** <term>a flat surface</term>, or a **Cone** on a **Plane**, or a **Globe** on a **Globe**. If you can conceive of any real touch smaller than another, let that be the measure of these **Minute Realities** in **Matter**. From this, it will follow that they must touch a whole side at once, and therefore can never leave any empty **gaps**.

Nor can we imagine any **corners** <term>original: "Angulosities"</term> or **round bumps** <term>original: "protuberancies"</term> in a quantity that is infinitely little, any more than we can in one that is infinitely great, as I have already declared in my Preface. I must confess, a man’s **Reason** in this speculation is mounted far beyond his **Imagination**; but since there are worse intricacies in theories constantly acknowledged to be true, it can...

...would be no prejudice to the present conclusion, according to the 4th and 7th Axioms.

8. Thus, we have clarified a full and distinct understanding of a **Spirit** with such undeniable accuracy that no Reason can claim it is impossible or incomprehensible. However, if this theory seems too laborious <note>original: "operose"</note> and tedious for impatient minds, or if the precision of the description seems risky and hard to believe—as if it were beyond our human faculties to reach such a precise conclusion on such an obscure subject—they may ease their understanding by being satisfied with what we established in Chapter 2, Sections 11 and 12. They should remember that the Wisdom and Power that created all things can make them of whatever nature He pleases. If God wills that there be a creature that is *penetrable and inseparable* <term>original: "indiscerpible"</term>, it is as easy for Him to make it so by its own nature as it is to make one *impenetrable and separable* <term>original: "discerpible"</term>. He may endow it with whatever other properties <note>original: "induments"</note> He chooses, according to His own will and purpose. Since these qualities are directly united with the subject they inhabit, Reason can ask no further how they are there, according to the 9th Axiom.

### CHAPTER VII.

1. *Regarding the self-motion of a Spirit.* 2. *Regarding self-penetration.* 3. *Regarding self-contraction and expansion <term>original: "dilatation"</term>.* 4. *The power of penetrating Matter.* 5. *The power of moving,* 6. *And of altering Matter.*

1. WE have proved that the **inseparability** <term>original: "Indiscerpibility"</term> of a **Spirit** is a very consistent and logical concept, whether we consider its **center** or its **outer edges** <term>original: "circumference"</term>, and whether we consider its **inner core** or its **extended presence** <term>original: "Primary as Secondary Substance"</term>. The next property is **self-motion**, which must necessarily be a quality of some substance or other. By *self-motion*, I mean nothing other than *self-activity*, which must belong to a subject that is active by its own nature. Now, whatever is active by its own nature can no more stop being active than it can stop existing. This is a sign that **matter** is not active by itself, because matter can be brought to a state of **rest**. This argument not only shows that *self-activity* belongs to a **spirit**, but also that there is such a thing as a **spirit** in the world, from which activity is passed on to **matter**. Indeed, if matter as matter had its own motion, nothing would hold together. Flints, diamonds <term>original: "Adamant"</term>, brass, iron, and even this whole Earth would suddenly melt into a substance thinner than the subtle **air**; or rather, matter would never have been compressed together into the solid form we find it in. But this is to anticipate my future goal of proving that spirits actually exist in the world. It is enough here to have asserted that *self-motion* or *self-activity* is just as easy to imagine belonging to a *spirit* as it is to a *body*—a fact that is plain at first sight to anyone who consults their own mental faculties. Nor should we hesitate to allow that something can *move itself*. Our opponents, who claim there is nothing but *matter* in the world, must of necessity (as I have already mentioned) admit that this *matter moves itself*, even though it is very illogical to say so.

2. The logic and possibility of **self-penetration** in a created **spirit**...

is to be conceived, partly from the finiteness <note>original: "limitableness"</note> of the Subject, and partly from the previously mentioned attributes of **inseparability** <term>original: "Indiscerpibility"; the quality of being unable to be divided into parts</term> and **self-motion**. For **self-penetration** cannot belong to **God**, because it is impossible for anything to belong to him that implies imperfection. **Self-penetration** cannot occur without lessening the presence of the thing that penetrates itself, or implying that some parts of that **essence** are not as well-off as they might be—which is a contradiction in a Being that is absolutely **perfect**. From the attributes of **inseparability** and **self-motion** (to which you may add **penetrability** from the general definition of a **spirit**), it is plain that such a **spirit** as we define—having the power of motion over the whole extent of its essence—may also determine this motion according to the property of its own nature. Therefore, if it directs its outer parts inward, they will return toward the center of its essential power. They may easily do this without resistance, as the whole subject is penetrable, and without damage, as it is also **inseparable**.

3. From this **self-penetration**, we do not only easily, but necessarily, understand **self-contraction** and **expansion** <term>original: "dilatation"</term> to arise. For this **self-moving substance** which we call a **spirit** cannot penetrate itself without also contracting itself; nor can it restore itself to its former state without thereby expanding itself. So, we do not need to dwell further on these **terms**.

4. That power which a **spirit** has to penetrate **matter** we may easily understand if we consider a **spirit** only as a **substance** whose immediate property is **activity**. For then it is no harder to imagine this active substance pervading this or that part of **matter** than it is to conceive of the spreading of motion itself within it.

5. The greatest difficulty is to imagine how this **spirit**, being so **bodiless** <note>original: "incorporeal"</note>, can be able to move **matter**, even though it is within it. For it seems so subtle that it will pass through, leaving no more footsteps of its presence than lightning does in a scabbard <note>original: "Scabbard"; a sheath for a sword</note>—though lightning may perhaps melt the sword because it finds resistance there. But a **spirit** can find no resistance anywhere, as the densest **matter** is easily penetrable and passable to a **bodiless substance**. The ground of this difficulty is based on the inability to conceive of any **union** that can exist between **matter** and a **substance** that can so easily pass through it. For if we could once imagine a **union** between **matter** and a **spirit**, the activity of the **spirit** would certainly have an influence upon the **matter**, whether for creating, increasing, or directing its motion.

But despite the **penetrability** and easy passage of a **spirit** through **matter**, there is still a capacity for a strong union between them, which is every bit as conceivable as the union between the parts of **matter** themselves. For what glue or cement holds the parts of hard matter together in stones and metals? Or, if you prefer, in something that is absolutely hard—having no pores or particles, but being one continued and perfectly uniform body, not only to the **senses** but according to the exact **rational concept** <term>original: "Idea of Reason"</term>—what cement holds together the parts of such

### CHAPTER VII. The Immortality of the Soul.

...such a body as this? Certainly nothing but *immediate union and rest*. Now, regarding *union*, there is no comparison between the union of *matter* with *matter* and this union of *spirit* with *matter*. For the first is only *superficial* <note>original: "superficiall"; occurring only on the surface level</note>; in the latter, the very inward parts are united point to point throughout. Nor is there any fear that the spirit will not take hold simply because it has the capacity to pass through the matter. For in this absolutely solid, hard <image-desc>A diagram of a geometric block or cube. A dotted line bisects the block horizontally. Points are labeled with letters: D at the top, C at the upper right, E on the left side where the dotted line begins, A in the center of the dotted line, and F at the bottom left.</image-desc> body—which we will call **A**—let us conceive of some inward surface <note>original: "superficies"</note>, such as **E A C**. This surface is so smooth that nothing can be conceived smoother. Why, therefore, does the upper part **E D C** not slide upon the lower <note>original: "neather"</note> part **E F C** at the slightest imaginable motion, especially if **E F C** is supposed to be held fast while the other is pushed against it? This ease of one body passing over another without sticking seems as necessary to our imagination <note>original: "Phansy"</note> as a *spirit* passing through all bodies without catching onto them. Therefore, it is plain by Axiom 7 <note>More refers to his own set of metaphysical axioms established earlier in this book</note> that a firm union of *spirit* and *matter* is very possible, even though we cannot fully conceive the manner in which it happens.

And as for *rest*, it is also compatible <note>original: "competible"</note> with this conjunction of *matter* with *spirit*, just as it is with the union of *matter* with *matter*. For suppose the whole body **A** moves with the same speed in every part; the parts of **A** are then—according to that sense of *rest* by which they would explain how the parts of *matter* stick to one another—truly at rest <note>original: "quiescent"</note>. In the same way, I say that in the *union* of *matter* and *spirit*, the parts of the *matter* receive from the *spirit* exactly the same velocity of motion that the *spirit* exerts, and no more. Thus, they both rest in a firm *union* with one another. This happens even when there is far less immediate *union* than what we are discussing. For if we simply lay a book on our hand—provided our hand does not move with a swifter motion than it communicates to the book, and the book is not pushed faster than the speed of our hand—the book and our hand will certainly maintain their union and move together. It is that natural and easy to conceive how a *spirit* may move a *body* without any more confusion or contradiction than is found in the *union* and *motion* of the parts of *matter* itself. See the Appendix to my <margin>Chapter 3, sections 7 and 8.</margin> *Antidote* <note>Henry More's book *An Antidote against Atheism* (1653)</note>.

6. The last term I included in the definition of a *spirit* is the *power of altering matter*. This necessarily follows from its power of *moving* it or *directing its motion*. For *alteration* is nothing more than varying either the shapes <note>original: "Figures"</note>, the positions, or the degrees of motion in the particles; all of which are simply the results of *local motion* <term>the movement of a physical object from one place to another</term>. In this way, we have clarified the *intelligibility* and *possibility* of all the terms belonging to the concept of a *created spirit* in general—at least those that can be rationally conceived to be the causes of any visible phenomena in the world. We will now move on to defining the chief types <note>original: "Species"</note> of spirits.

->### CHAPTER VIII.<-

1. Four main species of spirits. 2. How they are to be defined. 3. The definition of a *Seminal Form*. 4. Of the *Soul of a Beast* <note>original: "Brute"</note>. 5. Of the *Human Soul*. 6. The difference between the *Soul of an Angel* and a *Human Soul*. 7. The definition of an *Angelic Soul*. 8. <margin>1.</margin> We have listed four kinds of spirits: the *formative principles* <note>original: λόγοι σπερματικοί (logoi spermatikoi); literally "seed-reasons," a Stoic and Neoplatonic term for the internal blueprints of life</note> or **Seminal Forms**, the **souls of beasts**, the **human soul**, and that **soul or spirit** which activates or gives life to the "vehicles" <note>More uses "vehicle" to describe the airy or ethereal bodies used by spirits or angels</note> of **angels**. I consider angels to be truly composite beings, consisting of soul and body just like humans and animals. I will not attempt to prove their existence here, as that belongs to another discussion. My current goal is only to explain or define the concept of these things, enough to show that they are *possible ideas*—notions that contain no internal contradiction or impossibility. This will be very easy to do, as the main difficulty lay in the more *general concept* of a spirit, which we have already explained thoroughly in the previous chapters.

<margin>2.</margin> Now, this *general concept* can be divided into specific *types* only by identifying "differences"—that is, specific powers or properties belonging to one spirit but not another, according to Axiom 8. Therefore, it follows that if we describe these various kinds of spirits by their essential and internal properties, we have provided as good a definition for them as can be given for anything in the world.

<margin>3.</margin> We will begin with the simplest type: the **Seminal Forms** of things. Without deciding whether they actually exist yet, but considering them as a *possible idea* <note>original: "idea possibilis"</note>, we define them as follows: *A **Seminal Form** is a created spirit that organizes properly prepared matter into the specific life and growth <note>original: "vegetation"</note> of a particular kind of plant.* I cannot imagine any objection to this description, as it is entirely coherent and understandable. Because it is a *spirit*, it can move matter from within, or at least *direct its movement*. However, since it is not an all-powerful spirit, but rather *finite and created*, its power may be limited to *properly prepared matter* for both its vital union and its movement. The Creator who made these specific spirits varied their abilities to unite with life according to how the matter is prepared, limiting them so that none of them can be joined with just any matter. The same First Cause <note>referring to God</note> of all things who gives them the power to unite with and move *properly prepared matter* may also establish laws for this motion. Thus, when the spirit encounters the right kind of matter, it will produce a specific type of plant.

4. This is the first degree of *particular life* in the world—*if there are any beings that exist purely at this level. But now, as *Aristotle* noted somewhere, the essences of things are like numbers, whose species are changed by adding or taking away a single unit. Therefore, add another *intrinsic* power to this one of *vegetative growth* <note>original: "Vegetation"</note>—namely, *sensation*—and it becomes the *soul of a beast* <note>original: "Brute"</note>. For in truth, the bare substance itself cannot be calculated in explicit knowledge, being utterly inconceivable in itself; therefore, we will only count its powers. *A subject from which both growth and sensation originate is the general concept of the soul of an animal.* This is distributed into many kinds, with the effect of every *intrinsic* power being discernible in the constant shape and properties of every distinct kind of animal.

5. If we add *reason*, properly so called, to *growth* and *sensation*, we then have a settled notion of the *soul of man*, which we may more completely describe as: *A created spirit endowed with sense and reason, and a power of organizing terrestrial matter into human shape by vital union with it.*

6. And in this alone, I believe, does the spirit or soul of an angel (for I take the boldness to call whatever power it is that vitally animates matter a *soul*) differ from the *soul of a man*: the soul of an *angel* may vitally animate an *aerial* or *ethereal* body, but it cannot be born into this world in a *terrestrial* <note>earthly</note> one.

7. To finish our definitions: an *angelic soul* is very intelligibly described as: *A created spirit endowed with reason, sensation, and a power of being vitally united with and animating a body of air or ether only.* This power over an *aerial* or *ethereal* body is very easily understood from the general notion of a *spirit* in the previous chapters. For since it was established there that union with *matter* is not incompatible with a *spirit*—and consequently, neither is the moving of it, nor that kind of motion in a spirit which we call *contraction* and *dilation*—these powers, if carefully considered, will necessarily imply the possibility of the animation and union of an *angelic soul* with an *ethereal* or *airy body*.

8. The *Platonists* write of other orders of *spirits* or *immaterial substances*, such as the *Intelligences* <note>original: Νόες (Noës)</note> and *Unities* <note>original: Ἑνάδες (Henades)</note>. But since there is more subtlety than either usefulness or certainty in such speculations, I shall pass over them at this time. I have already, I think, irrefutably established that there is no incongruity or impossibility within the concept of *spirit* or *incorporeal substance*.

9. But there is yet another way of inferring the same thing, and it is the *argument of Descartes*, by which he concludes that there is in fact <note>original: "de facto"</note> a *substance* in us distinct from matter: namely, our own *mind*. For since every *real affection* or property is the *mode* <note>a specific state or quality of a substance</note> of some substance or another, and since real *modes* are inconceivable without their *subject*, he infers that, because we can doubt whether there is any such thing as *body* in the world (by which doubting we exclude *thought* <note>original: "Cogitation"</note> from *body*)...

<header>The Immortality of the Soul. BOOK I.</header>

...there must be some other substance distinct from the body to which *thinking* <note>original: "Cogitation"</note> belongs.

But I must confess this argument does not fully achieve *Descartes's* <note>original: "Des-Cartes his"</note> purpose, who intended to prove that in Man there is a *substance distinct from his body*. For since there may be *modes* <note>In 17th-century philosophy, a "mode" is a specific quality, state, or manner of being of a substance.</note> common to more than one subject, and this quality of *thinking* may be claimed to be compatible with physical <note>original: "Corporeal"</note> as well as non-physical <note>original: "Incorporeal"</note> substance, it may be conceived of separately from either, though not from both. And therefore his argument does not prove that the part of us which thinks or *perceives* is a substance distinct from our body, but only that there *can* be such a substance which has the power of *thinking* or *perceiving* that is not a *body*. For because it is impossible for there to be any real *mode* that exists in no subject at all, and since we clearly conceive of *thinking* as existing independently of physical substance, it is necessary that there can be some other substance on which it may depend; which must therefore be a *non-physical substance*.

# CHAPTER IX.

1. *That it is of no small consequence to have proved the possibility of the existence of a spirit.* 2. *The necessity of examining Mr. Hobbes's reasons to the contrary.* 3. *The first extract from Mr. Hobbes.* 4. *The second extract.* 5. *The third.* 6. *The fourth.* 7. *The fifth.* 8. *The sixth.* 9. *The seventh.* 10. *The eighth and last extract.* <note>original: "Excerption"</note>

I have been, I believe, surprisingly meticulous <note>original: "to admiration curious"</note> and concerned to prove that the existence of a spirit or non-physical substance is possible. But there is no reason anyone should wonder why I have taken so much trouble to make such a small and minor step as to bring the matter only to a *mere possibility*. For though I may seem to have gained little for my own case, I have thereby dealt a significant defeat to the opposing party, whose strongest position seems to be a firm confidence that the very notion of a *spirit* or *immaterial substance* is an utter impossibility and pure nonsense. From that view, they suggest consequences no better than these: That it is impossible for there to be any God, or Soul, or Angel (good or bad); or any immortality or life to come. That there is no religion, no piety or impiety, no virtue or vice, no justice or injustice, except for what the person with the longest sword <note>meaning the most military or political power</note> chooses to call so. That there is no freedom of the will, and consequently no rational remorse of conscience in any being whatsoever, but that all that exists is nothing but *matter* and *physical motion*; and that therefore every path of a human life is as *necessary* as the path of lightning or the strike of thunder—the blind *force* <note>original: "impetus"</note> of matter breaking through or being stopped everywhere with as certain and fixed a *necessity* as the flow of a torrent after mighty storms and showers of rain.

2. 3. The first passage I will note is in his * *Leviathan*: *"The word 'Body,' in its most general meaning, signifies that which fills or occupies some specific space or imagined place; it does not depend on the imagination but is a real part of what we call the Universe. For the Universe being the sum total of all bodies, there is no real part of it that is not also a body; nor is anything properly a body that is not also part of (that sum total of all bodies) the Universe. The same thing, because bodies are subject to change—that is, to appearing in various ways to the senses of living creatures—is called 'Substance,' meaning it is subject to various attributes* <note>original: "Accidents"; in 17th-century philosophy, "accidents" are non-essential properties like color, smell, or motion that can change while the underlying substance remains.</note>*, such as sometimes moving, sometimes standing still, and appearing to our senses sometimes hot, sometimes cold, or of one color, smell, taste, or sound, and sometimes another. And this variety of appearance (produced by the different ways bodies act upon our sensory organs) we attribute to changes in the bodies themselves, and we call them 'attributes' of those bodies. According to this understanding of the word, 'Substance' and 'Body' mean the same thing. Therefore, 'non-physical substance' are words which, when joined together, cancel each other out, as if a man should say an 'immaterial body.'"*

These have been, and still are, mistakenly accepted as real truths under the names of 'ghosts' and 'non-physical substances.'"*

But because they hold them to be incorporeal <term>without physical form</term> and lacking all dimension of quantity, and since all men know that a "place" is a dimension and cannot be filled by anything but a body, they are driven to uphold their reputation with a distinction: that these forms are not indeed anywhere "circumscriptively," but "definitively." <note>original: "Circumscriptivè, but Definitivè." These are Scholastic terms: circumscriptive presence means occupying a space with physical boundaries; definitive presence means being located in a place without occupying physical space.</note> These terms, being mere words and insignificant in this context, are used only in Latin so that their lack of meaning might be hidden. For the "circumscription" of a thing is nothing other than the determination or defining of its place, so both terms of the distinction mean the same thing. And in particular, regarding the essence of a man, which they say is his soul, they claim it is entirely in his little finger, and entirely in every other part (no matter how small) of his body, and yet there is no more soul in the whole body than in any one of these parts. Can any man think that God is served with such absurdities? And yet, all of this is necessary to believe for those who will believe in the existence of an incorporeal soul separated from the body.*

# The Immortality of the Soul. BOOK I.

The force of his argument lies in this: *that since everything in the universe is a body (the universe being nothing more than a collection of bodies), "body" and "substance" are merely names for the same thing. It is called "body" because it fills a physical space, and "substance" because it is the subject of various changes and characteristics <note>original: "Accidents"</note>. Therefore, if "body" and "substance" are the same, an "incorporeal substance" <term>a non-physical being</term> makes no more sense than an "incorporeal body"—which is a contradiction in terms.* But it is obvious to the whole world that this is not a proof, but merely an assumption of what needs to be proven: that the universe is nothing but a collection of bodies. Once he has proven that, we will acknowledge the conclusion; until then, he has proven nothing, and therefore this first argument must count for nothing.

2. Let us examine the strength of the second argument, which must be this, if anything at all: *anything that originates merely from dreams, fears, and superstitious fancies has no real existence in the world. But incorporeal substances have no other origin.* This first premise <note>original: "Proposition"</note> is an undeniable truth, but the second premise <note>original: "Assumption"</note> is as weak as the first was strong, whether you mean the actual origin of these substances or the principles by which we know they exist. Whatever their origin might be, it only matters to us insofar as we can know it <note>original: "it is cognoscible to us"</note>, according to my first axiom. Therefore, when he says they have no origin other than our own imagination <note>original: "Phansy"</note>, he must be understood as claiming there is no way to know they exist other than by our vain imaginings—which is completely false.

<margin>* See my *Antidote against Atheism*, the entire second book.</margin> 
For it is not from the dreams and fears of melancholic and superstitious people that philosophers and Christians have argued for the existence of spirits and immaterial substances. Rather, they argue from the evidence of external objects of sense—that is, the ordinary natural appearances <note>original: "Phenomena"</note> of nature. In these, such profound wisdom and planning <note>original: "Counsell"</note> are discoverable that they could not help but conclude that the order of things in the world came from a higher principle than the blind motions and collisions of matter and mere physical beings.

<margin>
* See my *Antidote*, the entire third book.
* *Antidote*, Book I, chapter 11.
</margin>
To this, you may add what are usually called *apparitions* <note>original: "Apparitions"</note>. These are so far from being merely the dreams and fancies of the superstitious that they are acknowledged even by those who most people consider overly atheistic—I mean *Pomponatius* <note>Pietro Pomponazzi, a Renaissance philosopher who sought natural explanations for miracles</note> and *Cardan* <note>Girolamo Cardano, a polymath who wrote on the supernatural</note>, and even by *Vaninus* <note>Lucilio Vanini, an Italian philosopher executed for atheism</note> himself. Though Vaninus was so devoted to atheism that he died for that despicable cause out of a perfect, mad zeal, he still admitted to them. I will omit mentioning the operations of the *soul* <note>original: "Soul"</note>, which have always appeared to the wisest of all ages to be of such a superior condition that they could not judge them to spring from so contemptible a source as a bare body or matter. Therefore, to ignore all of these and to represent only dreams and fancies as the reason the world concludes there are incorporeal substances is to imagine his reader is a complete fool, and to publicly admit that he intends to deceive him.

3. The third argument is this: *anything that appears to us while we are sleeping as well as when we are awake has no existence outside of ourselves. But ghosts—that is, immaterial substances—appear to us while sleeping as well as while awake.* This is the weakest argument produced yet, for both the first premise and the

...premise <note>original: "Assumption"</note> is false. For if the first proposition were true, the Sun, Moon, Stars, Clouds, Rivers, Meadows, Men, Women, and other living creatures would be nothing without us; for all these appear to us just as much when we are *sleeping* as when we are *waking*. But *incorporeal substances* <term>non-physical beings or spirits</term> do not appear to us as much when *sleeping* as when *waking*. For the concept of an *incorporeal substance* is so subtle and refined that it leaves little or no impression on the *imagination* <note>original: "Phansy"</note>; its representation is instead supported by the free power of *reason*, which seldom exercises itself in sleep, unless it is dealing with easy, imaginable *mental images* <note>original: "Phantasmes"</note>.

<margin>* Book 1, chapters 2 and 3.</margin>
4. The force of the fourth argument is briefly this: *Every substance has dimensions; but a spirit has no dimensions.* Here I confidently deny that premise. For it is not the defining characteristic of a *body* to have *dimensions*, but rather to be *impenetrable*. All substance has *dimensions*—that is, *length*, *breadth*, and *depth*—but not all substance has *impenetrability*. See my letters to Monsieur *Descartes*, besides what I have written here in this present treatise.

5. In the excerpts belonging to the fifth place, these arguments are comprised: 1. *That we have no principle of knowledge of any immaterial being, but such as a dream or a looking-glass provides us with.* 2. *That the word "spirit" or "incorporeal" implies a contradiction, and cannot be understood by a natural mind.* 3. *That nothing is understood by the mind except what enters through the senses; therefore, spirits—not acting upon the senses—must remain unknown and inconceivable.*

We have already answered the first point in our response to his second argument in the second objection.

To the second, I answer that *spirit* or *incorporeal* implies no contradiction. By those terms, we mean nothing more than *extended substance* that possesses *activity* and *indiscerpibility* <term>the quality of being impossible to tear apart or divide</term>, while excluding *impenetrability*. I have demonstrated above that this concept is *possible*, and I need not repeat what I have already written.

<margin>
* Antidote, Book 1, chapter 6. Appendix, chapter 2, sections 4, 5, 6, etc.
* Book 2, chapter 2, sections 9, 10, 11.
</margin>
To the third, I answer that *spirits* do really act upon the *senses* by acting upon *matter* that affects the *senses*. Since some of these operations are such that they cannot be rationally attributed to *matter* alone, *reason*—informed by the *senses*—concludes that there is some other, more noble principle distinct from *matter*. And as for the part of the argument asserting that there is nothing in the mind except what comes through the senses, I have—and shall again in its due place—demonstrated that this is a very gross error.

But in the meantime, I conclude that while the underlying substance of everything is utterly inconceivable (according to Axiom 8), we understand everything only by its immediate properties. Since the properties of *penetrability* and *indiscerpibility* are as easy to conceive as *divisibility* <note>original: "Discerpibility"</note> and *impenetrability*, and the power of communicating motion to *matter* is as easy to conceive as *matter's* reception of it, and the union of *matter* with *spirit* as easy as *matter* with *matter*; it plainly follows that the concept of a *spirit* is as naturally conceivable as the concept of a *body*.

...ridiculous the opinion of *Ghosts* and *Demons* <note>original: "Dæmons"</note>; but the strength of his argument, if it has any, is this: *If there be any such things as ghosts or demons, then they are (according to those who hold this opinion) either those images reflected from water or looking-glasses, clothing themselves in airy garments and so wandering up and down; or else they are living creatures made of nothing but air or some more subtle and ethereal matter.* One might well be amazed to observe such superficial and empty arguing come from so serious a philosopher, were one not well aware that his peculiar excellence, as he himself somewhere professes, lies in *politics*. In that field, the humors and rhetorical bravado of eloquence, especially among the simple-minded, are very effective and useful instruments. Certainly, such rhetorical flourishes as this cannot be intended for anyone but those of the very weakest capacity.

Those two groundless conceits that he would force upon the sober defenders of *spirits* and *demons* do not belong to them, but are the genuine offspring of his own brain. As for the first of them, it is most justly attributed to him as its original author; it is a rarity which neither I myself nor (I dare say) anyone else ever encountered outside of Mr. *Hobbes's* writings. And the second one he does not only fail to refute here, but makes a show of allowing it—for fear he should seem to deny Scripture—in Chapter 34 of his *Leviathan*. But those who assert the existence of *spirits* will not let Mr. *Hobbes* choose the definition for them; they will use their own reason and judgment to establish such an important concept.

7. In this seventh excerpt is contained the same argument that was found in the first; but to deal fairly and candidly, I must confess it is better supported than before. For there he assumes, but does not prove, the chief ground of his argument; but here he attempts a proof of it, expressed <note>original: "couched"</note>, as I understand it, in these words: [*and has the dimensions of magnitude, namely length, breadth, and depth*]. From this, he would infer that the whole *universe* is *corporeal* <term>made of physical matter</term>—that is to say, every thing in the universe—because there is nothing that does not have *length, breadth, and depth*. This, therefore, is the very final ground to which his argument can be reduced. But I have already pointed out how weak this is; it is not *three dimensions* <note>original: "Trinal Dimension"</note>, but *impenetrability* <term>the quality of a thing that prevents another thing from occupying the same space</term> that constitutes a *body*.

8. This last excerpt seems more significant than any of the former ones, or all of them put together; but when the force of the arguments contained within is duly weighed, they will be found to have as little power to prove his conclusion as the rest. The first argument runs like this: *Whatever is real must have some place; but spirits can have no place.* But this is very easily answered. For if nothing else is understood by *place* but *imaginary space* <note>the abstract idea of extension or "room" in which things exist</note>, then spirits and bodies may be in the same *imaginary space*, and so the premise is false. But if by *place* he means the *concave surface of one body immediately surrounding another body* <note>This refers to the Aristotelian definition of place as a physical "container"</note>, so that it is conceived to be the very essential nature of a *place* to immediately surround the physical surface of that substance which is said to be placed; then it is impossible that a *spirit* should be properly said to be in a *place*, and so the proposition will be false. Wherefore, there being these...

<meta>This page continues Henry More's critique of Thomas Hobbes's materialism, specifically addressing the philosophical definitions of how a spirit occupies space and its presence within a physical body.</meta>

# CHAPTER X. The Immortality of the Soul.

Based on these two interpretations <note>original: "acceptions"</note> of *Place*, the distinction of being there *circumscriptively* and *definitively* <note>original: "Circumscriptivè and Definitivè." These are Scholastic terms: "circumscriptive" means taking up space by filling it (like a body), while "definitive" means being present in a location without filling it physically.</note> is an allowable distinction, and the terms do not necessarily signify one and the same thing. But if we wish to follow Mr. *Hobbes* (and I see no great harm if we should do so) and confine the notion of *Place* to *imaginary space*, this distinction used by the Scholastic philosophers will be unnecessary here. We may, without any more fuss, assert that *spirits* are as truly in a place as *bodies* are.

His second argument is drawn from that Scholastic riddle—which I must confess seems to border on profound nonsense—stating that the soul of man is *the whole in the whole, and the whole in every part of the body* <note>original: "tota in toto and tota in qualibet parte corporis"</note>. This irrational slogan, it seems, so frightened Mr. *Hobbes* at some time or another that he never since could endure to come near the notion of a *spirit* again, nor even to consider whether it were a mere bugbear or a real being. But if passion had not overwhelmed his better faculties, he might have found a true, settled meaning for it, while still setting aside those wild intricacies with which the unnecessary Scholastic debates seem to have burdened it. For the *immediate properties* of a *spirit* are quite understandable without these enigmatic flourishes: namely, that it is a *substance* that is *penetrable* <note>Meaning it can occupy the same space as matter</note> and <term>indiscerpible</term> <note>original: "Indiscerpible"—a term More uses to mean something that cannot be torn apart, divided, or separated into pieces</note>, as I have already shown at length.

Nor is it necessary for that Scholastic riddle to be believed by everyone who wishes to believe in the existence of an *incorporeal soul*; nor do I believe Mr. *Hobbes's* interpretation of this riddle is necessarily the only one. It would have been only fair to ensure that the Scholastic schools actually held such a perfect contradiction before he pronounced that believing it was mandatory for all those who hold the soul of man to be *an immaterial substance, separable from the body*. I suppose they may mean nothing more by it than what *Plato* did when he described the soul as consisting *of divisible and indivisible substance* <note>original Greek: "ἐκ μεριστῆς καὶ ἀμερίστου οὐσίας"</note>. *Plato* meant nothing more by that *divisible and indivisible substance* than an essence that can be divided in the mind but cannot be actually pulled apart in reality.

9. We have now firmly established that the notion of a *spirit* implies no contradiction or impossibility within it; rather, it is the notion or *idea* of a thing that could possibly exist. I have done this so precisely and particularly that I have cleared every species of *incorporeal substance* from the accusation of being either obscure or inconsistent. And so that I might not seem to take advantage by pleading their cause while the opposing party is absent, I have brought in the most able and confident advocate for that side <note>referring to Thomas Hobbes</note> whom I have ever met. I now dare to appeal to any impartial judge to decide whether I have not demonstrated all his allegations to be weak and inconclusive. Therefore, having so clearly proved the *possibility* of a spirit's existence, we shall now take a step further and prove that it is not only a *possible* thing, but that it *really* and *actually* exists in nature.

### CHAPTER XI.

1. *Three grounds to prove the existence of an immaterial substance, of which the first is taken from the nature of God. 2. The second from the phenomenon of motion in the world. 3. That matter is not self-moving. 4. An objection that matter may be partly self-moved and partly not. 5. The first answer to the objection. 6. The second answer. 7. Other evasions answered. 8. The last evasion of all answered. 9. The conclusion: That no matter is self-moved, but that a certain quantity of motion was impressed upon it at its first creation by God.*

<margin>Book 1, chapters 7, 8.</margin>
1. **T**here are three main grounds from which a man may be assured of the *existence of spiritual* or *immaterial substance*. 
The first is the consideration of the transcendent excellence of the nature of God. According to the true *idea* of him, God is *an essence that is absolutely perfect*; he cannot possibly be a body, and consequently must be something *incorporeal*. Seeing that there is no contradiction in the notion of a *spirit in general*, nor in any of those kinds of spirits which we have defined (where the notion of God was included among the rest), and seeing that in the very notion of him there is contained the reason for his existence—as you may see at length in my *Antidote* <note>More refers here to his previous work, *An Antidote against Atheism* (1653).</note>—certainly if we find anything at all *exists*, we may safely conclude that He *exists much more*. For there is nothing besides him of which one can give a reason why it exists, unless we suppose him to be the author of it. Therefore, though God is neither *visible* nor *tangible*, yet his very *idea* represents to our intellectual faculties the necessary reason for his *existence*. By Axiom 5, even if we had no other argument drawn from our *senses*, we are to confidently conclude *that He exists*.

2. The second ground is the ordinary *phenomena* of nature, the most general of which is *motion*. Now, it seems demonstrable to me from this that there is some being in the world distinct from *matter*. For *matter* being of one simple, homogeneous <note>original: "homogeneal"; meaning of the same kind or nature throughout.</note> nature, and not distinguishable by *specific differences* (as the Scholastic philosophers <note>The "Schools" refers to the academic tradition of the Middle Ages and Renaissance based on Aristotelian logic.</note> say), it must have the very same *essential* properties everywhere. Therefore, of itself, it must all be either without motion, or else be self-moving in a certain pattern or measure of motion. There is no imaginable reason why one part of *matter* should move itself less than another; therefore, if there is any such difference, it can only arise from an external hindrance.

3. Now I say, if *matter* is utterly devoid of motion in itself, it is plain it receives its motion from some other substance, which is necessarily a substance that is not *matter*—that is to say, an *incorporeal* substance. But if it is moved by itself, in such or such a measure, the *effect* here being an *emanative effect* <note>An "emanative effect" is a result that flows necessarily and constantly from the very nature of a thing, like light from a fire.</note>, it cannot possibly fail to be wherever *matter* is, according to Axiom 17—especially if there is no external hindrance. And there is no hindrance at all that would prevent the *terrestrial* <note>Earthly or solid matter.</note> parts from regaining an activity...

<meta>This page continues Henry More’s argument against the idea that matter is self-moving. He is currently explaining that if planets possessed an inherent power of motion shared with the sun and stars, they would have been ground down into the same fine, fiery substance as the rest of the heavens.</meta>

...very nearly equal to the ethereal, or rather would never have lost it. For if the planets had only a common dividend of all the motion which they themselves, the sun, the stars, and all the ethereal matter possess (the matter of the planets being so small in comparison to that of the sun, stars, and ether), the proportion of motion that would fall to them would be far above what they actually have. It would be as if four or five poor men in a very rich and populous city should, by giving up the small estate they have to be shared equally, get an equal share with everyone else <note>More is referring to "leveling," a political concept of wealth redistribution popular during the English Civil War era</note>. Therefore, every planet could not fail to melt itself into a substance little less fine than the purest ether. But since they do not do so, it is a sign that they do not have that motion or agitation of themselves; therefore, they rest content with whatever has been externally added to them, whether it be less or more.

4. But those who love to argue, in order to evade the stroke of our *dilemma*, will resort to any bold shift; even though they insult their own reasoning faculties by saying so, they will say—and must say—that part of matter is self-moving, and part is without motion of itself.

5. But to this I answer that, first, this evasion of theirs does not agree with experience. As far as either our senses or reason can reach, there is the same matter everywhere. For consider the most subtle parts of *matter* discoverable here below—those which are invisible because of their subtlety and wonderful in their activity—I mean those particles that cause the violent agitation we feel in the *winds*. In time, they lose their motion, become a visible vaporous consistency, and turn to clouds, then to snow or rain, and perhaps eventually to ice itself. But then, in the course of time, they are first melted into water, then exhaled into vapors, and after being more fiercely agitated, they become *wind* again. And so we may not think that this cycling between *motion* and *rest* belongs only to *terrestrial* <note>original: "Terrestrial" — earthly</note> particles; that the *heavens* themselves are made of the same matter is apparent from the ejection of *comets* into our *vortex* <note>In 17th-century physics, a vortex was a whirlpool of "ether" that carried planets and comets around a star</note>, and the perpetual rising of those spots and scum upon the face of the sun.

6. But secondly, to return an argument that is even more forceful: this *matter* that is *self-moved*, in the process of impressing motion upon other *matter*, either loses some of its own motion or retains it all entirely. If the first is true, it may be stripped of all its motion; thus, that whose very nature is to *move* would *rest*, even though the entire cause of its motion (which is itself) still remains. This is a plain contradiction according to Axiom 17. If the second is true, no smaller an inconvenience than this will follow: the whole world would have been turned into pure *ether* by this time, if not into a perfect flame; or at least it will be in the end, leading to the utter destruction of all physical structures. For the fact that these *self-moving* parts of *matter* are quite numerous is proven by the results; they have already melted almost all the world into suns, stars, and *ether*, with nothing remaining but *planets* and *comets* to be dissolved. All of these put together hardly bear as great a proportion to the rest of the matter in the *universe* as an ordinary grain of sand does to the whole ball of the earth. Therefore, if such a potent principle of motion is constantly adding new motion to *matter*, and since no motion is lost once it is communicated (according to...

He further contends that if some matter moved itself without losing its own momentum, the entire universe would eventually be consumed by motion and heat.</summary>
