According to the laws of motion (no body loses any more motion than it communicates to another), it plainly follows that either the world would have been utterly burnt up by now, or it will be in an infinitely shorter time than it has already existed. Indeed, I may say absolutely that it would happen in a very short time and would never return to any organized structure of things again. While this could possibly be the case, no one but a madman would assert it, according to Axiom 2 <note>Axiom 2 in More’s work states that whatever is clear to the human mind is true.</note>. And the fact that this has not yet happened since the first epochs <note>original: "Epoches." Significant historical eras.</note> of history seems to be a demonstration that this second hypothesis is false.

7. There are still one or two more evasions, and once these are answered, there will be no doubt remaining regarding this point. The first is: *That matter is entirely homogeneous <note>original: "homogeneall." Uniform or of the same kind throughout.</note>, having the same nature everywhere, and that it is the common property of all matter to be, in itself, indifferent to motion or rest; therefore, it is no wonder that some of it moves, while other parts rest or move less than the others.* To this I answer that this *indifference* <note>The state of being neutral or having no inherent preference for one state over the other.</note> of *matter* to *motion* or *rest* may be understood in two ways: 

Either *privatively*—that is to say, that it has no real or active inclination toward *rest* more than toward *motion*, or vice versa, but is merely passive and capable of receiving whatever *motion* or *fixity* another agent grants it, keeping that state exactly and perpetually until another agent changes it again. (In this sense, I allow the assertion to be true, but it does nothing to oppose us; rather, it supports us, as it plainly implies that there is an *incorporeal substance* distinct from *matter* which must be the source of the *matter's* movement.) 

Or else, this *indifference* is to be understood *positively*—that is to say, that *matter* has a real and active inclination toward both *motion* and *rest*, so that it moves itself and stays still by its own immediate nature. From this, two absurdities follow: first, that two absolutely contrary properties are *immediately* seated in one simple subject. Nothing can seem more harsh and unappealing to our logical faculties than this, unless it is the second absurdity: that since *motion* and *rest* would be the *emanating* effects of this one simple subject, the *matter* would both *move and rest at once*. Or, if by *rest* they do not mean "fixity" but a mere absence of motion, it would both move and not move at the same time. For whatever is *immediate* to any subject will not cease to exist as long as the subject itself is not destroyed, according to Axiom 17.

Nor will they help themselves much by imagining that *matter*, necessarily exerting both these *immediate* powers or properties of *motion* and *rest* at once, moves itself at a certain speed and no faster. For this position coincides with the second part of the dilemma in Section 3 of this chapter; therefore, the same argument will serve for both places.

The other evasion is to suppose that part of *matter* is *self-moving* and part of it is *self-resting* (in a positive sense) or *self-fixing*. This is particularly directed against what we argued in Section 6, as they would use this to avoid the conclusion of that rapid and universal conflagration <note>A great fire or total destruction of the world by heat.</note> we inferred. But that this supposition is false is manifest from experience. For if there are any such *self-fixing* parts of *matter*, they would certainly be found in gold, lead, and similar metals; but it is plain that they are not found there.

there. For whatever is **self-fixing** will immediately be reduced to **rest** as soon as external violence is removed, according to **Axiom 17** <note>Axiom 17 likely states that a thing with an internal cause for a state will return to that state once external forces stop.</note>. From this, it would follow that although these **self-fixing** parts of matter may be carried along by other matter while they are attached to it, they would suddenly come to rest once they are free, since they contain the immediate cause of fixation within themselves. No one should doubt that this change would be sudden if they consider how suddenly an external force puts matter into motion. However, a **bullet** made of gold or lead, when put into motion—whether fast or slow—does not suddenly reduce itself to **rest**. Therefore, it plainly appears that this other evasion contradicts experience and has no force against our previous arguments.

8. The ultimate evasion the wit of man can possibly devise <note>original: "excogitate."</note> is that fiction of a certain **Divine Matter** dispersed throughout the world. Some imagine this to be the only **deity** <note>original: "Numen." A Latin term for a divine power or spirit.</note> of the world, and they claim its motions are not **necessary** but **voluntary**. By this, they hope to avoid that extreme inconvenience mentioned in the sixth section of this chapter. But this opinion seems very harsh and monstrous to me for the following reasons:

First, they seem very absurd in imagining this to be the *deity* of the world or God himself. It is inconsistent with **personality** and the **unity** of the Godhead to be made up of an infinite number of interspersed **atoms** scattered amid the matter of the world. This cannot be **one God** in any sense, nor can a single **divine atom** be an **entire deity**. From this, it would follow that there is no God at all.

Second, by acknowledging this "Divine Matter" to be **matter**, they also acknowledge its **impenetrability** <note>The quality of matter that prevents two objects from occupying the same space at the same time.</note> and the **side-by-side positioning** <note>original: "Juxta-position."</note> of its parts. They also acknowledge it has various shapes and, where there are no pores at all, absolute **solidity** and **hardness**. From this, it is manifest that whatever arguments are strong against **ordinary matter** being incapable of **perception** and **free action** (based on its nature and definition), those same arguments are just as strong against this matter to which they have given the title of "**Divine**."

<margin>* See Book 2, chapter 2, section 8.</margin>
Third and finally, effects and experiments plainly declare that there is no such **Divine Matter** interspersed among the subtle matter of the world that can act freely and knowingly, as I have abundantly noted in my *Antidote against Atheism.*

9. Therefore, it is most rational to conclude that no matter of any kind has any active **principle of motion** in its own nature, though it is capable of receiving it. Rather, when God created matter, he added an impression of **motion** upon it in a specific measure and proportion. This motion remains almost the same in quantity throughout the whole, although the parts of matter do not always have the same proportion of it as they collide <term>occursion</term> <note>original: "occursion." An archaic term for the clashing or meeting of bodies.</note> with one another. There is no more necessity for God to repeat this impression of **motion** on the created **matter** than there is for him to perpetually create the matter itself. Nor does his preservation of this quantity of motion imply a repetition or an increase of it any more than the preservation of matter implies adding new matter to it. Indeed, he only needs to preserve...

## CHAPTER XII.

1. *That the Order and Nature of things in the Universe argue for a Spiritual or Incorporeal Essence. 2. The evasion of this argument. 3. A preparation using Mr. Hobbes's own logic to answer the evasion. 4. The first answer. 5. The second answer. 6. Mr. Hobbes’s mistake in claiming that ignorance of secondary causes is the only seed of Religion.*

1. We have discovered, through the simple **phenomenon** of **Motion**, the necessity of the existence of some **Incorporeal Essence** <note>A spiritual substance that is not made of physical matter.</note> distinct from **Matter**. But there is a further assurance of this truth from the consideration of the order and admirable **Effect** of this motion in the world. Suppose **Matter** could move itself; would mere **Matter**, with **self-motion**, ever result in that admirably wise design of things which we see in the world? Can a blind **impulse** <note>original: "impetus"</note> produce such effects with such accuracy and constancy that the wiser a man is, the more he will be certain **that no wisdom can add, take away, or alter anything in the works of Nature to make them better?** How, therefore, can that which does not even have **Sense** <note>The capacity for basic perception or feeling.</note> achieve effects that reach the highest peak of **Reason** or **Intellect**? But I have spoken of this so fully and convincingly in the second book of my *Antidote* <note>Henry More's *An Antidote against Atheism* (1652), where he argues for God's existence from the design of the natural world.</note> that it would be a needless repetition to go any further on this subject.

2. Every evasion that I can imagine our adversaries might use here would be this: that **Matter** is capable of **Sense**, and the finest and most subtle matter is capable of the most refined **Sense**, and consequently of **Imagination** too—and perhaps even of **Reason** and **Understanding**. For since **Sense** is nothing else (as some imagine) but **Motion**, or rather the **Reaction** of one body being pressed upon by another, it would follow that all the **Matter** in the world has, in one way or another, the power of **Sensation**.

<margin>* Chapter 25.</margin>
3. Let us see now what this position amounts to. Those who make **Motion** and **Sensation** essentially the same thing must, of necessity, acknowledge that when there is no longer **Motion**, there is no longer **Sensation** (as Mr. Hobbes <note>Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679), a materialist philosopher who argued that all mental states are just physical motions.</note> has honestly confessed in his *Elements of Philosophy* <note>Referring to Hobbes's work *De Corpore* (1655).</note>). They must also admit that every **Motion** or **Reaction** must be a new **Sensation**, just as every stopping of **Reaction** is a stopping of **Sensation**.

4. Now, let us grant these busy, active particles of **Matter** that play around everywhere the advantage of having **Sense**. Let us see if, even with all their heads laid together, they can design the **anatomical structure** of any living creature. Assuredly, when everything is added up that can be imagined, they will fall short of the goal. For I ask: Does every one of these particles that must have a hand in framing the body of an animal possess the whole design of the work by the impression of some **phan-**

...mental image <note>original: "phantasm"</note> of it? Or, as they have several offices, do they each have different parts of the design? If the first is true, it is most certain—even according to the opinion of those we oppose—that there can be no knowledge or **perception** in **Matter** except what arises from the **Reaction** of one part against another. How then is it conceivable that any single particle of **Matter**, or many together (since no **Animal** yet exists in Nature), can have the **Idea** impressed upon them of that creature they are to frame? 

Or, if one or a few particles have the sense of one part of the animal—they appearing more capable of this, as the parts are far more simple than the whole **structure** <note>original: "Compages"</note> and contrivance—and other particles have knowledge of other parts, how can they compare notes? By what language or speech can they communicate their counsel to one another? Therefore, that they should mutually serve one another in such a design is more impossible than that many men, blind and dumb from birth, should join their forces and wits together to build a castle or carve a statue of a creature that none of them knew anything about, other than some of its smallest parts, without understanding how those parts related to the whole.

5. Besides this, **Sense** being really the same as **Physical** <note>original: "Corporeal"</note> **Motion**, it must change upon every new impression of motion. So, if a particle were carried in a certain line by its **Sense**, and it met with a counter-blow along the way, it would receive a completely different impression and "sense." It would thus forget what it was doing and divert its course another way. Indeed, even if it escaped such a collision, since **Sense** is merely **Reaction**, when the object it pushes against is removed, **Sense** must necessarily cease, and perfect forgetfulness <note>original: "Oblivion"</note> must follow. For it is not the same with these particles as it is with the spring of a watch or a bent crossbow, which retain the same **Reaction** (and consequently the same **Sense**) for a considerable time. 

And lastly, even if they could retain it, it is still irrelevant. For whatever their "sense" may be, their motion is necessary <note>Meaning "compulsory" or "automatic."</note> because it is merely physical; therefore, the result of their motion cannot come from any kind of knowledge. Physical motion comes first and is only felt—it is not directed by feeling. Therefore, whether Matter has any Sense or not, whatever is made out of it is nothing but the result of the wild jumbling and knocking of one part against another, without any purpose, counsel, or direction. Since the ordinary **phenomena** of Nature are guided according to the most exquisite wisdom imaginable, it is plain that they are not the **Effects** of the mere motion of Matter, but of some **Immaterial Principle**, according to Axiom 10.

6. And therefore, the **Ignorance of Secondary Causes** <note>Physical or mechanical explanations for natural events.</note> is not correctly called the **Seed of Religion** (as **Mr. Hobbes** would have it), but rather the seed of **Irreligion** and **Atheism**. For if we searched more precisely and particularly into their natures, we would clearly discern their insufficiency to produce such effects as we discover in the world. But when we have looked so closely and carefully into the nature of **Physical** <note>original: "Corporeal"</note> **Beings** and can find no **Causality** in them proportional to these effects we speak of, to still blame our own ignorance rather than the insufficiency of Matter and physical motion is to hold an opinion based on a whim <note>original: "humour"</note> and to violate our first and second Axioms.

### CHAPTER XIII.

1. *The last proof of incorporeal substances, based on apparitions. 2. The first excuse used to avoid the force of such arguments. 3. An answer to that excuse. 4. The second excuse. 5. The first kind of second excuse. 6. A description from the poet Virgil of that spirit <note>original: "Genius"</note> that suggests the principles of Epicurean philosophy. 7. The more complete and refined version of that philosophy today. 8. The great power of the stars (which they suppose consist of nothing but motion and matter) for the production of all kinds of creatures in the world.*

1. The third and last ground which I will use to prove the existence of **incorporeal substances** <note>original: "Incorporeal Substances"; beings not made of physical matter</note> consists of those extraordinary effects that we cannot easily imagine to be natural. Instead, we must conceive of some free or spontaneous agent as their cause, even though it is clear they come from neither humans nor animals. These include voices, knocking sounds, the opening of doors that were fast shut, and sudden lights floating in the air in the middle of a room and then vanishing. There are even sightings of the shapes of men and various kinds of animals that suddenly disappear after speaking and conversing. These and many similar extraordinary **effects** (which, if you like, you may call by the general term **apparitions**) seem to me to be an undeniable argument that there are such things as **spirits** or incorporeal substances in the world. 

I have demonstrated that this conclusion necessarily follows in the last chapter of the appendix to my *An Antidote Against Atheism* <note>original: "Treatise against Atheism"</note>. In the third book of that treatise, I produced so many unquestionable stories concerning apparitions that I consider it unnecessary to add anything more of that kind here; I take far more pleasure in exercising my reason than in recording history. Besides, I have already made such a careful choice of stories in that work that I cannot hope to select any that would prove more relevant or convincing. I recorded only those that I had compared with the strict rules I set for myself in the first chapter of that third book, in order to prevent all excuses and evasions <note>original: "tergiversations & evasions"</note> from those who would argue against them.

2. However, partly from my own observation and partly from information from others, I am well assured that there are only two ways people escape the force of such clear narratives. The first is a firm belief that the very **notion of a spirit or immaterial substance is an impossibility or a contradiction** in its very terms. Therefore, because such stories imply something they are confident is **impossible**, they judge the narrative to be false as soon as they hear it. Consequently, they think it more reasonable to conclude that all those who claim they have seen such things are madmen or frauds, rather than give credit to what they believe implies a **contradiction**.

3. But I have completely removed this excuse by so clearly demonstrating that the **notion of a spirit** implies no more **contradiction** than the **notion of matter**, and that its attributes are just as conceivable as the attributes of **matter**. So, I hope this loophole <note>original: "creep-hole"</note> is stopped forever.

4. The second excuse <note>original: "Evasion"</note> is not exactly a denial of the truth of these stories concerning **apparitions**, but rather a denial of the conclusions we draw from them. These skeptics willingly admit to the **apparitions** and **wonders** <note>original: "Prodigies"</note> recorded in history, but they deny that these are proof of a truly **spiritual** and **immaterial substance** <note>original: "Incorporeal Substance"</note> that is distinct from **matter**. They do not believe there is a spirit that can change matter into various shapes, or walk and speak; instead, they claim these events are special **effects** caused by the influence of the heavenly bodies (like stars and planets) upon this earthly region of birth and decay <note>original: "region of Generation and Corruption"</note>.

5. Those who offer this answer fall into two groups. The first group has a great deal in common with **Aristotle** and **Averroes** <note>Averroes was a 12th-century Islamic philosopher who commented extensively on Aristotle.</note>. They do not view the heavenly bodies as mere **physical substances**; rather, they believe they are moved by "Intelligences," which are **essences** that are separate and immaterial. However, this theory does not hurt my current argument at all, because they are essentially granting what I am arguing for: the existence of an **immaterial substance**. The purpose of this perverse theory is only to dismiss all arguments drawn from **apparitions** that prove the souls of men survive after death, or that there are any such things as **demons** or **spirits** <note>original: "Genii"</note> that have a permanent and immortal nature. I consider this theory easy enough to disprove, were it worth the time to challenge it.

The view held by the **Sadducees** <note>An ancient Jewish sect known for denying the resurrection and the existence of spirits.</note> is much more firm. They suppose their **effluences** <note>original: "$\alpha\pi o\rho\rho o\iota\alpha\iota$"; literal meaning: things that flow out or emanate</note> to be nothing more than the power of God’s presence altering **matter** into this or that apparition or manifestation. It is as if there were only one soul in all things, and God were that soul working in various ways within matter. But I have already disproven this in my *Philosophical Poems*, and I shall do so again in this current book. <margin>Book 3, chapter 16.</margin>

6. The other **believers in stellar influence** <note>original: "Influenciaries"</note> hold that the heavens have the same power as the previous group described. However, they do not assume such a high spiritual principle exists within the stars. Instead, they think physical influence is enough to explain all **earthly phenomena** <note>original: "Sublunary Phænomena"</note>, both ordinary and extraordinary. 

Truly, this is a very profound **secret**, and one not to be spoken or shared except by some old **Silenus** <note>In Greek mythology, Silenus was the tutor of Dionysus, often depicted as a wise but drunken satyr.</note> lying in his dark cave. Even then, it would only be told under the right circumstances and when he is in the right mood—when one might find him with his veins bulging from wine and his flower-garland fallen from his head because of his careless drowsiness. Then, if some young men like **Chromis** and **Mnasyllus**—especially if assisted by a beautiful and bold girl like **Aegle**, who as a joke smears the blood of mulberries on the sleeping satyr's forehead and temples while he pretends to sleep so he doesn't lose the pleasure of her touch—if these young men beg him enough, he will again sing that old song of **Epicurean philosophy** in a higher style than ever before. 

I declare that I would hate to repeat this song if it were not for the sake of disproving it; it is so monstrous and impious. But because no wound can be cured if it is hidden, I must bring this **theory** into view as well, which the poet **Virgil** briefly summarized in this passage:
<margin>Virgil, Eclogues, 6.</margin>

> For he sang how, throughout the great vacuum, the seeds of the earth, the air, the sea, and the liquid fire were all driven together; how from these first principles all things—and even the young orb of the world itself—took shape and grew. <note>original: "Namque canebat, uti magnum per inane coacta / Semina terrarumque animaeque marisque fuissent, / Et liquidi simul ignis ; ut his exordia primis / Omnia, & ipse tener mundi concreverit orbis."</note>

7. The fuller and more refined **sense** of this view nowadays is this: that **Matter** and **Motion** are the principles of all things whatsoever. By **Motion**, some **Atoms** or particles become more subtle than others, and more nimble and active. The motion of one Body against another everywhere necessarily produces **Sense**, with **Sense** being nothing more than the **re-action** of parts of **Matter**. The more subtle the **Matter** is, the more subtle the **Sense** becomes. The subtlest **Matter** of all is that which makes up the **Sun** and **Stars**; therefore, they must possess the purest and most subtle **Sense**. Whatever has the most perfect **Sense** also has the most perfect **Imagination** and **Memory**, because **Memory** and **Imagination** are really the same as **Sense**, the latter being just different modes of the former. Whatever has the most perfect **Imagination** has the highest **Reason** and **Providence**; for **Providence** and **Reason** are nothing more than a more precise sequence of **Phantasms** <note>original: "Phantafmes"; mental images or products of the imagination</note>, **Sensations**, or **Imaginations**. Therefore, the **Sun** and the **Stars** are the most **Intellectual Beings** in the world, and within them is the **Knowledge**, **Counsel**, and **Wisdom** by which all **earthly things** <note>original: "Sublunary things"; literally "under the moon," referring to the changing physical world</note> are formed and governed.

8. By their various influences <note>original: "impresses"</note> and infusions <note>original: "impregnations"</note>, these celestial bodies have filled the whole Earth with vital motion, raising innumerable kinds of flowers, herbs, and trees out of the ground. They have also generated the various kinds of living creatures. They have filled the seas with fish, the fields with beasts, and the air with birds. Earthly matter is as easily formed into the living shapes of these various **Animals** by the powerful influence of the **Imagination** of the sun and stars, as a developing fetus <note>original: "Embryo"</note> in the womb is marked by the strong fancy of the mother who carries it. Therefore, since these **celestial powers** are able to frame living shapes from earthly matter through the influence of their **Imagination**, it will be even easier for them to transform the vaporous air into similar shapes.

So, even if we admit that all these stories of **Apparitions** recorded by writers are true, it is no argument for the existence of any **incorporeal principle** <note>original: "Incorporeal Principle"; a non-physical or spiritual soul</note> in the world. For the piercing foresight of these glorious bodies, the **Sun** and **Stars**, is able to create whatever **Apparitions** or **Wonders** <note>original: "Prodigies"</note> they please to introduce the births or signal the deaths of the most important people in the world. **Pomponatius** <note>Pietro Pomponazzi (1462–1525), an Italian philosopher who explored naturalistic explanations for the supernatural.</note> himself acknowledges <margin>* *On the Immortality of the Soul*, chapter 14.</margin> that there are many true examples of this in both **Greek** and **Latin history**. This is the deepest secret that old **Silenus** <note>In Greek mythology, Silenus was a companion to Dionysus and a possessor of hidden wisdom.</note> could ever sing to trap the ears of gullible youth. It is indeed a **dreadful mystery** <note>original: "φρικτὸν μυϛήριον... Horrendum mysterium"</note> in the very worst sense—a very terrifying and dangerous mystery—except there is a great deal of hope that it may not be true. Let us, therefore, now examine it.

<header>CHAPTER XIV. The Immortality of the Soul.</header>

### C H A P T E R XIV.

1. *That the splendor of the celestial bodies proves no foresight or sovereignty that they have over us. 2. That the stars can have no knowledge of us, mathematically demonstrated. 3. The same conclusion demonstrated again more simply. 4. That the stars cannot communicate thoughts, neither with the sun nor with one another. 5. That the sun has no knowledge of our affairs. 6. Principles laid down for inferring that conclusion. 7. A demonstration that he cannot see us. 8. That he can have no other kind of knowledge of us, nor of the structure of any animal on Earth. 9. That even if the sun had the knowledge of the correct structure of an animal, he could not transmit it into terrestrial matter. 10. An answer to that instance of the "signature of the fetus" <note>original: "Signature of the Foetus"; the belief that a mother's imagination or celestial alignment could "stamp" or mark an unborn child</note>. 11, 12. Further answers to that point. 13. A short rebuke of those who confidently reject the idea of incorporeal substance <note>original: "Incorporeal Substance"; spirit or soul that exists without a physical body</note> from the world.*

<margin>* See *Enthusiasmus Triumphatus*, section 45 <note>original: "Enthusiasm. Triumphat."; a reference to Henry More's other work, which critiqued religious fanaticism</note>.</margin>

1. It must be acknowledged as truth that light is a very glorious thing, and the luster of the stars is very lovely to look upon, and that the body of the sun is so full of splendor and majesty that, without exaggeration, we must admit we are forced to look away, being unable to endure the brightness of his appearance. However, the idea that these are so many "eyes of heaven" watching over the Earth—so many kind and careful spectators and meddlers in human affairs—is a different matter. This is what the fanciful chemist <note>original: "Chymist"; here referring to an alchemist or early natural philosopher</note> Paracelsus imagines; he writes that not only princes and nobles, or men of great and singular worth, but almost everyone near death receives some prophetic sign or other (such as knockings in the house, the "dances of dead men," and the like) from these compassionate foreseers of his approaching fate. I must confess I am not so paganly superstitious as to believe a single syllable of this. Instead, I believe it can be demonstrated to be a mere fancy, especially based on our current hypothesis <note>original: "Hypothesis"; a proposed explanation or theory</note>: that the sun and stars have no spirit or immaterial being residing in them, but are mere matter consisting of the finest particles in constant, violent motion. If that is the case, then we can be certain there is nothing more divine in them than what is seen in other things that glow in the dark—such as rotting wood, glow-worms, or the flame of a cheap candle <note>original: "rush-candle"; a candle made from the pith of a rush dipped in fat</note>.

2. We will demonstrate at the very least that, whatever knowledge the sun and stars may have of other things, they have none at all of us or our affairs; this will completely remove this last excuse. That the stars can have no knowledge of us is exceedingly evident. For while the *Magnus Orbis* <note>original: "Magnus Orbis"; Latin for "Great Circle," referring to the Earth's orbit around the sun</note> of the Earth is but a tiny point compared to the distance from it to a fixed star—that is to say, the angle we might imagine being drawn from a star to the diameter of the Earth's orbit is to our senses no angle at all, but merely a line—how much smaller then is the Earth itself? And how utterly invisible must it be to any star, since the Earth's diameter is more than 1,100 times smaller than that of its orbit? From this it is clear that it is perfectly im-

...it is impossible that the *Stars*, even if they were gifted with sight, could even see the *Earth* itself (much less its inhabitants) to act as *Spectators* and *Interferers* <note>original: "Intermedlers"</note> in their affairs for good or evil. Since there is no higher Principle to inspire them with the knowledge of these things, it is evident that they remain utterly ignorant of them.

3. Or, if this demonstration (though undeniably true in itself) is not easily understood by everyone, we may add a more simple and familiar point: namely, that the *Stars* are bright bodies, and those of the largest size <note>original: "first magnitude"</note> are nearly a hundred times bigger than the *Earth*. Yet, they appear as such small things to us; from this, anyone may conclude that the dark <note>original: "opake"</note> *Earth* will either be completely invisible to the *Stars*, or at least appear so small that it would be impossible for them to see any distinct countries, let alone cities, houses, or inhabitants.

4. Therefore, we have plainly dismissed this numerous group of "celestial Senators" <note>original: "celestial Senators"; a metaphorical reference to the stars as a governing body or council</note> from having anything to do with consulting about or overseeing the affairs of mankind. Let them seem to wink and twinkle as thoughtfully <note>original: "cogitabundly"</note> as they like; we can rest assured that they have no plot concerning us, for either good or evil, as they have no knowledge of us. Even if they did, they could not *communicate their thoughts* to that supposed sovereign of the world, the *Sun*. They are as invisible to him as they are to us during the daytime. For it is nothing but his own light that prevents us from seeing such faint objects. This obstruction consists of nothing else but this: the motion caused by his *rays* in our *sense organs* <note>original: "Organ"</note> is so fierce and violent that the gentle vibration of the *Stars'* light cannot overcome it, nor even bear any significant proportion to it. What, then, could that starlight do in relation to the actual body of the *Sun* himself, where the matter has the most violent motion of anything in the world?

5. There is nothing left now but the *Sun* alone that could possibly be imagined to have any knowledge of, or any supervision over, our earthly affairs. I believe it is not difficult to demonstrate how incapable he is of this office as well. From this, it will clearly appear that those *apparitions* that are seen, whether in the *air* or on *Earth* (which are rightly viewed as an *argument for Providence and the existence of some Incorporeal Essence in the world* <note>original: "Incorporeal Essence"; a non-physical spirit or being</note>), cannot be attributed to the power and foresight of the *Sun*, assuming he is purely physical.

6. For it is a thing agreed upon by all sides that mere *Matter* has no innate *Ideas* <note>original: "connate Ideas"; concepts or knowledge present from birth or creation</note> within it of such things as we see in the world; instead, a kind of *sense* or *perception* arises from the *reaction* of one part of matter being moved by another. This opinion is the most rational to hold (assuming *Matter* has any sense in it at all) and is most consistent with experience. We see plainly that *sense* is always caused by some outward physical <note>original: "corporeal"</note> motion acting upon our organs, which are also physical. For it is plain that *light* comes from a physical motion, as shown by the reflection of its rays. No *sound* is heard except from the motion of the *air* or some other connecting *body*. No *voice* exists without the moving of the *tongue*; no *music* exists without either the blowing of wind,

...or the striking of strings, or something similar <note>original: "Analogical"</note> to these; and so it is with the other senses.

Therefore, if there is nothing but *physical matter* <note>original: "Body"</note> in the world, it is clear that *sensation* <note>original: "Sense"</note> arises merely from the *motion* of one part of *matter* against another. Motion always comes first, and *perception* follows; consequently, *perception* must necessarily follow the laws of *motion*, and no *perceiving being* <note>original: "Percipient"</note> can conceive of anything more than what is conveyed by physical <note>original: "Corporeal"</note> motion. Now, from these principles, it will be easy to prove that, even if we were to grant a power of perception to the *Sun*, it would not amount to any ability for him to be either a *spectator* or a *governor* of our affairs here on Earth.

7. According to the calculations <note>original: "Computation"</note> of *astronomers*—even those who speak more conservatively <note>original: "modestly"</note>—the *Sun* is more than one hundred and fifty times larger than the *Earth*. But every eye is able to judge how small he appears to us. How tiny, then, must the *Earth* appear to him? If he sees her at all, he will be so far from being able to notice any people or families that he cannot even clearly distinguish streets or cities—not even fields or countries. Whole regions, though of very great size, will vanish here, just like *Alcibiades’s* inheritance <note>original: "Patrimony"</note> in that map of the world *Socrates* showed him to humble the pride of the young heir. The *Earth* must appear considerably smaller to him than the *Moon* does to us, because the *Sun* appears smaller to us than the *Moon*. It would be easy to demonstrate that the Earth's *disk* <note>original: "discus"</note> would appear to the *Sun* nearly thirty, or even sixty times smaller than the *Moon* appears to us, according to the calculations of *Lansbergius* <note>Philip Lansbergen (1561–1632), a Dutch astronomer known for his tables of celestial motions</note>.

Now consider how little we can distinguish in that larger object of sight, the *Moon*, even when she is at her highest point—despite the fact that we are positioned in the dark, under the shadow of the *Earth*, which makes our sight more sensitive <note>original: "passive and impressible"</note>. How little, then, must the fiery eye of that *Cyclops* the *Sun*—which is entirely flame and light—distinguish on this smaller object, the *Earth*? His own power <note>original: "vigour"</note> and motion are so intensely strong and overpowering <note>original: "unyielding"</note>. We can judge what effect this would have on him by looking at ourselves: for although our eyes <note>original: "Organ"</note> are only moved or agitated by the reflection of his rays, we can hardly see the *Moon* when she is above the horizon during the day. What impression, then, can our *Earth* (an object smaller to him than the Moon is to us) make upon the *Sun*? His body is so furiously hot that he is like boiling fire, so to speak, and the solar spots around him are like the scum on a steaming cauldron.

Furthermore, our *atmosphere* is such a thick covering over us at that distance that nothing can appear but a white mist enveloping everything and shining like a bright cloud. In this mist, the rays of the *Sun* will be so lost that they can never reflect any clear representation of things back to him. Therefore, it is as evident to *reason* that he cannot see us as it is to our *senses* <note>original: "Sense"</note> that we see him; and therefore he can be neither an *overseer* nor an *interferer* <note>original: "Intermedler"</note> in our actions.

8. But perhaps you will reply that although the *Sun* cannot see the *Earth*, he may still have sensation and perception within himself (for he is a

fine glittering thing, and some strange matter must be presumed of him) that may amount to a wonderful large sphere of *Understanding*, *Fore-knowledge*, and *Power*. But this is a mere fanciful surmise, and such as cannot be made good by any of our faculties. On the contrary, the opposite is demonstrable by such principles as are already agreed upon. For there are no innate <note>original: "connate"</note> *Ideas* in *Matter*; therefore, from the collision and agitation of these *solar* particles, we cannot rationally expect any other effect in the *Sun* than what we experience in the striking <note>original: "percussion"</note> of our own eyes, which ordinarily results in the sensation of a confused light or flame. If the *Sun*, therefore, has any sense of himself, it must only be the perception of a very vigorous *Light* or *Fire*. Since this is always one and the same representation, it is a question whether he has a sense of it at all, any more than we have of our own bones, which we do not perceive because of our customary and uninterrupted sense of them—as *Mr. Hobbes* <note>Referring to Thomas Hobbes, author of Leviathan</note> ingeniously conjectures in a similar supposition.

But if you will say that there is a perception of the jogging or jostling, or of whatever touch or rubbing <note>original: "fridging"</note> of one *solar* particle against another—the body of the *Sun* being so exceedingly liquid, and consequently its particles never resting, but playing and moving this way and that—yet because they hit and chafe so randomly against one another, the perceptions that arise from this must be so various and accidental, so quick and short, so inconsistent, fleeting, and impermanent, that if any man were in such a condition as the *Sun* necessarily is according to this hypothesis, he would both be, and appear to all the world to be, stark mad. He would be so "off and on," so unsettled, and would do, think, and speak all things with such ungovernable rashness and recklessness <note>original: "temerity"</note>.

In brief, that the *Sun*, by this tumultuous agitation of his fiery *Atoms*, should hit upon any rational contrivance or right *Idea* of any of these living creatures we see here on *Earth* is utterly as hard to conceive as that the *Terrestrial* particles themselves should jostle together into <margin>* Chapter 12. sections 4, 5.</margin> such contrivances and forms—which is the very thing I have already sufficiently disproved.

9. And even if the *Sun* could stumble upon any such true frame or form of any *Animal*, or the proper first principles or design for one, it is still inconceivable how he should convey it into this "Region of Generation" here on *Earth*. This is partly because of the *Earth's* distance and invisibleness, and partly because—the deepest principle of all being mere motion without any superior power to govern it—this imagination of the *Sun* working on the *Earth* can be nothing but a simple straight-line impact <note>original: "Rectilinear impress"</note>. This could never result in such an inward, solid organization of parts in living creatures, nor could it hold together these *Phantoms* <note>original: "Spectres"</note> or *Apparitions* in the air in any more certain form than the smoke of chimneys or the fumes of *Tobacco*.

For whereas the mother has an explicit *Idea* of the *Fetus* and every part of it, the *Sun* and *Stars* have no distinct *Idea* at all of the parts of the *Earth*; nay—

10. I dare say that what we have already suggested will amount to a demonstration: that even if they [the sun and stars] possessed sensation, they do not even know whether this Earth we live on exists in the nature of things <note>original: "in rerum Naturâ"</note> or not.

13. Let insignificant pretenders to philosophy <note>original: "Philosophasters"</note> hoot at and deride it as much as their foolishness allows.

Having cleared the way thus far as to prove that there is no contradiction nor inconsistency in the notion of a *spirit*, but that it may *exist* in nature—nay, that *in fact* <note>original: "de facto"</note> there are *incorporeal substances* really existing in the world—we shall now move closer to our main design. We shall demonstrate that there is such an *immaterial substance* in *man*, which, from the power it is conceived to have in activating <note>original: "actuating"</note> and guiding the body, is usually called the *soul*. This truth we shall make good first in a more general way—but not a whit the less rigorous—by proving that such faculties or operations as we are conscious of in ourselves are utterly incompatible with *matter* considered in general, without any particular organization. And then afterwards we shall more precisely consider the body of man, and every possible fitness in the structure thereof that is worth

<header>CHAPTER I. The Immortality of the Soul.</header>

...worth taking notice of for the performance of *these operations* we ordinarily find in ourselves. And so that this may be done more plainly and convincingly, we will here add to the number of our axioms those that follow.

### AXIOM 20.

->*Motion or reaction of one part of matter against another—or at least a proper continuation of it—is really one and the same thing as sense and perception, if there is any sense or perception in matter at all.*<-

<margin>* Chapter 25, Article 2.</margin>
2. This axiom is plain enough in itself (assuming there were nothing but *body* in the world). Furthermore, it has the support of our most confident and potent adversary, Mr. Hobbes, in his *Elements of Philosophy*. I value his judgment in such cases as these, being persuaded by both reason and charity that because he sees so little into the nature of *spirits*, that defect is balanced by an extraordinary sharpness in discerning the best and most justifiable ways of explaining all *phenomena* <note>original: "salving all Phenomena," meaning to provide a rational explanation for observed events</note> from the ordinary, recognized properties of *matter*. Therefore, I shall not consider it irrelevant to bring in his testimony in matters of this nature; my demonstrations thereby become more attractive to men who share his conclusions. But since my design is not a specific victory over that sort of man, but an absolute establishing of the truth, I shall lay down no grounds that are merely *arguments directed at the person* <note>original: "Argumenta ad hominem"</note>; rather, I will use those that I am persuaded are evident to anyone who can judge impartially (upon this *hypothesis*, that there is nothing but *body* in the world). I have already provided the demonstration of this present axiom in my Preface, *Section 5*.

3. I cannot imagine any possible escape from this, unless one were to imagine that only a *general agitation* of the particles of *matter* would suffice to *stimulate* them to *thinking*, and that once they are thus stimulated, they can freely move on to other thoughts and *mental images* <note>original: "Phantasmes"</note> other than those that fully arise from the impact of *motion*.

But to this, one may briefly answer: First, since *sense* must necessarily arise from the *agitation* and *collision* of these particles (for since they are of nearly the same size, they will effectively act upon one another), the *conscious attention* <term>original: "Animadversion"; the act of the mind noticing or attending to something</term> of these particles will be so occupied and fixed upon their *sensible* perceptions that, even if they otherwise had the power of thinking freely, they would always be necessarily trapped in these *sensory images*.

<margin>* Chapter 6, Sections 4, 5, 6.</margin>
And then, secondly, all that is *perceived* is *perceived in common* by whatever is capable of being the *perceiver*. But nothing that is not really the same as physical motion, or an immediate and full effect of it, can be communicated to the common particles of this or that *matter*. Therefore, it is plain that there is no *collection* <term>original: "congeries"; a mass or gathering of many parts into one body</term> of *matter* that engages in *free thoughts*—whether they be coarse *mental images* or abstract *logical concepts*—because of the lack of mutual communication of those thoughts from one particle to another, as I have demonstrated more particularly in its *proper* place.

# The Immortality of the Soul. BOOK II.

Thirdly and finally, it is sufficiently clear from sense and experience that *matter* is a purely *passive* principle. It is only *moved* or *modified* insofar as some other thing moves and modifies it, but it cannot move itself at all. This is most easily demonstrated to those who argue for *sense* and *perception* within matter. For if it had any such *perception*, it would, by virtue of its *self-motion*, withdraw itself from the blows of hammers or the fury of fire. Or, of its own accord, it would move toward things that are most agreeable and pleasing to it—and do so without the help of *muscles*, since it would be immediately endowed with a *self-moving* power. But since *matter* is so "stupid" <note>original: "stupid," used here in the archaic sense of being inanimate or lacking sensation</note> as to lack *this power*, how can it be thought a subject in which a power and activity infinitely more *divine* should reside? I mean the free wandering into a *variety of thoughts*, the exercise of *invention*, *judgment*, and *memory*—and that regarding objects that are not supposed to be the *impressions* of the *motion* of particles hitting one another.

Nor should I be thought deceptive or dishonest for naming such *dense* and *massive matter* as is usually struck with hammers or hewn with axes, and concluding from that example that no *matter* at all—not even the most subtle—moves *itself*. For *self-motion* would be just as compatible with a *massive* piece of *matter* as with the most *minute* particle imaginable. This is because *force* will relate to force as *magnitude* relates to magnitude; therefore, the most *massive* pieces of *matter* would move themselves the most strongly and irresistibly. From this it appears that the *smallest* particle of any *massive* body, when separated from it, does not gain one bit of advantage toward *self-motion*; it only becomes less irresistible in its *self-motion*.

<margin>* See Book 4, chapter 11, section 8.</margin>
<margin>* See Preface, section 5.</margin>

4. Nor can you help your case by resorting to the *fiction* of a *matter specifically distinct* <note>meaning a fundamentally different type of matter</note> from what men ordinarily speak of (which * some decorate with the title of *Divine*, as if it were the very substance of the highest Godhead). For we may easily undeceive ourselves if we only contemplate a significant quantity of this *Divine Matter*—suppose a globe a few inches in diameter and perfectly *solid* (that is, its parts are immediately united without pores or gaps). Then, consider how it must be harder than an *ingot* <note>original: "Pig of Lead," a "pig" is a mass of metal cast into a simple shape</note> of lead or a *wedge* of gold (which I mention in my * demonstration of this axiom) and as opaque as any body whatsoever. Therefore, this *Divine Matter* will appear to our mind as incapable of *spontaneous motion* and of free *thoughts* and *perceptions* (unforced by physical motion) as the *ingot of lead* and *wedge of gold* mentioned there. Consequently, this *fiction* is but a mere mockery of words, and is as poorly put together in this sense as a "divine ingot of lead" or "divine wedge of gold" would be.

And what I have said of the whole globe applies for the same reason to *any particle of the same nature as it*. It will be no more capable of free thought than the particles of that *matter* that makes up *gold* or *lead*. For if there is any perception, it must be by *physical reaction* <note>original: "corporeal Re-action"</note> in both, if we impartially listen to the *dictates* of our own faculties. And let them say what they will, the *communication* of free perceptions will not be found possible in either; the most *divine* matter imaginable has no other union than the *juxtaposition* of parts <note>original: "Juxta-position," meaning parts simply sitting next to each other rather than being a unified being</note>, as our adversaries themselves will freely acknowledge.

# CHAP. I. The Immortality of the Soul.

<margin>* Book 2. ch. 2. sect. 8.</margin>
To these faithful presages and rational conclusions of our own mind, you may finally add the testimony <note>original: "suffrage"</note> of Nature in experiments. These clearly assure us that there is no such *Divine Matter* endowed with *free thought* <note>original: "cogitation"</note> and *free Agency* intermingled or interspersed within the *ordinary Matter* of the world, as I have plainly shown in my *Antidote* <note>Henry More's book, *An Antidote Against Atheism* (1652)</note>. And therefore we will conclude that no *Matter* whatsoever has any *perception* in any other manner, or according to any other laws, than what Mr. Hobbes has already defined, and I myself have declared in this twentieth Axiom—if *Matter* has any *perception* at all.

->AXIOM XXI.<-

*So far as this continued Reaction reaches, so far reaches Sense or Perception, and no farther.*

5. This Axiom is to be understood regarding the duration of time as well as the extension of the subject: namely, that *Sense* and *Perception* spread no further in *Matter* than *Reaction* does, nor do they remain any longer than this *Reaction* remains. This truth is fully evident from the foregoing Axiom.

->AXIOM XXII.<-

*Whatever diversity there is of Sense or Perception necessarily arises from the diversity of the Magnitude, Figure, Position, Vigor, and Direction of Motion in the parts of the Matter.*

<margin>Sect. 6. p. 8.</margin>
6. The truth of this is also clear from the 20th Axiom. For *Perception* being really one and the same thing as the *Reaction* of *Matter*—one part against another—and there being a diversity of *Perception*, it must imply also a diversity of modification of *Reaction*. And since *Reaction* is nothing but *Motion* in *Matter*, it cannot be varied except by such variations as are compatible with *Matter*. These are such things as *Magnitude*, *Figure*, *Posture*, and *Local Motion* (which includes any effort <note>original: "endeavour"</note> toward it), as well as the *Direction* of that either full motion or restrained effort, and the *Vigor* of it. If you run these down to the lowest degrees, you will at last come to *Rest*, which is therefore in some way referable to that category, just as you refer *Smallness* <note>original: "Littleness"</note> to *Magnitude*. These are the first conceivable properties in *Matter*, and therefore diversity of perception must of necessity arise from these.

->AXIOM XXIII.<-

*Matter, in all the variety of those Perceptions it is sensible of, has none but such as are impressed by physical <note>original: "Corporeal"</note> Motions; that is to say, they are Perceptions of some Actions or modified Impressions of parts of Matter bearing one against another.*

7. To this truth Mr. Hobbes sets his seal with all imaginable willingness, or rather eagerness, as do his followers. They stoutly contend that we do not have the perception of anything but *Phantasms* <term>Phantasms</term> <note>mental images or representations created by the senses</note> of...

of material objects, and of perceptible words or marks, which we make to stand for those objects. This would certainly be most true if there were nothing but *Matter* in the world; therefore, these thinkers speak very consistently with their own principles. I say this is not only true within that school of thought, but also rational in itself, provided one assumes there is nothing but *Matter* in the world and that *Perception* and *Reaction* are really the same thing. For if that *Reaction* exists in animals <note>original: "Brutes"</note> as well as in men, there must not be any difference in their perception of quite another kind, but only in their external way of communicating those perceptions. Therefore, the distinction between *Men* and *Beasts* must consist only in this: that the one can agree on some common mark—whether *Voices* or *Characters*, or whatever else—to express their *perceptions*, while the other cannot. However, the perceptions themselves must be of the same kind in both; neither of them perceives anything but *physical impressions* <note>original: "corporeal impressions"</note>, such as they feel by parts of matter pressing against one another.

### AXIOM XXIV.

->*The distinct impression of any significant extent of multi-colored matter cannot be received by a mere point of matter.*<-

<margin>Book 1, chapter 6.</margin>
8. BY a mere point of matter, I do not mean a mere mathematical point, but a *perfect smallness* <term>original "parvitude": the smallest possible physical unit of matter</term>, or the least *Reality* of matter (concerning which I have spoken already). Since this is the smallest quantity that *divisible matter* <term>original "discerpible": capable of being separated or divided</term> can consist of, no other particle of matter can touch it in an area smaller than itself. How, then, can this *smallness*, which is so tiny that it has no truly distinguishable internal parts, possibly be a subject capable of receiving a distinct view of—for example—half a horizon at once? Such a sight is caused by actual and distinct motions from the actual, distinct parts of the object being seen. But since this *perfect smallness* is the most minute quantity into which *Matter* can be divided, no more than one *actual* line of motion can be directed upon it; the rest will go past it. To this you may add that if this *perfect smallness* were distinctly capable of perceiving multi-colored objects, it would be a miracle if it could not also perceive the particles of the *Air* and the *Atmosphere*, the *globules* <note>original: "Globuli"; in Cartesian physics, these were the small round particles thought to transmit light</note> of light, and the most subtle structure of the parts of opaque bodies.

<margin>* Chapter 8, articles 4, 5, 6, 7, 8.</margin>
9. Again, this object we speak of may be so multi-colored—I mean with such various colors—that it may imply a contradiction for one and the same particle of *Matter* (suppose some very small round one, serving as the apex <note>original: "Cuspe"</note> of the visual pyramid or cone) to receive them all at once. The opposite kinds of those colors cannot be communicated to this round particle except by opposing motions, or by *Rest* and *Motion*, which are just as contrary. This is manifest from that excellent theorem concerning colors in Descartes' *Meteors* <note>René Descartes' *Les Météores* (1637), a work on atmospheric phenomena and optics</note>. Even if it were possible for that theorem to be false, it is still most certainly true that since *Motion* is the cause of sight, the contrast of objects regarding color must arise from contrary modifications of motion in this particle we are discussing, which immediately communicates the *object* to the *perceiving subject* <term>original "Sentient": the entity or organ that experiences sensation</term>. These opposing motions...

René Descartes' <note>original: "Des-Cartes his"</note> second element consists of these particles; since it is thus successively pushed against, things must then be as I have represented them in the accompanying figure. In the diagram, **C E A** is the *Object*, **G H** is the Sentient Matter <note>The physical matter of the brain or nerves capable of feeling.</note>, and **I** is the *Globulus* <term>globulus</term> <note>In Cartesian physics, "globuli" were tiny spherical particles believed to transmit light through the "second element" of the universe.</note>. 14. Lastly, this rapid alternation of impulse or impression would blur <note>original: "contaminate"</note> all the colors, making the whole object appear as if it were one blended <note>original: "confounded"</note> color, as a person may easily observe in a *painted wheel*. For what is it but a quick succession of one color upon the same part of the optic nerve where another color was just before that makes the whole *wheel* seem to be one blended color? 

But, not to mislead anyone, this example of the wheel has a specific advantage over this present theory for making everything seem like one blended color: the colors of the *wheel* do not only arrive at one and same part of the nerve, but they also arrive in one and the same line from the object. Therefore, in this regard, the example is less fitting. However, it is highly probable that *fluid* perceptive matter will still find the colors stained by one another to some degree in the whole object here as well—especially if it is near and very small—due to the instability of that particle that is successively acted upon by all its parts. 

At the very least, this example of the wheel is an indisputable confirmation of our first demonstration regarding the weakness of the second evasion: namely, the *necessity of a considerable stay* upon the percipient matter. Sensation cannot occur without some leisurely duration of this or that motion before it is wiped out. We might also add that there ought to be a proper permanency of the object that presses against the organ, even if no *new* impression suddenly followed to wipe out the former one. One may test this by quickly swinging a painted ball <note>original: "Bullet"</note> on a string, which will further confirm what we aim to prove. But this is more than enough to justify this 24th Axiom, whose evidence is so clear in itself that I believe very few people will fail to be convinced of it at first sight.

### AXIOM XXV.

*Whatever impression, or parts of any impression, that are not received by this perfect parvitude or physical point of matter, are not perceived by it at all.*

15. This is so exceedingly plain in itself that it lacks neither explanation nor proof.

### AXIOM XXVI.

*Whatever sense or motion currently exists in matter is a necessary impression from some other part of matter, and it necessarily continues until some other part of matter has pushed <note>original: "justled"</note> it out.*

<margin>* Part 1, Article 37.</margin>
16. That whatever *motion* exists in any part of *matter* is necessarily there, and continues there until some other part of *matter* changes or diminishes its *motion*, is plain from the laws of *motion* set down by René Descartes in his *Principles of Philosophy* <note>original: *Principia Philosophiæ*</note>. And there is the same reason for *sense* or *perception* (assuming there is nothing but *matter* in the world), as is plain from *Axiom* 20, which makes *motion* and *sense* or *perception* essentially the same thing.

## C H A P T E R II.

1. *That if matter is capable of sense, inanimate things are as well: and of Mr. Hobbes's wavering on that point. 2. An enumeration of several faculties in us that matter is utterly incapable of. 3. That matter, in no kind of temperature, is capable of sense. 4. That no single point of matter can be the common sensorium <term>common sensorium</term> <note>The hypothesized part of the brain where all the senses are unified into a single experience.</note>. 5. Nor a multitude of such points receiving the entire image of the object individually. 6. Nor yet receiving part by part, and the whole as a whole. 7. That memory is incompatible with matter. 8. That matter is incapable of noting some circumstances of the object which we remembered. 9. That matter cannot be the seat of second notions <term>second notions</term> <note>In logic, these are abstract concepts or "concepts of concepts," such as 'genus' or 'species'.</note>. 10. Mr. Hobbes's evasion of the previous demonstration clearly refuted. 11. That the freedom of our will proves that there is a substance in us distinct from matter. 12. That Mr. Hobbes therefore acknowledges all our actions are necessary.*

1. We have now added those axioms that are most useful for our current purpose. Therefore, according to the order we proposed, before we consider the structure <note>original: "fabrick"</note> and organization of the body, let us see if the operations we find in ourselves are compatible <note>original: "competible"</note> with *matter* when viewed in a more general way. That *matter*, by its own nature, is incapable of *sense* plainly appears from *Axioms* 20 and 21. For *motion* and *sense* being essentially one and the same thing, it will necessarily follow that wherever there is *motion*, especially any

<header>The Immortality of the Soul. Book II.</header>

For any significant duration of it, there must be *Sense* and *Perception*. This contradicts what we observe in a person in a trance <note>original: "Catochus," a term for a cataleptic state where the body is rigid but the soul seems absent.</note> and what we experience daily in dead carcasses; in both cases, even though there is physical *Reaction*, there is no *Sense*.

Briefly, if any *matter* has *Sense*, it follows that upon *Reaction*, all matter would have the same. A *bell* while it is ringing, a *bow* while it is bent, and every *jack-in-a-box* that schoolboys play with (while it is held in by the cover pressing against it) would be living *animals* or *sentient creatures*. This idea is so foolish and frivolous that simply stating the opinion should be considered enough to refute it for any sober person.

<margin>See his *Elements of Philosophy*, chapter 25, Article 5.</margin>
And indeed Mr. Hobbes <note>Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679), a philosopher who argued for a purely materialist view of the world.</note> himself, though he reduces *Sense* merely to the *Reaction* of *matter*, is ashamed of these odd consequences. He is very reluctant to be grouped with those philosophers (though, as he says, they are learned men) who have maintained that *all bodies are endowed with sense*. Yet he can hardly avoid saying that they are; he is only more hesitant to grant them *Memory*—which they would possess whether he liked it or not if he grants them *Sense*. For example, in the ringing of a *bell*, a tremor continues in the bell after every stroke. As this tremor fades, it must (according to <margin>* Chapter 25, Articles 7, 8.</margin> his *philosophy*) be *Imagination*; and when referring back to the stroke that has passed, it must be *Memory*. If another stroke hits it while this *Memory* still remains, what stops *Discrimination* or *Judgment* from following? But this *Conclusion* is consistent enough with his absurd principle: *that there is nothing but matter in the universe, and that it is capable of perception.*

2. But we will not satisfy ourselves only by exposing this one ugly inconvenience of this bold claim. We shall further endeavor to show that the hypothesis is false, and that *matter* is utterly incapable of the operations we find in ourselves. Therefore, there must be something *Immaterial* or *Incorporeal* within us. For we find in ourselves that one and the same thing hears, sees, tastes, and, in short, perceives all the variety of objects that nature reveals to us. Therefore, if *sense* is nothing but the impact of physical motion from external objects, that part of *matter* which must be the common *sensorium* <term>common sensorium</term> <note>The hypothesized part of the brain where all the senses are unified into a single experience.</note> must necessarily receive all those diverse impacts from objects. It must likewise *Imagine*, *Remember*, *Reason*, and be the source of *Spontaneous Motion*, as well as the seat of what the Greeks call *free will* <note>original: "τὸ αὐτεξούσιον" (to autexousion), meaning self-authority or the power of self-determination.</note>. We shall find this supposition involved in inescapable difficulties.

3. For first, we cannot imagine any *portion of matter* that is not either *hard* or *soft*. As for that which is *hard*, everyone dismisses it as being completely unlike anything that could possess the cognitive faculties we are conscious of. That which is *soft* will prove to be either *opaque*, *transparent* <note>original: "pellucid"</note>, or *shining* <note>original: "lucid"</note>. If it is opaque, it cannot *see*, as the outer surface acts as a barrier to the inner part. If it is transparent, like *air* or *water*, then it will indeed allow those *particles* and that *motion* (which convey the *sense* and distinction of *colors*) to enter, and *sound* will also penetrate it. But this *matter* being *heterogeneous* <note>original: "heterogeneall," meaning composed of different parts or elements.</note>—that is to say, consisting of parts with different natures and purposes—the *air*, for instance, being suitable for *sound*, and

# CHAP. II. The Immortality of the Soul.

...those round particles which *Descartes* <note>original: "Cartesius"</note> describes as color and *light*; the perception of these objects would be located in different places. However, there is some one thing within us that perceives both. Finally, if it were *luminous*, there would be much the same inconvenience as there is in *opaque* matter, for its own fieriness would repel the gentle touch of external impressions. Or, if it were so mild and thin that it was in some measure transparent, the same problems would return that were found in *clear* <note>original: "pellucid"</note> matter.

In short, any liquid *matter* has such a variety of particles in it that if the whole thing (as the common *sensorium* <term>the physical seat of sensation where all senses meet</term> must be) is affected by any impact from the outside, its parts must be affected in different ways. Consequently, no object would seem *homogeneous* <note>uniform or consistent in nature</note>, as appears from Axiom 22. I shall further illustrate this truth by a simple but very significant comparison. Suppose we should put feathers, bullets, and spur-rowels <note>the spiked wheel on a horseman's spur</note> in a box where they lie mixed together, but packed closely against one another. Upon any shake this box receives—supposing all the stuffing inside has *sense*—it is evident that the various things within it must be differently affected. Therefore, if the common *sensorium* were like that, no object in the world would seem uniform. Or, at the very least, these various particles would be the separate *receptors* of different kinds of motion from the outside—just as the air receives sounds, or the *Cartesian globules* <note>the spherical particles Descartes theorized were the medium for light</note> receive light and colors. But we are again at a loss, as before, to identify what receives all of these and so can judge all of them—unless we imagine it to be some very fine and *subtle matter*, so *light* and *thin* that it does not feel itself, yet so yielding and *passive* that it easily feels the various assaults and impressions of other bodies upon it or within it. Yet this would imply that this matter alone was *sensitive* and the others were not; and so it would be granted that not all *matter* (not even in fluid bodies) has *sense*.

<margin>But as for why it might not be so, something is suggested in the previous chapter, section 3.</margin>

Such a balanced *matter* as this is similar to the *animal spirits* <note>in early modern physiology, these were believed to be ultra-fine fluids that traveled through the nerves to facilitate sensation and movement</note> in humans. If *matter* could be the *soul*, these would be the very *soul* of the body and the *common perceiver* of all motions from within or without, because of their thinness, passivity, near uniformity, and *(perhaps)* the fact that no change or alteration is perceived from the playing together of their own thin and light particles; therefore, they would be very fit to receive all manner of impressions from others. From this, we may rationally conclude that some such subtle matter as this is either the *soul* itself or her immediate *instrument* for all kinds of perceptions. I shall prove the latter to be true in its proper place. I shall now demonstrate that the former part is false by proving more strictly that no *matter* whatsoever is capable of the kind of *sense* and *perception* we are conscious of ourselves.

4. For concerning that part of *matter* which is the common *sensorium*, I ask whether some one point of it receives the whole image of the object, or whether the image is wholly received into every point of it, or finally whether the whole *sensorium* receives the whole image through its spread-out parts (this part of the sensorium receiving this part of the image, and that part receiving that). If the first is true—seeing that the thing in us which perceives the external object also *moves* the body—it will follow that one little point of *matter* will give physical motion to what is countless millions of times bigger...

larger than itself; for which no example can be found or even imagined in Nature.

5. If we consider the second possibility, a difficulty arises that also affects the previous position: how could such a small point as we are discussing receive the images of such vast or varied objects all at once without them being erased or confused? This is impossible, as is clear from Axiom 24. Therefore, since it cannot receive them, it cannot perceive them, according to Axiom 25. But if every point or particle of this **matter** could receive the entire image, which of these innumerable particles—each receiving the image perfectly—should be considered "**I myself**" who perceives this image? If I am all those points, it would happen (especially with a small object very close by) that the line of impact reaching different and distant points would seem to come from several different places. Thus, one object would necessarily appear to be a cluster of objects. And if I am only one of these points, what becomes of the rest? Or **who are they**?

6. There remains, therefore, only the third way: that the different parts of the object's image are received by the different parts of this portion of matter supposed to be the common **sensorium** <term>the physical seat of sensation where all senses meet</term>. But this perfectly contradicts experience. We find that we perceive the whole object ourselves, whereas in this case, nothing could perceive the whole because every part would only perceive its own specific portion. Therefore, there would be nothing capable of judging the whole. It would be no different than if three men were imagined to sing a song in three parts, and none of them could hear any part but his own; they could never judge the harmony of the whole.

7. Regarding the **seat of imagination and memory**, especially **memory**, what kind of **matter** can be found that is fit for this function? If it be **fluid**, the images of objects will be prone to vanish suddenly, or to be distorted and turned the wrong way. For example:

The letter B is positioned to the left of the rectangle's midpoint. Inside the rectangle, point C is located within a shaded vertical strip on the left side, and point L is to the right of this shaded strip.</image-desc> 

If **C**, a particle of this **fluid matter**, receives an impression from **B**, it must feel it as coming from **B**. But in the shifting and tossing up and down that particles of **fluid matter** do, it might turn the side **EF** (which received that impression from **B**) toward **L**. Then it will feel as if the impression had come from **L**, for it must feel it as coming from the place directly opposite to itself (if it can feel it at all after the object is removed and the **reaction** has stopped). This same logic applies to other particles of this **fluid matter**, which must inevitably force a great deal of complete confusion upon both the **imagination** <note>original: "fancy"</note> and **memory**. 

If the matter be **hard**, it will soon settle into a state of **rest**, like a **bell** whose vibration <note>original: "tremor"</note> is gone in a short time; yet we remember things for many years together, even if we never think of them until the end of that time. If it be **viscid** <note>original: "viscid"; thick or sticky</note>, there is a similar problem; indeed, it is the least fit of all for either receiving **motion** or continuing it, and therefore unlikely to be the **seat** of either **imagination** or **memory**. For if **motion** (or **reaction**) and sense—whether internal or external—are one and the same, then when **motion** stops, **memory** must necessarily stop, according to **Axiom 21**. Nor can the matter remember any better when it is moved again in the same way, any more than a stone or a piece of lead that was flung into the air can become lighter or more prone to fly upward once it has stopped moving.

<summary>More argues that physical matter is incapable of perception or memory because a single point cannot contain a whole image, and multiple points would fragment consciousness. He further contends that neither fluid, hard, nor sticky matter has the physical properties necessary to store memories over time.</summary>

8. Lastly, we remember some things for which there can be no **physical imprints in matter** to represent them, such as **width** and **distance**. Regarding both of these, no mark can be made in the matter (represented by point **E**) by lines coming from the <image-desc>A geometric diagram representing visual perception or distance. 9. Consider those things commonly called **Second Notions** <term>abstract concepts about concepts, such as 'genus' or 'species,' which describe how we categorize things rather than describing the physical things themselves</term>. These are not physical objects, nor are they the **mental images** <note>original: "Phantasmes"</note> of any physical objects; they are merely our way of conceiving or reasoning about them. This category includes all **logical and mathematical terms**. These, I say, never entered the mind through the senses, as they are not the result of physical motion. Physical motion only triggers in us—just as it does in dogs and other animals—the sense of sounds, colors, heat, cold, and the like. Now, since **matter** is affected by no perception other than physical impressions caused by one body pressing against another, it is plain from Axiom 23 that these Second Notions, or mathematical and logical concepts, cannot be located in matter. Therefore, they must exist in some other substance distinct from it, according to Axiom 10.

10. Here Mr. Hobbes <note>Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679), a philosopher who famously argued that everything in the universe, including the human mind, is made of physical matter</note>, to avoid the force of this proof, has come up with a marvelously clever trick to fool his followers. He makes them believe that there is no such thing as these Second Notions separate from the **names** or **words** used to signify them. He claims there is no perception in us except for the mental images impressed by external objects—the kind of images shared by both humans and animals. As for the names we give to these objects or their mental images, he argues they are the same as any other marks, letters, or characters. Since these names enter through the senses, he tries to persuade people that it is a clear case: we perceive nothing except what is physically impressed upon us by objects. 

But how ridiculous an excuse this is can be easily seen if we consider that if these mathematical and logical notions were nothing but names, then mathematical and logical truths would not be the same in every nation, because they do not use the same names. For example, **Similarity** <note>original Latin: Similitudo</note> and **Likeness** <note>original Greek: ὁμοιότης</note>, **Analogy** <note>original Greek: ἀναλογία</note> and **Proportion** <note>original Latin: Proportio</note>, **Reason** <note>original Greek: λόγ. (logos)</note> and **Ratio** <note>original Latin: Ratio</note>—these names are utterly different, the Greek from the Latin. Yet the Greeks, the Romans, and every other nation do not differ in the concepts they hold under these different names. Therefore, it is plain that there is a **fixed concept** distinct from these words and names, as well as from those physical mental images impressed by the object; which was the point to be proven.

11. Lastly, we are conscious of that faculty which the Greeks call **free will** <note>original: αὐτεξούσιον (autexousion), meaning the power of self-determination</note>, or a **power within ourselves** to hold onto what is virtuous and honest, or to give in to pleasures and other lowly gains, regardless of any external pressure or persistent temptation. That we have this **liberty and freedom** in ourselves, and that we refuse the
