That we can choose the good and reject the evil when we might have done otherwise is evidenced by the natural sense of *remorse of conscience*. When a person has done something wrong, the pain, grief, or indignation they feel toward themselves is of a different kind than what we feel from misfortunes or insults we could not avoid. What pinches and vexes us so severely is the realization that we have brought such an evil upon ourselves when it was within our power to have avoided it. Now, if there is no sense or perception in us except what arises from the *reaction of matter* <note>original: "Re-action of Matter"; the materialist view that thoughts are just physical particles bumping into each other</note> against other matter, then every representation of things, every deliberation, and every determination we make would be—according to *Axiom 26*—purely necessary <term>in this context, 'necessary' means 'inevitable' or 'predetermined'</term>. Under this hypothesis, there is no more freedom while we deliberate or conclude than there is in a pair of scales, which rests just as inevitably at the end as it moved at the beginning. Therefore, it is manifest that this faculty we call *Free Will* is not found in *matter*, but in some other *substance*, according to *Axiom 10*.

12. To give him his due, **Mr. Hobbes** <note>Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679), a famous materialist philosopher who argued that everything in the universe, including the human mind, is physical matter in motion</note> consistently enough with his own principles, very flatly affirms *that all our actions are necessary*. But since I have proved the contrary by that faculty which we may call *internal sense* or *common notion*—which is found in all people who have not done violence to their own nature—my conclusion must stand as an undisputed truth according to *Axiom 5*, unless he can discover the contrary using some other approved faculty. He pretends, therefore, to offer some demonstration of reason which he would oppose against the dictate of this *inward sense*. It will be useful to examine this so that we may uncover his *sophistry* <term>clever but false reasoning intended to deceive</term>.

This is sufficient to support my last argument against Mr. Hobbes.

1. His first argument runs like this (I will repeat it in his own words, as well as the rest of them as they are found in his treatise *Of Liberty and Necessity*): "I conceive," says he, "that nothing takes its beginning from itself, but from the action of some other immediate agent outside of itself; and that therefore, when a man first has an appetite or Will for something for which immediately before he had no appetite or Will, the cause of his Will is not the Will itself, but something else not within his own control. So, while it is beyond controversy that the Will is the necessary cause of voluntary actions, and by what has been said the Will is also caused by other things which it does not control, it follows that voluntary actions all have necessary causes, and therefore are necessitated <term>predetermined by cause and effect</term>."

2. His second argument is this: "I hold," says he, "that to be a sufficient cause to which nothing is missing that is needed to produce the effect. The same is also a necessary cause. For if it were possible that a sufficient cause should not bring about the effect, then something was missing which was needed to produce it, and so the cause was not sufficient; but if it is impossible that a sufficient cause should not produce the effect, then a sufficient cause is a necessary cause, for something is said to produce an effect *necessarily* when it cannot help but produce it. From this it is obvious that whatever is produced, is produced necessarily. For whatever is produced has had a sufficient cause to produce it, or else it would not have existed." What follows is either the same, or so closely dependent on this, that I do not need to add it.

3. His third argument, therefore, shall be the one he urges from *Future disjunctions* <note>logical "either/or" statements about the future</note>. For example, let us take the case of the *Weather*: "It is necessary that tomorrow it shall rain, or not rain. If, therefore," says he, "it is not necessary it shall rain, then it is necessary it shall not rain; otherwise there is no necessity that the proposition, *It shall rain or not rain*, should be true."

4. His fourth is this: "That the denying of Necessity destroys both the decrees and the foreknowledge <note>original: "Prescience"</note> of Almighty God. For whatever God has purposed to bring to pass using man as an instrument, or foresees shall come to pass, a man—if he has liberty from necessity—might frustrate <term>thwart or prevent</term> and keep from happening. Then God would either not foreknow or decree it, or he would foreknow that such things shall happen that never will, and decree what shall never come to pass."

5. The beginning of his first argument is somewhat obscure and ambiguous: *Nothing takes its beginning from itself*. But I shall be as honest and faithful an interpreter as I can. If he means by "beginning," the *beginning of existence*, it is undoubtedly true that no substance, nor modification of substance, takes its beginning from itself; but this will not lead to the conclusion he aims for. But if he means that *nothing takes...*

...takes its beginning from itself, or of being affected or modified differently than before, he must mean by *nothing* either no Essence <note>original: "Essence"; the fundamental nature or substance of a thing</note> (neither *Spirit* nor *Body*) or no Modification of Essence. He cannot mean *Spirit*, since he does not admit such a thing exists in the entire scope of Nature. If he means *Body*, it will not prove what he intends, unless there is nothing but *Body* in the Universe. However, that is a mere unsupported principle of his, which he begs his gullible followers to accept but proves nowhere, as I have already noted. If by *Modification* he means the *Modification of Matter or Body*, that still relies on his previous principle—*that there is nothing but Body in the world*. Therefore, he proves nothing except by using a circular argument <note>original: "begg'd Hypothesis"</note>, and a false one at that, as I have demonstrated elsewhere. Therefore, the most favorable interpretation I can make is that he means by *nothing* "no Essence" or "no Modification of Essence," being willing to hide that dearly-held hypothesis of his (*that there is nothing but Body in the world*) under such general and vague terms.

6. Since the words in those other senses have no hope of proving anything, let us see how far they will succeed in this one: taking *no thing* to mean *no Essence*, *no Modification of Essence*, or (what is more relevant to the matter at hand) *no Faculty of an Essence*. From this two-fold meaning, let us examine two propositions that result from it: 
* First, *that no Faculty of any Essence can vary its operation from what it is, except by the action of some other immediate Agent outside itself*; 
* Or second, *that no Essence can vary its own Modification or Operation by itself, except by the action of some other immediate Agent outside it*. 

Of these two propositions, the latter seems to be the better and more natural interpretation. For it is very clumsy—and if truly examined, false—to say that the *Mode* or *Faculty* of any *Essence changes itself*. It is the *Essence itself* that exerts itself into these variations of Modes if no external Agent is the cause of these changes. And by Mr. Hobbes <note>Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679), the famous materialist philosopher</note> opposing an external Agent to this "Thing" that he says does not change itself, he naturally implies that he is speaking of *Substances* rather than *Faculties*.

7. Therefore, there only remains the latter proposition to be examined: *that no Essence can, by itself, vary its own Modification*. It is plain that some Essence must have had the power of *moving*, because there is *Motion* in the world, and that motion must be the *Effect* of some *Substance* or another. 

But that *Motion* in a broad sense—taking it to mean mutation or change—may proceed from the very Essence in which it is found, seems plain to me by *Experience*. For there is an Essence within us (whatever we choose to call it) which we find gifted with this property. This is apparent because it has a variety of perceptions—*Mathematical, Logical*, and I may also add *Moral*—which are not the imprints or traces of *Physical Motion* <note>original: "Corporeal Motion"</note>, as I have already demonstrated. 

Any person may observe in themselves, and discover in the writings of others, how the *Mind* has moved from one of these perceptions to another in very long chains of *Demonstration*. One can also see what stillness from physical movement is required when thinking through <note>original: "excogitation"</note> such a series of reasons. In these moments, the *Spirits* <note>original: "Spirits"; the 'animal spirits' thought to inhabit the nervous system</note> are not permitted to fall into any posture or motion other than what they are guided into by the *Mind itself*, where these immaterial and intellectual notions take the lead and rule.

Besides, in grosser phantasms <note>original: "Phantasmes"; mental images or sensory impressions stored in the mind</note>, which are supposed to be somewhere impressed in the brain, the composition of them, and the separation <note>original: "disclusion"</note> and various disposal of them, is plainly an arbitrary act. It implies an Essence <note>The soul or fundamental substance</note> that can, as it chooses <note>original: "lifts"</note>, excite in itself the variety of such phantasms as have been first presented to her from external objects, and change them and transpose them at her own will. 8. *But however, from this shaky ground he will infer that whenever we have a will toward a thing, the cause of this will is not the will itself, but something else not in our own disposal; the meaning of which must be that whenever we will, some bodily impression <note>original: "corporeal impress"</note>, which we cannot avoid, forces us to do so.* But the inference <note>original: "Illation"</note> is as weak as it is bold; it being built upon no foundation, as I have already shown. I shall only take notice how *Mr. Hobbes*, though he has rescued himself from the authority of the Schools <note>The Scholastic philosophers of the medieval universities, whose Aristotelian methods Hobbes often mocked</note>, and would gladly set up for himself, yet he has not freed himself from their fooleries in talking of *Faculties* and *Operations* (and the similar absurdities in both) as separate and distinct from the *Essence* they belong to, which causes a great deal of distraction and obscurity in the study of things. I speak this in reference to those expressions of his: that the *will is the cause of willing*, and that it is the *necessary cause* of voluntary actions, and of things not being in its disposal. Whereas, if a man would speak properly and desired to be understood, he would say, *that the subject in which is this power or act of willing (call it Man or the Soul of Man) is the cause of this or that voluntary action.* But this would reveal his sophistry, with which perhaps <note>original: "haply"</note> he has entrapped himself, which is this: *Something outside the power of the will necessarily causes the will; the will once caused is the necessary cause of voluntary actions; and therefore all voluntary actions are necessitated.*

9. Besides the fact that the first part of this argumentation is groundless (as I have already suggested), the second is sophistical <note>Deceptive or fallacious in its logic</note>, saying *that the will is the necessary cause of voluntary actions.* For by *necessary*, one may understand either *necessitated*—forced and made to act whether it wants to or not—or else it may signify that the will is a *requisite* cause of voluntary actions, so that there can be no voluntary actions without it. The latter of these may be in some sense true, but the former is utterly false. So, the conclusion being inferred from assertions of which one is groundless and the other sophistical, the inference cannot but be ridiculously weak and despicable. But if he had spoken in the *concrete* instead of the *abstract*, his sophistry would have been more grossly discoverable, or rather the train of his reasoning would seem sluggish and contemptible. Omitting, therefore, to speak of the *will* separately—which in itself is but a blind power or operation—let us speak of that *Essence* which is endowed with *will*, *sense*, *reason*, and other *faculties*, and see what face this argumentation of his will bear, which will then run like this:

10. *Some external, irresistible agent does ever necessarily cause that...*

# The Immortality of the Soul. BOOK II.

...*Essence* <note>The soul or fundamental substance</note> (call it *Soul* or what you please) which is endowed with the faculties of *Will* and *Understanding*, to *Will*: *This* Essence, endowed with the power of exerting itself into the act of *Willing*, is the necessary cause of *voluntary* actions: Therefore all voluntary actions are necessitated. The first *assertion* now at first sight appears to be a gross falsehood, the *soul* being endowed with *Understanding* as well as *Will*, and therefore she is not necessarily determined to will by external impressions <note>original: "impresses"</note>, but by the displaying of certain notions and perceptions she raises in herself, which are purely intellectual. And the second seems to be a very thin and weak piece of *Sophistry* <note>Deceptive or fallacious reasoning</note>. Both of these my reasons already alleged do so easily and so plainly reach, that I need add nothing more, but pass to his second *Argument*, the form of which in brief is this:

11. *Every* Cause is a sufficient cause, otherwise it could not produce its *effect*: Every sufficient cause is a necessary cause—that is to say, it will be sure to produce the effect, otherwise something was wanting to it, and it was no sufficient cause: And therefore every cause is a necessary cause, and consequently every *Effect* or *Action*, even those that are termed *Voluntary*, are necessitated. This reasoning looks clever at first view; but if we come closer to it, we shall find it a pitiful piece of *Sophistry*, which is easily detected by observing the ambiguity of that *Proposition*: "Every sufficient cause is a necessary cause." For the force lies not so much in it being said to be "sufficient," as in it being said to be a *Cause*; which, if it be a cause, it must of necessity have an *Effect*, whether it be sufficient or insufficient; this reveals the *Sophism* <note>A clever but false argument</note>. For these relative terms of *Cause* and *Effect* necessarily imply one another. But every *Being* that is sufficient to act in this or that way if it wills, and so to become the *C<unclear>aus</unclear>e* thereof, does neither act, nor abstain from acting, necessarily. And therefore if it does act, it adds *Will* to the *Sufficiency* of its power; and if it did not act, it is not because it had not sufficient power, but because it would not make use of it. So that we see that every sufficient *Cause*, rightly understood without trickery <note>original: "captiositie"</note>, is not a necessary cause, nor will it be sure to produce the *Effect*; and though there be a sufficiency of power, yet there may be something wanting—namely, the exertion of the *Will*. By this it may come to pass that what might have acted if it wanted to, did not; but if it did, *Will* being added to sufficient *Power*, it cannot be said to be "necessary" in any other sense than that *Axiom* in *Metaphysics*: "Whatever is, as long as it is, must necessarily be" <note>original: "Quicquid est, quamdiu est, necesse est esse"</note>. The reason for this is because it is impossible that a thing should be and not be at the same time. But before it acted, it might have chosen whether it would have acted or not; but it did determine itself. And in this sense is it to be called a *free Agent*, and not a necessary one. So it is manifest that though there is some clever perverseness of wit in the contriving of this argument, yet there is no solidity at all at the bottom.

12. And as little is there in his third argument. But in this, I must confess, I cannot so much accuse him of *Art* and *Sophistry*, as of ignorance of the rules of *Logic*; for he plainly asserts that the necessity of the truth of that *Proposition* named there depends on the necessity of the truth of the parts thereof; than which no grosser error can be committed in the

<summary>Henry More refutes Hobbes's claim that all causes are "necessary causes" by arguing that a free agent possesses the power to act but only does so when the Will is exerted, making the action voluntary rather than inevitable. He dismisses Hobbes's logic as sophistry and a misunderstanding of metaphysical axioms regarding existence and agency.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Henry More's critique of Thomas Hobbes's logic regarding necessity and free will, specifically addressing the nature of logical propositions and future events.</meta>

# CHAP. III. The Immortality of the Soul.

...the art of reasoning. For he might as well say that the necessity of the truth of a **connected** axiom <note>original: "Connex Axiome"; a conditional statement like "If A, then B"</note> depends on the necessity of the truth of its parts, as he does for a **disjunctive** axiom <note>original: "Disjunct"; a statement like "Either A or B"</note>. But in a **connected** axiom, even when both parts are not only false but impossible, the axiom itself is necessarily true. For example: *If Bucephalus <note>Bucephalus was the famous horse of Alexander the Great.</note> be a man, he is endowed with human reason*. This axiom is necessarily true, and yet the parts are impossible; for Alexander's horse can neither be a man, nor have the reason of a man, either potentially or actually. The necessity, therefore, is placed only upon the *connection* of the parts, not upon the parts themselves. 

So when I say, *Tomorrow it will rain, or it will not rain*, this **disjunctive** proposition is also necessary, but the necessity lies upon the *disjunction* of the parts, not upon the parts themselves. For since they are immediately disjoined, there is a necessity that one of them must occur, though there is no necessity that *this* one must be determined rather than *that* one. It is like a man kept in custody who has use of only two rooms; though there is a necessity that he be found in one of the two, he is not confined to either specific one of them. To be brief, and to prevent those frivolous answers and replies that follow in **Mr. Hobbes's** pursuit of this argument: just as the necessity of this **disjunctive** axiom lies upon the *disjunction* itself, so the truth (of which this necessity is a mode) must lie there too. For it is the *disjunction* of the parts that is affirmed, and not the parts themselves, as anyone who is even moderately in his right mind must acknowledge.

13. There is a more dangerous path that **Mr. Hobbes** might have taken, with more credit but hardly better success: the consideration of a simple axiom that speaks of a future **contingent** <note>An event that may or may not happen</note>, such as: *Tomorrow Socrates will dispute* <note>original: "Cras Socrates disputabit"</note>. Since every axiom is either true or false, as all agree, if this axiom is true now, it is impossible for **Socrates** not to dispute tomorrow; or if it is false now, it is impossible that he should. Thus, his action of disputing (or the omission of it) would be necessary, for the proposition cannot be both true and false at once. 

Some find it very difficult to untangle themselves from this trap. But if we more precisely examine the meaning of the proposition, the difficulty vanishes. He who affirms that **Socrates** will dispute tomorrow affirms it (to use the distinction of **futurities** that **Aristotle** suggests) either as **that which is likely to happen** <note>original: "tò méllon," meaning something that has a possibility of being otherwise</note> or as **that which will certainly come to pass** <note>original: "tò esómenon"</note>. If the latter, the axiom is false; if the former, it is true. Thus, the liberty of **Socrates's** action—as well as all similar contingent effects—is easily rescued from this logical entanglement. For every **future** axiom is as incapable of being judged unless we determine its sense by one of these two modes, just as an **indefinite** axiom is before we mentally add the marks of **universality** or **particularity**. We cannot say of either of them that they are true or false until we have completed and determined their meaning.

For if there is nothing but **body** or **matter** in the whole scope of things, it will be very hard to find any such **Deity** as has the **knowledge** or **foreknowledge** of anything. And therefore, I suspect that this last point is only included as an **argument directed at the person** <note>original: "Argumentum ad hominem"</note>, to puzzle those who have not dived to such a profound depth of natural knowledge as to imagine they have discovered there is no God in the world.

15. But let him vilify it as he will, it is the only argument he has brought that has any tolerable sense or solidity in it; and it is a subject that has exercised the wits of all ages: how to reconcile the **liberty** of man's **will** with the **decrees** and **foreknowledge** <note>original: "Præscience"</note> of **God**. But my **openness**, I hope, and **moderation** shall make this matter easier for me than it ordinarily proves to those who venture upon it. My **answer** therefore, in brief, shall be this:

16. First, that though there is such a faculty in the soul of man as **liberty of will**, yet she is not always in a state of acting according to it. For she may either degenerate so far that it may be as certainly known what she will do upon this or that occasion as what a hungry dog will do when a crust is offered him—which is the general condition of almost all men in most occurrences of their lives. Or else, she may be so **heroically good** (though that happens in very few) that it may be as certainly known as before what she will do or suffer during such emergencies. In these cases, the active use of **liberty of will** ceases.

17. Secondly, that the use of the faculty of **free will** is properly found where we find ourselves so near to a **state of balance** <note>original: "Æquiponderancy"</note>—being touched with the sense of **virtue** on one side, and the ease or **pleasure** of some vicious action on the other—that we are conscious to ourselves that we ought to, and that we may if we will, abandon the one and cling to the other.

18. Thirdly, that in this conflict the soul has no such absolute power to determine her own path toward one action or the other, but **temptation** or **supernatural assistance** may certainly carry her this way or that way; so that she may not be able to use that liberty of going indifferently either way.

19. Fourthly, that **divine decrees** either find men fit, or make them so, for the executing of whatever is absolutely purposed or prophesied concerning them.

20. Fifthly, that the **foreknowledge** <note>original: "Præſcience"</note> of **God** is so vast and so far exceeds the comprehension of our thoughts, that all that can be safely said of it is this: that this knowledge is most perfect and exquisite, accurately representing the natures, powers, and properties of the thing it foreknows. From this it must follow that if there is any creature who is free and undetermined, and who in such circumstances and at such a time may either act or not act, this perfect **foreknowledge** must discern from all eternity that the said creature, in such circumstances, may either act in this way, or that way, or not at all. And further to declare the perfection of this **foreknowledge**...

### CHAPTER IV. The Immortality of the Soul.

knowledge and omniscience of God; just as His omnipotence ought to extend so far as to be able to do whatever does not imply a contradiction, so His foreknowledge <note>original: "Præscience"</note> and omniscience ought to extend so far as to know precisely and fully whatever does not imply a contradiction to be known.

To conclude briefly, therefore: *free* or *contingent effects* either imply a contradiction if they are foreknown, or they do not. If they imply a contradiction to be foreknown, they are not an object of the *omniscience of God*; therefore, there can be no claim that His *foreknowledge* determines them, nor can it be argued that they are determined by it. If they imply no contradiction to be foreknown, that is to acknowledge that divine *foreknowledge* and free actions may very well exist together. And so, either way, despite divine *omniscience*, the *actions of men may be free*.

21. The sum of all this is: that human actions are sometimes *free* and sometimes *not free*. But the fact that they are at any time *free* is a *demonstration* that there is a *faculty* in us that is incompatible with *mere matter*—which is sufficient for my purpose.

# The Immortality of the Soul. BOOK II.

I shall first list the opinions and then examine the possibility of each in particular. Briefly, they are these: 1. That the whole body is the seat of the <term>common sense</term> <note>The "common sense" was a theorized internal power that unified the data from the five external senses.</note>. 2. The opening of the stomach. 3. The heart. 4. The brain. 5. The membranes. 6. The <term>transparent partition</term> <note>original: "Septum lucidum," a thin membrane in the center of the brain.</note>. 7. Some very small and perfectly solid particle in the body. 8. The <term>pineal gland</term> <note>original: "Conarion," the small gland in the brain Descartes famously identified as the seat of the soul.</note>. 9. The meeting of the nerves near the fourth ventricle of the brain. 10. The animal spirits in that fourth ventricle.

2. That the first opinion is false is evident from this: assuming we are nothing but *mere matter*, if we grant the whole body to be one common <term>center of sensation</term> <note>original: "Sensorium"</note> capable of perceiving all objects, the *motion* impressed upon the eye or ear must be transmitted into all parts of the body. For *sensation* is really the same thing as the *communication of motion*, according to Axiom 20. And since the variety of *sensation* arises from the modification of motion—which must necessarily be varied by the different temperaments of the body parts, according to Axiom 22—it plainly follows that the eye must be affected differently by the motion of light than the other parts to which this motion is transmitted. Therefore, if it is the whole body that perceives, it will perceive the object in every part of itself in several different ways at once; this contradicts all experience. It would also likely appear to be in several places at once, because of the many windings and turns that must occur during the transmission of this *motion*, which would act like so many refractions or reflections.

3. That the opening of the stomach cannot be the seat of the *common sense* is apparent from this: that which is the common *sensor* not only perceives all objects but also has the power of *moving* the body. Now, besides the fact that there is no organization in the mouth of the stomach that can overcome the strength of our arguments in the previous chapters—which took away all capacity from *matter* to have any *perception* at all—there is no imaginable mechanical reason to be found in the body to make it possible. Even if we supposed the mouth of the stomach were the common *perceiver* of all objects, it could not possibly *move* the rest of the limbs of the body as we find something in us does. This is so palpably plain that it is unnecessary to spend any more words on it.

4. The same may be said concerning the *heart*. For who can imagine that, if the *heart* were that *common perceiver*, there is any such mechanical connection between it and all the parts of the body that it could, by such or such a perception, command the motion of the foot or little finger? Besides that, the heart seems wholly employed in performing its <term>contraction and expansion</term> <note>original: "Systole and Diastole," the rhythmic beating of the heart.</note>, which causes such a great and alternating difference in the heart's position that, if it were the seat where the senses of all objects center, we would not be able to see things steadily or fix our sight in one place.

5. How incapable the *brain* is of being such an active principle of motion as we find in ourselves is plainly indicated by its *viscosity* <note>original: "viscidity"; the thick, gluey, or soft consistency of brain matter.</note>. Furthermore, physicians have discovered through experience that the brain is so far—

1. The essence of this misleading theory is, in short, that the **pineal gland** <note>original: "Glandula Pinealis"; also called the "Conarion" below.</note> is the <term>Common Percipient</term> <note>The central organ that receives and unifies all sensory information.</note> of all objects. This includes both the nerves that transmit sensations from outward objects and those that serve the **internal** needs of the **body**, such as hunger, thirst, and similar feelings. Thus, as the gland is moved in various ways, it determines the flow of the **spirits** into specific **muscles**, thereby moving the body.

2. It is demonstrable from **Descartes'** <note>original: "Cartesius"</note> own description of how an image is transmitted (for example, through the eye to the brain, and then to the **pineal gland** <note>original: "Conarion"; the Greek term for the pineal gland, which Descartes believed was the seat of the soul</note>) that the gland itself, without a soul, has no perception of any object. From this it is clear that the gland does not, and cannot, perceive the whole object, even if its various parts are admitted to perceive the various parts of the object. But something within us *perceives* the whole, which therefore cannot be the pineal gland.

The reason we do not *perceive* external objects as **double** is not so much because the image is united in the organ of **common sense** <note>The internal faculty that unifies diverse sensory inputs into a single experience.</note>, but because the lines of sight from the object to both eyes meet in such a way that it is felt in one place. Otherwise, if the object is very near and the direction of our eyes is not adjusted for that closeness, it will seem **double** anyway. This demonstrates that a person can see with both eyes at once; and for my own part, I am certain that I see better at a distance when I use both eyes than when I use only one.

5. We will not argue here that this might be a mere fancy—given that these **valves** in the **nerves** have not yet been discovered by any anatomist as part of the physical **structure** <note>original: "Organization"</note> of any animal's body. Instead, we will show that even if they did exist, they would not achieve what is intended. First, it does not seem that the spirits would move any faster out of **C** into **B** than the pressure caused in **B** (by the gland directing spirits there) forces them to move. Since all spaces are equally open for them to move in, they will go no further than they are driven or pressed, much like **air in a bladder**. How the **pineal gland** <note>original: "Conarion"</note> could drive or press the spirits into **B** with enough force to push the spirits out of **C** as quickly and sharply as we see in some physical actions is utterly inconceivable.

6. It would be impossible for a person to resist external force; even a tenth of the strength we normally use to open a man’s hand against his will would easily force it open, whether he wanted it or not. If our **body** were nothing but **mechanically organized matter**, a very ordinary strength moving limb **K** from **B** toward **C** would necessarily press the spirits in **B** so that they would pass through **E** into **C**. Therefore, it is the mere **command** <note>original: "Imperium"</note> of our soul that directs the spirits to one muscle rather than the other and holds them there despite external force. From this, it is manifest that **brute beasts** <note>Animals</note> must have souls as well.

# CHAPTER V. The Immortality of the Soul.

Only representing the **shape** <note>original: "Figure"</note> of a thing, not its **colors**. Besides, a person may take a hundred objects and view them from the same distance, keeping the **eye** in exactly the same position. This would force the images to occupy the very same spot in the **brain**. Despite this, we maintain a distinct memory of every single one. This would be impossible if there were no **soul** within us and we were composed of **mere matter**. 

The same can be said for many **names** or **words** directed, if you like, out of a **speaking tube** <note>original: "Trunk"; an early term for a tube used to direct sound</note> into the **ear**, which is held accurately in the same position. Even if the **sound** strikes perpetually upon the same parts of the hearing **organ**, a person can still have a distinct **memory** for five hundred different words. Such a power is perfectly beyond the limits of **mere matter**, for in a material system, there would be an unavoidable confusion of all those sounds.

8. Lastly, consider those imaginations or representations that do not correspond to any single object we have ever seen, but are instead made up of several different things that have left their own distinct marks in the **brain**—some (suppose) in the front and others in the back. How can the **pineal gland** <note>original: "Conarion"</note> join these together, and in whatever arrangement it pleases? 

Or rather, consider a single object, such as this **man** or that **house**, which we see in an upright position and which has left a signature or shape in the **brain** representing it that way. How can the **pineal gland** flip the orientation of the image and represent the house and man **upside down** <note>original: "with the heels upwards"</note>? Furthermore, there is the difficulty of representing the **distance** of an object, or its **breadth**, which we have already discussed *. It is impossible for the **pineal gland**, if it is **mere matter**, to perform any such operations. To do so, it would have to create motions within itself that are not necessarily triggered by the physical impact of another body, which plainly contradicts **Axiom 26**.

<margin>*On the Passions*, Part 1, Articles 17, 18.</margin>
9. Therefore, that serious and sensible mind **Descartes** does not dare to stretch the power of mechanical organization this far. He plainly confesses **that while there are some functions that belong to the body alone, there are others that belong to the soul**, which he calls **thoughts** <note>original: "Cogitations"</note>. According to him, these are of two sorts: **actions** and **passions**. 

The **actions** are all the operations of our **will**, just as in some sense all **perceptions** may be called **actions**. These **actions** of the will are either **purely intellectual operations** that take place only within the soul—such as the soul inspiring itself to **love God** or contemplating an immaterial object—or they are actions that influence the body, such as when we use our **will** to make ourselves go to a specific place.

This can happen during the day when our **imagination** <note>original: "Fancy"</note> wanders and we do not intentionally set ourselves to think about things, just as it happens in sleep at night. Those *perceptions* caused by the *soul* are either perceptions of its own *acts of will*, or its *contemplation* <note>original: "Speculation"</note> of things that are purely *intelligible* <note>concepts understood by the mind rather than through physical senses</note>, or *imaginations* created at will, or finally, *reminiscence*, when it searches for something that has slipped from its *memory*.

10. But as for the others, he
<margin>Descartes, *Discourse on Method* <note>original: "Dissert. De Methodo"</note>, Article 5, and *On the Passions*, Part 1, Article 16.</margin>
holds that they can be imitated, and he would have us believe they exist in the bodies of *animals* <note>original: "Brutes"</note>, which he considers mere *machines* <note>original: "Machinas"</note>. That is, that from the mere *mechanical structure* of their bodies, external objects of sense may open pores in their brains in such a way that they direct the *animal spirits* <note>a theoretical fluid in the nerves believed to cause movement and sensation</note> into specific muscles to cause spontaneous motion. He also suggests that the flow of spirits into the nerves of the intestines, stomach, spleen, heart, liver, and other parts may cause the exact same effects of *passion*—such as love, hatred, joy, or sorrow—in these animal *machines* as we feel in our own bodies, even though they, being without sensation, do not actually feel them. Thus, the twitching <note>original: "vellication"</note> of certain membranes <note>original: "Tunicles"</note> and fibers in the stomach and throat may affect their bodies just as ours are affected by the sensation of hunger or thirst. Finally, he argues that the spirits striking those parts of the brain marked by external objects may act on their bodies just as they act on ours during *imagination* and *memory*.

Now, if you add to this *machine* of *Descartes* the capacity for *sensation* and *perception* within matter (though I have already demonstrated that matter is incapable of this), it would result in exactly what *Mr. Hobbes* expects from the body alone. That is, all its motions being purely mechanical, its perceptions and inclinations would be fated, necessary, and unavoidable, just as he likes them to be.

But since none of the thoughts that *Descartes* calls *actions*, nor any of the *perceptions* he attributes to the soul, can be explained by any mechanical design, we should recognize them as a distinct category of arguments. Even if it were granted that the *souls of animals* were nothing but *sentient matter*, it would still follow that a *substance of a higher nature*—truly *immaterial*—must be the source of those nobler operations we find within ourselves, as is shown by Axioms 20 and 26.

# CHAP. VI.

*1. That no part of the* spinal cord <note>original: "Spinal Marrow"</note> *can be the* common center of sensation <note>original: "Common Sensorium"</note> *without a* soul *in the* body. *2. That the* animal spirits <note>a theoretical fluid in the nerves believed to cause movement and sensation</note> *are more likely to be that* common perceiver <note>original: "Common Percipient"</note>. *3. But yet it is demonstrable they are not: 4. As not being so much as capable of* sensation; *5. Nor of directing* motion *into the* muscles; *6. Much less of* imagination *and rational invention; 7. Nor of* memory. *8. An* answer *to an* evasion. *9. The* author’s *reason why he has refuted so particularly all the suppositions of the* seat of common sense, *when few of them have been asserted with the exclusion of a* soul.

1. **T**here remain now only two opinions to be examined: the one, that place of the *spinal cord* where *anatomists* conceive there is the nearest convergence <note>original: "concurse"</note> of all the *nerves* of the *body*; the other, the *animal spirits* in the *fourth ventricle* of the *brain*. As for the former—namely, *that part of the spinal cord* where the convergence of the *nerves* is thought to be—as I have answered in similar cases, I say again that besides what I have already demonstrated (that *matter* is incapable of *sense*, and that there is no modification of it in the *spinal cord* that would make it more likely to be endowed with that *faculty* than the pith of an *elder* tree or a bowl of *curds*), we must also notice that it is utterly unsuitable <note>original: "inept"</note> for *motion*. Nor is it conceivable how that part of it, or any other assigned to this office of being the *common perceiver* in us of all *thoughts and objects* (which must also have the power of moving our limbs), can move the parts of our *body* so nimbly and strongly when it has so little movement <note>original: "agitation"</note> in itself, appearing to be nothing but a kind of soft *mush* or *pulp* <note>original: "Pap or Pulp"</note>.

2. In this regard, the *animal spirits* seem much more likely to perform that office; and those whose insistent <note>original: "importunity"</note> and coarse imaginations force them to make the *soul physical* <note>original: "Corporeal"</note> nonetheless usually fixate <note>original: "pitch upon"</note> some subtle, thin *matter* to constitute her nature or *essence*. Therefore, they imagine her to be either *air, fire, light*, or some similar *physical substance* <note>original: "Body"</note>, with which the *animal spirits* have no small similarity.

<margin>* Chapter 2. sections 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, etc.</margin>

3. But this opinion, though it may seem plausible at first sight, is involved in insuperable difficulties. For it is manifest that all the arguments brought forward before will return with full force here. For there is no *matter* so perfectly liquid as the *animal spirits* that does not consist of particles only touching <note>original: "contiguous"</note> one another, and actually moving, playing, and turning around each other as busily as *atoms* in the *sunlight*. Now therefore, let us consider whether that *treasury* of pure *animal spirits* contained in the *fourth ventricle* is able to sustain so noble an office as to be the common *perceiver* in our *body*—which, as I have often repeated, is so complex a *function* that it does not only include the *perception* of external *objects*, but *motion, imagination, reason*, and *memory*.

4. Now, right at the start, the transmission of the image of the object...

An object entering this crowd of particles would inevitably hit them in various ways. Therefore, they would have several different *perceptions* among them: some perhaps perceiving part of the object, others all of it, others more than all, and others perceiving it in one place while some perceive it in another. But since the *percipient* <note>the perceiving subject or "sensor"</note> within *us* represents no such confusion or disorder in our beholding of objects, it is plain that the *animal spirits* are not that percipient.

5. Again, how could such a confused *percipient* be a proper principle for *directing motion* into the *muscles*? For besides the disorder that might happen in this *function* due to the distracted representation of present objects, the power of *thinking*, *contemplating*, and *deliberating* would also reside in these *animal spirits*. Yet they have no means of *communicating* with one another except by jostling against each other—which is about as effective as if men were to knock their heads together to communicate their *witty ideas* to one another. It must necessarily follow that they would have their *perceptions*, *inventions*, and *deliberations* separately. When they put these into execution, it would cause marvelous confusion in the body, with some of them commanding the parts to move one way and others driving them another way. Or, if their factions were split into many divisions and subdivisions, every one would be so weak that none of them would be able to command the body at all. But we find no such struggling or conflicting commands within us that would attempt to move our body one way when we intended another. It is not as if, when someone was about to write

->Sing, Goddess, of the wrath... <note>original: "Μῆνιν ἄειδε, θεά" — the opening line of Homer's *Iliad*.</note><-

something stronger in him, whose ideas he is *not aware of*, should take control of his hand and instead write down

->I sing of arms and the man... <note>original: "Arma virúmque cano" — the opening line of Virgil's *Aeneid*.</note><-

The same may be said of any other *spontaneous motion*. Because such motion is so constantly within our deliberation and command, it is a sufficient argument to prove that the cause of it is not a slippery substance like the *animal spirits*, nor something so fragmented, but rather something more perfectly *one* and *indivisible*.

6. We need not provide further examples concerning the power of *invention* and *reason*—how every particle of these *animal spirits* would have the liberty to *think* and *consult* with itself, as well as to *act* by itself, and how there is no possible means of *communicating* their thoughts to one another, unless it were, as I have said, by hitting against one another. But hitting can only communicate *motion*, not a specific *thought*, unless these particles were imagined to shape themselves into the form of the things they think of, which is impossible according to Axiom 26. Even suppose it were possible for one particle to shape itself, for example, into *St. George on horseback* with a *lance* in his hand, and another into an *enchanted castle*. This *St. George on horseback* would have to run against the castle to make the castle receive his impression and likeness. But what then? Truly, the encounter would be very unfortunate: for *St. George* might easily break his lance, but it is impossible that he should, by jostling against the particle in the form of a *castle*, convey the entire shape of himself and his horse. Yet we find ourselves able to imagine a man on horseback in its entirety. This is a truth as demonstrable

### Chapter VI: The Immortality of the Soul

...strable as any theorem in mathematics, but so plain at first sight that I do not need to use the precision of a longer demonstration to make it firmer.

Nor is there any plausible excuse <note>original: "colourable Evasion"</note> for trying a new approach, as if one particle could transform itself into a *castle* and another into a *horseman*, allowing all the others to see both and see each other. For *by what light, and in what small size would they appear, and in what different places, depending on the varying positions of the particles of the animal spirits? So, some of the *animal spirits* <note>a theoretical subtle fluid believed to carry messages through the nervous system</note> might think of one *mathematical demonstration* (or part of it) while others think of another. Consequently, if a *mathematician* were to write, while he intended to write one thing based on the decision of certain *animal spirits*, others might seize control of his hand to write something else, to whose thoughts and plans he was not at all privy. He would not be able to tell what they were thinking until those other *animal spirits* had written it down. Such absurdities are so mad and extravagant that a person would hardly stain their pen by recording them, were it not to wake those who obsess so much over the *power of matter* (thinking it sufficient for every *phenomenon* <note>original: "Phænomena"</note> in the world) into a proper sense of shame and disgust for their foolish principles.

7. The final faculty I will consider is *memory*, which is also necessarily joined with the others in the *common percipient* <note>the unified subject that experiences all sensations</note>. The animal spirits are utterly incapable of memory, not only because their parts are fluid but also because they dissipate so easily. For certainly, the *spirits*, due to their *subtlety* and *activity*, are very easily scattered and in all likelihood do not remain the same for even a week together. Yet, things that one has not thought of for many years will come as freshly into a person's mind as if they had happened just yesterday.

8. The only excuse <note>original: "Evasion"</note> they can devise <note>original: "excogitate"</note> here is this: that as there is a continual, gradual supply of *spirits*, those that arrive are seasoned, fermented, and tinted with the same *notions*, *perceptions*, and *inclinations* <note>original: "Propensions"</note> as the *spirits* already there. These are fine words, but they mean nothing except that the *spirits* currently present in the brain communicate their *notions* and *perceptions* to the newcomers—which is the very thing I have already proven impossible in the previous sections. Therefore, it is impossible for the *animal spirits* to be that *common percipient* that hears, sees, moves, remembers, understands, and performs the other functions of life that we experience within or through ourselves.

# CHAPTER VII. The Immortality of the Soul.

2. That there is some particular or restricted seat of the **Common Sense** <term>the mental faculty that unifies information from the five external senses</term> is an opinion that even all philosophers and physicians agree upon. It is a common comparison among them that the **External Senses** and the **Common Sense**, considered together, are like a circle with five lines drawn from the circumference to the center. Therefore, just as it was obvious for them to find specific organs for the **External Senses**, they have also attempted to assign some distinct part of the body to be an organ of the **Common Sense**. That is to say, as they discovered sight to be located in the eye, hearing in the ear, smelling in the nose, and so on, they believed there is some part of the body where seeing, hearing, and all other perceptions meet together, like the lines of a circle at the center. There, they believe, the soul also judges and distinguishes the differences between the objects of the outward senses. Therefore, they have rightly excluded all the **External** parts of the body from the slightest suspicion of being capable of performing such a general function. These parts are all employed in more specific tasks, acting as the organ for one of these five outward senses; they are affected only by what is pressed upon them, primarily by their own proper objects. Among these five, **Touch** (properly so called) has the largest share, being as large as the skin that covers us and reaching as deep as any membrane or nerve in the limbs and trunk of the body, as well as all the exterior parts of the head. None of these can see any more than the eye can hear, or the ear can smell.

3. Besides this, all those arguments that so clearly prove the place of **Common Sense** is somewhere in the head are a plain demonstration that the whole **Body** cannot be its seat; you shall hear what those arguments are shortly. All those opinions that have chosen any one part for the seat of **Common Sense** can be divided into two categories: namely, those that assign it to some particular place in the body, or those that place it in the **Head**. We will proceed in this order: first, we will refute those who have chosen any part for the seat of **Common Sense** outside of the **Head**; second, we will show in general that the common **Sensorium** <term>the sensory center of the brain</term> must be in some part of the **Head**; and lastly, from the many opinions concerning **what part of the Head** this common **Sensorium** should be, we will reject those that seem less reasonable and settle upon what we believe to be the most indisputable.

4. Those who place the common **Sensorium** outside of the head have located it either in the **upper opening of the stomach** or in the **Heart**. The former is Van Helmont’s opinion, and the other is Mr. Hobbes’s.

Nor can **frenzies** and **madnesses**, though they may sometimes be observed to take their rise from the stomach, prove that it is the seat of the **Common Sense** any more than **uterine frenzy** <note>original Latin: "furor uterinus," a historical medical term for female hysteria or hypersexuality</note>, apoplexies, epilepsies, and fainting spells proceeding from the **womb** prove that the common **sensorium** of women lies in that part.

6. And if we consider the great **sympathy** between the **orifice** of the **stomach** and the **heart**, whose **sufferings** <note>original Greek: "pathemata," meaning passions or disturbances of the mind and body</note> are so alike and joined that the ancients have given one name to both parts, calling them interchangeably **kardia** <note>original: καρδία; while this means heart, the ancients also used it to refer to the upper opening of the stomach</note>, and the pains of the stomach **kardialgiai** <note>original: καρδιαλγίαι</note> and **kardiogmoi** <note>original: καρδιωγμοὶ; medical terms for heartburn or stomach distress</note>; and also that the **heart** is that part from which the supplies of life clearly come—so that when the **pulse** ceases, life cannot long continue for want of warmth and spirits—here is an evident reason why a wound near the **mouth of the stomach** may kill a man more suddenly than a wound in the **head**. Even though both are supposed to be fatal, it does not mean the seat of the **Sensitive Soul** is primarily in that orifice. For partly because of the natural **sympathy** between the orifice of the **stomach** and the **heart**, and partly because of the horror and pain perceived by the soul in the common **sensorium** (which we will assume is in the **head**), the **heart** becomes so deadened that, as in the sudden passions mentioned before, it ceases to perform the ordinary functions of life. Thus, **pulse**, **sense**, and everything else is gone in a short time. However, when the **head** is mortally wounded, **perception** is so greatly diminished that the **heart** escapes the force of that **deadly passion** <note>original: "lethiferous passion"</note> more freely; and so, though **sense** is gone, it can continue the **pulse** for a longer time. This is a perfect answer to the stories **Van Helmont** recites in his *Sedes Animae* <note>original Latin: "Seat of the Soul"</note>.

7. To all of this I may add that Helmont himself acknowledges at the end of that treatise that the power of **motion**, of **will**, **memory**, and **imagination** is in the **brain**; and therefore, unless a man will say and deny the same thing at once, he must admit that the **Common Sense** is there also.

8. The opinion of **Mr. Hobbes** carries more credit and support, as it was asserted in the past by philosophers of great fame, such as **Epicurus**, **Aristotle**, and the school of the **Stoics**. But if we look closer at it, it will prove just as untrue as the other theory, especially in Hobbes's view, which holds that there is no soul in a man, but that all is merely **organized matter**. For let him declare any mechanical reason why his heart would be able to move his finger. But I have already refuted this opinion based on this hypothesis. It is more maintainable if a **soul** is granted to be in the body, and that the **heart** is its chief seat and the place of **Common Sense**, as **Aristotle** and others would have it, as well as the spring of **spontaneous motion**. But it is very unlikely that a part that is so continually employed in the natural motion of **contracting** and **dilating** itself should be...

# CHAP. VII. The Immortality of the Soul.

...be the seat of that principle which commands **free** and **spontaneous** movements. **Perceptions** would also be horribly disturbed by the heart squeezing itself and then relaxing again in cycles. Nor would objects appear in the same place—or at least our sight would not remain fixed on the same part of an object—when the **heart** is drawn up and then let down again, as I have suggested above. Furthermore, its extreme heat would not allow it to be affected by the gentle motions of the objects of sense, as the blood there is practically scalding hot. It is in this sense that the aphorism in **Aristotle** is to be understood: *The organ that judges variety must not itself be in a state of high temper or agitation* <note>original Greek: τὸ μέσον κριτικόν (to meson kritikon), meaning the judging medium or the neutral point of judgment</note>.

9. Therefore, it is a very reckless thing to assert that the **heart** is the seat of **Common Sense** <term>the faculty that integrates all five senses</term>, unless it could be proven by some clear experience. In fact, experiments are recorded to the contrary. For instance, if we bind a nerve, **sense** and **motion** will remain between the **binding** <note>original: "ligature"</note> and the **brain**, but not between the **heart** and the binding. Furthermore, the **crocodile**, even after its **heart** is cut out, will live for a considerable time, and will fight and defend itself. The same has been observed of the **sea-turtle** and the **wild goat**, as **Calcidius** <note>a 4th-century philosopher known for his commentary on Plato</note> writes. 

<margin>Galen, *On the Doctrines of Hippocrates and Plato*, Book 2.</margin>

To this you may add what **Galen** relates concerning sacrificed animals: that when their **hearts** were taken out and laid upon the altar, they were seen in the meantime not only to breathe and roar aloud, but also to run away, until the loss of blood finally made them fall down. To me, these narrations are all the more credible because I have seen with my own eyes a **frog** completely eviscerated <note>original: "exenterated"</note>—with heart, stomach, guts, and everything else taken out by an ingenious friend of mine who is a skilled **anatomist**. Afterward, the **frog** could see and would avoid any object in its way, and it skipped as freely and nimbly up and down as when it was whole, and continued to do so for a long time. However, a very small wound in the **head** deprives them immediately of **life** and **motion**. From this it is plain that the source of **sense** and **spontaneous motion** does not come from the **heart**.

<margin>* In his *Elements of Philosophy*, Part 4, Chapter 25, Article 4.</margin>

For if **motion** is cut off between the **brain** and the **heart**, by **Mr. Hobbes's** <note>Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679), the famous materialist philosopher</note> own admission, there will be no perception of the object. The same logic applies to the opening of the **stomach**. Thus, this one experiment clearly proves both of these opinions to be erroneous.

10. And so that no man hereafter may make any other unfortunate choice regarding the parts of the body, we shall now propose reasons which we hope will plainly prove that the **common sensorium** must necessarily be in the **head**—or rather, we shall repeat them. For some of the reasons by which we proved that the **heart** is not the seat of **Common Sense** will plainly demonstrate that the **head** is. 

<margin>Laurentius, *Anatomical History*, Book 4, Question 7.</margin>

As we noted from **Laurentius** <note>André du Laurens (1558–1609), a royal physician and anatomist</note>, if a nerve is tied, **sense** and **motion** will be preserved from the **binding** upward toward the **head**, but downward they will be lost. There is also that experiment with the **frog**: if you pierce its brain, it will immediately be devoid of **sense** and **motion**, even though it could skip around and use its senses as before when all its internal organs were removed. This is clear evidence that **motion** and **sense** are derived from the **head**. There is now no excuse to trace any motion to a further source like the **heart**, from which the...

# The Immortality of the Soul. BOOK II.

**Nerves** were once thought to branch out from the heart by **Aristotle**, but it is now certain that only the **Veins** and **Arteries** do, as is clear from every dissection <note>original: "Anatomie"</note>. Thus, the heart is rightly excused from that duty.

To this, we might add the consideration of those diseases that seize all the biological functions <note>original: "Animal functions"</note> at once, such as **Lethargy**, **Apoplexy**, **Epilepsy**, and the like. Physicians find the causes of these in the **Head** and apply remedies accordingly. This is a clear discovery that the **Seat of the Soul**, as far as it concerns biological faculties, is chiefly in the **Head**. The same may be said of **Frenzy** <note>original: "Phrensy"</note> and **Melancholy**, and similar disorders that corrupt a person's **Imagination** and **Judgment**. Physicians always conclude that something is wrong within the **Skull** <note>original: "Cranium"</note>.

Lastly, if it were nothing more than the close proximity of the outward **Senses** to the **Soul**, or her **discerning Faculty**, being so perfectly placed around her in the **Head**—this alone should be enough to convince anyone who is unbiased. Unless there were some significant argument to the contrary, one must conclude that the **Seat of Common Sense** <term>the internal faculty that integrates information from all five senses</term>, **Understanding**, and **command of Motion** is also there.

11. But now the greatest difficulty will be to define *in what specific part of the head it is to be located.* In this matter, unless we intend to work over-boldly and carelessly, we must have regard for physical logic <note>original: "Mechanical congruities"</note>. We should not settle on something just because it is *possible* under the assumption that there is a soul in man; rather, we must choose what is most fitting and appropriate.

12. That the whole **Brain** is not the **Seat of Common Sense** is clear from the wounds and cuts it may receive without destroying that faculty. For such injuries will not take away **Sense** and **Motion** unless they pierce deep enough to reach the **Ventricles of the Brain**, as **Galen** <note>a prominent Greek physician and philosopher in the Roman Empire</note> observed.

13. Nor is it located in the **small solid particle** proposed by **Regius** <note>Henricus Regius, a Dutch philosopher and physician</note>. For besides the fact that it is unlikely the center of perception would be so tiny, it is very inappropriate to place it in a body so perfectly **solid**—one harder than marble or iron. This invention was merely a recent whim of his irritable imagination. He aimed to create confusion regarding all of **Descartes'** metaphysical theories <note>original: "Metaphysical Speculations"</note>. Therefore, he found this rare quirk of wit to show how the **Soul** might be **incorruptible** and **immortal** even if it were nothing but **Matter**. It was not worth the effort to notice it here in this hypothesis, which we have demonstrated to be true: namely, *that there is a Soul in the Body whose nature is Immaterial or Incorporeal.*

14. Nor are the **Membranes** in the head the common sensory center <note>original: "Sensorium"</note>. This includes those that envelop the **Brain** (for if they were the seat, a person could see light through the hole made by a surgical drill <term>trepan</term>, even if the person who was **trepanned** had their eyes closed). Not to mention the path of the **Nerves**, the organs of external sense, which carry signals past these outer membranes and therefore point to a more inward place that must be the **recipient** of all their impressions. Nor is it any **internal membrane**, such as the one that seems the most likely candidate, the *Septum Lucidum* <note>original Latin: "clear partition"—a thin membrane separating the ventricles of the brain</note>, being in the middle of the upper ventricle. Yet, if the path of motion through the external senses is accurately considered, some signals will pass below it, and some at a distant...

### Chap. VII. The Immortality of the Soul.

parallel, so that this membrane will not be struck by all the objects of our **senses**. Besides, it seems odd and ridiculous that the **Center of Perception** should be either flattened into plates or stretched into hollow curves, as would be necessary if we made either the **external** or **internal membranes of the brain** the **Seat of Common Sense** <term>the internal faculty that integrates information from all five senses</term>.

15. The most likely place is one of those that the three last opinions point toward: namely, either the **Conarion** <term>the pineal gland</term>, the **meeting of the nerves in the fourth ventricle**, or the **animal spirits** <term>a hypothetical fluid then thought to transmit sensation and movement through the nerves</term> located there.

16. The first is the opinion of **Descartes**, and it is not to be hastily rejected; I have not found any arguments so far that are valid enough to disprove it. Those arguments recited from **Bartholin** <note>Thomas Bartholin, a famous Danish physician and anatomist</note> and supported by the learned author of ***Adenographia*** <note>Thomas Wharton, whose 1656 work *Adenographia* was a landmark study of the body's glands</note> do not, in my view, have the strength to ruin the theory. We will first repeat them and then examine them.

<margin>Wharton, *Adenographia*, chapter 23.</margin>
The first objection is that this **Gland** is too small to be able to represent the images <note>original: "Species"</note> of everything that the Soul has represented to her.

The second is that the external **nerves** do not reach the **Gland**, and therefore it cannot receive the impression of sensory objects.

The third is that it is located in a place of waste fluids <note>original: "excrements"</note> which would soil the images of things.

The fourth is that the images of things are perceived in the place where they are carried by the **nerves**. However, the **nerves** meet near the beginning or head of the **spinal marrow**, which is a more noble and ample place than the **pineal gland**.

<margin>See chapter 11, sections 4 and 5.</margin>
To the first objection, I answer that the size of the place where the **nerves** meet in the **spinal marrow** is not large enough to receive the distinct impressions of all the objects the mind retains in **memory**. (Furthermore, other parts of the **brain** may serve that purpose as well as any other part can.) But it must be the Soul herself alone who is capable of retaining such distinct and perfect representations of things, even if it were admitted that she might make occasional use of some private marks she impresses in the **brain**. These marks may happen to be nothing at all like the things she would remember, nor of any significant size or proportion to them—similar to what we observe in the words *Citadel* <note>original: "Arx"</note> and *Atom* <note>original: "Atomus"</note>, where there is no similarity in appearance or size between the words and the things represented by them.

To the second objection, I answer that although there is no physical continuation of **nerves** to the **Conarion**, there is a continuation of **spirits**. These are just as capable of conveying the impressions of motion from external sense to the **Conarion** as the air and **ether** are able to convey the light of the stars to the eye.

To the third, I answer that the **Gland** is conveniently enough placed as long as the body is healthy, for no waste fluids will then overflow or smear it. But in those illnesses where they do, **apoplexies**, **catalepsies**, or similar diseases will arise; we see these occur regardless of where the **Seat of Common Sense** is located.

To the last objection, I answer that once the **nerves** have entered any distance into the **brain**, they lose their **tunicles** <term>outer protective sheaths or membranes</term> and become so soft and spongy that the motion of the **spirits** can pass through them. Therefore, they may radiate through the sides and so continue their motion

17. But although these arguments do not sufficiently disprove the opinion, I am not so committed to it that I cannot think something more undeniable might be found. This is especially true since it is highly suspected that not all animals have this **Conarion**; and also because what pleased **Descartes** <note>René Descartes (1596–1650), the French philosopher who famously argued the soul was located in the pineal gland</note> so much about this invention was his belief that it was such a marvelous, fine instrument to drive the **animal spirits** <term>a hypothetical refined fluid then thought to transmit sensation and movement</term> into specific pores of the brain—a concept I cannot accept for the reasons mentioned above. Furthermore, stones have been found in this **gland**, and it is clear that it is surrounded by a network of veins and arteries, which are signs that it is a part assigned to some more humble function. Even so, I would not dismiss it without a fair hearing.

<margin>*Adenographia*, Chapter 23.</margin>
18. Therefore, the opinion of the previously cited author <note>Thomas Wharton, author of the 1656 anatomical work *Adenographia*</note>—who places the **Seat of Common Sense** <term>the internal faculty that integrates all five senses</term> in that part of the **spinal marrow** where the **nerves** are suspected to meet—is more straightforward and harder to refute. This assumes that the soul's center of perception could be conveniently located in such dull, pasty matter as the **pith of the brain**. Through this center, she not only understands all the **objects** of the external **senses**, but also imagines, reasons, and freely commands and directs the **spirits** into whichever part of the body she pleases. To be honest, this theory does not suit my taste at all. Therefore, I will also take my leave of this opinion and venture to declare: **That the chief seat of the soul—where she perceives all objects, where she imagines, reasons, and invents, and from which she commands all parts of the body—is those purer animal spirits in the fourth ventricle of the brain.**

### C H A P T E R VIII.

*1. The first reason for his opinion: the convenient location of these spirits. 2. The second reason: that the spirits are the immediate instrument of the soul in all her functions. 3. The proof of the second reason from the general authority of philosophers, and particularly of* **Hippocrates**; *4. From our sympathy with the changes of the air; 5. From the speed of motion and thought <note>original: "cogitation"</note>; 6. From what is observed generally in the generation of things; 7. From* **Regius's** <note>Henricus Regius (1598–1679), a Dutch philosopher and physician</note> *experiment of a snail in a glass; 8. From the spinning of images in vertigo <note>dizziness</note>; 9. From the structure of the eye and the motion of the spirits there; 10. From the dependency of the soul’s actions upon the body, whether in meditation or physical motion; 11. From the recovery of motion and sense in a numbed part; 12. And lastly, from what is observed in fainting fits, such as paleness and the sharpening of facial features, etc. 13. The conclusion from all this: that the spirits in the fourth ventricle are the seat of Common Sense, and that the main use of the brain and nerves is to preserve these spirits.*

### CHAPTER VIII. The Immortality of the Soul.

1. That which makes me embrace this opinion rather than any other is this: first, this situation of the **common sensorium** <term>the internal faculty where all senses meet and are processed</term> between the **head** and the trunk of the **body** is the most perfectly convenient for receiving the impressions of objects from both, as well as for imparting motion to the muscles in both the **head** and the **body**. In this regard, I consider it equal with the last opinion <note>referring to the spinal marrow theory mentioned on the previous page</note> and superior to all those that came before it. For whatever may be objected against it has already been answered in what I have said regarding the last objection against **Descartes** <note>René Descartes (1596–1650)</note>.

2. But now, in the second place (where this opinion of mine has a clear advantage over all others that I know), it is most reasonable that that matter which is the immediate **instrument** of all the **animal** functions of the soul should be the chief seat from which and where she exercises these functions. If there is any place where there is a more abundant supply of the purest sort of this matter, her peculiar residence should be there. Now, the **immediate instrument** of the functions of the soul is that thinner matter which is commonly called **animal spirits** <term>a refined, fluid-like substance then thought to transmit sensation and movement</term>, which are found in their greatest purity and plenty in the **fourth ventricle of the brain** <note>a cavity located in the upper part of the brainstem</note>. From this, it must follow that that precious and choice part of the soul which we call the **center of perception** is to be placed in that ventricle—not in any solid part of the brain nearby, but in the midst of these spirits themselves. For that is the most natural situation for commanding them into the parts of the **head** and **body**, besides allowing for a more delicate and subtle use of them "at home" in pursuing various imaginations and inventions.

<margin>Hippocrates, in the booklet *On the Heart*.</margin>

3. That this thin and **spirituous matter** <term>the animal spirits</term> is the immediate engine of the soul in all her operations is, in a sense, the general opinion of all philosophers. Even those who have placed the **common sensorium** in the **heart** felt secure in the truth of their idea because they took it for granted that the heart's left ventricle was the fountain of these pure and subtle spirits. They took great pleasure in imagining that the oracle of physicians, the grave and wise **Hippocrates**, spoke their own view so fully and significantly: "For the mind of man is naturally placed in the left ventricle; it is not nourished by foods or drinks from the stomach, but by a pure and luminous substance produced by the separation of the blood" <note>original Greek: Γνώμη γδ̄ ἡ τῦ ἀνθρώπε πέφυκεν ἐν τῇ λαιῇ κοιλίῃ· τρέφετ' δ' ὔτε σιτίοισιν ὔτε ποτοῖσιν ἀπὸ τῆς νηδύος, ἀλλὰ καθαρῇ κὶ φωτοειδεῖ περιεσίᾳ γεγονύῃ ἐκ τῆς διακρίσεως τῦ αἵματ☺</note>. This is exactly what happens in the brain; for the spirits there are nothing else but the more pure and subtle parts of the blood, whose thinness and movement cause them to separate from the rest of the mass and so fill the ventricles of the brain.

4. Moreover, our sensitive **sympathizing** with the **changes of the air**—which **Hippocrates** also noticed, observing that in clear **air** our thoughts are more **clear**, and in cloudy air they are more **obscure** and **dull**—is no slight indication that the substance which conveys **senses**, **thoughts**, and **passions** immediately to the soul is very thin and delicate, and of a nature very similar to the **air** with which it changes so easily.
