# The Immortality of the Soul. BOOK II.

<margin>*Lucretius, On the Nature of Things, book 3.*</margin>
5. The strange **agility** also of **motions** and **thoughts** <note>original: "cogitations"</note> that we find in ourselves has forced even the most sluggish wits—those who have been so dense as to judge the soul to be **physical** <note>original: "corporeal"</note>—to choose the freest, most subtle, and most active matter to compose her of that their imaginations could devise. And **Lucretius**, the most confident of the **Epicurean sect**, thinks he has hit the nail on the head in his choice:

->Now, therefore, since the nature of the mind is found to be exceptionally mobile, it must necessarily consist of small, light, and round bodies.<-
<note>original: "Nunc igitur quoniam est animi natura reperta / Mobilis egregiè, per quam constare necesse est / Corporibus parvis & levibus atque rotundis:"</note>

I value his testimony all the more in this case because he is such a materialistic <note>original: "crass"</note> philosopher. The necessity of the fineness <note>original: "tenuity"</note> of the particles that must pass through the body of a man is proven here to be so plain that even those with the dimmest eyes can easily discover it.

<margin>*Hermes Trismegistus, Poimandres, chapter 10, or "The Key."*</margin>
6. But we will advance higher to more forceful arguments; among which, I think, we may find some place for this: we cannot discover any immediate operation of any kind of soul in the world except for what it first performs upon **that matter** which shares in a very great measure this fineness and thinness of parts, which will easily yield and be guided. This may be observed everywhere in all **generations** <term>the biological process of creation and growth</term>, where the body is always **organized out of a thin, fluid liquid** that will easily yield to the formative <note>original: "plastick"</note> power of the soul. In this, I do not doubt that it takes the advantage of moving the most subtle parts of all first, such as the "first and second elements" of **Descartes** <note>René Descartes proposed that the universe was filled with particles of varying sizes; the first and second elements were the finest and most fluid</note>, which are never excluded from any such humid and thin substance. These elements of his are that true heavenly or ethereal matter which is **everywhere**, as **Marsilio Ficino** <note>Renaissance philosopher (1433–1499)</note> says somewhere that heaven **is**. It is that **fire** which **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with mystical philosophy</note> affirms is the most inward vehicle of the mind and the instrument that God used in the forming of the world, and which the soul of the world—wherever she acts—certainly still uses.

<margin>*Henricus Regius, Natural Philosophy, book 4, chapter 16.*</margin>
7. And to take yet another step further, that visual proof which **Henricus Regius** <note>Dutch philosopher and physician (1598–1679)</note> brings into view seems to me both ingenious and solid: it is found in a snail—specifically those that have no shells—moving in a glass. As soon as she begins to creep, certain bubbles are seen to move from her tail to her head; but as soon as she stops moving, those bubbles stop. From this, he concludes that a flow <note>original: "gale"</note> of spirits that circles from her head along her back to her tail, and then along her belly to her head again, is the cause of her forward motion.

8. That such **thin spirits** are the immediate instruments of **sensation** <note>original: "sense"</note> is also discovered by what is observed in **vertigo** <term>a sensation of spinning or dizziness</term>. For the **brain** itself is not of such a **fluid substance** as to turn round and make external objects seem to do so. Therefore, it is a sign that the immediate physical instrument for conveying the images of things is the **spirits** in the brain.

9. And that they are the chief organ of **sight** is plain in the exterior parts of the eye. For we may easily discern how full they are of that **pure and luminous essence** <note>original: "καθαρὴ καὶ φωτοειδὴς οὐσία"</note> which **Hippocrates** speaks of, though he places it in the wrong location; and how upon the passions...

# CHAP. VIII. The Immortality of the Soul.

<margin>* See *Antidote*, Book 3, chapter 3, section 8.</margin>
...depending on the state of the mind, these spirits ebb or flow in the eye and are otherwise wonderfully and significantly modified. In fact, the soul even seems to speak through them in that silent voice of angels, which some imagine to be nothing but silent gestures <note>original: "dumb shews"</note>, * but I do not believe that at all. It is also clear enough that dimness of sight comes from a deficiency of these spirits, even though the parts of the eye may otherwise be perfectly intact. The wider opening of the pupil of one eye when the other is shut also indicates the flow and more abundant presence of spirits there, as **Galen** <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–210 AD) was an influential Greek physician and philosopher in the Roman Empire.</note> has ingeniously concluded.

10. To which we may add that in those *more noble operations* of the mind, when she meditates and thinks through <note>original: "excogitates"</note> various theorems, she either uses some part of the body as an instrument then, or she acts freely and independently of the body. That the latter is false is obvious from the fact that, if it were true, a change of air, or illness and disease, could not hinder her in her *inventive* and purely *intellectual* operations. But it is manifest that they do, and that a man’s mind is much more cloudy at one time than another, and in one country than another; this is the source of that proverbial verse:

->*You would swear he was born in the thick air of the Boeotians.*<-
<note>original: "Bæotûm crasso jurares aëre natum." A reference to the ancient Greek region of Boeotia, whose inhabitants were stereotyped as being as dull as their foggy climate.</note>

If she uses any part of the body, it must be either these *animal spirits* or the *brain*. That it is not the *brain* is clearly demonstrated by its very consistency, which is so clammy and sluggish.

This point will have even more force if we consider what is certainly true: that the soul does not have any *power*, or at most very little, to *create motion in matter*. Instead, her peculiar privilege is *directing matter that is already in motion* <term>the soul acts as a "steersman" of the body's internal energy rather than the source of the physical energy itself</term>. The more subtle and active that matter is, the more easily it is directed by her because of its own mobility. For if it were an immediate faculty of the soul to provide *motion* to any matter—and since that faculty would never fail or diminish any more than the soul itself can fail or diminish—I do not understand how we should ever grow weary of movement. If that were the case, those nimble-footed *Maenads* <note>original: "Mænades," the female followers of Bacchus/Dionysus known for their ecstatic dancing.</note> or female priests of **Bacchus**, along with other agile young women of the countryside whom **Dionysius** <note>likely referring to Dionysius Periegetes, an ancient geographer.</note> describes dancing in the flowery meadows of **Meander** and **Cayster**, might—if life and limbs would last—be found dancing there to this very day, as free and playful as wild kids (as he likes to describe their activity), and that without any fatigue at all. For that immediate *motive* power of the soul could still impart motion to the whole body as freshly as ever, and would sooner consume the body into air or ashes by heating and agitating it than make the soul herself weary, or make the body seem so.

<margin>Hippocrates, *On Epidemics*, book 6.</margin>
Therefore, it is plain that the *motion* or *heat* that the soul voluntarily bestows upon the body is through the power of the *spirits*. When they are only playing and gently moving among themselves, she sends them out into the external members and so agitates and moves them. But because these spirits are so subtle and easily scattered, the soul uses them up in the process of using them; and when they are mostly spent, she can hardly move the body any longer. We call the sensation of this depletion *fatigue* <note>original: "laſſitude"</note>. These spirits are the "driving forces" <note>original Greek: τὰ ὁρμῶντα (ta hormonta)</note> or "internal movers" <note>original Greek: ἐνορμῶντα (enormonta)</note> mentioned by **Hippocrates** <note>The famous ancient Greek physician.</note>, and the soul’s immediate engine of motion through all parts of the body.

<summary>The author argues that the soul uses "animal spirits" as its primary tool for both sensory perception and intellectual thought, as the brain itself is too sluggish to be the direct instrument. He further asserts that the soul does not create motion but directs existing motion, which explains why we experience physical fatigue when our supply of spirits is depleted.</summary>

11. The spirits are also the cause of *Sensation* <note>original: "Sense"</note> in the more distant parts of the body as well as in the Head. This is gracefully suggested by Spigelius <note>Adrianus Spigelius (1578–1625) was a Flemish anatomist and physician.</note> through that common example of a man’s leg being numb or "asleep," as some call it, caused by compression or whatever else might hinder the movement of the *Spirits* into that part. As *Sensation* and *Movement* are restored, a man can clearly feel something creeping into the limb, tingling and stinging like ants <note>original: "Pismires"</note>, as he describes it. This sensation can be nothing other than the *Spirits* forcing their way back into the area. In this process, what the spirits experience is made felt by the Soul, as they are her immediate *Vehicle* of life and sensation.

12. Lastly, in *fainting spells* <note>original: "swooning fits"</note>, when *Movement* and *Sensation* fail, the external parts of the body become *pale* and *sunken*, and the face looks *leaner* and *sharper*. This can mean nothing else than that the favorable breeze of vital air that filled the body parts before is now absent and has retreated from them. That is to say, the *fluid Spirits* have withdrawn, without which no *Sensation* or *Movement* can be performed. From this, it is apparent that they are the immediate instrument of both functions.

13. I have proved that the *Animal Spirits* are the Soul’s immediate organ for *Sensation* and *Movement*. Therefore, if there is any place where these *Spirits* exist in the most appropriate abundance and purity, and in the most convenient location for *Animal functions*, that must, in all reason, be concluded the chief seat and *Acropolis* <note>Acropolis: A citadel or "high city"; here, the soul’s primary command center.</note> of the Soul. 

Now, the *Spirits* in the *middle ventricle* <note>ventricle: A cavity or chamber within the brain.</note> of the brain are not as ideally situated for both the Body and the Head as those in the *fourth ventricle* are; nor are they as pure. The *upper Ventricles*, being two separate chambers, are not as fit for this office, which is a very singular and unified task. Furthermore, the sensory impressions of movement through the eyes pass beneath them—not to mention that the *Spirits* here are less refined <note>original: "defecate"</note> than in the *fourth Ventricle*.

Therefore, because there is sufficient abundance, the *greatest purity*, and the *most ideal location of the Spirits in this fourth Ventricle*, it is clear that the *Center of Perception* is placed there, and that they are the *common Sensorium* <note>common Sensorium: The hypothetical part of the brain where all the senses were thought to be unified.</note> of the Soul. Just as the *Heart* perpetually pumps out *Blood* to supply the whole body with nourishment—maintaining the physical structure of this "building" for the Soul to dwell in—it also uses the more subtle and active parts of that blood to replenish the *Brain* and *Nerves* with *Spirits* (which are the Soul's immediate instrument for *Sensation* and *Movement*). Likewise, it is plain that the main use of the *Brain* and *Nerves* is to keep these subtle *Spirits* from dissipating too quickly. The *Brain* with its caverns is essentially one large, round *Nerve*, while the *Nerves* with their invisible microscopic channels <note>original: "porosities"</note> are merely smaller extensions or slender prolongations of the *Brain*. Altogether, they form one continuous receptacle or case for the *Animal Spirits*, which are the immediate instrument of the Soul’s sensory movements and the hidden *Vehicle* of life in this mortal body.

# CHAPTER IX. The Immortality of the Soul.

### 1. Several Objections against Animal Spirits. 2. An Answer to the first Objection touching the Porosity of the Nerves. 3. To the second and third, from the Extravasation of the Spirits and phlegm-like waste found in the Brain. 4. To the fourth, derived from the incredible swiftness of motion in the Spirits. 5. To the last, from the tying off of nerves. 6. Undeniable Demonstrations that there are Animal Spirits in the Ventricles of the Brain.

<margin>See chapter 6, Section 9.</margin>

1. **B**efore we proceed to our other two inquiries, we are forced to pause for a while and listen to a few objections made by some recent authors. These writers, going against the common consensus of all other philosophers, physicians, and anatomists, are not ashamed to deny that there are any such things as *spirits* in the body; or at least that there are any in the *ventricles of the brain*. For as for the *nerves*, they say, they have no pores or cavities to receive them. Besides, they argue it is plain that whatever fluid is in them is nothing but a milky white juice, as is observed when a *nerve* is pricked. And as for the *ventricles of the brain*, those cavities are too large; and the *spirits*, if they flow into them, will be like *extravasated* <note>original: "extravasated," meaning blood or fluid that has escaped from its proper vessel into the surrounding tissue.</note> blood, which would necessarily cause them to be spoiled and corrupt. Besides that, they argue the spirits would evaporate through those passages where the mucus or phlegm-like <note>original: "pituitous"</note> waste passes from the brain. The appearance of such waste there is, they say, another great argument that these ventricles were intended only as receptacles and channels for such waste-product humors which the brain discharges. Lastly, if *voluntary motion* <note>original: "Spontaneous Motion"</note> is created by means of these *spirits*, it could not be so extremely *sudden* as it is; for we can wag our finger as quickly as thought, but physical motion cannot be that swift. And if the *spirits* were continuous from the head to the finger, then, they say, if a nerve were tied off <note>original: "ligation"</note>, there would still be sensation from the tie to the fingertip; which they claim is against experience. These are the main objections I have met with in Hofman <note>Caspar Hofmann (1572–1648) was a prominent German physician and critic of traditional anatomical theories.</note> and others; but they are such that I think are very easily answered. Indeed, some of them even clash with one another.

2. For how can the *nerves* carry juice if they have no pores, or are not even passable to these thin, active *spirits* we speak of? Or from where can we better imagine that juice to arise than from these spirits themselves, as they lose their movement and collapse into a thicker consistency?

3. Neither can the *spirits* be looked upon as *extravasated* in the *ventricles* of the brain any more than the blood in the *chambers* <note>original: "Auricles or Ventricles"</note> of the heart. Nor is there any fear of them sliding away through the *infundibulum* <note>original: "Infundibulum," a funnel-shaped passage at the base of the brain once thought to drain waste from the brain to the nose or throat.</note>, since the phlegm-like waste only passes through there by its own weight, as well as its soaking moisture. This moisture always coats these parts, making them more impassable to the light spirits. Furthermore, the spirits' own agility and their balance with the outward air renders them incapable of leaving the caverns in which they reside.

# The Immortality of the Soul. BOOK II.

3. To argue that the brain's cavities were only made to hold useless waste because mucus-like <note>original: "pituitous"</note> waste is found there, is as foolish an inference as if a man should argue from what is found in the rectum <note>original: *Intestinum rectum*</note> that the stomach and all the intestines were made only to hold fecal waste <note>original: *Stercoreous excrement*</note>. The spirits in the ventricles <note>the chambers or cavities</note> of the brain, as they move about and hit against the sides of the caverns they are in, will over time lose some of their agitation—especially the thicker parts. These parts necessarily become a coarser substance and settle into a moist sediment like the waste found at the bottom of the ventricles. Nature discharges this through proper passages, leaving the spirits more pure. But because this necessary filth is found in these cavities, to conclude that this is their only use is as ridiculous as to infer that because I spit from my mouth or blow my nose, those were the chief purposes and uses of those two parts of my body—or that my eyes were not made for seeing, but for weeping.

4. The nature of the swiftness of motion in these spirits is much like that of *light*, which is a physical substance just as they are. However, the glowing matter in the sun does not fly many thousand miles in a moment to greet our eyes as soon as he appears on the horizon; instead, motion is passed along almost instantly from the sun to our eye through the "ethereal matter" <note>the subtle substance thought to fill all space</note> between them. Or, imagine a long tube, as long as you like, with someone blowing into it. At the very moment he blows at one end, the motion will be felt at the other. This works downward as well as upward, and just as easily. This answers that other frivolous objection I find in the works of Hofmann <note>Caspar Hofmann (1572–1648), a German physician and critic of then-modern physiological theories</note>, as if it were a difficult thing for these spirits to be commanded downward into the *nerves*. The opponents of this ancient and solid opinion are very simple and careless.

5. The argument regarding the *ligature* <note>tying off a nerve</note> proves nothing. For even though the *nerve* between the *ligature* and the finger might be well-supplied with spirits, the *center* of *perception* is not located there. Because there is an interruption and division between the spirits that connect to the *common sensorium* <note>the part of the brain where all the senses were thought to be processed together</note> and those on the other side of the *ligature*, it is no wonder that we feel nothing on this side of the tie. It is like seeing nothing in a neighbor’s garden when a wall is in the way, even though the sun shines clearly on both sides of the wall.

6. We see how weak their arguments are against this opinion, which is held by almost all *physicians* and *philosophers*. It is unnecessary to produce more evidence to confirm it; most of the arguments we have used to prove that spirits are the soul's immediate tools also prove their existence in the body.

Yet, as a bonus, I will briefly suggest the use of the *lungs*, which the best *physicians* and *anatomists* judge to be primarily for bringing "prepared air" to the heart. Consider also the "wonderful net" <note>original: *Rete mirabile*, a network of blood vessels at the base of the brain</note> and the choroid plexus <note>original: *Plexus Choroides*, a network of vessels in the brain's ventricles</note>; their very location reveals their use: they allow the thinner and more agile particles of the blood to evaporate more plentifully into the *ventricles* of the brain.

The expansion <note>original: *Diastole*</note> of the brain also keeps time with the *pulse* of the heart, which is a clear sign of what a powerful stream of spirits is driven by the direct

1. *That the soul is not confined to the Common Sensorium.* 2. *The first argument from the plastic power of the soul.* 3. *Which is confirmed from the gradual dignity of the soul's faculties, of which this plastic power is the lowest;* 4. *External sensation is the next;* 5. *After that, imagination, and then reason.* 6. *The second argument from passions and sympathies in animals.* 7. *An illustration of the manner of Natural Magic.* 8. *The third argument from the perception of pain in the exterior parts of the body.* 9. *The fourth and last argument from the nature of sight.*

1. **WE** are now at leisure to resume the two remaining inquiries. But for my own part, I cannot help but disagree; I find in neither of them any sufficient grounds for such a novel opinion, but rather apparent reasons to the contrary.

It is contrary to **Reason** to suggest that the random tumbling of atoms or physical particles should produce such exquisite forms of creatures. In these creatures, the sharpest mind is unable to find anything poorly designed <note>original: "inept"</note>; instead, everything is done exquisitely well everywhere, except where the foulness and coarseness of **Matter** has been at fault.

The fact that God is not the **direct** <note>original: "immediate"</note> Maker of these bodies is demonstrated by specific failures. For there is no matter so stubborn or perverse that His omnipotence could not tame it; if He were the direct maker, there would be no defects or deformities <note>original: "monstrosities"</note> in the birth of animals.

3. ### CHAP. X.

...on this side of **Will** and **Reason**, by which we correct and silence unacceptable fancies. Thus we see how the **Faculties** of the Soul rise by **Degrees**; which makes it even more easy and credible that the lowest faculty of all is as much a part of her as the **highest**.

6. Moreover, in my judgment, **Passions** and **Sympathies** are more easily explained by this **theory** <note>original: "Hypothesis"</note> of the Soul pervading the **whole Body**, than by restricting its essential presence to **one part** of it. * For to believe that a terrifying object—such as, for example, a bear or a tiger—could transmit motion through the eyes of an animal to the **pineal gland** <note>original: "Conarion"</note> and reflect back in a way that directs the animal spirits into the nerves, narrowing the opening of the heart and slowing the pulse to cause the symptoms of **fear**, seems to me little more than a piece of **mechanical gullibility** <note>original: "Mechanical Credulity"</note>. Those motions that represent the **images** <note>original: "Species"</note> of things are turned one way or the other without any physical force of matter sufficient to perform such feats as **Descartes** describes in his book *On the Passions*. In fact, the evidence he offers as a pledge of this truth is so false that it only encourages me further to disbelieve his theory. * For the waving of one’s hand near the eye of a friend is not sufficient proof that external objects will necessarily and mechanically force the animal spirits into the muscles without any faculty of the soul intervening. If a person is fully assured, or can keep themselves from the fear of being hurt by the waving of a friend's hand before their eye, they can easily refrain from blinking. But if fear surprises them, the Soul is responsible for the action, not the mere **mechanisms** of the body. Therefore, this is no proof that the **phenomena** of **passions**, with their consequences, can be explained in brute beasts by pure **mechanics**; and therefore, they cannot be explained that way in humans either.

But it is evident that these passions arise in us **against** both our **Will** and **Appetite**. For who would endure the torture of **fears** and **jealousies** if they could avoid it? Therefore, the Soul does not send or direct the spirits to her own torture from her seat in the head. From this, it is plain that it is the **effect** of the Soul as she resides in the **heart** and **stomach**, which sympathize with the horrifying representation in the **common sense-center** <note>original: "Common Sensorium"</note>, because of the exquisite unity of the Soul with herself and the continuity of animal spirits in the body, which are the necessary instruments of all her functions. And there is good reason for the **heart** and **stomach** to be so affected, as they are the primary seats of those faculties that maintain the **life** of the body; the danger to that life is the most significant object of **fear** in any animal.

<margin>* See Book 3, chapter 6, sections 7, 8, 9.</margin>

7. From this principle, I believe that not only the sympathy of parts within one person, but even the sympathy between different and distant subjects, can be understood. Such is the case between a wounded person and the knife or sword that wounded them, when the weapon is smeared with **weapon-salve** <note>A 17th-century medical theory where a wound was believed to be cured by applying ointment to the weapon that caused it rather than the body</note> and kept at a proper temperature. This is certainly not purely mechanical, but "magical"—though not in an unlawful sense. That is to say, it cannot be explained by mere matter, no matter how thin or subtle you imagine it to be. Instead, it must be attributed to the **Unity of the Soul of the Universe**, which is involved in all **formative** <note>original: "Plastick"</note> powers, and to the **continuity** of the **subtle matter**, which...

8. But we have an even clearer discovery that *our soul is not confined to any one part of the head, but possesses the whole body*, from the *perception of pain in its various parts*. For it is plainly impossible that a torture as intense as the prick of a pin could be communicated to the *center of perception* by mere mechanical means alone. Whether the immediate *instrument of sense* is the *core of the nerves* <note>original: "Pith of the Nerves"</note>, as **Descartes** would have it, or whether it is the *spirits*, which is more likely, it is ridiculous to think that the soul could feel such a sharp torment simply because parts that were joined were forcibly separated. 

This is especially true if that separation is not communicated to either the *spirits* or the *nerve cores* from the site of the puncture all the way to the seat of *common sense* <note>the faculty where all sensory information was thought to be unified</note>. The soul seated there could not feel such pain unless her very essence reached the part where the pain is actually felt. If she is present there, the reason is plain: it is the *unity of the soul possessing the whole body*, and the *continuity of the spirits*, that causes the sensation.

And it is no wonder—if the continuity and natural composure of the spirits bring rest and ease to the soul—that a violent disjoining and bruising of them (effectively stripping the soul of them, so to speak) should cause a very harsh and torturous sensation in the *center of perception*. This argument carries undeniable evidence if we only consider the soft texture of the *nerve cores* and the fluidity of the *spirits*, and how little stress or crowding a small thing like a pin or needle can cause in such soft and liquid matter. 

Considering this ought to eternally silence the doubts of those who are so puzzled that harms to the body should be felt as pains by the soul, while the body itself (being matter) feels nothing. For this is infinitely more conceivable than the idea that some part of matter in my head should feel pain from a prick in my finger, when the matter in my head is not harmed at all, or even moved in the slightest degree by it. And yet, it has been abundantly demonstrated that *perception occurs within the head alone*.

9. Lastly, unless the very essence of the soul reaches from the *common sensorium* <note>the central seat of sensation in the brain</note> to the *eye*, there will be very great difficulties in explaining how there could be such a distinct representation of any visible object. For it is very hard to conceive that *colors* will not be blurred, and the size of the object diminished—and indeed, that the image will not be entirely lost—before it can reach the soul, if the soul is only in the *common sensorium*. For it is plain, and experience will demonstrate, that there is a very perfect image of the object at the bottom of the eye, which is made by the *decussation* <term>the crossing or intersection of lines in the form of an X</term> of the lines of motion from it, in this way: the line A B from the object A C bears against that point in the bottom...

From this, the object is felt in the same length and breadth that can be perceived at such a distance from the eye. And just as the motion that is conveyed from **A** to **B** and from **C** to **D** is felt there, so also is the modification of that motion—by which the object in those parts may seem red, yellow, green, or any other color—felt there as well. From this, it is plain that there will be an exquisite impression, according to all the characteristics of the object, in the bottom of the eye. Therefore, if the soul receives the image there and conveys it from that spot to her *Center of Perception* entirely in the same state, the representation will be complete.

But if the soul is not present there, and the conveyance of that image must be left to the bare laws of *Matter*, the image will be much corrupted or lost before it can reach the *Common Sensorium* <note>the "common sensorium" was thought to be the place in the brain where all the senses were unified</note>. This is because the motion must be propagated from **B** and **D** until it reaches the hole **E**, passing into the *Optic Nerve* to be carried into the brain and finally to the seat of *Common Sense*. But between **B** and **E**, or **D** and **E**, there may be the coloring of various other colors; it would then be necessary for **F** to be tinted with the color **D**, and **G** with the color of both **D** and **F**, and so on for the rest of the lines drawn from the object to the eye. Thus, all their *colors* would be blended before they even reached **E**. Furthermore, at that sharp bend at **E**, where the visual line is as crooked as **BER**, according to the experiments of *reflection* and *refraction*, the breadth or length of the object **CA** would be lost. For we must expect that, as in *reflections* and *refractions* where the object appears in the line that immediately conveys the sense of it, it must also be so here; therefore, the points **C** and **A** would appear around **Q**, which would cause the object to essentially shrink away into nothing.

And even suppose it might appear in some tolerable width despite all this, the *brain* being an opaque substance would mean that as soon as the motion reached it, the image would be so changed or lost that it could not pass through that opacity with any splendor or wholeness. Therefore, I do not doubt that the image the soul perceives is the one in the eye, and not any other produced physically inside the brain (where *color* and *figure* would be so strangely corrupted, if not completely obliterated). I mean it is the meeting of the luminous spirits <note>original: "lucid Spirits"; subtle fluids once believed to facilitate vision</note> in the bottom of the eye with the outward light conveyed through the humors <note>the fluids within the eye</note> of the eye—which is the best meaning of the Platonic *synaugeia* <note>original: "συναύγεια"; a Greek term meaning a "meeting of rays" or "confluence of light"</note> that *Plutarch* speaks of—wherein the great mystery of sight consists.

Finally, it can be acquired by *voluntary attention*, when she very carefully and on purpose imprints the *idea* as deeply as she can into her inward sense. This *readiness* to think on such an *idea* will lessen in time and be so completely spent that when the same *idea* is represented again to the soul, she cannot tell that she ever saw it before.

But before this inclination is quite gone, based on this proneness to return to the same conception and its circumstances, the *relative sense* of having seen it before (which we call *memory*) necessarily emerges upon a fresh representation of the object.

9. We have now, as far as is necessary for our purpose, considered the *nature* and *functions of the soul*. We have plainly demonstrated that she is a *substance* distinct from the body, and that her very essence is spread throughout all its *organs*. We have also shown that the general instrument of all her operations is the subtle *spirits*. Although these spirits are not present in the same quantity or purity everywhere, they make the entire body so permeable to the impressions of objects upon the external organs that, like lightning, these impressions pass to the *common sensorium* <term>the brain's processing center where all senses meet</term>. It is not necessary for the *medium* to be as fine and thin as the matter where the most subtle motion begins. For example, light passes through both air and water, even though air alone is not enough for a motion like light, and water is almost incapable of being the source of it. This helps illustrate how sensation travels from the membranes (or wherever the spirits are most subtle and clear) through thicker parts of the body to the very *center of perception*.

10. Lastly, we have discovered a kind of *heterogeneity* <term>diversity of parts</term> in the soul, showing that she does not have the same power everywhere. Her *center of perception* is limited to the *fourth ventricle of the brain*; if the *sensory motions* we mentioned are not faithfully carried there, we have no knowledge of the object. Therefore, that part of the soul should be seen as the most precious. Since she is not an independent mass like matter, but one part resulting from another, the noblest part should logically be considered the cause of the rest. For this reason—just as *Synesius* <note>A 4th-century Neo-Platonist philosopher and bishop.</note> calls God, on whom all things depend, the "root of roots" <note>original Greek: "ῥιζῶν ῥίζαν"</note>—I believe this part may be called the *root of the soul*.

This understanding of ours will seem less strange if we consider that from the highest *Life*—namely, the Deity—there results that which has no *life* nor *sense* at all: namely, dull *matter*. Therefore, by a very good analogy, we may admit that the precious part of the soul (where *perception*, *sense*, and *understanding* reside) may send forth an *essential emanation from itself* that is completely devoid of all sense and *perception*. You might call these the *exterior branches of the soul*, or the *rays of the soul*, if you call that nobler and more divine part the *center*. This center might also well deserve the name *eye of the soul*, as all its other parts are merely darkness without it. In this way, like another *Cyclops*, it will resemble the world we live in, whose one eye <note>likely referring to the Sun</note> is visible to all who behold the light.

11. But to leave such playful <note>original: "lusorious"</note> considerations, which satisfy our imagination rather than our more serious faculties, we will hereafter content ourselves with the two well-known and perfectly different powers that philosophers recognize in the soul: *perception* and *organization*. We shall simply call the more noble part of the soul in the *common sensorium* the *perceptive* part, and all the rest the *plastic* <term>formative or shaping</term> *part of the soul*.

### CHAPTER XII.

1. An answer to an objection: that our arguments would prove the immortality of animal souls as well as human souls. 2. Another objection suggesting the preexistence of animal <note>original: "Brutes"</note> souls, and consequently our own. 3. The first answer to the objection. 4. The second answer, consisting of four parts. 5. First, that the hypothesis of preexistence is more consistent with reason than any other hypothesis. 6. And not only that, but that it is very solid in itself. 7. That the wisdom and goodness of God argue for its truth. 8. As does the state of providence in the world. 9. The second part of the second answer: that the preexistence of the soul has the support <note>original: "suffrage"</note> of all philosophers in all ages who believed it was incorporeal <term>not composed of physical matter</term>. 10. <margin>Chapter 10, section 7.</margin>
1. Now that I have established the nature of the soul and shown that she is a substance distinct from the body, I would be ready to discuss her separation *from it*. However, I feel obligated first to answer a hostile objection thrown in our way. By this objection, critics would have us believe that the arguments we have used—though they are no less than demonstrations—are merely logical fallacies. They claim this because some of them (and those of no small validity) seem to prove something very absurd and false: namely, that the souls of animals are also incorporeal substances distinct from the body. From this, it would follow that they are *immortal*. But I have already answered this in the *Appendix to my Antidote against Atheism*. In brief, I concluded *that they are technically no more immortal than dull matter, which never vanishes, and that once they are outside a physical body, they may have no more consciousness than matter itself*. For all these things depend on the will of their first Creator.

2. To this, they stubbornly reply that if the souls of animals continue to exist after death but are then senseless and inactive, it must follow that they enter into bodies again. For it is quite ridiculous to think that these souls—still existing in the world and needing nothing but appropriately prepared matter to live again—should be forever ignored and never brought back into play, while new ones are daily created in their place. This would mean that countless millions of souls would lie useless in the universe, with their numbers increasing forever toward infinity. But if they do return to bodies, it is obvious that they *preexist*. And if the souls of animals *preexist*, then certainly the souls of men do so too. My opponents consider this opinion so wild and extravagant that mockery and loud laughter—an argument that *any fool can use*—is enough to silence it and discredit it.

# CHAPTER XII. The Immortality of the Soul.

2. No wise person can ever harbor such an idea <note>original: "conceit"</note> as this, which every simple person <note>original: "Idiot," used here to mean an unlearned or common person</note> is able to disprove by consulting only their own *memory*. For a person is sure that if they had existed before, they would remember something of that past life. Besides, there is the difficulty of imagining the approach and entrance of these *preexistent* souls into the *matter* that they are to animate.

3. To this, two things may be answered. The first is that, although it cannot well be denied that granting the *preexistence* of the souls of animals <note>original: "Brutes"</note> is a very fair introduction to the belief in the *preexistence* of human souls as well, the conclusion is not at all necessary; one may be true without the other.

4. The second answer is this: that if the conclusion were granted, no absurdity can be found in it by reason, provided that the prejudices of education and the blind suggestions of irrelevant faculties—which have no right to vote here—are laid aside. To speak more explicitly, I say: this consequence of our soul’s *preexistence* is more agreeable to reason than any other hypothesis whatever. It has been accepted by the most learned philosophers of all ages; there were scarcely any of them who held the human soul to be *immortal* based solely on the light of nature and reason who did not also assert its *preexistence*. Furthermore, *memory* is not a fit judge to appeal to in this controversy. And lastly, *traduction* <term>the theory that souls are generated by parents like the body</term> and *creation* are just as intricate and inconceivable as this opposing opinion.

5. I shall prove all four parts of my answer in order. We shall understand the truth of the first if we compare it with those opinions that compete with it, of which only two are worth considering. The first is held by those who say the soul is transmitted from the parents <note>original: "ex traduce"</note>; the other by those who say it is *created* as the occasion arises. The first opinion is a plain contradiction to the *notion* of a soul, which is a *spirit*, and therefore an *indivisible*—that is, an *indiscerpible* <term>incapable of being torn apart or divided into pieces</term>—*essence*. The second opinion implies both an indignity to the *majesty* of God (by making Him the chief assistant and actor, in the highest and most particular way the Divinity can be conceived to act, in those abominable crimes of whoredom, adultery, incest, and even bestiality itself, by supplying those foul sexual acts with new created souls for that purpose) and also an injury to the souls themselves. It suggests that these souls, being thus created by the immediate hand of God and therefore pure, innocent, and immaculate, should be imprisoned in unclean, diseased, and disordered bodies. In such bodies, many of them seem so fatally overmastered and in such an utter incapacity for choosing what is good and virtuous that they must necessarily be sentenced to that extreme calamity which awaits all those who forget God. Therefore, since these two opinions are so inconsistent, what is left that can seem probable but the *preexistence* of the soul?

6. But I shall not press the *reasonableness* of this opinion only by comparing it with others, but also by the internal consistency that is found within it. For it is no greater wonder that every *particular* person's *soul* living now upon *Earth* should have existed since the creation of the world <note>original: "à mundo condito"</note> than that the *particular matter* of their *bodies* should have existed since then (which has perhaps undergone many millions of alterations and modifications before it ended up...

...[Which] into such a texture <note>original: "contexture"</note> as to prove the entire body of any one person in the world has been in places unimaginably distant. It has flowed, perhaps, through the triangular passages of as many vortices <note>original: "Vortices"; in Cartesian physics, these are whirlpools of celestial matter</note> as we see stars in a clear frosty night, and has once shone as bright as the sun (as the **Cartesian hypothesis** <note>The theory of René Descartes, who proposed that the solar system formed from the motion of swirling matter</note> would have all the Earth to have done). This is to such an extent that we eat, drink, and clothe ourselves with that which was once pure light and flame. So, the fact that the souls of animals <note>original: "Brutes"</note> truly <note>original: "de facto"</note> share the same start date as the creation of the world—an unavoidable certainty—fairly suggests the preexistence of human souls as well, according to the very concessions of our adversaries.

7. But this is not all. Both the **attributes of God** and the **appearance of things** in the world—from which his **Providence** is not to be excluded—are very strong demonstrations of this to an unprejudiced reason. For first, *if it is good for the souls of men to exist at all, the sooner they exist, the better. But we are most certain that the wisdom and goodness of God will do that which is best.* Therefore, if they can enjoy themselves before they come into these **earthly bodies** (it being better for them to enjoy themselves than not), they must exist before they come into these bodies. That is, they must be capable of enjoying themselves without these bodies for long periods of time before they appeared here in this age of the world. For nothing hinders them from living *before* they come into the body, just as they may live *after* leaving it; the latter of which is acknowledged even by those who deny **preexistence**.

Therefore, the **preexistence of souls** is a necessary result of the **wisdom and goodness of God**, who can no more fail to do that which is *best* than he can fail to *understand* it. Otherwise, his **wisdom** would **exceed** his **kindness** <note>original: "Benignity"</note>; indeed, there would be less reliance to be placed on **His goodness** than on the **generosity** of a very kind and good **man**, who, we may be well assured, will skip no opportunity of doing good that lies in his power—especially if it causes him neither damage nor trouble, both of which hindrances are incompatible with the Deity.

8. Again, the **appearance of Providence** in the world seems to suit this opinion very well. There is no account so natural and easy to give of those things that seem most harsh in the affairs of men as from this hypothesis: *that their souls once existed in some other state where, in various manners and degrees, they forfeited the favor of their Creator. And so, according to that just* **retribution** <note>original: "Nemesis"; the Greek goddess of divine retribution</note> *that He has interwoven into the constitution of the universe and of their own natures, they undergo various calamities and hardships of fortune, and the sad drudgery of fate, as a punishment inflicted or a disease contracted from the various wrongdoings of their* **apostasy** <term>the abandonment of a religious or moral principle</term>. This key is not only able to unlock the hidden mystery of why some men have an almost fatal aversion to all religion and virtue—their stupidity, dullness, and even invincible slowness to these things from their very childhood, and their incorrigible leaning toward all manner of vice—but also the reason for that wretched neglect and brutish barbarity that whole nations have lived under for many ages, and many still lie under at this very day.

### Chapter XII. The Immortality of the Soul.

This distressing state of affairs <note>original: "sad Scene of things"; referring to the apparent injustices and suffering in the world discussed on the previous page</note> must necessarily cloud and obscure the ways of **Divine Providence**, making them utterly unintelligible unless some light is provided by the hypothesis we are discussing.

8. It is plain, therefore, that very weighty reasons can be found to conclude the *preexistence of souls*. And since this opinion is so demonstrable through reason, and there is no other argument that can contradict it (for I shall prove shortly that the testimony of *memory* is invalid in this case), we are, according to the *Light of Nature* <note>The inherent human capacity for reason, independent of divine revelation</note>, undoubtedly to conclude *that the souls of humans preexist*, according to **Axiom 5.**

9. And as this hypothesis is *rational* in itself, it has also gained the support of all notable philosophers of all ages who have held the soul of man to be *incorporeal* <note>not composed of matter</note> and *immortal*. Therefore, I am not at all concerned with what either the *Epicureans* or *Stoics* held regarding this matter <note>The Epicureans and Stoics generally believed the soul was a subtle form of matter and would eventually perish or be reabsorbed</note>; this debate is only between those who agree on this truth: *that the soul is an immaterial substance.* Those among the philosophers who held it to be so unanimously agreed *that it preexists.* This is so plain that it is enough only to make this challenge: anyone who searches will satisfy themselves of its truth. I shall only add, to better support the case, a few instances here as a pledge of the truth of my general conclusion. Let us look into whatever corner of the world we wish that has been famous for *wisdom* and *learning* <note>original: "Literature"</note>, and you shall find the wisest of those nations were the *assertors* of this opinion.

10. In *Egypt*, 그 ancient nurse of all hidden sciences, the fact that this opinion was in fashion among the wise men there is sufficiently witnessed by the fragments of *Trismegistus* <note>Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary Hellenistic figure to whom various mystical and philosophical works were attributed</note>. For though some fraud and corruption may be suspected in several passages of that book regarding the interests of *Christianity*, this opinion of the *preexistence of the soul*—in which *Christianity* did not involve itself—cannot be judged as anything other than a branch of the *wisdom* of that nation. Not only were the *Gymnosophists* <note>original: "Gymnoſophiſts"; literally "naked philosophers," a term used by Greeks for certain ancient Indian or Egyptian ascetics</note> and other wise men of *Egypt* of this opinion, but also the *Brahmans* of *India* and the *Magi* of *Babylon* and *Persia*. This is plainly seen in those oracles called either *Magical* or *Chaldean*, which *Pletho* and *Psellus* <note>Gemistus Pletho and Michael Psellos, Byzantine scholars who preserved and commented on ancient Greek and Neoplatonic texts</note> have commented upon. To these you may add the hidden philosophy of the *Jews*, which they call their *Cabbala* <note>Kabbalah, a traditional system of Jewish mysticism</note>, of which the soul's *preexistence* forms a considerable part, as all the learned Jews confess. And I have, I hope, endeavored to show with some success in my *Conjectura Cabbalistica* <note>A work by the author (Henry More) attempting to interpret the book of Genesis through a philosophical and mystical lens</note> how naturally applicable this theory is to those first three mysterious chapters of *Genesis*.

11. First, if we can believe the *Cabbala* of the *Jews*, we must attribute this view to *Moses*, certainly the greatest *philosopher* who ever lived. To him you may add *Zoroaster*, *Pythagoras*, *Epicharmus*, *Em-* <margin>pedocles,</margin>

...principle we call the *soul*, and based on its nobility, he asserts that animals are more or less noble; this assertion, therefore, applies to human souls as well as those of beasts.

14. Nor can this text be dismissed by being so unfair to *Aristotle* as to claim he asserts there is only one Soul in the world, simply because he uses the singular word "soul" <note>original Greek: "psychēs"</note> rather than the plural "souls" <note>original Greek: "psychōn"</note>. For since the text allows for the explanation given by Sennertus <note>Daniel Sennert (1572–1637), a German physician who attempted to harmonize Aristotle's philosophy with early chemistry and atomism</note> as well as this other one, the most reasonable meaning should be attributed to him. Now, if his meaning was that there is only one Soul in the world that moves through all things and makes the universe one great animal—as the *Stoics* <note>A school of Hellenistic philosophy that taught that the universe is a single living being governed by divine reason</note> would have it—he would not need to say that all places are *in a manner* full of this Soul, but *absolutely* full of it, just as our body is *entirely* animated by the soul within it. Therefore, the sense must be that all places indeed are *in a manner* full of souls; not that they have the opportunity to animate matter and show their presence there through vital operation, but rather they remain there dormant, lacking any visible *energy* <note>original: "energie," here meaning active power or operation</note>, until *suitably prepared matter* engages them in more noticeable actions.

15. We will add a third passage that is even clearer, from the same treatise, where he raises this very question of the *preexistence of souls*, specifically the *sensitive* and *rational* souls; "concerning the sensitive soul and the intellectual soul" <note>original Greek: "peri aisthētikēs psychēs kai peri noētikēs"</note>, whether both kinds *preexist* <note>original Greek: "proüparchein"</note> before they come into the body, or whether the *rational* soul alone does. He concludes this way: "It remains that the mind alone enters from the outside and is alone divine; for no bodily activity has any connection with its activity" <note>original Greek: "Leipetai de ton noun monon thyrathen epeisienai kai theion einai monon; ouden gar autou tē energeia koinōnei sōmatikē energeia"</note>. Regarding this point, he concludes like a faithful student of his excellent master *Plato*; the closer he keeps to Plato's footsteps, the less he ever wanders from the truth. For in this very place, he plainly professes what many would prefer he not be so openly guilty of: that the soul of man is *immortal* and can perform its proper functions without the help of this *terrestrial body*.

And thus, I think I have fulfilled the first two parts of my answer to the objection raised. I have clearly proved that the *preexistence of the soul* is an opinion that is both the most rational in itself and has had the support of the most renowned philosophers in all ages of the world. Therefore, this conclusion, drawn from our arguments for the immortality of the soul, does not reveal any flaw in them.

# CHAPTER 13.

1. *The third part of the second Answer: That the forgetting of the former state is not a good argument against the Soul's Preexistence. 2. What the chief causes of forgetfulness are. 3. That they all combine, and to the highest degree, to destroy the memory of the other state. 4. That accidents and diseases have completely removed the memory of things in this life. 5. That it is impossible for the soul to remember its former condition without a miracle. 6. The fourth part of the second Answer: That the entrance of a preexistent soul into a body is as understandable as either creation or traduction.*

1. Regarding the last two difficulties—concerning the *soul's memory* of its former state and the manner of its entry into the body—I hope I shall resolve these with just as much ease, especially the first one. For if we consider the things that either completely remove or greatly diminish our memory in this life, we shall find that all of them are present—and to a higher degree or from stronger causes—during our descent into this *earthly body* than any we might encounter here. None of the causes here are so violent as to dislodge us from the body.

2. Now, the things that take away our memory here are chiefly these: First, *the lack of opportunity to be reminded of a thing*. This happens to many who wake up confident they *slept* without dreaming, yet before they go to bed again, they recover a whole series of images they had in their last sleep because of something that happened during the day; without that trigger, it would have been impossible for them to recall their dream. Second is the *lack of habit in thinking* <note>original: "Desuetude of thinking"</note> of a matter. Because of this, it happens that things we earnestly studied, labored over, and wrote down with our own hands when we were at school would be unrecognizable to us as adults if we did not see our names written on the exercise. Or lastly, *some significant change in the structure and condition of our body*, whether from an external accident, some violent disease, or old age (which is a disease in itself). These often exceedingly impair, if not completely take away, the memory, even though the soul remains in the *same* body.

3. All these principles of *forgetfulness*—namely, *the lack of something to remind us*, the *lack of habit in thinking*, and an *extraordinary change in the body*—are more prominently found in the *descent* of the soul into these *earthly prisons* than can happen to it during any time it lives within them. For there is, in all probability, a greater difference between the scenes the soul sees *outside* of the body and *inside* it than between what it sees while *sleeping* and *waking*. Furthermore, the constant distractions of this present life maintain a long period of not thinking about the former state. Besides that, their *descent* here, in all likelihood, only occurs during their state of *silence* and *inactivity*, in which myriads of...

4. And yet, that *diseases* and *accidents* <note>original: "Casualties"</note> have even completely taken away all *memory* is widely recorded in history. ...the opponent, who claims there are such great mysteries concerning the entrance of *preexistent souls* into their *bodies*.

### CHAP. XIV.

1. *The knowledge of the difference between* Vehicles <note>In this context, a "vehicle" is a subtle body or vessel that the soul inhabits (like air or light) before or after its time in a physical body.</note>, *and the soul's union with them, is necessary for understanding how she enters into this earthly body.* 2. *Although the name* Vehicle *is not found in* Aristotle, *the concept is present there.* 3. *A clarification of* Aristotle’s *notion of the* vehicle *using the philosophy of* Descartes. 4. *A full interpretation of his text.* 5. *Aristotle acknowledges only two* vehicles, *the* terrestrial *and the* ethereal; *which is more than sufficient to prove the soul’s forgetfulness of her former state.* 6. *The soul's usual* vehicle *after death is* air. 7. *The duration of the soul in her various* vehicles. 8. *The union of the soul with her* vehicle *is not based on mechanical fit, but on a "vital congruity."* 9. *What "vital congruity" of matter consists of.* 10. *What "vital congruity" of the soul consists of, and how, by changing, the soul may be freed from her airy* vehicle *without being violently cast out of it.* 11. *The manner in which souls descend into earthly bodies.* 12. *There is so little absurdity in the* preexistence *of souls that admitting it hardly harms our demonstrations of her immortality.*

1. However, I will spend my time better by clarifying the opinion I am defending here, rather than by complicating that other view which is so flawed in itself that no one who truly understands the nature of the soul can even allow it as a possibility. Therefore, to better understand how a *preexistent soul* may enter this *earthly body*, two things must be investigated: the differences between the *vehicles of souls*, and the *reason for their union with them*. The *Platonists* <note>Followers of the philosopher Plato.</note> primarily recognize *three* kinds of *vehicles*: *ethereal* (made of light or heavens), *aerial* (made of air), and *terrestrial* (made of earth). In each of these, there may be various degrees of purity and impurity, though these do not necessarily create an entirely new *species* <note>A distinct category or type.</note>.

<margin>Book 2, Chapter 3.</margin>
2. This notion of *vehicles*, although discussed most extensively in the school of *Plato*, is not completely ignored by *Aristotle*. This is evident in his work *On the Generation of Animals* where, although he does not use the specific term, he explicitly acknowledges the concept itself. He clearly affirms that every soul partakes in a body distinct from this organized earthly body, and that it is of a more divine nature than the common elements. He also argues that as one soul is more noble than another, there is a corresponding difference in this more divine body. For him, this is nothing other than that warmth or heat in the seed—"the heat inherent in the seed" <note>original Greek: τὸ ἐν τῷ σπέρματι ἐνυπάρχον τὸ καλέμενον θερμόν</note>—which is not fire, but a spirit contained in the frothy <note>original: "spumeous"</note> seed; and within this spirit is a nature similar to the element of the stars.

3. Neither *Aristotle* himself, nor anyone else, can have as clear an understanding of this as those who understand the first and second elements <note>This refers to the physics of René Descartes, where the "first element" is fine matter like fire/light and the "second element" is the subtle matter or aether that fills space.</note>...

# CHAP. XIV. The Immortality of the Soul.

...the element described by *Descartes*, which is the most subtle and active body in the world. It is of the very same nature as the Heavens and Stars—that is to say, it is the very Body of Light (which refers chiefly to the "First Element" <note>In Cartesian physics, the "first element" consists of the smallest, fastest-moving particles that form the sun and stars.</note>). Although it is so mingled with other matter here below that it does not shine, it is the basis of all natural warmth in all generations and the immediate instrument of the soul when it organizes matter into the shape of an animal. I have also <margin>* In this 2nd Book, chap. 8.</margin> suggested this elsewhere, when I proved *that the spirits are the soul's immediate instrument in all vital and animal functions. These spirits necessarily contain this celestial substance,* which keeps them from congealing (as it also does for all other liquid bodies) and must exist within their pores, as there is no *vacuum* <note>original: *vacuum* — a space entirely empty of matter.</note> in the whole scope of Nature.

4. Therefore, the full and express meaning of *Aristotle's* text must be this: that within the frothy, watery, or earthly moisture of the seed, there is a body of a more spiritual or airy consistency. Within this airy consistency is contained *a nature that is analogous or like the element of the stars* <note>original Greek: φύσις ἀνάλογ. θ. ἔσι τῷ τῶν ἄςρων ϛοιχεία (*physis analogos th. esti tō tōn astrōn stoicheia*)</note>, *namely, that which is by its very nature ethereal and light-filled.*

5. And it is this *Vehicle* <note>A "vehicle" is a subtle, non-physical body that the soul inhabits when not in a physical one.</note> that *Aristotle* seems to assert the soul acts in when separate from the body; as if she were always either in this *Terrestrial* body or in her *Ethereal* one. If this were true, such a vast change would surely erase all *Memory* of her former condition once she is plunged into this earthly prison. But it does not seem probable to me that Nature allows such a great gap; nor is it necessary to suppose it for this purpose. The descent of the soul out of her *Airy* vehicle into this *terrestrial* body, and the "smearing moisture" of the first rudiments of life, is sufficient to lull her into an eternal forgetfulness of whatever happened to her in that other condition—to say nothing of her long state of *Silence* and *Inactivity* before her turn comes to revive in an *earthly* body.

6. *Therefore*, without letting go of that more orderly idea of the *Platonists*, I shall make bold to assert that the soul may live and act in an *Airy Vehicle* as well as in the *Ethereal* one. There are very few who arrive at such high happiness as to acquire a *Celestial Vehicle* immediately upon quitting the *Terrestrial* one. That *Heavenly Chariot* necessarily carries us in triumph to the greatest happiness the soul of man is capable of; if simply parting with this *Earthly Body* could suddenly mount us into the *Heavenly* one, this would happen to all men indifferently, both the good and the bad. Therefore, by a just *Nemesis* <note>original: *Nemesis* — divine retribution or the distribution of what is due.</note>, the souls of men who are not heroically virtuous will find themselves restrained within the boundaries of this gloomy <note>original: "caliginous" — misty, dark, or foggy.</note> air, as both Reason itself suggests and the *Platonists* have unanimously determined.

7. We have adequately described the difference between those *three* kinds of *Vehicles* regarding their purity and consistency. The *Platonists* add to this the difference of *duration*, making some of them of such a nature as to hold the soul for a longer time, and others for a shorter time. The shortest of all is that of the *Terrestrial Vehicle*. In the *Airy* vehicle, the soul may inhabit—as they define it—for many ages, and in the *Ethereal* one forever.

<margin>Into generation <note>original Greek: εἰς γένεσιν (*eis genesin*)</note></margin>
8. But this does little to clarify the manner of the soul's descent, which cannot be better understood than by considering its *Union* with the generated body—or indeed with any kind of body whatever—where the soul is held captive and cannot release itself through the free command <note>original: *imperium*</note> of its own imagination and will. For what can be the cause of this cohesion, since the very essence of the soul so easily penetrates *Matter*, and the dimensions of all *Matter* are equally penetrable everywhere? 

There is no more body or matter in a vessel filled with *lead* than when it is full of *water*; nor is there more when it is full of *water* than when it is full of *air*, or any other more subtle body that can be imagined in the universe. It is manifest, therefore, that the density <note>original: *Crassities*</note> of matter is the same everywhere, and is equally penetrable and passable to the soul. Consequently, it is inconceivable how the soul's *union* with any part of matter should be such that it could not glide freely from one part to another whenever it pleases.

It is plain, therefore, that this *Union* of the *Soul* with *Matter* does not arise from any crude *mechanical* way—such as when two bodies stick to one another because of toughness, thickness, or a tight joining <note>original: *commissure*</note> of parts. Instead, it arises from a *congruity* <note>A "congruity" refers to a natural fitness or state of being in agreement or harmony.</note> of another nature, which I can best describe as *Vital*. This *Vital Congruity* exists chiefly in the *Soul* itself, as it is the noblest principle of life. However, it also exists in the *Matter*, where it is nothing more than a specific modification of that matter which fits the formative <term>plastick</term> <note>The "Plastic" part of the soul is its unconscious power to organize and shape biological matter into a living body.</note> part of the soul, drawing that faculty into action.

9. This does not mean there is any life within the matter itself with which the soul might sympathize and unite. Rather, it is termed *Vital* because it makes the *Matter* a fitting subject for the soul to reside in and exercise the functions of life. For that which has no life itself may still bind to it that which does have life. For example, some men are said to be "bound by the teeth" or "bound by the ear" when they are held captive by the pleasure they feel from good music or delicious food <note>original: *Viands*</note>. But the food they eat is not alive, nor is the thing that makes the music—neither the instrument nor the air that conveys the sound. In all of these, there is nothing but mere matter and physical motion; yet, our *vital* functions are affected by them. 

Now, just as we see that the *Perceptive* <note>The conscious, sensing part of the soul.</note> part of the soul is thus vitally affected by that which has no life in it, it is reasonable that the *Plastic* part of the soul may be affected in the same way. There may be a harmony between matter modified in a certain way and 그at power we call *Plastic*, which is entirely devoid of all conscious perception. In this alone consists what we call *Vital Congruity* in the prepared matter—whether it is waiting to be organized or is already shaped into the perfect form of an animal.

10. And that *Vital Congruity* which is in the soul—meaning in its *Plastic* part—is similar to the pleasure perceived by the senses, or rather to the capacity for receiving it. This occurs when the senses are greatly gratified by agreeable motions from outside or within the body itself, whether the mind wishes it or not. For there are some touches that will seem pleasant to our *perception*, regardless of whether our judgment wants them to be so. What this is to the *Perceptive* part of the

the Soul, that other *Congruity of Matter* is to the <term>Plastick</term> <note>original: "Plastick faculty"; the soul's innate, unconscious power to form and organize matter into a living body</note>. And therefore, that which ties the Soul and this or that specific Matter together is an irresistible and imperceptible pleasure, if I may call it so, arising from the *congruity of Matter to the formative faculty of the Soul*. As long as this *Congruity in the Matter* does not fail, nor that in the Soul, the *Union* is at least as necessary as the continuation of eating and drinking is so long as hunger and thirst continue and the food and drink prove good. But either fullness in the stomach or some foul taste in the food may break the *congruity* on either side, and then the action will cease along with the pleasure of it. And upon this very account, a Soul may be conceived to quit her <term>Aiery Vehicle</term> <note>In Platonist thought, a "vehicle" is a body of subtle matter—like air or light—that the soul inhabits when not in a physical, earthly body</note> within a certain period of ages, as the <term>Platonists</term> <note>Followers of Plato's philosophy, who believed in the pre-existence and immortality of the soul</note> hold she does, without any violent forcing of herself out of it.

11. What the *strings* or *cords* are that tie the Soul to the Body, or to whatever other Vehicle, I have declared as clearly as I can. From this, it will be easy to understand the *manner of her descent*. For assuredly, the same *cords* or *strings* that tie her there may also draw her there: *Where the carcass is, there the eagles will be gathered.* <note>A biblical reference (Matthew 24:28) used here to illustrate that the soul is naturally drawn to the matter it is destined to inhabit.</note> It is not that she needs to use her *Perceptive* faculty in her descent, as hawks and kites use their sight or smell to fly directly to the lure or the prey. Instead, because she is within the *Atmosphere* (as I may call it) of Generation, and so her *formative* power is reached and touched by such an invisible vapor <note>original: "reek"</note>—just as birds of prey smell their food from a distance—she may be carried by fate, with all *perceptions* ceasing in her, to that Matter which is so fit a receptacle for her to exercise her power of giving form <note>original: "efformative power"</note> upon. For in this <term>Magick-sphere</term> <note>A field of natural attraction or "sympathy" that draws souls toward physical embodiment</note>, as I may term it, which has this power of summoning down souls into *Earthly Bodies*, the nearer the center one is, the stronger the virtue is. And therefore the Soul will never cease until she has slid into the very Matter that sent out those rays or subtle vapors to allure her.

From this, it is easy to conceive that the souls of animals <note>original: "Brutes"</note> also, though they are not able to exercise their *Perceptive* faculty outside of a *Terrestrial* <note>Earthly</note> body, may still infallibly find the way back into the world as often as *Matter* is fitly prepared for birth <note>original: "generation"</note>. And this is one hypothesis, and most understandable to those who are so pleased with the opinion of those large spheres they conceive of <term>emissary Atomes</term> <note>Particles emitted from a body that extend its influence through the surrounding space</note>.

<margin>* Book 3, chapter 13, section 9.</margin>
There is also another theory, which is the *Power* and *Activity of the <term>Spirit of Nature</term>* <note>An unconscious, spiritual force that carries out God's laws in the physical world</note> or *<term>Inferiour Soul of the World</term>*, who is just as fit an agent to transmit particular souls as she is to move the parts of Matter. But of this, more * hereafter.

12. What has been said is enough for the present to illustrate the supposed obscurity and inconceivability of this Mystery. So I have fully made good all four parts of my answer to that objection which would have undermined the force of my strongest arguments for the Soul's Immortality. I have clearly proved that even if this conclusion necessarily resulted from them—namely, that the souls of both men and beasts did <term>Praeexist</term> <note>Exist in a spiritual state before being born into a physical body</note>—yet to an unprejudiced reason, there is no absurdity or inconvenience at all in the opinion. And therefore, this obstacle being removed, I shall the more cheerfully proceed to demonstrating the Soul's *actual separation* from the Body.

### CHAP. XV.

1. What is meant by the separation of the soul, along with a refutation of Regius, who would keep her trapped in the dead corpse. 2. An answer to those who claim to be puzzled by how the soul can leave the body. 3. That there is a threefold "vital congruity" found in three different subjects. 4. That this triple congruity is also compatible with one subject: namely, the human soul. 5. That under this hypothesis, it is very easy to understand how the soul may leave the body. 6. That her union with the <term>airy vehicle</term> <note>original: "Aereal Vehicle"; in Platonist philosophy, this is a body made of subtle matter that the soul inhabits after leaving the physical body.</note> can happen very suddenly, almost in a moment. 7. That the soul is actually separate from the body can be proved by either history or reason. Examples of the former from Pliny, Herodotus, and Ficinus. 8. Whether the <term>ecstasy</term> <note>original: "Ecstasie"; here referring to a trance state where the soul was believed to literally leave the physical body and then return.</note> of witches proves an actual separation of the soul from the body. 9. That this real separation of the soul during a trance is very possible. 10. How the soul may be released and leave the body, yet return to it again. 11. That although reason and will cannot release the soul from the body in this life, passion can—and in such a way that she may still return. 12. The unique power of desire for this purpose. 13. On Cardan’s trances, the ointments used by witches, and what truth may be found in their confessions.

<margin>*Natural Philosophy, Book 5, Chapter 1, pages 351, 352.*</margin>
1. Regarding the actual and physical separation of the soul from the body, it is clear that this refers to the **terrestrial body**. For to be in such a separate state as to be where no body or matter exists would be to exist outside the universe, since the entire universe is so densely packed with matter or substance that there is not the slightest vacuum to be found. The question, therefore, is simply whether at death the soul can move from the corpse to some other location. <term>Henricus Regius</term> <note>A 17th-century Dutch philosopher and physician who originally followed Descartes but later argued for a more materialistic view of the soul.</note> seems to trap her there based on a general law of nature called the **law of immutability**, by which everything is to continue in the same condition it is currently in until something else changes it. But applying this law here is completely inappropriate. For, as I have suggested before, the union of the soul with the body is based on certain conditions; not every piece of matter is suitable for every soul to join with, as <term>Aristotle</term> <note>The ancient Greek philosopher who taught that the soul is the "form" of a specific, organized body.</note> long ago correctly concluded. Therefore, when the necessary condition of the matter is no longer maintained, the soul is no longer bound to the body. His attempts to justify his position are so arbitrary, childish, and ridiculous that, based on their lack of merit, I shall ignore them entirely and move on, not even granting them the courtesy of a response.

2. Others are deeply puzzled by how the soul can escape the body, thinking of it as if it were imprisoned and locked within a secure fortress. But these people seem to forget the nature of the soul itself, the thinness of its "vehicle," and the actual anatomy of the body. For when we consider the soul’s nature and the fact that matter is equally penetrable everywhere, the soul can pass through solid iron and marble just as easily as through soft air and ether. Therefore, the thickness of the physical body is no obstacle to her. Besides, her **astral**
