# CHAP. XV. The Immortality of the Soul.

2. This <term>vehicle</term> <note>original: "Vehicle"; a subtle or spiritual body that carries the soul after it leaves the physical body.</note> is of such thinness that it can as easily pass through the smallest pores of the body as light passes through glass, or as lightning passes through the scabbard of a sword without tearing or scorching it. And lastly, whether we look upon the heart (the principal seat of the soul's <term>formative power</term> <note>original: "Plastick power"; the soul's unconscious ability to shape and organize physical matter.</note>) or the brain (the seat of perception); when a person dies, the soul may collect itself and the small residue of "spirits" (which may perhaps serve her in the beginning of her new vehicle) either into the heart, from which there is an easy passage into the lungs and out through the mouth; or else into the head, out of which there are more doors open than I will take the time to number. These things are very easily imaginable, though they are as invisible as the air in which they take place.

3. But so that these things may be more perfectly understood, I shall resume the consideration of that faculty in the formative part of the soul which we call <term>vital harmony</term> <note>original: "Vital Congruity"; the natural fitness or compatibility between the soul and a specific type of matter.</note>. Depending on the type of vehicle, we will define this as threefold: *Terrestrial* (earthly), *Aerial* (of the air), and *Ethereal* or *Celestial* (of the heavens). It is very plain that these vital harmonies are found in different kinds of spirits. For it is beyond dispute that the *Terrestrial* harmony is in the souls of animals and in our own. It is also clear that the *Aerial* harmony exists in that kind of beings which the ancients called *daemons* <note>original: "Δαίμονες" (daimones); in Greek philosophy, spirits that act as intermediaries between gods and mortals.</note>. And lastly, the heavenly and *Ethereal* harmony exists in those spirits that antiquity more properly called *gods* <note>original: "Θεοὶ" (theoi); referring here to divine inhabitants of the highest heavens.</note>, as they are inhabitants of the heavens. If we compare the nature of God with the observable <term>phenomena</term> <note>original: "Phænomena"; the observable facts or events in the natural world.</note> of the world, it is nothing less than a certain proof that there are such aerial and ethereal beings that are analogous to terrestrial animals.

For this Earth is replenished with living creatures; indeed, even if we include all the planets in the world and imagine them inhabited, they all joined together do not represent as great a proportion of the rest of the "liquid matter" of the universe (which is in a closer state of readiness to be a vehicle of life) as a single cumin seed does to the entire globe of the Earth. But how ridiculous would it be if, while the rest of the Earth was neglected, only one tiny piece of it—no better than the rest, nor bigger than the smallest seed—should be inhabited? The same may be said of the vast extent of the air; therefore, it is necessary to enlarge their territories and confidently pronounce that there are *Ethereal Animals* as well as *Terrestrial* and *Aerial* ones.

4. It is plain, therefore, that these three harmonies are to be found in various subjects. But what matters most for our purpose is to find them all in one: specifically, in the human soul. We can find a clear hint of this if we consider the vast difference between those faculties we are certain exist in the soul's *perceptive* part. We see how they emerge at different times, and how, when one is laid to sleep, others will spring up. There can be no greater difference between the highest and lowest of these *vital harmonies* in the formative part of the soul than there is between the highest and lowest of those faculties that result from the *perceptive* part. For some perceptions are the very same as those of *beasts*; others are little inferior to those that belong to *angels*, as we ordinarily call them. Some are perfectly brutish, while others are purely divine. Why, therefore, may there

# The Immortality of the Soul. BOOK II.

Could there not reside so great a range of capacities in the <term>formative part</term> <note>original: "Plastick part"; the soul's unconscious ability to shape and organize matter.</note> of the soul, that she may have within her all those three **vital harmonies** <note>original: "Vital Congruities"; the natural fitness or compatibility between the soul and a specific type of matter.</note>, by which she is able to unite livingly with a **celestial** and **aerial body**, as well as with this **terrestrial** one? Indeed, our nature being so free and diverse as it is, it would seem a slight against Providence to deny this capacity for living in these different **vehicles**; for that **Divine Justice** <note>original: "Nemesis"</note> which is supposed to rule in the world would seem defective without such a design.

But beyond all controversy, Eternal Wisdom and Justice has planned what is best. Unless we are to say nothing at all, we have nothing to judge by except our own faculties. Therefore, we must say that the divine plan follows what we, upon our most accurate investigation, conceive to be the best. For since there is no envy in the Deity (as *Plato* noted somewhere), we should not think otherwise than that He has framed our faculties so that, when we have rightly prepared ourselves to use them, they will correspond correctly with those things offered to them for contemplation in the world.

And truly, if we had the time here to consider it, I do not doubt it could be shown to be a very rational thing that there should be such an **amphibian** as the soul of man. Just as some creatures have the capacity to live either in the water or on the earth, the soul has the capacity to change her element. After her stay here in this **terrestrial vehicle** among men and beasts, she may ascend into the company of the **aerial spirits** <note>original: "Aereal Genii"</note>, in a body suited to their nature.

5. Supposing then this triple capacity of **vital harmony** in the soul of man, the manner in which she may leave this body is very easy to understand. For when the body's fitness to retain the soul is lost in death, the lower **vital harmony** in the soul loses its object and, consequently, its operation. And therefore, just as letting go of one thought in the **perceiving part** of the soul brings up another, so the ceasing of one **vital harmony** is the awakening of another—provided there is an object or subject ready to receive it. Certainly there is, partly in the body, but mainly outside of it. For there is a **vital air** that pervades all this lower world, which is connected to the life of all things and is the chief principle of it. This is why *Theon*, in his commentaries on *Aratus*, interprets that half-line of verse,

-> — **For we are also his offspring** — <-
<note>original: "Τοῦ γὰρ καὶ γένος ἐσμέν"</note>

in a secondary sense as referring to the **air**. He calls this **the natural Jupiter** <note>original: "Δία or Ζῆνα τὸν φυσικὸν"</note>, in whom, in an inferior sense, we may be said **to live, and move, and have our being**. For without **air**, neither fish, birds, nor beasts can survive; it provides the most immediate matter of life to them by feeding and refreshing their **animal spirits** <note>original: "Animal Spirits"; the refined fluids or energies believed to travel through the nerves to facilitate movement and sensation.</note>.

Wherefore, upon the cessation of the lowest **vital harmony**, that **aerial** capacity awakens into action. Finding such fit matter everywhere to employ herself upon, the soul will not fail to leave the body—either by choice, through the power of her own imagination and will, or else (supposing the very worst that can happen) by a natural kind of attraction,

# CHAP. XV. The Immortality of the Soul.

For the air outside is more wholesome and *vital* than in the corrupt caverns of the dead body, and yet there is a continuation between the internal and external air. It is therefore as easy to understand how—once the principle of joining with it in the <term>formative part</term> <note>original: "Plastick part"; the soul's unconscious ability to organize and animate matter.</note> of the soul is activated—she will naturally glide out of the body into the open air, as easily as fire ascends or a stone falls. For these motions are not merely mechanical, but vital or magical, and they cannot be reduced to mere matter, as I shall demonstrate in my Third Book.

<margin>Chapter 13, section 6.</margin>
6. And once the soul has recovered into this vast *ocean of life* and the *perceptive spirit of the world*, which is so full of enlivening *balsam*, it will be no wonder if she suddenly regains the use of her *perceptive* faculty. She is, as it were, regenerated in a moment into a natural power of life and motion by such a happy meeting of rightly-prepared matter for her <term>formative part</term> to unite with vitally. For even physical births are performed in a remarkably short time; if those histories are true of instant salads, sown and gathered not many hours before the meal at which they are eaten; or of the sudden birth of frogs following rain. Whole swarms of frogs, which did not exist before, have appeared perfectly formed and lively within the space of half an hour after oily raindrops fell upon the dry ground. I find this not only recorded by <term>Fallopius</term> <note>Gabriele Falloppio (1523–1562), a renowned Italian physician and anatomist.</note>, <margin>Scaliger, *On Subtlety*, Exercise 323.</margin> <term>Scaliger</term> <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger (1484–1558), a scholar who wrote on natural history.</note>, and others, but I have been personally informed of it by eyewitnesses. <term>Vaninus</term> <note>Lucilio Vanini (1585–1619), an Italian philosopher.</note> also claims to have been told by his friend Johannes Ginochius, who swore that in the month of July he saw with his own eyes a drop of rain suddenly turn into a frog. By such examples as these, it is evident that the reason why life takes so long to complete in earthly births is only the sluggishness of the matter the formative power works upon. Therefore, a soul once united with the air cannot fail to be able—in the blink of an eye—to exercise all its *perceptive* functions again, even if there was any interruption of them during the shocks of death.

7. How the soul may *live* and *act* apart from the body can be easily understood from what has been said. But to prove that she does so *in fact* <note>original: "de facto"</note>, there are only two ways: the testimony of *history* and *reason*. The historical evidence concerns either persons who were perfectly dead, or those subject to *ecstasies*—or rather to that high degree of ecstasy more properly called <term>separation</term> <note>original: "ἀφαιρεσία" (aphairesis); a Greek term meaning a taking away or withdrawal of the soul from the body.</note>, when the soul truly leaves the body and yet returns again. Of this latter sort is the example that <margin>Natural History, book 7, chapter 52.</margin> <term>Pliny</term> records of <term>Hermotimus of Clazomenae</term>, whose soul would often quit his body and wander here and there; after her return, she would tell many true stories of what she had seen during the time of her separation. <margin>History, book 4.</margin> <term>Maximus of Tyre</term> and <term>Herodotus</term> report the same of <term>Aristaeus of Proconnesus</term>. <margin>Platonic Theology, book 13, chapter 2. 8. *Bodin* <note>original: "Bodinus"; Jean Bodin (1530–1596), a French jurist and philosopher.</note> has a very great desire—even though it is so incredible to others—that this should be true, as it is such a powerful argument for the soul's immortality. He thinks this truth is evident from innumerable examples of the *ecstasies* of witches. We must admit with him that these are not natural, but that they amount to a perfect *separation* <note>original: $\alpha\phi\alpha\iota\rho\epsilon\sigma\iota\alpha$ (*aphaireseia*); a philosophical term for the soul's removal or withdrawal from the body.</note> or carrying away of the soul out of the body. However, their vivid sense of meeting, dancing, and worshipping the Devil, and the mutual memory of the persons who meet one another there at such a time, will be no infallible *demonstration* that they were actually there while their bodies lay at home in bed. The consistency of their confessions concerning the same secret meeting <note>original: "Conventicle"</note> is only a strong probability, provided it could once be proven that leaving their bodies were a thing possible.

For when they are out of them, they are in much the same condition as other *spirits* and can imitate whatever shape they please. Thus, many of these transformations into wolves and cats may as likely be the soul having left the body in this way as the Devil possessing the body and transforming it himself. And whatever these airy cats or wolves suffer—whether the cutting of their limbs, the breaking of their backs, or any such mischief—the witch in her bed suffers the same. This may very well arise from that magical *sympathy* seated in the unity of the *Spirit of the World* and the continuity of the subtle matter dispersed throughout; the *universe* in some sense being, as the *Stoics* and *Platonists* define it, *one vast entire animal*.

9. Now, that this real separation of the *soul* may happen in some *ecstasies* will be easily admitted if we consider that the soul, in her own nature, is separable from the body, being a substance really distinct from it. Furthermore, all bodies are equally penetrable and passable to her, since she lacks that physical property which is usually called *resistance* <note>original: $\alpha\nu\tau\iota\tau\upsilon\pi\iota\alpha$ (*antitypia*); the property of matter that prevents another object from occupying the same space.</note>; she can therefore freely slide through any matter whatsoever without any collision or resistance. Lastly, she does not so much provide heat and motion to the body as she provides *organization*. Therefore, when the body is well-organized and the blood is in a proper state, the heart and pulse will beat in some measure, and the brain will be replenished with "spirits" (and with them the whole body), even though the soul were out of it. In such a case (except for the fact that the *Spirit of Nature* cannot be excluded from there), it would be perfectly *Descartes's machine* <note>original: "Cartesius his Machina"</note> without sense, though seemingly as much alive as any living creature in a deep sleep. From this it appears that if the soul could leave the body, she might do it for a certain time without any harm to it,

10. But the real difficulty is to understand how the soul may be loosened from the body while the body is in a *fit* condition to retain her. That is a very great difficulty indeed, and in a sense impossible for any power except one that is supernatural. But it is not hard to conceive that this *vital fitness* in the body may be changed, either by way of *natural disease* or by *art* <note>original: "Art"; here meaning skill, medical technique, or perhaps ritual practice</note>. For why might some specific fermentation in the body not so alter the blood and spirits that the powers of the <term>plastic part</term> <note>the subconscious part of the soul responsible for forming and maintaining the physical body</note> of the soul cease to operate, just as the perceptive faculties sometimes do in cases of *catalepsy*, *apoplexy*, and the like? Therefore, this passing of the soul out of the body in *sleep* or *ecstasy* may sometimes be a certain disease, similar to that of the <term>night-walkers</term> <note>original Greek: νυκτοβάται (*nyktobatai*); sleepwalkers</note>.

Now, if it should happen that some such disorder should arise in the body that would greatly change its <term>vital congruity</term> <note>the soul's natural fitness or harmony with the physical body that keeps them joined</note> for a time, and if during this crisis that other disease of the *sleepwalkers* <note>original Latin: Noctambuli</note> should surprise the person, we can easily imagine what would happen. His imagination driving him to walk to this or that place, his soul may very easily be conceived—in this loosened condition it lies in—to be able to leave the body and pass through the air, as other inhabitants of that element do. It could act the part of separate spirits and exercise the same functions of the perceptive faculty as those who are entirely released from terrestrial matter. Only here is the difference: once that "damp" in the body that loosened the union of the soul is spent, the soul, by that natural *magic* I have mentioned more than once, will certainly return to the body and unite with it again as firmly as ever. But no man can pass out of his body like this whenever he pleases by the *command* <note>original: "Imperium"</note> of his will, any more than he can choose to walk in his sleep. For this capacity is pressed down deeper into the lower life of the soul, where neither *freedom of will* nor *free imagination* can reach.

11. *Passion* <note>intense emotion or physical sensation</note> is more likely to take effect in this case than either of the other two powers, as the seat of passions is originally in the heart, which is the chief fortress of these lower faculties. Therefore, by their proximity, they can more easily act upon the first principles of the *vital union*. The effect of these has been so great that they have completely carried the soul out of the body, as appears in various histories of that kind. For both *Sophocles* <note>the famous Greek playwright</note> and *Dionysius* the *tyrant of Sicily* died suddenly upon news of a victory for one of their tragedies. So too did *Polycrita*, a noblewoman of the Isle of *Naxos*; the poet *Philippides*; and *Diagoras of Rhodes*, upon a similar excess of *joy*. We might add examples of sudden *fear* and *grief*, but it is unnecessary.

It is a known and granted truth that *passion* has so much power over the vital state of the body as to make it an unfit mansion for the soul, from which her disunion from it will necessarily follow. Now, if *passion* will so utterly change the harmony of the blood and spirits as to completely release the soul from the body by a perfect death, why may it not...

# The Immortality of the Soul. BOOK II.

Consequently, it regains the soul back again by virtue of that *Mundane Sympathy* <note>the universal harmony or attraction between the soul and the physical world</note> I have so often spoken of.

12. Now, of all *passions* whatever, an excess of *desire* is most suited for this more harmless and momentary separation <note>original: "ablegation"</note> of the soul from the body. This is because its great strength is so closely aided by the imagination of traveling to the place where the person wishes to be. Thus, upon a disunion that does not amount to total death, the power of fancy may carry the soul to the intended place. Once satisfied and returned, the soul may rekindle life in the body to the same degree it had before it was overwhelmed by this excess of *desire*. If anything can explain it, this is what has caused dying men to visit their friends before their passing, even many miles away, while their bodies remain in their sickbeds; and it explains how healthy people have visited sick friends for whose health they have been overly anxious and concerned. 
<margin>See Helmont, *On the magnetic healing of wounds*, Paragraphs 74, 75, 76. <note>original: "De magnetica vulnerum curatione"</note></margin>
For this *ecstasy* really belongs to the *soul*, and not to the blood or the *animal spirits* <note>fine, vaporous substances then thought to transmit sensation through the nerves</note>; neither of these has any *sense* or *perception* at all. Therefore, this principle explains the story reported by *Martin Del-Rio* concerning a boy who, through the strength of imagination and the *desire* to see his father, fell into an *ecstasy*. After he regained consciousness, he confidently affirmed he had seen him and provided undeniable details of being present with him.

13. That *Cardan* <note>Girolamo Cardano, a 16th-century polymath known for his studies on the soul and occult phenomena</note> and others could fall into an *ecstasy* whenever they pleased, by the force of *imagination* and the *desire* to do so, is recorded and believed by very serious and sober writers. But whether they could ever do so to the point of a complete <term>separation</term> <note>original Greek: ἀφαιρεσία (*aphaire-sia*); a taking away or removal</note>, or a local disjunction of the soul from the body, I know of no one who dares to affirm. Such events are more often the accidents of nature and temperament—as seen in *sleepwalkers* <note>original Latin: *Noctambuli*</note>—rather than the effects of our *will*. However, we cannot certainly conclude that *skill* <note>original: "Art"</note> might not bring under our own power and control that which natural causes sometimes force upon us without our permission. But whether the *ointments* of *witches* have any such effect, or whether those unclean spirits they deal with—by their immediate presence in the witches' bodies—can for a time suppress or alter their *vital fitness* to such a degree that the soul is loosened, I leave for more curious investigators to explore. It is enough that I have demonstrated a very understandable possibility of this actual separation occurring without *death*, properly so called.

From this, the adamant *confessions* of *witches*—and the consistency of the stories told by several of them (both those who were there physically and those who left their bodies behind)—suggest a strong probability. This is especially true when, upon their return, they bring something home with them as a lasting sign of having been at that place. Although this might all be a delusion caused by their *familiars* <note>supernatural entities or demons believed to assist witches</note>, it is no small evidence that they were indeed where they claimed to be. For these are the greatest proofs that can be had in human affairs, and nothing has stopped men from believing this to be true as much as the supposed impossibility of it.

1. Examples of the other category—namely, the appearance of the ghosts of men after death—are so numerous and frequently discussed that it might seem unnecessary to list specific ones. These appearances occur either through dreams or *clear visions*. In dreams, we have the case of Avenzoar Albumaron <note>Ibn Zuhr, a famous 12th-century Arab physician</note>, an Arabian physician, to whom a recently deceased friend suggested in his sleep a highly effective <note>original: "soverain"</note> medicine for his sore eyes. Similar to this is the account in \* Diodorus concerning Isis, Queen of Egypt, whom he reports to have provided remedies to the Egyptians in their sleep after her death, just as she did while she was alive. Of this kind is also that memorable story from \* Posidonius the Stoic concerning two young men of Arcadia. Having arrived at Megara, one stayed with a tavern-keeper <note>original: "Victualler"</note> and the other at an inn. While the man in the inn was asleep, he dreamed that his fellow traveler earnestly begged him to come and help him, as he was being assaulted by the tavern-keeper and was in danger of being killed. However, after he fully woke up and found it was only a dream, he ignored it. But falling asleep again, his murdered friend appeared to him a second time, beseeching him that, though he had not helped him while alive, he would at least see his death avenged. The ghost told him how the tavern-keeper had thrown his body into a dung-cart, and that if he would get up early in the morning and wait at the town gate, he might discover the murder. He did exactly that, and so saw justice done to the murderer.

The first dream does not make the second one irrelevant to our purpose. While the first dream might have been caused by the strength of the distressed Arcadian's imagination and his desire for help being impressed upon the *Spirit of the World* <note>original: "Spirit of the World" (Spiritus Mundi); a concept of a universal medium that transmits thoughts or influences</note> and thus transmitted to his sleeping friend (a state best suited for such communication), it is clear that this explanation fails for the second dream after his death, unless his soul continued to exist and act. Therefore, it is obvious that the soul both existed and acted, and suggested this dream to seek revenge for the murder. There are infinite examples of this kind—I mean murders discovered by dreams where the soul of the murdered person seems to appear to someone asleep to make a complaint.

<margin>Marsilio Ficino, *Platonic Theology*, Book 16, Chapter 5.</margin>

2. We will add only an example or two of that other kind of *visions*, which are commonly called the *apparitions of the dead*. One such case is what *Pliny* relates at length in his *Letter to Sura* <note>Pliny the Younger, in a famous letter to Sura, described a haunted house in Athens</note>, concerning a house in *Athens* that was haunted and then freed by *Athenodorus* the philosopher. This occurred after the body of the person who appeared to him was dug up and buried with proper ceremony. It is not unlikely that most houses that are haunted are so mainly because of the souls of the deceased who have either been murdered, injured in some way, or have some hidden treasure to reveal, and the like. Individuals are haunted for similar reasons as houses; for instance, *Nero* was haunted after the murder of his mother, and *Otho* was pulled out of his bed in the night by the ghost of *Galba*. Such instances are infinite, as are those where the soul of a friend—perhaps a father, mother, or husband—has appeared to give good counsel and to inform them of the outcome of the greatest affairs of their lives. The ghosts of deceased lovers have also been reported to cling to their partners after they had left their bodies, taking all opportunities to meet them in solitude, whether by day or by night.

There are also other more chance encounters <note>original: "fortuitous occursions"</note> with these deceased spirits, for which one can give no explanation, unless it is because they find themselves in an easier position to appear. This may perhaps happen in fields after great slaughters of armies, and in public burial grounds. However, some would ridiculously dismiss these *apparitions* by claiming they are nothing but the mist or vapor <note>original: "reek or vapour"</note> of the bodies of the dead, which they imagine will take on the same height and shape as the man it came from. *Cardan* acts as foolishly in this regard as *Vanini* and others. * Cardan also acts foolishly in his account of those *specters* that appear so commonly in * *Iceland* <note>original: "Iseland"</note>, where the inhabitants meet their deceased friends in such a lifelike image that they greet them and embrace them as the same people. They do not know of their death until the figure suddenly disappears, or by later learning that they were dead at that time. He attributes this partly to the *density of the air* and partly to the foul food and heavy temperaments <note>original: "gross spirits," referring to the physiological "animal spirits" believed to drive the body</note> of the *Icelanders*. He implies that their imaginations are so strong that they convert the thick, vaporous air into the complete shape of their absent and deceased acquaintances, and so persuade themselves that they see them and talk with them. In his view, it is nothing more than an airy image created by the power of their own imagination from the rough remnants of these thick, flying vapors, just as men imagine shapes in broken clouds. But certainly, it would have been better to flatly deny the story than to give such a weak and improbable reason for the *phenomenon*. For neither do such visible vaporous forms near human height move close to the Earth, nor, if they did, could men be mistaken about an object so close at hand.

4. It is reasonable enough to think that the thickness <note>original: "Spissitude"</note> of the air in that place may contribute something to the frequency of these apparitions <note>original: "Spectra"</note>. Because the air there is more dense, it is more easily condensed into a visible form. However, this shape must be formed not by the imagination of the spectator (for that would be a monstrous power), but by the imagination of the Spirit that moves its own spirit-vessel <note>More uses the term "Vehicle" to describe the airy body a soul inhabits after death</note> made of that thick air. For the same reason, these apparitions also perhaps appear more often in the night than in the day, as the air is more damp and thick after the sun has been down for a while. To this also the custom of the Sami people <note>original: "Lappians"</note> of Scandinavia <note>original: "Scandia"</note> seems to agree; who, as Caspar Peucer <note>A 16th-century German physician and scholar</note> relates, are very much haunted with the apparitions of their deceased friends. They have no remedy for this trouble except burying them under their hearth. This ceremony can have no natural influence upon these spirits <note>original: "Lemures"</note> unless it forces them to stay in a warmer air, and consequently a more thinned air, than if they were buried elsewhere. Or rather, it may be because their bodies will rot sooner from the warmth of the hearth; otherwise, the coldness of that climate would allow the bodies to remain intact for a longer time. This would make them fit for the souls of the deceased to return to, refilling their spirit-vessels with a sticky moisture <note>original: "Cambium"</note> that makes the spirit far easier to be commanded into a visible form.

<margin>Book 3, chapters 8 and 9.</margin>
<margin>* *On Occult Philosophy* <note>original: *De occulta Philosoph.*</note>, book 3, chapter 41.</margin>
5. That this helps them to appear is evident from the well-known way these troublesome spirits return to their dead bodies. This is notorious in the history of Cuntius, which I have described at length in my *Antidote*, as well as in the story of the Silesian shoemaker and his maid. To this, you may add what Agrippa <note>Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, a famous 16th-century occultist</note> writes from the *Cretan Annals*: how there the *Catechanes* (that is, the spirits of deceased husbands) would be very troublesome to their wives and try to sleep with them as long as they could return to their dead bodies. This mischief was therefore prevented by a law: if any woman was haunted in this way, the body of her husband should be burned and his heart pierced with a stake. This also quickly ended the disturbances and tragedies that the ghost of Cuntius and others caused at Pentsch and Breslau in Silesia.

<margin>See *Magic of Specters* <note>original: *Magica de Spectris*</note>, Henning Gros, book 1, section 184.</margin>
Similar disturbances are reported to have happened in the year 1567 in Trutnov <note>original: "Trawtenaw"</note>, a city of Bohemia, caused by a man named Stephanus Hubener. He had grown amazingly rich (like Cuntius of Pentsch), and when he died, he did just as much damage to his fellow citizens. He would usually appear in the exact shape he was in when he was alive. Those he met, he would greet with such tight embraces that he caused many to fall sick and several to die from the "unkind hugs" he gave them. But burning his body rid the town of the dangerous encounters <note>original: "occursations"</note> with this malicious goblin.

All these instances prove not only that souls appear after they have left this life, but also that some thickening matter can make it much easier for them to appear. This matter might be obtained from living bodies, from bodies recently dead, or even from bodies that have been dead for some time (as Hubener’s body was, though it had lain 20 weeks in the grave), or finally from thick, vaporous air. This availability of matter invites them to play their tricks.

6. But regarding any private person who ever appeared for a specific purpose after his death, there is none who did so for a more noble reason than the distinguished Platonist Marsilio Ficino <note>original: *Marsilius Ficinus*; a celebrated Italian scholar and philosopher of the Renaissance</note>. After a warm dispute about the immortality of the soul, he had (as Baronius <note>Cesare Baronio, a 16th-century historian</note> relates) made a solemn vow with his fellow Platonist Michele Mercati <note>original: *Michael Mercatus*</note> that whichever of the two died first should appear to his friend and give him certain information of that truth. It being his fate to die first, and indeed not long after this mutual resolution, he was mindful of his promise once he had left the body. For while Michele Mercati was very focused on his studies early one morning, he heard a horse riding by at full speed and observed that it stopped at his window. With that, he heard the voice of his friend Ficino crying out aloud, "O Michael, Michael, those things are true, they are true!" <note>original: *o Michael, Michael, vera, vera sunt illa*</note>. Whereupon he suddenly opened the window and, seeing Marsilio on a white horse, called after him; but he vanished from his sight. He immediately sent word to Florence to inquire how Marsilio was doing, and learned that he died at the very hour he had called at his window to assure him of his own and other men's immortality.

7. The examples I have produced of the appearing of the souls of men after death—considering how clearly I have demonstrated their ability to be separated from the body and their capacity for vital union with an airy vessel <note>original: "Aiery Vehicle"; the medium or body a soul inhabits after death</note>—cannot but have their due weight of argument with those who are open-minded. And for others who do admit these things, prejudices from their upbringing—the belief that the soul, when it departs this life, is suddenly either snatched up into the Empyrean Heaven <note>The highest part of heaven, thought to be the dwelling place of God</note> or hurried headlong down toward the center of the Earth—makes the apparitions of the ghosts of men seem altogether incredible to them. They always substitute an angel or devil in their place, who they believe must impersonate the deceased, as if the souls themselves were not at leisure to act out any such part.

8. But misconception and prejudice, though they may hinder the force of an argument for those who are entangled by them, yet reason must prevail with those who are free. To them I dare appeal whether—considering the airy vessels of souls which are common to them and other spirits <term>Genii</term> <note>In this context, the term refers to various types of spiritual beings</note>, so that whatever they are imagined to do in their place, they may perform themselves—it is also appropriate that those persons who are most concerned should, when it is in their power, act in their own affairs. If a spirit appears in this way—claiming to be the soul of a specific person and resembling them in appearance—and if all this effort involves very just and serious matters, it would be unfit for a Devil to promote such care and kindness. It would be equally unfit for a good *Genius* <note>original: *Genius*; a protective spirit or guiding deity</note>, as it is beneath such a noble nature to tell a lie, especially when the matter could be handled just as effectively without one. I say, I appeal to anyone: if all these things are weighed together correctly, and the weight of prejudice does not tip the scales, the conclusion will certainly favor our cause. Any impartial judge ought to conclude that if these stories—which are so frequent everywhere and in all ages concerning the ghosts of men appearing—are true, then it is also true that they are indeed their ghosts. Therefore, the souls of men exist and act after they have left these earthly bodies.

### CHAPTER XVII.

1. *The superiority of arguments drawn from reason over those drawn from stories. 2. The first step toward a rational demonstration that the soul acts outside her body: that she is an immaterial substance separable from it. 3. The second step: that the immediate instruments for sense, motion, and the organization of the body are certain subtle and thin spirits. 4. A comparison between the soul in the body and the aerial spirits <note>original: "Aëreal Genii"</note>. 5. Concerning the nature of demons from the account of Marcus the Eremite <note>A 4th- or 5th-century ascetic monk</note>, and how the soul immediately becomes such a being once it has left this body. 6. An objection concerning the souls of animals <note>original: "Brutes"</note>, which is answered first by way of concession; 7. Secondly, by refuting the arguments for that concession. 8. That there is no rational doubt at all that the human soul acts after death. 9. A further argument for her activity outside this body, based on her conflicts with it while she is inside it. 10. Also from the general hope and belief of all nations that they shall live after death.*

1. **B**ut we proceed now to what is less subject to the excuses and misinterpretations of either the *profane* or the *superstitious*. For none but those who describe themselves as mere animals <note>original: "Brutes"</note> can reject the decrees and conclusions of philosophy and reason. They may think that, in matters of this nature, they can—with a great deal of applause and credit—refuse the testimony of other men's senses, if not their own. To them, all *apparitions* <note>ghostly sightings</note> are nothing but the powerful surprises of *melancholy and imagination* <note>In the 17th century, "melancholy" was seen as a physical imbalance that could cause hallucinations</note>. But they cannot so easily or creditably silence the deductions of reason by saying they are fallacies, unless they can show the sophism <note>original: *Sophisme*; a clever but false or deceptive argument</note>—which they cannot do where none exists.

<margin>* Chapters 2, 4, 5, 6.</margin>

3. In the next place, we should notice that the soul's immediate *instruments* are those thin <note>original: "tenuious"</note> and aerial particles that people usually call the *spirits*; these are what the soul uses to hear, see, feel, imagine, remember, and reason. By moving them—or at least directing their motion—she also moves the body; and by using them, or some similar subtle matter, she either completes or at least contributes to the organization of the body. For the idea that the soul should be the *vital architect* of her own house—maintaining a close connection and secure possession of it, distinct and safe from the invasion of any other particular soul—seems like a strong argument. And yet, while she is exercising that faculty, it seems reasonable that she may have a more than ordinary union or involvement with the *Spirit of Nature*, or the *Soul of the World*, insofar as it is *formative* <note>original: "Plastick"; the unconscious, life-giving force in nature</note>. This is asserted by *Plotinus* <note>A major Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 204–270 AD)</note> and may be suspected to be true if we consider the amazing effects of a mother's imagination on her *infant*. These effects are sometimes so great that, unless she stirred the *Spirit of Nature* into agreement, they might seem to exceed the power of any single cause. I will wait to provide examples until the proper place; in the meantime, I hope I may be excused for any perceived rashness in identifying the cause of those many and various marks found in nature, which so clearly point <margin>Chapter 10, section 7.</margin> to such a principle in the world as I have suggested *before.

4. But to return and focus on the subject at hand. It appears from the two previous conclusions that the soul—when considered as immediately clothed in this thin matter we are discussing, which is her inward *vehicle* <note>the "subtle body" or spiritual container that carries the soul</note>—has very little more difference from the aerial *spirits* <note>original: "Genii"</note> than a man in prison has from one who is free. The one can only see and breathe air through the grates of the prison and must be bothered by all the stench and unhealthy fumes of that miserable home; whereas the other may walk and take the fresh air wherever he finds it most convenient and pleasant.

This is the difference between the *spirits* <note>original: "Genii"</note> and an embodied *soul*. The *soul* is like a man fallen into a deep pit: he can have no better water, nor air, nor any longer enjoyment of the sun and its cheerful light and warmth than the size and quality of the pit allows him. Once imprisoned in the body, she cannot enjoy any better spirits (in which all her life and comfort consists) than the constitution of the body—after its cycles of refinement and digestion <note>original: "concoction"</note>—can provide for her. But those *spirits* of the air, who possess their *vehicles* without such harsh conditions, can (if they are not themselves at fault) use the power of their minds to provide themselves with more pure and unpolluted matter—matter that will more easily harmonize with the noblest and most divine functions of their spirit.

<margin>See Chapter 8, section 13.</margin>
Briefly, therefore, if we consider things correctly, we cannot help but strongly suspect that there is no more difference between a soul and an aerial *spirit* <note>original: "Genius"</note> than there is between a sword in its scabbard and one out of it. A soul is simply a *spirit* <note>original: "Genius"</note> inside the body, and a *spirit* is a soul outside the body—just as the ancients also defined them, using the same name,

5. This is very consistent with what Michael Psellus <note>An 11th-century Byzantine monk, philosopher, and historian</note> records, based on the exceptional knowledge and experience of Marcus the Eremite in these matters. Marcus describes the nature of these *Daimones* as being composed entirely of Spirit and Air; because of this, they hear, see, and feel in every part of their body. He justifies this with a reason, and wonders at the ignorance of men who do not notice it: "that the part which perceives is not in any bone or nerve, but the spirit that exists within them" <note>original: τὸ μὴ ἐπί τινι ὀστῷ ἢ νεύρῳ εἶναι τὸ αἰσθανόμενον, ἀλλὰ τὸ ἐν τούτοις ἐνυπάρχον πνεῦμα</note>. In other words, *it is neither bones, nor nerves, nor any gross or visible part of the body, nor any organ, through which the soul immediately performs the functions of sense; rather, it is the "spirits" <note>In early modern science, "spirits" were thought to be a subtle, fluid-like substance that carried signals between the soul and the body</note> that are her nearest and innermost instrument for these operations.* When the body is deprived of these spirits, no sense is found in it, even though the gross organs and parts remain in their usual physical state, as we see in cases of fainting <note>original: "Syncopes"</note> and strokes <note>original: "Apoplexies"</note>. This clearly shows that the immediate *Vehicle* <note>The "vessel" or medium through which the soul acts</note> of life is the spirits, and that the soul's connection with the body is through them, as the most learned physicians agree. From this, it follows that once this bond <note>original: "Vinculum"</note> is broken, the soul will be free from the body. It will then naturally be carried out of the corrupt carcass—which no longer has any harmony with the soul—into that element that is more similar to its own nature: the vital Air. This happens as naturally as fire rising upward, as I have <margin>* Chapter 14, section 5.</margin> already noted. Thus, when the principles of life are fully ignited in this thinner *Vehicle*, the soul becomes as complete for sensation and action as any other inhabitant of these airy regions.

6. There is only one stubborn objection against this easy and natural conclusion: that by this reasoning, the souls of animals <note>original: "Brutes"</note>—especially the more advanced ones—will not only continue to exist after death (for that difficulty has been resolved already), but will also live and enjoy themselves. To this, I dare boldly answer: it is a thousand times more reasonable that they do, than that the souls of men do not. Yet I will not confidently assert whether they do or do not; I will only briefly examine each hypothesis. First, for the sake of argument, let us say they do exist, and note the reasons that might lead one to think so. Among these, the two primary reasons are those mentioned in the objection: first, that they exist after death; and second, that the immediate instrument of their vital functions is their "spirits," just as in humans. To these we may add that, for the present, we are fellow-inhabitants of the same environment, the Earth, subject to the same disasters of fire, floods, and earthquakes. It seems improbable that the vast space of Air and Ether, which must be inhabited by living creatures, should have only one kind of inhabitant (the Angels or *Genii* <note>Spirits or guardian beings</note>, whether good or bad). That would seem as great a loneliness as if humans were the only inhabitants of the Earth, or mermaids the only inhabitants of the Sea. Furthermore, the periods of *Vital Congruity* <note>The natural "fit" or harmony between a soul and a specific type of body</note>—woven into the nature of their souls by that eternal Wisdom who is the creator of all things—may be shorter or longer, depending on the property of their essence and their relationship to the Universe; and so their descents and returns...

...may be accordingly swifter or slower. It is more in keeping with **Divine goodness** for things to be this way rather than otherwise, provided their natures allow it; for their existence would be in vain if they were deprived of vital activity when they could easily have it. They would be no more capable of **salvation** in the next state than they are of **conversion** here. The intellectual inhabitants of the air also possess external and bodily senses, and a variety of objects would serve them as well there as they do us here on Earth. Furthermore, historical accounts seem to imply that there are such kinds of **aerial animals** among them, such as **dogs**, **horses**, and the like. Therefore, to be brief, the idea that the souls of animals <note>original: "Brutes"</note> cease to live after they are separated from the body can have no other basis than **immorality**, the mother of **ignorance**—which is nothing but a narrowness of spirit born from excessive self-love and contempt for other creatures—that emboldens us to so confidently hold such a groundless conclusion.

7. This position indeed makes a plausible showing; so much so that if an objection forced someone to acknowledge it as truth, they would have very little reason to be ashamed of it. But this controversy is not so easily decided. For though it is clear that the souls of beasts are substances really separable from their bodies, if they have only one **vital congruity** <term>The natural suitability or "tuning" of a soul to a specific type of environment or body</term>—namely, the **terrestrial** one—they cannot recover life in the air. Whether they have one, two, or more vital congruities depends entirely on the wisdom and counsel of Him who made all things. Besides, the souls of animals seem to have a more passive nature than to be able to manage or enjoy this escape from **death**; that free and commanding imagination belongs only to us, as does **reminiscence** <note>The active, intentional recall of memories, as opposed to the passive memory found in animals</note>. But beasts have only a passive imagination and bare memory. Since these likely fail them in the "shipwreck" of their body, if they could live in the air, they would begin the world on a perfectly new slate, which is little better than death. In this sense, they might rightly be deemed mortal. Our being co-inhabitants of the same element, the Earth, proves nothing; by the same logic, worms and fleas should live outside their bodies, and fish should not. Yet fish, perhaps with their shapes slightly changed (for there is no necessity that these creatures in their **airy vehicles** <note>A subtle, spiritual "body" the soul was thought to inhabit after the death of the physical body</note> should look exactly as they do in their terrestrial ones), might act and live in the moister regions of the air.

As for the supposed loneliness that would exist in the air, it does not affect this matter. In the lower regions of the air, the various objects of the **Earth** and **Sea** will serve the purpose. The "winding up" of those various cycles of **vital congruity** may indeed pass for an ingenious invention—as something that is possible for the souls of animals—but, as the Scholastic philosophers say well, "From the possibility of a thing to its actual existence, the logical conclusion does not follow" <note>original: *A posse ad esse non valet consequentia*</note>. As for the argument from **Divine Goodness**, it does not exclude His Wisdom, which tempers itself to the natures of things. Since we do not know the nature of the souls of animals as perfectly as we know our own, we cannot easily be certain from that argument what the outcome will be in this case. A musician does not strike all strings at once; nor is it to be expected that everything in nature should act at all times. But when it is its turn, then being touched upon, it will give its sound; in

# CHAPTER XVII. The Immortality of the Soul.

...in the interim, it lies silent. And so it may be with the souls of animals <note>original: "Brutes"</note> for a time, especially when the vital balance of earth, air, and sea fails; yes, and at other times too, if none but intellectual spirits are fit to manage aerial vehicles <term>A subtle body made of air or light that a soul inhabits after leaving the physical body</term>.

I confess indeed that salvation can no more belong to the souls of animals than spiritual conversion can; but that is just as true of the souls of plants (if they have any distinct from the *Universal Spirit of Nature* <note>A common concept in 17th-century Platonism referring to a "world-soul" that animates the physical realm</note>). Yet, it does not prove that the souls of vegetables shall live and act in airy vehicles after a herb or tree has died and rotted here. Regarding the convenience of a variety of objects for the inhabitants of the air, I have already answered that. And as for the apparitions of horses, dogs, and the like, these may be the transformations of the aerial *genii* <note>original: "Genii"; celestial spirits or beings that inhabit the atmosphere</note> into these shapes. Although this is a sign that they would not be opposed to the use and company of such aerial animals if they had them, they can nevertheless do without them, as they are so well able to supply those roles themselves.

We will therefore briefly conclude that, from the mere light of reason, it cannot be infallibly demonstrated that the souls of animals do not live after death, nor that it is any contradiction in nature to say they do. This is sufficient to weaken the present objection.

8. But regarding the life and activity of the souls of men outside of this body, everything proceeds smoothly, without any check or stop. For we find that the aerial *genii* are so exceedingly similar to us in their faculties—we both being *intellectual creatures*, and both using the same immediate instrument of sense and perception (namely, *aerial spirits* <note>In early modern physiology, these were subtle fluids that carried messages between the soul and the body</note>)—that we can scarcely discover any other difference between us than there is between a man who is naked and one dressed in thick, heavy clothing. It is the easiest and most natural inference possible to conclude that when we are separated from the body and are clothed only in air, we shall be just like them and have the same life and activity they have. For though an animal falls short of this privilege, it should not discourage us; there is a greater kinship between the *intellectual* faculties and the *airy* or *ethereal vehicle* than there is between such vehicles and those lower, more sensual powers we share with beasts. And we find, when taking in the fresh air, that the more fine and pure our *spirits* are, the more noble, divine, and purely intellectual our thoughts become.

Nor is the step upward any greater than the step downward. For seeing that what is so *divine* and *angelic* in us may be united with the body of an animal (for such is this earthly clothing), why may the soul not be united with the vehicle of an *angel*, despite her *earthly suitability* <term>original: "Terrestrial Congruity"; the soul's natural adaptation to living in a physical, earthly body</term> (which, in new circumstances, may easily be imagined to cease acting)? So, there is no puzzle at all concerning the human soul; immediately upon death, she may join those aerial inhabitants, the *genii* or *angels*.

9. We may be even better assured of this if we consider how we possess faculties that the soul finds entangled, fettered, clouded, and obscured by her fated residence in this prison of the body. To such an extent that, as far as is lawful, she falls out with the body for those inconveniences...

...objections that the most robust physical health usually imposes upon it. Consider how its Will struggles against the impurity of the spirits that stir up bestial passions—passions which are, nevertheless, the peak and flower of enjoyment for other creatures. Consider how many times its whole life on Earth is nothing more than a perpetual warfare against the consequences of its union with this lump of Earth, which is so similar to other land animals. From this, it is plain that the soul finds itself in a wrong condition, and that it was created for a better and purer state. It could not reach this state unless it lived outside of the Body—which it does, in some sense, in *divine ecstasies and dreams*. In these cases, it makes no use of the *body’s organs*, but only of the purer spirits <note>original: "Spirits"; in the 17th century, these were believed to be subtle vapors that carried signals through the nervous system</note> in the fourth ventricle of the brain. There, it acts as if by itself and performs some preliminary exercises, similar to those it will perform in its *aerial vehicle* <term>A subtle body made of air or light that a soul inhabits after leaving the physical body</term>.

10. Add to all this that the *immortality of the soul* is the common, and therefore natural, hope and expectation of all nations. There are very few people so uncivilized as not to hold this as a truth, though they may be somewhat ridiculous in how they express it. For example, some say they shall retire after death to a certain grove or woods, or beyond a certain hill, or to a specific island—such as the *Race-course of Achilles* <note>original: "Δρόμος Ἀχιλλέως" (Dromos Achilleos), a peninsula in the Black Sea believed by the Greeks to be a haunting place of the hero's ghost</note>, the island where Achilles’ ghost was thought to wander, or the *Fortunate Islands* <note>original: "Insulæ Fortunatæ"</note>, the famous *Elysium* <note>The paradise of the ancient Greeks</note> of the ancients. 

And yet, perhaps if we should tell these people of the *Empyrean Heaven* <note>original: "Cœlum Empyreum"; in medieval cosmology, the highest part of heaven, composed of fire or light</note>, and calculate its height and distance from the Earth, and how many solid celestial spheres a soul must glide through before it can arrive there, these simple people would think our *scholarly opinions* <note>original: "Scholastick Opinion"; referring to the complex theological models of the Middle Ages</note> are just as odd as we think theirs are. Indeed, it is possible that someone with a more judicious and perceptive wit would laugh at both of us alike.

<margin>
*Antidote against Atheism*, Book 1, chapter 10, section 9.
</margin>
It is sufficient that, in the main, almost all nations are agreed that an *immortality* is to be expected, just as they agree that there is a *Deity* to be worshipped—even though ignorance of specific details makes religion vary, even to the point of being monstrous, in many parts of the world. But since both religion and the belief in its reward (which is a blessed state after death) are so generally acknowledged by all the inhabitants of the Earth, it is a clear argument that this belief is true according to the light of nature. This is true not only because they believe it, but because they so seriously either desire it or are so horribly afraid of it if they have offended their consciences. These traits would not exist so universally in men if there were no real objects in nature that corresponded to these mental faculties, as I have argued elsewhere in similar cases.

<summary>The author argues that the soul’s struggle against physical passions and its universal expectation of an afterlife across all cultures prove that immortality is a natural truth. He compares various cultural visions of the afterlife, noting that while the details differ, the core belief remains a constant human instinct.</summary>

<header>CHAP. XVIII. The Immortality of the Soul.</header>

## CHAPTER XVIII.

1. *That the powers of our souls, and the nature of their direct tools—the spirits—are so similar to those of spirits <note>original: "Dæmons"; used here in the classical sense of "daimon" or guiding spirit, not necessarily an evil entity</note>, that it seems reasonable that they would continue to act outside this earthly body, unless God purposefully prevented it. 2. Or if they could not, His power and wisdom could easily grant their essence a double or triple Vital Congruity <term>The soul's capacity to harmonize with and animate different types of matter, such as air or ether</term> to make it certain. 3. A further proof of this truth from the truthfulness of God. 4. An answer to an objection against the previous argument. 5. Another proof from His justice. 6. An answer to an objection. 7. An answer to another objection. 8. Another argument from the justice of God. 9. An objection answered. 10. An irrefutable proof of the soul's immortality from the Divine Goodness. 11. A more detailed application of that argument, and an identification of those people upon whom it will have the least effect. 12. That the most noble and virtuous spirit is the most certain of the soul's immortality.*

<margin>* Chapters 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.</margin>
<margin>* Chapters 8, 9.</margin>
1. Finally, to confirm everything, let us contemplate the Nature of *God*, who is the Author and Maker of all things. All things were created and are always ordered according to His goodness, wisdom, and power. Let us take special notice of how many steps toward this immortality are already impressed upon the very nature of the soul; and then seriously consider if it is possible that the Sovereign Deity should stop there and go no further, when there are such great reasons—if we understand anything at all—for Him to fulfill our expectations. For we have already clearly demonstrated that the Soul of man is a Substance actually *separable* from the Body, and that all her operations and functions are performed directly, not by those parts of the body that are made of earthly and gross matter, but by what is more aerial or ethereal: the *Vital* and *Animal Spirits* <note>original: "Spirits"; in 17th-century physiology, these were believed to be extremely subtle fluids or vapors that acted as the bridge between the immaterial soul and the physical body</note>. These are very similar to the "Vehicles" <term>The subtle, non-physical bodies inhabited by spirits</term> of the Angels or *Genii* <note>original: "Genii"; spirits or minor deities in classical mythology</note>. Indeed, if the Divine power simply left Nature to work on its own, it would seem very strange—considering those Divine and Intellectual powers in us (which are as similar to the souls of Angels as our animal spirits are to their subtle bodies)—if the soul, once separated from the body, did not immediately act within and give form to the air as easily as other spirits do. There is, after all, very little difference between their two natures.

2. Or, if one single *Plastic power* <term>The soul's innate ability to shape and organize the matter it inhabits</term> in a being so closely related to these "aerial people" is not enough to survive in both states, surely only a very small addition would be needed to help. And how easy is it for that Eternal Wisdom to design a double or triple Vital Congruity—namely, Aerial and Ethereal, as well as Terrestrial—within such an essence? Its powers and properties already clearly correspond with those purer inhabitants of both the Ether and the Air.

<summary>This page argues that the soul’s inherent structure and its use of "animal spirits" make it naturally suited for a life after death, suggesting that God has designed the soul with the potential to inhabit aerial or ethereal bodies.</summary>

<page-num>140</page-num>
<header>The Immortality of the Soul. BOOK II.</header>

3. But this is not all we have to say. For if there is one quality more precious in God than another, we should take it as a sure and undeniable guarantee of this current Truth: *that our souls will certainly prove to be immortal.* For my own part, I know nothing more precious in the Godhead than His *Truthfulness* <note>original: "Veracity"</note>, *Justice*, and *Goodness*. All three of these will assure and protect us, ensuring that we suffer no loss or harm when we leave these earthly bodies, whether in our life or our very being. It would be a great disgrace to that quality of God we call His *Truthfulness*—since He so clearly and universally promises a happy state after this life to all the nations of the *world* that have any *religion* at all—if, in reality, there were no such thing to be expected.

For He does not merely turn a blind eye to the error (if it were one) by failing to speak out against it—as any honest person would if someone else claimed, in their presence or hearing, that they intended to grant certain gifts and income to others when there was no such plan. Instead, He has, so to speak, intentionally endowed people with extraordinary talents and powers to establish this belief on Earth. All *prophets* and *miracle-workers* who have appeared in the world have, in one way or another, assured mankind of this very important truth. Furthermore, the most noble and virtuous souls in every age have been the most likely to believe it. This is not only because of their own self-interest. Anyone who has ever had the happiness to experience these things may observe that the clarity and purity of character—which mostly consists of the love and admiration of God and Virtue, and all those divine achievements that even those who never reach them still highly praise—I say, this more refined state of mind naturally creates a wonderful tendency, or even a necessity, to believe in the truth of the position we are defending. Therefore, if it is not true, God has arranged the natural order <note>original: "laid a train in Nature"</note> so that the most virtuous and pious people are the most certain to be deceived. This would be a direct contradiction to His quality of *Truthfulness*.

4. Nor can the strength of this argument be avoided by arguing *that* God might deceive people for their own good, just as parents do with their children; and that His *wisdom* might create such a natural error to be useful for states and governments, keeping the people in awe and thus making them more loyal and manageable. I must admit that a certain *usefulness* for holding together societies <note>original: "Commonweals"</note> does result from this divine truth as a secondary benefit. But to think that this is its main purpose, and that there is nothing more to it than that, is as foolish <note>original: "Idiotical"</note> and childish as concluding that because the stars—those massive lights—perform some small tasks for us at night, that this is their only meaning and they serve no other purpose.

Besides, no father would tell a lie to his child if he possessed a truth just as effective for his purpose. And if he told his child of something truly good as well as desirable to encourage obedience, he would certainly fulfill his promise if it were in his power to do so. But it is within God's power to fulfill whatever reward He has proposed; He has no need to use any falsehood in this matter.

<header>CHAPTER XVIII. The Immortality of the Soul.</header>

Therefore, if He were to do so, He would have less *truthfulness* <note>original: "Veracity"</note> than an ordinary honest man; this would be *blasphemous* and *contradictory* to the nature of the Deity.

5. Furthermore, regarding the point of *Justice*, God was obligated to design the nature and order of things so that the souls of men may live after death, and so that they may fare according to their behavior here on earth. For the Godhead, as the philosopher calls Him, is an <term>Impartial Law</term> <note>original Greek: Νόμος ἰσοκλινής (Nomos isoklines), a law that leans equally or fairly</note>, and He immutably and inevitably distributes justice—both *reward* and *punishment*—in the world. But everyone agrees that being good and living according to virtue is difficult. It is extremely hard to persuade anyone to do such violence to their own nature as to strive for a true sense of virtue. (While *cunning* and *politics* are easy enough, and other things exist that look like virtues when compared to their opposite vices but are not actually virtues.) However, to persuade people toward those things that truly are virtuous is, I say, extremely hard—if not impossible—without teaching this grand concern: the *state of the soul after death* and the *reward* that will then follow a *virtuous* life. If we are frustrated in these hopes by the soul's mortality, then we are defrauded of our reward, and God is robbed of the honor of His *Justice*.

6. Nor can the force of this argument be weakened by that high claim of *Stoicism*—*that virtue is a sufficient reward in itself*—nor by the idea that the very hope of this immortality (being accompanied by so much joy, peace, and contentment) will outweigh all the pain and trouble of either acquiring virtue or sticking close to it once it is gained. Regarding the first point: it is one thing to talk big and another to practice. For my own part, I think that in the main, *Epicurus*—who placed the highest good in *pleasure*—philosophized more solidly than the paradoxical *Stoics*. For without question, pleasure is what all men ought to aim for, if they had the right idea of it and knew where to find it, or could reach the purest and most justifiable sense of it. But there can be no *pleasure* (without a perfect miracle) while our spirits are disturbed and damaged by miserable poverty, imprisonment, sickness, torture, bad diet, and the many other hardships that those who are most virtuous have been most liable to in all ages. Added to this is the constant care and anxiety of standing on guard, the stings of slander and defamation, and the continual frustration of seeing the baseness and vileness of men's characters and the ugly, dishonest dealings of world affairs. These anxieties cannot be avoided by any remedy except one that is as bad as the disease (or worse), because it is completely incompatible with a truly heroic mind: I mean the Stoic *Apathy* <note>original: Apathy; here meaning a state of being unaffected by emotion or pain</note>. The best that can be said of this "apathy" is that it is a kind of constant and safe state of sulkiness, placing us only in the condition of those who are said to have neither won nor lost. Distressed and persecuted virtue is a poor reward indeed without the hope of future happiness.

7. But to say that the hope of it, without the actual enjoyment, is enough compensation is like the mockery that *Plutarch* records of *Dionysius* toward a fiddler. He had the man play before him and promised him a reward;

But when the performer demanded payment from him for his efforts <note>original: "pains"</note>, the ruler denied him, or rather said he had been paid already, dismissing him with this joke: "For as long as you pleased me with your singing, you were just as happy with your hoping for the reward; so you have been paid enough already." <note>original Greek: Ὅσον χρόνον εὔφραινες ᾄδων, τοσοῦτον ἔχαιρες ἐλπίζων</note> This kind of hurtful mockery <note>original: "injurious mirth"</note> might be acceptable in a trivial matter or from a tyrant, whose high status makes him a proud and forgetful mortal who looks down on his inferiors. But in a matter of this nature, which concerns not only this temporary life but the everlasting <note>original: "sempiternal"</note> duration of the soul, *injustice* is unspeakably grievous. It is all the more harsh and unfitting if we consider that this injustice is supposed to be committed not by a fragile earthly ruler—whose high honors might make him neglectful of small affairs and lowly people—but by the God of Heaven. He can attend to all things as easily as he can any single thing; he is perfectly and immutably just, never doing or omitting anything based on changing moods as happens with vain men, but always acting according to the supreme excellence and holiness of his own nature.

8. Neither is *Divine Justice* committed only to *rewarding*, but also to *punishing*. This cannot occur unless the souls of men exist after death. For there are undoubtedly many thousands who have committed the most enormous villainies: they have persecuted the good, taking away their possessions, liberties, or lives, sometimes adding the most barbarous tortures and insulting abuses. In all this, they have highly satisfied their own greed, ambition, and revenge. Indeed, it may be that the animal-like ferocity of their own spirits took great pleasure in bringing truly religious people into disgrace, laughing at all virtuous actions as the fruits of ignorance and folly. And yet, despite all this, they have died in peace in their beds, after lives filled as thickly with all the sensual enjoyments of honor, riches, and pleasure as their history <note>original: "Story"</note> is filled with frauds, thefts <note>original: "Rapines"</note>, murders, sacrileges, and whatever other crimes the wicked boldness of lawless people will attempt.

9. Such things as these happen proportionally through all the ranks and levels of men. Nor is it sufficient to reply that their own consciences, like so many Furies <note>In Greek mythology, the Furies were deities of vengeance who hounded wrongdoers.</note>, lash and scorch them in this life. For we are speaking of deep-seated and successful wickedness, where that principle of conscience is completely put to sleep. If it ever wakes and cries out, the noise of the world’s affairs, the hurry of business, the continual visits of friends and flatterers, and the false instructions of greedy priests or mercenary philosophers (who will shamelessly corrupt and pervert both the light of nature and the meaning of religion for money) will drown it out. The sound and clatter of these things, I say, will so preoccupy the ear of the successfully wicked person that the voice of conscience can no more be heard in this continual tumult than the crying <note>original: "vagient"</note> of the infant *Jupiter* could be heard amidst the wild dancing of the *Cretan Corybantes* and the tinkling and clashing of their bronze shields. <note>The Corybantes were mythical priests who clashed their shields to drown out the cries of the baby god Jupiter (Zeus) so that his father, Saturn, would not discover and eat him.</note> Therefore, if there is no life hereafter, the worst of men have the greatest share of happiness, as their passions and desires are continually satisfied to the fullest in those things that are agreeable and, in the right circumstances, even allowable to human nature.

...nature: such as the sweet reflection on the success of our political management of the affairs of the world; the general tribute of honor and respect for our policy and wit, and that ample testimony of it, our acquisitions of power or riches; that great satisfaction of foiling and defeating our enemies, and obliging and securing our more useful friends; to which finally you may add all the variety of mirth and pastime that flesh and blood can entertain itself with, from either *music*, *wine*, or *women*.

10. Thirdly and lastly, the mortality of the soul is not only inconsistent with the *veracity* <note>truthfulness</note> and *justice* of God, but also with his *goodness*, the most sovereign and sacred attribute in the Deity, and which alone is enough to demonstrate *that the soul of man cannot perish in death*. For suppose that God had made no promise to us—either by any extraordinary prophet or by the suggestion of our own natural faculties—that we shall be immortal, and that there was neither merit nor demerit in this life, so that all arguments from either the Divine *veracity* or *justice* were quite cut off; his *goodness* alone (especially if we consider how capable the soul is of existing afterward) is a sufficient assurance that we shall not fail to live after death. For how can that sovereign *goodness*, supported by all-powerful knowledge, fail to arrange it so? It is so much more consistent with His *transcendent bounty* to ordain things this way than otherwise. That is to say, as soon as he created the world, he made it so complete as to bring into being at once not only all *physical* <note>original: corporeal</note> substance (as all men agree he did) but also all *immaterial* or *incorporeal* substances. He created as many of them as can partake of life and of the enjoyment of themselves and the universe, setting them to living and working in all places and elements that their nature is able to function in. Therefore, among other beings of the intellectual order, he ordained that the souls of men also—wherever they were or ever should be, provided it were not their own fault <note>original: "not long of themselves"</note>—should have a power of life and motion. He ordained that no other *vengeance* <note>original: Nemeſis</note> should follow them except what they themselves set in motion; nor should this lead to utter annihilation, but only serve as discipline or punishment. Since souls are of such a complex nature—having faculties nearly related to animals <note>original: brutes</note> as well as those having a close affinity with the *spirits of the air* <note>original: Aëreal Genii</note> and *heavenly angels*—their *vital compatibility* <note>original: Vital Congruity; the soul's innate fitness to unite with different types of matter</note> should be just as complex. They are made capable of a living union with either *celestial*, *airy*, or *earthly bodies* <note>original: Vehicles</note>; and leaving one should be nothing more than taking up another, so long as the elements continue in their natural state and as soon as the laws of reproduction <note>original: generation</note> permit.

11. These ideas, and a long series of other things consistent with them, present themselves to the view of those who have the favor of beholding the more hidden treasures of the *Divine Benignity* <note>God's kindness or benevolence</note>. But since these points are more than the present occasion requires, I shall content myself with what precisely touches the matter at hand: that the soul of man is capable of acting after this life in an *airy body* <note>original: Aëreal Vehicle</note>, just as she does here in an *earthly* one. Because it is better that she live and act than that she be idle and silent in death, and because it depends merely upon the will of God whether she shall

whether [the world] shall [be so] or not; since He orders the natures of things infallibly according to what is best, He must of necessity ordain that the souls of men live and act after death. This is an unavoidable deduction of reason for those who acknowledge the existence of God and rightly appreciate that transcendent attribute in the Divine Nature. For those who have a true sense of it can no more deny this conclusion than they can deny the existence of the Deity itself. Nor can they ever be persuaded that He—who is so perfectly good in Himself and to whom they have so long remained faithful in obedience and loving <note>original: amorous</note> devotion—has made them with such a nature that, at the very moment they hope most to enjoy Him, they shall be unable to enjoy Him at all, or anything else, because they lack the capacity to act outside of an earthly body. But those who possess a merely animal temperament—who appreciate no love but for themselves and their own interests, and care for no one except those who are useful to them or provide profit—are prone to judge God according to the vileness of their own spirit. They will easily imagine <note>original: conceit</note> that God’s care and tenderness for us is only proportional to the benefit He receives from us—which is, in fact, nothing at all.

12. Therefore, this argument especially, as well as the previous two, are undeniable demonstrations in themselves. However, because they require a proper appreciation <note>original: resentment; here meaning a sensitive feeling or perception</note> of morality—that is, of *truthfulness*, *justice*, and *goodness*—in the person who is to be persuaded by them, it follows that those whose minds are most blinded and debased by vice will feel their force the least. Conversely, the *noblest and most generous spirit* will be the most firmly assured of the *immortality of the soul*.
