### CHAP. I.

*1. Why the Author treats of the state of the Soul after Death, and in what Method. 2. Arguments to prove that the Soul is ever united vitally with some Matter or other. 3. Further Reasons to prove the same. 4. That the Soul is capable of an Airy and Ethereal Body, as well as a Terrestrial. 5. That she ordinarily passes out of an Earthly into an Aerial <term>Vehicle: In Neo-Platonic philosophy, a "vehicle" is the subtle body or medium that the soul inhabits when it is not in a physical, earthly body.</term> Vehicle first. 6. That in her Airy Vehicle she is capable of Sensation, Pleasure, and Pain. 7. That the main power of the Soul over her Aerial Vehicle is the direction of motion in the particles thereof. 8. That she may also add or diminish motion in her Ethereal vehicle. 9. How the purity of the Vehicle contributes <note>original: confers to</note> to the quickness of Sense and Knowledge. 10. Of the Soul’s power of changing the constitution <note>original: temper</note> of her Aerial Vehicle; 11. As also the shape thereof. 12. The plainness of the last Axiom.*

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'W' featuring floral scrolls and foliage patterns.</image-desc>

WE have, I hope, with undeniable evidence demonstrated the Immortality of the Soul to those who, neither by their dullness of mind <note>original: slowness of parts</note> nor any prejudice toward immorality <note>original: prejudice of Immorality; likely referring to moral corruption which blinds one to spiritual truths</note>, are made incompetent judges of the truth of demonstrations of this kind. So, I have already finished my main purpose. But my own curiosity, and the desire of satisfying others who love to occupy themselves with speculations of this nature, call me out a bit further—especially if the very dignity of the present matter I am upon does not justly require it of me, as will be best seen after finishing it. This subject concerns the State of the Soul after Death. In this, though I may not perhaps <note>original: haply</note> be able to plant my foot as firmly as in the previous part of this treatise, yet I will assert nothing but what shall be reasonable, even if not demonstrable, and which far outweighs whatever shall be argued to the contrary, and in such clear order and

[...my] method, so that if what I write is not worthy to convince, it at least will not be able to deceive or confuse by complexity and obscurity. Therefore, I shall present for view all at once the main principles upon which I shall build the rest of my discourse.

### AXIOM XXVII.

->The Soul, when separated from this earthly <note>original: "Terrestrial"</note> body, is not released from all vital union with matter.<-

2. This is the general opinion of the *Platonists*. *Plotinus* indeed dissents, especially concerning the most divine souls, as if they at last were perfectly stripped of all matter and had no union with anything but God himself. I look upon this as a whim proceeding from the same unevenness of temperament that made him suppose that the most degenerate souls eventually slept in the bodies of trees and grew up merely into a *plant-like life* <note>original: "Plantal life"</note>. Such fictions of imaginative men have much corrupted the ancient *Cabbala* and sacred doctrine which the *Platonists* themselves claim to be "given by God" <note>original: *theoparadoton* (Greek: θεοπαράδοτον); a holy tradition received from the mouth of God or angels</note>. However, even *Plotinus* himself does not deny that until the soul arrives at such an exceeding height of purification, she acts in either an *airy* or *celestial body*.

But the idea that she is never released so perfectly from all *matter*—however pure and thin <note>original: "tenuous"</note> it may be—is a stronger conclusion drawn from her condition of operating here in this life than can be found anywhere else. For we find plainly that her most subtle and most *intellectual* operations depend upon the *fitness of the condition* <note>original: "fitness of temper"</note> in the *animal spirits* <note>original: "Spirits"; in 17th-century physiology, these were subtle fluids or gases in the body thought to be the medium of thought and sensation</note>. It is the *fineness and purity* of these spirits that invites her and enables her to love and seek after *divine* and *intellectual objects*. If she could perform these kinds of motions directly by her own proper power and essence, what would hinder her, since she has a will, from bringing them to effect? Yet we find she cannot do so if the *spirits* are *indisposed* <note>original: "indisposed"; meaning out of balance or in poor condition</note>. 

As I said, the soul could not be hindered by the improper condition of the spirits in these acts if they were of such a nature that they belonged to the bare essence of the soul, completely separated <note>original: "prescinded"</note> from all union with *matter*. For then, regarding these acts, it would be all the same where the soul is—that is, in what *matter* she is (and she must be in some, because the universe is everywhere densely packed with *matter*)—whether she be raised into the purest regions of the *air*, or plunged down into the foulest depths of earth or water. Her *intellectual* actings would be the same in both; for this physical union likely only engages the *plastic* <note>original: "Plastick"; the soul's unconscious power to shape and organize the body</note> and *sensitive* powers of the soul, even when she is vitally united with *matter*. What else is there imaginable in the body that can hinder her in her nobler operations?

Therefore, it is plain that the nature of the soul is such that she cannot act except in dependence on *matter*, and that her operations are, in one way or another, always modified by it. And therefore, if the soul acts at all after death (which we have demonstrated she does), it is evident that she is not released from all *vital union* with every kind of *matter*.

<summary>Axiom 27 argues that the soul is never entirely separated from matter, maintaining that even after death, it requires a "vehicle" (airy or celestial) to function. The author supports this by noting how intellectual activities in life are dependent on the physical state of the body's spirits.</summary>

whatsoever. This is not only the opinion of the *Platonists*, but of *Aristotle* as well, as can be easily gathered from what we have cited from him above.

<margin>Book 2, chapter 14, sections 4, 5</margin>
3. Besides, it seems like a very wild leap in nature for the human soul to go from being so deeply and muddily immersed in matter as to keep company with beasts—through its vital union with gross flesh and bones—and then suddenly change so much that it would not adhere to any matter whatsoever. It would then ascend into an immateriality <note>original: *aylotes* (Greek: ἄϋλότης); a state of being entirely without matter</note> that is perhaps compatible with no one but God himself—unless there are such creatures as the *Platonists* call *Intellects* <note>original: *Noes* (Greek: Νόες); pure, disembodied minds</note> or *pure intellects*. This must seem very harsh and inconsistent to any impartial person, especially if we consider the noble beings that exist just below the level of the *Intellect* <note>original: *Noos* (Greek: Νόος)</note> or *Intellects*. All philosophers who have ever written about them acknowledge that these beings are vitally united with either *aerial* or *ethereal vehicles* <note>In Neo-Platonic philosophy, a "vehicle" is a subtle body—made of air or light—that carries the soul after it leaves the physical body.</note>. All *Genii* <note>spirits or guardian spirits</note> or Angels are of this condition.

It is enough, therefore, that the soul never exceeds the immateriality of those higher orders of beings. The ignorance of nature shown by those who deny that the lower spirits are vitally united to vehicles made of air seems to clearly reveal <note>original: "bewray"</note> their mistake. It would have been an easy thing, and better for their reputation, to have informed their followers about the mysteries of nature; but they themselves were ignorant of these things. They would have realized this if they were not bound to their airy bodies. For if they were not, they would not be forced to move along with the entire flow of the air. Instead, by keeping themselves steady and being disconnected from all matter, they could have perceived in a single moment both the *daily* <note>original: "diurnal"</note> and *yearly* <note>original: "annual"</note> motion of the *Earth*. By doing so, they could have saved the reputation of their followers by sharing this theory with them. The lack of this knowledge ruins their credibility with those who understand the system of the world better than they do, despite their boasting that their philosophy is like the dictates of the highest angels.

### AXIOM XXVIII.

->*There is a triple vital suitability <note>original: "congruity"</note> in the soul: namely ethereal, aerial, and terrestrial.*<-

<margin>Book 2, chapter 14, section 1</margin>
4. I have previously noted that this is the common opinion of the *Platonists*. That this opinion is also true in itself appears from the preceding axiom. There can be no doubt about the *terrestrial suitability*; and it is just as certain that at least one of the other two must be granted, otherwise the soul would be released from all *vital union* with matter after death. Therefore, the soul has a *vital aptitude* at least to unite with *air*. However, *air* is a common container for both bad and good spirits (just as the *earth* is for all sorts of humans and animals). In fact, it is more a place for those who are in some way bad than for the good, just as it is on *earth*. But the soul of man is capable of very high refinements, even reaching a condition that is purely angelical. For this reason, logic judges it appropriate—and all of antiquity has voted for it—that the souls of men who have reached such a high level of purification must at last obtain *celestial vehicles*.

<summary>More argues that the soul does not become entirely disembodied after death but moves into "aerial" or "ethereal" bodies depending on its level of purity. He suggests that if spirits were truly matterless, they would have easily discovered the Earth's rotation and orbit long ago.</summary>

### AXIOM XXIX.

->*According to the usual custom of Nature, the soul awakes in an orderly way into these Vital Congruities, not passing from one extreme to another without any stay in the middle.*<-
<note>Vital Congruities: The soul’s inherent fitness or natural compatibility with a specific type of body (earthly, aerial, or ethereal).</note>

5. **T**his truth, besides the fact that at first sight it cannot but seem very reasonable according to that well-known aphorism, *Nature does not make leaps* <note>original: *Natura non facit saltum*</note>; so if it is further examined, its solidity will more fully appear. For considering how small a degree of purification the souls of almost all men achieve in this life—even those who are commonly considered honest and good men—it will plainly follow that very few arrive at their *Ethereal Vehicle* <note>A "vehicle" is a subtle body used by the soul; the ethereal vehicle is the highest form, made of pure light or fire.</note> immediately upon quitting their *Terrestrial Body*. That is a privilege that has belonged to none but very noble and heroic spirits indeed, of which history records very few. But that there may be degrees of purity and excellence in the *Aerial Bodies* is a thing that cannot be denied, so that a just *Nemesis* <note>original: *Nemesis*; here referring to the natural law of divine justice or retribution that determines the soul's state after death.</note> will find everyone after death.

### AXIOM XXX.

->*The soul in her Aerial Vehicle is capable of sensation properly so called, and consequently of pleasure and pain.*<-

6. **T**his plainly appears from the 27th and 28th Axioms. For there is a necessity that *sensation* results from the vital union of the soul with any body whatsoever. And we may remember that the immediate instrument of *sensation*, even in this earthly body, are the *spirits* <note>In 17th-century science, "animal spirits" were thought to be a very thin, subtle fluid that flowed through the nerves to carry sensory information to the brain.</note>; so there can be no doubt of this truth. And since *pleasure* and *pain* are the proper modifications of *sensation*, and since there is no body that is not *capable of being affected* <note>original: "passible"</note>, it is evident that these *Vehicles of Air* are subject to *pain* as well as *pleasure* in this region where bad things are to be met with as well as good.

### AXIOM XXXI.

->*The soul can neither give to nor take away from the matter of her Vehicle of Air any considerable degree of motion, but she can still direct the particles already in motion whichever way she pleases by the command of her will.*<-
<note>original: *Imperium* (command/authority)</note>

7. **T**he reasonableness of this Axiom may be proven <note>original: "evinced"</note> partly from the former one; for considering the *roughness* <note>original: "brushiness"</note> and *angularity* <note>original: "angulosity"</note> of the parts of the *air*, a more than ordinary motion or a compressive rest may very well prove painful to the soul and discordant to her touch. It can also be proven partly from what we may observe in our own spirits in this body, which we can only direct, not give motion to, nor diminish their motion by our imagination or will. (For no man can imagine himself into heat or cold—the sure consequences of extraordinary motion and rest—by willing his spirits to move faster or slower; but he may direct them...

## AXIOM XXXII.

->*Although the soul can neither give nor take away any significant degree of motion from the matter of her **Aerial Vehicle**, nothing prevents her from doing both in her **Ethereal Vehicle**.*<-

8. The reason for this is that the particles of her *Ethereal Vehicle* consist partly of smooth, spherical shapes and partly of thin matter so incredibly fluid that it yields to anything without resistance. In contrast, the *air* (as can be observed in **air guns** <note>original: "Winde-Guns"</note>) has parts so stubborn and stiff that even after they have been compressed until the barrel of the gun grows hot, they lose neither their shape nor their force. Instead, like a steel spring, when they are released, they return to their natural state with such violence that they fire a bullet with as much force as gunpowder does. Furthermore, we may rightly believe that the goodness of that Deity on whom all beings depend has granted the *Ethereal Vitality* <note>original: "Æthereal Congruity of Life"; the state of being naturally suited to a celestial body.</note>—which awakens only in perfectly obedient souls who can be trusted as entirely faithful to His empire—a greater power than the other, as there is no unsuitability in such a subject possessing it. For it is as easy to conceive that God may endow a soul with the power of moving or stopping matter as it is to conceive of Him granting the power to direct its motion.

## AXIOM XXXIII.

->*The purer the Vehicle is, the more quick and perfect are the Perceptive Faculties of the soul.*<-

9. We can, in a sense, experience the truth of this in this life. We find that the sharpness of hearing, seeing, tasting, and smelling, as well as the quickness of **memory** <note>original: "Reminiscency"</note>, reason, and all other *perceptive* faculties, are increased or decreased by the clarity, foulness, or dullness of the **spirits** <note>In 17th-century physiology, "spirits" were a subtle, fluid substance in the nerves that acted as the medium between the soul and the body.</note> of our body. Forgetfulness and mental dullness arise from their thickness and earthiness, or wateriness, or whatever other heavy consistency they might have. When this imbalance <note>original: "distemper"</note> is removed and the body is replenished with a sufficient amount of pure spirits, the mind recovers her activity again. She remembers what she had forgotten and understands what she was previously incapable of; she sees and hears at a greater distance; and so it is with the rest of the senses.

### AXIOM XXXIV.

> *The soul has a marvelous power not only of changing the temperament of her **Aerial Vehicle**, but also its external shape.*

10. The truth of the first part of this axiom is evident from daily experience. We can frequently observe how strangely the *passions* of the mind affect our "spirits" <note>original: "Spirits"; in 17th-century physiology, these were subtle fluids believed to transmit the soul's commands to the body.</note> in this state. We see how *anger*, *grief*, and *envy* can alter the body, not to mention other *emotions*. Surely, the finer and more subtle a body is, the more easily it is changed by these influences. Therefore, the passions of the mind must have a very great influence upon the soul's **Aerial Vehicle** <note>original: "Aëreal Vehicle"; the body composed of air that the soul was thought to inhabit after the death of the physical body.</note>. Although these passions cannot change the vehicle into anything other than air, they can change the quality of this air into conditions as vastly different as *virtue* is from *vice*, *sickness* from *health*, *pain* from *pleasure*, *light* from *darkness*, or the stench of a jail from the *fragrant* <note>original: "Aromatick"</note> scents of a flourishing *paradise*.

11. The truth of the second part is demonstrable from the latter part of Axiom 31. If we assume the soul has the power to direct the motions of the particles of her fluid vehicle, it must follow that she also has the power to shape it, to some extent, according to her own will and imagination. To this, you may add a significant piece of evidence: what our will and imagination already do in this life. For example, simply because I will and imagine moving my mouth, foot, or fingers, I can move them, provided I have enough "spirits" to direct that motion. The entire vehicle of the soul is, in a sense, nothing but these spirits.

### AXIOM XXXV.

> *It is rational to think that just as some faculties are put to sleep at or after death, others may awake that are more suitable for that state.*

12. The truth of this axiom appears from the fact that our souls do not exist by chance. They are made by an all-wise God who, foreseeing all their future states, has coordinated the *awakening* or the *slumbering* <note>original: "Excitation or Consopition"</note> of their powers and faculties to fit the specific conditions they will inhabit.

### CHAPTER II.

1. *Regarding the dimensions of the soul considered purely in itself.*
2. *Regarding the shape of the soul’s dimensions.*
3. *Regarding the diverse nature of its essence.*
4. *That there is a diversity in its form-giving part that is distinct from its perceiving part.*
5. *Regarding the action of this form-giving part in framing its vehicle.*
6. *The excellence of Descartes' philosophy.*
7. *That the vehicles of ghosts have as much solid, physical substance in them as the bodies of men.*
8. *The foolishness of the opposite opinion is demonstrated.*
9. *The advantage of the soul regarding the matter of its body in the next state compared to this one.*

---

1. To gain a clearer and more definite understanding of the soul's nature and condition after it leaves the body, let us first consider for a moment what it is in its own essence, without reference to any body at all. We shall find it to be a *substance that occupies space and cannot be divided* <note>original: "extended and indiscerpible"; in More's philosophy, the soul takes up space but cannot be physically torn apart or separated into pieces.</note>, as can be easily gathered from what <margin>Book 1. ch. 3, 5, 8. Also Book 2. chap. 1, 2.</margin> we have written above. It is a timely meditation here (where we consider the soul as having left this *earthly body*) to realize that it has just as many, if not more, dimensions of its own than are visible in the body it has left. I believe this is worth noting to silence those who—with good reason—laugh at the inconceivable and ridiculous theories of the Scholastic philosophers. These thinkers first rashly strip all *extension* <note>original: "Extension"; the property of taking up space.</note> from spirits, whether souls or angels, and then argue about how many of them, wearing boots and spurs, could dance on the point of a needle at once. Such follies greatly detract from the truth. They squeeze our perception into such an intolerable narrowness and faintness that we cannot imagine anything regarding our own being. If we try, we are prone to fall into despair or self-contempt, imagining ourselves to be nothing more than insignificant specks of dust in a sunbeam.

2. It is very obvious that the *soul has dimensions*, yet they are *not infinite*; therefore, it is necessarily bounded by some *shape* or another. However, it is very uncertain whether there is any specific *shape* natural to it that matches a *living form*, or whether the soul is naturally of a *round* or *oval shape* and changes its form as the occasion requires. It is not necessary to define this question further than this: when the soul acts upon *earthly matter*, its *form-giving* <note>original: "Plastick"; referring to the 'plastic power,' the soul's unconscious capacity to organize and shape matter into a body.</note> part is directed to organize the body into a *human form*. However, in the *air-like* or *heavenly* <note>original: "Aëreal or Æthereal"</note> realms, the soul is no more restricted to a specific shape than the *spirits* <note>original: "Genii"</note> or angels. If their vehicles <note>original: "Vehicles"; the subtle bodies composed of air or light that the soul inhabits after death.</note> are naturally guided into one shape more than another, the soul's vehicle is in the same condition. Thus, in its visible vehicle, it will take the ordinary form of *angels*, with a similar appearance and clothing.

<margin>Book 2. ch. 11. sect. 10, 11.</margin>

3. What is *more significant* <note>original: "more material"</note>, I think, is easier to define: whether the Soul is one *uniform substance* <note>original: "Homogeneal Substance"</note>, or whether it is in some way *varied in nature* <note>original: "Heterogeneal"</note>. That the latter is true to some extent is clear from what we have written elsewhere—namely, that the *perceiving faculty* does not extend through the *whole Soul* but is confined to a certain part. We called this the *Center* or *Eye of the Soul*, and also its *perceptive part*; but all the rest we called *form-giving* <note>original: "Plastick"; in More's philosophy, the "plastic" power is the unconscious ability of the soul to shape and organize a physical or spiritual body.</note>. But here a further doubt arises: whether there is not also a *diversity of nature* in the very *form-giving* part of the Soul as well. The *Aristotelians* seem confident there is not, and they claim that if there were an eye in the toe, the toe would see as well as the head. I doubt this very much. For if it were true, it would follow that some creatures would have a glimmering light all over their bodies, since they are largely transparent. Furthermore, people with thin and clear complexions might perhaps perceive light through the lower parts of their fingers, which are somewhat translucent. Therefore, because life and spirits are continuous from those parts to the *pineal gland* <note>original: "Conarion"; the pineal gland, which many 17th-century philosophers believed was the seat of the soul.</note> (as they are) or to the fourth ventricle of the brain, it would follow that the Soul would perceive some glimmerings of light from there. This would mean it would *see* there as well as *feel*.

4. Therefore, it seems more rational to admit a *diversity of nature* in the *form-giving* part of the Soul as well. We should acknowledge that every distance from the Seat of *Common Sense* <note>The "Common Sense" was thought to be the internal faculty where all five external senses were unified and processed.</note>—that is to say, every circle that surrounds the *Center* of the Soul—does not have the same power in terms of variety or extent. Instead, there is a gradual decline from the first excellence, which is the *perceptive* part of the Soul. The circle closest to it is that part of the *form-giving* faculty capable of conveying objects of *sight* as well as *touch* and *hearing*, and whatever other senses may exist in the Soul. The next circle allows *hearing* without *sight*, though not without *touch*; for *touch* spreads through everything. But in its outermost region, which is by far the largest, it transmits the specific perceptions of no objects except those that are *tactile*. To other senses, this region acts only as a dead medium, just as the circle of *hearing* is merely a dead medium for objects of *sight*. So, if we wish to indulge our imagination with *Ficino* <note>original: "Ficinus"; refers to Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), a Renaissance Neo-Platonist philosopher.</note> by imagining the Soul as a star, we shall do so more perfectly if we look upon it as having an *aura* <note>original: "Halo"</note> around its circles. To our *reason*, the Soul is no more *uniform* than that celestial sight is to our *vision*.

5. But if we look upon the Soul as always leaning toward some personal shape, the direction of its *form-giving rays* must then tend toward a kind of organization, insofar as it serves the state the Soul is in—whether in an *Airy* or *Ethereal Vehicle* <note>More believed the soul inhabited subtle bodies made of air or ether after departing the physical body.</note>. We can see that the *form-giving power* omits or changes certain things as it is influenced by the nature of the matter it acts upon in the way it organizes our bodies here. For in all likelihood, the Soul in itself is as much of one sex as the other. This causes it sometimes to mark the *matter* with both sexes, though that happens very seldom. Therefore, it is clear that she omits one part of her *form-*

From this, it is easy to conclude that, assuming her *form-giving* <note>original: "Plastick"; the soul's unconscious ability to organize matter into a living body.</note> power naturally shapes the *ethereal* or *aerial vehicle* <note>In 17th-century Neoplatonism, a "vehicle" is the subtle body composed of air or ether that the soul inhabits when not in a physical body.</note> into any *animal shape*, it may only produce such features of that creative power as are suitable and fitting for an *angelic nature*.

However, according to this hypothesis, perhaps all *objects of sense* will not reach the *center of the soul* from every part of the horizon; not even if this organization were not natural but merely chosen by the soul. But whether the soul is imagined as bound up in an *animal form* or spread out in a loose, circular shape—depending on how her rays display themselves in her *vehicle of air* or *ether*—the *seat of sight* will still be properly limited, which is a consideration of no small importance.

6. This general explanation may be enough regarding the very nature of the soul itself, its *extension* <note>The property of taking up space.</note> and its *varied nature* <note>original: "Heterogeneity"</note>. I will only add one more observation concerning her *airy* and *ethereal vehicle*, and then I will move on to more specific investigations. Rash fantasies and false conclusions from misunderstood experiments have made some people very confident that there is a *vacuum* in nature, and that the lighter a body is, the less actual substance it contains. This is a very foolish and irrational idea at first sight to anyone even reasonably well-versed in the incomparable philosophy of *René Descartes* <note>original: "Renatus Des-Cartes." Descartes argued that the universe is a "plenum," meaning it is entirely full of matter, and there is no such thing as empty space.</note>. His clever wit and thorough insight into the nature and laws of matter have so perfected the explanations for those *phenomena* that *Democritus*, *Epicurus*, *Lucretius*, and others puzzled over, that nothing more seems to be needed regarding that way of philosophizing except patience and an unbiased judgment to read what he has written.

7. Therefore, according to his philosophy—and the truth—there is always as much matter or body in one state of consistency as another. For example, there is as much matter in a cup of air as in the same cup filled with water, and as much in a cup of water as if it were filled with lead or *quicksilver* <note>Mercury.</note>. I mention this here so that I may free the human imagination from that common and ignorant misunderstanding people have about *spirits* that appear. They think spirits are as vanishing and devoid of substance as the shadows of our bodies cast against a wall, or our images reflected in a river or mirror. Because of this error, they have given them names accordingly, calling the ghosts of men that appear to them *images* <note>original Greek: "Εἴδωλα" (*Eidola*)</note> and *shadows* <note>original Latin: "Umbræ"</note>. People think that the more visible these are, the more substantial they are. They imagine that the *air* is so condensed that there is not only more of it, but that there is simply more matter or substance when it becomes visible than there was in the same space before. Consequently, they must imagine that death reduces us to a pitiful, thin scrap of being—that our substance is essentially lost, and nothing remains but a thin vapor, no more in proportion to us than what a sweating horse leaves behind him as he 

gallops...

...gallops by on a frosty morning. This must certainly be a very lamentable consideration to those who love this thick and plump body they carry around with them, and who are pleased to remember how many pounds they outweighed their neighbor the last time they were weighed together on the scales.

8. But if a sort of uncertain *transparency* is thought to prove a lack of physical substance, then a pillar of *crystal* would have less substance than a pillar of *tobacco smoke*. Though smoke may be such a doubtful and vanishing <note>original: "evanid"</note> object to the eye, if we test it by hand, it will prove to be much less solid than the crystal. Similarly, those *ghosts* that are said to appear in this transparent manner have proved their solidity to those who have touched them, or have been touched by them. For it is ridiculous and unworthy of a philosopher to judge the quantity of physical *matter* by how it appears to our *sight*; for by 그 that logic, *air* would be nothing at all. Nor should we judge it by how it feels to our hands or how much it weighs; for if we did, a cup of mercury <note>original: "Quick-silver"</note> would seem to have infinitely more matter in it than one filled only with air, and a vessel of water would seem to have less matter when it is plunged under the water in a river than when it is carried through the *air*. But we must remember that regardless of what consistency matter takes—even if it is as thin and pure as the flame of a candle—there is no less physical *substance* in it than there is in the same dimensions of silver, lead, or gold.

9. So we do not need to mourn the shriveled condition of the deceased, as if they were stripped of almost all physical substance and were too thinly clothed to enjoy themselves or any object of the senses. For they have no less "body" than we ourselves have; the only difference is that this body is far more active than ours, being more *spiritualized*. That is to say, it has greater degrees of motion communicated to it. Since all the matter in the world receives its motion from some *spiritual being* or another, matter may be said to more closely resemble that *immaterial being* the more motion is communicated to it. This resemblance also appears in the effect of that motion: namely, the thinness and subtlety of its particles. Through this fineness, the body is enabled to imitate, in some way, the special privilege of spirits—the ability to pass through all bodies whatsoever. These "vehicles of the soul," <note>In More's philosophy, the "vehicle" is the subtle body (made of air or ether) that the soul inhabits after leaving the gross physical body.</note> because of the thinness of their parts, may easily pass through matter that seems solid and impenetrable <note>original: "impervious"</note> to us, though it is not actually so to them. For matter reduced to such a fluid subtlety of invisible particles may easily enter through pores that are too small to be seen.

From this it is manifest that the soul, speaking in a natural sense, loses nothing by death, but is a very considerable gainer by it. For she does not only possess as much "body" as before, with just as full and solid dimensions, but she also receives the added benefit of having this body more invigorated with life and motion than it was formerly. I could not help but take notice of this consideration, so that I might wipe away that false notion <note>original: "conceit"</note> that haunts most people's imaginations: the idea that the afterlife is a state of vanishing and starved weakness.

## CHAPTER III.

*1. That the natural home of the Soul after death is the Air. 2. That it cannot leave the Aerial Regions until the Ethereal Congruity of life is awakened in it. 3. That all Souls are not in the same Region of the Air. 4. Cardan's idea of placing all Daemons in the upper Region. 5. The use of this idea for showing the reason for their seldom appearing. 6. That this phenomenon is explained by a more rational hypothesis. 7. A further refutation of Cardan's opinion. 8. More tending to the same goal. 9. The origin of Cardan's error concerning the remote operations of Daemons. 10. An objection: how Daemons and separate Souls can be in this lower Region, where winds and tempests are so frequent. 11. A preparation for an answer from the consideration of the nature of the winds. 12. Particular answers to the objection. 13. A further answer from the nature of the Static Faculty of the Soul. 14. Another from the sudden power of activating its Vehicle. 15. What discomforts it suffers from hail, rain, etc.*

1. The more specific inquiries we intend to address can be reduced to these few topics: namely, *the place where the soul lives, its employment, and its moral condition after death.* That the place of its residence is the *air* is the constant opinion of ancient philosophers and natural theologians, who unanimously make that element the home of departed souls. For this reason, they called it <term>Hades</term> <note>original: <term>ἀΐδης</term></note>, which means <term>invisible</term> <note>original: <term>ἀϊδὴς</term></note>, because deceased people are in a state of *invisibility*, just as the place they are confined to is an element utterly *invisible* by its own nature, and is also filled with dark mists and enveloped by the rotating dark shadow of the Earth. The truth of this opinion of theirs is plainly demonstrable from the 29th and 31st Axioms <note>Earlier in the book, More established "axioms" regarding how souls connect to matter</note>. For since nature makes no enormous jumps, it must follow that separate souls must take their first station in the *air*, because that *Vital Congruity* <note>The soul's natural fitness or "tuning" to a specific type of body</note> that fits an *Aerial Vehicle* <note>A spirit-body made of air</note> naturally awakens immediately upon leaving the *earthly body*.

2. Therefore, since the soul is thus vitally united with a *body* or *vehicle* of *air*, it is impossible for it to move out of those regions. This is because its motions are limited by the capacity of its vehicle; it is not able to change the consistency of that vehicle into any state more subtle or pure than the *air* will allow while still remaining its own kind. The soul can only *thicken* <note>original: "conspissate"</note> the *air* by directing its motion toward itself, and by squeezing out a considerable part of the "first and second element" <note>In the science of the time, these were the finest, most subtle particles of matter</note>, it may retain more air than usual. But it cannot command the air away from itself entirely so as to inhabit those two finer elements alone (or any significant part of them), because the *Ethereal Congruity* of life—the fitness for a body of pure light or ether—is still entirely asleep. Nor is it in the power of the soul to awaken this state whenever it pleases. Therefore, it would be pain and death to the soul to attempt to remove the *Aerial matter* entirely from itself. Besides, it

3. Therefore, it is necessary that the soul, having departed this life, should be somewhere in the **Air**, though it is not at all necessary that all souls should inhabit the same region of it. For as some souls are more purified than others when they leave the body, so a more pure degree of **Vital Congruity** <note>The soul’s natural resonance or "fitness" for a particular type of body or environment.</note> will awaken in them. From this, by that **Divine Nemesis** <note>The natural law of cause and effect or divine retribution that balances the universe.</note> that runs through all things, they will be naturally conveyed to such places and be associated with such company as is most suitable to their **nature**. They will be as distinctly sorted by that Eternal Justice that God has so deeply engrafted into the very essential fabric of the **Universe**, just as human laws dispose of people here—sending some to **Prisons**, some to **Pest-houses** <note>Hospitals for those with contagious diseases like the plague.</note>, and others to the **Prytaneum** <note>original: "Prytaneum"; a public hall in ancient Greece where distinguished citizens and heroes were honored and fed at the public's expense.</note>.

4. It will therefore, in all likelihood, fall to the lot of some souls to be fatally fettered to this **lower region of the air**, as I do not doubt many other **Spirits** are. However, **Cardan** <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), an Italian polymath.</note> greatly pleases himself with a peculiar idea of his own: he suggests that the **highest region of the air** is the only habitation of all **Demons** <note>original: "Daemons"; in this context, spirits or supernatural beings, not necessarily evil.</note> or **Spirits** whatsoever. He argues that their descent to us is as rare as **humans** diving to the bottom of the **Sea**, and almost as difficult. He believes this thick **air** we breathe is as unsuitable to their thin, subtle consistencies as **water** is to us, in which we are forced to hold our breath and, consequently, make a very short stay in that **element**.

Besides this, he imagines that passing through the **Middle Region** of the air is tedious to them because of its coldness. Therefore, he says it is like a fence between us and them, just as the **Sea** is between the **Fish** and us. Although we far exceed fish in **intelligence** and **industry**, and have a great desire to catch and kill them, we actually get very few into our hands compared to those that escape us. And so these **Demons**, though they wish us no good, can hurt none of us through physical conflict (it being so difficult for them to reach us), and very few of us are harmed by their **skill** and **industry**.

For this fanciful philosopher claims they only attempt to target us as we do **fish**, using **baits**, **nets**, and **eel-spears**, or similar **engines** which we cast into the bottom of the **water**. So, he says, these **Aerial Spirits** <note>original: "Aëreal Genii"</note>, keeping their station above in the **third region of the air** (just as we stay on the bank of the **river**, or in a **boat** on the **sea** when we fish), may entangle some men by sending down **dreams** and **apparitions**. By causing frights and mental disturbances, they may—even at this distance—eventually work a person's ruin and destruction.

5. I suppose he framed this hypothesis to explain why the appearance of **Spirits** <note>original: "Genii"</note> is so rare, and why they do so little harm. An answer would be ready for him: that this **lower air** is no **element** for them to live in. He argues that it is just as foolish for people to say there are no **spirits** because they are so seldom seen, as if...

6. This parable holds true, though not for the same reasons, simply by substituting a *difference of condition* for a *distance of place*; the comparison will prove just as sound as before. For a spirit to **condense** his <term>Vehicle</term> <note>The "Vehicle" is the subtle body composed of air or light that a soul inhabits after death.</note> to a nearly earthly thickness and visibility is as rare and strange as for land animals to dive to the bottom of the sea, and it is likely just as difficult. Therefore, the reason is obvious why so few are seen, and the confident denial of their existence is as rash and foolish by those who have not seen them. It is as if the fishes should debate among themselves about the existence of humans and their diving into the water, and whether there were any "haunted" places in the sea—thinking that those places where people fish for pearls, or that cause frequent shipwrecks, or are most pleasant to swim in, would be the most famous. We must reasonably conclude that only some notable occasion, accident, or weighty purpose—the kind that occurs only rarely—would be the only invitations to the **Genii** <note>Spirits or guardian beings.</note> to expose themselves to our view.

7. That there is so little harm done by them need not be blamed on the *distance of their home*, but rather on the **Law of the Universe**, whose force penetrates through all levels of being. Besides, it is too trivial and naive a thought—and far below the level of a philosopher—to think that all **Aerial Spirits** are haters of mankind who take delight merely in destroying them. After all, humans do not hate fish because they live in a different element, but catch them merely out of self-interest, for profit and food—which the airy **Genii** cannot aim for by destroying us. To do mischief merely for the sake of mischief is such an extreme enormity that some doubt whether it is even compatible with any **Intellectual Being**. And therefore <term>Cardan</term> <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), a famous Italian physician and polymath who wrote extensively on the nature of spirits.</note> ought to have proved that first. For we may observe among ourselves that even men who are quite wicked still shrink from things that are uselessly and grossly destructive to either man or beast. They themselves would help to destroy, punish, or at least hinder anyone attempting such wild and outrageous acts that have no basis in reason, but are merely an exercise in cruelty and the harassment of other creatures.

He must also show that at least a **Civic Goodness**—the kind that ensures the safety of people and their property—is not significantly more prevalent even in these **Kingdoms of the Air** than gross injustice. 7. To claim that these aerial inhabitants are too perfect for this world is a flawed assumption. In short, he should have had to prove that **Political Order**, in its full exercise, did not extend from **Heaven** to **Earth**, and even reach into the **subterranean regions** <note>original: "Subterraneous Regions"</note> if there are any intellectual creatures there. This order is a sufficient reason for why so little harm is done, even though all places are full of **aerial spirits**.

8. Add to all this that although they may not be permitted to do any gross evil themselves, or to kill men at their pleasure without their consent, they may still support people in such ways, or invite them to such courses, as will prove destructive to them. But perhaps they do this with no greater malice than we have when we set dogs against each other, fight cocks, bait bears and bulls, race horses, and the like. In these cases, it is often by our doing—as the animals are excited and animated by us—that they pursue their own inclinations to the point of losing their lives.

But though we do not care if a dog or a cock is killed in this way, there are none so barbarous as to club these creatures on the head merely because they wish to do so. Similarly, these worse kinds of **Genii** <note>original: "Genii" - spirits or guardian beings, often thought to influence a person's character or fate.</note>, depending on their tempers, may perhaps follow certain men who are prone to specific vices. They may drive these men into contests, or to please their own fancies, to the furthest extreme they can go. Taking sides, they amuse themselves by making one man overcome another in dueling, in drinking, in craftiness and undermining others, in womanizing <note>original: "wenching"</note>, in gathering riches, in climbing to positions of honor, and so on. In these situations, it may be their pastime to see the person they have favored achieve victory. If that person perishes in the rush of their temptations and encouragements, it is a thing they intended no more, perhaps, than someone who puts his cock into the pit desires for its neck to be broken. But if it happens so, the sorrow is much the same in both cases.

Therefore, these spirits may do enough mischief in the world by supporting the men who act it out, though perhaps they neither take pleasure in doing it on any other terms, nor—if they did—are they able to do it, because there are so many watchful eyes over them. For these **aerial legions** are just as capable of **political honesty** <note>The idea that even spirits follow certain social norms or "honor among thieves."</note>, and may value it as deeply as the nations of the Earth do, and perhaps even more deeply.

9. But if these creatures were removed as far away as **Cardan** <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), an Italian polymath who wrote extensively on the nature of spirits.</note> would have them, I do not see how they could have any communion at all with us to do us either good or hurt. For the idea that they are able to send **apparitions** or **dreams** from such a distance is itself but a dream. It is an idea born from that primary error in **Aristotelian philosophy** which claims that God and the "Intelligences" act from the heavenly spheres to produce all these effects of nature below. Such things can never be done except by a present **divine power** <note>original: "Numen"</note> and **Spirit of Life** that pervades all things.

10. ### CHAPTER III: The Immortality of the Soul

Souls will not be able to keep their *Vehicles of Air* <note>original: "Vehicles of Aire" — in More’s philosophy, the "vehicle" is the subtle, non-physical body or envelope that the soul inhabits after death.</note> around them, but instead, they will be blown to pieces by the roughness of these storms. But we may be easily delivered from this anxiety if we consider the nature of the *Winds*, the nature of these *Vehicles*, and the *Static* power of the Soul. To say they will manage as well as the *Genii* <note>original: "Genii" — spirits or guardian beings.</note> do here is not fully satisfactory, because a person would also willingly understand how the *Genii* themselves are not liable to this inconvenience. My answer, therefore, shall address both.

11. That *Winds* are nothing other than watery particles in their state of greatest agitation, Cartesius <note>original: "Cartesius" — the Latinized name of the French philosopher René Descartes.</note> has very convincingly demonstrated in his *Meteors* <note>original: "Meteors" — referring to Descartes’s 1637 scientific work *Les Météores*, which discussed atmospheric phenomena.</note>. These particles do not so much drive the *Air* before them as pass through it, like a flight of arrows or showers of hail or rain. Therefore, one part of the *Air* is not driven away from another; rather, it is as if one should imagine many little pieces of hair twirling on their middle point like a quarterstaff <note>original: "quarter-staffe" — a long pole used as a weapon; More is using it to describe the rotational motion of particles.</note>, and so passing through the *Air*. This motion would pass freely without carrying the *Air* along with it. This being the nature of *Wind*, the *Air* is not torn to pieces by it, even though we find its force <note>original: "impetus"</note> moving against us, because it cannot penetrate *our* bodies with the same ease that it does the *Air*.

12. But the *Vehicles* of the *Genii* and deceased souls are very much of the same nature as the *Air*; therefore, it is plainly impossible that the *Wind* should have any more force on them than it has on the rest of that element. Consequently, the smallest thing imaginable will hold all the parts together. This is also true even if the *Wind* did carry the *Air* along with it; for then the *Vehicles* of the *Genii* would move along with the stream, suffering little or no violence at all, unless they tried to force themselves against it. They are not forced to do this, nor indeed are they even required to enter the wind, or at least not to stay in it. They may take shelter, as other living creatures do, in houses, behind walls, in woods, valleys, caverns, rocks, and other convenient places. They can do this quite early, as changes in the air and the signs of coming storms are more perceptible to them than to any land animal.

13. And yet they need not be so cautious about staying out of danger, as they have the power to grapple with the greatest of it through their *static* faculty. This faculty arises from the power of *directing the motion* of the particles of their *Vehicle*. Since they have the power of *directing the motion* of these particles whichever way they please (by Axiom 31), it necessarily follows that they can determine their course inwards, or toward the center. By this direction, the particles will all be kept close together, firm and tight; this ability I call the *Static* power of the Soul. If the soul can direct the entire agitation of the particles of the Vehicle—both those of the first and second element as well as those of the Air—partly toward the center and partly in a counter-tendency against the storm, this force and firmness will be far greater than the strongest *Winds* she could possibly encounter.

14. Therefore, the Soul's Vehicle is in no danger from the boisterousness of the winds, and even if it were, there is still no fear that life would cease. For as the wind blows off one part of the Air, it brings on another which

1. THE next thing we must inquire into is the activity of the soul after death; how she can entertain herself and pass the time, whether in *solitude*, in *company*, or as a political member of some kingdom or empire. Concerning all these in general, we may conclude that it is the same for her as it is for the rest of the aerial spirits. As Maximus Tyrius, Xenocrates, Philo, and others expressly affirm, "For the soul, having stripped off the body, is a divine spirit" <note>original: "ἡ γὰρ ψυχὴ ἀποδυσαμένη τὸ σῶμα δαιμόνιόν ἐστι"</note>. But we shall consider these things more particularly.

2. As for those activities with which she may entertain herself in *solitude*, they are either objects of the external *senses* or of the inward *mind*. Concerning the former, it is easier to ask questions than to satisfy them—such as whether she possesses the same number of senses she had in this life. I believe there can be no doubt that she is endowed with hearing, sight, and touch, because these will necessarily belong to her whether her *vehicle* is organized <note>original: "organized" — structured with specific organs like eyes or ears.</note> or not. <margin>* Chap. 2. sect. 3, 4.</margin>
Touch is the most certain <note>original: "incontrovertible"</note> of all the senses. Sight is revealed to us by the transmission of motion through spherical particles. These particles travel from an object through the air to our very organ of sight, which sees only because these particles are vitally united with the soul. Since these same particles permeate the soul's entire vehicle, it is impossible for her not to see. But the question is: does she see through every part of that vehicle? To which I must answer, no. This is partly due to what I have * already explained concerning the *diversity* <note>original: "heterogeneity"</note> of her *formative part* <note>original: "plastick part" — the part of the soul responsible for shaping and organizing the body</note>, and partly because of a major inconvenience that would follow such a supposition. For if we granted that the soul saw through every part of her vehicle, every nearby object would not only appear double, but a hundredfold or a thousandfold. This would be a hideous deformity and a corruption of sight. Therefore, we have very good reason to believe the soul's *visual faculty* is restricted in this state of separation, just as it was in the *earthly body*.

<margin>* Chap. 2. sect. 5.</margin>
3. However, this does not prevent the soul—when she exists in one *uniform sphere of air* <note>original: "homogeneal orb of Aire"</note> without a specific structure—from seeing all around her: behind, before, above, beneath, and in every direction. But if she organizes her vehicle into a specific shape, *sight* may perhaps be restricted, just as it is in us, since we cannot see behind ourselves. We touched upon this consideration * previously.

4. It is plain, therefore, that these *aerial spirits*, though we cannot see them, cannot fail to see us. Indeed, they may see us from a great distance if they can transform their vehicle, or their organ of sight, into an advantageous shape similar to what is achieved with *telescopic lenses* <note>original: "Dioptrick Glasses"</note>. This power would infinitely exceed the contracting and dilating of our own pupils, which is a weaker and more limited attempt toward the high privilege we are discussing. Such a feat seems very possible for *spirits*, according to Axioms 31 and 34. The same may be said of their *hearing*. For the same principle may enable them to shape organs for receiving *sounds* with greater skill and excellence than the most accurate *acoustic device* <note>original: "Acoustick"</note> we have read about or can imagine.

Therefore, it is a very childish mistake to think that because we neither see the shape nor hear the speech of *spirits*, they neither *hear* nor *see us*. For soft bodies can be impressed upon by hard ones, but not the other way around; just as melted wax will receive the impression of a seal, but the seal is not impressed by the wax at all. Similarly, a solid body will stop the flow of air, but the air will not stop the course of a solid body. Every small earthly object will reflect light, but light hardly moves any earthly body out of its place; instead, it is bounced back by it. Therefore, that which is most thin and subtle is most easily acted upon <note>original: "passive"</note>. Consequently, if such a subtle substance serves as the vehicle for the senses, it is the most sensitive.

From this, it follows that since the reflection of light from objects is able to move our own organs, which are not as fine, it will even more certainly move the organs of the *spirits* <note>original: "Genii"</note>, even at a greater distance. But because their bodies are made of transparent *air*, it is impossible for us to see them unless they choose to take the trouble of condensing their bodies into a more *earthly consistency*, which would allow them to reflect light. Nor can we easily hear their

And therefore, unless they intend to be heard on purpose <note>original: "datâ operâ"</note> (of <margin>* See *Antidote*, Book 3. chap. 3. sect. 8.</margin> which the "Devil of *Mascon*" <note>A famous 1651 account of a poltergeist or "demon" in Mâcon, France, that allegedly spoke and sang to residents.</note> is a notorious * example), that impact on the air in their usual discourse can naturally never strike *our* auditory organs.

5. And so that we do not seem to say all this for nothing; it appears that they will have the sense of hearing as well as *seeing* from what I have indicated <margin>* Chap. 2. sect. 4.</margin> * above: that *this faculty* is located near the *common sensorium* <term>the supposed part of the brain or soul where all the senses are integrated</term> in the vehicle, as well as that of *sight*. Therefore, since the vehicle is made entirely of air, such vibrations <note>original: "percussions"</note> of it as cause the sense of sound in us will necessarily do the like in them. They may hear even more accurately, perhaps, if they organize their vehicle for that purpose, which would correspond to the raising <note>original: "arrection"</note> of the ears of animals to better take in sound.

6. That they have the sense of *touch* is inevitably true; otherwise, how could they feel resistance? Resistance is necessary when one body bears against another, because they are impenetrable. And to speak my mind freely, it will be very difficult to prove that they do not have something analogous to *smell* and *taste*, which are very closely related to *touch* properly so-called. For since *fumes* and *odors* pass so easily through the air, they will very naturally penetrate into their vehicles as well. If these *fumes* are thicker and moist, they may cause that variation of *touch* which we mortals call *tasting*; if they are more subtle and dry, they cause what we call *smelling*. If we should admit this, we are still within modest bounds <margin>* *On the Variety of Things* <note>original: "De rerum varietate"</note>, book 16. chap. 93.</margin> compared to others, such as *Cardan* <note>Girolamo Cardano, a 16th-century Italian polymath.</note>, who affirms outright that the *aerial spirits* <note>original: "Aëreal Genii"</note> are nourished, and that some of them enter the bodies of animals to fatten themselves there on their blood and spirits. This is also asserted by Marcus the *Mesopotamian Hermit* in *Psellus* <note>Michael Psellus, a Byzantine monk and scholar.</note>, <margin>* In his *On the Operation of Demons* <note>original: "περὶ ἐνεργείας δαιμόνων"</note>.</margin> who tells us that the purer sort of the *spirits* are nourished by drawing in the air, just as our spirits are in the nerves and arteries; and that other *spirits*, of a coarser kind, suck in moisture—not with the mouth as we <margin>* In his *The Guide for the Perplexed* <note>original: "More Nevochim"</note>, part. 3. chap. 46.</margin> do, but as a sponge sucks in water. And *Moses the Egyptian* <note>Moses Maimonides, the Jewish philosopher.</note> writes concerning the *Sabians* <note>original: "Zabii"; an ancient religious group.</note> that they eat the blood of their sacrifice because they thought it was the food of the *demons* they worshipped, and that by eating it they were better able to communicate with them. If these things could be believed, it would solve that difficult problem concerning the *familiars* of witches—specifically, why they suck from them. But such curiosities, not being much to our purpose, I willingly omit.

7. The conclusion of what has been said is this: it is certain that the *spirits*, and consequently the souls of departed men (who by that very fact <note>original: "ipso facto"</note> are of the same rank as spirits), have the senses of *seeing*, *hearing*, and *touching*, and probably of *smelling* and *tasting*. These faculties being granted, they need not be at a loss for how to spend their time, even if they only focused on external objects; all the furniture of heaven and earth is clearly exposed to their view. They see the same sun and moon that we do, behold the people and conversation of all men, and, if no special law forbids them, may pass from town to town and city to city, as the poet *Hesiod* also suggests:

7. There is nothing that we enjoy but they may have their share <note>original: "fees"</note> of it: fair fields, large and trackless <note>original: "invious"</note> woods, pleasant gardens, high and healthful mountains where the purest gusts of air are to be found, crystal rivers, mossy springs, formal entertainments, theatrical pomps and shows, public and private discourses, and the exercises of religion, whether in temples, families, or hidden cells.

They may also be (and perhaps are not disinterested) spectators of the glorious and mischievous hazards of war, whether sea-fights or land-fights; besides those soft and silent, though sometimes no less dangerous, combats in the camps of *Cupid* <note>The Roman god of desire and erotic love; the author refers to the "battles" of romance.</note>; and a thousand more particulars that it would be too long to list, where they perhaps are not mere spectators but abettors <term>those who encourage or assist another, often in doing something wrong</term>, as *Plutarch* writes. Like old men who are past wrestling, tossing the bar, or playing at cudgels <note>A traditional English sport of fighting with wooden sticks.</note> themselves, yet will assist and encourage the young men of the parish at those exercises, so the souls of departed men—though they have put off the capacity for the ordinary functions of human life along with the body—may still assist and abet those functions, pursuing some design through them. This may be for either evil or good, according to how they were inclined when they were in the body.

8. In brief, whatever is the habit and desire of the soul in this life sticks and adheres to her in the one to come; and she will be sure, so far as she is capable, either to act it out, or to be at least a spectator and abettor of such kinds of actions.

Which, rightly understood, is no poetical fiction but a declared truth in *Plato*'s philosophy. However, he says that every *genius* does not perform every office; rather, as their natural inclinations and habits were in this life, they exercise the same in some manner in the other. And therefore he believes *Aesculapius* <note>The Greek god of medicine.</note> still practices medicine, *Hercules* exercises his strength, *Amphilochus* prophesies, *Castor and Pollux* navigate, *Minos* hears legal cases, and *Achilles* goes to war. 

This opinion is as likely to hold true for bad souls as for good ones; and then it follows that the souls of the wicked make it their business to assist and abet the exercise of such vices as they themselves were most addicted to in this life, and to animate and tempt men toward them. From this it would follow that, since they are spirits (or "demons") in their separate state, if they are also tempters to evil, they will differ very little from actual devils.

...mathematical or metaphysical. For assuredly *knowledge* is not so easy and cheap in this state of separation <note>The state of the soul after it has left the physical body.</note> that they may not advance and improve themselves by exercise and meditations. And since they are capable of forgetting due to disuse <note>original: "desuetude"</note>, it will be a new pleasure for them to recall to mind their almost obliterated speculations. And for those who take more pleasure in *outward sense* than in the operations of their *understanding*, there is so much change in nature and so many various qualities of the air and these inferior elements—which must inevitably act upon their *aerial bodies* to cause more or less gratification or dislike—this also will keep them from being idle. It will set them on a quest for such refreshments and delights as nature will provide for the various inclinations <note>original: "multifarious presages"</note> and desires of their shifting vehicles <term>In this context, a "vehicle" is the airy body or vessel that carries the soul after death.</term>.

10. Not that they do not keep constant to some general inclination, which has divided these aerial wanderers into so many orders or tribes. The ancient philosophers and poets (who are philosophers of the oldest standing of all) assigned proper places to each order: the sea, rivers, and springs to one; mountains and groves to others; and so on for the rest. Because of this, they also gave them those names of *Nereids* <note>Sea nymphs.</note>, *Naiads* <note>Water nymphs found in springs and rivers.</note>, *Oreads* <note>Nymphs of mountains and caves.</note>, *Dryads* <note>Tree nymphs.</note>, and the like. To these you may add the *guardian deities* <note>original Latin: "Dii tutelares"</note> of cities and countries, and those who love the warmth of families and the homely conversation of men, such as they called *household spirits* <note>original Latin: "Lares familiares"</note>. All of these, and hundreds more which there is no need to list—though they are always engaged in one natural tendency—yet because there is such a great variety of occasions to satisfy it more or less, their thoughts may be employed in acquiring and improving those delights that are most agreeable to their own nature. To run over every detail of this would be as endless as it is useless.

These short suggestions are sufficient to make us understand that the *spirits* <note>original: "Genii"</note> and *separate souls* need not lack *employment*, even in *solitude*; for their stay among us must be considered "solitude" when they do not noticeably and personally converse with us.

# CHAPTER V: The Immortality of the Soul.

## 11. That considering how the Soul organizes the fetus in the womb, and moves our limbs at pleasure, it would be a wonder if Spirits did not have such command over their airy bodies as is believed. 12. A further argument from an excessive power some have attributed to the Imagination.

1. But the state of separation <note>The state of the soul after it has left the physical body.</note> does not condemn the soul to this solitude. Instead, being admitted into the Order of the **Spirits** <note>original: "Genii"</note>, she possesses their privileges, which include conversing personally with these **aerial** people, and also, when the occasion arises, with the inhabitants of the Earth—though the latter is much more difficult.

2. As for her conversation with the **aerial spirits** and other separate souls, it must reasonably be concluded to be much more frequent than her interaction with men. Yet, this latter interaction is in some ways easier to understand; because it is certain she can see us, as light is reflected from our opaque bodies to her senses. By **thickening** <note>original: "conspissating"</note> her vehicle <term>The "vehicle" is the airy body or vessel that carries the soul after death.</term>, she may even make herself visible to us. However, since the vehicles of the spirits and souls are naturally and purely **aerial** in their consistency, and since air is a transparent body, it will transmit light entirely. Because no reflection is made from these airy bodies, they can have no perception of one another's presence, and therefore no society or communion with each other.

3. This seems like a significant difficulty at first glance. But it is easily resolved if we consider that **air** allows for many degrees of **rarefaction** <note>The process of becoming less dense.</note> and **condensation** <note>The process of becoming more dense.</note>, and yet it still appears equally invisible to us, as one may observe in a **weather glass** <note>An early scientific instrument, similar to a thermometer or barometer, used to show changes in air pressure or temperature.</note>. It would be even more appropriate to consider the experiment of the **air gun** <note>original: "Wind-gun"</note>, in which the **air** is compressed to a much higher degree of **condensation** than its natural state. Within many of these degrees of compression—if not the very highest—the **air** remains invisible to us. But there is no reason to doubt that during these stages of **condensation**, the **air** (if it were in a glass tube) might become visible to the **spirits** because of the tenderness and delicacy of their senses, long before it would be visible to us.

From this, it follows that the vehicles of the **spirits** may have a consistency different from the surrounding **air**, which is perceptible to them—that is, to one another's sight—even though it is as imperceptible to us as the rest of the **air** is. For example, a man with poor eyesight might not be able to distinguish ice submerged in water from the water itself by sight alone, though he might by touch. Or, if we suppose their vehicles are purer and finer than the rest of the **air**, their presence might be perceptible by that means too. For this vaporous **air** undoubtedly has a confused reflection of light within it, similar to a mist or when the sun shines "waterishly" and predicts rain. Since these reflections <note>original: "repercussions"</note> of light are far more sensible to the **spirits** than to us, any lessening of them would be more noticeable. Therefore, even a small decrease in the reflection from their vehicles would be enough for them to discover one another's presence. To illustrate this hypothesis, the experiment of the **weather glass** is most fitting.

# BOOK III: The Immortality of the Soul

But I consider the other supposition more likely to be true: that just as the aquatic animals that live in the sea have a consistency denser than the element they move in, so it is with these spirits that live in the air—though there is not nearly as great a difference in density here as there is in the water.

4. It is plain, therefore, that the forms of the spirits <note>original: "Genii"</note> and separate souls are visible to one another. Yet they cannot see each other at any great distance, and therefore it is necessary for them to approach one another for mutual conversation. This forces us to say something of their physical movement <term>original: "Local Motion"; the ability of an object to move from one place to another.</term>. This movement is achieved neither by fins nor wings, as it is with fish or birds, who must use those instruments to keep themselves from sinking to the bottom of their respective elements. Instead, it is done merely by directing the agitation of the particles of their vehicle <term>vehicle: In Neo-Platonic philosophy, the "vehicle" is the subtle, airy body that the soul inhabits after leaving the physical body.</term> toward the place they aim for. They move at whatever speed or leisure best pleases them and is compatible with their natures. For they can go no faster than the total movement of the particles of their vehicle will carry that much matter. Indeed, they cannot even go quite that fast; for if they did, it would imply that their vehicles would turn into an absolutely hard body, such as brass or iron, or whatever we find even harder. If that happened, they would necessarily fall down to the Earth as dead as a stone. 

Therefore, those are merely fanciful ideas that attribute such agility to spirits as if they could be here, there, and everywhere at once—skipping from one pole of the world to another and returning to the Earth in a moment. In truth, they can pass with no greater swiftness than is permitted by the movement of the particles of their vehicles, after accounting for the energy required to keep their bodies within a tolerable state of airy fluidity.

5. And this alone will be enough to make them far more active and swift than us. For their whole vehicle is perhaps at least as thin and mobile as our animal spirits <term>animal spirits: In early modern medicine, these were believed to be extremely fine, subtle fluids that traveled through the nerves to facilitate sensation and movement.</term>, which are very few in comparison to this heavy burden of an earthly body that they must drive along with them. But the spiritual bodies of the spirits <note>original: "Genii"</note> have nothing to drive along but themselves. Therefore, they are more free and light compared to us than a spirited horse that has thrown its rider compared to a packhorse laden with a heavy sack of salt.

6. The next thing to be considered regarding the mutual conversation of these aerial spirits is what shape or form they appear in to one another, and whether that form is natural, arbitrary <note>meaning chosen by the spirit's will</note>, or a mixture of both. It is plain that they must appear in some form or another, since their vehicles are not infinite in size. It is the more general opinion that there is no particular form that belongs to them naturally, unless it is that which is the simplest of all forms and the easiest to maintain by external forces: the equal compression of the air on every side of the vehicle. This is the same process by which drops of dew, rain, and hailstones usually take a spherical shape. 

This would also handsomely match the nature of the soul, assuming she consists of a "central" and "radial" essence <note>More’s theory that the soul has a central point of consciousness with powers extending outward like rays.</note> as I have described above, with the "common sensorium" <term>common sensorium: The hypothetical part of the brain or soul where all different sensory inputs (sight, sound, etc.) were thought to meet and be processed into a single experience.</term> placed in the center. In this form, the soul may reside in the air, and perhaps even melt herself—I mean her vehicle—

# CHAPTER V: The Immortality of the Soul

vehicle, into almost as much of a fluid state as the part of the element [air] next to her, so that it may be similar to our retiring into secrecy from the sight of men when we wish to be private by ourselves.

7. But she can, if she wishes—and likely with much more ease—change the consistency of her **Airy Body** <note>original: "Aëreal Body"</note> to such a degree of thickness that there may be a faint sighting of her, like a glimpse of a fish under water. She may even make herself more visible to her fellow **spirits** <note>original: "Genii"</note>, while still keeping this simple, sphere-like <term>original: "orbicular"</term> form. But what conversation there can be between two such masses of living **air**, I do not know. They might indeed communicate their **emotions** <note>original: "Affections"</note> to one another in the same way as is seen in the **eye**, where the movements of the **spirits** <term>In 17th-century physiology, "spirits" were subtle, invisible fluids thought to carry signals between the soul and the physical organs.</term> clearly show the **passions** of the **mind**. So, it seems possible that in this simple shape, they could make known their joy or grief, peaceableness or wrath, **love** or **dislike**, by modifying the movement of the spirits within their vehicle. But how any **intellectual** or **rational conversation** could be held without further organizing their **airy bodies** [into speech organs], I confess I am at a loss to understand.

8. Therefore, the **spirits** and **separate souls**, whatever their shape may be in private, appear in a more elaborate and articulate form when they are to talk with one another. For they can change their **figure** almost as they please, according to **Axiom 34** <note>A logical principle established earlier in More's book regarding the soul's power over its vehicle.</note>. I believe this power is used not only for service but for beauty and decoration. And without doubt, the most perfect beauty is that of **man** in the best examples (choose whichever sex you like), which is far above the rest of the creatures. This is not just our opinion, but the opinion of Him who made us. For He would certainly give the **chief of earthly animals** the noblest **form** and shape. Although this form is much obscured by our unfortunate **Fall** <note>The "Fall of Man" in the Garden of Eden, which More believes corrupted human physical perfection.</note>, we can certainly still guess what it once was. It is most rational, therefore, to conclude that the **airy spirits** converse with one another in **human shape**, at least the better sort of them.

9. But the difficulty now is whether that **human shape**—into which the soul transforms its vehicle—is simply the effect of the **command** <note>original: "Imperium"</note> of her **will** over the matter she animates, or whether her **will** is limited or restricted in its effect by a simultaneous use of her **formative power** <term>original: "Plastick power"; the soul's innate, unconscious ability to organize and shape matter into a living body.</term>. Perhaps the soul's **will** only gives the general command for the vehicle to take an **animal form**, while the fact that it takes the shape of a **man** arises more naturally from the soul's own **formative virtue**. I say this happens in a more easy and natural way; for a strong desire to change the figure into something else might make the appearance look like another creature. But no forced thing can last for long.

The more easy and natural shape that the better **spirits** appear in, therefore, is **human**. If this is granted, it is likely that one specific **human shape** may be more easy and natural than another, and that the soul, when she **wills** to appear in a personal form,

<summary>Henry More argues that while spirits can exist as simple spheres of air, they take on human form to communicate rationally.
