# The Immortality of the Soul. BOOK III.

9. The soul will transform her **vehicle** <term>In Neo-Platonic philosophy, the "vehicle" is the subtle, airy body that carries the soul after it leaves the physical body.</term> into one constant likeness, unless she disguises herself on purpose. That is, the **formative** <note>original: "Plastick"</note> power of every soul, whether of men or of other **spirits** <note>original: "Genii"</note>, naturally displays itself in a specific modification of the **human shape**, which is the proper **signature** <term>A "signature" was a 17th-century term for a physical mark or form that identifies the true nature or individual identity of a thing.</term> of every particular or individual person. Although this shape may be slightly changed during biological reproduction by the imagination of the parents or the quality of their seed, once the soul is set free from the body she acquired here, she may perfectly recover her ancient form again.

10. This does not mean that the **formative** <note>original: "Plastick"</note> virtue, awakened by the **command** <note>original: "Imperium"</note> of her **will**, shall renew all the features it did in this earthly body. Many of those features are useless and serve no purpose in that state; therefore, as Providence ordains, they will remain inactive in this **airy form** <note>original: "Aiery figuration"</note>. Only those features will operate that are fit for this separate state, such as those required to perfect the visible appearance of a person, giving him all the parts needed for ornament or for the pleasure of rational conversation. Nor does this **shaping** <note>original: "Efformative"</note> power determine the whole appearance alone, for these **aerial spirits** appear in various clothing—some like beautiful virgins, others like valiant warriors with their helmets and plumes of feathers, as **Philostratus** <note>Flavius Philostratus (c. 170–250 AD), a Greek scholar who wrote the *Life of Apollonius of Tyana*.</note> would have us believe **Achilles** appeared to **Apollonius**. Instead, there is a combined action and effect resulting partly from the freedom of the **will** and **imagination**, and partly from the natural tendency of the **formative** virtue to cast the vehicle into a personal shape.

11. This prerogative of the soul—having the power to shape her vehicle at will—may seem very strange because we do not see it done before our eyes, nor do we often think of such things. Yet, it is not much more wonderful than the fact that the soul organizes the **fetus** in the womb, or that we can move the parts of our body merely by our **will** and **imagination**. As for the fact that **aerial spirits** can do these things—that they can shape their vehicles and transform themselves into various appearances—I need not bring any new examples. The narrations I have recited in my *Third Book against Atheism* sufficiently prove this truth. Truly, considering the great power acknowledged in **imagination** by all philosophers, nothing would seem more strange than if these **airy spirits** did *not* have this command over their own vehicles to transform them as they please.

12. For there are some philosophers, and those of significant reputation, who attribute such wonderful effects to the faculty of imagination when it is armed with **confidence** and **belief**. (To these passions, **fear** may be compared, as it is a strong belief in an imminent evil that will surely happen; likewise **vehement desire**, which is accompanied by a strong persuasion that we may obtain what we want, otherwise desire would not be so active.) I say, they attribute such wonderful force to **imagination** that they claim it will not only alter a man’s own body, but act upon another person's even at a distance. They claim it can inflict diseases on the healthy and heal the sick; that it can cause hail, snow, and winds; that it can strike down a horse or camel and throw their riders into a ditch; and that it can perform all the feats of **witchcraft**, even to the point of making ghosts and spirits appear by transforming the nearby air into the shape of a person...

To such an extent as this have Avicenna, Algazel, Paracelsus, Pomponazzi, Vanini, and others exalted the power of human **imagination**. ## CHAPTER VI.

1. *More credible instances of the effects of imagination.* 2. *A special and peculiar instance in the "signatures" or birthmarks on a fetus.* 3. *That what Fienus grants, who has so cautiously limited the power of imagination, is sufficient for the present purpose.* 4. *Examples approved of by Fienus.* 5. *Certain examples rejected by him, and yet approved of by Fernelius and Sennertus.* 6. *Three notorious stories of the power of the mother’s imagination on the fetus, from Helmont.* 7. *A conjectural inference from those stories: what influence the Spirit of Nature has in all formative operations.* 8. *A further confirmation of the conjecture from birthmarks on the fetus.* 9. *An application of this to the transformation of the vehicles of demons.*

1. BUT I shall keep my belief within more moderate bounds, as that which the most sober authors agree upon is sufficient for our purpose; and that is the power of **imagination** on our own bodies, or what is contained within our own—namely, the **fetus** <note>original: "Fœtus"</note> in the mother's womb. For it is plain that imagination will bring real and sensible effects to pass, in that some have caused diseases in their own bodies by too strongly imagining them; by fancying bitter or sour things, they have brought those real flavors into their mouths; at the memory of some filthy object, they have begun vomiting; at the thought of a medicinal potion, they have begun purging; and many other such things of a similar nature. Among these, the act of setting a time for oneself to wake up in the morning is no less admirable than any other. These alterations of the **spirits** <term>In 17th-century physiology, "spirits" (animal spirits) were fine, subtle fluids thought to carry messages and life-force through the body.</term> to produce such qualities is just as difficult as arranging them into new figures or postures.

Philosoph." referring to Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa's *De Occulta Philosophia*</note>. I would not have repeated this here had I not been credibly informed of a more recent example of a similar effect of imagination, though based on more fanciful grounds. That **fear** has killed some and turned others gray is also to be attributed to imagination. This latter example is a sign that the **formative** <note>original: "Plastick"</note> power of the soul has some influence even on the hair itself. This makes it less marvelous that the soul's vehicle may be turned into the living likeness of a man; not a hair that is necessary to...

2. But of all examples, those regarding the **birthmarks** <note>original: "Signatures"</note> of the **fetus** <note>original: "Fœtus"</note> caused by the **mother's imagination** come closest to our purpose. For we may easily conceive that just as the plastic power in the fetus is directed or misled by the force of the mother’s fancy, so the **shaping power** <note>original: "Efformative virtue"</note> in departed souls and **spirits** <note>original: "Genii"</note> may be governed, directed, or even distorted by the force of their own imagination. This is all the more certain because the union between the soul's imagination and its own plastic faculty is much closer than the union between a mother and the plastic power of another soul (the child's). Furthermore, the capacity for change is much greater in the yielding **airy vehicle** <term>The subtle, non-physical body inhabited by a soul after death.</term> than in the denser, physical beginnings of a fetus in the womb.

<margin>Fienus, *On the Power of the Imagination*, question 22.</margin>
3. Even so, the effects of the mother’s imagination on the marking of the fetus are quite wonderful and almost beyond belief to those who have not examined these matters. However, the more learned sort of both physicians and philosophers agree on its truth—including **Empedocles, Aristotle, Pliny, Hippocrates, Galen**, and all modern physicians—having been forced to agree by daily experience. These "signatures" or marks of a less extreme nature are frequent enough, such as a resemblance to cherries or mulberries, or the color of claret wine spilled on a pregnant woman, along with many similar instances. If we only accept what **Fienus** <note>Thomas Fienus (1567–1631), a famous physician and professor at Leuven.</note> has concluded on this matter—who, I think, has conducted himself as cautiously and modestly as possible—enough will be granted to assure us of what we aim to prove. For he acknowledges that a mother's imagination can change the shape of the fetus so that it resembles an ape, pig, or dog, or any such animal, though the resemblance might not be absolutely perfect. He affirms the same regarding colors, hair, and various types of **growths** <note>original: "excrescencies"</note>: that imagination can produce things very similar to horns and hoofs, and that it can increase the size and number of the parts of the body.

<margin>Fienus, *On the Power of the Imagination*, question 13, examples 5, 7, 18, 19, 27; and question 22.</margin>
4. For instance, he cites the case of the hairy girl from **Marcus Damascenus**; another from **Guillaume Paradin** of a child whose skin and nails resembled those of a bear; and a third from **Boudewijn Ronsse** of a child born with many growths colored and shaped like those of a turkey-cock; and a fourth from **Ambroise Paré** of one born with a head like a frog; and finally, one from **Avicenna** regarding chickens with heads like hawks. All these deviations of the plastic power happened due to the force of imagination in the females, either at the time of conception or while carrying their young.

<margin>Fienus, *On the Power of the Imagination*, question 13, example 14.</margin>

6. But the most notorious instances of this sort are those recorded by **Van Helmont** <note>Jan Baptist van Helmont (1580–1644), a chemist and physician from the Spanish Netherlands.</note> in his work *On Injected Materials*. One tells of a tailor’s wife at **Mechelen** <note>original: "Mechlin"</note> who, while standing at her door, saw a soldier’s hand cut off in a fight. Struck with horror at the sight, she immediately went into labor and gave birth to a child with only one hand; the other arm was a bleeding stump without a hand, and the infant died from that wound due to the great loss of blood. Another woman, the wife of Marcus De Vogeler, a merchant of Antwerp, in the year 1602 saw a soldier begging who had lost his right arm in the **Siege of Ostend**. He showed his still-bloody stump to the people, and the woman immediately went into labor. She gave birth to a daughter with one arm struck off, leaving nothing but a bloody stump for the **surgeons** <note>original: "Chirurgions"</note> to treat. This woman later married a merchant of Amsterdam named Hoochcamer and was still alive in the year 1638, as Helmont writes. He adds a third example of another merchant's wife whom he knew. Hearing one morning that thirteen men were to be beheaded (this happened at Antwerp during the time of the **Duke of Alba** <note>original: "Duke D’Alva," the Spanish governor of the Netherlands known for his harsh rule.</note>), she had the curiosity to see the execution. Taking a place in the room of a certain widow, a friend of hers who lived by the marketplace, she watched this tragic spectacle. She suddenly went into labor and gave birth to a perfectly formed infant, except that the head was missing; the neck was bloody, just like the bodies she had seen of those who had been beheaded. And what makes the wonder even greater is that the hand, arm, and head of these infants were nowhere to be found. From this, Van Helmont would infer a **penetration of physical dimensions** <note>A philosophical concept where two physical objects occupy the same space simultaneously.</note>, but I will not argue how groundless that theory is here.

7. If these stories he recites are true—and I must confess I do not know how to deny them, since he reports them with such honest and credible details—they are notable examples of the **power of Imagination**. Such cases not only win belief for themselves but also for other stories that **Fienus** <note>Thomas Fienus (1567–1631), a physician who wrote extensively on the power of the imagination.</note> would reject—not only regarding wounds to the infant's body, but also more **unusual shaping** <note>original: "exorbitant conformation"</note> of body parts, of which we shall provide an instance or two shortly.

<margin>* Book 2, chapter 10, section 1.</margin>
In the meantime, as I more carefully contemplate this strange virtue and power of the mother's soul (in which there is no such level of purification or spiritual height that it should be able to perform such **miracles**, as I may call them, rather than **natural effects**), I cannot help but be more than usually inclined to think that the **plastic faculty** <term>The innate, unconscious power of a soul to shape and organize physical matter.</term> of the infant's soul—or whatever influences come from the mother's imagination—is not the **complete** <note>original: "adequate"</note> cause of the formation of the **fetus** <note>original: "Fœtus"</note>. This is something that **Plotinus** <note>A major Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> mentions in passing elsewhere, as I have already noted: namely, that the **Soul of the World** <note>original: "Anima Mundi"</note>, or the **Spirit of Nature**, assists in this process.

For we may easily conceive that the deeply impassioned imagination <note>original: "Fancy"</note> of the mother draws the *Spirit of Nature* into agreement. This Spirit may rationally be acknowledged to play a role in the formation <term>original: "efformation"; the process of giving shape or form to a living being</term> of all living beings in the world, and is perhaps the only agent in the forming of all types of *plants*.

8. But this is not the only argument that would move one to think that this *Spirit of Nature* is involved with the formation of the *fetus*. For those *signatures* <term>physical marks or birthmarks believed to be impressed upon the fetus by the mother's mental state</term> that are passed to the infant from the mother's imagination during the act of conception cannot be well understood without this hypothesis. For what could be the subject of that *signature*? It is not the *formative* <note>original: "Plastick"; referring to the soul's ability to give shape to matter</note> part of the mother’s soul; for it is not the mother's soul that shapes the *embryo*. As **Sennertus** <note>Daniel Sennert (1572–1637), a German physician.</note> cleverly suggests from the way birds are formed—which happens in their eggs, separate from the hen, and they may just as well be hatched without any hen at all, a practice common in *Egypt*. Nor is it the *body* of the embryo, for it has no body yet. Nor is it *its own soul*, for the soul—if we believe **Aristotle**—is not yet present there. But the *Spirit of Nature* is present everywhere; when it is drawn into agreement by the force of the mother's imagination, it retains the mark and will be sure to seal it upon the body of the infant.

Regarding the rough beginnings <note>original: "rude inchoations"</note> that the *Soul of the World* <note>original: "Anima Mundi"; a philosophical concept of an intrinsic spirit that connects all living things</note> has started in the matter of the *fetus*, this *signature* is included in the whole design. It is later completed by the presence and operation of the individual *soul of the infant*, which cooperates according to the pattern of the *Soul of the World* and follows in its footsteps. Having once begun any hint of a complete design, the Soul of the World is able to pursue it in any place, as she is everywhere alike, or rather, the same as herself. For just as our soul is one, yet—depending on the various temperaments of the spirits—expresses itself in various imaginations and conceptions; so the Soul of the World, being perfectly the same everywhere, is committed to exerting her *formative* power everywhere alike, where the matter is exactly the same.

Therefore, it would have been no wonder if those chickens mentioned above with hawks' heads had been hatched a hundred miles away from the hen whose imagination was disturbed during the act of conception. This is because the *Soul of the World* had begun a rough draft, which it would necessarily pursue everywhere, just as a geometer certainly knows how to draw a circle that will fit three given points.

This would lead a man to believe that she may not stand idle during the transformation of the "vehicles" <note>the subtle, quasi-physical bodies that souls or spirits were thought to inhabit</note> of the *spirits*, but assists their imaginations and de-

## CHAPTER VII.

1. *Three notable examples of signatures, rejected by* **Fienus**; 2. *And yet so far allowed as possible as will fit our design.* 3. *That* **Helmont's** *cherry and* **Licetus's** *crab-fish are strong arguments that the Soul of the World has to do with all formations <note>original: "Efformations"</note> of both animals and plants.* 4. *An example of a most exact and lifelike signature from* **Kircher**; 5. *With his judgment upon it.* 6. *Another example from him of a child with gray hair.* 7. *An application of what has been said so far, concerning the signatures of the fetus, to the transformation of the airy bodies <note>original: "Aiery Vehicles"</note> of separate souls and spirits <note>original: "Dæmons"</note>.* 8. *Concerning their personal transformation visible to us.*

1. Those other examples of the marking <note>original: "Signation"</note> of the fetus by the mother’s imagination, which Fienus rejects, include one from Weyer. He tells of a man who threatened his wife when she was pregnant, saying she carried the *Devil* in her womb and that he would kill him. Consequently, not long after, she gave birth to a child that was well-shaped from the middle downwards, but from the middle up was covered with black and red spots. It had eyes in its forehead, a mouth like a *Satyr*, ears like a *dog*, and curved horns on its head like a *goat*. The other story is from Ludovicus Vives, about a man who returned home disguised as a *Devil* (a role he had played on stage). Having sexual relations with his wife while in that costume, and saying he would father a *Devil* with her, he impregnated her with a monster that had a clearly diabolical shape. The third and most remarkable story is from Peramatus, concerning a monster born at St. Lawrence in the *West Indies* in the year 1573. The account of this was brought to the Duke of *Medina Sidonia* from very reliable sources. A child was born there at that time who, besides having horrible deformities of the mouth, ears, and nose, had two horns on its head like those of young goats and long hair on its body. It had a fleshy, double-layered girdle around its middle, from which hung a piece of flesh like a purse. In its left hand, it had a bell made of flesh, similar to those the *Indians* <note>The indigenous peoples of the Americas</note> use when they dance, and white "boots" of flesh on its legs, folded down. In short, the entire shape was hideous and diabolical. It was believed to have resulted from some fright the mother took from the "antic" <note>strange, grotesque, or ancient-style</note> dances of the *Indians*, in which the *Devil* himself is said to sometimes appear.

<margin>*On the Power of the Imagination*, question 22.</margin>

3. But *Fortunius Licetus* is more generous in his concessions, allowing not only that the births of women may be very accurately distorted in some of their parts into the likeness of those of *animals* <note>original: "Brutes"</note>, but that fantastical <note>original: "Chimærical"</note> imaginations in dreams may also cause it, as well as fancies or external objects seen while they are awake. This was told to him by a person of credit who both knew the woman and saw the *crab* she produced.

*Helmont’s Cherry*, which he mentions so often, and how it was green, pale, yellow, and red at the times of year when other *cherries* are, is something of this nature. That is to say, it comes close to the perfect species of a *cherry*, just as the other case did of a *crab*. The plant life of a *cherry* was present in some measure in the one, as the life of an *animal* was perfectly in the other. This confirms what we said before: that the strength of our *desire* and *imagination* may pull the *Spirit of Nature* <term>the subconscious plastic power that shapes matter</term> into agreement and make it act. Once it has begun, it does not stop if there is *matter* to work upon; and being the same in all places, it acts the same upon the same *matter* under the same circumstances. For the root and soul of every *plant* <note>original: "Vegetable"</note> is the *Spirit of Nature*; by virtue of this, this *cherry* flourished and ripened according to the seasons of the country where the person who bore that living mark <note>original: "Signature"</note> was located.

These two instances are very strong arguments that the *Soul of the World* <term>the universal life force or Anima Mundi</term> has something to do with all *formations* <note>original: "Efformations"</note> of either *plants* or *animals*. For in all likelihood, neither the child's soul nor the mother's could frame that *crab*. However, the mother might—by that strange power of *desire* and *imagination*—excite the *Spirit of the World*, which attempts to make something out of any matter fitted for generation. Being directed by the fancy of the woman, it might mark <note>original: "sign"</note> the fluid materials in her womb with the image of her mind.

*A Pope sitting on his Throne, with a Dragon under his feet, and an Angel putting a Crown on his head.*

Therefore, a man who was eager to hear a further confirmation of these hopes (which he had developed from the favorable guesses of others) by the expert opinion <note>original: "suffrage"</note> of such a learned man, was willing in private to take off his doublet and show his arm to *Kircher*. After viewing it with all possible care, *Kircher* declared that the *Signature* <term>A "signature" was believed to be a physical mark on a person or plant that revealed its inner nature, origin, or destiny.</term> was so perfect that it seemed more like a work of *Art* than of nature straying from its normal path <note>original: "exorbitating Nature"</note>. Yet, based on certain observations he made, he was well assured it was the work of *Nature* and not of *Art*, even though it was an artistic piece that *Nature* had imitated. Specifically, it was the picture of Pope *Gregory* the Thirteenth, who is sometimes depicted exactly as this *Signature* vividly represented: namely, on a throne with a dragon under his feet, leaning with one hand on his seat, and holding the other in the posture used for giving a blessing, with an angel pulling back a curtain and reaching a crown toward his head.

5. *Kircher*, therefore, setting aside the superstitions and follies of the fake <note>original: "spurious"</note> *Kabbalists* and *Astrologers*, told the man the truth—though it was not nearly as pleasant as their lies and flatteries. Namely, he explained that this *Signature* was not impressed by any influence of the *Stars* or seals of *Angels*. Instead, it was the effect of the *Imagination* of the mother who bore him. In a moment of more than ordinary affection for this Pope, whose picture she saw in a chapel or some other place of devotion, and having some occasion to touch her own arm, she printed 그 image onto the arm of her child, as often happens in such cases. This was undoubtedly the true solution to the mystery.

6. The same *Author writes how he was invited by a friend to contemplate another "strange miracle" (as the friend who invited him termed it) so that he might give his judgment upon it. It was nothing other than an abandoned infant, only about fourteen days old, that had gray hair on both its head and eyebrows. His friend, an apothecary, looked upon this as a great omen <note>original: "prodigy"</note> until he was informed of the cause. The mother who gave birth to the child was married to an old man whose head was entirely white; the fear of being caught in the act of adultery by her snowy-headed husband caused her to imprint 그 color onto the child she carried. I could not omit reciting this story, as it witnesses the exact precision with which the power of *Fancy* <note>original: "Fancy" here refers to the creative power of the imagination.</note> works to fashion and modify physical matter, not missing even the specific colors of the hair, as I have already noted elsewhere.

7. To finally conclude and leave this rich theme: whether it is the *Power of Imagination* leading the *Spirit of Nature* <term>The "Spirit of Nature" was thought to be an unconscious force that organized matter according to higher mental patterns.</term> into agreement, or the *Soul of the Infant*, or both, it is evident that the *Effects* are remarkable. These effects sometimes very accurately match the *Idea* of the pregnant woman, as it is impressed upon the moist and malleable <note>original: "ductil"</note> matter in the womb. Furthermore, the mother's soul is not as uniquely united to the infant's body as a separated soul is with its own vehicle <term>In this philosophy, the "vehicle" is the subtle, airy body inhabited by the soul after it leaves the physical body.</term>, nor does it have any closer or more mysterious connection with the *Spirit of Nature* than she has

The soul has this power when her **plastic** <term>In 17th-century philosophy, the "plastic" part of the soul is its unconscious power to form and organize matter, similar to how an embryo grows in the womb.</term> part, by the **command** <note>original: "Imperium"</note> of her **will** and **imagination**, is to organize her **vehicle** into a certain shape and form. This is a kind of momentary **birth** of the distinct **personality** of either a **separate soul** or any other **spirit** <note>original: "Daemon"</note>. It follows that we may be very certain that there is such a power in the **spirits** and **separate souls** that they can, with ease and accuracy, transform themselves into shapes and forms agreeable to their own temper and nature.

8. All of what I have meant so far refers to their **visible** interactions with one another. But they are sometimes visible to us also, in some **animal** shape, which is undoubtedly much more difficult for them than that other **visibility** among themselves. Yet this is also possible, though far more unusual, as it is more unnatural. For it is possible through technical means to **compress** air so much that it is reduced to a visible opacity. This has been done by some, and particularly by a friend of **Descartes**, whom he mentions in his letters as having made this experiment; the air gains this opacity by squeezing the **particles** <note>original: "Globuli"</note> out of it. While **separate souls** and **spirits** may do this by that **directive faculty** (Axiom 31), it would surely be very painful. Because the "first element" <note>In Cartesian physics, the "first element" consists of the finest, most agitated particles of matter.</note> would be exposed, if the **air** is not drawn together very tightly, it will cause an unpleasant heat; and if it is, an equally unnatural cold. Such a small change in timing will make the "first element" too much or too little, so that it may perhaps be very hard—at least for these inferior spirits—to keep steadily in a balanced middle state. Therefore, when they appear, it is not unlikely that they soak their **vehicles** in some vaporous or sticky moisture or other, so that they may become visible to us at an easier rate.

These spirits appeared not in a personal shape, but by showing a light to the eyes of their abominable spectators and worshippers. I suppose the spirit stirred up this light within the limits of his own vehicle. By the power of his will and imagination (according to Axiom 31), he commanded the thicker particles of the air and earthly vapors, along with the "globules" <note>In the physics of René Descartes (Cartesius), "globuli" are the secondary particles of matter that make up the sky and air.</note>, to pull back in every direction from a central point. From this, the "first element" <note>In Cartesian physics, the "first element" is the finest, most agitated matter, which produces light and heat.</note> is left exposed to a significant degree. The activity of this element must inevitably catch and consume some particles of the vehicle bordering it. Thereby, it does not show a pure, star-like light (which would happen if the first element were unmasked in pure air without being mixed with other matter). Instead, because of the foulness of the parts it wears away and turns into fuel, and the dirtiness of the surrounding vehicle through which it shines, it shows a red and fiery appearance—like the sun on the horizon seen through a thick mass of vapors.

This fiery splendor might either simply slide down among the people and pass by with the motion of the demon's vehicle (which seems to be Psellus's main point), or it might stay a while and speak with those it approaches, as I have heard in some accounts. Since the reason for these glowing appearances is so easy to understand using the principles of Descartes's <note>original: "Cartesius"</note> philosophy, we do not need to imagine that they are nothing but the deceptive tricks of the imagination <note>original: "fancy"</note> rather than real objects, as...

...as Psellus would have them; it being no more incompatible for a spirit <note>original: "Dæmon"</note> to produce such a light in his subtle body <note>original: "Vehicle"</note>, and one even purer than I have described, than it is for a wicked man to light a candle with a tinderbox.

4. What we have said concerning the purity and impurity of this light reminds me of a related topic that is more appropriate to discuss here: the **splendor** and **beauty** of **personal appearance** in the **better** sort of **spirits** <note>original: "Genii"</note>. **This beauty is undoubtedly greater or lesser according to their degree of virtue and moral character.** For even in this physical body, which is not as responsive to the powers of the mind, a person may observe that the air of their face changes significantly based on whether they are well-inclined or ill-inclined. Vicious habits, by defacing the soul's inward beauty <note>original: "pulchritude"</note>, even change the outward countenance to a repulsive appearance.

This must therefore necessarily take place to a much greater degree in the next state, where our outward form is entirely shaped by the inward **command** <note>original Latin: "Imperium"</note> of our mind. The more pure the mind is itself, the more it will display a flawless beauty in the outward features and fashion of the body—both in the proportion of its parts, the spirit and expression of the face, and the ornament of clothes and attire. In the soul, there is an inseparable connection between these three things: **virtue**, **love**, and **beauty**. The soul herself is the first root of all three; and especially in the **state after death** <note>original: "Separate state"</note>, she is the source of outward **beauty** itself. Therefore, the conversation and company of the most **virtuous** spirits there must provide the highest pleasure and satisfaction, not only in terms of rational communication but also regarding external and personal delight. For if **virtue** and **vice** could ever be seen with outward eyes, it would be in these **airy bodies** <note>original: "Aëreal Vehicles"</note>, which are so responsive to the will and the idea of good and pure affections that the soul, in a sense, becomes perfectly transparent through them, revealing her lovely **beauty** in all its blossoming glory to the indescribable enchantment of the observer.

<margin>*An Antidote Against Atheism, Book 3, chapter 16, sections 4, 5, 6, 7, etc.*</margin>

5. I do not mean that there is any necessity for their subtle body to be like a statue of fluid **crystal**. Rather, those **impressions** of **beauty** and **ornament** will be so faithfully and vividly represented, according to the dictates of the soul's inward sense and imagination, that if we could see the soul herself, we could know no more of her than what she displays to our eyes. This personal shaping of the outermost parts—which represent the body, face, and clothing—can be adjusted to such a fine opacity that it may reflect light in colors more perfect than any earthly body can. Yet, the whole subtle body is so weightless that it will naturally keep its position in the air. We cannot find this surprising when we consider how **clouds** hang there, which are much less **airy** <note>original: "Aëreal"</note> than the density we are discussing—to say nothing of **airy apparitions** as high as the clouds, appearing in the same colors and shapes as are seen here below, and yet are not reflections of earthly objects, as I have proved in my third book against atheism.

2. Hence it will follow that the souls of deceased men and the rest of the spirits of the air <note>original: "Aëreal Dæmons"</note> may provide much contentment to one another through mutual conversations concerning the nature of things, whether *moral*, *natural*, or *metaphysical*. For to think that quitting the earthly body entitles us to *omniscience* <note>The state of knowing everything.</note> is a fable that can never be laughed at enough. Even *Socrates*, somewhere in *Plato's* writings, predicts that he shall continue his old trade when he comes into the other world, convincing and confounding the idle and boastful *Sophists* <note>Teachers and philosophers often accused of using clever but fallacious arguments.</note> wherever he goes. By the same reasoning, *Platonists*, *Aristotelians*, *Stoics*, *Epicureans*, and whatever other sects and temperaments exist on the Earth may likely be met with there, so far as that state will permit—though they cannot doubt all the things we doubt here. For these spirits of the air know that they themselves *exist*, and that the souls of men *survive* and *act* after death, unless they are too deeply stained with *Averroism* <note>The philosophy of Averroës, which argued for a single collective human intellect, leading some to believe individual souls do not survive death.</note>.

But it may also be a great controversy among them whether *Pythagoras’s* or *Ptolemy’s* hypothesis is true concerning the motion of the Earth, and whether the stars are as large as some define them. For these lower spirits <note>original: "Dæmons"</note> have no better means than we do to assure themselves of the truth or falsehood of these opinions. Besides this, they discuss news of the affairs of both the *Earth* and the *Air*. For the inhabitants of the air cannot be less active than those on *Earth*, nor less busy, whether in the performance of some solemn exercises or in carrying out designs of one party against another, whether private or public. The events of these actions will fill the aerial regions with a quickly spreading fame. I say nothing of the wise conjectures concerning future successes beforehand, and innumerable other topics of conversation, which would be too long to list, but which bear a very near resemblance to how men pass their time here.

3. But of all *Pleasures*, none are comparable to those that proceed from their joint exercise of *Religion* and *Devotion*. Because their bodies surpass ours so much in thinness and purity, they must be a fitter soil for the *divinest* thoughts to spring up in, as well as the most delicate and ravishing affections toward their Maker. When these feelings are heightened by sacred *hymns* and *songs*, sung with voices perfectly imitating the sweet, passionate expressions of their devout minds, they must even melt their souls into divine love and make them swim with joy in God. But since these kinds of exercises are so highly rapturous and ecstatic, transporting them beyond the ordinary limits of their nature, they cannot in reason be thought to be extremely frequent; but are instead like a solemn feast <note>original: "Repaſt"</note>,

4. Therefore, there are other entertainments which, although they are of a lower nature than these, still far exceed the greatest pleasures and satisfactions of our current state. Since the *animal life* <note>The aspect of the soul governing vital functions and instincts, as opposed to the purely intellectual mind.</note> is as essential to the soul as its union with a body (which it is never without), it follows that there are appropriate gratifications for it in the other world. None greater can be imagined than *sociability* and *personal enjoyment* <note>original: "complacency"</note>, not only in rational discussions—which are so suited to the philosophical mind <note>original: "Ingeny"</note>—but also in innocent pastimes, in which *musical* and *romantic* <note>original: "Amorous"</note> inclinations may also be refreshed. These three dispositions are the best <note>original: "flowr"</note> of all the rest, as *Plotinus* <note>A major Neoplatonist philosopher of the 3rd century.</note> has noted somewhere. > *Now you arrive at the blessed meetings*

Consequently, their food must be very thin and insipid <note>original: "flashie"</note>, more of a mockery than any real satisfaction or pleasure.

8. They may perhaps enjoy this desirable sight in a more perfect way whenever they are admitted into those higher regions of the air.

For the very soil beneath them shall then be *transparent*. In it, they may see with their own eyes the very roots of the trees of this *Higher Paradise*. If it does not bother them, they may even see this opaque Earth through it, their vision ending with a faint white glow like that seen in the moon—with the difference in brightness coming from the distinction between land and water. For they will certainly find the "blood of the grape" <note>Wine or grapes.</note>, ruby-colored cherries, and nectarines there.

### CHAP. X.

*1. How hard it is to define anything concerning the aerial or ethereal Elysiums. 2. That there is political order and laws among these spirits of the air. 3. That this chain of government reaches down from the highest ethereal powers through the aerial spirits to the very inhabitants of the Earth. 4. The great security we live in because of this. 5. We have no other grounds for their existence than the fact that, otherwise, the largest and most noble part of the universe by far would lie uncultivated, like a desert of sand where a man can see neither plant nor living creature. It would seem as strange as if Nature had restricted all the varieties she could produce to one humble molehill, and made all the rest of the Earth a single, uniform surface of dry clay.

# CHAP. X. The Immortality of the Soul.

...clay or stone, on which not one sprig of *grass*, much less any *flower* or *tree*, should grow, and where no *bird* nor *beast* could ever be found to set their foot. Yet, because the *spirits* of us *mortals* are too weak-spirited <note>original: "pusillanimous"</note> to be able to grapple with such vast objects, we must resolve to remain either ignorant or *skeptical* in this matter.

2. Therefore, let us instead consider what will more easily fall under our comprehension: the *social organization* <note>original: "Polity"</note> of the *aerial spirits* <note>original: "Aiery Daemons"</note>. Regarding this, it is most certainly true that such a thing exists among them, and it is very useful for us to be persuaded of it. To know their particular *ranks* <note>original: "Orders"</note> and *customs* is a needless curiosity. However, the idea that they live under the restraint of *government* is not only the opinion of the *Pythagoreans*—who, with the precision of *grammatical criticism*, assigned distinct names to the *law* belonging to three distinct ranks of beings: humans, spirits, and gods <note>original Greek: ἄνθρωποι, δαίμονες and Θεοί</note>, calling the law of the first *Human Law* <note>original Greek: Νόμος (Nomos)</note>, the second *Justice* <note>original Greek: Δίκη (Dikē)</note>, and the third *Divine Law* <note>original Greek: Θέμις (Themis)</note>—but it is also the easy and obvious suggestion of ordinary reason. It must necessarily be so, especially among the *aerial spirits* <note>original: "Genii"</note> in these lower regions. They are a mixed rabble of good and bad, wise and foolish, in the same sense that we say the inhabitants of the Earth are. Therefore, they must naturally fall under a government and submit to laws, for the same reasons that men do. Otherwise, they cannot passably survive, nor enjoy whatever rights may belong to them in one way or another.

Since the souls of deceased men and these *spirits* are endowed with physical senses (according to *Axiom* 30), they are capable of *pleasure* and *pain*. Consequently, they are capable of both *injury* and *punishment*. It is manifest that, having the use of reason, they cannot fail to organize themselves into some *political form*. Thus, they are divided into nations and provinces, having their officers of state, from the King on his throne to the very lowest and most abhorred executioners of justice.

<margin>Chapter 3, section 7.</margin>
3. This invisible government is not limited to the *aerial regions*, but also has authority over the inhabitants of the *Earth*, just as the government of men has authority over various types of brute beasts. Furthermore, the *heavenly powers* <note>original: "Æthereal Powers"</note> also have the right and practice of ruling over the *aerial spirits*. Because of this, nothing can be committed in the world against the most essential laws without a severe and inevitable punishment following. Every nation, city, family, and person is, in some manner, the <term>peculium</term> <note>Latin: a private property or a special charge/territory under one's care.</note>—and therefore under the guardianship—of some invisible power or another, as I have suggested above.

4. We may be assured that transgressions against those laws, without which the creation could not survive, are punished with intolerable *torture*. This punishment is infinitely greater than any *pleasure* the evil *spirits* <note>original: "Genii"</note> could imagine taking in doing mischief to those of their own rank, or to us mortals. From this, it is clear that we are as secure from their major outrages—such as the burning of our houses, the stealing of our jewels or necessary tools, the murdering of ourselves or our children, or the destroying of our cattle and corn—as if they did not exist in the nature of things <note>original Latin: "in rerum natura"</note>. This remains true unless they have some special permission

# The Immortality of the Soul. BOOK III.

For their greatest opportunity to do mischief depends on that relationship; yet this is very limited, because all these actions must involve the consent of a visible person—someone not difficult to discover in these unlawful practices, and easy to be punished by the laws of men.

5. And the aerial spirits <note>original: "Aëreal Genii"</note> can just as easily inflict punishment on one another as we mortals can arrest, imprison, and punish those who break our laws. For though these spirits <note>original: "Demons"</note> are invisible to us, they are not invisible to their own kind. Nor can the activity and cunning of the wicked ones overpower the good citizens there who uphold the laws better than they are upheld among us. Nor can changing their shapes conceal their identities any more than the disguises used by fraudulent men. For they are as able to distinguish what is fake from what is true and natural among themselves as we are among ourselves. And since every aerial spirit is part of some political district <note>original: "Political Subdivision"</note>, if any outrage is committed, it will be an easy matter to track down the criminal. No spirit <note>original: "Demon"</note> is able to change his shape so much that he would not be forced to appear in his natural and usual form upon command, nor would he dare to deny, under examination, which particular district he belongs to. Therefore, the easy discovery of their crimes and the certainty of unbearable <note>original: "insupportable"</note> torment will secure the world from all the disorder that some skeptical thinkers <note>original: "scrupulous wits"</note> suspect would arise from these kinds of creatures, if they actually existed.

6. To this we may also add that what we have is useless to them, and it is very hard to imagine that there are many rational beings so corrupt as to take pleasure in evil when it brings them no personal benefit. Socrates’ aphorism, "Every wicked man is ignorant" <note>original Greek: Πᾶς ὁ μοχθηρὸς ἀγνοεῖ</note>, may be just as true in the other world as it is in this one. All that these evil spirits desire may only be our fall into as great a degree of rebellion <note>original: "Apostasy"</note> from God as they themselves have fallen, so that we might fully share in their false liberty—just as debauched people in this life love to make converts <note>original: "Proselytes"</note> and to be respected by those they have nurtured in wickedness. There are several other considerations that help to remove this panic regarding the invasions and harassments of these aerial inhabitants, which might further silence the suspicious atheist, but I will willingly omit them, having already said more than enough on this subject.

# CHAPTER XI: The Immortality of the Soul.

...the underground caverns of the Earth are used as dungeons for punishing wicked demons. It is as if various volcanoes, such as Etna, Vesuvius, Hecla, and many others (especially in America), were prisons or houses of correction for unruly spirits <note>original: "Genii"</note>.

It is beyond any doubt that they suffer a long and intolerable restraint for the villainies they have committed. Since they possess physical senses <note>original: "corporeal Sense"</note> that are sharper and more sensitive than ours, they are more susceptible to the highest degrees of pain. They are not only confined and guarded in the caverns of burning mountains, where the heat of those infernal chambers and the steam of sulfur <note>original: "Brimstone"</note> must torture them exceedingly, but they are also ordered into various other hollows in the ground, made foul-smelling <note>original: "noisome"</note> by various fumes and vapors. These can torture them in different ways and degrees, fully proportional to the greatest crimes they are capable of committing—far beyond what the cruelest tyranny on Earth has inflicted on either the guilty or the innocent. However, how these confinements and torments are inflicted, and by what degrees or periods of relief they are granted, is something that is neither easy to determine nor necessary to understand.

Therefore, we will stop pursuing such an unproductive subject and move to the third general topic we mentioned: **What the moral condition of the soul is after it has left this body.**

## CHAPTER XI.

10. *That the logic is proportionally the same in matters of less importance.* 
11. *What harm people may cause themselves in the next world through their misguided religious zeal <note>original: "zealous mistakes"</note> in this one.* 
12. *That even if there were no memory after death, the way we live here may sow the seeds of the soul’s future happiness or misery.*

However, the opposite is true, as appears from what we have already proved in my second book: specifically, *that the immediate home of Memory is the soul itself, and that all representations along with their circumstances are preserved in her, not in the spirits* (a fact which *Vanini* <note>original: "Vaninus"; Giulio Cesare Vanini was an Italian philosopher whose views on the soul were controversial</note> himself cannot deny), nor in any part of the body. Therefore, by the 33rd Axiom, it follows that her *memory* will actually be more perfect after death, and her *conscience* more active in excusing or accusing her according to the deeds she performed here.

2. It is also relevant to note that the natural and usual shape of the soul’s *aerial vehicle* <note>The "aerial vehicle" is the subtle, spirit-like body that Neo-Platonic philosophers believed the soul inhabited after leaving the physical body</note> resembles the features of the person during their life. It is most natural for the *formative power* <note>original: "Plastick part"; the soul's unconscious capacity to shape matter or its own spirit-body</note>—acting at the command of the *will* to take on a personal shape—to become as similar to that life as the new state will allow. In this act, the *Spirit of Nature* <note>More’s term for a universal, non-conscious force that executes God's laws in the physical world</note> perhaps concurs, just as it does in the formation of a *fetus*. However, this occurs within the limits of *aerial suitability* for life, which we have already discussed. We also discussed how the unique essence or shape of every soul (though it may deviate slightly due to the power of the parent’s imagination during conception or pregnancy) may return more closely to its distinct appearance afterward, thus serving as an unmistakable *mark of individuality*.

3. To all this, we will add the retention of the same name which the deceased had here, unless there is some special reason to change it. Thus, their persons will be as precisely distinguished and defined as any of ours in this life. All of these things are highly probable in themselves—that they will naturally occur this way—and they are very convenient for the administration of justice and the maintenance of *order* in the next state.

4. With these points established, it will not be difficult to understand how the soul's condition after this life depends on her *moral* behavior here. Because memory does not cease, *conscience* may very likely awake more furiously than ever. The mind will become a clearer judge of past evil actions than she could be while in the flesh, being now stripped of all those circumstances and distractions that prevented her from holding herself accountable or perceiving the ugliness of her own ways. Besides, there is such communication between the *Earth* and the *Air* that at least the reputation <note>original: "fame"</note> of things will reach the knowledge of those who have left this life. The subsequent failure of their wicked enterprises and unreasonable dealings may arm their tormenting conscience with new whips and stings. This happens when they either hear or see with their own eyes that what they unjustly built up has collapsed in shame, and they behold all their designs come to nothing and their reputation ruined on Earth.

5. This is the state of such souls as are capable of a sense of dislike...

# Chapter 11. The Immortality of the Soul.

...of their past actions. One would think they need no other punishment than this, if he considers the mighty power of the mind over its own *Vehicle* <term>the "aerial vehicle" or spirit-body the soul inhabits after death</term>, and how vulnerable that vehicle is to the mind itself. These *passions* of the soul that follow an evil conscience must inevitably bring her aerial body into intolerable distress, worse than death itself. Nor can she die even if she wanted to—neither by fire, nor sword, nor any means imaginable—not even if she were to fling herself into the flames of smoking *Etna* <note>original: "Ætna"; a volcano in Sicily often used in literature to symbolize the entrance to the underworld or extreme physical torment</note>. For suppose she could stay there long enough to endure the hideous pain of destroying the *vital congruity* <term>the specific state of the spirit-body required for the soul to remain connected to it</term> of her vehicle by that sulfurous fire; she would be no sooner released than she would catch life again in the air, and all the former troubles and vexations would return, in addition to the extra weight of those pangs of death. For *Memory* would return, an ill conscience would return, and all those busy Furies—those disordered passions which follow it—would return as well. And so it would be, even if the soul should kill herself a thousand and a thousand times; she could only pain and punish herself, not destroy herself.

6. But if we could suppose some people’s consciences were *seared* <note>hardened or unfeeling</note> in the next state as well as this (for certainly there are those who make it their business to erase all sense of the difference between good and evil from their minds, and hold it to be a high sign of wit—though it is nothing but a piece of brutish stupidity—to think there is no such thing as *Vice* and *Virtue*, and that it is a primary part of perfection to be so degenerate as to act according to this principle without any remorse at all); these men may seem to have an excellent privilege in the other world, being thus armor-proof against all the fiery darts of that domestic devil. It would be as if the greatest security in the next life were to have been completely wicked in this one.

But it is not beyond the reach of mere reason and philosophy to discover that such bold and shameless wretches who have lost all *inward* sense of good and evil may, against their wills, feel a lash from the *outside*. For Divine Retribution <note>original: "Nemesis"; the Greek goddess of inescapable justice</note> is excluded from no part of the universe; and *Goodness* and *Justice*, which they despise here, will make themselves known to them in that other state, whether they want them to or not. I speak of such coarse spirits who can swallow murder, perjury, extortion, adultery, sodomy <note>original: "Buggery"</note>, and similar gross crimes without the least disgust, thinking they have a right to satisfy their own lusts even if it causes the greatest injury to their neighbor. If these men were to escape with impunity, there would really be no Providence, and they themselves would be the truest prophets and most faithful instructors of mankind, revealing the most choice *secret* <note>original: "Arcanum"</note> they have to share: namely, *that there is no God.*

# The Immortality of the Soul. BOOK III.

...officers of Justice, who are as devoid of all sense of what is good as those they shall punish. So, their penalty shall be inflicted by those who share the same principles as themselves—beings who watch for such plunder as this and, when they catch it, "dress" and "adorn" <note>Here, "dress and adorn" is used sarcastically to mean preparing the soul for various forms of torture.</note> their victims according to the varied spite of their own unpredictable moods. Taking a special pride and pleasure in making and seeing creatures miserable, they fall upon their prey with total eagerness and speed, like hungry lions attacking a condemned criminal <note>original: "malefactour"</note>, but with far more ferocity and mockery. For having more wit and, if possible, even less goodness than the soul they assault, they satisfy their wanton cruelty with every kind of abuse and torment they can imagine, giving the soul only enough rest to ensure she feels their new inventions with a sharper and more distinct pain. Neither reason nor persuasive speech can prevail with them—no protest, petition, or submission works. For what purpose could it serve to protest against injury and violence to those whose deepest understanding is this one main principle: *That every person’s lust, when he can act without fear of punishment, is the most sacred and sovereign law?* Or what can either petitions or submissions do with those who believe it is the most contemptible piece of foolishness and stupidity to be talked into abandoning their own interests? Since they acknowledge no such thing as virtue or vice, they make it their only interest to please themselves in whatever fits their own desires; and their main pleasure is to agonize and torture, in the most exquisite ways they can, as many people as opportunity delivers into their power.

And thus we see how, in the next life, the arrogant and self-important *Atheist* <note>In the 17th century, "Atheist" often referred not just to those who denied God's existence, but those who lived as if there were no divine moral law.</note> may at last feel the tragic inconvenience of his own practices and principles. For even those who took pleasure in helping him toward that high level of wickedness while he was in this life may perhaps take just as much pleasure in seeing him punished by those grim executioners in the other world. It is like that "playful" cruelty (which some attribute to the person of *Nero* <note>The Roman Emperor Nero, often cited as a paragon of cruelty.</note>) of ordering the *Vestal* virgins <note>Priestesses in ancient Rome sworn to celibacy; breaking their vows was a capital offense.</note> to be raped, and then putting them to death for having been so.

7. But this subject would be too long and too tragic to dwell on any further. Let us turn our eyes toward a more tolerable object: the state of the soul that has lived virtuously and conscientiously, according to the best opportunity she had for knowledge, in whatever part or age of the world she lived. For though this *Moral Innocence* among the *Pagans* <note>Non-Christians, particularly those of the classical Greek and Roman world.</note> will not amount to what our religion calls *Salvation*, it must still be advantageous to them in the other state, according to their different degrees of goodness. They will be more or less *Happy* or *Miserable* based on how *Virtuous* they have been in this life. For we cannot imagine why God should be harsher to them in the other world than in this, since nothing has happened to turn his affection away from them except death—which was not in their power to avoid and looks more like a punishment than a fault. This is especially true for those who are well-meaning and conscientious, who do not intentionally reject the healthy suggestions of the *Light of Nature* <note>The inherent sense of right and wrong or reason believed to be implanted in all humans by God.</note>, but are lovers of humanity and virtue. For to these people, death is only an entrance into another life...

# CHAPTER XI. The Immortality of the Soul.

-> — *To the pleasant green spaces*
*Of the fortunate groves, and the blessed seats.* <note>original: "Ad amœna vireta / Fortunatorum nemorum, sedésque beatas" — Virgil, Aeneid VI.638-39.</note> <-

This is a truth I could not conceal, as it would be a great discredit to *Divine Providence* to think otherwise. For to those who are free-thinking, God's ways will seem as incomprehensible in overloading the simple with punishment as they would in failing to reward the more perfectly righteous and enlightened <note>original: "illuminate"</note>. For a failure in either case would tempt people to disbelieve the whole system and hold that there is no *Providence* at all.

8. Therefore, let there be special privileges for *morality* everywhere for those who pass into the next state. For unless *God* makes a deliberate stop, it will naturally follow that *Memory* after *death*, suggesting nothing but what the *Conscience* approves of, must result in great *tranquility of mind*. This also brings a certain *health* and *beauty* to the *aerial vehicle* <note>The "aerial vehicle" refers to the subtle, non-physical body the soul was thought to inhabit after leaving the physical body.</note>, as well as better *company* and *conversation*, and more pleasant *territories* and *regions* to live in. For what *Plotinus* says of the extreme degrees of character is also true of those in the middle; otherwise, Divine Justice would be very incomplete <note>original: "maime"</note>. *For a man,* he says, *having once made a depraved temper his own and united with it, is known well for what he is; and according to his nature, he is thrust forward toward what he is inclined to, both here and after he has departed from this life. Thus, he shall be pulled by the attractions of Nature into a suitable place. But the good man's reception and interactions shall be of another sort, guided as if by the pulling of certain hidden strings moved and pulled by Nature's own fingers. So admirable is the power and order of the Universe that all things are carried on in a silent way of Justice, which none can avoid. The wicked man has no perception or understanding of this, but is drawn along, knowing nothing of where in the Universe he ought to be carried. But the good man both knows and goes where he ought, and discerns before he departs from here where he must live, and is full of hopes that it shall be with the gods.* This long paragraph from *Plotinus* is not without some small truth in it, if correctly limited and understood; but it does not seem to reach at all the specific circumstances and increases of *happiness* for the *soul* in the next state, which will naturally follow from her actions in this life.

9. For certainly, according to the various degrees of *kindness* <note>original: "benignity"</note> of *spirit* and the desire to do good to mankind in this life—and the more ample opportunities one has of doing it—the happiness of the other *world* is doubled for them, since there is such a certain communication and interaction between both. Therefore, those who act or suffer deeply for such causes as *God* will maintain in the *world*, and who are just and holy at their core (and there are some *principles* that are essentially so, which *Providence* has supported through *miracles*, the agreement of the wisest men in all ages, and the common voice of *nature*); those who have been the most heroic supporters and promoters of these things in this life will naturally receive the greater contentment of *mind* after it. They will be conscious of how seriously they have assisted what *God* will never desert, and that *truth* is mighty and must at last prevail—a fact they are better assured of when out of the *body* than when they were in it.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the afterlife, moving from the general rewards of the virtuous to the specific ways that earthly actions—such as political service, military defense of one's country, and the promotion of lasting truths—contribute to a soul's happiness in the next world.</meta>

### The Immortality of the Soul. BOOK III.

10. Nor is this kind of increase in happiness to be limited only to our promotion of what is of the highest and most essential importance here on earth. Rather, it affects, in due proportion, all actions that spring from a virtuous and good principle, of which there are several degrees. Among these, we should not consider those that relate to a *National* good to be the least significant. Therefore, for those who—out of a natural nobility of spirit and successful courage in *War*—have delivered their country from slavery, or have been so wise and understanding in *Politics* as to have designed healthy laws for the greater happiness and comfort of the people; while such a nation prospers and exists, it cannot help but be an increase of happiness to these significant benefactors. We would have to imagine them to be less generous and good in the other world than they were here—where they actually have the advantage of being better—to think otherwise. And what I have said in this more notable example is, to a degree, true in matters of smaller concern, which would be endless to list. However, whole nations, along with their laws, social orders, and families, may eventually fail, and therefore these additions to happiness might be cut off. But he who spends his efforts in this life to carry out such designs as will remain relevant as long as the world endures, and which must achieve a complete triumph at last; such a person lays the groundwork for an *Everlasting* advantage in the other *World*, which, despite all the tosses and turns of unstable fortune, will be sure to take effect.

11. But this matter requires judgment as well as passion and eagerness. For meddling ignorance, even when accompanied by some measure of sincerity and good intentions, may set things in motion in the world—or record principles that are either false, or irrelevant and poorly timed—which, being put to bad use, may greatly harm the cause one desires to promote. This will be a sad sight for them to witness in the next state. For though their lack of sophistication may be pardonable, they will still experience the ill effects of their mistake upon themselves. Just as a man who kills a friend instead of an enemy may satisfy his conscience (which rightly pleads his innocence), yet he cannot avoid the feeling of shame and sorrow that naturally follows such a disastrous error.

12. There may be such additions to our enjoyments in the other *World* from the lasting traces of our actions in this one, provided we have any *Memory* of things after death—as I have already demonstrated that we have. But even if we did not, and the opinion of *Aristotle* and *Cardan* <note>original: "Cardan" — referring to Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), an Italian polymath who, like some interpretations of Aristotle, questioned the persistence of individual memory after death.</note> were true, *Virtue* and *Piety* would still not prove useful *only* for this present state. This is because, according to how we live here, we shall hereafter be drawn—by a hidden chain <note>original: "concatenation"</note> of causes—to a condition that matches the purity or impurity of our souls in this life. That silent *Nemesis* <note>In Greek mythology, Nemesis is the goddess of retribution; here, More uses it to describe a natural, inescapable law of cause and effect that balances the universe.</note> that passes through the entire fabric of the universe is always inevitably arranging us into such a state as we ourselves have prepared ourselves for by our habitual actions. It is of such great consequence, while we have the opportunity, to strive for the best things.

# CHAP. XII. The Immortality of the Soul.

### CHAPTER XII

*1. What* The Spirit of Nature *is. 2. Experiments that argue for its real existence, such as that of two strings tuned to the same pitch. 3. Sympathetic cures and tortures. 4. The sympathy between the earthly and astral body. 5. Monstrous births. 6. The attraction of the magnet and the roundness of the sun and stars.*

1. We would have completely finished our discussion now, if I did not think it appropriate to address two expectations of the reader. The first concerns *The Spirit of Nature*; the second is the presentation of objections that may be made against our concluded assertion of the soul’s immortality. Regarding the former, I can easily imagine that the reader may well desire a more precise <note>original: "punctual"</note> account of that principle I have had recourse to so often than I have given so far. He will think it fitting that I should somewhere more fully explain what I mean by the terms, and show him my strongest grounds for why I believe there is any such being in the world. To hold him no longer in suspense, I shall do both in this place.

*The Spirit of Nature*, therefore, according to the notion I have of it, is: *An incorporeal substance, but without sense or conscious awareness <term>original: "Animadversion"; meaning the ability to perceive or reflect on its own actions</term>, pervading the whole matter of the universe, and exercising a plastic power <term>a "plastic power" is the ability to mold, shape, or organize matter into specific forms, like a seed growing into a tree</term> within it according to the various predispositions and occasions in the parts it works upon. It produces such phenomena in the world—by directing the parts of matter and their motion—as cannot be explained <note>original: "resolved"</note> by mere mechanical powers.* This rough description may serve to convey to anyone a clear enough conception of the nature of this thing. And that it is not a mere idea, but a real being, there are several considerations that may persuade us, besides what I have occasionally hinted at already (and shall here confirm again with new instances).

2. The first of these shall concern those experiments of *sympathetic pains, reliefs, and cures*. There are many examples of these, approved by the most cautious claimants to sobriety and judgment. Regarding all of these, I cannot help but declare that I suspect them to happen by some power similar to that which makes *strings* that are tuned as *unisons* <note>original: "Unisons"; two strings tuned to the same note</note> (even on different instruments) behave as they do: when one is touched, the other trembles and moves very noticeably, even casting off a straw or pin or any such small thing laid upon it. This cannot be explained by any mechanical principle, though some have ingeniously attempted it. For before they attempted to show the reason why a string that is *not* a unison to the one struck should not leap and move as the one that *is* does, they should have demonstrated that the unison string can be moved at all by the mere *vibration of the air*. If it could, these vibrations would not fail to move other bodies that are far more movable than the string itself. For example, if one hung a small thread of silk or a hair with some light thing at the end of it near the string that is struck, these would surely receive those reciprocal vibrations that are communicated to the unison string at a far greater distance—

<summary>The author defines the "Spirit of Nature" as a non-physical force that shapes the universe and explains why certain phenomena, like sympathetic resonance in musical strings, prove that the world is governed by more than just mechanical laws.</summary>

stance, if the mere motion of the material **air** caused the vibration <note>original: "subsultation"</note> of the string tuned in **unison**—which is, in fact, contrary to experience.

Besides that, if it were the mere **vibration of the air** that caused this tremor in the **unison** string, the effect would not be significant unless both strings lay almost in the same plane, and the vibration of the string being struck moved within that same plane where they both lie. However, if the string is struck so as to cut the plane perpendicularly by its trembling excursions, or if both strings are in two different planes at a significant distance above one another, the result is much the same. This is true even though the air cannot rationally be conceived to **vibrate** backwards and forwards in any way other than almost exactly in the very planes in which the strings move.

All of these things clearly show that purely **material** <note>original: "Corporeal"</note> causes cannot produce this effect. Therefore, we must suppose that **both** strings are united with some one **incorporeal** being, which has a different **unity** and **activity** from **matter**, yet still possesses a **sympathy** with it. When this **immaterial** being is affected, it causes it to affect the matter in the same way in another place, wherever the matter corresponds <note>original: "symbolize"</note> with the first in some predisposition or quality—just as these two strings do by being tuned in **unison** to one another. And it does this without sending any particles to the matter it acts upon. This is similar to how my thought of moving my toe is represented within my brain; by the power of my soul, I can move my toe as I please without sending spirits <term>In 17th-century physiology, "spirits" were thought to be subtle, thin fluids that traveled through the nerves to move the body.</term> into my toe, but only by making use of those that are already there. I can do this because of that **unity** and **activity** which is peculiar to my soul as a spiritual substance that pervades my whole body. From this, I would also conclude that there is some such principle as we call **The Spirit of Nature**, or the inferior **Soul of the World**, to which such **phenomena** as these are to be attributed.

3. And I consider **sympathetic cures**, pains, and reliefs to be of the same kind. For example, when in the use of those **magnetic remedies**, as some call them, they can make a wound painfully hot or cold at a great distance, or can put it into perfect ease, this is not by any agency of **emissary atoms** <note>particles sent out from a source</note>. For these hot **atoms** would cool sufficiently in their journey to the person through the cold air; and cold **atoms**, if they could be active enough to travel so far, would be warmed enough by their journey in the summer sun. Furthermore, the inflammation of a cow's udder caused by milk boiling over into a fire, or the scalding of men's entraals at a distance by the burning of their waste—along with other tricks of a similar nature—cannot be rationally explained by the movement of the spirits of men or cattle mingled with fiery atoms and then re-entering the affected parts. This is because the extreme smallness <note>original: "minuteness"</note> of those atoms suggests they would be extinguished suddenly, just as the smallest wires made red-hot cool down the fastest.

To all this you may add (if it proves true) that notable example of wine reacting <note>original: "working"</note> when the vines are in flower, and the idea that this **sympathetic** effect must come from the vines of the country from which the wine originated. If so, these exhalations of the vineyards must spread as far as from **Spain** and the **Canary Islands** to **England**, and by the same logic, must reach all around in every direction as far from the **Canaries**,

# CHAPTER XII. The Immortality of the Soul.

...besides their journey upwards into the air. So there will be a hemisphere of wine-based atoms <note>original: "vineal Atoms"</note> of an incredible extent, unless they divide themselves into groups and march only to those places where their **wines** are carried. But what material <note>original: "corporeal"</note> cause can guide them there? The same question may be asked of other phenomena of a similar nature. This again makes it necessary to establish the principle I am aiming for; even if the effects were caused by the movement of atoms.

4. The most notable examples of this **Universal Sympathy** <note>original: "Mundane Sympathy"</note> are found in histories that are more uncertain and obscure. Although I have been very credibly informed of them, as I have already declared, I only dare to vouch for them as possibilities: namely, the souls of men leaving their bodies and appearing in the shapes of, <margin>See Book 2, chapter 15, sections 8, 9, 10.</margin> for example, *cats*, *pigeons*, *weasels*, and sometimes *men*. They say that whatever hurt befalls them in these *Astral* bodies (as the followers of *Paracelsus* <note>original: "Paracelsians"</note> like to call them), the same injury is inflicted upon their *earthly* bodies while they lie, in the meantime, in their beds or on the ground. For instance, if their *Astral* bodies are scalded, wounded, or have their backs broken, the same thing certainly happens to their *earthly bodies*.

If these things are true, they are most likely explained by the principle we are discussing: that *the Spirit of Nature* is drawn into agreement with the imagination of the souls in these *Astral* bodies or *Airy Vehicles* <note>original: "Aiery Vehicles." In Neoplatonism, this is a subtle, intermediate body that the soul inhabits when outside the physical body</note>. This act of imagination must be strong in them, as it is driven and assisted by sharp pain and fright during these scaldings, woundings, and strikes to the back. Something similar happens to pregnant women, whose imaginations, sharpened by a sudden fear, have deprived their children of arms or even heads. This is also shown in two remarkable stories Sir Kenelm Digby relates in his witty and eloquent *Discourse on the Cure of Wounds by the Powder of Sympathy*, <margin>Chapter 6, section 6.</margin> in addition to what we have already quoted from Van Helmont <note>original: "Helmont"</note>.

5. I suppose these effects are beyond the power of any human imagination if it is not assisted by some more forceful agent. This includes the extraordinary birth Digby mentions of a woman from Carcassonne who, by playing too much with an *ape* while she was pregnant, gave birth to a monster exactly in that shape. If we agree with that learned writer that it was a real *ape*, it is no more wonderful—and perhaps less so—than the birth of a crab or lobster we mentioned earlier from Fortunius Licetus <note>An Italian physician who wrote a famous treatise on "monsters" or birth defects</note>; as we might also note other more common, though no less "monstrous" births for women to bear. The mother's soul cannot be suspected as the cause of these, since she is not even the direct creator <note>original: "Efformer"</note> of her own fetus, as the judicious naturalist Dr. William Harvey <note>The famous physician who discovered the circulation of blood</note> has determined. And if the mother's soul could be the creator of the fetus, her formative <note>original: "Plastick"</note> power would, in all reason, always be as specific and unique as the soul itself.

What remains, therefore, but the *Universal Soul of the World* or *Spirit of Nature* that can perform these feats? This Spirit, like *Vertumnus* <note>original: "Vertumnus-like." A Roman god of the seasons and change, known for his ability to change his shape at will</note>, is ready to change its own activity and the yielding matter into any mode or shape as the occasion requires. Thus, it prepares a dwelling—or at least the rough outlines of one—for any specific soul whatsoever, in any place where the matter will yield to its operations. But the time when that particular guest arrives, it is intended...
