### CHAPTER XIII. The Immortality of the Soul.

Then that by which the Earth is carried around in twenty-four hours, it would necessarily break out in a straight line through the thin air and never return to the Earth again, but escape just as a *comet* does out of a *vortex* <note>In Cartesian physics, a "vortex" was a whirlpool of subtle matter that carried planets around the sun.</note>. And Descartes admits as a true experiment that, *in fact* <note>original: "de facto"</note>, a cannonball has been shot so high that it never fell back to the ground. For my part, I can imagine no other undeniable reason for this, except that at a certain distance the *Spirit of Nature* in some respects leaves the motion of *matter* to the pure laws of *mechanics*, but within other boundaries checks it—which is why the water does not spill <note>original: "swill"</note> out of the Moon.

7. Now, if pure *mechanical* powers in *matter* and physical motion cannot even account for a phenomenon as simple as a stone falling to Earth, how can we hope they will be the sufficient cause of various types of *plants* and other things that possess far more craftsmanship and complexity <note>original: "curiosity"</note> than the direct descent of a stone to the ground?

Nor are we forced back by this discovery into that foolishness of the confused *Schools* <note>The "Schools" refers to Scholasticism, the medieval system of philosophy and theology based on Aristotle.</note>, who endowed almost every different object of our senses with a distinct *substantial form* <note>An Aristotelian concept where an internal "form" gives an object its essential properties.</note>, and then puzzled themselves with endless trivialities about their generation, decay, and mixing. For I agree with *Descartes* that nothing affects our senses except such variations of *matter* as are created by differences in motion, shape, and the position of parts, etc. However, I disagree with him in this: I hold that it is not mere and pure mechanical motion that causes all these sensible modifications in matter. Instead, many times the immediate director of this motion is this *Spirit of Nature* (which I am discussing)—which is one and the same everywhere, and always acts the same way on similar occasions, just as a clear-minded man of solid judgment always gives the same verdict in the same circumstances.

<margin>* Chapter 6, sections 7, 8; Chapter 7, section 3.</margin>

For since this *Spirit of Nature* meddles with the formation of the *fetus* of animals (as I have * already shown more than once)—where, despite this, there seems to be less need for it because they possess a more specific agent for that purpose—it is extremely rational that all plants and flowers of all kinds (for which we have no evidence of individual souls) should be the effects of this *Universal Soul of the World*. This hypothesis is not only most reasonable in itself, according to that common axiom, "It is pointless to do with more what can be done with fewer" <note>original: "Frustra fit per plura quod fieri potest per pauciora"</note>, but it is also very useful for preventing many difficult problems regarding the *divisibility* of the souls of plants, their *transformations* into other species, the growing of *cuttings* <note>original: "slips"</note>, and the like. For there is one soul ready everywhere to take advantage of prepared matter. This is the common and only <term>seminal reason</term> <note>original Greek: "λόγος σπερματικός" (logos spermatikos)</note> of all *botanical* appearances, or of whatever other *phenomena* there may be, large or small, that exceed the pure mechanical powers of *matter*. We except only *humans* and *beasts*, who—having the capacity for some kind of enjoyment—rightly possess individual souls to multiply the experience of those enjoyments which the transcendent wisdom of the Creator has designed.

8. I have now clearly enough explained what I mean by *The Spirit of Nature*,

Nature, and sufficiently proved its existence. From what has been said, it may be easily understood why I give it this name, as it is a Principle that has such great influence and activity in the *birth* <note>original: "Nascency"</note> and *formation* <note>original: "Coalescency"</note> of things. This is true not only in the production of *Plants*, along with all other solid structures <note>original: "Concretions"</note> of a lower nature that are still above the mere *mechanical* laws of *matter*, but also in respect to the birth of *Animals*, for which it prepares and assists.

I do not know whether I may also credit it with the guidance of *Animals* in the most important of those actions which we usually attribute to *natural Instinct*. Among these, none is so famous as birds making their nests, and particularly the artistic structure of the martins' <note>Martins are small birds in the swallow family known for building complex mud nests.</note> nests under the arches of church windows. In these nests, there is such a notable design unknown to the birds themselves, and so little immediate pleasure for their senses. It looks as if they were driven <note>original: "actuated"</note> by another power—inspired and carried away in a natural trance by this *Spirit of Nature* to do they know not what. Yet, it is really a necessary provision and accommodation for laying their eggs and hatching their young. In the shaping <note>original: "efformation"</note> of those eggs, this *Inferior Soul of the World* <note>A term More uses interchangeably with the "Spirit of Nature" to describe a universal, unconscious soul that organizes the physical world.</note> is so rationally conceived to assist and intervene. Therefore, she <note>More personifies the Spirit of Nature as "she," following the tradition of "Mother Nature" or the "Anima Mundi."</note> may be better supposed to overpower the bird's *imagination* <note>original: "Fancy"</note> and make use of its limbs to build these convenient containers—acting as workshops to store the material upon which she intends to work, namely the eggs of these birds whom she thus guides in making their nests.

9. For there is no reason or ground for anyone to imagine <note>original: "conceit"</note> that this building of their nests in such a way comes from acquired *Art* and observation, or from the instruction of the parent birds, rather than from *natural Instinct*. Just because their actions aim toward such a significant goal is no argument that they know it or ever consulted about it. It is no more evidence of thought than when *Ivy* or *Bindweed* wind around the nearest plant that can support them, having never calculated <note>original: "cast up with themselves"</note> beforehand either the necessity or convenience of such close embraces. Nor does it follow at all that because young birds might see the old ones make their nests before they begin to make theirs, that they actually "see" them in the sense of taking notice or learning. Indeed, who can produce even one example of a parent bird tutoring or teaching her young in this kind of *Architecture*? Or who has spied a young bird applying her mind to learn that art by observing what the older one does? Therefore, a man might as well argue—indeed, much better—that the *songs* of birds are not by *Instinct*, but by learning and art, because they may have heard the older birds sing or whistle before them. Yet, they will naturally take up such notes as belong to their species on their own, without ever hearing the older birds. So, it is not based on any *Reason*, but is a mere vain and shallow guess <note>original: "surmise"</note>, to think that the *Architecture* of birds in building their nests is not *natural Instinct*, but acquired *Art* and *Imitation*.

But on the other side, there are very plain and positive reasons to convince us that this *Architecture* of theirs comes from *Instinct* and is not an acquired faculty. First, this is because, in general, brute *Animals* are of such a nature that they lack that free and reflective *reason* which is required for acquired *Art* and *deliberation* <note>original: "Consultation"</note>. For if they had any such principle,

Fourthly, the peculiar inability to be taught <note>original: "Indocility"</note> seen in those birds that are the most ingenious architects in building their nests is a plain indication that it is not free **Reason** but **Instinct** that guides them. **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman author and natural philosopher.</note> observes this in the **swallow**: how impossible she is to train, and yet how admirable she is at framing her little mansions of mud.

Fifthly, the fact that this architecture is not a piece of learning passed down from older birds to their offspring, but is instead the immediate effect of Nature, is further proven by the fact that in all parts of the world, the same kinds of birds make the same kinds of nests. It cannot be supposed that they learned this from birds in remote countries, whom the vastness of the seas kept from any mutual conversation.

Sixthly and lastly, no man can think or speak of examples of natural architecture without the **martin's nest**, the **honeycombs of bees**, the **webs of spiders**, and the **cocoons** <note>original: "Bags"</note> **of silk-worms** bringing each other to mind, as they are all of the same kind and nature. This led **Pliny**, **Cardan**, and **Nierembergius** <note>Gerolamo Cardan and Juan Eusebio Nieremberg were prominent Renaissance and early modern scholars of natural history.</note> to join them in one list as examples of the same category. This may well lead us to conclude they are so closely related that if one is **natural instinct**, all the rest must be so too. Our previous argument is incredibly strong in these last three instances. For we can be sure that all the **bees** in the world did not come out of a single hive, and therefore could not have learned their architectural skill from the same teachers; yet they all make their combs with the same craftsmanship—if I may call it that—and with the same geometric exactness. As for **spiders**, it is evident that they are among <term>the things generated spontaneously</term> <note>original: "τὰ αὐτομάτως γενόμενα"</note>, as **Aristotle** phrases it, and are generated out of mere filth <note>original: "sluttery" (OCR: "fluttery")</note> and decay. Yet these insects, as soon as they are born, can set up shop and begin their trade of weaving without any teacher or instructor.

The nests of birds are remarkable not only for their construction but also in regard to their purpose and design. This purpose is not for the comfort of the *Individual* bird, but a plan for the propagation of the *Species*. Consider the insect we call the **silkworm**: after she has passed through various changes and names—such as *worm*, *caterpillar*, *silkworm-cocoon*, *chrysalis*, *nymph*, *larva*, and *butterfly* <note>original Greek: "σκώληξ, κάμπη, βομβύλιος, χρυσαλλὶς, νύμφη, νεκύδαλος, ψυχὴ"</note>—she ends this final stage and transformation with a plentiful provision for the continuation of her kind.

For when she has reached her third change, in which she is called a *silkworm-cocoon* <note>original: "βομβύλιος" (bombylios)</note>, she works from her mouth and with her forefeet that *cocoon* <note>original: "Folliculus"</note> or ball of silk mentioned before. In doing so, she builds her own tomb, which yet becomes the womb or cradle for herself. Having passed the state of a *chrysalis* <note>original: "χρυσαλλὶς"</note> (during which she *remains motionless* <note>original: "ἀκινητίζειν" (akinētizein)</note>, as **Aristotle** says, and approaches the shape and nature of an egg), she emerges afterward with a closer resemblance to her intended animal form and is called a *nymph* <note>original: "νύμφη"</note>. After this, acquiring a greater degree of life and motion, she is styled a *nekydalos* <note>original: "νεκύδαλος"</note>, as if her dead body had caught vital fire again. In this state she does not lie loose but sticks again to the cavity of the silk ball; once grown to full maturity, she breaks through and shows herself in the complete form of a **Butterfly**.

When they have reached this peak of perfection, they enjoy it for only a very short time. For after three or four days of indulgence in the delightful rituals of **Venus** <note>Meaning mating.</note>, the *Male* immediately says goodbye to the world; the *Female* follows him soon after, but only after she has left behind several hundred eggs, small like grains of millet, as a numerous pledge and provision for the continuation of their kind. How then, according to this account, can the old silkworm ever teach the young ones their trade of spinning or weaving?

I understand this mainly regarding the *structure* of their *nests*, though their choice of where to build them may not come merely from the lightness of their bodies or their habit of living near buildings, trees, or bushes. It also comes partly from the dictate of that **Instinct** which suggests to them everywhere what is best for their safety, making them many times more wise <note>original: "sagacious"</note> than we can understand. This appears in what **Pliny** writes concerning a kind of **swallow** that builds nests near *Coptos* in Egypt: they either do not build or they abandon their nests many days in advance, *if the rising river is going to reach them.* <note>original: "si futurum est ut auctus amnis attingat"</note>

That there is such a thing as **Instinct** in brute animals is, therefore, very plain. That is to say, there is an *instigation* or *impetus* in them to do things without counsel, deliberation, or acquired knowledge—things that, according to our own reason and best consultation, we cannot help but approve as the fittest things to be done. **Scaliger** <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger (1484–1558), a renowned scholar.</note> seems to parallel this principle in general to Divine Inspiration, saying: *Instinct is said to come from Nature, just as inspiration comes from the Gods.* <note>original: "Instinctus dicitur à Naturâ, sicut à Diis Afflatio."</note> But I think it is most safely and most unexcep-

<header>CHAP. XIII. The Immortality of the Soul.</header>
<sig>A a a</sig>

...unquestionably applied where the *Instinct* respects not so much the welfare of the *Individual* as the common good of this or that *Species*. For if there is any *Impulse* from an external principle upon any particular *Animal*, it is most certain to happen when that *Animal* is moved from the pursuit of its own individual comfort to serve a more public end. From where else could this motion come, if not from That which is not a particular Being, but something in whose Essence the scope and purpose of the general good of the World and of all the *Species* within it is vitally contained? This force binds all particulars together by that common *Essential Law*, which is the Spirit itself, occasionally prompting them to such actions and services (either beyond their knowledge or against their private interests) as lead most effectively to the preservation of the whole. 

And this is what we have called the *Spirit of Nature*, which moves through and assists all physical beings. It is the *vicarious power of God* (who is that *impartial Law* <note>original Greek: "Νόμος ἰσοκλινής" (Nomos isoklinēs), referring to God as a universal, stabilizing law that weighs all things equally</note>, as the Philosopher calls Him) upon the universal matter of the world. This suggests to the *Spider* the idea of spinning and weaving her web, and to the *Bee* the framing of her honeycombs, but especially to the *Silkworm* the gathering of her thread <note>original: "clue," meaning a ball of yarn or thread</note>, which serves as both a coffin and a cradle. It also guides *Birds* in building their nests and in the diligent hatching of their eggs. But I have dwelt on this argument for too long.

10. The most notable of those tasks that can be assigned to *The Spirit of Nature*—fittingly given its name—is the movement of the souls of animals into such matter as is most suitable for them. This Spirit is the common *matchmaker* <note>original: "Proxenet," a go-between or broker</note> or *contractor* of all natural pairings between *Forms* and *Matter*, if we may also use metaphors just as *Aristotle* did, whose aphorism states that *matter desires form as a woman desires a man* <note>original Latin: "Materia appetit formam ut fœmina virum"</note>.

This *Spirit* therefore may have not only the power of directing the motion of matter nearby, but also of *transporting* particular souls and spirits (while they are in a state of *silence* and *inactivity*) to such matter as they are prepared to find life in once again. This *transportation* or *transmission* may very well occur over immense distances. The effect of this *sympathy* and *shared activity* is seen in the fermentation of wines, as has been noted above (though that is a less important matter); or, in a more undeniable example, in the way magnetic particles are conducted from one pole of the Earth to the other.

Whence, to conclude, we may look upon this *Spirit of Nature* as the great *Quartermaster-General* of Divine Providence. It is able, on its own and without any subordinate officers, to lodge every soul according to her rank and merit whenever she leaves the body. This would prove a very useful hypothesis for those who believe in the *pre-existence* of human souls to explain how they may be conveyed into bodies here, regardless of the distance they were at before. It also explains how matter might perhaps be so prepared that the best of them may be brought from the purest *ethereal regions* into a human body without serving any long apprenticeship in the intervening *air*. Likewise, it shows how the souls of animals need not lie forever useless in the universe, even if the Earth were made perfectly unsuitable for the life of any animal.

But such speculations as these are of such vast comprehension and unfathomable mystery that I cannot bring myself to linger on them any longer; especially since they do not touch directly on our current purpose and are more suited to fill a volume of their own than to be squeezed into the narrow limits of my now nearly finished discourse.

### CHAP. XIV.

1. *Objections against the soul's immortality based on her condition in infancy, old age, sleep, and sickness.* 2. *Other objections taken from experiments that seem to prove her discerpibility* <term>the quality of being able to be torn apart or divided into pieces</term>. 3. *Also regarding the rare appearance of the souls of the deceased.* 4. *And regarding our natural fear of death.* 5. *An evasion used by the opposing party, who suppose there is only one soul common to all creatures.* 6. *An answer concerning the "smallness" of the soul in infancy.* 7. *Also concerning the weakness of her intellectual faculties then, and in old age.* 8. *That sleep does not at all prove the soul's mortality, but rather illustrates her immortality.* 9. *An answer to the objection regarding strokes* <note>original: "Apoplexies"</note> *and trances* <note>original: "Catalepsies"</note>. 10. *Also to the objection regarding madness.* 11. *That the various impairments of her intellectual faculties no more prove her mortality than the changes in matter prove its capacity to be naturally annihilated. And why God created souls that sympathize with matter.*

I. As for the objections that are usually made against the immortality of the soul, to list them all would be both tedious and useless, since there is scarcely one in twenty that would seem important to anyone of even average intelligence and judgment. But I shall examine the greatest difficulties that can be raised, so that the truth we maintain may be more fully cleared and more firmly believed. The most significant objections I know against the soul's immortality are these five:

The first is from the consideration of the condition of the soul in infancy and old age, as well as in madness, sleep, and strokes. For if we only observe the great difference in our mental operations in infancy and senility compared to what they are when we are in the prime of our years—how our wit grows by degrees, flourishes for a time, and at last decays, keeping the same pace with the changes that age and years bring to our body (which follows the same laws as flowers and plants)—what can we suspect but that the human soul, which is so grandly described among the learned, is nothing more than a physical temperament <note>original: "Temperature of Body," referring to the idea that the "soul" is merely a specific balance of physical elements or humors</note> of the body? 

This view suggests that the soul grows and spreads with the body, both in size and ability, and withers and dies as the body does; or at least that it depends entirely on the body for its operations, and therefore there is no sense or perception of anything after death. Furthermore, even when the soul has the best advantage of years, she is not exempt from those "eclipses" of the mind's powers that proceed from sleep, madness, strokes, and other diseases of that nature. All of which show her...

...her condition, whatever more exalted wits imagine of her—that she is but a poor mortal and physical thing.

2. The Second Objection is taken from such experiments as are thought to prove the soul *divisible* in the grossest sense—that is to say, *discerpible* <term>original: discerpible; capable of being torn into pieces or divided</term>. And it seems a clear case in those more lowly *animals* which are called *insects*, especially the "long and many-footed creatures" <note>original Greek: τὰ μακρὰ κᾲ πολύποδα</note>, <margin>*On the History of Animals, Book 4, Chapter 7.*</margin> as *Aristotle* describes them. He acknowledges that if they are cut into pieces, each segment will have its own motion and sense. The most notable instance of this kind is in the centipede <note>original: *Scolopendra*</note>, whose parts <margin>*Ibid.*</margin> *Aristotle* affirms will live a long time after being divided, and even run backward and forward. Therefore, he considers it to look like many living creatures growing together, rather than one single one: "For such animals seem like many living creatures grown together" <note>original Greek: Ἐοίκασι γὰρ τὰ τοιαῦτα τῶν ζώων πολλοῖς ζώοις συμπεφυκόσι</note>. <margin>*On Youth and Old Age, Chapter 2.*</margin> But yet he will not grant them the privilege of plants, whose cuttings will live and grow when set in the earth. But the instances that belong to this objection ascend higher, for they claim that the parts of "perfect" <note>historically, "perfect" animals referred to complex creatures like mammals and birds</note> animals will also live separately.

There are two main instances of this. The one is that of the eagle which <margin>*Fromondus, On the Soul, Book 1, Chapter 4, Article 1, Section 6.*</margin> *Fromondus* <note>Libert Froidmont (1587–1653), a Belgian scientist and theologian</note> mentions, whose head being chopped off by an angry countryman for quarreling with his dog, the body flew over the barn near the place of this crude execution. This happened at *Fromondus's* father's house; nor is the story improbable if we consider what normally happens to pigeons and ducks when their heads are cut off. The other instance is of a criminal beheaded at *Antwerp*, whose head—when it had given a few jumps into the crowd and a dog began licking the blood—caught the dog's ear in its teeth and held it so fast that the frightened dog ran away with the man's head hanging at its ear, to the great astonishment and confusion of the people. This was told to *Fromondus* by an eyewitness of the event. From these two examples, they think it may be safely inferred that the souls of men, as well as those of the more "perfect" kind of beasts, are also *divisible*.

That example in the same author from *Joseph Acosta* <note>José de Acosta (1540–1600), a Jesuit missionary who wrote about the Americas</note>, if true, is ultimately for this purpose. For the speaking of a sacrificed captive when his heart was cut out may be a further confirmation indeed that the <margin>*See Book 2, Chapter 7, Section 9.*</margin> brain is the seat of the common sense <term>the internal faculty that integrates information from the five senses</term>, but it is no argument for the *divisibility* of the soul. She remains at that time entire in the body after the cutting out of the *heart*, whose office it is to provide *spirits* <note>vital fluids or "animal spirits" believed to transmit life and motion</note>, which were not yet so far dissipated that they failed to suffice for that sudden operation of life.

3. The Third Objection is from the rare appearance of the souls of the deceased. For if they can appear at all, why do they not do so more often? If they never appear, there is a strong suspicion that they do not exist at all.

4. The Fourth is from the fear of death, and an inward, depressing sense in us at some times that we are utterly mortal, and that there is nothing to be expected after this life.

5. The Fifth and last is more of an evasion than an objection: that there is but *One Common Soul* in all men and beasts, which operates according to the variety of animals and persons it animates and brings to life.

They argue that once this individual body is lost, this specific man or beast is lost, and so every living creature is properly and entirely mortal. These are the most significant and relevant *objections* I have ever encountered, or can devise, concerning the soul's immortality. I shall answer them in order.

6. Regarding the first objection, which seems the most clever, I say that neither the *contracted state* of the soul in *infancy*, nor the *weakness* of her *intellectual operations* either *then* or in extreme *old age*, are sufficient proofs of her *corporeality* <note>original: corporeity; the quality of being physical or having a body</note> or *mortality*. For why should we wonder that the soul—having fallen into this low and fatal condition where she must submit to the course of nature and the laws governing animals born here on Earth—should reveal herself by degrees? She grows from smaller dimensions to the ordinary size of men, yet the faculty of contracting and expanding <note>original: dilating</note> themselves is part of the very essence and definition of all *spirits*, 
<margin>Book 1, chapter 5.</margin>
as I have noted already. Thus, she merely performs this growth slowly and naturally now, being subjected to the laws of this earthly fate; whereas, when exempt from this condition, she does so suddenly and freely. She does not grow by *juxtaposition* <note>the physical adding of one part next to another</note> of parts or the *intromission* <note>the taking in of external matter</note> of matter, but by enlarging her own substance along with the body, which remains one and the same substance always.

7. As for the *weakness* of her *intellectual faculties* in *infancy* and *old age*, this consideration has even less power to prove her a mere physical essence than the previous one. It does not challenge our principles at all, because we have already accounted for the worst possible suspicions regarding the operations of the mind. I have freely acknowledged that these operations depend very closely on the condition and quality of the soul's immediate instrument: the *spirits* <note>In 17th-century physiology, "spirits" were highly refined substances in the blood thought to carry out the soul's commands</note>. Because these spirits are more sluggish and "watery" in *children* and *old men*, they must necessarily hinder the soul in any operations that require a different constitution of spirits than what is usually found in *age* and *childhood*. However, I will not say I am absolutely certain that the soul cannot act without any dependence on matter at all. But if it does not—which is most probable—it must follow that its operations will follow the laws of the body it is united with. From this, we can demonstrate how necessary *purity* and *temperance* are for preserving and improving a man’s mental abilities.

<margin>Aelian, *Various History*, Book 2, Chapter 35.</margin>
8. As for *sleep*, which the dying philosopher called *the brother of death* <note>original: A reference to the Greek philosopher Gorgias, recorded by Aelian, who said "Sleep is already beginning to hand me over to his brother [Death]"</note>, I do not see how it proves the soul’s mortality any more than a man's inability to wake up again would. Rather, it helps us conceive how the shocks and agonies of death may seem to utterly take away all hope of the soul living afterward; yet, upon recovering a more agile *vehicle of air* <note>More believed the soul inhabited a body of "fine air" after the physical body died</note>, she may suddenly awake into a fuller and fresher experience of life than before. I may also answer that *sleep* is only the binding <note>original: ligation</note> of the outward senses and the interruption of signals from the external world. This no more proves a fundamental lack of life or immortality in the soul than having a man's sight confined within the walls of his room by closed shutters <note>original: shuts</note> proves any blindness in the person inside. That person is perhaps busy reading by candlelight, and doing so with such ease that he can read print so small it would trouble an ordinary person to read it by daylight.

Without doubt, if human souls were once restored to the sobriety they are capable of, they would be as ashamed of the desires and ideas they are now fully engaged in as any madman, restored to his right senses, is of the antics he played when he was out of his mind.

1. Nor do those instances in the second objection prove anything to the contrary—as if the soul itself were actually *divisible*. The most powerful example is that of the *Scolopendra* <note>original: "Scolopendra," a genus of large centipedes</note>, where the motion of the divided parts is so quick, nimble, and long-lasting. But it is easy to imagine that the activity of the spirits <term>spirits: in early modern science, these were subtle fluids or vapors thought to facilitate movement and sensation</term> within the mechanical structure <note>original: "conformation"</note> of the pieces of that *insect*, until motion has exhausted them, will necessarily make them run up and down, just as gunpowder in a firework <note>original: "squib"</note> causes its movement. Therefore, the soul of the *Scolopendra* will only be in one of those segments—it is uncertain which, though likely determined by how the segments were cut. For if you cut a wasp’s head off from its body, the soul retires from the head into the body. But if you cut her at the waist, leaving the upper part of the body attached to the head, the soul then retires into that front part of the wasp. Therefore, it is no wonder that after the head is cut off, the wasp's body will fly and flutter for so long, since the soul is still in it and perhaps contributing to the direction of the spirits for motion—not out of conscious sense, but from habit or nature. This is similar to how we walk without thinking about it, or play the lute while our mind is focused on something else, as I have noted * previously. But when the waist is left attached to the head, it is even less surprising, for then the animal may not be lacking sense and imagination <note>original: "fancy"</note> to direct the spirits to move the wings.

3. To this second objection, one might have added those *monstrous births* <note>monstrous births: A historical term for infants born with significant physical deformities or conjoined twins.</note> which seem to imply that the *perceptive part* of the soul is actually divided into two or more parts. For *Aristotle* seems to expressly affirm that a monstrous birth that has two hearts is two *animals*, but that which has only one heart is only one. From this, it would follow that there is also only one soul in that one-hearted monster, even though it has two or more heads. From this, it is also evident that the *perceptive part* of that one soul must be actually divided into two or more. Daniel Sennert <note>Daniel Sennert (1572–1637) was a famous German physician and chemist.</note> subscribes to this opinion of *Aristotle*. Therefore, he conceives that the monstrous child born at *Emmaus* in the time of the Emperor *Theodosius*, who had two heads and two hearts, was two *persons*; but that other child born in the year 1531 with two heads and only one heart, who lived until he was a man, was only one *person*. He believes this appears more clearly because both heads professed their perpetual agreement in the same actions: they had the same appetite, the same hunger and thirst, spoke alike, had the same desire to lie with their wife, and performed all other acts of relieving themselves <term>original: exonerating nature</term> together. But for the other that had two hearts and was divided down to the navel, there was not this identity of affection and desire; instead, sometimes one would want something and sometimes the other. Sometimes they would play with one another, and sometimes they would fight.

<margin>
*On the Generation of Animals, book 4, chapter 4.*
*On Youth and Old Age, chapter 3.*
*Book 2, chapter 7, sections 8, 9.*
</margin>
4. But I answer—and first regarding *Aristotle's* authority—that he does not so confidently assert that every monster that has only one heart is only one *animal*. For his words run thus: "In cases where the animal is monstrous, or where several are grown together, we must judge according to the primary principle; for example, if the heart is such a part, that which has one heart is one animal." <note>original: Ἐν ᾗ δὲ τὸ ζῶον τὸ τερατῶδες ἢ πλείω συμφεφυκότα δεῖ νομίζειν κατὰ τὴν ἀρχήν, οἷον εἰ τοιοῦτόν τί ἐστιν ἡ καρδία μόριον, τὸ μὲν μίαν ἔχον καρδίαν ἓν ζῶον.</note> Here he only speaks hypothetically, not decisively, suggesting the heart is that part where the first principle of life resides, and from which the rest of life in soul or body is derived. For indeed, he makes it elsewhere the seat of the *Common Sense* <term>Common Sense: The internal faculty where all the physical senses (sight, touch, etc.) were thought to meet and be integrated.</term>; but we have already demonstrated that this is a mistake, and he himself seems unsure of his own opinion. Therefore, we may reject it with less offense and affirm (without any hesitation) that a monster is either one or more *animals* according to the number of its heads, and that there are as many distinct souls as there are heads in a monstrous birth. But from the heads downward, the body and the heart being one, there must necessarily be a wonderful and exact

5. The weakness of the third objection is obvious because it denies the existence of all spirits, as well as the souls of the deceased. No one can doubt their existence unless they are blindly skeptical. We say, therefore, that the souls of men—being in the same condition as other spirits—do appear sometimes, though only rarely. The cause in both cases is partly the difficulty of bringing their "vehicles" <term>spiritual bodies: Neoplatonists believed the soul inhabited different "vehicles" or bodies (ethereal, aerial, terrestrial) depending on its state of purity.</term> to an unnatural density <note>original: consistency</note>, partly because they have no occasion to do so, and finally because they are not permitted to do as they please or to be wherever they wish.

6. As for the *fear of death*, and that oppressive feeling that sometimes so uncontrollably suggests to us that we are entirely mortal: To the first, I answer that it is a necessary result of our union with the body. If we were to admit it is one of the imperfections or infirmities we acquire by being in this state, that would be a solid answer. Therefore, this fear and the dread of something bad in death is no argument that there is any actual evil in it; it is no more to be heeded than the predictions of any fanatic who pretends to prophesy. Besides this, it is fitting that we should have this fear and abhorrence to make us keep the station Providence has placed us in; otherwise, every little frustration <note>original: pet</note> would invite us to pack ourselves out of this world and try our fortunes in the next, leaving the earth to be inhabited only by beasts, even though it is meant to be managed and cultivated by humans.

7. To the second point, I answer that such stubborn conclusions are nothing but the deceptions of *melancholy* <note>melancholy: In this period, depression was thought to be caused by an excess of "black bile," a physical humor that could cloud the mind and imagination.</note> or some other dull and gross imbalances of the blood that corrupt the imagination. Such fantasies prove nothing, according to Axiom 4. Even though the soul, when enthroned in her *ethereal vehicle*, is a very magnificent thing—full of divine love, majesty, and tranquility—in her present state, she is clogged and overburdened with the filth and darkness of this *terrestrial body*. She is subject to many fears, jealousies, and other disturbing passions; though the objects of these fears are mere mockeries, they cause real distress to her mind during this captivity and imprisonment.

<margin>Virgil's *Aeneid*, Book 6.</margin>

This is the sad state of the more deeply fallen <note>original: "lapſed"</note> souls upon Earth; who are so entirely mastered by the motions of the body that they are carried headlong into agreeing with all the suggestions and imaginations that the body so confidently forces upon them. Among these, the belief in our mortality is not the weakest.

But such melancholy fancies—which would stubbornly convince us that we are utterly extinct at death—are no more an argument for it than the fancies of those who have been persuaded they were dead already while they were still alive. For example, some have refused to eat because they thought the dead never take any nourishment, until they were tricked into an appetite by seeing some of their friends, disguised in burial shrouds <note>original: "winding-ſheets"</note>, eating heartily at the table. Following their example, they then thought it appropriate to eat, and so were kept alive.

8. I cannot help but confess that the tragic display and preparation for dying—which destroys the operations of the mind, throwing her into fits of senility <note>original: "dotage"</note> or fury, making the very face look ghastly and distracted, or at best sadly pale and wasted, as if life and soul were almost quite extinct—cannot help but leave strange impressions even on the strongest mind, raising suspicions that all is lost in such a great change. But the knowing and kind spirit, though he may weep at such a dismal spectacle, does not lose his hope and confidence in the soul’s safe passage into the other world. He is moved in the same way as the more emotional spectators of a cleverly crafted tragedy on stage. There, characters whose virtue, misfortunes, or both have won the affection of the audience are finally seen rolling in their blood, and after some horrific groans and gasps, lie stretched out completely dead upon the stage. But once they are pulled off-stage, they find themselves well and alive, and are ready to enjoy a cup of wine with their friends in the dressing room <note>original: "attiring room"</note> to truly comfort themselves after their fictional pangs of death. They leave the easily-moved crowd to indulge their soft emotions for an evil that never actually befell the actors.

9. Therefore, the fear and hatred we have of death, and the sorrow that accompanies it, is no argument against our living after it. These are merely the appropriate feelings for those who are spectators of the great Tragi-Comedy of the World. Since the entire plot is designed by Infinite Wisdom and Goodness, we cannot help but suspect that the most sorrowful scenes are only a show, but the delight is real for those who are not wicked

## CHAPTER XVI.

1. *That what we truly are is both* **Sensitive** *and* **Intellectual**. *2. What the true concept of a soul being "One" is. 3. That if there be but* **One Soul** *in the world, it is both* **Rational** *and* **Sensitive**. *4. The most favorable representation of the opinion of those who hold there is but* **One Soul**. *5. A refutation of the previous representation. 6. A reply to the refutation. 7. An answer to the reply. 8. That the* **Soul of Man** *is not properly any ray of either* **God** *or the* **Soul of the World**. *9. And yet, even if she were so, it would not harm her immortality; from which the folly of* **Pomponatius** <note>original: "Pomponatius"; referring to Pietro Pomponazzi (1462–1525), an Italian philosopher who argued that the soul's immortality could not be proven by reason</note> *is noted. 10. A further observation upon* **Pomponazzi's** *folly in admitting a certain number of distant* **Intelligences** <note>In this context, "Intelligences" refers to celestial or angelic beings that govern the planetary spheres</note> *while denying* **Particular Immaterial Substances** *in* **Men** *and* **Animals** <note>original: "Brutes"</note>.

1. As for the last objection—or rather, the excuse—of those who have no desire to find their souls immortal, they claim indeed that they have no soul distinct from that *one Universal Soul of the World*. Even so, they acknowledge that the operations we are conscious of—reason and our other faculties—cannot exist without a soul. We shall easily discover either the falsehood or the uselessness of this idea for their purpose; they wish so desperately to slink out of existence after the mad antics <note>original: "freaks"</note> they have played in this life. For it is clearly true that a person is most properly whatever it is that *perceives* <note>original: "animadverts"; the faculty of conscious awareness and attention</note> within them; for that is an operation that no being but oneself can do for them. And that which perceives in us does not only notice its *intellectual* and *rational* operations, but all sensations whatsoever that we are conscious of, whether they end in our body or in some outward object. From this, it is plain that *that which we are* is both *sensitive* and *intellectual*.

2. Now, if we rightly consider what is included in the true and common concept of the *unity* of a soul, it is very obvious that it mainly consists in this: that its *perceiving faculty* <note>original: "Animadversive"</note> is only *one*, and that there is no *sensation* or *perception* of any kind in the soul that is not communicated to and perceived by the whole perceiving faculty.

3. These things having been established, it necessarily follows that if there were *but one soul in the world*, that soul would be both *rational* and *sensitive*, and there could be no pain, pleasure, or thought in *one man’s* soul that would not also be in *all others*. Indeed, a man could not whip a dog or spur a horse without feeling the sting of it himself—which is flatly against all experience and therefore obviously false. Regarding this wild theory, I have spoken so fully in my *Poems* that I need add nothing here in this place, having sufficiently refuted it there.

### CHAPTER XVI. The Immortality of the Soul.

4. However, to avoid being too brief with them, let us imagine the most favorable version of their opinion we can. Let us suppose that although this *Soul of the World* <note>original: "Anima Mundi"; the idea that a single spiritual essence inhabits the entire universe</note> is in itself everywhere the same, and that the *perceptive faculty* <note>original: "Animadversive faculty"; the soul's power to turn its attention to and perceive objects</note> is equally strong throughout, it is nevertheless restricted to that specific part of matter which it currently inhabits. In this view, the soul would be dull and unaware of all other operations—whether sensory or intellectual—that are performed by her outside of that person in other people. This is very difficult to conceive and completely contrary to the idea of the *Unity* of a soul: that it would not be conscious of its own perceptions. But let us grant it as a possibility. Let us suppose that one part of the *Soul of the World* informs one man, and another part informs another—or at least that some vital ray does. Even so, this opinion will be burdened with very harsh difficulties.

For if different parts of the *Soul of the World* inhabit different parts of Matter, then when a man moves from one place to another, he either tears one part of the *Soul of the World* from another, or else he changes souls with every step. If the latter were true, it is a wonder that he does not change his intelligence <note>original: "Wits"</note> as well and lose his memory. This could only be avoided if they say that every part of the *Soul of the World*, upon entering a new body, acts exactly as the part it replaced did (assuming the body hasn't changed). In that case, every part of the *Soul of the World* would have the exact same thoughts, errors, truths, memories, pains, and pleasures that the previous part had in the body it just left. Thus, a man would always imagine he is himself wherever he goes, even though this "self" is nothing but the *Soul of the World* acting in a specific body, retaining and renewing the memory of all accidents, impressions, motions, and thoughts she perceived within that particular piece of organized matter. This is the most advantageous way this opinion could possibly be devised <note>original: "excogitated"</note>. But I leave it to those who enjoy confusing themselves with such mysteries to see if they can make any real sense of it.

5. And if someone can imagine this as possible, I would ask him: based on this supposition, who is *himself*? He cannot deny that he is a being capable of perception and *attention*, which the *Body* is not; therefore, he himself is not the *Body*. He must, then, be that within him which is properly called the *Soul*. But he is not the soul's operations, for the same reason—because the operations perceive nothing, while the soul perceives them as it performs them. Nor is he the *Faculties*, for they do not perceive each other's operations; rather, that which is a man's *Self* perceives them all. Therefore, he must say he is the *Soul*. And if there is only one Soul in the world, he would be forced to boast that he is the *Soul of the World*. But this pride must quickly fall if he simply considers that the *Soul of the World* would be every man's personal *self-identity* <note>original: "Ipseity"; from the Latin 'ipse', meaning 'self'</note> as well as his own. Consequently, every single man would be all men, and all men would be but *one* individual man—which is a perfect contradiction to all the laws of *Metaphysics* and *Logic*.

6. Reminded of these inconveniences, such a person will speak more cautiously. He will affirm that he is not the *Soul of the World* in its entirety, but only insofar as she carries out or exerts herself through the *Sense* and Remembrance of all those notions or impressions that happen to her...

wherever the soul is joined with his body; but as soon as this body of his is dissipated and dissolved, the soul will no longer produce any such specific thoughts or senses that refer to that union. Consequently, the memory of such actions, notions, and impressions—which were held together in relation to a particular body—is lost and set aside upon the failure of the body to which they referred. Thus, this *selfhood* <term>original: "Ipseity"; the quality of being oneself or having a distinct identity</term> or *personality*, which consisted mainly in this, necessarily perishes at death.

This certainly is what many libertines <note>original: "Libertines"; individuals who rejected moral and religious restraints, often favoring materialist or pantheist views to avoid the idea of post-mortem judgment</note> would prefer (if they even understand their own meaning), as they are afraid to meet themselves in the other world for fear they should quarrel with themselves there for their actions in this one. It is the most attractive theory <note>original: "Hypothesis"</note> they can construct in their own favor, and it is far superior to that dull idea *that there is nothing but mere matter in the world*, which is infinitely more easy to disprove.

7. And yet, this is too thin a covering to shelter them and secure them from the sad consequences <note>original: "after-claps"; unexpected strokes of misfortune or consequences following an event</term> they may justly suspect in the next life. For first, they must admit that they have in this life as specific and proper a sense of torment, of pleasure, of peace, and of pangs of conscience, and of other impressions, as if they had an individual soul of their own distinct from that of the world and from everyone else’s; and if there are any *spirits* or *genies* <note>original: "Dæmons or Genii"; in this context, neutral terms for supernatural beings or guiding spirits</note>, as there certainly are, the same is true for them as well. We have also demonstrated that all *sense* and *perception* are immediately triggered in the soul by the *vital spirits* <note>original: "Spirits"; the subtle fluids then believed to circulate through the nerves to facilitate sensation and movement</note>. Therefore, with what confidence can they promise themselves that the death of this earthly body will completely erase all traces of their existence here on earth? In all likelihood, the subtler remains of that body may direct the thoughts of the *Soul of the World* in the same course as before, drawing from her the memory of all the transactions of this life, and making her exercise her judgment upon them. This would cause her to shape the most vital vapors <note>original: "exhalations"</note> of the terrestrial body into an *aerial vehicle* <term>original: "Aëreal Vehicle"; a subtle, semi-material body composed of air or "ether" that the soul was thought to inhabit after the physical body died</term>, which would share the same nature as the biological "ferment" of these material beginnings of life saved from the ruins of death.

For even a slight touch is enough to prompt the soul to complete the entire scene; and so a man shall be represented to himself and others in the next state whether he wants to be or not, and he will have as distinct a personal *selfhood* there as he had in this life. From this it is plain that this false *theory*—*that we are nothing but the Soul of the World acting in our bodies*—will not serve the purposes of those who wish it were true, nor will it secure them from future danger, even if it were admitted to be true. But I have already demonstrated it to be false based on the concept of the *Unity* of a soul.

We shall be even more assured of the truth of this demonstration if we consider that the subtle elements, which are the immediate conveyors of *perceptions* in our souls, are continuous throughout the *Soul of the World* and permeate all living creatures. Therefore, the *Soul of the World* would necessarily be informed in every part of what she thinks or feels everywhere, if she were the only soul that animated every *living creature* <note>original: "Animal"</note> upon Earth. Consequently, the Sun, stars, and planets would appear to us in the actual size they really are, because they are perceived in that size by those...

8. That other notion, that our souls are a *Vital Ray* of the *Soul of the World*, may gain much support from expressions in ancient authors that seem to favor the opinion. For instance, **Epictetus** says that the souls of men are "united with God, as being his parts and fragments" <note>original: "συμφυεῖς τῷ Θεῷ, ἅτε αὐτοῦ μόρια ἔσαι καὶ ἀποσπάσματα"</note>. And **Philo** calls the Mind of Man "a fragment and inseparable part of the divine soul" <note>original: "τῆς θείας ψυχῆς ἀπόσπασμα καὶ ἀδιαίρετον"</note>. **Trismegistus** also says, "the mind is not cut off from the essence of God, but is spread out like the light of the sun" <note>original: "ὁ νοῦς οὐκ ἔστιν ἀποτετμημένος τῆς οὐσίας τοῦ Θεοῦ, ἀλλ᾽ ὥσπερ ἡπλωμένος καθάπερ τὸ τοῦ ἡλίου φῶς"</note>. All these expressions make the soul of man a ray or beam of the *Soul of the World* or of *God*. 

But we must take notice that these are merely metaphorical phrases. What is actually understood by them is *that there is an emanation of a secondary substance from the various parts of the Soul of the World, resembling the rays of the Sun*. This way of thinking, though it is easier to grasp than the other, still has enough difficulties. For this *Vital Ray* must have some source from which it is stretched. If so, the body would be like a bird on a string, which would be drawn to a great length when one takes long voyages—to the *East* or *West Indies*, for example. Yet even those are nothing compared to the length of our yearly journey on the Earth as it moves from *Libra* to *Aries* <note>The author is referring to the Earth's orbit around the sun, which covers a massive distance through the zodiac signs over six months</note>. Or, if you prefer not to see it as a *linear ray* but as an "orb" or sphere of individual life, every such sphere must be incredibly vast so that the body does not travel out of the soul's reach. Besides, this sphere would strike through other bodies as well as its own, and its own body would occupy only several small parts of it. Such inconsistencies and lack of harmony are very harsh and unpleasing to our rational faculties.

Therefore, the notion that is infinitely more elegant and certain is the one that proportions the soul to the dimensions of the body and makes her independent of anything but the Will and Essence of her Creator. Because God is exactly the same everywhere, and His power is as well, the soul's sustaining support is exactly the same as what she had at the very first moment of her creation and placement in the world. In this respect of dependence, she may be called a *Ray* of Him, just as the rest of creation is; but in no other sense that I know of, except for likeness and similarity, she being the *Image of God*, just as the rays of light are the image of the *Sun*.

9. But even if every particular soul were a "ray" of the *Soul of the World*, what do the skeptics gain by this? These *rays* would be just as capable of maintaining the various functions of life as the soul is in the sense we have described. Therefore, *personality, memory*, and *conscience* will just as surely return or continue in the next state under this hypothesis as they do in the more common one. <margin>*On the Immortality of the Soul, chapter 14.*</margin> 

This also reveals the great folly of **Pomponatius** <note>Pietro Pomponazzi (1462–1525), an Italian philosopher who questioned the soul's immortality based on Aristotelian logic</note> (and of all those influenced by his thinking). He is modest and judicious enough not to deny the existence of *apparitions* <note>ghosts or spirits</note>, but he attributes them all to the influence of the stars, or rather the *Intelligences* of the celestial orbs. He argues that since these celestial forces give life and animation to brute animals, why might they not also, when the occasion arises, animate and move the air into a specific shape and form—even making these shapes speak and converse with one another? For Pomponatius argues this in his book *On the Immortality of the Soul*, based on the concession of **Thomas Aquinas** that angels and separated souls may shape the air into a form and speak through it. <margin>*On the Immortality of the Soul, chapter 14, pages 114, 115.*</margin> "Why therefore should the Intelligence—" <note>original Latin: "Quare igitur Intelligentia"</note>

<header>The Immortality of the Soul. BOOK III.</header>

"Can the intelligences moving the celestial bodies—which possess so many and such great instruments—not do these things, they who make parrots, woodpeckers, crows, and blackbirds speak? <note>original Latin: *telligentiæ moventes corpora cælestia hæc facere non possunt cum suis instru- mentis quæ tot ac tanta possunt, quæ faciant Psittacos, Picos, Corvos & Merulas, loqui?*</note>" And a little after, he plainly reasons from the power the *Intelligences* <term>Intelligences: In medieval and Renaissance cosmology, these were immaterial beings or angels believed to govern the motion of the planets and stars.</term> have of generating animals, that it is not at all strange that they should raise such kind of *apparitions* as are recorded in *history*.

But if these *celestial intelligences* are confined to their own spheres <note>original: "Orbs"</note>, so that no *secondary essence* reaches these lower regions, it is impossible to conceive how they can act upon the matter here below. But if there are any such *essential emanations* from them, by which they give life to the matter in these living *species* we see in the world, such as men and animals <note>original: "Brutes"</note>; nothing hinders those same *emanations* from remaining and giving life to the air when this earthly body <note>original: "fabrick"</note> fails, and retaining the memory of things done in this life. Thus, our *personality* will be preserved as perfect and distinct as it was here.

10. But this idea <note>original: "conceit"</note> of *Pomponatius* <note>Pietro Pomponazzi (1462–1525), an Italian philosopher who questioned the traditional proofs for the immortality of the soul.</note> is far more foolish than theirs who claim there is only one *Soul of the World* <term>Anima Mundi: The "Soul of the World," an underlying spirit that some philosophers believed animated all nature.</term> that passes through all the matter of the world and is present in every place to perform all the feats that are to be done. To acknowledge as many distinct *intellectual beings* as there are imagined celestial spheres, yet to hesitate—or rather to seem confident—that there are not as many individual souls as there are men here on Earth, is nothing but whim and madness. For it is just as rational to acknowledge eight hundred thousand myriads of *intellectual* and *immaterial beings*, really distinct from one another, as it is to acknowledge eight; and an infinite number is as rational as acknowledging only one that could not create the matter of the world. For then two substances, wholly independent of one another, would be granted, as also the infinite parts of matter that have no dependence one on the other.

Why may there not be, therefore, infinite numbers of spirits or souls that have as little dependence on one another as those eight intelligences? Especially since the motions and operations of every animal are a more certain argument for an *immaterial being* residing there than the motions of the heavens are for any distinct *intelligences* in their spheres—if they could even be granted to have any. It is no stranger a thing to conceive of an infinite multitude of *immaterial* as well as *material essences* independent of one another, than to conceive of but two: namely, matter and the Soul of the World. But if there exists such an excellent principle as one that can create beings—as there certainly is—we are still the more assured that there are such multitudes of spiritual essences surviving all the chances of this present life, just as the most sober and knowledgeable men in all ages have declared there are.

<meta>catchword: CHAP.</meta>

**1.** We have now, despite <note>original: "maugre"</note> all the opposition and objections made to the contrary, safely conducted the soul into the next state and installed her in the same condition as the **aerial spirits**. I might be very well excused if I took my leave of her here and committed her to the fortune that awaits those of the invisible world; it is more appropriate for those who are there to meditate on and imagine all future events belonging to them than for us who are on this side of the passage. It is enough that I have demonstrated that neither the essence nor the operations of the soul are extinguished by death, but that they either do not cease <note>original: "intermit"</note> or suddenly revive upon the recovery of her **airy body**.

**2.** But seeing as those who take any pleasure at all in thinking of these things can seldom command the range of their thoughts within whatever limits they please, it is common for them to doubt whether the soul can be secure in her permanence of life in the other world. 3. The soul seems vulnerable to death for three reasons. The first we have already mentioned, which concerns an internal principle: the *periodic limits* of her *vital congruity* <term>vital congruity: the soul's natural capacity to be united with and animate a specific type of body (physical or aerial)</term>, or else the *fickleness* and *failure* of her own *will*. 5. His father Fazio Cardano, who confessed that he had the company of a familiar spirit for about thirty years, often told him the following story while he was alive; after his death, Girolamo found the exact account of it committed to writing, which was this: *On the 13th day of August 1491, after I had performed my religious rites, at the 20th hour of the day, seven men appeared to me in their usual manner. They were clothed in silk garments, with cloaks in the Greek style, purple stockings, and crimson coats <note>original: "Cassocks"</note> that were red and shining on their breasts. They said the thinness <note>original: "tenuity"</note> of their bodies was such that they can do us neither good nor harm, except for what they may be able to do through* **apparitions** *and* **terrors**, *and the sharing of knowledge. They were both public professors in an* **Academy**, *and the one of smaller stature had 300 disciples, while the other had 200. When my father asked them why they would not reveal the treasures they knew to men, they answered that there was a special law against it, carrying a very heavy penalty.*

7. Cardano found the record of this apparition among his father's papers, but he seems unwilling to decide whether it is a true history or a fable. 8. Regarding the death of the great god Pan, you may read of it in Plutarch's *On the Obsolescence of Oracles* <note>original Latin: "De defectu oraculorum"</note>. There, Philippus, as proof of the mortality of **demons** <note>original: "Dæmons"; in this context, referring to supernatural beings between gods and humans, not necessarily evil spirits.</note>, recites a story he heard from a Roman named Emilianus, a man far removed from both stupidity and vanity. He told how his father, Epitherses, was sailing for Italy in the evening near the Echinades islands when the wind failed them. Their ship was carried by an unpredictable course toward the island of Paxi. While most of the passengers were awake and many were drinking merrily after supper, a voice was suddenly heard from the island calling "Thamus" by name. Thamus was an Egyptian by birth and the pilot of the ship. The passengers were greatly astonished, as few of them had noticed the pilot’s name before. He was called twice before he gave any sign that he was listening, but after he gave his full attention, a clear and distinct voice was heard from the island uttering these words: **"When you reach Palodes, announce that the great Pan is dead"** <note>original Greek: "Ὅταν γίνῃ κατὰ τὸ Παλῶδες, ἀπάγγειλον, ὅτι Πὰν ὁ μέγας τέθνηκεν"</note>. The company was much astonished upon hearing the voice. After much debate among themselves, Thamus resolved that if the wind blew fair, he would sail past and say nothing; but if they were becalmed there, he would deliver his message. Therefore, being becalmed when they came to Palodes, with neither wind nor tide moving them, Thamus looked out from the stern <note>original: "poop"</note> of the ship toward the shore and delivered his message, telling them that the great Pan was dead. Upon this, there was suddenly heard a collective groaning of a multitude together, mixed with a murmuring of wonder.

<margin>See Plutarch, *On the Obsolescence of Oracles*.</margin>

This is the maximum that anyone allows them; most people allow less. Plutarch, speaking through the voices of others, has polished this opinion into a more elaborate and distinct form. Based on the mortality of the spirits and the various ranks of rational beings Hesiod mentions—namely **Gods, spirits, heroes, and men** <note>original Greek: "Θεοὶ, δαίμονες, ἥρωες, and ἄνθρωποι"</note>—he has assigned a specific law and manner for their passing from one state to another, making them change their elemental forms as well as their status. From demons, a few, after a long time and being entirely purified through virtue, come to participate in divinity <note>original Greek: ὁρᾶται, τῆς οὐσίας ἄνω φερομένης˙ οὕτως ἐκ μὲν ἀνθρώπων εἰς ἥρωας, ἐκ δ᾽ ἡρώων εἰς δαίμονας αἱ βελτίονες ψυχαὶ τὴν μεταβολὴν λαμβάνουσιν, ἐκ δὲ δαιμόνων ὀλίγαι μὲν ἔτι χρόνῳ πολλῷ δι᾽ ἀρετῆς καθαρθεῖσαι παντάπασι θεότητος μετέχον.</note>. But others, he says, not having sufficient command of themselves, are again brought down into human bodies to live there a fleeting and obscure life, having a lightless and dim existence <note>original Greek: ἀλαμπῆ καὶ ἀμυδρὴν ζωὴν ἴσχουσαι</note>, as he phrases it.

10. These are the most notable testimonies for the mortality of demons that I have encountered, and they are therefore well worth our review. That vision of Facius Cardanus, if it is not a mere fable, contains many paradoxes.

<margin>
*On the Variety of Things, Book 16, Chapter 93.* <note>original Latin: *De rerum varietate lib. 16. cap. 93.*</note>
</margin>

First, **that these aerial spirits are born at set times just as we are.** This does not mean that "she-demons" go into labor to give birth to them, but rather that they seem to have a beginning to their existence, from which their age may be measured—some living more years and some fewer. This is inconceivable, unless we imagine that there is a constant "lapse" or descent of souls out of the higher regions of the air into these lower ones, or that those who leave these earthly bodies join the ranks of the aerial spirits. Similarly, their death cannot be easily understood unless we imagine that their souls pass into more pure <term>vehicles</term> <note>In Neoplatonic philosophy, a "vehicle" is the subtle body or "casing" that carries the soul.</note>, or else descend back into terrestrial bodies. For Cardano himself acknowledges that they do not truly perish, which is consistent with his opinion on the pre-existence of our souls.

Secondly, **that these aerial spirits live for only about 300 years.** This contradicts the poet Hesiod and the majority of the Platonists, unless they were speaking specifically of the particular order of spirits to which they belonged. It is likely that there is as much difference in their lifespans as there is in the lifespans of various kinds of birds and beasts.

Thirdly, **that our souls are mortal to the extent that nothing uniquely "us" remains after death.**

Fourthly, **that they were far more closely allied to the gods than we are, and that there was as much difference between them and us as there is between us and beasts.** This must be understood in terms of the excellence and natural activity of their "vehicles," rather than the superiority of their intellectual faculties. If it does refer to intellect, it must only apply to the better sort of those aerial spirits. Or, if they mean it applies to all their ranks, it may be a mistake born of pride—much like how the rich, powerful, and academic among us take it for granted that they are more judicious and discerning than the poor and lowly, no matter how wise those poor men may be.

Fifthly, **that they know all secret things, whether hidden books or buried money.** Humans might do this as well if they could stand by unseen while someone else hid them.

Sixthly, **that the lowest sort of these spirits were the guardians of the noblest men, just as the lowliest humans are the keepers and trainers of the best kinds of dogs and horses.** This part of the vision is also shrouded in mystery, as they have not defined whether this "lowliness" of the guardian spirits should be understood in a **political** or **physical** sense...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "Averroistical spirits" encountered by Fazio Cardano. It explores their philosophical views on the soul's survival after death and posits that human souls may exist in a state invisible even to these supernatural beings.</meta>

...well hold to it, as some do among us. For Pomponazzi <note>Pietro Pomponazzi (1462–1525), an Italian philosopher who argued that the immortality of the soul could not be proven by reason.</note> and others of the *Averroists* <note>Followers of the medieval philosopher Averroes, who believed in a single, universal "active intellect" shared by all humans rather than individual immortal souls.</note> are as ridiculously stubborn as they are.

And therefore these *Averroistical spirits* <note>original: "Dæmons"</note> answered exactly according to the conclusions of their own school of thought: *that nothing belonging to any individual survives after death.* <note>original Latin: "Nihil proprium cuiquam supereſſe poſt mortem."</note> For the Mind or Soul being a substance common to all, and now separated from those earthly bodies which it animated in *Plato*, suppose, or *Socrates*—and these bodies being dead and decayed, and only the common Soul of the World surviving—there being nothing but this Soul and these bodies to make up *Socrates* and *Plato*, they conclude it is a plain case that nothing unique to the individual survives after death. And therefore, though they see the representation of *Socrates* and *Plato* in the other world, claiming their own personalities along with all the actions they did and accidents that befell them in this life, yet according to the gloomy subtleties and curiosities of their school, they may think and profess that, to speak accurately and philosophically, it is none of them. They believe there is no substance unique to them remaining after death, but only the *Soul of the World*, renewing the thoughts to itself of what belonged to those parties in this life.

12. This is one hypothesis consistent enough with the honesty of these *spirits*; but there is also another, not at all impossible: namely, that the *spiritual bodies* <note>original: "Vehicles"</note> of the souls of men who have died are as invisible to this order of *spirits* <note>original: "Genii"</note> that conversed with *Fazio Cardano* as that order is to us. And therefore, though the ghosts of deceased men appear to them as well as to us, yet it being only for a time, it moves them no more than our hardened *Epicureans* <note>Philosophers who believed the soul was material and died with the body.</note> in this world are moved by such things. Especially since it is easy for them to think that these are nothing but some playful spectacles that the universal Soul of the World represents to itself and other spectators, when and for how long she pleases, and that the vaporous remains of the dead body provide the occasion.

Now, it may appear from the following that the *spiritual bodies* <note>original: "Vehicles"</note> of the souls of men who have departed this life—after they have come to a settled condition—may be far thinner and more invisible than those of the previously mentioned *spirits*, without causing any inconsistency in nature. For the excellence of the inward Spirit is not always according to the thickness of the Element with which it is joined. Otherwise, those fish that have a human shape, and are taken at certain times in the *Indian Sea*, should have a higher degree of Reason and Religion than we who live upon Earth and have bodies made of that element. From this, nothing hinders the spirit of man from being more noble than the spirit of some of the *aerial spirits*. And since Nature does not always move in linear steps <note>original: "Arithmetical... Progreſſion"</note>, but also in exponential leaps <note>original: "Geometrical Progreſſion"</note>, one step in one being may reach far above what is currently ahead of it in other degrees of progress. Just as a creeping worm is above a caddis-worm, and any four-footed beast is above the birds until the birds can use their legs as well as the beasts; but as soon as they are equal to them, they are immediately far above them, and can not only walk, but fly. Just as a peasant is above an imprisoned prince and has more command; but this prince can be no sooner set free and become...

And so it may be naturally with the souls of men when they are freed from this prison of the body: their progress being made in geometrical progression <note>A mathematical metaphor suggesting that as the soul's refinement increases, it does so at an accelerating rate.</note>, as soon as they seem equal to that order of *daemons* <note>original: "Dæmons"; here referring to supernatural spirits or beings, not necessarily evil demons.</note> we speak of, they may mount far above them in fineness and subtlety of body, and so become invisible to them. Therefore, this leaves the spirits in a position of falsely assuming that souls do not exist at all, simply because they cannot see them.

13. But if they thought that there is either some particular ray of the "Soul of the World" that belongs peculiarly (suppose) to *Socrates* or *Plato*, or that they had individual souls really distinct, then it is evident that they either spoke ambiguously or lied. Their pride and scorn of mankind—they looking upon us as little more than beasts in comparison to themselves—might easily permit this. They would feel no more guilt in deceiving us than we do when we play a trick <note>original: "put a dodge upon a dog"</note> on a dog to amuse ourselves. But if they had a design to lead us into some dangerous error, it is very likely that they would shuffle it in among many truths, so that those truths, being examined and found solid at the bottom, might prevent us from suspecting any one of their dictates to be false. Therefore, if this vision was ill-intentioned, the intended poison was the doctrine of the soul's mortality; the dangerous falsehood of that opinion was to be covered by a mixture of other things that are true.

<margin>*On the Obsolescence of Oracles* <note>original: "De Defectu Oraculorum," a work by Plutarch.</note></margin>
14. As for that account of *Aemilianus*, which he heard from his father *Epitherses*, it would be even more relevant to our purpose if the conclusion of the scholars at *Rome* could be thought authentic. This occurred after *Thamus* had been sent for and confirmed the truth of the story to *Tiberius Caesar*—namely, that this *Pan*, the news of whose death *Thamus* told to the spirits at *Palodes*, was the son of *Mercury* and *Penelope*. For then it is plain that *Pan* was a human soul, and therefore concerns the present question more nearly. But because this narrative is applicable to a more sacred and venerable subject <note>A reference to the Christian tradition that the "death of Pan" coincided with the crucifixion of Christ, signifying the end of pagan oracles.</note>, it loses some of its force and fitness for our present use. That which *Demetrius* adds, concerning certain holy islands near *Britain*, would have been more fitting in this regard. When *Demetrius* arrived there, a great commotion of the air suddenly occurred, with mighty tempests and prodigious whirlwinds. After these ceased, the inhabitants declared, "That one of the superior beings has died" <note>original Greek: "Ὅτι τῶν κρειττόνων τινὸς ἔκλειψις γέγονεν"</note>. Upon this *Plutarch*, according to his usual eloquence, comments in this manner: *For just as the lighting of a lamp brings no trouble, but its extinction is distressing to many; so great souls, while they remain kindled into life, shine forth harmlessly and kindly, but their extinction or decay often stirs up winds and tempests, as in this present example, and often infects the air with poisonous plagues* <note>original Greek: "Ὡς γὰρ λύχνου ἀναπτόμενου φάναι δεινὸν οὐδὲν ἔχει, σβεννύμενου δὲ πολλοῖς λυπηρός ἐστιν· οὕτως αἱ μεγάλαι ψυχαὶ τὰς μὲν ἀναλάμψεις εὐμενεῖς καὶ ἀλύπους ἔχουσιν, αἱ δὲ σβέσεις αὐτῶν καὶ φθοραὶ πολλάκις μὲν, ὡς νυνὶ, πνεύματα καὶ ζάλας τρέπουσι, πολλάκις δὲ καὶ λοιμικοῖς πάθεσιν ἀέρα φαρμάττουσιν."</note>.
