<meta>This page continues the discussion on the soul's progression through different states of existence, specifically focusing on the transition between the physical, aerial, and ethereal realms, and whether the soul is truly immortal or subject to a form of "death" when changing its spiritual "vehicle" or body.</meta>

<header>The Immortality of the Soul. BOOK III.</header>

15. Whether the souls of men that leave these *earthly* bodies are *virtuous* or *vicious*, they must eventually "die" to their *aerial vehicles* <note>The author uses the term "vehicle" to describe the "body" or vessel the soul inhabits in different states of existence—first earthly, then made of air, then of light or ether.</note>. This seems like a sad story at first glance, as if *righteousness* could not *deliver one from death*. But if it is carefully examined, the terror will be found to concern only the *wicked*. For the deepest level of *death* is the *descent into this terrestrial body*. In this body, besides the fact that we necessarily forget whatever has passed, we lead for the present "a dark and obscure life" <note>original: "ἀλαμπῆ κὴ ἀμυδρὴν ζωήν"</note>, as *Plutarch* says, dragging this weight of Earth along with us, just as prisoners and criminals drag their heavy shackles in their filthy and secluded jail cells. 

But in our return back from this earthly state, *life* is naturally more expansive for those who are prepared to make good use of the advantage they have in their *airy vehicle*. However, if they are not masters of themselves in that state, they will eventually be fatally sent back to their former prison; this is the most total *death* imaginable. But for the *good* and *virtuous* souls that after many ages change their *aerial vehicle* for an *ethereal* one, that is no *death* to them, but a higher ascent into *life*. One might as well say of an infant who has left the dark womb of his mother that this change is *death*, as say that a *genius* <note>term: Here meaning the individual human soul or spirit.</note> dies by leaving the thick *air* and emerging into that vehicle of light which is commonly called *ethereal* or *celestial*.

16. There may be, therefore (according to Axiom 36), a dangerous relapse from the *aerial vehicle* back into the *terrestrial*, which is properly the *death* of a soul that moves backward in its progress. But for those who ever reach the *ethereal* state, the periods of life there are infinite. Although they may have their *perigees* as well as *apogees* <note>term: Astronomical terms used metaphorically. A "perigee" is the point in an orbit closest to the Earth, while an "apogee" is the point farthest away.</note>, these circuits are of such vast scope, their *perigees* so rare and short, and their return to their former *apsis* <note>term: The highest or lowest point in an orbital path.</note> so certain—like that of the celestial bodies—that their *ethereal* awareness never leaves them even when they are at their lowest point near the Earth. It is clear that they have arrived at that *life* which is justly called *eternal*.

17. From this it is plain that *perseverance in virtue*, if no external *fate* hinders it, will carry a man to an *immortal life*. But whether those who are thus *heroically good* become so through discipline and effort, or "by some divine dispensation" <note>original: "θείᾳ τινὶ μοίρᾳ"</note> (a special favor and irresistible design of God), is not to be disputed here, though it is discussed at length in the dialogues of *Plato*. But in the meantime, we will not hesitate to conclude that there is no *internal impediment* for those who are highly and *heroically virtuous* that would prevent them, in the course of time, from arriving at an everlasting security of *life* and *happiness* after they have left this *earthly body*.

<summary>The author argues that for the virtuous, leaving the physical body is an ascent into higher life rather than death, while the wicked risk a "death" that consists of being reborn into the physical world. True immortality is achieved when the soul reaches an ethereal state of constant awareness and virtue.</summary>

<header>CHAPTER XVIII. The Immortality of the Soul.</header>

# CHAPTER XVIII.

1. *The burning of the world as an opinion of the Stoics.* 2. *Two ways of destroying the world noted by the ancients, especially by fire.* 3. *That the burning of the world, as it relates to us, is to be understood only as the burning of the Earth.* 4. *That the goals of the Stoics' burning of the world are applicable only to the Earth’s burning.* 5. *An acknowledgment that the Earth may be burnt, though the proof of it is irrelevant <note>original: "impertinent"</note> to this section.* 6. *That its burning will prove very fatal to the souls of wicked men and demons.* 7. *Five different opinions concerning their state after the burning; the first being that they are quite destroyed by fire.* 8. *The second, that they are annihilated by a special act of God's power.* 9. *The third, that they lie senseless in an eternal death.* 10. *The fourth, that they are in a perpetual, furious, and painful dream.* 11. *The fifth and last, that they will revive again, and that the Earth and Air will be inhabited by them.* 12. *That this last seems to be formed from the fictional rebirth <note>original: "παλιγγενεσία" (palingenesia)</note> of the Stoics, who were very poor metaphysicians and equally bad naturalists.* 13. *A critical comment on a self-contradicting sentence by Seneca.* 14. *The lack of clarity regarding the state of the souls of the wicked after the burning.* 15. *That the inhabitants of the Ether will be safe. And what will then become of good men and demons on the Earth and in the Air. And how they cannot be delivered except by a supernatural power.*

**1.** As for external obstacles, we shall now examine them to see what force they have, and if they exist at all. The first of these is *The Conflagration <note>term: A large, destructive fire; specifically, the predicted end of the world by fire.</note> of the World*. This is an ancient opinion, believed and entertained not only by religions but by philosophers as well—especially the *Stoics*, who affirm that the souls of men do indeed survive after death, but cannot continue to exist any longer than the time when the world burns. However, it is not so much important what they thought as it is to consider the actual condition of the souls of men and *demons* <note>original: "Dæmons"; in this context, the author refers to spiritual entities inhabiting the air, which could be good, neutral, or evil, rather than just "devils."</note> after that tragic fate.

<margin>Seneca, cited in Lipsius, *Physiologia Stoicorum*, book 2, dissertation 21.</margin>
**2.** Those who do not believe the world is eternal have found two ways to destroy it: by water or by *fire* <note>original: "ἐξυδατώσει or ἐκπυρώσει"</note>. These, they say, happen as naturally in a vast period of time (which they call the *Great Year* <note>original: "Annus Magnus"</note>) as winter and summer do in our ordinary year. *“A flood comes, just as winter and summer do, by the law of the world”* <note>original: "Inundatio non secus quàm Hyems, quàm Æstas lege Mundi venit."</note>. But as for this destruction by water, since it is not as famous, nor as frequently spoken of, nor as destructive, nor as likely to end the world as the other way—and since it does not belong properly to our inquiry—we shall let it pass. The general prediction now concerns *Fire*, held not only by the Stoics such as *Zeno, Cleanthes, Chrysippus, and Seneca*, but also by several of different sects, such as *Heraclitus, Epicurus, Cicero, Pliny, Aristocles, Numenius*, and many others.

<margin>Justus Lipsius, *Physiology of the Stoics*, book 2, dissertation 22.</margin>

3. But though there is such great and unanimous agreement that the *World* shall be burnt, they do not all express themselves the same way in the matter. *Seneca's* vote is the most extravagantly explicit of any, describing the very *Stars* as running and crashing into one another, thereby setting everything on fire. But *Posidonius* and *Panaetius* had more sense; they did not hold to that <term>universal conflagration</term> <note>original: "ἐκπύρωσις τῶν ὅλων" (ekpyrosis tōn holōn)</note> which the other *Stoics* did. For the destruction of the *Ethereal Regions* by *Fire* is as foolish a fancy as sentencing an *eel* to be drowned, because the matter of the *Ether* is too fine and subtle for *Fire* to rage in, being indeed nothing but pure *Light* or *Fire* itself. And yet this *Ethereal Matter* is by far the greatest portion of the *World*. Therefore, the *World* cannot properly be said to be liable to destruction by *fire* from any natural causes, as the *Stoics* would have it. This is demonstrably true according to *Descartes's principles*, as he makes *Fire* nothing but the motion of certain little particles of *Matter*, and holds that there is no more motion at one time in the *World* than at another; because one part of *Matter* cannot impress any agitation upon another without losing just as much itself. This frightening talk of the *Conflagration of the World*, therefore, must be restricted to the firing of the *Earth* only, so far as it concerns us. For there is nothing else combustible in the *Universe* but the *Earth* and other *Planets*, and whatever *vapors* and *exhalations* arise from them.

<margin>Justus Lipsius, *Physiology of the Stoics*, book 2, dissertation 22.</margin>

4. This *Conflagration*, therefore, which *philosophers*, *poets*, *Sibyls*, and everyone else have filled the *World* with the reputation of, is nothing but the burning of the *Earth*. And the goals the *Stoics* claim for their <term>conflagration</term> <note>original: "ἐκπύρωσις" (ekpyrosis)</note> may be applicable to it, but not to the burning of the *Heavens* or *Ether* at all, as anyone even slightly skilled in *Philosophy* must acknowledge. For their nature is so simple that they cannot decay, and therefore they require no renovation, as the *Earth* does. Nor do the inhabitants of those *Heavenly Regions* pollute themselves with any vice; or if they do, they sink from their *physical* station as well as their *moral* one, and fall toward these *terrestrial dregs*. And therefore that part of the happy <term>rebirth</term> <note>original: "παλιγγενεσία" (palingenesia)</note> that *Seneca* speaks of—

> Every living creature will be generated anew, and man will be given back to the earth, innocent of crimes and born under better omens <note>original: "Omne animal ex integro generabitur, dabitúrque terris homo inſcius ſcelerum, & melioribus auſpiciis natus"</note>—

will not apply to those *Ethereal Creatures*.

5. We are willing, then, to be carried along by this common and loud cry of *Fire* that must burn the *World*, into an acknowledgment that the *Earth* may, within a certain period of time, be burnt, along with all those things that are upon it or near it. But what combination of natural causes may contribute to this dismal *spectacle* is not for me to argue, especially in this place. I shall only take a view of what sad effects this *Conflagration* may have upon the *Souls* of *Demons* and *Men*. For it is evident that those who have recovered their *Ethereal Vehicles* <note>The "ethereal vehicle" refers to the subtle, celestial body the soul inhabits after being purified from earthly attachments.</note> are exempt from this fate; the remoteness of their habitation secures them from both the rage and the foulness of these *sulfurous flames*.

6. The most certain and most destructive execution that this *Fire* will perform must be upon the unredeemed *Souls* of *Wicked Men* and *Demons*—those who are so deeply sunk and drowned <term>into the world of physical existence</term> <note>original: "εἰς γένεσιν" (eis genesin)</note> that the very

<header>CHAPTER XVIII. The Immortality of the Soul.</header>

The density of their spiritual bodies <note>original: "Vehicles"</note> imprisons them within the limits of this thick, misty air. These souls or spirits, therefore, who have so inextricably entangled themselves in the fate of this lower world—giving up all their senses to the fleeting pleasures of the most luxurious principle, which is the very seat of death—are, in the mystical philosophy of the ancients, called *Nymphs*. Although the ancients allot them a long series of years, they do not exempt them from mortality and fate. And *Demetrius* in *Plutarch's* writings declares specifically, citing *Hesiod*, that their life will end with the *Conflagration* <note>The prophesied end of the world by fire.</note> of the world. This is based on what the Poet hints at enigmatically: "The argument overall seems to be hinted at by Hesiod regarding the conflagration, at which time it is likely that the Nymphs will fail along with the moisture." <note>original Greek: Καὶ ὁ λόγος ὅλως ἠνίχθαι δοκεῖ τῷ Ἡσιόδῳ πρὸς τὴν ἐκπύρωσιν, ὁπηνίκα συνεκλείπειν τοῖς ὑγροῖς εἰκός ἐστι τὰς Νύμφας</note>

---
-> Who dwell in the beautiful groves, <-

<note>original Greek: Αἵ τ᾽ ἄλσεα καλὰ νέμονται / Καὶ πηγὰς ποταμῶν καὶ πείσεα ποιήεντα.</note>
---

7. But to move past these poetic riddles and take a more serious and distinct view of the soul's condition after the *burning* of the Earth, we shall find five different opinions concerning it. The first holds *that this unmerciful heat and fire will at last destroy and consume the soul as well as the body.* But this seems impossible to me—that any created substance should utterly destroy another substance so as to reduce it to nothing. No part of *matter*, even when acting most violently upon another part, can do that. It can only thin out, scatter, and disperse the parts, making them invisible. But the substance of the soul is *incapable of being scattered* <note>original: "indissipable"</note> and *cannot be torn apart* <note>original: "indiscerpible"</note>; therefore, it remains whole, whatever happens to the body or its spiritual container <note>original: "Vehicle"</note>.

8. The second opinion is *that after long and tedious torture in these flames, the soul is annihilated by a special act of God's power.* But, it seems to me, this relies too much on God having to find a way out of a problem. It is as if God were so stuck by creating a creature that is naturally immortal that he must then "uncreate" it or annihilate it. Furthermore, the divine *Nemesis* <note>The principle of divine justice and cosmic order.</note> that is understood within philosophy never assumes such forced outbursts of the Deity to create extraordinary effects. Instead, everything is brought about by a wise and inevitable chain of secondary causes, whether they are natural forces or the choices of free agents.

9. The third opinion, therefore, to avoid these absurdities, denies both *destruction by fire* and *annihilation*. Instead, it suggests *that the boredom and extremity of pain eventually make the soul, on its own, pull away from all connection with matter.* This connection is the immediate principle of union which we call *Vital Congruity* <note>The natural harmony or "fit" between a soul and its body.</note>, consisting of a specific state of the body (or spiritual vehicle) as well as the soul. When this state is ruined and lost, and the soul is thereby completely loosed from all sympathy with the body or matter, she becomes perfectly dead and senseless to all things (following Axiom 36) and, as they say, *will remain so forever.* But this does not seem rational; for, as *Aristotle* says somewhere, "Everything that has a function exists for the sake of its work." <note>original Greek: Ἕκαστον, οὗ ἔστιν ἐνέργεια, ἔστιν ἕνεκα τοῦ ἔργου.</note> Therefore, many whole immaterial substances would continue to exist for all eternity for no end or purpose, even though they could be used to animate matter again just as well as ever.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of five theories regarding the soul's state after the world is destroyed by fire, specifically focusing on the possibility of a restoration of life on Earth.</meta>

<header>The Immortality of the Soul. BOOK III.</header>

...that after this dissolution <note>original: "solution," meaning the loosening or separation</note> of the souls or spirits of *wicked men* and *demons* from their spiritual bodies <note>original: "Vehicles"</note>, their pain continues even in that separate state. They fall into an unquiet sleep, full of furious, tormenting dreams that act as fiercely upon their spirits as the external fire did upon their bodies. 

But others object to this opinion as a very uncertain conjecture. It assumes something that seems unsound to them: namely, that the soul can act when it has lost all vital union with matter. This seems contrary to the soul’s intimate and essential nature, which is suited for union with matter. Furthermore, the soul's dreams while in the body do not happen without the help of the animal spirits <note>In early modern science, "animal spirits" were fluids in the nerves thought to facilitate sensation and movement.</note> in the brain, which usually reflect their physical condition. From this, they conclude that there is no certain ground to establish this opinion.

11. Therefore, to make everything certain—so there may be no problem in admitting that the souls or spirits of *evil demons* and *wicked men*, separated from their spiritual bodies by the force of that fatal *conflagration*, may continue to exist—a final group has devised a strange and unexpected hypothesis. 

They suggest that once this fire has finished its work on that unfortunate crew, and long, terrible torture has worn out their afflicted ghosts until they completely withdraw from all matter and enter a profound sleep or death, nature will eventually recover. After a long series of years, the fury of the fire will be completely extinguished. The vast atmosphere of smoke and vapors sent up during the Earth's burning will return in heavy showers of rain. These rains will recreate the seas and rivers, solidify the ground, and fall so plentifully that the soil becomes pleasant and fruitful, and the air becomes cool and healthy. 

Nature, recovering to her advantage and becoming youthful again, full of life-giving <note>original: "genital," meaning generative or creative</note> salt and moisture, will cause the souls of all living creatures belonging to these lower regions of the earth and air to wake up in their proper places. The seas and rivers will be replenished with fish; the earth will produce all kinds of birds, four-footed beasts, and creeping things. The souls of men shall then catch life from the purer and more healing parts of the earth and be clothed again in physical bodies. Finally, the spirits of the air <note>original: "Aëreal Genii"</note>, once that element becomes healthy and vital again, shall revive in the cool, dewy <note>original: "rorid"</note> air in due time and order. This awakening into life is accompanied, they say, by inclinations matching the resolutions they made during those fiery torments before falling into their long sleep.

<margin>
*Lipsius, Stoic Physiology, book 1, dissertation 6; book 3, dissertation 13; book 2, dissertation 14.*
</margin>

12. But this whole hypothesis seems to be built out of the Stoics' dream concerning the *restoration* <note>original Greek: apokatastasis</note> or *rebirth* <note>original Greek: palingenesia</note> of the world after its *rising up* <note>original Greek: anastasis</note> or *conflagration* <note>original Greek: ekpyrosis</note>. It is as if this passage from *Seneca* applied to this case: *Epistle 36*: "Death, which we fear and shrink from, interrupts life, but does not take it away. A day will come again that will return us to the light—a day which many would refuse, were it not that it brings us back having forgotten our past." <note>original Latin: "Mors, quam pertimescimus ac recusamus, intermittit vitam, non eripit. Veniet iterum qui nos in lucem reponet dies, quem multi recusarent, nisi oblitos reduceret."</note> 

However, one can easily see how poorly the Stoics philosophize once they leave their usual path of moral teachings, if one is even moderately skilled in nature and metaphysics. For what errors could be more obvious than those they hold regarding *God*, the *soul*, and the *stars*? They consider the first two to be *physical substances* <note>original: "Corporeal Substances"</note> and believe the stars are fed by the vapors of the...

### CHAPTER XIII. The Immortality of the Soul.

Earth; affirming that the Sun sucks up the water of the great Ocean to quench his thirst, but that the Moon drinks from the smaller Rivers and Brooks. This is as true as the story of the Donkey that drank up the Moon <note>A traditional folk tale or proverb about an animal drinking from a bucket and "swallowing" the moon's reflection.</note>. Such conceits are more fitting for *Anacreon* <note>An ancient Greek poet famous for his drinking songs.</note> to stumble upon in a drunken fit—who, to invite his companions to tipple, composed that song:

> Drink! The sea drinks the breezes,
> And the sun drinks the sea,
<note>original: Πῖνε θάλασσα δ' αὔρας, Ὁ δ' ἥλιος θάλασσαν</note>

—than to be either discovered or owned by a serious and sober Philosopher. And yet *Seneca* <note>A Roman Stoic philosopher.</note> mightily triumphs in this notion of feeding the stars with the thick fogs of the Earth, and declares his opinion with no small amount of eloquence. However, because I love solid sense better than fine words, I shall not take the trouble to recite them.

13. The quality of his understanding may be easily discerned by my last quotation, in which there seems to be a clear contradiction: *The day will come again which will restore us to light, a day which many would refuse, unless it brought them back forgetful.* <note>original: Veniet iterum qui nos in lucem reponet dies, quem multi recusarent, nisi oblitos reduceret.</note> If it is *us*, how can we be *forgetful*? If we are *forgetful*, how is it *us*? For we are not ourselves unless we remember that we are so. And if madmen may be said—and truly so—to be "beside themselves" or "not themselves" because they have lost their wits, certainly those who have completely lost the memory of themselves will be far from being themselves; they would exist as if they had never been before. As *Lucretius* <note>A Roman poet and Epicurean philosopher.</note> has excellently declared:

<margin>On the Nature of Things, book 3.</margin>
> Even if time should collect our matter after death,
> And rearrange it to be as it is now,
> And once more the light of life were given to us,
> It would still not concern us at all,
> Since the memory of our former selves would have been once broken.
<note>original: Nec, si materiam nostram conlegerit ætas Post obitum, rursumque redegerit ut sit ac nunc est, Atque iterum nobis fuerint data lumina vitæ, Pertineat quicquam tamen ad nos id quoque factum, Interrupta semel cum sit retinentia nostri.</note>

In this passage, the Poet seems to industriously demolish all hopes of any benefit from this Stoic rebirth <note>original: παλιγγενεσία (palingenesia), meaning a periodic restoration or rebirth of the world.</note>. He professes that a person who cannot remember having ever lived before is the same as if he had never been. From this it would follow that even if the souls of men should revive after the *Conflagration* <note>The predicted destruction of the world by fire.</note> of the world, they have still not escaped a perpetual and permanent death.

14. We see, therefore, how desperately impossible it is to prove the condition of the soul after the *Conflagration* of the Earth, as all five of these opinions are accompanied by such instability and uncertainty. Therefore, they should be looked upon more as some nighttime landscape to feed our wandering melancholy, rather than a clear and distinct draft of understandable truth to inform our judgment.

15. All that we can be assured of is this: that those souls that have obtained their *Ethereal Vehicles* <note>original: Æthereal Vehicles; in this context, spiritual bodies made of the highest, purest matter (ether), which are immune to physical fire.</note> are out of the reach of that sad fate that follows this *Conflagration*; and that the wicked souls of *Men* and *Demons* will be involved in it. But there is a middle sort between these, concerning whom not only curiosity but good will would make a man anxious. For it is possible that the *Conflagration* of the world may surprise many thousands of souls that have not yet—through the course of time, nature, or any higher principle—reached an *Ethereal* state of life, but who may yet be very holy, innocent, and virtuous.

<header>The Immortality of the Soul. BOOK III.</header>

We may easily believe this if we consider that these very *earthly bodies* are not such great obstacles to the goodness and sincerity of the mind, but that many, even in this life, have given great examples of it. Nor can that *aerial* state be less capable of—nor easily exist without—the good *spirits* <note>original: "Genii"</note>, any more than the Earth could exist without *good men*, who are the most immediate ministers of the goodness and justice of God. But exemption from certain fates in the world is not always granted because of *innocence*, but most ordinarily depends upon *natural power*. Therefore, there may be many *good spirits*, and very holy and harmless souls of the departed, whose spirit-bodies <note>original: "Vehicles"; the Neoplatonic idea that the soul inhabits a subtle "vehicle" or body made of air or light.</note> are of such a consistency that they can no more leave these aerial regions than we, who have heavy bodies without wings, can fly into them. This is to say nothing of those virtuous and pious men who may happen to be alive at that time, and so be liable to be overtaken by this storm of fire.

Undoubtedly, unless there appears—before this fate approaches—some visible *Zeus the Savior* <note>original: "Zeus σωτὴρ"</note> or *Jupiter the Preserver* <note>original: "Jupiter Sospitator"</note>, as the heathens would call him, they must necessarily be involved in the ruin of the wicked. That would be a great flaw in the exact and blameless frame of Providence that all people expect who acknowledge that there is a God. Therefore, according to the light of reason, there must be some supernatural means to rescue those harmless and kind spirits out of this common calamity. But to describe the manner of how it must be done here would be to credit human reason <note>original: "natural Light"</note> and philosophy with greater abilities than they actually possess; therefore, that subject must be reserved for its proper place.

### CHAP. XIX.

*1. That the extinction of the sun is no irrational fear, but may be rationally suspected from historical records and the grounds of natural philosophy. 2. The sad influence of this extinction upon man and beast, and all the aerial spirits <note>original: "Dæmons"</note> imprisoned within their several atmospheres in our system <note>original: "Vortex"; referring to the Cartesian theory that stars and planets are centers of rotating celestial matter.</note>. 3. That it will do little or no damage to the inhabitants of the heavens <note>original: "Æthereal Inhabitants"</note> regarding heat or warmth. 4. Nor will they find much need of its light. 5. And if they did, they may pass out of one solar system into another by the privilege of their celestial bodies. 6. And that without any labor or toil, and as early as they please. 7. The vast incomprehensibility of the paths and reaches of the ways of Providence. 8. A short summary of the entire discourse. 9. An explanation of the Persians' two principles of Light and Darkness, which they called **God** <note>original: "Θεὸς"</note> and **Spirit** <note>original: "Δαίμων"</note>, and when and where the principle of Light achieves full victory. 10. That philosophy, or something more sacred than philosophy, is the only guide to a true **divinization** <note>original: "Ἀποθέωσις"; the process of a human soul becoming a god.</note>.*

<margin>1.</margin>
The last danger that threatens the *soul after death* <note>original: "Separate Soul"</note> is the *extinction of the sun*. Although this may seem like a mere *irrational fear* <note>original: "Panick feare"</note> at first sight, yet if the matter is examined, there will appear no small reasons that may induce men to suspect that it may at last happen.

# CHAPTER XIX. The Immortality of the Soul.

...could happen, there having been, at certain times, such near occurrences in Nature toward this sad accident already. <margin>Pliny, *Natural History*, book 2, chapter 30.</margin> Pliny, though he highlights only one example, yet speaks of it as a thing that comes to pass several times. "There occur," he says, "prodigious and prolonged failures of the Sun, such as happened when Caesar the Dictator was killed, and during the war of Antony, when there was a continuous paleness for a whole year." <note>original Latin: "Fiunt, prodigiosi & longiores Solis defectus, qualis occiso Dictatore Caesare, & Antoniano bello, totius anni pallore continuo."</note> The like happened in Justinian’s time, as Cedrenus <note>Georgius Cedrenus, an 11th-century Byzantine historian.</note> writes; when, for a whole year together, the Sun was of a very dim and dusky hue, as if he had been in a perpetual Eclipse. And in the time of Irene the Empress, it was so dark for seventeen days together that the ships lost their way on the sea and were ready to run against one another, as Theophanes relates. But the late accurate discovery of the Sunspots <note>original: "Spots of the Sun"</note> by Scheiner <note>original: "Shiner"; Christoph Scheiner was a Jesuit priest and astronomer who was among the first to observe sunspots.</note>, and the appearing and disappearing of fixed Stars, and the excursions of Comets into the remoter parts of our Vortex <note>In the physics of René Descartes, a "vortex" is a large circular motion of cosmic matter that carries planets around a star.</note>, as also the very internal structure of that admirable Philosophy of Descartes, all argue it is more than possible that, after some vast periods of time, the Sun may be so inextricably enveloped by the Sunspots <note>original: "Maculæ"</note> that he is never free from, that he may quite lose his light.

2. The beginnings of this extinction will be very hideous and intolerable to all the inhabitants of the planets in our vortex, if the planets have any inhabitants at all then. For this defect of light and heat, coming on by degrees, must necessarily weary out poor mortals with heavy lingering suffering, both for want of the comfort of the usual warmth of the Sun—by which the bodies of men are refreshed—and also by reason of his inability to ripen the fruits of the soil. From this must necessarily follow famine, plagues, sicknesses, and at length an utter devastation and destruction of both man and beasts.

Nor can the *aerial spirits* <note>original: "Aëreal Demons"; in this context, "demons" refers to any supernatural beings inhabiting the air, not necessarily evil ones.</note> escape free; because the vital tie to their spirit-bodies <note>original: "Vehicles"</note> necessarily confines them to their various atmospheres, they will be inevitably imprisoned in more than Cimmerian darkness <note>A classical reference to a legendary land of perpetual mist and darkness.</note>. For the extinction of the Sun will put out the light of all their Moons, and nothing but ice, and frost, and flakes of snow, and thick mists—as palpable as the plague of Egypt—will possess the regions where they live. Though those "twinkling eyes of heaven," the stars, might be compassionate spectators of that sad sight, yet they cannot send out one ray of light to help or visit them; their faint and remote beams are not able to pierce, much less to scatter, the clammy and stiff consistency of that long and fatal night.

3. Therefore, calling our mind away from such a dismal sight, let us focus it upon a more hopeful object; let us consider the condition of those souls that have reached their ethereal spirit-body <note>original: "Æthereal Vehicle"</note>, and see how far this fate can affect them. It is plain at first sight that they are out of the reach of this misty dungeon, as they have already ascended into the secure mansions of the purer ether.

The worst that can be imagined for them is that they may find themselves in a condition somewhat like ours when we walk out on a clear, starlight, frosty night, which to those who are healthy is a pleasure rather than an offense. And if we can bear it with some delight in these earthly bodies, whose parts will grow hard and stiff for want of due heat, it can prove to be nothing else but a new modification of tactile <note>original: "tactual"</note> pleasure...

## The Immortality of the Soul. BOOK III.

...to those *ethereal inhabitants* whose bodies are not densely packed <note>original: "constipated"; here meaning solid or tightly crowded together</note> like ours, but are themselves a kind of *agile light and fire*.

All that can be imagined is that the spherical particles of their *spiritual bodies* <term>Vehicles</term> <note>The "vehicle" of the soul refers to the subtle, non-physical body that the soul inhabits after leaving the physical body.</note> may stand a little more closely and firmly together than usual. Because of this, the triangular spaces between the particles would become narrower, and the subtlest element would move somewhat more quickly through them. This would actually create a sense of greater vigor and cheerfulness than usual. Thus, this fate is not at all frightening to them in this regard.

4. But you might say that their light will be obscured if the *Sun* is extinguished, since its shining seems to concern the *gods* as well as *men*, as *Homer* suggests:

> He rose up to bring light both to the immortals and to mortals. <note>original Greek: Ὤρνυθ’ ἵν’ ἀθανάτοισι φάος φέρῃ ἠδὲ βροτοῖσι.</note>

But I answer that Homer’s words are chiefly to be understood as referring to the *aerial daemons* <note>In 17th-century philosophy, "daemons" were intermediate spirits inhabiting the air, not necessarily evil beings.</note>, not the *ethereal deities*. These higher deities can turn themselves into a pure, actual light whenever they please. So, there is no fear that their personal interactions will be any less cheerful or distinct than before; white letters are just as legible on black paper as black letters are on white. 

Even if we assume they are in the dark, they are actually in a softer and milder light. This is merely a change of pleasure, much like seeing the *Moon* shine brightly into a room after a *candle* has been blown out. Certainly, the light contributed by the *Stars* is more significant to their quick and tender senses than the clearest *moonlit* night is to ours—even if we suppose they are no nearer to any *star* than we are. 

Such great changes as these may have their advantages for those whom *Providence* favors, as well as their disadvantages. The *extinction of our Sun* may lead to the increase of light in some *star* of a neighboring *vortex* <note>In Cartesian physics, a "vortex" is a large whirlpool of cosmic matter carrying planets around a star.</note>. While that light may not be able to pierce those "Cimmerian prisons" <note>A reference to the Cimmerians of mythology, who lived in perpetual darkness; here referring to the dense, dark physical world.</note> I spoke of before, it may still provide sufficient light to those *spirits* who are free. Besides, the breaking apart <note>original: "discerption"</note> and ruin of our *vortex* that will happen then will necessarily bring us much nearer to the center of another vortex. That neighboring star will provide enough light to the *ethereal spirits* <note>original: "Æthereal Genii"</note>, even if it is too weak to help those in the *air*.

We can see that such a remote distance from these central suns <note>original: "central Luminaries"</note> of the *vortices* is consistent with perfect happiness. This is partly because the celestial matter above *Saturn*, reaching to the very edge of the *vortex*, is more strongly agitated than the matter between Saturn and the Sun; therefore, it has less need of the *Sun’s* beams to maintain its movement and fluidity. It is also partly because those huge, vast regions of *ether* would be wasted and essentially useless if they were not inhabited by *ethereal inhabitants*. In all likelihood, these inhabitants are of the noblest kind, matching the nature of their environment. Therefore, all the *ethereal people* may retire there during such an emergency and rest secure in joy and happiness, in those true "spaces between the worlds of the gods" <note>original Latin: "Intermundia Deorum." Epicurus used this term to describe the peaceful, empty spaces where gods resided, unaffected by the world's chaos.</note> that *Epicurus* dreamed of.

5. We can easily accept this if we consider the grand privileges of the *ethereal vehicle*. In this state, such a great power of the *soul* is awakened that she can regulate the motion of its particles as she pleases by adding or subtracting degrees of agitation (Axiom 32), where...

<summary>Henry More argues that ethereal beings are not threatened by the Sun's eventual extinction because they can generate their own light and migrate to more stable regions of the cosmic vortices.</summary>

# CHAPTER XIX. The Immortality of the Soul.

By which she is also able to adjust the density of her *Vehicle* <term>Vehicle</term> <note>The "vehicle" of the soul refers to the subtle, non-physical body that the soul inhabits after leaving the physical body.</note> and, according to this adjustment of her body, to ascend or descend in the *Vortex* <term>Vortex</term> <note>In the physics of the time, a "vortex" was a swirling system of cosmic matter that carried planets around a star.</note> as she pleases, and that with a great variety of speed, according to her own will. By using this privilege, she may also, if she wishes, pass from one *Vortex* into another and receive the warmth of a new *Sun* <note>original: "Vesta"; the Roman goddess of the hearth, used here to represent a central star or sun.</note>, so that no imaginable fate shall ever be able to seize her.

6. Nor will this be any more effort for her than sailing down a stream. For once she has adjusted the movement and density of her *Vehicle* for her celestial voyage, she will be as naturally carried where she is bound as a stone falls downward or fire rises upward. So there is no fear of any fatigue <note>original: "lassitude"</note>, any more than there is from being rowed in a boat or carried in a sedan chair. For the celestial matter that surrounds her *Vehicle* carries her upward or downward, toward the center or away from the center of a *Vortex*, at its own effort and expense. Lastly, the senses of the *ethereal inhabitants* are so fine and subtle that their foresight and wisdom must be beyond all imagination, far above our own. Besides, there will be many warnings and premonitions of any future disaster—visible and constant—long before the Sun fails to the point that they would be affected by its decay; so that the slightest blast of misfortune shall never touch them, nor shall any imaginable evil overtake them.

7. This is a small glimpse into the mysteries of Providence, whose strategies <note>original: "fetches"</note> are so wide-ranging and whose cycles are so immense that they may well seem completely incomprehensible to the *skeptical* and the *uninformed* <note>original: "Incredulous and Idiots"; here meaning those lacking spiritual or scientific education.</note>. Such people are very prone to thinking that all things will always remain as they are, and they desire them to be so. However, this is as crude and irrational as if someone who goes to a *ball* and is very impressed with the first dance he sees were to demand that no other dance be performed, or that the dancers move no further from one another than they did when he first entered the room. In reality, they are meant to move closer together or further apart according to the measures of the *Music* and the laws of the dance they are performing. And all the matter of the *Universe*, and every part of it, is constantly *moving* in such a dance. Its patterns, moving backward and forward, cover a vast distance; and what seems to have stood still the longest must move again, according to the rhythms and accents of that *Music*—which is indeed beyond the hearing of the sharpest ears, but is nevertheless perceptible by the purest minds and the sharpest wits. No one would dare oppose the truth of this if the breath of the critic could only tell its own story and reveal how many stars and *Vortices* it passed through before its particles met, only to be misused in forming such a rash contradiction.

8. We have now finished our entire *Discourse*, the summary of which is this: *That there is a non-physical substance—which we call the Soul—within Man. This Soul survives and acts after the death of his Body, usually first in an aerial vehicle, just as other spirits <note>original: "Daemons"</note> do. In that state, she is not entirely exempt from fate, but she becomes perfect and secure once she has obtained her ethereal vehicle, for she is then out of the reach*

# The Immortality of the Soul. BOOK III.

...of that evil Principle <note>original: "Principle"; here meaning a fundamental cosmic force</note>, whose dominion is equal <note>original: "commensurable"</note> with misery and death. The Persian Magi <note>Ancient Iranian priests and sages</note> called this power Arimanius <note>Arimanius is the Latinized form of Ahriman, the spirit of evil and darkness in Zoroastrianism</note> and compared him to Darkness, just as they compared the other good Principle, whom they called Oromazes <note>Oromazes is the Latinized form of Ahura Mazda, the supreme god of light and wisdom in Zoroastrianism</note>, to Light—naming one a *Spirit* <note>original: "Δαίμων" (Daimōn)</note> and the other *God* <note>original: "Θεός" (Theos)</note>.

<margin>Plutarch, *On Isis and Osiris*.</margin>
9. There can be no other acceptable meaning for this than as a foreshadowing <note>original: "adumbration"</note> of those two grand parts of Providence: the one working in the *Demonic* and the other in the *Divine Orders*. Between these two natures, there is perpetually more or less strife and contest, both inwardly and outwardly. But if the prophecy of Theopompus <note>A Greek historian of the 4th century BCE</note> is true—as recorded in Plutarch, who was initiated into these secrets <note>original: "Arcana"</note>—the power of the Benign Principle will get the upper hand at last, and at length Hades or Arimanius will be left behind <note>original: "Τέλος δ᾽ ἀπολείπεσθαι τὸν ᾅδην", meaning "At last Hades shall be abandoned"</note>, who so strongly holds us captive. And then men shall be perfectly happy, neither needing food nor casting any shadow <note>original: "καὶ τοὺς μὲν ἀνθρώπους εὐδαίμονας ἔσεσθαι, μήτε τροφῆς δεομένους, μήτε σκιὰν ποιοῦντας"</note>. For what shadow can that body cast that is made of pure and transparent light, such as the *Ethereal Vehicle* <term>Ethereal Vehicle</term> <note>The subtle, luminous body the soul is thought to inhabit in the afterlife.</note> is? Therefore, that Oracle is fulfilled when the soul has ascended into that condition we have already described, in which alone it is out of the reach of ***Fate*** and ***Mortality***.

10. This is the true *Deification* <note>original: "Ἀποθέωσις" (Apotheosis); the process of a human soul becoming divine</note>, to speak according to the Persian language. The Emperors and great potentates of the Earth have been ambitious to adorn their memory with this empty title after death; but it is such a high privilege of the human soul that mere "political virtues" (as Plotinus <note>A major Neoplatonist philosopher</note> calls them) can never advance her to that level of happiness. Either *Philosophy*, or something more sacred than *Philosophy*, must be her guide to such a transcendent condition. Without caring to dispute whether the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of the philosopher Pythagoras, who believed in the transmigration of souls</note> ever arrived at it by living according to the precepts of their Master, I shall nevertheless confidently assert that what they aimed at is the sublimest felicity our nature is capable of. Since this is the furthest discovery this treatise could hope to reach, I shall conclude everything with a couplet <term>Distich</term> of theirs (which I have noted elsewhere on a similar occasion). It contains the furthest scope, not only of their philosophy, but of this present discourse.

> If you leave the body behind and go to the free ether, 
> You shall be an immortal, deathless god, no longer mortal. 
> <note>original: "Ἢν δ᾽ ἀπολείψας σῶμα ἐς αἰθέρ᾽ ἐλεύθερον ἔλθῃς, Ἔσεαι ἀθάνατος, θεὸς ἄμβροτος, οὐκέτι θνητός."</note>

->To this sense:<-

> *Whoever, after death, reaches the Ethereal Plain,*
> *Is immediately made a God, and never dies again.*

He cites Persian and Pythagorean wisdom to argue that true happiness and immortality are achieved when the soul escapes the physical realm for the ethereal one.</summary>

### TO
## The eminently Learned and truly Religious
# **Dr. CUDWORTH**,
## Master of *Christ’s* College, and Hebrew Professor in the University of *Cambridge*.

SIR,

Concerning the choice of the *subject matter* of my present labors <note>original: "pains"</note>, I think I have spoken enough in the following *Preface*. Concerning the choice of my *Patron*, I shall say no more than that the sole motivation for it was his exceptional <note>original: "singular"</note> learning and piety. The first of these is so evident to the world that it is universally acknowledged by everyone; and as for the second, no one can be ignorant of it who has ever had the happiness, even in a small way, of his more open and intimate conversation <note>original: "converse"</note>. For my own part, I cannot but publicly declare that I have never yet met anyone so truly and appropriately religious, where the right knowledge of God and Christ guides the enlightened mind so steadily <note>original: "even"</note> that it is as far removed from *superstition* as from *irreligion* itself. And my present labors cannot find a better welcome or more wise <note>original: "judicious"</note> acceptance from anyone than from people such as these. For such free and unprejudiced spirits will neither dismiss truth as old-fashioned <note>original: "antiquate"</note> because the concept is old, nor disregard her for looking young or having the appearance of novelty.

Besides, there are none who can be better assured of the sincerity and effectiveness of my present project <note>original: "Design"</note>. For as many as are born of the *Spirit*, and are not merely sons of the *Letter* <note>The "Letter" refers to a literal, surface-level reading of the Bible, while the "Spirit" refers to its deeper spiritual meaning.</note>, know very well how much the more inward and mysterious meaning of the text contributes to the reverence of the Holy Scripture and the benefit of piety <note>original: "Godliness"</note>; whereas the insistence on the bare literal sense has either created or confirmed many an *atheist*. And assuredly, those men see very little in the affairs of religion who do not plainly discover that it is in the *atheist’s* highest *interest* to have it taken for granted that there is no spiritual meaning, either in Scripture or the Sacraments, that extends further

They might also think that the *Mosaical philosophy* <note>The philosophy derived from the books of Moses in the Bible.</note> regarding God and the nature of things is nothing other than what most obviously presents itself in the mere *letter* <note>The literal, surface-level reading of the text.</note> of *Moses*. 

If the *atheist* could have these points fully granted to him on all sides, and also gain this as part of the bargain—that there is no knowledge of God except what the text of *Moses* established in the world, or what is *traditional*—he cannot help but think that religion, in this form, is so empty, objectionable <note>original: "exceptionable"</note>, and contemptible, that it is only right for those who are not total fools to look upon it as some melancholy whim <note>original: "conceit"</note> or clever fiction. Nor does it follow at all that because a truth is delivered by way of tradition, it cannot be reached by *reason*. # THE PREFACE
## to the READER.

1. What is meant by the term *Cabbala*, and how warrantably the *Literal Exposition* of the text may be so called. 2. That *optional speculations* <note>original: "dispensable speculations"; ideas that are not essential to core religious dogma</note> are best proposed in a *skeptical* <note>original: "Sceptical"; meaning cautious or investigative rather than dogmatic</note> manner. 3. A clear description of the nature and dignity of *Reason*, and what the Divine *Logos* <note>original: "Logos"; the Greek term for "Word" or "Divine Reason"</note> is. 4. The general probabilities of the truth of this present *Cabbala*. 5. The design of the author in publishing it.

->READER,<-

<margin>1.</margin> I present you here with a triple interpretation of the *first three chapters of Genesis*, which in my *title page* I have termed a *Threefold Cabbala*. For your better direction and satisfaction, I think it is not out of place to say a few things by way of a *preface*—things that you yourself would likely be inclined to ask me. *Such as, for example, why I call this interpretation of mine a* Cabbala, *and from whom I received it; what the probabilities of its truth may be; and what my purpose is in publishing it.*

To the *first* question I answer: the *Jewish Cabbala* is understood to be a *traditional doctrine* or *exposition* of the *Pentateuch* <note>the first five books of the Bible</note>, which *Moses* received from the mouth of God while he was on the Mount with Him. *And this sense or interpretation of the Law or Pentateuch—as it is a doctrine received first by Moses, and then from him by Joshua, and from Joshua by the seventy elders, and so on—was called Cabbala from the Hebrew word* <term>kibbel</term> <note>original Hebrew: קבל</note>, *meaning "to receive." But as it was delivered as well as received, it was also called "Massora," which signifies a "tradition." This latter term more properly refers to the critical and grammatical skill of the learned among the Jews; therefore, it was useful for explaining the literal sense as well as the more mysterious meaning of the text where it was intended. From this, without any boldness or abuse of the word, I may call the literal interpretation which I have come upon a "Cabbala," just as I do the philosophical or moral ones. The literal sense itself is not so plain and certain that it would not seem to require some traditional doctrine or exposition to settle it, just as much as those other senses that are more mystical.*

*And therefore I thought it fit to call this threefold interpretation that I have developed "Cabbalas," as if I had indeed discovered the true Cabbala of Moses in all three senses of the text—the kind of message that might have suited his own mouth to utter for the instruction of a willing and well-prepared disciple. Therefore, for the greater elegance and solemnity of the matter, I present Moses speaking his own mind in all three separate expositions.*

<margin>2.</margin> *And yet I call the whole interpretation but a "conjecture," having no desire to seem more definitively wise than others can bear or approve of. For*

<summary>Henry More introduces his "Threefold Cabbala," explaining that the term refers to a tradition received from Moses. He argues that even the literal meaning of Genesis requires a traditional guide to be understood and explains why he frames his interpretations as if spoken by Moses himself.</summary>

<keywords>Cabbala, Genesis, Moses, Pentateuch, Massora, Literal Exposition, Philosophical sense, Moral sense, tradition, interpretation</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the preface of Henry More's "Conjectura Cabbalistica." It explains the author's philosophical approach: why he proposes speculative ideas cautiously rather than dogmatically, the role of reason in faith, and the definition of human reason as a reflection of divine wisdom.</meta>

# THE PREFACE

<margin>2.</margin> Though in such things as are *Necessary* and *Essential* to the *Happiness* of a man—such as the belief that there is a *God*, and similar truths—it is not enough for a man only to provide undeniable *Reasons* for what he seeks to prove. He must also profess plainly and dogmatically that he himself fully *assents* <note>agrees or gives belief</note> to the *Conclusion* he has demonstrated. This ensures that those who do not fully understand the power of *Reason* may nonetheless be encouraged to share the same *Faith* with those who do, as it is of such great consequence for them to believe the proposition. 

Yet, I believe that regarding *Speculative* and *Optional Truths* <note>original: "Dispensable Truths"; ideas not essential for salvation</note>, a man not only may, but rather ought to propose them *Sceptically* <note>cautiously or as a hypothesis rather than absolute fact</note> to the world. There is more prudence and modesty in offering the strongest *Arguments* he can without being dogmatic at all, or appearing to be obsessed with his own *Conclusion*, or too earnestly seeking to win *Proselytes* <note>converts to a particular opinion</note> to his own view. For where the force of the *Arguments* is perceived, *Assent* will naturally follow in proportion to how clearly the force of the *Arguments* is discovered. Furthermore, agreeing to opinions that are merely *Speculative*, without understanding the *Reasons* for them, provides neither pleasure nor any real accomplishment for a rational creature.

<margin>3.</margin> To your second demand I answer: although I call this *Interpretation* of mine *Cabbala*, I must confess I received it neither from *Man* nor *Angel*. Nor did it come to me by *Divine Inspiration*—unless you are so wise as to use the name "Inspiration" for those timely suggestions of that *Divine Life* and *Sense* that resides vigorously in the *Rational Spirit* of free and well-meaning *Christians*. But *Inspiration* such as this does not distract from the *human faculties*; rather, it fulfills and enlarges them. 

I may add that this is the great *mystery of Christianity* that we are called to participate in: the perfecting of *Human nature* through participation in the *Divine*. This cannot be understood as referring to this gross flesh and the external senses, but rather to our *Inward humanity*—namely, our *Intellect*, *Reason*, and *Imagination* <note>original: "Fancie"</note>. To exclude the use of *Reason* in the search for *Divine truth* is not a command of the *Spirit*, but of headstrong *Melancholy* and blind *Enthusiasm* <note>original: "Enthusiasme"; in the 17th century, this referred to a state of irrational religious frenzy or claiming direct private revelation from God</note>. This is a religious *Frenzy* that men fall into by remaining passive, waiting to receive "impressions" that have no proportion to their actual *Faculties*. Once people give in to this mistake and irregularity, they put themselves in a position where they might admit anything indiscriminately. In time, they grow either dull or mad, and under the pretense of being "highly *Christian*" (the true *Mystery* of which they do not understand), they actually degrade themselves to a level lower than the lowest of men.

For my own part, *Reason* seems to me to be so far from being a contemptible *Principle* in man that it must be acknowledged, in some sense, to exist in *God* himself. For what is *Divine Wisdom* but the steady comprehension of the *Ideas* of all things, along with their mutual relationships, their agreements and disagreements, and their dependencies and independencies? These relationships necessarily arise from the natures of the *Ideas* themselves. The *Divine Intellect* looks through both the ideas and their relations all at once, thereby discerning the order and coherence of all things. And what is this but *Stable Reason* <note>original: "Ratio stabilis"</note>—a kind of steady and immovable *Reason* discovering the connection of all things at once? In contrast, the reason in us is *Moving Reason* <note>original: "Ratio mobilis"</note>, or *Reason* in *evolution* <note>the process of unfolding or developing over time</note>, because we are only able to apprehend things in a successive manner, one after another. But

<summary>More argues that while core religious truths should be stated firmly, speculative ideas are best proposed cautiously. He defends the use of Reason in Christianity, arguing that human reason is a developing reflection of God's own eternal, stable Reason.</summary>

# To the READER.

...so many as we can comprehend at a time, while we plainly perceive and carefully view their *Ideas*, we know how well they fit, or how much they disagree with one another, and so prove or disprove one thing by another. This is really a participation in that *Divine Reason* in *God*, and is a true and faithful principle in man when it is perfected and polished by the *Holy Spirit*; but before that, it is very earthly and obscure, especially in *Spiritual things*.

But now, seeing that the *Logos* <note>original: *Logos*; the Word or Divine Wisdom</note>, or steady, comprehensive *Wisdom* of *God*, in which all *Ideas* and their relationships are contained, is simply universal, stable *Reason*, how can there be any pretense of being so highly inspired as to be lifted above *Reason* itself? Unless, of course, men will imagine themselves wiser than *God*, or their *Understandings* superior to the natures and reasons of things themselves.

Therefore, to frame a brief *Answer* to your *Second* demand: I say, this threefold *Cabbala* <note>original: *Cabbala*; here referring to More's three-part interpretation (Literal, Philosophical, and Moral) of the book of Genesis</note> you inquire after is the dictate of the free *Reason* of my *Mind*, heedfully considering the written *Text* of *Moses*, and carefully examining the *Expositions* of such *Interpreters* as are ordinarily to be found. And I know nothing to the contrary, but that I have been so successful as to have actually hit upon the true ancient *Cabbala*.

4. Regarding this, in the *Third place*, I will set down some general *Probabilities*, referring you for the rest to the *Defense* of the *Cabbalas* themselves, and the *Introduction* to them.

And first, it is no insignificant *Argument* that the *Literal Cabbala* is true because it is carried out so evenly and consistently from one part to another. Everything is also represented so suitably to the capacity of the people, and so advantageously for keeping their minds in the fear of *God* and obedience to his *Law*, as shall be particularly shown in the *Defense* of that *Cabbala*. So that according to the sense of this *Literal Cabbala*, *Moses* is discovered to be a man of the highest *Political* accomplishments and true, justifiable *Prudence*.

Nor does he fall short in *Philosophy*. And therefore the *Philosophical Cabbala* contains the most noble *Truths*, both *Theological* and *Natural*, that the *Mind* of man can entertain herself with. Indeed, *Moses* seems to have been ahead of his time, anticipating the most subtle and deep *Inventions* of the most excellent *Philosophers* who ever appeared after him to this very day. A further reason to believe in the truth of this *Philosophical Cabbala* is that the grand mysteries contained therein are mostly the same as those that those two distinguished <note>original: *eximious*</note> *Philosophers*, *Pythagoras* and *Plato*, brought out of *Egypt* and parts of *Asia* into *Europe*. It is generally acknowledged by *Christians* that they both received their *Philosophy* from *Moses*. And *Numenius* the *Platonist* speaks out plainly concerning his *Master*: "What is *Plato* but *Moses* speaking Attic Greek?" <note>original: *Moses Atticus*; Numenius suggested Plato was simply Moses in a Greek form</note>. As for *Pythagoras*, it is an incredible thing that he and his followers should make such a great fuss <note>original: "such a deal of doe"</note> over the mystery of *Numbers* had he not been favored with a sight of *Moses’* account of the *Creation of the World* in *six days*, and had the *Philosophical Cabbala* of it shared with him—which mainly consists of *Numbers*, as I shall explain more particularly in the *Defense* of this *Cabbala*.

# The PREFACE

<margin>Iamblichus, *On the Life of Pythagoras*, chapters 28 and 29.</margin>
*And the* Pythagoreans' *oath, swearing by him who taught them the* mystery <note>original: *mystery*; a secret religious rite or teaching</note> *of the* Tetractys <note>original: *Tetractys*; a mystical symbol consisting of ten points arranged in a triangle, representing the number four</note>, *or the number* Four—*what a ridiculous thing would it have been if it referred merely to dry numbers? But it is exceedingly probable that under that* mystery *of* Four, Pythagoras *was first himself taught the meaning of the fourth day's work in the* Creation, *and afterward delivered it to his disciples. In this* Cabbala <note>original: *Cabbala*; a mystical or traditional interpretation of the Bible</note> *of the fourth day,* Pythagoras *was instructed, among other things, that the* Earth *was a* Planet *and moved around the* Sun. *It is notoriously well known that this was always the opinion of the* Pythagoreans, *and so in all likelihood it was a part of the* <margin>Aristotle, *On the Heavens*, book 2, chapter 13.</margin> Philosophical Cabbala *of* Moses. *This you will more fully understand in my* Defense *of it.*

*In brief, all those* conclusions *that are comprised in the* Philosophical Cabbala—*being such as best suit the sublime and comprehensive understanding of* Moses, *and also being so plainly consistent with the* phenomena <note>original: *Phænomena*; observable facts or events in nature</note> *of nature and the* attributes *of* God, *as well as being continually agreeable, without any force or distortion, to the* historical text—*this, I believe, suggests no small probability that this* Cabbala *is true. For what could be the* properties *of the true* Philosophical Cabbala *of* Moses, *if not these which I have named?*

*Now for the* Moral Cabbala, *it carries its own evidence with it throughout, representing* Moses *as being as well-experienced in all* godliness *and* honesty *as he was skillful in* politics *and* philosophy.

5. *And the edifying* usefulness *of this* mystical *or* moral Cabbala, *to answer your* last *demand, was no small invitation among the rest to publish this present* exposition. *For* moral *and* spiritual truth *that so nearly concerns us being so strangely and unexpectedly, and yet so fitly and appropriately, represented in this* history *of* Moses, *it will in all likelihood make a more forceful impression upon the* mind. *It will more powerfully carry away our* affections <note>original: *Affections*; our emotions or desires</note> *toward what is good and justifiable, instructing us with delight concerning the true way to* virtue *and* godliness.

*Neither the* philosophical *nor the* literal Cabbalas *are destitute of their honest uses. For in the former—to the amazement of the mere* naturalist <note>original: *Naturalist*; one who studies the physical world without considering the divine</note> (*who commonly imagines that pious men and* patrons *of* religion *have no ornaments of the* mind *except for scrupulousness about* virtue *and* melancholy <note>original: *Melancholick*; relating to the "humor" of black bile, often associated with gloom or religious obsession</note> *fancies concerning a* deity)—Moses *is found to have been a* master *of the most sublime and generous* speculations <note>original: *Speculations*; theoretical or scientific contemplations</note> *that exist in all* natural philosophy. *Besides that, he places the* soul *of* man *many degrees out of the reach of fate and mortality. And by the latter* <note>the literal interpretation</note>, *there is a very charitable provision made for those who are so prone to expect rigid* precepts <note>original: *Precepts*; rules or principles</note> *of* philosophy *within* Moses's *outward* text. *For this* literal Cabbala *will steer them away from the toil of trying to make the bare* letter *of the text speak in harmony with the true frame of* nature. *When they attempt this with more zeal than knowledge, they both disgrace themselves and wrong* Moses. *For there are unalterable and indelible* ideas *and* notions *in the* mind *of* man; *when we are awakened to these and apply them to the known course and order of* nature, *we can no more forsake the use of them than we can the use of our own* eyes, *nor can we disbelieve their dictates more (or even as much) as we might those of our outward* senses. *Therefore, for men who have recovered a proper command of their* reason, *and...*

# To the READER.

<sig>Eee 4</sig>

...well-skilled in the contemplation and experience of the nature of things, to propose to them the kind of *Mosaical Philosophy* <note>original: *Mosaical Philosophy*; the belief that the foundations of all true science and philosophy were revealed by God to Moses</note> that some have boldly and superstitiously dared to put forward—for lack of a proper *Literal Cabbala* <note>original: *Literal Cabbala*; a traditional interpretation of the Bible's plain, historical meaning</note> to guide them—is, as much as they are able, to risk making not only *Moses* but *Religion* itself contemptible and ridiculous.

From this, I think it is clear enough why it is so useful to carefully distinguish between the *Literal* and *Philosophic Cabbala* <note>original: *Philosophick Cabbala*; a deeper, symbolic interpretation of scripture that aligns with philosophical and scientific truths</note>, and to explain the meaning of each so plainly and fully on its own, so that there will be no confusion or mistake in the future. For besides the fact that discovering these significant *Truths* and high, but irrefutable, *Paradoxes* <note>original: *Paradoxes*; statements that seem contradictory but may be true, often used here to describe scientific ideas—like the movement of the Earth—that contradict common sense</note> in *Moses’s* text supports *Religion* and clears her from that shameful accusation of *Ignorance* in *Philosophy* and the knowledge of things; it also justifies those more noble results of free *Reason* and *Philosophy* against the common suspicion of *Impiety* and *Irreligion*.

...middle of its course around noon; and then, fading in brightness toward the west, it finally disappeared entirely. 4. And God saw the *Light* (for it is a very visible thing) and saw that it was good. 5. And he called the return of the light *Day*, and the return of darkness he called *Night*; and the evening and the morning made up the *First* natural day.

6. Now, after God had made the *Basis* or floor of this great building <note>original: "edifice"</note> of the *World*—the *Earth*—he set to work on the higher parts of the structure. He commanded, therefore, that there should be a hollow *Expansion* <term>original: Expansion; here referring to the atmosphere or "firmament" envisioned as a solid but transparent canopy</term>, firm and transparent, which by its strength would support the Waters above and keep them from falling upon the *Earth* in excess.

7. And so it became a barrier between the *Upper* and the *Lower* waters; so that by virtue of this hollow *Firmament*, humanity might live safe from the violence of such destructive floods <note>original: "inundations"</note>, like someone sheltered in a well-secured tent from rainstorms. For the danger of these waters is obvious to the eye: this cerulean <note>original: "ceruleous" or azure blue</note> sea that covers the translucent <note>original: "diaphanous"</note> Firmament can be easily seen through it. Furthermore, frequent and heavy showers of rain fall from above, even though no water is seen rising up there; therefore, it must all come from that upper sea, if we simply trust our outward senses.

8. Now, therefore, regarding this translucent canopy or firmly-stretched tent over the whole floor of the Earth: although I cannot strictly say that God saw it was "good" (since it is indeed invisible by nature), its use shows it to be exceedingly good and necessary. And God called the entire space of this hollow *Firmament* "*Heaven*." And the evening and the morning made up the *Second* natural day.

9. And now that such a sure defense had been made against the flooding of the *Upper* waters so they would not fall upon the *Earth*, God turned his attention the next day to ordering the *Lower* waters, which were still spread over the whole face of the world. At his command, therefore, the *Waters* gathered into one place, and the dry land appeared.

10. And God called the dry land *Earth*; and the gathering together of the waters he called the *Sea*. I may now properly say that God saw that it was good, for the *Sea* and the *Land* are visible enough and are proper objects for our sight.

11. And immediately, before he made the *Sun*, *Moon*, or *Stars*, God commanded the earth to bring forth *Grass*, *Herbs*, and *Flowers* in their full beauty, and *Fruit-trees* yielding delicious fruit—even though there had not yet been any cycle of *Spring*, *Summer*, or *Autumn*, nor any sunlight to ripen and develop <note>original: "concoct"</note> the fruit of those trees.

### CHAPTER III. The Literal Cabbala.

1. And truly, it must be quite obvious for you to often consider among yourselves, not only how this *shame of nakedness* came into the world, but also the toil and drudgery of farming and agriculture <note>original: "Tillage and Husbandry"</note>; the grievous pangs of childbirth; and lastly—what is most terrible of all—death itself. Regarding all of these things, as well as some others, I shall give you such plain and intelligible reasons that your own hearts could not wish for anything more clear. You have already heard what a happy condition *Adam* was created in; how he was placed by God in a garden of delight, where all his senses were gratified with the most pleasing objects imaginable: his eyes with the beauty of trees and flowers, and various delightful forms of living creatures; his ears with the sweet musical accents of the singing <note>original: "canorous"</note> birds; his smell with the fragrant odors of aromatic herbs; his taste with a variety of delicious fruit; and his touch with the soft breathing of the air in the flowery alleys of this ever-springing *Paradise*. Add to all this that pleasure of pleasures, the delightful conversation of his beautiful bride, the enjoyment of whose love created no anxiety for him, nor pangs of childbirth for her. For all the functions of life were performed with ease and delight; and there had been no need for man to sweat for the provision of his family, for in this Garden of *Eden* there was a perpetual spring, and the natural strength of the soil outpaced human effort <note>original: "prevented mans industry"—in this period "prevented" meant to go before or anticipate</note>. Youth and jollity would never have left the bodies of *Adam* and his descendants <note>original: "seed"</note>, because old age and death were to be kept away forever by that sovereign power <note>original: "virtue"</note> of the *Tree of Life*. And I know that just as you heartily wish this state could have continued forever for *Adam* and his descendants, you also eagerly expect to hear the reason why he was deprived of it. In short, it is this: *his disobedience to a commandment which God had given him*; the circumstances of which I shall declare to you as follows.

Among those several living creatures which were in Paradise, there was *the Serpent* also, whom you know to this very day to be full of subtlety. Therefore, you will be less surprised to learn that when he was in his state of perfection, he possessed not only the use of *reason*, but the power of *speech*. It was, therefore, this Serpent that was the first occasion of all this mischief to *Adam* and his descendants. For he cunningly came to the woman and said to her, "*Is it really true that God has commanded you that you shall not eat of any of the trees of the garden?*"

2. And the woman answered the Serpent, "*You are mistaken; God has not forbidden us to eat of all the fruit of the trees of the garden.*"

3. "*But indeed, regarding the fruit of the tree in the midst of the garden, God has strictly charged us: 'You shall not eat of it, nor shall you touch it, lest you die.'*"

4. But the Serpent said to the woman, "*Nonsense! I assure you <note>original: 'Tush, I warrant you'</note> this is only to frighten you and restrict you from that liberty and happiness you are capable of; you shall not certainly die.*"

5. "*For God knows the power <note>original: 'virtue'</note> of that tree very well: that as soon as you eat of it, your eyes shall be opened, and you shall become like gods, knowing good and evil.*"

6. And when the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was pleasant to the eye, and a tree to be desired to make one wise, she took some of the fruit and ate it. She also gave some to her husband with her, and he ate it.

7. And the eyes of both of them were opened, and they realized they were naked and were ashamed. Therefore, they sewed fig leaves together and made themselves aprons to cover their nakedness <note>original: "parts of shame"</note>.

8. And the Lord God came into the Garden toward the cool of the evening, and as He was walking in the Garden, He called for *Adam*. But as soon as *Adam* heard His voice, he and his wife ran away into the thickest part of the trees of the Garden to hide themselves from His presence.

9. But the Lord God called to *Adam* a second time and said to him, "*Adam*, where are you?"

10. Then *Adam* was forced to answer and said, "I heard Your voice in the Garden, and I was afraid because I was naked, and so I hid myself."

11. Then God said to him, "Who has made you so wise that you should know you are naked or lack any covering? Have you eaten of the forbidden fruit?"

12. And *Adam* excused himself, saying, "The woman whom You recommended to me as a suitable helper <note>original: "meet help"</note>, she gave me some of the fruit, and I ate it."

13. And the Lord God said to the woman, "What is this that you have done?" And the woman excused herself, saying, "The *Serpent* deceived me, and I ate."

14. Then the Lord God gave sentence upon all three. To the *Serpent* He said, "Because you have done this, you are cursed above all livestock <note>original: "cattel"</note> and above every beast of the field. And whereas until now you have been able to carry your body high <note>original: "bear thy body aloft"</note> and walk upright, from now on you shall crawl upon your belly like a worm, and you shall eat dust all the days of your life.

15. And there shall be a perpetual hostility <note>original: "Antipathy"</note> not only between the woman and you, but between her offspring <note>original: "seed"</note> and your offspring. All of mankind shall abhor you and hate all the cursed generations that come from you. Your kind shall busily lie in wait to sting men's feet, though their skill in medicinal herbs shall be able to cure it; but men shall strike all serpents on the head and kill them without pity or remorse, deservedly treating your offspring as their deadly enemy."

16. And the judgment <note>original: "doom"</note> of the woman was her sorrow and pangs in child-bearing, and her subjection to her husband. This law of subjection is generally observed in the nations of the world to this very day.

17. And the judgment of *Adam* was the toil of farming <note>original: "Husbandry"</note> upon barren ground.

18. For the earth was cursed for his sake, which is the reason that it brings forth thorns and thistles and other weeds that farmers could wish would not clutter <note>original: "cumber"</note> the ground upon which they bestow their toilsome labor.

### CHAP. III. The Literal Cabbala.

19. Thus, by the sweat of his brow <note>original: "sweat of his face"</note> was *Adam* to earn his food <note>original: "eat his bread"</note>, until he returned to the dust from which he was taken.

20. And *Adam* named his wife *Eve*, because she was the mother of all people who were ever born into the world and lived upon the face of the earth.

And the Lord God spoke concerning *Adam*, mocking <note>original: "deriding"</note> him for his disobedience, saying, "Look, *Adam* has become like one of us, knowing good and evil. We must watch him now, so he does not reach out for the *Tree of Life* and make himself immortal."

23. Therefore, the Lord God sent him out from the Garden of *Eden* to farm <note>original: "till"</note> the ground from which he had been taken.

24. So He drove out *Adam*, and his wife was forced to follow him. They could no longer stay in *Paradise* because the place was terrifyingly haunted by spirits, and frightening apparitions appeared at the entrance—winged men <note>These are the Cherubim described in Genesis 3:24.</note> with fiery, flaming swords in their hands, waving them in every direction. Because of this, *Adam* never dared to try and go back to taste the fruit of the *Tree of Life*. This is why humanity has remained mortal to this very day.
