# The Defense of the Literal Cabbala. CHAPTER I.

Just as a head is the first part of a living creature, so *Reshit* <note>original Hebrew: ראשית (reshit)</note> signifies that which is placed first in anything else. Thus, the creation of the world is the Head or the opening part of the history that Moses intends to record.

Since Moses intended (as is clear from the title of this book, *Genesis*, as well as its contents) to write a history and genealogy from the beginning of the world until his own time, it is very easy and natural to understand that, in reference to what he would later add, he said, *In the beginning*; as if his whole train of thought were this: First of all, God made the heavens and the earth, with all they contain—the sun, moon, and stars; the day and night; the plants; and the living creatures in the air, water, and on the earth. After all these, he made Adam, and Adam fathered Cain and Abel, and so on through the full history and genealogies.

I believe this sense is more easy and natural than that of St. Augustine <note>original: Austin</note>, Ambrose, and Basil, who argue that *In the beginning* means "In the Beginning of Time" or "In the Beginning of the World." Nevertheless, I thought it worth mentioning these views so the reader may choose for themselves.

<margin>Manasseh Ben Israel, *On the Creation*, Problem 4, section 5.</margin>
*God made Heaven and Earth.* Maimonides and Manasseh Ben Israel observe three words used in Scripture when the creation of the world is attributed to God: *bara*, *asah*, and *qanah* <note>original Hebrew: ברא, עשה, קנה</note>. They note that *bara* signifies the "production of things out of nothing," which is the definition of creation used in the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to medieval Scholastic theology.</note>. *Asah* is the "making of a thing perfect and complete, according to its own nature and properties." *Qanah* suggests the "dominion and rightful possession that God has over all things created or made." However, although *bara* signifies "creation" in its strictest sense according to the learned Jews, the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the early Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> did not observe such precision. They translated it as "he made" <note>original Greek: ἐποίησεν (epoiēsen)</note>, which means no more than "made." Ordinary people do not have the time for such subtle distinctions. Therefore, I accept this latter meaning as the common, literal sense, and the former as the philosophical one. Whenever I use the word "Creation" in this *Literal Cabbala*, I mean only the common and general notion of "making a thing," regardless of the specific circumstances.

Neither do I translate *Elohim* <note>original Hebrew: אלהים</note> in the plural as "the Trinity." As Vatablus <note>François Vatable, a 16th-century French scholar.</note> observes from the Hebrew doctors, when a subordinate speaks of a superior, he speaks of him in the plural number. For example, Isaiah 19:4: "I will give over Egypt into the hand of cruel lords" <note>original Latin: *Tradam Ægyptum in manum dominorum duri*</note>; and Exodus 22:11: "And its owners shall accept it" <note>original Latin: *Et accipiet domini ejus*</note>, where "owners" is used for "owner." Since the text does not strictly require the sense of the Trinity, and because that mystery is so profound, it is rightly left out of this *Literal Cabbala*.

**Verse 2.** In the first verse, there was a summary proposal of the entire creation in its two main parts: *Heaven* and *Earth*. Now he begins the specific account of each day's work. It is not necessary for him to repeat here the "making of the earth," for that was the last word he spoke in his general summary. It would have been awkward or unnecessary to repeat it immediately. This is the reason why there is no command stating, "And the Lord said, Let there be an Earth," before the Earth is made. This omission, I believe, has led some ignorant or careless people to believe that this confused, muddy heap called the Earth was an eternal *First Matter*,

<meta>This page continues the author's "Literal Cabbala," a commentary on the first chapter of Genesis. Having previously discussed the meaning of "In the beginning," the author now moves to the description of the primitive state of the Earth and the creation of Light (Genesis 1:2-5).</meta>

# CHAPTER I. The Defense of the Literal Cabbala.

Matter is not independent of God, nor was it never created by him. If a person appeals to their own reasoning faculties, such a thing is impossible, as I will mention again when I come to the *Philosophic Cabbala* <note>The "Philosophic Cabbala" is a later section where the author provides a metaphysical, rather than literal, interpretation of the text.</note>.

The meaning, therefore, is that the *Earth* was made first, which was covered with *Water*; upon the *Water* was the *Wind*, and in all of this was a thick *Darkness*. And God was present in this dark, windy, and wet night. So this globe of *Earth*, *Water*, and *Wind* was simply one dark tempest and sea-storm—a night of confusion and chaotic agitation. For "the Spirit of God" <note>original Hebrew: רוח אלהים (ruach elohim)</note> is not, in the *Literal* sense, anything more than *a great and mighty wind* <note>original Latin: *Ventus ingens*</note>. Just as the "Cedars of God" and "Mountains of God" refer to *tall cedars* and *great mountains*, by analogy, the *Wind of God* means *a great wind*.

*Verse 3.* In the midst of this stormy darkness, God, intending to set to his work, essentially lights his lamp, or sets up a candle and lantern for himself in this dark workshop. Everything mentioned so far consists of words that strongly appeal to the imagination and senses; they are easily understood by uneducated people, who might be reminded of the dismal state of things before God commanded the comforting daylight to spring forth—the sole source of Light that so pleases the eyes and cheers the spirits of humanity—by every dark and stormy night.

The idea that daylight is something independent of the *sun*, just as the *Night* is independent of the *stars*, is a concept perfectly suited to the imaginations of common people, as I have found myself when talking with them. They are also prone to think that unless there is a noticeable wind blowing, there is nothing between the Earth and the clouds, but that it is a mere void. Therefore, I have not translated "the Wind of God" <note>original Hebrew: רוח אלהים (ruach elohim)</note> as "the *Air*," as the philosopher *Maimonides* <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a famous Jewish scholar and philosopher.</note> does in some places, but as *a mighty wind*. This is something that uneducated people can perceive; by making the initial, unformed state of things so dismal and stormy, it will cause them to remember the first morning light with more thankfulness and devotion.

*Verse 4.* For it is a very visible thing. See what is said in the commentary on verse eight.

*Verse 5.* By "Evening" and "Morning" is meant the *Artificial Day* <note>the period of light</note> and the *Artificial Night* <note>the period of darkness</note>. This is an example of a synecdoche <note>a figure of speech where a part represents the whole, or vice versa</note>, as the scholar *Castellio* tells us in his *Notes*. Therefore, this artificial day and night put together make one *full twenty-four hour period* <note>original Greek: Νυχθήμερον (nychthemeron), literally a "night-day"</note>, or *Natural Day*. The Evening is placed before the Morning, and Night before Day, because darkness existed before light. However, that *primitive darkness* was not strictly "Night." For *Night* is *one great shadow* <note>original Greek: μία μεγάλη σκιά (mia megale skia)</note>, as *Aristotle* describes it: a shadow cast by the Earth, which implies there is light on one side of it. Therefore, *Night* (properly so called) could not exist before Light. But uneducated people do not trouble themselves with such technicalities, nor do they easily understand the difference between the specific cone-shaped shadow of the Earth (which is *Night*) and that infinite *Primitive Darkness* that had no boundaries before there was any light. Therefore, that same darkness added to an artificial day makes up one *Natural Day* to them. This is an idea that the poet *Hesiod* also accepts without much thought—whether he was following his own imagination or this text by *Moses*, I do not know.

*Verse 6. This Basis or Floor.* That the Earth seems like a round *Floor*, plain and extending in every direction so as to join with the bottom of the Heavens, I have already hinted to you in my *Introduction*; and it is looked upon as such in the phrasing of Scripture, accommodating itself to our outward senses and common notions <note>original: "vulgar conceit," meaning the way an average person perceives the world through their senses rather than scientific theory.</note>. Upon this *Floor* stands the hollow Firmament, like a *Tent* pitched upon the ground; which is the very expression of the Prophet *Isaiah*, describing the Power of God: <margin>Isaiah 40:22.</margin> *Who stretches out the Heavens like a Curtain, and spreads them out as a Tent to dwell in.* And the word *Raquiya* <note>original Hebrew: רקיע</note>, which is usually translated as *Firmament*, signifies *extension, expansion*, or *spreading out*. 

But as to how the *Seventy* <note>The "Seventy" refers to the Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> came to <margin>Book 1. chapter 7.</margin> interpret it as *stereoma* <note>original Greek: στερέωμα, meaning a solid structure</note>, or *Firmamentum* <note>Latin: "Firmament"</note>, *Fuller* in his *Miscellanies* gives a very ingenious reason, and one that serves our purpose well. *For the heaven or Raquiya* (*he says*), *since it is very often compared to a Tent in the Sacred Scriptures, is said to be "fixed"* <note>original Greek: πήγνυσθαι (pegnusthai)</note> *insofar as it is spread out. For in this way Tents are usually spread out, when they are stretched by ropes tied to pegs driven into the ground, and in this way they are also made firm. Therefore, the Raquiya* <note>original Hebrew: הרקיע</note> *might not inappropriately be called a certain immense "frame"* <note>original Greek: πῆγμα (pegma)</note>, *as it were, and therefore also a "firmament"* <note>original Greek: στερέωμα (stereoma)</note>. 

The sense of this, in brief, is simply this: *That the Seventy translate Raquiya as stereoma—that is, Firmament—because the Heavens are spread out like a well-fastened and firmly-pitched Tent.* And I add also, that they are so stiffly stretched that they will strongly bear against the weight of the *Upper waters*; so that the waters are not able to break them down and thereby drown the world. This notion, as it is easy and agreeable with the imagination of the people, is so far from doing them any harm that it will make them more sensible of Divine Power and Providence. It suggests that God, by main force, keeps off a Sea of water that hangs over their heads—which they can see through the transparent Firmament (for it looks blue as other Seas do)—and which would rush down at once and drown them if the Power of God and the strength of the Firmament did not hold it back.

*Verse 7.* See what has been already said regarding the sixth verse. I will only add here that the nearness of these *Upper waters* makes them even more formidable, and so they are greater incentives to devotion. For as they are brought so near as to touch the Earth at the bottom, so—with our outward sense still being the judge—they are perceived to be within a small distance of the Clouds at the top. And that these *Upper waters* are no higher than that is manifest from other passages in Scripture that place the habitation of God only among the Clouds, yet He is called *the most High*. <margin>Section 5.</margin> See *Psalm 104:3, Deuteronomy 33:26, Nahum 1:3,* and *Psalm 68:4*. But I have treated this so fully in my *Introduction* that I consider it unnecessary to add anything more.

*Verse 8.* I cannot say properly that *God saw it was good*. In the whole story of the first three Chapters, it is evident that God is represented in the form of a Man, speaking with a mouth and seeing with eyes. Because of this, since the Firmament is of itself *invisible*, *Moses* omits the saying.

Thus, the people, judging by their sight, may very well imagine the *firmament* <note>The expanse of the sky, once thought to be a solid dome.</note> to be between the lights of heaven and the upper waters (that blue sea they look upon), rather than on this side of them, or strictly between the lights and stars.

*Verse 16. Two great lights, etc.* This is intended to distinguish them from the *stars*, which indeed seem much smaller to our sight than the *sun* or *moon*. This is true despite the fact that many *stars*, according to astronomers' calculations, are larger than the sun, and all are far larger than the moon. So, it is plain that the Scripture speaks sometimes according to the appearance of things to our *sight*, and not according to their absolute *natures* and *properties*. Anyone who will not admit this to be true is, I think, justly suspected of having more ignorance than religion, and more superstition than reason.

*Regarding their smallness, etc.* The stars indeed seem very small to our sight, and therefore *Moses* seems to include them only in passing <note>original: "cast them in but by the by"</note>, complying with the ignorance of the unlearned. But astronomers, who have made it their business to understand their sizes <note>original: "magnitudes"</note>—even those who make the most conservative <note>original: "frugal"</note> calculations concerning the larger stars—declare them to be no less than sixty-eight times larger than the Earth, and others say much more.

### Verse 27. In his own shape. 
It was the opinion of the *Anthropomorphites* <note>A group of early Christians who believed God possessed a physical human body.</note> that God had all the parts of a man, and that we are, in this sense, made according to His image. This opinion is in itself—if not rightly understood—vain and ridiculous. Yet, the views of those who imagine God to be a *finite being* seem little better to me. They take care to place Him far away from the "stink" of this earthly globe, so that He may sit *pure in a pure place* <note>original Greek: καθαρὸς ἐν καθαρῷ χώρῳ</note>, and so they confine Him to Heaven. *Aristotle* seems to do this, if he is indeed the author of the book *On the World* <note>original Latin title: De Mundo</note>. It is a contradiction to the very idea of God for Him to be *finite*, and consequently to have a *shape* or *physical parts*. 

However, it is so difficult for the uneducated masses to grasp the *notion* of a *being who is immaterial and infinite* that it seems to be for their benefit to conceive of God as an all-powerful person. In this view, He can do whatever He pleases: He can make heavens and earths, bestow His blessings in whatever measure and manner He chooses, and (most importantly) if necessary, He can personally appear to them, scold them, and rebuke them—and if they are stubborn, He can execute terrible vengeance upon them. This, I say, will more strongly strike the internal senses and imagination of the common people than the idea of omnipotence existing in a thin, subtle, invisible, immaterial being, of which they can have no perception at all, nor any manageable conception.

Therefore, since it is necessary to permit the ignorant to have some finite and shaped understanding of God, what could be more fitting than the human form in its highest possible excellence of *beauty, strength, and stature?* And the prophet *Isaiah* <note>original: "Esay"</note> seems to speak <margin>Isaiah 40:22</margin> of God according to this notion when he says, *God sits upon the circle of the Earth, and the inhabitants thereof are as grasshoppers;* suggesting that men bear as little proportion to God as grasshoppers do to a man when he sits on the grass among them. Since it is necessary to permit the people to have such understandings of God (and it is true wisdom and godly policy to accommodate their weakness for their own good), there were also the most strict injunctions laid upon them against *idolatry* and the worship of images.

But if anyone should say that this was the quickest way to lead them into *idolatry*—allowing them to entertain a conception of God in *human* shape—I would say that it is no more dangerous than acknowledging a man to be God, as our religion does in the person of *Christ*. Indeed, I would add that *Christ* is the true *Figured God* <note>original Latin: Deus Figuratus; a term for God represented in a visible form or shape</note>, and for His sake, the *Jews* were more easily permitted to think of God in the shape of a man.

And I think it is most reasonable that there should be such a being as *Christ*—that is, *God in human form*—so that He may visibly visit the Earth and, to their very physical senses, overwhelm the atheist and unbeliever at the last day. As He witnesses of Himself, <margin>John 5:22</margin> *The Father judges no one, but He has given all judgment to the Son:* <margin>John 6:46</margin> and that *No man can see the Father except as he is united to the Son.* For the eternal God is immaterial and invisible to our outward senses, but He has thought it good to deal with us, in both mercy and judgment, through a *Mediator* and *Vicegerent* <term>A person appointed by a ruler to act as their deputy or representative.</term> who partakes of our nature as well as His own. Therefore, it is

It is not at all absurd for Moses to allow the Jews to conceive of God as having a physical and human shape, since all people shall be judged by God in that shape on the last day <note>This refers to the Christian belief that Christ, in human form, will judge the world.</note>.

He made females as well as males. That story in Plato’s *Symposium* <note>original: *Symposion*. This refers to the myth told by Aristophanes in Plato's dialogue where humans were originally spherical, double-gendered beings before being split in two.</note>—about how men and women grew together at first until God cut them apart—is a very probable argument that the philosopher had seen or heard something of this Mosaic history. But I see no probability at all that this was actually his opinion. The story is told by that ridiculous comedian Aristophanes, with whom I believe Plato is essentially getting even for the way Aristophanes abused his good old friend and tutor Socrates. Aristophanes had brought Socrates onto the stage "walking on air" <note>original Greek: ἀεροϐατῶντα (*aerobatounta*)</note> in a basket to make him a laughingstock to all of Athens <note>A reference to Aristophanes' play *The Clouds*.</note>.

The text is indeed capable of being interpreted that way; however, since there is no reason to force that meaning upon it, and because it is not an idea well-suited to the understanding and notions of common people, I thought it best not to include it, even here in this *Literal Cabbala*.

*Verse 29.* **Fruit-bearing** <note>original: *Frugiferous*</note>. Sebastian Castellio <note>A 16th-century French theologian and Bible translator.</note> translates it this way, *fruit-bearing herbs* <note>original Latin: *Herbas frugiferas*</note>, which must refer to the kinds of plants I have named: strawberries, wheat, rice, and the like.

## CHAPTER II.

*7. The meaning of "soul" <note>original Greek: ψυχὴ (*psyche*)</note> corresponds to the breathing of Adam's soul into his nostrils. 8. The exact location of Paradise. That the Gihon is part of the Euphrates; the Pishon is the Phasis or Phafitigris. That the Midianites are called Ethiopians. Six reasons why Paradise was located near Mesopotamia. In the first four verses, everything is so clear and plain that there is no need for further explanation or defense, except to note that in the second verse, where I write *Within six days*, the Septuagint <note>original: the Seventies Translation</note> warrants it, as they translate it "on the sixth day" <note>original Greek: τῇ ἕκτῃ (*tē hektē*)</note>.

*Verse 5.* See what has been said regarding the eleventh verse of the first chapter.

*Verse 6.* **A mighty torrent of water.** The Septuagint renders the Hebrew word *ed* <note>אד</note> as "fountain" <note>original Greek: πηγὴ (*pēgē*)</note>. Aquila <note>A 2nd-century translator of the Old Testament into Greek.</note> translates it as "outburst" or "eruption" <note>original Greek: ἐκφλυγμὸς (*ekphlygmos*)</note>. The common occurrence of springs erupting from the ground may be a popular proof that the water covering the face of the Earth first broke out from there, but was afterward driven into one place by the power of God so that there might be dry land. ### CHAPTER II: The Defense of the Literal Cabbala

...[omnipoten]ce of God might be the more manifest in the making of Adam out of this dry dust.

But this objective might be more concisely reached even if the Hebrew word *Ed* <note>original Hebrew: אד (*’ed*)</note> were translated as *Vapor* (as most do translate it); if the negative in the previous verse might be repeated as being shared between clauses <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ κοινοῦ (*apo koinou*), a grammatical term where a word is understood to apply to two parts of a sentence</note>, as Rabbi Saadia <note>original: *R. Schadiah*</note> reads it: "Neither was there anyone who cultivated the land, nor did a vapor ascend, etc." <note>original Latin: *Nec quisquam erat qui coleret terram, nec vapor ascendebat, &c.*</note> To this sense Rabbi David Kimhi <note>original: *R. D. K.*</note> gives his approval very willingly. See Paul Fagius <note>A 16th-century German scholar of Hebrew.</note> on this passage.

<margin>Matthew 3:9</margin>
*Verse 7. The dust.* The Hebrew word means exactly that, and I make no mention of any moistening of it with water; for God is here portrayed acting according to His absolute power and omnipotence. It is just as easy to make men out of dry dust as out of hard stones; and yet God is able *even from stones to raise up children for Abraham.*

*Blew into the nostrils.* Breathing is so obvious an effect of life that the early, unrefined Greeks also gave the Soul its name from that action, calling it *psyche* from *psycho*, meaning *to breathe or to blow.* <note>original Greek: ψυχὴ (*psyche*) from ψύχω (*psycho*).</note>

*Verse 8. Eastward of Judea.* For this is how interpreters explain the word "Eastward" in Scripture, always in reference to Judea.

To prevent any further trouble in justifying the meaning I have given to the following verses concerning Paradise, I shall here all at once set down what I find most probable concerning its location <note>original: *situation*</note>, based on the works of François Vatable <note>original: *Vatablus*</note> and Cornelius à Lapide <note>A famous 17th-century Jesuit biblical commentator.</note>, adding also something from Dionysius the Periegete <note>original: Dionysius the Geographical Poet</note>. In general, we are led by the four rivers to the correct location of Paradise. And the Gihon, says Vatable, "is a lower stretch or stream of the Euphrates flowing into the Persian Gulf" <note>original Latin: *est tractus inferior Euphratis illabens in sinum Persicum*</note>. The Pishon <note>original: *Pison*</note> is the Phasis or Phasi-Tigris, which runs through Havilah, a region near Persia; so that the Pishon is a branch of the Tigris, just as the Gihon is a branch of the Euphrates. This is Vatable's view. And so that the Gihon may have its Ethiopia <note>original: *Æthiopia*</note>, Cornelius à Lapide notes that the Midianites <note>original: *Madianites*</note> and others near the Persian Gulf are called Ethiopians; and therefore he concludes, first, that Paradise was broadly located around Mesopotamia and Armenia, for the following reasons:

First, because these regions are called "Eastern" in Scripture (which, as I have said, is always to be understood in reference to Judea) according to the rule of the commentators. And the Lord is said to have planted this Garden of Paradise "Eastward."

Secondly, because after man was cast out of Paradise, these regions were inhabited first—both before the Flood (for Cain is said to inhabit Eden, Genesis 4:16) and also after the Flood, as they were nearer to Paradise and more fertile (Genesis 8:4, and also 11:2).

Thirdly, Paradise was in Eden, but Eden was near Haran (Ezekiel 27:23: *Haran, and Canneh, and Eden*). Haran was in Mesopotamia, being a city of Parthia where Crassus was slain; authors call it *Carrhae* <note>original: *Charra*</note>.

Fourthly, Paradise is where the Euphrates and Tigris are. And these are in Mesopotamia and Armenia. They give Mesopotamia its name, as it lies between them.

# The Defense of the Literal Cabbala. CHAPTER II.

->As much land as lies between the Euphrates and the Tigris,<-
->The inhabitants call this "Mesopotamia," the land between the rivers.<-
<note>original Greek: Ὅσση δ' Εὐφρήτῃ καὶ Τίγριδι ἔνδοθι γαῖα, Τήνδε Περικτίονες μέσην ποταμῶν ἐνέπεσι.</note>

That is,
> *The land between the Tigris and Euphrates streams,*
> *All this they name Mesopotamia.*

Fifthly, because these regions are most fruitful and pleasant. And that *Adam* was made not far from there is not improbable, given the excellence of that place—as much for the handsomeness of the men it produces as for the fertility of the soil.

->Such a harvest is produced upon that land; it causes to grow<-
->Grass and flowery pastures, and also a race of men,<-
->The most beautiful and like the immortals.<-
<note>original Greek: Τοίη ἐπὶ κείνης ἄρεσις πέλει, ἐν μὲν ἀέξειν Ποίην, ἐν δὲ νομὸς εὐανθέας, ἐν δὲ καὶ ἀνδρῶν Φύτλην, καλλίστην τε καὶ ἀθανάτοισιν ὁμοίην.</note>

That is,
> *So excellent is that soil for green herbage,*
> *For flowery meadows, and such fair, handsome men,*
> *As if they had been the offspring of the gods.*

->As the same geographer writes.<-

Sixthly and lastly, there is yet a further probability alleged: that *Paradise* was near *Mesopotamia*, as that country is not far distant from *Judea*. For it is the tradition of the Church Fathers that *Adam*, when he was cast out of *Paradise*, traveled over various parts of the world and came at last to *Judea*, where he died. He was buried on a mount which his posterity called *Mount Calvary* (because the head of the first man was laid there), where *Christ* was later crucified to atone for the sin of *Adam*, the first transgressor. If the story is not true, it is a pity it should not be; it has such venerable supporters as *Cyprian*, *Athanasius*, *Basil*, *Origen*, and other Fathers, as *Cornelius* <note>Cornelius a Lapide, a prominent 17th-century Jesuit biblical exegete.</note> affirms.

But now, for the more exact situation of *Paradise*, the same author ventures to place it at the very meeting point of the *Tigris* and *Euphrates*, where the city of *Apamia* now stands in *Ptolemy's* maps—at eighty degrees *longitude*, and some thirty-four degrees and thirty minutes <note>original: "scruples" — an archaic term for minutes of a degree</note> *latitude*.

Thus, according to the *Letter* <note>The literal interpretation of the text.</note>, we have found the *Paradise* which *Adam* lost; but if we find no better one in the *Philosophical* and *Moral Cabbala* <note>The author's deeper symbolic and ethical interpretations of the same text.</note>, we shall have gained nothing but "labor for our travel." <note>A play on the phrase "labor for our pains," suggesting the physical search is useless without spiritual insight.</note>

*Verse 9. That stood planted in the midst of the garden.* For in this verse, the *Tree of Life* is planted in the midst of the garden, and in the third verse of the third chapter, the *Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil* is placed there as well.

*For the Lord God had so ordained.* Commentators do not seem to suspect any inherent harm in the *Tree* itself; they believe the fruit was naturally good, but that God forbade it only to test the goodness of *Adam*. So this law that prohibited *Adam* from eating the fruit was merely <term>thetical</term> <note>original: "thetical" — a law based on a specific decree or "position" (Greek: thesis) rather than natural morality.</note> or *positive*, rather than *indispensable* and *natural* <note>Meaning it wasn't a law against something naturally evil (like murder), but a test of obedience to a specific command.</note>.

*Verse 10. From there it was parted.* This is the reason *Paradise* is thought to have been located where *Apamia* stands, as I have suggested above.

### CHAPTER II. The Defense of the Literal Cabbala.

**Verse 11. Phasis.** See the note on verse 8.

**Chaulateans.** The similarity of the name is apparent between *Havilah* and the *Chaulateans*, whom the geographer *Strabo* places in *Arabia* near *Mesopotamia*.

**Verse 13. Arabian Ethiopia.** See the note on verse 8.

**Verse 17.** See the note on verse 9.

**Verse 18. High praise for Matrimony.** *Moses* clearly recommends the use of *marriage* to the *Jews* and, in a way, encourages them toward that state; he does this like a proper Law-giver and Father of the people. For *in the multitude of people is the King’s honor, but in the lack of people is the destruction of the Prince*, as *Solomon* says in *Proverbs 14:28*. Besides, there was significant political wisdom in religiously commending something to them that most people would be inclined toward anyway. Laws are best liked when they suit the pleasure of the people, and the people will have a better opinion <note>original: "conceit"</note> of the Law-giver for it.

**Verse 19. These he brought to Adam.** Namely, the *Beasts* and *Birds*; but there is no mention of the *Fish*, as they were not suited to travel in the same element. It would have been too harsh and forced <note>original: "affected"</note> to have either brought the *Fish* from the *Sea* or to have carried *Adam* to the *Shore* to assign names to all the *Fish* flocking there to him. But later he might have had the opportunity to give them names as they occasionally came into his view.

**Verse 20.** See the note on verse 18.

**Verse 21. Fell into a dream.** For the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament</note> have, "God cast a trance upon Adam" <note>original Greek: Ἐπέβαλεν ὁ θεὸς ἔκστασιν ἐπὶ Ἀδὰμ</note>; and in that trance <note>original: "ecstasie"</note> he might very well see what God did during the entire time he slept.

**Verse 23.** See the notes on verses 21 and 24.

**Verse 24. So strict and sacred a bond, etc.** That is the goal of the story: to create a very fast and unbreakable affection between man and wife, so that they should look upon one another as one and the same person. In this, *Moses* has wisely provided for the happiness of his people by instilling a principle that is the root of all domestic <note>original: "Oeconomical"</note> order, delight, and contentment; while the husband looks upon his wife as himself in the *feminine* gender, and she on her husband as herself in the *masculine*. For *Grammarians* can discern no other difference between them than that between *Ish* and *Ishah* <note>original Hebrew: איש and אשה</note>, or *Man* and *Man-ess* <note>original Latin: Vir and Virissa</note>. 

But *Rabbi Abraham Ben Ezra* has found a mystery in these names beyond mere grammar. For in *Ish* and *Ishah*, he says, the contracted name of *Jehovah* is contained—namely, *Yah* <note>original Hebrew: יה</note>—for there is the letter *Yod* <note>י</note> and the letter *He* <note>ה</note>. So long, therefore, as the married couple live in God’s fear and mutual love, God is with them as well as in their names. But if they cast God off through disobedience and do not fulfill what they owe to one another, then their condition is what their names indicate to them once the name of God is taken out: namely, *Esh* and *Esh* <note>original Hebrew: אש and אש</note>—the fire of discord and contention in this life, and the eternal fire of Hell hereafter. This is the clever thought <note>original: "conceit"</note> of that pious and witty *Rabbi*.

**Verse 25. And were not ashamed.** *Marriage* and the physical union of men and women being so effectively recommended to the *Jews* in the preceding story, the wisdom of *Moses* foresaw that it would be natural for the people to think to themselves how so good and commendable a...

### CHAPTER III.

1. *How much it saves the reputation of our first parents that the Serpent was found to be the primary author of the transgression. That according to* St. Basil, *all the living creatures of Paradise could speak: undeniable reasons that the Serpent could, according to the Literal Cabbala.* 9. *The opinion of the Anthropomorphites* <term>Anthropomorphites: those who believe God has a human form or physical body</term> *is true, according to the Literal Cabbala.* 14. *That the Serpent walked upright before the Fall was the opinion of* St. Basil. 16. *A story of the easy delivery of a certain poor woman of* Liguria <note>A region in North-West Italy</note>. 19. *That the general calamities that weigh upon mankind came by the transgression of a <term>Positive Law</term> <note>A law based on a specific divine command rather than natural morality</note>; how well-suited this is to the purpose of* Moses. 23. *That Paradise was not the whole Earth.* 24. *The apparitions in Paradise called by* Theodoret *bogeymen or terrible phantoms* <note>original Greek: Μορμολύκεια</note>.

IN this third chapter, causes are laid down for some of the most notable and most concerning events in nature: such as the hard labor and toil of men to earn a livelihood; the antipathy between men and serpents; the burden of the ground with troublesome weeds; the shame of sexual intercourse <note>original: "Venery"</note>; the pangs of childbirth; and death itself. Of all these, *Moses’s* wisdom held it fit to give an account suited to the capacity of the people. For these issues fall into that grand question in philosophy, *Whence comes evil?* <note>original Greek: πόθεν τὰ κακὰ;</note>—a question which has exercised the wits of all ages to this very day. Every fool is able to ask the question, but few men are wise enough to be either able to give, or fit to receive, a sufficient answer to it, according to the depth of the matter itself.

But it was very necessary for *Moses* to continue his history and to communicate to them those plain and intelligible causes of the *evils* that always lay before their eyes. He had already so fully asserted that God is the Creator of Heaven and Earth and the contriver of all things that we see, adding also that the *laws* he proposed to them were delivered to him from God, and that all prosperity and happiness would accompany them if they observed those laws; that they should eat the good things of the land and live to a long and healthful age.

Now it was easy for the people—though they were unrefined <note>original: "rude"</note> and recently taken from making bricks for *Pharaoh* in *Egypt*—to think to themselves: "If God made all things, how is it that they are no better than they are? Why do our wives bring forth their children with pain? Why are we liable <note>original: "obnoxious"</note> to be stung by serpents? Why might God not give us an endless life, as well as a long life?" and the like. To which *Moses* in general...

### CHAPTER III. The Defense of the Literal Cabbala.

...general answers (to the great advantage of the people, and to bind them more firmly to the *Laws* he delivered to them from God): namely, that it was *disobedience* to God’s *will* that brought all this trouble <note>original: "mischief"</note> into the world; which is most certainly true. But by what particular circumstances it is laid out, you may read here in this third chapter.

*Verse 1. The Serpent also.* It would have been too harsh and violent <note>original: "boistrous"</note>, and would have too greatly reflected dishonor upon our first parents, *Adam* and *Eve*, if they had immediately violated such an express command from God and shown themselves to be professed rebels against him. Their descendants would scarcely have been able to remember them without curses and bitterness for being such bold and open authors of so much misery for them. But as it happened, it was not of their own doing, but by the subtlety of the *Serpent* that they were deceived into disobedience, being outwitted by his false suggestions. So their mistake may be looked upon with pardon and pity, and we ourselves are fairly warned to take heed that we do not forfeit what remains.

*But the power of Speech.* I cannot be as broad in my belief as *St. Basil*, who affirms that all living creatures in Paradise could speak and understand one another. But according to the *Literal Cabbala*, I think it is manifest that the *Serpent* could; and that it was not the *Devil* in the *Serpent*, as some interpreters would have it. For why should the *Serpent* be cursed for the *Devil’s* sake? And besides, the whole business is attributed to the cunning and subtlety of the Serpent, as doing it by the power of his own nature. Therefore, to talk this way of the *Serpent* and the *Devil* at once would be to confuse two *Cabbalas* <note>The literal and the philosophical interpretations</note> into one.

*Not eat of any of the Trees.* So say *Chrysostom*, *Rupertus*, and *St. Augustine*; as if the cunning Serpent had made use of that damnable maxim, *Slander boldly, something will stick* <note>original Latin: "Calumniare fortiter, aliquid adhaerebit"</note>. So, at first, he lays his charge high against God, as if He would debar them of necessary food and starve them; he did this so that at last he might gain at least this much: that God had unnecessarily restricted them from what contributed greatly to their pleasure and perfection.

*Verse 4. See verse 1.*

*Verse 7. And the eyes of them both were opened.* Some gather from this that *Adam* and *Eve* were blind until they tasted the forbidden fruit. This is such a foolish interpretation <note>original: "glosse"</note> that none but a blind man could ever have stumbled upon it; for the greatest pleasure of Paradise would have been lost if they had lacked their sight. Therefore, as gross as it is, that can be no part of any *Literal Cabbala*, as it has no probability at all; it is not a probable argument <note>original Greek: "λόγος πιθανός"</note>.

*Verse 9.* God's walking in the Garden, his calling after *Adam*, his pronouncing the doom upon him, his wife, and the Serpent, and various passages before, do again and again instill the opinion of the *Anthropomorphites* <term>Anthropomorphites: those who believe God has a human form or physical body</term>—that God has a human shape. I have already acknowledged this to be the meaning of the *Literal Cabbala*.

*Verse 13.* Here the first origin of trouble is resolved into the *Serpent*, whereby *Adam* and *Eve’s* reputations are somewhat saved, and the root of misery to mankind is plainly discovered.

*Verse 14. Creep upon thy belly.* It is plain according to the *Letter* <note>The literal text</note>,

# The Defense of the Literal Cabbala. CHAPTER III.

...that the Serpent went upright, which is also the opinion of Saint Basil. Otherwise, his doom signifies nothing if he had already crept upon his belly before.

*Verse 15. Perpetual Antipathy <note>original: "Antipathy"</note>. See verse 1.*

<margin>Historical Library, book 4, page 227.</margin>
*Verse 16. Her sorrows and pangs in child-bearing. See verse 1.* But these pains are much increased for women by their luxury and corrupt <note>original: "rotten"</note> delicacy, which weakens nature and enfeebles the spirits so that they can endure nothing; whereas those who are used to hardship and labor fare better. There is a famous <note>original: "notorious"</note> instance of this in a woman of Liguria who (as Diodorus Siculus writes) while working hard in the field, was overtaken by the labor of childbirth. She simply stepped aside for a moment and, delivering the child with quick dispatch, laid her baby as handily <note>original: "gainly"</note> as she could in some fresh leaves and grass. She immediately returned to her task and would not have stopped her work, except that her employer, out of pity for the infant, paid her the whole day's wages just to be rid of her. It was as if Providence had released her from the curse of Eve because she voluntarily underwent so much of Adam's curse, which was sweating in the field.

*Verse 18. See verse 1.*

*Verse 19. Observe the great wisdom of Moses.* The statutes and ordinances which he delivered to the people were, for the most part, not by nature <note>original: "φύσει"</note> but by decree <note>original: "θέσει"</note>—that is, not naturally and intrinsically good, but positive <note>term: A "positive law" is a rule created by a person or authority, rather than one existing in nature, like a ceremonial rule.</note> and changeable in themselves. Here, according to this history, all those great evils of toil and labor on barren ground, the pains of childbirth, and death itself are blamed on the transgression of a law that was merely "positive." By this means, the Lawgiver skillfully encourages the people to observe all the ceremonies and ordinances he gave them from God with great care and diligence. All of Adam's descendants experience the harm caused by breaking just that one positive law in Paradise—eating the fruit of the forbidden tree—whereas otherwise, positive laws might have been easily ignored or neglected.

*Verse 20. Called his wife Eve.* Life <note>original: "חוה" (Chavah)</note> signifies life.

*Verse 21. The use of which God taught.* The two great comforts and necessities of life are food and clothing. Therefore, it was appropriate to record this passage as well, to endear the people's minds to God and increase their devotion and thankfulness to Him, who was so specifically and in such detail the Author of those great supports of life.

*Verse 23. Out from the Garden of Eden.* This shows plainly that Paradise was not the whole Earth, as some would claim. For he was brought into Paradise by God, and now he is driven out again; but he was not driven out of the world.

*Verse 24. Haunted with spirits.* This phrase is very significant in expressing the nature of the event, and aptly describes the condition of Paradise when Adam was driven out. He could no longer return there because of those spirits that had visibly taken possession of the path and the place. I am not alone in this interpretation; Theodoret and Procopius agree with me, calling these apparitions at the entrance of Paradise scary monsters <note>original: "μορμολύκεια" (mormolykeia)</note> and ghosts of terrible form <note>original: "Spectra terribili formâ"</note>. I think that this may very well serve as the literal sense of this verse, as the existence of spirits and apparitions is acknowledged in all nations, no matter how uncivilized or slow-witted they may be.

### CHAPTER I.

# The Defence of the Philosophick Cabbala. CHAP. I.

his *Pentateuch* <note>The first five books of the Bible, traditionally attributed to Moses</note> with anything more proper and more relevant to his scope and purpose than this. And it is nothing but the ignorance of the atheist that can make him look upon it as contemptible, it being in itself as highly removed above contempt as true Prudence and stability is above madness and folly.

And yet I confess, I think there is still a greater depth and richness of wisdom in it than has been hitherto opened in this *Literal Cabbala* <note>The interpretation of the text based on its plain, historical, or moral surface meaning</note>, and such as shall represent *Moses* as profoundly skilled in *Philosophy* and divine *Morality* as he is in *Politics*. Against this, the atheist shall have nothing at all to allege, unless ignorance and overconfidence furnish his brain with irrelevant arguments.

For he shall not hear *Moses* in this *Philosophic Cabbala* either tasking God to a *six* days' labor, or bounding the world at the clouds, or making the moon bigger than the stars, or numbering days without suns, or bringing in a serpent talking with a woman, or any such like passages, which the atheists' misunderstanding and perverseness makes them take offense at. But they shall find him more expansive and more free than any other, and laying down such conclusions as the wisest *Naturalists* <note>Scientists or observers of the natural world</note> and *Theosophers* <note>Those who study divine wisdom and the nature of God</note> in all ages have looked upon as the choicest and most precious. Such, I say, are those in the *Philosophic Cabbala* you have read; and I am now come to defend it, and make it good that it is indeed the meaning of *Moses's* text. And one great key for the understanding of it in this first chapter will be those *Pythagorean Mysteries of Numbers*, as I have already suggested in my *Preface*.

<margin>Section 4.</margin>
*Verse 1.* I mean the same thing by both. And there is good reason there should be meant the same thing by both. For, besides that those actual, conspicuous lights are in heaven—namely, the sun and stars—*Heaven*, or the *Ethereal Matter*, has in it all over the principles of *Light*, which are the round *particles*, and that very fine and subtle *matter* that lies in the *intervals* of those round *particles*. He that is but a little acquainted with the *French Philosophy* <note>original: "French Philosophy"; this refers to the physics of René Descartes, who theorized that light was transmitted through spherical particles in the ether</note> understands the business plainly. And in the expounding of *Moses*, I think I may lay down this for a safe principle: that there is no considerable truth in Nature or Divinity that *Moses* was ignorant of; and so if it be found agreeable to his text, I may very well attribute it to him. At least the Divine Wisdom wherewith *Moses* was inspired anticipates all the inventions of men.

<margin>Of the City of God, book 11, chapter 9 <note>original: "De Civit. lib. 11. cap. 9"</note></margin>
But now that I understand this *Heaven* and *Earth* in the **First** verse as things distinct from the *Heaven* and *Earth* afterwards mentioned, I am not alone in it, but have the authority of *Philo* <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish philosopher who sought to harmonize the Torah with Greek philosophy</note>, who interprets not this *Heaven* and *Earth* as the visible and tangible *Heaven* and *Earth* which are mentioned on the second and third day, but as a *Heaven* and *Earth* quite different from them. I also have the support <note>original: "suffrage"</note> of *St. Augustine*, who likewise understands by *Heaven* and *Light* one and the same thing—to wit, the *Angels*—and by *Earth* the *First Matter*. This is something like the sense of this present *Cabbala*, only where he sets down *physical matter*, we set down a *metaphysical* one (that other belonging most properly to the second day); and for *Angels*, we have *The World of Life*, which comprehends not *Angels* only, but all *Substantial Forms* and *spirits* whatever.

# CHAP. I. The Defence of the Philosophick Cabbala.

It is no surprise that *Heaven* or *Light* should be symbols of *The World of Life* or *Form*. You can find a sufficient reason for this in the *Cabbala* itself, at the fifth verse of this present chapter; and *Plotinus* <note>A major Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 204–270 AD) who influenced Christian and Jewish thought</note> compares *Form* to *Light*, saying, "For the reason-principle is light" <note>original Greek: "ὁ γὰρ λόγος φῶς"</note>, meaning that *Form is Light*.

Finally, in the second verse of this same chapter, there are also clear reasons laid down why the mere *possibility* of the outward creation is called the *Earth*, following the description of the *Earth* in the second verse of the first chapter of *Moses's* text. To this, you may further add that just as the *Earth* is viewed as the *foundation* <note>original: "Basis"</note> of the world, so the *possibility* of the outward creation is, in some sense, its *foundation*.

**The Triune Godhead.** The Hebrew words "God created" <note>original: "ברא אלהים" (Bara Elohim)</note> elegantly suggest both a plurality and a singularity, as the *Noun* is plural while the *Verb* is in the singular number. From this, I believe the mystery of the *Trinity* and the *Unity* of the Godhead—or "The One" <note>original Greek: "τὸ ἕν" (to hen)</note>—is very likely included here. Even *Vatablus* <note>François Vatable (d. 1547), a French humanist and Hebraist</note> himself, though he hesitates over these grammatical points, openly acknowledges three persons in one God in his commentary on the twenty-sixth verse of this chapter. It is a strong argument that this was the *Philosophic Cabbala* of *Moses* and the learned and pious *Jews*, because the concept of the *Trinity* is so strongly emphasized by the *Platonists* and *Pythagoreans*. Everyone acknowledges (and I think I shall make it clearer than ever) that these philosophers obtained their philosophy from *Moses*.

**By His Eternal Wisdom.** *Ambrose*, *Basil*, and *Origen* <note>Prominent early Church Fathers and theologians</note> interpret "In the beginning" <note>original Latin: "In Principio"</note> to mean the same as "In the Son" <note>original Latin: "In Filio"</note>. In the first chapter of *Colossians*, the Apostle [Paul], speaking of the Son of God, says that he is the *firstborn of every creature*, and that *by him all things were created that are in heaven and on earth*; that *he is before all things, and by him all things consist*. This is the *Wisdom of God*, or the *Idea* according to which He framed all things. Therefore, he must be the *Beginning* of the *Creatures of God* before all other things. Very similar to the Apostle's words are the two attributes *Philo* <note>Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BC – 50 AD), a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher</note> gives to the same subject, calling him "The first-born word of God" <note>original Greek: "πρωτόγονον θεοῦ λόγον"</note> (or "the first-born form of God") and "the Beginning" <note>original Greek: "ἀρχὴν"</note>. He also calls him simply "The Word" <note>original Greek: "Λόγον" (Logon)</note>, which signifies *Word*, *Form*, *Reason*, or *Wisdom*. One of the Chaldee Paraphrasts <note>Translators or commentators of the Hebrew Bible into Aramaic</note> also interprets "In the beginning" as "In Wisdom" <note>original Latin: "In Sapientia"</note>. This agrees perfectly with the words of *Solomon* in <margin>Proverbs 8:22.</margin> "The Lord possessed me" <note>original Hebrew: "יהוה קנני ראשית דרכו" (Adonai kanani reshith darko)</note>, "at the beginning of his way" <note>original Latin: "Principium viae suae"</note>, which means "of his works," as *Vatablus* explains it, and the text confirms: "The sunrise of his works of old" <note>original Hebrew: "קדם מפעליו מאז" (kedem miph'alav me'az)</note>. There is no necessity to treat the Hebrew words for "beginning" and "before" <note>original: "ראשית" (reshith) and "קדם" (kedem)</note> as adverbs; they are substantives [nouns]. Here, *Wisdom* is called the *Principle* and the *Morning* of the works of God—not to diminish its status, but because the *East* and the *Morning* are the womb of light, from which all *Light* and *Form* spring. And as I mentioned before from *Plotinus*, *Form is Light*.

<margin>In his *Virgin of the World* <note>original Greek: "Κόρη Κόσμου" (Korē Kosmou), a Hermetic text</note>.</margin> This notion of "the East" or "the Beginning" <note>original Hebrew: "קדם" (kedem)</note> suits the passage in *Trismegistus* where *Hermes* <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary figure associated with ancient esoteric wisdom</note> speaks thus: "But I, having come from the sunrise, to those who see all..." <note>original Greek: "Ἐγὼ δ' ἐξ ἀνατολῆς γεנוμένης, τοῖς πᾶντα βλέπειν" (More translates 'sunrise' as synonymous with the spiritual origin of form)</note>

# CHAP. I. The Defence of the Philosophick Cabbala.

...having beheld the things of the East with [soulful] eyes, etc. <note>original Greek: "πεσιν ὀφθαλμοῖς τὰ τ' ἀνατολῆς θεωρήσας" — More is quoting Philo Judaeus, who associates the "East" with the Divine Word</note> where "East" <note>original Greek: "ἀνατολὴ" (anatole)</note>, which is the same as the Hebrew word *Qedem* <note>original: "קדם"</note>, must signify the **Divine Intellect**, the **bright Morning Star**, the **Wisdom of God**. To this **Wisdom**, called in the eighth chapter of *Proverbs* "the Beginning" <note>original: "ראשית" (Reshith)</note> and "the Ancient" <note>original: "קדם" (Qedem)</note>—the *Beginning and Morning of his Works*—the creation of the world is attributed by Solomon, as you may see there at length. I will only add that what the Hebrew text here in *Genesis* calls *Reshith* ("the Beginning"), the *Chaldee* <note>The Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Bible</note> calls *Qadmin*, which is essentially the same as *Qedem*. Therefore, the "Beginning" is the **Essential Wisdom of God**, not merely a habit or property, but a **Substance** that *is* Wisdom. For true Wisdom is Substance: "True wisdom is substance, and true substance is wisdom" <note>original Greek: "Ἡ ἀληθινὴ σοφία οὐσία, καὶ ἡ ἀληθινὴ οὐσία σοφία"</note>; this is the same point that *Plotinus* <note>A Neoplatonic philosopher</note> makes. This is why he is called in the *Apocalypse* <note>The Book of Revelation 1:4</note>, "the one who is, and who was, and who is to come" <note>original Greek: "ὁ ὢν καὶ ὁ ἦν καὶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος"</note>, which is but a description <note>original: "Periphraſis"</note> of **Jehovah**, **Essence**, or *Ousia* <note>Substance/Being</note>. This name **Jehovah** <note>original: "יהוה"</note> contains the future, present, and past tense within it, in the letters *Vav* and *He*, as *Zanchius* <note>Girolamo Zanchi (1516–1590), a prominent Italian Protestant theologian</note> observes. This is the second person <note>original: "Hypoſtaſis"</note> in the **Holy Trinity**, the **Logos**, which was in the beginning of the world with God. *All things were made by him, and without him was nothing made that was made* (John 1).

**First created this.** I cannot attribute it to any reason at all, except for a slowness of imagination and the heavy clumsiness of melancholy—or perhaps the weight of blood and flesh—that makes men imagine that **Creation** is impossible even for God himself. In contrast, I believe I have clearly demonstrated in my <margin>Book 1, chapter 7, section 4.</margin> *Antidote against Atheism* that it is impossible for God *not* to have the power of Creation; otherwise, he would not be God. But because our own will and mind can create no substance distinct from ourselves, we foolishly conceive—measuring the **Power of God** by our own—that he cannot create any substance distinct from himself. This is merely a weak conclusion resulting from our own dullness and lack of attention.

**Ver. 2. Solitude and Emptiness.** The very word signifies this in the original Hebrew <note>referring to *Tohu* and *Bohu*</note>, as *Vatablus* <note>François Vatable, a renowned 16th-century Hebrew scholar</note> will tell you. These being abstract terms (as the scholastic philosophers <note>original: "Schools"</note> call them) very fittingly agree with the definition we have given to this **Symbolical Earth**. We affirm it is not a real, actual subject—neither spiritual nor corporeal—that could be said to be *void and empty*; rather, it is **Vacuity and Emptiness** itself, joined only with a capacity of becoming something. It is, as I have often suggested, the **Potential Being** <note>original Latin: "Ens Potentiale"</note> of the entire outward Creation.

**But the Spirit of God.** This refers not to a great wind, but to the **Holy Ghost**. This is the general interpretation of the Church Fathers. It is a sign that this aligns with the true **Mosaical Cabbala**, as it is so consistent with **Plato’s School**; I suspect that school currently possesses more of that Cabbala than the Jews themselves have today.

**Having hovered awhile.** The word in the original is *Merachephet* <note>original: "מרחפת"</note>, which signifies a hovering or brooding over a thing, just as a bird does over her nest or her young ones. This is likely the origin of the "Egg" mentioned by the Greek playwright **Aristophanes**.

->To this sense:<-

> Under the wind below in darksome shade,
> There the black-winged Night her first Egg laid.

# CHAP. I. The Defence of the Philosophick Cabbala.

And this manner of brooding in this way is an emblem of the deepest affection; and who knows but that from this text the poets took the occasion of inventing that ancient **Cupid**, the father of all the gods, the creator of all things, and the maker of mankind? For he is described this way by **Hesiod** and **Orpheus**, and here in this passage from **Aristophanes**, from which I took the previously cited verse.

**Simmias of Rhodes** describes this ancient Love in verses that represent a pair of wings. I will not say this is according to the metaphor <note>original: "conceit"</note> of **Aristophanes's** Egg, which they were meant to brood and hatch. But the longest feather of one of them writes thus:

-> Behold me, the king of the broad-breasted Earth, who established the sky and the sea. <note>original Greek: "Λεῦσσέ με τὸν γᾶς τε βαθυστέρνυ ἄνακτ', ἀκμονίδαν τὰν ἅλα θ' ἑδράσαντα·"</note> <-

-> To this sense, <-

> I am the King of the deep-bosomed Earth,
> My strength gave to the Sea both bounds and birth.

This Spirit of God, then, or the **Divine Love** which was from everlasting, will prove to be the **Third Divine Hypostasis** <term>Hypostasis: a person or distinct substance within the Trinity</term>. The first was *Elohim* <note>original Hebrew: "אלהים"</note>, which signifies "strength," a word generally applied to the whole Trinity. But *Jehovah*, as the Rabbis observe, is a name for God as He is merciful and gracious, which may correspond to **Plato's** *The Good* <note>original Greek: "Ταγαθόν"</note>—though that name is also applied to Christ, as we have already acknowledged. The second is *Reshith* <note>original Hebrew: "ראשית"</note>, which is **Wisdom**, as has been proved from the Book of Proverbs, and answers to the Platonic *Mind* <note>original Greek: "Νῦς"</note>. We have now come upon the third, which must be **Love**; and it has a fortunate alignment <margin>Enneads 3. book 6. also Enneads 4. book 4. chapter 9.</margin> with the third *hypostasis* in the Platonic Triad, the **Soul** <note>original Greek: "Ψυχὴ"</note>, whom **Plotinus** calls the **Celestial Venus** <note>original Greek: "οὐρανίαν Ἀφροδίτην"</note>. And it is to this Soul, in a more immediate way, that the creation of the world is attributed by that philosopher, as well as by Plato; just as here in Moses, the Spirit of God is said to lie close, brooding upon the watery <note>original: "humid"</note> matter for the physical production of this outward world.

*Verse 3. Exist independently of Physical Matter.* That which exists first is clearly independent of what follows, and **Philo** considers all immaterial beings to have been created on this first day. Thus, the souls of men are removed far from any fear of fate or mortality, which is the grand tenet of Plato's school.

*Verse 5. Matter merely Metaphysical.* See the term *Hyle* <term>Hyle: the Greek word for raw, unformed matter</term> in my "General Interpretation" at the end of my *Poems*. There you shall find that I have established the same concept I use here, though at that time I had no intention of explaining the books of Moses.

*Monad or Unity.* The suitability of the number to the nature of each day's work will be found to be wonderful. From this we may well conclude that it was ordered so on purpose, and that in all probability **Pythagoras** was acquainted with this **Cabala**. This was likely the reason the **Pythagoreans** made such a great fuss <note>original: "deal of doe"</note> over numbers, attributing concepts to them that no other mathematicians <note>original: "Arithmeticians"</note> do. Therefore, if such theorems as the Pythagoreans held are found to be suitable and compatible with Moses's text, there is a strong indication <note>original: "shrewd presumption"</note> that this is the correct **Philosophical Cabala** of the passage.

Nicomachus of Gerasa in Photius’s *Bibliotheca*.

*Spiritual Beings* of the *intellectual world*—taking that term in a broad sense—or the *World of Life*, as *Ficino* calls it: *The World of Life and Forms*. The *Pythagoreans* call a "Unit" (the number one) the *Form* <note>original Greek: "εἶδος"</note> and *Life* <note>original Greek: "Ζωὴ"</note>. They also call it the *Tower of Jupiter* <note>original Greek: "Ζανὸς πύργος"</note>, giving the same name to a "Point" or "Center." By this, they mean the *vital formative center* of things, the *seminal principles* <note>original Latin: "Rationes Seminales"</note>. They also call a Unit the *seminal reason* <note>original Greek: "λόγος σπερματίτης"</note>, which is the *seminal form*. A very short and sufficient explanation for *Philo’s* claim that spiritual substances were the first day’s work is this: just as a "Unit" is *indivisible* in mathematics, so is the nature of *spirits indivisible*. You cannot make two out of one of them, as you can with a piece of *physical matter* by actually dividing or severing one piece from another. Therefore, what was truly and properly created on the first day was *immaterial*, *indivisible*, and *independent* of matter, ranging from the highest *angel* to the lowliest <note>original: "meanest"</note> *seminal form*.

As for the *potential* for the outward creation to exist, since it is not strictly a real "being," it presents no difficulty. Whatever it is, it can be appropriately linked to *incorporeal* (non-physical) things, because it is an object of the intellect rather than the senses. It is also unchanging <note>original: "impassible"</note> and cannot be diminished, and so is in a way indivisible. Since the power of God cannot be diminished, the *possibility* of the creature existing must also be undiminishable, as it follows directly from His power. Therefore, because this *potentiality* is always
<margin>
Nicomachus of Gerasa, *Theology of Arithmetic*, in Photius’s *Bibliotheca*, no. 187.
</margin>
one, it is rightly referred to the first day. In this respect, the *Pythagoreans* call a "Unit" *matter* <note>original Greek: "ὕλη"</note>, as they do the "Binary" (the number two). They also call it *darkness* <note>original Greek: "ἀλαμπία"</note> and *murkiness* <note>original Greek: "σκοτωδία"</note>. These names clearly refer to the dark *potentiality* of things described by *Moses* in the first day's creation.

<margin>
\* Concerning the production of this physical matter, see Plotinus, *Enneads* 4, book 3, chapter 9. See also my *Treatise on the Immortality of the Soul*, Book 3, chapter 16, section 8.
</margin>
*Verse 6. Created a vast amount, etc.* He \* creates *physical matter* now (just as he previously created *The World of Life*) out of nothing. This *universal matter* may well be called the *Expanse* <note>original Hebrew: "רקיע" (Raki'a)</note>, for *extension* is a defining property of *physical matter*. *Castellio* translates it as *fluid* <note>original Latin: "Liquidum"</note>, and this *universal matter* is still mostly *fluid* all over the world, but at first, it was universally fluid.

*Between the aforementioned fluid potential, etc.* But here you may ask: how can this *physical matter* be imagined to be between the *waters above* and the *waters underneath*? What could the *waters above* be? *Maimonides* argues that we do not need to find such a consistent literal analogy in the hidden sense of Scripture, as you may see in his preface to *The Guide for the Perplexed* <note>original title: "More Nevochim"</note>. But I do not need to rely on that general excuse. It seems to me that the *seminal forms* which descend through *matter*—thereby reaching the *potential* of the parts of the physical creation and making them spring into action—are not unlike raindrops. These drops descend through the heaven or air and make the earth fruitful. Furthermore, the *seminal forms* of things are at first contracted into a round shape, so to speak, but they spread out when they bring any part of the *potential* of the physical creation into action, just as raindrops spread when they fall to the ground. So the analogy is clear enough, even if it seems a bit elaborate and detailed. We may add to all this what the ancients said concerning the *Naiads* or *Water-Nymphs*: they understood them to be *all souls in general that descend into matter and the process of generation* <note>original Greek: "τὰς εἰς γένεσιν κατιούσας ψυχάς κοινῶς ἁπάσας"</note>.

# CHAP. I. The Defence of the Philosophick Cabbala.

See *Porphyrius* in his *On the Cave of the Nymphs*.

<margin>Hymn 3.</margin>

<margin>* See the *Appendix to the Defence*, chapter 7, section 8.</margin>
*Demetrius*, in the works of *Plutarch*, also describes souls involved in physical birth <term>generation</term> as being so many *water nymphs*. And this is not a mere metaphor, but also points to a physical truth: namely, the moisture of the <term>vehicles</term> <note>In More’s philosophy, a "vehicle" is the subtle, semi-material body that a soul inhabits to interact with the physical world.</note> of those souls or spiritual powers that are engaged in *generation*. Therefore, all those immaterial beings—whether the Universal Spirit of Nature or the souls of humans and animals—are endowed or invested with such a <term>genital moisture</term> <note>original: "genital moisture." Here, "genital" refers to the power of generating or creating life, rather than its modern anatomical meaning.</note> in their framing of any visible structure out of matter here below. They descend into this matter by virtue of the vital attachment of this humidity. Thus, they are more than metaphorically called *water*, just as the angels and other spirits created on the first day are more than symbolically called *heaven* and *light*, as I have noted in the appropriate place.

And because of this birth-moisture that these spiritual essences are involved in when they frame any earthly structure, I believe that excellent Platonist *Virgil* makes that description of the task or exercise of the *water nymphs* in the River *Peneus*:

> Around Cyrene, the nymphs were carding Milesian wool, dyed with a deep glassy-green color. While they were captivated by this song, they unrolled their soft tasks from their spindles, etc.
> <note>original Latin: "Cyrenen circum Milesia vellera Nymphæ / Carpebant hyali saturo fucata colore. / Inter quas curam Clymene narrabat inanem / Vulcani, Martisque dolos & dulcia furta; / Atque Chao densos Divûm numerabat amores; / Carmine quo captæ fusis dum mollia pensa / Devolvunt, &c."</note>

In these passages, that knowledgeable poet certainly means nothing else but this: that the spinning and weaving of the first structure of things occurs within a certain primordial or birth-moisture in which these spiritual powers, the *water nymphs*, work. This is why he portrays them teasing, spinning, and singing love songs about the hidden and stolen romances of the gods—that is, those parts of the celestial creation that descend into physical existence <term>physical existence</term> <note>original Greek: "γένεσιν"</note>—under the waters of the River *Peneus*.

To conclude, therefore, it is very easy and appropriate to conceive that just as the angels, the souls of men not yet sunk into physical birth, and all those spiritual beings created on the first day are called *heaven* and *light* in reference to their innermost vehicles; so likewise, all souls as they descend into physical existence <note>original Greek: "εἰς γένεσιν"</note>, and all spiritual powers as they apply themselves to terrestrial formation (which requires this birth-moisture), are by the same analogy called the *Upper Waters* in this second day's work, as Man...

# The Defence of the Philosophic Cabbala. CHAP. I.

...in respect to his outward body, he was called *Adam*, which is to say, *Earth*.

*Verse* 7. *What harm straying souls suffer*. The frequent complaints that the noble spirit in the *Pythagoreans* and *Platonists* makes against the burdens and disadvantages of the body make this *Cabbala* <note>original: Cabbala; here meaning a mystical or philosophical interpretation of scripture</note> very probable. And it is somewhat like our theologians imagining *Hell* to be created on this day.

*Verse* 8. *Activated and moved*. This is consistent with *Plato's* school, which holds that *matter* is immovable by itself; this is most reasonable. For if matter were movable by its own nature, nothing would hold together for a moment, but would dissolve into infinitely small particles. From this, it is obvious that there must be something besides *matter*—either to bind it or to move it. Thus, the creation of *immaterial beings* <note>Spiritual substances or souls</note> is also necessary in that regard.

*Rightly called Heaven*. I mean *Shemayim* <note>Hebrew: שמים</note>. For this movement of matter brought it to *Descartes's* second principle, which is the true *Aether*, or rather *Shemayim*. For it is liquid as *water*, and yet contains the fierce principle of *fire*, which is the first element and the most subtle of all. This is understood at first sight by *Cartesians* <note>Followers of the physics of René Descartes</note>, who will easily accept the explanation <note>original: Notation</note> of the Rabbis regarding the word *Shemayim*, as being derived from *Esh* <note>Hebrew: אש</note>, *fire*, and *Mayim* <note>Hebrew: מים</note>, *water*. For so *Rabbi Bahya* says: "*The Heavens*," says he, "*were created from the beginning, and are called* Shemayim, *because they are* Fire and Water." No philosophy proves this as well as the *Cartesian* system. For the round particles, like *water* (though they are not the same shape), temper the fierceness of the first principle, which is the purest *fire*. And yet this *fire* always lies, to some extent, within the triangular intervals between the round particles, as that philosophy explains at length.

<margin>
Nicomachus Gerasenus, *The Theology of Arithmetic*, book 1.
</margin>
*And the Binary*. How appropriately again does the number two agree with the nature of the work of this day, which is the creation of *physical matter*? The *Pythagoreans* call the number two *Hyle* <note>Greek: ὕλη; matter</note>. *Simplicius*, in his commentary on *Aristotle's Physics*, says of the *Pythagoreans*: "They might well call One, 'Form,' as it defines and limits whatever it takes hold of to a certain shape and property; and Two they might well call 'Matter,' as it is indeterminate and the cause of size and divisibility." <note>original Greek: Εἰκότως ἓν μὲν τὸ εἶδος ἔλεγον, ὡς ὁρίζον ὅπερ ἂν καταλάβῃ καὶ περατοῦν· δύο δὲ τὴν ὕλην, ὡς ἀόριστον, καὶ ὄγκου καὶ διαιρέσεως αἰτίαν.</note> And they have extensively applied to the number *two* such names as are most appropriate to *physical matter*, such as *unformed*, *undetermined*, and *unlimited* <note>original Greek: Ἀσχημάτιστος, Ἀόριστος, Ἄπειρος</note>. For such is matter by itself, until *form* takes hold of it. It is also called *Flow* <note>original Greek: Ῥόα</note>, from the fluidity of matter; *Airy* <note>original Greek: Ἀερία</note>, because it provides the substance for the heavens and stars; and *Contention*, *Fate*, and *Death* <note>original Greek: Νεῖκος, Μόρος, Θάνατος</note>, for these are the consequences of the soul being joined with *physical matter*. They also call it *Motion*, *Generation*, *Nature*, and *Division* <note>original Greek: Κίνησις, Γένεσις, Φύσις, Διαίρεσις</note>, which are properties clearly belonging to bodies. They call this number also *Endurance* <note>original Greek: Ὑπομονὴ</note>, because it is the *subject* or *substratum* <note>original Greek: ὑποκείμενον</note> that endures and undergoes all the changes and alterations that the active *forms* impose upon it. Therefore, it is plain that the *Pythagoreans* understood *physical matter* by the number *two*...

# The Defence of the Philosophic Cabbala. CHAP. I.

Since the Moon and other **Planets** are related, she may well be referred to this fourth day’s Creation.

<margin>* On Creation, Problem 1. <note>original: *De Creatione Problem. 1.*</note></margin>
This will not seem bold or harsh at all if we consider that the most learned scholars have already agreed that the entire Creation was made all at once. For example, this is held by the most rational of all the **Jewish Doctors**, **Moses Maimonides** <note>original: *R. Moses Ægyptius*</note>, **Philo Judaeus**, **Procopius of Gaza**, **Cardinal Cajetan**, **St. Augustine**, and the schools of **Hillel** and **Shammai**, as **Manasseh Ben Israel** writes. Consequently, that slow order of days is essentially removed, along with all the difficulties that might arise from such a theory.

Therefore, I say the **Earth**, as one of the **primary Planets**, was created on this fourth day. I translate the Hebrew word *Ha-kokhavim* <note>original: הכוכבים</note> as **Primary Planets**. I call them "Primary" because of the emphatic Hebrew letter *He* (meaning "the"); and "Planets" because the very origin of their name implies their nature. For the Hebrew word for star, *Kokhav* <note>original: ככב</note>, is clearly derived from *Ko* <note>original: כו</note>, meaning **burning**, and *Kav* <note>original: כב</note>, meaning **extinguishing**; these are nouns formed from the roots *Kavah* and *Kabah*, according to a flawless linguistic analogy. The nature of the **Earth**, as well as the rest of the **Planets**, is such that they seem to have once been burning and shining Suns; but once their light and heat were extinguished, they later became opaque Planets. This conclusion seems to be plainly contained here in the writings of **Moses**, but it is demonstrated at large in the philosophy of **Descartes** <note>original: *Des-Cartes*</note>. This linguistic explanation is not weakened by the claim that the word is ordinarily used to signify the **fixed stars** as well as the **planets**. I do not deny that in a common sense it may apply to them as well. For the **fixed stars**, according to the imagination of uneducated people, may be said to be "lighted up" and "extinguished" whenever they appear and disappear. Such people measure everything by obvious sense and fancy; they may well look upon the stars as so many candles set up by divine Providence in the night, but frugally put out during the day to avoid waste. I remember that **Theodoret**, in his work *On Providence* <note>original: περὶ Προνοίας</note>, swallowed this idea so easily that he uses it as a special argument for Providence: that stars can burn with their heads downwards and not immediately melt away <note>original: "sweal out"</note> and be extinguished, as our ordinary candles are. Therefore, the word *Kokhav* may very well be attributed to all the stars—both **Fixed** and **Planets**—but to the **Fixed** stars only based on common, superficial appearances, while it applies to the **Planets** based on true and natural grounds. We may be sure that this is what **Moses** would aim for and emphasize in his **Philosophic Cabbala**.

Briefly, then, the emphatic "the" in *Ha-kokhavim* contains a double **Emphasis**: it points to those true *Kokhavim* or **Planets**, and specifically the **most eminent** among those **truly** so-called. It is not at all strange that such deep scientific conclusions should be hidden in this **Mosaic text**. As I have suggested elsewhere, **Moses** was ahead of **Descartes**. The ancient Patriarchs had the intelligence, and because of their long lives, the leisure time to invent as precise and subtle theories in philosophy as any of their descendants ever could, besides what they might have received by tradition from **Adam**. And if we find that the **Earth** is a **Planet**, it must be immediately acknowledged that it orbits the Sun. This is pure **Pythagoreanism** <note>The ancient Greek theory that the Earth revolves around a central fire or the Sun.</note> once again, and a strong indication that Pythagoras was taught that mystery by this **Mosaic Cabbala**. But regarding the fact that the **Earth** is a **Planet**,

Besides the etymology <note>original: "Notation"</note> we have already emphasized, the necessity of the Earth being created on this fourth day among the other planets is a further argument. For there is no mention of its creation on any other day according to this Philosophic Cabbala.

Thus, no grammatical violence is done to the text of Moses during this entire explanation.

Four is the first "body" in numbers, representing an **equilateral pyramid** <note>A tetrahedron, which has four faces</note>; this figure is also a fitting symbol of **light**, as rays enter the eye in a pyramidal form. And lights are now set up in all the vast region of the ethereal matter, which is **heaven**.

They suggest that all things are so sweetly and fittingly ordered in the world that its various motions are like a beautiful dance or ravishing music.
