<note>original Greek: Οὐ μὰ τὸν ἡμετέρᾳ ψυχᾷ παραδόντα τετρακτύν, Παγὰν ἀενάου φύσεως ῥιζώματ’ ἔχουσαν.</note>

> *By him that did to us disclose*
> *The Tetrad’s mystery,*
> *Where Nature’s Fountain that ever flows*
> *And hidden root does lie.*

They swore by Pythagoras, as is believed, because he taught them this mysterious tradition. And do you really think it would have been such a "venerable mystery"—worthy of the solemnity of religion and an oath—simply to understand that 1, 2, 3, and 4 make ten, and that ten is "everything"? Even primitive <note>original: "rude"</note> mankind first learned that by counting on their fingers; indeed, mathematicians still recognize this by calling them **digits** <note>from the Latin *digitus*, meaning finger</note> to this very day.

There is no likelihood that a man as wise as Pythagoras would place such emphasis on such trifles, or that his scholars would be such fools as to be impressed by them. However, it is well known that the Pythagoreans held that the **Earth moves** around the **Sun**, which is plainly implied according to the *Philosophic Cabbala* of this **Fourth** day’s work. That much of his secrets reached common knowledge and fame. But it is very highly probable that he had the entire *Philosophic Cabbala* of Creation explained to him by some knowledgeable priest or philosopher (as we now call them) in the East. These teachers, using this mystery of numbers, set out for him the most excellent and precious conclusions in **Natural Philosophy**. I believe they interpreted the Text of **Moses** in a way similar to what I have discovered, proving all those noble and vast conclusions through demonstration and reason. Thus, Pythagoras, being well-equipped with the knowledge of things, was willing to share them with those whose piety and intellect were fit to receive them—without discarding the outward form of **numbers** through which they were first conveyed to him. But to believe that such arithmetical trivialities <note>original: "nugacities"</note> as are usually recorded as his were actually the riches of the wisdom of such a famous philosopher is something beyond all belief or probability.

Therefore, I believe that the most choice and precious treasures of knowledge are laid open in the Cabbala of the **Fourth day**, from which it...

You can see that the former and simpler **Tetractys** is still included and used here, for **four** again determines the assignment of the masculine and feminine numbers. From this, I further believe that under the number of this more complex **Tetrad** (which also contains the other within it), he taught his disciples the mystery of the **whole creation**, revealing to them the nature of all things, both **spiritual** and **physical**. <margin>Anonymous commentary on Ptolemy’s *Tetrabiblos*, Book 1</margin> *For an even number carries with it divisibility and passivity; but an odd number carries indivisibility, impassivity, and activity. Therefore, the latter is called masculine, and the former feminine,* <note>original Greek: Ὁ γὰρ ἄρτιος ἀριθμὸς τὸ τμητικὸν ἔχοι καὶ παθητικόν, ὁ δὲ περισσὸς τὸ ἄτμητον καὶ ἀπαθὲς καὶ δραστήριον. Διὸ ὁ μὲν θῆλυς ὀνομάζεται, ὁ δὲ ἄῤῥην</note> as a certain author writes.

<margin>A description of this conjunction can be seen in Plotinus, *Enneads*, Book 5, Tractate 1, Chapter 2; also Book 4, Tractate 3, Chapter 10</margin>
Therefore, the putting together of the first four masculine numbers with the first four feminine numbers is the **joining of the active and passive principles** together, matching the parts of **matter** with appropriate **forms** from the **world of life**. So I believe the **Tetractys** was a symbol of the entire system of Pythagoras’s **philosophy**, which we may very justly suspect to be the same as the **Mosaic Cabbala**. And the root of this **Tetractys** is **six**, which again corresponds to **Moses** and reminds us of the **six days** of work in the creation.

**Verse 20.** ***Fish and birds <note>original: "fowl"</note> are made on the same day.*** And here Moses plainly acts the part of the **philosopher** by joining them together; for there is more affinity between them than is easily noticed by the thoughtless common people. For besides the fact that birds frequent the waters very much (many kinds of them, I mean), these elements themselves—**air** and **water**—are very similar to one another due to their thinness and liquidity. Besides, the fins of **fish** and the wings of **birds**, the feathers of one and the scales of the other, are very similar <note>original: "analogical"</note>. They are both also lacking **ureters** properly so called, as well as **teats** <note>original: "dugges"</note> and **milk**, and they lay eggs <note>original: "oviparous"</note>. Furthermore, their motions are mostly alike: the fish as it were **flying** in the water, and the birds **swimming** in the air, according to the words of the poet concerning Daedalus, when he had made himself wings:

> *By an unaccustomed path he swam out to the frozen North.*

<margin>Juan Eusebio Nieremberg, *Natural History*, Book 11, Chapter 35</margin>
Consider also that just as some **birds dive** and swim under water, so some **fish fly** above the water in the air for a considerable time, until their fins begin to become stiff and dry.

But it is a strange coincidence, if it was not intended, that living creatures should be said to be made on the **fifth** and **sixth** days, since those numbers, according to the **Pythagorean mystery**, are so fitly significant of their nature. For **five** is acknowledged by them to be **male** and **female**, consisting of **three** and **two** (the first two masculine and feminine numbers). It is also an emblem of **generation** <note>reproduction</note>, for the number **five** multiplied by **five** brings back **five** again, as you see in **five times five**, which is **twenty-five**. <margin>Nicomachus of Gerasa, *Theology of Arithmetic*, Book 2. Plutarch, *On the E at Delphi*.</margin>

Concerning the number **Six**, I shall speak in its proper place.

*Vers. 26. That it is so free, so rational.* That the Image of God consists in this, rather than in dominion over the creatures, I take to be the correct and more **philosophical** sense; the other interpretation is more **political**. **Philo** <note>Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BCE – 50 CE), a Jewish philosopher who sought to harmonize the Torah with Greek philosophy.</note> interprets it in the manner we have chosen, which is also more suitable to **Platonism** and **Pythagoreanism**—the best **Cabbala** <note>In this context, "Cabbala" refers to a traditional or mystical interpretation of Scripture.</note> that I know of regarding **Moses'** text.

*Vers. 27. Male and Female.* It is a wonder, says **Grotius** <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a Dutch legal scholar and theologian.</note>, to see how the explanations of the **Rabbis** on this passage and those passages in **Plato's** *Symposium* agree with one another. Nevertheless, he says that regardless of where they originated, he has no doubt they are false and vain; and I must confess I am fully of the same opinion. But this strange agreement between **Aristophanes'** narration in the aforementioned *Symposium* and the comments of the **Rabbis** on this text is no small argument that **Plato** had some knowledge of **Moses**, which may well add greater authority and credit to this **Cabbala** of ours. But it was the wisdom of **Plato** to keep the true **Cabbala** for himself, while casting the questionable fantasies that might arise from the text onto a ridiculous and shallow character like **Aristophanes**; it was good enough for him to utter such things in that **"Club of Wits,"** the **Philosophic Symposium** of **Plato**.

*Vers. 28. They lorded it.* The **Septuagint** <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> uses the word *katakyrieusate* <note>original: κατακυριεύσατε</note>, which means to domineer with a high hand (as in **Matthew 20**).

<margin>Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* (Miscellanies), Book 6.</margin>
*Vers. 31. And the Senary denotes.* The **Senary**, or the number **six**, has a double reference: the one to this particular day's work, the other to the whole Creation. Regarding the particular day's work, it is the Creation of various sorts of **land animals**, divided into **male** and **female**. And the number **Six** is made up of **male** and **female**, for **two** multiplied by **three** is **six**. This idea belongs to **Philo**; and hence the **Pythagoreans** called this number *Gamos* <note>original: Γάμος</note>, or **Matrimony**, as **Clement** also observes. Clement adds, moreover, that they did this in reference to the **Creation of the World** as described by **Moses**. This number also, in the same way as the number **Five**, is a fitting emblem of procreation, for **six** multiplied by **six** makes **thirty-six**. This idea is found in **Plutarch's** *On the E at Delphi*, though he speaks of it regarding an inferior kind of generation; but I believe it is most appropriate to **animals**. There is something here also that respects **Man** particularly, who is the finest result of this sixth day's labor. The number of the brutish nature was **five**, according to **Philo**; but here a **Unit** <note>original: Unite</note> is added to **Man**—**Reason**, which reaches out to the knowledge of a God. And this **Unit** added to the former **five** makes **six**.

<margin>Nicomachus of Gerasa, *Theology of Arithmetic*, Book 2.</margin>
But now, regarding the reference that **Six** bears to the whole Creation: it appears the **Pythagoreans** believed it was significant of this based on the titles they gave it. For they call it *Diarthrosis tou pantos*, *Akmōn*, and *Kosmos*—that is, **the articulate and complete formation of the universe**, **the Anvil**, and **the World**. I suppose they call it the **Anvil** from that indefatigable...

# CHAP. I. The Defence of the Philosophic Cabbala.

<margin>Euclid, *Elements of Geometry*, Book 7, Definition 22.</margin>
...capable of shaping out new forms and figures upon the matter of the universe, by virtue of the *Active Principle* that ever busies itself everywhere. But how the *Senary* <note>The number six.</note> should symbolize the *world*, you shall understand thus: The *world* is *self-complete*, filled and perfected by its own *parts*; so is the *Senarius* <note>The Latin term for the number six.</note>, which has no denominated parts except a *sixth*, a *third*, and a *second* (that is, 1, 2, and 3), which when put together make *six*. *Euclid* defines a perfect *number* by this property: "A perfect number is that which is equal to its parts" <note>original: Τέλιος ἀριθμός ἐστιν ὁ τοῖς ἑαυτῦ μέρεσιν ἴσος ὤν</note>. Therefore, this number represents the perfection of the *world*; and you know that at the conclusion of everything, God saw that all he had made was *very good*.

<margin>Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, Book 6.</margin>
<margin>Nicomachus of Gerasa, *Theology of Arithmetic*, Book 2.</margin>
Furthermore, the *world* is *Male and Female* <note>original: Ἄῤῥην καὶ Θῆλυς; Latin: Mas and Fœmina</note>; that is, it consists of an *Active* and a *Passive Principle*, the one brought down into the other from the *world of life*. The *Senary* is created by multiplying the first *masculine number* by the first *feminine number*, for *three* times *two* is *six*.

Thus you see consistently that the property of the *number* reflects the nature of the *work of every day*, according to those mysteries that the *Pythagoreans* observed in them. Besides this, the *numbers* have ordinarily received names corresponding to each day's work. As I have often suggested, this provides a very high probability that the *Pythagoreans* possessed a Cabbala <note>A traditional mystical or philosophical interpretation.</note> referring to the text of *Moses* and the history of the Creation. Even *Philo* <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish philosopher who harmonized Greek philosophy with Hebrew scripture.</note>, though not in such a detailed way, attempted to reveal the mind of *Moses* using this key. I hope I have made it so plain that it will not hereafter be doubted that this is the genuine way of interpreting the philosophic meaning of the *Mosaic text* in this first chapter of *Genesis*.

# The Defense of the Philosophic Cabbala. CHAPTER 2.

In this second chapter, Moses, having spoken of the Sabbath, returns to a more detailed declaration of the creation of Adam, which is related to the work of the **Sixth** day. Then he moves into that mysterious story of **Paradise**, which continues into the next chapter.

<margin>* In his *Mosaic Cosmopoeia* <note>original: *Cosmopæia Mosaic.*</note>.</margin>
Verse 3. *And the number declares the nature.* The *Hebdomad* or *Septenary* <term>The number seven.</term> is a fitting symbol of God, as He is considered having finished these six days of creation. For then, as this *Cabbala* <term>A traditional Jewish mystical or philosophical interpretation of the Bible.</term> suggests, He creates nothing further. And therefore, His condition is then very fittingly represented by the number *Seven*. All numbers within the Decad <term>The number ten.</term> are categorized into three ranks, as *Philo* <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish philosopher who sought to harmonize the Torah with Greek philosophy.</note> observes: "Some beget, but are not begotten; others are begotten, but do not beget; the last both beget and are begotten" <note>original: Οἱ μὲ̄ γεννῶσιν, οὐ γεννώμενοι· οἱ δὲ γεννῶντ’ μὲ̄, οὐ γεννῶσι δέ· οἱ δὲ ἀμφότερα, καὶ γεννῶσι καὶ γεννῶντ’.</note>. The number *Seven* is the only exception; it is neither begotten, nor begets any number, which is a perfect emblem of God celebrating this *Sabbath*. For He now creates nothing new, just as He Himself is uncreatable. So, the idea that God is constantly *creating and infusing souls* into bodies as the occasion arises is quite contrary to this *Mosaic Cabbala*. But the Cabbala is very consistent with itself, declaring that all souls were created at once on the first day, and it will also declare the manner of their falling into the body in these following chapters.

Verse 4. *Productions of the Heavens.* The original has it *Generations of the Heavens* <note>original: תולדות השמים (Toldot HaShamayim)</note>. Here, the *suns* and *planets* are plainly said to be generated by the *heavens* or *ethereal matter*, which is again wonderfully consistent with *Cartesian philosophy* <note>The scientific and philosophical system of René Descartes, which described the universe in terms of matter and motion.</note>; you may see there at length how planets and stars are generated in this way. It must be acknowledged that there was a fathomless depth of wisdom in Moses, whose skill in philosophy thus plainly anticipates the subtlest and most expansive reaches of all the wits of the world who ever wrote after him.

*Take upon me to define.* It has already been witnessed from approved authors that no fixed time is understood by the *six days* of creation; and the present *Cabbala* plainly confirms it, showing that the mystery of numbers is intended, not the chronological order or succession of days.

Verse 6. *Like dewy showers of rain. Vatablus* <note>François Vatable, a renowned 16th-century French Hebrew scholar.</note> plainly interprets this passage as referring to *rain*. But I believe it is better interpreted as something analogous to the common rain that now descends upon the earth, though much less oily and not so full of vital vigor and the principles of life.

Verse 7. *And Man himself rose out of the Earth.* That God should shape *earth* with His own hands, like a sculptor <note>original: Statuary</note>, into the figure of a *man*, and then blow breath into its nostrils to make it alive, is not likely to be the *Philosophic Cabbala*; that version is more obviously adapted to a common or popular understanding <note>original: vulgar conceit</note>. However, the mention of *rain* immediately before the making of *man* may very well suggest that such preparations of the ground played some causal role in his production. And if it is at all credible that other living creatures rose out of the *earth* in this manner, it is just as likely that *man* did so as well; for the same words are used regarding both of them. For the text of Moses in verse 19 says, *That out of the ground*

That *Euripides* was influenced by the same doctrines found in the schools of *Pythagoras* and *Plato* is suggested by both his friendship with *Socrates* and the *moral and philosophic maxims* <note>original: Γνῶμαι</note> in his tragedies. # The Defense of the Philosophic Cabbala. CHAPTER II.

...very fruitful, and there are ever new occasions that add experience of things,
->I grow old always learning many things. <note>original: Γηράσκω δ᾽ αἰεὶ πολλὰ διδασκόμενΘ.</note><-
According to our English proverb, *The older the wiser*.

*In the Land of Havilah.* From the Hebrew words *Havah* and *El* or *Eloah*: *God has shown it* <note>original Latin: *Deus indicavit*</note>.

*Verse 12. Pure Gold, etc.* An easy emblem of *tried experience*, the mother of true *wisdom* and *prudence*. And the virtue of *Bdellium* <term>A fragrant, bitter resin similar to myrrh, used in ancient medicine.</term> is not improper for diseases that arise from phlegmatic laziness; and the very name and nature of the *Onyx* stone also points out its significance. Though there is no necessity—as I have told you already, citing *Maimonides* <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent Sephardic Jewish philosopher and scholar.</note>—to give an account in this manner of every particular passage in an allegory or parable. Therefore, if any man thinks me too curious, they may omit these expositions and let them count for nothing.

*Verse 13. The river is Gihon.* According to the history or the literal letter of the text, we have identified *Pison* as the *Phasis* and *Gihon* as a branch of the *Euphrates*. But the ancient Fathers—*Epiphanius*, *Augustine*, *Ambrose*, *Jerome* <note>original: *Hieronymus*</note>, *Theodoret*, *Damascene*, and several others—identify *Pison* as the *Ganges* and *Gihon* as the *Nile*. And they have no contemptible arguments for it. 

First, in *Jeremiah 2:18*, *Sihor* is a river of Egypt, which is unquestionably the *Nile*. Its *etymology* <term>The study of the origin and history of words.</term> seems to reveal the truth of it, coming from the Hebrew word *shachar*, meaning "to be blackened," <note>original Hebrew: שחר</note> because of the muddy blackness of the river. The Nile is notorious for this quality and therefore has its name in Greek, as if it were "new mud" <note>original Greek: νέα ἰλὺς (*nea ilus*)</note>. According to this, *Dionysius* <note>Dionysius Periegetes, an ancient geographer and poet.</note> wrote:
->For no river can compare with the Nile,<-
->For casting up mud and increasing the soil’s wealth.<-
<note>original Greek: Οὐ γάρ τις ποταμῶν ἐναλίγκιΘ ἔπλετο Νείλῳ, / Οὔ τ᾽ ἰλὺν βολέειν, ἔτε χθονὸς ὄλβον ἀέξειν.</note>
That is,
> *For there is no river that can compare with the Nile,*
> *For casting mud and fattening the soil.*

But now, to recite the very words of the Prophet: *What have you to do with the way of Egypt, to drink the waters of Sihor?* The Latin version has it, *to drink the muddy water* <note>original Latin: *ut bibas aquam turbidam*</note>; this is the Nile. But the *Seventy* <note>The Septuagint, the earliest Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> translate it *to drink the water of Gihon* <note>original Greek: πιεῖν ὕδωρ Γηῶν</note>, which is the name of this very river of Paradise. And the *Abyssinians* <note>People of Ethiopia.</note> even to this day call the Nile by the name of *Guion*. 

Add to this that the Gihon runs through *Ethiopia*, as does the Nile; and it is called *Siris* as it runs through Ethiopia, which is likely derived from *Sihor*. Then the Greek ending makes it *Sioris*, and later by contraction *Siris*.
->He is called Siris by the Ethiopians; but the inhabitants<-
->of Syene, when he turns, call him by the name of the Nile.<-
<note>original Greek: Σῖρις ὑπ᾿ Αἰθιόπων κικλήσκεται, οἱ δ᾿ Συήνης / Ἐνναέται στρεφθέντι μετ᾿ οὔνομα Νεῖλον ἔθεντο.</note>
That is,
> *The Ethiopian calls him Siris,*
> *Syene calls him Nilus as he crawls past her.*

As the same author writes in his geographical poems. And that *Pison* is the *Ganges* also has its probabilities—the Ganges being in *India*, a country famous for gold and precious stones. Besides, the notation of the name agrees with the nature of the river, *Pison* being from the Hebrew word *push*, meaning "to multiply" <note>original Hebrew: פוש</note>. And there is no less a number than ten—and those great rivers—that flow into <note>original: exonerate</note>

### Chapter II: The Defense of the Philosophic Cabbala.

...flow into the *Ganges*; just as there must be a gathering of *varied experience* to fill up and complete the virtue of *Wisdom* or *Prudence*. Thus, we shall see that the four rivers of Paradise have been given names that are most advantageous and favorable to the mysterious <note>meaning: allegorical or hidden</note> sense of the story.

Therefore, regardless here of all geographical concerns, we will say that *Gihon* is the *Nile* <note>original: Nilus</note> or *Siris*, the river of the *Ethiopians*—that is, the river of the *Just*. Here, the virtue is clearly distinguished from the subject in which it resides. For by the reputation of the *justice* and innocence of the *Ethiopians*, we are assured which of the cardinal virtues is meant by *Gihon*. Indeed, the ancient reputation of their honesty and uprightness was such that *Homer* made it their descriptive title, calling them "the blameless Ethiopians" <note>original Greek: ἀμύμονας Αἰθιοπας</note>. He further added that *Jupiter* used to banquet with them, being so taken with the integrity of their behavior. *Dionysius* also calls them "the divine or God-like Ethiopians" <note>original Greek: Θεουδέας Αἰθιοπας</note>; and they were so named "because of their justice" <note>original Greek: διὰ δικαιοσύνην</note>, as *Eustathius* <note>A 12th-century Byzantine scholar and archbishop.</note> comments on that passage. *Herodotus* also, speaking of them, says they are very handsome men, highly civilized, and live very long lives, which is the reward for righteousness. Thus, by the place where the *Gihon* runs, it is plainly shown to us which cardinal virtue is to be understood by it.

**The Etymology of its Name.** The name *Gihon*, as you have seen, clearly encourages us to recognize it as a river of *Ethiopia*. Its derivation also suitably agrees with the nature of *Justice*, for it comes from the Hebrew word *Giah* <note>original: גיה</note>, meaning "to break out" <note>original Latin: erumpere</note>. As the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> notes, Justice is "another person's good" <note>original: ἀλλότριον ἀγαθὸν, *Bonum alienum*</note>; it is not confined within a person's self but rather breaks out toward others, bestowing upon everyone what is their due.

*Verse 14. Is Hiddekel.* The word is compounded, says *Vatablus* <note>François Vatable, a 16th-century French humanist scholar.</note>, from two words that signify "swift" and "rapid" <note>original Latin: *velox* and *rapidum*</note>. This virtue, like a swift and rapid stream, bears down everything before it, as explained in the *Cabbala*.

<margin>* In his *Allegorical Interpretation*, Book 1.</margin>
*And stoutly resists.* * Philo uses the word "to wrestle against" or "resist" <note>original Greek: ἀντιπαλεῖν</note> here, which he takes the opportunity to use based on the *Septuagint's* <note>The Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> phrase "opposite the Assyrians" <note>original Greek: κατέναντι Ἀσσυρίων</note>, which he interprets as "against the *Assyrians*." The Hebrew text says "Eastward of Assyria," which means *Assyria* is located *Westward* of it. Now, the *West* is that quarter of the world where the sun says goodbye to us and leaves us to darkness; this is why the word for the *West wind* in *Eustathius* is derived from the words for "darkness" <note>original Greek: ζόφος</note> and "upon," meaning the wind that blows from the dark *quarter*. *Assyria*, therefore, represents that false state of seeming happiness and the power of wickedness, which is called the *Kingdom of Darkness*. The most noble objective of *Fortitude* is to destroy or resist the power of this kingdom within ourselves. This is the strength and power to resist the suggestions of the *body*, which may be represented by the *West* <note>original: Occident</note>, just as the *Intellect* is represented by the *East* <note>original: Orient</note>; the *Evening* in the previous chapter also denoted the corporeal or material principle throughout.

*Perath. From the Hebrew word Parah:* "It has borne fruit" <note>original: פרה; Latin: *Fructificavit*</note>.

*Verse 17. In process of time, etc.* This is according to the view of the *Pythagoreans* and *Origen*. And that *Pythagoras* had the favor of...

### # *The Defense of the Philosophic Cabbala.* Chapter II.

...having the *Mosaic Cabbala* <note>original: Mosaicall Cabbala; a term for a hidden, mystical interpretation of the laws of Moses</note> communicated to him by some knowledgeable Priest of the Jews, or some other holy man, I think I have consistently made it exceedingly probable in the previous chapter.

<margin>"The body is a bond and a tomb to the soul, and the world is a cave for it." <note>original Greek: Τῇ δὲ ψυχῇ δεσμὸς τὸ σῶμα καὶ τάφος, καὶ ὁ κόσμος αὐτῇ σπήλαιον.</note> Plotinus, *Enneads* 4, book 8, chapter 3.</margin>

*The region of mortality and death.* Nothing is more common with the Platonists than calling the body a *sepulcher* <note>original: Sepulchre; a tomb or burial vault</note>, and *this life* we live here upon Earth either *sleep* or *death*. These expressions are so suitable to this *Cabbala*, and the *Cabbala* is so consistent with the text of *Moses* (which mentions the death and *sleep of Adam*), that there is a strong presumption these phrases and notions first originated there. <margin>Philo, *Allegorical Interpretation*, book 1.</margin> And *Philo* <note>A Jewish philosopher from Alexandria who harmonized Greek philosophy with Jewish scripture.</note> acknowledges that *Heraclitus*—that mysterious and obscure philosopher whom *Porphyry* also cited for the same purpose in his *On the Cave of the Nymphs*—actually hit upon the very meaning that *Moses* intended regarding this *death of Adam* in his famous saying: *"We live their death (namely, the death of souls out of the body), but we are dead to their life."* <note>original Greek: Ζῶμεν τὸν ἐκείνων θάνατον, τεθνήκαμεν δὲ τὸν ἐκείνων βίον.</note> And *Euripides*, that friend of *Socrates* and fellow traveler of *Plato*, speaks much to the same purpose in his tragedies: <margin>Clement of Alexandria, *Miscellanies*, book 3.</margin>

> Who knows whether to live is actually to die,
> And to die is to live? <note>original Greek: Τίς οἶδεν, εἰ τὸ ζῆν μέν ἐστι κατθανεῖν, / Τὸ κατθανεῖν δὲ ζῆν?</note>

Therefore, the philosophic sense concerning *Adam's death* must be this: that he shall be dead to the *ethereal* <note>original: Æthereal; referring to the heavenly or spiritual realm</note> life he lived before while he is confined to the *terrestrial* <note>earthly</note> life. Furthermore, whereas he might have lived forever in the *ethereal life*, he shall certainly die to the *terrestrial* in a shorter time. Thus, the sons of men cannot escape either the certainty or the speed of death.

*Verse 18. Both good for himself, etc.* For the words of the text do not confine this benefit to *Adam's* convenience alone, but speak broadly without any restraint in this present verse. Therefore, because there was a double benefit, it was more explicit to mention both in the *Cabbala*.

*Verse 19. Fallen and unfallen Angels.* The *fallen angels* are compared here to the *beasts of the field*, and the *unfallen* to the *birds of the air* <note>original: Fowls of the Air</note>. How appropriately the *fallen spirits* are counted among the *beasts of the field*, you shall understand more fully in the following chapter. In the meantime, you may notice that the *Platonists*—indeed, *Plato* himself in his *Phaedrus*—describe the soul of man as a *winged creature* before it falls into this terrestrial region. Phrases such as "the shedding of wings" <note>original Greek: πτεροῤῥυεῖν</note>, "the growing of wings" <note>original Greek: πτεροφυεῖν</note>, "the loss of wings" <note>original Greek: ἡ πτερῶν ἀποβολὴ</note>, and "the soul's plumage" <note>original Greek: ὃ τῆς ψυχῆς πτέρωμα</note> are common expressions in that school. And *Plato* very plainly defines what he means by these *wings of the soul* (and the same logic applies to all other spirits whatsoever) in this manner: *"The nature of the wing is such that it can carry what is heavy upward, lifting it aloft to where the race of gods dwells."* <note>original Greek: Πέφυκεν ἡ πτεροῦ δύναμις τὸ ἐμβριθὲς ἄγειν ἄνω, μετεωρίζουσα ᾗ τὸ τῶν θεῶν γένος οἰκεῖ.</note> This means the wing's power is able to carry upward that which would otherwise sink downward, bearing it high to where we may have more sensible communion with God and His holy angels. For the word "gods" <note>original Greek: Θεοὶ</note> in the plural is most suitably translated as *angels* in such passages, being most consistent with the subject matter and the truth of Christianity. It may seem less strange that "gods" should signify *angels* in the writings of the Greek philosophers...

# CHAP. II. The Defence of the Philosophick Cabbala.

...philosophers, especially those who have been acquainted with *Moses*, since for him *Elohim* <note>original Hebrew: אלהים</note> signifies the same thing—namely, *Angels* as well as *God*. Therefore, to conclude: losing the principle that keeps us in this divine state is the *losing of our wings*. This is what the fallen *angels* have done, and therefore they may very well be compared to *terrestrial* <note>original: Terrestrial; earthly</note> *beasts*.

*Verse* 20. *A faculty of being united, etc.* This vital aptitude in the soul for being united with physical matter is so essential and proper to her, that invigorating the exercise of that faculty must be very pleasing and acceptable to her, and a significant part of her happiness. Otherwise, what is the meaning of the *Resurrection of the dead* or of *bodies* in the next world? Yet this is a core article of the Christian faith.

*Verse* 22. *This new sense of his Vehicle.* According to the *Platonists*, there are three principles in man: *Intellect*, *Soul*, and the *Image of the Soul* <note>original Greek: Νῦς, Ψυχὴ, εἴδωλον Ψυχῆς</note>. The first is *Intellect*, *Spirit*, or *Divine Light*. The second is the *soul herself*, which is *Adam*, the *Man*—as the saying goes, "The soul of each person is the person" <note>original Latin: Animus cujusque is est quisque</note>. The third is the *Image of the Soul*, which is her vital energy acting upon the body to give it life. If that life is in good tune and vigor, it provides a very pleasing sensation to the soul, whether in this physical body or in a more refined "vehicle" <note>In Neoplatonism, a "vehicle" is a subtle or spiritual body that carries the soul.</note>. *Marsilio Ficinus* <note>An Italian priest and influential philosopher of the Renaissance who revived Platonism.</note> identifies this as our *Eve*. This is the *feminine faculty* in the human soul, which is most easily awakened into action when the soul falls asleep to intellectual things.

<margin>* *Nicomachean Ethics*, book 10, chapter 7.</margin>
*Verse* 24. *Overly tedious aspirations.* "To think human thoughts as a human being" <note>original Greek: Τὰ ἀνθρώπινα φρονεῖν ἄνθρωπον ὄντα</note> is a common warning criticized by *Aristotle* in his *Ethics*. Nevertheless, it is a great point of wisdom and absolutely necessary to know the true laws and boundaries of human happiness. We must ensure that the heat of melancholy <note>In the 17th century, "melancholy" was often associated with religious fanaticism or over-ambition.</note> does not drive men beyond what is compatible with human nature and the reach of all its faculties. At the same time, we must beware that the overly savory taste for the pleasures of the flesh—the *animal life*—does not keep them down many thousands of degrees below what they are capable of. But the person who truly fears God will be delivered from both extremes. What I have spoken is directed more properly to the soul in the *flesh*, but it can be understood by analogy for a soul in any *vehicle*, for they are capable of sinning in all of them.

*Verse* 25. *Stood naked before God.* *Adam* was as truly clothed in *corporeality* <note>The state of having a physical body</note> then as he ever was afterward, for the *ether* <note>A subtle, celestial substance believed to fill the upper regions of space.</note> is as much a body as the *earth*. But the meaning is that *Adam* had a sense of the divine Presence; he felt intensely certain in his own mind that his whole being lay naked and bare before God. He knew that nothing could be hidden from God’s sight, which pierced into his very thoughts and the inner frame of his spirit. Yet, even though *Adam* stood naked before Him in this way, he did not find any need for a covering to hide himself from that present-making sense of Him. Indeed, he did not feel "naked" in the negative sense of the word. That sense of nakedness—the desire for a further covering and shelter from the divine presence—arose only from his later disobedience and rebellion against God's commands, which he had not yet committed.

<margin>*Attic Nights*, book 19, chapter 6.</margin>
*Not at all ashamed.* Shame is "the fear of just blame" <note>original Greek: φόβος δικαίου ψόγου</note>, as *Aulus Gellius* <note>A 2nd-century Roman author and grammarian.</note> defines it, following the philosophers. But since *Adam* had not yet acted randomly or followed the impulses of his own will, he...

## CHAP. III.

*1. The Serpent "Ophioneus" <note>original Greek: 'Oφιωνεύς; a serpent-like titan</note> in Pherecydes Syrus. Iyyim, Tziyyim, Se'irim, Ochim, and Lilith <note>original Hebrew: איים, ציים, שעירים, אחים and לילית</note>, names of Spirits haunting fields and desolate places. The correct meaning of Se'irim. 13. That Satan, upon tempting Adam, was cast down lower towards the Earth with all his accomplices. 15. Plato's prophecy of Christ. How inappropriate it is for Divine Goodness to sarcastically insult frail Man after he has fallen into tragic misery. 24. That it is a great mercy of God that we are not immortal upon Earth. **Verse 1.** *This old Serpent therefore.* In the writings of Pherecydes Syrus (who was the master of Pythagoras), there is mention of one *Ophioneus*, the "Prince of Evil" <note>original Latin: Princeps mali</note>, as Grotius cites him on this passage. This is a further argument that Pythagoras was acquainted with this *Mosaical Philosophy*; and that according to the *Philosophick Cabbala*, it was an evil Spirit—not a *natural serpent*—that tricked *Adam* and brought such mischief upon mankind.

<margin>Isaiah 13:21.</margin>
*The Beasts of the Field.* Regarding the idea that these evil spirits should be counted as "beasts of the field," besides the reasons given in the Cabbala itself, we may add further that these unclean spirits are known to haunt solitudes, wasteland fields, and desolate places. This is evident in the Prophet *Isaiah’s* description of the desolation of *Babylon*, where he says it shall be a place for the *Iyyim* and *Tziyyim* <note>original Hebrew: איים and ציים; desert creatures or island-dwellers</note>—which Castellio translates as "Fauns and Wood-spirits" <note>original Latin: Fauni and Sylvani</note>, and the *Seventy* <note>The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> translate as "Centaurs and Demons" <note>original Greek: ὀνοκένταυροι and Δαιμόνια</note>. These *Onocentauri* (Centaurs) are described by *Hesychius* as "a kind of spirit that frequents the woods and has a dark appearance" <note>original Greek: δαιμόνων τι γένος κάθυλον καὶ σκοτεινὸν τῇ ἐπιφανείᾳ</note>. 

The Prophet also mentions (in the same description) the *Se'irim*, the *Ochim*, and *Lilith* <note>original Hebrew: שעירים, אחים, and לילית; wild goats/satyrs, howling creatures, and night-monsters</note>, all of which commentators interpret as Spirits. For the *Se'irim* are interpreted by the *Seventy* as "Demons" <note>original Greek: Δαιμόνια</note> and by *Castellio* as "Satyrs" <note>original Latin: Satyri</note>. *Castellio* renders *Ochim* as "Fauns," while the *Seventy* call them "Echoes" or "Cries" <note>original Greek: ἠχάς; Latin: Clamores, Strepitus</note>; *Grotius* suspects they originally wrote "Noises" <note>original Greek: ἠχία</note>. From both, you may guess that they were a kind of spirit that causes noise and a stir in those desolate places, according to the words of *Lucretius*:

<margin>Lucretius, On the Nature of Things, Book 4.</margin>
> The neighbors imagine that goat-footed Satyrs and Nymphs 
> inhabit these places, and say that Fauns are there;
<note>original Latin: Hæc loca capripedes Satyros Nymphásque tenere / Finitimi fingunt, & Faunos esse loquuntur;</note>

But the Poet <note>Lucretius</note> seems to dismiss this with the idea that it is only the shepherds being merry with their girls. However, no man can comment <note>original: "glosse"</note> upon this Text in that manner: For the Prophet says, *No shepherd shall pitch his fold there, nor shall any man pass through it for ever.* The last strange creature in these dreadful solitudes is *Lilith* <note>original Hebrew: לילית</note>, which interpreters ordinarily translate as *Lamia*, a *Witch*; and for my own part, I give so much credit to various stories that I have read and heard, that I would rather interpret those noises in the night, which Lucretius speaks of, to be the secret meetings <note>original: "Conventicles"</note> of witches and devils, rather than the merriment of shepherds and their shepherdesses re-echoed from rocks and hills, while they themselves remain unseen in the midst of their music and mirth. And what I have alleged already, I conceive is authority enough to support the sense of the *Cabbala*, which supposes evil spirits to be reckoned among, or to be analogous to, the *beasts of the field*.

But something may be added yet further from Matthew 12:43. There our Savior Christ plainly allows this doctrine: that evil spirits have their haunts in the wide fields and deserts. Grotius observes this to be the opinion of the Jews, and that *Daemones* (demons) <note>original Hebrew: שדים, *Shedim*</note> have their name for that reason, from the word for *Field* <note>original Hebrew: שדה, *Sadeh*</note>. For if the name were derived from the word meaning "to destroy" <note>original Hebrew: שדד, *Shadad*</note>, the grammar would require the word to be *Shiddim* rather than *Shedhim*.

**Verse 2.** *And Adam answered him.* Although the Serpent here is looked upon as a person distinct from Adam, approaching him from the outside, yet it is not at all inconsistent to make *Eve* merely an *Internal Faculty* of him. For just as she is said to *proceed from him*, so she is said still to *be one with him*: which is wonderfully consistent with the faculties of the soul; for though they come *from the soul*, yet they are really *one with it*, as anyone who understands anything of philosophy will easily admit.

<margin>Aristotle's Metaphysics, Book 1.</margin>
**Verse 5.** *Know all things.* *All men by nature desire to know* <note>original Greek: Πάντες ἄνθρωποι τοῦ εἰδέναι ὀρέγονται φύσει</note>. This is an aphorism from Aristotle, and this desire is strongest in those whose spirits are most thin and subtle. And therefore this bait could not help but be very attractive to Adam in his "thinner vehicle" <note>In Platonic philosophy, the "vehicle" is the subtle, airy, or celestial body that the soul inhabits before descending into a physical, earthly body</note>. But whatever is natural to the soul, unless it is regulated and bounded by the divine Light, will prove to be its mischief and ruin, whether in this lower state or whatever state the soul is placed in.

...the pure frame of his *ethereal* or *heavenly vehicle* <note>vehicle: In Neoplatonic philosophy, the "vehicle" is the subtle body or carrier of the soul as it descends through the spheres of heaven toward Earth.</note>, and worked himself into a dislike of the sordid ruins and disordered remains of it; and in some measure awakening that lower *plant-like life* <note>original: "Plantal life"; the vegetative faculty of the soul that governs growth and physical form.</note>, which had not yet come near enough to *terrestrial matter*, and with which he was not yet clothed, he found himself naked of what he predicted would suit him very well and ease the trouble of his current condition. See *2 Corinthians 5:1, 2, 3, 4*.

**Verse 8. That they hid themselves.** They hate the light because their deeds are evil. This is true of all rebellious spirits, no matter what *vehicle* they inhabit.

**Verse 9. Pursued him.** *The more excellent faculty of the soul is the leader of man and his guiding spirit* <note>original Latin: "Præstantiorem Animæ facultatem esse ducem hominis atque Dæmonem."</note>. This is Ficino’s <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), an influential Italian Renaissance philosopher.</note> interpretation from Plato's *Timaeus*: namely, that the best faculty to which the soul is awakened is its guide and good spirit <note>original: "Genius"; a guardian spirit or internal divine spark.</note>. But if we are rebellious toward it, it becomes our "demon" in the worst sense, and we are afraid of it and cannot endure the sight of it.

**Verse 10. No power nor ornaments.** For he found that although he could spoil and disorder his *vehicle*, it was not in his power to bring it back into order so easily.

**Verse 12. It was the vigor and impetuosity.** There is some attempt at a real excuse by *Adam*; but it is manifest that he cannot clear himself from sin, because it was in his power to have regulated the motions of the life of his *vehicle* according to the rule of the divine light within him.

**Verse 13. What work has she made here?** *Adam*, touched in some way with the conviction of the divine light, bemoans that sad *catastrophe* <note>catastrophe: Here meaning a sudden downturn or disastrous turning point.</note> which the vigorous life of the vehicle had caused. But then he again excuses himself due to the deceptiveness of that faculty, especially since it was influenced by so cunning and powerful an assailant as the old *serpent, the Devil*.

**Imagination for ever.** That is, *forever* <note>original Hebrew: "le-olam" (לעולם); original Greek: "eis ton aiona" (εἰς τὸν αἰῶna)</note>.

**The Eternal God.** It is an acknowledged fact that God speaks both *within a person* (as he does in other *intellectual* creatures) by his divine light residing there, and that he also speaks *within himself* concerning things or persons. These "speeches" are nothing other than his *decrees*. It is not at all harsh, when reading *Moses* <note>Referring to the Book of Genesis.</note>, to understand the speakings of God according to what the circumstances of the matter naturally imply; nor is it necessary to represent God as a third person in a physical and visible shape, unless there was an urgent reason that forced it upon us. 

Philosophy will more easily admit God's *inward word*—by which he either creates or decrees anything that shall happen, as well as the divine light by which he instructs those souls that receive him—as the "speakings" of God, rather than any audible, articulate voice pronounced by him in human form, unless it were by *Christ himself*; for otherwise, in all likelihood, it is simply a message delivered by an *angel*.

**Verse 14. The Prince of the rebellious Angels.** For the mighty shall be mightily tormented <note>A reference to Wisdom of Solomon 6:6: "For mercy will soon pardon the meanest: but mighty men shall be mightily tormented."</note>; and the nature of the situation also implies it, because disgrace, adversity, and being trampled upon is far more painful and distressing to those who have held great positions than to those of a lower rank.

It also argues that God's "voice" in Genesis is best understood as an internal divine light or decree rather than a physical, audible sound.</summary>

*Christ* bruises the *head of Satan* by destroying his kingdom and sovereignty, and by being so highly exalted above all powers whatsoever. **Verse 20.** *Euripides*, the friend of *Socrates* and a supporter of *Pythagorean philosophy*, writes somewhere in his tragedies (as I have already mentioned) to this effect: *"Who knows,"* he says, *"whether living is actually dying, and whether dying is not actually living?"* This question aligns perfectly with this present *Cabbala* <note>Cabbala: Here referring to a mystical or traditional interpretation of scripture.</note>. For *Adam* is described here as if he were dying to that better world and state of life he was in. Just as someone here on Earth on their deathbed often prophesies and declares what they foresee about their own future state—that they shall be with God, that they shall be in Heaven among the holy angels and the departed saints, and the like—so *Adam* here utters his defensive prophecy. He suggests that this change of his and departure from his current state, though it may prove bad enough for himself, nevertheless has its use and convenience, and that it is better for the *Universe*. For he shall live upon Earth and be a ruler there among the *earthly* creatures, helping to order and govern that part of the world.

**The Life of his Vehicle, EVE.** For **EVE** signifies *Life*—that life which the soul grants to whatever physical form <note>original: vehicle</note> or body it inhabits and animates.

**Verse 21. Skin of Beasts.** *Origen* <note>Origen (c. 185–253 AD), an early Christian scholar and theologian.</note> understands this as *Adam* being embodied and clothed in human flesh and skin. *"For it is ridiculous to say,"* he writes, *"that God was Adam’s tanner and a tailor of skins."* <note>original: *Ridiculum enim est dicere, quòd Deus fuerit Adami coriarius & pellium sutor.*</note> No one will be surprised by the confidence of this pious and learned Father if they consider that the *pre-existence* of souls <note>pre-existence of souls: The belief that the soul existed in a spiritual realm before entering a physical body.</note> before they enter the body is generally held by all the learned Jewish scholars, and so it was likely part of this *Philosophical Cabbala*. ...gross consistency. See *Origen's Against Celsus, book 4* <note>original: *Origen. Cont. Cels. lib. 4.*</note>. This is consistent with what is found in *Cornelius*, which I believe he took from *Epiphanius*.

**Verse 22. But play and sport.** I consider this a much better *decorum* <term>the requirement of a story or character to behave in a fitting way</term> than to make God *sarcastically* jeer at *Adam* and triumph over him in the midst of such a great and universal disaster—as some interpreters suggest—leaving him without any source of comfort. This is especially true since there was a principle in *Adam* that was so easily deceived, which surely serves as a kind of excuse for him. To jeer at a man who, through his own weakness and the overwhelming cunning of his adversary, has fallen into such a dreadful and tragic state of misery is something so far from the nature of God that it would be utterly unbecoming of any good man.

**Verse 24. He made sure he should not be immortal.** For it is to our advantage, as *Rupertus* has observed regarding this passage (citing *Plotinus*): *It was the mercy of God that he made man mortal, so that he might not be forever tormented by the miseries and sorrows of this present life* <note>original: *Miſericordia Dei fuiſſe, quod hominem fecerit mortalem, nè perpetuis cruciaretur hujus vitæ ærumnis*</note>.

This refers to passing through the condition of being reclothed with his fiery *vehicle* <term>the "subtle body" or spiritual vessel that carries the soul</term>. The following words explain the meaning of the *Cabbala*; it is in accordance with the views of that "*Plato* among the poets" (as *Severus* called him), *Virgil*, in the sixth book of his *Aeneids*:

> *Until a long day, when the cycle of time is complete,*
> *Has removed the ingrained stain, and left the pure*
> *Ethereal sense, and the fire of simple air.*
> <note>original: *Donec longa dies perfecto temporis orbe / Concretam exemit labem, purúmque reliquit / Æthereum ſenſum, atque auraï ſimplicis ignem.*</note>
>
> ->Regarding this idea:<-
>
> *Until that long day finally arrives*
> *That has washed away all filth and foul desire,*
> *And leaves the Soul Ethereal throughout,*
> *Bathing her senses in pure, liquid Fire.*

We shall further support this very appropriately with the last two *Golden Verses* (as they are called) of the *Pythagoreans*, who associate *Immortality* with this *Ethereal* condition:

> *If, having left the body, you reach the free Ether,*
> *You shall be an immortal God, undying, no longer mortal.*
> <note>original: Ἤν δ᾿ ἀπολείψας σῶμα ἐς αἰθέρ᾿ ἐλεύθερον ἔλθῃς, / Ἔσσεαι ἀθάνατος Θεὸς ἄμβροτος, οὐκέti θνητός.</note>
>
> *Rid of this body, if the free Ether*
> *You reach, from now on you shall be Immortal.*

The Greek text says, *you shall be an Immortal God*, which *Hierocles* interprets to mean: *you shall imitate the Deity in this, by becoming Immortal*. And *Plutarch*, in his *The Obsolescence of Oracles* <note>original: *Defect of Oracles*</note>, pursues this *apotheosis* <term>the elevation of a human to divine status</term> according to the order of the elements: Earth refined to Water, Water to Air, Air to Fire. So man, from being a *terrestrial animal*, becomes one of the *Heroes*; from a *Hero* he becomes a *Daemon* or *good spirit* <note>original: *Genius*</note>; and from a *spirit* he becomes a *God*. This he calls <margin>R. Maimonides, *The Guide for the Perplexed*, part 1, chapter 49.</margin> *to partake of divinity* <note>original: *μετασχᾶν θεότητος*</note>, which is nothing more than to become one of the *Elohim* <note>original: אלהים</note>, or *Immortal Angels*, who are *like a flame* <note>original: *inſtar flammæ*</note>, as the Hebrew Doctors declare in *Bereshith Rabbah* <note>A midrashic commentary on the book of Genesis</note>. According to their *vehicles*, they are a *versatile fire*, turning themselves like *Proteus* <term>a Greek sea-god capable of changing shape at will</term> into any form. These are the very words of *Maimonides* regarding this passage.

In yet another place, he says that "Soul," "Genius," and "Angel" <note>original: *Psychē, Daimōn, Angelos*</note> are three words that signify one and the same thing. Similarly, the philosopher *Xenocrates* made "Soul" and "Genius" <note>original: *Daimōn*</note> identical, adding that a man was "happy" <note>original: *eudaimōn*</note> if he possessed a "virtuous soul" <note>original: *spoudaian psychēn*</note>.

Therefore, not to weary my reader or myself with too much scholarly study <note>original: philology</note>, we conclude that the meaning of *Moses* in this last verse is this: that *Adam* is condemned here to a mortal, fleeting, and temporary state until he reaches his **Ethereal** or pure fiery **vehicle** <term>in Neoplatonic philosophy, the 'vehicle' is the subtle, celestial body that carries the soul</term> and becomes, as our Savior Christ says, "equal to the angels" <note>original: *isangelos*</note>. This, I say, is the condition of mankind, according to the **Philosophical Cabbala of Moses**.

### AN
## APPENDIX to the DEFENCE
### OF
# The Philosophic Cabbala.

### CHAPTER 1.

<margin>1.</margin>
*1. The strength of the Philosophic Cabbala <term>A philosophical interpretation of the biblical creation story, suggesting it contains hidden ancient wisdom</term> argued from the nature of the Truths contained within it. 2. The dignity of Pythagoras. 3. That he was acquainted with the Mosaic Philosophy. 4. Pythagoras's miracles. 5. Of Plato, that he was acquainted with Jewish learning; and what was miraculous about him. 6. Of Plotinus: his turning of Olympius's magical practices back upon him; his great esteem for Origen. 7. The folly of men in adhering to some private judgment more than to the Church Fathers, Churches, performers of miracles, and to Reason itself. 8. The Cartesian philosophy <term>The natural philosophy of René Descartes</term> as a restoration of the physical part of the Mosaic philosophy, and regarding Descartes being inspired.*

<margin>1.</margin>
<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial letter 'L' featuring scrolling acanthus leaf motifs.</image-desc>
Let us now take a general view of this entire *Cabbala* and more briefly consider its strength. We may categorize this strength under three main headings: namely, the nature of the *truths* contained in it; the dignity of those *persons* who have owned them in previous *ages*; and lastly, *the invalidity of the most significant objections that can be made against it.*

As for the *truths themselves*: *First*, they are of the kind that would befit such a holy and worthy person as *Moses*, if he were to *philosophize*. They are very precious and choice truths, positioned far above the understanding <note>original: "conceit"</note> of common people <note>original: "the vulgar"</note>. Therefore, it is more likely they were delivered to him (or to *Adam* first) by God as a special *mystery*.

*Secondly*, they are such that the more they are examined, the more irrefutable they will be found. No *hypothesis* ever proposed to humanity agrees so perfectly with the *phenomena* of nature, the *attributes of God*, the *workings* <note>original: "passages"</note> *of Providence*, and the *rational faculties* of our own minds.

*Thirdly*, there is a consistent suitability and applicability to the text of *Moses* throughout, without any force or violence done to *grammar* or *literary criticism*.

<meta>catchword: Fourthly</meta>

<summary>This page introduces an appendix defending the "Philosophic Cabbala," outlining three main arguments for its validity: the profound nature of its truths, the high status of the philosophers who held them, and its rational consistency with nature and scripture.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the defense of the Philosophic Cabbala, transitioning from the inherent truth of the doctrines to the character and divine inspiration of the ancient philosophers—specifically Pythagoras—who held these views, and their connection to Jewish wisdom.</meta>

<header>The Defense of the Philosophic Cabbala. CHAPTER 3.</header>

Fourthly and lastly, there is a great usefulness, if not a necessity, for at least some of these doctrines. They serve as such substantial supports for religion and as great encouragements for the diligent purification of our minds and the study of true piety.

2. Now, regarding the *dignity* of the *persons*—such as *Pythagoras*, *Plato*, and *Plotinus*—this is evidenced by the enduring reputation for a high degree of virtue, righteousness, and devout love of the Deity that is everywhere acknowledged in them, in addition to whatever miracles happened to them or were performed by them.

<margin>See Iamblichus, *On the Life of Pythagoras*, Chapter 1.</margin>
And as for *Pythagoras*, if you consult his biography by *Iamblichus*, he was held in such great admiration by his contemporaries that some thought him to be the son of *Apollo*, whom the god allegedly fathered with *Parthenis*, his known mother. This opinion was shared by *Epimenides*, *Eudoxus*, and *Xenocrates*. *Iamblichus* soberly and earnestly rejects this notion, but he later acknowledges that Pythagoras’s looks and speeches so wonderfully captivated the minds of everyone who conversed with him that they could not help but affirm he was a son of God <note>original: "Θεοῦ παῖς"</note>. This is not to be taken in our strict theological sense, but according to the customs of the ancient *Greeks*, who looked upon men who were heroically and eminently good and virtuous as *divine souls* and of a celestial lineage. *Aristotle* particularly notes that the *Lacedemonians* <margin>Nicomachean Ethics, Book 7, Chapter 1.</margin> termed those who were very good <note>original: "σφόδρα ἀγαθοὶ"</note> as divine men <note>original: "θείους ἄνδρας"</note>. According to this sense, Aristotle interprets that verse in *Homer* concerning *Hector*:

->— He did not seem to be<-
->The son of a mortal man, but of a god.<-
<note>original: "— οὐδὲ ἐῴκει / Ἀνδρός γε θνητοῦ παῖς ἔμμεναι, ἀλλὰ θεοῖο."</note>

But to return to the man we were speaking of before. This eminence of Pythagoras, acknowledged among the heathens, will seem more credible if we consider the benefit of his conversations with the wisest men then on Earth—namely, the *Jewish priests and prophets*, who received their knowledge from God, just as *Pythagoras* received it from them. From this, I believe that what *Iamblichus* writes concerning the philosophy of *Pythagoras* is true: that it is "a philosophy delivered from the gods at the beginning" <note>original: "φιλοσοφία ἐκ θεῶν παραδοθεῖσα τὸ κατ’ ἀρχάς"</note>.

3. Furthermore, there is ample testimony in literature that *Pythagoras* was acquainted with the *Mosaic* or *Jewish* philosophy. This is mentioned by *Aristobulus* (an *Egyptian Jew*) in the writings of *Clement of Alexandria*, and by *Josephus* in his work against *Apion*. *St. Ambrose* adds that Pythagoras was a *Jew* himself. *Clement* calls him "the Hebrew philosopher" <note>original: "Ἑβραίων φιλόσοφον"</note>. To this I might add the supporting views of *Justin Martyr*, *John Philoponus*, *Theodoret*, *Hermippus* (quoted in *Origen’s* work against *Celsus*), *Porphyry*, and *Clement* again, who writes that there was a common rumor that *Pythagoras* was a disciple of the prophet *Ezekiel*. And although Clement does not believe the report, that learned antiquarian *Mr. Selden* <note>John Selden (1584–1654), a famous English jurist and scholar of ancient law.</note> seems inclined enough to think it true in his first book, *On Natural Law according to the Hebrews* <note>original: "De Jure Naturali juxta Hebraeos"</note>, where you may read the citations of the aforementioned authors more fully. Besides all these, <margin>On the Life of Pythagoras, Chapter 3.</margin> *Iamblichus* also affirms that Pythagoras lived at *Sidon*, his native country, where he fell...

4. But there is yet another argument to further prove the likelihood of his conversing with the prophets, which will also further highlight the dignity of his person: the miracles recorded of him. For it would seem Pythagoras was not only initiated into the Mosaic Theory, but had also attained the power of working miracles, just as Moses and the succeeding prophets did. Very strange facts are recorded by both Porphyry and Iamblichus. For instance, when Pythagoras was crossing a river with several of his companions (Iamblichus calls the river the Nessus, while Porphyry calls it the Caucasus), he spoke to the river, and the river answered him back with an audible and clear voice, "Greetings, Pythagoras" <note>original: "Χαῖρε, Πυθαγόρα"</note>. Another account says he showed his thigh to Abaris the Priest, and Abaris affirmed that it glistened like gold, and from this declared that Pythagoras was the god Apollo. It was also known that he conversed with his friends at Metapontum and Tauromenium (one a town in Italy, the other in Sicily, many days' journey apart) on the very same day. To these and many others which I willingly omit, I shall only add his predictions of earthquakes; or rather (because that may seem more natural) his immediate quenching of plagues in cities, his silencing of violent winds and tempests, and his calming the rage of seas and rivers. Because his followers Empedocles, Epimenides, and Abaris acquired this skill from him, they became so famous that Empedocles was surnamed the "Wind-Averter" <note>original: "Alexanemus"</note>; Epimenides, the "Purifier" <note>original: "Cathartes"</note>; and Abaris, the "Air-Walker" <note>original: "Æthrobates"</note>, due to the power they had in suppressing storms, freeing cities from the plague, and walking high in the air. This last skill enabled Pythagoras to visit his friends in that manner at Metapontum and Tauromenium on the same day.

Their philosophy was the same as Pythagoras's and is likewise applicable to the text of Moses. Plato’s exemplary life and virtue, together with his profound knowledge of the more sacred mysteries of God and the state of the human soul in this world and the next, deservedly earned him the title of "The Divine Plato" <note>original: "ὁ θεῖος Πλάτων"</note>.

If they were capable of understanding these reasons, they could not take any offense at my admittance of the *Cartesian* philosophy <note>The philosophy of René Descartes (1596–1650)</note> into this present *Cabbala*. משה *Moshe*, which is commonly <note>original: "ordinarily"</note> *Moses*; this aligns again with Mr. *Selden’s* <note>John Selden (1584–1654), a renowned English jurist and scholar of ancient history.</note> opinion and further confirms his conjecture. Regarding the kind of natural philosophy this *Moschus* taught his followers, <margin>* In his *On the Greek Historians*, book 3; Strabo, book 16.</margin> *Vossius* <note>Gerardus Vossius (1577–1649), a Dutch classical scholar.</note> has expressly noted this from *Strabo*, who mentions one *Moschus* of *Sidon* who lived in the ages before the *Trojan War*. He was the first author of the *Atomic Philosophy*—the philosophy that explains all natural *phenomena* through the shape and motion of particles. Therefore, there must be a significant connection between this ancient *Moschical* (or rather *Mosaical*) *physiology* <note>The study of nature or physical science.</note> and the *Cartesian Philosophy*, which has so often and so naturally played a part in this *Philosophic Cabbala*.

Furthermore, that the *natural philosophy* of *Pythagoras* was atomic can be proven from what we find in *Diogenes Laertius* concerning *Democritus*. It is well known how much influence his "Atoms" have had in the world. But as *Diogenes* writes (citing *Thrasyllus*), *Democritus* was such a great admirer and imitator of *Pythagoras*, and seems to have taken so much from him, that one would think he had been his student or listener, if the chronology allowed for it. But even though he was not a direct disciple of *Pythagoras* himself, *Glaucus Rheginus* writes that he was a student of one of the *Pythagoreans*; and *Apollodorus of Cyzicus* reports that he was very intimately familiar with *Philolaus*. In the catalog of the books he wrote, one was titled *Pythagoras*, and another *Tritogenia*—a mystical term used among the *Pythagoreans*. Additionally, when *Plato* wanted to burn the writings of *Democritus*, it was two *Pythagoreans*, *Amyclas* and *Clinias*, who dissuaded him from carrying out his plan—certainly out of an honest, though mistaken, zeal. I believe these facts provide solid ground for a strong suspicion that the *physics* part of *Pythagoras’s* philosophy was atomic. And it is already well known that he held that the Earth is in motion. Let us consider the rest of the teachings of *Democritus* and see how they all align with those of *Descartes* <note>original: "Cartesius"</note>.

If *Democritus* received all his philosophy from the writings or traditions of *Pythagoras*, then Pythagoras must also have held: That there are infinite worlds; that they can be created and destroyed, but that matter itself is imperishable; and that there are infinite numbers of atoms or particles, differing in size and shape, "and that they are moved in the universe in the manner of vortices" <note>original Greek: "φέρεσθαι δ’ ἐν τῷ ὅλῳ δινώμεναι"</note>. For that is the proper meaning of *Dine* <note>original Greek: "Δίνη"</note>, namely, a *vortex* or whirlpool. "And thus all combinations generate fire, water, air, and earth" <note>original Greek: "Καὶ οὕτω πάντα συγκρίματα γεννᾶν πῦρ, ὕδωρ, ἀέρα, γῆν"</note>. By the rotation of these vortices of particles, "fire" (*pyr*) is generated <note>the term for the Sun among the Pythagoreans, as I have noted in the proper place</note>, and then afterwards Earth, Water, and Air. As it is said more expressly: "The composition of the Sun and Moon was the result of these vortices or spherical masses" <note>original Greek: "τόν τε ἥλιον καὶ τὴν σελήνην ἐκ τοιούτων δινῶν καὶ περιφερῶν ὄγκων συγκρίσθαι"</note>—referring to these immense and vastly rolling vortices. And lastly, "that all things are produced by necessity, the vortex being the cause of the generation of all things, which he calls necessity" <note>original Greek: "πάντα τε κατ' ἀνάγκην γενέσθαι, τῆς δίνης αἰτίας οὔσης τῆς γενέσεως πάντων, ἣν ἀνάγκην λέγει"</note>. That is to say, all things are made by a mechanical necessity, this vortical motion being the cause of the generation...

Being even ravished with admiration of his transcendent mechanical inventions for explaining the *phenomena* in the world, I should not hesitate to compare him with *Bezalel* and *Oholiab* <margin>Exodus 35:32.</margin> <note>Biblical craftsmen chosen by God to build the Tabernacle.</note>, those skillful and clever workers of the Tabernacle who, as *Moses* testifies, were filled with the Spirit of God and possessed an excellent understanding to create all manner of curious works.

Nor is it any more an argument that *Descartes* was not inspired because he did not say he was, than it is that others are inspired just because they say they are—which to me is no argument at all. But the suppression of what happened would suggest much more sobriety and modesty; whereas the profession of it among sober men would be suspected as a touch of melancholy and distraction, especially in Natural Philosophy, where the grand pleasure is the evidence and exercise of Reason, not a bare belief, or (as in other cases) an inexpressible sense of life, in respect of which every true Christian is inspired.

### CHAPTER 2. Of the Philosophical Cabbala.

*...numbers through the whole decad <note>original: "Denary" — referring to the number ten.</note> is Jewish as well as Pythagorean.*
6. *And that neither the Jews nor Pythagoreans confine themselves to ten; therefore this objection regarding inadequacy is found to be very invalid.*

1. And thus we have briefly considered the nature of the truths comprised in the *Philosophical Cabbala*, as also the quality of those persons who have championed them in previous ages. Now for the *objections*: these seven are certainly the most significant, if not the only, claims that can be made against it: namely,

**First,** That both the *Pythagorean* numbers and names are inadequate to the six days of Creation.

**Second,** That the *Pythagorean* philosophy does not correspond exactly to the *Jewish Cabbala* in its main points, specifically that the *Jewish writers* make no mention of the *motion of the Earth*.

**Third,** That the interpretation of the first day's Creation is different in kind from all the rest, as it alone is symbolic. Here, three additional questions are also proposed regarding the *metaphysical matter* <note>original: "Hyle" — the Greek word for matter or substance.</note> created on the first day.

**Fourth,** That the order of the *Cabbala* is backwards <note>original: "preposterous" — literally meaning "behind-before," or out of its natural order.</note> in placing the *Earth before the Sun*.

**Fifth,** That the works of the fifth and sixth days are too common and trivial to be the subject of a *Philosophical Cabbala*.

**Sixth,** That there is an unjustifiable reversal of order <note>original: "ὑστερολογία" (*hysterologia*) — a rhetorical term for putting the last thing first.</note> committed in our interpretation of *Paradise*, as we assume it was planted before *Adam* was made out of the earth.

**Seventh and last,** That our interpretation of the *cherubim and flaming sword* is forced, in that we make them a means for *Adam* to regain *Paradise*, even though they seem intended to keep him out.

2. But to these I shall fully answer in order. And first, to the first part of the first objection, which would suggest that because the *Pythagoreans* continued their *mysteries of numbers* through the whole *decad* <note>original: "Denarius" — the number ten.</note>, while the days of Creation are only *six*, the six-day Creation is therefore not at all involved in the mystery of their *numbers*. To this I answer that their continuing their mysteries of numbers through the whole *decad* does no harm to *our cause*. For whether we assume the *symbols* <note>original: "Hieroglyphicks"</note> of *numbers* were in use before the *Cabbala of Moses*, and that the first author took only as many of them as served his purpose (just as someone writing a sentence takes only the letters of the alphabet that suit his needs), or whether the first author of the *Cabbala* started these *numerical symbols*, and the mysteries of *numbers* were afterward expanded for smaller designs—neither *hypothesis* counts for anything against our interpretation. For does it follow that because *Moses* made *symbolic notes* of *six numbers* only, to be reminders of the nature of certain *phenomena* of the world, those who follow that *Cabbala* shall never use their *imagination* to expand these *numerical mysteries* and similarities to other matters? Certainly not—not even when, in the process of time, they had lost the original purpose and scope of these...

If this knowledge were merely the number of the *four* elements (*fire, water, earth,* and *air*), or the similarity that *Mind, Soul, Opinion,* and *Body* bear to the first *four* numbers (1, 2, 3, 4)—which is actually quite weak or shallow in all but the last, if we were to examine things strictly; and even if it were exact, it would be a mere trifle; also, the things themselves grouped together to make up the *Tetractys* are only forced together, as they are not all of one nature, but some are *substances* and others are *accidents* <note>In philosophy, "substances" are things that exist in themselves, while "accidents" are qualities or properties that exist only in a substance.</note>—I say, if this were all, these pretended *mysteries* would be of such small importance that it is impossible they could have inspired such great reverence for the first person who shared them, to the point that the *initiates* <note>original: "Mystæ"</note> would religiously swear by him in their serious conversation.

By this, it is necessarily implied that the *planets* must be so many *Earths*, along with the rest of those noble conclusions of *philosophy* that depend on that idea. This

was the belief of *Pythagoras’s* school, as plainly appears from *Aristotle* in his *On the Heavens*; where he says the *Pythagoreans* assert that the *fire*—that is, the *Sun*—is in the middle of the world, "that the Earth is among the stars," <note>original Greek: "τὴν γῆν ἐν τῷ ἄστρῳ εἶναι"</note> and that the *Earth* is one of the *stars*; he means *planets*. And that they made the *planets* also *Earths* appears from what he adds: "Furthermore, they establish another Earth opposite to this one, which they call the 'Counter-Earth,'" <note>original Greek: "Ἔτι δ᾽ ἐναντίαν ἄλλην ταύτῃ κατασκευάζουσι γῆν, ἣν ἀντίχθονα ὄνομα καλοῦσιν"</note>

# CHAP. II. of the Philosophical Cabbala.

<margin>
* Macrobius, *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio*, book 1, chapter 11.
* Plutarch, *Concerning the Face Which Appears in the Orb of the Moon*.

Moreover, they describe another Earth, which they call *Antichthon* <note>The "Counter-Earth," a hypothetical body in Pythagorean cosmology.</note>, opposite to our own. This was undoubtedly nothing other than our opposite neighboring planet or earth, the *Moon*. For she is called by the ancients the *Ethereal Earth* <note>original Latin: *Terra Ætherea*</note>, as in *Plutarch* she is called the *Olympian Earth* <note>original Greek: *γῆ ὀλυμπία*</note>. This side of her is called *Antichthon* <note>original Greek: *Ἀντίχθων*</note> and *Persephone* <note>original Greek: *Περσεφόνη*</note>, while the other side is called the *Elysian field* <note>original Greek: *Ἠλύσιον πεδίον*</note>. Over the course of time, these ideas have corrupted this very solid philosophy with superstitious fancies. But this is enough to reveal Pythagoras’s opinion concerning the planets: that he viewed them as so many *Earths*.

<margin>
See Johannes Meursius, *The Pythagorean Decad*, chapter 6.
</margin>

The *Tetractys* <term>A symbolic triangular figure representing the number ten, made of the first four integers (1+2+3+4=10).</term> is therefore used to represent the *Cabbala* of this *Fourth Day's* work. When this is fully and methodically explained, and the *initiates* <note>original: "Mystæ"</note> find their natures so perfected and their minds so illuminated by it, it might well draw from them such a veneration that it would religiously lead them to swear by its first author. It is said that Pythagoras himself used this form of oath; and I could charitably believe that all the early *Pythagoreans* swore in the same sense that Pythagoras did—namely, by the First Communicator of such a high and stupendous piece of *Wisdom*. This wisdom (as I have noted from *Iamblichus*) is said to be *god-given* <note>original Greek: *θεοπαράδοτος*</note>, delivered first from God himself. This makes their swearing irreproachable and blameless.

4. Since there is such an exquisite fitness and appropriateness in applying these *Pythagorean Numbers* (even if we do not use all of them) to the six days' work of Creation, it serves as a demonstration that Pythagoras’s philosophy was essentially the same as the ancient *Jewish Cabbala* regarding the structure of the *World*.

<margin>
* See also Philo Judaeus, *On the Preliminary Studies*. <note>original Greek: Περί τῶν εἰς τὰ προπαιδεύματα συνόδω</note>
</margin>

5. Furthermore, there are more numbers from the *Pythagorean Decad* <note>original: "Denary"; referring to the group of ten.</note> employed in this mystery than is claimed. I have demonstrated that the number *Seven* is very significant for the *Seventh Day’s Rest*. And the number *Ten* emerges out of the *Tetractys*, as noted above. Thus, *eight* numbers of the *Decad* are clearly shown to belong naturally to the *Jewish Cabbala*. It seems very plain to me that the ancient wisdom of the *Jews* made a mysterious use of the number *Eight* in their religion, given that *circumcision* was appointed for the *eighth day*. Since eight is the first *cube* <note>2 x 2 x 2 = 8. In Pythagorean thought, the cube represents stability because it sits firmly on any side.</note>, it is a fitting *hieroglyph* for the *stability* of that *Covenant* made with the Jews through circumcision. The Pythagoreans call the number eight *security* <note>original Greek: *ἀσφάλεια*</note>, which signifies the safety found in a *Covenant*. And unless I were to seem overly concerned with a minor matter, I believe it would not be difficult to produce passages from Holy Scripture where the number *Nine* may be rightly thought to possess a *mystical* meaning. There is very little reason to claim that the symbolic use of the first *ten* numbers is only *Pythagorean* and does not concern the *Jewish Cabbala*.

6. To all of this, you may add that neither the *Pythagoreans* themselves nor the holy writers of the Bible confine the *mystical* use of *numbers* to the first *ten*; instead, both expand into other, more complex numbers. This provides further evidence of how groundless and invalid the *claim* <note>original: "Allegation"</note> is against the truth of the *Philosophical Cabbala*—that argument which tries to dismiss the amazing fitness and consistency of the *numbers* used as *symbols* for each day of Creation by saying: *That there are more mystical*

It is as if, whenever there are several mystical numbers that far exceed the number of seven days, they should all be applied to these seven; or that, because some are unapplicable, therefore those that are so manifestly applicable were not rightly applied.

And thus I hope I have fully satisfied the first part of this first objection concerning the numbers themselves. I think that if these are duly considered, they are alone (by reason of their fitness and the significance of their natures and properties) sufficient to assure us of that part of the Philosophic Cabbala which is comprised in the first chapter of *Genesis*. In that chapter, there is also a prelibation <note>original: "prelibation"; a preliminary taste or foretaste</note> of those illustrious truths which are more fully and circumstantially delivered in the second and third chapters. This shows that the whole philosophy of *Pythagoras* is of one piece and from one fountain: the ancient Cabbala of *Moses*.
