# CHAP. III. of the Philosophic Cabbala.

People have invented mysteries in new numbers upon the occasion of having those that pertain to the *Creation* communicated to them. I repeat the same thing here concerning the giving of new names to those first numbers, by imagining they will represent this or that in either *Morality*, *Nature*, or *Metaphysics*.

These irrelevancies <note>original: "impertinencies"</note> certainly would grow the fastest, as I said before, when the original purpose and use of these names were hidden in oblivion. For then, having no *guiding star* <note>original: "Cynosura"; the constellation Ursa Minor, used for navigation</note> to lead them, they would be blown toward every small and trivial resemblance that this or that number might have with this or that object, according to whatever direction their flighty imaginations carried them, and their desire to make the dry mysteries of numbers grow into some collection of superstitious knowledge. "Once one has gone beyond the limit, there is no boundary" <note>original Greek: Τῆϛ ἅπαξ ὑπὲρ τὸ μέτρον ὅρος οὐδείς ἐστιν (Tes hapax hyper to metron horos oudeis estin)</note>. For once they had lost the standard for dealing in the names of numbers, their additions would be infinite.

2. But things have turned out in this matter much as they have with the sober truths of the Christian religion. Although innumerable human inventions have been added to Christianity, the grand truths of the faith itself have been preserved among them, discoverable by the testimony of Holy Scripture. Similarly, though there have been many irrelevant *names* of the first *seven* numbers invented by ignorant and superstitious *Pythagoreans*, they have also retained the true and useful ones. These are likewise discoverable by applying them to the text of *Moses*, according to either the *philosophic* sense or the literal wording of it. This is eminently plain in the *First Day's* work, where I truly think I shall find more names relevant to the work of that day than irrelevant ones, despite the fact that ignorance has added so many.

3. For while there are nearly fifty names for a *Monad* or *Unit* <note>a "Monad" is the number one, representing unity or the source of all things</note>, over half of them are significant of the nature of those things comprised in the *First Day's* work. To the names relevant to what we call there the *World of Life* <note>original Latin: "Mundus vitae"</note> (which encompasses the entire *Immaterial Creation*), besides **Life**, **Form**, **Tower of Jove**, and **Seminal Reason** <note>original Greek: Ζωὴ (Zoe), Εἶδος (Eidos), Ζανὸς πύργος (Zanos pyrgos), Λόγος σπερματικός (Logos spermatikos)</note>, which we have noted already, you may also add: **Mind**, **Form-giver**, **Seed**, **Substance**, **Cause of Truth**, **Simple Pattern**, **Now**, **Memory**, **Prometheus**, and **Male-female** <note>original Greek: Νῦς (Nous), Μορφώ (Morpho), Γονὴ (Gone), Οὐσία (Ousia), Αἴτιον ἀληθείας (Aition aletheias), Ἁπλοῦν παράδειγμα (Haploun paradeigma), Νῦν (Nun), Μνημοσύνη (Mnemosyne), Προμηθεύς (Prometheus), Ἀρρενόθηλυς (Arrenothelus)</note>.

**Mind**, because all *immaterial beings* are **intelligible** <note>original Greek: νοητὰ (noeta)</note>, meaning they are understood by the mind and not perceived by the **senses**. **Form-giver**, because they are what give *form* to *matter*. **Seed**, because all *generation* <note>the creation or production of things</note> comes chiefly from this principle, and *matter* can produce nothing of itself. (These are the words of *Plotinus*: <margin>* Plotinus, *Enneads*, book 3, chapter 6, section 19.</margin> "For only form is productive, while the other nature <note>matter</note> is barren." This was the reason, he says, why the ancients depicted Mercury "always holding the organ of generation ready for work, showing that it is the intelligible reason that generates within the realm of sense perception.") **Substance**, because *immaterial beings* are the truest *substance*, as the *Platonists* rightly argue; and so **Cause of Truth** for the same reason. **Simple Pattern**: **Pattern** for the same reason as **Form** and **Form-giver**; and **Simple**, because *immaterial beings* are devoid of complex parts. **Now**, because intellectual life exists all at once, "ignorant of the shifts of time, always consisting in a single, ever-present age," <margin>* Macrobius, *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio*, book 1, chapter 8.</margin> as *Macrobius* speaks. **Memory**, if it be not pedantically...

# An Appendix to the Defense CHAP. III.

...superstitious men. If the name of the Mother of the Muses <note>original: "Mnemosyne"</note> was pedantically popped in—whose children's names are also scattered throughout the <term>Pythagorean Denary</term>—I suspect the reason for that name is because the highest and deepest seat of *Memory* resides in our immaterial nature. He is called Prometheus <note>original: "Προμηθεύς"</note> because the Soul, clothed in her fiery spirits, like Prometheus, enlivens this body—this statue of clay. And lastly, he is called Androgynous <note>original: "Ἀρρενόθηλυς" (Arrenothelus)</note>, because all *immaterial* orders fundamentally contain that division of faculties into *Masculine* and *Feminine*, as is expressed more at length concerning *Adam*.

4. And as for that which is the fluid, indeterminate capacity of things—that dark *Abyss* which we may briefly call the <term>Metaphysical Hyle</term>, or the *possibility of creatures in the outward world*—besides the names we have already produced, such as Matter <note>original: "Ὕλη" (Hyle)</note>, Lightlessness <note>original: "Ἀλαμπία" (Alampia)</note>, and Gloom <note>original: "Σκοτωδία" (Skotodia)</note>, you may also add Chaos, Confusion <note>original: "Σύγχυσις" (Synchysis)</note>, Mixture <note>original: "Σύγκρασις" (Synkrasis)</note>, Proteus <note>original: "Πρωτοὺς"</note>, and All-receiver <note>original: "Πανδοχεύς" (Pandocheus)</note>. All of these denote the confusion, indeterminacy, and mixed capacity of this *Metaphysical Hyle*, or the mere *potentiality of the external creature*. But then, for that dark *Abyss* mentioned in that *First Day's Creation*, what terms are more significant than Chasm <note>original: "Χάσμα" (Chasma)</note>, Tartarus, Styx, and the Pit <note>original: "Βάραθρον" (Barathron)</note>? These are so appropriate to the text that nothing could be more so, and it is utterly unlikely they would have been names for a *Unity* unless in reference to this. Add to Styx also Oblivion <note>original: "Λήθη" (Lethe)</note>, because when things are resolved into this *First* Day's state, they are overwhelmed with forgetfulness; the souls of Men and Angels are then in silence, and so thoroughly drenched in the Lake of *Lethe* that they can never remember anything from the past.

<margin>* Philosophic Cabbala, chapter 1, verse 5.</margin>
5. There are yet two very significant terms remaining: Unmixedness <note>original: "Ἀμιξία" (Amixia)</note> and Virgin Seed <note>original: "Σπορὰ παρθένος" (Spora parthenos)</note>, which exactly describe the condition of the *First* day's Creation. For when considering those immaterial beings as not yet united with Matter, what better describes their state than "Virgin Seed"—a dry and rigid virginity? Or what better than "Unmixedness," following that phrase in *Hesiod*, "to be joined in love" <note>original: "φιλότητι μιγῆναι" (philotēti migēnai)</note>? Furthermore, the unmixed nature of the *Active* and *Passive* principle proper to this Day is famously signified by the name "Unmixedness," as you may see in the *Cabbala itself. So, in addition to those seven appropriate names we were satisfied with before, we have gained at least twenty more just as fitting through this examination.

6. But for those names that do not serve our purpose, the explanation for them is very easy. After the *Pythagoreans* lost the knowledge of the true goal of naming those numbers—which was to remember the nature of those things said to be created on those various days—they then devised names without any clear aim, based on any slight similarity between the number and the things it might represent. For example, because there is but *one God*, they called a *Unity* God <note>original: "Θεός" (Theos)</note>, Zeus, Piety <note>original: "Εὐσέβεια" (Eusebeia)</note>, and perhaps Happiness <note>original: "Εὐδαιμονία" (Eudaimonia)</note>. And then in *natural* things, because there is but *one Sun*, they called a *Monad* Sun <note>original: "Ἥλιος" (Helios)</note>, Fiery-sun <note>original: "Πυράλιος" (Pyralios)</note>, and Apollo; and because of Apollo, they also called it Eloquent <note>original: "Λόγιος" (Logios)</note>. In *morals*, because love and goodwill consist of a kind of unity of affections, they call a *Unity* Friend <note>original: "Φίλος" (Philos)</note>, Friendship <note>original: "Φιλία" (Philia)</note>, Love <note>original: "Ἔρως" (Eros)</note>, and Harmony <note>original: "Ὁμόνοια" (Homonoia)</note>.

# CHAPTER III. Of the Philosophical Cabbala.

And because there is Unity in *artificial order*, they call it the order of harmony <note>original: "Τάξις συμφωνίας" (Taxis symphonias)</note>, a ship <note>original: "Ναῦς" (Naus)</note>, or a chariot <note>original: "Ἅρμα" (Harma)</note>. I cannot better imagine why they should call it Atlas <note>original: "Ἄτλας"</note> and Axle <note>original: "Ἄξων"</note> than because the Poles that are said to support the world, upon which it hangs and turns, are two points—that is, two fixed *units*. But why they call it the Equal <note>original: "Ἴσον" (Ison)</note>, the Middle <note>original: "Μέσον" (Meson)</note>, and the Moderate <note>original: "Μέτριον" (Metrion)</note> is very plain. "Equal," because those things that are equal have one quantity; "Middle" and "Moderate," because that which is exactly in the *middle*, or perfectly moderate, is but *One*. However, let anyone judge what an insipid and unsatisfactory cleverness <note>original: "Arguteness"</note> there is in such conceptions as these, and how unworthy they are of so profound a philosopher as *Pythagoras*—to whom the <margin>* Pliny, *Natural History*, Book 34, Chapter 6.</margin> *Roman Senate* erected a statue as the wisest man in all *Greece*.

7. As for the *names of the Binary* <note>The number two</note>, I have already listed over a dozen that are very significant of the nature of the work of the *Second Day* of Creation. To those that signify the most dismal things, you may further add Audacity <note>original: "Τόλμα" (Tolma)</note>, Endurance <note>original: "Τλημοσύνη" (Tlemosyne)</note>, Misery <note>original: "Δύη" (Dye)</note>, Dissension <note>original: "Διχοστασία" (Dichostasia)</note>, Strife <note>original: "Ἔρις" (Eris)</note>, and Ignorance <note>original: "Ἄγνοια" (Agnoia)</note>. To Rhea also would be referred (except that it seems like a reckless and superstitious piling up of synonyms by later, unskillful *Pythagoreans*) the names Dindymene <note>original: "Δινδυμήνη"</note>, Mother of God <note>original: "Διομήτωρ" (Diometor)</note>, Phrygia <note>original: "Φρυγία"</note>, and Hesto <note>original: "Ἑστώ"</note>. All these terms mean nothing else but the goddesses *Cybele* or *Vesta*. But anyone who has noticed that *Vesta* represents the *Sun* in true *Pythagoreanism* can see how <margin>* See Chapter 8, section 6.</margin> un-Pythagorean this is.

The rest of the titles are such dull fooleries that it is tedious to recite them; yet I will give you more than a taste of them, so you may see with what pitiful trifles the *pseudo-Pythagoreans* entertained themselves once they had lost the true meaning of their *Cabbala*. For just as it was a fine thing for them previously to call the *Monad* (the number one) by the name of Apollo, or the *Sun*; so now, for no better reason, I think, than because they had already done so, they call the *Binary* (the number two) Artemis, Isis, Demeter, the Eleusinian, Dictynna, and Hera. All of these may signify no more than the *Moon*, which is the *second* great light in the heavens. Likewise, because any agreement or kind affection requires *two parties*, they call the Binary the fountain of harmony <note>original: "Πηγὴ τῆς συμφωνίας" (Pege tes symphonias)</note>, Erato, Harmony, Aphrodite, Dione, Cytherea, Fellowship <note>original: "Κοινωνία" (Koinonia)</note>, and Marriage <note>original: "Γάμος" (Gamos)</note>. In this list, "Marriage," and as many other words as sound that way, is very forcedly and unskillfully thrust in. 

Because the conjunction of two *units* in the *Binary* is either the conjunction of two *masculines*—as some would have the *unit* to be (and then certainly no *Pythagoreans*, unless they are the successors of that <margin>* See Tacitus, *Annals*, Book 15, section 37.</margin> *Pythagoras* <note>A freedman of the Emperor Nero who participated in a mock marriage ceremony with him.</note> whom *Nero* was married to, would call the Binary "Marriage")—or else it is the conjunction of two *hermaphrodites*, which is ridiculous. For <margin>* In *The Dream of Scipio*, Book 1, Chapter 6.</margin> *Macrobius* declares, according to the thinking of the *Ancients*, that a unit is both male and female. "However, the one which is called the monad—that is, Unity—is both Male and Female, both even and odd, not a number itself, but the fountain and origin of numbers" <note>original: "Unum autem, quod μονὰς, id est, Unitas, dicitur, & Mas idem & Fæmina est, par idem atque impar, ipse non numerus, sed fons & origo numerorum"</note>. Concerning this, <margin>* Aristotle, *Metaphysics*, Book 1, Chapter 5.</margin> *Aristotle* also affirms the same: "For the 'one' comes from both of these, for it is both even and odd; and number comes from the one" <note>original: "Τὸ γὰρ ἓν δὴ ἐξ ἀμφοτέρων εἶναι τούτων, καὶ γὰρ ἄρτιον εἶναι καὶ περιττόν· τὸ δ’ ἀριθμὸν ἐκ τοῦ ἑνός"</note>. This reveals their folly in also calling the *Ternary* (the number three) "Marriage." For it would then be the marriage of a female with a hermaphrodite, and of a number with something that is not even a number. "Now griffins will be mated with horses" <note>original: "Jungentur jam gryphes equis" — a quote from Virgil used to describe an impossible or absurd pairing</note>. Thus, it is clear that the names Aphrodite and Marriage are the specific titles of the *Quinary* (the number five) and *Senary* (the number six), as they have a

### An Appendix to the Defense — CHAPTER III.

special congruity also to the *Fifth* and *Sixth* days' work. But let us not be so strict, and instead admit that a *Unit* <note>The number one</note> is rather *masculine*; even then, the *Binary* <note>The number two</note> will still be excluded from the title of Marriage <note>original: "Γάμος" (Gamos)</note>, and the *Ternary's* <note>The number three</note> title admitted only with difficulty, representing the male and female among plants, which more perfectly fits the nature of the *Third* day's work.

Furthermore, because the *Binary* is made by adding one unit to another, it is called Increase <note>original: "Αὔξησις" (Auxesis)</note>, Composition <note>original: "σύνθεσις" (Synthesis)</note>, and Addition <note>original: "Ἐπίθεσις" (Epithesis)</note>. And because judgment <note>original: "Dijudication"</note> implies a *duality* in the object being judged, it is called Discrimination <note>original: "Διάκρισις" (Diakrisis)</note>. And because Opinion tends toward *two* ways at once, it is styled Opinion <note>original: "Δόξα" (Doxa)</note>; and since Demonstration has *two* main parts—the premises and the conclusion—it is termed Knowledge <note>original: "Ἐπιστήμη" (Episteme)</note>. Lastly, because the number *two* is divided into *two* equal parts, it is named Justice <note>original: "Δίκη" (Dike)</note>. The self-proclaimed *Pythagoreans* fell into such petty speculations once they lost sight of the true goal that the Mystery of Numbers aimed for in the *Binary*.

8. Let us also look a little deeper into the *Ternary*, where we will find similar trivialities. The most tolerable of these are the names relating to moral considerations, such as Wisdom <note>original: "Μῆτις" (Metis)</note>, Good Counsel <note>original: "Εὐβουλία" (Euboulia)</note>, and Prudence <note>original: "Φρόνησις" (Phronesis)</note>, with which the *Ternary* is adorned; this is because whoever wishes to advise well must look upon things *past, present*, and *to come*. It is also called Friendship <note>original: "Φιλία" (Philia)</note>, Peace <note>original: "Εἰρήνη" (Eirene)</note>, and Concord <note>original: "Ὁμόνοια" (Homonoia)</note>, since the *union* of two parties is made by some *third* thing or person. It is also called Piety <note>original: "Εὐσέβεια" (Eusebeia)</note>, I suppose because of the frequent use of the number *three* in religious rites. The terms Three-bodied <note>original: "Τρίσωμος" (Trisomos)</note> and First Breadth <note>original: "Πρῶτον πλάτος" (Proton platos)</note> are mathematical considerations, just as Two-bodied <note>original: "Δίσωμος" (Disomos)</note> and First Length <note>original: "Πρῶτον μῆκος" (Proton mekos)</note> are for the *Binary*. However, these terms serve no greater purpose than to inform us that the *Binary* represents two mathematical points and the first and shortest line, while the *Ternary* represents three points and the first and simplest geometric figure, which is the *Triangle*. These are certainly notions that cheerfully edify and deliciously feed the human mind; yet what follows is even more worthless and trivial. For the *Ternary* is called the festival of Saturn <note>original: "Κρονία" (Kronia)</note> because *Saturn* had three sons—*Jupiter, Neptune*, and *Pluto*; and Hades <note>original: "Ἅιδης" (Haides)</note> because *Pluto* was the third son. It is also called Latona <note>original: "Λατώ" (Lato)</note> and Hecate <note>original: "Ἑκάτη" (Hekate)</note> because *Latona* was the mother of *Hecate*, who had three titles: *Luna, Diana*, and *Proserpina*. It is called the Graces <note>original: "Χαριτία" (Charitia)</note> because there are three Graces: *Aglaia, Thalia*, and *Euphrosyne*. It is called the festival of the Dioscuri <note>original: "Διοσκορία" (Dioskoria)</note> after the three *Dioscuri*: *Trittopatreus, Ebuleus*, and *Dionysius*. Finally, it is named after Phorcus <note>original: "Φορκία" (Phorkia)</note> and the Gorgons <note>original: "Γοργονία" (Gorgonia)</note> because *Phorcus* was the father of the three *Gorgons*: *Medusa, Stheno*, and *Euryale*. The *Ternary* was made a repository for such pitiful trash by the *pseudo-Pythagoreans*, who did not know the ancient *Cabbala*.

9. Finding Female-formed <note>original: "Θηλυμορφὸς" (Thelymorphos)</note> recorded among the titles of the *Ternary*, they also included Thetis <note>original: "Θέτις"</note> and *Angopeza* (which I believe should be Silver-footed <note>original: "Ἀργυρόπεζα" (Argyropeza)</note>, an epithet of *Thetis* in *Homer*). Even *Ovid* notes the beauty of the feet of *Thetis* in that five-beat line of poetry <note>A pentameter</note>:

> *And such feet as I scarcely believe even Thetis had.* <note>original: "Et Thetidis quales vix reor esse pedes."</note>

They also added *Naitis* <note>A water nymph</note> and *Crataeis* <note>A personification of a river or rocky power</note>, I think aiming for the same meaning. These names make no sense at all except in reference to the *Third* day's work, when the distinction between *Land* and *Sea*—and consequently *Rivers*—was made.

But though there has been so much trash until now, there is yet one

### CHAPTER III. of the Philosophic Cabbala.

There is one name remaining that will compensate for the trouble of searching through this mess <note>original: "raking in this dunghill"</note>: and that is *Loxias* <note>original: "ΛοξίαϚ," a title for Apollo meaning "oblique" or "slanting"</note>. Considering the importance of its meaning and its easy reference to the oblique motion of the Earth (upon which depends the nourishing of the world with plants and flowers), and seeing that
<margin>* Plutarch, *On the Opinions of the Philosophers*, book 2, chapter 12.</margin>
*Pythagoras is said to have been the first to observe the tilt <note>original: "obliquity"</note> of this motion, I can willingly admit it to be an ancient and authentic title of the Ternary <note>The number three</note>.

10. And it will not be unseasonable to take notice that the very
<margin>* See Paul Fagius's commentary on the text.</margin>
* derivation <note>original: "Notation"</note> of the word *Eretz* <note>original: "ארץ" (Earth)</note> supports our theory. It is derived, as the ancient Hebrews have observed, from *Rutz* <note>original: "רוץ," meaning "to run"</note>; certainly because of the Earth's constant course around the Sun, and not because the Heavens run around her. We may be even more certain of this if we also consider the derivation of *Shemesh* <note>original: "שמש" (Sun)</note>, which is most likely from *Sham* and *Ush*—meaning "to stand" <note>original: "ἱστάναι" (histanai) or "μεῖναι" (meinai), as the Septuagint often renders it</note> and "fire" <note>original: "אש" (Esh)</note>. This is consistent with how the Pythagoreans usually call the Sun *fire* <note>original: "πῦρ" (pyr)</note>, as you may see in 
<margin>* Aristotle, *On the Heavens*, book 2, chapter 13.</margin>
* Aristotle: "For they say that in the center of the earth there is fire," <note>original: "Ἐm μ͂ γῆ τῆ μέσε πῦρ εἶναί φασιν"</note> and
<margin>* Plutarch, *In the Life of Numa*.</margin>
* Plutarch: "They believe that fire is situated in the middle of the universe, and they call this Hestia." <note>original: "Κατὰ μέσον τῆ κόσμε πῦρ ἱδρυ̑σθαι νομίζειν, κὶ τῆτο Ἐσίαν καλε͂σιν"</note> So his "Fixed Fire" <note>original: "ἱδρύμνον πῦρ" (idrymnon pyr)</note> exactly answers to *Shemesh*, which has the same meaning, just as all Suns are acknowledged to be fixed stars <note>original: "Stellæ Fixæ"</note>.

And the fact that this fixed fire is called *Hestia* <note>original: "Ἐσία"</note> by the Pythagoreans is a further discovery of where they obtained their concept: namely, from the Hebrews, who call fire *Esh* <note>original: "אש"</note>, and the Chaldeans call it *Eshta* <note>original: "אשתא"</note>, which is essentially the same as the word *Hestia* or *Vesta*. Nor was it necessary to retain the whole word *Shemesh*; the element *Esh* in *Hestia*, having been transplanted into the Greek tongue, acquired a strong affinity with *isemi* <note>Greek: "I know" or "I am certain," here linked by the author to the Hebrew concept of placing/standing</note>, which is the same as *Sham* in Hebrew. Thus, it alone carries the same sense as *Shemesh*: for even the best words are but reminders of the nature of things.

But none are so philosophical as these words *Eretz* <note>Earth</note> and *Shemesh* <note>Sun</note>. I may also add *Kokhav* <note>original: "כוכב" (Star/Planet)</note>. The easy and genuine derivations of these terms set out the hidden natures of the things they belong to, showing the exact opposition they have to one another: that of *Eretz* implying the Earth's motion; that of *Shemesh* implying the Sun's fixedness; that of *Kokhav* implying the extinction of light or fire in all the planets; and that of *Shemesh* implying the innate light and heat in all the Suns or fixed stars. The wonderful consistency of the philosophical derivations of these three words (to say nothing of *Shamayim* <note>original: "שמים" (Heavens)</note>) cannot but gain further belief both for the derivations themselves and for the truth of the physical part of the Cabbala. Nor is *Shamayim* of less philosophical importance, even if it were admitted to be from *Shamah* <note>original: "שמה," meaning "to be high"</note> and not from "fire and water" <note>original: "אש and מים"</note>. For then its being a dual noun <note>Hebrew nouns ending in -ayim are dual, implying two</note> would suggest the same thing as before: namely, the two Cartesian elements or parts of which Heaven consists, as is observed in other words denoting things consisting of two parts, such as "stones," "ranges," "stalls," <note>original: "אבנים, כירים, משפתים"</note> and the like. Also, it suggests the two kinds of Heaven: the one created on the first day, the other on the second. Just as *Mayim* <note>water</note> likewise denotes two kinds of water: that from the clouds, and that in the sea, rivers, and wells; but in a more philosophical sense, the waters visible and invisible. By "invisible," "Stygian," or "Celestial," I mean that part of the "World of Life" <note>original: "Mundus vitae"</note> that descends into the realm of physical generation <note>original: "εἰς γένεσιν" (eis genesin)</note>.

## CHAPTER IV.

1. *Four more names for the Tetrad that are relevant. 2. An account of those that are irrelevant. 3. That such trifles—whether regarding numbers or names—could not have won such reverence from Pythagoras as to induce him to swear by the first person to share the* Tetractys <note>The "Tetractys" refers to the mystical number four, or the sum of the first four numbers (1+2+3+4=10), which was central to Pythagorean philosophy.</note>. 4. *Marriage* <note>original: "Γάμος" (Gamos)</note> *is a name proper to the Quinary (five) and Senary (six), and how the Binary (two) and Ternary (three) came by that title. 5. Two more relevant names for the Quinary, with an account of the irrelevant ones. 6. That if the nature of numbers alone, and not the nature of things, had been intended by the* Tetractys, *the Pentad (five) would have better deserved the religious reverence of an oath. 7. The irrelevant names for the Senary. 8. Names of the Senary referring to* Marriage <note>original: "Γάμος" (Gamos)</note> *and the* World <note>original: "Κόσμος" (Kosmos)</note>. *9. Six other names for the Senary most fitly interpreted from the text of* Moses. *10. Eight names for the Septenary (seven) referring to the same text. 11. Of the irrelevant names of the Septenary, and why that number is called Pallas, and why Apollo* Seventh-born <note>original: "ἑβδομαγενής" (Hebdomagenes)</note>.

1. We come now to the *Quaternary* [the number four], of which—besides what we have noted already—there are four more titles that are not altogether unsuitable or insignificant: *Connection* <note>original: "Ἔξαμμα" (Examma)</note>, *Nature* <note>original: "Φύσις" (Physis)</note>, *Variegated* <note>original: "Ἀιόλα" (Aiola)</note>, and *Key-bearer of Nature* <note>original: "Κλαδδοῦχ. τῆς φύσεως" (Kladdouchos tes physeos)</note>. 
*Connection*, because the distinct and articulate fitting together of the parts of the Universe took place on the *Fourth Day*. *Nature*, as denoting the universal comprehension of all things. *Variegated*, as suggesting the variety of objects in the Universe discoverable by the Lights of Heaven—which are the work of the *Fourth Day*, and are themselves a most eminent part of that variety. This is why Sophocles uses the phrase "variegated Night" <note>original: "αἰόλα Νὺξ"</note> because she is so dappled with stars. And lastly, the *Tetractys* is called the *Key-bearer of Nature* because explaining the work of the *Fourth day* is indeed the *Key* to the most excellent secrets of *Nature*; or rather, it is an entrance into the truest and most important knowledge of *Universal Nature*, both *Metaphysical* and *Physical*. For this reason, the *Tetrad* is not only said to be the "source of natural completions" <note>original: "φυσιϰῶν ἀποτελεσμάτων πηγὴ"</note>, but (if I do not mistake the meaning of Photius) it is also called "full of many gods" <note>original: "πολυθεὸς"</note>, or rather "all-encompassing god" <note>original: "πανθεὸς"</note>, being full of *immaterial beings* everywhere—*daemons*, or *angels*, or whatever you wish to call them; though the Greeks commonly called them "gods" <note>original: "Θεοί" (Theoi)</note>.

<margin>Nicomachus Gerasenus, *Theology of Arithmetic*, book 1.</margin>
2. But while these names produced here and elsewhere are relevant to our purpose, there are others that are quite irrelevant. For I find that the ignorance of later generations abused the *Tetrad*—as much as it was religiously admired by the knowledgeable *Pythagoreans*—making it a repository for superstitious and useless trifles. For example, because *Mercury* was born on the fourth day of the month, the number was called *Hermes*, *Maiades* [son of Maia], and *Sokos* [the strong]. Also, because *Hercules* was born then, it was called *Herakles*, *Savior from Hunger* <note>original: "Ἀλιμωσώτη" (Alimosote)</note>, *Manly* <note>original: "Ἔπανδρος" (Epandros)</note>, *Masculine* <note>original: "Ἀῤῥενεϱὸς" (Arreneros)</note>, and *Undefiled* <note>original: "Ἀϰήλυντος" (Akelyntos)</note>. Because *Bacchus* was *twice* born, and the *Tetrad* is generated by *two* (for two times two is *four*), the *Tetrad* is called *Dionysos*, *Bassareus* [the fox-clothed], *Twice-mothered* <note>original: "Διμάτωρ" (Dimator)</note>, and *Woman-shaped* <note>original: "Θηλύμορφος" (Thelymorphos)</note>; it is also called *Dioskoros* [son of Zeus], perhaps in reference to both *Hercules* and *Bacchus*. And lastly,

Lastly, because fire has a pyramidal form, and **four** makes the **first body** <note>original: "πρῶτον σῶμα" (proton soma)</note> which is a pyramid—one **unit** <note>original: "Unite"</note> laid on the other three (a shape like a mound, for which it is also called **a heap** <note>original: "Σωρείτης" (Sorites)</note>)—they call the Tetrad **Hephaestus** <note>The Greek god of fire (original: "Ἡφαιστὸς").</note>.

3. But what a pitiful business would it have been for **Pythagoras** <note>An ancient Greek philosopher (c. 570–495 BC) known for his focus on mathematics and the mystical properties of numbers.</note> if these were the only riches of that **Tetractys** <note>The "Tetractys" is a triangular figure consisting of ten points arranged in four rows: one, two, three, and four. It was a sacred symbol to the Pythagoreans.</note> which he held in such high esteem that he swore a religious oath by the person who first shared it? Would this satisfy that famous report made by **Plutarch**? <margin>* In his *On Isis and Osiris*.</margin> **"The so-called Tetractys was the greatest oath, as is famously reported, and was named the World."** <note>original: "Ἡ δὲ καλουμένη τετρακτὺς μέγιστος ἦν ὅρκος, ὡς τεθρύλληται, καὶ Κόσμος ὠνόμασαι."</note> (He speaks there of the compound Tetractys, but the oath applied equally to both.) The Tetractys, so called, was a grand oath, as is famed, and was named **The World** <note>original: "Κόσμος" (Kosmos)</note>. And certainly, it was that clear and pleasant view into the order and nature of the **System of the World** arising out of the union of the **active** and **passive** principles—and then extending to all objects, both **metaphysical** and **physical**, which were declared in the account of the **fourth** day's creation. This, I say, was certainly that Tetractys which is called *Kosmos* or the **Universe** (that is, the **Cabbala** <note>Here used to mean a secret or traditional oral teaching.</note> of the genuine and satisfying knowledge of it), by the first communicator of which mystery both Pythagoras himself and the succeeding Pythagoreans so religiously swore. But as for those other toys and niceties that are merely **numerical**, it is utterly incredible that the sharing of them should ever have earned such considerable respect from so wise a man as Pythagoras was judged to be by everyone.

4. Concerning the titles of the **Quinary** [the number five], those that we have already noticed are the most famous in literature, as you may see in the many citations of **Meursius** <note>Johannes Meursius (1579–1639), a Dutch classical scholar and antiquary who wrote *Denarius Pythagoricus*.</note>, and they are so appropriate to the work of that day <margin>* *The Pythagorean Decad*, chapter 7.</margin> that nothing could be more so. As for the **Binary** [two] and **Ternary** [three] being called **Aphrodite** <note>original: "Ἀφροδίτη"</note> and **Marriage** <note>original: "Γάμος" (Gamos)</note>—since they are not as applicable to the days of creation, nor as compatible with the nature of those numbers as I have **previously demonstrated** <margin>* Chapter 3, section 7.</margin>—they fall proportionately short in the testimony of the ancients. They were certainly the additions of some idle and uninspired pretenders to Pythagoreanism in later ages. This was also the case with the daring attempt to call the Quinary **Androgyny** <note>original: "Ἀνδρογυνία"</note>, when **Male-female** <note>original: "Ἀρρενόθηλυς" (Arrhenothelus)</note> would have been more proper, if they had known the original purpose of these names.

5. To those few titles of the Quinary which we have produced, two more may be added, which I think are relevant. One is **Nature** <note>original: "φύσις" (Physis)</note> as it signifies **the genitals** <note>original: "τὰ αἰδοῖα" (ta aidoia). This relates to the fifth day of creation, when life was commanded to multiply.</note>; the other is **the smallest peak of life** <note>original: "ἀκρότης ἐλαχίστη τῆς ζωῆς" (akrotes elachiste tes zoes)</note>, alluding to the five senses, which the Pythagoreans would easily acknowledge as the lowliest and most fleeting part of life that is capable of perception.

But there are several other names of the Quinary that are, I must confess, irrelevant to the fifth day's work, though it may not be altogether irrelevant to mention them so that no deception is suspected in hiding them. They are intended as notes of either **physical** or **mathematical** observation. The physical ones show how unreliable they are by relying on a supposition that is so **un-Pythagorean**—namely, that there are four elements, an idea that the motion of the Earth naturally breaks to pieces. But yet, based on this **Aristotelian** <note>Referring to the philosophy of Aristotle, who maintained there were four earthly elements and a fifth heavenly one.</note> conceit that there are four, they consider the **Ether** a fifth, and from that, they call the Quinary **Nemesis** <note>original: "Νέμεσις"</note>, as if it distributes the world into these **five orders**: **Earth**, **Water**, **Air**,

Air, Fire, and **Æther** <note>The "fifth element" or quintessence believed by ancients to fill the universe beyond the terrestrial sphere.</note>. Regarding this **fifth** element, they call the **Quinary** <note>The number five (original: "the Quinary").</note> **Pallas** <note>original: "Παλλάς" (Pallas)</note> and **Solitary** <note>original: "Ἄζυξ" (Azyx), meaning unyoked or a virgin</note>, as it is a "virgin-element" that does not mix with the creation of earthly things. It is also called **Immortal** <note>original: "Ἄμβροτος" (Ambroto)</note>, because it is the region of immortality, and **Not of the Flesh** <note>original: "Ἀχρεῶτις" (Achreotis), implying a place where biological needs do not exist</note>, because flesh and blood cannot live there. They also call it **Balanced** <note>original: "Ἀτάλαντος" (Atalantos)</note>, because the bodies of its inhabitants are in equilibrium with the region and do not sink by any weight. Finally, it is called the **Tower of Jupiter** <note>original: "Ζανὸς πύργος" (Zanos pyrgos)</note> because, although Jupiter fills all things, his highest dwelling is the **Æther**. However, this last point is spoken in a way that is not very Pythagorean; for when interpreted through the study of nature, the "Tower of Jupiter" is the **Sun**, not the Æther—the same thing **Aristotle** <note>Ancient Greek philosopher (384–322 BC).</note> calls the **Guard of Jupiter** <note>original: "Διὸς φυλακὴ" (Dios phylake).</note>.

<margin>* On the Heavens, Book 2, Chapter 13.</margin>
<margin>* See chapter 5, section 2, where the Decad (Ten) is called **God** <note>original: "Θεὸς" (Theos).</note></margin>
As for the mathematical names—**Division** <note>original: "Δίχησις" (Dichesis)</note>, **Unpaid** <note>original: "Ἀμισθὸς" (Amisthos)</note>, **Twin** <note>original: "Διδυμαία" (Didymaia)</note>, **Of the Heart** <note>original: "Καρδιάτις" (Kardiatis)</note>, **Circular** <note>original: "Κυκλικός" (Kyklikos)</note>, and **Stable Axis** <note>original: "Ἄξων ἑδραῖα" (Axon hedraia)</note>—all six of these names merely suggest one simple point: that **Five** divides **Ten** into two equal parts, just as a diameter divides a circle, as justice decides equally, and as the heart is in the middle of the body. Truly profound ideas! The names that follow are more significant, namely: **Unconquerable** <note>original: "Ἀνikία" (Anikia)</note>, **Upright** <note>original: "Ὀρθιάτις" (Orthiatis)</note>, **Justice** <note>original: "Δίκη" (Dike)</note>, and **Providence** <note>original: "Πρόνοια" (Pronoia)</note>. All of these refer to Five because it is the **hypotenuse** <note>The longest side of a right-angled triangle.</note> of the first right-angled triangle that has its sides (3, 4, and 5) relating to each other in whole numbers. It is called "Upright" because it spans the right angle; "Unconquerable" because its mathematical power is greater than the powers of either side; "Justice" because it equals the power of both sides combined; <margin>* Aristotle's *Ethics*, book 5, chapter 6.</margin> for **the equal is just** <note>original: "τὸ δ' ἴσον δίκαιον" (to d' ison dikaion).</note>; and finally "Providence" because there is such deliberate design in achieving exactly the same result through means that seemed so different and unlikely to work.

<margin>* Diogenes Laertius, *Life of Pythagoras*.</margin>
6. For this mathematical discovery, **Pythagoras** is said to have **sacrificed a hundred oxen** <note>original: "sacrificed an Hecatomb"</note> to the **Muses** <note>The nine goddesses of the arts and sciences.</note>. This discovery in numbers (which was likely the mother of the one in geometry) so far surpasses the mere numerical trivialities of the **Tetractys** <note>The sacred Pythagorean number ten, made from 1+2+3+4.</note> that if the Tetractys had no deeper meaning than those dry details, Pythagoras's students surely would have chosen to swear by him as the teacher of the **Pentad** <note>The number five.</note> rather than the **Tetrad** <note>The number four.</note>. We are so well assured from every side that it was the nature and mystery of **reality**, not just **numbers**, that was contained in the Pythagorean Tetractys.

<margin>* Johannes Meursius, *The Pythagorean Denary*, chapter 8.</margin>
<margin>* Clement of Alexandria, *Miscellanies*, book 6.</margin>
7. Among the titles belonging to the **Senary** <note>The number six.</note>, the most dry and irrelevant are **Amphitrite** <note>A sea goddess, wife of Poseidon (original: "Ἀμφιτρίτη").</note>, **Near-Justice** <note>original: "Ἀγχιδίκη" (Anchidike)</note>, and **Middle-Way** <note>original: "Μεσόδυς" (Mesodus)</note>. Six is called Amphitrite **because it contains two triads around itself** <note>original: "ὡς ἀμφὶς ἑαυτῆς δύο περιέχουσα τριάδας" (hos amphis heautes dyo periechousa triadas).</note>; it is called "Near-Justice" because it is the number next to the Quinary (Five), which is called "Justice"; and finally it is called "Middle-Way" because it is at an equal distance from 10 and 2—six exceeds two by the same amount (four) that ten exceeds six.

Those names based on the study of nature are **Choir-Division** <note>original: "Διχορονία" (Dichoronia)</note> and **Half of Everything** <note>original: "Ἥμισυ παντός" (Hemisy pantos)</note>. Both of these refer to the signs of the **Zodiac**. The first refers to both the six signs visible in the night and the other six visible in the day (for six signs always rise by night and six by day). The second refers to the division of the world into two halves by the horizon line, with six signs always remaining in each half.

Those names that refer to pagan superstition are **Far-Darter** <note>original: "Ἑκατηβελέτις" (Hekatebeletis)</note>, **Of the Crossroads** <note>original: "Τριοδῖτις" (Trioditis)</note>, and **Three-Formed** <note>original: "Τρίμορφος" (Trimorphos)</note>. These all refer to **Trivia** <note>The Roman name for Hecate, goddess of magic and crossroads, often depicted with three faces.</note>, as she was said to have been born on the sixth day of the month.

<summary>This page explores the Pythagorean symbolism of the numbers five (Quinary) and six (Senary), linking them to the Æther, the geometry of right-angled triangles, and the astronomical division of the Zodiac.</summary>
<keywords>Pythagoras, Quinary, Senary, Æther, Tetractys, geometry, hypotenuse, Zodiac, Hecate, Trivia, Aristotle</keywords>

<margin>Nicomachus of Gerasa, *The Theology of Arithmetic*, book 2.</margin>
8. As for those names of **Aphrodite**, **Zygia**, **Philiosis**, **Philetosia**, **Zygitis**, and **Gamelia** <note>original: *’Αφροδίτη*, *Ζυγία*, *Φιλίωσις*, *Φιλητοσία*, *Ζυγίτις*, *Γαμηλία*. These names relate to love, yoking, friendship, and marriage.</note>, they are all referable to **Marriage** <note>original: *Γάμος* (Gamos)</note>, which we have already taken notice of in our *Defense of the Cabbala*. To which you may also refer **Lachesis** <note>original: *Λάχεσις*; in Greek mythology, the Fate who measured the thread of life.</note>, the spinner of life from birth. To **World** <note>original: *Κόσμος* (Cosmos)</note> also you may refer **Truth**, **Harmony**, and **Self-Sufficiency** <note>original: *’Αλήθεια* (Aletheia), *’Αρμονία* (Harmonia), and *Πανάρκεια* (Panarceia).</note>: the two former as respecting God’s general approbation of all that He had made as **consonant** to His **mind** and **will**; and the last as implying a perfection and self-sufficiency in the world to subsist by virtue of those powers and parts God had framed it of.

9. The titles that follow are more particular, and most of them cannot well be made sense of without reference to Moses’s text. Such are **Beginning**, **Male-Female**, **Form of Forms**, **Soul-maker**, **The Instiller of the Vital Habit**, and **Health** <note>original: *’Αρχὴ* (Arche), *’Ανδρογυναία* (Androgynaia), *Εἶδος εἴδους* (Eidos eidous), *Ψυχοποιὸς* (Psychopoios), *Τῆς ζωτικῆς ἕξεως ἐμποιητική* (Tes zotikes hexews empoietike), and *Ὑγεία* (Hygeia).</note>. For why should **Six** be called **Beginning**, but that Adam’s dominion over the creatures is mentioned on the Sixth Day? **Male-Female** also answers **word-for-word** to *male and female created He them*. And what sense can there be that **Six** is called **Form of Forms**, but that Adam on the sixth day was created the image of the likeness of God? *Let us make man in our image after our likeness*. For this reason, **Clement** and **Philo**
<margin>* Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, book 5.
* In his *Mosaical Creation of the World*.</margin>
also call him **the image of an image** <note>original: *εἰκὼν εἰκόνος* (eikon eikonos)</note>. And why should it be called **Soul-maker** and **The Instiller of the Vital Habit**, but that the creation of man was on the **Sixth** day, and so described by Moses, as that Adam being but a statue of earth, an image of clay at first, God **breathed into him the breath of life, and man became a living soul** <note>original: *καὶ ἐγένετο ἄνθρωπος εἰς ψυχὴν ζῶσαν* (kai egeneto anthropos eis psychen zosan)</note>? And perhaps in this respect also the **Senary** <note>The number six.</note> may be called **Form of Forms**, the soul being the very form of that form or image of earth that God had made. And lastly, it is extremely probable that **Health** refers also to the sound constitution Adam was made in, health being before diseases, according to that song in **Maximus Tyrius**,

->**Health, most venerable of the blessed ones**, &c.<-
<note>original: *’Υγεία πρεσβίστα μακάρων* (Hygeia presbista makaron). Maximus Tyrius was a 2nd-century Greek philosopher.</note>

<margin>Wisdom 1:14.</margin>
And suitably to that in the Book of **Wisdom**, *For God created all things that they might have their being, and the generations of the world were healthful*, etc. Thus it is plain from these instances that Pythagoras's mysteries of numbers had relation to Moses’s text.

10. As for the **Septenary** <note>The number seven.</note>, we produced no names for it, which omission we will now supply. For some of them seem very appropriate and naturally referable to the **Mosaical doctrine**. Such as **Wholeness**, **Bringer of Perfection**, **Inevitable**, and **Fortune** <note>original: *Οὐλομέλεια* (Oulomeleia), *Τελεσφόρος* (Telesphoros), *’Αδράστεια* (Adrasteia), and *Τύχη* (Tyche).</note>. For the **Septenary** may well be called **Wholeness** and **Bringer of Perfection** because it is said on the **seventh** day God ended His work, all things being then entire and perfect. It is also fitly called **Inevitable**,
<margin>See *Philosophic Cabbala*, chapter 2, verses 2, 3.</margin>
**from not acting** <note>original: *παρὰ τὸ μὴ δρᾷν* (para to me dran), *à non agendo*</note>, because God **rested on the seventh day** from all His work. Or if **Adrasteia** <note>The Greek name for the goddess of inevitable fate or Nemesis.</note> signifies the same as **Nemesis**, the sense will be that though God sits still and creates nothing further, yet there is such a law of things in the creation itself that, whether by free agents or by natural ones, no man shall escape punishment; which is suggested by **Adrasteia**, deriving the word **from not escaping** <note>original: *παρὰ τὸ μὴ διδράσκειν* (para to me didraskein), *à non fugiendo*</note>. **Fortune** also has some affinity with this notion, it being a result of God’s resting on the **seventh day**.

But there are also other names, as **Reverence**, **Guardian**, **Opportunity**, and **Dream** <note>original: *Σεβὰς* (Sebas), *Φυλακῖτις* (Phylacitis), *Καιρὸς* (Cairos), *Ὄναρος* (Onaros).</note>.

<summary>This page argues that Pythagorean number symbolism for the numbers six and seven is derived from the Genesis creation account, linking Greek terms like "Form of Forms" and "Inevitable" to Adam's creation and the Sabbath rest.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the author's exploration of Pythagorean number symbolism and its connection to the biblical Creation story in Genesis. Having previously discussed the number six (the Senary), the author now examines the names and mystical meanings associated with the number seven (the Septenary) and begins a new chapter on the number ten (the Denary).</meta>

<header>An Appendix to the Defense CHAPTER 5.</header>

<margin>* See *Philosophic Cabbala*, chapter 2, verse 3.</margin>
The first of these names is a <term>Pythagorean</term> notation of the number **Seven** <note>original: *Ἑπτάς* (Heptas)</note> rather than a new name. It signifies **Worship of the Seven** <note>original: *Cultus Septenarii*</note>, derived from the words **to worship** <note>original: *σέβειν* (sebein)</note> or **an object of worship** <note>original: *σέβασμα* (sebasma)</note>, which corresponds to the passage: *God blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it*. Furthermore, because God so strictly commanded the people **to keep the Sabbath** <note>original: *φυλάξαι τὸ σάββατον* (phylaxai to sabbaton)</note>, it is not improbable that the <term>Septenary</term> <note>The number seven.</note> may be called **The Guardian** <note>original: *Φυλακῖτις* (Phylakitis)</note>. Alternatively, the name may come from the **Watchmen** <note>original: *φύλακες* (phylakes) or *Vigiles*</note>, or **Angels, into whose hands the government of the world is committed during this Sabbath of God**. Lastly, it is called **The Season** <note>original: *Καιρὸς* (Kairos)</note>, **in the highest sense** <note>original: *κατ’ ἐξοχὴν* (kat’ exochen)</note>, because the Seventh day is a sanctified season or opportunity carved out of the whole sum of time to focus our thoughts on the best things and meditate on the wisdom of God. If they called this kind of celebration of holy rest and repose a **Dream** <note>original: *Ὄνειρος* (Oneiros)</note>, it is because such divine contemplations are clearest when the senses of the body are most restricted, similar to what happens during sleep. However, it is more likely that this refers particularly to Joseph's explanation of Pharaoh's dreams of the **seven cows** and the **seven ears of corn**; the history of the Jewish nation, whose philosophy was so sacred to the Pythagoreans, would not have seemed unworthy of their memory.

11. As for the names **Utterance** <note>original: *Ἀυδὴ* (Aude)</note> and **Voice** <note>original: *Φωνὴ* (Phone)</note>, the reason for these is very simple, coming from the seven vowels in the Greek alphabet. **Judgment** <note>original: *Κρίσις* (Krisis)</note> refers to the "critical days" in the course of diseases. **The Horn of Amaltheia** <note>original: *Κέρας Ἀμαλθείας* (Keras Amaltheias); the cornucopia or "horn of plenty."</note> is attributed to the <term>septenary</term> as the number in which the universe is said to be perfected, just as it was attributed to the <term>ternary</term> <note>The number three.</note> regarding the fullness and abundance of the Earth.

The other names are those belonging to either **Pallas Athena** or **Apollo**, both of whom signify the same thing: **Wisdom**. I cannot guarantee that Apollo’s being called **born on the seventh day** <note>original: *ἑβδομαγενὴς* (hebdomagenes)</note> and the Septenary being called **Pallas** did not have their true and original source in this <term>Cabbala</term> <note>A secret or traditional mystical interpretation of the Hebrew Scriptures.</note> of Moses. The most divine wisdom owes its origin to rest and freedom from worldly tasks, which God commands His people to cease from on the Seventh day. Thus, the more we consider those names of the <term>Pythagorean numbers</term> that correspond to the Days of Creation, the more we find them fit and applicable to Moses’s text.

# CHAPTER 5. Of the Philosophic Cabbala.

1. We are not at all concerned with the **Octonary** <note>The number eight.</note> and **Novenary** <note>The number nine.</note>, as they have no reference to any of the **Days of the Creation**. However, the **Denary** <note>The number ten.</note> is so closely connected to the **Quaternary** <note>The number four.</note>—in that ten is the sum or "power" of the first four numbers ($1+2+3+4=10$)—that it would be a blameworthy omission if I did not bring all its titles into view. I have already observed the appropriateness and significance of the names **The World** <note>original: *Κόσμος* (Kosmos)</note>, **Heaven** <note>original: *Οὐρανὸς* (Ouranos)</note>, **Full Perfection** <note>original: *Παντέλεια* (Panteleia)</note>, and **The All** <note>original: *Τὸ πᾶν* (To pan)</note>. 

Of the remaining titles, those least relevant to our purpose are <margin>* Johannes Meursius, *The Denary*, chapter 12.</margin> **The First Quadrature** <note>original: *Πρῶτος τετραγωνισμὸς* (Protos tetragonismos)</note>, **Mnemosyne** <note>The personification of Memory.</note>, and **Memory**. It is called **The First Quadrature** (or the first squaring) only because it is composed of the first four numbers: 1, 2, 3, and 4. It is adorned with the title of **Mnemosyne** because she is the mother of the nine Muses; and these shallow **false-Pythagoreans**, it seems, thought it a clever thing to assign one of the daughters to each of the other nine numbers within the **Denary**. However, they have placed the **Mother** at both the **rear** and the **front** of the sequence; so inconsistent are they in these worthless foolishness. I do not need to point out that **Memory** <note>original: *Μνήμη* (Mneme)</note> was simply added as a synonym for **Mnemosyne**.

2. But the rest of the titles for the **Denary**, or **Decad**, are not such rubbish. Instead, they reflect—as the **Decad** should, being the power of the **Tetrad** <note>The number four.</note>—upon the **Fourth Day’s** Creation, which was the organizing of the **Universe** into form, shape, and right order. Therefore, just as this **number ten** (as I noted before) was called **The World** for the broadness of the title, I believe the following names are related to this concept: **Fate** <note>original: *Εἱμαρμένη* (Heimarmene)</note>, **The Heavenly** <note>original: *Οὐρανία* (Ourania)</note>, **Eternity** <note>original: *Αἰὼν* (Aion)</note>, **Power** <note>original: *Κράτος* (Kratos)</note>, **Necessity** <note>original: *Ἀνάγκη* (Ananke)</note>, **Atlas**, **Untiring** <note>original: *Ἀκάμας* (Akamas)</note>, **The All-Souled** <note>original: *Πάμψυχος* (Pampsychos)</note>, and **God** <note>original: *Θεὸς* (Theos)</note>. From this last name, the **Quinary** <note>The number five.</note> is also called <margin>* See also chapter 1, section 8, and chapter 8, section 7.</margin> **Pure** <note>original: *Ἀμιδὴς* (Amides)</note>. All of these titles have a comprehensive meaning.

**Fate** and **Necessity** suggest the laws of destiny and the fixed order of the Universe; and **The Heavenly** suggests the celestial music or harmony of that Order (assuming it wasn't just thrown in as one of the nine Muses to fill space). **Eternity**, **Power**, **Atlas**, and **Untiring** denote the permanence and stable endurance of the world, showing there is no fear that it will ever fail by its own nature. This sense matches the expressions in the **Pythagorean Oath**: **The source and root of ever-flowing nature** <note>original: *Πηγή, ῥίζωμά τε ἀενάου φύσεως* (Pege, rhizoma te aenaou physeos)</note>. **Ever-flowing nature** plainly corresponds to **Eternity** <note>original: *Αἰὼν* (Aion)</note>, which is the same as saying **Always being** <note>original: *ἀεὶ ὢν* (aei on)</note>; while **Power**, **Atlas**, and **Untiring** correspond to the **Root** and **Source**. For these four—namely, **The Spirit of Nature**, **Suns**, **Planets**, and **Vortices**—are rightly said to be everything these names express. The agreement is exact: just as the **Tetrad** and **Decad** are actually the same **Tetractys** <note>A mystical triangular figure of ten points arranged in four rows, symbolizing the organization of the universe.</note>, so their names also carry the same weight and point to the same things. 

Finally, **God** and **The All-Souled** (if **The All-Souled** is **The Lord** <note>original: *ὁ Κύριος* (ho Kyrios)</note>, as the scholar Hesychius translates it) harmonize with the same idea. They are most clearly understood from these **four lines by the Sibyl** <note>Ancient female prophets; here referring to the Sibylline Oracles.</note>:

> ->I am He who is (consider this in your heart);<-
> ->I am clothed in heaven, and wrapped in the sea;<-
> ->The Earth is the support for my feet; around my body flows<-
> ->The Air, and the dance of the stars runs around me on every side.<-

This is also the sense found in <margin>* Plotinus, *Enneads*, Book 2, chapter 3, section 10.</margin> **Plotinus**: **God is the whole when the separate soul is included; but the rest is a great spirit, and the passive elements within**

<sig>P p p</sig>
<meta>catchword: him (original Greek: ἀυτῷ)</meta>

# An Appendix to the Defence CHAP. V.

...demons to him. <note>original: "αὐτῷ δαιμόνια" (autō daimonia). This is the conclusion of a Greek passage from the previous page.</note> It is so evident that all those names respect the whole universe in all its features.

<margin>
* See Philo Judaeus, *On Dreams*.

3. But there is something so sacred in those *Sibylline* verses <note>A collection of oracular utterances written in Greek hexameters ascribed to the Sibyls, prophetesses who uttered divine revelations in a frenzied state.</note> that I cannot let them pass without further observation. Though this may seem somewhat like a digression, it is not altogether irrelevant to our present purpose. I do not doubt that the *Sibyl*, in this description, alludes to the priestly vestments of *Aaron*. *Philo Judaeus* <note>A Hellenistic Jewish philosopher from Alexandria (c. 20 BCE – 50 CE) who sought to harmonize the Torah with Greek philosophy.</note> makes Aaron a type or figure of the only-begotten Son of God, whom he calls **the first-born of God** <note>original: "τὸν πρωτόγονον Θεοῦ" (ton prōtogonon Theou)</note> and **the divine Word** <note>original: "τὸν θεῖον λόγον" (ton theion logon)</note>. He makes him the eternal High Priest of this vast temple, the universe, and styles him **the image of Him who is** <note>original: "εἰκόνα τοῦ ὄντος" (eikona tou ontos)</note>—the image of *Jehovah* and the maker of the world: **The Word is the image of God, through whom the whole world was created** <note>original: "Λόγος δέ ἐστιν εἰκὼν Θεοῦ δι᾽ οὗ σύμπας ὁ κόσμος ἐδημιουργεῖτο" (Logos de estin eikōn Theou di' hou sympas ho kosmos edēmiourgeito)</note>. 

And yet, in a complex sense, Philo also makes the universe itself the Son of God. After a detailed description of the meaning of *Aaron’s* vestments and priestly ornaments—where he argues that the two precious stones on his shoulders signify the two hemispheres (each having six names of the Tribes, just as the hemispheres have six signs apiece divided by the horizon); the twelve stones in the breastplate signify the twelve signs of the Zodiac, arranged in four groups of three to denote the four seasons of the year; his blue robe to symbolize the air; the flower-work at its hem to symbolize the earth; the **pomegranates** <note>original: "Ῥοίσκοι" (rhoiskoi). Philo links this to the word "rheō" (to flow).</note> to symbolize water; and the bells to represent the harmonious mixture of water and earth for the purpose of generation—he finally adds this reason for the attire: **So that in the sacred rites, the whole world might minister together with him** <note>original: "Ὅπως ἐν ταῖς ἱερουργίαις συλλειτουργῇ πᾶς ὁ κόσμος αὐτῷ" (Hopōs en tais hierourgiais sylleitourgē pas ho kosmos autō)</note>. 

To this, he immediately adds: "For it is most fit for him who supplicates the Father **to bring in the one who begot him for his service** <note>original: "καὶ τὸν ἐπάγεσθαι πρὸς θεραπείαν γεγεννηκότος" (kai ton epagesthai pros therapeian gegennēkotos)</note>," as if the universe were the Son of God. This saying is unsound unless he whom Philo elsewhere calls the "first-born of God" and the **Divine Logos** is included to make the concept complete.

<margin>
* Pomegranates.
Philo, *Life of Moses*.
</margin>

For thus it will appear that the **Divine Logos** is the true High Priest indeed, whose garments are (according to those verses of the *Sibyl*) all the parts of the universe; and that *Aaron* was but a figure of him. Furthermore, the phrase **I am He who is** <note>original: "Εἰμί δ᾽ ἐγὼ ὁ ἐών" (Eimi d' egō ho eōn)</note> corresponds to the engraving of the four letters <note>The Tetragrammaton (YHWH), the name of God.</note> in the golden plate upon the front of *Aaron's* mitre, which *Philo* says was **the name of Him who is** <note>original: "ὄνομα τοῦ ὄντος" (onoma tou ontos)</note>. The *Sibyl’s* phrase **He who is** <note>original: "ὁ ἐών" (ho eōn)</note> reflects this, and by it was understood **Jehovah the Son** <note>original: "Jehova Filius"</note>. 

When the Sibyl says, **I am clothed in the heavens** <note>original: "οὐρανὸν ἐνδέδυμαι" (ouranon endedymai)</note>, it refers to Aaron's blue robe. This is not merely the "air," but rather that part of the "heavens" which lies between the Sun and any planet or Earth in the same **vortex** <note>In Cartesian physics, a vortex was a large whirlpool of celestial matter that carried the planets around the sun.</note>. Similarly, those pomegranates are not just "water," but the whole globe of Earth and water, which is found everywhere at the lowest parts or hem of this blue garment of the eternal *Aaron*. These pomegranates fitly represent the **seminal fullness** <note>The reproductive or creative potential.</note> of the Earth, the mother of all things. Because there are many of them, they suggest the plurality of Earths or planets in their respective vortices. 

Nor does the scarlet interwoven in the **Ephod** <note>A ceremonial vest worn by the Jewish High Priest.</note> and **Breastplate** signify the element of fire, as *Philo* would suggest; rather, the texture of scarlet and purple with gold and white silk, of which the Ephod and Breastplate consisted, denotes the intense heat and shining light of the Sun. This is what the **Pythagoreans** call **the fire established in the center** <note>original: "τὸ πῦρ ἐν μέσῳ ἱδρυμένον" (to pyr en mesō hidrymenon)</note>.

<summary>This page discusses how Philo Judaeus interpreted the vestments of the High Priest Aaron as symbols of the entire universe and the Divine Logos. The author critiques Philo's interpretation, arguing that these garments represent a "vortex" cosmology and identify the Logos as the true High Priest whose "clothing" is the cosmos.</summary>

# CHAP. V. of the Philosophic Cabbala.

Since the Ephod and Breastplate have their place in the middle of the body—which is the region of the heart, the "Sun" of the lesser world <note>The "lesser world" or microcosm refers to the human body, which philosophers often compared to the "greater world" or macrocosm (the universe).</note>—and lastly, the *Tunica Ocellata*, or robe of "eye-work," as I may call it, reached further than the blue robe (even as far as possible), it is apparent that it represented the starry heaven. The stars are fitly compared to eyes, as Plato elegantly compared them in his well-known couplet:

->“You gaze at the stars, my star; I wish I were the heavens, to look at you with many eyes.” <note>original: "᾿Αστέρας εἰσαθρεῖς ἀστὴρ ἐμός, &c." (Asteras eisathreis astēr emos). This is a famous epigram attributed to Plato.</note><-

And though the Earth in the *Sibyl* <note>Referring to the Sibylline Oracles mentioned on the previous page.</note> is called "a support for the feet," <note>original: "γαῖα... στήριγμα ποδῶν" (gaia... stērigma podōn)</note> yet because it is said to be "poured around the body," <note>original: "περὶ σῶμα κεχύσθαι" (peri sōma kechysthai)</note> it implies the loose flowing of it, like those pomegranates at the hem of the priestly robe. Nor can the air be said "to run around everywhere" <note>original: "περιδραμεῖν πάντῃ" (peridramein pantē)</note> (which certainly here means "in every direction") <note>original: "πανταχῆ" (pantachē)</note> so closely joined with the chorus of the planets, unless it implies the mobility and plurality of Earths; which therefore clarifies the meaning of the previous verse.

<margin>Exodus 28:34</margin>
But regarding the fact that there is *a golden bell and a pomegranate, a golden bell and a pomegranate*, no better sense can be made than what Philo has given in another place: <margin>* Philo, *On Monarchy*.</margin> "The bells represent the harmony, symphony, and resonance of the parts of the universe." <note>original: "Τὴν δ᾿ ἁρμονίαν καὶ συμφωνίαν καὶ συνήχησιν τῶν τοῦ κόσμου μερῶν οἱ κώδωνες ἐμφαίνουσιν"</note> For this reason, the Pythagoreans called the *Tetractys* "Harmony." <note>original: "῾Αρμονία" (Harmonia). The Tetractys is a triangular figure of ten points, symbolizing the organizational deck of the universe.</note> And that ridiculous rumor of Pythagoras’s <margin>* Macrobius, *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio*, Book 2, Chapter 1.</margin> "music of the spheres" was, without question, nothing but the poorly reflected echo of the sound of these golden bells hanging on Aaron’s robe. For Pythagoras held no belief in physical celestial spheres at all, but was misunderstood because he spoke the mystical language of Jewish philosophy. He was also misunderstood in the mystery of numbers; the world generally imagined that he made numbers the actual principles of all things, whereas he understood them only as symbols of things. But Aristotle attacks this opinion <margin>* Aristotle, *Metaphysics*, Book 13, Chapters 3, 4, 5, 6.</margin> as if Pythagoras seriously held it, providing as much amusement to intelligent bystanders as if they saw someone fiercely charging his lance against a suit of armor, mistaking it for a living soldier. But this is only an aside; we will return to the business at hand.

4. The phrase "that the whole world joins in the liturgy," <note>original: "πᾶς ὁ κόσμος συλλειτουργῇ" (pas ho kosmos sylleitourgē)</note> which I cited above from Philo, is to be understood in a complex way, also including the *Eternal Logos*. This is plain from a parallel passage where Philo, again describing the priestly vestments, speaks as before: <margin>Philo, *On the Life of Moses*.</margin> "In this way the High Priest, having been so adorned, is prepared for the sacred rites, so that when he enters to offer prayers, the whole world may enter with him." <note>original: "Τοῦτον τὸν τρόπον ὁ ἀρχιερεὺς ἀγηκοσμηθεὶς στέλλεται πρὸς τὰς ἱερουργίας, ἵν᾿ ὅταν εἰσίῃ τὰς εὐχὰς ποιησόμενος, συνεισέρχηται πᾶς ὁ κόσμος αὐτῷ"</note> In the conclusion of this passage, he expressly includes "the Word that contains and governs the whole." <note>original: "τὸ σύμπαν συνέχοντα καὶ διοικοῦντα λόγον" (to sympan synechonta kai dioikounta logon)</note> He immediately adds: "For it is necessary for him who would supplicate the Father of the world to use as an intercessor a Son perfect in virtue, for the forgiveness of sins and the supply of most abundant blessings." <note>original: "παρακλήτῳ χρῆσθαι τελειοτάτῳ τὴν ἀρετὴν υἱῷ, πρός τε ἀμνηστείαν ἁμαρτημάτων καὶ χορηγίαν ἀφθονωτάτων ἀγαθῶν." (paraklētō chrēsthai teleiotatō tēn aretēn huiō...)</note> Given this, it is no wonder that the *Decad* (the number ten), which is the symbol of the universe, is called "God" <note>original: "Θεός" (Theos)</note> by the Pythagoreans; this is the specific point I was aiming at.

But the most admirable thing to consider is the exquisite reason why the *Eternal Logos*—who was the Framer of the World and is, as it were, clothed in His own work—is considered the true High Priest according to this symbolic type of Aaron. For who is so fit and effectual an intercessor

...for [he pleads] with the Father for the faults and offenses of the world as the one who made it, and in whose heart is contained the blueprint <note>original: "Platform"</note> of it. He is the one who thoroughly understands why certain unholy or imperfect events or passages occasionally occur, which are not as desirable as one might wish. Out of his perfect knowledge of the nature of things, he can clearly plead that various unfortunate emergencies are unavoidable due to that *Incompossibility* and *Incommensurability* <term>Incompossibility refers to things that cannot exist together; incommensurability refers to things that cannot be measured by the same standard. Here, the author suggests the physical world is inherently imperfect compared to the divine plan.</term> that is immovably embedded in that stubborn and unrefined matter <term>original: "Hyle" (Greek: hūlē), the ancient philosophical term for the fundamental "stuff" or primal matter of the universe, often seen as resistant to divine order.</term>.

Besides, by presenting himself in his priestly <note>original: "Sacerdotal"</note> vestments—which represent the structure <note>original: "Compages"</note> and harmonious fitting of all the parts of the *Universe*—he also, in a special manner, pleads for the particular failures of a few parts, since the rest of the parts of Creation are so healthy and lovely. Those parts that are out of order are no more than a passing discord in good music, which makes the next note sound even sweeter. It is as if he should argue to his Father that, taking one thing with another and viewing the outcomes and completions <note>original: "Periods"</note> of all things together, everything is in a way acceptable and good. Even those parts that seem most dark and dismal, it is the prerogative of the Sovereign *Goodness* to bring light out of them, and for those to whom much is forgiven, their love will also be great.

<margin>Baruch 3:35–37.</margin>
I have no doubt that *Aaron* symbolized such a High Priest as this in his priestly garments. This serves as a special confirmation of the divinity of our blessed Savior:
> *This is our God, and none other shall be held in comparison to him. He has found out all the ways of knowledge, and has given it to Jacob his servant, and to Israel his beloved. Afterward, he showed himself upon Earth, and lived among men.* <note>These verses from the Book of Baruch (in the Apocrypha) were frequently cited by early Christian writers as a prophecy of the Incarnation of Christ.</note>

He appeared as a prelude in the Cloud and in the Bush, but fully and completely by being incarnated of the blessed Virgin. *Aaron* also represented both of Christ's natures: his Divine nature through his priestly vestments, which could symbolize no clothing but that of God; and his human nature in his own person, *Aaron* being merely a man.

And yet, because he was to represent the person of him who was truly God, the Lord *Jesus*, there were some rules <note>original: "injunctions"</note>, or rather privileges, placed upon him that assumed he was, in a sense, elevated above human nature. Upon considering this, *Philo* <note>Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BC – 50 AD), a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher who used allegorical interpretation to fuse Greek philosophy with Jewish scripture.</note> breaks out into expressions that are as descriptive of the condition of Christ—the *God-man* <note>original: "Θεάνθρωπος" (Theanthrōpos)</note> and true High Priest—as any that can be spoken:

->“For the Law intends that the High Priest should share in a nature greater than human, approaching closer to the Divine, or (to speak accurately) to be the boundary between both; so that through a mediator partaking of both natures, people might appease God, and God, by using his ministry, may reach out and provide the supplies of His grace to mankind.” <note>original Greek: Βούλεται γὰρ ὁ νόμος τὸν ἀρχιερέα μείζονος μεμοιρᾶσθαι φύσεως ἢ κατ' ἄνθρωπον, ἐγγυτέρω προσιόντα τῆς θείας, μεθόριον, εἰ δεῖ τἀληθὲς λέγειν, ἀμφοῖν· ἵνα διὰ μέσου τινὸς ἄνθρωποι μὲν ἱλάσκωνται θεόν, θεὸς δὲ τὰς χάριτας ἀνθρῶποις ὑποδιακόνῳ τινὶ χρώμενος ὀρέγῃ καὶ χορηγῇ.</note><-

So clearly is the divinity of Christ foreshadowed in the Law of *Moses*.

# CHAPTER V. Concerning the Philosophical Cabbala.

<sig>Ppp 3</sig>

...more pardonable. For it is not a mere digression, but an explanation <note>original: "Exposition"</note> of what I had alleged to prove the meaning of *God* <note>original: "Θεὸς" (Theos)</note>, one of the names of the *Decad* <term>Decad: The number ten. In Pythagorean philosophy, ten was considered the most perfect number because it contains all the numerical building blocks of the universe.</term> that refers to the *integral* or more *universal features* <note>original: "Lineaments"</note> of the world.

5. But *Sun* <note>original: "Ἥλιος" (Helios)</note>, and *Revealer* <note>original: "Φάνης" (Phanes)</note>, and *Sphere* <note>original: "Σφαῖρα" (Sphaira)</note> may very well particularly hint at the *Lights* made on the *Fourth day*. These are not without the whirling of the round *Vortices* <term>Vortices: In 17th-century physics, it was believed that planets were carried around the sun by "whirlpools" of invisible matter.</term>, which is suggested by the name *Sphere*. And lastly, *Key-bearer* <note>original: "Κλαδοῦχος" (Kladouchos)</note>, (which was also the name of the *Tetrad* <term>Tetrad: The number four.</term>), I conceive that they all refer to the *Tradition of the Tetractys* <term>Tetractys: A sacred Pythagorean symbol consisting of ten points arranged in a triangle of four rows (1+2+3+4=10), representing the harmony of the universe.</term>. That is, they refer to the *opening of the mystery of Creation* by unfolding the properties of that number applicable to the *Fourth Day's* work. This is seen more as a *general sketch* of the *Universe* than as a description of the literal things said to be created on the Fourth Day. 

But the names of the *Decad* (which is the direct power of the *Tetrad*) plainly imply that the *Fourth Day* encompasses the *whole Creation*. All those names tend in that direction; otherwise, they are drily and ridiculously forced upon the number without such a reference. For why should the *Decad* be called *Sun*, *Revealer*, *Fate* <note>original: "Εἱμαρμένη" (Heimarmene)</note>, *Necessity* <note>original: "Ἀνάγκη" (Ananke)</note>, *Eternity* <note>original: "Αἰών" (Aion)</note>, etc., unless it refers to the law and order of the *Universe*, and its furnishing with suns and planets? 

The *Decad*, being the sum of all simple numbers, may be a symbol of the *Universe*. On that account, it is called *Heaven* <note>original: "Οὐρανὸς" (Ouranos)</note>, *World* <note>original: "Κόσμος" (Kosmos)</note>, *The All* <note>original: "Τὸ πᾶν" (To Pan)</note>, and *Perfect Completion* <note>original: "Παντέλεια" (Panteleia)</note>, and also *Sphere*. This is also because of the *recycling* <note>original: "ἀνακύκλωσις" (anakyklosis)</note> or *revolution* in counting from *ten* to *ten* again, and so *forever*, as is easy to observe. Yet, if there were no further purpose or more serious reference to something else, the mere comparison of this number *ten* to the *world* or a *sphere* would be a very lifeless and trivial thing.

<margin>The number ten is the greatest according to the Pythagoreans, being the Tetractys, etc. —*Athenagoras, Apology for Christians*.</margin>

6. In brief, therefore, the *Cabbala* of the *Decad* or *Tetractys* (for they are all one, as *Athenagoras* has observed) is called *Key-bearer* for two reasons. First, because it was the *explanation* of that part of the *Mosaic* Creation which was most closely locked up. 

Admitting a *philosophical* sense of the text, the *first* day's Creation consists only of *immaterial beings* (as the *Monad* <term>Monad: The number one, representing unity and the divine mind.</term> naturally implies). If this is true, it follows that the *Earth* is not mentioned as being created at all, unless it can be placed in the *Fourth day*. Moreover, the text also says generally of the *Lights* that were made, *That they were to be for signs and for seasons and for days and years*. This hardly makes good sense if applied to each light individually, because these roles would overlap in some. Nor can it be an enumeration of the jobs or properties belonging to every one of the lights of Heaven, unless there are planets or Earths orbiting all the *Suns* (which we usually call fixed stars). 

Yet these things are so faintly and obscurely hinted at, and that individual sense—though more harsh and improper—is so far possible, that the work of the *Fourth* day will seem only like a particular creation of the lights of heaven as they are commonly understood, unless we are warned otherwise by some knowledgeable *Guide to the Mysteries* <note>original: "Mystagogus"</note>. And therefore, because the meaning lacks such clarity...

Because of this, the *Cabbala* of the *Tetractys* <term>Tetractys: A sacred Pythagorean symbol of ten points arranged in a triangle, representing the organization of the universe.</term>, or the traditional explanation <note>original: "Explication"</note> of the *Fourth* day's work, must be acknowledged to be rightly titled *Key-bearer* <note>original: "Κλειδῦχος" (Kleidouchos)</note>, as being the opener of the most concealed mysteries of the Creation.

7. And then secondly, the *Tetractys*, in reference to the nature of the number itself and its properties (though it be but a trifle, and such as *Lucian* <note>Lucian of Samosata: A 2nd-century satirist known for mocking philosophy and religion.</note> might justly mock if there were no further usefulness in it), may well be called *Key-bearer*, in that it is so elegantly and expressly expressive <note>original: "significative"</note> of the *Cabbala* of the *Fourth* day's Creation. And indeed, the analogy here between the sign and the thing signified is admirable: for as the *Fourth* day's Creation in its external appearance is but part of the Creation allotted to the *Fourth* day, as other parts are to other days, in a more hidden <note>original: "recondite"</note> meaning it is indeed the fashioning and ordering of the whole *Universe*, the framing of it into *Suns*, *Planets*, and *Vortices* <term>Vortices: In 17th-century physics, these were giant whirlpools of ethereal matter that carried planets around stars.</term>. Similarly, the *Tetractys* or *Four*, the symbol of this, is at first view but one certain number, part of the *Decad* <term>Decad: The number ten.</term>, but in the hidden power contained within it, it is the whole *Decad*—since 1, 2, 3, and 4 put together make up *Ten*.

<margin>* Section 3.</margin>
To which you may add, that as the work of the *Fourth day* seems at first view to be only the *making of Lights*, whose rays are received in a *pyramidal* form, whereas it was indeed the *framing of the World* and the arranging of it into so many round *Vortices*; so the *Tetrad* or *Tetractys* in its obvious nature is only the *first pyramid* (for *four* is the first pyramidal number), but in its more abstruse power it is a *Sphere*, as was noted above.

And lastly, as the *Fourth day's* Creation seems only to respect the visible and material world according to the external sense, but necessarily implies an immaterial principle ordering matter into that frame of things; so the *Tetrad* is only *feminine* in its open or exterior nature, but in its parts, by which it grows into a *Decad*, it is both *masculine* and *feminine*. Both 1 and 3 (as *Zaratas* <term>Zaratas: An ancient name for Zoroaster, the Persian prophet, whom some Renaissance thinkers believed taught Pythagoras.</term> would have it) are *masculine*, and 2 and 4 are *feminine*. Just as in the more complex *Tetractys* of 36, there are four *masculine* numbers (1, 3, 5, 7) and four *feminine* (2, 4, 6, 8). This, as in the former consideration, suggests the necessity of joining the *active* and *passive* principles in the *Fourth* day's work—that is, in the fabric of the *Universe*. But because the composition of these parts adds up to *thirty-six*, which is a "circular number" in an easier sense than *ten*, it may be suggested that the whole six days of Creation are comprised together in the fourth, and that the framing of the world is done by the rotation <note>original: "circumgyration"</note> of the ethereal matter into repeated *Vortices*. But this complex *Tetractys* does not belong to this present investigation <note>original: "inquisition"</note>. The analogy between the simple Tetrad and the Fourth Day's Creation in the philosophical sense is so perfectly clear that I think it is apparent by now why it has gained the title of *Key-bearer* among the *Pythagoreans*, its very property so fitly opening the right meaning of the *Work of the Fourth Day*.
