<meta>This page continues the author’s argument that the names and properties attributed to numbers by the Pythagoreans—specifically the number ten (the Decad) and the number four (the Tetrad)—are not arbitrary, but are keys to understanding the "Natural Cabbala" or the physical structure of the universe as described in the Fourth Day of Creation.</meta>

### CHAPTER 5: On the Philosophic Cabbala.

The Fourth Day was intended chiefly and more directly as a universal *Natural Cabbala*, the great principles <note>original: "Theorems"</note> of *Nature* being contained there, just as the *Metaphysical principles* were in the *First Day's Work* and in the two following Chapters. Based on these considerations, the reason is clear for all those names given to the *Denarius* <term>Denarius: In Pythagorean numerology, the number ten.</term> which signify the *Universal Law* or the *Structure of Nature* <note>original: "Compages of Nature"</note>, which must be assigned to the *Fourth Day*, since there is no *Tenth Day* of Creation to assign them to. And *Ten* is the *Tetractys* <term>Tetractys: A sacred Pythagorean symbol representing the number ten (1+2+3+4), often depicted as a triangle of ten points.</term> as well as the *Tetrad* <term>Tetrad: The number four.</term> itself. <margin>* Plutarch, *On Isis and Osiris*.</margin> Just as *Thirty-Six* is called the *Tetractys*, as are the first four *masculine* numbers and first four *feminine* numbers from which it results.

<margin>* See Johannes Meursius, *The Pythagorean Denarius*, chapter 11.</margin>
9. Regarding why the *Decad* <term>Decad: The number ten.</term> should also be called *Pruner* <note>original: "Κλαδεύς" (Kladeús), from a root meaning to branch or prune.</note>, the reason is very easy and natural if we refer to the *Fourth Day's Cabbala*. For by grasping that root or trunk, so to speak, we also grasp the branches. For the Cabbala of the *Tetractys* will naturally branch out into the consideration of the first, second, and third days, as well as the fifth, sixth, and seventh days; the nature of the *World* cannot be rightly understood without including them as well, as they are the *Branches* <note>original: "Κλάδοι" (Kladoi)</note>, the sprigs or branches on either side of the Cabbala of the *Fourth Day*.

10. And as for that third and last name, *Faith* <note>original: "Πίςις" (Pistis)</note>, it is a further argument that the names of the *Decad* refer to the *Fourth Day*. It suggests that the *Decad* is also that very *Tetractys* by whose inventor and communicator *Pythagoras* and his followers were said to swear; for the *Decad* is called *Faith* just as the *Tetractys* is called an *Oath* <note>original: "Ορκος" (Horkos)</note>, and *Faith* is the assurance given by an oath. For *to pledge faith* <note>original: "πίςιν ἐπιτιθέναι" (pistin epitithenai)</note> is the same as to swear an oath in the *Greek language*. So strangely and easily do things align everywhere, naturally coming together in a joint confirmation of the truth of the *Philosophic Cabbala*. It is clearly evident what special reason *Pythagoras* had to mention the *Tetrad* rather than the *Pentad* <term>Pentad: The number five.</term>, or any other number, in that form of swearing by him who first shared the *Cabbala*. For if the mystery had ended in the numbers themselves, and had not been the symbols and repositories of some real knowledge of *Natural* or *Divine* things, the *Pentad* would have deserved the fame of an oath more than the *Tetractys*, as I suggested above. <margin>* Chapter 4, section 6.</margin>

To conclude generally regarding the *Pythagorean Names* of numbers, I dare appeal to anyone whether I have not gained a hundred times more ground than I have lost by being held to this strict account. I ask whether there has not been a large addition of very relevant names to those I had previously produced, as well as a clear discovery of how those names entered the *Pythagorean Titles* that are not relevant to our present *Cabbala*. This precise account cannot help but give complete satisfaction to all those who know when to be satisfied.

### CHAPTER VI.

1. *The Second Objection, regarding the unsuitableness of the Pythagorean Philosophy to the Jewish Cabbala, which makes no mention of the Motion of the Earth; along with the first answer to it.* 2. *A second answer, showing how easily—if not inevitably—the Motion of the Earth could have been lost from the Jewish Cabbala.* 3. *Regardless, there is that in the Jewish Cabbala which necessarily implies the Motion of the Earth.* 4. *The Ancient Sages of the Jews held the Motion of the Earth, as shown by Pythagoras having drawn his doctrine from that source.* 5. *That* Numa Pompilius <note>The second king of Rome, traditionally associated with religious and cultural foundations.</note> *was descended from the Jews.* 6. *And that the Temple he built to* Vesta <note>The Roman goddess of the hearth; the author argues the design of her temple represented the sun at the center of the universe.</note> *is proof he held the Earth's Motion.*

The second objection against our *Cabbala* <term>Cabbala: Here referring to a secret or traditional oral interpretation of the scriptures, which the author believes contains ancient scientific truths.</term> is based on the incompleteness <note>original: "Maimedness"</note> of the doctrine that I claim to be *Jewish* or *Mosaic*. This doctrine is supposed to consist of two main parts: *the Motion of the Earth* (along with the things necessarily involved in it) and the *Preexistence of the Soul*. The first part, the objectors say, is not found in *Jewish* writings. To this I answer:

First, it is beneath the true ambition <note>original: "Generosity"</note> of my design merely to apply to the text of *Moses* those truths that remain in the writings of the *Jews* and might be considered relics of the ancient *Cabbala*. Rather, my ultimate goal, through the method I have taken, was to restore to their knowledge that noble part of their *Cabbala* which was lost, yet which *Pythagoras* once received from their ancestors—as is abundantly confirmed by the testimonies of historians. Truly, this *physical* part of the *Cabbala* which I have applied fits the text of *Moses* so well and adheres to it so closely—not only regarding the things themselves but also through the consideration of the names and properties of *Pythagorean* numbers—that by this device <note>original: "Artifice"</note> (like iron clamps holding a structure together), both parts of the *Cabbala* are joined so firmly into one that it is obvious to any impartial <note>original: "indifferent"</note> eye that the whole *Cabbala* is of a single structure and piece, and belongs entirely to the text of *Moses*.

2. And then, secondly, I ask: what is the *physical* part of the *Jewish Cabbala* if it is not this? (For they will not deny that *Moses* philosophizes in this first chapter of *Genesis*.) What other principles, so great and so true, can they apply to his text as I have? If they answer that such principles did exist and were applicable, but are now lost, I say that the very fact the *physical* part was lost is a strong <note>original: "shrewd"</note> indication that this is the very part we have recovered. No part of the *Cabbala* was as likely to be lost as this, because it is much harder to teach someone the *Pythagorean* system of the world than the *Preexistence of the Soul*. This is evident because it was a piece of philosophy too large for the capacity of *Aristotle* himself; though he could name the opinion and attribute it to the *Pythagoreans*, he could not accept <note>original: "close with"</note> it. For the prejudice of the senses is great against it, and then the philosophical and mathematical—

# CHAPTER VI. of the Philosophic Cabbala.

Mathematical preparations are much more extensive than what is required for receiving the doctrine of the Soul’s *Preexistence*. This is why, although *Platonism* is derived from *Pythagoreanism*, it has left out the theory of the Earth’s *Motion*. Indeed, the *Pythagoreans* themselves

<note>original: "Τᾶ δ’ ἐν μένῳ ἱδρυμῴα, ἑςίᾳ Θεῶν, ὅρος τε ὄρφνας καὶ ἡμέρας γίνεται."</note> That which is established in the middle, the hearth of the Gods, becomes the boundary of darkness and day. Timaeus Locrus, *On the Soul of the World*.
</margin>
had lost it over time, as appears in *Timaeus Locrus* <note>A Pythagorean philosopher to whom a treatise on the world-soul was attributed.</note>, *Apollonius Tyaneus*, and in some of the titles the *Pythagoreans* gave to their numbers.

And yet even fewer *Jews* than *Pagans* would be found capable of receiving this part of the *Cabbala*. For them, it was necessary not only to have the preparations required for the other doctrines, but also a special resilience to endure seeing the *Cortex* <term>Cortex: The outer shell or literal meaning of a text.</term> of the *Mosaic* letter break into pieces, so to speak, in order to give up this hidden kernel for them to feed upon. Meanwhile, they could be taught the *Preexistence* of the *Soul* with little or no violence to the outward letter of *Moses*—that is to say, to its literal sense. Therefore, the fact that the *Motion of the Earth* has been lost and does not appear in the remains of the *Jewish Cabbala* is no argument against it having once been a part of it.

And fourthly and lastly, that they did expressly hold the *motion of the Earth* is, in my view, sufficiently proven already by what I have produced to show that *Pythagoras* was either a *Jew* himself, or at least received his doctrine from the *Jews*. It is no wonder, as I have already noted, that time wore it away, or let it sink and be lost, since there were so few who were fit or who felt concerned enough to receive it.

# An Appendix to the Defense CHAPTER VI.

(On this last point) although the reputation of this part of the *Cabbala* <term>Cabbala: Also spelled Kabbalah; here referring to a secret, oral tradition of mystical or scientific knowledge passed down from Moses.</term> is almost extinct among the *Jews*, the idea that it was once the hidden doctrine of the scholars of that nation seems sufficiently credible to me based on what *Plutarch* writes about *Numa Pompilius*. Numa's strict prohibition of using images in divine worship is very clearly *Mosaic* <note>original: "Mosaical"; meaning following the laws or customs of Moses.</note> in nature. Also, his principle that **"it is not good for secret mysteries to be carried in lifeless writings"** <note>original: "Οὐ καλῶς φορεῖσθαι τὰ ἀπόρρητα ἐν ἀψύχοις γράμμασιν"</note> shows that he was taught Cabbalistically through oral tradition. It is a well-confessed fact that there was once a secret tradition of more profound, hidden learning among the *Jews*.

Furthermore, *Numa*’s instructor is said to have been not a *Greek*, but **"some barbarian greater and better than Pythagoras himself"** <note>original: "βάρβαρός τις βελτίων Πυθαγόρου"</note>. Where, I ask you, could such a person be found, unless they were descended from the *Jews*? I must confess there is another tradition that he was taught by *Pythagoras*. However, this was not the famous *Pythagoras* of Samos (who lived some centuries later), but a different *Pythagoras* who was a *Lacedaemonian* <term>Lacedaemonian: A Spartan.</term>, just as *Numa* himself was. For the *Sabines* were a colony of the *Lacedaemonians*, as *Plutarch* affirms.

<margin>
* In the *Life of Numa*.
1 Maccabees chapter 12, verse 21.
Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews*, book 13, chapter 11.
</margin>

To get straight to the point, the *Lacedaemonians* themselves were descended from the *Jews*, as appears both in the first book of *Maccabees* and in the writings of *Josephus*. *Areus*, King of the *Lacedaemonians*, in his letter to *Onias* the High Priest, expressly affirms that it was found in writing that the *Lacedaemonians* and *Jews* were brothers, and that they were of the lineage of *Abraham*. The letter of *Jonathan* the High Priest acknowledges this kinship and confirms they found it so in their own records. He adds further that they remember the *Lacedaemonians* in their sacrifices and prayers, as is fitting for brothers.

6. "Well, let it be so then," you might say, as it seems very probable from these circumstances that *Numa* was both descended from the *Jews* and steeped in *Jewish religion* and learning. But what is the purpose of this? How does it prove that the *Motion of the Earth* was once part of the *Jewish Tradition* or *Cabbala*? Only in this way: *Numa* so religiously respected the truth of this theorem that he knew there was no temple of God as grand as the universe itself. Because the universe appears round from every perspective to all its inhabitants, and because there must be an ever-shining fire—meaning a Sun—in the middle of it, he built a round temple in imitation of this. This was called the Temple of *Vesta*, about which *Plutarch* speaks very plainly and openly:

<note>original Greek: "Νουμᾶς δὲ λέγεται καὶ τὸ τῆς Ἑστίας ἱερὸν ἐγκύκλιον περιβαλέσθαι τῷ ἀσβέστῳ πυρὶ φρουράν, ἀπομιμούμενος οὐ τὸ σχῆμα τῆς γῆς ὡς Ἑστίας οὔσης, ἀλλὰ τοῦ σύμπαντος κόσμου, οὗ μέσον οἱ Πυθαγορικοί τὸ πῦρ ἱδρῦσθαι νομίζουσι, καὶ τοῦτο Ἑστίαν καλοῦσι καὶ Μονάδα. Τὴν δὲ γῆν οὔτε ἀκίνητον, οὔτε ἐν μέσῳ τῆς περιφορᾶς οὖσαν, ἀλλὰ κύκλῳ περὶ τὸ πῦρ αἰωρουμένην, οὔτε τῶν τιμιωτάτων οὔτε τῶν πρώτων τοῦ κόσμου μορίων ὑπάρχειν."</note>

**"It is reported that Numa built a circular Temple of Vesta to house an eternal fire in its center. In doing so, he was not imitating the shape of the Earth (as if the Earth were Vesta), but rather the shape of the Universe. The Pythagoreans believe that fire is placed in the center of the Universe, and they call this fire 'Vesta' or 'the Monad.' They believe the Earth is neither stationary nor at the center of the orbit, but is suspended and revolves in a circle around the fire, and that the Earth is not one of the most significant or primary parts of the world."**

## CHAPTER VII.

<margin>See Iamblichus on this passage; also more on this in Porphyry and Stobaeus.</margin>
1. *The Third Objection, taken from the inconsistency <note>original: "Heterogeneousness"</note> of the exposition of the First Day's Creation compared to all the rest, it alone being symbolic.* 2. *The answer to the objection.* 3. *That the description of the Earth on the first day suggests a symbolic sense; and how the popular imagination holds the same idea regarding Light or Day and Heaven.* 4. *That "Heaven" on the first day signifies the immaterial orders of beings, as expressly proved from Origen.* 5. *The same further confirmed from Parmenides, the disciple of Diochaetes the Pythagorean, who was likely acquainted with the text of Moses.* 6. *That the Jewish Rabbis also support this view.* 7. *Scriptural testimony that the creation of angels and of human souls is signified by the Light created on the first day.* 8. *That "Heaven" and "Light," when understood as the World of Life <note>original: "Mundus Vitæ"</note>, do not signify merely symbolically.* 9. *A further consideration proving the same conclusion.* 10. *That whether "Heaven" and "Light" signify symbolically or not, the first day's work will not be so inconsistent with the rest, as "Evening" and "Morning" are derived from it for every day of creation.* 11. *That the metaphysical matter <term>original: "Hyle"; the underlying substance or potentiality of the universe.</term> in the first day's creation is not called "Earth" merely symbolically—a point not difficult to prove, but unnecessary.*

1. THE third objection is against our explanation of the first day's work. For they argue that it is very inconsistent and strangely different from the interpretations of all the other days, where the things mentioned are not **symbolical**, but are literally what they are said to be. However, "Heaven," "Earth," and "Light" are not literal in the first day's creation, but are symbols of something else. This makes the *Cabbala* seem disjointed, as if it were not all of one piece.

2. <margin>Plotinus, *Enneads* 3, book 6, chapter 14. The same in Plotinus, book 4, chapter 1.</margin> But I answer: the question is not whether the interpretation may seem harsh to a fastidious <note>original: "nice"</note> and squeamish imagination, but whether it is true. I think I have already produced significant proof of its truth, and I must further remind you how many people there are who, while interpreting the story of *Adam* and *Eve* in *Paradise* literally, nonetheless do not think it harsh to explain the story of the *Serpent* symbolically. Furthermore, there was a necessity to speak of the creation of **immaterial beings** in a symbolic way, as *Moses* intended not to mention anything difficult or subtle in the literal letter of the text, as is acknowledged by all interpreters. Neither could there be a **philosophical** as well as a **literal Cabbala** without taking this liberty, which ought to be freely granted, as no uncertainty or obscurity arises therefrom,

3. And so that the *Earth* might not disrupt that sense of the Cabbala, its description is such that it very naturally favors the *Philosophical* meaning, for the text calls it *Vacuity or Emptiness itself*, as I have already noted. Nor is it at all strange that *Heaven* and *Light* are made symbols of the same thing. I have already offered reasons for this that come closer to philosophy (the most important being that Heaven or *Ether* <note>original: "Æther"; the material of the upper sky</note> is the very body of *Light*, or *Light* itself when properly moved). However, this also follows from the concept that naturally arises from the literal text according to popular understanding. Most people certainly have the same *idea* in their mind regarding that *illuminated hollow* <note>original: "illuminated Concave"</note> which is *Heaven* as they have regarding *Day* as distinct from the Sun. And there was no visible *hollow* at first except that of *Day*, since there were then neither Moon nor stars to enlighten the night.

And that this idea of ours is sound appears further in the fact that *Jupiter* and *Diespiter* <note>Latin: "Father of Day"</note> are the same deity <note>original: "Numen"</note> among the pagans. And yet *Jupiter*—that is, *Jovis Pater*, or Father *Jovis*—is the arched Heaven. "They call the whole circle of heaven Zeus," <note>original: Τὸν πάντα κύκλον τοῦ οὐρανοῦ Δία καλέουσιν</note> as Herodotus says of the Persians. And what can *Dies Pater*—that is, Father *Day* (for, as Varro has interpreted it, "Dies" is the nominative case here, as in *Marspiter*, *Neptunuspater*, or *Januspater*)—be but this illuminated hollow or arch which is called *Day*? This was a distinct deity among the pagans just like *Night*, for they turned the prominent phenomena of nature into various gods. Macrobius expressly states, "The Cretans call the day Zeus <note>original: Δία</note>, and the Salii, in their song, call Jupiter 'Lucetius' <note>Latin: Light-bringer</note>." From this, *Dijovis* is in all likelihood the same as *Diespiter*.

But we will not dwell upon these trifles <note>original: "toyes"</note>. It was sufficient to have noted that *Heaven* <note>original: Οὐρανὸς</note> and *Day* <note>original: Ἡμέρα</note> are one and the same as *Zeus* <note>original: Ζεὺς</note> in pagan theology, and therefore the same as each other. It is now more important to consider that without any light at all, nothing can be perceived; therefore, *Heaven* must be popularly conceived as this luminous hollow. This hollow is called *Day* because of its brightness, and termed *Heaven* because of its height and curvature (for *Cælum* <note>Latin: Heaven</note> is essentially the same as *Koilon* <note>Greek: hollow</note>). Thus, they are one combined object, especially in the First Day's creation. *Heaven* was not discoverable anywhere except in this newly created *Day*, whose combined appearances made up one and the same luminous *hollow*, as I mentioned before.

From this, the literal sense of the First Day's work—serving as the symbol or representation of the Philosophical meaning—is very easy and natural if you take it this way: namely, that first it is summarily stated, *God created Heaven* (that is, this *Luminous Hollow*) *and the Earth. But this Earth was nothing*

# CHAPTER VII. of the Philosophical Cabbala.

But then, after coming to the other part, he tells us how *God* commanded the *Light* to be made—that is, this luminous expanse <note>original: "Concave"</note>, *Heaven*. (For in their *Idea* they are really the same, as I have said, and therefore the words *Light* and *Heaven* are merely synonyms here). He also tells how He called this Light or *Luminous Heaven*, *Day*, etc. When this structure and the sense of things are considered, it must take away all doubt and the notion of any harshness in making *Heaven* and *Light* symbols of the same thing—namely, of that which the *Platonists* call *Mundus vitae*, or the *World of Life and Form*.

Nor can it be objected that this *literal sense* is inconsistent with the *Literal Cabbala* <note>The author distinguishes between a plain reading (Literal) and a deeper symbolic reading (Philosophical)</note> we have framed already, where the *Heaven* is made on the *Second* day, and therefore cannot be literally made on the *First*. For by the *Literal sense* here, I do not mean that continuous popular meaning or *Literal Cabbala*, for that is not supposed to be the basis of the Philosophical interpretation. (For these three distinct *Cabbalas*—Literal, Philosophical, and Moral—are not intended to either agree or disagree with one another, as they have no mutual reference at all; rather, they grow out of the *Letter* of the text which is common to all three, like three different types of flowers growing out of one garden bed.) 

But by the *Literal sense* here, I mean such a sense as may be crafted out of the text when it is prepared by a skillful hand to fitly and naturally exhibit any part of either the *Literal* (specifically so called), the *Philosophical*, or the *Moral Cabbala*. This preparation may be made through grammar and criticism, or else by conceptual or true notions. For the *Letter* of the text, as I said, is common to all three *Cabbalas*, but it is to be prepared and fitted in each instance—not to match the sequence of things in the other two interpretations, but to match the things within that specific *Cabbala*. This is a principle that any man who considers it well must acknowledge as both rational and necessary.

4. Now, the fact that we have given the right sense of the first Day’s Creation in our *Philosophical Cabbala* appears further (beyond what we have already produced) from the writings of *Clement of Alexandria* and *Origen*. Comparing the *Second* Day’s work with the *First*, they write: "And indeed, in the Monad <note>The 'Monad' refers to the first day or the principle of unity</note> He established an invisible heaven, a holy earth, and an intellectual light; but in the creation of the sensible world, He crafted a solid heaven" <note>original Greek: Καὶ ἐν μὲν τῇ μονάδι συνίσησιν οὐρανὸν ἀόρατον, καὶ γῆν ἁγίαν, καὶ φῶς νοητόν· ἐν δὲ τῇ κοσμογονίᾳ τῇ αἰσθητῇ ςερεὸν οὐρανὸν δημιουργεῖ</note>. 

*Origen* follows this interpretation exactly: "Since God had made heaven before," he says, "He now makes the firmament, that is, the corporeal heaven. This, therefore, is that *World of Life* which is the highest Throne of God. The *Pythagoreans* also call this the *Tower of Jupiter* <note>original Greek: Ζανὸς πύργος</note>, it being His highest habitation. It is also termed His *External Framing* <note>original Greek: Δημιουργικὴ φρουρὰ</note>, because the framing of the *World* in all its parts is performed by it, either immediately or as an instrument, just as a *Fetus* is formed in the womb.

# An Appendix to the Defense, CHAPTER VII.

...two Principles, "Fire and Earth" <note>original: "πῦρ καὶ γῆ"</note>, which in *Hebrew* would be "Light and Earth" <note>original: "אור וארץ"</note>, *Light and Earth*, or (which I have shown to be the same thing) *Heaven and Earth*. He adds further, "And the one has the rank of creator, the other that of matter" <note>original: "Καὶ τὸ μὲν δημιουργοῦ τάξιν ἔχειν, τὸ δὲ ὕλης"</note>. This matches the *Text of Moses in the philosophical sense so perfectly that it is hard to doubt that he took these two principles from there: the one *Active* or *Creator-like*, the other *Passive* or *Material*. The one is symbolically called "Fire" <note>original: "πῦρ"</note>, "Light" <note>original: "אור"</note>, Light, or Ether; the other "Earth" <note>original: "γῆ"</note>, which is "Earth" <note>original: "ארץ"</note>, *Earth*; *Heaven* and *Earth*.

Then, let them judge how right a scent <note>original: "sent"</note> we have been on in the pursuit of the meaning of the *Physical* part of the *Philosophic Cabbala*, and whether *Pythagoras* did not understand things the same way. For this *Parmenides* was a *Pythagorean*, having been an intimate friend of one *Diochaetes*, a follower of *Pythagoras*. This *Diochaetes*, as *Sotion* writes, was indeed poor, but a singularly honest and good man. For this reason, *Parmenides* stayed so close to him for his company while he lived, and held him in such great honor that he built a chapel <note>original: "Ἡρῷον"</note> for him when he died.

From this, *Parmenides* might have taken the opportunity to divide *Philosophy* into that which is accurately and intellectually true, and that which is according to the appearance of things to the common people: "Philosophy is twofold: one according to truth, the other according to opinion" <note>original: "Διττὴν τε εἶναι τὴν φιλοσοφίαν, τὴν μὲν κατ' ἀλήθειαv, τὴν δὲ κατὰ δόξαν"</note>. The latter of these, were it not for the reasons I have suggested, would not have been noticed by *Parmenides* as a piece of wisdom or philosophy at all. And that "opinion" <note>original: "δόξα"</note> signifies external appearance is plain in that *Epicurus* divides that which appears from the outside into "evidence" <note>original: "ἐνάργεια"</note> and "opinion" <note>original: "δόξα"</note>. Furthermore, *Democritus* in *Laertius* has defined it: "The principles of the universe are atoms and the void; all other things are matters of custom and opinion" <note>original: "ἀρχὰς εἶναι τῶν ὅλων ἀτόμους καὶ κενόν· τὰ δ' ἄλλα πάντα νενομίσθαι, δοξάζεσθαι"</note>; that is to say, they are "appearances" <note>original: "φαίνεσθαι"</note>, or "external appearances" <note>original: "φαινόμενα"</note>.

<margin>

To this "Fire and Earth" <note>original: "πῦρ καὶ γῆ"</note> of *Parmenides* exactly corresponds that pair of principles among the *Pythagoreans*, "Light and Darkness" <note>original: "φῶς & σκότος"</note>. These plainly point at the *Light* and *Darkness* in the beginning of *Genesis*. The *Pythagoreans* translate the Hebrew word for light <note>original: "אור"</note> as "light" <note>original: "φῶς"</note>, while *Parmenides* uses "fire" <note>original: "πῦρ"</note>. One calls the <term>Hyle</term> <note>The primary, unformed matter of the universe</note> "earth" <note>original: "γῆ"</note>, and the other "darkness" <note>original: "σκότος"</note>, but both reflect on the Text, where *Hyle* is denoted by both those terms. And that *Parmenides* did not mean this physical Earth is plain from *Aristotle*, who says that *Parmenides* ranked his first principle, Fire, "according to being" <note>original: "κατὰ τὸ ὂν"</note>, and the other "according to non-being" <note>original: "κατὰ τὸ μὴ ὂν"</note>, which is how *Plotinus* describes *Hyle* to be. *Theodotion* also translates the Hebrew phrase for "waste and void" <note>original: "תהו ובהו"</note> as "emptiness and nothing" <note>original: "κένωμα καὶ οὐδέν"</note>. But I have wandered too far; let us return to *Origen*.

6. Consistent with that interpretation by *Origen* is the general doctrine of the *Jewish Rabbis*: "The throne of God's glory was created before the creation of the world" <note>original: "Solium gloriæ Dei creatum esse ante creationem Mundi"</note>.

And *Menasseh Ben Israel* assures us that the *Cabbalists* explain the "Creation of Heaven" to be the creation of angels, and he cites the *Targum* <note>an ancient Aramaic translation or paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible</note> on *Job* and *Moses the Egyptian* <note>Moses Maimonides</note> to the same effect.

7. Tell me, if you have understanding. When the morning stars sang together, and all the sons of God shouted for joy?* Anyone would have to be blind not to see what is meant by the *morning stars* from the following explanation <note>original: exegesis</note>—namely, the *sons of God*, which is the same as the *angels*. They are called morning stars *symbolically*, in allusion to the *first day's* creation—the creation of *Light*—which was the *morning* of the world and the birth of spiritual and *angelic beings*. And therefore, in verses 19 and 21, regarding this *first day's* creation of *Light*, He asks *Job* another similar question: *Where is the way to the dwelling of light? And as for darkness, where is its place?*—certainly alluding to the *light* and *darkness* mentioned on the *first day*. For He then asks further, *Do you know that you were then born or made, and that the number of your days is great?* This is how the learned *Jews* read it, and from this text they confidently conclude the *pre-existence of souls*. If they are correct, there is no question that their creation is involved in the creation of *Light* during the *first day's* work. From these testimonies, I think it is plain enough that by the "Creation of Heaven or Light" is meant—as *Origen* ventured to affirm—the creation of all *spiritual substances*.

8. Furthermore, to address the objection more directly, I do not believe it is necessary to admit that *Heaven* and *Light* are merely *symbolic*. Instead, the things created on the *first* day may be called by those names most truly and properly, even though the words were first applied to the material heaven and visible light. This is just as the words *Spirit* <note>original: Spiritus</note>, *Soul* <note>original: Anima</note>, and *Psyche* <note>original: Ψυχὴ</note> were terms first given to material things—meaning a gust of *air*, *wind*, or *breath*—but now truly and properly signify: the first, any *immaterial substance*; the latter two, the *soul* of *man*, which is spiritual and immaterial. And so it may be with *Heaven* and *Light*: that which we conceive of heaven belongs more truly and excellently to the *World of Life* <note>original: Mundus Vitae</note> than to the material heaven itself. * For the generations of earthly <note>original: sublunary</note> things—their fates and lifespans, that vital influence, and the measuring of time—I do not doubt that all these are more truly, primarily, and properly attributed to the *World of Life* (in which all the *seminal forms* <note>the spiritual blueprints or "seeds" of all things</note> of things exist) than they are to the physical heaven. 10. This luminous *Heaven* or *Heavenly Light* is symbolically called the *Morning* of each Day’s Creation, just as the *material* part or *passive principle* is called the *Evening*. This *Morning* is always a portion of that *full Day* which was first created; it is restrained and softened by its conjunction with *dark matter* into a moderate *morning splendor* <note>original: Matutine Splendour</note>. Several parts of matter, shaped and modified to fit the various capacities of that dark *emptiness* and *vacuity* (which was the *Midnight* opposite to that *full Day*), are raised to a state of *physical existence* <note>original: actual Materiality</note>. These may be considered the "evening twilight" of every Day's Creation. The *possibility* of this external and material creation is the <term>borderland</term> <note>original: μεθόριον</note> between the *World of Life* <note>original: Mundus vitae</note> (or *Full Day*) and that *Metaphysical Matter* <note>original: Metaphysical Hyle; "Hyle" is the Greek word for "wood" or "raw material," used in philosophy to mean prime matter without form.</note> (or *Midnight*), as soon as its parts have even a *material existence*. Just as the dusk of the evening is the <term>borderland</term> <note>original: μεθόριον</note> between Day and Night.

## CHAPTER VIII.

1. *That Hyle <term>Original: Hyle. A Greek term for "matter," specifically the "prime matter" or raw potentiality of the universe before it takes form.</term> or first Matter is mere Possibility of Being, according to Aristotle.* 2. *That the same is but Empty Space or Capacity of Body, according to Plato and Plotinus; and how fitly the description of Hyle in their works agrees with Moses's description of the "Earth, without form and void" <note>original: Terra inanis & vacua</note>.* 3. *What in Plotinus's description answers to the "Abyss," "Darkness," and "Waters" in Moses's account.* 4. *That Plotinus seems to make Hyle a mere Non-Entity.* 5. *But that his more express opinion is that it is the Potentiality of Corporeal Beings, and Entity in reversion <note>An "entity in reversion" refers to something that does not exist yet but has the potential to become a real thing in the future.</note>.* 6. *How this Hyle may be said to be created.* 7. *Why Moses would take notice of so scanty and fleeting a business as this Hyle seems to be in his Six Days of Creation.* 8. *That "Incompossibility" <term>The state of two things being unable to exist at the same time or in the same way; a logical contradiction in the nature of things.</term> is involved in the notion of the Mosaic Hyle, with a special reason why the Pythagoreans might call the number ten "Necessity" <note>original: Ananke / Ἀνάγκη</note>.*

<margin>Book 6, chapters 3 & 7.</margin>
1. Now, regarding those three additional questions concerning this *Metaphysical Hyle*: The first of them concerns its name—why I would venture to give so substantial a name as *Hyle*, which is the same as saying *Matter*, to something that I acknowledge has no existence but a *Metaphysical* one, and such a *Metaphysical* one that it is not truly any "Being" at all, but a mere capacity for it. But I answer that I have rather surnamed the "Hyle" of the ancients as *Metaphysical*, than transplanted the name of Hyle to a mere *Metaphysical Entity*. For as far as I can find, the ancients usually allow their *Hyle* no more "Being" than I have allotted to it in my description. Namely, that it is only the capacity for the existence of the corporeal or sensible world, but is itself neither a substance nor anything else actually existing. "I call matter that which of itself is called neither a 'what,' nor a quantity, nor any other thing by which being is defined" <note>original: Λέγω δ' ὕλην ἣ καθ' αὑτὴν μήτε τὶ, μήτε ποσὸν, μήτε ἄλλο μηδὲν λέγεται οἷς ὥρισται τὸ ὄν</note>. This is *Aristotle's* definition of Matter in his *Metaphysics*. And again, not far after: "The possibility of being and not being, that is the Hyle or Matter in everything" <note>original: Τὸ δυνατὸν εἶναι καὶ μὴ εἶναι, τοῦτό ἐστιν ἡ ἐν ἑκάστῳ ὕλη</note>.

Plotinus, insisting upon this notion of space, makes Matter relate to the bodies of the world as an empty room relates to our senses. He affirms that it is "impassive" <term>incapable of being affected or suffering change</term>, saying: "Just as when people strike one another in the same house, the house is unaffected, and so is the air within it" <note>original: Οἷον ἐν οἴκῳ τῷ αὐτῷ ἀλλήλους παιόντων ὁ οἶκος ἀπαθὴς καὶ ὁ ἐν αὐτῷ ἀὴρ</note>. In accordance with this idea, he calls Matter "the shadow and phantom of bulk" <note>original: εἴδωλον καὶ φάντασμα ὄγκου</note>; and adds further that it is "a thing that has no resistance" <note>original: τὸ ἀντερεῖδον μὴ ἔχον</note>. This lack of resistance matches what he says to the same purpose in his sixth *Ennead*: "For they do not grant it any resistance at all" <note>original: Οὐδὲ γὰρ ὅλως τὸ ἀντίτυπες αὐτῇ διδόασιν</note>. Therefore, in his second *Ennead*, he describes Matter as only "a suitability or capacity for bulk" <note>original: ὄγκου ἐπιτηδειότητα</note>, which is evident when he also calls it "empty bulk" <note>original: κενὸν ὄγκον</note>, and in the eighth chapter, he flatly denies that it has rarity, density, or magnitude.

Further expressing the desolate condition of Matter in his third *Ennead*, he calls it "an ever-craving penury and universal desolateness" <note>original: τὴν ἀεί πεισαν αὐτῇ πενίαν, and τὴν πάντων ἐρημίαν</note>, whose lack is mocked rather than supplied. The "Forms" it seems to receive are like echoes in hollow, solitary places; they are not absorbed but bounced back. Nothing of what it participates in actually sticks to it; instead, it acts like a looking glass, which reflects images rather than receiving them. This is consistent with what he writes elsewhere: "The nature of Hyle <term>Prime Matter</term> must not be composite, but simple and one in its own nature, so that it may be void of all things" <note>original: Δεῖ δὲ αὐτὴν μὴ σύνθετον εἶναι, ἀλλὰ ἁπλοῦν καὶ ἕν τι τῇ αὑτῆς φύσει, ἔστω γὰρ πάντων ἔρημος</note>. This shows how fitly it is categorized within the work of the *First Day* of creation. Besides, he plainly declares in both his second and third *Ennead* that "Hyle or Matter is in the rank of Incorporeals" <note>original: Ὅτι ἡ ὕλη ἐν τῇ τῶν ἀσωμάτων</note>—meaning things that have no physical body.

We have already suggested that Hyle is called a "foundation" <note>original: ὑποβάθρα</note> and a "seat" <note>original: ἕδρα</note>, which corresponds to the stability of the "Earth," the first name given to the Mosaic Hyle. Plotinus is very clear in that comparison to an echo, to which he likens the "Forms" that Matter is said to receive: "But the Matter remained the same, receiving nothing, but reflecting the approach [of the forms], like a seat that pushes back" <note>original: Ἀλλ’ ἔμεινεν ἡ αὐτὴ ἡ ὕλη οὐδὲν δεξαμένη, ἀλλ’ ἐπιχέουσα τὴν πρόσοδον, ὡς ἕδρα ἀπωθουμένη</note>. In these words, he compares Matter to a fixed seat against which the Forms strike but do not sink in, so that he intends for Matter to remain as it was before: unchanged and immovable.

* *Ennead* 1, book 8, chapter 7.
* Book 4, chapter 10.
</margin>
3. That also suits very well with the third name for the *Mosaic Hyle* <note>original: "Hyle" refers to the Greek concept of primordial "wood" or "matter" from which the world was crafted.</note> (namely, the *Abyss*), which *Plotinus* uses in his second *Ennead*: "The depth of every thing is the Matter; and therefore it is entirely dark" <note>original: Τὸ δ' βάθος ἑκάστη ὑλη, διὸ καὶ σκοτεινὴ πᾶσα</note>. He calls this "the ultimate" <note>original: τὸ ἔσχατον</note> elsewhere; and therefore it is ever dark. This *Darkness* is a fourth property of the *Mosaic Matter*, which *Plotinus* discusses quite extensively in this second *Ennead*. He contends that we can have no other notion of it, as it is "as darkness is to the Eye" <note>original: τῇ ὀφθαλμῷ τὸ σκότος</note>; and he says the Soul can see it in no other way than "as deformity, as uselessness, and as a lack of light" <note>original: ἢ ὡς ἀσχημοσύνην καὶ ὡς ἀχρείαν καὶ ὡς ἀλαμπές</note>. A little after, he writes, "This perceives the dim dimly, and the dark darkly, and perceives what it perceives" <note>original: Τοῦτο νοεῖ ἀμυδρῶς ἀμυδρόν, καὶ σκοτεινῶς σκοτεινὸν, καὶ νοεῖ ἃ νοοῦσα</note> as a man sees darkness. Finally, so that he does not seem to have missed even one part of the *Mosaic* description of the *First Matter*, what *Moses* may mean by the mobility of the *Waters*, *Plotinus* has expressed as "the Indefiniteness" or "the Undeterminedness of Matter" <note>original: τὸ ἀόρισον, or ἡ ἀορισία</note>.

<margin>
* Book 6, chapter 7.
* Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, book 5.
</margin>
4. Truly, I think what we have produced so far offers strong proof that he considers *Matter* to be no more "substantial" a being than what might be called *Metaphysical*. But he speaks even more broadly, yet more concisely, in his third *Ennead*, where (as *Clement* <note>Clement of Alexandria, a Christian theologian who integrated Greek philosophy with scripture.</note> also says Plato styles it) he calls it "That which is truly Non-Entity" <note>original: τὸ ἀληθινῶς μὴ ὄν; literally "that which truly is not."</note>. A little later, he describes it further as "whose being, existing only in imagination, is no Being" <note>original: ἔ' τὸ ὂν ἐν φαντασίᾳ οὐκ ὂν ἐςί</note>. And in chapter thirteen, he declares that if Matter would remain what she is, "she must necessarily be unreceptive to all Beings; indeed, if there is even a shadow of them, she must not share in it, so that she may preserve her own property" <note>original: ἀνάγκη αὐτὴν μὴ μόνον τῶν ὄντων ἄδεκτον εἶ, ἀλλὰ καὶ εἴ τι μίμημα αὐτῶν, καὶ τότε ἄμοιρον εἰς οἰκείωσιν εἶ</note>.

<margin>
* Book 1, chapter 27.
* Book 5, chapter 5.
</margin>
5. But the Philosopher is so severe in such expressions that he seems to strip *Matter* more naked than she really ought to be. However, he is more moderate in other passages, where he allows her to be the *Potentiality* of the outward and sensible World. He only argues her to be no *Entity* because she is only this *Potentiality*. As in the sixth *Ennead*: "For if that which is to come is only Potentiality, and that which is to come is no Essence or Substance; then Matter, which is but Potentiality, is no Substance or Essence" <note>original: Εἰ γὰρ δύναμίς ἐσιν ὃ μέλλει ἔσεσθαι, ἐκεῖνο δὲ μὴ οὐσία, οὐδ' ἂν αὐτὴ οὐσία</note>. And in the second *Ennead*, he will allow *Matter* to be *Essence in Reversion* <note>A legal term meaning a property that will eventually return to its owner; here, it means a being that does not yet fully exist.</note>. "The Being of Matter is only an expected or promised Being" <note>original: Τὸ εἶναι αὐτῇ μόνον τὸ μέλλον ἐπαγγελλόμενον</note>, or, as I said, a *Being in reversion*. Toward the end of the chapter, he concludes, "If, therefore, it must exist, it must not exist in actuality, so that by departing from true being, it may have its being in non-being" <note>original: Εἴπερ ἄρα δεῖ αὐτὸ εἶ, δεῖ αὐτὸ ἐνεργείᾳ μὴ εἶ, ἵνα ἐκβεβηκὸς τοῦ ἀληθινῶς εἶ τῷ μὴ εἶ ἔχῃ τὸ εἶ</note>. And in the close of all, "If, therefore, one must keep matter imperishable, matter herself..." <note>original: Εἴπερ ἄρα δεῖ ἀνώλεθρον τὴν ὕλην τηρεῖν, ὕλην αὐτὴν... <meta>This page concludes the discussion of the metaphysical status of "Hyle" (Matter) as described by Plato and Plotinus, comparing it to the Mosaic "First Day's Creation." # An Appendix to the Defence CHAPTER VIII.

"...one must keep it, that is, say that it exists only in potentiality so that it may be what it is" <note>original: δεῖ τηρεῖν, τουτέστι, δυνάμει λέγειν αὐτὴν εἶναι μόνον ἵνα ᾖ ὃ ἔστιν</note>. The meaning of both these sentences is simply this: that the *Essence* of *Matter* excludes real *Existence* and consists only in the *Capacity* or *Possibility* of *Being*. From this, it is clear that this *Platonic Hyle* <note>original: "Hyle" is the Greek term for primordial matter or the underlying substance of the universe.</note> which I have applied to the *First Day’s Creation* may rightly be called *Metaphysical*. Or, if you prefer, that which has only the most fading <note>original: "evanid"</note> *Metaphysical Entity* may be called *Hyle*, which was the goal of this discussion.

<margin>* Aquinas, *Summa Theologica*, Part 1, Question 45.</margin>
6. However, a more dangerous *query* <note>original: "Quære"</note> now arises from the answer to the previous one: namely, how this mere *Capacity* or *Possibility* of bodily and sensible beings can be said to be created. For this *Possibility* and *Capacity* seems to exist on its own and requires no *Creation*. But I answer that *Creation* is nothing other than an *emanation* <note>A "flowing out" or proceeding from a source; in theology, the idea that the universe flows from God's own being or power.</note> of the Creature from God, as *Aquinas* has determined. I say that this *Possibility* and *Capacity* of things is the furthest *projection* or *emanation* from the *Divine Existence*, and would not exist without Him. For if He did not exist, every thing else would be impossible to be. Therefore, this *Possibility* depends on Him; and since it is not a mere nothing (according to the *Metaphysicians*, who allow *being in potentiality* <note>original: "Ens in potentia"</note> to be truly *being*, just as much as *being in actuality* <note>original: "Ens actu"</note>), it is rightly said to be created by Him. And if *Creation* is *out of nothing* <note>original: "ex nihilo"</note>, then this is far more strikingly so than any other kind, since what lies below it is the most absolute *non-being* <note>original: "Non-ens"</note> conceivable—which is, as I said, *Impossibility*. That would be the state of all things if there were no God.

7. The third and last *query* is why *Moses* would take notice of such a thin and fading matter as this mere *Possibility* of the external Creation. For what good does it do to consider that the *Possibility* of a house or a statue exists before the masons and sculptors make them? But I answer: the reason is not the same, as there is an infinite difference between the whole Universe and a house or statue, and between God and a mason or sculptor. Therefore, in such vast subjects as God and the Universe, every tiny consideration will be significant; and we see that human understanding has always thought so. For men's minds have been much puzzled and immersed in diving down to the lowest and final ground of all things, which they call *Hyle*, and have commonly defined it as I have described: *a mere Potentiality*.

Furthermore, is it a contemptible notion or speculation to consider that the very *Possibility* of *other Beings* comes from God, and that it is impossible for anything to exist without Him? For as this is a most true aphorism, it is also very closely connected to piety and religion; and we should expect such a philosophy from a man as holy as *Moses*.

And lastly, when we say this *Hyle* is the *Potentiality* or *Capacity* of things, it also involves *incompossibility* <note>A philosophical term for the state of things that cannot coexist, often used here to imply that finite things are limited by their own nature and cannot be everything at once.</note>, as it is a *finite capacity* or *possibility*. Therefore, from this, there will be a necessary consequence of those things that are considered evil in the world. For such a *Capacity* or *Possibility* that is only *finite* lives next door to *Necessity*, the Mother of Mischief, as is hinted at in the *Pythagorean* verses (though on a different occasion):

->—For power dwells near to necessity.<-
<note>original: Δύναμις γὰρ ἀνάγκης ἐγγύθι ναίει</note>

### Chapter VIII: Of the Philosophical Cabbala

<margin>* Plutarch, *On the Procreation of the Soul*.</margin>
Nor can I find any acceptable sense in Plato's <note>original: "Ἀνάγκη πολλὰ τῷ θεῷ δυσμαχοῦσα καὶ ἀφηνιάζουσα"</note> *Necessity that stubbornly and untamedly resists and opposes God*, except for this *Incompossibility of the Creation* <note>The philosophical idea that certain things are logically impossible to create together, even for God.</note>. But when he calls it a "disorderly and evil-doing soul" <note>original: "ἄτακτον ψυχὴν & κακοποιὸν"</note>, and "a soul contrary and opposed to the one that works good" <note>original: "ψυχὴν ἐναντίαν καὶ ἀντίπαλον τῇ ἀγαθεργῷ"</note>, it is either a piece of exaggerated rhetoric—or rather poetry—or else a gross mistake in reading Moses's text. (I have already mentioned that he was acquainted with it.) He interpreted <term>Ruach Elohim</term> <note>Hebrew for "Spirit of God."</note> in the same sense as the *Literal Cabbala* <note>The literal, surface-level reading of the creation story in Genesis.</note> has expressed it, which he imagined to be the effect of this "disorderly and evil-doing soul."

8. But the appearance of the *First Matter* in Moses’s account is horrid and dismal enough without such whimsical ideas fetched from a misunderstanding of the *Literal Cabbala* to make it reveal its own guilt and complicity in the evils that happen in the world. Being nothing other than what has been described so far from Plotinus, Plotinus himself nevertheless complains lamentably of the mischiefs arising out of it. In his essay *On what evils are, and from where they come* <note>original: "Περὶ τοῦ τίνα, καὶ πόθεν τὰ κακὰ"</note>, he defines this *Hyle* <note>The Greek term for primordial matter.</note> to be "the essence of evil" <note>original: "κακοῦ οὐσία"</note>, and "the first or original evil" <note>original: "τὸ πρῶτον κακὸν"</note>. Giving a reason for the evil that exists in the world, he writes <margin>Ennead 1, book 8, chapter 7.</margin> thus: <note>original: "Μεμιγμένη γὰρ δὴ ἡ τοῦδε τοῦ κόσμου φύσις ἔκ τε νοῦ καὶ ἀνάγκης, καὶ ὅσα παρὰ θεοῦ εἰς αὐτὸν ἥκει ἀγαθὰ, τὰ δὲ κακὰ ἐκ τῆς ἀρχαίας φύσεως τῆς ὕλης λεγομένης"</note> "The nature of this world is mixed of Intellect and Necessity; those things that come from God are good, but the evils are from that ancient nature called Hyle [Matter]." 

<margin>* See *Psychozoia* Canto 1, Stanzas 9, 44, 45.</margin>
But I must confess, it is a bit odd of him to call this *Hyle* "ancient," unless he refers merely to the particular, vanishing appearances in the world. For the world itself is as ancient as this *Hyle* according to his own doctrine elsewhere. For example, in his fifth <margin>* Book 9, chapter 12.</margin> *Ennead*, he makes the universe a necessary emanation from God and the *natural image of the Eternal Intellect*. From this he infers, <note>original: "Πᾶσα δὲ φύση εἰκών ἐστιν ὅσον ἂν τὸ ἀρχέτυπον μένῃ"</note> "Every nature is an image as long as the archetype remains." And in <margin>* Ennead 3, book 2, chapter 3.</margin> *another place*: "The World exists of necessity, and was not made by calculation, but by a superior nature producing something naturally similar to itself" <note>original: "Ἐξ ἀνάγκης ἐστὶν ὁ Κόσμος, καὶ οὐκ ἐκ λογισμοῦ γενόμενος, ἀλλὰ φύσεως ἀμείνονος γεννώσης κατὰ φύσιν ὅμοιον ἑαυτῇ"</note>. And in the chapter before this citation, he says the very same thing: "The World was not made by deliberation that it ought to be so, but by the immediate necessity of the emanation of a secondary nature" <note>original: "Γέγονε δὲ ὁ Κόσμος οὐ λογισμῷ τοῦ δεῖν εἶναι, ἀλλὰ δευτέρας φύσεως ἀνάγκῃ"</note>. If these conclusions of Plotinus are true, I should think this is as significant a reason as any why the *Pythagoreans* called the *Decad* <note>The number ten, which Pythagoreans viewed as the mystical symbol of the universe.</note> "Necessity" <note>original: "Ἀνάγκη"</note>.

I have more willingly made this detour because it makes it easier to understand what I was about to add to further prove that Plotinus makes *Hyle* the root of all evils. In the first <margin>* Book 8, chapter 7.</margin> *Ennead*, as mentioned before: <note>original: "Ἐπεὶ γὰρ οὐ μόνον τὸ ἀγαθὸν, ἀνάγκη τῇ ἐκβάσει, τῇ παρ᾽ αὐτοῦ ὑποστάσει, ἢ, εἴ τῳ φίλον λέγειν, τῇ ἀεὶ ὑποβάσει καὶ ἀποστάσει, τὸ ἔσχατον, καὶ μεθ᾽ ὃ οὐκ ἦν ἔτι γενέσθαι ὁτιοῦν, τοῦτο εἶναι τὸ κακόν· ἐξ ἀνάγκης δὲ εἶναι τὸ μετὰ τὸ πρῶτον, ὥστε καὶ τὸ ἔσχατον. τοῦτο δὲ ἡ ὕλη μηδὲν ἔτι ἔχουσα αὐτοῦ, καὶ αὕτη ἡ ἀνάγκη τοῦ κακοῦ."</note> "For since the Sovereign Goodness is not alone, it must follow—by a progression, or a gradual sinking, or descent, or distance from it—that there exists a lowest point, after which nothing else can come into being; and this is evil. It is by necessity that there is something after the first, and thus also a last point. This last thing is Matter, which no longer possesses anything of the Good; and this is the necessity of evil." # An Appendix to the Defence CHAPTER IX.

It is possible that if anything exists, this must be the Evil. And of necessity, there is something that comes after the *First* <note>The "First" refers to God or the original source of all existence.</note>, so there must be an "Extreme" or lowest point. This is *Hyle* or *Matter*, which possesses nothing of the *First*, and this is the "Necessity of Evil"—namely, in that this *Hyle* has nothing of the *First* within it, nor is it capable of containing it. This is as much as to say that the <term>incompossibility</term> <note>original: "Incompossibility"; the logical impossibility of two things existing together.</note> or lack of proportion in the lowest creation of things (such as this *Physical World*) is this <note>original: "Ἀνάγκη"</note> *Necessity* of Evil. There would be a total impossibility of all things if there were no God, but there is still an incompatibility or lack of proportion in these lower things despite the fact that He exists—just as it is impossible for the edge of a knife and the back of it to be equally strong.

These considerations of this *Metaphysical Hyle* are not trivial; indeed, they are so significant that they may well be considered worthy of Moses's distinct notice. He presents this *Hyle* or *First Matter* in the grim and horrific appearance it takes in the First Day’s Creation, and for these reasons, he made it part of the *First Day’s work*. For this is a truth that deserves serious meditation. It is not unfitting for a philosopher to contemplate the primary grounds for those effects for which all-foreseeing Providence has so expressly prepared humanity—furnishing us with those intense and theatrical emotions of laughter and weeping to handle such strange and difficult occurrences. It is quite plain, then, that interpreting this *Metaphysical Hyle* as the *void and formless Earth* enveloped in waters and darkness is a sound and undeniable interpretation.

***

1. *A new supposition concerning Hyle, as if it were an actual material substance, and how applicable Moses's description is to it.* 2. *How it can be referred to the First Day’s Creation, characterized by a Unit.* 3. *How it will be found to be the Interior Waters in the philosophical sense.* 4. *What coagulated the single-particle consistency of this Physical Hyle into a capacity for becoming Ether, or the Second Day’s work.* 5. *That the supposition of this Physical Hyle is very acceptable if it has a single-particle consistency; otherwise, it is intolerable.*

<margin>* *Immortality of the Soul*, Book 1, chapter 6. Also Preface, section 3.</margin>
1. But if it would be a relief to anyone's mind to have a more solid and perceptible object represented by this name *Hyle*, the text is perhaps not entirely incapable of it. For suppose we should treat this *Hyle* as real and actual Matter, consisting of those perfect <term>parvitudes</term> <note>original: "Parvitudes"; extremely small, indivisible particles or atoms.</note> (which I have described elsewhere) that are actually divided from one another and filled with roughly as much motion as is currently preserved in the world; the attributes of that *Hyle* described by Moses will agree with it very well.

### CHAPTER 9. Of the Philosophical Cabbala.

...term *Earth*. It will also be such a <term>Depth</term> <note>original: "Βάθος" (Bathos)</note> or *Profundity* as the name *Abyss* may well reflect upon, it being the deepest or lowest of the real Creation. Then regarding *Vacuity* and *Emptiness*, this *Hyle* <note>The Greek word for "matter." In this context, it refers to the most basic, unformed substance of the universe.</note> is utterly empty of all sensible forms (assuming it is not yet joined with any substantial ones). It is not even thin or thick to the touch, because it is not perceptible at all. It is truly <note>original: "τὸ μετ᾽ ἀναισθησίας ἁπτὸν" (to met' anaisthesias hapton)</note> "that which is tangible with a lack of perception," which <margin>* Chapter 8, section 2.</margin> *Plato* ventured to describe; it is indeed tangible in itself, but not to the touch of man or Angel, because of the infinite subtlety of its consistency. Therefore, it must necessarily be like a void *Solitude* and empty *Space*, a mere *Vacuum* to the search of any created sense. Any sense roaming up and down could find no <term>density</term> <note>original: "crassitude"</note> anywhere except what these perfect <term>tiny particles</term> <note>original: "Parvitudes"</note> have. These are so infinitely subtle that no touch can perceive them, so that everything will seem absolutely empty and void.

Thirdly, this vast *Solitude* will be as dark as pitch. Even if the Sun were where it is now, and the rest of the *Vortex* <note>In 17th-century physics, a "vortex" was a large-scale swirling motion of matter that carried planets along.</note> were made of this consistency of *Matter* I describe, it would be as black as midnight, as I could easily demonstrate.

And lastly, regarding its *Fluidity* or *Waterishness*, it is infinitely more like water—that is to say, more fluid than water itself. If the opinion of <term>Thales</term> <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher who believed water was the primary substance of all matter.</note> had any truth in it, it must be found here. But <margin>* Aristotle, Metaphysics, Book 1, Chapter 3.</margin> *Aristotle* seems to attribute this to even more ancient sages. He says they made *Oceanus* and *Tethys* (the sea deities) the <note>original: "τῆς γενέσεως πατέρας" (tēs geneseōs pateras)</note> "fathers of generation," and taught that *Water* (namely the river *Styx*) was the oath of the Gods. He writes, <note>original: "Τιμιώτατον δὲ τὸ πρεσβύτατον, ὅρκος δὲ τιμιώτατόν ἐστιν" (Timiōtaton de to presbytaton, horkos de timiōtatón estin)</note> "That which is oldest is most honorable, and an oath is the most honorable thing." Certainly, such a *Water* as this *Hyle* I have described—which the Sun cannot enlighten enough to be seen through—must be a *Stygian* water indeed. It is notable here that the *Pythagoreans* called the <term>Monad</term> <note>The number one, representing unity or the first principle of all things.</note> "Styx." Thus, the nature of this *Physical Matter* described here fits perfectly with those attributes in the text of *Moses*.

2. But you will ask, how will you make it suit the character of the Day—namely, with a *Unit* or *Monad*? And how will you carry things down into the *Second Day's* work as you do with your *Metaphysical Matter*? You make that the *Waters under the Firmament*, and you make that *Firmament* the vastly extended matter, which is properly divisible and therefore represented by the *Binary* (the number two). You say that, being framed into an *Ethereal* consistency, it is called *Heaven*, which surrounds every *Earth* and lies next to its *Physical* waters, which are everywhere gathered together into one place, and so on.

I must confess that since the nature of *Physical Matter* is divisible, and the *Binary* is such a clear sign of it, while the *Metaphysical* is <note>original: "ἕν τι καὶ ἁπλοῦν καὶ ἀσώματον" (hen ti kai haploun kai asōmaton)</note> "something one, simple, and incorporeal," as <margin>Chapter 8, section 2. * Plotinus, Ennead 2, Book 4, Chapter 8.</margin> *Plotinus* has described it, I could not help but conclude that the *Metaphysical Matter* belonged to the *First* day, and the *Physical* to the *Second*. This is a very sober and safe interpretation, based on what has been said. However, I shall continue and see how tolerable the other view might be.

I say, therefore, that this *Physical Matter*, as I have described it, is also "something one, simple, and incorporeal" in a very significant sense. It is *one* and *simple*—that is to say, exactly uniform everywhere, and indivisible into any...

# An Appendix to the Defence CHAPTER 9.

...parts that are of a different nature; whereas the Firmament on the Second Day is distinguishable into the *First* and *Second Element*. And then again, for all practical purposes, it is as good as incorporeal, being only "tangible with a lack of perception" <note>original Greek: "ἄπλον μετ' ἀναισθησίας" (aplon met' anaisthesias). 3. But now as touching the *Waters under the Firmament*: This <term>Physical Hyle</term> <note>The fundamental, unformed matter of the universe.</note>, thus considered with all that <term>indeterminateness</term> <note>original Greek: "ἀορισία" (aorisia)</note> and *fluid lack of form*—the potential for physical creatures which is necessarily inherent in it—will be accurately and expressly described as those inferior *Waters*. And the "Firmament" <note>original Hebrew: "הרקיע" (ha-raki'a)</note> or "the Heaven" <note>original Hebrew: "השמים" (ha-shamayim)</note> will be an order of being between this *Physical Hyle* (which contains the aforementioned *possibility* and *indeterminateness* of things) and those immaterial beings that descend "into the realm of physical birth" <note>original Greek: "εἰς γένεσιν" (eis genesin)</note>, and are noted by the name of *Superior Waters* or *Waters above the Firmament*. For this thin, primordial water consisting of mere *Physical Monads* existed before the Firmament and filled everything. Out of this, and in the next order above it, was the *Heaven* or *Firmament*, or, as the Greeks call it, *Ether*; and next above this *Ether*, which was created before it, is that part of the *World of Life* that descends into *generation*. This is the order of things; and it is easily understood, you will say, that the *Ether* is a middle term between those two extremes: the *Physical Hyle* and the *World of Life*.

4. But you will further demand how this *Primordial Water*—this *Hyle* consisting of mere *Physical Monads*—should ever coagulate or curdle into that consistency of the *Ether*, which is made up of globular particles and of that thinner element, both being much coarser than the first consistency of the matter. But to this I have nothing to answer except that the same power which, in the formation of *animals*, coagulates the first moist matter into an organized consistency of several degrees and uses, also coagulated this primordial matter of the world into such different degrees of thickness as was fit to produce those two elements of which the *Ether* consists. And though the world is a *machine* <note>original Latin: "Machina"</note>, the *Mechanic* or *Artificer* is not *Matter*, but some other principle within the *World of Life*.

Therefore, the monad-like consistency of the matter being lost in the production of the *Ether*, and it clearly falling into two distinct principles—which *Descartes* <note>original: "Cartesius"</note> has wisely noticed—the creation of this *Ether* or *Heaven* naturally falls under the character of the number two, and is fittingly placed in the *Second Day*.

Nor is it necessary to add how all things will now proceed orderly as before, and how this *Ether* will surround the *physical* or *sensible waters* that cover the Earth. At this point, the *Literal* and *Philosophical Cabbala* <note>The "Cabbala" here refers to the author's tradition of mystical and philosophical interpretation of the Bible.</note> easily align, just as they do in the creation of the Fifth and Sixth Days. Nor does it belong to this place to consider how, after the "hellish darkness" <note>original: "Stygian Darkness," referring to the gloom of the underworld river Styx.</note> of these *Primordial Waters*, the *Matter* was coagulated, as was said above,

# CHAPTER 10. of the Philosophical Cabbala.

...said, and set into **vortical motion**, **light** dawned throughout infinite parts of the world, and the whole heavens at last glistened brightly with innumerable **suns** or **stars**. This speculation belongs entirely to the **fourth day’s work**.

5. In the meantime, it is clear that this new interpretation is quite acceptable. And although the authority of **Plotinus** and the **Platonists** leans strongly toward the first view—and their support may rightly seem more significant since they follow the lineage of the **philosophical Cabbala**—yet that venerable Father of the Church, Saint **Augustine**, favors this second view. Furthermore, **Plato** himself, by calling **matter** a "matrix and mother" <note>original Greek: "ἐκμαγεῖον & μητέρα" (ekmageion & mētera). In Platonic philosophy, this refers to matter as the receiving substance that takes on the form of the Ideas.</note>, seems to suggest that it is more than just **metaphysical**. Likewise, **Plutarch** affirms that both **Plato** and **Aristotle** make **matter** "body-like" <note>original Greek: "σωματοειδῆ" (sōmatoeidē)</note>. 

But if this **physical matter** <note>original: "Hyle"</note> is not understood as having had a **monadic consistency** <note>Composed of primary, indivisible units.</note> at first, this interpretation—which is so plausible or even unexceptionable under that hypothesis—will be found unacceptable without it. For this **matter** would then necessarily be reduced to the **binary** <note>In Pythagorean numerology, the 'binary' or number two represented division, strife, and the material world, as opposed to the 'monad' or unity.</note>, or else the **Pythagorean numbers** would mean nothing at all. But admitting it to have had such a consistency at first, all things follow smoothly and easily, and either explanation will prove fitting and rational to any impartial judgment; I leave it to the reader to choose which to prefer. Yet I cannot help adding this in favor of the latter view: *that creation comes from that which is more liquid than the thing created; and there is nothing more liquid than the heavens, unless it is this primordial water of monadic consistency—this ancient Styx, the solemn oath of the gods, as you heard from Aristotle* <note>Aristotle noted that ancient poets made the gods swear by the River Styx because water was considered the most ancient and fundamental element.</note>.

### CHAPTER 10.

1. **The fourth objection, concerning the seemingly backward placement of the suns on the fourth day and the earths on the third.** 2. **The answers: First, that the rigid order of those six mystical numbers of the creation was intended only as a storage system for memory and secrecy, not as a textbook of a precisely organized methodology.** 3. **Secondly, that the method is not as flawed as is claimed, as the Earth correctly follows the æther (the work of the second day) as its direct result;** 4. **Just as the decorating of the Earth also follows (as the first certain result of the union of the active principle with the æther on the second day), but rightly precedes the fourth day’s work as its goal or purpose.** 5. **That it was not necessary, nor perhaps possible, for the same text to carry three different meanings with the exact same sequence of events in each sense.**

# An Appendix to the Defense — CHAPTER 10.

...suns and planets, and planets must exist before there can be Earths to be decorated with rivers, plants, and flowers. Therefore, according to the priority of nature, the creation of *suns* and *planets* should have been placed before the decorating of the *Earth* with seas, rivers, and plants.

2. However, I answer that this objection is based on a misunderstanding. It assumes the external shell <note>original: "Cortex"</note> of the text of *Moses*, regarding the order of the six days of creation, is like a covering made of flexible silk, rather than a cabinet made of hard materials. A cabinet is so shaped and framed that every part cannot equally receive every thing put into it. Therefore, the rule for placing things must be dictated by the cabinet itself, not by *our desire* or *fancy* that would place them elsewhere. This is exactly the case in this *mystical repository* made up of the first six numbers, whose natures are *immutable* and *inflexible*, and whose order cannot be *transposed* or *inverted*. Therefore, those noble truths of philosophy that are to be hidden or concealed under them must be placed in whichever numbers are *most representative* of them, and in the *same order* as the numbers themselves stand. 

Because of this, it was necessary that the decorating of the Earth precede the adorning of the universe with suns and planets, simply because the number *three* precedes the number *four*. These were the *fittest numerical boxes*, so to speak, for receiving those great truths hidden in the third and fourth day’s creation within this mysterious cabinet. This cabinet is only a *repository for memory* and *mystical concealment*, not a book of natural and accurately organized scientific method; yet it is no less useful for occasionally sharing these mysteries with those thought worthy of them. Such sharing could not happen without a deeper conversation, where all things would be unfolded in an orderly and methodical way.

3. I consider this answer so substantial that I think it is unnecessary to add anything more, though I might also argue that the order of the things themselves is not as unnatural as is claimed. For the *second* day’s work is the *ether* or *heaven*, which consists of the first and second elements of *Descartes* <note>René Descartes (1596–1650), whose physics proposed that the universe was filled with "ether" made of particles of different sizes.</note>. His third element—which is nonetheless the effect of the first—is the substance that makes up the planets and Earths. In what a natural order, then, does the consideration of the Earth follow that of the *firmament* or *heaven* as its effect, and so take place on the *third* day? 

Admittedly, due to certain circumstances—namely the gathering of the subtler parts of the *ether* into the form of a sun as the *vortex* <note>In Cartesian physics, a vortex is a large circling motion of ethereal matter that carries planets around a central sun.</note> recedes—the Earth might be seen as the third thing produced after the *ether*. For this reason, the *ternary* <note>The number three.</note> is fittingly called "Born of the Third" <note>original Greek: <term>Τριτογένεια</term> (Tritogeneia). In Pythagorean thought, this epithet for Athena was interpreted numerically to mean she was "born of the number three."</note> in the school of *Pythagoras*. Yet the Earth is also really an immediate product of that subtle principle in the *ether*, and it is just as much *ether* as the other principles within it. Therefore, placing the Earth immediately after the *ether* is, in this respect, according to the natural order and may count as a tolerable method.

4. Furthermore, decorating the Earth with land and sea, trees, grass, and flowers is the first confirmed effect of that *active principle* <note>Likely referring to the "Spirit of God" or the "Anima Mundi" (World Soul) mentioned in philosophical interpretations of Genesis 1:2.</note> united with matter, which was mentioned in the *second* day’s work. So, the Earth and its vegetative decorations follow the making of the heaven or *ether* in a logical enough order. It does not need to be said that they were created on the *third* day be—

Because an Earth and a *Primary Planet* are one and the same, it is included in the Creation of the Fourth Day. Therefore, the Earth’s features <note>original: "furniture"</note> follow the *Second Day's* creation as an *effect* of it, but precede the *Fourth Day's* creation because they are the *object* of the things said to be created then. For the *Sun*, *Moon*, and *Stars* are made to shine upon the Earth and send down their influences for the seasonal revival <note>original: "resuscitations"</note> of the life-giving powers <note>original: "Seminal Powers"</note> of plants and herbs. Thus, the *Earth* seems to be the *intended purpose* <note>original: "Finis Cui"</note> for the creation of the *Luminaries of Heaven* as light-bearers. Therefore, according to the *natural priority* <note>original: "Priority of Nature"</note>, the Earth rightly comes first, whether as the *Final Cause* or the *object* of their *influence*. Similarly, both the *features of the Earths* and the *Luminaries of Heaven* come first in order as *objects* of the *senses of man* and other *animals* that are said to be created on the *fifth* and *sixth days*.

And so, the order of the entire *six days* of creation in the philosophical sense is natural enough and logically coherent, even if it does not always follow the concept of *causality*, nor is this *causality* always that of the *efficient cause* <note>the direct force that brings something into being</note>.

5. It would have been a needless miracle—and perhaps impossible—to design a single text to perfectly correspond to the popular appearance of things, the strictness of philosophical truth, and the moral allegory all at once. Yet, the text of *Moses* is charged with all of these, and it fulfills this design admirably for all significant purposes. However, an exact chain <note>original: "concatenation"</note> of the series of things throughout is more than should be expected. Such precision was not intentionally aimed for; rather, the *order* of numbers, according to their significance, was meant to be a *repository* of *notes* and *reminders*. The management of the Cabbala itself (that is, the ancient philosophy of the *Jews*) was left to the skill of the *teacher of the sacred mysteries* <note>original: "Mystagogus"</note> whenever he was consulted, who would not fail to explain everything in a proper and natural method.

### An Appendix to the Defense: CHAPTER 11

1. Regarding the supposed triviality of the **Fifth** and **Sixth** Day’s work: I believe it is evident from what we noted on the **Fifth Day** that Moses's categorization of **Fish** and **Birds** together is not a commonplace or trivial observation, but a **philosophical** one. His **distinct** assignment of a **Morning** and **Evening** to them—representing an **Active** and **Passive** principle—points toward a very significant and useful truth. It provides a timely check against the dangerous mistake of believing that mere **Matter** is capable of sense and thought, a belief that would greatly undermine the existence of human souls themselves.

2. As for the **Sixth** day’s work, there is even less reason for such criticism. First, the author is **philosophically** sound in classifying **Man** among the land-dwelling animals <note>original: "Mediterranean Animals," referring to creatures that live in the middle of the land rather than the sea or air</note>. This is because the internal structure of their organs is much more similar to one another than to either **Birds** or **Fishes**. Furthermore, the external resemblance between **Mankind** and **Apes** (of which there are many species) is so close, and transitions so gradually into species that are more strictly **four-legged** <note>original: "Quadrupedal"</note>, that it is clear that humans and apes are naturally held together in one subordinate rank and **series**.

Secondly—and this is of great importance—despite this close affinity in the outward and inward structure of parts between **Humans** and **Beasts** (especially certain kinds of **Apes**), the text distinctly and expressly declares that **Man** is nevertheless of a condition **highly elevated** above them. He possesses a nature that is **clearly Divine**, being, in respect to his soul, the **Image** and **Likeness** of God. It is also remarkable that the soul is no less the image of God for its role in animating this **earthly** body, just as God animates the **World**. This idea is hinted at in the **Cabbala** <note>the author's specific philosophical interpretation of mystical Jewish tradition</note> itself and is such a profound philosophical truth that it is not suitable for everyone to contemplate.

Furthermore, the mention of their reproduction—which refers to the design of the reproductive organs in all creatures—in both the **Fifth** and **Sixth** day, as well as the provision of food, are not low or trivial matters. They are noble subjects for contemplation and the great evidence of Divine Providence. Those who think so poorly of what is mentioned in the **Fifth** and **Sixth** days of Creation are widely mistaken.
