# An Appendix to the Defense, Chapter 11

The text only says that God placed *Cherubim* and a *flaming sword* to keep the way of the *Tree of Life*. This does not imply a total prohibition of all passage, but rather a condition for it: namely, that there is no passage except through this *Fiery Guard*. And it is just as much the role of a gatekeeper or guard to let people in as it is to keep them out; thus, there is very little contradiction in the interpretation we have provided in that respect.

And that these *fiery, flaming Cherubim* are a symbolic representation <note>original: "Hieroglyphick"</note> of a certain state into which the earthly man must pass before he can enjoy a blessed immortality is no private whim of mine. It has the support of no fewer than five different interpreters on this passage—namely, *St. Ambrose, Origen, Lactantius, Basil,* and *Rupertus*—as *Cornelius à Lapide* <note>A 16th-century Jesuit exegete known for his massive Bible commentaries</note> affirms. He says it is the joint opinion of them all, based on this text: namely, that a fire is set before the entrance into Heaven through which all souls must pass (St. Peter and St. Paul not excepted) so that they may be tried and purged if there is any impurity in them. It is quite valid, therefore, to make these *fiery Cherubim* an emblem of some state or condition of the soul that must prepare it for tasting the *fruit* of the *Tree of Immortality*. But the imagining of this to be a passage through an *external flame* or *fire* is, I must confess, too <term>mythical</term> <note>original: "Μυθῶδες" (myth-like or fabulous)</note> and <term>childish</term> <note>original: "Παιδαριῶδες" (childish or juvenile)</note> to be accepted as the meaning of the *Philosophical Cabbala*.

Therefore, I interpreted it as the *fiery* or *ethereal vehicle* <note>original: "Æthereal Vehicle"; in Neoplatonic philosophy, this refers to the "luminous body" or refined spiritual substance the soul inhabits as it ascends to higher realms</note>, or the condition of the *flaming Cherubim*—namely, that we cannot attain the state of immortality until we pass into this order of beings and become like them.

Thus, when it is said that these *flaming Cherubim* keep the way to the Tree of Life by being placed before the Garden of *Eden*, it is meant in the same sense as *Hesiod* says:

->*The gods have placed sweat before virtue,* <note>original Greek: "Τῆς δ’ ἀρετῆς ἱδρῶτα θεοὶ προπάροιθεν ἔθηκαν"</note><-

*That God has made Labor the gatekeeper of the Gate of Virtue*; and in the same way that *Virgil* places *Grief*, *Care*, *Sickness*, and *Old Age* at the entrance of the underworld:

->*Before the entrance itself and in the first jaws of the underworld*<-
->*Grief and vengeful Cares have placed their beds, etc.* <note>original Latin: "Vestibulum ante ipsum primisque in faucibus Orci / Luctus & ultrices posuere cubilia Curae, &c."</note><-

In both places, the meaning is surely nothing else but that by being industrious, a man shall attain *Virtue*, and in no other way; and that by being overwhelmed with *care, grief, sickness*, or *old age*, a man shall be sent packing into the state of the dead. Similarly, *Spenser* <note>Edmund Spenser, author of the allegorical epic *The Faerie Queene*</note>—to omit several other instances in his work—makes those two serious figures, *Humilta* <note>Humility</note> and *Ignaro* <note>Ignorance</note>, the gatekeepers of the *House of Holiness* and the *Castle of Duessa*, respectively. He can mean nothing else by this than that he who would enter the House of Holiness must be like *Humilta*, an humble man; and he who can conscientiously pass into the company of the deceptive *Duessa* must be a very *Ignaro*.

In like manner, the meaning of placing these *flaming Cherubim* before Paradise and the gate to the Tree of Life is only that they may serve as a symbolic representation to show what kind of person a man must be, or what state or condition he must partake of or pass into, before he can arrive...

# Chapter 11: Of the Philosophical Cabbala

...arrive at a blessed immortality; namely, that he must recover his fiery *vehicle* <note>In Neoplatonic philosophy, the "vehicle" is the subtle or celestial body that carries the soul</note>, be made *angelic*—equal to the angels <note>original: "ἰσάγγελος" (isangelos)</note>—and enter, as it were, into the order and condition of the *celestial angels*. I think this is such an easy and unexceptionable sense that nothing could be clearer.

Unless, perhaps, it seems even easier if we also add that being made like these *cherubic orders* involves considerable *struggle* <note>original: "colluctation"</note> and *conflict*. The soul is not able to approach the *angelic nature* in her *inward progress* except with pain and agony.
<margin>Isaiah 33:14–15</margin>

This *struggle*, or, if you prefer, *sword-fight* <note>original: "digladiation"</note>, may be represented by the *flaming sword turning every way*. It is as if the meaning were that whoever would recover the capacity of eating of the *fruit of the Tree of Life* must first undergo combat with the *fiery angelic nature*. One must pass through this state before he can come to be made a partaker of life and immortality. It is so common and obvious that *external things* and *people* in *Holy Scripture* are the *symbols* and *hieroglyphs* of *internal spiritual states* <note>original: "dispensations"</note> that I do not need to dwell on it further.

6. By this time, I hope I have made everything smooth and plain in my *Philosophical Cabbala*. I have removed every imaginable doubt concerning the fitness and harmony <note>original: "concinnity"</note> of these matters and the clarity of the grounds I stand on. I have so explicitly and clearly fitted a *philosophical* meaning to the *literal letter of the text* in every *minute detail* <note>original: "punctilio"</note> that I must confess I do not think it likely that *Pythagoras* or anyone else had such a specific and detailed account of its *Cabbala* from any *Jewish priest* or *prophet* (assuming they had any at all) as I have given here. Not that I am so conceited as to imagine that I have a more certain knowledge of the meaning of the *Mosaic text* in this *philosophical* way than they did; but rather, it was not necessary for them to insist on fitting a sense so precisely to every clause as I have done. They were able to persuade their inquisitive *initiates* <note>original: "mystæ"</note> based on the faith of a continuous *tradition* that this or that was the *philosophical* meaning intended by *Moses*. However, since this *tradition* has been interrupted for so many *ages*, I was forced to find a rational explanation or meaning for *everything*, otherwise the probability of the truth might be doubted in *its entirety*.

If anyone thinks this is too much attention to detail <note>original: "curiosity"</note>—as perhaps it is (and yet why should a man think he has found anything fitting that was not intended by that *Wisdom* that anticipates all thoughts?)—he may satisfy himself with the plainer and more general outlines of the *Cabbala*, without expecting to find every passage of the text tied to such a *philosophical sense*. In this way, the whole structure will be like an *apple of gold in a setting of silver*, as I have already noted from *Maimonides* <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher</note>. But if I have fitted a *philosophical* sense to every clause with such lack of objection that he can hardly withhold his agreement, I hope he has no reason to complain that the *Cabbalist* has placed in his hand a **ball of pure and continuous gold.**

### Chapter 12

1. This concludes the defense of my *Philosophic Cabbala* <note>The "Philosophic Cabbala" is the author’s term for his rational, Neoplatonic interpretation of the Book of Genesis</note>. It will not be inappropriate to add something as an apology for the *Cabbalist* himself. I find myself vulnerable to no fewer than three different accusations: namely, *trivial curiosity*, *rashness*, and *inconsistency of judgment*.

Regarding the first, I know that men who are more strictly philosophical and rational will condemn me for taking too much detailed trouble in applying *natural* and *metaphysical truths* to an uncertain and slippery <note>original: "lubricous"</note> *text* or *literal meaning*. They might argue that these truths are better known and more appropriately conveyed through their own proper proofs and arguments, rather than by imagining they are intended in such obscure and enigmatic writings.

But I answer: there is such a fitting and complete agreement between the *Cabbala* and the text—further supported by the history of the origins of *Pythagorean* or *Platonic philosophy*—that it should not be considered a mere whim. Rather, it is a very high probability that such a *Cabbala* as this belongs to the *Mosaic literal text*. This is especially true if you recall how successfully the nature of *numbers* highlights the work of each day, according to the sense of the *Cabbala*.

Furthermore, for my own part, I consider no effort either too detailed or tedious if it serves the common good. I believe that a significant portion of mankind is affected by my labors—the entire Jewish nation and all of *Christendom*—to say nothing of the clever *Persian*, nor do I despair for the *Turk* <note>The author is likely referring to the Safavid and Ottoman Empires, hoping his philosophical approach might bridge religious divides</note>, though at present he is no friend to allegories.

Therefore, we have not applied our efforts thoughtlessly, having recommended such weighty and useful truths in such a religious manner to so great a portion of the world.

2. Regarding the accusation of *rashness* in making it my business to reveal those secrets or *mysteries* that *Moses* had so carefully <note>original: "sedulously"</note> hidden in his obscure text: I say it is the privilege of Christianity—and the current times require it more than ever—to pull off the *veil from Moses’s face* <note>A biblical metaphor for revealing the spiritual meaning behind the literal laws of the Old Testament</note. Although these are grand *truths* that I have discovered, they are as useful as they are sublime, and they cannot help but highly please every good and holy man who is capable of judging them.

Indeed, it is a part of that virtue called constancy, for it is the constant purpose of a good man to embrace that which is best and truest. Conversely, to persist in what we find to be false is nothing but per-

...perverseness and pride. It will prove to be a strong argument for the truth of this present *Cabbala* <note>original: "Cabbala," referring here to the author's philosophical interpretation of Genesis</note> that the evidence for it has drawn me away from my previous opinion, in which I once seemed settled.

To tell the truth, I am not at all inconsistent. I still believe that the literal text of the Scripture does not teach any philosophical principle that men might argue about. When you venture beyond the *literal sense*, you are not being taught by the Scripture itself; rather, you are applying what you have learned elsewhere to the text. Such ideas should not be worthless or trivial notions, nor should they be easily disproven by reason or more solid principles of philosophy, if a man dares to apply them to so sacred a text. Instead, they must be ideas that one is certain will withstand the strictest examination—ideas that lead to a fuller knowledge of God, more clearly align the natural phenomena and outward providence with His most precious *attributes*, and tend toward the furthering of the *holy life*. This, I profess once more, is the sole purpose of the Scripture. Anyone who ventures beyond the *letter* without that guide will soon be bewildered and lose himself in his own fantasies.

4. I would have been satisfied with the *Moral Cabbala* alone. For the *divine life* is superior to all *natural* and *metaphysical* knowledge whatsoever. A man is truly complete when he is genuinely righteous and prudent; I know I can only please such a person with the *Moral Cabbala* that follows. However, if any more zealous pretender to prudence and righteousness—lacking either the time or the ability to examine my *Philosophic Cabbala* to its depths—should nevertheless either condemn it or admire it, he has inappropriately and recklessly stepped outside his own area of expertise. I cannot excuse him from the charge of *injustice* or *folly*.

The holy and divine life either cannot exist at all, or is easily lost in man, if it is not produced and preserved by a deep-rooted <note>original: "radicated"</note> acknowledgment of those grand truths in the *Philosophic Cabbala*: namely <note>original: "viz."</note>, the existence of the *Eternal God* and the certain expectation of a more complete happiness after the dissolution of this mortal *body*. **Verse 1. *A Microcosm or little world.*** <term>Microcosm: a miniature representation of the entire world or universe, often applied to humanity</term>. Nothing is more common or trivial than to compare Man to the universe and make him a little, condensed world in himself. Therefore, it was not difficult to assume what is so easily understood. The Apostle also assumes this when he applies the creation of light in this chapter to the illumination of the soul, as you will hear later.

<margin>1 Corinthians 15:46, 47.</margin>
**Verse 2. *But that which is animal or natural operates first.*** According to the words of the Apostle: *That which is spiritual is not first, but that which is animal or natural; afterward that which is spiritual. The first man is of the earth, earthy; the second man is the Lord from heaven.* But what this earthy condition is, is very vividly described by Moses in this first day’s work. For here we have earth, water, and wind—one tumultuous, dark chaos and confusion of dirt and water, blown into heaps and waves; an unquiet night-storm, an unruly black tempest.

And it is noteworthy that it is not said of this deformed globe, *Let there be Earth; Let there be Water; Let there be Wind:* but all this is the subject matter <note>original Greek: τὸ ὑποκείμενον (*to hypokeimenon*)</note>, a thing already made—namely, *the raw soul of man in the disorder described.* A sad melancholy, like the drowned earth, lies at the bottom, from which care, grief, discontent, agonizing suspicion, and horrid fear are washed up by the restless, watery desire or the irregular suggestions of the *concupiscible* <term>concupiscible: the part of the soul associated with desires, especially for physical or sensory pleasures</term>. In this part is most prominently located base lust and sensuality. Above these is boisterous wrath, stormy revengefulness, foolhardy confidence, and tireless fighting over trivial things. In short, whatever passion and disorder is found in fallen man can be compared to these elements. But God does not leave his creature in this evil condition. So that all this disorder may be discovered, quelled in us, and avoided by us, he says, *Let there be Light*, as you read in the following verse.

<margin>2 Corinthians 4:6.</margin>
**Verse 3. *The daylight appears.*** St. Paul alludes to this when he says: *God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness, shine in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.* In this, the Apostle seems to me to have captured the essence of all *six* days of this spiritual creation at once. The highest manifestation of that light created on the first day is the face of *Jesus Christ*, the *Heavenly Adam*, fully completed on the *sixth* day. Therefore, when it is said, *Let there be Light*, that light is understood as the one that enlightens every man who comes into the world. This is the *divine intellect* as it can be shared with human souls. The first day is its first appearance, still weak and too separated from our emotions; but at last, it grows into the true and plain image and character of the Lord from *Heaven*—*Christ* according to the *Spirit*.

**Verse 4. *And God has framed the nature of man so that he cannot but say, etc.*** Since God works through secondary causes <term>second causes: the natural laws or human actions through which God achieves his purposes in the physical world</term>, nothing is more common...

# The Defense of the Moral Cabbala. Chapter I.

...then to attribute to Him what is actually done by men, even when those actions seem less consistent with the nature of God. Therefore, it should not seem strange if, in this *Moral Cabbala* <note>original: *Cabbala*; here referring to a spiritual or symbolic interpretation of the Bible</note>, we acknowledge that man performs—through the power of God working within the soul—the very things the text says God does. Examples include the *approving of the light as good* and the *distinguishing between light and darkness*, and similar actions. In a *mystical* sense, these actions apply to both God and man. When we speak in a *moral* or *mystical* sense of God acting within us, the nature of the situation requires that whatever He is said to do there, we should also be understood to do through His assistance.

For the human soul is not merely passive like a piece of wood or stone, but is immediately made active by being acted upon by God. Therefore, if God rules within us, we rule with Him; if He contends against sin in us, we also contend along with Him against that same sin. If He sees what is good or evil within us, we, *by that very fact* <note>original: *ipso facto*</note>, see through Him. *In His light, we see light*; and so it is with everything else. Consequently, it is a very easy assumption in this *Moral Cabbala* to take the liberty—where the meaning or a more concise expression requires it—to attribute to man (though not to man alone) what God alone does when we refer to the *literal* meaning of the text. This is entirely consistent with the Apostle’s words: *I live, and yet not I* <note>Galatians 2:20</note>. For if the life of God or Christ was in him, he certainly lived; otherwise, what was that life doing there? He simply did not proudly attribute that life to himself as his own, but acknowledged it to be from God.

# The Defense of the Moral Cabbala. CHAPTER 1.

The fact that **Venus** <note>The Roman goddess of love and beauty.</note> was born from the sea is an emblem suggesting that the **desiring part of the soul** <note>original: "Concupiscible"</note> is rooted in moisture. This would not be so relevant if natural philosophy and experience did not confirm that **sexual desire** <note>original: "Concupiscence"</note> is located in the body's "moisture." This is the origin of Heraclitus’s saying, *A dry soul is the wisest* <note>original Greek: Ξηρὰ ψυχὴ σοφωτάτη; original Latin: *Anima sicca sapientissima*</note>, found in Porphyry's *On the Cave of the Nymphs*. Without question, the disordered use of this desiring part of the soul greatly dulls the mind and makes it incapable of divine perception and knowledge. And yet, to strive for a complete lack of feeling regarding the pleasures of the body is equally groundless and unjustifiable. I shall speak more fully on this in the notes for verses 22 and 31 of this chapter.

**Verse 21. Winged Prayers.** <note>original: "Ejaculations," meaning short, sudden, and intense prayers or thoughts directed toward God.</note> Whether these are mental or vocal, they are fittingly compared to **birds** <note>original: "Fowls"</note>, according to the words of Homer:

->—he spoke winged words.<-
<note>original Greek: —ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα.</note>

And if **spoken words** have wings, the **inward desires** of the soul may well be said to have wings also. These are the **words of the mind**, just as the others are the words of the mouth; they generally fly further and reach Heaven sooner than the spoken ones.

Note also that Origen likewise makes a distinction here between the **fish** and the **birds**. He considers the **birds** to be good thoughts and the **fish** to be evil ones. However, I consider them both to be neutral—things that should be regulated, not destroyed, by the **Mystical Adam**, which is **Christ**, the **Image of God** in man. Furthermore, these strong spiritual heats and prayers are the effects of **Melancholy** <note>In the 17th century, "melancholy" was seen as a physical temperament that could lead to deep reflection or religious ecstasy, as well as sadness.</note>. When the divine principle in man activates this temperament, it works very fiercely and sharply. It is a great consumer of the "delightful moisture" of the desiring part of the soul and greatly weakens physical pleasures. This is to the great advantage of the mind if done with discretion and proper moderation; otherwise, if this passion is indulged in too much, it may lead to fevers, frenzies, and mental distractions.

The structure of the text, which mentions only such birds as frequent the **waters**, naturally points to the meaning we have given. But if our imagination expands to other winged creatures, such as the birds of the mountains and various other sorts of birds, they may also have their own proper meanings. They are a part of those **animal-like symbols** <note>original: "Animal Figurations"</note> that are to be subdued and regulated by the **Mystical Adam**, the Spirit of **Christ** within us.

**Verse 22. Might have something to order.** If you take away all the **passions** from the soul, the mind of man will be like a General without an army, or an army without an enemy. The **Pythagoreans** <note>Followers of the philosopher Pythagoras.</note> define **Righteousness** as *the peace of the whole soul, its parts being in good tune or harmony* <note>original Greek: εἰρήνα τᾶς ὅλας ψυχᾶς μετ᾿ εὐρυθμίας</note>. This matches another definition of theirs, describing **Righteousness** as *the harmony or agreement of the irrational parts of the soul with the rational part* <note>original Greek: ἁρμονία τῷ ἀλόγῳ μέρεος τᾶς ψυχᾶς ποτὶ τὸ λόγον ἔχον</note>. To completely remove all the passions of the mind, instead of bringing them under the right rule of Reason and Divine Light, is as if a man should cut away all the strings of an instrument instead of tuning it.

**Verse 24. *And makes the spirited part fruitful.*** <note>original: "Irascible," referring to the part of the soul associated with anger, courage, and vigor.</note> Religious devotions helped along by Melancholy dry out the body very much and heat it, and make it very—

This more fierce and fiery affection in man is <margin>Enneads, Book 1, Chapter 8.</margin> what **Plotinus** <note>A major Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 204–270 AD).</note> calls "the beast-like and lion-like nature within us" <note>original Greek: *tò thēriōdes kaì leontōdes*</note>. If **Adam** <note>Here representing the rational mind or the soul in its state of governance.</note> keeps this nature in subjection, there is no harm in it, but rather good. It is evident in the Gospel that our Savior Christ was at one time deeply moved with **Sorrow**, and at another time very strongly carried away with **Zeal** and **Anger**, as you may observe in the accounts of his raising **Lazarus** and whipping the money-changers out of the Temple. This is not an imperfection, but rather a perfection; the **divine Life**, when it has reached the passions and body of a man, becomes more tangible, full, and sensible. The only danger lies in being uncontrollably passionate, or when the body is carried away by its own imbalance—or by the hypocrisy of the mind—and one still imagines or pretends that it is the impulse of the **divine Spirit**. This is a too frequent mistake, God knows, but such a thing was impossible to happen in our Savior. Therefore, the passions of his mind were perfections rather than imperfections, as they are for all those who are close and sincere followers of him, especially when they have reached the **Sixth Day’s progress** <note>In the author's allegorical system, the Sixth Day represents the final stage of spiritual development where the soul fully reflects the divine image.</note>.

There are all three parts of that divine image—**Knowledge**, **Righteousness**, and **Holiness**—which are mentioned in the previous description by **Plato**, as if Plato had been pre-instructed by men of the same Spirit as the Apostle.

**The true and perfect Man.** **Plotinus** calls that divine principle within us "the true man" <note>original Greek: *ton alēthinon anthrōpon*</note>. The rest is the "brutish nature," the "lion-like and beast-like nature" <note>original Greek: *to leontōdes kai thēriōdes*</note>, as I said before.

Thus, the description might read: "To be like God is to be holy and just, together with wisdom and power." However, I suspect that this **Power** is already included in **Holiness** and **Justice**. For unless we have reached the power to be able to act constantly according to these virtues, we are merely well-wishers of holiness and righteousness, rather than being properly and formally righteous and holy.

> "For God wills that this remarkable creation of God, Man, should not only be stainless from these, but also rule over them" <note>original Latin: *Vult enim Deus ut insignis ista Dei factura, Homo, non solùm immaculatus sit ab his, sed & dominetur eis*</note>.

For it is the Will of God, says Origen, not only that we should be free from any stain from these passions (which would be more certainly achieved if we were utterly rid of them and they were quite rooted out of our nature), but that we should rule over them without being at all blemished or unsettled by them. And for my own part, I do not understand how the Kingdom of Heaven, which is to be within us, can be any kingdom at all if there are no subjects there to be ruled over and to obey. Therefore, the passions of the body are not to be quite extinguished but regulated, so that there may be a greater fullness of life in the whole man.

And those who strive after such a still, silent, and demure condition of mind—those who wish to feel nothing but peace and rest, and who try to make their whole nature empty of all **Animal Figurations** <note>The specific shapes or expressions of our physical and emotional nature.</note> whatsoever—what do they achieve but a clear day shining upon a barren heath that feeds neither cow nor horse? Neither sheep nor shepherd is to be seen there, but only a wasted, silent solitude, and one uniform dryness and emptiness. And yet, while a man fancies himself thus wholly **divine**, he is not aware how he is even then held down by his **Animal Nature**. He does not realize that it is nothing but the stillness and fixity of **Melancholy** <note>One of the four "humors" or temperaments in ancient medicine, associated here with a heavy, brooding, or overly-withdrawn spiritual state.</note> that deceives him. In place of the true Divine Principle, this melancholy would take the government for itself and, in this usurped tyranny, cruelly destroy all the rest of the animal expressions. But the true Divine Life would destroy nothing that is in Nature, but only regulate and order things for the fuller and more sincere enjoyment of man. It reproaches nothing but sinfulness and excess, granting **Sanguine** and **Choler** <note>Two other humors: Sanguine (active/cheerful) and Choler (energetic/angry).</note> as much virtue and religion as either **Phlegm** or Melancholy. For the Divine Life, just as it is to take up human nature in general, is not repelled by any of the temperaments. Indeed, the squabbles in the world are ordinarily not about true piety and virtue, but about which of the complexions or which humor shall

### Chapter 1. The Defense of the Moral Cabbala.

...ascend the Throne, and sit there instead of Christ himself. But I will not speak too much on one theme; I shall instead take a short view of the whole allegory of the chapter.

In the **First day**, there is Earth, Water, and Wind, over which and through which there is nothing but disconsolate darkness and tumultuous agitation. The winds ruffle the waters into mighty waves, and the waves wash up the mire and dirt into the water—all becoming merely a rude heap of confusion and desolation. This is the state of the <term>Earthly Mind</term> <note>original Greek: *νῦς χοϊκός* (nous choikos). A term used by Philo to describe the unrefined, physical intellect or the "man of dust."</note>, or "Earthly Adam," as **Philo** calls him, until God commands the Light to shine out of Darkness, offering him a guide to a better condition.

In the **Second day**, the **Firmament** is created, dividing the upper and the lower waters, so that the soul may feel the strong impulses or taste the different flavors of either. Thus, the Will of man is touched from both above and beneath. This is the day in which Life and Death, Good and Evil, are set before him, and he may reach out his hand and take his choice.

<margin>Matthew 7:20.</margin>
In the **Third day**, the Earth is uncovered from the waters so that fruit-bearing trees may be planted. *By their fruits you shall know them,* says our Savior—that is, by their works.

In the **Fourth day**, there appears a more full arrival of Divine Light, and the **Sun of Righteousness** warms the Soul with a sincere love for both God and man.

In the **Fifth day**, so that this light of Righteousness and the "bright eye of divine Reason" does not shine its rays upon an empty field where there is nothing to subdue or to guide and order, God sends out whole shoals of fish in the waters and numerous flights of birds in the air. This also includes part of the **Sixth day’s** work, in which all kinds of beasts are created.

In these creatures are revealed the various suggestions and thoughts of the mind, which spring from these lower elements of human nature—namely, Earth and Water, or Flesh and Blood. A person beholds all of these in the light of the Sun of Righteousness, discovers what they truly are, knows what to call them, and can rule over them; he is not driven to be over-ruled by them. This is **Adam**, the masterpiece of God's creation and Lord of all creatures, framed after the image of God. He is "Christ according to the Spirit," under whose feet the entire animal life—with its various motions, forms, and shapes—is subdued. 

He will call everything by its proper name and set every creature in its proper place. <margin>Isaiah 32:5.</margin> *The vile person shall no longer be called generous, nor the miser called bountiful.* <margin>Isaiah 5:20.</margin> *Woe be unto those who call evil good, and good evil; who call darkness light, and light darkness.* 

He will not call bitter passion "holy zeal"; nor call fake, seductive courtesy "friendship"; nor call a false, soft hesitation to punish the undeserving "pity"; nor call cruelty "justice"; nor call revenge "magnanimity" <note>Greatness of spirit or courage.</note>; nor call unfaithfulness "shrewd policy"; nor call talkativeness either "wisdom" or "piety." But I have run into the second chapter before I was aware of it.

In this first chapter, Adam is said only to have dominion over all living creatures and to feed upon the fruit of the plants. And what is **Pride** but a mighty, mountainous whale? What is **Lust** but a goat? The **Lion**, **Eagle**, and **Bear** represent willful dominion; the **Fox** represents craft; and the **Ox** represents worldly toil. Over these and a thousand more is the rule of Man—I mean of Adam, the Image of God.

# CHAPTER II. The Defense of the Moral Cabbala.

...example of *disobedience* and *unbelief*. For the Greek word <term>disobedience</term> <note>original: *Ἀπείθια* (apeitheia)</note> may well include both *meanings*—namely, *disobedience*, or the failure to do the will of God according to the measure of power and knowledge He has already given us; and *unbelief*, the doubt that the divine Life and Spirit within us is able to subdue the whole creation of the *microcosm* <note>original: "little World"</note> under us. This "world" includes all the *animal impulses* and *forms* <note>original: "Animal Motions and Figurations"</note>—be they *lions*, *bears*, *goats*, or *whales*, or whatever else they may be—as well as the ability to cast out the children of *Anak* <note>In the Bible, the Anakim were a race of giants; here they represent formidable spiritual obstacles</note> before the *Israelites*, as seen in that other archetype <note>original: "Type"</note> of Christ and of His Kingdom in the *souls of men*.

**Verse 4.** *The generations of the animal life when God created them.* For these are as truly the works of God as the Divine Life itself, though they are nothing compared to it. Indeed, they are but a heap of confusion without it. Therefore, the great achievement is to have these in proper order and subjection to the Spirit or Heavenly Life within us, which is *Christ*. And so that you may have a more specific understanding of these generations of the *animal life*, I shall give you a list of some of them, though in no particular order, just as they first come to my memory.

Such things include *anger*, *zeal*, *indignation*, *sorrow*, *mockery* <note>original: "Derision"</note>, *mirth*, *seriousness* <note>original: "Gravity"</note>, *open-heartedness*, *reservedness*, *stoutness* <note>here meaning courage or determination</note>, *flexibility*, *boldness*, *fearfulness*, *mildness*, *sharpness* <note>original: "Tartness"</note>, *candor*, *suspicion*, *stubbornness* <note>original: "Peremptoriness"</note>, *despondency*, and *triumph* or *boasting* <note>original: "Gloriation"</note>. Also, all the *inclinations* <note>original: "Propensions"</note> toward physical exercise or bodily activity, such as *running*, *leaping*, *swimming*, *wrestling*, *jousting* <note>original: "Fusting"</note>, *racing* <note>original: "Coursing"</note>, and the like. This is in addition to all the courtly introductions, necessary accompaniments, and delightful consequences of marriage, which spring up from the love of women and the pleasure of children. This says nothing of those enjoyments that arise from shared affections and simple natural friendship between one man and another, or larger circles of acquaintances—their *friendly feasting*, *sports*, *music*, and *dancing*. All these, and many more that I do not have time to list, are but the natural sproutings <note>original: "pullulations"</note> of the *animal life*, and in themselves they have neither good nor evil in them. In fact, to speak more truly and impartially, they are good, according to the approval of Him who made them. They become bad only to those who are bad and act either without moderation, for unjustifiable ends, or under improper circumstances; otherwise, they are very good in their kind when they are regulated and moderated by the divine principle within us.

And I think it is of great importance for men to notice this truth for these reasons: First, because the boundaries of sin and the innocent motions of nature are not plainly and openly set out and defined. When men count the various *animal forms* and natural motions as *sins*, they take upon themselves such a task—namely, the complete rooting out of that which would be neither good nor perhaps even possible to utterly destroy—that they seem in truth to imply that it is impossible to enter into that *Rest* or *Sabbath* of the people of God. Therefore, by carelessly sheltering themselves under this confused cloud of "sins" and "infirmities," where they exaggerate everything as if every action were equally sinful, if they are but zealous and punctual in some...

# The Defense of the Moral Cabbala. CHAP. II.

They consider it quite well, and a high testimony of their sanctity. And their hypocrisy will be sure to focus on that which is least relevant to the purpose; that is, a man will spend his zeal on behalf of some natural temperament <term>complexion</term> <note>original: "Complexion"; in the 17th century, this referred to a person's natural physical and mental constitution or "humors."</note> he himself possesses, and against the opposite disposition. But as for the essential dictates of the Divine Light, he will be sure to neglect them because they are harder to perform, even though they are of more importance both for himself and the common good. But if it were more clearly defined what is sin and what is not sin, a man might fight against his enemy with more heart and courage, as the enemy would not appear so numerous and formidable; and he would have less opportunity for perverse excuses and hypocritical evasions <note>original: "tergiversations"</note>.

The second reason is that men may not think better of themselves than they actually are for their hatred of things that have no inherent harm in them; nor think worse of others than they deserve when they do things that are approved by God and the Divine Light. This is of very great importance for maintaining Christian love and unity among men.

The third and last reason is that they may observe the madness and hypocrisy of the world, whose religious disputes or secret judgments are commonly nothing more than the conflict and antipathy between opposite expressions <note>original: "Figurations"</note> of the *Animal Life*. These, like wild beasts without a master to keep order among them, are very eager to devour one another. But by this, every man shall know whether it is temperament or religion that reigns within him: if he loves God with all his heart and all his soul, and his neighbor as himself, and can give a sufficient reason for all his actions and opinions based on that *Eternal Light*, the *Love of God* poured into his heart. If not, it is merely a faction of the *Animal Life*, fed and fostered by either natural temperament or custom; and he is far from having arrived at the Kingdom of Christ or entering into 그 true rest of the people of God.

# The Defense of the Moral Cabbala. Chap. II.

<margin>Revelation 21:2</margin>
*Adam*, *Seth*, *Enos*, *Cainan*, *Mahalaleel*, and *Jared* all died, not enjoying the richness of God’s goodness in their physical bodies. But *Enoch*, who was the *Seventh* from *Adam*, was taken up alive into Heaven and seems to enjoy that great bliss in his body. Therefore, the world in the *Seventh Chiliad* <term>Chiliad: a period of one thousand years</term> will be taken up into God, snatched up by His Spirit, and enacted by His Power. The *Jerusalem* that comes down from Heaven will then flourish upon Earth in a most glorious and eminent manner. God will, as I said, pitch His tabernacle <term>tabernacle: a dwelling place; specifically, God's presence among humanity</term> among men. And for God to be in us and with us is the same as us being lifted up into God.

But to come now to the mystery of the Septenary <term>Septenary: the number seven, or a group of seven</term>, or the number *Seven*; it is of two kinds: the first is the "seven within the decad" <note>original: ἡ ἐντὸς δεκάδος ἑβδομάς; "decad" refers to the number ten</note>, the other is the "one outside." The Septenary within the Decad is merely *seven units*; the other is a *Seventh Number*, *beginning from a unit and continuing in a steady geometrical proportion until you have gone through seven proportional terms*. Regarding the *seventh term*, there is this second kind of Septenary, 
<margin>* In his *Cosmopoeia Mosaic*.</margin> 
whose nature *Philo* <note>Philo Judaeus, a first-century Jewish philosopher who interpreted the Bible allegorically</note> fully expresses in these words: 

> *For always beginning from a unit, and continuing in double, or triple, or whatever proportion you choose, the seventh number of this rank is both Square and Cube, containing both kinds: the incorporeal and the corporeal substance. It contains the incorporeal according to the surface area <note>original: superficies</note> which the squares exhibit; but the corporeal according to the solid dimensions which are set out by the cubes.* <note>original Greek: Αἰεὶ γὰρ ὁ ἀπὸ μονάδος συντιθέμενος ἐν διπλασίοις ἢ τριπλασίοις ἢ συνόλως ἀναλογοῦσιν, ἕβδομος ἀριθμὸς κύβος τε καὶ τετράγωνός ἐστιν, ἀμφότερα εἴδη περιέχων τῷ τε ἀσωμάτῳ καὶ σωματικῆς οὐσίας· τῆς μὲν ἀσωμάτου κατὰ τὸ ἐπίπεδον ἣν ἀποτελοῦσι τετράγωνοι, τῆς δὲ σωματικῆς κατὰ τὴν ἑτέραν, ἣν ἀποτελοῦσι κύβοι.</note>

As for example, 64 or 729: these are numbers that arise in this manner. Each of them is a *Seventh* term from a unit; one arises from a double proportion <note>1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64</note>, and the other from a triple proportion <note>1, 3, 9, 27, 81, 243, 729</note>. If the proportion were quadruple, quintuple, or any other, the same reason applies: some other *Seventh* number would arise that would prove to be of the same nature as these. They would prove to be both *Cubes* and *Squares*—that is, both *Corporeal* <term>corporeal: relating to the physical body</term> and *Incorporeal* <term>incorporeal: spiritual or without a physical body</term>. For instance, 64 is made either by multiplying eight by eight, making it a *Square*, or else by multiplying four cubically (for four times four times four is again 64), making it a *Cube*. And so 729 is made either by squaring 27 or by cubically multiplying 9, for either way 729 will be produced; thus it is both Cube and Square, Corporeal and Incorporeal. By this, it is suggested that the world shall not be reduced in the *Seventh* day to a mere spiritual consistency—to an incorporeal condition—but that there shall be a cohabitation of the Spirit with Flesh in a mystical or moral sense, and that "God will pitch His tent among us." Then everlasting righteousness shall be settled and rooted in the Earth for as long as mankind shall inhabit its face.

And this truth of the *Reign of Righteousness* in this *Seventh thousand years* is still more clearly set out to us in the *Septenary within Ten*, the "seven within the decad" <note>original: τῇ ἐντὸς δεκάδος ἑβδομάδι</note> as *Philo* calls it: the simple number *Seven*. For the parts it consists of, and into which it is most equally divisible (or rather, only divisible into different numbers), are 3 and 4, which put together...

Whatever others *might suggest* to the contrary, there is nothing so safe for a man who is truly sincere as to refuse to be "led by the nose" by others. We see the sad result of such behavior in *Eve's* listening to the outward suggestions of the *Serpent*.

*Verse* 22. *The greatest part of that Paradise a man is capable of upon Earth.* This is a truth of perception and experience. It can no more be proven by logic than the fact that White is White or Black is Black.

# CHAPTER II. The Defense of the Moral Cabbala.

<margin>See *The Immortality of the Soul*, Book 3, Chapter 1, Section 2.</margin>
<margin>Commentary on Plotinus's *Enneads*, Book 2, Volume 8, Chapter 8, and elsewhere. <note>original: *Comment. in Plotin. Ennead. 2. lib. 8. cap. 8.*</note></margin>

*Verse* 23. *Essential operation of the Soul.* The very nature of the Soul, insofar as it is a Soul, is a capacity for shaping or giving life to a Body. Though *Aristotle* says the soul must always inhabit an organized Body, he does not actually prove it. For my part, I am very inclined to think that the Soul is never entirely without some *Vehicle* <note>original: "Vehicle". In Neoplatonic philosophy, a "vehicle" (*ochema*) is a subtle, quasi-material body that carries the soul and allows it to interact with different levels of reality.</note> or another, even though *Plotinus* is of a different mind. He believes that the Soul, at its highest peak, is joined with God and nothing else, resting nakedly in His arms. I am bold enough to disagree with him on this "exaltation" of the soul, just as I am confident in rejecting his other suspected "extravagance"—his debasement of souls. He suggests that souls can eventually become so drowsy and senseless that they grow out of the ground in the dull state of life found in trees and plants. I am not alone in this freedom to disagree with *Plotinus*. Besides my own intuition (for I must admit I have no absolute logical proof against his opinion), I am encouraged by the example of *Ficinus* <note>original: "Ficinus". Marsilio Ficino was a famous Renaissance philosopher who translated and commented on the works of Plato and Plotinus.</note>, who is a great admirer of that author.

What I was about to say is this: *the shaping or animating of a Body is such a necessary and essential act of the Soul* that the condition and health of the Body it inhabits must be of great importance to the Soul. The Soul is conscious of the Body's state and feels its joy or sorrow through a universal touch and an inward sense that rises into her awareness and attention. We can easily imagine how much the *health and good condition of the Body matters to the Mind* that lives there if we simply consider the state of *plants*. We cannot help but imagine that plants are in a more pleasant state when they flourish and are sweet and pleasing to the eye than when they are withered by age or drought, or beaten down to the earth by heavy rainstorms. It is the same with the human body (where there is a Soul to notice its condition): it is far better when it is healthy through careful judgment and moderation in diet and exercise than when it is either parched by religious gloom <note>original: "superstitious melancholy"</note> or <term>slocken</term> <note>original: "slocken". An archaic word meaning quenched, drenched, or overwhelmed.</note> and drowned in sensuality and excess. Both extremes diminish the joys of life and lessen that full happiness that a person is capable of through their *Mystical Eve*—the "woman" (or sensitive soul) that God has given everyone to take delight in.

<margin>1 Timothy 4:8.</margin>
*Verse* 24. *So far as they are incompatible with the health of the body.* This is an undeniable truth; otherwise, how could the Apostle’s words be true, *that Godliness is profitable for all things, having the promise of this world and that which is to come*? Without the health of the Body, there is nothing at all to be enjoyed in this present world. Certainly, God does not bind us to the laws governing Angels or higher creatures, but to rules suitable to human nature.

*Obedience to the Precepts of that Superior Light.* If the life of the Body grows so strong that it extinguishes or hinders our sense of divine things—our dependence on God and the joyful hope of the life to come—it has then become disorderly. It must be disciplined and kept in check so that it does not pull us down into a hatred of all piety or sink us into a total forgetfulness of God and the divine life.

*Verse* 25. *Without any shame or blushing.* See what has been said regarding the *Philosophic Cabbala*.

# THE DEFENSE OF THE MORAL CABBALA. CHAPTER III.

# CHAPTER III.

A story of a dispute between a prelate and a blacksmith concerning Adam’s eating of the apple. 1. What is meant by the subtlety or deceit of the serpent. That religion, when practiced to its full extent, is a very cheerful state; it is only human hesitation and hypocrisy that have generally placed such a sour and sad mask <note>original: "vizard"</note> upon it. 5, 6. That worldly wisdom, not philosophy, is criticized <note>original: "perstringed"</note> in the mystery of the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil. 10. The meaning of Adam’s flight after he found himself naked. 20. Adam as the earthly-minded man, according to Philo. 21. What is meant by God clothing Adam and Eve with hairy coats in the mystical sense. 23. *Paradise of Luxury* <note>original: "Παράδεισος τρυφῆς"</note>, or the Paradise of Pleasure. That scripture history is written very concisely and therefore allows for modest and judicious supplements to clarify the meaning. 24. What is meant by the cherubim and the flaming sword. Plato’s definition of philosophy: *The practice of death* <note>original: "Μελέτη θανάτου"</note>. A more extensive description of dying to sin and the life of righteousness. That the Christian religion, even as it refers to the physical person of Christ, is under no pretext to be abolished until the final destruction <note>original: "conflagration"</note> of the world by fire.

In this third chapter, we reach the tragic conclusion of the story: the Fall of Adam and the origin of all the misery and calamity that has befallen mankind since the beginning of the world. This was of such horrific consequence because our mother Eve could not suppress her longing, but by the easy persuasion of the serpent, ate the forbidden fruit—as a famous prelate in France once very tragically argued to his attentive audience.

<margin>
See Jean Bodin, *On the Demon-mania of Sorcerers*, Book 2, Chapter 2, pages 123, 124, 125. <note>original: "Jo. Bodin. Mag. Dæmono-man."</note>
</margin>
But it seems, as Bodin relates, that a certain blacksmith in the church heard from this venerable preacher that all of mankind—except for a small handful of Christians—was irrevocably lost to eternal damnation because Adam ate an apple. This blacksmith had the boldness to argue the matter with the prelate. Receiving no satisfaction from the prelate's handling of the literal sense of the text (and his skill, it seems, went no further), the blacksmith finally burst out with these words: "So many quarrels foolishly stirred up over such a tiny thing!" <note>original: "Tam multas rixas pro re tantilla ineptè excitari"</note>; as if he had said in plain English, "What a lot of fuss has there been here about the eating of an apple?" This blasphemous saying, as Bodin writes, had no sooner reached the ears of the French court than it became a proverb among the courtiers. Such a dangerous thing is an ignorant and indiscreet preacher combined with a bold, immodest listener. Bodin, in the same passage, professes it is his judgment that the unskilled insistence of our theologians <note>original: "divines"</note> upon the literal sense of Moses’s writings has produced many hundreds of thousands of atheists. For this reason, I hope that men who are not merely ignorant or impulsive <note>original: "humorous"; in the 17th century, this referred to being governed by the "four humors" or temperaments</note>, but are sincere lovers of God and divine truth, will receive these interpretations of mine <note>original: "Cabbalas"</note> with more favor and acceptance—especially this moral one, as its meaning is significant enough to silence any

**"What a rigid and severe thing," etc.** This is the notion of those who are either complete strangers to religion, or have not yet reached the comforting outcome that may be expected from it. For God takes no delight in the perpetual torment <note>original: "rack"</note> of those souls He came to redeem. Instead, He came to redeem us from that pain and torture which self-love, our untamed desires, and pride of spirit make us liable <note>original: "obnoxious"</note> to. Because men are reluctant to part with these things, and do not have the heart to let them be cut to the core <note>original: "the very quick"</note> and pulled up by the roots, the work is not accomplished according to the full mind and purpose of God. Thus, there are still the seeds of perpetual anxiety, sadness, and inevitable pain. For to be dead is a relief, but to be constantly dying is painful; and it is most often merely the due punishment for hesitation and hypocrisy. When men's spirits have been soured and made sad for so long, their profession and behavior are such that they frighten all inexperienced young people away from any tolerable commitment to religious matters. **Verses 2, 3. *But the womanly part in Adam.*** It is simply the same Soul in man holding a dialogue with itself that is represented by these three parts: *The Serpent, Adam, and the Woman.* <note>In More’s "Moral Cabbala," these are internal faculties: the Serpent is the sensory drive, the Woman is the emotions/will, and Adam is the intellect/reason.</note> And here the Soul, recollecting itself, cannot help but confess that religion denies her no honest or fitting pleasure that does not endanger her greater happiness. She reflects on the peril she is in of losing the divine life and the proper sense of God if she ventures so recklessly to follow her own will, rather than measuring all her actions and purposes by the divine light that is currently available to guide her.

**Verse 4. *But the Serpent, &c.*** The meaning of this verse is that the eager desire for *pleasure* had worked itself so far into the sweetness of the *animal life* that it clouded the man’s judgment. It made him foolishly hope that being so freely devoted to his own will did no harm to the will of the Spirit and the life of God within him. Yet, despite this, the Apostle expressly writes: *What fellowship is there between righteousness and unrighteousness? What communion between light and darkness? What agreement between Christ and Belial?* And he tells us elsewhere *that Christ gave himself for his Church, so that he might thoroughly purge and sanctify it, so that it should have neither spot nor wrinkle, but that it should be holy and blameless—a true Virgin-Bride clothed with his divine life and glory.* Those men who are so willing to waver between the two—the *flesh* and the *spirit*—and have enough room in their hearts to entertain both (as if there could be any friendship and communion between them), let them seriously consider whether this opinion is not the same one that deceived *Adam*. Let them fear the same sad outcome and acknowledge that it arises from the very same principle: the excessive desire to please their own wills without the permission of the divine light or consulting the will of God.

But that the careful exercise of *Reason* in the knowledge of God’s marvelous works in *Nature*, or those innocent, delightful conclusions in *Geometry* and *Arithmetic*, and the like—that these parts of knowledge should be criticized <note>original: "perstringed"; to be censured or touched upon disparagingly</note> by *Moses* in this history—seems to me to have not the least probability. For there are so very few in the world whose minds are seriously focused on such objects that it would not have been worth mentioning. And then again, it is plain that the failure comes from the desire for the kind of knowledge that the *Woman*—the flowering life of the *Body*—caused *Adam* to sin through. Therefore, it is the fulfilling of the various desires of the flesh, not a high aspiration for intellectual contemplations, that made way for the transgression; for intellectual pursuits involve the *Masculine faculties*, not the *Feminine* <note>In More's allegory, "Masculine" refers to the rational mind and "Feminine" to the sensory or emotional nature of the soul</note>.

Therefore, I say, the *Wisdom* that the *Serpent* promised here was not *Natural Philosophy* <note>The precursor to modern science</note>, or *Mathematics*, or any of those harmless and noble achievements of the human understanding. Instead, it was the *Knowledge* of the world and the *Wisdom* of the flesh. For the *life of the body* is full of desires and expectations of satisfaction in gaining this or that external thing, whether it be *honor*, *riches*, or *pleasure*. And if they cast off the divine Guide within them, they will have it by hook or by crook. And this worldly *wisdom* is so plausible in the world, and so sweetly relished by the merely natural man, that it would be temptation enough for a novice—if only to be considered *wise*—to venture into such things as would initiate him into it.

<margin>Romans 8:7.</margin>

This wisdom of the flesh, he says, is *at enmity with God*. For again, these kinds of contemplations are not so much the knowledge of *Good* and *Evil* as they are of *Truth* and *Falsehood*. The knowledge of *Good* and *Evil* refers to that experience we gather in *moral* or *political* encounters.

<margin>Enthusiasm Triumphatus, sections 21, 23.</margin>

I think animals like *baboons* and *satyrs* <note>More refers to mythological satyrs as if they were real lecherous animals</note> and such lustful creatures have these pleasures to an even higher degree. And I fear no men are as prone to such misinterpretations of Scripture as the boldest *religionists* and *mock-prophets*, who are very full of heat and physical energy, and have their *imagination* too often infected with the fumes of those lower body parts, whose intense sensations and pleasures they prefer over all the subtle delights of *Reason* and noble contemplation.

# The Defense of the Moral Cabbala. CHAPTER III.

...deception <note>original: "gullery"</note> of their own corrupted fancy, let us listen and keep close to Him who can neither deceive nor be deceived—I mean *Christ* and his holy Apostles. And now in particular, let us consider that grave and pious 
<margin>1 Peter 2:11</margin> 
warning <note>original: "Monition"</note> of *St. Peter: "Beloved, I beseech you, as strangers and pilgrims, abstain from fleshly lusts that war against the soul."* In this passage, this holy man, instructed by God, plainly suggests that the soul in this world is like a traveler in a foreign country, and that she is journeying toward a state more suitable to her than this one in the body. From this it follows that the tender nurturing of those pleasures that are mortal and die with the body is a sign of a poor, base, and degenerate mind—one unacquainted with its own nature and dignity.

*Verse 7. How naked he was now, and stripped of all strength and power for divine and holy things.* This was *Adam’s* mistake: he thought he could serve two masters—*the will of God* and *the dictates of the flesh*. But 
<margin>Wisdom of Solomon 1:5</margin> 
thus he became estranged from the divine life and power, which *will not dwell in a body that is subject to sin. For the holy spirit of discipline will flee from deceit, and withdraw from thoughts that are without understanding (namely, those that are suggested and pursued at random), and will not remain when unrighteousness enters.*

*Verse 8. Could not endure the presence of it.* For the *divine Light* was now only a convincer of his failures, but provided nothing of divine love and power, as it does for those who are obedient and sincere followers of its commands. Therefore, *Adam* could no more endure the presence of that Light than sore eyes can endure the sun or candlelight.

*Verse 9. Persisted and came up closer to him.* This divine Light is God, as He is manifested in the conscience of man. However, His *love* and *power* are not fit to be shared with *Adam* in this dissolute and disobedient condition he is in—only conviction is shared, to bring him to repentance. And after the rush of his excessive pleasures and passions, when he was for a time "left in the suds" <note>An old English idiom meaning to be left in a state of embarrassment, difficulty, or helpless confusion</note> as they say, this *light of conscience* did more strictly and particularly sift and examine him. He might well wonder to himself why he found himself so afraid to commune with his own heart.

*Verse 10. Honestly confessed.* For he immediately discovered the reason why he was thus estranged from the divine Light: he found himself naked of that power and good affection he had toward divine things before. He had lost those by indiscriminately following the wild suggestions of his own disordered will, as you see in the following verse. Therefore, he had no desire to be convinced of any obligation to things he felt he had no power left to perform, nor any inclination toward.

*Verse 11. The sad outcome of his disobedience.* Adam's conscience traced all this mental confusion back to his disobedience and his choice to follow his own will, without any rule or guidance from the will of God.

*Verse 12. His Rational Faculties, and said.* Like that line in the comic playwright <note>Terence, a Roman playwright</note>,

# CHAPTER III. The Defense of the Moral Cabbala.

And so, men commonly reason themselves into an allowance for sin by claiming human infirmities or natural frailties.

*Verse 13. That he kept his feminine faculties in no better order. That is,* the foolish and mischievous sophistry used by men, by which they trick themselves into thinking that because certain things *can* be done, and because they are merely the suggestions of nature—which is God's work in the world—they may therefore do them in whatever way and measure they please. But here, the *divine Light* does not punish *Adam* for exercising his *feminine* faculties <note>In More’s system, the "feminine" represents the sensory and emotional part of the soul, while the "masculine" represents higher reason.</note>, but because, in exercising them, they were not regulated by a higher and holier rule, and because he did not keep them in subjection to the *masculine*.

To which he had nothing to say, except... [etc.]. The meaning is that *Adam's* temptations were very strong and so well-suited <note>original: "accommodate"</note> to the vigorous life of the body that he believed he could not resist. But what can the human will not accomplish if it is sincere and assisted by God, as *Adam's* was?

*Verse 14. Then the divine Light began to punish the Serpent.* From this 14th verse to the 20th, there seems to be a description of a person's conscience plainly convicting him of all the ugliness and trouble caused by the sinful paths he has taken. There are also hints of the advantages of the *better life* if he were to convert to it—which is like a sudden flame kindled in his mind for a time. However, because the true love of the divine life and the power of grace are not also communicated to his soul, and his body remains unpurified of the filth it has contracted through previous evil ways, this flame is quickly extinguished. All those warnings and visions of what so nearly concerned him are drowned in oblivion, and he immediately settles back into his old, bad ways.

*That it crept basely upon the belly.* See what has been said regarding the writings of *Philo* <note>Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BCE – 50 CE) was a Jewish philosopher who pioneered the allegorical interpretation of Hebrew Scripture.</note> on verse 1.

*Verse 15. But if I might once descend so far.* The divine light could well be said to speak these words within *Adam*. For his conscience might well remind him of the pleasant sense of the *harmless joys of the body* he experienced while in a state of obedience and sincerity. If the *divine light* had worked itself into a more full and universal possession of all his faculties, the regulated joys of the *body*—which were the offspring of the "woman"—would have so far exceeded the tumultuous pleasures of disordered desires that they would have extinguished their heat, just as sunlight playing upon a fire puts it out, as was already mentioned regarding this 15th verse.

*Verse 16. So that the natural joy of the body's health shall be greatly corrupted.* The divine light within *Adam's* conscience might very well say all this, since he likely already had a taste of it. After immoderately satisfying his furious desires for pleasure, he found himself in a dull, sluggish, and nauseating condition—even though fresh impulses <note>original: "recruits"</note> spurred him on to new follies. For the *Moral Cabbala* does not assume it was one single mistaken act that brought *Adam* to this confusion of mind, but rather general disobedience and leading a life unguided by the light and law of God.

*Earthly-minded Adam.* *Philo* calls him "the earthly mind" <note>original Greek: *gēinon noun* (γήϊνον νοῦν)</note>, page 332.

<summary>More interprets Adam's excuse for sin as a failure to govern his sensory "feminine" side with his rational "masculine" spirit, arguing that conscience warns against sin but is often overwhelmed by bodily habits.</summary>

# The Defense of the Moral Cabbala. CHAPTER III.

*Verses 17, 18, 19.* Adam’s conscience was so awakened by the *divine Light* and *Reason*, and his *experience* so instructed him at that moment, that he could easily see his own fate if he continued in these disobedient ways. He realized he would be stung and troubled in his wild pursuit of excessive <note>original: "inordinate"</note> pleasure so long as the *earthly mind* was his guide. However, despite this conviction, the path Adam would eventually choose—unless God visited him with a higher degree of additional <note>original: "superadvenient"</note> grace that would give him *faith*, *power*, and *devotion*—is revealed in the very next verse.

*Verse 20.* Adam was not sufficient. For the mere conviction of light, when separated from *faith*, *power*, and *devotion*, may indeed disturb and confuse the mind, but it cannot by itself calm or settle a person toward doing good if they have developed a habit of evil.

<margin>* In his *Who is the Heir of Divine Things?* <note>original: "Quis rerum divinarum hæres"</note></margin>
*Called her, My life.* As soon as this correction and punishment from the *divine Light* manifested in Adam’s conscience was over, he immediately returned to his previous way of thinking and followed the same intentions he had before. He emotionally concluded that however true his conscience might be, nothing could be truer than this: *that the joy of his body was a necessary comfort in life, and therefore he would base his happiness on indulging it.* By clinging to this desire, he considered it *his very life*, believing life was not worth living without it. These are almost the exact words of \*Philo, speaking of the physical senses which contain this bodily joy: "For the earthly mind, named Adam, having seen it and being deceived, called that 'life' which was actually his own death" <note>original: "Ἡν γὰρ ὁ γήϊνος νοῦς, ὄνομα Ἀδάμ, ἰδὼν ἀπατηθεὶς, τῷ ἑαυτοῦ θάνατον, ζωὴν ἐκείνην ὠνόμασεν"</note>. This is Philo’s interpretation of this verse.

<margin>Psalms 35:26 and 109:29.</margin>
*Verse 21. Put on hairy coats.* The *Philosophical Cabbala* and the biblical text fit together perfectly and easily here. This *moral interpretation* will not seem difficult if you consider scriptural phrases like: *“But as for his enemies, let them be clothed with shame,”* and elsewhere, *“Let them be clothed with rebuke and dishonor,”* among other similar passages. Is it not standard and natural to describe people as "clothed" according to their character and status? For instance, fools are traditionally dressed in a *fool's coat*. Since Adam’s will and desires were so firmly set on a *brutish life*, it is fitting to think that when the *divine Light* judged them to be like animals, the rebuke it gave them is described as *“clothing them with the skins of beasts.”*

The meaning of this verse is that the *divine Light* in Adam’s conscience struggled with him once more, and Adam was convinced that he would become a kind of *brute* by following the paths he intended. In fact, he was content with this, as one might imagine, because the pleasure of sin had so weakened his higher faculties that there was little to no strength left, at least for the time being, to lift him toward heaven and holiness.

Truly, vile *Epicureanism* <note>A philosophy often misinterpreted in this era as the pursuit of crude sensory pleasure.</note> and *sensuality* will make the soul of man...

# CHAPTER III. The Defense of the Moral Cabbala.

...so degenerate and blind that he will not only be content to slide into animalistic <note>original: "Brutish"</note> immorality, but even please himself with the opinion that he is a real animal <note>original: "Brute"</note> already—an ape, a satyr, or a baboon. Such a person believes that the best of men are no better, except that "civilizing" them and a hardworking education has made them appear in a more refined shape, and that long-instilled <note>original: "inculcate"</note> precepts have been mistaken for innate <note>original: "connate"</note> principles of honesty and natural knowledge. Otherwise, they argue, there are no essential grounds for religion and virtue, but only what has happened to be adopted by overpowering custom. These things, I dare say, are as easily disprovable <note>original: "confutable"</note> as any conclusion in mathematics is demonstrable. But as many as are thus foolish <note>original: "sottish"</note>, let them enjoy their own wilderness and ignorance; it is sufficient for a good man that he is conscious within himself that he is more nobly descended, better bred and born, and more skillfully taught by the purified faculties of his own mind.

*Verse 22. Designed the contrary.* The mercy of the Almighty is such toward poor humanity that our weak and dark spirit cannot always be as resolutely wicked as we might wish to be. Therefore, it is a foolish <note>original: "fond"</note> assumption of desperate men who do all the violence they can to the remains of that light and principle of religion and honesty left in them, hoping thereby to find rest and tranquility of mind by killing or completely erasing all the rules of godliness and morality from their souls. For it is not in their power to do so, nor do they have any reason to promise themselves they are thereby secure from the pangs of conscience. For some events of Providence or another may so awaken them that they shall be forced to acknowledge their error and rebellion with unexpressible bitterness and confusion of spirit. And the longer they have run in the wrong direction, the more tedious a journey they have to return back.

Wherefore, it is safer to commit to that life early on—the life that, once attained, neither deserves nor is subject to any change or death; I mean when we have reached the proper measure of it. For this is the natural accomplishment of the soul; all else is but rust and dirt that lies upon it.

*Verse 23. Out of this Paradise of Luxury.* The English translation takes no notice of any more Paradises than one, calling it always the *Garden of Eden*. But the Seventy <note>the Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note>—who are more favorable to our *Moral Cabbala*—what they call a "Garden in Eden" at first, they later name the *paradise of luxury* <note>original Greek: παράδεισον τρυφῆς (*paradeison tryphēs*)</note>. But whether there is any linguistic force in this or not, the supplement I made in the previous verse will justify the sense of our *Cabbala*. Even in the literal letter and history of the Scripture, if a man pays attention, he must of necessity fill in the gaps of something or other to move to what follows with proper cohesion and clarity of sense.

For example, in the very next chapter, where God sentences Cain to be a vagabond, Cain cries out that *everyone who meets him will kill him*. According to the brief account of the text, there was no one but Adam and Eve in the world to meet him, and yet a mark is set upon him by God as if there had been several people in the world into whose hands he might fall and lose his life. And then again at verse 17, Cain...

# The Defense of the Moral Cabbala. CHAPTER III.

...had no sooner arrived in the *Land of Nod* <note>The place where Cain was exiled after killing Abel (Genesis 4:16).</note>, but he has a wife and a child by her, and he is immediately said to build a city, even though there is no mention of anyone but himself, his wife, and his child to be the builders <note>original: "Artificers"</note>. But any discerning <note>original: "ingenious"</note> reader will easily provide fitting supplements for himself, always assuming appropriate distances of time and the right preparations for everything that is said to have happened. And so in the story of *Samson*, where he is said to take three hundred foxes, it may be rationally supposed that the country was full of such creatures, that he had a sufficient amount of time, a large enough number of people to help him, and similar practical details. No one can deny that the history of Scripture is very concise; therefore, where easy, natural, and agreeable supplements will clarify the sense, I believe it is very justifiable to assume such supplies, and for a commentator <note>original: "Paraphrast"</note> to judiciously weave them into the text.

But now, that *Paradise* should at first signify a state of divine pleasure, and afterward a state of *sensual indulgence* <note>original: "voluptuousness"</note>, is no more harsh than the fact that *Adam* is at one time the *Spiritual* or *Intellectual Man*, and at another time the *Earthly* and *Carnal Man*. For one and the same natural thing may be a symbol of contrary spiritual mysteries. So a *lion* and a *serpent* are figures of Christ as well as of the Devil. Therefore, it is not so hard to admit that this *Garden of Eden* may symbolize <note>original: "emblematize"</note> the *delights of the Spirit* while *Adam* is discussed as innocent and obedient to God; but after his forsaking of God, it symbolizes the *pleasures of the flesh*. Consequently, the fruit of the *Tree of Life* in the first state may be *perseverance and establishment in the divine life*, while in the second state, it represents *a settlement and fixedness in the animalistic <note>original: "brutish"</note> and sensual life*.

**Verse 24. The manly faculties of Reason and Conscience. These, I believe, may be understood as the Cherubim and the flaming sword.** For the *Cherubim* bear the image of a *man*, and *Reason* is a cutting, dividing thing like a *sword*. The Stoics <note>A school of Hellenistic philosophy that emphasized logic and ethics.</note> call it *dividing reason* <note>original: διαιροῦντα λόγον (diairounta logon)</note>, meaning a dividing and distinguishing logic. For *Reason* is nothing but a distinct discernment of the ideas of things, by which the mind is able to sever what does not fit and lay together what does. But if anyone prefers the interpretation of *Philo* <note>Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BCE – 50 CE), a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher who used allegorical methods to interpret the Bible.</note> regarding the *Cherubim* and *flaming sword*—who makes the *Cherubim* signify the *Goodness* and *Power of God*, and the *flaming sword* the *divine word* <note>original: θεῖον λόγον (theion logon)</note>, the effectual and operative wisdom or Word of God—it does not at all clash with what we have already set down. For I myself also suppose that God, by his *Son*, the *Eternal Word*, works upon the reason 
<margin>Hebrews 4:12, 13.</margin> and conscience of man. *For that Word is living and powerful, sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is the discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart; neither is there any creature that is not manifest in his sight, but all things are naked and open unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do.*

That he could not settle into his state of sin <note>original: "set up his rest"</note> forever. Assuredly, a man's heart is not so much in his own hand that he can do himself all the mischief he is willing to do. For we belong more to God than to ourselves, and His goodness and power have dominion over us. And therefore, let not a man vainly imagine that by violently running into all enormity of life, and extinguishing all...

For though a man may happen to forget God for a time, God can never forget us, since all things lie open to His sight. And the power of His *ever-living Word* will easily cut through all that thickness and darkness in which we shroud ourselves. It will wound us so as to make us look back with shame and sorrow at a time when we least expected it.

But so that our pain may be less and our happiness may begin sooner, it will be wise for us to comply with the *divine Light early*. The sooner we begin, the easier the work will be, and it will be more quickly completed through the power of God working within us. But this I must confess—and I think myself bound to testify to such a true and useful mystery wrapped up in this *Mosaic covering* <note>original: "Mosaical covering"; More refers to the symbolic or allegorical layer of the writings of Moses.</note>—that there is no other path or return to happiness except through death. This is why *Plato*, who was familiar with these Holy writings, defined *Philosophy* as the meditation on death <note>original: *Meletē thanatou*</note>. By this, he meant dying to the lusts of the flesh and the disordered desires of the *body*. If we were to pass through this purgation <note>original: "Purgatory"; here used as a process of spiritual cleansing or testing rather than a specific location.</note>, there would soon spring up that *Morning Joy*: the Resurrection from the dead, and our arrival at everlasting life and glory. There is no other way than this that can be demonstrated by *Scripture, Reason*, or *Experience*.

But there are those who, through the grace of God and an intense thirst for divine righteousness, have borne the Cross until the perfect death of the "body of sin." They make it their business to have no more awareness or taste for themselves or their individual persons than if they did not exist at all. Once they are thus demolished in regard to themselves and turned into a *Chaos* or a dark *Nothingness*, so to speak, they become fitted for the *new Creation*.

When this *personal life* is thus destroyed, God calls to them in the dead of the night, when all things are silent around them. He awakes them, raises them up, and breathes into them the breath of everlasting life. From then on, He moves them by His own Spirit and takes all human faculties unto Himself, guiding or permitting all their operations. He always holds up the spirit of man so that he will never sink into sin; from this point forward, death and sorrow are swallowed up forever, for the sting of death is sin.

But whatever liberty and joy men take for themselves that is not founded in this new life is false and frivolous. It will end only in sadness, bitterness, and intolerable enslavement. For the *bodily life* <note>original: "Corporeal life"</note> and its senses will have sunk so deeply into the soul that it will be painfully difficult to disentangle her.

But as many as have passed through this *Death* have arrived at that *Life* which abides forever and ever.

And this *Life* is pure and immaculate *Love*. This *Love* is God, as He can be communicated to man, and it is the sole life and essence of *virtue* truly so called. Or rather, just as all colors are but the reflection of the rays of the sun, so all virtue is but this One Love, appearing in various colors and shapes according to the diversity of *objects* and *circumstances*. <meta>This page continues Henry More’s "Defense of the Moral Cabbala," where he personifies the "divine life" as a feminine force of wisdom and love that seeks to transform the human soul.
